title: Model cards are not primary artifacts: stereochemistry in the MoLFormer and SMI-TED chemical foundation models
author: Nathan Kaplan
text:
Pretrained chemical language models are selected, embedded with, and fine tuned on the basis of what their documentation says they are. We report that the released model card for MoLFormer, one of the most widely used chemical foundation models, states that isomeric information was removed from its training data, and that this statement is contradicted by artifacts distributed in the model's own repository. The shipped token frequency table records the tetrahedral stereocentre token [C@H] occurring 669,642,207 times, making it the twelfth most frequent token in a corpus of 47.2 billion tokens, ahead of fluorine, and stereochemical tokens account for 3.17% of all token occurrences. The described stripping is real but occurs at a different pipeline stage: isomeric = False is hardcoded into the fine tuning scripts and applied to downstream benchmark data, not to pretraining. We find a related divergence in SMI-TED, whose released vocabulary contains 2,393 tokens rather than the 2,988 reported, and whose shipped frequency table is identical to MoLFormer's, byte for byte, across all 2,357 shared tokens, despite the paper describing a different corpus. We release the extracted frequency table and an audit tool, and recommend that chemical model cards state stereochemistry handling separately for pretraining, fine tuning, and inference.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

Chirality is not a detail in medicinal chemistry. Roughly half of small molecule pharmaceuticals are chiral compounds, and for those, handedness frequently determines whether a substance is the therapeutic agent or an inactive, sometimes harmful, contaminant. A practitioner selecting a pretrained molecular representation for virtual screening triage, similarity search, or library deduplication therefore has a concrete question to answer: can this model distinguish enantiomers?

For models built on SMILES, the question reduces to whether the stereochemical characters @, @@,/and \ were present in the training corpus and are representable in the vocabulary. The natural place to look is the model card, which for models distributed through HuggingFace is the document practitioners actually read.

We report that for MoLFormer [1], the model card's answer is wrong, and that the error has propagated.

The model card foribm-research/MoLFormer-XL-both-10pctstates, under Training Details, Data:

“Molecules were canonicalized with RDKit prior to training and isomeric information was removed.”

The MoLFormer repository distributestraining/pubchem_canon_zinc_final_vocab_sorted.pth, a dictionary sorted by frequency that maps each vocabulary token to its occurrence count in the pretraining corpus. It is loaded at training time bytraining/pubchem_encoder.py, whose sequence bucketing thresholds are derived from its counts. Read directly, it gives: 56 token types contain @. Together with/and \ they account for 1,495,080,848 of 47,163,650,949 occurrences, or 3.17% of the corpus. [C@H] alone is 1.44 times as frequent as fluorine (Table1).

The distributed vocabulary filetraining/bert_vocab.txtreconstructs from this table exactly, element by element, as['<bos>','<eos>','<pad>','<mask>'] + list(counts) + ['<unk>'], confirming that the vocabulary the model was trained with is this table's ordering.

Two statements in the MoLFormer paper [1] foreclose the alternative reading, that the frequency table might describe a corpus prior to a stripping step. The paper defines the vocabulary as derived downstream of canonicalisation:

“All molecules from both PubChem and ZINC are converted to a canonical format utilizing RDKit then tokenized. All unique tokens extracted from the resulting output gives us a vocabulary of 2357 tokens plus 5 special tokens…”

And the paper's dataset statistics table, captioned “Minimum, maximum and mean and standard deviation of sequence length for the datasets considered in this work. The vocabulary size after tokenization is also given in the last column,” reports the number of unique tokens observed in each pretraining corpus, noting explicitly that a corpus “might only contain a subset of the model vocabulary capacity.” For PubChem and ZINC combined, the corpus MoLFormer-XL was trained on, the observed count is 2362, the entire vocabulary. Every stereochemical token appeared in training.

We note that the paper itself makes no claim that isomeric information was removed, and its introduction states that “chirality information [is] explicitly represented in SMILES strings.” The divergence is specific to the model card, not to the publication.

The card's description is not fabricated; it is misplaced. Stereochemistry removal is hardcoded in the fine tuning pipeline:

It is a literal, not a configurable argument, and it is applied to every MoleculeNet dataset. In the pretraining path, by contrast,training/pubchem_encoder.pycontains no RDKit call;normalize_smilesis defined attraining/utils.py:50and has zero call sites undertraining/; and the sole call site ofrandomize_smiles, atdataset_pubchem.py:91, lies within a block that is commented out.

The practical consequence differs sharply between the two readings. Under the card's claim, MoLFormer's pretrained representation could not encode stereochemistry at all. In fact the pretrained representation was exposed to 1.42 billion stereochemical tokens, while the reference fine tuning protocol discards stereochemistry from the evaluation data. Users following the released fine tuning scripts obtain a downstream model blind to stereochemistry from a pretrained model that was not blind to it, and no published benchmark result distinguishes these cases.

A caution for anyone reproducing this:training/pubchem_canon_script.pyis named as though it performed canonicalisation. It does not. It is a HuggingFace datasets.ArrowBasedBuilder that reads lines of text and imports no cheminformatics library.

The identical sentence appears on the model card foribm-research/GP-MoLFormer-Uniq. The claim has also entered the literature: Li et al. [2] state that “many existing CLMs are intentionally trained on SMILES stripped of stereochemical information,” citing MoLFormer and SMI-TED.

Examining SMI-TED [3] for the same class of divergence, we find two.

The shipped vocabulary is 2,393 tokens, not the “2988 tokens plus 5 special tokens” the paper reports and offers as evidence of an improved curation process relative to MoLFormer's 2362. The actual difference is 31 tokens, all rare metal hydrides.

The shipped frequency table is MoLFormer's. pubchem_canon_zinc_final_vocab_sorted_curated.pth totals 47,163,651,386 occurrences against MoLFormer's 47,163,650,949; all 2,357 shared tokens carry identical counts, byte for byte, with zero differing. SMI-TED's paper describes a corpus of 91 million PubChem molecules, a different source composition and an order of magnitude fewer molecules than the table it distributes.

Separately, and relevant to any user of the public API:normalize_smiles(smi, canonical = True, isomeric = False)is defined atmodels/smi_ted/inference/smi_ted_light/load.py:39and applied insideencode()at line 601. Users callingencode()on a pair of enantiomers receive identical embeddings, without warning, from a model whose vocabulary and pretraining fully support stereochemistry. The behaviour differs by entry point:extract_embeddings()performs no normalisation. This has been raised independently by users on the project's issue tracker.

Model cards for chemical language models should state stereochemistry handling separately for pretraining, fine tuning, and inference. A single sentence cannot describe all three, and conflating them is the error documented here. Where a frequency table or vocabulary is distributed, it should be cited in the card as the authoritative answer.

Inference APIs that modify chemical structure should say so at the call site. Silent canonicalisation inside an encode() method is indistinguishable, to the caller, from a model that cannot represent the discarded information.

Documentation claims about preprocessing are checkable, and should be checked. The evidence in this Comment required no model training and no specialised hardware, only reading files that the model's authors distributed. Where a shipped artifact and its documentation disagree, the artifact is authoritative.

If stereochemistry or canonicalisation handling differs between training stages, or between training and inference, authors should analyse the effects of those differences and explain the rationale for the process.

This includes the extracted MoLFormer pretraining token frequency Table (2,357 token types with corpus occurrence counts, released as CSV), the output of the stereochemistry canonicalisation experiment, the audit software, and a verification protocol allowing every figure reported in this Comment to be regenerated from the original source artifacts. The secondary data underlying this study are artifacts distributed by the model authors and are publicly available in the IBM/molformer repository athttps://github.com/IBM/molformerand the IBM/materials repository athttps://github.com/IBM/materials, both under an Apache 2.0 license. All claims were verified against those artifacts on 31 July 2026, at IBM/molformer commit 3b9ac434db387fadf2cf99b99def654cbf193841 and IBM/materials commit dc01519f434c0c10227a1d1955cd8a025b136151. title: Molecular function-guided unsupervised similarity-based enrichment for low-data virtual screening
author: Alexander Hagg; Dirk Reith; Matthias Preller; Karl N. Kirschner
text:
Identifying bioactive compounds for orphan or understudied protein targets remains a significant hurdle in drug discovery due to the lack of sufficient structure-activity relationship (SAR) data. We present MolFuSE (Molecular Function-guided Similarity Explorer), an unsupervised, projection-based enrichment framework designed for low-data virtual screening and ligand repurposing. MolFuSE leverages manifold learning—specifically uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)—to create low-dimensional similarity spaces based on a reference set of ligands known to bind proteins with the same molecular function as the target. Through systematic evaluation across nine protein targets and their functional classes, we demonstrate that UMAP embeddings of Mordred 2D descriptors act as a strong “potency filter”, significantly outperforming traditional topological fingerprints in the early enrichment of high-potency inhibitors (<100 nM). While extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFP4) fingerprints achieve superior global ranking (receiver operating characteristic (ROC)-area under the curve (AUC) 0.961 vs. 0.863), the descriptor-based approach provides more robust early recognition (enrichment factor at 1% (EF@1%)) when the reference set itself is small. Crucially, we identify a critical point in data scaling: performance peaks at a reference set size of approximately 10,000 compounds and degrades for larger sets due to descriptor-space dilution from structurally diverse weak binders. MolFuSE provides a computationally efficient, interpretable tool for prioritizing high-affinity candidates when target-specific data is unavailable.

We introduce a data-pooling strategy for low-data virtual screening and ligand repurposing that uses molecular-function annotations to aggregate “pseudo-active” reference sets, bypassing the need for target-specific ligands or structural data. Evaluating this framework across eight diverse protein families, we show that non-linear UMAP projections of physicochemical descriptors act as a robust potency filter, preferentially prioritizing high-affinity binders (< 100 nM) in early enrichment compared to traditional topological fingerprints. We provide evidence of a critical scaling threshold where reference sets exceeding approximately 10,000 diverse compounds dilute the descriptor space, establishing a practical blueprint for unsupervised screening across distinct target classes.

Identifying novel bioactive compounds for emerging therapeutic targets remains a persistent challenge in early-stage drug discovery. For well-characterized protein targets with extensive SAR data, machine learning approaches have demonstrated remarkable success in virtual screening campaigns [6,8,15,27,56]. However, the majority of potential therapeutic targets—particularly those in understudied protein families or emerging disease pathways—lack the hundreds to thousands of known bioactive molecules required for robust supervised learning models  [46].

This low-data regime problem is particularly acute for novel targets like myosins, orphan G-protein-coupled receptors, [20,54] and other undruggable proteins, [45,61] for which experimental screening campaigns have yet to be conducted at scale. While large pharmaceutical companies may leverage proprietary databases, this data remains inaccessible to the broader research community. Furthermore, for truly novel targets—such as those identified in emerging pathogens or rare diseases—historical screening data may not exist. Traditional ligand-based virtual screening (LBVS) methods rely on thesimilar property principle: structurally similar compounds are likely to exhibit similar biological activities [21,25,59,60] and proteins with the same function bind the same set of small molecules [52]. This principle underpins similarity searching, where known active compounds for a specific target protein serve as queries to identify novel candidates from large chemical libraries. Compounds are typically encoded as fingerprints (e.g., ECFP4 [48]) or physicochemical descriptors, enabling rapid comparison via metrics such as the Tanimoto coefficient [55]. However, if few or no ligands are known, then the pairwise similarity comparison becomes undefined. Structure-based virtual screening (SBVS) via molecular docking [1,24,30] offers an alternative pathway through the lock-and-key principle [10], but requires high-quality experimental structures—frequently unavailable for novel targets—and computationally expensive pose optimization. To reduce the SBVS computational cost, an LBVS prefiltering can be done. In practice, early retrieval performance in virtual screening is commonly quantified using the enrichment factor at 1% (EF@1%). Literature analyses indicate that traditional 2D LBVS methods typically yield median EF@1% values of approximately 16.3 (10%/90% percentiles [12.7, 21.7]), whereas 3D shape-based methods can achieve higher median values near 27.8 (10%/90% percentiles [27.6, 28.0]) on custom benchmarking sets [50]. Crucially, these metrics are not directly comparable across studies due to differing target compositions and baseline difficulties. For instance, structure-based molecular docking protocols evaluated on distinct, potentially more challenging benchmarks like the DUD-E dataset show mean EF@1% values of approximately 8.09 for standard tools like AutoDock Vina [40], though multi-reference implementations can yield higher rates. These historical metrics establish a performance context for low-data screening frameworks.

Homology-based similarity search has been used to identify ligands for a reference target when no initial ligands are known, by screening compounds that bind to homologous targets [49]. The authors introduce a descriptor based on four molecular features and calculate the molecular similarity between the candidate compound and the reference set by measuring the distance to its nearest neighbor(s). While the method yields high-quality rankings, the linear similarity space is entirely determined by the four features. Consequently, it may not perform well in highly diverse molecular spaces.

Following developments in chemogenomics, which have identified that certain molecular families can bind similar proteins, cross-target supervised approaches have been developed to screen the chemical space against entire protein families when known ligands for a target protein are absent [19]. When comparing binding affinity predictions using family-specific versus generic protein–ligand complexes, the family-specific models consistently yielded better predictions [58].

Supervised approaches, as described above, require datasets with affinity annotations, whereas unsupervised approaches can benefit from richer datasets. Herein, we exploit unsupervised learning methods, specificallymanifold learning, from functionally related proteins. We define the set of functionally related proteins as thefunctional classof a target protein. For example, if a novel transferase target has no known inhibitor, one might leverage the 100,000+ known transferase inhibitors from associated target proteins to guide the screening. To our knowledge, this “functional class based transfer” concept – defined as using collections of bioactive compounds, the reference set (RS), grouped by molecular function of their target protein (e.g., KW-0808 transferase proteins; KW-0560 oxidoreductase proteins), as annotated by UniProt,Footnote1which itself is based on the Gene Ontology [13]—has not been extensively explored as a manifold learning method in virtual screening, particularly for non-linear approaches.

While using functional annotations to group proteins is an established concept [12], our approach specifically applies this concept to bootstrap virtual screening by enriching an ample, diverse purchasable chemical space (i.e., from ZINC [18]) with a targeted set of functionally relevant compounds. We hypothesize that a non-linear similarity space derived from the combined ZINC and functional class-specific datasets provides a more informative chemical landscape, enabling the identification of promising candidates, even for targets with few known ligands. In the search for ligands that show affinity to novel or orphan target proteins, we define a RS as the set containing ligands with known affinity values for proteins within the same functional class. Aggregating known ligands for all proteins associated with a target’s function yields a significantly larger and more diverse RS of “pseudo-active” compounds, guiding the search more effectively and covering a larger portion of the potentially active molecular space. However, to better characterize such a diverse set, a richer (i.e., higher-dimensional) descriptor set is needed, which in turn poses its own problem.

High-dimensional descriptors (i.e., encoding spaces) suffer from the curse of dimensionality, where pairwise distances converge to the same magnitude, making comparisons meaningless [3,5]. To mitigate this information loss, (non-)linear projections can be used to find an embedding space whose dimensionality is close to the number of dimensions necessary to fully describe the data (a.k.a., the “intrinsic dimensionality”) [4]. Since projection methods are lossy by themselves, and it is usually not possible to determine the intrinsic dimensionality, the embedding space dimensionality can be chosen to allow a certain amount of information loss. For example, in principal component analysis (PCA) the dimensionality reduction is achieved by retaining the number of principal components required to account for a predefined percentage of the total data.

Recent advances in projective dimensionality reduction, particularly UMAP [36], enable the construction of low-dimensional molecular similarity spaces that preserve both local neighborhoods and global structure. This technique has been successfully applied to chemical space visualization (i.e., chemography) [38,41] and has very recently been benchmarked against other non-linear projection methods for that purpose [42].

Unlike linear techniques such as PCA, which often struggle to preserve non-linear local similarity relationships [33,42], or alternative non-linear methods like t-SNE, which do not preserve global spatial relationships and are computationally difficult to scale to large datasets [26], UMAP balances local and global structures while facilitating out-of-sample mapping without model retraining [2]. While modern deep learning representation methods—such as Graph Neural Networks and pre-trained Transformer models like ChemBERTa or MolBERT—capture highly complex chemical features [7,9,32], they typically require substantial computational resources and many training examples for fine-tuning, alongside offering limited direct interpretability compared to explicit distance-based metric spaces. This makes unsupervised manifold learning an attractive alternative to navigate these limitations. However, whether embeddings trained on a generic RS can effectively prioritize high-potency compounds for specific low-data targets remains an open question. In this work, we investigate this problem using MolFuSE.

MolFuSE (Molecular Function-guided Similarity Explorer) is a projection-based enrichment framework designed explicitly for low-data virtual screening scenarios. MolFuSE operates under the following three core design principles:

Projection-only strategy: Dimensionality reduction models are fit exclusively on the large RS plus decoy libraries, ensuring that held-out target actives do not influence the learned similarity space—mimicking realistic prospective screening conditions.

Exact nearest-neighbor scoring: Compounds are ranked according to their minimum Euclidean distance to the RS within the manifold (i.e., the embedded space). This provides interpretable retrieval paths and facilitates post-hoc analysis of enrichment drivers.

Potency-stratified evaluation: Performance is assessed separately for high-potency (affinity\(< 100\)nM), medium-potency (100–1000 nM), and weak (1000–10000 nM) actives, revealing method-specific biases toward different potency regimes.

Through four systematic experimental phases, we explore MolFuSE’s performance using several criteria: (1) hyperparameter optimization of dimensionality reduction methods (i.e., PCA vs. UMAP) and molecular representations (i.e., 1,611 Mordred 2D descriptors vs. 2048-bit ECFP4 fingerprints), (2) sensitivity to RS affinity cutoffs before scoring (i.e., filtering RS by affinity thresholds), (3) robustness to RS size (i.e., random subsampling from 10 to 100,000+ compounds with full model retraining), and (4) cross-target generalization (i.e., across eight target proteins from various functional classes with varying natural RS sizes).

Our findings reveal that UMAP embeddings of Mordred descriptors achieve good enrichment for high-potency ligands, substantially outperforming both traditional fingerprint methods and literature-reported 3D docking benchmarks. We demonstrate that adequate screening is achievable with an RS as small as 1,000 compounds, and identify a previously unreported critical point where an extensive RS degrades performance–likely due to descriptor space dilution from structurally diverse low-affinity binders. These results establish MolFuSE as a practical, computationally efficient tool for hit discovery in low-data regimes, with implications for orphan-target prioritization and early-stage drug-discovery workflows. In other words, MolFuSE is a ligand-repurposing tool that projects compounds with known activity against a particular protein class onto low-data targets, thereby suggesting candidates for experimental exploration.

Our experimental framework relies on the interplay between three distinct compound sets: (1) the RS, comprising known binders to a functional class of proteins; (2) the Target Actives Set, a held-out collection of ligands with known affinity for a specific target protein (e.g., tyrosine-protein kinase ABL1) that is used for evaluation; and (3) the Decoy Set, a large library of presumed non-binders used to challenge the retrieval capability. The transferase functional class is used to illustrate and evaluate MolFuSE.

For Phase 1–3 experiments, we selected Tyrosine-Protein Kinase/Transferase ABL1 (CHEMBL1862) as the primary evaluation target since it has many known actives, making it a convenient target for this work. Known actives were retrieved from ChEMBL using the P00519 identifier, requiring affinity measurements between 1 and 10,000 nM and theremovalof active compounds from the RS dataset, via canonical SMILES matching, to prevent data leakage between training and test sets. We also divided the active set into three potency tiers for evaluation:

High: affinity < 100 nM (N = 1,562 compounds, 46.9%)

Medium: 100 nM\(\le\)affinity\(< 1,000\)nM (N = 729, 21.9%)

Weak: 1,000 nM\(\le\)affinity\(\le 10,000\)nM (N = 975, 29.3%)

By removing all known ligands of the target protein, we mimic a low-data environment where the models lack any prior binding information. We did not artificially prune structurally similar analogs between RS and active set because our objective was specifically to evaluate whether the manifold could leverage information from related binders in the same functional class to enrich the target’s actives.

For the Tyrosine-Protein Kinase/Transferase ABL1 (CHEMBL1862) target protein, the UniProt functional class KW-0808 Transferase was selected. The target-specific RS was constructed from ChEMBL (version 34) [14] by querying all compounds with reported bioactivity with human transferase target proteins. Compounds were required to have standard binding affinity measurements (EC\(_{50}\), IC\(_{50}\), K\(_i\), or K\(_d\)) in nanomolar units, and valid SMILES strings with successful RDKit parsing.

For compounds with multiple measurements against the same or different transferase targets, we applied median affinity deduplication: the median affinity across all assays was computed and assigned as the compound’s representative value. This approach provides robustness against multi-assay variability and batch effects common in large-scale screening databases [11]. In an uncharacterized or orphan target setting, the true binding site topology is unknown. If a compound shows strong affinity against one specific target protein but weak affinity across five other proteins in the same functional class, recording its “best” value would mischaracterize it as a universally potent binder for that functional class. The final RS contained approximately 191,000 unique transferase inhibitors with median affinity values ranging from sub-nanomolar to\(>10\)\(\mu\)M.

For Phase 4’s cross-target validation, we selected eight additional targets spanning diverse structural families and RS sizes (43,000–425,000 compounds): ABL2, EGFR, ERBB2, SRC, LCK, YES1, FYN and LYN.

To simulate realistic screening conditions, we incorporated a decoy library from the ZINC database [18], representing commercially available “screening-like” compounds with no known transferase activity. After removing overlap with the RS or target actives (by canonical SMILES), the final decoy set contained 1,293,566 compounds. The decoy-to-active ratio is 58:1 with strict SMILES-based deduplication.

To capture diverse aspects of chemical similarity, we utilized two distinct encoding strategies—explicit physicochemical descriptors (Mordred) to capture molecular properties, and topological fingerprints (ECFP4) to capture substructural features.

A total of 1,611 two-dimensional (2D) molecular descriptors were utilized in this study, calculated via the Mordred library [39]. These descriptors are summarized by category, descriptor family, and weighting properties in the supporting information. For a full listing, we refer to the code repository (see Sect.Limitations and future directions).

Preprocessing the resulting data consisted of the following steps:

Zero-variance filtering: Descriptors with variance\(< 10^{-12}\)(effectively constant across all compounds), or those where no descriptor values were calculable, were removed, yielding approximately 1,611 informative descriptors.

Median imputation: Missing descriptor values, around 5.95% on average per descriptor (e.g., from SMILES parsing failures or undefined mathematical operations), were replaced with the median descriptor value computed across the RS and decoy set.

Standardization: The remaining descriptors were z-score normalized, fit exclusively on the combined RS and decoy set. Held-out target actives were transformed using the same scaler parameters, ensuring no data leakage.

StandardScaler was appliedonlyto Mordred descriptors. Fingerprint representations (see below) were used directly without scaling.

For comparison, we generated 2048-bit Extended Connectivity Fingerprints with radius 2 (ECFP4) [28,48]. Fingerprints were stored as binary vectors (0/1 for absence/presence) and used without preprocessing.

PCA and UMAP models were fit on the combined RS and decoy set (N = 1,484,566 compounds: 191,000 RS + 1,293,566 decoys). Held-out target actives were projected into the learned embedding space using the respectivetransformmethod, ensuring strict separation between training and test sets. Both methods were used to project the dataset into 2D, 5D, 10D and 20D embedding spaces. Both methods used either the binary fingerprints directly or z-score-normalized Mordred descriptors.

The following key UMAP hyperparameters were optimized in Phase 1:

n_neighbors\(\in\){10, 20, 50, 100, 500}: Controls local vs. global structure preservation. Lower values emphasize tight local clusters; higher values capture broader manifold geometry.

min_dist\(\in\){0.0, 0.01, 0.1}: Minimum distance between embedded points. Lower values allow tighter clusters; higher values produce more dispersed embeddings.

n_components\(\in\){2, 5, 10, 20}: Dimensionality of the target embedding space.

metric: Distance metric for manifold construction. Employed were theeuclideanmetric for Mordred descriptors, andjaccardfor ECFP4 fingerprints due to their binary bit-vector nature.

random_state: Set toNoneto enable parallel processing across independent replicates and for variance assessment.

To ensure reproducibility, all UMAP runs used five independent replicates, while the deterministic PCA runs are reported as single values. The RS subsampling (Phase 3) used five independent random samples per size, and the cross-target validation (Phase 4) used five replicates per target. Performance metrics are reported as mean ± standard deviation across replicates.

After embedding, all compounds (i.e., RS, decoys, and held-out actives) were represented as points in the low-dimensional space. For each held-out active compound, we computed its ranking score as:

where\(d(x_{\text {active}}, x_{\text {RS}})\)is the Euclidean distance in the embedded space. The negative sign ensures that compoundscloserto the RS receivehigherscores. This exact 1-nearest-neighbor (1-NN) approach was implemented using a kd-tree for computational efficiency with Euclidean metrics. The evaluation set compounds (i.e., target actives and decoys) were ranked by descending score, and enrichment metrics were subsequently computed.

All preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, and scoring were implemented in Python 3.12. SMILES parsing, ECFP4 fingerprint generation [48], EF@1%, ROC-AUC, and Boltzmann-enhanced discrimination of ROC (BEDROC) were computed using RDKit 2023.03.1 [29]. Mordred community edition 2.0.6 [39] was used for 2D descriptor computation. Data manipulation and numerical computation were done using Pandas [37,43] and NumPy [16]. The scikit-learn 1.3.0 package [44] was used to compute PCA, StandardScaler, KDTree, imputation and zero-variance filtering. The fast umap-learn 0.5.3 library [17,36] was used for computing UMAP.

While global metrics like ROC-AUC and precision-recall (PR)-AUC assess overall ranking quality, they can fail to capture “early enrichment”—the ability to find true actives in the topx% of predictions [23,31,35,50,57]. A high global AUC does not guarantee that actives are positioned early enough for experimental validation [57]. Consequently, we utilize EF@1% and BEDROC to specifically evaluate early enrichment. The EF@1% quantifies how many true actives appear in the top 1% of ranked compounds relative to random selection [57].

where\(N_{\text {total}}\)represents the total number of compounds, andnrepresents the number of compounds in the respective subsets.

It was noted that EF@1% is not sensitive to ranking performance before and after the cutoff threshold [57]. The BEDROC metric was introduced to address this limitation by giving more weight to top-ranked compounds. Consequently, it provides a more robust measure of early enrichment that is less sensitive to a specific, arbitrary cutoff value. It is defined as:

The\(\alpha\)is a tunable exponential weighting factor,\(r_i\)is the rank of the\(i^{th}\)active compound (from 1 to\(N_{\text {total}}\)),nis the number of active compounds, and\(N_{\text {total}}\)is the total number of compounds within the dataset [47,57]. The “early enrichment” factor\(\alpha\)controls the weight given to the top-ranked compounds, tuning the metric towards quantifying early enrichment. A higher\(\alpha\)places greater importance on compounds at the top of the ranked list. An\(\alpha = 20\)is a common assignment where approximately 80% of the BEDROC score is determined by the top 8% of the ranked compounds. An\(\alpha \approx 160\)is a highly stringent setting where 80% of the score is derived from just the top 1% of the ranked list.

To assess method-specific biases, we computed separate EF@1% values for high-potency (affinity < 100 nM), medium-potency (100–1000 nM), and weak (1000–10,000 nM) actives. This stratification reveals whether methods preferentially retrieve tight binders vs. weaker inhibitors – a critical distinction for hit-to-lead optimization.

We performed a systematic grid search across the following methods, representations, and hyperparameters:

Dimensionality reduction methods: PCA and UMAP

Molecular representations: Mordred (1,611 descriptors) and ECFP4 (2048-bit)

UMAP hyperparameters: n_neighbors\(\in\){10, 20, 50, 100, 500}, min_dist\(\in\){0.0, 0.01, 0.1}, and n_components\(\in\){2, 5, 10, 20}

PCA hyperparameters: n_components\(\in\){2, 5, 10, 20}

This yielded 515 total experimental runs. For each configuration, we computed overall EF@1% and potency-stratified EF@1% values. The optimal configuration was selected as the highest-performing method assessed using the overall EF@1%, with secondary analysis of high-potency-stratified performance.

Using the optimal hyperparameters identified in Phase 1, we investigated if filtering the RS by affinity thresholds improves the enrichment. We re-scored thesamePhase 1 embeddings (i.e., no model retraining) using RS filtered to include affinities a)\(\le\)100 nM (i.e., high-potency compounds), b)\(\le\)1,000 nM, c)\(\le\)10,000 nM, and d)\(\le\)100,000 nM. For each cutoff, exact 1-NN distances were recomputed to the filtered RS, and enrichment metrics were re-evaluated. This design isolates the effect of RS potency composition from embedding geometry.

To assess robustness to RS size, we performed the following systematic ablation study:

Random subsampling: The full RS was randomly subsampled to target sizes: 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, and 100,000. Subsampling was performedwithout replacementfrom RS to test generalization capacity across diverse RS scales.

Model retraining: For each RS subsample, we restandardized the values and retrained the dimensionality reduction model (UMAP or PCA) from scratch using the optimal hyperparameters found in Phase 1 (i.e., UMAP 2D, n_neighbors=10, min_dist=0.0 for Mordred descriptors).

Evaluation: Held-out actives were projected into each newly trained embedding space and scored via exact 1-NN against the subsampled RS. The stratifying potency enrichment was then evaluated based on the optimal affinity cutoff (i.e., 100 nM).

Replicates: 5 independent random subsampling and retraining runs were performed per RS size to assess the variance.

This design tests the following hypothesis that larger RS provides better coverage of chemical space, improving retrieval, and, conversely, smaller set sizes degrade performance. The random subsampling approach (rather than curation or active learning) ensures that observed effects reflectscale alone, not content quality.

To validate generalizability beyond a single target, we applied the optimal hyperparameters from Phases 1–3 (i.e., see above plus 100 nM affinity cutoff) to eight additional targets with varying RS sizes: ABL2 (\(\sim 43,000\)), EGFR (\(\sim 86,000\)), ERBB2 (\(\sim 95,000\)), SRC (\(\sim 180,000\)), LCK (\(\sim 225,000\)), YES1 (\(\sim 280,000\)), FYN (\(\sim 340,000\)), and LYN (\(\sim 425,000\)compounds). For each target, we:

constructed target-specific RS by excluding compounds with known activity against the held-out target (i.e., leakage prevention),

retrained the UMAP model on target-specific RS + ZINC decoys, and

evaluated potency-stratified enrichment on held-out actives (5 replicates per target).

We computed Spearman correlation between natural RS size and high-potency EF@1% to quantify the relationship between the RS scaling and the screening performance. This design tests whether the Phase 3 findings (optimal size 10,000, degradation at 100,000+) generalize across targets with naturally occurring RS sizes spanning 1–2 orders of magnitude.

In this phase, we validated MolFuSE’s approach by conducting three control experiments that tested the necessity of dimensionality reduction and the magnitude of decoy bias.

To test if MolFuSE exhibits systematic bias toward ChEMBL-like compounds regardless of target specificity, we scored non-transferase actives against transferase-trained models. We selected seven diverse non-transferase target families from Phase 4 and scored their known actives using the respective transferase RS. Under the null hypothesis of no database bias, we expect random performance of EF@1%\(\approx\)1.0. Elevated enrichment would indicate the model preferentially ranks ChEMBL compounds over ZINC compounds, independent of biological relevance. However, critically, if this enrichment remains substantially lower than the target-specific performance, the databases are onlypartiallyseparable with functional class specific-models increasing enrichment.

To determine if UMAP dimensionality reduction is necessary, we scored candidates using the raw 1,611-dimensional Mordred descriptors with scaled Euclidean distance (1-NN). This control (35 replicates across seven Phase 4 target families) directly tests whether high-dimensional descriptor spaces provide adequate discrimination without the need for manifold learning. We compare raw descriptor performance against Phase 4 (descriptors + UMAP, averaged across all targets) using identical descriptors and scaling, isolating UMAP ’s contribution. The Phase 4 results represent an average behavior over diverse protein families, and thus provides a generalizable baseline rather than target-specific optimization.

To benchmark MolFuSE against established standards, we implemented raw ECFP4 fingerprint similarity using Tanimoto/Jaccard distance (1-NN, no UMAP). We compare against Phase 1 (ECFP4 + UMAP) across five replicates to quantify if UMAP’s learned metric provides meaningful improvement over established methods. This control also verifies that MolFuSE’s performance gains are not simply due to the use of ECFP4 representations.

The raw descriptor baseline and database bias control experiments used all eight Phase 4 target families (i.e., Antimicrobial, Antioxidant, Cytokine, Heparin-binding, Lyase, Motor Protein, Oxidoreductase, and Transferase; 35 total replicates) to assess generalizability across diverse protein families. The fingerprint baseline experiment (raw ECFP4 vs. Phase 1 ECFP4 + UMAP) used ABL1 transferase (UniProt: P00519) exclusively, with 3,325 ABL1 actives and 1,293,529 ZINC decoys (5 replicates).

For each experiment, we computed enrichment metrics (EF@1% and ROC-AUC) across multiple replicates and performed independentt-tests comparing Phase 5 (no UMAP) against Phase 1/4 baselines (with UMAP). Significance thresholds are set to *\(p<0.05\), **\(p<0.01\), ***\(p<0.001\).

Results are reported in the same order as described in the previous section. It is important to understand what values the metrics would assume in the worst case, where the screening model would produce a uniform-randomly distributed ranking (see Table1). In that case, the expected value of the first term in Eq.3is exactly 1.0. For Phases 1, 2, 3 and 5, the same expected BEDROC metric will result since the same number of actives (\(n=5,505\)) and total molecules (\(N=1,718,819\)) were used.

Performance variation was determined through systematic evaluation of 515 hyperparameter configurations. This evaluation comprehensively covered two dimensionality reduction methods (PCA, UMAP) and two molecular representations (Mordred descriptors, ECFP4 fingerprints). The extensive hyperparameter grids revealed substantial performance variation.

Examination of enrichment performance across embedding dimensionalities shows that ECFP4 fingerprints consistently outperform Mordred descriptors when evaluated on enrichment (Fig.1). The optimal configuration for EF@1% was UMAP with ECFP4 fingerprints (20 dimensions, n_neighbors=10, min_dist=0.0, Jaccard metric), achieving a value of 33.94 ± 0.56. PCA baselines performed substantially worse. The best performance for descriptors was an EF@1% of 24.27 at 2D and for fingerprints an EF@1% of 13.08 at 20D), confirming that non-linear manifold learning is critical for enrichment.

Fingerprints’ structural encoding provides a consistent advantage across all dimensionalities for general retrieval. However, as detailed in the subsequent section, this trend starts to invert when specifically targeting high-potency compounds.

An important shift in performance emerges when evaluating enrichment stratified by compound potency. While fingerprints dominate global metrics, Mordred descriptors coupled with UMAP achieve better enrichment for high-potency actives (affinity < 100 nM), at least relative to the mean enrichment over the entire set.

Error bars represent standard deviation across replicates

As shown in Fig.2, the scores for Mordred descriptors on high-potency targets exceed those of medium and weak potency tiers. Conversely, ECFP4 fingerprints show better performance for the medium potency tier. This suggests that while fingerprints effectively retrieve topologically similar scaffolds, the physicochemical properties encoded by Mordred descriptors are better suited for clustering the tightest binders in the embedding space. However, fingerprints still seem to outperform descriptor-based UMAP similarity spaces.

Analysis of the 515-run grid (Fig.3) revealed clear topological preferences for the embedding. Low values for the number of neighbors (n_neighbors=10–20) consistently performed best, indicating that preserving local neighborhood structures is more critical for 1-NN retrieval than preserving the global manifold geometry. Furthermore, tight clustering parameters (min_dist=0.0–0.01) outperformed dispersed embeddings (min_dist=0.1), suggesting that dense packing of the RS aids in creating discriminative decision boundaries for the 1-NN scorer.

Phase 1—optimal hyperparameters and sensitivity. EF@1% values for all UMAP hyperparameter configurations. Low values for the number of neighbors (n neighbors=10–20) consistently performed best

Using the optimal embeddings from Phase 1, we investigated the impact of RS quality on retrieval performance. We rescored held-out actives against subsets of the RS, filtered by varying affinity thresholds (100–100,000 nM).

Figure4shows a strong negative correlation between the inclusion of weak binders (affinity\(> 1\)\(\mu\)M) into RS and enrichment performance. Including weak binders creates “noise” in the embedding space, allowing decoys to score well by appearing similar to weak, non-specific binders. The same effect is also clearly seen in Fig.5, where the performance for the different potency tiers of the target compounds is plotted. While medicinal chemistry programs routinely optimize weak initial hits when no alternatives exist, virtual screening benchmarks and early-hit workflows place a premium on prioritizing strong binders (blue line) over weak binders (red line). In benchmark evaluations, distinguishing potent from weak binders of the same target is formally defined and evaluated as “ranking power” [53]. From a practical screening standpoint, experimentally validating weak, micromolar-range hits requires elevated assay concentrations where non-specific artifacts such as colloidal aggregation are prevalent [51]. Conversely, computational prioritization of high-affinity matter seeks to directly identify cleaner, more verifiable starting points [34]. Descriptor-based UMAP similarity spaces outperform fingerprint-based similarity spaces in terms of EF@1% and BEDROC (\(\alpha = 20\)) scores but fingerprints still outperform descriptors for the stricter BEDROC (\(\alpha = 160\)) score.

Phase 2—Affinity cutoff sensitivity for all metrics and methods, shaded area shows 95% confidence interval

One can also note that the choice of metric leads to different choices for UMAP, either for descriptors or fingerprints. Filtering the RS to include only high-potency compounds (< 100 nM) resulted in the highest enrichment across all metrics for the UMAP methods. Consequently, we adopted the 100 nM affinity cutoff as the default for subsequent experiments to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio in the reference manifold. PCA on descriptors is influenced the least by changing the filtering of RS and PCA on fingerprints is generally the worst performer. We therefore choose to ignore PCA in the rest of the experiments.

Phase 2—Affinity cutoff sensitivity for stratified potency sets using UMAP

To test the limits of the “low-data” assumption, we systematically subsampled the RS from 10 to 100,000 (about 50,000 fewer than the original data set) compounds and retrained the models. Figure6illustrates the relationship between RS size and enrichment metrics, revealing a striking non-monotonic trajectory. At all RS sizes, Mordred descriptors outperformed ECFP4 fingerprints for high-potency retrieval, reinforcing the conclusion that rich physicochemical descriptor spaces better capture affinity-relevant features than structural fingerprints. These trends are consistent across all metrics employed.

Phase 3—Sensitivity to RS size for all potency tiers, all metrics and methods. Metric values are plotted on y-axes

Robustness in Low-Data Regimes:MolFuSE demonstrates remarkable efficiency with small datasets. Using UMAP on the descriptors of a small RS of just 1,000 compounds achieves an EF@1% of 41.77 ± 1.38. This strengthens the method’s applicability to orphan targets where limited bioactivity data is available.

However, contrary to the assumption that “more data is better”, when applying UMAP on descriptors, performance peaks at approximately 10,000 compounds (EF@1% 53.62 ± 1.70) and significantly degrades as the set size increases to 100,000+ compounds. This degradation (Fig.6, right columns) suggests a descriptor space dilution effect. As the RS grows to encompass the full range of transferase inhibitor space, the UMAP embedding must accommodate increasingly diverse molecular structures. This forces the manifold to change in ways that disperse the high-potency clusters, making the 1-NN distance less discriminative. This finding highlights a critical trade-off between chemical space coverage and embedding specificity. Consequently, curating RS to exclude very weak binders (e.g., affinity > 10\(\mu\)M) may improve performance, even if it reduces the total compound count.

To ensure that the results are not artifacts of the ABL1 target, we applied the optimal configuration (i.e., UMAP 2D, Mordred, n_neighbors=10, min_dist=0.01, 100 nM cutoff) to eight additional functional classes with varying natural RS sizes (43,000 to 425,000 compounds). For each target protein’s data set, we trained a UMAP model. Figure7summarizes the cross-target performance. Phase 3 overestimated the generalization capability on smaller RS; however, the linear trend of the correlation between RS size and enrichment is clearly visible. Furthermore, the models were retrained without rehyperparameterizing UMAP for the other targets since this is a very computationally expensive operation.

When using hyperparameters from Phase 3 (left), their generalization performance (EF@1%) is tested in Phase 4 (right) on other target proteins with other RS from other molecular functions

Two additional notable observations include:

Consistency: The trend line (dashed red) indicates a positive correlation between available data and performance, although the gains plateau, mirroring the saturation effects seen in Phase 3.

Metric Stability: The method maintains high early enrichment (EF@1%) across diverse transferase sub-families, validating the generalizability of the manifold learning approach.

These results confirm that the parameters optimized on ABL1 transfer effectively to related protein targets, supporting the utility of MolFuSE as a algorithmic tool for protein functional class-wide screening.

Table2shows that non-transferase actives scored against transferase-trained models achieved EF@1% = 13.5 ± 11.2 and ROC-AUC = 0.655 ± 0.107 across seven target families. This substantially exceeds random performance (EF@1% = 1.0, Table1), confirming the presence of database bias: the model preferentially ranks ChEMBL compounds over ZINC decoys independent of target-specific biological relevance.

This bias likely arises from two sources: (1) ChEMBL compounds are drug-like compounds with measured bioactivity, exhibiting restricted physicochemical properties (e.g., Lipinski’s rule of five), while ZINC contains broader chemical diversity that includes non-drug-like structures; (2) RS itself is derived from ChEMBL, creating implicit training set homogeneity. Future work should explore alternative decoy sets (e.g., property-matched DUD-E decoys) to isolate target-specific signals more cleanly, though such matched sets introduce their own biases.

However, it is important to note that this bias effect (EF@1% = 13.5) is approximately 2.5-foldlowerthan target-specific performance (EF@1% = 30–34 for matched transferase targets). This quantitative difference demonstrates that the ChEMBL and ZINC databases are onlypartiallyseparable, not fully trivially distinguishable. Target-specific biological signals clearly dominate MolFuSE’s predictions. The model is not merely learning to distinguish “ChEMBL-like” from “ZINC-like” compounds, but instead capturing genuine protein-ligand interaction patterns superimposed on a non-negligible background of database bias.

Using the raw 1,611-dimensional descriptors without UMAP achieved an EF@1% of 7.8 ± 9.1 and ROC-AUC of 0.504 ± 0.121 across the 7 target families (Table2). In contrast, the descriptors + UMAP achieved an average EF@1% = 20.7 ± 14.7 and ROC-AUC = 0.729 ± 0.130 over the same targets and descriptors (\(p < 0.001\), 166% relative improvement). These results reflect average behavior across all target families, capturing UMAP ’s generalizable benefit rather than target-specific tuning. This improved performance demonstrates that UMAP is not merely a computational convenience but is necessary for effective descriptor-based screening.

The poor performance of using only high-dimensional descriptors can be attributed to the curse of dimensionality: in 1,611-dimensional space, the Euclidean distance metrics become uninformative as all pairwise distances converge [5]. The nearest-neighbor search in such spaces approaches random selection because the ratio of nearest-to-farthest neighbor distances tends toward 1.0. UMAP addresses this by learning a low-dimensional manifold that preserves local neighborhood structures, effectively denoising the descriptor space and recovering biologically meaningful similarity relationships. Without this manifold learning step, the high-dimensional descriptor space is notably less useful in ligand-based screening.

Raw ECFP4 fingerprints with Tanimoto similarity (i.e., without UMAP) achieved EF@1% = 30.1 ± 0.0 and ROC-AUC = 0.961 ± 0.000 (Table2). This represents strong performance and establishes a high baseline for comparison. Completion of Phase 1 (ECFP4 + UMAP) achieved an EF@1% = 33.9 ± 0.5 (\(p < 0.001\)), an 11% improvement, and a ROC-AUC = 0.863 ± 0.004. Comparison of these metric values shows an unusual pattern: raw ECFP4 has higher global ranking quality (\(\Delta \text {ROC-AUC} = +0.1\); +10%). In contrast, ECFP4 + UMAP has superior early enrichment (\(\Delta EF@1\% =+3.8\); +11%). This indicates UMAP prioritizes top-ranked predictions—the most critical region for practical virtual screening where experimental validation costs dominate. The trade-off is acceptable: a 10% reduction in global AUC is offset by an 11% gain in the actionable top 1% of predictions.

Akin to tools like the SwissSimilarity web tool [62], which predicts the targets of bioactive compounds based on a combination of 2D and 3D similarity measures and linear projections with known ligands, we introduce a web application, shown in Fig.8, designed for interactive MolFuSE navigation and analysis of the RS-guided similarity spaces. This goes beyond applications such as VSFlow [22] that do not involve dimensionality reduction techniques.

The MolFuSE Explorer.aUser selects workspace, model and input candidates.bThe resulting similarity space is calculated by the backend.cCandidates are scored, and top candidates are revealed

The primary interface is an interactive 2D scatter plot that visualizes the selected space. Points are color-coded to distinguish between known binding ligands for the functional class, ZINC decoys, and user-uploaded compounds. Users can dynamically filter the displayed data based on activity thresholds and other properties. A key capability is the projection of user-uploaded custom compounds into the current RS-guided space using a trained UMAP model. This allows users to assess their novel compounds in the context of known RS-relevant actives and the broader purchasable chemical space. To aid candidate identification, a 1-Nearest Neighbors (1-NN) search can be performed within the 2D space to find the most similar ZINC or custom compounds to the aggregated set of ChEMBL actives.

This study demonstrates that in low-data virtual screening regimes, high-performing prediction models can be developed using manifolds learned from homologous protein data. Our findings regarding potency stratification, data saturation, and embedding dimensionality suggest that MolFuSE operates more robustly through a similarity-based scoring mechanism governed by physicochemical compatibility (using Mordred descriptors) rather than pure substructural analogy ECFP4 fingerprints, although the latter encoding strategy should always be considered, especially with larger RS sizes.

A central finding in the hyperparameter and representation analysis (Phase 1) is the performance divergence between topological fingerprints (ECFP4) and physicochemical descriptors (Mordred) when evaluated against high-potency targets. While fingerprints generally offer robust global retrieval—evidenced by high ROC-AUC scores in baseline comparisons—descriptor-based UMAP embeddings demonstrated a specific advantage in concentrating sub-100 nM binders at the very top of the active rankings. This advantage, reflected in the higher high-potency discrimination of descriptor-based UMAP embeddings at optimized RS sizes, suggests that tight binding is driven by specific physicochemical property profiles that are explicitly encoded by Mordred descriptors, whereas fingerprints excel at broader structural retrieval. While fingerprints excel at identifying structural analogs (scaffold hopping), descriptor-based manifold learning appears to filter the potency better, resulting in clustering compounds with the requisite physical properties for tight binding regardless of their scaffold similarity, especially when RS size is small. This distinction supports the use of descriptor-based embeddings specifically for the early recognition problem, where limited experimental data hinders the prediction of top-ranked candidates.

Contrary to the prevailing big data paradigm in deep learning, where performance typically scales with dataset size, our reference set (RS) ablation studies (Phase 3) identified a critical performance ceiling. The observation that enrichment peaks at an RS size of approximately 10,000 compounds and significantly degrades as the set expands to 100,000+ provides a nuanced view of the “Similar Property Principle” [52] in low-dimensional embeddings. We attribute this degradation to descriptor space dilution. As the RS grows to encompass the historical diversity of a functional class’s active compounds, it inevitably incorporates a wider array of distinct molecular structures and weaker binders. In the context of a fixed-dimensional UMAP embedding, preserving the global structure of this heterogeneous data forces the manifold to expand, dispersing the dense local clusters of high-potency compounds required for effective 1-NN retrieval. This is further supported by Phase 2 results, where excluding weak binders (\(\ge 100\)nm) from the scoring set improved performance. Consequently, for embedding-based similarity search, the quality and physicochemical specificity of the reference data appear more critical than volume. This finding is particularly relevant for “low-data” targets, as it implies that massive historical datasets are not required if a smaller, curated set of highly specific ligands is available.

Dimensionality reduction: necessity and trade-offs The ablation study clarifies the role of UMAP not merely as a visualization tool, but as a necessary pre-processing step for physicochemical screening. The failure of raw high-dimensional descriptors (EF@1%\(\approx 7.8\)) compared to their UMAP-projected counterparts (EF@1%\(\approx 20.7\)) confirms that the “curse of dimensionality” renders Euclidean metrics ineffective in the raw 1,611-dimensional space. UMAP mitigates this by learning a manifold that preserves local neighborhood structures, effectively denoising the descriptor space. However, this gain in early enrichment comes at the cost of global ranking quality. While the ECFP4-based MolFuSE workflow improves early enrichment EF@1% by 11% over the raw Tanimoto baseline, the descriptor-based approach provides more actionable prioritization of high-potency hits at the cost of a lower global ROC-AUC. This trade-off is consistent with UMAP’s algorithmic focus on local versus global structure preservation. For practical virtual screening, where only the top 0.1% to 1% of a library is typically screened, optimizing for EF@1% and BEDROC is operationally more valuable than maintaining a correct ranking order among non-active decoys.

Finally, the detection of a moderate baseline preference for ChEMBL compounds over ZINC decoys underscores the challenge of database bias in retrospective validation. While the target-specific biological signal was found to be approximately 2.5-fold stronger than this background bias, absolute performance metrics must be interpreted with this inflation in mind. Despite this, the consistent performance across eight diverse protein targets (Phase 4) demonstrates that the method generalizes beyond the optimization target (ABL1), with performance dropping with the size of RS. It should be noted that the cross-target validation was performed without rehyperparameterizing UMAP for each specific functional class; thus, the reported results likely represent a conservative lower bound of the method’s potential performance when tuned for specific target families.

The Phase 5 controls establish three key findings:

Partial database bias exists but does not dominate. MolFuSE exhibits moderate ChEMBL-over-ZINC enrichment for irrelevant targets (EF@1% = 13.5), confirming database provenance introduces bias. However, this effect is 2.5-fold weaker than target-specific performance (EF@1% = 30–34), demonstrating that biological signals dominate over database artifacts. Absolute performance metrics should be interpreted with this bias acknowledged.

UMAP is essential for descriptor-based screening. Compared to the 1,611-dimensional raw descriptors (EF@1% = 7.8), UMAP embeddings increase performance by 166% (EF@1% = 20.7,\(p < 0.001\)). The curse of dimensionality renders high-dimensional Euclidean spaces ineffective for nearest-neighbor search; manifold learning is necessary, not optional. Notably, Phase 4 UMAP results represent average cross-target performance, suggesting this benefit generalizes across protein families.

MolFuSE modestly improves upon industry-standard Tanimoto. Raw ECFP4 fingerprints with Tanimoto similarity provide a strong baseline (EF@1% = 30.1), which UMAP integration improves by 12.6% (EF@1% = 33.9,\(p < 0.001\)). The gain is concentrated in early enrichment (top 1%), the most critical region for experimental validation. While UMAP introduces a trade-off by reducing global ROC-AUC (0.863 vs. 0.961), it notably improves actionable, top-ranked predictions, representing a good compromise for practical screening applications.

These results validate MolFuSE’s core hypothesis, that manifold learning enhances ligand-based virtual screening, while honestly characterizing limitations and establishing that simpler baselines (Tanimoto) remain competitive.

Herein, we introduced MolFuSE, a projection-based virtual screening framework (i.e., for ligand-repurposing) that leverages a reference set (RS) of ligands that bind proteins with the same molecular function as the target protein. By capitalizing on UMAP’s dimensionality reduction, this method constructs a lower-dimensional embedding space that significantly enhances early recognition performance, achieving good enrichment of high-potency compounds in low-data regimes. Through systematic evaluation across four experimental phases, we demonstrate that this model has:

High-potency discrimination: UMAP embeddings of Mordred 2D molecular descriptors’ explicit encoding of binding-relevant properties (LogP, hydrogen bonding, electronic distribution) substantially outperforms topology-focused ECFP4 fingerprint-based methods in the early recognition (EF@1%) of tight binders, although topological fingerprints maintain better global ranking quality (ROC-AUC).

RS size vs. performance: Effective screening is achievable with RS as small as 1,000 compounds, enabling application to orphan targets and understudied protein families. Performance peaks at 10,000 compounds and degrades at 100,000+, suggesting that feature space dilution from structurally diverse weak binders impairs retrieval—challenging the assumption that larger RS are universally better. Instead, MolFuSE refines the ’similar property principle’ [52] by demonstrating that for high-potency retrieval, the quality and physicochemical specificity of RS are more critical than its size.

MolFuSE addresses a challenging problem in early-stage drug discovery: effective virtual screening for targets with limited SAR data. By transferring knowledge from related functional classes via RS, MolFuSE achieves good enrichment performance without direct knowledge of known binders. The method’s interpretability—via exact 1-NN scoring and traceable similarity paths—further enhances its utility for medicinal chemistry hit triaging.

While MolFuSE demonstrates robust performance, several avenues for refinement remain. First, UMAP hyperparameters were optimized to a single protein target and then held constant across all targets to ensure a standardized benchmark. Consequently, target-specific rehyperparameterization could yield improved results. While we also identified a bias in the decoy dataset, its impact on MolFuSE’s performance was minimal.

A primary limitation is the reliance on Mordred’s 2D descriptors:

Shape and Stereochemistry: The current model does not explicitly encode 3D volume/curvature, shape moments, or chiral centers (i.e., enantiomers may receive identical embeddings).

Conformational Flexibility: Conformer preferences and flexibility are currently unrepresented.

All results in this study are retrospective. While high enrichment of ChEMBL-sourced actives is valuable, the ultimate utility of MolFuSE must be confirmed through prospective experimental validation. Future efforts will focus on the testing of compounds to confirm that top-tier enrichment translates into viable experimental hit rates (\(>10\%\)) and successful lead optimization campaigns. MolFuSE could be extended to look at off-target effects and toxicity by finding similar compounds with a shared scaffold but differing substitution patterns. It could also be used to suggest molecules that balance substructure similarity and differing extended/branching scaffolds. This next step would be a multi-objective LBVS strategy. In conclusion, by leveraging non-linear manifold learning, MolFuSE offers a beneficial path to accelerate hit discovery in data-constrained virtual screening workflows, particularly for under-explored therapeutic targets.

title: ADMET property prediction and toxicity profiling of CDK2 inhibitors: a practical cheminformatics tutorial using ADMET-AI 2.0 and RDKit
author: Festus O. Ogungbemiro; Jane O. Anebi; Felix O. Okunlola; Love A. Onyekwere; Evna M. M. Pereira
text:
Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity (ADMET) prediction plays a central role in modern computer-aided drug discovery by enabling early evaluation of pharmacokinetic behaviour and safety liabilities. This tutorial presents a reproducible computational workflow for large-scale ADMET profiling using ADMET-AI 2.0, a graph neural network-based prediction platform, applied to 200 cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) inhibitors curated from ChEMBL release 35. Implemented within an annotated Jupyter notebook, the workflow integrates cheminformatics preprocessing, physicochemical property analysis, drug-likeness evaluation, structural alert screening, absorption and distribution profiling, CYP450-mediated metabolism prediction, excretion assessment, toxicity evaluation, Tox21 pathway analysis, DrugBank percentile benchmarking, and composite multi-parameter optimisation scoring. A total of 104 ADMET-related outputs were generated per compound, including 52 predictive endpoints and 52 corresponding DrugBank approved-drug percentile rankings. The 200 curated CDK2 inhibitors exhibited 100% Lipinski Ro5 compliance, 38.5% predicted CYP3A4 inhibition, 73.5% predicted hERG liability, and 99.5% predicted DILI risk, with a mean composite ADMET score of 0.46 and a mean traffic light green flag count of 9.5/13. The workflow provides an accessible and FAIR-compliant framework for ADMET analysis, cheminformatics education, and reproducible computational drug discovery.

Scientific contribution

This work contributes a structured educational framework for teaching and implementing computational ADMET analysis in modern drug discovery. To be explicit about the nature of this contribution: the novelty is pedagogical and integrative rather than methodological, no new prediction model, algorithm, or endpoint is introduced. The study demonstrates how an existing graph neural network-based prediction model (ADMET-AI) can be integrated with open-source cheminformatics workflows to support interpretable and reproducible pharmacokinetic assessment. Beyond endpoint prediction, the tutorial emphasises practical data handling, workflow automation, compound prioritisation, and transparent result interpretation within a Jupyter notebook environment. The inclusion of DrugBank percentile benchmarking, traffic-light visualisation, and composite scoring strategies provides learners and researchers with practical, worked examples of established multi-parameter decision-making approaches during lead optimisation, rather than new decision frameworks in their own right. By combining methodological clarity with FAIR and reproducible research principles, the workflow serves as a scalable resource for cheminformatics education, computational pharmacology training, and ADMET-guided drug development studies.
