The translation of a promising chemical compound from a laboratory hit into an approved therapeutic requires not only that the compound binds its biological target with sufficient potency [1], but also that it survives the complex physicochemical and biological environment of the human body long enough to reach that target at effective concentrations [1,2], remain there for an adequate duration, and be safely eliminated without producing harmful effects. These requirements are collectively captured by the acronym ADMET: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity, representing the five pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic domains that determine whether a compound can function as a drug in a living organism [2,3,4]. Despite decades of progress in medicinal chemistry, ADMET-related failures remain the leading cause of drug candidate attrition: Waring and colleagues reported in 2015 that pharmacokinetic and toxicological failures account for approximately 40% of drug terminations across four major pharmaceutical companies [2,3], and more recent analyses confirm that this proportion has remained high despite widespread ADMET screening adoption [3]. Given that average drug development costs exceed $2.6 billion per approved drug [4], and that late-stage clinical failures are dramatically more expensive than early-stage failures, there is an overwhelming incentive to identify and eliminate ADMET liabilities computationally as early as possible.

Computational prediction of ADMET properties has evolved substantially over the past two decades, progressing from early empirical rules such as Lipinski's Rule of Five [5] which identified molecular weight, lipophilicity, and hydrogen bonding as determinants of oral bioavailability through descriptor-based QSAR models, to modern graph neural networks trained on thousands of experimental measurements across all five ADMET domains [6]. The Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC), introduced by Huang and colleagues in 2021 [7], established curated, standardised benchmark datasets for 22 ADMET prediction tasks enabling systematic model comparison. ADMET-AI, introduced by Swanson and colleagues in 2024 [8], leverages the Chemprop-RDKit graph neural network architecture [9] to predict 52 ADMET endpoints simultaneously, uniquely providing percentile rankings against 2,579 FDA-approved drugs from DrugBank [10] that enable direct contextualisation of predictions against the approved drug landscape.

Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 2 (CDK2) was selected as the tutorial target for compelling scientific and pedagogical reasons. CDK2 (UniProt P24941, ChEMBL CHEMBL301) is a serine/threonine protein kinase forming active complexes with Cyclin E to drive the G1-to-S phase transition, and with Cyclin A during S phase progression [11]. Dysregulated CDK2 activity is a hallmark of breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and leukaemia [12], and CDK2 has one of the largest public bioactivity datasets in ChEMBL, with over 2,000 unique inhibitors spanning sub-nanomolar clinical candidates to micromolar inactive compounds ideal for demonstrating ADMET profiling across all activity classes.

The tutorial uses ADMET-AI 2.0 [8] as the sole prediction engine rather than web tools such as pkCSM [13] or SwissADME [14] for three reasons: ADMET-AI runs fully locally after a single pip install with no compound number limits; its DrugBank percentile ranking feature provides an immediately interpretable benchmark unavailable in web tools; and it predicts 52 endpoints simultaneously in a single programmatic call. The prediction engine treats each molecule as a mathematical graph using atomic-level message-passing operations [9], generating molecular representations that incorporate both local chemical environment and global molecular topology, concatenated with 200 RDKit-computed physicochemical features before prediction. Compared with ADMETlab 2.0 [15] and ADMETlab 3.0 [16], which offer broader endpoint coverage through a web API, ADMET-AI’s offline capability and programmatic Python interface are uniquely suited to the reproducible educational workflow demonstrated here.

The tutorial adheres to five pedagogical principles detailed in “Educational design principles” section: concept-before-code (every code cell preceded by a scientific explanation); realistic-data (genuine ChEMBL variation, not sanitised data); validation-first (five-anchor ground truth validation before any analysis); reproducibility (pinned software versions, embedded dataset, FAIR archive); and progressive-complexity (18-cell sequential structure from fundamentals to integrated reporting).

All analyses used Python 3.11 in a conda-managed environment (cdk2_admet_tutorial) reproducible from the pinned environment.yml file supplied in the repository. Confirmed package versions: RDKit 2026.03.3 [17] for molecular parsing, descriptor calculation, and SVG visualisation; ADMET-AI 2.0.1 [8] for ADMET prediction; pandas 3.0.3; NumPy 1.26.4; matplotlib 3.11.0; seaborn 0.13.2; scikit-learn ≥ 1.4.2, chembl-webresource-client 0.10.9. The numpy < 2.0 constraint is necessary because RDKit conda-forge builds for Python 3.11 are compiled against NumPy 1.x; NumPy ≥ 2.0 causes an AttributeError at RDKit import. Cell 0 suppresses PyTorch Lightning GPU availability messages, validates all package versions via Python assert statements with quantitative range checks, and defines a global PALETTE dictionary for consistent visualisation. Cell 0 also includes an optional, commented-out CPU-only override (os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "") for users who encounter PyTorch/CUDA-related errors when ADMET-AI attempts to initialise a GPU device with a misconfigured driver (this is a runtime setting only and requires no change to environment.yml. All imports are consolidated in Cell 0; no import statements appear in later cells. The notebook has been tested on Windows 11, macOS 15.x, and Ubuntu 22.04 (all cells pass). Environment reproduction:

Cell 0B provides a structured four-part introduction covering: (1) Python data structures for chemistry lists, dictionaries, and DataFrames demonstrated with three reference drugs; (2) SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) notation [18] parsing, canonical SMILES generation, and molecular graph inspection with RDKit; (3) the five ADMET domains in plain language with clinical examples for each endpoint; and (4) ADMET-AI 2.0 architecture, training data (TDC [7]), and the 104-property output structure. This cell is specifically designed for students with basic Python familiarity but no prior cheminformatics or pharmacokinetics exposure, following the progressive pedagogy recommended by Perkel [19] for Jupyter notebook-based science education.

The tutorial dataset comprises 200 CDK2 inhibitors retrieved from ChEMBL release 35 [20] targeting CDK2 (CHEMBL301, UniProt P24941, Homo sapiens), a serine/threonine kinase essential for cell cycle regulation. CDK2 forms active complexes with Cyclin E at the G1/S transition and with Cyclin A during S phase, making it a validated oncology target. The dataset was curated prior to this tutorial using a six-step pipeline—IC50 standardisation, unit filtering, exact-relation filtering, duplicate removal, invalid record removal, and geometric mean aggregation of replicate measurements [21] and is loaded directly from a companion CSV file (cdk2_inhibitors_200.csv), separating data management from analysis code as a reproducibility best practice.

To ensure broad coverage of biological activity space, compounds were selected using a stratified sampling strategy across five potency strata: 25 very potent compounds (IC50 < 10 nM), 55 potent (10–100 nM), 60 moderate (100–1000 nM), 40 weak (1–10 µM), and 20 inactive (IC50 > 10 µM). Upon loading, pIC50 values were computed as −log₁₀(IC50 in Molar) and compounds were classified into three activity categories (Active: pIC50 > 6.0; Intermediate: 5.0–6.0; Inactive: pIC50 < 5.0). Nine RDKit physicochemical descriptors were then calculated for each compound molecular weight (MW), lipophilicity (clogP), [22] hydrogen bond donors (HBD), hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), topological polar surface area (TPSA) [23], rotatable bond count, fraction of sp3carbons (Fsp3) [24], heavy atom count (HAC), and ring count—providing the structural context for all subsequent ADMET analyses.

To address reproducibility and transparency requirements, Cell 1B performs a programmatic provenance analysis of the 200-compound dataset using the ChEMBL web resource client (v0.10.9) [20]. For each of the 200 ChEMBL IDs, all IC50 activity records against CHEMBL301 are retrieved via the ChEMBL REST API, collecting the source document identifier (document_chembl_id), assay identifier (assay_chembl_id), assay type code, and assay description. A total of 580 activity records were retrieved across 185 unique assays.

Counting unique document_chembl_id values established that the 200 compounds originate from 124 independent peer-reviewed publications, confirming the broad chemical and pharmacological diversity of the dataset rather than dependence on a small number of studies. The assay type distribution shows that 555 of 580 records (95.7%) derive from Binding assays (type B), with a minority from Functional assays (type F, n = 24) and a single ADMET record (type A, n = 1).

Regarding binding mode, ChEMBL assay descriptions do not systematically annotate binding site identity, and keyword-based searches for ATP in assay text are not a valid proxy since ATP appears routinely as a cofactor in kinase assay buffers rather than as a descriptor of compound binding site. The attribution of all dataset compounds to the ATP-binding pocket is therefore established on mechanistic grounds: CDK2 possesses a single well-characterised druggable site the ATP-binding cleft between the N- and C-lobes of the kinase domain and no allosteric small-molecule binding site has been established for CDK2 in the structural or pharmacological literature [11,15,16]. All IC50-active compounds selected against CHEMBL301 are therefore conventionally attributed to the ATP-binding cleft, consistent with all published CDK2 co-crystal structures bearing small-molecule ligands.

ADMET-AI 2.0.1 [8] predicted 104 properties for all 200 compounds via ADMETModel.predict(). The model ensemble of two Chemprop-RDKit graph neural networks [9] processes each molecule as a directed graph: atoms as nodes with features (element, charge, aromaticity, hybridisation, H-count) and bonds as edges (type, conjugation, ring membership). Message-passing iteratively aggregates neighbour information into molecular representations, concatenated with 200 RDKit physicochemical features before prediction. The 104 outputs comprise 52 raw predicted values (binary probabilities [0,1] or continuous) and 52 DrugBank percentile rankings benchmarking each prediction against 2,579 FDA-approved drugs from DrugBank 5.0 [10]. Pipeline validation used five reference drugs spanning all ADMET domains (Table1); a pass/fail criterion of probability ≥ 0.5 for known positives and < 0.5 for known negatives was applied.

Before interpreting predictions for the 200 CDK2 inhibitors, the predictive performance of ADMET-AI 2.0 must be considered so that predictions are not taken at face value. Supplementary Table S3 (Table_S3_ADMET_Endpoints.xlsx, submitted alongside this manuscript) provides a comprehensive reference of all 55 endpoints and descriptors analysed in this tutorial (46 ADMET-AI predictions + 9 RDKit computed descriptors), annotated with: source, domain, training dataset name and size, endpoint type, unit, published TDC benchmark metric, and interpretation threshold. Endpoints are categorised into confidence tiers: High confidence (AUROC ≥ 0.85, e.g. AMES n = 7,255 AUROC = 0.877, HIA n = 578 AUROC = 0.984, BBB n = 1,975 AUROC = 0.916); Moderate confidence (AUROC 0.70–0.85, e.g. Bioavailability n = 640 AUROC = 0.748); Low-moderate confidence (n < 500, e.g. DILI n = 475, Carcinogens n = 278). A formal per-compound Tanimoto similarity analysis between the CDK2 inhibitors and TDC training sets requires the PyTDC package, which introduces a dependency conflict with admet-ai =  = 2.0.1 in the same conda environment. A formal, scaffold-split-aware overlap analysis using the exact PyTDC train/test partitions therefore still requires installing PyTDC in a separate environment, and readers requiring that level of rigour should compute Tanimoto similarity (ECFP4, threshold ≥ 0.85; Maggiora et al. [30]) between query compounds and the TDC training sets accordingly. A lightweight but executed compound-level nearest-neighbour similarity assessment against the full 41-dataset TDC training pool—which does not require PyTDC—is now implemented directly in Cell 2C (“Executed applicability domain analysis: chemical space and k-NN Tanimoto similarity (Cell 2C)” section).

For QSAR/GNN models, the applicability domain (AD) defines the chemical space within which predictions are considered reliable  [31]. Two complementary AD methods are described. Method 1: k-NN Tanimoto similarity (ECFP4, k = 5); compounds with mean Tanimoto < 0.35 to training-set neighbours are flagged out-of-domain. Method 2: PCA-based distance; compounds beyond the 95th percentile of Euclidean distance from the training-set centroid in 10-component PCA space are flagged as structural outliers. A full, scaffold-split-aware execution of these methods against the exact PyTDC train/test partitions requires PyTDC, which conflicts with the reproducible conda environment (“ADMET-AI model performance and training data context (Cell 2B)” section). Method 1 (k-NN Tanimoto, k = 5, threshold 0.35) is now executed in full in Cell 2C (“Executed applicability domain analysis: chemical space and k-NN Tanimoto similarity (Cell 2C)” section) against the complete 41-dataset TDC training pool, without PyTDC. Method 2 (PCA-based centroid-distance outlier flagging) remains a candidate for future extension; Cell 2C instead provides a 2-component PCA chemical-space visualisation (not a formal outlier flag) as an accompanying, purely descriptive view of the same chemical space. Cell 2B additionally provides TDC training set sizes and benchmark performance per endpoint, serving as a complementary model-level AD proxy: endpoints with small training sets (n < 500) and lower benchmark performance carry higher prediction uncertainty, effectively identifying the soft edges of the applicability domain at the endpoint level.

Cell 2C addresses a basic visualisation of the chemical space covered by the 200 CDK2 inhibitors relative to the ADMET-AI training data, without requiring PyTDC or breaking the single-command reproducible environment. The 41 single-task TDC ADMET datasets used to train ADMET-AI (“ADMET-AI model performance and training data context (Cell 2B)” section) were downloaded directly from the ADMET-AI Zenodo archive (https://zenodo.org/records/10372419/files/data.zip?download=1) and merged into a single reference file, data/tdc_admet_all.csv, containing one row per unique training SMILES across all 41 datasets combined (52,665 unique compounds). This file requires no PyTDC installation. Two analyses are executed: (1) ECFP4 Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2048 bits) were computed for the 200 CDK2 inhibitors and for a random subsample of the TDC training compounds, and both sets were projected into two dimensions by PCA to visualise the CDK2 inhibitors relative to the training chemical space; (2) for every CDK2 inhibitor, the mean Tanimoto similarity to its five nearest neighbours (k-NN, k = 5) among the full 52,665 TDC training compounds was computed using RDKit's BulkTanimotoSimilarity, and each compound was flagged in-domain (mean similarity ≥ 0.35) or out-of-domain (< 0.35), following the threshold already specified in “Applicability domain assessment” section [31]. This is a lightweight, dependency-free approximation of a full scaffold-split-aware PyTDC analysis, not a replacement for it, and is presented as such.

Nine physicochemical properties were analysed. Five are computed by RDKit (molecular weight via Descriptors.MolWt(), logP via Wildman-Crippen [22], HBD, HBA, TPSA via Ertl fragment method [23]) and four are predicted by ADMET-AI 2.0 trained on experimental datasets (QED [32], aqueous solubility Solubility_AqSolDB [33], lipophilicity at pH 7.4 Lipophilicity_AstraZeneca, hydration free energy HydrationFreeEnergy_FreeSolv [34]). Table S3 lists the source for every endpoint analysed in this tutorial. Histograms were generated stratified by activity class to reveal whether potent CDK2 inhibitors occupy distinct physicochemical space.

Drug-likeness was assessed using the Lipinski Rule of Five (Ro5) [5]. Note: QED was analysed in “Physicochemical profiling (Cell 3)” section and is not repeated here to avoid redundancy. Three structural alert systems implemented via RDKit substructure matching (not ADMET-AI predictions) were applied: PAINS (480 substructure alerts for pan-assay interference via redox cycling, metal chelation, and covalent modification [35]); BRENK alerts (105 alerts for reactive or metabolically unstable functional groups [36]); and NIH alerts (NIH Molecular Libraries programme diversity filters [37]). As emphasised by Baell and Holloway [35], structural alerts indicate statistical risk and require expert structural review rather than automatic exclusion, flagged compounds may contain electrophilic moieties essential for their binding mechanism.

Five absorption endpoints were profiled. Caco-2 permeability (Caco2_Wang): log cm/s, threshold > −5.15 [38]. HIA (HIA_Hou): binary, HIA ≥ 30% [39]. Oral bioavailability F20% (Bioavailability_Ma): binary, F > 20% [40]. PAMPA permeability (PAMPA_NCATS): passive membrane permeability from NCATS pharmaceutical collection [41]. P-gp substrate (Pgp_Broccatelli): binary efflux prediction, non-substrate preferred for CNS and oral targets [42].

Three distribution endpoints: BBB penetration (BBB_Martins): binary classifier trained on 1,975 compounds [43]. Plasma protein binding (PPBR_AZ): regression, % bound; only unbound fraction is pharmacologically active [44]. Volume of distribution (VDss_Lombardo): regression, L/kg; >1 L/kg indicates extensive tissue distribution [45].

Seven CYP450 endpoints were profiled covering five isoforms responsible for approximately 75% of drug metabolism [46]. Inhibition of CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 was predicted using Veith dataset models [47]. Substrate prediction for CYP2C9, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 used Carbon-Mangels dataset models [48]. A compound-by-endpoint heatmap was generated for 60 active CDK2 inhibitors alongside a positivity rate bar chart for all 200 compounds.

Three excretion endpoints: hepatocyte clearance (Clearance_Hepatocyte_AZ, uL/min/10⁶ cells, AstraZeneca dataset); microsomal clearance (Clearance_Microsome_AZ, uL/min/mg protein, AstraZeneca dataset); plasma half-life (Half_Life_Obach, hours, Obach dataset [49]). Clinical half-life categories: <1 h very rapid; 1–8 h short; 8–24 h moderate; >24 h long-acting.

Six binary and one continuous toxicity endpoint: hERG inhibition [25]; AMES mutagenicity (Salmonella typhimurium test, ICH S2(R1) requirement [29]); DILI (FDA DILIrank-trained model [50]); ClinTox clinical failure (FDA-approved vs withdrawn drugs [51]); carcinogenicity (Lagunin dataset [52]); skin sensitisation (Mansouri dataset [53]); acute oral toxicity LD50 (Zhu dataset [54], log mol/kg; higher = less toxic).

Twelve Tox21 endpoints from the NIH/EPA/FDA collaboration [55] covering: nuclear receptor panel (NR-AR, NR-AR-LBD, NR-AhR, NR-Aromatase, NR-ER, NR-ER-LBD, NR-PPAR-gamma) unintended activation causes endocrine disruption; and stress response panel (SR-ARE, SR-ATAD5, SR-HSE, SR-MMP, SR-p53) indicators of oxidative stress, genotoxicity, and mitochondrial toxicity.

ADMET-AI 2.0 automatically benchmarks each predicted value against 2,579 FDA-approved drugs from DrugBank 5.0 [10], providing a percentile ranking that contextualises predictions against the approved drug landscape. Ten key endpoints were analysed. For favourable properties (HIA, BBB, bioavailability, solubility, half-life, QED), a higher percentile indicates performance superior to a greater proportion of approved drugs. For unfavourable properties (hERG, AMES, DILI, CYP3A4 inhibition), a lower percentile indicates lower predicted risk relative to approved drugs importantly, a low hERG percentile indicates lower cardiac risk than most approved drugs (favourable), not high risk. This percentile ranking is an ADMET-AI-derived descriptive feature rather than an independently validated risk-stratification tool, and is used here for interpretive context and teaching purposes rather than as a standalone prioritisation criterion.

Binary green/red decision rules following Gleeson et al. [44] were applied to 13 endpoints, yielding a maximum of 13 green flags per compound. The 13 endpoints and their green criteria are as follows: 8 safety endpoints flagged green when predicted probability < 0.5 (predicted not a risk): hERG, AMES, DILI, ClinTox, Carcinogens_Lagunin, Skin_Reaction, PAINS, BRENK; 3 PK/absorption endpoints flagged green when predicted probability ≥ 0.5 (predicted absorbed or penetrant): HIA, Bioavailability, BBB; 1 drug-likeness endpoint flagged green when Lipinski score ≥ 0.5 (Ro5 compliant); 1 efflux endpoint flagged green when predicted probability < 0.5 (non-substrate preferred): Pgp substrate. Red is assigned for the opposite condition in each case. The 13-endpoint framework was selected to span all five ADMET domains and two structural alert systems, providing a comprehensive multi-parameter overview. It should be understood explicitly as a didactic decision-support heuristic built on predefined, literature-informed thresholds, intended to support teaching, exploratory analysis, and hypothesis generation—not as a validated, experimentally confirmed compound-prioritisation algorithm. Top 30 compounds by green count were displayed as a heatmap with G/R cell annotations.

An Multi-Parameter Optimisation (MPO)-inspired [56] composite ADMET score was constructed from 11 endpoints using desirability functions mapping each predicted value onto [0, 1]. Safety endpoints (hERG, AMES, DILI, ClinTox, PAINS, BRENK): d = 1−min(val/0.5, 1). PK endpoints (HIA, Bioavailability, Lipinski): d = min(val/0.5, 1). Caco-2 (continuous log cm/s, range [− 8, −4]): linear normalisation; default −6.0 for missing values (not 0.5, which is dimensionally incorrect for a non-probability endpoint). QED used directly as bounded in [0, 1]. Weights sum to exactly 1.0 (verified by assertion): hERG, AMES, DILI, ClinTox 0.15 each (60%); HIA, Bioavailability, Caco-2 0.08 each (24%); Lipinski, QED 0.05 each (10%); PAINS, BRENK 0.03 each (6%). Tiers: Excellent ≥ 0.80; Good 0.65–0.79; Moderate 0.50–0.64; Poor < 0.50. As with the traffic light dashboard (“ADMET traffic light dashboard (Cell 12)” section), this composite score is an author-defined desirability function with manually assigned weights and predefined tiers; it is presented as a didactic device for teaching multi-parameter trade-offs and generating hypotheses, not as an experimentally validated compound-prioritisation model, and should not be used as a sole or definitive basis for compound selection decisions.

Cell 14 rendered the twelve top-scoring compounds as a 2D SVG structure grid using RDKit’s rdMolDraw2D.MolDraw2DSVG Cairo-free renderer [17], annotated with pIC50, ADMET score, and hERG probability. Cell 15 exported the integrated CSV report (cdk2_integrated_admet_report.csv) containing all 200 compounds with 119 columns: 13 physicochemical descriptors, 52 raw ADMET-AI predictions, 52 DrugBank percentile rankings, 13 traffic light flags, composite ADMET score, ADMET tier, and 2 applicability-domain columns (AD_mean_knn_tanimoto, AD_flag; Cell 2C), following FAIR data principles [57].

Cell 0 confirmed all required packages at specified versions. ADMET-AI 2.0.1 loaded successfully and warning suppression correctly filtered PyTorch Lightning messages. Cell 0B demonstrated SMILES parsing for Aspirin, Ibuprofen, and Caffeine, showing canonical SMILES standardisation, molecular graph inspection (atoms, bonds, rings), and the ADMET domain taxonomy across all 52 ADMET-AI endpoints. The four-part fundamentals cell successfully bridges basic Python programming and cheminformatics concepts, providing the conceptual scaffolding required for all subsequent cells.

All 200 CDK2 inhibitor SMILES parsed successfully into valid RDKit Mol objects from data/cdk2_inhibitors_200.csv. Dataset statistics: pIC50 range 4.208–9.523; mean MW 419.3 Da; mean logP 3.39; mean TPSA 92.5 Å2, all within Lipinski Ro5 space [5] and consistent with published CDK2 inhibitor analyses. The activity distribution across potency strata is summarised in Table2. The 200 compounds originate from 124 independent ChEMBL experimental studies employing ATP-competitive CDK2 binding assays and 185 unique assays. The dominant assay type is Binding (B, direct CDK2 binding), with a minority of Functional (F) assays measuring kinase activity. Because CDK2 has no characterised allosteric site for small molecules, inhibition measured by IC50 against CHEMBL301 is mechanistically attributed to the ATP-binding cleft across all compounds in this dataset confirming broad chemical and pharmacological diversity. The deliberate inclusion of Inactive compounds provides essential negative controls for ADMET comparison across activity classes, demonstrating how property profiles differ between compounds with genuine target engagement and those lacking sufficient CDK2 affinity.

ADMET-AI ran in approximately 60–90 s on the CPU-only test system, generating a 200 × 104 prediction matrix. All five ground truth validation anchors passed both directional and quantitative range assertions (Table3): Verapamil hERG = 0.969 (confirmed strong hERG inhibitor [25]); Caffeine BBB = 0.982 (confirmed highly CNS-penetrant [26]); Metformin HIA = 0.289 (confirmed low intestinal absorber [27]); Atorvastatin CYP3A4_substrate = 0.666 (confirmed major CYP3A4 substrate [28]); Ibuprofen AMES = 0.009 (confirmed non-mutagenic [29]). Cell 2 applies real unit-test assertions with quantitative ranges calibrated against the admet-ai =  = 2.0.1 environment, providing rigorous pipeline validation beyond directional sanity checks. These results confirm pipeline integrity across all five ADMET domains before CDK2 dataset analysis.

Applicability domain analysis generated by Cell 2C (admet_chemical_space_pca.png). PCA projection of ECFP4 fingerprints for the 200 CDK2 inhibitors against a random subsample of the 52,665 TDC training compounds; CDK2 inhibitors highlighted in red

The k-NN (k = 5) Tanimoto similarity analysis executed in Cell 2C found that 45.0% (90/200) of the 200 CDK2 inhibitors met the in-domain threshold (mean similarity to their five nearest TDC training neighbours ≥ 0.35), with a mean k-NN similarity of 0.383 across the full dataset (range 0.245–0.875). The remaining 110 compounds (55.0%) fell below this threshold and are flagged out-of-domain. The PCA chemical-space visualisation (Fig.1) shows the CDK2 inhibitors distributed across two regions: the majority overlap with the central, densely populated region of TDC training chemical space, while a distinct cluster of inhibitors occupies a separate region at positive PC1/PC2 values with comparatively sparse training-set coverage, consistent with the roughly even split between in-domain and out-of-domain compounds by the k-NN criterion. This is consistent with the aminopurine, aminopyrimidine, and oxindole kinase-inhibitor scaffolds in this dataset being only partially represented within general bioactivity training data, and indicates that ADMET-AI predictions for a substantial fraction (55.0%) of the CDK2 inhibitors in this tutorial should be interpreted with additional caution, as they fall in an under-represented region of training chemical space. These compounds are identified individually via the AD_flag column in the integrated report (Cell 15, Table S1).

The nine-panel histogram (Fig.2) revealed clear activity-class-dependent property distributions. Mean MW 419.3 Da (range 184.2–835.9 Da) and mean logP 3.39 placed the dataset well within Lipinski Ro5 space [5]. All 200 compounds achieved 100% Lipinski Ro5 compliance. Mean QED was 0.585, with 38.5% of compounds exceeding the 0.6 drug-likeness threshold [32]; Active compounds showed higher mean QED than Inactive compounds, demonstrating that ChEMBL CDK2 optimisation campaigns have been conducted under integrated property design principles [44]. Mean aqueous solubility was −4.47 log mol/L (std 0.80), with the majority of compounds near the −4.0 threshold for adequate oral formulation [33]. Mean hydration free energy was −15.72 kcal/mol (std 3.17), consistent with the polar CDK2 ATP binding site. Five physicochemical descriptors (MW, logP, HBD, HBA, TPSA) are computed by RDKit; four (QED, solubility, lipophilicity, hydration free energy) are predicted by ADMET-AI 2.0.

Drug-likeness and structural alert profiles generated by Cell 4 (admet_druglikeness_alerts.png). Left: QED distribution with 0.6 threshold [32]. Right three panels: Clean vs Flagged counts for PAINS [35], BRENK [36], and NIH [37] alert systems

Lipinski Ro5 compliance was 100% (200/200 compounds), confirming the ChEMBL curation effectively selected drug-like compounds. PAINS screening flagged 10 compounds (5.0%), BRENK flagged 32 (16.0%), and NIH alerts flagged 8 (4.0%); 165 compounds (82.5%) were clean across all three systems (Fig.3). The flagged compounds were annotated rather than automatically excluded, consistent with Baell and Holloway [35], who emphasised that PAINS alerts require expert structural review. Several flagged CDK2 inhibitors contain electrophilic moieties required for covalent or pseudo-covalent binding mechanisms, illustrating the context-dependence of alert interpretation that is a key pedagogical point of Cell 4.

Absorption profiles generated by Cell 5 (admet_absorption.png). Six-panel figure: Caco-2 histogram [38]; PAMPA histogram [41]; HIA bar chart [39]; bioavailability F20% bar chart [40]; Pgp substrate bar chart [42]; Caco-2 vs PAMPA scatter coloured by activity class

Caco-2 permeability (Caco2_Wang) showed mean −5.17 log cm/s (std 0.35, range −7.10 to −4.55), with the majority of compounds near the −5.15 threshold for acceptable permeability [38]. HIA (HIA_Hou) predicted 198/200 compounds absorbed (99.0%) [39], consistent with the Lipinski-compliant physicochemical profile of the dataset. Oral bioavailability F20% (Bioavailability_Ma) was 98.5% (197/200) [40]. Pgp substrate prediction (Pgp_Broccatelli) identified 46.0% (92/200) as P-gp substrates, with 54.0% predicted as non-substrates [42]; P-gp efflux is a clinically significant resistance mechanism for kinase inhibitors. Mean PAMPA permeability was 0.767 (std 0.18), and the PAMPA versus Caco-2 scatter plot revealed a positive but imperfect correlation, consistent with Siramshetty et al. [41], who demonstrated that active transport components in Caco-2 cells introduce systematic differences relative to purely passive PAMPA measurements.

Distribution profiles generated by Cell 6 (admet_distribution.png). BBB bar chart [43]; PPBR histogram [44]; VDss histogram [45]; BBB vs PPBR scatter by activity class

BBB penetration (BBB_Martins) predicted 140/200 compounds (70.0%) as BBB-penetrant [43]. For CDK2 inhibitors targeting peripheral oncology indications, CNS penetration represents a potential safety liability rather than a therapeutic benefit, motivating scaffold modification to reduce BBB penetrance while maintaining potency. Mean PPBR was 89.5%, with 55.0% of compounds (110/200) showing PPBR ≥ 90% [44], indicating high plasma protein binding that restricts free drug concentration. Mean VDss was 7.72 L/kg (std not shown), with 91.0% (182/200) exceeding 1 L/kg, indicating extensive tissue distribution beyond the plasma compartment [45].

CYP450 metabolism profiles generated by Cell 7 (admet_cyp450_metabolism.png). Left: heatmap of 7 CYP450 predictions for 60 active CDK2 inhibitors [47,48]. Right: positivity rate bar chart for all 200 compounds; red bars indicate rates above 50%

CYP3A4 inhibition (Veith dataset) predicted 38.5% (77/200) as inhibitors. CYP1A2 inhibition was 37.5% (75/200), CYP2C19 31.0% (62/200), CYP2C9 27.0% (54/200), and CYP2D6 10.5% (21/200)—the lowest inhibition rate, consistent with the narrow CYP2D6 active site being less accommodating of bulky CDK2 inhibitor scaffolds. CYP3A4 substrate prediction (Carbon-Mangels dataset) identified 78.5% (157/200) as CYP3A4 substrates, directly paralleling the CYP3A4 substrate status of approved CDK4/6 inhibitors (Palbociclib, Ribociclib, Abemaciclib) that require dose adjustments with CYP3A4 modulators [46,47]. The heatmap (Fig.6) of the top 60 Active compounds (sorted by pIC50) visually demonstrates co-occurrence patterns of CYP inhibition and substrate prediction across the most potent CDK2 inhibitors.

Excretion profiles generated by Cell 8 (admet_excretion.png). Histograms for hepatocyte clearance, microsomal clearance, and plasma half-life [49]; red dashed lines indicate medians

Hepatocyte clearance (Clearance_Hepatocyte_AZ) showed mean 28.7 µL/min/10⁶ cells (median 21.4). Microsomal clearance (Clearance_Microsome_AZ) showed mean 34.9 µL/min/mg protein (median 29.4). Half-life (Half_Life_Obach) showed mean 52.2 h (median 45.1 h): 2.0% very rapid (< 1 h), 0.5% short (1–8 h), 15.0% moderate (8–24 h), 82.5% long-acting (> 24 h). The predominance of long predicted half-lives (82.5%) is mechanistically consistent with the high predicted VDss (mean 7.72 L/kg) observed in “Distribution property profiling (Cell 6, Figure 4)” section: extensive tissue distribution reduces plasma clearance rate, prolonging apparent half-life. This combined finding is an important positive attribute for CDK2 inhibitor development, supporting once-daily dosing regimens.

Toxicity profiles generated by Cell 9 (admet_toxicity.png). Binary bar charts for hERG [25], AMES [29], DILI [50], C linTox [51], carcinogenicity [52], skin sensitisation [53]; LD50 histogram [54]; multi-flag count histogram

hERG inhibition risk was 73.5% (147/200) [25], reflecting the documented structural overlap between nitrogen-containing kinase inhibitor pharmacophores and hERG channel binding motifs. This high rate underscores the importance of early hERG profiling for CDK2 inhibitor programmes. AMES mutagenicity risk was 31.0% (62/200) [29]. DILI risk was 99.5% (199/200) [50] an exceptionally high rate consistent with the known hepatotoxic liability of nitrogen-rich heterocyclic scaffolds that dominate CDK2 inhibitor chemical space. ClinTox clinical failure risk was 40.5% (81/200) [51]. Carcinogenicity risk was low at 2.5% (5/200), and skin sensitisation at 6.5% (13/200). Multi-toxicity analysis showed 0 compounds with zero flags (0.0%), 38 with exactly one flag (19.0%), and 162 with two or more flags (81.0%). Mean LD50 was 2.73 log mol/kg (median 2.80), indicating moderate acute toxicity (Fig.8).

A compound-by-endpoint heatmap was chosen because it reveals co-activation patterns which compounds simultaneously activate multiple Tox21 pathways that are invisible in individual endpoint bar charts. NR-AhR (aryl hydrocarbon receptor) showed the highest nuclear receptor activation at 36.5% (73/200), consistent with polycyclic aromatic ring systems common in CDK2 inhibitor scaffolds [55]. NR-Aromatase activation was 8.5% (17/200). All other nuclear receptor endpoints (NR-AR, NR-AR-LBD, NR-ER, NR-ER-LBD, NR-PPAR-gamma) showed 0.0% activation, indicating low endocrine disruption risk. SR-ARE (antioxidant/oxidative stress response) was 32.5% (65/200), SR-MMP (mitochondrial) 29.0% (58/200), SR-p53 (DNA damage) 5.5% (11/200), SR-ATAD5 and SR-HSE each 0.5%. Compounds with zero Tox21 flags across all 12 endpoints constituted 48.0% (96/200) of the dataset, identifying the most mechanistically clean subset. In Fig.9, the 10% dashed line marks endpoints where more than 10% of all 200 CDK2 compounds are predicted active, this is a class-level dataset signal, not a per-compound risk threshold; individual compound risk must be assessed from the per-compound probability values in the integrated report CSV.

DrugBank percentile analysis generated by Cell 11 (admet_drugbank_percentiles.png). Left: box plots for 10 endpoints vs 2,579 approved drugs [10]; red line at 50th percentile. Right: median percentile radar chart; red circle at 50th percentile = average approved drug

CDK2 inhibitors compared favourably against approved drugs on PK: mean HIA percentile 55.1, mean oral bioavailability percentile 69.0 (better than 69% of approved drugs), mean half-life percentile 76.1, and mean QED percentile 58.4. However, they compared unfavourably on safety: mean hERG percentile 74.4 (higher predicted hERG inhibition than 74% of approved drugs, which is a concern), mean DILI percentile 83.5 (higher DILI risk than 83% of approved drugs), and mean CYP3A4 inhibition percentile 76.1 (stronger CYP3A4 inhibition than 76% of approved drugs). Mean AMES percentile was 65.2 and mean BBB percentile 40.7. The radar chart (Fig.10) captures this asymmetric profile: favourable absorption and PK, elevated metabolic and safety liabilities. This pattern is class-characteristic of nitrogen-containing kinase inhibitors and directly explains why post-marketing cardiac and hepatic safety monitoring is required for approved CDK4/6 inhibitors. Note: for hERG and DILI, a higher percentile indicates higher predicted risk (unfavourable); for HIA and bioavailability, a higher percentile indicates better absorption (favourable).

Mean green flag count was 9.5/13 across all 200 compounds. Compounds with 10 or more green flags constituted 47.0% (94/200) of the dataset, and 25 compounds (12.5%) achieved 12 or more green flags. No compound achieved all 13 green flags simultaneously, illustrating the fundamental property trade-offs inherent in drug-like chemical space (Fig.11). Programmatic analysis of the 25 compounds with 12/13 green flags confirms that DILI is the most common single red flag, consistent with the 99.5% DILI prediction rate identified in “Toxicity property profiling (Cell 9, Figure 7)” section. This finding is consistent with the known hepatotoxic liability of nitrogen-rich CDK2 inhibitor scaffolds [50].

Composite ADMET score distribution generated by Cell 13 (admet_composite_score.png). Left: histogram by tier [56]. Right: ADMET score vs pIC50 scatter by activity class; green dashed line at 0.65 (Good threshold)

Composite ADMET scores (Fig.12) ranged from 0.2986 to 0.7224 (mean 0.4604, median 0.4265, std 0.1121). Tier distribution: Excellent 0.0% (0 compounds), Good 8.5% (17), Moderate 27.0% (54), Poor 64.5% (129). The top 10 compounds by ADMET score were predominantly small MW (193–340 Da), logP 1.5–3.0 compounds, consistent with the composite score penalising large lipophilic compounds through the Caco-2 and DILI desirability functions. The dominance of the Poor tier reflects the near-universal DILI prediction (99.5%) which heavily penalises the composite score given its 0.15 weight. No compound achieves the Excellent tier (≥ 0.80) because the 0.60 combined toxicity weight virtually precludes a perfect composite score for compounds predicted DILI-positive. This finding has direct implications for CDK2 inhibitor optimisation: scaffold redesign to reduce DILI liability is the highest-priority intervention for improving composite ADMET quality.

2D structure grid of top 12 CDK2 inhibitors by ADMET score, generated by Cell 14 (admet_top12_structures.svg). MolDraw2DSVG renderer [17]. Legends: ChEMBL ID, pIC50, ADMET score, hERG probability

The twelve top-ADMET-scoring compounds (Fig.13) showed consistent structural characteristics: HAC 22–32, NH/OH donors for hinge contacts, limited lipophilic bulk. Aminopurine and aminopyrimidine scaffolds dominated, consistent with their established CDK2 pharmacophore properties [11]. Even among top-scoring compounds, hERG probabilities ranged 0.18–0.44, confirming that some cardiac safety risk is essentially unavoidable for nitrogen-containing CDK2 scaffolds. The integrated report (Tables4, S1) provides 121 columns across 200 compounds, constituting a complete ADMET-annotated CDK2 inhibitor reference resource directly usable for downstream machine learning, virtual screening, or SAR analysis.

Five pedagogical principles shaped the tutorial design; their implementation is demonstrated throughout the Methods and Results sections and is summarised here for reference. (1) Concept-before-code: each code cell is preceded by a markdown cell providing scientific rationale, clinical context, and interpretation guidance [19]. (2) Realistic-data: the ChEMBL-derived dataset includes genuine property variation rather than a sanitised teaching subset. (3) Validation-first: five-anchor ground truth validation with quantitative unit-test assertions spanning all ADMET domains precedes dataset analysis. (4) Reproducibility: all package versions are pinned in environment.yml; the dataset is provided as data/cdk2_inhibitors_200.csv, provides FAIR-compliant permanent access [57]. (5) Progressive-complexity: the 16-cell structure progresses from Python fundamentals to composite ADMET scoring.

]The tutorial occupies a unique position at the intersection of computational toxicology, ADMET cheminformatics, and open-source education. To reiterate the scope of the contribution stated in Scientific Contribution above: this positioning is claimed for the tutorial's pedagogical integration and workflow design, not for any new predictive method—ADMET-AI, RDKit, PAINS/BRENK/NIH filters, and the MPO-style composite scoring framework are all established tools and methods, applied here in a documented, validated, and reproducible combination. Web-based tool tutorials [13,14] lack programmatic integration and impose compound limits. Theoretical ADMET reviews [6] provide no executable code. General ML tutorials cover property prediction without focusing on ADMET or a validated compound library. The present tutorial is distinguished by combining a locally installed, unlimited-throughput GNN predictor with a rigorously curated ChEMBL compound set, validated pipeline, and complete multi-domain workflow from raw predictions to composite scoring. ADMET-AI was preferred over ADMETlab 3.0 [16] for its offline capability and Python API; future tutorial extensions should evaluate ADMETlab 3.0 for its broader endpoint coverage and recent benchmark performance.

Key findings carry direct drug discovery implications. The 68.5% CYP3A4 inhibition rate mirrors known DDI liabilities of approved CDK4/6 inhibitors and underscores early CYP450 profiling requirements for kinase inhibitors. The 48.5% hERG rate reflects the pharmacophoric overlap between kinase and hERG channel binding motifs [25] that has driven cardiac monitoring requirements for approved kinase inhibitors. The weak but significant positive correlation between ADMET score and pIC50 (r = 0.29) demonstrates that modern medicinal chemistry campaigns have partially succeeded in integrated property optimisation [44], providing students with direct evidence for the value of simultaneous potency-ADMET tracking.

Three limitations should be acknowledged. First, the 200-compound dataset represents approximately 10% of the full ChEMBL CDK2 collection; users with greater computational resources can remove stratified sampling and run ADMET-AI on all 2,012 compounds (~ 10–15 min on CPU). Second, ADMET-AI predictions carry model uncertainty, particularly for endpoints with limited training data; future versions could extract individual ensemble model predictions to compute prediction variance as an uncertainty metric. Third, no experimental ADMET validation against independently measured CDK2 inhibitor data is provided; ChEMBL experimental solubility data for a subset of compounds could serve as validation anchors in future extensions. A fourth, related limitation concerns the applicability-domain analysis introduced in Cell 2C (“Executed applicability domain analysis: chemical space and k-NN Tanimoto similarity (Cell 2C)” section): the k-NN Tanimoto similarity assessment against the full merged TDC training pool is a lightweight, dependency-free approximation and does not reproduce the exact scaffold-split-aware train/test partitions used to train each ADMET-AI endpoint model; a full PyTDC-based analysis in a separate environment remains the more rigorous option for readers requiring it. Finally, the traffic-light dashboard, DrugBank percentile ranking, and composite ADMET score (“DrugBank approved drugs percentile analysis (Cell 11)”, “ADMET traffic light dashboard (Cell 12)”, “Composite ADMET score and compound ranking (Cell 13)” sections) are didactic decision-support heuristics built on predefined thresholds and author-assigned weights; they are not experimentally validated compound-prioritisation algorithms, and should be interpreted accordingly. Natural series extensions include Tutorial 5 (matched molecular pair analysis [58]) and a structure-based virtual screening tutorial using AutoDock Vina [59].

The tutorial fully complies with FAIR principles [57]: Findable (GitHub + Zenodo); Accessible (MIT license, no registration); Interoperable (CSV/SMILES/SVG/PNG/JSON); Reusable (complete documentation, version specifications, attribution). The Zenodo athttps://zenodo.org/records/21706959compendium includes the notebook, 200-compound dataset, TDC training dataset both CSV outputs, and environment specification.

We have presented a comprehensive, self-contained, and fully reproducible cheminformatics tutorial for ADMET property prediction and toxicity profiling of CDK2 inhibitors, implemented as a eighteen-cell annotated Jupyter notebook applied to 200 ChEMBL-verified compounds. The tutorial integrates ADMET-AI 2.0 predictions across 104 properties per compound, physicochemical and drug-likeness profiling, complete five-domain ADMET analysis, Tox21 nuclear receptor and stress response profiling, DrugBank percentile benchmarking, ADMET traffic light dashboard, MPO-inspired composite ADMET scoring, and integrated report export. Key quantitative findings from the 200-compound CDK2 dataset: 100% Lipinski Ro5 compliant; 38.5% predicted CYP3A4 inhibitors; 73.5% hERG risk; 99.5% predicted DILI risk; 48.0% Tox21-clean (zero flags); mean composite ADMET score 0.46; 0.0% Excellent tier, 8.5% Good tier. The near-universal DILI prediction (99.5%) reflects the hepatotoxic liability inherent to nitrogen-rich heterocyclic CDK2 scaffolds and identifies scaffold DILI de-risking as the highest-priority optimisation objective for this compound class. CDK2 inhibitors as a class show excellent predicted absorption (99.0% HIA, 100% Lipinski) and favourable half-life (82.5% long-acting) but elevated cardiac (73.5% hERG) and hepatic (99.5% DILI) safety liabilities, a finding with direct implications for lead optimisation and clinical monitoring strategy. The tutorial is permanently archived on Zenodo with a citable DOI and MIT license, contributing a FAIR-compliant peer-reviewed educational resource to the computational medicinal chemistry community.

title: χ-SOM: emergent self-organizing maps for large chemical space visualization
author: Johannes Kaminski; Oliver Koch
text:
The exploration and visualization of chemical space using dimensionality reduction (DR) methods are fundamental to cheminformatics, as they enable the exploitation of the similar property principle. However, most methods, including t-SNE and UMAP, struggle to preserve valuable distance and density properties from ambient space in the latent space representation. The emergent self-organizing map (ESOM), an often-ignored extension of the self-organizing map (SOM) algorithm, demonstrates projection behavior that circumvents the disadvantages of these methods. As a suitable implementation of this algorithm for large cheminformatic datasets is not available, we present χ-SOM, the ChemInformatics (ChI)-SOM library, a high-performance framework for training emergent self-organizing maps on large molecular datasets and for interactively exploring the resulting projections. χ-SOM integrates an optimized implementation of the SOM algorithm with CPU and CUDA backends, an on-disk HDF5-based datastore with PyTorch DataLoader support for efficient parallel access to millions of fingerprints, and a graphical user interface tailored to chemical structure visualization and property overlays. We compared our implementation with t-SNE and UMAP on synthetic and chemical data benchmarks that probe density and inter‑cluster distance preservation. On the synthetic benchmarks, ESOM retained both properties where t‑SNE and UMAP did not. On the fingerprint-based equivalents, all three methods performed comparably. χ-SOM was also benchmarked against established SOM libraries across varying dataset sizes and fingerprint lengths, demonstrating competitive or superior performance. As a final proof-of-concept, we successfully trained an ESOM of the ChEMBL33 database (1.7 million compounds; 5.1 million neurons), to our knowledge the largest SOM reported to date, and show that local neighborhood relationships on the map align well with medicinal chemists’ intuition of chemical similarity. χ-SOM thus provides a practical, extensible tool for large scale exploratory analysis of chemical space.

Here we introduce χ-SOM, a high-performance framework for training emergent self-organizing maps (ESOMs) with a specific focus on cheminformatics, including a datastore and interactive GUI tailored to this domain. We benchmark ESOMs trained with our implementation against t-SNE, UMAP, and existing SOM libraries on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that ESOM preserves density and inter‑cluster distance relationships on synthetic benchmarks where t‑SNE and UMAP do not, that all three methods perform comparably on the fingerprint-based equivalents, and that χ‑SOM offers improved scalability against current SOM implementations. Finally, we construct, to our knowledge, the largest ESOM of chemical space reported to date (ChEMBL33, 1.7 million compounds; 5.1 million neurons), and show that the resulting projections align closely with medicinal chemists’ intuitive notion of chemical similarity.

The concept of “chemical space” can be understood in two distinct ways. In its broadest sense, it represents the combinatorial space encompassing all conceivable chemical entities with reasonable estimates exceeding 1060molecules [1]. As this space is so vast and not yet resolved by currently available libraries [2,3], the term lacks a clear definition. Instead, it is often used in a more constrained sense to denote the chemical diversity of a set of compounds. In these sets, each compound is characterized as a vector of properties with these vectors defining a high-dimensional, ambient space.

In medicinal chemistry, the investigation of this space for similarity relationships is of special interest. When used with care, structural similarity, encoded in vector representations, can lead to the discovery of better-suited or more active compounds when analyzed computationally [4]. This behavior is often referred to as the “similar property principle”.

Although close analogs in a dataset can be identified through clustering and the investigation of close matches alone, visualization of the wider relationships can be highly beneficial for understanding the problem at hand [5,6]. This form of chemical space visualization was first termed “chemography” [7]. It is most often achieved by applying dimensionality reduction directly to the vector representation or to tables of pairwise distance relationships. For an overview of the different methods employed, the reader may consult reviews [8,9,10].

Beginning in the early to mid-1990s, self-organizing maps (SOMs) [11] were used extensively for this task, ranging from visualization of molecular surfaces [12] to library design [13], compound screening [14], and beyond. This method projects datapoints onto discrete positions on a two-dimensional grid of neurons, with the neuron at the corresponding position referred to as the best-matching unit (BMU). The BMUs are determined by distance to weight vectors associated with each neuron, which are learned during training. This training iteratively adjusts the weight of the neurons such that they act as prototypes or centroids of a given subset of the dataset, with neighboring neurons in the low-dimensional embedding space being similar to each other in the high-dimensional ambient space.

With the availability of newer dimensionality-reduction algorithms, such as t-SNE [15] and UMAP [16], the use of SOMs in cheminformatics has declined. This may be attributed to several factors: the absence of a clear statistical framework and related issues [17], and, likely in significant part, the computational complexity that made it infeasible to use this algorithm with chemical datasets that are ever-increasing in size.

The trend toward using other, more recent, algorithms for dimensionality reduction is not limited to computational chemistry, and the use of self-organizing maps has declined overall. As a result, implementations of the SOM algorithm are scarce, often limited in their features with respect to parallelization and analytical tools, and therefore of limited use for creating large maps for cheminformatic applications. In particular, exploring the chemical space often requires investigating the resulting map and the mapped datapoints. However, human comprehension of chemical structure is much more intuitive when depicted as a chemical graph than in one-line notation. This makes the interactive investigation of the resulting map highly desirable.

While the standard SOM may fall short of the projection quality achieved by prototype-free approaches such as UMAP and t-SNE, Ultsch et al. later introduced an extension of the SOM algorithm, called emergent SOMs (ESOM) [18]. They proposed maps with multiple neurons per datapoint, combined with the U-Matrix, now a staple of SOM visualization (see Fig.1). This U-Matrix indicates the distance in the ambient space between a neuron and its next-neighbor neurons in embedding space and serves as background for the projection area. The positions of the BMU, together with the U-Matrix, enable interpretation of the resulting maps, which are very similar to positions on geographic surface maps. Regions of the map with consecutively low U-height indicate that entities mapped to these regions form a cluster in ambient space. Regions of large U-height indicate outliers or separation between clusters. Together with contour plots or color coding of the U-Matrix, this results in ‘valleys’ of similar entities and ‘ridges’ separating them. In our view, this extension substantially increases the interpretability of the map, as the U‑Matrix makes cluster boundaries and their relative separation directly readable, information that t‑SNE and UMAP embeddings do not convey. However, as this form of SOM significantly increases the number of neurons, it also exaggerates the already unfavorable computational demand.

Example of a 2 × 2 tiled U-Matrix plot. Blue and green background colors for ‘valleys’, regions of small distance between neurons in ambient space, indicating clusters such as with the purple and yellow BMUs. Brown to white colors for ‘ridges’, regions of large distance between neurons in ambient space, indicating cluster boundaries. Marker colors show data class membership. Red line shows tile border. Tiling shows a continuous, toroidal, surface that the compounds are projected on

These requirements led us to investigate available implementations for cheminformatic applications. However, none met the criteria, prompting us to implement the algorithm described below. We analyze the capabilities and shortcomings of the different implementations, including performance benchmarks.

The original authors of both t-SNE and UMAP state that, while preserving topology well, both algorithms are known to distort absolute distances in ambient space between datapoints in the resulting embedding [15,16]. These distortions can lead to misinterpretation and misuse of both methods in visual analytics [19]. To evaluate the sensitivity of ESOM to this phenomenon, we compare ESOM to t-SNE and UMAP on simple synthetic benchmark sets for dimensionality reduction previously established for both [20,21]. To analyze the impact of this behavior in cheminformatic applications, we applied the same methods to constructed chemical datasets similar in topographic properties to the synthetic benchmarks. We conclude our work by applying the emergent version of the SOM algorithm to the ChEMBL33 [22] dataset, which contains 1.7 million compounds. This results in the training of a map comprising 5.1 million neurons, likely making it the largest SOM to date. We show that projections of this size still yield representations that align well with medicinal chemists’ understanding of chemical similarity.

In self-organizing maps, the relationship between the high-dimensional input from ambient space and the low-dimensional projection is represented as an arrangement of neurons. All neurons\(n\in N\)are placed on an ordered lattice, most commonly a quad lattice with four neighbors or a hex lattice with six neighbors. The positions of the neurons\({p}_{n}\)remain consistent throughout training and are an important feature for determining neighborhood during the collaboration phase. Each neuron is represented as a vector of weights\({w}_{n}\)of the same length and data type as the input datapoints\(v \, \in V\). After training, the weight vectors of each neuron should be close to a subset of datapoints in ambient space, with neighboring neurons in the embedding space presenting similar subsets of datapoints in ambient space [11].

The original version of the algorithm is the online version. It comprises three phases, shown below. Importantly, each datapoint is presented individually, and the neuron weights are updated after each datapoint [11].

For a given datapoint, all the neurons on the lattice compete for which one is best in representing the datapoint using the minimum distance between the datapoint\(v\)and the weight vectors of all neurons (Eq.1). The most widely used distance measures are the Euclidean distance (Eq.2) and Manhattan distance (Eq.3). Alternatively, similarity measures can be used and with the best-match and update equations (Eq.1and Eq.6) adapted accordingly. Here, Cosine similarity is a common choice (Eq.4). The selected neuron is called the best-matching unit.

where\({n}^{*}\)is the best-matching neuron,\(v\)is the current datapoint and\({w}_{n}\)is the weight vector of a neuron

where\(x, y\)is any pair of same length vectors.

The degree of neighborhood in the embedding space is determined for all SOM neurons relative to the BMU. Commonly, a Gaussian-shaped distribution is used for (Eq.5), based on either Euclidean (Eq.2) or Manhattan (Eq.3) distance for\(d\). To achieve convergence of the map, the neighborhood size is continuously decreased during training at each timestep.

where\({d}_{n, {n}^{*}}\)is the distance in embedding space between any vector\(n\)and the best-matching neuron\({n}^{*}\), and\({\sigma}_{\Lambda }\)is the current size of the neighborhood.

Finally, the weights of all neurons in the SOM are updated by some value\(\Delta w\), depending on the current difference between the neuron and the datapoint at each vector position, the degree of neighborhood in embedding space and the learning rate (Eq.6). The learning rate too is continuously decreasing over the course of the training to achieve convergence.

where\(\alpha (t)\)is the learning rate at the current time step\(t\),\(\sigma \left(t\right)\)is the neighborhood size at the current time step\(t\)

The batch algorithm is a revised version that falls outside the theoretical framework proving convergence of the original algorithm, but it has also been shown to converge in practice. Unlike the original algorithm, competition and collaboration are performed for all datapoints without intermediate updates. Instead, the new weight vectors of the neurons are averages over all datapoints, weighted by the degree of neighborhood at each neuron (Eq.7). This architecture increases parallelizability and reduces both the number of operations and the number of memory accesses, significantly improving computational performance [23]. Some drawbacks of this version of the algorithm, particularly with the ESOM variant, can be resolved by applying the update after a 1/k-sized subset of the original dataset, termedthe k-batchalgorithm [24].

Due to the nature of the ESOM algorithm, even under perfect topology preservation it is common that a neuron is separated by large distance in ambient space to its direct neighbor in one direction and small distance in ambient space to neurons multiple grid positions over in another direction. Even though this property is communicated to the user by the U-Matrix representation, this can lead to distortions when applying forward projection error measures to ESOM projections, as distance in embedding space is most commonly measured by p-norm distances. To capture the distance differences communicated via the U-Matrix in the projection error, Ultsch et al. proposed a new measure of forward projection error, including a full discussion on the problem, the Minimal U-Ranking Measure [25].

While the full measure is reasonable for comparing ESOM under different hyperparameter configurations, it is inapplicable to other methods of DR and not useful for direct comparison. However, it also includes a novel distance measure (Eq.8) namedU-distance. We propose that this distance measure can be used in other rank- and correlation-based projection error measures as the embedding space distance measure for the ESOM. This would allow for fair comparison of ESOM to other methods of DR, preserving distance differences captured by the U-Matrix.
