First, the obtained data was used to benchmark the output from the ML model qmdesc against DFT data (B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-mSVP). This was done for the nitrogen atom-centered Fukui coefficient for electrophilic attack, f( −) (Fig.5B), and for the bond order of the N–H bond (Fig.5C). In both cases, the linear correlation is good, with R2values of 0.738 and 0.798. Interestingly, for both primary and secondary aromatic amines, the correlation in f( −) is notably higher than for the aliphatic subgroups. Conceivable explanations could be the higher conformational flexibility of aliphatic amines, which was not recovered by the ML model, or the possibly higher prevalence of aromatic amines in the training set of qmdesc. In contrast, for the bond order, this trend could not be detected and only the primary aliphatic amines stood out with a higher R2value. Analyses like these are important to monitor the performance of much faster ML models against the respective QM data to assert the applicability of the model for a given dataset and to ensure that the gain in computational efficiency does not come at the cost of predictive reliability of the descriptors themselves or of downstream models. BONAFIDE facilitates such analyses.

Second, the calculated features were used to visualize the investigated chemical space by means of dimensionality reduction. For that, the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)[78] was chosen to compare a 20D atom and bond descriptor space sourced through BONAFIDE from six individual featurization tools (Fig.5D) with an atom-rooted Morgan fingerprint representation (Fig.5E, see Chapter S3 in the SI for details). The latter embedding is sparse, mostly reproducing the basic chemical categories of amines (cyclicvs.non-cyclic, primaryvs.secondary, and aromaticvs.aliphatic). The former also resembles these categories to a certain extent but is more continuous. At the same time, it maps out, for example, the average local ionization energy (ALIE) as an important property of amines for describing their nucleophilicity/basicity by continuously increasing from the bottom right to the top left of the plot.

To illustrate the difference between the two representations with a concrete example, the relative location of the cyclic amines I and II in the two 2D-UMAP spaces were compared. In panel E of Fig.5, they are placed closely together due to their high structural similarity, whereas in D they are far away from each other. In fact, the ring size of cyclic amines can have a significant influence on the properties and reactivity of the amine nitrogen as for example demonstrated in organocatalysis [79]. This could be reflected by the underlying chosen features of Fig.5D. Furthermore, the primary aliphatic amines III and IV were found clearly separated from their cluster located in the bottom of panel D. In both cases, the formation of a hydrogen bond with free hydroxyl groups in close proximity to the amine nitrogen atom is conceivable (cf.the structures of III and IV in box at the bottom of Fig.5). Indeed, visual inspections of the 3D molecular structures after conformer generation and structure optimization confirmed this hypothesis with the conformers exhibiting the intramolecular hydrogen bond being clearly the lowest energy ones for both compounds. This important structural detail is reproduced by the selected atom and bond features, which demonstrates their usefulness in effectively exploring amine chemical space. For comparison, in panel E, compounds III and IV were found clustered with the rest of the primary aliphatic amines.

In summary, these examples show how different feature spaces can lead to distinct molecular representations, which must be selected based on the given problem at hand as well as with respect to,e.g., availability of computational resources or model runtime restrictions. With BONAFIDE, the individual representations can easily be accessed, benchmarked, and assessed for their application in downstream tasks.

Dedicated features for atoms and bonds in molecules are important local descriptors,e.g., for modelling the selectivity of chemical reactions [25]. They are a valuable complement to global molecular features widely used in digital chemistry. This work presents the Python-based BOnd aNd Atom FeaturIzer and Descriptor Extractor (BONAFIDE). BONAFIDE provides a consistent API for local descriptor generation and supports, in its current state (version 0.2.4), 11 external dependencies for feature calculation resulting in a total of 590 features. It also includes direct access to quantum chemistry software for single-point energy calculations at various levels of theory. Features can be obtained from 2D or 3D molecular structures or from the results of electronic structure simulations. Therefore, BONAFIDE brings together structure/steric descriptors and data from quantum chemistry – an often-recognized powerful combination, especially for smaller datasets [17,22,31,80,81,82]. With the development of the presented software package, we aim to facilitate and standardize the combination of features from different sources to accelerate the construction of robust and increasingly generalizable ML models in chemistry across a variety of use case scenarios [83]. Flexible input and output formats as well as the possibility of implementing custom featurizers increases the amenability of BONAFIDE for the integration into (already existing) overarching data workstreams and emerging agentic AI architectures. Moreover, the broad diversity of descriptors will allow the investigation of less explored features for certain research questions beyond the typically deployed features; for example driven by fine-grained mechanistic understanding in the context of chemical reactivity modeling [3]. We investigated the runtimes of BONAFIDE for different descriptor calculation scenarios and demonstrated how it can be used to target and featurize a predefined area of chemical space with a multi-step featurization pipeline.

A current limitation of BONAFIDE is that bond features can only be calculated for actual chemical bonds rather than for an arbitrary pair of atoms, which might be disadvantageous for specific use cases. Due to that, the featurization of non-equilibrium configurations such as transition structures could be complicated as well, depending on the desired set of features [17,82]. Future work can focus on the inclusion of additional dependencies such as Gaussian [77], ORCA [84], or g-xTB [85] as quantum chemistry engines, the Natural Bond Orbital (NBO) program [86] for feature generation, or machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIP) [87,88]. BONAFIDE already includes two ML models for atom and bond property prediction, and we believe that the continuous integration of ML models into BONAFIDE (and overarching frameworks in general) in a sustainable and well-documented manner will decrease the hurdles of employing such tools and will therefore facilitate their widespread adoption across the entire chemical research landscape. Future releases of the package can also work toward the inclusion of a command line interface (CLI), which is currently not implemented or to dedicated functionality for batch-processing.

The BONAFIDE source code is publicly available, and we encourage the scientific community to make active use of the package as well as to report potential bugs, request new features, or contribute ideas for further extensions. We are planning to actively maintain the online documentation and GitHub repository of BONAFIDE. The package is already utilized in several internal AstraZeneca projects, and we are confident that it will prove equally valuable to the broader scientific community, fostering further innovation in data-driven chemistry.

title: Research EnzyPred: a general model for predicting enzyme–substrate interactions using deep learning, parallel LoRA, and, natural language processing-inspired approaches
author: Luis Fernando Salas Nuñez; Alvaro Barrera-Ocampo; Paola A. Caicedo; Natalie Cortes; Edison H. Osorio; Oscar Alberto Alvarez Solano; Maria F. Villegas-Torres; Andrés Fernando  González Barrios González Barrios
text:
Enzyme–substrate interaction (ESI) prediction is a critical challenge in biocatalysis, with applications in metabolic engineering and drug design. This prediction is valuable because it allows avoiding experimental characterization, a process that can be complex and expensive. In this work, we present EnzyPred, an ESI prediction tool based on Natural Language Processing (NLP), Deep Learning (DL), fine-tuning, Low Range Parallel Adapter (LoRA-P), and Inference-time Prioritized Fine-tuning (PFT) techniques, using representations generated through Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM) for enzymes and Extended Connectivity Fingerprinting (ECFP) for substrates. This approach allows training the model with evolutionary, structural, and chemical features, improving performance in identifying interactions. The model was trained on a dataset of 32,833 positive enzyme–substrate pairs, complemented by 32,833 negative pairs generated using soft clustering, molecular descriptors, and Tanimoto similarity. EnzyPred achieved an average accuracy of 86.97%, proving to be competitive with previously presented tools, standing out for its generalization capacity, computational efficiency, and adaptability. Two case studies were used to validate the tool experimentally. In the first, the enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of 4'-O-methylnorbelladine to N-desmethylnarwedine in Amaryllidaceae was sought. For this, the substrate was fixed and tested with predicted enzymes from different transcriptomes reported in the literature for this family. The predicted ones were tested in the laboratory, identifying the enzyme, which contributed to the knowledge of the synthesis pathway of galantamine, a drug used in the treatment of Alzheimer's. In the second case, we searched for compounds that may interact with the enzyme acetylcholinesterase (AChE), for which the enzyme was fixed and we used the ZINC22 database as a search space. 747 compounds with activity were predicted, of which nine were prioritized through clustering for experimental testing, and all presented activity. These results confirm the relevance of this approach to predict molecular interactions, opening new possibilities for the design of enzymatic and synthetic pathways.

Scientific contribution

This study introduces EnzyPred, an adaptive deep learning framework for enzyme–substrate interaction prediction that jointly integrates protein language model, molecular fingerprints, and a novel activity-free negative sampling strategy to address data imbalance and false negatives. Unlike previous ESI models, EnzyPred incorporates low-rank adaptation and Inference-time Prioritized Fine-tuning, enabling rapid and targeted model specialization for specific enzyme–substrate pairs without retraining from scratch. The framework is validated across enzyme identification and virtual screening tasks, with experimental confirmation, demonstrating its potential to accelerate biocatalysis discovery and pathway elucidation beyond existing methods.

Enzymes are biological catalysts of biochemical reactions that have evolved to efficiently mediate metabolic pathways, a fundamental capability of living organisms that has enabled significant advances in biotechnology [1,2,3]. Furthermore, enzymes can act on multiple substrates beyond their primary function, a phenomenon called enzymatic promiscuity [4,5]. This has important implications in fields such as biocatalysis, metabolic engineering, and drug design [4]. Enzymatic promiscuity can be exploited to design new metabolic pathways for compounds of interest; or it can cause the accumulation of unwanted byproducts that impair the efficiency of a metabolic pathway [6,7]. Consequently, understanding and predicting this promiscuity is a significant challenge due to the limited availability of experimental data and the costs associated with systematically characterizing enzyme–substrate relationships [1,8].

Significant advances in enzyme and substrate characterization using machine learning (ML) have made it possible to address the challenge of understanding and predicting the dynamics of their interactions [9,10]. Machine learning techniques such as deep learning (DL), convolutional neural networks (CNN), active learning, and natural language processing (NLP) have shown promising results in analyzing and extracting features from complex data, including protein amino acid sequences and molecular representations of substrates [6,11,12,13,14]. These ML techniques have automated analysis, reduced costs and time, and allowed the identification of unknown relationships between enzymes and substrates, thus expanding our understanding of the enzymatic chemical space. However, these methodologies are often limited by the lack of negative data and the low diversity of training sets, which affects their generalization capacity [9,15,16].

The development of neural networks with transformer architecture has not only allowed the creation of large, advanced, and accurate natural language models, but has also demonstrated their ability to characterize, understand, and predict interactions between residues in enzyme sequences, allowing the development of protein language models (pLMs) [17,18]. These models, specifically designed to analyze protein amino acid sequences, interpret an entire protein sequence as a sentence and its constituents (amino acids) as individual words [19]. Proving to be very effective in capturing the complex relationships present in such sequences. These models have been trained on large protein sequence datasets, allowing them to understand the subtle relationships and patterns present in amino acid sequences [17]. Some of the most prominent protein language models in this field include Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM) [20,21], Transformer-based Protein Sequence Predictor (TAPE) [22], ProtBERT, ProtT5, ProtXLNet, and ProtALBERT [19].

The application of pLM to amino acid sequence characterization and subsequent use in enzyme–substrate interactions (ESI) has shown the ability to identify and generalize essential features of the Enzyme Substrate (ES) complex [13]. This is due to its ability to capture the complex relationships between the structural and functional characteristics of enzymes and their substrates, but since these interactions are very varied and specific, the tools reported in the literature are often limited to training compounds [6,11], certain types of enzymes such as phosphatases or kinases [23], inhibitors or drugs [24,25,26,27,28].

In recent years, the representation of chemical space has seen a transition from classical molecular fingerprints to deep learning architectures that treat SMILES as a language, such as ChemBERTa and Chemformer [29,30]. These models have shown significant promise in predicting bioactivity and toxicity by learning global molecular features. In parallel, frameworks like TransDTI have demonstrated that combining transformer-based protein embeddings with chemical descriptors can significantly improve drug-target interaction (DTI) workflows [31].

In this context, we present EnzyPred, an ESI prediction tool that uses a combination of methods such as recurrent neural networks (Long Short Term Memory, LSTM, typically used in NLP and time series), fine-tuning, low-rank parallel adapter (LoRA-P) together with Inference-time Prioritized Fine-tuning (PFT) and Deep learning (DL), which represents an imoprovement in terms of efficiency and accuracy [32,33,34]. The integration of LoRA-P and PFT into this pipeline optimizes computational efficiency, improves accuracy on relevant data, and allows for the use and tuning of any ES pair, distinguishing this work from previous approaches. This model is designed to predict enzyme–substrate interactions by integrating advanced protein and molecular representations [35,36,37]. The model leverages the ESM to analyze amino acid sequences and Extended Connectivity Fingerprinting (ECFP) to encode molecular features from SMILES representations [20,38]. While chemical Transformers have gained popularity, ECFP remains a relevant standard for substrate encoding; it effectively captures the structural motifs to model enzyme–substrate recognition and, unlike Transformer-based architectures, offers a higher degree of interpretability by linking features directly to specific molecular fragments. By employing an initial dataset of 32,833 enzyme–substrate pairs with documented activity, complemented with a dataset generated artificially using soft clustering techniques, the limitations of biased data were addressed, significantly improving the accuracy of the predictions. This approach allows capturing complex relationships between enzymes and substrates, offering a flexible and adaptative framework to investigate enzyme promiscuity and develop new applications in biocatalysis.

The developed tool was validated using a diverse dataset, achieving a LoRA-P accuracy of 86.97%, outperforming several previously published tools and enabling the activity prediction of ES pairs not present in the trained dataset. Additionally, two experimental validations were carried out, defined by ongoing projects of the research group: the first aimed to address the synthesis of galantamine in plants of the Amaryllidaceae family by identifying the enzyme that catalyzes the reaction of 4′-O-methylnorbelladine to n-desmethylnarwedine; the second validation consisted of the identification of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitors using compounds from the ZINC database [39]. These validations highlight the practical applicability of EnzyPred in real-world scenarios. In addition to these applications, the model has the potential to transform biocatalysis, enabling the discovery of new substrates, enzymes, and metabolic pathways for sustainable chemical processes. The integration of the model into synthetic biology opens new possibilities to address the challenges related to the production of drugs and chemicals in a sustainable manner [7,8,12,40].

The main goal of this work is to address current limitations in ESI prediction by overcoming the lack of experimental data, interaction variation [27], and the computational challenges [22,23]. Additionally, this study aims to highlight its potential to significantly lower development costs and duration in industrial and biotechnological applications [41]. The objectives include not only the development of an efficient predictive model that allows the entry of any ES pairs but also their experimental validation in different biochemical contexts, laying the groundwork for future research integrating artificial intelligence and biology.

The approach addressed in this work represents a significant advance in the use of artificial intelligence for biology in the fields of synthetic pathway elucidation, biotechnology, and the discovery of uncatalogued enzyme interactions, providing an important tool for exploring the field of biochemistry and promoting innovation in metabolic engineering [42]. The experimental results demonstrate the robustness of EnzyPred and its relevance for addressing complex biological problems.

Selecting the training data for the model was a challenge since experimental data with activity (positive) exist in different databases. Still, data without activity (negative) and experimental validation do not exist since they are not relevant for traditional studies, so the development of the database for the model took two different approaches one for the selection of data with activity and another for the selection of data without activity.

For the samples of enzyme–substrate pairs with activity, the BRENDA database was initially explored, which provides detailed information on enzyme–substrate relationships, including EC numbers to classify the enzymes and common chemical names of the substrates [43]. The amino acid sequence of proteins was downloaded from UniProt and the Simplified Molecular Entry Line Entry System (SMILES) chains of the substrate were searched in PubChem and the Open Parser for Systematic IUPAC Nomenclature (OPSIN) database, using the common name provided by BRENDA, this gave us 11,080 known enzyme–substrate activities [11,44,45,46].

To increase the positive data set, the Gene Ontology (GO) annotation database was explored [47]. The UniProt IDs corresponding to experimentally confirmed annotations of the catalytic activity of the enzymes were searched. From these identifiers, the substrates involved in the reactions catalyzed by these enzymes were extracted. The data contained information on reversible reactions, so the reactants and products were treated as substrates. For reactions labeled as irreversible, only the reactants specifically annotated as substrates were extracted. The SMILES of the substrates were then captured by searching PubChem and OPSIN as previously performed. This gave us a total of 21,753 new enzyme–substrate pairs with activity, which provided us with a total of 32,833 positives [6].

To eliminate redundancies between BRENDA and GO, a deduplication process was performed. An enzyme–substrate pair was considered a duplicate if it featured the same canonicalized SMILES for the substrate and a sequence similarity ≥ 80% between the enzymes. Detected duplicates were removed, maintaining a single entry per unique enzyme–substrate combination.

The 80% sequence identity threshold was selected conservatively. According to previous studies, general enzymatic function may begin to diverge below 50% sequence identity, while for the reliable transfer of more specific functions higher thresholds near 70–80% are recommended [48,49]. Thus, an 80% threshold enables the removal of significant redundancies without risking the loss of relevant functional variations, while simultaneously preserving the functional diversity of the dataset.

Due to the lack of experimental databases for negative interactions, a smart negative sampling strategy was chosen instead of the commonly used random sampling approach. A workflow based on unsupervised learning, molecular descriptors, and similarity measures was developed. We started with the positive dataset and separated it into enzymes and substrates. For the substrates, the ECFP was calculated from SMILES, along with the Tanimoto similarity index among all substrates [38]. Regarding the enzymes, protein amino acid sequences were used to calculate molecular descriptors based on physicochemical properties, scoring matrices, n-grams, and kernels (see Supplementary Material). With these data, flexible clustering was performed using the K-means algorithm with 100 clusters. Euclidean distance was employed as the similarity metric after standardizing the features. The optimal number of clusters was determined using the elbow method and the silhouette coefficient, seeking a proper balance between intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separation [20,50].

After processing the substrates and enzymes, non-active enzyme–substrate pair samples were created for each active pair. To achieve this, a positive sample was selected, and the three most dissimilar substrates were identified based on Tanimoto similarity. Similarly, for the enzyme, the three most dissimilar enzymes were identified based on the greatest Euclidean distance to the class containing the positive sample and the lowest probability of belonging to the class with the active enzyme. Six possible negative pairs were generated for each positive pair using these candidates. In the event of ties in distance or similarity, the pair was selected randomly. Finally, duplicate records were removed, and 32,833 unique negative pairs were randomly selected, providing us with a balanced dataset.

This approach seeks to generate plausible and difficult negatives, maximizing the probability of them being true negatives by combining enzymes and substrates with characteristics significantly different from those of the positive pair. This helps the model learn the actual boundaries of the interaction, rather than easy negatives that provide little value during training. Once our model data and input types were defined, we performed a qualitative and quantitative characterization of the enzyme–substrate pairs. To do this, we used an ECFP description of the substrates, which provided us with structural information about them. For enzymes, we used ESM, which gave us dense numerical representations of each residue in the amino acid sequence of each protein [20,38].

ECFP are a type of topological fingerprint that allows capturing structural and chemical features relevant to substrate activity by searching for substructures of the substrate [38]. These are circular fingerprints, based on the Morgan algorithm, that allow capturing the presence or absence of particular substructures in the substrates and encode all the groups of connected neighboring atoms. The circular structure can have different diameters; for example, diameter 0, which will capture the identity of the atoms at each position in the substrate; ECFP with diameter 2 captures the direct bonds of each atom and its neighboring atoms; the diameter 4, which was used in our case, allows capturing larger substructures of up to 2 chemical bonds away, describing the substrate by means of simple fragments or specific interactions [51,52,53]. Each of the substructures found is encoded in a 2048-bit binary vector, where each position indicates the presence or absence of a specific substructure present in the substrate. A position of 1 means that there is a substructure associated with this position in the compound; if it is at 0, it indicates its absence.

ESM is a Transformer network-based pLM designed to analyze protein sequences and capture relevant evolutionary and structural patterns [21,54]. This model uses unsupervised learning to learn the dependencies between the amino acids of a protein, allowing it to identify biological features related to its structure and function [54]. It generates detailed numerical representations using each residue within a protein as context.

In our case, each amino acid sequence of the proteins was processed by ESMC, generating embeddings, which are high-dimensional vectors that describe the structural and functional context of each residue in the sequence [20]. The output is a matrix of dimensions L × D, where L represents the length of the sequence and D the dimensionality of the embedding generated for each residue [21].

As a classification model, we will use LSTM recurrent neural networks together with dense layers to learn the relationship between the characteristics of the enzyme–substrate pair and the activity. LSTM networks have the advantage that they allow us to analyze the sequential dependencies of amino acids in enzymes by capturing the contextual interactions between residues in the sequence of a protein. In our case, LSTMs will process the representations generated by ESM to extract relevant features of the enzyme, learning patterns that may be related to its catalytic activity [35,36].

On the other hand, the ECFP vector, which describes the structural and chemical properties of the substrate, will be processed by dense layers that transform its information into a compact representation [55,56,57,58]. Then, the outputs of both are concatenated by means of dense layers and will culminate in a sigmoid output layer to perform the binary prediction of interaction or non-interaction.

Since there are many different types of enzymes and interactions, we added two additional architectures to the base model that add specificity to the model based on the enzyme, substrate, or enzyme–substrate pair. The first approach involves fine-tuning, which is retraining the model with a reduced data set that has similarity to the enzyme, the substrate, or both, allowing the model to be fine-tuned by giving greater weight to specific characteristics of the enzyme and the substrate. The second approach is based on Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA), which enables the model to be tailored to an enzyme, substrate, or both, without altering base model capabilities.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a technique designed to adapt large LLMs to specific tasks by keeping the pre-trained model weights frozen and training only low-rank matrices that fine-tune the model's behavior to the desired application [33]. This approach significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters, facilitating model specialization with lower computational and memory costs. In our work, we have adapted this concept to develop a novel variant, called Low-Rank Parallel Adapter (LoRA-P), which allows our general model based on LSTM networks and dense layers to be specialized to specific enzymes, substrates, or enzyme–substrate pairs, addressing the high variability of their characteristics and the unique interactions that are often specific to a particular class.

Unlike classic LoRA, which was originally designed for Transformer networks specifically to modify the projection matrices in the self-attention module, LoRA-P adapts to our architecture, which combines LSTM networks to process enzyme sequence representations (generated by ESMC) and dense layers to handle ECFP representations of the substrates. Instead of directly altering the weight matrices of the base model, as in classic LoRA, LoRA-P introduces a parallel model that operates independently. This parallel model takes the same inputs as the base model (ESMC representations for enzymes and ECFP representations for substrates) and projects them to a low-rank space using reduced-dimensional matrices. The results of the parallel model and the base model are combined in an additional dense layer, which is optimized during fine-tuning to integrate both representations effectively.

The integration of LoRA-P into our tool is achieved by keeping the base model weights unchanged, ensuring that the original architecture, trained to capture general patterns of enzyme–substrate interactions, remains intact. In contrast, the parallel LoRA-P model allows for specific adaptation to the distinctive features of an enzyme, a substrate, or an enzyme–substrate pair by learning complementary representations in a low-rank space. To explore the impact of the dimensionality of this space, we experimented with ranks of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32, allowing us to evaluate the trade-off between model adaptability and parametric efficiency. The dense fusion layer, which combines the outputs of the base model and LoRA-P, is co-trained with the parallel model, allowing for optimized integration of representations to improve binary interaction/non-interaction prediction.

This approach offers several advantages. First, by keeping the base model static, LoRA-P preserves the general knowledge learned during pre-training. In contrast, the parallel model provides the flexibility to capture task-specific patterns without requiring complete retraining. Second, projection to a low-rank space significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters, which decreases computational resource consumption and facilitates scalability to multiple fitting tasks, a critical aspect given the high number of possible enzyme–substrate combinations. Finally, LoRA-P is especially useful in data-limited scenarios, such as enzyme–substrate interaction datasets, as it enables efficient fitting without the need for large volumes of class-specific data. Workflow of the PFT algorithm with LoRA-P

To evaluate an alternative general model adaptation strategy, a fine-tuning experiment was performed, which consisted of retraining the LSTM-based model and dense layers using PFT-selected enzyme–substrate pairs. Unlike the LoRA-P approach, described in a previous section, which keeps the base model weights frozen and employs a low-rank parallel model, fine-tuning optimizes all general model weights, allowing direct specialization toward the features of prioritized pairs. This process sought to capture specific enzyme–substrate interaction patterns, leveraging the ability of LSTM networks to model sequential dependencies in ESM representations of enzymes and of dense layers to process ECFP representations of substrates. This approach is significantly more computationally expensive compared to LoRA-P due to the complete optimization of model parameters. This approach complements the proposed efficient adaptation strategies, offering a robust alternative for scenarios where computational resources are not a limitation.

To find the best hyperparameters for the model, a two-step strategy was adopted. In the first step, the number of LSTM and dense layers was modified, along with the dimensionality of the layers. In the second step, a grid search was used with different learning rates, epochs, optimizers, and dropout rates. 1000 iterations were performed until the best model was found. After this, different PFT sizes were tested for prediction.

To optimize LoRA-P hyperparameters, a specific process focused on the configuration of the parallel model and the dense fusion layer was carried out. A systematic search was performed to determine the optimal range of the low-rank space, evaluating values of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32, to balance adaptive capacity with parametric efficiency. Additionally, the learning rate, number of epochs, and dropout rate of the dense layer that combines the outputs of the base model and LoRA-P were tuned using a grid search with 500 iterations to identify the configuration that maximized accuracy and sensitivity in the binary prediction of enzyme–substrate interactions.

For the model evaluation, we independently divided the global dataset into three main sets: a training set (90%, randomly selected), a test set we call general (8%, randomly selected), and a test set called underrepresented (2%, fixed). For training, we used cross-validation, splitting the data into 10 folds. In each iteration of hyperparameter optimization, 9 folds were used for training and the remaining fold for validation. This process was repeated 10 times, so that each fold was used once as a validation set [62].

The underrepresented dataset allows for evaluating the model's performance in more complex scenarios. This set was generated as follows:

The Tanimoto similarity was calculated between all substrates (using their ECFP fingerprints).

The sequence similarity was calculated between all enzymes.

The 1% of pairs with the lowest substrate similarity and the lowest frequency of occurrence in the total dataset was selected.

The 1% of pairs with the lowest sequence similarity and the lowest frequency of occurrence in the total dataset was selected.

The final set of underrepresented pairs consists of 1,313 pairs, which exhibit low similarity at both the enzyme and substrate levels compared to the majority of the training data.

Consequently, the data reserved for evaluation were independently divided; a test set we call general (composed of 8% randomly selected pairs) and a test set called underrepresented (composed of 2% uncommon pairs in the set). This strategy allows for evaluating separately both the general performance of the model and its specific capacity to handle rare cases within the training data, reporting both results independently in Table1.

The performance metrics used were those traditionally used in classification problems, such as accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Accuracy measures the proportion of correct predictions among all predictions made. Sensitivity refers to the model’s ability to correctly identify enzyme–substrate pairs with activity, and specificity refers to the ratio of pairs without activity correctly classified [63,64].

The metrics were calculated for both the validation and test sets, allowing the evaluation of the overall performance and the model's ability to generalize.

The applied methodology allowed Enzypred to successfully capture enzyme sequence patterns and substrate structural features, achieving high accuracy in both paired and underrepresented test sets. Comparing the results obtained with similar tools presented in recent studies shows that the tool allows for high adaptation to specific data. At the same time, validations focused on particular enzymes and substrates demonstrate their competitive performance and practical utility in elucidating synthesis pathways in biological systems.

The proposed model achieved good performance, outperforming several of the previous approaches for general prediction models reported in the literature for enzyme–substrate interaction prediction (see Table1). We first trained a model without PFT and LoRA-P to serve as a base model, then applied a fine-tuning approach to this model, and finally, used the proposed approach with different ranges. In addition to the performance with a general test dataset, we tested the model with a test dataset of enzyme–substrate pairs that were less represented in the training dataset (underrepresented), also obtaining good results.

The statistical analysis across multiple independent runs (Table1) highlights the stability of the LoRA-P architecture. While full fine-tuning achieved high accuracy in the general set, it exhibited greater variability in the underrepresented set (SD: 2.35% for Accuracy). In contrast, LoRA-P 8 and LoRA-P 16 provided more consistent results, suggesting that restricting the trainable parameters to low-rank matrices prevents over-fitting and enhances generalization in data-scarce scenarios.

The model was shown to effectively capture the sequential information of enzymes as well as the structural features of substrates. Furthermore, the incorporation of PFT contributed to a higher performance of the model.

In addition to the above analysis, we compared the results of our model with other tools and architectures reported in the literature. The model developed in this study, which we have named EnzyPred, achieved an accuracy of 86.97% (LoRA-P r = 8) on the general test set and 82.07% on the underrepresented test set, placing it among the best reported approaches.

To validate our tool in real-world settings, we performed two types of validations: one by fixing the substrate and varying the enzymes to complete the ES pair, and the second by fixing the enzyme and varying the possible substrates. We defined the substrate and enzyme for experimental testing based on projects our research group has been developing with plants from the Amaryllidaceae family. The complete experimental protocols are described in detail in previous publications [39,65].

To test the prediction of our model, we decided to evaluate it in the identification of the enzyme that catalyzes the reaction of 4'-O-Methylnorbelladine to N-Demethylnarwedine (Fig.5), which is part of the galantamine synthesis pathway in Amaryllidaceae. Galantamine is a highly therapeutically relevant compound used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease symptoms, so its production by biocatalysis has a significant impact [66,67].

The figure illustrates the enzymatic reaction in the galantamine synthesis pathway in Amaryllidaceae, the conversion of 4′-O-methylnorbelladine to N-desmethylnarwedine, a key step in the production of the compound

With the substrate defined, we established the enzymatic search space within the predicted proteins in the transcriptomes of several Amaryllidaceae plants. This approach is strategic, since these species are known for their natural ability to produce galantamine, which increases the probability of finding relevant enzymes in their transcriptomes. By restricting the search space, the experimental validation is optimized, decreasing both the computational resources required and the analysis time, and avoiding the exhaustive exploration of the entire chemical space.

The transcriptomes used in this study were extracted from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database on November 16, 2022. The selected species includedCrinum asiaticum var. pedunculatum (PRJNA1327645), Lycoris radiata (PRJNA579622), Lycoris longituba (PRJNA490415), Narcissus pseudonarcissus (PRJNA301357), and Narcissus aff. pseudonarcissus (MK2014) (PRJNA264603)[68]. Additionally, predicted proteins from the Crinum transcriptome, previously assembled by the research group, were included, where galantamine production was also verified by metabolomic analysis (The assembled transcriptome of Crinum is shared with the NCBI under Bioproject ID PRJNA1327645).

Once the enzymatic search space was defined, the model processed the substrate by matching it with the enzymes in the transcriptomes, obtaining a total of 711 transcripts with predicted activity. These sequences were grouped by homology into 21 categories, which were identified by BLAST analysis in NCBI [69]. Subsequently, a phylogenetic analysis was performed that allowed 10 transcripts to be prioritized for experimental testing, which are presented in Table3. It should be noted that the names of the enzymes in the table were assigned based on the BLAST results.

The experimental validation strategy follows the approach described in the article “Machine learning-assisted discovery of cytochromes P450 putatively involved in the biosynthesis of Amaryllidaceae alkaloids inCrinum asiaticum”, developed by the research group. As a result, it was possible to identify among the prioritized enzymes the one that catalyzes the target reaction in Amaryllidaceae (Cytochrome P450 96 T) [65].

Another validation we performed consisted of fixing the enzyme and varying the substrates. In this case, we set out to identify compounds with activity on acetylcholinesterase (AChE) [40,66]. To do this, we set the enzyme as a constant and defined the search space using the ZINC22 commercial compounds database [70]. Only those compounds in stock with a molecular weight equal to or less than 500 Da were selected, resulting in a total of 11012710 molecules.

Once the enzyme–substrate pairs were generated, they were processed by our model, which predicted activity for 747 molecules. From the compounds identified by the tool, a clustering was performed using molecular descriptors, classifying them into 10 categories. The descriptors used are detailed in the supplementary material. From each category, one compound was prioritized, selecting the most representative, except in the galantamine category, which was used as a positive control. This allowed us to prioritize a total of 10 compounds for experimental tests.

The experimental validation protocol used follows the one described in the article "dyphAI: Dynamic pharmacophore modeling with AI: The latest tool for efficient screening of new acetylcholinesterase inhibitors", developed by the research group. The results are reported in Table4. Seven of the prioritized compounds were confirmed to show activity against AChE.

Regarding molecules ZINC10274013 and ZINC17245175, the experimental results were inconsistent, likely due to solubility issues in the experimental setup, which prevented a definitive determination of their inhibitory potential.

The results and validations presented demonstrate the robustness and reliability of EnzyPred, making it a fundamental tool for elucidating biosynthetic pathways, drug discovery, and understanding metabolomics. The robust performance across diverse datasets and evaluation metrics underscores the model's generalizability, further supporting its potential to advance research in enzyme–substrate interaction prediction. In this work, we developed a tool that integrates molecular feature extraction using ECFP and ESM, along with a combination of natural language processing-based approaches such as LSTM and LoRA-P networks, and PFT to address ESI prediction, demonstrating its potential for addressing complex biological problems.

The construction of the training data plays a fundamental role in the performance of our model. Being diverse and not focused solely on specific types of enzymes or interactions allows it to capture relevant information from the entire enzyme space. Therefore, the data were selected from different databases. Furthermore, due to the lack of a truly experimentally validated negative dataset, we developed a strategy based on molecular descriptors, similarity, and unsupervised learning to create the non-interacting samples. This allowed us to establish a negative sample for each positive sample, helping the tool identify the ES pair patterns that prevent activity. Furthermore, the combination of balanced data (positive and negative pairs) and strategies such as PFT allowed the model to perform well on data underrepresented to the training data.

Describing the ES pair using ECFP and ESM allowed it to capture relevant characteristics of the pair. These characteristics, along with the ability to process both sequential and non-sequential data, facilitate its application to various problems related to biocatalysis and drug design, demonstrating robust results in practical validations. Defining an adaptation base through similarity and diversity criteria, using a prioritization function (enzyme, substrate, or ES pair), and developing LoRA-P enabled the model to select relevant compounds. This allowed it to prioritize characteristics influencing a specific case, thereby adapting and improving prediction performance. Furthermore, this feature enables the addition of more samples, even those not included in the training data, without modifying the base model.

The model showed robust performance for different types of enzymatic and molecular interactions, especially for ES pairs that were well represented in the training data (83.17%), whereas for underrepresented ES pairs EnzyPred may show a decrease in performance (73.53%), as shown in Table1. This difficulty was addressed through substrate substructure characterization and similarity-based PFT, showing that the model improves by 8.54% for these data (see Table1). However, performance is still lower than for well-represented data; this may be because there are not enough samples yet to establish the characteristics that determine the interaction, or not fully, but this difficulty can be solved by adding more data representing the enzyme, substrate, or underrepresented ES pair to the LoRA-P fitting base. Nevertheless, the specificity remains good, allowing for the rule out of activity of many pairs; Likewise, the result can be improved and false positives ruled out using other methods such as phylogenetic analysis, which provides additional context on the enzyme–substrate relationship.

Now, regarding the general model (83.17%), the fine-tuning model (86.57%), and the LoRA-P models (4, 8, 16, and 32) (> 83.37%), we observe in Table1that the adapted models perform better. This is due to the adaptation base, since it allows the model to focus on a specific problem without losing generality. Regarding fine-tuning and LoRA-P models (4, 8, 16, and 32), they have similar performance; however, fine-tuning takes much longer to training compared to LoRA-P models, since it modifies all the parameters of the general model (refer to Table S1 in the Supplementary Material for a detailed comparison). Likewise, among the LoRA-P models, the high-rank models (8, 16, and 32) perform best, possibly due to their greater number of trainable parameters. LoRA-P 8 achieves excellent performance on both the general (86.97%) and underrepresented (82.07%) datasets, indicating an optimal balance, providing flexibility for modeling ES, as larger models can introduce redundancy and noise.

The low variance observed in the LoRA-P configurations (specifically ranks 8 and 16) indicates that the model is less sensitive to initial weight initialization compared to traditional approaches. This reproducibility is crucial for enzyme–substrate interaction prediction, where identifying rare but biologically significant interactions requires a model that reliably captures underlying structural features rather than statistical noise.Regarding the comparison of EnzyPred with other tools reported in the literature, it presents competitive performance, outperforming other tools.

When comparing EnzyPred with other architectures reported in the literature for similar problems, it shows superior performance due to strategies like LoRA-P and PFT used as adaptation mechanisms. These allow fine-tuning without altering the base model and enable better capture of complex enzyme–substrate interaction patterns compared to traditional methods such as SVM-based baselines or dense and convolutional layers. This underscores the potential of the adaptation mechanism as a key factor for the tool's strong performance while maintaining generality, especially on diverse datasets, outperforming other proposed models.

Another key feature of Enzypred, compared to other tools cited in the literature, is that it is not limited to predicting activity for the trained dataset, specific enzyme families, or a single group of compounds, such as drugs. Instead, it also enables the prediction of any pair of ESs. For example, it identified enzymes in the galantamine metabolic pathway in Amaryllidaceae (see Table3) and substrates that interact with AChE (see Table4), positioning itself as an alternative for enzyme annotation when a reference enzyme is not available for BLAST.

One of the model's most significant contributions is the reduction in time and resources required to identify relevant enzymes for biocatalysis, as well as potential substrates with the desired activity.

Regarding the experimental validations, these were chosen based on tests the research group has been conducting with the Amaryllidaceae species. In the first experimental test, using the substrate 4'-O-methylnorbelladine, the enzyme responsible for its conversion to N-desmethylnarwedine in Amaryllidaceae was identified, demonstrating the model's efficiency in complex biological contexts and highlighting its potential to optimize the search for relevant enzymes in specific transcriptomes. The second validation, focused on enzymes (such as AChE), highlights the tool's adaptability, allowing the exploration of a broad chemical spectrum. In this validation, all the molecules prioritized for laboratory testing showed activity, demonstrating that this approach has important implications for the design of new enzyme inhibitors, with potential applications in the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. Finally, we consider that restricting the molecular and enzymatic search space to transcriptomes, metabolic networks, or specific databases optimizes the necessary computational resources, making the model suitable for large-scale studies.

EnzyPred represents an advance in enzyme–substrate interaction prediction. However, several limitations must be considered to properly contextualize these findings. The main limitations relate to the composition of the dataset. Despite the good performance observed in multiple scenarios, EnzyPred is based on ESI datasets available from two metabolic pathway and enzyme databases (BRENDA and GO). This reliance may introduce biases toward well-studied enzyme families and metabolic pathways. As a result, predictions for poorly characterized enzymes or rare chemotypes may be less reliable.

Although the proposed negative sampling strategy without activity reduces the risk of false negatives compared to random sampling, it cannot completely exclude the presence of undiscovered true interactions. Therefore, predictions of enzyme–substrate pairs classified as non-interacting should be interpreted with caution.

Experimental validation was performed only in selected case studies and does not constitute comprehensive biochemical validation across all enzyme classes. Finally, EnzyPred predicts the probability of enzyme–substrate interaction rather than catalytic efficiency or kinetic parameters. Consequently, the framework should be regarded as a prioritization tool to guide experimental efforts, rather than a replacement for experimental characterization.

EnzyPred is a major advance in the field of biocatalysis and bioinformatics, enabling the prediction of enzyme–substrate interactions using cutting-edge techniques such as pLM, ECFP, ESM, LSTM, PFT, and LoRA-P. It achieves a competitive performance (86.97% for overall datasets, 82.07% for underrepresented datasets) compared to other tools presented in the literature. Its ability to adapt and process diverse datasets allows it to go beyond the limits of enzyme families or specific compounds, such as drugs, allowing the prediction of any ES pair and tailoring to an enzyme, substrate, or ES pair. It stands out in applications such as the identification of enzymes in the galantamine metabolic pathway in Amaryllidaceae and virtual screening with AChE. Experimental validations with 4′-O-methylnorbelladine and AChE confirm its efficiency in identifying relevant enzymes in complex biological contexts and exploring a broad chemical spectrum, with implications for biocatalysis and drug discovery. The negative and balanced data generation strategy, combined with molecular descriptors and similarity, improves the model's robustness and allows it to improve the positive class by reducing false positives in the face of sparse or underrepresented data. Furthermore, using LoRA-P allows for rapid adaptation without modifying the base model, optimizing computational resources and facilitating large-scale studies. Potential future improvements could include integrating methods such as phylogenetic analysis to reduce false positives, and incorporating more representative data for underrepresented pairs. This would consolidate EnzyPred position as a versatile tool for computational biology research. While EnzyPred does not replace experimental validation, it provides a powerful computational framework to accelerate hypothesis generation, enzyme prioritization, and pathway elucidation.

title: Computational applications in secondary metabolite discovery (CAiSMD) 2026: focus on secondary metabolites towards drug discovery
author: Fidele Ntie-Kang; Jude Y. Betow; Donatus B. Eni; Jonathan A. Metuge; Albisto Adriano; Mary Anti Chama; Hans Denis Bamal; Philippe Belle Ebanda Kedi; Lívia Mendes Campos; Abubakar Sadiq Abdullahi; Gabriel Francisco Filippin Medina; Seraphin B. N. Mbeket; Yemi A. Adekunle; Alice Rhelly V. Carvalho; Bruno D. A. Akamba; Christianah Adebimpe Dare; Yoshua B. Mtulo; Edgar López-López; Yannick Djoumbou-Feunang; Clovis S. Metuge; Solange Ndamo; Daniel M. Shadrack; Bakary N’tji Diallo; Boris D. Bekono; Marilia Valli; James A. Mbah; Saheed Sabiu; Samuel A. Egieyeh; José L. Medina-Franco; Jutta Ludwig-Müller
text:
TheComputational Applications in Secondary Metabolite Discovery (CAiSMD) 2026workshop was held from 24 to 26 March 2026 in a hybrid format, combining onsite participation at the University of Buea Center for Drug Discovery with global virtual attendance. Building on previous editions,CAiSMDcontinues to promote the application of bio/cheminformatics and computational chemistry in natural product-based discovery, with a strong emphasis on capacity building for researchers in resource-limited settings.

The scientific program featured three keynote lectures, seven oral presentations, two hands-on training sessions, two roundtable discussions, and a session dedicated to Young Investigators. Key themes included chemoinformatics resources (databases, webservers, packages, codes, etc.) for natural product research, antimicrobial drug discovery, integrated computational bioprospection, virtual screening, network pharmacology, and multi-target drug design. The hands-on sessions provided practical training in chemical space exploration and virtual screening using the Latin American and African natural products databases.

A major highlight was the Young Investigator session, which showcased innovative research from emerging scientists (MSc students, PhD students, and early postdocs) across diverse therapeutic areas, emphasizing the growing adoption of computational approaches worldwide. Interactive discussions further addressed challenges related to data accessibility, interdisciplinary collaboration, and training needs. Complemented with relevant experimental models, the introduction of bioinformatics, and computational systems biology have accelerated therapeutic innovations through the elimination of time-consuming, expensive, challenging, and inefficient processes that are consistent with the conventional drug discovery systems.

Overall,CAiSMD2026successfully combined scientific exchange with practical training, reinforcing the role of computational tools in accelerating secondary metabolite research and empowering young and emerging scientists, particularly in developing countries, to contribute to global drug discovery efforts.

This workshop particpates actively in capacity building fo next generation scientists for the use of computational technologies for secondary metabolite discovery with diverse applications.
