The central design choice in NHAMP is to introduce safety during generation rather than only after generation. Many AMP-discovery pipelines first optimize for activity and only later apply toxicity predictors or heuristic filters. That strategy can work, but it is inefficient when the overlap between antimicrobial activity and non-hemolytic behaviour is already narrow. By incorporating both objectives into the reverse diffusion trajectory, NHAMP shifts the search itself toward that overlap while keeping property evaluators outside the generation loop. The reported libraries are therefore not the product of an additional end-stage screen.

The guidance signals also produce a chemically interpretable shift. Triple guidance repeatedly moves the model toward peptides that are more cationic yet less hydrophobic and less aggregation-prone than the alternatives. This is consistent with experimental and biophysical work showing that AMP selectivity depends on how charge, amphipathicity and hydrophobicity are balanced, and that excessive hydrophobicity often increases hemolytic liability [7,8,9,10]. The embedding projections and structural-confidence analyses are compatible with the same reading: NHAMP appears to remain near a plausible peptide manifold while redistributing probability mass within it.

The ablation results further suggest that the three guidance branches are complementary rather than redundant. The dual-property branch localizes the activity-safety overlap, whereas the AMP and non-hemolytic branches contribute additional directional information that the smaller dual-property subset cannot provide by itself. In practical terms, the guidance scales act as controls on the efficacy-safety trade-off. In this dataset, separating where the overlap lies from how the sampler moves toward it appears to work better than relying on the dual label alone.

Within the broader AMP-design literature, NHAMP sits between two common strategies: generate large libraries and filter heavily afterwards, or couple property predictors tightly to the generator. Both approaches have been productive, but both are vulnerable to predictor bias and to the scarcity of reliable multi-property labels. Recent multi-property generators such as Multi-CGAN show the value of partially labelled data in this setting [18,19,21,22,24]. Our choice was to leave evaluators outside the generator while injecting multi-objective information into sampling itself. That does not remove predictor dependence, but it makes the source of improvement easier to interpret and keeps the generative claim separate from the screening claim.

Accordingly, NHAMP does not remove the need for downstream evaluation. Selectivity, stability and developability remain major causes of attrition in peptide discovery, even after a candidate is recognized as antimicrobial [5,6,18,19]. What NHAMP can do is reduce the number of clearly misaligned sequences that enter that later screening funnel.

These conclusions remain provisional. The central evidence in this study is in silico: AMP assignment, hemolysis prediction, MIC ranking and structural confidence all depend on models with their own biases and blind spots. Agreement among predictors provides a useful computational benchmark, but it does not equate to experimental selectivity. A generator evaluated repeatedly within one predictor ecosystem can, in principle, learn that ecosystem as much as the underlying biology. Cross-method benchmarking is informative, but still limited, because differences in source data, library construction and prior filtering are only partly controlled by rescoring under a common screen. Finally, the present study addresses only one safety liability. Peptides predicted to be non-hemolytic may still fail later because of serum instability, proteolysis, immunogenicity or manufacturability constraints. The operational grouping of weakly hemolytic records with non-hemolytic records may also make the predicted safety label more permissive, so the reported non-hemolytic fractions should be read as reduced predicted hemolytic liability rather than guaranteed absence of red-blood-cell lysis.

Beyond the general predictor caveats above, our two structural analyses each carry their own limitations. The α-helix and β-sheet propensity values shown in Fig.6are Chou–Fasman-style sequence-level estimates and therefore reflect intrinsic residue-level tendencies rather than the conformation an individual peptide adopts in any specific environment; they do not account for membrane interaction, oligomerisation or other context-dependent folding behaviour that is central to AMP biology. The pLDDT values shown in Fig.7come from AlphaFold 3 predictions; many AMPs are conformationally flexible and may not adopt a single stable structure in solution, while AlphaFold 3 was developed and validated primarily on full-length, well-ordered protein systems. Consequently, pLDDT values in this study should be interpreted only as approximate indicators of structural plausibility for ranking purposes, rather than as definitive measures of peptide stability or functional conformation in physiological environments. We therefore do not use AlphaFold 3 outputs to infer mechanism of action, membrane-bound state, oligomerization or experimental stability.

The next step is therefore prospective validation. A focused NHAMP library should be tested in matched antimicrobial and hemolysis assays, ideally together with sequence-diversity analysis and orthogonal predictors. Methodologically, the framework should also be challenged with additional objectives, such as serum stability or salt tolerance, where trade-offs may be sharper and guidance conflicts more explicit. More broadly, the present results support a simple design principle: treat safety as part of generation rather than only as a terminal filter. The same logic may prove useful in other peptide-design settings constrained by competing objectives. A concrete first validation tranche would synthesize 20–25 candidates chosen for dual-positive predictions, low APEX-Pathogen-predicted MIC, high sequence diversity and absence of training-set duplicates. We would test Gram-negative Escherichia coli ATCC 25922, Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 or ATCC 27853, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii, together with Gram-positive Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213 and a methicillin-resistant S. aureus isolate, using broth microdilution MIC assays, time-kill assays for the strongest hits, and human or sheep red-blood-cell hemolysis assays to estimate HC10, HC50 and selectivity indices.

In summary, NHAMP establishes a protein language model–fused latent diffusion framework for the controllable generation of antimicrobial peptide candidates under explicit efficacy–safety constraints. By accumulating antimicrobial, non-hemolytic, and dual-property guidance during denoising, the model directs sampling toward the narrow overlap between predicted antimicrobial activity and reduced hemolytic liability, rather than maximizing one property and removing liabilities only after generation. Within a shared post hoc evaluation pipeline, NHAMP retained a high predicted AMP-positive rate (83.8%) while improving the predicted non-hemolytic fraction (71.4%), and triple guidance achieved the highest dual-positive yield among the tested settings (64.7%). In a separate ablation experiment using independently generated sequence sets, triple guidance achieved the highest mean dual-property fraction among the tested guidance settings (60.4 ± 3.05%). Compositional, physicochemical, and embedding-space analyses further support the interpretation that this improvement reflects a redistribution of generated sequences toward more cationic, less hydrophobic, and less aggregation-prone peptide regions, rather than merely inflating evaluator-specific scores.

These findings should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously. The evidence presented here remains primarily in silico, and agreement among predictive models is not equivalent to experimental proof of antimicrobial potency, selectivity, or broader developability. The principal contribution of NHAMP is therefore methodological: it shows that safety-related constraints can be incorporated into the generative trajectory itself and that doing so can improve the practical yield of candidate libraries for downstream prioritization. Future work should focus on prospective antimicrobial and hemolysis assays, alongside broader developability testing, including serum stability, proteolytic resistance, salt tolerance, and manufacturability. Overall, this study supports a pragmatic design principle for peptide engineering: when key objectives conflict, incorporating safety during generation may be more effective than relying on terminal filtering alone.

We trained NHAMP on the two sequence resources bundled with the project snapshot: antimicrobial.csv (22,536 sequences) and Mixed_data.csv (6,038 sequences). All sequences were stripped of whitespace and restricted to the 20 canonical amino acids. To ensure label consistency across these heterogeneous sources, we adopted an operational low-hemolysis thresholding strategy in which peptides labeled as "weakly hemolytic" were grouped with the "non-hemolytic" class for model training. This grouping minimizes potential noise introduced by variations in experimental assays, such as differences in red blood cell sources or measurement protocols. To further validate the integrity of the integrated labels, we performed a cross-dataset consistency check using the HemoPI-2 model as an independent benchmark. We found a 98.4% concordance rate between the labels in the DRAMP-derived collection and the HemoPI-2 predictions [17], confirming that the biological signals for non-hemolytic activity are highly aligned between the two datasets. The antimicrobial collection was assigned label 0 (AMP) to provide broad coverage of antimicrobial sequence space, whereas Mixed_data.csv supplied labels 0, 1 and 2 corresponding to AMP, non-hemolytic and dual-property peptides. After concatenation, the effective class counts before reweighting were 22,712 label-0 peptides, 646 label-1 peptides and 4,217 label-2 peptides. To reduce overfitting, on-the-fly mutation augmentation was applied during diffusion training with probability 0.2 and mutation rate 0.1, replacing a small subset of residues with randomly chosen canonical amino acids. This is an operational low-hemolysis label: weakly hemolytic entries were retained with the non-hemolytic class to reduce threshold noise across heterogeneous assays, but this choice can inflate predicted safety estimates and therefore requires experimental hemolysis confirmation.

Diffusion training used variable-length residue embeddings rather than a globally fixed token length. Each peptide was tokenized with the pretrained ESM-2 tokenizer using boundary tokens, encoded with esm2_t6_8M_UR50D, and the CLS and EOS positions were removed so that the denoiser operated on an 320 residue embedding. Within each minibatch, sequences were padded dynamically to the longest peptide and accompanied by a binary attention mask that was propagated through training and sampling. A separate decoder-adaptation stage used max_length = 72, corresponding to up to 70 peptide residues plus the two boundary tokens [31].

NHAMP learns a denoising diffusion probabilistic model in ESM embedding space rather than directly over discrete amino-acid tokens. Starting from a clean peptide embedding, Gaussian noise is added progressively across 1,000 diffusion steps with a monotone schedule (s = 0.008), and the model is trained to reconstruct the clean embedding from a noisy intermediate state together with the timestep, the condition label and the attention mask. The loss is a masked mean-squared error computed only over valid residues [32].

The denoiser is a lightweight transformer that reuses the attention modules from the ESM-2 encoder as an inductive bias for protein-like long-range dependencies. Timestep and condition signals are injected by feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM): sinusoidal timestep embeddings are combined with label embeddings, projected to per-layer scale and shift vectors, and applied before each reused attention block. A position-wise multilayer perceptron with dimensions 320-1024-320 then maps the attended representation back to the denoised embedding estimate [31,40].

We trained the denoiser with classifier-free guidance by randomly dropping the condition label with probability 0.2 and replacing it with a dedicated unconditional token (ID 3). During sampling, an unconditional prediction is combined with one or more conditional predictions to form an accumulated guidance direction. For triple-guidance sampling, the AMP, non-hemolytic and dual-property signals were summed with scales 0.4, 1.5 and 1.2, respectively. This design allows the reverse trajectory to be influenced simultaneously by potency, safety and their intersection rather than relying on post hoc filtering alone. Keeping the three terms separate is useful because the dual-property subset alone is much smaller and more restrictive than the AMP-only or non-hemolytic subsets, so the single-property guidance contributes complementary high-signal directions during denoising [33].

These specific scales were selected through a pilot empirical optimization process that balanced predicted dual-property yield, perplexity, decoded-sequence validity and latent-space stability. Because experimentally verified non-hemolytic sequences are substantially rarer than general AMP sequences, the non-hemolytic branch was assigned the largest scale (1.5) to provide a stronger steering signal toward sparse low-hemolysis regions. The AMP branch used a lower scale (0.4) because the AMP label was more abundant and otherwise tended to dominate the combined update, whereas the dual-property branch used an intermediate scale (1.2) to anchor sampling near the predicted activity-safety overlap. Higher scales were avoided when pilot samples became repetitive, low-complexity or visibly out of the ESM-2 latent distribution, so the final values reflect an empirical trade-off rather than universal constants.

Peptide length was controlled explicitly. For each sample, a target length was drawn from the empirical length distribution of the antimicrobial dataset and clipped at 70 residues. The corresponding attention mask kept padded positions inactive throughout denoising and decoding, so a single model could generate peptides of different lengths without changing model parameters. In practice, the same mask is carried through both guidance accumulation and the reverse diffusion update, ensuring that guidance never leaks into padded positions.

For transparency and reproducibility, the exact guided denoising step and the full reverse sampling loop are written explicitly below. Algorithm 1 defines the multi-guidance accumulation used at a single timestep, and Algorithm 2 shows how that operation is embedded within the full DDPM-style reverse process.

Relative to standard single-condition CFG, this formulation makes the set of active objectives explicit and allows their scales to be tuned independently. In the present work, the dual-property term anchors sampling toward the overlap between activity and safety, whereas the AMP and non-hemolytic terms contribute complementary directional corrections; together they define the triple-guidance sampling strategy used throughout the main benchmark and ablation analyses.

Training of diffusion model with classifier-free guidance

Multi-condition denoising sampling

The diffusion model was trained with AdamW (learning rate 1 × 10−6, weight decay 1 × 10−12) for 500 epochs with batch size 128. To counter class imbalance, batches were drawn with a weighted random sampler (class weights 1 for label 0, 10 for label 1 and 5 for label 2; replacement enabled). To address the class imbalance, particularly for the non-hemolytic class, weighted random sampling was selected as the optimal strategy after evaluating several alternatives. Initially, under-sampling the majority AMP group was attempted, but this resulted in a significant loss of structural diversity and triggered mode collapse, yielding repetitive sequences within a narrow chemical space. Alternatively, supplementing the minority classes with generic non-hemolytic protein fragments introduced a large distribution mismatch—specifically, a significant latent-space distance between generic proteins and functional AMPs—which weakened the guidance effect and degraded the biological potency of the generated peptides. Ultimately, weighted sampling was adopted as it ensures the model frequently encounters rare non-hemolytic features without discarding the rich structural information inherent in the majority AMP class. We applied gradient clipping at norm 1.0, maintained an exponential moving average of parameters (decay 0.995), and saved EMA-smoothed checkpoints every 10 epochs for downstream sampling, The weighted sampler changes the frequency with which minority-class examples are seen during training, but it does not create a physically duplicated stored dataset; on-the-fly mutation augmentation further reduced repeated presentation of identical rare peptides.

To decode denoised embeddings into amino-acid sequences, we used the ESM-2 masked-language-model head. Because diffusion outputs are not guaranteed to lie exactly on the encoder manifold, the LM head was adapted by reconstructing tokens from embeddings corrupted with Gaussian noise (standard deviation 0.2) while the encoder remained frozen. Decoder adaptation used the antimicrobial dataset for 5 epochs (batch size 64, learning rate 1 × 10−4) with cross-entropy loss ignoring padding. Unless stated otherwise, each method was used to collect 1,000 valid sequences by sampling batches of up to 128 candidates from masked Gaussian noise, running 1,000 denoising steps, decoding with temperature-scaled multinomial sampling (temperature 1.3), and filtering out sequences shorter than 10 residues, sequences containing invalid symbols and low-complexity outputs in which a single residue class (G, C, A, K, L, M or R) exceeded 60% of the sequence.

Primary evaluate metrics were obtained from an external post hoc evaluation pipeline applied uniformly to all generated libraries, rather than from an internal classifier coupled to NHAMP during sampling. AMP-positive rate was computed with AMP Scanner vr.2, a deep learning predictor for AMP recognition [14]. Hemolytic propensity was assessed with HemoPI-2, which reports binary hemolysis predictions and estimated values [17]. non-hemolytic fraction denotes the fraction of generated peptides predicted to be non-hemolytic by HemoPI-2, and dual-property fraction the fraction simultaneously classified as AMP-positive by AMP Scanner vr.2 and non-hemolytic by HemoPI-2. Because no additional end-stage property filtering was applied before scoring, these metrics quantify the raw generated libraries under a shared evaluation pipeline rather than method-specific scoring heads. AMP Scanner vr.2 and HemoPI-2 were selected because they are publicly accessible, widely used for AMP and hemolysis triage, provide sequence-level binary calls suitable for library-scale rescoring, and were not used as trainable components inside NHAMP. Other binary predictors were not used as primary endpoints in this revision because their thresholds, supported sequence ranges and output calibration are not directly interchangeable; APEX-Pathogen, PLM perplexity, physicochemical descriptors and embedding analyses were used as independent downstream checks rather than as replacement binary classifiers.

MIC values were obtained from a separate in silico predictor and were used only for candidate prioritization, not for training or guidance tuning. Perplexity under a pretrained protein language model was used as a plausibility proxy. Physicochemical descriptors, including net charge, isoelectric point, hydrophobic ratio, instability index and aggregation propensity, were computed with standard peptide descriptor libraries. Embedding-space analyses used t-SNE and UMAP on ESM-2 representations. Secondary-structure propensity and 3D structural confidence were assessed by two distinct procedures, described separately in the next two subsections [36,37,39]. For Fig.5, the APEX-Pathogen stage was applied after dual-positive classification, and the displayed top 25 were the candidates with the lowest mean predicted MIC across the evaluated pathogen panel.

Because experimental structures are not available for the bulk of the training-set AMPs, the α-helix and β-sheet content reported in Fig.6was estimated from sequence using a Chou-Fasman-type residue-propensity scheme. Each amino acid was assigned its tabulated α-helix and β-sheet propensity values. For every peptide we then slid a 4-residue window along the sequence for the helix calculation and a 3-residue window for the sheet calculation, computed the mean propensity within each window, and flagged the window as helix-prone or sheet-prone when the mean exceeded 1.05. The α-helix propensity content and β-sheet propensity content reported per peptide are the fractions of windows passing this threshold. These are sequence-level estimates of structural tendency, not assignments derived from any predicted 3D structure; the same procedure was applied identically to training-set AMPs, training-set non-hemolytic peptides, training-set dual-property peptides and NHAMP-generated peptides, so that all groups in Fig.6are directly comparable [41].

Separately, for the analyses shown in Fig.7, 500 representative generated peptides were folded with a local installation of AlphaFold 3 [39], using the official open-source release from the Google DeepMind GitHub repository (https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3, version 3.0.1). The publicly released AlphaFold 3 model parameters were obtained under the standard non-commercial research licence and stored locally; no remote inference was performed. Sequence databases used by the data pipeline were installed locally as instructed in the AlphaFold 3 documentation and consisted of UniRef90 (2022_05 release), UniProt (2021_04 release), MGnify clusters (2022_05), BFD (first non-consensus sequences subset), PDB seqres (2022_09_28), PDB mmCIF templates, RNAcentral (active sequences clustered at 90% identity/80% coverage), Rfam (release 14.9, clustered at 90% identity/80% coverage) and the NCBI nt-RNA subset (2023_02_23, clustered at 90% identity/80% coverage). All inference was performed on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU (24 GB VRAM).

For each peptide an input JSON was generated in the AlphaFold 3 dialect (version 1), specifying a single protein chain containing the peptide sequence in the canonical 20-letter amino-acid alphabet, with no modifications, ligands, ions or counter-chains, and with modelSeeds [1]: to fix the random seed for reproducibility. A representative example of the input format is: {"name": "seq483", "sequences": [{"protein": {"id": ["A"], "sequence": "KKLKKKILKKPNLKLEWLYKLKP"}}], "modelSeeds": [1], "dialect": "alphafold3", "version": 1}. The pipeline was invoked via the standard run_alphafold.py entry point in two stages: a data-pipeline step (–run_data_pipeline = true, –run_inference = false) that built per-peptide MSAs against the local sequence databases above using the default jackhmmer/nhmmer search settings provided by the AlphaFold 3 distribution, followed by an inference step (–run_data_pipeline = false, –run_inference = true) using the released model parameters. Default values were used for –num_recycles and –num_diffusion_samples; no templates were forced beyond the default PDB template search, and no manual energy minimisation was applied to the output structures.

For each peptide AlphaFold 3 returned a ranked set of predicted structures together with per-residue confidence (pLDDT) and an overall ranking score. We retained the top-ranked model per peptide (highest ranking score) and extracted the per-residue and sequence-mean pLDDT; these are the quantities visualized in Fig.7. For the structural gallery in Fig.7b, the 20 peptides with the highest sequence-mean pLDDT were selected from the 500 folded peptides and arranged in a 4 × 5 grid in descending order of confidence. Cartoon renderings shown in Fig.7were prepared with PyMOL (Schrödinger, LLC), colouring each residue by its AlphaFold 3 per-residue pLDDT value (dark blue, pLDDT > 90; light blue, 70–90; yellow, 50–70; orange, < 50).

No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. All reported metric values and perplexity scores were computed on independently generated sequence sets using fixed random seeds for each method, and distribution plots summarize the generated-sequence populations rather than repeated wet-lab measurements. Because post hoc predictors can introduce systematic biases, the most defensible interpretation of the present metrics is comparative: they prioritize candidate sets for follow-up but do not replace orthogonal predictors or experimental assays. For the guidance ablation (Table2), uncertainty is reported as mean ± standard deviation computed across five non-overlapping groups of 100 generated sequences for each guidance setting.

title: Data-centric training enables meaningful interaction learning in protein-ligand binding affinity prediction
author: Matheus Müller Pereira da Silva; Lincon Onório Vidal; Isabella Alvim Guedes; Camila Silva de Magalhães; Fábio Lima Custódio; Laurent Emmanuel Dardenne
text:
Predicting protein–ligand binding affinity remains a fundamental challenge in drug discovery, where deep learning models have become central. However, these models often struggle with protein and ligand biases, and their generalization to unseen targets remains limited. Here, we introduce a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based scoring function trained with principled data-centric strategies as a controlled case study to investigate model bias, diagnostic evidence of interaction learning, and the comparative rigor of out-of-distribution evaluation protocols. We propose molecular dropout, a novel regularization technique that, combined with random rotation augmentation, mitigates rotational variance and reduces bias toward isolated protein or ligand features. Together, these strategies promote the learning of meaningful interaction patterns using only experimental structures and measured affinities, without requiring artificial data such as cross-docked poses, decoy generation, or assumed binding labels. In-depth analyses show that the model achieves low false-negative rates for strong binders, supporting its applicability in virtual screening. On the PDBbind v2016 core set, the model achieves a Pearson correlation (RP) of 0.839, and under the stringent Pfam-CV out-of-distribution protocol, it reaches RP= 0.573, performing competitively with existing methods on both benchmarks. Among the out-of-distribution protocols evaluated, Pfam-CV is the more rigorous benchmark. Analysis of interaction fingerprint similarity between training and test sets suggests that performance degradation under more stringent splitting schemes is largely driven by insufficient coverage of diverse binding landscapes in the available training data, rather than by an intrinsic inability of the model to capture meaningful intermolecular interaction patterns.

Scientific contribution

This work demonstrates that a straightforward CNN architecture, trained with principled data-centric strategies on experimental structures alone, can achieve competitive performance across diverse benchmarks without requiring complex preprocessing pipelines, synthetic data generation, or elaborate architectural designs. Ablation studies and in-depth analyses provide converging evidence that the model captures genuine protein–ligand interactions rather than merely exploiting molecular biases or dataset artifacts. Furthermore, analysis of interaction fingerprint similarity across splitting schemes suggests that the generalization gap observed under stringent out-of-distribution benchmarks reflects insufficient diversity of binding profiles in the available training data. This finding points to data coverage, rather than model capacity, as the main bottleneck to generalization.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

Accurately predicting the binding affinity of protein–ligand complexes is central to computational drug discovery, guiding the selection of promising candidates for experimental validation. Fast and accurate binding affinity estimation can enhance every stage of the drug development pipeline—from identifying hits within ultra-large virtual screening libraries (containing billions of compounds) [1] to optimizing leads, where predictions must ideally match the accuracy of rigorous yet computationally expensive alchemical free energy perturbation (FEP) methods [2,3,4]. Additionally, recent advances in generative models are reshaping de novo drug design, with scoring functions playing a crucial role in estimating the binding affinity of the generated compounds and guiding the design process toward high-affinity candidates [5,6].

With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, machine learning-based scoring functions (MLSFs) have gained significant traction. Two prominent deep learning methods for binding affinity estimation are convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [7,8,9] and graph neural networks (GNNs) [10,11,12,13]. CNN-based scoring functions offer a straightforward framework for modelling protein–ligand complexes by processing voxelised 3D grid representations, capturing spatial features such as cavities, surface topology, and interaction interfaces. Notably, the implicit representation of empty space in voxel grids may encode solvent-accessible regions and pocket volumes, features relevant to entropic effects that are often overlooked in deep learning models [2]. In contrast, GNNs operate on atomic graphs, naturally respecting molecular topology and enabling permutation-invariant learning, while incorporating chemically informed inductive biases. Their ability to model long-range dependencies and incorporate domain knowledge through engineered edges makes them highly expressive and well-suited for capturing fine-grained interaction patterns [14]. Moreover, many GNN architectures are inherently invariant or equivariant to 3D rotations, allowing them to produce consistent predictions regardless of molecular orientation. However, this flexibility can come at the cost of increased sensitivity to graph construction rules, such as distance thresholds or interaction definitions, potentially introducing rigidity or bias into the modelling process [14,15]. Conversely, CNNs operate on a more direct, volumetric representation of the complex, preserving raw spatial information and aligning with the deep learning paradigm of learning relevant features hierarchically from minimally processed inputs.

Despite their potential, CNN-based scoring functions face notable challenges. CNNs tend to be more computationally intensive than GNNs [16,17]. Moreover, unlike many graph-based methods, CNNs are not inherently invariant to 3D rotations, leading to inconsistent predictions for the same complex across different orientations [16,17,18,19]. To address this, researchers have explored different rotation-based data augmentation techniques [7,8,9,20,21,22,23], but a comprehensive comparison of their capacity to mitigate rotational variance in affinity prediction has not been published yet.

Another concern in the MLSF literature is whether these models genuinely learn meaningful interaction patterns or make predictions based on spurious correlations. Research has demonstrated that CNNs and GNNs can overfit ligand or protein features rather than capture their intermolecular interaction patterns [15,16,24,25], raising questions about whether models capture binding mechanisms or exploit dataset artifacts. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored various data augmentation techniques designed to increase the diversity of protein–ligand pairs [26] or to explicitly guide the focus of the model toward protein–ligand interactions [27]. However, these approaches frequently rely on strong assumptions, such as assuming binding affinities to cross-docked complexes or labelling incorrect poses of actual ligands as decoys. Since these assumptions are not always reliable, they risk introducing unwanted noise into the model.

Moreover, the ability of MLSFs to generalise to out-of-distribution examples remains a topic of debate [16,28,29,30,31]. Several data-splitting strategies aimed at minimising the similarity between training and test sets have recently been proposed [28,32,33,34,35,36,37]. As many studies have reported, when evaluated on these challenging test sets, the performance of several state-of-the-art MLSFs is drastically reduced, raising questions about their true applicability [30,34,36,38,39,40].

In this study, we introduce a CNN-based scoring function (DockTDeep), built on a standard architecture and trained with principled data augmentation and regularization, as a well-controlled case study to address three open questions in the evaluation of ML-based scoring functions. First, which rotation augmentation strategy most effectively reduces rotational variance in CNNs, and can existing practices be improved? Second, can diagnostic evaluations provide converging evidence that a model trained solely on experimental data (without requiring artificial data such as cross-docked poses, decoy generation, or assumed binding labels) captures genuine protein–ligand interaction patterns, rather than exploiting molecular biases? Third, how stringent are current out-of-distribution splitting schemes, and what drives performance degradation under distributional shift? To address the second question, we propose molecular dropout, a novel regularization technique that imposes minimal assumptions while directing the model's focus toward intermolecular interactions. Addressing the third question, our comparative analysis of splitting schemes identifies Pfam-CV as the more stringent of the two protocols examined here, enforcing a level of distributional separation that exceeds alternative strategies. Moreover, interaction fingerprint similarity analysis suggests that degradation under more stringent protocols is largely driven by gaps in training coverage of diverse binding landscapes, rather than by an intrinsic inability of the model to capture meaningful interaction patterns. The resulting model performs competitively with top-performing scoring functions on both standard and out-of-distribution benchmarks, demonstrating that principled training alone can match more architecturally elaborate approaches. The source code and trained weights of the model are available at [41].

We built a 3D CNN model to predict absolute protein–ligand binding affinity values in kcal/mol. The network input consists of voxel grids representing the protein–ligand complex. Each input tensor includes channels for different atom types: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, and another channel for other atoms. Figures S1-S4 exemplifies the molecular representation used (seeMethodsfor details on model architecture and molecular data encoding).

We used the PDBbind v2020 [42] dataset for training, validation, and testing. PDBbind is divided into three subsets: the “general” set, containing all protein–ligand data; the “refined” set, a higher-quality selection from the general set; and the “core” set, a small group of top-quality complexes for testing docking and scoring methods.

Our models were primarily trained on the general and refined sets. Model selection was performed using the validation subset of the refined set. Testing was done on multiple test sets, including the 2013 and 2016 core sets, a randomly split test set, and a time-based split set created by comparing the 2019 and 2020 PDBbind versions. To minimise data leakage between training and test sets, we also applied two different splitting schemes that aim to reduce the overlap of similar instances across splits, namely, the Pocket Pfam-Based Cross-Validation (Pfam-CV) split scheme [33] and the PDBbind CleanSplit scheme [37].

In contrast to some GNN models, CNNs are not invariant to rotations in input data. While rotation-based data augmentation approaches have been discussed in the literature, no study has systematically compared and measured their effectiveness in minimising rotational variance in CNNs for predicting protein–ligand binding affinities. Here, we describe and evaluate possible strategies to address this issue.

The first approach involves applying a random rotation directly to the atomic coordinates of the protein–ligand complex before voxelisation (referred to herein as “random rotation”), similar to other approaches [8,23]. This method benefits from slightly altering parts of the input visible to the model each time (see Fig.1a). In this work, this data augmentation method was applied “on the fly” for every input structure during training.

Comparison of strategies to mitigate rotational variance in CNN predictions for protein–ligand binding affinity.aThe blue shade represents the portion of the molecular structure within the voxel grid, while the pink shade denotes parts outside the grid. In the 90-degree rotation, no information is lost nor added after rotation. In the random rotation, pink portions that were once outside appear now inside the grid, preserving all possible information.bBoxplot of predicted affinities for 15 validation set examples under baseline, 90-degree, and random rotation strategies.cMean standard deviation (SD) and range of predictions for the validation set (N=904).dComparison of RMSE (lower is better) and Rp (higher is better) across strategies

Another widely adopted strategy is to rotate the grid using only right angles (90-degree rotations), producing 24 distinct orientations of the same input. The great majority of CNN-based MLSFs in the literature employ this method [7,9,20,21,43], claiming it makes CNNs resilient to input rotations. However, while this adds variations of the same protein–ligand complex, it provides little new information to the model (see Fig.1a).

Finally, an alternative approach [22] relies on the use of a limited set of random rotations (9 different configurations), likely due to the cost of applying transformations to the entire dataset before training. Because our setup allows for on-the-fly transformations with minimal overhead, we did not explore this restricted augmentation scenario.

To determine whether the 90-degree and random rotation strategies effectively reduce rotational variance in CNNs, the same CNN was trained on the refined set using both data augmentation approaches and compared them to a baseline model without augmentation. To assess the impact on rotational variance, 30 random rotations were applied to the coordinates of each protein–ligand complex in the randomly split validation set. The standard deviation (SD) and the range (difference between the maximum and minimum values) of each model’s predictions on these configurations were then measured. Figure1b illustrates the boxplot distribution of predicted values for 15 randomly selected validation set examples. Figure1c shows prediction performances regarding Pearson’s R (Rp) and root mean square error (RMSE).

The results on the entire validation set (Fig.1c) indicate that the random rotation strategy significantly reduced prediction variance (mean SD: 0.236, mean range: 0.967) compared to the baseline model (mean SD: 0.548, mean range: 2.265) and the 90-degree rotation strategy (mean SD: 0.630, mean range: 2.555). Finally, the 90-degree strategy showed no improvement concerning rotational variance metrics over the baseline and even performed slightly worse on average. This may result from overfitting to the limited set of orientations (24 in total), particularly since 90-degree rotations provide little to no new information to the model. The 90-degree approach exhibits high prediction variability, with a mean range of 2.56 kcal/mol, translating to approximately a 1.8-fold difference in the inhibition constant. Consequently, such models are unable to address rotational variance effectively. On the other hand, random rotation from SO(3) is a continuous augmentation that makes memorization impossible and forces the model to learn features that are approximately invariant, especially when coupled with a large number of training epochs to maximize the exposure to different orientations (in this work, we used 1500 training epochs).

As shown in Fig.1d, the random rotation strategy yielded superior results (Rp = 0.798, RMSE = 1.594) compared to the 90-degree rotation and baseline models, which achieved Rp values of 0.784 and 0.709, respectively. Based on these results, we adopted the random rotation strategy over the 90-degree approach for all subsequent experiments, highlighting this as an efficient strategy to reduce rotational variance in CNNs. Moreover, we do not recommend using the 90-degree rotation approach due to the significant variation in predicted values of the same protein–ligand complex in different orientations.

CNNs and GNNs have been shown to achieve high correlation values in binding affinity predictions even when using only the ligand or protein information rather than the full complex [15,16,25,27]. This has raised concerns that their performance may rely more on memorising ligand or protein structural similarities than learning genuine protein–ligand interaction patterns [33,44,45].

To address this issue, we developed a new regularisation technique called molecular dropout. Conceptually similar to the dropout technique commonly used in fully connected layers of neural networks, molecular dropout randomly omits, with a probabilityp, either the protein or ligand from the input during training and assigns a binding affinity label of zero to those examples. This method is straightforward to implement in CNNs. It avoids the complexities and assumptions of other approaches, such as docking or decoy poses with assumed binding affinities [8,26,27,46] or sharing labels across different inputs [26].

Figure2a compares the Rp values of the baseline (B) model against random rotation models trained with and without molecular dropout (B + RR + MD and B + RR, respectively) in the refined set. These models were tested on the randomly split validation set in three configurations: the full protein–ligand complex, the protein alone, and the ligand alone while keeping the original label values unchanged, similar to other approaches [27]. We also compared the CNN models to a ligand-basedk-NN (k-nearest neighbours) baseline. Thek-NN baseline estimates binding affinities by averaging the affinity values of thek=5 nearest ligand molecules in the training set (seeMethods). Thek-NN baseline makes its predictions entirely based on the features of the ligand alone, disregarding any intermolecular interaction.

The results indicate that although part of the baseline model's predictive power was recovered using only ligand (Rp = 0.355) and protein (Rp = 0.241) structures, the correlation remains weak. Random rotation further reduced these correlations, with a significant drop for the protein alone (Rp = 0.035)—where the correlation was nearly eliminated—and for the ligand (Rp = 0.278). Moreover, the incorporation of the molecular dropout approach effectively pushed the correlation values for both the ligand (Rp = 0.1) and protein (Rp = −0.117) to negligible levels while also yielding a correlation of Rp = 0.804 in the full complex setup (compared to Rp = 0.797 for random rotation and Rp = 0.709 for the baseline).

A particularly informative comparison is with the ligand-basedk-NN baseline: in the ligand-only scenario, all three CNN variants underperformed it (Fig.2a). Because thek-NN baseline predicts affinity from ligand similarity alone, a CNN exploiting ligand identity would be expected to at least match it when the protein is withheld. However, none of the CNN variants reached the performance of the k-NN baseline, most notably the molecular dropout model, whose ligand-only correlation dropped to Rp = 0.10, suggesting that their predictive performance is not primarily driven by memorization of ligand structures.

We also designed an additional experiment in which only the protein atoms closest to the ligand were masked (specifically, any protein atom within 5 Å of any ligand atom—see Fig.2c) while keeping the original label values unchanged. Similarly to the experiment above, models that accurately capture intermolecular interactions are expected to perform poorly in this test, as the key interactions have been eliminated. Figure2b presents the RMSE for each model across the entire validation set, as well as for different binding affinity ranges: weak/inactive, moderate, and strong (seeMethodsfor specific range boundaries and the number of examples in each category).

The results show that the model trained with molecular dropout (B + RR + MD) experienced the most significant RMSE deterioration across the entire validation set, with RMSE rising from 1.580 to 3.695. Random rotation without MD (B + RR) also experienced an increase in RMSE, from 1.594 to 2.965, though the effect was less pronounced. The baseline model (B) exhibited the smallest rise in RMSE, increasing from 1.841 to 2.474.

This effect becomes even more pronounced when examining the RMSE values within different binding affinity ranges. In the strong affinity group, the molecular dropout model (B + RR + MD) shows a dramatic RMSE jump from 1.676 to 5.463. A similar trend is observed in the moderate range, where RMSE rises from 1.468 to 2.965. In contrast, the weak/inactive group shows a slight RMSE decrease, from 1.591 to 1.386. The random rotation (B + RR) and baseline (B) models follow a similar pattern, consistent with the trends seen in the overall dataset.

Assigning a zero label when dropout occurs creates an implicit auxiliary task, where the model must learn that zero affinity corresponds to the absence of one binding partner, which means any nonzero prediction must ideally rely on information from both. Overall, these results demonstrate that the model trained with molecular dropout achieves accurate predictions not by relying on either ligand or protein features alone, but requires meaningful information from both to make accurate predictions. Based on these findings, we adopted the combined approach of random rotation with molecular dropout (B + RR + MD) for all subsequent experiments.

To investigate the assumption that the model incorporates information from protein–ligand interactions to perform its predictions, we performed redocking experiments on all protein–ligand complexes in our validation split from the refined set using the DockThor program [47]. Then, we selected the worst poses, based on root mean square distance (RMSD), from the top 10 poses ranked by the algorithm for each complex. These poses had an average RMSD of 8.285 Å compared to their crystal structure counterparts, representing sub-optimal conformations that likely fail to perform important interactions. Despite this, all poses remained physically plausible and free of steric clashes. Figure3illustrates the percentage change in binding affinity predictions for the docked poses relative to their crystal pose predictions.

Sensitivity of predicted compound strength to suboptimal poses reflects protein–ligand interaction recognition. A scatter plot comparing the reference prediction (i.e., the prediction for the crystal structure, dashed line) with the prediction difference (i.e., the percentage change in potency) for the worst poses generated from a docking experiment. Negative values represent a decrease in compound potency, while positive changes represent increase in potency

In the strong binders range, most protein–ligand complexes showed worse predicted values than their respective crystal poses, with some exhibiting nearly an 80% drop in the predicted potency. Only a few strong binders retained predictions close to those of their crystal structures. A similar trend, though less pronounced, was observed for the moderate affinity range. In the weak/inactive range, predictions varied widely, with differences ranging from approximately −80 to +70%.

These observations align well with expectations for a model that accounts for intermolecular interaction patterns and shows evidence that the model is sensitive to the geometric arrangement of the two partners, not just their co-presence. Interactions formed by strong binders play a critical role in stabilising the protein–ligand complex, often through the formation of well-defined and kinetically stable bound states. By contrast, weak or inactive compounds typically fail to induce such stabilisation, resulting in transient and poorly defined binding states rather than a single dominant bound configuration [48,49]. Enhancing accurate pose-dependent predictions for weak or inactive binders may require expanding the dataset in this range or incorporating information about protein–ligand flexibility and dynamics to reflect their more transient nature.

The results reinforce the rationale that our scoring function successfully identifies key interactions, especially those made by strong binders, since incorrect ligand conformations significantly reduce predicted binding affinity potencies in most cases.

A single worst-pose comparison, however, may not be able to separate sensitivity to genuine intermolecular contacts from sensitivity to gross changes in ligand geometry, since a large displacement could alter both at once. We therefore examined the full dose–response of the predicted potency as a function of pose RMSD, binned from 0–1 to 6–8 Å, and repeated the perturbation with a model trained without molecular dropout (Fig.4a). The predicted potency degrades monotonically with increasing pose RMSD, and, decisively, the molecular dropout model (MD-on) is significantly more sensitive to pose degradation than an otherwise identical model trained without it (MD-off)—specifically beyond 3 Å, with MD-on showing the larger potency drop (per-complex paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test:p< 0.05 at 3–4 Å andp< 0.001 at 4–6 and 6–8 Å). These results further confirm that molecular dropout sharpens the model's sensitivity to the intermolecular contacts that a mis-docked pose disrupts.

To confirm that this behaviour is a property of the model rather than of a particular docking protocol, we repeated the dose–response using poses generated by an independent docking engine, smina [69], instead of DockThor. The two engines yield closely overlapping dose–response curves within every affinity class (Fig.4b), showing that the interaction-sensitivity signal is docking-engine independent. Both docking programs also achieve comparable, good re-docking success rates, with DockThor superior overall (Supplementary Fig. S9), and every RMSD bin is well populated for both engines (Supplementary Table S4).

To further elucidate the model behaviour within distinct affinity categories, we calculated the Rp and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (Rs) for each affinity range (strong, moderate, weak/inactive) separately in the randomly split validation set. All subsets have a similar number of instances (seeMethods).

Figure5a, b presents the model’s correlation results. Notably, while the correlation coefficients for the entire dataset are high (Rp = 0.804, Rs = 0.796), they drop significantly within the individual activity ranges. For the strong category, the coefficients drop to Rp = 0.565 and Rs = 0.533; for the moderate category, Rp = 0.350 and Rs = 0.363; and for the weak/inactive category, Rp = 0.516 and Rs = 0.508. This pattern suggests that the scoring function effectively distinguishes broad categories of data but struggles with finer ranking within these ranges. This limitation is likely due to insufficient high-quality training data within the ranges. It could also reflect inherent label uncertainty, estimated at around 0.58 kcal/mol (0.44 pKiunits) [50]. This uncertainty could be large enough to impact performance metrics within the specific ranges.

Figure5c displays the confusion matrix generated from categorising the model's predictions into the predefined binding affinity categories. The model correctly classifies the majority of strong complexes (74%), with 21.7% misclassified as moderate and only 4.3% as weak/inactive. Similar trends were observed for correctly classified moderate (60.4%) and weak/inactive complexes (69.9%). Notably, the model demonstrates low false negative and false positive rates, with only 4.3% of strong complexes misclassified as weak/inactive, and 2.7% of weak/inactive ligands incorrectly predicted as strong complexes.

Interestingly, upon examining the strong complexes misclassified as weak/inactive (13 instances) and the weak/inactive instances misclassified as strong (8 instances), we found that many of these errors were due to wrong data annotation, structural issues in the PDBbind database itself or complex mechanisms of interaction (e.g., allosteric modulation).

For instance, the complex of compound3with the human carbonic anhydrase II (hCAII, PDB code 5eij) was predicted as a false-positive with predicted ΔGbindof −11.60 kcal/mol. However, the affinity data attributed to this complex by PDBbind (−7.25 kcal/mol, Ki~ 5 uM) is, in fact, the experimental affinity of the same compound against hCAI. For hCAII, compound3is more potent, with an experimentally measured Kiof 1 uM. Other examples of false-positive and false-negative in our validation set that are wrongly labelled in PDBbind are 3n9s and 4o2c.

As an example of structural error, the structure of the hexauridine substrate complexed with Hfq (PDB ID 2ylc) is provided in PDBbind as a monomer, whereas in the biological assembly the ligand is homohexameric (see Figure S5). Considering the monomeric structure of the ligand, our model predicted 2YLC as a weak complex (predicted ΔGbind= −6.55 kcal/mol) instead of a strong instance (experimental ΔGbind= −10.75 kcal/mol). After fixing the structure, our model correctly predicted it as a strong complex (ΔGbind= −12.64 kcal/mol).

Some misclassifications in binding affinity arise from allosteric effects occurring far from the binding site represented in the grid search space, as seen in PDB ID 4xoe, thus being outside the predictive scope of the model. Tables S1 and S2 provide a detailed list of misclassified examples and the probable issues. As these annotation and structural inconsistencies originate in PDBbind itself, they affect all methods evaluated on this benchmark equally and do not impose a performance ceiling specific to DockTDeep.

These results highlight that while the developed scoring function has limitations in distinguishing compound affinities within narrow ranges, it still performs effectively in broader categorisation tasks. This suggests that the model may face challenges in applications requiring fine discrimination, such as detecting activity cliffs, ranking compounds within the same affinity range, or optimising compounds through small structural changes—likely due to the limited availability of high-quality data in these ranges or high experimental label uncertainty. However, the models’ overall solid categorisation behaviour suggests potential utility for high-throughput virtual screening, where reliably identifying strong/moderate binders with low false negative rates remains a key priority.

As a preliminary indication of its potential utility in virtual screening, we evaluated DockTDeep retrospectively on three DUD-E targets [70]: Factor Xa, thrombin, and MMP-13 (Supplementary Fig. S10; Methods). Although DockTDeep was trained only on experimental protein–ligand complex structures, with no exposure to docked poses or artificially generated decoys, it enriched known actives above random for all three targets, with AUROC values ranging from 0.69 to 0.91. This behavior was observed consistently when poses were generated either with DockThor or with smina.

These results should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously. The evaluated target families are represented in the training set, and the observed enrichment may therefore reflect target-family familiarity as well as learned recognition of protein–ligand interaction patterns. Thus, this analysis does not by itself establish generalization to novel targets in a prospective virtual-screening setting. In addition, widely used virtual-screening benchmarks such as DUD-E contain known hidden biases that can affect the apparent performance of deep-learning models [44]. A broader evaluation on leakage-controlled and less biased benchmarks, together with rigorous prospective validation, remains an important direction for future work.

A growing critique in scientific literature is that traditional cross-validation methods allow for excessive overlap between training and test sets, especially when proteins in both sets share substantial structural similarities, as seen in commonly employed benchmarks [24,25,28,36,40,51,52]. This “data leakage” could inflate performance metrics by allowing models to be tested on data that is not entirely novel. Stricter validation methods, such as Pfam-CV [33], have been proposed to address this problem. Pfam-CV clusters proteins based on binding pocket structures, using the Pfam database to group evolutionarily related protein families. It aims to evaluate machine learning models rigorously by testing how well they predict binding affinities for structurally distinct proteins.

As extensively demonstrated in prior literature, training MLSFs with more data improves their prediction performance despite increased noise and lower quality [24,26,53,54]. Lower data quality arises mainly from two factors: less reliable binding affinity measurements (e.g., IC50values) and poorer structural integrity of the protein–ligand complex (e.g., low-resolution PDB structures). By holding out a high-quality evaluation set, we show that adding lower-quality training data still improves model performance (Figure S6). Therefore, we included all complexes from the larger PDBbind’s general set for the remaining generalisation results, in line with previous studies in the literature (seeMethodsfor more information on splitting and the number of training instances).

We present our model’s generalisation capabilities from multiple perspectives. Assessing model performance across diverse testing regimes rather than relying on a single benchmark is key to understanding where models can deliver practical utility in real-world scenarios. Our model achieved an Rp of 0.775 and RMSE of 1.639 on the randomly split test set and an Rp of 0.674 and RMSE of 1.813 on the time-based test set. This performance reduction reflects the challenge of predicting newly added complexes, which often have differing characteristics. On the PDBbind core sets from 2013 and 2016 (which exhibit greater train-test similarity), the model demonstrated consistent performances with Rp values of 0.859 and 0.839, respectively, aligning well with the values reported for other methods (Fig.6b and c). We note that all such benchmark comparisons draw on values reproduced from the original publications of the competing methods, obtained under their own data preparation and exact training set composition.

Under the stringent Pfam-CV protocol, our model achieved a competitive average Rp of 0.573 and a low average MAE of 1.247, comparable to those reported for established methods, including graph-based models (Fig.6d and e). This underscores the model’s generalisation ability in an extreme out-of-distribution scenario.

Despite the promising results on the Pfam-CV split, the performance of the model lags behind that observed in the other test sets. This is unsurprising given that stringent splits like Pfam-CV represent a particularly demanding regime for out-of-distribution generalisation. Machine learning relies on identifying patterns and relationships, and removing all similarity between training and test sets can deprive the model of crucial information needed for accurate predictions [31,52,55]. Figure7highlights this, showing the distribution of maximum interaction fingerprint (IFP) similarities between test and training sets. The Pfam-CV split (green) nearly eliminates shared interaction patterns, unlike the other splits where greater overlap is observed.

Finally, results under the PDBbind CleanSplit protocol show a mean Rp of 0.777 and a mean RMSE of 1.383, remaining competitive with the other reported methods (Fig. S7). However, this split scheme allows for substantially higher train-test similarity, as illustrated in Fig.7, which helps explain the improved performance metrics observed relative to the more stringent Pfam-CV split. Notably, the overall distribution of maximum train-test IFP similarity in PDBbind CleanSplit closely resembles that of the random split, with similarity values spread broadly across the range. This is not the case for Pfam-CV, which exhibits a markedly skewed distribution, indicating a far more structurally disjoint separation between training and test sets. The performance metric values obtained under PDBbind CleanSplit are also comparable to those from the random train-test split (Fig.6a), further supporting this observation. Consequently, contrary to the premises suggested in its original proposal [37], we argue that the CleanSplit protocol may not provide a sufficient basis for drawing definitive conclusions regarding the generalization power of AI-based scoring functions in out-of-distribution contexts. In our view, Pfam-CV provides a more rigorous benchmark for assessing out-of-distribution generalization.

The sharp performance drop of MLSFs under stringent, low-similarity evaluation is frequently interpreted as evidence that these models largely exploit dataset biases and memorising ligand and protein features rather than learning transferable protein–ligand interactions [15,16,36,38,44]. Our diagnostic analyses provide further evidence that this gap is closely linked to incomplete coverage of interaction-pattern diversity in the training data. In particular, the IFP similarity analysis shows that held-out protein families remain poorly covered under Pfam-CV, while the scaling experiment in Fig.8shows that performance improves only when training subsets progressively broaden the coverage of interaction-pattern space, not when training-set size is increased uniformly. Together, these results add quantitative evidence to an actively debated question and support the view that data coverage is a major bottleneck for real-world generalization, rather than model capacity or architectural sophistication alone [24,25,31,39,52].

To test this coverage hypothesis directly, we performed a scaling experiment within Pfam-CV, progressively increasing the training fraction from 25 to 100% under two subsampling schemes, while keeping the test folds fixed throughout the experiments (Fig.8). In the first scheme, training complexes were sampled uniformly from the original training pool. This increased the amount of training data while approximately preserving the overall diversity of the full training set. Under this uniform subsampling scheme, the held-out Rp remained essentially unchanged, ranging from 0.52 to 0.53 across all training fractions. This indicates that performance was not limited by training-set size alone. In the second scheme, we explicitly varied the coverage of the interaction-pattern space. Training subsets were expanded outward from the densest region of IFP space by adding nearest neighbours first. As a result, smaller subsets were concentrated in a narrow and internally redundant region of the interaction-pattern space, whereas larger subsets progressively incorporated more diverse interaction patterns. Under this coverage-broadening scheme, the held-out Rp increased monotonically, from 0.47 at 25% of the training data to 0.53 when the full training set was used.

Importantly, this manipulation changed only which training complexes were included, it did not make the training set more similar to the held-out test families. The maximum train-test IFP similarity remained low throughout the experiment, with a mean value of approximately 0.25, consistent with the disjoint-family separation shown in Fig.7. Thus, the complexes whose addition improved performance were still dissimilar to the test families. The improvement therefore resulted from broader coverage of the interaction-pattern space, rather than from increased similarity between training and test examples.

Together, these results support the conclusion that generalization under stringent splitting protocols is constrained primarily by the coverage of diverse interaction patterns in the available training data, rather than simply by model capacity or data volume alone. This experiment was performed using a single random seed and three distinct Pfam-CV folds.

Despite several recent advances introduced by modern deep learning techniques, predicting binding affinities of small molecules against protein targets using MLSFs still remains a challenging task in computational drug discovery. In this work, we introduced DockTDeep, a CNN-based scoring function that combines a standard architecture with principled data-centric training. The results demonstrate that it performs competitively against top-performing methods on both standard and out-of-distribution benchmarks. In-depth analyses show that predictions strongly deteriorate when protein atoms near the ligand are masked, and drop to negligible correlations when only ligand or protein information is provided. Furthermore, predicted binding affinities degrade substantially for suboptimal docked conformations, particularly for strong binders, confirming that the model is sensitive to the geometric quality of protein–ligand interactions and not just their co-occurrence. Together, these results offer converging evidence that the model captures genuine intermolecular interactions rather than exploiting molecular biases. The training pipeline relies on straightforward data augmentation strategies that use only experimental structures and measured affinities, without the need for cumbersome synthetic data generation, also facilitating model retraining as new structural and affinity data become available.

The results in narrow binding affinity ranges suggest that for tasks requiring fine-grained discrimination, such as activity-cliff prediction or lead optimization, the PDBbind v2020 dataset may be insufficient, regardless of algorithmic sophistication; accordingly, we do not recommend DockTDeep for these applications. For virtual screening, where the goal is enrichment of strong binders rather than precise ranking, large-scale datasets can still be effective, even when affected by some degree of noise, provided that training strategies mitigate bias and that the training data adequately cover the target binding landscape. Consistent with this, the model's low false-negative rate for strong binders, with only 4.3% misclassified as weak or inactive, supports its practical utility in this context.

To rigorously assess generalization, we evaluated our model across challenging train-test splits designed to reduce shared patterns between training and test sets. The recently proposed CleanSplit scheme permits substantially higher train-test similarity, which likely contributes to the improved correlation (Rp = 0.777). In our view, CleanSplit alone is insufficient to support definitive conclusions about the out-of-distribution generalization of AI-based scoring functions. As expected, performance decreased under more stringent evaluation regimes, with Pfam-CV emerging as the most challenging benchmark for out-of-distribution assessment (Rp = 0.573). Thus, of the two protocols examined here, Pfam-CV provides the more rigorous benchmark for out-of-distribution evaluation. An Rp near 0.57 under such a stringent protocol is a substantive result and is indicative of the generalization challenges faced by current models when applied to prospective virtual screening experiments, particularly for target protein families that are poorly represented or absent from the models’ training sets. Our results suggest that the degradation observed under stricter splitting schemes reflects limitations in the available training data, which do not adequately sample the diversity and complexity of binding landscapes required for robust generalization. More broadly, generalization may depend on factors that are implicitly encoded yet substantially more complex than simple protein–ligand atomic contacts, including protein flexibility and water-mediated interactions; likewise, the current voxel encoding groups halogens and metal ions into a single channel, collapsing chemically distinct interactions such as halogen bonding and metal coordination. Whether such models learn genuine interactions or mainly exploit dataset biases remains actively debated. Our diagnostic analyses provide further evidence that the performance gap under stringent evaluation protocols is closely linked to incomplete coverage of interaction-pattern diversity in the training data. These results support the view that data coverage is a major bottleneck for real-world generalization, rather than model capacity or architectural sophistication alone.

We conducted all experiments using the 2020 version of the PDBbind database, which compiles binding affinity data for protein–ligand complexes from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Affinity data are reported as either the inhibition constant (Ki), dissociation constant (Kd) or the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50), depending on available experimental measurements. For model training, the affinity values were converted to free energy of binding (ΔGbind) given in kcal/mol using the equation ΔGbind= RTln(Kd), with R = 1.987 × 10−3kcal · mol−1· K−1and T = 298 K. When Kdor Kivalues were unavailable, IC50was used instead. Because IC50depends on assay conditions such as substrate concentration and inhibition mechanism, this substitution introduces a systematic approximation; IC50-derived entries account for 36.98% (7,190 of 19,443) of the general set, whereas the refined set and both core sets contain none.

PDBbind [42] is organised into three subsets, each defined by progressively considering structural and binding affinity quality criteria. The “general set” comprises 19,443 protein–ligand complexes from all available data. The “refined set,” containing 5,316 complexes, is filtered based on properties such as structural quality (e.g., X-ray crystallography structures with resolution better than 2.5 Å), binding affinity accuracy (e.g., excluding less reliable data like IC50), and biochemical criteria, such as restricting entries to binary complexes. The “core set”, a widely used benchmark for docking and scoring evaluation, is systematically sampled from the refined set to ensure representativeness and reduce redundancy. The 2016 core set is the latest version and has 290 structures from 65 distinct proteins, while the previous 2013 version contains 195 instances.

Protein–ligand complexes from PDBbind were obtained from the Protein Data Bank [56] and originally prepared through an automated procedure by Li et al. [57]. These complexes were protonated at neutral pH by deprotonating carboxylic acid and phosphate groups while protonating aliphatic amine, guanidine, and amidine groups. Since the correct assignment of protonation and tautomeric states is crucial for accurate binding mode and affinity predictions, an improved preparation protocol was implemented in our work.

Our preparation protocol used the Protein Preparation Wizard from Maestro (Maestro, version 9.7, Schrödinger, LLC, New York, NY, 2014). Protonation states and hydrogen-bond networks were optimised with ProtAssign and PROPKA [58], taking into account the presence of the bound ligand. Epik [59] (Epik, version 2.7, Schrödinger, LLC, New York, NY, 2014) was used to calculate the protonation and tautomeric states of each ligand. All water molecules were removed, and metal ions were treated as cofactors. Finally, an energy minimisation step was performed to optimise the positions of hydrogen atoms. Due to preparation errors, 340 structures were removed from the dataset.

For hyperparameter selection, we employed only examples from the refined set due to its superior quality. The refined set was split into training and validation sets (3,599 training examples, 904 validation examples). All architectural and training decisions were made solely on the basis of this refined-set validation split; no performance on the core sets, the Pfam-CV folds, or the CleanSplit folds informed any design choice, and these benchmarks were used only for final evaluation.

To evaluate the model's performance across different binding affinity ranges, we divided the refined validation set of 904 examples into three groups: strong, medium, and weak/inactive. The classification was based on the following binding affinity thresholds [60]:

ΔGbind≤ −9.981 kcal/mol (45 nM)

-9.981 kcal/mol (45 nM) < ΔGbind≤ −7.395 kcal/mol (3.6 µM)

ΔGbind> −7.395 kcal/mol (3.6 µM)

Each group contains the following number of examples: 304 in the strong category, 308 in the medium category, and 292 in the weak/inactive category.

For model testing, we randomly split the general set into training and test subsets (15,699 training examples, 3404 test examples). A time-based split was also applied using the general set, differentiating between structures released before and after 2019. This resulted in a training set of 17,317 examples and a test set of 1786 examples.

To evaluate out-of-distribution generalisation, we employed the Pocket Pfam-Based Cross-Validation (Pfam-CV) split scheme [33] and the PDBbind CleanSplit cross-validation scheme [37]. Pfam-CV provides a more stringent partitioning of the PDBbind dataset into training, validation, and test sets by clustering proteins based on the structural features of their binding pockets, leveraging the Pfam database to group evolutionarily related protein families. This approach proposes to assess how effectively protein–ligand scoring functions predict binding affinities for structurally diverse proteins. PDBbind CleanSplit, on the other hand, takes a different approach to remove structural similarities, focusing on creating a training set that is structurally and chemically distinct from the 2013 and 2016 versions of the PDBbind core sets. Its approach is based on a series of sequential filtering using a combination of Tanimoto ligand similarity, protein similarity (TM scores) and a pocket-aligned ligand RMSD to to quantify and eliminate overlap in ligand and protein 3D structures [37].

To compare our results in terms of the mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) with other scoring functions presented in the original Pfam-CV and PDBbind CleanSplit papers, we converted our predictions from kcal/mol to pKi. The performance metrics, Pearson's correlation coefficient (Rp), MAE, and RMSE were computed and averaged across all splits according to the methodologies described in the original papers.

Interaction fingerprints (IFP) for all protein–ligand complexes were computed using the protein–ligand extended connectivity (PLEC) fingerprint method [61]. The PLEC fingerprints capture atomic environments by pairing atoms from the ligand and protein within a 4.5 Å distance. The surrounding atomic environments—up to a predefined depth—are generated for each interacting atom pair and then hashed into a final bit position. We used an IFP of size 4096, with a bond depth of 4 for the protein and 2 for the ligand. This method is implemented in the Open Drug Discovery Toolkit (ODDT) Python package (version 0.7) [62].

The Dice similarity coefficient was used to determine the maximum IFP similarity between any two datasets. The maximum IFP similarity was calculated by iterating over each complex in the first dataset and measuring its similarity coefficient against all examples in the second dataset to generate a distribution of maximum similarity values. We employed voxel grids to represent protein–ligand complexes, treating the molecular encoding problem from a computer vision perspective. Each voxel grid is a four-dimensional tensor of three spatial dimensions, width, height, and depth, and a fourth dimension for multiple channels. These grids were constructed at a 1.0 Å resolution within a 24 Å cube centred on the ligand’s geometric centre, capturing the interaction region between the protein and ligand. The grids were generated using our open-source tool, DockTGrid [63,64].

The encoding consists of 21 channels. Six channels represent the ligand alone, with separate channels for carbon (C), hydrogen (H), oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), and sulfur (S) and an "Additional Elements" channel for other atoms such as halogens and metal ions. Another six channels represent the protein alone, using the same atomic categories. Additionally, six channels capture the protein and ligand together, allowing for shared representation. Finally, three channels capture the total excluded volume, with separate channels for the ligand, protein, and the entire protein–ligand complex, independent of specific atomic properties.
