The β3-adrenergic receptor (ADRB3) is a G protein-coupled receptor involved in the regulation of energy expenditure, lipolysis, and glucose metabolism, and has therefore attracted interest as a potential therapeutic target in metabolic disease and related disorders. In addition to its established role in adipose tissue, ADRB3 is highly expressed in bladder smooth muscle, where its activation relaxes the detrusor muscle, reduces afferent bladder signaling, and increases bladder capacity [1]. Clinically, β3-agonists are already used for overactive bladder [1], and the receptor is also being explored in broader urinary, metabolic, and cardiovascular contexts. Beyond the bladder, β3-adrenoceptor agonism activates thermogenesis and lipolysis in human brown and beige adipose tissue, and the agonist mirabegron increases resting metabolic rate in healthy volunteers [2]. Beyond synthetic agonists, several plant-derived compounds have been reported to modulate ADRB3-dependent lipolysis or thermogenesis, including the ginsenoside Rb1 from Panax ginseng [3] and the flavonoids quercetin and fisetin, which potentiate beta-adrenergic-mediated lipolysis [4], suggesting that plant extracts and botanical preparations represent an underexplored source of ADRB3-active ligands. This makes ADRB3 an attractive target for ligand discovery, motivating a computational screening tool capable of prioritizing candidate agonists, including constituents of plant extracts, for further pharmacological evaluation. Despite this relevance, the identification of selective and potent ADRB3 agonists remains challenging.

One major reason is the structural and pharmacological complexity of adrenergic receptor ligands. Many compounds active at ADRB3 share physicochemical and structural features with ligands of other β-adrenergic receptor subtypes, making subtype-specific activity difficult to predict. At the same time, publicly available bioactivity data are heterogeneous, as they originate from different assays, laboratories, and reporting conventions. This complicates direct use of raw activity records for machine-learning applications and highlights the need for transparent curation and consensus labeling strategies.

Ligand-based machine learning offers a practical framework for prioritizing candidate compounds from chemical structure alone. However, predictive performance in cheminformatics depends strongly on how molecules are represented and how models are validated. In particular, random train-test splits can substantially overestimate performance when closely related analogues occur in both training and test sets. More stringent evaluation strategies based on scaffold-aware splitting provide a more realistic estimate of generalization to previously unseen chemotypes and are therefore especially relevant for medicinal chemistry applications.

Another unresolved question is which type of molecular representation is most informative for ADRB3 activity prediction. Circular fingerprints such as Morgan fingerprints capture local substructural environments efficiently and are widely used in ligand-based modeling [5]. In contrast, physicochemical descriptors summarize broader molecular properties such as lipophilicity, polarity, charge distribution, and topological complexity. Although both feature classes are commonly used, their relative value for ADRB3 agonist prediction has not been systematically benchmarked in a scaffold-aware setting.

In the present study, we constructed a curated ADRB3 activity dataset from ChEMBL [6], assigned consensus activity labels, and benchmarked multiple machine-learning classifiers across five predefined feature sets, including fingerprint-only, descriptor-only, and hybrid representations. Performance was assessed using scaffold-aware cross-validation and a held-out scaffold-grouped test set. In addition, Y-randomization [7] was used to evaluate the risk of chance correlation, and SHAP analysis was applied to interpret the best-performing model [8]. The goal of this work was not only to identify a high-performing ADRB3 classifier, but also to determine whether ADRB3 agonist activity is better captured by topological fingerprint space, physicochemical descriptor space, or a combination of both.

Bioactivity data for human adrenergic beta receptors were retrieved from ChEMBL. Separate activity tables were downloaded for ADRB1, ADRB2, and ADRB3, and standardized fields relevant to ligand-based modeling were retained, including compound identifiers, canonical SMILES, target identifiers, assay identifiers, document identifiers, activity type, relation, value, and units.

Reported activity values were converted to a logarithmic potency scale:

where\(C\)is the molar activity concentration.

Labeling followed a two-level strategy: At the measurement level, per-row pharmacological votes were assigned based on assay type, inferred assay direction, and potency. Agonist evidence required an EC50 measurement from a functional agonist assay with pEC50 ≥ 6.0 (relation =, >, or ≥). Assay direction was inferred automatically from the assay description text; keywords triggering agonist assignment includedagonistic,agonism,cAMP,adenylyl cyclase,stimulat-, andrelaxat-(the latter capturing beta-3-mediated smooth-muscle relaxation readouts). Antagonist measurements in antagonist-labelled assays (pAntag ≥ 6.0, where pAntag denotes the negative log10potency pooled across these antagonism-type readouts). Inactive votes required weak potency (pEC50 ≤ 5.0, relation =, <, or ≤) with no directional assay assignment. Only rows with valid structures, interpretable measurement types, valid relations, supported units, and positive activity values were retained for further processing.

Compounds were grouped by canonical SMILES, and a pharmacology label was first assigned from the per-molecule vote profile. Confirmed agonists required at least two agonist votes with ≥75% agreement, a median pEC50 ≥ 6.0, and no antagonist votes. Single-evidence agonists (label:agonist_single) required exactly one agonist vote with pEC50 ≥ 6.0. Analogous criteria defined antagonist and inactive categories. Compounds not meeting any confirmed criterion were labelledambiguous. The machine-learning label (ml_label) was then assigned independently from the pharmacology label. Confirmed and single-evidence agonists formed the positive class (ml_label = 1). Pharmacologically confirmed non-agonists formed an initial control set (ml_label = 0). Ambiguous compounds with zero agonist votes were reassigned to the control class with reduced sample weight (0.5), as they show no agonist signal despite having measurable ADRB3 activity data. Ambiguous compounds with at least one agonist vote were excluded to protect positive-class precision.

To supplement the control class, confirmed agonists of ADRB1 and ADRB2 that lacked any ADRB3 agonist evidence were added as decoy controls (sample weight = 0.8). These molecules are structurally drug-like, functionally active at closely related β-adrenergic receptor subtypes, and represent the subtype selectivity discrimination that the model must learn. Decoys were excluded if they appeared as ADRB3 agonists in any measurement. As a final quality step, any control molecule—whether from ADRB3 data or the decoy set—with a maximum Tanimoto similarity ≥ 0.90 to any training agonist (ECFP4, radius 2, 2048 bits) was removed to prevent near-duplicate label conflicts across classes.

For machine learning, the positive class comprisedagonistandagonist_singlecompounds (ml_label = 1), whereas the control class (ml_label = 0) comprised pharmacologically confirmed non-agonists, ambiguous compounds with zero agonist votes, and ADRB1/ADRB2 decoy controls. Sample weights reflected label confidence: 1.0 for confirmed agonists and confirmed pharmacological controls, 0.6 for single-evidence agonists, 0.7–1.0 for single-evidence pharmacological controls, 0.8 for decoy controls, and 0.5 for rescued ambiguous controls.

Structures were curated from the ADRB3 training subset before feature generation. Canonical SMILES were standardized using RDKit (RDKit: Open-source cheminformatics;https://www.rdkit.org; version 2026.3.1,https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19250388), and only compounds yielding valid molecular graphs were retained. Sanity filtering excluded chemically implausible structures: molecular weight outside 100–900 Da, fewer than 8 or more than 70 heavy atoms, TPSA > 250 Å [2], rotatable bonds > 20, or metal-containing compounds. Duplicate entries after curation were collapsed to a single representative at the curated-structure level, preferring higher-confidence pharmacology labels when multiple source rows mapped to the same structure. The final modeling set comprised 2147 curated structures with valid binary labels (1086 agonists and 1061 controls).

Morgan circular fingerprints were calculated from curated structures using RDKit with 2048 bits and chirality encoding enabled [5]. Two radii were used:

Both fingerprint types were generated with 2048 bits and chirality encoding enabled. Only compounds with valid curated structures and valid binary labels were retained for fingerprint generation.

A broad RDKit descriptor panel was calculated for all curated compounds. Descriptors with excessive missingness or near-zero variance were removed after filtering. In the final modeling matrix, 189 RDKit descriptors were retained. Descriptor values were median-imputed where necessary and standardized within the modeling pipeline when used by descriptor-containing models.

Descriptors directly encoding target activity or derived potency information were excluded to avoid information leakage.

Five feature sets were benchmarked:

RDKit descriptors only

ECFP4 + RDKit descriptors

ECFP6 + RDKit descriptors

For the hybrid representations, the 2048-bit fingerprint block was concatenated with the filtered RDKit descriptor block.

Six classifier variants were benchmarked: Random Forest (RF, [9]), support vector machine with radial basis function kernel (SVM-RBF, [10]), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost, [11]), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM. [12]), RF + SMOTE [13], and XGBoost + SMOTE.

RF and SVM were implemented usingscikit-learn, XGBoost usingxgboost, LightGBM usinglightgbm, and SMOTE usingimbalanced-learn. Morgan fingerprints and RDKit descriptors were calculated withRDKit, and SHAP analyses were performed using theshappackage.

The benchmark script defined Random Forest with 500 trees,max_features="sqrt",balanced class weights, and parallel execution; SVM with RBF kernel, C =1.0, and balanced class weights; XGBoost with 500 estimators, learning rate 0.05, maximum depth 6, and subsampling; and LightGBM with 500 estimators, learning rate 0.05, maximum depth 6, and 31 leaves. SMOTE augmentation was applied only to the Random Forest and XGBoost pipelines specifically defined for oversampling. Oversampling was performed strictly within training folds to prevent information leakage.

Model evaluation was designed to assess generalization to unseen chemotypes. Bemis-Murcko scaffolds [14] were generated from curated structures and used as grouping variables. A scaffold-grouped held-out test split was first created, after which the remaining development set was evaluated by grouped cross-validation. Thus, compounds sharing the same scaffold were assigned either to training or validation/test partitions, but never split across them. The held-out test set comprised 379 compounds across 179 unique scaffolds, and the development set comprised 1771 compounds across 712 unique scaffolds. No scaffolds were shared between the two partitions (scaffold overlap = 0), ensuring that test-set evaluation reflected genuine generalization to previously unseen chemotypes. Agonist prevalence was 49.5% in the development set and 55.1% in the held-out test set, reflecting the modest class-balance shift introduced by the scaffold-grouped split rather than a fundamental sampling bias.

For each feature-set/classifier combination, 5-fold grouped cross-validation on the 1771-compound development set was used to generate out-of-fold (OOF) predictions. A final model was then trained on the full development set and evaluated once on the held-out scaffold-grouped test set.

Performance was quantified using:

The best overall model was selected based on OOF MCC, with balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC used as secondary ranking criteria. The held-out test set was used only for final evaluation and not for model selection.

To test whether model performance could arise from chance correlations, Y-randomization [7] was performed across all benchmark combinations using the same scaffold-aware validation framework. For each feature-set/classifier combination, the true labels were randomly permuted and the full grouped cross-validation procedure was repeated. In the final practical run, 20 permutations were used per combination.

For each model, the real ROC-AUC was compared with the distribution of permuted ROC-AUC values, and an empirical one-sided permutation p-value was computed as:

\({N}_{perm}\)is the number of permutation runs

\({n}_{\text{p}\text{e}\text{r}\text{m}\ge \text{r}\text{e}\text{a}\text{l}}\)is the number of permutation runs in which the permuted ROC-AUC was greater than or equal to the observed ROC-AUC

Model interpretation was performed for the selected best model using SHAP(SHapley Additive exPlanations, [8]). SHAP values were computed on development-set samples for the final fitted model. For tree-based models, TreeExplainer was used; the selected best model was a Random Forest trained on ECFP4 fingerprints, and SHAP feature contributions were therefore obtained in a tree-based explanation framework.

To keep computation practical, SHAP analysis was performed on a sampled subset of compounds, with a separate background subset used for explanation. Feature importance was summarized by the mean absolute SHAP value of each variable. Results were visualized using:

A bar plot of the top-ranked features

A beeswarm plot showing the distribution of SHAP contributions across compounds

The pipeline was implemented in Python using open-source tools, including RDKit, scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, imbalanced-learn, and SHAP. All major workflows were organized into nine numbered scripts: ChEMBL target data retrieval (00); two-level consensus label construction with pharmacological annotation and ML-pragmatic labeling, including ADRB1/ADRB2 decoy controls and Tanimoto-based similarity filtering (01); structural curation and sanity filtering (02); molecular featurization across five feature sets (03); scaffold-aware benchmark training across six classifier variants (04); result summarization (05); benchmark figure generation (06); Y-randomization and SHAP-based model interpretation (07); and applicability domain assessment (08). A master runner script (09) coordinated end-to-end execution with configurable start, end, and skip options.

A systematic benchmark across all predefined feature-set and classifier combinations identified Random Forest (RF) trained on ECFP6 fingerprints (radius 2, 2048 bits) as the best-performing model under scaffold-aware evaluation. Table1shows out-of-fold performance for all six classifier variants on ECFP6, sorted by MCC. RF achieved the highest OOF MCC (0.880) with a ROC-AUC of 0.976, PR-AUC of 0.965, balanced accuracy of 0.940, and a Brier score of 0.054 (Table1).

When evaluated on the held-out scaffold-grouped test set—comprising 379 compounds across 179 scaffolds with zero overlap to the development set—performance remained high.

Thus, the ECFP6 fingerprint representation yielded the best overall balance of ranking performance, threshold-dependent classification accuracy, and calibration, with ECFP4-based models performing similarly and hybrid descriptor-containing sets offering no consistent advantage.

The held-out test-set behavior of the selected Random Forest model is shown in Fig.1. The ROC curve indicated strong discrimination between agonist and control compounds, consistent with a test-set ROC-AUC of 0.99. Similarly, the precision-recall curve remained clearly above the level expected from class prevalence, with an average precision of 0.98 (Fig.1).

Performance of the selected best model on the held-out scaffold-grouped test set.AROC curve.BPrecision-recall curve.CConfusion matrix

The confusion matrix showed that the model correctly classified 237 control and 249 agonist compounds, while producing only 7 false positives and 5 false negatives (Fig.1). This pattern indicates that the model generalized well to previously unseen scaffolds, achieving consistently high performance across both classes, with only 11 misclassifications out of 379 test compounds.

Taken together, these results suggest that the model generalized strongly to novel scaffold groups, maintaining high sensitivity and specificity simultaneously with only marginal misclassification in either class.

To assess whether the observed benchmark performance might arise from chance correlations, Y-randomization was performed across all benchmark combinations using the same scaffold-aware validation framework. In the permuted runs, ROC-AUC values were centered near a mean of 0.496 (range: 0.475–0.506;n= 600 permutation runs across 30 model combinations), as expected under random label assignment. In contrast, the real models showed a mean ROC-AUC of 0.968 (Fig.2).

Y-randomization across all benchmark combinations. Histogram of ROC-AUC values obtained from permuted-label runs. The dashed line indicates the mean ROC-AUC of the corresponding real models

This produced a clear separation between the empirical null distribution and the performance of the real models. For all benchmarked combinations, the empirical one-sided permutationp-value was 0.0476, corresponding to the minimum attainable value under the reduced setting of 20 permutations (Table3). Although this limits p-value resolution, the absence of permuted runs matching the performance of the corresponding real models strongly argues against a purely random explanation of the observed signal.

Overall, the Y-randomization analysis supports the conclusion that the benchmark models capture a genuine structure–activity relationship rather than chance label structure.

To improve interpretability, SHAP analysis was performed for the selected best model—Random Forest trained on ECFP6 fingerprints (radius 3, 2048 bits)—using TreeExplainer on a sample of 300 development-set compounds. All 15 highest-ranked features by mean absolute SHAP value were ECFP6-derived fingerprint bits, with no physicochemical descriptor among the top contributors (Figs.3and4). The most influential bit was ecfp6_191 (mean |SHAP|= 0.0218), followed by ecfp6_1475 (0.0198), ecfp6_1581 (0.0188), ecfp6_1607 (0.0155), and ecfp6_1602 (0.0139). All top-ranked features were fingerprint-derived (Figs.3and4).

SHAP feature importance bar plot—top 20 ECFP6 fingerprint bits for the selected Random Forest model (RF + ECFP6). Bar length represents the mean absolute SHAP value (mean |SHAP value|) across 300 randomly sampled development-set compounds, quantifying the average magnitude of each feature's contribution to model predictions regardless of direction. Features are ranked from highest (top) to lowest (bottom) importance. All 20 displayed features are ECFP6-derived fingerprint bits (radius 3, 2048-bit encoding); no physicochemical descriptor appears among the leading contributors. The most important feature, ecfp6_191 (mean |SHAP|= 0.022), contributes approximately 4.2-fold more than the 20th-ranked feature (ecfp6_1168, mean |SHAP|= 0.005), indicating a gradual rather than step-wise decay in feature importance. The top five bits (ecfp6_191, ecfp6_1475, ecfp6_1581, ecfp6_1607, ecfp6_1602) collectively account for the largest share of predictive signal. The directionality of each bit's contribution—i.e., whether its presence drives predictions towards the agonist or control class—is shown in the accompanying beeswarm plot (Fig.4)

SHAP beeswarm plot of the top 20 ECFP6 fingerprint features for the selected Random Forest model. Each row corresponds to one ECFP6 fingerprint bit (radius 3, 2048 bits), ranked by mean absolute SHAP value (top to bottom). Each point represents one compound from the 300-compound development-set sample used for explanation. The horizontal position indicates the SHAP value, i.e. the contribution of that feature to the model output on the log-odds scale: positive values push the prediction towards the agonist class, negative values towards the control class. Point colour encodes the feature value: since ECFP6 bits are binary, red/pink indicates that the substructural environment encoded by the bit is present in the molecule (bit = 1), and blue indicates its absence (bit = 0). Agonist-associated bits such as ecfp6_191, ecfp6_1581, and ecfp6_839 show a pattern in which bit presence shifts predictions towards the agonist class, whereas control-associated bits such as ecfp6_1475, ecfp6_1607, and ecfp6_1602 display the inverse pattern

These results indicate that prediction of ADRB3 agonist activity by the RF model is driven entirely by local substructural environments encoded in the ECFP6 fingerprint, with no contribution from physicochemical descriptor features. The consistent dominance of fingerprint bits across all top-ranked positions independently confirms the benchmark finding that fingerprint-based representations outperform descriptor-based representations for this classification task. To decode the specific bits involved, RDKit substructure images were generated for the ten most important bits using an example compound that sets each bit (Additional file 1: Supplementary Figure S1; Supplementary Table S1). Several of the highest-ranked bits (ecfp6_1475, ecfp6_1607, ecfp6_1602) center on a phenolic or benzylic hydroxyl group adjacent to an amine-bearing side chain, a pattern visually consistent with the aryl-ethanolamine motif shared by catecholamine-type β-adrenergic agonists; other top bits (ecfp6_191, ecfp6_1350) involve conjugated NH/heteroaromatic environments.

The benchmark identified Random Forest trained on ECFP6 fingerprints as the best-performing model under scaffold-aware validation. All fingerprint-based models (ECFP4, ECFP6) consistently outperformed the descriptor-only set, and hybrid combinations of fingerprints with RDKit descriptors provided no consistent improvement over fingerprints alone. OOF MCC values ranged from 0.784 (RDKit descriptors + SVM-RBF) to 0.880 (ECFP6 + RF), with all top-ranked combinations based on fingerprint features (Table1).

This result suggests that ADRB3 agonist activity is captured effectively by local substructural environments encoded in circular fingerprints. Morgan fingerprints encode atom neighbourhoods and substituent patterns at a radius-defined depth, likely reflecting the specific structural requirements for receptor engagement. The absence of added benefit from physicochemical descriptors further suggests that the physicochemical properties relevant to ADRB3 recognition are already implicitly represented within the structural fingerprint features. The near-perfect class balance throughout the dataset (~ 50.6% agonists) also explains why SMOTE-augmented variants offered no consistent advantage: oversampling is primarily beneficial under severe class imbalance, a condition not present here, as reflected in the marginal difference between RF and RF+SMOTE (OOF MCC 0.868 vs 0.866).

The held-out scaffold-grouped test set, sharing zero scaffolds with the development set, provides the most stringent estimate of generalization to previously unseen chemotypes. Performance remained near OOF levels across all metrics: test MCC 0.941 versus OOF MCC 0.880, and test ROC-AUC 0.990 versus OOF 0.976. The modest OOF-to-test gap reflects the expected effect of scaffold extrapolation rather than a fundamental limitation of the model (Table2).

Sensitivity and specificity were near-equally high (0.976 and 0.965 respectively), with only 11 misclassifications out of 379 test compounds (5 false negatives, 6 false positives). This balanced error profile is consistent with the near-equal class prevalence throughout the dataset (~ 50%), and contrasts with the conservative, specificity-biased profiles often observed in models trained on imbalanced datasets. For prospective virtual screening, the combination of high sensitivity and high specificity means that the model is unlikely to miss genuine ADRB3 agonists or to generate excessive false leads.

The Y-randomization experiment provides an important internal validity check. Real models performed far above the corresponding permuted-label runs: the empirical null distribution was centered at a mean ROC-AUC of 0.496 (range: 0.475–0.506), whereas real models ranged from 0.947 to 0.976 with a mean of 0.968 (Fig.2). The separation between the two distributions is complete—no permuted run came close to any real model—yielding the minimum attainable empirical p-value of 0.0476 for all benchmark combinations (Table3).

Accordingly, the benchmark results are unlikely to be driven primarily by random correlations or trivial artifacts of dataset composition. This strengthens confidence that the observed model performance reflects a meaningful signal related to ADRB3 agonist activity.

The SHAP results decisively reinforce the benchmark findings. All 15 highest-ranked features by mean absolute SHAP value were ECFP6-derived fingerprint bits; no physicochemical descriptor appeared among the top contributors (Figs.3and4). This is consistent with the benchmark result that fingerprint-based models (ECFP4 and ECFP6 alike) outperformed descriptor-only and hybrid feature sets, and provides independent, post-hoc confirmation that the model’s predictions are grounded in local structural information rather than in global molecular properties.

This finding is chemically interpretable. Circular ECFP6 fingerprints at radius 3 capture atom-centred environments up to three bonds from each atom, encoding local functional-group patterns, ring systems, and substitution motifs. RDKit-based visualization of the atom environments underlying the ten most important bits showed that several of the highest-ranked bits (ecfp6_1475, ecfp6_1607, ecfp6_1602) center on a phenolic or benzylic hydroxyl group adjacent to an amine-bearing side chain, a pattern visually consistent with the aryl-ethanolamine motif shared by catecholamine-type β-adrenergic agonists, while other top bits (ecfp6_191, ecfp6_1350) involve conjugated NH/heteroaromatic environments (Additional file1: Supplementary Figure S1; Supplementary Table S1). These observations indicate that the bits contributing most strongly to ADRB3 agonist prediction correspond to structurally and pharmacologically plausible features rather than uninterpretable artifacts.

To our knowledge, no prior study has developed a dedicated, fingerprint-based machine learning classifier for ADRB3 agonist activity using a structurally diverse, ChEMBL-derived dataset under scaffold-aware validation. Existing computational work on ADRB3 is limited to ligand-based 3D pharmacophore modeling combined with molecular docking and small-scale in vitro validation [15], and classical 2D-/3D-QSAR (CoMSIA) analysis restricted to a single, structurally homogeneous congeneric series of indolylethylamino-phenylethanol compounds [12]. Broader multi-target GPCR classification frameworks pool agonists and antagonists across many receptor families simultaneously but do not address ADRB3-specific agonist/control discrimination, subtype selectivity against ADRB1/ADRB2, or scaffold-grouped generalization. Our work is therefore, to our knowledge, the first to combine a large, structurally diverse ADRB3 dataset with scaffold-aware cross-validation, an independently held-out scaffold-grouped test set, and bit-level SHAP interpretability linked to explicit RDKit substructure visualization. Given emerging evidence that plant-derived compounds such as ginsenoside Rb1 and dietary flavonoids can modulate ADRB3-dependent lipolysis and thermogenesis3,4, a fingerprint-based classifier of the kind developed here could support the computational triage of botanical extracts or isolated phytochemical constituents for ADRB3 agonist activity prior to in vitro testing. We note, however, that our model was trained and validated exclusively on single, well-defined small-molecule structures from ChEMBL; its applicability to complex, multi-component plant extracts, as opposed to individual phytochemical constituents, has not been evaluated in this work and would require dedicated validation.

Several limitations of this study should be considered:

First, while the curated modeling set of 2150 compounds is well-suited for classical machine-learning classifiers, it remains modest in scale relative to datasets used for deep learning approaches. The held-out scaffold-grouped test set comprised 498 compounds, which, although adequate for the metrics reported, may limit precise estimation of performance in low-confidence subregions of chemical space. Although scaffold-aware splitting provides a more realistic estimate of generalization than random splitting, performance estimates on a limited test set remain subject to sampling variability. Accordingly, the reported metrics should be interpreted as a robust but still finite-sample estimate of predictive performance rather than as a definitive measure of model generalization.

Second, the activity labels were derived from public ChEMBL measurements and therefore inherit the limitations of heterogeneous literature and assay data. Despite the use of a consensus-based labeling strategy and potency thresholds, residual assay variability, experimental noise, and inconsistencies between studies cannot be excluded. The resulting labels are thus best understood as curated approximations of biological activity rather than as error-free ground truth.

Third, the present benchmark was restricted to ligand-based molecular representations derived from 2D structure, namely circular fingerprints and RDKit physicochemical descriptors. No receptor-based information, docking-derived descriptors, or experimentally validated binding-mode information was incorporated. Consequently, the models capture statistical structure–activity relationships, but they do not directly explain the molecular mechanism of receptor activation.

Fourth, Y-randomization was performed with a reduced number of permutations for practical reasons. Although the real models were clearly separated from the permuted null distribution, the empirical p-values therefore have limited resolution. The permutation analysis should accordingly be interpreted primarily as a qualitative and semiquantitative validation of non-random signal rather than as a high-precision inferential test.

Fifth, SHAP analysis improves model interpretability but does not establish causal relationships. The identified fingerprint bit contributions indicate which local structural environments were important for the trained model, not which molecular properties are necessarily causal determinants of ADRB3 agonism. Interpretation of these features should therefore remain chemically informed and hypothesis-generating.

Sixth, the control class was supplemented with confirmed ADRB1 and ADRB2 agonists as decoy controls to increase negative-class diversity. While these molecules lack ADRB3 agonist evidence in ChEMBL, undetected or unreported cross-reactivity at ADRB3 cannot be fully excluded for all decoys, which could represent a source of label noise in the control class. Future work incorporating selectivity data could address this limitation explicitly. Finally, the present study focused on binary activity prediction and did not explicitly model selectivity versus other adrenergic receptor subtypes, efficacy differences, partial agonism, or signaling bias. These aspects may be highly relevant for pharmacological translation and should be addressed in future work.

ADRB3 agonist activity can be predicted robustly using scaffold-aware ligand-based machine learning on a curated dataset of 2150 compounds. The best-performing model was a Random Forest trained on ECFP6 fingerprints, achieving an OOF MCC of 0.880 and a test-set MCC of 0.941 (ROC-AUC 0.990, sensitivity 0.976, specificity 0.965) on a held-out scaffold-grouped test set with zero scaffold overlap to the development set.

Held-out test performance, Y-randomization, and SHAP analysis consistently reinforced this result. ECFP6 fingerprints (closely matched by ECFP4) outperformed physicochemical descriptor sets across all classifier variants; hybrid feature combinations offered no consistent improvement. SHAP analysis confirmed that all top-ranked features were ECFP6-derived fingerprint bits, indicating that ADRB3 agonist activity is captured primarily through local structural environments rather than global physicochemical properties. These findings support ECFP6-based Random Forest models as a practical and effective strategy for prioritizing novel ADRB3-active compounds.

title: Using MR-chordless circuits for efficient enumeration of autocatalytic cores in large chemical reaction networks
author: Richard Golnik; Nicola Vassena; Peter F. Stadler; Thomas Gatter
text:
Autocatalysis is an important property of chemical reaction networks (CRNs) that is particularly prevalent in metabolic networks. A set of well-definedautocatalytic coresprominently features minimal subsystems that determine the autocatalytic capabilities. Recently, a graph-theoretic characterization has become available that enabled the enumeration of moderate-sized autocatalytic cores in real-life metabolic networks. Such an approach relies on enumerating and properly assembling elementary circuits in the bipartite graph associated to a CRN. Here, we improve on this approach in two ways: (1) We elaborate on algorithms for the enumeration of elementary circuits restricted to so-called MR-chordless circuits. These circuits do not have a chord from a Metabolite to a Reaction vertex, and are the only candidates to find autocatalytic cores. (2) We interleave our new algorithm with tests for autocatalysis to further limit the number of circuits that need to be stored for the construction of autocatalytic cores more complex than elementary MR-chordless circuits. Combined, these innovations achieve a performance gain of several orders of magnitude and make it possible to exhaustively enumerate all autocatalytic cores in real-life metabolic reaction networks comprising several hundred metabolites and reactions. Importantly, we find that reaction networks with irreversible reactions contain complex autocatalytic cores comprising more than a single “cycle with an ear”. Such structures exceed the established classification of autocatalytic cores for fully reversible networks into five types.

Scientific contribution

We developed a new graph-theoretic algorithm for enumerating autocatalytic cores that can handle large genome-scale metabolic models. Implemented in the Python programautogatito, it is up to four orders of magnitude faster than previous methods. Applications to large metabolic network models that involve both reversible and nonreversible reactions reveal that more complex autocatalytic cores exist than predicted by existing classification schemes for reversible reactions.

Autocatalytic reaction networks comprise sets of reactions in which the products collectively catalyze their own formation. Apart from food and waste metabolites, they form self-maintaining sub-structures in chemical reaction networks (CRNs) that are of key interest for the analysis of contemporary metabolic networks [1,2,3,4] and for studies of the transition between non-living and living matter [5,6,7,8]. Until recently, several alternative definitions of structural autocatalysis in chemical reaction networks were in use [2,9,10,11], complicating the comparison of computational results. The definition given in [10], which exhibits several convenient mathematical properties [12], has been widely accepted in recent years. It also forms the basis of practical algorithms to analyze empirical networks, including a heuristic based on combinations of cycles [13], an ILP enumerating minimal autocatalytic subnetworks [11], a SAT-solver based approach [14], and a combinatorial algorithm to enumerate irreducible autocatalytic subnetworks [15]. The latter approach, implemented in the Python projectautogato[15] is based on the explicit enumeration of elementary circuits in the directed bipartite König representation of the CRN. This representation assigns one class of vertices to species (Metabolites) and the other to Reactions. There is a directed edge (MR) from a speciesxto a reactionrifxis a reactant ofr, and a directed edge (RM) from a reactionrto a speciesxifxis a product ofr. While the number of elementary circuits in a digraph can grow super-exponentially with size, e.g., in complete digraphs, the number of autocatalytic cores may stabilize depending on the size and connectedness of the network (see Fig.1). The reason – informally – is that the minimality condition inherent to autocatalytic cores becomes more difficult to satisfy for larger subsystems.

Theautogatosoftware includes a modified algorithm to determine only autocatalytic cores instead of enumerating all irreducible autocatalytic subsystems [15]. It enumerates all elementary circuits up to a particular, user-defined size, engaging a modification of Johnson’s algorithm [16]. The computational cost of enumerating a very large number of elementary circuits to find a relatively small amount of cores, however, becomes disproportionate (Fig.1). It was already noted in [15] that elementary circuits contributing to autocatalytic cores cannot have directed chords connecting a reactant (metabolite) vertex to a reaction vertex, so called MR-chords. We therefore call such circuits MR-chordless. This observation suggests replacing the enumeration of all elementary circuits with a dedicated enumeration procedure for MR-chordless circuits. We therefore developed a specific algorithm to enumerate this type of elementary circuits in bipartite graphs. To this end, we use ideas similar to the approach of Dias et al. [17] for enumerating chordless circuits in general.

Ratio (left) of the number of autocatalytic cores over the number of elementary circuits and the absolute counts (right) of both, depicted as a function of the number of metabolites in the autocatalytic cores and elementary circuits, indicated on the horizontal axis. The reference metabolic networks areHelicobacter pylori[18] (H.p., 208 metabolites and 333 reactions),Methanosarcina barkeri(M.b., 249 metabolites and 402 reactions [19]),Staphylococcus aureus(S.a., 270 metabolites and 456 reactions [20]),Lactococcus lactis(L.l., 264 metabolites and 448 reactions [21]), andPlasmodium falciparum Ljungdahlii(P.f., 297 metabolites and 530 reactions [22]), after removal of the set of most highly interconnecting metabolites. For details on the networks, see the supplementary information

This contribution is organized as follows: we briefly summarize the key mathematical results underlying the combinatorial algorithm for computing autocatalytic cores withautogato[15] in sectionTheoretical background. In sectionThe algorithmwe describe our algorithm and in particular the necessary modifications to the approach of Dias et al. [17] for enumerating general chordless circuits towards enumerating only MR-chordless elementary circuits in bipartite digraphs. We also provide a self-contained proof that our algorithm, indeed, identifies only MR-chordless elementary circuits, determines them exhaustively in a given bipartite graph, and avoids duplications. Finally, we introduce a modification of our enumeration algorithm designed for the efficient detection of autocatalytic cores. This variant, termedautogatito, is provided as part of theautogatoPython project. Extensive benchmarking in sectionBenchmarkingshows that our algorithm enumerating MR-chordless elementary circuits directly outperforms the combination of Johnson’s algorithm with post-processing by up to 4 orders of magnitude. The integration of this feature intoautogato[15], together with avoiding the enumeration of larger MR-chordless elementary circuits that cannot be part of cores because they contain the vertex set of a smaller autocatalytic elementary circuit, results in a further performance improvement.

Achemical reaction network(CRN)\(\Gamma\)is a pair of sets\(\Gamma =(X,R)\), whereXis the set ofspeciesormetabolites, andRis the set ofreactions. Any reaction\(r\in R\)is an ordered association between nonnegative combinations of the species:

where the nonnegative constants\(s^{-}_{xr}\)and\(s^{+}_{xr}\)are thestoichiometric coefficients. A speciesxis areactantof the reactionrif\(s^-_{xr}>0\)and aproductofrif\(s^+_{xr}>0\). For simplicity of presentation, we excludeexplicit catalystsin this contribution. That is, we assume that there is no speciesxsuch that\(s^-_{xr}>0\)and\(s^+_{xr}>0\)for some reactionr, no species is both reactant and product of the same reaction. In this case, the associatedstoichiometric matrix\(\textbf{S}\in \mathbb {Z}^{|X|\times |R|}\), defined as\(s_{xr}:=s^{+}_{xr}-s^{-}_{xr}\), fully encodes the network\(\Gamma\). In particular,\(s_{xr}=s^{+}_{xr}\), wheneverxis a product ofr,\(s_{xr}=-s^{-}_{xr}\)wheneverxis a reactant ofr. Otherwise\(s_{xr}=0\). It is possible to extend the theory of autocatalytic subsystems to CRN with explicit catalysis, see [23] for details.

We write\(X'\)and\(R'\)to refer to subsets ofXandR. The set of metabolites participating in a set of reactions\(R'\)is denoted by\(X(R'):=\{x \in X \ | \ \exists \ r\in R: s_{xr}\ne 0 \}\). The network\(\Gamma\)is conveniently represented by its bipartiteKönig graph\(\textbf{K}=(V,E)\)with vertex set\(V:=X\cup R\)and edge set\(E:=E_1\cup E_2\), where\((x,r)\in E_1\)iff\(s_{xr}<0\)and\((r,x)\in E_2\)iff\(s_{xr}>0\). We call\(E_1\)themetabolite-to-reactions(MR) edges, and\(E_2\)thereaction-to-metabolite(RM) edges. Similarly,\(E'_j\)refers to subsets of\(E_j\),\(j=1,2\). In the following, we use some notation and terminology that is standard in graph theory. We refer to the SI (Sect.Graph Theory) for definitions of these concepts.

An elementary circuit with an MR-chord from\(x_3\)to\(r_6\)is depicted in teal, while an MR-chordless elementary circuit in blue. The blue and the teal elementary circuits, together, yield a fluffle. However, this is not an induced fluffle, precisely due to the MR-chord from\(x_3\)to\(r_6\). With a proper column ordering, the MR-chord in the elementary circuit appears as a negative off-diagonal entry.Lower right:The stoichiometric matrix associated with the induced fluffle (and autocatalytic core) is marked in red. With the proper column ordering, the matrix is a Metzler matrix, i.e., with nonnegative off-diagonal entries

We use the notation\(\textbf{S}'\)to refer to the submatrix of\(\textbf{S}\)indexed by species-rows\(X'\subseteq X\)and reaction-columns\(R'\subseteq R\). A vectorvis calledstrictly positive, denoted by\({\textbf {v}}>0\)if all of its entries are strictly positive. A submatrix\(\textbf{S}'\)isautocatalytic[10] if

for all columns\(r\in R'\)there are rows\(x,y\in X'\)such that\(s_{xr}<0\)and\(s_{yr}>0\), and

there is a strictly positive vector\(\textbf{v}>0\)such that\(\textbf{S}'\textbf{v}>0\)is again strictly positive.

Anautocatalytic core(equivalently a PAC in [14]) is an autocatalytic matrix\(\textbf{S}'\)that possesses no proper autocatalytic submatrix. As shown in [10,12], there is a 1-1 correspondence of species and reactions in\(\textbf{S}'\)such that each\(x\in X'\)is the unique reactant in\(X'\)of a uniquely defined reaction\(r_x\in R'\). Therefore,\(\textbf{S}'\)is square and the columns of\(\textbf{S}'\)can be reordered such that the resulting matrix\(\textbf{A}\)is a matrix with strictly negative diagonal entries and nonnegative off-diagonal entries. Up to the proper ordering of the columns, the latter property defines\(\textbf{S}'\)as aMetzler matrix. Further, such Metzler matrix is irreducible. The closely relatedminimal autocatalytic subnetwork(MAS) [11] is a subnetwork\((X(R'),R')\)that contains an autocatalytic core and\(R'\)is inclusion-minimal with this property. Hence, the reaction set\(R'\)of a MAS is the reaction set of at least one autocatalytic core. The enumeration of autocatalytic cores thus also yields a complete list of MAS.

The square sub-matrices of the stoichiometric matrix which, up to re-ordering of their columns, can be written as Metzler matrices, are in 1-1 correspondence with the inducedflufflesof the bipartite König graph\(\textbf{K}\)[15]. AFluffleis a subgraph\(G=(X'\cup R',E'_1\cup E'_2)\)of\(\textbf{K}\)satisfying the following properties:

Gis a strongly connected block,

every\(x\in X'\)has out-degree 1 and every\(r\in R'\)has in-degree 1.

See theGraph Theorysection in the SI for a self-contained presentation of the standard concepts ofinduced subgraphs,strong-connectedness, andin- and out-degree. The crucial observation here is that the subgraph\(\textbf{K}[X(C)\cup R(C)]\)induced by an elementary circuitCis a fluffle if and only ifCis MR-chordless, i.e., if there is no edge\((x,r)\in E_1\)which is not inE(C). A graphical summary about the relationship of (induced) fluffles and Metzler matrices is shown in Fig.2. Finally, with an iterative argument based on theear-decompositionof strong blocks, it can be shown that all induced fluffles are a superposition of MR-chordless circuits. The detailed arguments are published in [15]. The search for candidate autocatalytic cores, therefore, can be restricted to elementary circuits without MR-chords and their superpositions. Moreover, by minimality of cores, autocatalytic elementary circuits do not need to be combined with other elementary circuits.

A more efficient enumeration of autocatalytic cores should thus be achievable by replacing Johnson’s algorithm for listing all elementary circuits [24] by a variant that produces MR-chordless circuits only. A natural starting point for this endeavor is an algorithm by Dias et al. for the enumeration of chord-free circuits [17]. In the following section, we describe the modifications necessary to adapt this algorithm for our purposes.

The algorithm described in [17] forbids all kinds of chords. In bipartite digraphs, however, there are two classes of directed edges, distinguished by vertices that form the heads and tails, respectively. The implementation below is independent of the identifiers of the two disjoint vertex sets. Nevertheless, in the setting of CRNs we refer to the two types of edges, and thus also of chords, as metabolite-to-reaction (MR) and reaction-to-metabolite (RM). For better readability, we refer to elements of the two disjoint vertex setsXandRas metabolites and reactions, respectively.

In fact, the assumption of a bipartite graph considerably simplifies some special cases that have to be accommodated in the general case:

Self-loops cannot occur in a bipartite graph and thus do not have to be handled.

Elementary circuits of length 2, so-calleddigons, are chordless and thus can be easily collected in a preprocessing step (see Alg.1). However, Digons cannot be removed from the original graph, in contrast to [17], because its MR-edge, might appear as an edge along an elementary circuit, while the corresponding RM-edge constitutes an acceptable chord.

Bipartite graphs are triangle-free and hence quadrangles are the smallest elementary circuits that can exhibit an MR-chord. Quadrangles, therefore, are the smallest structures detected by the main enumeration function of our algorithm.

The graph\(\textbf{K}\)is first decomposed into its strongly connected components (SCCs), which can be analyzed separately. Since SCCs with less than 4 vertices cannot encounter two reactions and reactants, they are omitted. For each larger component, our goal is to enumerate all MR-chordless circuits. The key building blocks arestems, defined as directed paths of length three that initiate and terminate in metabolite vertices,xandy, and have an interior reaction vertex, denoted asr. For a given reactionr, the set of stems, denoted as\(\mathcal {S}_r\), is obtained as the cartesian product of the predecessor and successor vertices ofr, i.e., the reactants and products of the reactionrin a CRN. An element of\(\mathcal {S}_r\)is denoted as\(S =(x,r,y)\). A stack\(\textbf{T}\), composed of sets of vertices that remain to be visited along the nascent path\(\textbf{P}\)is utilized for efficient vertex traversal, modifying the concept of classiciterativedepth-first-search as follows. Vertices can be visited more than once if the path to reach them is changed. Hence, we cannot rely on global visited markers. Instead, sets of successors that have yet to be visited for each node in the current path are tracked in the stack.\(\textbf{T}\)itself is processed in first-in-last-out (FILO) order. Any visited successor of the current terminating vertex of the growing path\(\textbf{P}\)is removed from the leading set of\(\textbf{T}\).

Upon initialization, the set of all successors ofyis pushed onto\(\textbf{T}\). All successors in the leading set of\(\textbf{T}\)are visited consecutively until a valid amendment is found, which is added to the nascent path while the set of its successors is loaded onto the stack in turn. Upon backtracking, i.e., if the leading set of\(\textbf{T}\)is exhausted, it is removed from\(\textbf{T}\), and the algorithm continues by processing the new top element of\(\textbf{T}\).

A reaction\(r_i\)is processed only if\(F[r_i]=1\), implying that exactly one of the metabolites on the current path\(\textbf{P}\)is a reactant for\(r_i\), while a metabolite\(x_i\)is processed only if\(B[x_i]=0\), in particular if it is not a reactant for any reaction that has already been added to\(\textbf{P}\). The initial vertexxis therefore never visited due to initialization ofB(see Lemma2, Claim 2 and Claim 4). In addition,rcan also never be revisited since\(F[r]=1\)by initialization and any additional traversal would require another predecessor ofrand hence\(F[r]\ge 2\), which violates general processing requirement for reactions. Forywe obtain\(B[y]=1\)directly after addition of the necessary fourth vertex to obtain at least a quadrangle, which prevents a second visit.

Further processing of vertices depends on their particular type. For a reaction vertex\(r_i\), it is initially verified ifxis a successor (product) for\(r_i\)since this would imply that an MR-chordless elementary circuit has been found. The corresponding circuit is subsequently returned to the main function. Since RM-chords are specifically allowed, we extend the search by adding\(r_i\)to the current path, and the set of vertices consisting of successors of\(r_i\)is pushed to the stack, as it is performed in case thatxis not a successor of\(r_i\). Whenever none of the out-neighbors of the ultimate vertexvof\(\textbf{P}\)can extend the current path,vis removed from\(\textbf{P}\), its set of successors removed from the stack, andFandBare updated as described previously.

We are now in the position to prove the main result of this section.

LetGbe a bipartite digraph. Then Alg.1enumerates all MR-chordless elementary circuits. Moreover, it generates each MR-chordless elementary circuits exactly once.

Every elementary circuit, and thus every MR-chordless elementary circuit is contained in a unique strongly connected component ofG. It therefore suffices to consider the strongly connected component\(G'\)ofGindividually. Moreover, if\(V(G')<4\), it can contain only digons, hence it suffices to run\(\texttt {MRChordlessCircuitSearch()}\)for all stems contained in a strongly connected components with\(|V(G')|\ge 4\). To see that every MR-chordless circuits is constructed exactly once, we note that the set of digons is disjoint from the set of longer circuits produced byMRChordlessCircuitSearch(), and moreover the circuit sets for the different connected components are pairwise disjoint. The only remaining candidates for possible duplicate production, therefore, are two circuitsCand\(C'\)with stems (x,r,y) and\((x',r',y')\)such that\(r\in V(C')\)and\(r'\in V(C)\)with\(r\ne r^{\prime}\)Constraining the successor function such that\(r^\prime\in E(C)\)implies\(r'>\)ifris the reaction-vertex in the stem used to produceC, thus\(r'>r\)and\(r>r'\), a contradiction. In the following we adapt this base algorithm to enumerate MR-chordless elementary circuits for the efficient enumeration of autocatalytic cores. To this end we recall from sectionTheoretical backgroundthat (i) all autocatalytic cores are MR-chordless superpositions of MR-chordless elementary circuits, and (ii) no extension of an autocatalytic core can again be an autocatalytic core. As a consequence, further exploration of a path can be abandoned as soon as an MR-chordless circuit with autocatalytic sub-matrix has been identified.

We therefore modify Alg.2in the following way (see Alg.3): Upon detection of an MR-chordless elementary circuitCin\(\textbf{K}\), we retrieve the associated sub-matrix\(\textbf{S}[C]\)of the stoichiometric matrix and examine its autocatalytic capacity by checking condition (A2) (see section Theoretical background), as described in [15].

Modification ofMRChordlessCircuitSearch()forautogatito.

If\(\textbf{S}[C]\)is autocatalytic,\(r_k\)is not appended to the current path\(\textbf{P}= (x_1,r_1, \ldots , x_k)\), and the next potential neighboring reaction vertex of\(x_k\)is considered. Otherwise,\(r_k\)is appended to\(\textbf{P}\)and the search continues as described above. This avoids the enumeration of non-core autocatalytic Metzler matrices for which a smaller autocatalytic core has already been found. These non-autocatalytic MR-chordless elementary circuits are subsequently used for the assembly offlufflesto obtain autocatalytic cores comprising more than one elementary circuit using Alg. 1 of [15].

The benchmarking of the presented algorithm follows a two-step approach. First, we compare the efficiency of our algorithm as a stand-alone Python implementation (MRChordlessCircuits.py) against Johnson’s well-established algorithm for enumerating all elementary circuits in two different graph models: i) random graphs of different sizes and connectedness, and ii) in fluffles, where all elementary circuits are MR-chordless to warrant equal conditions. Secondly, we include the algorithm into a Python packageautogatitofor enumerating autocatalytic cores. We remark at this point thatautogatitobuilds on the Python packageautogato, which has been published previously [15].

To evaluate the efficiency of our algorithm for enumerating MR-chordless circuits in bipartite graphs, we compared it as a stand-alone Python implementation (MRChordlessCircuits.py) to Johnson’s algorithm for the enumeration of elementary circuits with a post-processing step that identifies MR-chords and terminates as soon as an MR-chord has been detected.

ID (RID), OD (ROD), and D (RD) specify the selective method for choosing a reaction vertex of the currently considered strongly connected component in Alg.1. In particular, for ID, OD, and D, the reaction vertex with maximum in-, out-, and total degree, respectively, in the König graph is chosen, while for RID, ROD, and RD, the reaction vertex with the highest in-, out-, and total degree, respectively, in the R-Graph is chosen. Johnson+ refers to enumeration of all elementary circuits with Johnson’s algorithm and additional post-processing for identifying the MR-chordless among those

As a test set, we generated random bipartite Erdős-Rényi graphs of different sizes, ratios of vertex set sizes, and edge probabilities engaging NetworkX’s random-bipartite graph generator [25,26]. Ratios of metabolites to reactions were 2 : 1, 1 : 1, and 1 : 2 while the total size of the graphs encompassed 30, 60, 90, 120, and 150 vertices with edge probabilities ranging from\(0.5\%\)to\(2.5\%\). In the description of Alg.2, successors of a vertex are treated as sets returned by the function\(\texttt {Succ}_\mathcal {D}()\). This choice was made to achieve the optimal theoretical complexity, as sets allowO(1) search and deletion of elements. Yet, in practical terms hashing of every member creates a large overhead. As successor sets are generally very small, i.e.,\(|\texttt {Succ}_\mathcal {D}()| \ll |X|\), linear search and deletion costs may be lower than hashing costs. Hence, both lists and sets were tested in the implementation. As expected, for all three algorithms, time requirements grow exponentially. Nevertheless, our new algorithm outperformed Johnson’s enumeration of all elementary circuits with post-processing by up to 4 orders of magnitude for graphs surpassing\(10^4\)MR-chordless elementary circuits. In addition, we did not observe a significant difference in the running-times of the algorithm when using a set or a list to determine the successors of a vertex.

To improve the performance of our algorithm we also investigated different orderings of reaction vertices according to their degree in the bipartite graph and in the associated R-graph. To this end, we selected for each strongly connected componentGthe vertex with the maximum in-degree, out-degree, or total degree (i.e., the sum of in- and out-degree) in the bipartite Kőnig graph or the R-graph, i.e., the digraph with vertex setR(G) and edge-set\(F:=\{(r,q) \ | \ \exists x\in X(G): s^+_{xr}>0\,\wedge \, s^-_{xq}>0\}\). However, none of these modifications showed a clear performance improvement in comparison to choosing a reaction vertex at random in random bipartite Erdős-Rényi graphs (see Fig.3, upper panels). However, an advantage might only be detectable for more densely connected graphs.

Clearly, the stronger performance of our algorithms can be primarily attributed to the growing number of elementary circuits in contrast to MR-chordless circuits (see Fig.3, lower panels). As observed for autocatalytic cores, growing network size and increasing interconnectivity increases the likelihood for MR-chords within elementary circuits, naturally limiting the number of MR-chordless circuits and contributing to the strong divergence between the number of elementary circuits and MR-chordless elmentary circuits.

In contrast to fluffles, the number of elementary circuits and MR-chordless elementary circuits are not necessarily the same in randomly generated bipartite graphs. To provide equitable conditions, we benchmarked the performance of our algorithm against Johnson’s algorithm in fluffles, which we generated randomly using the following construction, starting from an elementary bipartite circuit composed of 2 reactions and 2 metabolites. Then RM-ears, i.e., ears initiating in a reaction vertex and terminating in a metabolite vertex, are added. In each step, either a metabolite and a reaction vertex or an MR-edge is chosen at random. Subsequently, a bipartite path of even length\(k \ge 2\)is inserted between the selected starting reaction and terminating metabolite node, or the MR-edge is split, and a metabolite and reaction vertex picked for the described path insertion. The value ofkis chosen (with equal probabilities) as a random even integer between 2 and a tuneable maximum length parameter, here 20. This procedure ensures that only fluffles are produced and thus all elementary circuits are MR-chordless.

As expected and depicted in Fig.4(upper left panel), the number of elementary circuits computed using Johnson’s algorithm equals the number of MR-chordless elementary circuits computed using Alg.1. Even in the case of fluffles, our algorithm outperformed Johnson’s algorithm with a subsequent check for MR-chordlessness, in particular for larger network sizes (see Fig.4). In the case of fluffles, however, the test for MR-chordlessness is not necessary. In contrast, Johnson’s algorithm alone showed tremendously reduced time requirements for the enumeration of MR-chordless elementary circuits in fluffles and was superior to our enumeration algorithms, where no additional vertex sorting was enforced (Fig.4upper middle and right panel). However, these limitations could be overcome by selecting reaction vertices for stem generation with respect to their degrees. In particular, the best performance, equal to Johnson’s algorithm, was achieved when always the vertex with the highest in-degree in the R-graph was selected (Fig.4lower middle panel).

To demonstrate the usefulness of the algorithms developed in sectionThe algorithm, we comparedautogatitowithautogato’s core enumeration algorithm [15]. Figure5summarizes the results for the metabolic networks used in Fig.1. In contrast toautogato, which depends on the enumeration of all elementary circuits,autogatitowas able to enumerate all MR-chordless elementary circuits independent of their size and obtained a complete list of all autocatalytic cores that are represented by a single elementary circuit directly forHelicobacter pylori[18],Methanosarcina barkeri[19], andStaphylococcus aureus[20]. Moreover, for these species, we were also able to enumerate all autocatalytic cores that are superimpositions of non-autocatalytic MR-chordless elementary circuits. For all other species depicted,autogatitosignificantly increased the size (e.g. doubled forLactococcus lactis) of all enumerated autocatalytic cores represented by MR-chordless circuits and their superimpositions. Thus, the number of elementary circuits necessary to detect the same number of autocatalytic cores of a particular size was reduced dramatically (Fig.5, upper left panel).

The middle left panel of Fig.5shows the ratio of MR-chordless elementary circuits to autocatalytic cores. Surprisingly, the majority, (\(70\%\)in H.p.\(67\%\)in M.s., and\(61\%\)in S.a.), of all autocatalytic cores were represented by elementary circuits. The remainder was composed mainly of two elementary circuit. In particular, more than 99% of the autocatalytic cores are either an elementary circuit or a superimposition of two elementary circuits (Fig.5, right panels). We note, however, that even if an autocatalytic core was induced by a single elementary circuit, the induced fluffle might exhibit more elementary circuits (see e.g. a type V core with 5 elementary circuits). We, thereby, always refer to the size of the smallest circuit-net, i.e., the minimum number of elementary circuits, required for composing the particular autocatalytic core.

Metabolites are depicted with circles and reactions as squares, and an alternating sequence of metabolites and reactions as one symbol composed of a square and a circle. If not otherwise specified above the edges, stoichiometries are trivial. A classification of autocatalytic cores infully reversiblenetworks stipulates the existence of exactly five distinct classes [10], consisting of either a single elementary circuit or a superpositions of two circuits (type III). Here, we consider the general case of RNs composed of both reversible and irreversible reactions. The structure of autocatalytic cores in this setting may be more complex. Indeed, our computational survey uncovers a small number of such more complex autocatalytic cores that appear as superpositions of three, and in a few cases even four elementary circuits, as shown in the lower-left panel in Fig.5.

Figure6shows two autocatalytic cores closely resembling a type III core. Since acetolactate-synthetase requires two pyruvate molecules and all other stoichiometries are trivial, two elementary circuits are not sufficient for the corresponding fluffle to be autocatalytic. In both cases, the upper wing is composed of two elementary circuits. The additional elementary circuit (green) shares the common MR-path of the other two as well as additional paths with the blue circuit, and thereby compensates for the non-trivial educt stoichiometry of pyruvate in acetolactate synthesis.

Figure7shows an even more complex example of an autocatalytic core formed by four elementary circuits. Again, the composed fluffle exhibits many similarities with a type III core from [10]. All elementary circuits share a common central MR-path. However, in addition to an elementary circuit connecting the upper and lower part (green), the upper wing is composed of two elementary circuits which are both doubled in their productivity by an additional RM-shortcut, which is essential to compensate for the 5 isopentenyl-diphosphate molecules necessary for octaprenyl-pyrophosphate synthesis, in order to ensure that the emerging fluffle is autocatalytic.

Metabolites are depicted as circles and comprise PYR: pyruvate, GLU: glutamate, IPDP: Isopentenyl-diphosphate, MAL: Malate, 5MTA: 5-methylthioadenosine, while reactions are depicted as rectangles and comprise ME: malate-enzyme, ARGSL: argininosuccinate lyase, DKMPPD: 2,3-diketo-5-methylthio-1-phosphopentane degradation reaction, HSERTAr: homoserine O trans acetylase reverse, OCTDPS: octaprenyl pyrophosphate synthase, SPMS: spermidine synthase. An alternating sequence of metabolites and reactions is depicted as a square and a circle in one symbol

Autocatalytic cores are an important characteristic of chemical reaction networks and may serve as a key discriminating feature between the metabolic networks of living organism and inanimate chemical systems. The algorithmic advances described here make it possible to obtain the (nearly) complete inventory of autocatalytic cores for large graphs, thus enables a systematic investigation of autocatalysis in chemical reaction network data. In our own benchmarks we enumerated datasets comprising up to\(3\cdot 10^7\)MR-chordless circuits and\(10^7\)autocatalytic cores. Owing to the high memory overhead of Python data-structures and other language restrictions, the current implementation is limited mainly by its RAM requirements. This, unfortunately, also limits parallelization, as RAM usage increases linearly with the number of subprocesses. Hence, computations were distributed to set of servers with each 512GB of RAM.

Empirically, we observe that the overwhelming majority of autocatalytic cores are either formed by a single MR-chordless elementary circuit or constitute the superposition of a pair of such circuits. Structurally, these cases conform the classification of autocatalytic cores infully reversiblenetworks [10]. For very large networks, the limiting resource is the memory required to store the elementary MR-chordless circuits that are not autocatalytic for the second stage ofautogatito, i.e., for testing autocatalysis of pairwise or even larger combinations. We observe, however, that the majority of autocatalytic cores are formed by a single elementary circuit in the König graph\(\textbf{K}\). Enumeration of MR-chordless elementary circuits thus provides a reasonable approach towards characterizing autocatalysis, even for network sizes that render the exhaustive generation of larger autocatalytic cores via superimposition of MR-chordless elementary circuits computational infeasible.

An important result of our computational survey in real-life metabolic networks is the fact that autocatalytic cores beyond the classification given in [10] do exist if irreversible reactions are included. Although formally all chemical reactions are reversible, the differences in free energies between reactants and products is so large in many cases that the ratio of product to reactant concentrations required to drive the reaction energetically “up-hill” are not achievable in practice. The capability to handle irreversible reactions, therefore, is of key practical relevance. This begs the question of whether autocatalytic cores can at least in principle become arbitrarily complex in partially irreversible RNs, or whether there is a finite list of discernible types.

Complete metabolic networks are likely to contain much larger sets of reactions than the models used here. The Human Metabolome Database [28], for example, lists more than 200,000 substances as of Jan. 2026. Since the number of (long) elementary circuits increases exponentially with size of the König graph\(\textbf{K}\), complete enumerations are bound to fail eventually as larger and larger network models become available. Nevertheless, it will remain feasible to list MR-chordless elementary circuits at least up to a certain maximum length, storing the non-autocatalytic ones on disc. Such a strategy will then require dedicated algorithms to efficiently identify composite autocatalytic cores composed of two or more elementary circuits. Whileautogatitoalready performs well on contemporary datasets, we plan a low-level implementation to improve on memory consumption and parallelization in future.
