title: MoActiPred: an AI-Based bioactivity prediction model applied to the development of influenza neuraminidase inhibitors
author: Zeqi Zhang; Jiqing Ye; Qingyu Zou; Chenyi Ji; Stephanie Holt; Patrice Guillon; Larissa Dirr; Long Yin Lam; Tsz Fung Tsang; Xue Yang; King Hong Chan; Mark von Itzstein; Xiao Yang; Cong Ma
text:
Accurate prediction of small-molecule bioactivity is critical for accelerating drug discovery. Here, we report MoActiPred, a multimodal AI framework that integrates 2D molecular graphs, physicochemical descriptors, and 3D E (3)-equivariant geometric representations. Using a curated ChEMBL-derived influenza virus neuraminidase (NA) inhibitor dataset (1245 compounds; IC50threshold 20 nM), MoActiPred showed the strongest overall performance among the evaluated methods, including traditional machine-learning models (Random Forest, SVM, and XGBoost), SMILES-based language models (ChemBERTa, ChemFM, and PolyBERT), and graph-based baselines (MolCLR and SEGNN). On the public test set, MoActiPred obtained an accuracy of 0.952, MCC of 0.797, and F1 score of 0.898, while retaining high average precision, supporting the value of combining 2D and 3D representations. To evaluate its practical utility, MoActiPred was applied prospectively to 26 oseltamivir analogues designed, experimentally synthesised and evaluated against influenza A (H3N2) NA. The model correctly predicted 6 of 7 high-activity compounds (IC50< 20 nM) and 18 of 19 inactive or weakly active derivatives, yielding 92.3% accuracy. Enzymatic assays showed that most derivatives were active, with 5b and 5f emerging as the most potent inhibitors (IC504.31 and 6.49 nM, respectively). In MDCK.2 cell-based assays, 5b and 5f exhibited strong H3N2-selective antiviral activity, with EC₅₀ values of 0.72 nM and 3.04 nM, respectively, and no detectable cytotoxicity (CC50> 100 μM). Docking, MD simulations, and water-map analyses indicated that the oseltamivir core of 5b occupies the conserved active site while itsN-substituent engages the 150- and 430-cavities, with solvation-driven binding particularly favouring N2. These results support that MoActiPred’s utility in drug discovery research and identify 5b as a promising lead for further optimisation against influenza A (H3N2).

Scientific contribution

MoActiPred advances bioactivity prediction by integrating 2D molecular graphs, physicochemical descriptors, and 3D E (3)-equivariant geometric representations within a single multimodal framework. Compared with conventional machine-learning models, SMILES-based language models, and graph-based baselines, MoActiPred achieved stronger classification performance on the curated and public neuraminidase inhibitor datasets, demonstrating the value of combined 2D/3D molecular representation learning. Its prospective utility was further supported by in-house synthesis of a focused oseltamivir-analogue series followed by enzymatic and cell-based biological activity testing.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

Prediction of small-molecule bioactivity has become a cornerstone of modern drug discovery. Its roots can be traced to the 1960s, when Hansch and Fujita introduced the first quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models. These early approaches relied on linear relationships between simple physicochemical descriptors, such as logP and steric parameters, and biological activity. As computational power and chemical databases expanded in the 1990s and 2000s, machine learning (ML) methods such as random forests, support vector machines (SVMs), and neural networks began to exploit increasingly sophisticated molecular fingerprints and descriptors. The emergence of large-scale datasets, such as MDDR and ChEMBL, which now contain millions of compounds and associated bioactivity measurements, further accelerated the development of predictive bioactivity models.

The rise of deep learning around 2015 marked a turning point in bioactivity prediction. With the introduction of benchmarks such as MoleculeNet, researchers began to apply end-to-end learning directly to raw molecular representations, including graphs and sequences. Today, artificial intelligence (AI) models can predict binding affinities (e.g., pIC50, Kᵢ), classify compounds as active or inactive, and even generate multi-target activity profiles. These advances have markedly accelerated hit identification, with AI-driven approaches achieving hit rates 10–100 times higher than traditional random screening. Notably, AI-designed kinase inhibitors have progressed to clinical trials (e.g., work by Insilico Medicine), and AI-powered platforms have rapidly identified antiviral leads against emerging threats such as SARS-CoV-2 (e.g., Atomwise).

Fundamentally, bioactivity prediction asks whether, given a small molecule (e.g., SMILES or graph) and a target (e.g., protein sequence or binding pocket), we can accurately estimate the likelihood and strength of their interaction. This task is complicated by several challenges, including sparse data (with most targets having fewer than 100 known actives), the presence of activity cliffs (where small structural changes cause large shifts in activity), target drift over time, and the need for interpretability to support decision-making in medicinal chemistry and regulatory settings.

To address these challenges, a diverse array of AI methodologies has emerged. Classical machine learning approaches use fixed-length molecular fingerprints (such as ECFP or MACCS) and physicochemical descriptors to train models like random forests [1], XGBoost [2], and SVMs [3]. These models are relatively fast and often interpretable but may struggle to capture 3D structural nuances. Sequence-based models tokenise SMILES strings for input to RNNs or Transformer architectures (e.g., ChemBERTa [4], ChemFM [5], PolyBert [6]) and support both predictive and generative applications, although they typically lack explicit 3D awareness. Graph neural networks (GNNs), now considered state-of-the-art, operate directly on molecular graphs, learning local chemical environments and enabling transferability across tasks, particularly when large datasets are available. Many graph-based models further incorporate 3D geometry, using equivariant GNNs or 3D CNNs to capture spatial relationships critical for accurate prediction (e.g., MolCLR [7], SEGNN [8]). Finally, generative models, often built on variational autoencoders (VAEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and reinforcement learning, can propose novel compounds optimised for bioactivity and drug-likeness, opening new avenues for de novo drug discovery.

Despite remarkable progress, key challenges remain, including data sparsity, the need for robust generalisation to novel targets and chemotypes, and the requirement that AI-driven predictions be interpretable and actionable for medicinal chemists. Nevertheless, the integration of AI into bioactivity prediction is reshaping drug discovery, enabling faster, more efficient, and more innovative exploration of chemical space than was previously possible.

In this study, we develop MoActiPred, a multimodal bioactivity prediction model (Fig.1). MoActiPred integrates complementary molecular information from 2D topological structures, physicochemical descriptors, and 3D geometric configurations, enabling a more comprehensive characterisation of small molecules. In particular, the inclusion of a 3D equivariant neural branch allows the model to explicitly capture spatial and stereochemical features closely associated with bioactivity. Benchmark experiments on a curated public dataset show that MoActiPred outperforms a range of baseline methods, achieving the highest accuracy, MCC, and F1 score while maintaining competitive average precision.

Overall architecture of MoActiPred integrating 2D graph features, molecular descriptors, and 3D equivariant molecular representations

To further assess its practical utility, we benchmarked MoActiPred on a series of anti-influenza candidates synthesised in our laboratory. Influenza is a highly transmissible acute respiratory disease responsible for seasonal epidemics and occasional pandemics, causing up to an estimated 650,000 deaths annually [9,10]. Among the three human-infecting types (A, B, and C) [11], influenza A is most strongly associated with severe disease and global outbreaks, with multiple HA (18) and NA (11) subtypes implicated in historic pandemics such as the 1918 H1N1 “Spanish flu” and the 1968 H3N2 “Hong Kong flu” [12,13].

Current prevention and treatment strategies rely on vaccines and small-molecule antivirals. Vaccines are constrained by the need to predict circulating strains [14], whereas neuraminidase （NA）-targeted antivirals can shorten illness and reduce complications [15]. The continued emergence of resistant and novel strains underscores the need for new influenza antivirals, making accurate bioactivity prediction especially valuable in guiding anti-influenza drug discovery.

In this study, we synthesised a series of neuraminidase inhibitors (NAIs) to further evaluate our AI models [16]. To date, several NAIs have been approved for clinical use (Fig.2) [17], including oseltamivir phosphate (i, the ethyl ester prodrug of oseltamivir carboxylate, OC) [18], zanamivir (ii) [19], laninamivir (iii) [20], and peramivir (iv) [21].

Chemical structures of clinically marketed NA inhibitor

In 2006, Russell et al. reported that the 150-loop (residues 147–152) of NAs from the N1 and N4 subtypes adopts an open conformation, creating a 150-cavity adjacent to the active site [22]. Further studies also demonstrated that the 150-loop could be locked open by unsaturated C-3 modified N-acetylneuraminic acid inhibitors that successfully block influenza virus infection [23]. Subsequent studies showed that the 150-cavity in N2 NAs can also open upon binding of OC to the active site [24]. Structural analyses of OC–NA complexes revealed that the C-5-NH₂ group of OC lies in close proximity to the 150-cavity, suggesting this moiety as a suitable handle for introducing 150-cavity-binding substituents. Accordingly, numerous OC derivatives modified at the C-5-NH₂ position have been synthesised, exemplified by compounds v–viii (Fig.3) [25,26,27,28,29,30].

Representative OC derivatives modified at the C-5-NH₂ position

Our previous work identified a series of heterocycle-bearing secondary amine derivatives of OC, including compounds vi and vii (Fig.3), and showed that a substituted furan ring is a favourable motif for occupying the 150-cavity. Building on this, we selected compound vi as the scaffold for systematic derivative design, synthesis, and biological evaluation.

To further assess its practical utility, MoActiPred was applied to 26 newly-designed oseltamivir derivatives targeting NA. Of the 7 compounds predicted to be active, 6 were experimentally confirmed to exhibit high activity. Across all 26 derivatives, MoActiPred achieved an accuracy of 92.3% and correctly identified 18 of 19 experimentally inactive compounds. These results indicate that MoActiPred offers a robust and practically useful framework for screening and prioritising influenza antiviral candidates.

We developed MoActiPred, a predictive model that integrates 2D and 3D molecular structure with physicochemical descriptors (Fig.1). To better capture spatial information, we incorporated SEGNN, a 3D equivariant neural network, allowing the model to explicitly encode molecular geometry. As outlined in Fig.1, MoActiPred combines complementary information from molecular graphs and handcrafted descriptors to obtain a comprehensive representation of each compound.

For the 2D molecular graph branch, atom and bond features are embedded and passed through multiple relational graph attention layers to learn local chemical environments and topological dependencies. In parallel, global structural descriptors are normalised and fed into a separate module, supplying physicochemical information that may not be fully captured by the graph alone. The molecular graph is also processed by an SEGNN module to extract geometry-aware features and higher-level substructure patterns. The 2D graph branch and the SEGNN branch encode different molecular information. The 2D graph branch operates on atom-bond connectivity and learns topology-dependent local chemical environments, whereas the SEGNN branch operates on 3D conformer geometry and uses E (3)-equivariant message passing to encode spatial relationships. Thus, SEGNN-derived features are not a duplicate of the 2D graph features but a complementary geometric representation. Finally, graph-based features, descriptor features, and SEGNN-derived features are fused via fully connected layers, followed by pooling and a prediction head. By jointly modelling fine-grained atomic interactions, 3D structural patterns, and global molecular properties, MoActiPred yields robust, expressive representations for bioactivity prediction.

In this study, we curated an NA inhibition dataset by collecting bioactivity data from ChEMBL (Fig.4A) [31]. The final dataset contains 1245 molecules with annotated IC50values. Compounds with IC50< 20 nM were labeled as active, and those with IC50≥ 20 nM were labeled as inactive. The resulting curated dataset contained 204 active and 1041 inactive compounds.

During dataset curation, we found that stereochemical annotations strongly affected structure de-duplication. Because stereoisomers are encoded by different SMILES strings, molecules with distinct configurations can appear as separate entries. While stereoisomers may indeed have different biological activities, this only adds value if the reported activity can be unambiguously assigned to the correct stereochemical form.

In practice, we identified cases in ChEMBL where this assignment was ambiguous. For instance (Fig.4B), CHEMBL163966 is linked to multiple compounds reported in the literature [32], including 4ar and 4at, which differ in the configuration of the pyrrolidine moiety. Compound 4ar is the SR (cis) isomer, whereas 4at is the SS (trans) isomer, and they exhibit markedly different activities against influenza A, with IC50values of 5 nM and 110 nM, respectively. Aggregating such stereochemical variants under a single structural record can introduce bias into the dataset and compromise the reliability of activity labels.

A seemingly straightforward alternative for duplicate identification is to rely on molecular similarity. However, we found that similarity-based approaches can also introduce ambiguity, particularly when Morgan fingerprints are computed with small radii (e.g., 2 or 3). Under these settings, some structurally distinct molecule pairs may nevertheless be regarded as effectively identical.

For example (Fig.4C), CHEMBL4473618 and CHEMBL4425127 [33] share related core scaffolds but differ substantially in linker length. Despite these clear structural differences and their distinct SMILES representations, they are treated as the same when similarity is assessed using Morgan fingerprints with radii below 9. Only when the radius is increased to 9 do the two molecules become distinguishable. This observation indicates that similarity-based de-duplication with small-radius fingerprints may fail to capture important structural differences, especially those arising from extended substructures such as linkers.

To mitigate this source of inconsistency, we adopted a 2D structure-based de-duplication strategy that ignores stereochemical distinctions during duplicate removal and represents molecules using canonical SMILES. This procedure enhances representational consistency at the dataset level, while allowing potential activity differences arising from stereochemistry to be examined at a later stage. Consequently, the curated dataset should be understood as reflecting 2D structure-level de-duplication, rather than a stereochemistry-preserving definition of molecular identity.

We evaluated MoActiPred on the curated test set and compared its performance with a range of baseline methods. To examine the contribution of the 3D equivariant branch, we also included MoActiPred_2D, a variant that omits the 3D equivariant representation. The main results are summarised in Table1, and the complete metrics, including sensitivity and specificity, are reported in Supplementary Table S1.

Traditional machine-learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM) achieved relatively high AUC values, indicating reasonable ability to rank positive samples ahead of negatives. However, their performance on threshold-dependent metrics such as accuracy, MCC, and F1 score was less competitive, suggesting limited suitability for direct classification. ChemBERTa yielded the lowest false discovery rate, reflecting high precision among predicted positives, but its sensitivity was only 0.400, indicating that a substantial fraction of true positives was missed.

In contrast, MoActiPred achieved the highest accuracy on the test set and delivered the best overall performance on comprehensive classification metrics, including MCC and F1 score. Although MoActiPred_2D obtained the best average precision, MoActiPred showed comparable AP while offering a more balanced and consistently superior performance across evaluation metrics. Collectively, these results highlight the advantages of MoActiPred and support the added value of incorporating 3D equivariant molecular representations. The MCC values of zero for MolCLR and SEGNN reflected their threshold-dependent behaviour on the imbalanced held-out test set rather than an expectation that all graph-based models should behave similarly. As shown in Supplementary Table S1, both models assigned no test-set compounds to the active class under the selected classification threshold, yielding zero sensitivity, perfect specificity, and consequently MCC = 0. MoActiPred differed from these graph-only baselines by fusing 2D topology, global descriptors, and 3D equivariant geometry before classification, which improved the sensitivity/specificity balance and threshold-dependent metrics such as MCC and F1.

To evaluate MoActiPred in a real-world setting beyond the curated ChEMBL dataset, we designed and synthesised three subseries of N-substituted furans derived from oseltamivir. These subseries incorporate diverse heterocycles directly connected to the furan ring (Figure.5and6), as well as aliphatic or aromatic groups attached to the furan moiety via amide or ether linkages (5a–i, 10a–h, and 15a–i). The derivatives feature 0–2-atom linkers extending the C-5–NH₂ furan substitution to generate more drug-like structures with potential for further optimisation and development. The newly designed compounds were subsequently evaluated in bioactivity prediction by MoActiPred and other baseline models, enzymatic neuraminidase inhibition assays and antiviral assays to determine their biological activity.

Given the strong predictive performance of MoActiPred on the curated dataset, we next applied the model to evaluate the activity of 26 newly designed oseltamivir derivatives against NA. As shown in Table2, MoActiPred predicted 7 compounds to be active (IC50< 20 nM) and 19 to be inactive. These compounds were then tested in an in vitro NA inhibition assay using MUNANA as the substrate, with NA from A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2) and OC as the reference inhibitor.

In the first series of OC derivatives (5a–i), bearing heterocycles directly attached to the furan ring, all compounds exhibited mild to strong NA inhibitory activity with IC50values below 40 nM, except 5c, which contains a pyrazole ring. When the substitution on the pyrazole moiety was shifted from 5- to 4-position (compounds 5e and 5f), the inhibitory activity increased markedly, with IC₅₀ values of 10.24 and 6.49 nM, respectively. These results suggest that the pyrazole ring participates in binding and that the additional methyl group at the 1-Nposition in 5f further enhances activity. Electron-donating heteroaryl rings (5a, 5b) conferred higher inhibitory activity than electron-withdrawing heteroarenes (5 g, 5 h). Among them, 5b, bearing a 1H-pyrrol-2-yl group, was the most potent (IC50= 4.31 nM).

For the amide-linked series 10a-h, most compounds showed moderate inhibitory activity, with IC₅₀ values in the range of 19 nM to 246 nM. Compound 10a, incorporating anN, N-diethylamino group, was the most active (IC50= 19.64 nM). Overall, IC₅₀ values increased with the size of the substituents (10b < 10c < 10d and 10f), indicating that smaller substituents are favored when the carbonyl linker is attached to the C-5–NH2furan.

In the ether/thioether-linked series 15a–i, which contain an oxomethylene linker and aryl or heteroaryl rings, compounds 15a-g inhibited NA with IC₅₀ values of 20 nM to 75 nM. Electron-donating substituents at the para-position of the phenyl ring were preferred (IC50: 15a < 15b ≈ 15c), and a meta-substituent further improved activity (IC50: 15d < 15c). By contrast, 15e, bearing 3, 4-diF substituents, was less active than 15b (4–F), likely due to the stronger electron-withdrawing effect of fluorine, which appears unfavourable for NA inhibition. Replacement of the ether linker with a thioether and introduction of 3, 4-diCl groups, with weaker electron-withdrawing character, yielded 15 h as the most potent member of this series (IC50= 12.37 nM).

Among the 26 derivatives, 6 of the 7 compounds predicted by MoActiPred to be active indeed showed high activity (IC50< 20 nM), whereas 18 of the 19 compounds predicted to be inactive exhibited IC50> 20 nM. This corresponds to a prediction success rate of 92.3%, underscoring the effectiveness of MoActiPred in prioritising active oseltamivir derivatives.

In summary, most of our designed compounds exhibited inhibitory activity against A/Wisconsin/67/2005 (H3N2) NA. In particular, compounds 5b and 5f, bearing 1H-pyrrol-2-yl and 1, 3, 5-trimethyl-1H-pyrazol-4-yl substituents, respectively, showed the lowest IC50values. The results indicate that the linker length at the C-5–NH₂ furan does not correlate linearly with bioactivity; instead, precise selection of substituents tailored to each linker length is required to achieve optimal inhibition. Notably, MoActiPred prospectively identified the majority of highly active derivatives with a 92.3% success rate, underscoring the power of AI-guided design in efficiently prioritising potent NA inhibitors. Such accurate AI-based bioactivity prediction can substantially support medicinal chemists in designing new drugs and reduce both time and synthetic effort.

We next evaluated MoActiPred and the baseline models on the 26 newly synthesised oseltamivir derivatives with experimentally measured IC₅₀ values. This experimental set contained 7 active and 19 inactive compounds using the same activity threshold as the public benchmark. MoActiPred correctly classified 24 of the 26 compounds, including 6 of 7 active compounds and 18 of 19 inactive compounds. The resulting accuracy was 0.923, with a Wilson 95% confidence interval of 0.759–0.979. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals were 0.469–1.000 for MCC, 0.729–1.000 for macro F1, 0.882–1.000 for AUC, and 0.773–1.000 for AP.

Compared with the baseline models on the same 26 experimental compounds, MoActiPred achieved the highest accuracy, MCC, macro F1, positive-class F1, AUC, and AP (Table3). MoActiPred_2D was the closest comparator, correctly classifying 23 of 26 compounds and achieving the same AUC to three decimal places. The full MoActiPred model showed a modest numerical improvement over MoActiPred_2D in accuracy (0.923 vs 0.885), MCC (0.805 vs 0.697), macro F1 (0.902 vs 0.846), and AP (0.948 vs 0.937). To further assess whether these differences were robust to the small experimental sample size, we performed paired non-parametric bootstrap comparisons between MoActiPred and each comparator using 2,000 resamples of the 26 experimental compounds (Table S6). The bootstrap analysis showed consistently positive performance differences for MoActiPred across most comparators. In particular, compared with XGBoost, SVM, ChemBERTa, PolyBERT, and MolCLR, the 95% confidence intervals for MCC, macro F1, AUC, and AP remained above zero, supporting a more balanced and reliable classification behaviour. Exact McNemar tests also indicated stronger paired binary correctness for MoActiPred than XGBoost, SVM, ChemBERTa, and PolyBERT. By contrast, the differences between MoActiPred and MoActiPred_2D were small and their bootstrap confidence intervals included zero, indicating that the full model provided a modest numerical improvement but not a statistically supported advantage in this limited 26-compound validation set.

MoActiPred misclassified two compounds. Compound 5 g was a false positive with an IC50of 32.15 nM, whereas compound 10a was a false negative with an IC50of 19.64 nM. Both compounds were close to the activity-label boundary, suggesting that the observed errors occurred near the experimental decision threshold. Taken together, the experimental validation supports the use of MoActiPred for prioritising focused oseltamivir-derived analogues, while the sample size and chemical scope of the validation set limit broader claims of external generalisation.

We further assessed whether the experimental derivatives overlapped with the model-training molecules at the scaffold level. None shared an identical Bemis-Murcko scaffold with the training molecules under the implemented scaffold definition. Their nearest-neighbour ECFP6/Tanimoto similarities to the training set were moderate, with a median of 0.599 and a range of 0.537–0.766. These results indicate that the experimental molecules were not scaffold duplicates of the training compounds and showed relatively low nearest-neighbour similarity to the final model-training set. Thus, the prospective validation reflects focused analogue prioritisation in a chemically related but non-duplicated oseltamivir-derivative space, rather than simple recall of training-set structures.

To provide a more stringent assessment, we performed an additional single scaffold-disjoint evaluation. The curated dataset was divided at the scaffold-group level, such that no Bemis-Murcko scaffold appeared in both the training and test sets. This scaffold-based split contained 1120 training molecules, including 181 active and 939 inactive compounds, and 125 held-out test molecules, including 23 active and 102 inactive compounds. The training set contained 218 scaffold groups, whereas the test set contained 125 scaffold groups. No scaffold was shared between the two sets, and each held-out test molecule represented a distinct scaffold group.

Under this scaffold-disjoint evaluation, MoActiPred retained strong predictive performance and achieved the highest AP, accuracy, MCC, and F1 score among the compared models (Supplementary Table S4). MoActiPred correctly classified 116 of 125 held-out molecules, including 18 of 23 active compounds and 98 of 102 inactive compounds. This corresponded to an AP of 0.808, sensitivity of 0.783, specificity of 0.961, accuracy of 0.928, MCC of 0.756, and F1 score of 0.878. Compared with the graph-only variant MoActiPred_2D, the full model showed higher AP (0.808 vs 0.764), specificity (0.961 vs 0.931), accuracy (0.928 vs 0.912), MCC (0.756 vs 0.723), and F1 score (0.878 vs 0.860), although MoActiPred_2D showed slightly higher sensitivity (0.826 vs 0.783).

No single model dominated all scaffold-split metrics. SVM achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.928), and MoActiPred_2D achieved the highest mean sensitivity/specificity (0.879). However, SVM detected fewer active compounds at the selected classification threshold, while ChemFM's perfect specificity reflected very low sensitivity rather than balanced classification. Overall, the scaffold-disjoint experiment indicates that MoActiPred did not rely solely on scaffold overlap in the random split and retained useful threshold-dependent predictive performance for held-out scaffold classes within the curated neuraminidase inhibitor dataset.

To examine whether comparative model performance transferred beyond the ChEMBL-derived benchmark and the focused synthesised series, we evaluated all models on the public neuraminidase-inhibitor dataset reported by Zhang et al. [34].

On this external benchmark, model performance varied across metrics, indicating different ranking and classification trade-offs (Supplementary Table S9). Random Forest achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.969) and accuracy (0.923), SVM achieved the highest AP (0.850), highest specificity (0.996), and lowest FDR (0.091), and XGBoost achieved the highest sensitivity (0.971), mean sensitivity/specificity (0.915), and MCC (0.614). MoActiPred nevertheless showed competitive and balanced external performance, achieving the highest macro F1 (0.801), the second-highest MCC (0.604), and the third-highest AP (0.713), sensitivity (0.706), and mean sensitivity/specificity (0.824). It correctly classified 24 of 34 active compounds and 260 of 276 inactive compounds, corresponding to an accuracy of 0.916 and specificity of 0.942.

Compared with MoActiPred_2D, the full multimodal model showed higher AP (0.713 vs 0.570), specificity (0.942 vs 0.902), accuracy (0.916 vs 0.894), MCC (0.604 vs 0.594), and macro F1 (0.801 vs 0.784), together with a lower FDR (0.400 vs 0.491). MoActiPred_2D showed higher ROC-AUC (0.903 vs 0.898), sensitivity (0.824 vs 0.706), and mean sensitivity/specificity (0.863 vs 0.824). These results suggest that the 3D branch improved precision-oriented and overall classification metrics on this external set, although with some reduction in sensitivity. Thus, the full model provided a more conservative but more precise classification profile rather than a uniform gain across all individual metrics.

Although no exact molecule was shared with the training data, the external benchmark was not scaffold-disjoint. The 310 compounds comprised 79 Bemis–Murcko scaffolds, of which 25 (31.6%) were also present in the training set. These shared scaffolds accounted for 217 external compounds (70.0%; 32 active and 185 inactive), whereas the remaining 93 compounds occupied 54 previously unseen scaffolds and included only two active molecules.

Six shared-scaffold groups contained both activity labels, and 66 of the 217 shared-scaffold external compounds had at least one oppositely labelled compound with the same scaffold in the curated dataset. Thus, scaffold identity alone was insufficient to determine activity. Substituent-dependent changes in steric fit, electrostatics, hydrogen bonding, protonation state, conformational preference, and desolvation may alter activity even when the core scaffold is retained. The external benchmark therefore combines two complementary challenges: discriminating molecule-disjoint compounds that share a core scaffold and extrapolating to previously unseen scaffolds.

Because the scaffold-unseen subset contained only two active compounds, the external results should not be interpreted as robust evidence of sensitivity to novel active scaffolds. Moreover, the activity labels were aggregated from published records spanning different assay conditions and NA subtypes; therefore, within-scaffold label discordance may reflect both genuine substituent-dependent SAR and inter-assay heterogeneity. Accordingly, the external benchmark supports transfer within neuraminidase-inhibitor chemical space, but does not by itself establish broad out-of-distribution generalisation.

To summarise performance across the three complementary evaluation settings, we calculated an unweighted arithmetic mean for each metric and model using the point estimates reported for the public ChEMBL-derived test set (Table1), the prospective 26-compound experimental set (Table3), and the 310-compound external benchmark (Supplementary Table S9). Each evaluation setting contributed equally to the mean, irrespective of sample size, so that the summary reflected cross-setting consistency rather than being dominated by the largest dataset.

In this cross-benchmark summary, MoActiPred achieved the strongest mean performance for every summarised metric (Table4). It obtained a mean AUC of 0.943, AP of 0.844, mean sensitivity/specificity of 0.868, accuracy of 0.930, MCC of 0.735, and macro F1 of 0.867, together with the lowest mean FDR of 0.223. MoActiPred_2D ranked second across the same averaged measures, followed most consistently by Random Forest. Relative to MoActiPred_2D, the full multimodal model increased mean AUC by 0.015, AP by 0.048, mean sensitivity/specificity by 0.010, accuracy by 0.025, MCC by 0.051, and macro F1 by 0.030, while reducing mean FDR by 0.063.

These results indicate that, although individual baseline models led selected metrics on the external benchmark, MoActiPred provided the most consistent overall performance when the internal benchmark, prospective experimental validation, and external dataset were considered together. The improvement over MoActiPred_2D in the cross-benchmark analysis further supports the contribution of the 3D geometric branch to overall model robustness, particularly for AP, MCC, macro F1, and FDR.

Nevertheless, these averages should be interpreted cautiously. They are descriptive, unweighted summaries of heterogeneous datasets with different sample sizes, class distributions, assay origins, and chemical compositions. They should therefore not be interpreted as pooled performance estimates, formal significance tests, or evidence of universal superiority. Rather, Table4supports the conclusion that MoActiPred maintained the most balanced and consistent performance across the complementary evaluation settings considered in this study.

Compounds 5b and 5f were also selected for determination of IC₅₀ values against purified NAs from pandemic A/H1N1 (A/California/04/2009) and A/H3N2 (A/Babol/36/2005), as well as A/H5N1 (A/Anhui/01/2005), with zanamivir used as the drug control. As shown in Table5, both 5b and 5f exhibited good inhibitory activity against H1N1 and H3N2 NAs; however, their effectiveness was reduced against H5N1 NA.

Inhibitory activities of compounds 5b and 5f were further evaluated against a panel of influenza virus strains using an MDCK.2 cell-based ELISA assay: H3N2 A/Perth/16/2009, H1N1 A/Brisbane/59/2007, H1N1 A/Hong Kong/1870/2008, A/Hiroshima/48/2008, A/Auckland/526/2009, and H1N1 A/California/04/2009. Oseltamivir and zanamivir were included as reference drugs. As shown in Fig. 6A, both 5b and 5f proved to be potent inhibitors of A/H3N2 virus, with geometric mean EC₅₀ values of 0.72 nM and 3.04 nM, respectively, comparable to those of oseltamivir (1.04 nM) and zanamivir (7.12 nM). This indicates that the strong neuraminidase inhibition of these oseltamivir derivatives against A/H3N2 NA effectively translates into antiviral activity in infected cells.

Compounds 5b and 5f showed only mild inhibition of A/Brisbane/59/2007 (EC₅₀ = 865.5 nM and 2298 nM, respectively; Fig. 6B) and A/Hong Kong/1870/2008 (EC₅₀ = 1910 nM and 2067 nM, respectively; Fig 6C), and did not exhibit significant activity against A/Hiroshima/48/2008, A/Auckland/526/2009, or A/California/04/2009 (EC₅₀ > 10 μM). Cytotoxicity assessment in MDCK.2 cells using alamarBlue revealed no detectable toxicity for either compound (CC₅₀ > 100 μM). Overall, these results demonstrate that 5b and 5f possess specific antiviral activity predominantly against influenza H3N2 strains.

Typically, the 150-loop of N1, which belongs to group-1 NAs, adopts an open conformation, whereas that of N2, a group-2 NA, is closed. Although early structural studies suggested that 09N1 does not possess a 150-cavity [35], more recent work has shown that the 150-loop of N1 subtypes is highly mobile and can adopt a more open conformation in solution than is evident in crystal structures [36].

To further elucidate how the synthesised compounds interact with those NAs that showed experimental inhibition, the most promising ligand, 5b, was subjected to computational docking into N1 (H5N1), 09N1 (H1N1), and N2 (H3N2) using Maestro. Initial IFD-MD results indicated that compound 5b engages with NA subtypes N1, 09N1, and N2 with interaction energies of − 1.3, 8.3, and 8.2 kcal/mol, respectively.

As shown in Fig.7A–C, the oseltamivir core of compound 5b is positioned within the active site of each NA, while itsN-substituent occupies a similar region adjacent to the catalytic pocket. In 09N1 and N2 (Fig.7B and 7C), the 150-loop adopts an open conformation, which may be induced by binding of 5b. As illustrated in Fig.7D–F, the side chain of 5b extends into the opened, canonical 150-cavity through the open 150-loop, with its furan ring forming a hydrogen bond with Asp151 and engaging in π-cation interactions with Arg118 or Arg156. These docking models are consistent with the experimental observation that 5b inhibits NAs from all tested influenza strains.

In particular, 5b exhibited approximately fivefold stronger inhibitory activity against the NAs of 09N1 and N2 compared with N1. To further elucidate the binding modes of 5b with these NAs, we carried out molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on the respective protein–ligand complexes, followed by MM-GBSA binding free energy calculations. The RMSD plots for each NA-5b complex (Supplementary Fig. S1) indicated that all systems reached equilibrium. Trajectories from the final 5 ns of each simulation (10,000 snapshots) were then used for binding free energy estimation (Supplementary Fig. S1), and the MM-GBSA results are summarised in the Supplementary Table S10. Overall, 5b displayed binding free energies of − 58.28, − 59.06, and − 38.14 kcal/mol with N1, 09N1, and N2, respectively, indicating that 5b binds more strongly to 09N1 than to N1, consistent with its superior inhibitory activity.

To reconcile the apparent difference between the MM-GBSA results and the experimental data for N2, we conducted a WaterMap analysis to gain deeper insight into the thermodynamic properties of the hydration layer in the active site. As shown in Fig.7I, we identified several high-energy water sites within the N2 binding pocket. The binding pose of 5b in N2 allows it to effectively displace these unfavourable water molecules. The release of such high-energy waters into the bulk solvent generates a substantial solvophobic driving force, which enhances the overall binding affinity and complements the relatively lower direct protein–ligand interaction energy estimated by MM-GBSA.

In contrast, the water molecules in the binding pockets of N1 and 09N1 are more stable (Fig.7G–H), so water displacement contributes less strongly to binding in these systems. Altogether, these findings indicate that the interaction between 5b and N2 is predominantly solvation-driven, whereas its binding to N1 and 09N1 is more enthalpy-driven through direct contacts. This dual contribution of favourable solvation and direct interactions provides a coherent explanation for the particularly strong inhibitory activity of compound 5b against the influenza H3N2 strain.

We curated NA-targeting activity data (IC₅₀ values) for influenza virus from the ChEMBL database. By filtering entries with the ‘Target Name’ specified as Neuraminidase, we obtained 3,489 records. Because multiple influenza virus strains exist, some molecules appeared with more than one activity record. To standardise these data, we first binarised IC₅₀ values using a 20 nM threshold: molecules with IC₅₀ < 20 nM were labelled as “1” (active against neuraminidase), and those with IC₅₀ ≥ 20 nM as “0” (inactive).

We then consolidated multiple records corresponding to the same molecule by assigning the most positive label observed. This was accomplished by removing stereochemical information and using canonical SMILES as unique identifiers. We note that Morgan fingerprint-based similarity was not always reliable for duplicate detection in certain cases, whereas canonical SMILES provided a more robust basis for de-duplication (further discussed in the Discussion section). Consequently, if any record associated with a molecule was labelled “1,” the molecule was classified as active; otherwise, it was classified as inactive.

After this processing, we obtained a curated dataset of 1,245 labelled molecules, comprising 1,041 inactive and 204 active compounds. For the original public benchmark, the dataset was randomly divided into a training set of 1,182 molecules, including 194 active and 988 inactive compounds, and a test set of 63 molecules, including 10 active and 53 inactive compounds.

To evaluate the possible influence of scaffold overlap, we additionally constructed a single scaffold-disjoint split using Bemis-Murcko scaffold grouping. In this split, scaffold groups rather than individual molecules were assigned to the training or test set, and a scaffold group was not allowed to appear in both sets. The scaffold-based training set contained 1,120 molecules, including 181 active and 939 inactive compounds, whereas the scaffold-based test set contained 125 molecules, including 23 active and 102 inactive compounds. The training and test sets contained 218 and 125 scaffold groups, respectively, with no scaffold overlap between them.

In MoActiPred, each molecule is represented as a graph, where heavy atoms serve as nodes and bonds as edges. To increase the expressiveness of this molecular graph, we augmented both nodes and edges with additional descriptors beyond basic atom and bond types. The full set of features is summarised in Table6. These enriched node and edge features provide a more detailed characterisation of molecular structure, enabling the model to better capture complex chemical properties and intermolecular interactions.

The ring-type feature set comprises a diverse collection of ring structures extracted from the dataset. For each molecule, ring fragments are identified and converted into canonical SMILES strings, and duplicate structures are removed to generate a non-redundant library of ring motifs.

The 2D graph branch operates on atom-bond connectivity and learns topology-dependent local chemical environments. In contrast, the SEGNN branch operates on 3D conformer geometry, interatomic displacement vectors, and E (3)-equivariant message passing, thereby capturing spatial information that is not encoded by the 2D graph alone. We leveraged the E (3)-equivariant molecular representation provided by SEGNN. For each molecule, a 3D conformation was first generated using the ETKDGv3 method in RDKit, and a 2 Å radius graph was then constructed based on these coordinates. In this radius graph, nodes correspond to heavy atoms, and an edge is created between any pair of atoms separated by a distance of at most 2 Å.

To construct the geometric features required by SEGNN, edge attributes were derived from the relative spatial relationships between connected atoms. For each edge, we computed the relative position vector from the 3D coordinates of the two atoms and calculated the squared interatomic distance as an additional scalar descriptor. Using these relative position vectors, spherical harmonics were applied to obtain rotation-equivariant edge features under the specified irreducible representations, thereby encoding angular information about the local geometry. Node attributes were then computed by aggregating the edge attributes of all incoming edges using a mean reduction operation.

The descriptor set used in our model was designed to capture multiple complementary aspects of molecular structure and physicochemical behaviour.

First, EState descriptors (MaxAbsEStateIndex, MaxEStateIndex, MinAbsEStateIndex, and MinEStateIndex) characterise the electronic environment of atoms by combining intrinsic electronic states with their topological context.

Second, several VSA-based descriptors were included to describe how molecular surface area is distributed across different physicochemical property ranges. Specifically, SlogP_VSA descriptors reflect the partitioning of van der Waals surface area according to atomic contributions to lipophilicity, PEOE_VSA descriptors quantify the surface area associated with different partial charge intervals, and SMR_VSA descriptors capture surface area distributions related to molar refractivity and polarizability.

In addition, general structural descriptors such as MolWt, LabuteASA, NumRotatableBonds, and NumAromaticHeterocycles were incorporated to represent molecular weight, accessible surface area, conformational flexibility, and aromatic heterocycle content, respectively.

To further characterise molecular shape and connectivity, we included Kier shape indices (Kappa1, Kappa2, and Kappa3) and connectivity indices (Chi0, Chi0n, Chi0v, Chi1, Chi1n, and Chi1v), which together provide information on molecular branching, topological structure, and atomic valence patterns.

Model optimisation was performed using the AdamW optimiser with a learning rate of 1e-4 and a weight decay of 1e-4. The model was trained with the cross-entropy loss function for 500 epochs, and the final trained model was used for all reported held-out test, scaffold-split, and experimental-validation predictions.

We benchmarked MoActiPred against representative baseline methods from three categories.

First, traditional machine learning models including SVM, Random Forest, and XGBoost were evaluated using molecular fingerprints as input features. For each molecule, we generated 2048-bit ECFP fingerprints with a radius of 3 and concatenated them with MACCS keys, yielding a 2215-dimensional feature vector.

Second, language-based models, including ChemBERTa, ChemFM, and PolyBERT, were fine-tuned using molecular SMILES strings as input to assess the performance of large-scale pre-trained chemical language models.

Third, graph-based models, including MolCLR and SEGNN, were evaluated using molecular graph representations constructed according to the specific input requirements of each method.

To comprehensively assess classification performance, we employed a diverse set of evaluation metrics. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was used to quantify the overall discriminative ability between active and inactive compounds across all thresholds, while Average Precision (AP) emphasised performance on the positive (active) class. Sensitivity and specificity measured the proportions of correctly identified active and inactive molecules, respectively, and their average (Mean_sen_spe) provided a balanced view of performance across both classes.

We further used the false discovery rate (FDR) to quantify the proportion of false positives among all predicted actives, which is particularly relevant in virtual screening scenarios where reducing unnecessary experimental validation is crucial. Overall predictive correctness was summarised by accuracy, whereas the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 score offered more stringent and balanced assessments by jointly accounting for true and false predictions across both classes. Collectively, these metrics provide a robust, multi-faceted evaluation of model performance in terms of discrimination, class-wise behaviour, reliability, and overall classification balance.

To assess the stability of the classical machine-learning baselines, Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM were first evaluated by five-fold stratified cross-validation on the model-development training partition (Table S8). The same five-fold protocol was also applied within the scaffold-split training partition as an internal stability check before scaffold-disjoint held-out testing. In each fold, the model was trained on four folds and evaluated on the remaining fold. Cross-validation was used to verify the effectiveness of the fixed baseline configurations. After cross-validation, each final baseline model was trained on the complete corresponding training partition and evaluated on the held-out public test set, scaffold-split test set, and experimental validation set as appropriate. The input representations, preprocessing steps, fixed hyperparameters, and validation policy for Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM are summarised in Supplementary Table S7. Language- and graph-based baselines were evaluated using their corresponding implemented model configurations to provide a reproducible comparison.

For the scaffold-based evaluation, all models were trained and evaluated using the same scaffold-disjoint partition. Active and inactive labels followed the same IC₅₀ threshold definition used in the original benchmark. Model performance was summarised using ROC-AUC, AP, sensitivity, specificity, mean sensitivity/specificity, FDR, accuracy, MCC, and F1 score. ROC-AUC and AP were used to assess ranking performance, whereas the remaining metrics were used to assess threshold-dependent classification behaviour.

For the 26-compound experimental validation set, binary predictions were used to compute sensitivity, specificity, precision, FDR, negative predictive value, accuracy, MCC, macro F1, and positive-class F1. Prediction scores were used to compute ROC-AUC and AP. Uncertainty in the experimental validation metrics was assessed by non-parametric bootstrap resampling of the 26 compounds with replacement using 2000 resamples (Table S5). Accuracy was additionally reported with a Wilson binomial 95% confidence interval. For paired model comparisons on the experimental dataset, differences in accuracy, MCC, macro F1, AUC, and AP were estimated as MoActiPred minus each comparator. Confidence intervals were obtained by paired non-parametric bootstrap resampling of the 26 compounds with replacement using 2000 resamples. Exact McNemar tests were used to compare paired binary correctness.

To assess the applicability domain of the experimental compounds, we compared the 26 synthesised derivatives with the final model-training set. Bemis-Murcko scaffolds were computed from canonical SMILES using RDKit, and exact scaffold overlap between the experimental and training molecules was recorded. We also computed 2048-bit Morgan fingerprints with radius 3 (ECFP6) for both training and experimental molecules. For each experimental molecule, the maximum Tanimoto similarity to any training-set molecule was recorded. This analysis was used to determine whether the experimental compounds were exact scaffold duplicates of training molecules or chemically related but non-identical analogue cases.

To evaluate model generalisation to unseen chemotypes, compounds were grouped by Bemis-Murcko scaffold using canonical SMILES. Scaffold groups, rather than individual molecules, were assigned to the training or test set, and a scaffold group was not allowed to appear in both sets. A single scaffold-disjoint partition was used for the scaffold split experiment. The resulting scaffold split contained 1120 training molecules and 125 test molecules. The training set contained 181 active and 939 inactive compounds across 218 scaffold groups, whereas the test set contained 23 active and 102 inactive compounds across 125 scaffold groups. Train/test scaffold overlap was zero in the final split. The same evaluation protocol was used as in the original benchmark.

The external benchmark was derived from the public influenza neuraminidase-inhibitor dataset reported by Zhang et al. [34]. Compounds identified as overlapping with the final MoActiPred training set were removed, multiple IC50 records corresponding to the same molecule were consolidated using the same record-resolution procedure as the main dataset, and binary activity labels were assigned using the study threshold of IC50< 20 nM. This process yielded 310 non-overlapping compounds, comprising 34 active and 276 inactive molecules. To characterise structural overlap beyond exact molecular identity, Bemis-Murcko scaffolds were generated from canonical non-isomeric SMILES using RDKit. Exact scaffold matches between the external compounds and the model-training set were recorded. Empty scaffolds generated for acyclic molecules were excluded from unique-scaffold counts.

Predictions from MoActiPred, MoActiPred_2D, and the eight baseline models were evaluated against the same external labels. Performance was summarised using ROC-AUC, AP, sensitivity, specificity, mean sensitivity/specificity, FDR, accuracy, MCC, and macro F1. ROC-AUC and AP were interpreted as ranking metrics, whereas the remaining measures described threshold-dependent classification behaviour. The external comparison was treated as a descriptive matched benchmark; pairwise statistical superiority was not inferred from point estimates alone.

For each model and each metric shared by the three test tables, we calculated the unweighted arithmetic mean of the reported point estimates from the public ChEMBL-derived test set (Table1), the prospective experimental set (Table3), and the external benchmark (Supplementary Table S9). AUC, AP, mean sensitivity/specificity, FDR, accuracy, MCC, and macro F1 were averaged separately; values were not pooled across compounds, and no single composite score was calculated across metrics. Each evaluation setting received equal weight regardless of sample size. These averages were used only as descriptive summaries of cross-setting consistency and were not treated as inferential comparisons.

The NA inhibitory assay was performed using the commercially available NA‐Fluor™ Influenza Neuraminidase Assay Kit as described previously [28].

For determination of inhibitory effect of compounds on purified neuraminidase activity, home-made reagents were utilised instead. In a black 384-well plate, purified neuraminidase was diluted in reaction buffer (50 mM NaOAc, 6 mM CaCl2, pH 5.5) by predetermined dilution factor. The neuraminidase dilution was subsequently used to serially dilute 1 mM compound stocks by a factor of 3.5, and the plate was incubated at room temperature for 20 min. In each well of the plate, 6 μL of compound dilution and 4 μL of 0.25 mM MUNANA solution were added in duplicate and mixed by centrifugation at 1000 ×gfor 20 s. The plate was then incubated at 37 °C and agitated at 1100 rpm. After 20 min, 50 μL of stop buffer (0.25 M glycine, pH 10.4) was added to each well. Fluorescence with excitation wavelength at 370 nm and emission wavelength at 450 nm was measured by Tecan Infinite M200 PRO plate reader. IC50values were determined by constructing a compound versus response curve with variable slope, four parameters using non-linear regression analysis from GraphPad Prism software (Version 10).

100 μl of MDCK.2 cells in culture media [DMEM supplemented with 5% FBS, 1% glutamine (2 mM), 1% non-essential amino acids, 1% sodium pyruvate, 1% Anti-Anti (Gibco)] were seeded in 96-well cell-binding plates at a cell density of 17,500 cells/well. Plates were then incubated overnight at 37 °C, 5% CO2. Cell supernatant was aspirated and 50 μL of influenza A virus diluted in infection media [DMEM supplemented with 1 μg/mL of TPCK trypsin, 1% glutamine (2 mM), 1% non-essential amino acids, 1% sodium pyruvate, 1% Anti-Anti (Gibco)] was added to infect MDCK.2 cells at a final virus concentration of 200 FFU/well. Plates were then incubated at 35 °C, 5% CO2for 1 h and gently tapped at 15-min intervals. Viral inoculum was aspirated and 100 µL of compound of desired concentrations were added to each well. Plates were then incubated at 35 °C, 5% CO2for about 24 h. On the next day, MDCK2 cells were fixed by adding 100 μL of 8% formaldehyde solution (37% formaldehyde diluted by PBS) to each well. Plates were incubated at room temperature for 20 min. All liquids in wells were then discarded and the plates washed with PBS. 50 μL of IGEPAL/H2O2solution (1% IGEPAL, 1% of 35% H2O2solution in PBS) was added to each well and the plates were incubated at 37 °C for 20 min. The solution was then discarded, and the plates washed with 0.02% PBS Tween 20 (PBST). 50 µL of mouse monoclonal anti-influenza A virus nucleoprotein (BioRad MCA400, clone AA5H, 0.5 µg/ml) and 50 µL of Goat polyclonal anti-mouse IgG-HRP (BioRad 170–6516, 1:5000 dilution) diluted in PBST with 5% skim milk were added to all wells in succession, with plates incubated at 37 °C for 45 min and washed with 0.02% PBST after each antibody addition. 50 μL TMB substrate (BD OptEIA TMB Substrate Reagent Set, with Substrate Reagent A and Substrate Reagent B mixed in 1:1) was added to each well, and plates were incubated at room temperature for 2–3 min. Reaction was then stopped by adding 25 μL of 1 M H2SO4and absorbance at 450 nm and 570 nm correction were recorded by Bio-Rad xMark Microplate Spectrophotometer. EC50values were determined by constructing a compound versus response curve with variable slope, four parameters using non-linear regression analysis from GraphPad Prism software (Version 10).

MDCK.2 cells were prepared and incubated overnight as advised in the cell-based ELISA method. On the next day, compounds were serially diluted threefold in culture media starting from 100 μM. 100 μL of the dilution series was added to each well after cell supernatant was aspirated. The plates were then incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2for 36–42 h. All liquids in wells were discarded and the plates washed with PBS. 75 μL of culture media containing 10% alamarBlue reagent was added into each well and the plates were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2for 2–4 h. IFD-MD of compound 5b into N1 (PDB: 2HU0), 09N1 (PDB: 4B7J) and N2 (PDB: 4GZP) was performed using Maestro (Schrödinger). The protein structures and 5b were prepared with the Protein Preparation Wizard and LigPrep, respectively, and the OPLS4 force field was applied to all atoms.

To capture mutual conformational adaptation between the proteins and5b, the Induced Fit Docking–Molecular Dynamics (IFD-MD) workflow was used. Final protein–ligand complexes were selected based on a combination of the IFD score, Glide GScore, and visual inspection of binding-mode stability during IFD-MD refinement. These optimised complexes were then used as starting structures for long-timescale MD simulations.

Each selected complex was solvated in an orthorhombic TIP3P water box with a 10 Å buffer and neutralised with 0.15 M NaCl. MD simulations were carried out using Desmond in the NPT ensemble (300 K, 1.01325 bar). After the default relaxation protocol, a 1000 ns (1 μs) production run was performed, and trajectories were saved every 100 ps for analysis. The final 100 ns of each trajectory were analysed with the Simulation Interaction Diagram (SID) tool to evaluate long-term stability and binding persistence, including RMSD, RMSF, and the time evolution of protein–ligand hydrogen bonds.

Binding free energies (ΔGbind) were estimated using the Prime MM-GBSA module. For each system, the final snapshot of the 1000 ns trajectory was extracted as a representative stable conformation. MM-GBSA calculations were performed with the OPLS4 force field and the VSGB continuum solvation model.

This work presents MoActiPred as a target-focused multimodal framework for neuraminidase-inhibitor prioritisation. By integrating 2D graph features, physicochemical descriptors, and 3D equivariant representations, the model achieved a strong overall balance of performance across the public and prospective evaluations. The model delivered high accuracy and MCC while maintaining balanced sensitivity and specificity, making it suitable for hit triage and library prioritisation. Performance was further supported by a matched external benchmark on 310 non-overlapping neuraminidase-inhibitor compounds derived from a published virtual-screening study. MoActiPred achieved the highest macro F1 (0.801) and second-highest MCC (0.604) among the compared models, supporting balanced transfer within the tested neuraminidase-inhibitor chemical space rather than broad target-independent generalisation. When the reported point estimates were averaged equally across the public, prospective, and external evaluations, MoActiPred also achieved the highest mean AUC (0.943), AP (0.844), mean sensitivity/specificity (0.868), accuracy (0.930), MCC (0.735), and macro F1 (0.867), together with the lowest mean FDR (0.223). These cross-benchmark averages summarise consistency across the three tested settings but do not replace dataset-specific analysis or formal statistical comparison.

Prospective validation on 26 novel C-5-aminoN-substituted furan oseltamivir derivatives confirmed the translational value of the model: MoActiPred correctly predicted the activity class of 24 compounds, enriching for potent inhibitors and minimising unnecessary syntheses and assays. Structure–activity relationship analysis revealed that both the nature of the heterocycle and linker architecture at the C-5-NH₂ furan moiety critically modulate NA inhibition, without a simple dependence on linker length. Among all analogues, 5b and 5f emerged as standout inhibitors with low-nanomolar IC₅₀ values against group-1 and group-2 NAs and sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar EC₅₀ values against H3N2 in cell culture, while maintaining low cytotoxicity. Compound 5b, in particular, surpassed oseltamivir and zanamivir against H3N2 in the cellular context, positioning it as a compelling lead candidate.

Computational modelling showed that 5b’s oseltamivir core anchors in the conserved active site, whereas itsN-substituent probes the 150- and 430-cavities, with distinct enthalpic and solvation-driven contributions across NA subtypes. These insights provide a mechanistic rationale for its subtype-selective potency and suggest clear directions for further optimisation, including tuning cavity interactions and improving activity against resistant variants such as H274Y. Overall, the combination of MoActiPred-guided design, targeted synthesis, and mechanistic modelling provides a practical framework for prioritising focused neuraminidase-inhibitor analogues and offers a model for future prospective validation in other target systems.

Several limitations should still be considered when interpreting the model performance. First, the prospective experimental validation set contained only 26 newly synthesised oseltamivir derivatives, so confidence intervals around the prospective performance estimates remain wide. Second, although the external validation set was independently sourced and filtered to remove training-set overlap, it was retrospectively curated from published neuraminidase-inhibitor records and remains within neuraminidase-inhibitor chemical space. Future work should continue to evaluate MoActiPred on broader non-overlapping chemotype collections and prospective external assay datasets.

title: The impact of reward scalarization and weight scheduling on optimization dynamics in multi-objective molecular design
author: Lucas Leuschner; Oscar Palomino-Hernandez
text:
Inverse molecular design imposes multiple property constraints, requiring them to be combined into a scalar reward for reinforcement-learning (RL) fine-tuning; a step that can be highly sensitive to the reward formulation. Here, we systematically analyze how scalarization choices and stabilization mechanisms shape optimization dynamics in RL fine-tuning for multi-parameter optimization (MPO). We evaluate three scalarization schemes (arithmetic mean, geometric mean, and Chebyshev) under multiple target regimes that vary in constraint tightness and prior support. While broad targets yield stable behavior across scalarizations, narrow and weakly supported targets expose sharp failure modes. We further show that these failure modes can be prevented through the usage of target-aware weight scheduling. Collectively, our results highlight critical interactions between scalarization choice and weight dynamics, and provide mechanistic insight and actionable guidance for stabilizing RL fine-tuning in constrained molecular MPO.

Scientific contribution

This work examines different reward formulations in multi-objective reinforcement learning for molecular design, going beyond the designs typically considered in prior studies. We further show how these formulations influence convergence behavior and collapse modes, and how their effects depend on the size and constraint structure of the multi-dimensional optimization space.
