Allosteric regulation, in which small-molecule effectors or mutations modulate activity at sites spatially distant from the orthosteric pocket, is a pervasive mechanism of biological control and an attractive avenue for drug discovery and protein engineering. The systematic curation of allosteric proteins, modulators and complexes in the Allosteric Database (ASD) and related resources has broadened our view of allosteric mechanisms and enabled quantitative analyses of their sequence, structural and network features [1]. Despite these advances, prospectively locating allosteric sites and functionally relevant mutations across diverse proteins remains difficult, largely because allostery is encoded in subtle, distributed changes in conformational ensembles.

From a physical perspective, allostery is increasingly viewed as an ensemble-level phenomenon in which ligand binding, mutation or post-translational modification redistributes conformational populations and residue–residue coupling patterns rather than simply triggering a single rigid structural transition [2,3,4]. This view links allosteric regulation to protein dynamics, thermodynamic coupling, frustration, coevolution and network-like communication across distant structural regions [5,6,7,8]. Biologically, allostery enables proteins to integrate cellular and mutational signals while preserving the core architecture of functional sites [9,10]. These properties also make allosteric sites attractive for therapeutic intervention, offering opportunities for improved selectivity, tunable efficacy and modulation of proteins that are difficult to target through orthosteric sites alone [11,12,13,14].

Classical computational approaches infer allosteric communication from structure and dynamics. La Sala et al. combined extensive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with coevolutionary analysis to prioritise cryptic allosteric pockets by integrating structural, dynamic and evolutionary metrics [15]. Qi et al. developed CorrSite 2.0, which identifies collective motions that connect candidate pockets to functional sites, thereby improving allosteric-site prediction [16]. Complementing these dynamics-based strategies, Xie et al. introduced KeyAlloSite, which exploits weak but specific evolutionary couplings between orthosteric and distal pockets to detect multi-site and weakly coupled allosteric regulation [17]. Reverse perturbation strategies have also been developed to identify allosteric sites by probing how local perturbations influence distal functional regions, providing another physics-inspired route for allosteric-site detection [18]. Although powerful, such methods are computationally demanding and are not designed to systematically predict how individual amino-acid substitutions strengthen, weaken or rewire allosteric communication.

In addition to MD-, coevolution- and network-based approaches, several physics-informed and statistical-mechanical models have been developed to quantify perturbation-induced allosteric effects. Structure-based statistical mechanical models of allostery, including SBSMMA, estimate residue-level allosteric free-energy changes and provide interpretable maps of how ligand binding or mutation redistributes energetic coupling across a protein structure [19,20,21]. Public resources such as AlloSigMA further implement these concepts to support residue-level analysis of mutation- or ligand-induced allosteric free-energy changes [22,23,24]. Related studies on allosteric mutations have shown that amino-acid substitutions can perturb protein function through long-range energetic and dynamic coupling rather than only through local structural disruption [25,26,27,28]. These methods provide valuable physical interpretability, but they are generally not designed as unified deep-learning frameworks for ligand-conditioned residue-level binding-site prediction and mutation-effect prioritization across curated datasets.

Pocket-centred supervised learning provides a complementary route to allosteric-site discovery. Early work relied mainly on geometric and physicochemical cavity descriptors. Tian et al. developed PASSer and PASSer2.0, which systematically leverage ASD-derived benchmarks to explore pocket features and model-selection strategies, thereby improving pocket-level allosteric-site prediction [29,30]. Qiao et al. further proposed AllosEC, which augments pocket descriptors with secondary-structure and environmental features to robustly classify enzyme allosteric pockets [31]. Khokhar et al. developed DeepAllo, which combines FPocket descriptors with embeddings from a fine-tuned protein language model (PLM) in a multi-task learning framework, thereby achieving strong allosteric-site prediction performance across several datasets [32]. More recently, Hu et al. introduced Allo-PED, where PLM-based residue embeddings and structural features are integrated in a two-stage framework that first identifies allosteric pockets and then refines predictions to the residue level [33]. However, most existing methods remain pocket-centred and rarely model the functional consequences of sequence variation at or near allosteric sites. Many also rely on a limited set of modalities, without jointly exploiting PLM embeddings, residue–residue interaction graphs and local structural environments [32,33,34].

Multimodal deep learning has recently shown strong potential for residue-level functional-site prediction. Models integrating PLM-derived sequence embeddings with structural or regulatory context have improved the prediction of functional phosphorylation and glycosylation sites, highlighting the value of fusing sequence, structure and contextual information for site-specific regulation [33,35]. Nonetheless, a unified framework that performs residue-level allosteric binding prediction, evaluates mutation effects on allosteric regulation and combines PLM embeddings with graph-based structural representations remains lacking.

Therefore, we introduce MMAllo, a multimodal deep learning framework designed to address these gaps. MMAllo comprises two complementary modules. MMAlloBind integrates PLM-based residue embeddings, graph-based structural and interaction features, and ligand molecular fingerprints to predict ligand-specific allosteric binding residues. MMAlloMut extends these multimodal representations to mutation-centred graphs to infer the functional consequences of amino-acid substitutions at allosteric or allosterically coupled positions. Benchmarking on the AlloBench and ASD-derived datasets shows that MMAlloBind reliably identifies residue-level allosteric sites using ANKH embeddings on AlphaFold3-predicted structures, while MMAlloMut effectively prioritizes curated allosteric mutations over putative negative mutations using sequence encodings and structural graphs. Application of MMAlloBind to PTPN2-FRJ (9C56) and CBLB-compound 9 (8QTG) demonstrates that it can recover spatially coherent allosteric pockets from AlphaFold3 models without ligand coordinates. A mutation-centred analysis of the P10828 V264D variant (6KKB/6KNU) further shows that MMAlloMut can prioritise experimentally validated allosteric mutations from predicted wild-type structures alone. Together, these results establish MMAllo as a general framework for identifying allosteric sites and quantifying mutation effects on protein function, providing a practical tool for protein engineering, variant interpretation and rational design of allosteric therapeutics.

We constructed two curated datasets to train and evaluate MMAllo.

For allosteric binding-site prediction (MMAlloBind), experimentally validated protein–ligand allosteric complexes were collected from the AlloBench database [36], including UniProt identifiers [37], PDB structures [38], ligand SMILES strings and residue-level allosteric annotations. For each protein, the corresponding predicted structure was downloaded from the AlphaFold3 database [39], andCαcoordinates and sequences were extracted with Biopython. Ligand SMILES were retrieved via the PDBe API and converted into 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints (radius = 2) using RDKit [40]. Because AlloBench records allosteric residues in PDB numbering, we mapped each annotation to UniProt sequence indices by building a residue-level correspondence between PDB and UniProt. Quality control involved (i) removing proteins without available AlphaFold3 structures (23 in total), (ii) checking sequence consistency between AlphaFold3 models and database records, (iii) verifying that annotated allosteric residues matched the residue names in the structures, (iv) discarding proteins longer than 1,500 residues, and (v) eliminating duplicate protein–ligand pairs. Residues annotated as allosteric were labelled as positive samples; all other residues were treated as negatives. To prevent information leakage, we applied protein-level five-fold group cross-validation (GroupKFold) [41], ensuring that all complexes for a given protein appeared in the same fold.

For allosteric mutation prediction (MMAlloMut), curated allosteric mutation records were extracted from the AM dataset of the Allosteric Database (ASD). To ensure reliable sequence and structure mapping, we retained records with complete UniProt identifiers, mutation-site information, wild-type and mutant residue identities, and available structural information from PDB or AlphaFold3. Each retained mutation was mapped to the corresponding residue position in the wild-type protein sequence, and the residue identity at the mutation site was verified before feature construction.

For each recorded mutation, the wild-type sequence was obtained from the corresponding AlphaFold3-predicted wild-type structure, the residue identity at the mutation position was verified, and a mutant sequence and unique mutation identifier were generated; these constituted the curated positive set. To construct putative negative mutations, we randomly selected residue positions and substituted them with one of the remaining 19 amino acids, excluding any combination that coincided with a curated positive mutation. Within each protein, grouped by UniProt ID, we then subsampled putative negatives to match the number of positives, yielding a 1:1 class ratio. The same protein-level five-fold GroupKFold scheme [41] was used so that all mutations from a given protein were restricted to a single fold. This balanced design was adopted to provide a controlled computational training setting. However, because experimentally validated allosteric mutations are expected to be much rarer than non-allosteric variants in natural or clinical mutation populations, the putative negative set should not be interpreted as a fully verified collection of experimentally inactive mutations.

To further characterize the structural scale of the curated dataset, we analyzed the protein-length distribution after removing duplicated UniProt entries. The dataset contained 127 unique proteins with lengths ranging from 108 to 1,500 residues, and 110 proteins (86.6%) were longer than 300 residues. This analysis indicates that a substantial fraction of the dataset consists of relatively large or potentially multidomain proteins. For large proteins, particularly those longer than 300 residues, we further inspected the AlphaFold3-predicted structures before graph construction, focusing on residue-level sequence consistency, structural coverage of annotated regions and mapping consistency at labeled mutation or allosteric-site positions. The corresponding protein-length distribution and secondary inspection of large AlphaFold3-predicted structures are provided in Fig. S1 and Table S1.

We considered three complementary strategies for encoding protein sequences, tailored to the requirements of MMAlloBind and MMAlloMut. First, one-hot encoding represents the 20 standard amino acids as 20-dimensional binary vectors, yielding an L × 20 matrix for a sequence of length L. This simple representation gave the best performance for MMAlloMut, indicating that local sequence patterns are highly informative for mutation-effect prediction. Second, we used the ESM2 protein language model [18] (esm2_t6_8M_UR50D) to obtain 320-dimensional residue embeddings. ESM2 was pre-trained on the UniRef50 database and captures evolutionary conservation and context signals. For each sequence, we extracted residue-level embeddings from the last layer after removing special start and end tokens. Third, we employed the ANKH protein language model (ankh-large) to generate 1,536-dimensional residue embeddings. ANKH is optimised for structure-aware representation learning and provided the best performance in MMAlloBind. Residue-level features were taken from the last_hidden_state of the T5EncoderModel [42]. All sequence embeddings were generated through a unified preprocessing pipeline and stored in.npy format for efficient reuse.

Ligand features were represented by Morgan molecular fingerprints computed with RDKit [40], using a radius of 2 and a bit length of 1,024. These fingerprints encode local substructures within two bonds of each atom and capture chemical patterns relevant to ligand preference in protein binding.

The three-dimensional structure of each protein was modelled as a geometric graphG=(V, E), where nodes correspond to residues and edges represent spatial or sequential proximity [43]. Node features were given by the chosen sequence representations (20,320 or 1,536 dimensions), and the number of nodes equalled the sequence length. Undirected edges were created between residuesiandjwhen theCα-Cαdistance was ≤ 10 Å, excluding self-loops and spurious edges at termini. Each edge was annotated with a 15-dimensional feature vector comprising: (i) a 3-dimensional direction vector encoding the normalised displacement from residueito residuejin the local coordinate frame of residuei, defined from backbone atoms [44]; (ii) a 4-dimensional quaternion describing the relative orientation between the local frames of residuesiandj[44]; and (iii) an 8-dimensional radial basis function (RBF) expansion [45] of theCα-Cαdistance, implemented with eight Gaussian basis functions whose centres are uniformly spaced between 0 and 20 Å. The direction and quaternion features capture relative spatial orientation and backbone geometry, whereas the RBF features provide a smooth, differentiable representation of inter-residue distances suitable for gradient-based optimisation.

For the mutation dataset, node features were constructed by concatenating the wild-type and mutant embeddings at each residue position. This design enables MMAlloMut to directly learn feature differences induced by amino-acid substitutions along the protein sequence.

MMAlloBind is a multimodal graph neural network [46,47] that integrates protein structural graphs, sequence embeddings and ligand fingerprints to predict residue-level allosteric binding probabilities. The input consists of a ligand Morgan fingerprint (1,024 dimensions) and a protein graph whose nodes carry PLM-based residue embeddings and whose edges are annotated with the 15-dimensional geometric descriptors described above. A three-layer MLP first projects the ligand fingerprint into a 512-dimensional latent space. In parallel, node and edge encoders map the PLM embeddings (ANKH: 1,536; ESM2: 320; one-hot: 20) and 15-dimensional edge features into the same 512-dimensional space.

The protein graph is then processed by a Cov2ProtMPNN-style encoder composed of two stacked ProtMPNN layers [48,49]. In each layer, node updates aggregate messages from neighbouring nodes and connecting edges, while edge updates combine features from incident nodes with the original edge descriptors. Residual connections and LayerNorm are applied to stabilise training.This architecture mimics signal propagation in allosteric communication networks, where node updates correspond to information diffusion across residues and edge updates capture changes in coupling strength. Two message-passing layers allow information to propagate over approximately two graph hops (~ 10–20 Å in space).

Following graph encoding, the updated node embeddings are reshaped into a residue sequence and passed to a protein–ligand cross-attention module. Specifically, a TransformerBlock [50] is used in which protein features serve as queries and the encoded ligand vector provides keys and values. The cross-attention employs four heads (128 dimensions per head); the attention weights can be interpreted as residue-specific affinities for the ligand, with different heads potentially focusing on distinct interaction types (e.g. hydrophobic contacts, electrostatics, hydrogen bonds). A subsequent protein self-attention layer integrates sequence context so that the model can recognise allosteric motifs spanning multiple residues. Finally, a two-layer MLP (512 → 256 → 1) followed by a Sigmoid activation maps residue features to allosteric binding probabilities.

Because the fraction of annotated allosteric residues is typically less than 5% of all residues in a protein, MMAlloBind faces a strong residue-level class imbalance, with far fewer positive allosteric residues than background residues. We therefore trained MMAlloBind with a weighted binary cross-entropy loss, applying masks so that only valid non-padding residues contributed to the loss. For evaluation, we emphasized AUPR, F1 score and MCC in addition to accuracy, because accuracy alone can be misleading under severe class imbalance. Optimisation used AdamW [51] with a learning rate of 1 × 10⁻4and weight_decay = 0.01. Unless stated otherwise, models were trained with a batch size of 12, hidden dimension 512 and dropout rate 0.1 for up to 100 epochs, with early stopping based on validation AUPR (patience = 10) to prevent overfitting.

MMAlloMut is designed to assess whether a single-point mutation perturbs the allosteric regulatory network of a protein. To explicitly encode mutation-induced changes, we adopt a dual-stream sequence representation: at each residue position, the wild-type and mutant PLM embeddings are concatenated along the feature dimension (320/1,536/20 → 640/3,072/40). This allows the model to directly learn pre- versus post-mutation differences while retaining the full wild-type context.

Structural features are derived from the wild-type three-dimensional structure, as mutant structures are often unavailable and AlphaFold3 predictions are generally more reliable for wild-type proteins [39]. Thus, the structural impact of the substitution is captured implicitly through the sequence-embedding differences. Node and edge encoders project the concatenated residue embeddings and 15-dimensional edge features into a 256-dimensional latent space. The resulting protein graph is then processed by the same Cov2ProtMPNN-based encoder used in MMAlloBind to extract structure-aware features, followed by a sequence self-attention layer [50] that integrates long-range contextual information along the chain.

A mutation-indexing layer then selects the feature vector corresponding to the mutated residue from the sequence representation; this vector has already aggregated information from its structural neighbourhood via graph message passing and from global sequence context via self-attention. Finally, a two-layer MLP classifier (256 → 128 → 1) maps this vector to a probability that the mutation exerts an allosteric effect.

Because the mutation dataset was constructed to be balanced, with equal numbers of curated positive mutations and putative negative mutations, we used a standard unweighted binary cross-entropy loss. MMAlloMut was trained using the AdamW optimizer [51] (learning rate 1 × 10⁻4), with a batch size of 40, hidden dimension of 256, and dropout rate of 0.1. Models were trained for up to 100 epochs with early stopping based on validation accuracy (patience = 8).

To assess the impact of different protein language model embeddings, we compared ANKH (ankh-large, 1,536 dimensions), ESM2 [18] (esm2_t6_8M_UR50D, 320 dimensions), and one-hot encoding (20 dimensions) under the same conditions. For each configuration, the graph topology, edge features, model architecture, and training protocol were held fixed, and full five-fold cross-validation [48] was performed to ensure an unbiased comparison. To evaluate the contribution of structural information, we performed a series of ablation experiments targeting graph connectivity and edge features. In the no-edge variant, edge-feature updates are removed, and message passing is restricted to node aggregation alone, resulting in a simplified propagation scheme [52]. In the no-graph variant, graph convolution layers are entirely omitted, and the original node features are passed directly to the subsequent attention and prediction modules. By comparing the performance of the full model with the no-edge and no-graph variants, we quantified the respective contributions of graph topology and explicit edge features to predictive performance.

All models were evaluated on independent test sets using multiple complementary performance metrics, including the F1-score (the harmonic mean of precision and recall), accuracy (ACC), the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR, which is more informative for imbalanced datasets), and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), which accounts for all entries of the confusion matrix. Performance scores are reported as the average of the five cross-validation folds.

PTPN2–FRJ (PDB ID: 9C56) [42,53] and CBLB–compound 9 (PDB ID: 8QTG) [44,54] were selected as independent MMAlloBind case studies to evaluate the ability of MMAlloBind to recover experimentally characterized allosteric binding pockets. PTPN2, also known as T-cell protein tyrosine phosphatase (TC-PTP), is a non-receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase that negatively regulates cytokine and immune-related signaling pathways. Recent structural studies have recognized PTPN2 as a promising target for cancer immunotherapy and reported the crystal structure of human PTPN2 in complex with an allosteric inhibitor, corresponding to the 9C56 structure used here. CBLB, also known as Cbl-b, is a RING finger E3 ubiquitin ligase that negatively regulates T-cell, B-cell and NK-cell activation through ubiquitin-mediated signaling control [42]. Pharmacological inhibition of CBLB has therefore emerged as a promising immuno-oncology strategy to enhance antitumor immune responses, and the 8QTG structure captures CBLB in complex with an arylpyridone allosteric inhibitor, compound 9 [54].

For each MMAlloBind case-study system, we prepared the experimental complex structure, ligand SMILES string, protein sequence and the corresponding AlphaFold3-predicted structure. We note that the model inputs consisted only of the protein structure and ligand SMILES, whereas the spatial coordinates of the ligand on the protein surface were not provided to the model. After obtaining residue-level allosteric binding probabilities from MMAlloBind, all residues within 4 Å of the ligand in the experimental structure were collected as experimentally observed ligand-contact residues. The overlap between the top 10% residues ranked by predicted probability and the experimentally observed binding residues was quantified using the Jaccard similarity index.

For the independent MMAlloMut case study, we examined the V264D mutation in human thyroid hormone receptor beta (THRβ/THRB, UniProt ID: P10828). THRβ is a ligand-regulated nuclear receptor that mediates thyroid hormone signaling and plays important roles in endocrine regulation, metabolism and hormone-dependent transcriptional control. Dysregulation of thyroid hormone receptor signaling has also been implicated in cancer biology, and recent studies have highlighted TRβ as a potential tumor suppressor and therapeutic target in several solid tumors [55]. However, the V264D mutation analyzed here is primarily a disease-related mutation associated with defective ligand binding and resistance to thyroid hormone, rather than a mutation assigned to a specific cancer type.

The 6KKB/6KNU structural pair provides an experimentally characterized system for studying this mutation-induced allosteric mechanism [38]. We therefore used the AlphaFold3-predicted wild-type structure [39] and the experimentally resolved mutant structure 6KNU to evaluate whether MMAlloMut could prioritize a structurally characterized disease-related allosteric mutation. One-hot encodings were extracted for the wild-type and mutant sequences and concatenated into 40-dimensional node features, and the protein graph was constructed using the wild-type structure. MMAlloMut assigned V264D an allosteric mutation probability of 0.732, exceeding the default binary classification threshold of 0.5. This above-threshold positive prediction was obtained using only the predicted wild-type structure, suggesting that the framework can prioritize candidate allosteric mutations even when experimentally resolved mutant structures are unavailable. By comparing the experimental wild-type and mutant structures, we further analyzed how the introduction of a negatively charged aspartate at position 264 disrupts the original hydrophobic core [45], providing additional structural support for the predicted allosteric effect.

To provide a physics-based validation of MMAllo, we carried out all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on three representative systems: the PTPN2–FRJ allosteric inhibitor complex (9C56) and the CBLB–compound 9 allosteric inhibitor complex (8QTG) for MMAlloBind, and the THRβ V264D wild-type/mutant structural pair (6KKB/6KNU) for MMAlloMut. All simulations were performed in AMBER22 with the GPU-accelerated pmemd.cuda engine using the ff99SB force field for proteins and GAFF parameters for ligands prepared by Antechamber in AmberTools22. Each complex (or apo protein) was solvated in a cubic TIP3P water box with at least 15 Å padding; Na⁺/Cl⁻ counterions were added to neutralise the system [56].

After system setup, 1,000 steps of energy minimisation (500 steepest-descent + 500 conjugate-gradient) were followed by gradual heating from 0 to 300 K over 25,000 steps (50 ps, NVT, 2 fs timestep) using SHAKE-constrained bonds to hydrogen and a Langevin thermostat (collision frequency 2.0 ps⁻1). This was followed by 50 ps density equilibration and 500 ps slow-release equilibration with progressively relaxed positional restraints. Production simulations were initially performed for 450 ns for all systems in the NPT ensemble at 300 K and 1 atm with particle-mesh Ewald electrostatics, an 8 Å cutoff for short-range non-bonded interactions, periodic boundaries and a Berendsen barostat. To address concerns regarding simulation length and trajectory stability, both apo/free and ligand-bound simulations of PTPN2–FRJ (9C56) and CBLB–compound 9 (8QTG) were further extended to 1 μs. Coordinates were saved every 10 ps throughout the production simulations. The revised RMSD, Rg, SASA and RMSF analyses for 9C56 and 8QTG were therefore based on the extended 1-μs trajectories.

We analyzed MD trajectories using a graph neural-network-based neural relational inference (NRI) model [58]. For each protein system, Cartesian positions and velocities of allCαatoms were extracted from all-atom MD simulations and assembled into node feature sequencesxi={xi1,xi2,…,xiT},i=1,…,NforNresidues overTtime steps. These trajectories were provided to an encoder-decoder architecture that treats residues as nodes in a fully connected latent interaction graph. The encoder is a graph neural network that performs repeated node-to-edge and edge-to-node message passing to infer a categorical distribution overKedge typeszij∈ {1,2,…,K},i ≠ jbetween residue pairs, implemented as a variational posteriorqΦ(z∣x). The decoder is a recurrent graph neural network with GRU units that conditions on sampled edge types and past states to reconstruct future framespθ(xt+1∣x≤t,z). Model parameters were optimised by maximising the evidence lower bound, which combines a Gaussian reconstruction loss on atomic coordinates with a Kullback–Leibler regulariser that enforces sparse edge priors. After training, residue-residue interaction strengths were obtained by averaging posterior edge probabilities across time and trajectories to yield a weighted interaction graph. Domain-level contact maps, candidate shortest paths between predefined allosteric and functional regions, and node centrality measures were then computed on this weighted graph to identify putative communication routes and mediating residues underlying long-range allosteric regulation in the systems analyzed in this study, including PTPN-FRJ, CBLB-compound 9 and the 6KKB/6KNU wild-type/mutant pair. Because allosteric communication may involve multiple partially redundant routes and collective conformational changes, additional near-degenerate paths were considered in the supplementary analysis when their probabilities were comparable to the top-ranked route.

For MMAlloBind, data preparation includes the construction of a protein-graph, the extraction of PLM embeddings, and the calculation of ligand fingerprints. The prepared inputs are passed sequentially through the five models trained on different cross-validation folds, each evaluated in inference mode to generate residue-level probabilities following Sigmoid activation. The final prediction for each residue is obtained by averaging the probabilities produced by the fivefold-specific models, yielding an ensemble estimate. For each protein–ligand pair, MMAlloBind outputs a ranked list of residue indices together with their associated allosteric binding probabilities. The workflow is shown in Fig.1a.

Overview of the MMAllo framework for multimodal prediction of protein allosteric sites and mutations.aMMAlloBind. The AlphaFold3-predicted structure and ligand SMILES are used as inputs. PLM embeddings combined with a protein MPNN yield residue-level representations, which are fused with the ligand Morgan fingerprint via a cross-attention block. A self-attention layer produces the final residue binding probabilities for the allosteric ligand.bMMAlloMut. The model adopts a similar structure-aware protein-encoding architecture but additionally incorporates both wild-type and mutant residue embeddings

The workflow of MMAlloMut follows an analogous procedure but produces a single probability for each mutation, as shown in Fig.1b. As in MMAlloBind, predictions from the fivefold-specific models are averaged to obtain an ensemble score for each mutation. This five-fold ensemble strategy enhances stability in prediction and improves generality across diverse protein environments.

The two modules of MMAllo are complementary. MMAlloBind provides residue-level allosteric binding probabilities conditioned on both the protein and ligand, while MMAlloMut evaluates whether specific amino-acid substitutions at candidate sites are likely to modulate allosteric regulation. Although MMAlloBind and MMAlloMut are trained independently on task-specific datasets with separate loss functions, the two modules follow a unified modeling philosophy based on residue-level protein representations and structure-aware graph encoding. Thus, their relationship lies in the shared architectural design and representation strategy, rather than in joint optimization or parameter sharing during training.

The overall architecture of MMAlloBind is shown in Fig.1a. Protein residues are first embedded using a PLM and subsequently processed by a protein message passing neural network (MPNN) operating on the residue-residue interaction graph to generate structure-aware residue representations. The ligand is encoded separately by a Morgan fingerprint. A protein–ligand cross-attention block then integrates residue-level features with the ligand fingerprint, followed by a protein self-attention layer that aggregates sequence-context information and produces residue-wise binding probabilities for the allosteric ligand binding.

MMAlloMut reuses the protein encoder from MMAlloBind but augments it with mutation-specific information (Fig.1b). For each candidate mutation, the wild-type and mutant PLM embeddings of the index residue are concatenated and provided as node features, while all other residues use the wild-type embedding. Following message passing on the residue-residue graph and subsequent sequence self-attention pooling, the representation corresponding to the mutated residue is extracted and passed through a multilayer perceptron to predict whether the mutation exerts an allosteric effect.

To understand the performance of MMAlloBind on predicting the allosteric binding sites within different protein environments, we compared ANKH, ESM2, and One-hot encoding embeddings with MMAlloBind (Fig.2and Table1). As shown in Fig.2and Table1, the ANKH-based model achieved the best overall performance, with an F1-score of 0.318, AUC of 0.830, AUPR of 0.267, and MCC of 0.316. ESM2 embeddings also improved performance over one-hot encoding but remained clearly inferior to ANKH (F1 = 0.212, AUPR = 0.195, MCC = 0.215). Although one-hot encoding yielded a slightly higher overall accuracy (0.969), its F1-score, AUPR, and MCC were all near zero, indicating that it rarely identifies true allosteric binding residues in this highly imbalanced case. These results suggest that powerful PLMs, particularly ANKH, provide rich contextual information that is critical for accurate prediction of allosteric binding residues.

The contribution of graph-based structural information is evaluated by using an ablation study, as mentioned in the Methods section (Fig.3and Table2). As shown in Fig.3, removing the structural graph components from MMAlloBind leads to a reduction in F1, MCC, and AUC scores, suggesting its worse performance in the prediction of allosteric binding sites. Panels Fig.3a and c compare the F1 score and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), respectively, for the full model, a variant without residue edge features (noted as No edge in Fig.3), and a variant without the structural graph branch (noted as No graph in Fig.3). Eliminating the entire graph module (No graph in Fig.3) causes a notable drop in both F1 and MCC, while removing only the edges but retaining residue-level structural descriptors (No edge in Fig.3) yields only a minor decrease. This pattern indicates that node-level structural information contributes more than explicit edge features, but that graph-based modeling still provides an overall benefit. Consistent with these trends, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves in Fig.3b show that MMAlloBind attains the highest AUC (0.830), followed by No edge (AUC = 0.807) and No graph (AUC = 0.786). The precision–recall curves in Fig.3d further demonstrate that the full model achieves the best area under the PR curve (AUPR = 0.267), closely followed by the No edge variant (AUPR = 0.265), while No graph performs worse (AUPR = 0.242) on this highly imbalanced allosteric binding-residue prediction task. Clearly, the full model achieved the best performance across all metrics, as shown in Table2. The No edge variant has very similar results compared to the full model, indicating that node-level structural descriptors contribute the most, while explicit graph connectivity contributes a smaller but consistent increment to the accuracy. In contrast, the No graph model (without any structural information) exhibited significantly lower F1, AUC, AUPR and MCC values, despite a slightly higher accuracy, highlighting the importance of structural graphs in accurately predicting allosteric binding sites. These results suggest that incorporating AlphaFold3-based structural graphs could improve the identification of allosteric binding residues. To evaluate the performance of MMAlloBind in predicting allosteric binding sites, we conducted two case studies using experimentally resolved allosteric inhibitor-bound complexes: PTPN2 in complex with FRJ and CBLB in complex with compound 9, as shown in Figs.4and5. These two systems were selected because they contain experimentally characterized allosteric inhibitor-binding pockets and are directly related to human immune regulation and cancer-immunotherapy-relevant signaling.

For PTPN2 in complex with FRJ (PDB ID: 9C56, Fig.4), [42,56] MMAlloBind suggested that there are high probabilities of allosteric binding on Leu193, Asn194, Phe197, Glu201, Glu274, and Gly275 residues, as shown in the right panel of Fig.4. These residues are ranked among the top candidates and form a spatially contiguous pocket surrounding the allosteric inhibitor FRJ (Fig.4). Most of these residues are in direct contact with the ligand and in accordance with the experimentally observed allosteric site, indicating that MMAlloBind not only identifies possible residues that can participate in allosteric binding, but also points out the real allosteric pocket identified in experiments, instead of unrelated regions at the protein surface.

As shown in Fig.4b–e, both the apo/free and ligand-bound PTPN2 trajectories were extended to 1 μs to better assess the stability of the FRJ-associated allosteric pocket. The extended simulations showed that both systems remained globally compact, with narrowly distributed Rgvalues and modest changes in SASA. The RMSF profiles further indicated that the predicted allosteric pocket did not undergo large-amplitude local fluctuations during the simulated timescale. These results support the persistence of the MMAlloBind-predicted FRJ-associated pocket during the extended simulations, while avoiding the interpretation that the finite trajectories exhaustively sample the full conformational ensemble.

According to UniProt annotations, Cys216 is the catalytic cysteine of PTPN2 and was therefore chosen as the reference active-site residue in our analysis. Building on this residue-level prediction, we further examined whether the MMAlloBind pocket lies on a plausible allosteric communication route. Using NRIMD on the extended ligand-bound trajectory, we identified a representative high-probability candidate communication path connecting the predicted allosteric residue Asn194 to the catalytic residue Cys216 via Gly210, forming a three-residue relay Asn194 → Gly210 → Cys216 (Fig.4f). This path should be interpreted as a graph-theoretical route inferred from the NRIMD-derived residue interaction network, rather than as evidence that allosteric signaling occurs exclusively through this single pathway. Nevertheless, its location within well-packed secondary-structure elements provides a plausible structural context through which perturbations near the FRJ-stabilized pocket could be coupled to the catalytic loop containing Cys216.

Another case study was conducted on protein 8QTG. The results further highlight MMAlloBind’s capability in capturing spatially coherent allosteric sites (Fig.5). For the CBLB-Compound 9 complex (PDB ID: 8QTG; Fig.5), MMAllo suggests there are high probabilities of allosteric binding at Lys145, Leu148, Glu232, and Ile235 residues. Similar to the previously mentioned case study with PTPN2, these residues are also ranked among the top candidates in CBLB and form a coherent pocket in three-dimensional space rather than being dispersed along other positions in the protein, as shown in Fig.5. These residues may represent key allosteric binding residues that can be further investigated to understand compound-9-mediated regulation of CBLB. This spatial organization is consistent with an allosteric site identified in experiments, suggesting that, with MMAllo, we can easily understand higher-order structural dependencies instead of only individual residue patterns.

As shown in Fig.5b–e, both the apo/free and ligand-bound CBLB trajectories were extended to 1 μs to better evaluate the conformational behavior of this system. The ligand-bound trajectory showed an initial conformational adjustment followed by a relatively more stable later-stage regime. Although the RMSD reflected a substantial deviation from the starting structure, the Rgdistribution remained confined to a narrow range, suggesting that the complex did not undergo large-scale unfolding or collapse. RMSF and NRIMD analyses were therefore focused on the later segment of the extended trajectories, providing a more appropriate basis for evaluating the candidate allosteric communication route associated with compound 9 binding.

According to UniProt annotations, Cys376 is a key catalytic residue in CBLB and was therefore chosen as the reference active site in our analysis. An analogous analysis was performed for CBLB in complex with compound 9. NRIMD analysis of the later segment of the extended ligand-bound trajectory identified a representative high-probability candidate communication route linking the MMAlloBind-predicted allosteric residue Lys145 to catalytic Cys376 through Leu65, Leu307 and Glu346, yielding the route Lys145 → Leu65 → Leu307 → Glu346 → Cys376 (Fig.5f). This route spans both N- and C-terminal regions and provides a plausible graph-based connection between the predicted allosteric pocket and the catalytic site. Because allosteric regulation is expected to involve collective conformational coupling and potentially multiple partially redundant pathways, this route is interpreted as a candidate communication path rather than a unique causal signal-transmission pathway.

To justify the final architecture and residue representation used in MMAlloMut, we next examined the contributions of graph-based structural modeling and sequence-encoding strategies.

To separate the contribution of different components in MMAlloMut, we performed an ablation study on the independent test set (Fig.6). The full MMAlloMut model produced a balanced confusion matrix, correctly identifying the majority of allosteric mutations, while maintaining a reasonable false positive rate. In terms of precision-recall performance, MMAlloMut achieved the highest AUPR score (0.850), while removing the graph module (No graph in Fig.6) resulted in a drop in AUPR score to 0.806, indicating that graph-based structural representations are essential for capturing the long-range dependencies underlying allosteric mutations.

The No edge variant, in which explicit edge features are removed while graph connectivity is retained, exhibited a modest reduction in precision-recall performance (AUPR = 0.845) but achieved a ROC-AUC comparable to that of the full model (0.881 vs 0.878). This behavior suggests that edge-level interaction descriptors provide fine-grained improvements mainly in the high-precision regime. Taken together, these results confirm that integrating protein language model embeddings with graph-based structural modeling is critical for accurate allosteric mutation prediction.

We quantitatively evaluated the contribution of different components in MMAlloMut using an ablation study (Table3). The full MMAlloMut model achieved an F1 score of 0.811, an accuracy of 0.806, an AUC value of 0.878, an AUPR value of 0.850, and an MCC value of 0.614, indicating robust performance on allosteric mutation prediction. Removal of explicit edge features (No edge in Fig.6) yielded performance metrics that were largely comparable to those of the full model, with slightly higher ACC, AUC, and MCC but a modest reduction in AUPR (0.845 vs 0.850). This trend suggests that edge-level interaction descriptors primarily contribute to refining predictions in the high-precision regime under class imbalance, while having a limited impact on overall ranking. In contrast, eliminating the entire graph module (No graph) resulted in a consistent degradation across all metrics, underscoring that graph-based structural modelling is critical for capturing long-range dependencies and accurately identifying allosteric mutations.

We further examined how different sequence encodings influence MMAlloMut’s performance (Fig.7and Table4). We examined how different sequence encodings influence the performance of MMAlloMut (Fig.7). When one-hot encodings was used for residue features, MMAlloMut achieved the strongest overall performance, with an AUC of 0.878 and an AUPR of 0.850. ANKH embeddings led to intermediate performance (AUC = 0.784, AUPR = 0.764), whereas ESM2 embeddings produced the lowest scores (AUC = 0.701, AUPR = 0.679). These results indicate that the choice of sequence representation substantially influences allosteric mutation prediction and that simpler one-hot encodings can be highly effective when combined with graph-based structural modeling. At the same time, ANKH consistently outperforms ESM2, suggesting that ANKH captures sequence features that are more relevant to allosteric regulation in our dataset.

We also evaluated the impact of various sequence encoding strategies on MMAlloMut using standard classification metrics (Table4). When ANKH embeddings were used as residue features, MMAlloMut achieved an F1-score of 0.707, ACC of 0.728, AUC of 0.784, AUPR of 0.764, and MCC of 0.461, consistently outperforming ESM2 embeddings (F1 = 0.617, ACC = 0.656, AUC = 0.701, AUPR = 0.679, MCC = 0.319).

Notably, the strongest overall performance was obtained using simple one-hot encodings, which yielded an F1 score of 0.811, an accuracy of 0.806, an AUC of 0.878, an AUPR of 0.850, and an MCC of 0.614. These trends, which are consistent with the corresponding ROC and precision-recall curves, indicate that under the current dataset size and model configuration, low-level one-hot representations can be highly effective when combined with graph-based structural modeling, while ANKH remains a more informative PLM choice than ESM2 for this task.

To further evaluate the behavior of MMAlloMut in scenarios where only predicted wild-type structures are available, we analyzed the V264D mutation in the protein with UniProt ID P10828, for which an experimentally resolved mutant structure is available (Fig.8). Using the AlphaFold3-predicted wild-type structure together with one-hot encodings of the wild-type and mutant sequences as input features, MMAlloMut classified V264D as an above-threshold positive allosteric mutation with a probability of 0.732, exceeding the default decision threshold of 0.5.

Because the AlphaFold3-predicted wild-type model and the experimentally resolved mutant structure may represent different conformational states and differ in unresolved or flexible regions, Fig.8a,b were used only to illustrate the local structural environment surrounding residue 264. These panels were not intended as a direct global structural comparison between the wild-type and mutant proteins. Substitution of the non-polar valine by a negatively charged aspartate side chain introduces an unfavourable charge into this hydrophobic environment and is expected to destabilise local packing. Consistent with this interpretation, comparison of the wild-type and mutant structures suggests that the V264D substitution disrupts the original hydrophobic core around residue 264, thus making the mutation of V264 capable of modulating long-range allosteric communication. The agreement between the prediction by MMAlloMut and the experimental results suggests that MMAlloMut performs very well in identifying possible allosteric mutations. The Rgprofiles of the wild-type and V264D systems were broadly similar (Fig.8d,e), indicating that the mutation did not induce large-scale unfolding or global collapse during the simulated timescale. However, Rgmainly reports overall compactness and is not expected to capture local packing disruption or changes in long-range communication topology. Therefore, comparable Rgvalues do not contradict the mutation-associated local structural perturbation and NRIMD-inferred network changes.

Previous biochemical and structural studies have shown that the V264D mutation in THRβ exhibits a ligand-dependent loss-of-function phenotype, conferring resistance to T3 while retaining activation by roxadustat, consistent with a selective disruption of conformational coupling rather than a global reduction in ligand affinity. Consistent with this view, and to quantify how this mutation reshapes ligand recognition, we analysed per-residue MM/PBSA binding free-energy decompositions for 6KKB and 6KNU (Fig.8h,i). In the wild-type complex, several hydrophobic residues in the pocket, including Leu330, Ile276, Phe272 and Leu346, contribute strongly favourable interaction energies, while Val264 makes only a small contribution. In the V264D mutant, many of these stabilising contributions are attenuated and Asp264 itself becomes weakly destabilising, yielding an overall less favourable binding profile. Together with the published ligand-dependent phenotype of V264D, the MM/PBSA results suggest that the mutation perturbs the energetic balance of ligand recognition rather than simply abolishing all protein–ligand contacts. These energetic changes provide supporting evidence for the MMAlloMut prediction, but they should be interpreted as computational estimates that require further experimental validation.

To further characterise the mechanistic impact of V264D, we carried out Gaussian accelerated MD simulations on 6KKB and 6KNU followed by MD-based allosteric network analysis (Fig.8). For 6KKB, the domain-domain edge probability matrix shows relatively weak and nearly uniform couplings between most domains, with only a modest enhancement between the allosteric domain and a small subset of neighbouring domains (Fig.8j). Consistently, the residue-level edge probability map within the allosteric community is dominated by narrow vertical stripes, indicating that communication is channelled through a few local hub residues and that long-range cross-links between different parts of the pocket are sparse (Fig.8k).

Compared with the wild-type system, the V264D mutant displayed altered NRIMD-inferred communication patterns, including increased coupling involving the domain containing residue 264 and a denser residue-level interaction map within the allosteric community (Fig.8l,m). We further compared the NRIMD-derived representative candidate shortest communication paths starting from residue 264 in the wild-type and V264D mutant systems. In the wild-type 6KKB system, the candidate path followed the route Val264 → Thr327 → Arg243 → Gln235 → Ala279, suggesting that the communication from residue 264 is mediated through a multi-step relay involving residues distributed around the local structural environment. In contrast, the V264D mutant 6KNU system adopted a shorter and topologically distinct route, Asp264 → Phe451 → Phe455 → Ala279. This shift from a Val264-centred polar/charged residue-containing relay to an Asp264-centred route involving distal phenylalanine residues indicates that V264D not only changes the local physicochemical environment at residue 264, but also redirects the inferred allosteric communication pathway toward a different set of mediating residues. Together with the MM/PBSA energy analyses, these GaMD-derived network and path changes indicate that V264D perturbs long-range allosteric communication patterns while simultaneously weakening the original binding energetics, providing a coherent mechanistic picture of V264D as a ligand-dependent, deleterious allosteric mutation in line with the effects predicted by MMAlloMut.

To further examine the applicability of MMAlloMut beyond the main validation examples, we additionally tested four recently reported allosteric mutation cases that were not included in either the training set or the principal validation systems. These cases included catalase P9WIE5_S457I, falcipain Q8I6U4_M245I, rat odorant-binding protein 3F1Q_T112A and human Gαs 6NBF_E392K. MMAlloMut assigned above-threshold probabilities to all four cases (0.665–0.922), supporting its potential applicability to independent allosteric mutation examples (Table S2). Because these additional cases were used only as an external supplementary check, the main mechanistic validation remains focused on the structurally characterized PTPN2–FRJ (9C56), CBLB–compound 9 (8QTG) and THRβ V264D (6KKB/6KNU) systems.

In this work, we developed MMAllo, a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates residue-level protein representations, graph-based structural information and ligand molecular fingerprints to support allosteric binding-residue prediction and allosteric mutation prioritization. For MMAlloBind, the ANKH-based model achieved the best overall performance among the tested sequence representations, with an F1 score of 0.318, AUC of 0.830, AUPR of 0.267 and MCC of 0.316 on the curated benchmark dataset. These results indicate that structure-aware PLM embeddings can provide useful contextual information for residue-level allosteric binding-site prediction, particularly under the strong class imbalance caused by the small fraction of annotated allosteric residues.

For MMAlloMut, the revised pan-cancer dataset expanded the original BLCA/UCEC setting to include UCEC, BLCA, SKCM, COAD, LUAD, LUSC, STAD, BRCA and GBM, thereby improving cancer-type diversity while preserving ASD-AM allosteric annotation quality and sequence/structure mapping requirements. In the mutation-prediction task, MMAlloMut combined wild-type and mutant residue representations with graph-based structural encoding to prioritize curated allosteric mutations over putative negative mutations. The ablation and encoding analyses further supported the contribution of graph-based structural modeling and clarified the representation choices used in the final model configuration.

In case studies of PTPN2-FRJ (9C56) and CBLB-compound 9 (8QTG), MMAlloBind recovered spatially coherent residue clusters around experimentally characterized allosteric ligands. Extended ligand-bound simulations further supported the persistence of these predicted pockets during the simulated timescale. NRIMD analysis identified representative high-probability candidate communication paths connecting predicted allosteric residues to annotated catalytic residues. These paths provide interpretable graph-based hypotheses for long-range coupling, but they should not be interpreted as unique causal routes of allosteric signaling, because real allosteric communication may involve multiple redundant pathways and collective conformational changes.

For the P10828 V264D mutation, MMAlloMut assigned an above-threshold allosteric mutation probability using only the predicted wild-type structure. Subsequent structural inspection, GaMD-based network analysis and MM/PBSA calculations provided supporting evidence that V264D perturbs local packing, ligand-interaction energetics and inferred long-range communication patterns. However, the current validation remains computational, and the functional necessity of individual intermediate residues or network edges will require future site-directed mutagenesis or biochemical experiments.

Overall, MMAllo provides a practical framework for linking residue-level allosteric site discovery with mutation-effect prioritization. Its ability to operate on predicted wild-type structures makes it useful for proteins lacking experimentally resolved complex or mutant structures. At the same time, the present study has several limitations, including the use of putative rather than experimentally verified negative mutations, uneven ASD-AM annotation density across cancer types, finite simulation timescales and the lack of direct mutational validation for the predicted communication-path intermediates. Future work will integrate larger variant resources, more realistic class distributions, expanded experimental validation and longer-timescale simulations to further improve the robustness and applicability of MMAllo in allosteric drug discovery and functional variant interpretation.

title: Reinforcement learning for de novo RET inhibitor design: potency-focused optimization and polypharmacological multi-parameter optimization against resistance mutations
author: Surendra Kumar; Vinay Pogaku; Mi-hyun Kim
text:
Despite their role as oncogenic drivers and predictive biomarkers, alterations in rearrangement during transfection (RET), a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK), remain significant challenges due to off-target effects and reduced efficacy against emerging mutations, necessitating more selective and innovative drug design. Herein, we report a multi-layered framework encompassing both reinforcement learning (RL) training and post-processing phases, for the efficient de novo design of RET inhibitors striking a balance between structural novelty and predictive reliability. We evaluated two RL strategies: potency-focused optimization (PFO) and polypharmacological multi-parameter optimization (PMPO), with the latter integrating 131 predictive models for off-target selectivity and phenotypic activity. For the 23 kinase targets, pIC50classification thresholds were defined using Youden's J statistic (mean J = 0.762, range 0.679–0.918). The 108 NSCLC phenotype models showed limited discriminative performance (mean AUC = 0.550). After applicability domain filtering, the increased mean AUC allowed the use of the phenotype models as a confidence-weighted filter in the generative workflow. Post-hoc similarity distribution analysis confirmed that the generated candidates represent structurally novel yet domain-consistent chemotypes, as evidenced by peak densities situated within the Tanimoto similarity range of 0.20–0.40 (generated vs known). Notably, PMPO significantly enhanced multi-parameter consistency (CV: 5.1% vs. 16.5%) and selectivity control (p < 0.0001) without compromising primary target potency. A central achievement of this work is the observation of independent scaffold convergence across diverse optimization settings, providing orthogonal validation of the identified quinoxaline core as a robust RET-inhibitory chemotype. After the common post-processing phases, including hinge-core analysis, scaffold novelty assessment, drug-likeness filtering, and drug-target affinity prediction, RL-1185 compounds were identified and prioritized as a lead molecule exhibiting high potency against multiple RET alterations (IC50: 0.78 nM for RETV804M, 142 nM for RETG810R), the novelty (Tanimoto coefficient: 0.579), and favorable synthetic tractability.

Scientific contribution

This work provides three key contributions: (1) Establishment of a multi-layered technical safeguard framework that ensures computational reliability and structural novelty through training constraints and post hoc validation. (2) A reward-design strategy integrating target potency, predicted off-target selectivity, and an exploratory phenotypic baseline constraint establishing a general RL-based inverse design framework in which predictive models both rank generated molecules, and shape the explored chemical space. (3) Experimental evaluation of computationally prioritized compounds identified a novel aminoquinoxaline scaffold with sub-nanomolar inhibitory activity against the RET wild-type and gatekeeper mutant (IC50 < 1 nM).

Biomarkers serve as indispensable guides for the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of various human diseases. In oncology, these molecular signatures are particularly vital for identifying patient subpopulations most likely to benefit from targeted therapies, thereby significantly increasing clinical success rates [1]. However, despite these merits, the high frequency of genetic alterations and the emergence of acquired resistance continue to pose persistent challenges, often impeding the design of innovative and durable therapeutics [2]. Rearrangement during transfection (RET), a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK), is one such therapeutically important biomarker because its frequent alterations complicate the development of durable targeted treatments. RET alterations function both as oncogenic drivers and as predictive biomarkers for targeted treatment [3,4]. Early RET-trageting agents inhibited multiple kinases but often showed limited selectivity, resuling in  off-target effects and reduced efficacy against specific RET mutations [5,6,7]. For example, cabozantinib inhibited RETWTwith an IC50of 18.4 nM but was markedly less potent against the RETV804Mgatekeeper mutation (IC50= 229 nM) [8]. Vandetanib likewise showed reduced activity against RET mutants [4] (Fig.1).

Three-dimensional overview of protein–ligand interactions  in  RET kinase complexes with clinically evaluated RET inhibitors with their potencies.

The development of second-generation RET inhibitors, together with their protein crystal structures, led to the identification of a cryptic “post-lysine” pocket adjacent to the catalytic lysine (K758), a site previously unexploited by first-generation inhibitors [9]. By selectively targeting this pocket, second-generation inhibitors, such as selpercatinib and pralsetinib have achieved major clinical success and have shown improved selectivity and potency against RET-driven cancers [10,11], particularly RETWTand RETV804M/Lmutants. Even so, solvent-front mutations at Gly810 (e.g., G810A/C/D/S/R), remain a major obstacle because these inhibitors show reduced activity against RETG810variants, limiting their therapeutic potential [12,13]. Next-generation inhibitors, including vepafestinib and TPX-0046, have therefore been developed to address these resistance mechanisms, and have shown promising inhibitory activity against RETG810R(149 nM for vepafestinib and 17 nM for TPX-0046) [12,14] (Fig.1). Notably, while vepafestinib maintains inhibitory potency against G810 mutation, it faces limitations due to resistance involving the I788N mutation (IC50= 1,640 nM), as well as potential resistance variants that may complicate its therapeutic efficacy [12].

In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), RET fusions, such as KIF5B-RET, CCDC6-RET, act as prominent oncogenic drivers [15,16], producing constitutive RET activation and uncontrolled cellular proliferation. Inhibitors capable of addressing these RET alterations therefore remain important for the treatment of NSCLC patients with RET-driven disease [17]. Designing RET inhibitors that are both selective and effective against resistant mutations remains challenging because diverse structural changes in the kinase can introduce steric clashes and weaken binding affinity [3,4]. In addition, although DFG (Asp-Phe-Gly)-in and DFG-out conformations are widely used concepts in kinase inhibitor design, selpercatinib and pralsetinib do not follow the typical type II mechanism associated with DFG-out binding [18,19]. Instead, they bind RET kinase in the DFG-in conformation, while exploiting the post-lysine pocket adjacent to lysine (K758), as demonstrated by their high selectivity and efficacy in RET-driven cancers [9]. Ponatinib, by contrast, is a type II inhibitor that targets the DFG-out state and has shown activity against certain resistance mutations such as RETV804M, a frequent gatekeeper mutation in RET-rearranged cancers [20]. Even so, variants including I788N and G810R continue to pose substantial challenges and motivate the search for new inhibitor scaffolds [9].

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning have accelerated drug discovery by reducing the time and costs associated with conventional development workflows [21]. Generative deep-learning models, which learn the probability distribution of molecular datasets, have become increasingly useful for proposing novel candidate compounds [22,23,24]. Within this context, de novo design has emerged as an important strategy for generating new chemical entities with optimized properties [25,26]. Motivated by these developments, we sought to incorporate AI-driven design into our effort to discover inhibitors for actionable RET mutations. In our recent study, we analyzed protein–ligand interaction patterns (PLIP) and investigated side-chain modifications of the imidazo[1,2-b]pyridazine [27] hinge binder. One of the central challenges in RET inhibitor design is that key resistance residues such as V804 and G810 are positioned distally (13.126 Å), while productive binding also requires access to residues associated with the active conformation, including the cryptic pocket adjacent to K758. To address these challenges, we extended the substituents at the 2- and 6-positions of the selpercatinib hinge-binding framework [27]. Those compounds showed nanomolar potency against mutant RET kinases, which prompted us to explore a new scaffold with potential advantages in both novelty and developability.

In this study, we systematically compared two distinct reinforcement learning (RL) strategies for de novo design of RET inhibitors while incorporating prior knowledge of RET protein–ligand interactions into scaffold design [28] (Fig.2):

Potency-Focused Optimization (PFO)focused on maximizing predicted RETG810Rpotency through a scoring function incorporating: (i) an in-house regression model for RETG810RpIC50prediction, (ii) molecular docking scores, (iii) QED score, and (iv) custom alert filters. This approach prioritizes target engagement while relying on post-hoc filtering including PAINS [29] filtering, ADMET profiling[30], Bemis-Murcko scaffold analysis [31] and predictions from our in-house drug-target affinity models (SMPLIP-Score [32] and ChargeNET [33]).

Polypharmacological Multi-Parameter Optimization (PMPO)extended the PFO framework by incorporating: (i) 23 off-target kinase classification models for prospective selectivity optimization and (ii) 108 NSCLC cell-line phenotype classification models to estimate cellular efficacy. This approach was intended to address the practical reality that target potency alone does not guarantee therapeutic success.

Realized workflow of potency-focused optimization (PFO) and polypharmacological multi-parameter optimization (PMPO) reinforcement learning approaches with identical downstream selection logic

Both approaches employed identical downstream filtering and prioritization workflows, enabling a direct comparison of their outputs. This design was intended to distinguish the efficiency of potency-focused progression from the broader property control achieved with the extended multi-parameter framework.

Compounds were ultimately selected for synthesis from the PFO campaign on the basis of predicted target potency, favorable drug-likeness metrics, and moderate structural novelty relative to known RET inhibitor scaffolds, enabling experimental validation of the computational methodology.

To develop a regression model for the G810R mutation of the proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase (RET), datasets were selected from BindingDB [34] and ExCAPE-DB [35] (Table1). All RETG810Rbioactivity data were sourced exclusively from patent publications originating from a single pharmaceutical company (Array BioPharma Inc.), so that the IC50measurements were generated under identical assay protocols and experimental conditions. This uniform data source eliminates the inter-laboratory variability and methodological inconsistencies commonly encountered in multi-source datasets compiled from diverse literature sources, thereby minimizing systematic errors that would otherwise require complex normalization procedures. Dataset preprocessing was carried out with RDKit [36] and included duplicate removal, SMILES canonicalization, salt stripping, and molecule neutralization. Structures yielding invalid SMILES after standardization were excluded. After preprocessing, a structurally dataset comprising 870 molecules with bioactivity (pIC50) data was obtained for regression model development. As shown in Fig.3a and b, the dataset exhibit substantial representation across the entire activity range. Additional details on dataset are provided in Figure S1 andS2.

Dataset description of this study.apIC50 (M) Distribution of RETG810Rinhibitors.bt-SNE visualization of chemical space diversity for RETG810Rinhibitors (Clusters 0–5).cPreparation  of the off-target dataset (n = 94,213 unique compounds after staged filtering).dPreparation procedure of phenotype dataset from Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) database (108 NSCLC cell lines, 429 drugs, 41,352 compound-cell line observations)

For polypharmacological multi-parameter optimization, additional classification models were developed. Off-target kinase classification models utilized 188,217 raw compound-target pairs (after excluding RET data from 196,531 total entries) as the initial input; after staged cleaning, including exact deduplication, invalid SMILES removal, and stereo-insensitive deduplication (InChIKey first block), the final training set comprised 94,213 unique compounds (Tables S1–S2) from BindingDB [34] across 23 kinases associated with binding affinities (pIC50) (Fig.3c). NSCLC phenotype classification models were trained on 41,352 compound-cell line observations (429 drugs × 108 NSCLC cell lines) from the CancerRXGene database [37] (Table1, Table S1 and Fig.3d). Table S1 and Figures S3 and Figure S4 provide detailed information on the dataset curation workflows. All classification datasets were preprocessed with the same RDKit-based workflow used for the regression dataset, including duplicate removal, SMILES canonicalization, salt stripping, and molecule neutralization.

For training the generative model, data exclusively from ChEMBL-DB version 31 [38] (Table1) was utilized. Preprocessing followed the standard REINVENT 3.2 protocol with RDKit [26,52] and included SMILES canonicalization, salt stripping, molecule neutralization, and removal of stereochemical information (isomericSmiles=False). Stereochemistry was omitted so that prior training focused on constitutional molecular structure and general SMILES syntax. Because REINVENT 3.2 was used in its standard non-stereochemical configuration, stereochemical information was removed during preprocessing to maintain a consistent token vocabulary and focus training on constitutional SMILES grammar. Additionally, molecules with SMILES strings longer than 200 characters were excluded. The dataset was filtered based on several structural and chemical criteria, including number of atoms (6 ≤ num_atoms ≤ 70), number of rings (num_rings ≤ 10), largest ring size (size_largest_ring < 9), longest aliphatic carbon chain (longest_aliph_c_chain < 6), carbon atom ratio (c_atom_ratio ≥ 0.5), token count (num_tokens ≤ 100), and exclusion of tokens appearing in less than 5% of the dataset[28]. This token-frequency filter removes only very rare bracket tokens, such as unusual isotopic or coordination notations that can destabilize sequence generation, while leaving standard organic chemistry tokens unaffected. This resulted in a final dataset of 2,047,768 molecules.

To develop a robust regression model for RETG810Rinhibitor prediction, a systematic evaluation was conducted across multiple machine learning algorithms, molecular representations, and data partitioning strategies using the curated dataset of 870 molecules. Three regression algorithms were assessed: Random Forest [39], ExtraTrees [40], and ElasticNet [41], each representing different ensemble and regularization approaches. Four molecular fingerprint representations were examined: Avalon [36], Extended Connectivity Fingerprint (ECFP) [42], ECFP count vectors [42], and Molecular ACCess System (MACCS) keys [43], all compatible with the REINVENT scoring framework. To ensure model robustness and generalizability, four data partitioning strategies were implemented: random splitting for baseline performance assessment, Butina clustering-based splitting to evaluate performance on structurally dissimilar molecules, scaffold-based splitting to test generalization to novel chemical scaffolds [36], and UMAP-based clustering to assess performance across chemical space clusters [44]. Evaluation across all model combinations (Fig.4, Figure S5-S7 and TableS3) showed that Random Forest with ECFP Count fingerprints gave the best performance under random splitting (test R2= 0.591, RMSE = 0.408). Because the different splitting schemes evaluate different aspects of model behavior, their metrics are not directly comparable: random splitting reflects interpolation within known chemical space, whereas scaffold- and cluster-based splits assess extrapolation to structurally distinct compounds [45]. The lower performance under scaffold-based and Butina cluster-based splitting therefore indicates the greater difficulty of generalizing to novel chemotypes, rather than model failure. For the RL production run, the random-split model was selected as a pragmatic choice to maximize coverage of the available active chemical space.

To enable polypharmacological multi-parameter reinforcement learning, additional predictive models were developed. The 23 off-target kinase models and 108 NSCLC cell-line models were trained independently as single-task binary classifiers, with one model for each target. This design was chosen because data size and class balance varied markedly across targets, making joint multi-task training less suitable without substantial recalibration. Independent training also allowed the optimal algorithm-fingerprint combination to be selected for each target separately, improving per-target AUC. Binary classification was used because activity labels are less sensitive than continuous pIC50values to inter-assay variability in heterogeneous multi-target and multi-cell-line datasets.

1. Off-Target Kinase Classification Models.Twenty-three classification models were trained to predict activity against kinases associated with clinical toxicities (JAK1/2/3, TYK2, ABL1, PI3K-α/δ/γ, RAF/MAPK kinases, and others) [46,47]. Multiple machine learning algorithms and molecular fingerprints were systematically evaluated across random, scaffold-based, and cluster-based data partitioning strategies. As in the regression workflow, the random-split model was selected for production, whereas scaffold-based and cluster-based splits were retained as more stringent indicators of generalization [45]. Output probability values (0–1) indicate predicted activity, where lower values represent selectivity for RET. Across all split strategies and 23 kinase targets, the mean test AUC was 0.799 (per-strategy mean AUC: Random 0.893, Scaffold 0.856, Butina 0.771, UMAP-cluster 0.675), above the 0.70 utility threshold;  the models were therefore used in the RL workflow. Figure5, Figure S8-S10 and Table S4 present the comprehensive model evaluation and selection process.
