2. NSCLC Phenotype Classification Models.One hundred eight classification models were trained on NSCLC cell-line viability data to predict cellular efficacy. Multiple machine learning algorithms and molecular fingerprints were systematically evaluated using random, scaffold-based, and cluster-based data partitioning strategies. The random-split configuration was also used for RL integration, while scaffold-based and cluster-based splits were retained as stricter assessments of generalization [45]. Output probability values (0–1) indicate predicted anti-cancer activity, with higher values representing greater cellular efficacy. Figure6, Figure S11–S14 and Table S5 present the comprehensive model evaluation, generalization assessment, and selection process. To interpret these results, it is important to consider the impact of class imbalance across the NSCLC phenotype datasets. Because class balance varied substantially, threshold-dependent metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 vary substantially across cell lines and are more sensitive to inter-cell-line differences in class balance than AUC [48,49]. AUC was therefore used as the primary criterion for model selection, as it evaluates ranking performance independently of the classification threshold and is less sensitive to class imbalance [50,51]. Accuracy was not used as the principal metric because it can be inflated by correct assignment of the majority inactive class [48], as reflected in the metric distributions shown in Fig.6d. This approach is consistent with established practice for imbalanced cheminformatics classification tasks [52,53]. Models were trained using a Z-score threshold of 0 on the NSCLC training dataset (429 drugs × 108 cell lines), yielding a mean test AUC of 0.550 across all configurations (Fig.6, Table S6). GDSC drug-sensitivity data are characterized by substantial class imbalance, with drug-sensitive cell lines accounting for approximately 10% of observations in the full GDSC database [54] (our NSCLC Z = 0 subset: mean 37.6%; Table S10). Following established practice in GDSC drug-sensitivity modelling, where class imbalance is commonly addressed through sample reweighting [54,55], models were also trained with class-frequency inverse weights (sklearn sample_weight = 'balanced'). This yielded a mean test AUC of 0.552 (ΔAUC =  + 0.002, ΔMCC =  + 0.003; Table S6, Figure S15 and S16), indicating only a marginal improvement and no material change in model performance. Methods that combine cell-line genomic features with drug fingerprints, including gene expression, mutation status, and copy number variation, consistently outperform fingerprint-only approaches in GDSC modelling [55,56,57]. This indicates that chemical structure alone does not capture sufficient molecular context for reliable phenotypic prediction. Applicability domain filtering was applied using the CLASS-LAG method [58], which assigns each test compound a confidence score of min(p, 1 − p) from a per-cell-line Random Forest trained on AVALON fingerprints. Restricting predictions to the 20% most chemically confident compounds increased the mean AUC from 0.561 to 0.585 (+ 0.024) for the unweighted model and from 0.554 to 0.584 (+ 0.029) for the weighted model (Table S7); the unweighted model reached 0.674 at 1–2% coverage (gain: + 0.113; Table S7, Figure S17) and 0.616 at 10% coverage (+ 0.055); the weighted model reached a best AUC of 0.710 at 3% coverage (Table S7). Extending this analysis to a 12-model consensus ensemble (AVALON, ECFP, MACCS × RF, LR, SVM, XGBoost; Table S8), the CLASS-LAG method applied to the weighted ensemble reached a mean AUC of 0.769 at 1–2% coverage, exceeding the 0.70 practical-utility threshold for that structurally confident subset; the unweighted CONS-STD-PROB reached 0.692 at 1–2% coverage (+ 0.133 over baseline). These results show that the phenotype model contains discriminative signal within a narrow applicability domain (top 1–3% most structurally representative predictions), supporting its use as a confidence-weighted filter in the PMPO generative workflow. At broader coverage levels (> 5%), AUC values converged toward the global baseline, consistent with a tight structural boundary on predictive reliability. CONS-STD restriction provided no improvement over the ensemble baseline of 0.560, indicating that model instability was not the primary cause of the global performance limitation. Models trained at a stricter Z-score threshold (Z ≤  − 0.75; ~ 13% sensitive, weighted) yielded a mean test AUC of 0.559 (Figure S18 and Table S9), confirming that model performance was insensitive to the labelling threshold. AUC showed no significant correlation with class balance across cell lines (Pearson r =  − 0.137, p = 0.16; per-cell-line active fractions in Table S10; correlation statistics in Supplementary Note 1). A weak positive correlation between training set size and mean cell-line AUC was detected (r =  + 0.197, p = 0.04; Supplementary Note 1), but it explained only 3.9% of AUC variance. Together with the variance decomposition in Supplementary Note 1, these results suggest that 2D fingerprints do not contain enough information to model cell-line-specific drug response reliably. We therefore treated the phenotype models as a workflow-level PMPO component rather than as validated predictors of phenotypic activity; with a mean test AUC of approximately 0.55, they should not be interpreted as reliable guides for phenotypic optimization. Supplementary Note 1 provides the diagnostic analysis supporting this interpretation and indicates that future phenotype models should incorporate cell-line genomic or transcriptomic features.

The generative model was based on the REINVENT framework, using a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture. Prior model training used an initial learning rate of 5 × 10–4, with adaptive decay (gamma = 0.8), a minimum learning rate of 1 × 10–5, early stopping with a patience of 8 epochs, a batch size of 128, and maximum of 100 epochs. SMILES augmentation was applied throughout training (randomize=True), allowing each molecule to be presented as a different valid SMILES string across epochs [28]. In combination with early stopping, this strategy reduces memorization of fixed token sequences, limits model overfitting, and promotes learning of broader structural syntax.

The REINVENT framework was then used for reinforcement learning with two distinct scoring-function configurations (Table2). In this policy-based reinforcement learning approach, the generative model is optimized to maximize a composite reward function [28]. As summarized in Fig.7, the architecture combines dedicated scoring heads for docking, drug-target affinity (DTA) prediction, and molecular filters with an experience buffer that tracks molecular history and diversity metrics. The component scores are combined through weighted fusion to generate the reward signal that guides policy optimization.

For PFO campaigns, the composite scoring function used the weighted product formulation (custom_product), corresponding to Eq.4of the REINVENT scoring framework [28];

where\({p}_{i}\left(x\right)\)represents the score of componenti(RETG810Rregression, QED, docking scores), for molecule x,\({w}_{i}\)is the weight corresponding to componenti, and\(S\left(x\right)\)is the final composite score guiding molecular generation. This formulation computes a weighted geometric mean of all component scores, normalized by the sum of weights. For PMPO campaigns, component scores were instead combined via the weighted sum (custom_sum), corresponding to Eq. 5 of the REINVENT scoring framework [28], in which each transformed score was multiplied by its weight and the results were divided by the sum of all component weights, yielding a weighted arithmetic mean.

The weighted sum (Eq.5) differs from the weighted product (Eq.4) in that a low score on one component can be offset by higher scores on others, so no single objective is strictly enforced. This is a known limitation relative to the product formulation, in which low scores penalize the total reward through the geometric mean and all criteria must be at least partially satisfied simultaneously. The weighted sum was used in the PMPO campaigns and this trade-off should be considered when interpreting the results; future implementations should evaluate the weighted product to achieve stricter per-component enforcement.

A mutant-specific regression model was employed to predict the bioactivity of generated SMILES strings during the reinforcement learning. This model utilized features derived from extended-connectivity fingerprint (ECFP) counts [42], with radius of 3 and fingerprint length of 2048 bits. A sigmoid transformation was applied to scale the predicted bioactivity values.

The QED score [59] was calculated to assess the drug-likeness using the RDKit library with values ranging from 0 to 1 (higher values indicating a greater drug-likeness).

Custom structural alerts were included in the RL scoring function to penalize molecules containing moieties associated with acute toxicity, chemical reactivity, or irreversible covalent binding. Fourteen SMARTS-based alert patterns were used in two categories: macrocycle exclusion (8–17 membered rings) and reactive or electrophilic functional groups (13 patterns), including peroxides, disulfides, carbocations, hydrazine-type N–N bonds, anhydrides, and heteroatom-flanked sp3 carbons associated with undesirable reactivity or metabolic instability [60]. The full SMARTS definitions and structural descriptions are provided in Table S11.

The REINVENT diversity filter [28] (IdenticalMurckoScaffold; minscore=0.4, minsimilarity=0.4, nbmax=25) was applied during training to discourage repeated scaffold generation, reinforcing only molecules that exceeded the total reward threshold across all campaigns.

To bias the generative model toward biologically relevant regions of chemical space, inception (experience replay) memory was employed using three curated subsets: (1) 70 selpercatinib-like molecules representing known hinge-binding chemotypes; (2) high-affinity RET inhibitors with pIC50≥ 8.0, and (3) 249 structurally diverse RET inhibitors including selpercatinib and vepafestinib analogs. These compounds were pre-validated to achieve high scores across both experimental and predicted metrics, ensuring they were retained within the inception memory.

Three docking programs were utilized at two distinct and non-overlapping stages: Schrodinger's Glide [61], OpenEye's Hybrid Docking tools [62], and Autodock Vina [63]. Molecules were prepared using LigPrep [64], from the Schrodinger2020-4 suite. The RET kinase structure (PDB ID 7JU6) [65], was prepared using the Protein Preparation Wizard [66]. For the RETG810Rmutant, the Residue and Loop Mutation tool was used to mutate glycine  810 with arginine with local minimization for residues within 5.0 Å of the mutation site.

Docking role assignments:Docking was used at two distinct stages. During RL training, OpenEye Hybrid docking (Chemgauss4) was included only in PFO-JOB05, and AutoDock Vina [63] only in PMPO-JOB05, to test the effect of a structure-based docking term within the reward function. In all other campaigns, docking was not part of the RL reward. During post-generation filtering, Glide XP [61] was applied uniformly to all ten campaigns as a ligandability screen, and the OpenEye Hybrid score (threshold <  − 10.0 kcal/mol) was used as part of the Stage 2 activity filter for PFO-JOB05. These downstream docking criteria were applied sequentially as independent pass/fail filters.

A filtering strategy was applied based on hinge-binding interactions and scaffold-based patentability analysis. Hinge-binding core motifs were evaluated for potential to form key hydrogen bonds with the kinase hinge region, specifically targeting backbone atoms of residue A807. Fused ring systems containing hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA) functionalities appropriately oriented toward the hinge were prioritized, while molecules bearing sterically bulky substituents at this position were excluded. To assess scaffold novelty and reduce redundancy with known kinase chemotypes, Bemis-Murcko scaffold analysis was performed and compared against a curated set of known hinge-binding cores. Scaffolds with TC = 1.0 relative to any reference core were excluded as structurally identical to known chemotypes.

Generated molecules were screened against ADME and PAINS [29] criteria: Molecular Weight > 700; SlogP within 1.5—6.5; NumLipinskiHBD ≤ 5; Hydrogen Bond Acceptors ≤ 14; Rotatable Bonds ≤ 15; Heavy Atoms between 15—55.

In-house convolutional neural network (CNN) [33] and machine learning models [32] were employed to predict the binding affinity of the selected molecules. The models were rigorously trained and validated on diverse datasets, enabling reliable generalization to unseen molecules.

Biochemical kinase inhibition assays were performed by Reaction Biology Corporation (Pennsylvania, USA) using three recombinant RET kinase constructs: wild-type RET (RETWT), the gatekeeper mutant (RETV804M), and the solvent-front mutant (RETG810R). All assays were conducted in a cell-free system in the presence of ATP (10 µM). For IC50determination, compounds were evaluated in duplicate across a 10-point, threefold serial dilution series with a maximum concentration of 10 µM. In addition, percent residual kinase activity was measured at a single concentration (1 µM, duplicate) for preliminary inhibition assessment. A pan-kinase inhibitor was included as a positive control to verify assay performance. Reported IC50values represent the mean of duplicate measurements. Measurements were performed in duplicate (n = 2), and SEM values should therefore be interpreted as minimum estimates of variability; independent confirmation of the reported potency values is recommended as part of future validation work. Detailed synthetic procedures and assay protocols are described in the associated patent application [67].

Figure2summarizes the de novo design strategy used to generate RET inhibitor candidates through potency-focused optimization (PFO) and polypharmacological multi-parameter optimization (PMPO). For both approaches, the REINVENT prior was first trained on approximately 2.3 million molecules from ChEMBL DB [38], yielding a SMILES validity rate of approximately 98% at a learning rate of 3.2 × 10–4 (Figure S19 and Figure S20). Reinforcement learning was then performed with two distinct scoring-function configurations. In the PFO setting, the  reward function incorporated (i) an in-house regression model for RETG810RpIC50prediction, (ii) a docking score from the RET-specific DockStream pipeline [68], (iii) a QED score, and (iv) custom alert filters. In the PMPO setting, the reward further incorporated (v) 23 off-target kinase classification models and (vi) 108 NSCLC-focused phenotype classification models.

Inception memory was used to bias the generative model toward biologically relevant regions of chemical space [28], whereas scaffold novelty was enforced later through Bemis-Murcko scaffold analysis and Tanimoto similarity-based exclusion. The parameter settings used for RL-based molecule generation are listed in Tables S12 and S13. As shown in Figure S21, approximately 89% of RL runs achieved 100% validity, with an additional 7.7% reaching 99% validity (PFO-JOB01), indicating that the generative model consistently produced chemically valid structures.

To compare the PFO and PMPO strategies systematically, five parallel RL campaigns were conducted under each approach with different scoring-function parameterizations (Table3). This setup allowed the influence of the optimization objective on the quantity, quality, and diversity of the generated molecules to be examined directly.

The five PFO and five PMPO campaigns were run with distinct hyperparameter and scoring-function settings (Table3), including different combinations of QED, HBA, HBD, SlogP, custom alerts, and, in one campaign for each strategy, an in-RL docking term. These campaigns were intended to sample the effect of different reward formulations on the quantity and character of the generated molecules rather than to serve as strict replicate runs. Molecules from each campaign were first processed through the same downstream filtering cascade independently (Stages 2–5, Fig.2), after which the surviving candidates from all five campaigns within each strategy were considered together.

The quantity and quality of generated molecules depended strongly on both hyperparameter settings and optimization objectives. Comparison of prior-generated molecules with those generated after reinforcement learning showed that incorporation of the in-house scoring models, particularly the RETG810Rregression and docking term, improved the quality of the RL-generated molecules (Figure S22). Under comparable settings, PMPO campaigns also tended to generate more molecules than PFO campaigns (e.g., PMPO-Job1: 351,396 vs. PFO-Job1: 9,888), likely because the multi-dimensional reward landscape provides more routes to favorable scores. All RL-generated molecules were then passed through the same sequential filtering cascade (i) predicted activity threshold (pIC50> 7.0 and Hybrid Score < –10.0) together with hinge-binder requirements, (ii) docking-based ligandability screening (Glide GScore ≤ –8.0), (iii) physicochemical property and PAINS filtering, (iv) Tanimoto similarity-based filtering against a reference set of 49 known kinase inhibitor hinge-binding cores, excluding molecules with identical hinge-binding motifs (TC = 1.0), and (v) final activity threshold refinement (pIC50> 7.4).

The filtering analysis highlights several differences between the two strategies (Fig.8): (1)Generation-to-Final Attrition:PMPO campaigns showed higher attrition rates (e.g., PMPO-Job1: 351,396 → 3; 99.999% reduction) compared to PFO campaigns (PFO-Job1: 9,888 → 7; 99.93% reduction), consistent with the stricter constraints imposed by simultaneous optimization of potency, selectivity, and phenotype. (2)Final candidate yield:Across the five campaigns, PFO yielded 1,270 final candidates, whereas PMPO campaigns yielded 35, indicating that the expanded objective set substantially narrowed the accessible chemical space. (3)Parameter sensitivity:Among the tested parameterizations, the “QED + Regression Model” configuration (Job1) gave the most efficient campaign behavior for both strategies, with the lowest overall reduction rates.

Among the regression-guided PFO campaigns (JOB01–04, n = 221), the predicted pIC50averaged 7.56 ± 0.09, comparable to 7.03 ± 0.03 for the PMPO set, indicating that multi-parameter optimization maintains target potency while incorporating additional selectivity and phenotype constraints. Tanimoto coefficient analysis showed that the two strategies sampled chemical space in different ways (Fig.9, Table S14). PFO campaigns covered a broader similarity range to the reference hinge-binding cores (mean range: 0.125–0.498, CV: 0.407), whereas PMPO campaigns were more concentrated within a moderate-similarity regime (mean range: 0.401–0.568, CV: 0.140). Most PFO campaigns showed negative skewness (4/5 campaigns: JOB01 =  − 0.156, JOB02 =  − 0.910, JOB03 =  − 0.346, JOB04 =  − 1.243), indicating molecules clustering toward higher similarity despite explicit novelty control, whereas PFO-JOB05 was strongly positively skewed (+ 1.685) and produced  82.59% of molecules with Tanimoto < 0.30, indicating a structurally distinct set of molecules. By contrast, most PMPO campaigns showed positive skewness (4/5 campaigns: JOB01 = 0.480, JOB02 =  + 1.141, JOB04 =  + 1.142, JOB05 =  + 0.399), consistent with more consistent sampling in the moderate-novelty range (0.30–0.60).Table S15and Table S16 summarize the Morgan fingerprint [42] Tanimoto similarities between generated scaffolds and the reference kinase cores.

The Tanimoto coefficient distributions calculated against the 49 known hinge-binding cores (Fig.9c and f) were used as a heuristic measure of structural distance from established RET inhibitor chemotypes. Under this analysis, PFO-JOB01 molecules were primarily distributed within a moderate similarity range to known cores (42.9% with Tanimoto 0.30–0.45 and 57.1% with Tanimoto 0.45–0.60), with no candidate exceeding Tanimoto 0.60. In contrast, 33.3% of PMPO-JOB01 candidates showed Tanimoto values above 0.60, indicating somewhat greater overlap with known scaffolds. These distributions suggest that the two optimization strategies sampled partially overlapping but distinct regions of RET inhibitor scaffold space.

Because the QSAR models used during RL were trained on whole-molecule representations, assessing proximity to their training domain requires full-molecule rather than fragment-level comparison. Accordingly, the Tanimoto similarity distributions were computed for all 9,888 molecules generated in PFO-JOB01 against RETWTand RETG810Rinhibitor reference sets at the whole-molecule level (Figure S23). Both distributions peaked in the TC = 0.20–0.40 range (KLD = 0.503), indicating that the generated molecules, while structurally novel, remained within the broader chemical neighborhood of known RET inhibitors throughout the generation process [70].

Murcko scaffold decomposition further showed that the quinoxaline core emerged independently in all five PFO campaigns and in three of the five PMPO campaigns despite differences in starting points and reward parameterization (Fig.9c and f, Table3). This recurrent appearance suggests that the quinoxaline framework occupies a favorable region of RET-focused chemical space under multiple optimization settings. Fisher's exact test supported significant over-representation of this scaffold class relative to random expectation (p < 0.001).

PMPO reinforcement learning (N = 35, five campaigns) maintained predicted RETG810Rpotency while improving the kinase selectivity profile; the NSCLC phenotype component was analyzed as an exploratory workflow-level signal because of its limited predictive performance. All molecules remained within the high predicted RETG810Rpotency range (mean pIC50: 7.03 ± 0.03, 100% ≥ 7.0), comparable to the PFO set (7.6 ± 0.09), demonstrating that multi-parameter optimization preserves primary target engagement (Fig.10). Integration of the 23-kinase classification models encompassing toxicity-associated families (JAK, ABL, PI3K, RAF/MAPK) achieved favorable selectivity profiles, with 77% meeting the off-target probability threshold (≤ 0.3, mean: 0.276 ± 0.039, Fig.10a). This threshold was used as a conservative prioritization threshold to favour candidates with lower predicted off-target probabilities. It was not derived from the distribution of the evaluated candidates themselves. Retrospectively, the value of 0.3 lies below the Youden's J optimal probability threshold for all 23 off-target kinase classifiers (mean Youden point = 0.503 ± 0.075, range 0.360–0.690; ECFP_COUNT + RandomForest). This provides a model-derived, non-circular basis for using 0.3 as a conservative operating point: at this threshold, the classifiers achieve a mean sensitivity of 94.5% (94.5% of genuinely off-target-active compounds are correctly flagged) and a mean negative predictive value (NPV) of 93.5% (93.5% of compounds passing the filter are truly inactive on the off-target panel), with lower specificity (76.7%). Nevertheless, this threshold is not a priori validated selectivity boundary; experimental profiling against the full kinase panel would be required for definitive validation. The 108 NSCLC cell-line models were also evaluated within the PMPO reward as an exploratory phenotype component. All molecules exceeded the phenotype threshold of ≥ 0.3 (mean: 0.338 ± 0.016; Fig.10b). However, because these models showed near-random predictive performance (mean AUC ≈0.55; Fig.6d), mainly reflecting the limited information content of 2D fingerprints relative to cell-line biology, this component provided limited phenotypic information. The phenotype threshold was therefore treated as an exploratory workflow-level readout rather than as a validated measure of cellular efficacy or on-target mechanism. All 35 PMPO candidates exceeded the exploratory phenotype threshold. Considering potency and off-target selectivity as the validated predictive objectives, 77% (27/35) of PMPO molecules met both criteria, and 77.1% exhibited novel core scaffolds (Table4).

We compared PFO and PMPO strategies by retrospectively evaluating the PFO molecules (N = 1,270) with multi-kinase classifiers and phenotype models, and contrasting those results with the prospectively generated PMPO set (N = 35) (Fig.11). The retrospective PFO evaluation revealed substantial multi-parameter performance despite RET-only optimization: max off-target selectivity 0.686 ± 0.126, phenotypic activity 0.945 ± 0.093, with 16.5% achieving good selectivity (≤ 0.5) and 90.6% high phenotype (≥ 0.9). PMPO optimization produced moderate improvements: selectivity 0.555 ± 0.084 (19.2% better, p < 0.0001), phenotype 0.969 ± 0.053 (+ 2.5%, p = 0.54), with 54.3% meeting selectivity criteria. Both maintained comparable RET activity (SMPLIP: PFO 7.74 ± 0.34 vs PMPO 7.39 ± 0.44; ChargeNET: PFO 7.52 ± 0.52 vs PMPO 8.09 ± 0.68).  Campaign-level analysis revealed PFO variability (selectivity CV: 16.5%) versus PMPO consistency (CV: 5.1%), validating feasibility of the simplified approach. This comparison establishes that potency-focused optimization provides practical lead generation with acceptable multi-parameter performance, while PMPO offers enhanced consistency for applications requiring stringent selectivity control at increased computational investment.

The generated compound set from PFO-JOB01 was examined systematically to identify candidates for experimental validation. Property distributions were examined following application of a stepwise filtering cascade, including hinge binder requirements and predicted pIC50thresholds (Figure S24). To ensure developability and patentability, stringent selection criteria were applied: (1) predicted inhibitory potency against RETG810R(pIC50≥ 7.4) and (2) structural specificity for the kinase hinge region, evaluated using a hinge-core filter based on experimentally characterized motifs [69,71,72] (Fig.12). Bemis-Murcko scaffold analysis identified seven molecules representing three unique core scaffolds (Table5), all of which showed limited similarity to known scaffolds. Among the analyzed cores, CORE2-based molecules gave the highest predicted binding affinities (SMPLIP-Score: 8.188; ChargeNET: 8.230), although synthesis assessment suggested increased chemical complexity. In contrast, CORE3-based molecules demonstrated favorable docking profiles while maintaining established synthetic feasibility. CORE3 (aminoquinoxaline, represented by RL-1185) was ultimately selected based on: (1) scaffold convergence across PFO-JOBS; (2) competitive activity across models (SMPLIP: 7.36, ChargeNET: 8.12, RETG810R: 7.45); (3) optimal Tanimoto similarity (0.579); (4) favorable docking with predicted hinge hydrogen bonding (Ala807, 2.2 Å); and (5) synthetic tractability. The complete selection cascade is summarized inTable S17. Briefly, PFO-JOB01 candidates were first reduced from 1,270 to 49 molecules using the predicted pIC50threshold and hinge-binding core requirement, then to 17 structurally distinct candidates after Tanimoto filtering against known kinase hinge-binding cores. Bemis-Murcko clustering grouped these candidates into three scaffold families, from which seven representatives were evaluated using the three DTA models. CORE3 was selected on the basis of scaffold convergence, predicted affinity, Tanimoto novelty, docking geometry, and synthetic tractability. Two CORE3 analogs, RL-1185-a and RL-1185-b, were synthesized to examine the effect of the C-6 ethylamino versus amino substituent.

PMPO campaigns produced 35 candidates spanning 19 unique scaffolds, with successful multi-dimensional optimization, including a maximum multi-Kinase selectivity score of 0.7, and phenotype probability of 1.0 (Fig.13and Table S16). These structurally novel candidates, however, would require dedicated synthetic campaigns and are therefore positioned for follow-up validation after the PFO proof-of-concept. This staged strategy reflects practical resource constraints: synthesis-tractable PFO candidates were prioritized for initial validation, whereas PMPO candidates remain reserved for subsequent optimization studies.

Using the CORE3 scaffold, two optimized analogs (RL-1185-a,RL-1185-b) were designed to enhance binding with wild-type RET (RETWT) and clinically relevant solvent-front mutant RETG810R.

Glide XP docking indicated both molecules adopted binding poses resembling those of the clinically used RET inhibitors selpercatinib and pralsetinib, with engagement of both the hinge region and DFG loop (Fig.14). The aminoquinoxaline core formed hydrogen bonding with Ala807 (2.11 Å and 2.15 Å, respectively) together with π-cation interactions involving Lys758, and both molecules gave favorable docking scores (RL-1185-a: − 9.8 kcal/mol; RL-1185-b: − 10.2 kcal/mol). In the RETG810Rmodel, the Ala807 hydrogen-bonding interaction was retained (2.27 Å and 2.31 Å), suggesting that the compact scaffold can accommodate the steric effects of the Gly810 to Arg substitution without gross disruption of the binding pose.

Following computational analysis, RL-1185-a and RL-1185-b were synthesized and evaluated against the RET kinase family, including wild-type RET (RETWT) and clinically relevant drug-resistant mutants (RETG810Rand RETV804M) using the protocol described in the associated patent filing [67]. Initial screening at 1 µM showed strong inhibition by both compounds. RL-1185-a gave residual activities of 0.14% for RETWT, 11.37% for RETG810R, and 0.63% for RETV804M, whereas RL-1185-b gave 0.51%, 24.47%, and 1.72%, respectively. Full dose–response analysis confirmed the potency of both compounds (Fig.14c,andd). RL-1185-a showed sub-nanomolar activity against RETWT(IC50= 0.52 ± 0.05 nM) and RETV804M(IC50= 0.78 ± 0.10 nM) while maintaining nanomolar activity against RETG810R(IC50= 142 ± 10 nM). RL-1185-b was less potent overall but showed the same rank order of activity, with IC50values of 3.93 ± 0.15 nM, 4.21 ± 0.31 nM, and 275 ± 1 nM against RETWT, RETV804M, and RETG810R, respectively. Values are reported as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) from duplicate experiments (n = 2).

Structurally, RL-1185-a and RL-1185-b share the same quinoxaline core and differ only at the C-6 position, where RL-1185-a bears an ethylamino (–NHCH2CH3) substituent and RL-1185-b bears a primary amino (–NH2) group. Docking analysis indicated that both compounds adopt closely related poses within the ATP-binding pocket of RETWT(Fig.14), including a key hydrogen bond to the hinge region residue A807 (2.11 Å). In the RETG810Rmutant model (Fig.14b), this hydrogen bonding interaction was preserved (2.27 Å), although the solvent-front (G810R) substitution likely contributes to the reduced potency observed experimentally. Both compounds nevertheless retained strong activity against the gatekeeper mutant RETV804M, indicating favorable accommodation within the modified binding site.

A central challenge in AI-driven de novo design is navigating the inherent trade-off between structural novelty and the predictive reliability of the underlying models [73]. While excessive out-of-domain generation can lead to unreliable artifacts, stifling exploration hinders the discovery of truly novel chemotypes [28]. To achieve a dynamic equilibrium between structural novelty and predictive reliability, we implemented a multi-layered framework of technical safeguards throughout both the RL training and post-processing phases. By strategically initializing the replay buffer with curated RET active chemotypes and employing a performance-gated diversity filter, we effectively constrained the agent’s exploration to pharmacologically relevant regions of chemical space without stifling structural novelty. Specifically, the inclusion of high-affinity RET inhibitors (pIC₅₀ ≥ 8.0) and structurally diverse chemotypes, including clinical-stage inhibitors, within the replay buffer guided the generation of high-scoring compounds and promoted sampling within RET-relevant chemical space during learning [28,74,75]. Throughout the training, a performance-gated diversity filter was also applied to prioritize molecules with high total rewards, effectively acting as a practical constraint on the exploration of chemical space. Furthermore, our approach to stereochemistry and the use of randomized SMILES augmentation as a rigorous overfitting control served to focus the model on learning generalizable structural syntax rather than memorizing specific token sequences. This strategy effectively prevented rote memorization, thereby enhancing the robustness and generalization of the generative prior. In summary, the integration of inception memory was designed for strict alignment with the reward function. The effectiveness of this approach was confirmed through empirical verification from RL outputs, which demonstrated that inception-derived compounds consistently occupied the targeted high-reward regimes. To address concerns regarding structural mimicry, a robust novelty safeguard was enforced by excluding any molecules with hinge cores identical to known reference scaffolds. These combined measures demonstrate that our workflow does not merely reproduce established inhibitors, but successfully navigates the tension between exploitation and exploration. Consequently, the final candidates represent structurally novel compounds that demonstrate both high predicted potency and computational reliability within the defined predictive domain. In summary, while no explicit applicability domain metric was used, our multi-layered approach provides a practical and rigorous solution to the problem of controlling  out-of-domain generation. As a result, highly potent and structurally innovative RL-1185 compounds were generated under the multi-layered framework within a statistically reliable predictive domain.

This study demonstrated that a multi-layered RL framework can support de novo drug design for RET alterations under implicit domain control through strategic use of inception memory and performance gating. Our two prospective multi-parameter optimization campaigns demonstrated that the off-target activity and phenotypic activity models were incorporated into the reward function without substantially compromising primary target potency. The kinase selectivity models provided the main validated multi-parameter signal (mean AUC = 0.799). Meanwhile, the NSCLC phenotypic models exhibited limited predictive performance, as 2D drug structural features accounted for only 3.7% of the phenotypic response variance. These phenotypic models served as exploratory baseline constraints rather than predictive signals. Downstream selection and experimental validation identified novel quinoxaline derivatives with potent inhibitory activities against multiple RET alterations. These results highlight the potential of this framework for application to other challenging oncological targets and biomarkers such as RET alterations.

title: Synthetic data for more accurate deep learning models in molecular science: a test case of protein-ligand binding affinity prediction
author: Prakul Agrawal; Prathit Chatterjee; U. Deva Priyakumar
text:
Deep learning models are data-hungry, and synthetic (artificial) data has been shown to be invaluable when data availability is low. While this has been demonstrated in certain technology areas, adopting such an approach is new in machine learning (ML) applications in chemistry, except for some pre-training tasks. In drug discovery, predicting binding energy between proteins and ligands is crucial. Many ML-based studies have been proposed to predict protein-ligand binding affinity using existing experimental data. However, these models suffer from inherent biases. Recent efforts have produced PLAS-20k, a synthetic dataset of multiple protein-ligand complex (PLC) conformations generated using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations as a viable option to complement existing experimental data and improve binding affinity prediction. For the binding affinity prediction task, we employ Pafnucy, a deep convolutional neural network, and propose using multiple structures for each PLC from PLAS-20k for training. We compare four different statistical and ML-based result-aggregation techniques. This work demonstrates the utility of dynamic datasets in enhancing binding affinity predictions, laying the foundation for future improvements in predicting similar protein properties using synthetic datasets and more sophisticated models and methods. We propose that physics-based synthetic datasets can significantly help develop more accurate data-driven methods.

Scientific contribution

This study shows that incorporating synthetic molecular dynamics data improves deep learning models for protein–ligand binding affinity prediction beyond static experimental structures. By systematically evaluating frame selection and prediction aggregation strategies, we demonstrate that training on diverse conformational snapshots significantly enhances generalization and accuracy. Our results highlight that dynamic synthetic datasets can enable deep learning models to outperform conventional methods such as MM-PBSA while remaining computationally efficient.

Deep learning (DL) has become an indispensable tool that enables learning patterns and deriving information from observations regarding various properties of the studied systems. However, DL models often require immense amounts of well-curated data to accurately grasp the properties they are being trained for and generalize effectively. Unfortunately, real-world data frequently presents challenges such as scarcity, human error, and subjectivity [1]. These issues with real-world datasets can lead to problems in developing and applying machine learning (ML) models. For instance, supervised learning for autonomous vehicles requires diverse datasets, and instance segmentation performance relies on a vast amount of well-annotated data [2,3]. It has been shown that these biased or low-data scenarios can be aided by using synthetic data. Synthetic or artificial data can be described as data that, instead of being recorded from purely natural observations, has been generated artificially using various algorithms or simulations to mimic a natural setting or help solve specific tasks [4,5]. Just as synthetic data can aid learning in areas such as computer vision, even in the fields of human analysis and health care, it can help meet the demand for large-scale and publicly available datasets [6,7]. However, synthetic data is less commonly utilized in fundamental sciences, with most of its usage being in pre-training various models [8,9,10,11]. As such, there is plenty of scope to leverage synthetic datasets in domains like molecular science, such as aiding in predicting protein-ligand binding affinity.

Identifying molecules that effectively bind to specific receptors is a pivotal challenge in drug design [12,13,14]. Protein-ligand interaction scoring functions, crucial for assessing the binding efficacy of various ligands with a given protein receptor binding pocket, directly impact the identification and optimization of potential therapeutic compounds [14,15,16,17,18,19,20]. Traditional physics-based approaches like molecular dynamics (MD) simulations [21,22] and enhanced sampling protocols such as replica-exchange MD (REMD) [23,24], random accelerated MD (RAMD) [25,26], umbrella sampling [27,28], steered MD [29,30], and metadynamics [31,32,33] have been widely used to calculate binding affinities of PLCs [34]. Besides these, more generalized computational approaches involve approximate methods like molecular-mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area (MM-PBSA) [14,35,36]. However, these methods can be computationally expensive and time-consuming, limiting their scalability for high-throughput screening exercises [37]. Simple scoring functions are typically used to virtually screen large libraries via docking; however, such methods are very approximate [38]. In recent years, ML-based scoring functions have been used in the hope that they will be more accurate and efficient [37,39].

ML and DL approaches have emerged as preferred tools for developing the scoring functions [37,40,41,42,43,44,45,46], leveraging publicly available protein-ligand binding affinity datasets [47,48] for accurate and faster predictions. However, despite the advancement of DL models in the drug design domain, it has been observed that the datasets used to train these models themselves harbor latent biases that impact their practical utility, particularly in virtual screening [49,50,51,52,53]. These biases have been systematically investigated, emphasizing the significance of accounting for sequence, protein-ligand interaction, and pocket structure similarities when constructing data splits. The analysis also sheds light on the observed high performance of protein-only and ligand-only models in some datasets, indicating that the models were seemingly not learning the interactions between the ligands and proteins [49]. Another bottleneck in binding affinity prediction is that most datasets feature only the static structure of PLCs [54,55], while the actual affinities generally depend on protein-ligand thermodynamic ensembles. These challenges show that models developed based on limited experimental data are not robust. However, determining experimental binding affinities at a large scale involving diverse proteins/ligands is expensive, and increasing the size of the dataset is not feasible. Hence, synthetic data approaches could be employed to improve binding-affinity datasets, similar to how they are used in fields like computer vision [1].

MD data can be utilized as a viable source of synthetic data. Dynamic information captured by MD simulations can provide a more comprehensive representation of the binding process, improving prediction accuracy. The graph-based DL model Dynaformer utilized this fact and leveraged geometric features from MD trajectories to outperform static models [40]. Beyond direct supervised use of MD trajectories, the authors of ProtMD have also explored self-supervised pretraining approaches: an equivariant graph-matching network pretrained on MD trajectories via a prompt-based denoising task and a snapshot-ordering task, whose learned representations are subsequently linearly probed or fine-tuned for binding-affinity and ligand-efficacy prediction [56]. Recent studies have published systematically computed datasets such as PLAS-5k and PLAS-20k, comprising binding affinity derived from MM-PBSA of about 5000 and 20,000 PLCs, respectively, with trajectories obtained from MD simulations [55,57]. These datasets pave the way for utilizing the dynamic information of simulated trajectories for a heterogeneous and larger subset of existing PLCs to enhance the accuracy and generalizability of ML-aided binding affinity predictions. In our work, we utilize the Pafnucy model [58] and train it on about 6000 unique PLCs from the PLAS-20k dataset to examine one aspect of the dataset, which is the utility of the dynamic trajectories (synthetic data) to improve the model performance.

Our study demonstrates how using synthetic data from the MD simulations can improve the performance of ML models compared to static structures. We harness a deep convolutional neural network, Pafnucy, to predict the binding affinities of the PLCs. We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate different methods of selecting snapshots or frames from the available MD trajectories in PLAS-20k, assess the impact of varying the number of frames on prediction accuracy, and compare various aggregation techniques for combining predictions from multiple frames. Our results showcase a significant improvement in model performance upon training it on a larger number of frames per PLC with appropriate frame selection methods. These results suggest that incorporating dynamic data through simple data augmentation can significantly enhance the predictive power of DL models, providing a basis for future research in this area and exploring the possibilities of leveraging synthetic datasets in drug discovery and other ML tasks in fundamental sciences.

The PLAS-20k dataset is derived from MD simulations and offers an opportunity for integrating MD simulations with ML techniques [57]. With close to 19,500 protein-ligand structures, this dataset encompasses a wide range of PLCs. This information allows us to utilize the dynamic nature of biomolecular systems and incorporate a broader range of data in ML applications. The binding affinities reported in this dataset, computed with the MM-PBSA method and averaged over multiple simulation runs per PLC, are segregated into polar and non-polar components and accompanied by the respective MD trajectories. In addition to the PLAS-20k dataset, we also use the PDBBind dataset [19] to obtain the experimental (ground state) binding affinity of the selected PLCs.

The PLAS-20k dataset provides 200 frames (MD trajectory snapshots) generated through five independent MD simulation runs for each PLC. These 200 frames are drawn from the production phase of each MD run, after the system has undergone energy minimization and equilibration [55,57]. These frames are stored as PDB files containing the spatial coordinates for both protein and ligand structures. Since the Pafnucy model, which is being used for the binding affinity prediction task, also requires protonation states, partial charge information, and the separation of protein and ligand structures into individual files in MOL2 format, preprocessing of the data was required. We supplemented the protonation states and partial charge information by incorporating the PRMTOP parameter files of the PLCs, which also contained the connectivity, atom-type, and residue-type information, along with the corresponding PDB files. As the original PDB files store both protein and ligand structures in a single file, we separated these into distinct files. We utilized the VMD software [59] to achieve both of these tasks using TCL scripts, and for each PLC, we generated 200 MOL2 files for the protein structure and 200 MOL2 files for the ligand structure.

The PLAS-20k dataset reports the binding affinities in the units of kcal/mol. We converted the binding free energies to align with the Pafnucy model’s prediction of binding affinities in terms of\(-\log (K_d)\)using the Eq. [60]:

Here,\(K_d\)represents the dissociation constant for each PLC,\(R\)is the universal gas constant, and\(T\)denotes the absolute temperature in Kelvin.

The Pafnucy model utilizes 3D grids as input, with each grid point characterized by 19 atomic features. These features were computed from the MOL2 files using Open Babel [61] and thetfbio.datapackage [58]. The feature data and corresponding binding affinity labels were stored in HDF files to train the ML model. Approximately 6000 PLCs were selected for training and testing the model after the preprocessing stage. This subset corresponds to all PLAS-20k PLCs for which an experimental binding affinity was available in PDBBind (SectionDataset), as this is the ground-truth label used for supervised training. A list of the specific PLCs used is provided in our code repository for reproducibility.

As described in PLAS-5k and PLAS-20k studies [55,57], the initial system preparation involves the preparation of the complexes of proteins and ligands. While these complexes are further subjected to energy minimization, we train Pafnucy on these single-frame PLCs obtained before the energy minimization stage (essentially experimental structures) for the baseline model. This baseline could allow us to evaluate the effectiveness of the availability of multiple frames in improving the data quality.

In addition to the baseline DL model, we also utilize the MM-PBSA values (obtained by harnessing the Poisson-Boltzmann equation for depicting free energy differences between two states of a system [35]), available as part of the PLAS-20k dataset, for comparing the performance of our multi-frame approach.

As mentioned, the PLAS-20k dataset consists of 200 frames or snapshots obtained from the MD simulations for each PLC. While all of these frames can be used to train the Pafnucy model, training the model on all 200 frames is computationally expensive and time-consuming. Also, many snapshots may be closer in overall structure to each other. Therefore, we selected a smaller sample set from these 200 frames per PLC. In this study, we compare the effects of the number of frames chosen to train the model and the method used to choose these frames from all the available ones. Both the number of frames and the method of selection influence the diversity of the conformations captured by the model. We look at the different techniques of frame selection below.

In this method, we randomly select a specified number of frames from the total number of frames for each PLC. This way of randomly selecting a subset of frames does not impose any specific criteria for the selection. However, it provides no control over whether the chosen frames are similar to one another.

This method allows us to evaluate how a continuous selection of frames performs compared to more distributed frame selections by choosing the required quantity of frames from only the initial trajectory run corresponding to each PLC. However, it also suffers from not considering the possible diversity in the remaining frames.

In this approach, we select frames at uniform intervals across the 200 frames in order to capture a more representative set of frames. This could potentially help capture the overall distribution of conformations rather than focusing on one particular region of the trajectory. After determining the interval size, we select frames spaced by this interval, ensuring that the total number of selected frames does not exceed the predefined number per PLC.

This method uses clustering algorithms to group similar frames and choose frames from these clusters. For each PLC separately, we first compute the pairwise root mean square deviation (RMSD) of the coordinates across the 200 frames. Then, we use the K-medoids algorithm [62] on the resulting 200x200 matrix of pairwise RMSD values to cluster the frames. For our purposes, we find K-medoids to be more suitable than methods such as K-means [63], as the K-medoids algorithm selects actual data points as cluster centroids and is more robust to outliers [64]. Since the number of clusters is not predetermined, we use the silhouette-score metric to determine each PLC’s optimal number of clusters [65,66]. Once the clusters are formed, frames are arbitrarily chosen from within each cluster. The number of frames selected from each cluster is in proportion to the size of the cluster and the total number of frames decided to be chosen.

Pafnucy is a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) model consisting of 3-dimensional convolutional layers and fully connected dense layers, which is used to estimate the binding affinity of ligand-receptor complexes [58]. It represents each PLC as a 4D tensor containing the x, y, and z spatial coordinates and a vector of 19 features, such as atom type, hybridization, partial charge, etc. The input molecule first passes through three 3D convolutional layers, with 64, 128, and 256 filters combined with max-pooling layers. The output is then flattened and passed through three fully connected dense layers containing 1000, 500, and 200 neurons, respectively. A dropout rate of 0.5 is applied to all dense layers to prevent over-fitting. When tested on the PDBbind database v. 2016 core set [19], Pafnucy obtained a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 1.42 and a Pearson correlation of 0.78. The model also outperformed all 20 scoring functions provided by the CASF-2013 ‘scoring power’ benchmark [67].

Schematic diagram of the modified binding affinity prediction pipeline.AThe Pafnucy architecture serves as the primary deep convolutional neural network for predicting binding affinity.BDuring training, multiple frames from each PLC are provided as separate inputs to the model, which is trained to predict the same experimental binding affinity for all frames.CSubsequently, a feed-forward neural network is trained to aggregate the CNN outputs corresponding to each PLC.DOnce fully trained, the complete model can take multiple snapshots from a single PLC and, using a specified aggregation method, combine their predictions to produce a final binding affinity estimate

We utilized the Pafnucy model in our study to predict binding affinity values by feeding multiple frames of a PLC into the model instead of using a single frame. One can refer to Table3in Appendix B for the hyperparameters. We performed a 9:1 train-test split of the dataset. We ensured that there is no PLC overlap between the train and test sets, and that all frames belonging to a single PLC are assigned entirely to either the training or test set. This split is therefore performed at the protein–ligand complex (PLC) level. We note that a complex-level split does not by itself guarantee protein-level separation. Because the PLCs are drawn from PDBBind, which contains many complexes of the same protein bound to different ligands, a given protein sequence may appear (with different ligands) in both splits. Quantifying this, the mean of the per-protein maximum sequence identities between a test protein and the training set is 92.7%, and 77.5% of test proteins have an identical-sequence counterpart in the training set (full analysis in Appendix D). As shown in Appendix D (Fig.4), the improvement from multi-frame augmentation over the single-frame baseline is nonetheless preserved within every sequence-identity stratum, including test proteins with low identity (< 30%) to the training set. Therefore, the qualitative conclusions of this study are not an artifact of protein redundancy, although the absolute error values should be interpreted in light of it. For ligands, we observed a Jaccard similarity of only 0.035 between the training and testing sets. Each PLC was selected based on the number of frames and the selection method (SectionTrajectory frames), allowing for performance comparison across these different approaches.

As shown in Fig.1, basic data augmentation was applied for training by assigning the same binding affinity value corresponding to the reported experimental ground-truth to every frame of a given PLC. These frames were treated as independent molecular complexes when input into the architecture. This architecture then maps each frame individually to the specified binding affinity. For testing, we input the various frames of the complexes into the trained model. The model outputs a predicted binding affinity for each frame in terms of\(-\log (K_d)\). We then convert these values back to kcal/mol (Eq. (1), SectionData preparation). Since multiple frames were provided for each protein-ligand complex, we obtained several predicted values for each complex. To generate a single final prediction, we aggregated the results using methods such as Gaussian kernel density estimation, arithmetic mean, Bayesian Gaussian mixture models, and feed-forward neural networks (SectionPrediction aggregation). Following this, we evaluated model performance by calculating the mean squared error (MSE) and Pearson correlation coefficient (\(r_p\)) to assess accuracy.

Pafnucy (SectionPafnucy) was selected for this study as a simple, well-characterized architecture that lets us isolate the effect of the data pipeline (frame selection, frame count, aggregation) from architectural complexity, rather than for state-of-the-art performance. Several more recent architectures for this task are discussed in SectionIntroduction. To test whether the trends reported in SectionResults and discussiongeneralize beyond this specific architecture, we additionally trained and evaluated the Geometric Interaction Graph Neural Network (GIGN) model [68] using the same frame-selection and aggregation protocol on the same dataset. GIGN is a more recent graph neural network that explicitly encodes covalent/non-covalent interactions and is rotation/translation-invariant by construction. Full methodological details and hyperparameters (Table4) are presented in Appendix C. The purpose of this cross-architecture experiment is to test whether the qualitative trends associated with frame selection, frame count, and aggregation transfer to a structurally different model, not to maximize absolute predictive accuracy or to rank the two architectures against each other. As detailed in Appendix C, the two are trained under different protocols and their absolute error values are not directly comparable.

When multiple frames of the same protein-ligand complex are provided to the model, a predicted binding affinity for each frame is produced separately. As a result, multiple binding affinity predictions are made for the same complex. Therefore, we aggregated the predictions for each complex to produce a single output and evaluated the performance of three different aggregation methods, as discussed below.

Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) calculates the probability density function of a random variable by assigning a kernel to each data point. A kernel is a real-valued, non-negative function where the area under the curve equals one, and it is usually symmetric around the data point to which it is assigned. The estimated overall density is obtained by first summing the values of the kernels across the entire range of data and then normalizing the sum by the number of data points [69,70].

In Gaussian KDE, each kernel is modeled as a Gaussian function centered at the corresponding data point. A tunable parameter called the bandwidth controls the variance of these kernels.

Here,\(K(x)\)represents the overall KDE at point\(x\),\(\mathcal {K}\)is the Gaussian kernel,\(n\)is the number of data points, and\(h\)is the bandwidth.

In this study, we take the predicted binding affinities for each PLC and compute the Gaussian KDE for these predictions, as shown in Fig.2. Then, we select the binding affinity corresponding to the peak of this density estimate as the final binding affinity for each complex.

Calculating the arithmetic mean of the data points is a commonly used aggregation method. Using this standard method of central tendency, we aggregate the predicted binding affinities for each PLC by evaluating their unweighted arithmetic mean (Fig.2).

Here\(x_i\)represents the predicted binding affinity for the\(i\)-th selected frame, and\(n\)is the number of frames chosen for a given complex.

Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) assumes that all the data points are generated from a mixture of a finite number of Gaussian distributions to cluster points. Based on this assumption, it assigns a probability of belonging to a particular cluster to each data point, thereby acting as a soft clustering algorithm. This approach contrasts with hard clustering methods like K-means, which assign each data point to exactly one cluster. The GMM algorithm utilizes the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate parameters such as mean, covariance, and weight of each component [71,72].

In many cases, the number of clusters to be formed is unknown, which can be a challenge. This issue can be tackled possibly by using a Bayesian GMM, which applies variational inference to calculate the posterior distributions of the parameters of the Gaussian mixture [73,74].

In our work, we fit a Bayesian GMM on the output predictions that identifies different Gaussian components to obtain predicted binding affinities for each PLC. Once these components are identified, the one with the highest weight is selected, as shown in Fig.2, and the mean of this component is taken as the final aggregated binding affinity for the respective complex.

A Feed-Forward Neural Network (FFNN) is a type of artificial neural network where data travels in a single direction, from the input to the output, without forming any loops. It’s composed of an input layer, one or more intermediate hidden layers, and an output layer. Each neuron in these layers applies a non-linear function to the weighted sum of its inputs.

Our work employs an FFNN with four hidden layers of sizes 256, 128, 64, and 32. Each layer uses the SiLU (Sigmoid Linear Unit) activation function, and dropout regularization is applied at each layer with rates of 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1, respectively. The network is trained on the frame-level binding affinity predictions generated by Pafnucy for the training set. We also include statistical features such as the minimum, maximum, mean, median, and standard deviation of the frame-level predictions to enhance representation. All input features are scaled using a MinMax scaler. This FFNN learns to map the set of frame-level predictions for each PLC to a single aggregated binding affinity, providing a machine learning-based alternative to rule-based aggregation methods.

The performance of the traditional MM-PBSA technique to calculate the binding free energies of the various PLCs is much worse than that of the deep learning model trained using multiple frames. It is well known that naive MM-PBSA free-energy estimates carry a large systematic offset relative to experimental values [35,75]. The uncorrected predictions in our dataset have a test-set MSE of 1176.0\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)(Table1, footnote), reflecting this offset. To enable a fair comparison, we apply a standard linear transformation (slope/intercept fit on the training set; full derivation in Appendix A) to the MM-PBSA predictions before comparing them to the DL approach. As shown in Fig.3A, even after this correction, the linearly-transformed MM-PBSA predictions show a larger deviation from the experimental values, and a higher test-set MSE (5.38\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)), than the multi-frame DL approach (best test MSE 3.46).

When comparing the method of the baseline approach, which uses complexes prior to energy minimization (experimental structures) from the PLAS-20k dataset without multiple frames, with those that utilize several frames and aggregation techniques, we see that the former’s predictions are more scattered away from the ideal predictions than the latter’s (Fig.3B, C). The baseline shows higher MSE (5.1\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)for the testing set) and lower\(r_p\)(0.6 for the testing set) values, showcasing the advantage of using multiple frames for more accurate binding affinity predictions (Tables1and2).

Out of the four methods we used for selecting frames for each PLC, we observe that the approaches that rely on frames that are either randomly selected or selected from the initial trajectory run have low MSE and high\(r_p\)for the training set. However, they perform notably poorer on the testing set (Tables1and2). Choosing frames specifically from the initial trajectory coordinates likely suffered due to these being too similar, leading to an over-representation of a limited conformational region. Similarly, it seems that the random selection also resulted in insufficient representation of the conformational diversity for the chosen PLCs. These results suggest that learning representation of similar frames is more straightforward for Pafnucy, improving training performance but reducing generalizability to unseen testing data.

Based on the results in Tables1and2, we believe the uniform selection method improves upon the previous two frame selection approaches by sampling evenly across the entire trajectory, possibly capturing a broader range of conformations. However, we observe that the best performance is achieved using the clustered selection method. Unlike the previous approaches, this method specifically groups similar frames together and selects representatives from these groups, possibly giving a higher probability of having a more structurally diverse set of input. Therefore, the clustering approach supports the testing data’s lowest MSE (3.5\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)) and highest\(r_p\)(0.7) values.

On varying the number of frames selected per PLC for different deep learning models and comparing their performances, we observed that, similar to using a static structure, using a single frame results in higher MSE across the randomized selection, starting-frames selection, and baseline approaches than when multiple frames are used (Table1). While increasing the number of frames generally leads to higher training error up to 40 frames, training error plateaus thereafter (e.g., 1.77, 1.77, and 1.75\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)for 40, 50, and 60 frames, respectively, using mean aggregation, clustered selection), while test error does not improve further and, in most configurations, is worse than at 30 frames. We extended our experiments up to 60 frames using the clustered selection approach (our best-performing strategy) to verify this trend. Rather than a continued decline, performance beyond 30 frames fluctuates (test MSE of 3.99, 3.67, and 3.86\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)at 40, 50, and 60 frames, respectively, versus 3.50 at 30 frames), but in no case surpasses the 30-frame result within the range tested. In our experiments, we therefore obtain the best performance (i.e., lowest MSE and highest\(r_p\)) on unseen test data by selecting 30 frames using the clustered selection approach. Even for the uniform selection approach, we notice that selecting 30 frames leads to better results.

A plausible explanation for this performance trend of the different models is that with limited data, the models tend to overfit and result in low training error but high test error. Overfitting is reduced as the number of frames increases up to a point, and the model begins to generalize better with lower test errors [76,77]. However, this benefit does not continue indefinitely: beyond 30 frames, test performance does not improve further and instead fluctuates without exceeding the 30-frame optimum. This is possibly due to the introduction of redundant or highly similar frames at higher counts, which add training cost without adding genuinely new conformational information, or due to a mismatch between the increased input diversity and the fixed capacity of the CNN/aggregation pipeline [78]. To elaborate, Pafnucy projects each complex onto a fixed 1Å grid (Table3), meaning that conformational differences smaller than the grid spacing are largely flattened out, causing closely related frames to map to near-identical input tensors. Moreover, because Pafnucy is not rotation-invariant, every input is presented in 24 rotations during training (Table3). A 30-frame training set thus already yields 720 distinct input tensors per complex, capturing much of the diversity that additional frames would otherwise introduce. As such, Pafnucy showcases a capacity limitation rather than a data shortage, and its training error plateaus beyond roughly 40 frames instead of continuing to decline. Consequently, the optimal frame count depends heavily on both the network architecture and its input representation, a conclusion supported by the higher optimum observed for the rotation-invariant, graph-based GIGN model (Appendix C). Hence, while increasing the number of frames improves accuracy up to an architecture- and selection-strategy-dependent point, identifying the optimal number of frames is likely necessary to achieve the best performance [79].

We compared the performance of four methods for aggregating the predictions from multiple frames: Gaussian KDE, arithmetic mean, Bayesian GMM, and a Feed-Forward Neural Network (FFNN). Based on the testing data MSE values, the simple mean method consistently outperforms the KDE and Bayesian GMM approaches in most cases. For example, under the clustering-based frame selection approach for 30 frames, the mean method yields an MSE of 3.50, compared to 3.63 and 3.54\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)for Gaussian KDE and Bayesian GMM, respectively (Table1).

The KDE method, which estimates a probability density function over the predictions and selects the peak value, generally performs worse than the mean and Bayesian GMM methods across most configurations. For the training data, both the mean and Bayesian GMM methods perform comparably—MSEs of 1.52\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)each, with the same\(r_p\)values of 0.92, under the 10-frame uniform selection strategy. However, on the testing set, Bayesian GMM slightly underperforms compared to the mean (e.g., MSEs of 4.61, 4.63, and 4.81 for mean, GMM, and KDE, respectively), reinforcing the practical advantages of the mean method due to both its performance and computational simplicity.

When introducing the FFNN-based aggregation, we observe that it initially lags behind the statistical methods in most configurations. However, its performance improves significantly as the number of frames increases, especially under the clustering-based frame selection approach. Notably, the FFNN achieves the best overall results—an MSE of 3.46 and an\(r_p\)of 0.72—under the clustered 30-frame setup (Tables1and2). Although the FFNN shows lower performance in other frame quantity and selection combinations, it consistently follows the same trend as the statistical methods: error generally decreases with more frames until a certain point, after which it starts increasing. This behavior suggests that the FFNN’s success heavily depends on the quality of initial frame-level predictions generated by Pafnucy. Although the arithmetic mean is still the most practical and reliable aggregation method, the FFNN shows potential under optimized conditions, such as a carefully chosen frame selection strategy and frame count. Importantly, both statistical and machine learning-based aggregation methods highlight similar performance trends, underlining the critical role of selecting the right number of frames and an appropriate frame selection strategy for effective prediction aggregation.

Our results demonstrate that utilizing multiple snapshots of each PLC from MD simulations in a DL model, such as Pafnucy, improves the predictive accuracy compared to solely relying on static structures. Different variations of the Pafnucy model, achieved by training with diverse frame quantities and approaches, can replace methods such as MM-PBSA due to improved results and lower computational costs. Moreover, with sufficient frames and appropriate frame selection and output aggregation techniques, it is seen that the dynamic information in the PLAS-20k could possibly be used more effectively, leading to greater generalizability of the model and higher precision of binding affinity predictions of PLCs. Notably, these trends are not specific to the Pafnucy architecture. Repeating the same frame-selection and aggregation experiments with GIGN, a structurally distinct and more recent graph neural network, yields the same qualitative improvement over a single-frame baseline. The clustered, multi-frame training and simple mean aggregation again outperform the alternatives (Tables5and6, Appendix C). This cross-architecture consistency reinforces that the benefit we observe stems from the synthetic MD data itself, rather than from properties specific to the Pafnucy model. These observations emphasize how crucial synthetic datasets are, particularly those that incorporate dynamic information, in understanding the complexities of the protein-ligand binding process. More generally, this illustrates the potential of synthetic data to advance numerous scientific fields.

For ML techniques applied in the domains of chemistry and biology, obtaining large amounts of high-quality experimental data for model training is often infeasible. Augmenting the data with synthetic datasets can help in solving such low-data issues. As a test of the usage of synthetic data, this work focuses on the task of protein-ligand binding affinity prediction. Since predicting binding affinity between proteins and ligands is a crucial aspect of drug discovery, several non-ML and ML techniques have been developed to achieve this task. Various ML methods have already shown great promise in improving the efficiency and accuracy of these predictions. However, further enhancement of these models may require moving beyond the traditional usage of static structures usually available in most commonly used datasets. This limitation of static structures could lead to moving on to synthetic datasets with dynamic (MD) trajectories, such as the PLAS-20k dataset. Our findings clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data in enhancing data augmentation techniques, significantly improving binding affinity predictions. A cross-architecture check using a second, more recent model (Appendix C) supports the generality of this conclusion beyond the specific architecture used in our main analysis, while also showing that some configuration choices (e.g., the precise optimal frame count) are architecture-dependent and should not be over-generalized from a single model. Overall, our results highlight the invaluable role synthetic datasets can play in future research and applications.

While this study shows the benefits of utilizing the dynamic information present in datasets such as the PLAS-20k by training the simple Pafnucy model, further improvements to the deep learning approach can include making use of more sophisticated prediction models, which could incorporate techniques that allow them to learn the relationships between snapshots of the same PLC. One could also train the models on negative samples, allowing the models to understand the unstable configurations in addition to the stable ones. These improvements could potentially allow DL to generalize even better to unseen PLCs and lead to higher efficiency of the drug discovery pipeline. Besides binding affinity, one could take up similar ideas of utilizing synthetic datasets to study other protein properties and use a combination of experimental and synthetic data to develop better models.

The majority of hyperparameters used for our work are the same as those used by the original Pafnucy model. Table3provides a list of hyperparameters along with their values and descriptions. Additionally, we set the random seed to 42 for all tasks involving randomness.

To assess whether the trends reported in SectionResults and discussionare specific to the Pafnucy architecture, we repeated the central frame-selection and frame-count experiments using a second, more recent architecture, GIGN [68], on the same dataset, the same frame selections, and the same train/test split used throughout the main text. Throughout this appendix, the GIGN results should be read as a qualitative check on the trends reported in the main text rather than as a head-to-head performance comparison with Pafnucy. The two models were trained under different protocols, and GIGN was not optimized for absolute accuracy on this dataset.

GIGN (Geometric Interaction Graph Neural Network) represents a PLC as a graph in which covalent (intramolecular) and non-covalent (intermolecular) interactions are passed through a dedicated heterogeneous interaction layer, rather than being treated identically. The model is invariant to translation and rotation of the input structure by construction, so, unlike Pafnucy, which requires explicit rotational data augmentation (Appendix B), no rotation augmentation is needed for GIGN.

We trained GIGN using the same Baseline, Uniform, and Clustered frame-selection configurations evaluated for Pafnucy, using the identical frame indices and the identical PLC-level train/test split. All other modeling choices (architecture, optimizer, hyperparameters; Table4) were held fixed across every configuration, and only the frame-selection strategy and frame count were varied, mirroring the controlled design of the main Pafnucy study. The one procedural difference from the Pafnucy training protocol is that, for GIGN, a validation set comprising 10% of the training PLCs was carved out (at the PLC level) and used for early stopping and checkpoint selection. Pafnucy’s original training protocol did not use a held-out validation split. Aggregation across frames during inference (KDE, Mean, Bayesian GMM, FFNN) was performed in the same way as in the main text.

The results are reported in Tables5and6. Consistent with the main-text Pafnucy results, multi-frame training substantially outperforms the single-frame Baseline, and arithmetic Mean aggregation is the best or tied-best aggregation method in nearly every configuration, matching the robustness of simple averaging reported for Pafnucy. Notably, improvement over the baseline is sustained rather than tapering off: the best GIGN result is obtained at 60 frames using the clustered approach, the largest frame count we tested, rather than at an intermediate value, indicating that additional well-selected synthetic frames continued to help up to the range we evaluated.

These results support the paper’s primary assertion by employing a structurally distinct, more recent architecture. They show that incorporating multiple MD-derived synthetic frames per PLC, chosen via clustering, meaningfully enhances binding-affinity prediction compared to a static-structure baseline, and that this advantage is not exclusive to Pafnucy. The exact frame count at which performance is maximized differs between the two architectures (30 for Pafnucy, 60—the upper edge of our tested range—for GIGN), which we note as a crucial fact that cautions against overgeneralizing a single optimal configuration across architectures.

We further note that GIGN exhibits a substantially larger train-test gap than Pafnucy, with training MSEs of\(0.05-0.22\)\((\text {kcal} \cdot \text {mol}^{-1})^2\)with\(r_p = 0.99-1.00\), against test MSEs of\(3.98-4.63\)with\(r_p = 0.57-0.63\)(Tables5and6). This reflects the fact that GIGN’s hyperparameters (Table4) follow the values reported by the original authors for PDBbind and were not re-tuned for the PLAS-20k dataset, and that GIGN has a larger effective capacity relative to our roughly 6000-PLC training set than the more heavily regularised Pafnucy (dropout 0.5, weight decay, 24-fold rotational augmentation; Table3). Early stopping on the held-out validation split (Section C.2) limits but does not remove this effect. Because every frame-selection configuration is trained and evaluated under identical conditions, this gap does not affect the qualitative comparisons drawn here. However, the absolute GIGN errors should not be read as the best achievable performance for this architecture on PLAS-20k.
