We quantified the protein-level similarity between the training and test sets. Our splits are performed at the level of PLCs: no complex appears in both sets. However, because the PLCs are drawn from PDBBind, in which the same protein frequently appears in complex with several different ligands, complex-level separation does not imply protein-level separation. To assess residual similarity, a single representative sequence was extracted from each PLC. For every test protein, the maximum pairwise sequence identity to any training protein was determined via local (Smith-Waterman) alignment, where identity was defined as the count of identical residues divided by the shorter sequence’s length. The mean of these per-protein maximum identities is 92.7%, and 77.5% of test proteins have an identical-sequence counterpart in the training set, confirming that the dataset is substantially redundant at the protein level, as is characteristic of PDBBind-derived data.

This redundancy raises a natural question: is the improvement from multi-frame augmentation a genuine effect, or does it reflect the model recognizing proteins it has already seen? We therefore partitioned the test proteins into identity strata (< 30%, 30–50%, 50–90%, 90-<100%, and =100%) and, within each stratum, compared the single-frame baseline against the multi-frame (clustered) model, with per-PLC predictions aggregated by arithmetic mean. Because our concern here is whether the qualitative benefit is present in each stratum rather than its exact magnitude, we report the Pearson correlation (\(r_p\)) and the Spearman rank correlation (\(\rho\)) metrics between predicted and experimental affinities. Together, they capture both value-level and ranking-level agreement, the latter of which is especially relevant to virtual screening. Figure4reports both metrics, for the baseline and multi-frame models, at three frame counts spanning the range we tested (20, 40 and 60 frames, clustered selection).

Two observations hold consistently. First, in every stratum and at every frame count, both correlations increase substantially under multi-frame training relative to the baseline. This includes the low-identity (< 30%) stratum of typically structurally novel proteins, where the Pearson correlation rises from 0.29 for the baseline to 0.70–0.83 for the multi-frame models and the Spearman correlation from 0.15 to 0.58–0.70. Second, the improvement is of comparable magnitude between the novel proteins and the near-identical ones. We note that the 30–50% and 50–90% strata contain relatively few test proteins (\(n=18\)and\(n=19\), respectively), so the values in these two buckets are correspondingly noisier. It is the consistency of the trend across all five strata and across three independent frame counts, rather than any single bucket, that supports the conclusion.

These results indicate that the improvement from multi-frame MD augmentation is preserved across the full range of train-test sequence similarity, including for proteins with little similarity to the training set. Therefore, it is not an artifact of the protein-level redundancy in the dataset. We emphasize that this analysis supports the qualitative conclusions of the paper, that augmentation with well-selected MD frames improves prediction, rather than the absolute error values, which are influenced by the dataset’s redundancy and should not be read as estimates of performance on entirely novel targets. Establishing the latter would require a protein-clustered split, which we identify as a direction for future work.

title: pyMSscreen: an interactive interface for automated quality control and prescreening in mass spectrometry workflows
author: Anjana Elapavalore; Parviel Chirsir; Emma H. Palm; Martin Jakubec; Emma L. Schymanski
text:
Reliable quality control of mass spectrometry data remains a major bottleneck in target, suspect and non-target screening workflows. In non-target analysis, thousands of features can be extracted through automated peak picking, many of which require manual verification to exclude artefacts arising from noise, co-elution, inconsistent chromatographic behavior or statistical prioritization. Similarly, suspect screening workflows depend on effective chromatographic and spectral quality control to support confidence in annotated features. However, existing quality control practices are often fragmented across vendor software and custom scripts, limiting reproducibility and scalability. This article describes pyMSscreen, a unified framework that enables automated and reproducible chromatographic quality control across target, suspect, and non-target mass spectrometry workflows. The backend leverages RDKit and pyOpenMS for compound validation and spectral extraction, while the frontend provides a web-based interface for systematic inspection of chromatograms and mass spectra. The development of pyMSscreen draws on experience gained from the earlier R-based Shinyscreen, which showed that accessible graphical user interface can greatly simplify the review of liquid chromatography mass spectrometry data. However, the practical limitations of the Shiny framework, including difficulties with deployment, motivated the creation of a more flexible and modern solution. pyMSscreen employs a modular architecture that supports target, suspect, and non-target screening by accommodating both SMILES orm/zonly input lists. Automated quality control metrics are applied consistently across workflows, enabling assessment of peak shape, signal intensity, retention-time alignment, and background noise prior to downstream interpretation. Container-based deployment ensures reproducible installation and execution across computational environments. The performance and applicability of pyMSscreen is illustrated using a representative non-target dataset and suspect screening workflow demonstrating consistent results relative to established approaches, while substantially reducing manual data handling and review time. Overall, pyMSscreen provides an efficient, transparent, and reproducible platform for chromatographic quality control and data curation in high resolution mass spectrometry based cheminformatics workflows. The code is openly available (Artistic 2.0 license) athttps://gitlab.com/uniluxembourg/lcsb/eci/pymsscreen.

Scientific contribution

pyMSscreen presents a unified framework for chromatographic quality control that integrates automated quality metrics with interactive visual inspection of mass spectrometry data. The central contribution is the consistent evaluation of chromatographic peak quality and spectral alignment across target, suspect, and non-target screening workflows within a single methodology. This work builds on earlier developments in interactive mass spectrometry data review while establishing a scalable and reproducible approach to feature-level quality control.

Environmental and metabolomics samples are often highly complex, containing a wide variety of known and unknown chemicals derived from biological processes and/or anthropogenic sources. Many of these substances have the potential to affect human health or disrupt ecological balance, making their detection and characterization a critical task for analytical scientists [1]. Non-target screening (NTS) via liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS) has become a central analytical approach in the identification of small molecules and chemicals of emerging concern [2]. NTS enables researchers to comprehensively screen complex mixtures and search for both known and unknown chemicals with one acquisition method. Despite its strengths, confidently identifying chemicals in the samples remains challenging, largely due to the sheer number of detected features in each dataset [1]. A typical NTS workflow includes sample collection, preparation, instrumental analysis, and data processing. Of these stages, data processing is often the most challenging bottleneck highlighted by researchers, as it involves several interconnected tasks, including peak detection, alignment, integration, and ultimately linking the observed features to chemical structures [2]. While advanced computational tools have helped to automate many steps, the inherent complexity of data processing continues to impede routine implementation of NTS [1].

To meet these challenges, common data processing workflows in NTS often use a combination of vendor-specific software, open source platforms, and in-house resources. Vendor specific software such as Xcalibur for Thermo instruments [3] provide user-friendly inspection tools but are restricted by licensing, limited compatibility, and a narrow focus on specific instruments. In contrast, open source platforms such as xcms [4], MZmine [5], RforMassSpectrometry [6], and patRoon [7], offer more flexible solutions by allowing users to directly configure and adapt data-processing workflows [8]. However, one key challenge in NTS is not the software itself but the lack of standardized quality control (QC) procedures. Reliable NTS interpretation requires consistent quality metrics, including reproducible signal intensity, adequate signal-to-noise ratios and robust retention-time (RT) alignment between extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) and corresponding tandem mass spectral fragments MS2. These QC steps are essential for confirming true chemical signals during screening, yet are often applied inconsistently across workflows. This gap highlights the need for tools that explicitly support high-confidence QC checks, especially for screening-level confirmation based on EIC and MS2peak quality.

One possible solution is the use of Shinyscreen, an open source R Shiny based application, introduced a graphical interface for semi-automated screening, intended to lower the barrier for researchers to perform robust QC without extensive programming experience and enabled rapid validation of MS data [8]. Although the R/Shiny framework of Shinyscreen facilitated rapid prototyping and user interaction, Shiny applications are typically single-threaded, and extending functionality beyond the R environment increases architectural complexity [9]. Although the introduction of a Docker image simplified installation, challenges remained with performance and adaptability.

Building on this foundation and to overcome the limitations of earlier approaches, the current article describes pyMSscreen, a Python-React based framework that extends the functionality of Shinyscreen in a Python-based implementation. pyMSscreen is implemented as a full-stack framework consisting of a Python-based backend and a web-based frontend. The backend is implemented using Flask and is responsible for data processing, automated QC, and data management, while the frontend is implemented in React and provides an interactive interface for visual inspection and user interaction. The backend integrates RDKit [10], a widely used open source cheminformatics toolkit, for structure-based preprocessing tasks such as parsing SMILES strings, calculating exact masses, and generating molecular formulas. Another used library, OpenMS [11] is a robust open source framework for MS data analysis, and the pyOpenMS bindings expose these algorithms within Python. pyOpenMS naturally supports the standard mzML format, aligning with open data standards that are crucial for reproducibility and long-term data access. The framework is built around the principle of combining the computational robustness of Python with the flexibility of a modern web interface, ensuring that both expert users and students can efficiently interact with complex HRMS datasets. Collectively, these features allow pyMSscreen to bridge the gap between restrictive commercial solutions and other open source packages, offering a versatile and user-friendly environment for QC in HRMS. Selected case studies show representative functionality where pyMSscreen could be used to complement current workflows.

pyMSscreen combines pre-screening and automated QC within a single, modern framework with Python Flask as the backbone, offering access to a variety of scientific and cheminformatics libraries like pyOpenMS [12] for data processing and RDKit for structural handling [10]. The frontend is built with React and integrates Plotly.js [13] offering a responsive interface for real-time interaction with results and intuitive data visualisation. Compared to its predecessor Shinyscreen [8], this new framework is designed to improve computational efficiency and analytical flexibility, while maintaining ease of use. Its modular architecture ensures compatibility across operating systems and computational infrastructures, making it broadly applicable to target, suspect screening and NTS workflows. These are the main modes of HRMS data interpretation, each requiring distinct levels of prior mass or structural information and QC. To support NTS workflows, pyMSscreen operates on feature lists of masses generated during prior feature extraction and peak-picking workflows using external software, where the detected features remain unknown. pyMSscreen was designed to support all three modes through a unified QC approach, enabling consistent evaluation of MS1intensity, retention time (RT) alignment of MS2scans, and noise detection, irrespective of the starting information.

Figure1illustrates the operational workflow of the full-stack framework. Experimental data in mzML format is ingested by the backend, where the Flask application orchestrates input configuration and initiates signal extraction and prescreening using pyOpenMS and RDKit. The processed results are exposed through a RESTful application programming interface (API) and retrieved by the React frontend, which manages quality assessment and renders chromatographic and spectral visualisations with Plotly.js [13]. The complete environment is distributed within Docker containers, ensuring reproducible execution and consistent deployment across heterogeneous computing platforms.

pyMSscreen—full stack framework and application workflow

The server side is built with Flask, a lightweight Python web framework for rapid development of RESTful APIs. Flask’s minimalist “microframework” design provides essential functions (routing and HTTP handling) without excessive overhead, making it easy to integrate scientific libraries. All core functionality is exposed through well-defined REST API endpoints, keeping the backend stateless and client-agnostic. Structure-based preprocessing is performed using RDKit [10], including parsing of SMILES strings, calculation of exact masses, and generation of molecular formulas The resulting values are then combined to construct a comprehensive compound list, which guides subsequent spectral extraction. Configuration files (inputs and settings) are serialized in human-readable YAML and CSV formats to ensure reproducibility and interoperability with other tools.

For HRMS data processing, the backend leverages pyOpenMS (the Python bindings for the OpenMS C +  + library) to parse mzML files and extract spectral information. Thus, the backend’s MS data processing pipeline combines OpenMS’s powerful algorithms with the approachability of Python.

The frontend is implemented in React, a JavaScript library for building interactive user interfaces. React enables a dynamic single page application that responds immediately to user input without requiring full page reloads. The interface is organised into modular components aligned with the application workflow. Core modules include data setup for uploading mzML files and compound lists, extraction and prescreening configuration for adjusting processing parameters, and a visualisation dashboard for plot visualization and manual revision of QC results. This modular structure promotes code reuse and extensibility, allowing common elements such as file upload widgets or compound tables to be deployed across multiple views, while additional functionality can be introduced without modifying existing modules.

React’s declarative paradigm ensures that the interface remains tightly coupled to the analysis state. For example, when extraction is completed, the change in state automatically triggers the rendering of plots and summary tables. State management is achieved through the Context API, which maintains shared information such as working directories, uploaded files, and extracted results. This approach provides consistency across workflow stages while preserving modular independence, allowing users to move seamlessly between tasks with their inputs and results retained throughout the session.

Visualisation of HRMS data is a central feature of pyMSscreen, implemented with Plotly.js [13] through its React integration. Plotly was chosen for its ability to generate interactive, publication-quality plots within the browser. Within the Visualisation Dashboard, users can examine EICs and MS2spectra for each compound in an interactive environment. These plots allow detailed inspection, such as zooming into chromatographic peaks to assess their shape or overlaying multiple EIC traces to compare e.g., data from reference standard mixtures with sample measurements. The peaks are aligned using Plotly’s subplot functionality and each EIC is displayed together with its corresponding MS2spectrum in a stacked view, with synchronised axes to facilitate RT comparison. This is achieved by preparing the plot data in the browser after retrieval from the Flask API and rendering combined layouts through the Plotly interface. Interactivity is further supported by features such as double-clicking legend entries to isolate specific traces and mark the associated peaks. Users can also filter and group plots according to metadata such as sample tag or adduct, which enables focused evaluation of subsets within larger datasets.

A design choice was made to handle configuration (run-specific parameters) and state using simple files in standard formats. A JSON file (state.json) maintains the list of input files and compounds in a given session, allowing the stateless server to reconstruct analysis context on each request. The rationale is that configuration in YAML (for extraction settings like mass tolerances, intensity thresholds, retention time windows, etc.) makes the analysis setup transparent. The users or reviewers can open the extract_config.yaml file and immediately see the exact parameters used for peak picking and QC. This YAML config is written by the backend whenever the user updates settings via the UI (through a /save_extract_config endpoint) and is read back on each analysis run to ensure reproducibility of results. Using file-based JSON/YAML, pyMSscreen remains lightweight and deployable. All state files reside in a single folder that can be zipped for archival or debugging. This approach also aligns with best practices in maintaining human-readable files, allowing the users to directly inspect the input parameters.

Communication between the frontend and backend occurs exclusively through HTTP requests. The backend exposes a RESTful API with endpoints corresponding to each key operation in the workflow, and the React frontend interacts with these exclusively through HTTP requests. Axios, a JavaScript client for asynchronous communication, is used to transmit JSON payloads, manage responses, and handle errors. Its compatibility with React’s asynchronous programming model enables concise implementation, and the calls are encapsulated within a dedicated utility module (api.js) to preserve clarity and maintainability of the interface code. The use of Axios across all communication ensures consistency and facilitates global configuration of network parameters. The stateless design of the REST API, in which each request contains all necessary contextual information such as working directory and chemical identifiers, enhances scalability and reliability. Independent requests can be processed in parallel or distributed across computational resources without the need for shared state.

The entire pyMSscreen framework is packaged as a Docker container, which encapsulates all dependencies and environment settings to ensure reproducible installation across platforms. This containerization simplifies deployment on local machines, institutional servers, or cloud infrastructures, and supports both single-user and multi-user setups with minimal configuration. By adopting a full-stack architecture, pyMSscreen overcomes the scalability and extensibility limitations inherent to R/Shiny applications, offering a sustainable solution for both high-throughput workflows and exploratory research.

The workflow begins with the specification of input data (Fig.2). The configuration page accepts two resources: (i) a compound list in CSV format and (ii) mass spectrometry data files in mzML format. The compound list can be provided either as a set of precursorm/zor neutral exact mass values for NTS (obtained in advance from peak picking output generated by other software e.g., patRoon output) or annotated compound entries including chemical identifiers and SMILES strings for target or suspect screening workflows. An example compound list with supported input fields is provided as a reference input file, with corresponding mzML files on Zenodo. The MS data need to be annotated with sample tags and adducts via the interface. File paths are stored in a state.json file, which defines the working context for all subsequent operations. By default, all inputs and generated outputs are stored in the working directory `/app/uploads`, which is used internally by the application. In the Docker based deployment, this directory is mapped to a user defined location on the host system through a volume mount configured via environment variables specified in the.env file prior to building and starting the docker container. This configuration ensures persistent storage of uploaded data and generated results outside the container across restarts and updates. Further details are explained in the README.

pyMSscreen—user input configuration

The backend validates SMILES strings (where present in the compound list) and uses RDKit to calculate exact masses and molecular formulas. Adducts are selected from a drop-down menu in the application, and the corresponding mass-to-charge ratios are calculated for each mzML file for the target and suspect screening workflows. The results are compiled into a comprehensive table (comprehensive_table.csv) that links structural information with analytical metadata and provides the basis for spectral extraction.

Spectral extraction is carried out with the pyOpenMS library. Each mzML file is loaded into an MSExperiment object, which is separated into MS1and MS2scans. For every mass, EICs are constructed by summing intensities within the specified mass tolerance across MS1scans, while MS2spectra are simultaneously screened for precursor ions within a defined tolerance (Fig.3). For spectra that match, fragment lists, total intensities, and retention times are recorded. The resulting spectral data are exported as CSV files for downstream inspection. For visualization and peak prioritization, EICs are evaluated using a local maximum based peak detection approach with a 5-point moving average window, a minimum peak prominence of 5% of the maximum EIC intensity, a minimum chromatographic separation of 0.15 min, and a minimum peak width of 3 consecutive data points. The peak selection criteria help reduce noise and avoid closely overlapping or low intensity signals, while retaining the most representative chromatographic features within the EIC. In cases where multiple chromatographic signals are present within the same EIC, the most intense signal is prioritized for automated QC evaluation, while the top three most intense chromatographic peaks are retained and visualized to support manual inspection of chromatographic complexity and potential co-elution effects.

Extraction and prescreening parameters

The extracted data are then evaluated by a prescreening module using parameters defined in YAML configuration file. By default, spectral extraction is performed using a precursor mass tolerance of 5 ppm, whereas the prescreening parameters are set to a minimum MS1intensity threshold of 105, a maximum retention time deviation of 0.5 min between corresponding MS1 and MS2 signals, and a signal-to-noise ratio threshold of 3. These parameters can be adjusted by the user depending on the instrument configuration and dataset characteristics (Fig.3). MS2 spectra are associated with the closest chromatographic peak apex within the specified retention time tolerance window. If no MS2 signal is detected within the defined retention time tolerance, the feature is retained in the summary table but flagged accordingly during QC evaluation. Each criterion produces a binary flag, and these flags collectively determine the overall classification. The results are consolidated into a summary table (summary_table.csv), which can be reviewed and, when necessary, manually adjusted by the user.

The visualisation dashboard (Fig.4) serves the user with the comprehensive compound list and QC summary for client side rendering and streams per compound EIC/MS2CSVs for on demand plotting. The frontend, implemented in React with Plotly.js [13], consumes these endpoints to produce interactive chromatograms, MS2spectra, and fragment distributions in the browser, enabling rapid review without platform specific desktop software. The settings pane includes the option for the user to visualise the Plots filtered per tag.

Overview of visualisation dashboard

The summary table gives an overview of different QC flags that the user can check/uncheck after visual inspection of the chromatogram. When a single tag is filtered by using sample and compound tags, the Export Peak List button is enabled for the users to copy the MS2peak list to be copied to the clipboard which can further be used for subsequent workflows, for e.g., in silico spectral matching using MetFrag [14]. The Plotting pane represents the EIC, MS2scans and MS2fragments as subplots. The legend also marks the trace which can be selected by double clicking. This allows the user to manually do QC after inspecting the plots and the RT information. The interactive plots can be saved as individual plots based on the current selection or a summary of plots can be downloaded by clicking the Export Summary PDF button.

The performance of pyMSscreen is demonstrated using two representative use cases. The first use case covers a workflow applied during teaching activities, where expected amino acids can be identified in reference standards (to determine experimental RTs) then screened in yeast samples to assess changes in intensity in different scenarios. pyMSscreen was used to perform automated QC of the corresponding chromatographic peaks, including assessment of peak shape, signal intensity, RT consistency, and background noise and compared with MZmine 4.8.0 [5]. This use case was designed to assess the suitability of pyMSscreen for systematic QC and provides the basis for subsequent evaluation of processing speed relative to vendor-based software, Xcalibur [3]. The second use case demonstrates the application of pyMSscreen within a suspect screening workflow using the surface water dataset from Aurich et al. [15], where candidates were annotated using patRoon (version 2.3) and subsequently evaluated with pyMSscreen for chromatographic quality and signal reliability. This example illustrates how chromatographic QC can be integrated downstream of suspect annotation to support the interpretation of suspect screening results and identify potential peak-picking artefacts.

Two batches of the yeast strain FY4 wild-type (WT) and the DLD3 knockout (KO) mutant, a model for D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, were analyzed. This mutation alters levels of α-ketoglutarate, D-2-hydroxyglutarate, and several other cofactors. The analysis of amino acids in these strains provides a critical snapshot of the downstream metabolic shifts caused by this mutation. Both strains were cultured under identical conditions and normalized to an optical density of 2 prior to extraction. Data were acquired using standard LC Glasgow method [16] and a Q Exactive™HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) operated in both positive ( +) and negative ( −) electrospray ionization modes. Raw files were converted to mzML format for subsequent analysis using Proteowizard (version 3.0.21075) [17].

Twenty proteinogenic amino acids were evaluated in both positive and negative ionization modes using a target input list containing SMILES and Name entries for each compound. RT and intensity obtained with pyMSscreen were compared with those from the non-target workflow in MZmine 4.8.0. as shown in Fig.5.

Retention time comparison between pyMSscreen and MZmine

pyMSscreen detected all 20 amino acids across the dataset while MZmine detected 18 of the 20 amino acids. For compounds detected by both tools, RTs were highly consistent, indicating comparable chromatographic alignment (Fig.5). The two amino acids not reported by MZmine were observable in the EIC generated by pyMSscreen, highlighting the benefit of interactive visual inspection of the chromatographic peaks.

An illustrative example is provided by the isomeric amino acids leucine and isoleucine, which share the same exact mass and therefore produce identical precursorm/zvalues. Isoleucine was not detected by MZmine due to its close elution with leucine. In the EIC form/z132.1019 generated by pyMSscreen, two closely eluting peaks are clearly visible at approximately 4.3 and 4.6 min (Fig.6). Comparison with individually analyzed standards enabled unambiguous RT based assignment of the earlier peak (4.3 min) to leucine and the later peak (4.6 min) to isoleucine. The visualization dashboard further enables direct inspection of the associated MS1and MS2acquisitions for each peak. During automated processing, the algorithm prioritizes the most intense chromatographic signal for downstream evaluation while retaining the top three most intense peaks within the chromatogram. This approach transparently displays the underlying chromatographic complexity and supports QC by enabling inspection of co elution effects, while still preserving access to lower intensity but analytically relevant features.

EIC for m/z 132.1019 showing two peaks at approximately 4.3 and 4.6 min, consistent with the presence of the isomeric amino acids leucine and isoleucine

Beyond improvements in feature interpretability, pyMSscreen minimizes manual processing associated with vendor-based workflows by integrating chromatographic inspection, MS1/MS2evaluation, and QC within a single web interface. pyMSscreen was compared against the standard vendor-based workflow for this dataset (Thermo Scientific™Xcalibur™). In Thermo Xcalibur, chromatographic data extraction can be performed using Quan Browser by manually defining targetm/zvalues and retention time windows in the processing setup, after which multiple files can be processed together. Once a processing method is established, the chromatographic peaks are integrated automatically and can be manually inspected for each file and compound. Qual Browser additionally allows inspection of chromatographic traces and MS1and MS2spectra across multiple files by creating templates. However, the setup and management of processing methods and templates can be time consuming, particularly when working with large suspect lists or when iterative updates are required. In addition, systematic inspection of MS2spectral quality and its alignment is not fully integrated within a single workflow.

In contrast, pyMSscreen automates chromatographic extraction across all files and ionization modes using a compound file, thereby removing the need for manual configuration of processing methods or templates. All data files are processed simultaneously in a single run, reducing user input and enabling rapid analysis of complete datasets. The pyMSscreen visualisation dashboard integrates chromatographic and spectral review within a browser based environment, allowing users to filter samples by metadata, isolate individual chromatographic traces, and inspect MS1and MS2spectra within a unified interface. This allows focused inspection of individual samples within large datasets, making the review process considerably faster and more consistent.

Overall, this use case demonstrates that pyMSscreen serves as an effective visualization tool that enables rapid determination of accurate retention times for target compounds and facilitates efficient QC. For the dataset used in this study (6 mzML files and 20 amino acids), automated QC in pyMSscreen was completed in less than 2 min. Based on iterative evaluation across different user groups, pyMSscreen complements comprehensive workflows such as MZmine by enabling plot generation and supporting QC through an interactive web-based interface. By reducing the need for manual inspection across multiple data files, the use of pyMSscreen improves the efficiency of data processing in HRMS workflows.

To further demonstrate the performance of pyMSscreen in NTS, the QC evaluation was applied to the June 2020 surface water dataset from Aurich et al. [15]. In the original study, patRoon was used to annotate features using MS1detection, spectral libraries, and diagnostic fragments. Candidate compound structures were ranked by MS2spectral similarity scores and assigned identification confidence to Levels 2, 3a, and 3b following an adapted scheme by Talavera Andújar et al. [18], which was based on confidence levels defined in 2014 [19]. Specifically, Level 2 corresponds to a good MS2library match with a MassBank of North America (MoNA) similarity score of atleast 0.9, Level 3a to a fair match with MoNA scores between 0.7 and 0.9, and Level 3b defined with MonA scores between 0.4 and 0.7 (described further in [15]). These identification levels were retained unchanged in the present study to ensure consistency with the original dataset.

While this approach is powerful for assigning plausible structures, patRoon does not directly assess chromatographic signal quality, which is critical for confirming whether annotated features represent robust detections. To address this, all features annotated as Level 2, 3a and 3b were reevaluated using pyMSscreen’s built-in QC module. pyMSscreen applies standardized rules for QC using instrument-specific thresholds, in this case MS1intensity > 105, RT window between MS1and MS2should be within 0.5 min, and the signal to noise ratio is set to be 3. By evaluating features without prior blank subtraction, the pyMSscreen workflow provides a transparent assessment of chromatographic quality, ensuring that QC metrics reflect the actual spectral data rather than processing artifacts. Figure7a illustrates significant variability in chromatographic quality across all identification levels. While patRoon provides plausible structural assignments, the subsequent QC analysis showed that only circa 50% of these features passed the spectral and intensity thresholds. This discrepancy demonstrates that automated workflows alone are insufficient for robust feature validation, as it may include signals that lack the chromatographic integrity required for reliable quantification.

apyMSscreen QC outcome on patRoon annotated compounds.bpyMSscreen QC consistency with user-validated peak quality assessment

pyMSscreen also supports a semi-automated workflow in which users can visually inspect chromatographic peaks and manually override QC flags where justified. This provides a practical balance between automation and expert oversight, particularly valuable for ambiguous or borderline chromatographic features. To assess the reliability and flexibility of pyMSscreen’s QC framework, the fully automated QC output was compared with the manual review of QC flags directly within the application. The default automated QC flags (“auto QC”) were compared with the user-reviewed QC annotations (“semi-automated QC”), which represent the final curated decisions made after visual inspection within pyMSscreen itself. This comparison does not constitute external manual validation, but rather evaluates how well the automated rules agree with expert decisions when both are embedded in the same workflow environment.

The resulting confusion matrix (Fig.7b) demonstrates a high level of concordance between automated and user-validated QC outcomes. pyMSscreen’s automated QC correctly matched the user’s final decision for 2223 out of 2240 features. Specifically, the automated QC accepted 987 peaks that were also confirmed by user inspection (true positives) and rejected 1236 features that were also rejected after manual review (true negatives). Notably, the automated algorithm produced no false positives (FP = 0), meaning it never approved a peak that the user subsequently deemed unacceptable. Only 17 features initially rejected by the automated QC were later accepted upon user review (false negatives); these typically displayed borderline peak morphology judged acceptable after visual inspection.

The automated QC achieved perfect precision (1.00) and specificity (1.00), indicating that the rule-based system does not falsely classify poor-quality features as acceptable. Accuracy was 0.992, reflecting strong overall agreement between automated and user-validated QC decisions. The recall of 0.983 reflects pyMSscreen’s intentionally conservative QC behavior: while it occasionally flags borderline peaks that users later deem acceptable, it never incorrectly passes poor-quality signals, based on the default settings used here, which are selected based on instrument knowledge.

This evaluation highlights the complementary strengths of fully automated and semi-automated modes in pyMSscreen. The automated QC provides a rigorous, reproducible baseline that eliminates false positives and enforces strict chromatographic standards. At the same time, the user-adjustable interface allows domain experts to override automated decisions when appropriate, supporting a flexible, semi-automated workflow. Together, these features make pyMSscreen a robust and transparent QC framework that enhances confidence in suspect and non-target screening results.

This use case illustrates that pyMSscreen provides an essential QC complement to patRoon. While patRoon efficiently generates structurally plausible annotations, pyMSscreen helps identify which of these annotations correspond to true, high-quality chromatographic features. When combined, the two tools form a more reliable and reproducible workflow for NTS studies.

pyMSscreen establishes a unified and transparent framework for automated QC and visualization of HRMS data. By combining the computational strength of Python with a flexible React-based frontend, the application delivers an accessible yet powerful environment for both target, suspect and non-target screening applications. Its modular architecture and containerized deployment make it reproducible, scalable, and easily adaptable across research environments. Beyond usability, pyMSscreen introduces a comprehensive QC framework that evaluates MS1peak characteristics, MS2peak alignment, RT consistency, and noise behavior in a transparent and reproducible manner. The development of pyMSscreen was informed by the pros and cons of its predecessor, Shinyscreen, which demonstrated the value of an intuitive graphical interface for HRMS data review. While Shinyscreen substantially improved accessibility, its reliance on the R/Shiny ecosystem imposed important limitations in scalability, multi-user performance, and extensibility. pyMSscreen addresses these issues through a full-stack implementation that decouples data processing from visualization, thus enabling more efficient computation, interactive browser-based review, and seamless integration into diverse research environments.

Future refinement of pyMSscreen will focus on the inclusion of blank evaluation to improve background discrimination and the robustness of QC metrics, alongside the potential addition of automated tag detection and peak quality scoring to support feature prioritization. In addition, planned extensions include an identification module with a focus on evaluation of QC metrics, supporting more informed feature prioritization in large datasets. The React frontend is well suited for embedding interactive predictive components, enabling dynamic feedback between computational inference and expert validation. Such developments will allow pyMSscreen to evolve from a rule-based QC framework into a learning system capable of supporting semi-automated annotation, accelerating data-driven discovery in metabolomics, environmental analysis, and cheminformatics. It bridges the gap between restrictive commercial tools and complex open source pipelines, offering a future-ready platform for robust and efficient HRMS screening.

title: Phyfold: environment aware mathematical modeling for protein folding dynamics integrated with physics informed neural network
author: Jamshaid Ul Rahman; Iqra Noureen; Abdul Mannan; Rongin Uwitije
text:
Protein folding remains a fundamental problem in computational biology, where understanding folding trajectories and dynamic behavior under physiological conditions is critical for linking structure to function. Recent advances such as AlphaFold have revolutionized sequence to structure prediction, establishing a powerful and robust foundation for computational protein modeling. Building upon this success, we introduce a novel physics informed computational framework that expands static structure prediction toward dynamic and physically consistent modeling of protein folding processes. The proposed framework unifies a mathematically grounded reaction diffusion model of folding kinetics with deep sequence embeddings through a physics informed neural network (PINN), ensuring consistency with governing physical laws while remaining biologically grounded. We refer to this unified framework as PhyFold. Our results illustrate that the proposed approach effectively captures environment dependent folding dynamics and shows strong agreement with both numerical reference solutions and experimental fluorescence measurements under physiologically relevant conditions. By explicitly integrating environmental factors such as temperature, pressure, and pH, PhyFold enables realistic, physics aware simulation of protein folding dynamics. This approach offers a natural extension of modern structure prediction methods and opens new directions for protein design, structure guided drug discovery, and personalized medicine. The code to reproduce the work is available athttps://github.com/jamshaidwarraich/PhyFold.git.

Scientific contribution

PhyFold introduces a hybrid Bio-Physics Informed Neural Network framework that models protein folding kinetics as a reaction diffusion partial differential equation with environmentally modulated kinetic coefficients, integrated with ProtT5 sequence embeddings for sequence specific spatiotemporal prediction an approach not previously demonstrated in the literature. Unlike purely data driven or static structure prediction methods, PhyFold explicitly encodes temperature, pH, and pressure dependence into governing kinetic coefficients, enabling physically interpretable simulation of cooperative folding transitions across diverse physiological conditions. Dual validation against finite difference reference solutions and experimental GFP fluorescence measurements confirms mathematical consistency and biological relevance, establishing PhyFold as a computationally efficient surrogate for environment aware protein folding dynamics.

Indeed, the protein molecules, the classic molecular machines of life, mediate almost all biological phenomena such as catalytic activity, structural function, immunity, and signaling because of the unique folding abilities of these molecules to achieve a specific three-dimensional structure [1]. This complex folding mechanism converts a linear arrangement of amino acids into an accurate spatial form so that the protein may assume its functional form. The ability of the most complex of molecular structures that make up a living system to assemble with precision and fidelity is one of the signatures of a living system, which has since been observed in Nature as noted by Dobson [2]. It is important to note that even the slightest deviation in the folding dynamics [3], which can be caused by the presence of foreign substances and/or other biological agents, can have disastrous effects on the transformation, as demonstrated in the case of aggregation, misfolding, and degradation, underpinning the causes of numerous diseases, including, but not limited to, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s [4], and other prion diseases [5].

Protein folding as a fundamental mechanism has been focused on under the approach of energy landscape [6] theory extensively so as to understand its mechanics as a fundamental mechanism of protein folding itself has been the subject of study under the energy landscape theory approach. Known as the new view of protein folding, this viewpoint holds that folding is not a series of compulsory steps between particular partially folded states but is rather a stochastic search of the numerous conformations available to a polypeptide chain [7]. The energy landscape is encoded in the amino acids sequence that allows proteins to evolve in a way that allows them to fold fast and efficiently in a trial and error process. This theoretical framework has transformed our views on the formation of correct folds out of underlying structural transitions.

It has been a key problem in computational biology and biophysics [8] to understand and predict the dynamics of protein folding processes under conditions of strong dilution, which may be facilitated by the repulsive long range forces the protein must resist without collisions . Simulations A wealth of information on folding pathways and energy landscapes [9,10] has been obtained with classical molecular dynamics (MD) [11] simulations. These atomistic methods are able to describe the fine details of folding mechanisms and some simulations have shown that local structural units such as the alpha-Helices can be formed in less than 100 nanoseconds. Nevertheless, the computational cost of these techniques is prohibitive, limiting its time and space resolution to large biomolecules and folding pathways with timescales ranging between micro and seconds long [12,13] and respectively, which demand deep learning in science and biotechnology .

Such constraints have triggered the development of mathematical and machine learning methods that can fill the gap between atomistic and computational efficiency. The recent advances in the area of deep learning have transformed protein structure prediction field [14]. AlphaFold2 proved to be highly accurate at predicting tertiary structures directly off amino acid sequences [15] with unprecedented accuracy, and RoseTTAFold [16] built upon these achievements with three track neural architecture. Equally, based models such as ProtT5 [17], and ESM-2 [18] generate syntactic forms of evolutionary and biophysical data using large protein sequence corpora as potent priors to downstream prediction tasks [19]. Such frameworks as DeepProtein offer detailed benchmarks of learning protein sequences that allow to systematically analyze different architectural methods of learning protein sequences [20,21].

Even with these impressive developments, the vast majority of data driven methods are merely correlative and are concerned with the structure of a static equilibrium of folding pathways as opposed to dynamic ones, which are the required structures in nature [22]. As stressed by Dill and MacCallum, it is not only the protein folding problem but also an understanding of how the structure actually folds, not only the prediction of structure but also the folding of a protein structure [23]. The limitation is especially important given the fact that folding is also related to a lot of biological processes such as molecular homeostasis and cell regulation. In addition, traditional machine learning methods do not explicitly incorporate physical laws that guarantee that the variables interact in biophysical plausible ways within the changing environmental conditions [24,25,26].

To overcome these, we propose a new hybrid framework, namely, PhyFold, that fills the gap between data driven learning and physics based modeling that uses reaction diffusion physics [27] and deep learning embeddings [28], which combine reaction diffusion physics with environmental parameters. Adding to the classical data driven models, physics based models simulate the folding by RDEs and energy landscape theory use of the folding problem in the physical language of RDEs and energy landscapes [29,30]. They give mesoscopic images of the kinetics of folds, where the conformational population is a diffusive process with temperature, pH, and solvent interactions acting as modulation factors, as illustrated in the literature [24,25]. These models are simple to use because they include key features such as nucleation, cooperative folding, and spatial diffusion yet can be constrained by simple potential functions and boundary conditions.

PINNs have become a disruptive computational model to bring together these complementary paradigms and unify them in a cohesive framework for computing physics and chemistry processes and properties through a single computational system and algorithmic approach [31,32]. Based on this, our PhyFold framework directly incorporates partial differential equations (PDEs) into its architecture and restricts biophysical modeling to obey the known physics while also being able to learn using minimal experimental information provided by the data [33,34]. The hybridization allows simultaneous enactment of PDE residual minimization, fulfillment of boundary conditions, and the fitting of empirical data [35] and practically turns the model into a physics consistent surrogate solver. The latest comparative assessment of PINN based techniques and classical numerical methods, including finite difference techniques, have undergone a thorough test in solving nonlinear reaction diffusion problems applicable in biological systems and have proven to have a great capacity to predict the solution to such problems [36].

The achievements of this neural network in epidemiological simulation and modeling [37,38] are strong incentives to implement the method in protein folding dynamics: it has been demonstrated to be successful and effective in epidemiological applications and in the analysis of molecular systems in general, including lipid molecules and their dynamics, among others, where this method can be utilized to gain an advantage. Moreover, the latest developments in the sphere of the graph neural networks to predict molecular properties, such as Enhancing Molecular Property Prediction via Hybrid Deep Learning and Domain Knowledge prove the possibility of the hybrid methods that will combine the domain knowledge with data driven learning. This paper builds on these ideas by creating a physics informed model that is particularly adapted to study spatiotemporal protein folding in the many different environmental conditions with a critical transition between physical modeling and biological verification.

The PINN method allows the study of the dynamics of conformational change in space and time without using atomistic simulation only in the context of protein folding. The PhyFold model provides the mapping between spatial location, temporal dynamics and folding dynamics using a reaction diffusion [39] mathematical model that describes cooperative folding dynamics as well as environmental modulation. This model combines diffusion with spatial propagation and nonlinear reaction terms in its formulation and is effective in the description of the process of unfolded to folded states and includes environmental parameters like temperature, pH, and pressure in its formulation [40].

Coupled with experimental or embedding derived datasets, PhyFold can offer an essential interface between mathematical modeling and biological validation [41] by combining this physics based framework with such data. Not only do the predictions presented by the framework provide numerically consistent predictions, but it is also possible to interpret them biologically, especially when compared to fluorescence based folding metrics benchmarked against real biology data structure measurements [42,43]. The recent developments in AI techniques of protein interaction modeling only emphasize the usefulness of such hybrid strategies, which the paradigm that PhyFold directly illustrates is an example of multistate protein folding via AI technologies [44]. The whole framework of PhyFold is given Fig.1

The PhyFold workflow integrates ProtT5 based sequence embeddings with PINN to predict spatiotemporal protein folding dynamics from fluorescence data, incorporating environmental modulation

Although PINNs are conceptually elegant and a number of challenges have been tackled, there are a number of barriers to using PINNs that has prevented the direct implementation of this technology in the field of protein science. Conventional PINN models tend to be based on idealized PDEs [45] having fixed coefficients (whereas these should be more comprehensively modeled with probability distributions) and have a resemblance to coarse grating mechanisms in complex systems [46,47]. Also, there is no empirical connection between sequence derived features and features of physical states to restrict their biological validity and generalization power, as well as their biological validity and generalization power, respectively [11].

Moreover, prior research has seldom tried to directly validate PINN learned folding dynamics with a test of experimental fluorescence measurements or large scale sequence embeddings. This gap shows the need for hybrid approaches that combine the mathematical strength of physics based PDEs with the biological richness of deep sequence embeddings.

Significance and contribution to the field: In this paper, a hybrid framework is developed to model the folding of proteins under varying environmental conditions called PhyFold, which involves a PINN and protein sequence embeddings. As in Fig.1, we combine a reaction diffusion equation with ProtT5 sequence embeddings so that both types of information can be utilized in the same learning pipeline. This is an early version published as a preprint in [48].

Proposed model is validated via two different complementary levels.

Mathematical Validation: PINN prediction results are compared with the solution of Finite Difference Method (FDM) to validate whether the neural network is able to follow the governing reaction diffusion equation.

Biological Validation: In order to validate the model using the real folded state of the proteins, the comparison between the fraction of proteins that can fold as predicted by PhyFold and the experimental fraction of proteins that can fold as measured from the change of fluorescence measurement is done. This double validation approach allows PhyFold to learn physical consistency as well as biological meaning in protein folding, which cannot be achieved using the modeling approach of data and physics separately. The environmental factors, including pH, temperature, and pressure, are considered directly in the PhyFold model, allowing us to learn about their impact on protein folding.

Protein folding is one of the most basic processes in the field of molecular biology, and has remained a central subject in the field of structural bioinformatics and biophysics [1]. Previously developed theoretical models explained the basic energy landscape theory which demonstrates that proteins are folded in a pathway mediated by thermodynamic [49] stability and kinetic accessibility [24] to the foldamers. These initial systems related the physicochemical [50] properties of folding with chaperone assisted models and pathological misfolding of neurodegenerative diseases [3,51].

Atomistic insights of folding transitions are available only through traditional computational approaches like MD simulations, which is limited by the cost of calculation and temporal scaling, as well as by scale and computational expense [17]. These limitations inspired the introduction of machine learning into protein structure prediction, dynamics models [26] and prediction of protein structure. Models such as AlphaFold have shown that deep learning models can predict residue level 3D structures of primary sequences with exquisite accuracy [15], but usually predict equilibrium conformations and not kinetic folding pathways [30].

Later studies have investigated the dynamics of protein folding by applying ML-based generative models to protein folding [32]. Simultaneously, self supervised protein language models have become a reality resulting in biologically meaningful sequence embeddings [43]. These embeddings deliver high dimensional representations which are able to capture evolutionary and structural dependencies, which are reflected in protein sequences and structures, respectively [52].

PINNs [53] was propsed in order to add physical consistency to data driven frameworks. The strategy offers a means of deep learning governing PDEs into neural loss functions. Later works have used this neural network to address other complicated biophysical systems [16]. This neural network can simulate kinetics of folding when perturbed by the environment under reaction diffusion dynamics and still exhibit physical interpretability [13], by constraining learning: this capability is known as folding kinetics modeling of physical processes, given that reaction diffusion dynamics can be interpreted as physical processes that can be learned by running simulations and understood through physical laws governing equilibrium driven processes.

However, although much has been achieved, the majority lack dynamic prediction of the folding in real time, or do not incorporate the adaptability of the environment, by not considering the influence of differing physiological conditions, which has been accomplished by most current models. Contrarily, the given study will address this issue by co-training a reaction diffusion based PINN model with bioinformatics derived fluorescence measurements as a biological proxy. The hybrid methodology does not only maintain thermodynamic fidelity but also can be tailored to the different physiological conditions to provide a single methodology to model protein folding and stability under environmental state variation.

Most of the available studies in protein folding utilize fixed equilibrium states using experimental or simulated data to analyze the time independent equilibrium states of the process but not to examine the time dependent evolution of the process. The PhyFold model becomes dynamical since the biological drive to understand the underlying structural dynamics of proteins and the transitions between states requires the model to be informed by environmental changes, i.e. temperature, pH and pressure. This method is essential because it includes the shortcomings of the static analyses, which is the dynamic folding kinetics that is experienced when subjected to real cellular conditions. Combining reaction diffusion equation (RDE) and a PINN, we create a predictive model that is validated with experimental fluorescence data and this represents a considerable improvement as it describes the ongoing changes of the folding landscape. The RD partial differential equation (PDE) controls the protein folding process:

It is important to clarify that the spatial coordinate\(x \in [0,1]\)represents a normalized dimensionless reaction coordinate describing the abstract progression of conformational states within the reduced order mesoscopic formulation, rather than a literal physical spatial dimension in three dimensional Euclidean space. This abstract coordinate parametrizes the evolution of the folding state variable from unfolded to folded conformations and should not be interpreted as representing physical distances between residues or atomic positions. The unidimensional depiction of the reaction coordinate is in agreement with the energy landscape theory for protein folding, which views protein folding as diffusion along a dominant reaction coordinate instead of atom by atom simulations [1,6].

whereu(x,t) represents the folding fraction with the following biophysical interpretation:\(u = 0\)denotes completely unfolded state (random coil conformation),\(u = 1\)represents fully folded state (native tertiary structure), and\(0< u < 1\)indicates partially folded intermediate states. The domain is defined as\(x \in [0, 1]\)(normalized spatial coordinate along protein chain) and\(t \ge 0\)(folding time).

The diffusion term\(D \frac{\partial ^2 u}{\partial x^2}\), models the spatial propagation of folding information along the polypeptide chain, accounting for the cooperativity of folded regions stabilizing adjacent regions via long range interactions. The diffusion coefficientDis a parameter that reflects the conformational change rate and depending on the flexibility of the chain, the dynamics of the backbone, the accessibility of the chain to the solvent and the viscosity of the micro environment, as well as the temperature dependent dynamics and collision rate of molecules. The constant diffusion coefficient D was intentionally adopted as a first-order approximation to maintain mathematical tractability, numerical stability, and physical interpretability of the learned PINN dynamics. Introducing spatially varying or anisotropic diffusion coefficients would significantly increase model complexity and parameter identifiability challenges, particularly in the absence of residue-resolved experimental kinetic measurements. Neumann boundary conditions enforce no flux across domain boundaries.

Although real protein N-termini and C-termini exhibit asymmetric physicochemical properties, the homogeneous Neumann conditions adopted here represent a mathematically consistent first-order approximation within the reduced-order mesoscopic framework their purpose is to prevent nonphysical flux of folding-state information across computational boundaries rather than to assert biological equivalence of the two termini. Terminus-specific sequence context is implicitly incorporated through the ProtT5 embeddings, which encode residue-level physicochemical and structural properties including terminal region characteristics derived from large-scale evolutionary and structural corpora, thereby partially compensating for the simplified boundary formulation at the biological level.

The model parameters are informed by experimental fluorescence data to ensure biological relevance and accuracy. The proposed framework connects molecular scale folding events to continuum level kinetic dynamics, and provides a physically interpretable and computationally efficient way to simulate the protein folding behavior under diverse environmental conditions.

We analyze the well posedness of the proposed reaction diffusion model introduced in the above section under the prescribed Gaussian initial condition and homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. The governing equation is semilinear parabolic, consisting of a linear diffusion operator and a nonlinear reaction term. Since the diffusion coefficient is strictly positive, the equation satisfies the parabolicity condition.

Letf(u) denote the nonlinear reaction term defined in the proposed model. To establish existence and uniqueness, we verify thatf(u) is continuous and satisfies a Lipschitz condition with respect touon the physically admissible domain.

which confirms that the nonlinear reaction term is Lipschitz continuous with respect touon the admissible domain.

The Gaussian initial condition prescribed in the model is smooth, bounded, and lies entirely within the admissible folding interval. Consequently, the initial data belongs to the appropriate function space required for classical parabolic theory. The homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions are compatible with the diffusion operator and ensure a closed system.

By standard results for semilinear parabolic PDEs, the continuity and Lipschitz continuity of the nonlinear term together with the parabolic diffusion operator guarantee the existence of a unique solution to the initial boundary value problem. Moreover, the bounded initial data and no flux boundary conditions allow the application of the parabolic maximum principle, ensuring that the solution remains bounded within the physically meaningful folding interval for all times.

Thus, the proposed reaction diffusion model is mathematically well posed and admits a unique, bounded, and physically meaningful solution.

The PINN forms the computational core of our framework, designed to solve the spatiotemporal dynamics of protein folding by directly embedding the governing RDE into the learning objective as illustrated in Fig.2.

The network employs a fully connected feedforward architecture comprising: an input layer receiving the concatenated vector\([x, t, {\textbf{e}}]\), wherexis the spatial coordinate,tis the temporal variable, and\({\textbf{e}} \in {\mathbb {R}}^{1024}\)is the ProtT5 sequence embedding yielding 1026 input neurons in total; two hidden layers each containing 64 neurons with hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation functions; and a single output neuron with sigmoid activation constraining the predicted folding fractionu(x,t) within the physically admissible range [0, 1]. Xavier normal initialization was applied to all weight matrices to ensure stable gradient propagation.

This architectural design enables the PINN to learn a conditional mapping from spatiotemporal coordinates to folding fractions explicitly conditioned on the protein specific biological context rather than solving a single generic reaction diffusion problem. The predicted folding dynamics\(u(x,t,{\textbf{e}})\)therefore vary across proteins according to their unique embedding representations, enabling genuine sequence specific modulation of folding behavior. The shared reaction diffusion parametersD,\(\alpha _0\), and\(\beta _0\)represent universal physical mechanisms governing folding kinetics, while protein specific variability is captured through the high dimensional embedding conditioning. This integration effectively transforms the standard PINN into a Bio-Physics Informed Neural Network.

While the governing PDE operates in a one dimensional abstract coordinate space, three dimensional structural and evolutionary context is implicitly incorporated through the ProtT5 sequence embeddings, which encode residue level physicochemical dependencies derived from large scale structural corpora, thereby partially compensating for the reduced dimensionality of the governing PDE. The use of this approach, combining reductionist physics models with high dimensional biological embedding, is based on the theoretical principle that mesoscale kinetic phenomena can be described by low dimensional systems provided that sequence information is conditioned [24].

The optimization goal is designed as a composite loss,

The loss weighting parameters are selected to maintain an effective balance between biological supervision and physical consistency. The data fidelity weight (\(\lambda _{\text {data}} = 190\)) ensures sufficient influence of the experimental fluorescence signal at discrete observed points, while the combined physics weights PDE compliance (\(\lambda _{\text {PDE}} = 10\)), initial conditions (\(\lambda _{\text {IC}} = 100\)), and boundary conditions (\(\lambda _{\text {BC}} = 50\)) — amount to a total physics regularization weight of 160, which is comparable to the data loss weight. This configuration ensures that the learned solutions remain physically consistent with the governing reaction-diffusion equation while remaining biologically grounded.

The validity of this weighting configuration is empirically confirmed through an ablation study reported in "Ablation study and parameter sensitivity analysis" section, demonstrating that removal of the PDE loss term or redistribution of weights leads to measurable degradation in predictive performance.

The PDE residual loss enforces satisfaction of the RDE at collocation points throughout the domain. The initial condition loss ensures the solution matches the Gaussian initial distribution specified in Eq. (5). The boundary condition loss enforces the Neumann conditions defined in Eq. (6) at the domain boundaries. An optional data loss term incorporates biological validation when experimental fluorescence data is available.

Training configuration employs the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of\(5\times 10^{-3}\), complemented by a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler that reduces the learning rate by a factor of 0.5 after 5000 epochs of no improvement. Early stopping with a patience of 5000 epochs prevents overfitting, while random sampling of collocation points ensures robust training.

Schematic architecture of the PINN for protein folding dynamics. The network integrates physical modeling with data driven learning through: (i) multi modal inputs (spatial temporal coordinates and sequence embeddings), (ii) hidden layers with physics informed activation, and (iii) output constrained folding fraction prediction. The composite loss function simultaneously enforces PDE compliance, initial/boundary conditions, and experimental data fidelity through balanced weighting terms

To validate and compare the PINN performance, the same RD model governed by Eq. (1) was solved numerically using the implicit backward Euler Finite difference (FDM) scheme in MATLAB. The spatial domain [0, 1] was discretized intoJintervals, and the temporal domain\([0,T_{\max }]\)was divided into uniform time steps\(\Delta t\). The discretized system can be expressed as in Eq. (8)

with Neumann boundary conditions following Eq. (6) and an initial condition implementing the Gaussian distribution specified in Eq. (5), representing local initiation of the folding process. The numerical implementation iteratively updates\(U_i^{n+1}\)at each time step and stores the results for quantitative comparison with the PINN predictions.

The fluorescence dataset employed in this study is the publicly available GFP fluorescence dataset originally introduced by Sarkisyan [57] and accessed via the DeepProtein benchmark [17]. The dataset comprises 21,446 protein sequences with experimentally measured logarithmic fluorescence intensity labels. The dataset was partitioned using a standard random split with fixed random seed (random seed=1234) into training (80%) and test (20%) subsets yielding approximately 17,157 training sequences and 4,289 test sequences. The test set was strictly held out from all training procedures. Regarding sequence identity between splits the fluorescence dataset comprises single and multiple point mutations of the Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP), meaning all sequences are variants of a single parent protein. Conventional 30% sequence identity filtering designed to prevent leakage between evolutionarily distant protein families is not directly applicable in this context, as all sequences are by definition highly similar variants of the same protein. The relevant generalization challenge is therefore prediction across different mutational combinations rather than across protein families. The biological validation metrics reported in this study were computed on the full held out test set of 4,289 sequences, ensuring statistically representative validation results. ProtT5 embeddings captured high dimensional biophysical context, while the PINN predicted the effective folding fractionu(x,t) as a function of spatial coordinate (x) and time (t). The predicted folding fraction\({\bar{u}}\)represents a normalized conformational progression from unfolded to folded states. Since fluorescence intensity in the Sarkisyan [57] dataset serves as an experimentally established proxy for folding dependent structural integrity, the spatially and temporally averaged folding fraction\({\bar{u}}\)was computed as a scalar summary per protein sequence and compared against normalized experimental fluorescence labels. The fluorescence dataset is incorporated as a biologically grounded validation tool to confirm consistency between predicted folding dynamics and experimentally observed biological behavior, rather than as a competitive benchmark for fluorescence intensity prediction. The predicted fluorescence (\({\hat{y}}\)) was statistically compared against the true experimental values (y) using root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), coefficient of determination (\(R^2\)), and Pearson correlation (r):

Although the FDM-PINN benchmark comparison is presented under optimal physiological conditions as a representative case, the mathematical validity of the PINN framework extends consistently across all environmental stress conditions. This follows from a fundamental property of the governing reaction diffusion equation: the environmental stress conditions sub-optimal, thermal stress, acidic, and alkaline do not alter the mathematical structure of the PDE. Rather, they exclusively modify the environmentally modulated kinetic coefficients\(\alpha (\Theta )\)and\(\beta (\Theta )\), which are deterministic scalar functions of temperature, pH, and pressure defined in Eq. (3) and Eq. (4). The spatial differential operator, diffusion coefficientD, boundary conditions, and initial conditions remain mathematically identical across all tested environmental scenarios. The mathematical validity established under optimal conditions therefore directly extends to all stress condition simulations by the structural invariance of the governing equation not as an assumption, but as a mathematical consequence. The physically consistent and monotonically degrading predictive performance observed across all conditions in Table2further corroborates this, as mathematically unstable PINN solutions would produce irregular or physically implausible folding predictions which are not observed in our results.
