The moderate Pearson correlation value (\(r=0.650 \pm 0.015\)) and the negative value of the\(R^2\)(−0.264) value indicate that there is a linear relationship between the two variables although predictions by the model are less precise as when the simple mean values are used to predict the variable.

The comparatively stronger predictive performance under acidic stress (\(r = 0.775\),\(R^{2} = 0.573\)) relative to alkaline stress (\(r = 0.650\),\(R^{2} = -0.264\)) reflects a fundamental asymmetry in the underlying destabilization mechanisms. Under acidic conditions (pH 6.5), the dominant effect involves protonation of ionizable residues a localized and relatively predictable perturbation that is reasonably approximated by the symmetric Gaussian decay in\(\alpha (\Theta )\). Under alkaline conditions (pH 8.0), multiple concurrent mechanisms operate simultaneously including deprotonation of ionizable residues, disruption of electrostatic networks, perturbation of hydrogen-bonding patterns, and alteration of hydrophobic packing producing highly nonlinear and heterogeneous conformational responses that exceed the representational capacity of the current symmetric pH-response formulation. The domain of reliable applicability of the PhyFold framework therefore encompasses physiological, mild sub-optimal, thermal stress, and acidic stress conditions. Under extreme alkaline stress (\(\textrm{pH} \ge 8.0\)), quantitative prediction accuracy is reduced, and this is explicitly acknowledged as a current limitation of the framework.

This limitation originates primarily in the functional form of Eq. (3), which employs a symmetric Gaussian pH-response function that does not explicitly model the asymmetric multi-mechanism destabilization characteristic of extreme alkaline environments. Experimental fluorescence variability under alkaline conditions further compounds this limitation. Future extensions incorporating asymmetric pH-response functions and explicit electrostatic interaction operators are identified as important directions.

It is important to note that Pearson correlation (r) and\(R^{2}\)evaluate distinct aspects of predictive performance. The positive Pearson correlation (r = 0.650) under alkaline stress indicates that meaningful directional correspondence between predicted folding behavior and experimental fluorescence trends is preserved, even when absolute magnitude agreement reflected in\(R^{2}\)deteriorates. The monotonic degradation of predictive performance across increasingly extreme environmental conditions confirms that PhyFold captures environmentally modulated folding complexity in a physically interpretable manner.

The high folding rate constant of both alkaline and other stress conditions is a\(\alpha =1.671\), although this is still a lower folding rate than physiological optima would be. The very high prediction errors (MAE =\(0.279 \pm 0.010\), RMSE =\(0.296 \pm 0.012\)) and negative value of\(R^2\)(−0.264) identify alkaline stress as the most difficult situation to predict. This weakness of the performance indicates that existing physical models could be failing to represent the multi mechanism destabilization effects caused by high pH environments, which is an important area that requires future model enhancement.

The PhyFold frame can capture the dynamics of folding of a protein, which observe major biophysical principles of the formation of protein structures. The sigmoidal folding curves and the propagation of the spatial structure are representative of the cooperative folding process and are preceded by a rapid structural consolidation due to the nucleation processes. These conditions are perturbed and the kinetics of folding are delayed, the steady state folding fractions are reduced, which agrees with previous experimental measurements and indicates that there are increased energetic barriers and destabilisation of native conformations.

The sensitivity analysis on the environmental condition also shows that physio-chemical conditions play a crucial role in determining folding behavior. Optimal temperature and pH also maximize the rates of effective folding whereas atypical alkaline stress specifically disrupts electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonding network that provide stability to the structure. The extreme loss of predictive accuracy in high pH regimes demonstrates the complexity inherent in the folding landscapes under chemically perturbed conditions, and the necessity to consider the effects of the environment on the folding landscape models.

PhyFold uses explicitly physical limitations to a data driven learning model, so that biologically interpretable folding predictions are being made by PhyFold beyond structure determination. This allows modeling of physiologically relevant and stress induced conditions of folding pathways more realistically, which is of use in protein engineering, structure guided drug discovery, and in the study of folding related dysfunctions.

To empirically validate the contribution of physics informed constraints, the adopted loss weighting scheme, and the robustness of baseline parameters, a systematic ablation and sensitivity analysis was conducted.

Three alternative loss weight configurations were evaluated against the nominal PhyFold framework: (1) removal of the PDE residual loss (\(\lambda _{\text {PDE}}=0\)), (2) equal weighting of all loss terms (\(\lambda _{\text {data}}=\lambda _{\text {PDE}}= \lambda _{\text {IC}}=\lambda _{\text {BC}}=100\)), and (3) physics-heavy weighting (\(\lambda _{\text {data}}=100\),\(\lambda _{\text {PDE}}=50\),\(\lambda _{\text {IC}}=100\),\(\lambda _{\text {BC}}=50\)). All other training configurations were kept identical. Results are summarized in Table3.

Removal of the PDE loss term leads to reduction in Pearson correlation from\(r=0.822\)to\(r=0.699\), confirming that physics-informed constraints contribute meaningful predictive value. Both alternative weighting configurations similarly degrade performance, confirming that the adopted loss weights represent a principled optimal balance.

A local sensitivity analysis was conducted by independently perturbing each baseline parameter (D,\(\alpha _0\),\(\beta _0\)) while keeping remaining parameters fixed at nominal values. Results are summarized in Table4.

The nominal parameter configuration (\(D=0.01\),\(\alpha _0=2.0\),\(\beta _0=0.2\)) yields the strongest predictive performance. Perturbations ofDbetween 0.005 and 0.02 preserve Pearson correlation above 0.82, confirming robustness to diffusion coefficient variation. Perturbations of\(\alpha _0\)and\(\beta _0\)produce systematic and physically interpretable performance changes, confirming that nominal values represent physically meaningful choices rather than arbitrary selections.

This study presents PhyFold, a hybrid framework that unifies PINN with deep learning embeddings to model protein folding dynamics under varying environmental conditions. By coupling data-driven learning with physical constraints, PhyFold bridges the gap between empirical fluorescence data and the underlying biophysical processes governing folding kinetics. The framework explicitly incorporates environmental parameters temperature (T), pH, and pressure (P) into the RDE governing protein folding, enabling physically consistent simulation of environmental influences on folding stability. Mathematical validation against finite difference solutions confirmed close adherence to the governing physics, establishing the reliability of the PINN based solver. Optimization with the Adam optimizer ensured smooth and stable convergence while maintaining the balance between data loss and physical consistency. Using fluorescence data as a biologically grounded validation proxy, the model achieved a Pearson correlation of\(r = 0.822\)and MAE\(= 0.101\)across the held out test set of 4,289 GFP variant sequences, demonstrating strong agreement with experimentally observed biological trends. These results highlight that integrating physics informed constraints into neural computation enhances both predictive accuracy and interpretability. The framework reproduces the spatiotemporal dynamics of protein folding and captures environmentally modulated folding behavior in a physically interpretable manner. The framework demonstrates its strongest predictive reliability under physiological and near physiological conditions, including mild sub optimal, thermal stress, and acidic stress environments. Under extreme alkaline stress (pH\(\ge\)8.0), the current symmetric pH response formulation represents an acknowledged limitation, as the model does not fully capture the multi mechanism destabilization at high pH, reflected in the negative\(R^2\)observed at this condition. The one dimensional reaction coordinate is based on energy landscape theory and Kramers’ diffusion formalism and is appropriate for two state folders, like GFP. However, it cannot resolve the three dimensional structural complexity and nonlocal contacts. In order to apply the one dimensional reaction coordinate to multi domain and intrinsically disordered proteins, an important future direction is to develop higher dimensional collective variable spaces. Future extensions incorporating asymmetric pH response functions, sequence dependent diffusion coefficients, higher dimensional representations, and validation across diverse protein families are identified as important directions for advancing the framework.

title: Fast intermolecular interaction energy calculation with the OPLS-AA force field
author: Mirco Daniel; Hannah Kullik; Martin Urban; Christoph Steinbeck; Achim Zielesny
text:
A fast pipeline based on the OPLS-AA force field is presented that enables the automated calculation of non-bonding intermolecular (dimer) interaction energies derived from a set of small organic (monomer) molecules. To calculate the non-bonding contributions, optimized geometries of the monomer molecules as well as their OPLS-AA van der Waals and atomic partial charge parameters are required. The key advantage of the new pipeline lies in its fast, highly parallelized in-memory computations without slow I/O operations, which make it possible to thoroughly process comparatively large numbers of (more than a hundred) monomer molecules within acceptable time frames (hours and days): Compared to an analogous, more versatile, and comprehensive approach, the new computational scheme delivers comparable results while being more than two orders of magnitude faster. For locally estimating the required OPLS-AA force field parameters with the LigParGen and BOSS software packages, a user-friendly graphical user interface for the Windows operating system is provided.

Scientific contribution

Rapid calculation of mutual intermolecular energies for a set of monomer molecules based on the widely used OPLS-AA force field enables a considerable expansion of this type of calculation for practical purposes. The performance improvement can be used to achieve significant improvements of interaction energy averages as well as considerable expansions in the size of the monomer molecule set.

The quantitative estimation of intermolecular interactions between (small organic) molecules substantially supports both their theoretical understanding and practical design purposes, from materials science to life sciences [1,2]. Compared to the total energy of a configuration of a molecular dimer (i.e., a non-covalently bound pair of monomer molecules) or the covalent bonds within its constituent monomers, the contribution of intermolecular non-bonding interactions is typically orders of magnitude smaller, as it only includes dispersed variations of electromagnetic interactions due to van der Waals forces or partial atomic charges.

A recent work presented an automated molecular force-field based calculation pipeline for the estimation of mutual intermolecular interaction energies of a set of small to medium-sized organic monomer molecules [3], openly available on GitHub [4]. The calculation pipeline consists of a computing backbone programmed in Java, with all force-field-based calculations being performed by stand-alone, task-based executables of the Tinker Molecular Modelling package [5]. This architecture relies heavily on comparatively slow file I/O operations for communication between the different executables. This creates a severe performance bottleneck when extending the workflow to larger monomer sets, as the computational effort scales quadratically with the number of monomers.

The aim of this work is to introduce an algorithmically simplified variant of this calculation pipeline specifically for the OPLS-AA (Optimized Potentials for Liquid Simulations–All Atom) force field [6,7], where the final dimer geometry optimization is skipped. The new variant is again highly parallelized and thoroughly exploits modern multi-core workstation processors. Unlike the established pipeline, however, it performs all calculations exclusively in memory within the Java backbone, without invoking an external Tinker executable file, thereby completely avoiding comparatively slow communication-based I/O operations. For obtaining the OPLS-AA force field parameters of the organic monomer molecules, the LigParGen calculation engine (either locally or via a webserver) can be utilized [8].

For local LigParGen calculations with the Windows operating system, a supplementary, standalone open graphical user interface (GUI) application based on a local executable of the BOSS software [9] is provided, that alleviates parameter calculation for large sets of monomer molecules. A convenient Windows installer is available in addition.

The force-field-based intermolecular energy\({E}_{ij}^{C}\left(r\right)\)between two monomer molecules\(i\)and\(j\)depends on the intermolecular distance\(r\)between the centers of the molecules as well as their relative spatial configuration\(C\). For a specific distance\({r}_{fix}\)there is a minimum energy configuration\({C}_{min}\)with\({E}_{ij}^{{C}_{min}}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\le {E}_{ij}^{C}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\)which is smaller than all other configuration energies\({E}_{ij}^{C}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\)at that distance. An averaged intermolecular energy at a fixed intermolecular distance\({r}_{fix}\)can be obtained by approximating the infinite number of possible spatial dimer configurations with a subset of configurations according to an elaborated scheme developed in [3], where configuration sampling at each fixed distance\({r}_{fix}\)involves evaluating\({N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{rot}\)distinct spatial configurations. First,\({N}_{sphere}\)evenly spaced points are generated on a unit sphere around each monomer's center using a Fibonacci lattice. The molecules are aligned along an axis connecting their centers and one surface point from each sphere, creating\({N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{sphere}\)orientations. The second molecule is then rotated around this axis by\({N}_{rot}\)different angles. These\({N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{rot}\)configurations can be averaged with Boltzmann weights\({w}_{C}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\)for a defined temperature (with\({\text{k}}_{\text{B}}\), the Boltzmann constant, and\(\text{T}\), thermodynamic temperature)

to obtain an averaged intermolecular energy\(\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle \left({r}_{fix},T\right)\)for the fixed distance\({r}_{fix}\). Among these\({N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{rot}\)averaged configurations, the one with the minimal intermolecular energy is denoted\({E}_{ij}^{{C}^{*}}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\). Note that\({E}_{ij}^{{C}^{*}}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\ge {E}_{ij}^{{C}_{min}}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\), because the sampled configuration\({E}_{ij}^{{C}^{*}}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\)may only be an approximation–though usually an acceptable one–rather than the true minimum energy configuration\({E}_{ij}^{{C}_{min}}\left({r}_{fix}\right)\)at the fixed distance\({r}_{fix}\). The global minimum energy dimer is characterized by a distinct distance\({r}_{min}\)so that\({E}_{ij}^{min}={E}_{ij}^{{C}_{min}}\left({r}_{min}\right)\le {E}_{ij}^{C}\left(r\right)\), i.e.,\({r}_{min}\)is the distance between the centers of two molecules\(i\)and\(j\)when the dimer geometry corresponds to the global energy minimum. The corresponding averaged minimum energy distance\({r}_{\langle E\rangle ,min}\)with\({\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle }^{min}\left(T\right)=\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle \left({r}_{\langle E\rangle ,min},T\right)\le \langle {E}_{ij}\rangle \left(r,T\right)\)does not necessarily coincide with minimum distance\({r}_{min}\)of the global minimum energy dimer but will generally be located in its vicinity.

The OPLS-AA force field estimates the intermolecular interaction energy\({E}_{ij}^{C}\)between two monomer molecules\(i\)and\(j\)as a sum of an electrostatic Coulomb\(\left({E}_{ij}^{Coulomb}\right)\)and a Lennard–Jones 6–12\(\left({E}_{ij}^{LJ}\right)\)contribution [6]

\({k}_{e}\), Coulomb's constant\(\frac{1}{4\pi {\varepsilon}_{0} } \left[\frac{N{m}^{2}}{{C}^{2}}\right]\);\({N}_{A}\), Avogadro's constant\(\left[\frac{1}{mol}\right]\);\({f}_{cal}\), conversion factor from Joule to Calorie\(\left[\frac{cal}{J}\right]\);\(e\), elementary charge\(\left[C\right]\);\({q}_{a}e\), partial charge of atom\(a\)in molecule\(i; {q}_{b}e\),partial charge of atom\(b\)in molecule\(j\);\({\varepsilon}_{0}\), vacuum permittivity\(\left[\frac{{C}^{2}}{N{m}^{2}}\right]\);\({r}_{ab}\), distance between atom\(a\)in molecule\(i\)and atom\(b\)in molecule\(j\)\(\left[m\right]\);\({\varepsilon}_{ab}\), depth of the potential well between atom\(a\)in molecule\(i\)and atom\(b\)in molecule\(j\)\(\left[\frac{kcal}{mol}\right]\);\({\sigma}_{ab}\), distance at which the potential energy between atom\(a\)in molecule\(i\)and atom\(b\)in molecule\(j\)is zero\(\left[\text{m}\right]\).

The parameters\({\varepsilon}_{ab}\)and\({\sigma}_{ab}\)for pairs with different atoms are obtained with the (geometric mean) combination rules of the self-interaction parameters:

The new simplified variant of the intermolecular energy calculation pipeline starts with optimized geometries of all monomer molecules and their corresponding OPLS-AA (\(q\),\(\varepsilon\)and\(\sigma\)) force field parameters. The optimized molecule geometries may be obtained by a priori quantum chemical or molecular mechanics calculations to result in a set of monomer PDB-files, each containing the 3D coordinates of its monomer atoms. The OPLS-AA force field parameters\(q\),\(\varepsilon\)and\(\sigma\)of each monomer molecule for the non-bonding contributions are taken from publicly available parameter sets (e.g., [10]) or obtained with the LigParGen calculation engine. LigParGen calculations are available via the new local LigParGen-GUI application (see below), the direct use of the native Linux LigParGen CLI or the LigParGen web server, which all take a monomer PDB-file as an input and generate the corresponding monomer xyz- (3D coordinate) and key-(parameter)-files for the calculation pipeline. The set of monomers xyz- and key-files is then copied to the input directories/Moleculesand/tinker/params/OPLSAALIGPARGENto calculate the mutual interaction energies.

A typical estimation procedure for averaged interaction energies is sketched in Fig.1for the acetic acid (HAc) dimer: To estimate\({r}_{\langle E\rangle ,min}\)and corresponding\({\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle }^{min}\), an initial scan is performed with various intermolecular distances (typically in the range from about 3 to about 16\(\text{\AA }\), in steps of 0.5\(\text{\AA }\)). For each distance,\({N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{rot}\)dimer configurations are calculated according to the scheme in [3] to determine each averaged\(\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle \left(r\right)\)value. The determined global averaged energy minimum is then refined using a two-stage minimization procedure (where the step size is initially set to 0.1\(\text{\AA }\)and subsequently to 0.01\(\text{\AA }\)in the second refinement stage) to obtain an approximate value for\({\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle }^{min}=\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle \left({r}_{\langle E\rangle ,min}\right)\)with an accuracy of two decimal places (0.01\(\text{\AA }\)) for\({r}_{\langle E\rangle ,min}\). If desired,\({\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle }^{min}=\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle \left({r}_{\langle E\rangle ,min}\right)\)can finally be approximated by an increased number of\({N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{sphere}\times {N}_{rot}\)dimer configurations.

Estimation of\({\text{r}}_{\langle \text{E}\rangle ,\text{m}\text{i}\text{n}}\)and corresponding\({\langle {\text{E}}_{\text{i}\text{j}}\rangle }^{\text{m}\text{i}\text{n}}\left(\text{T}=298\text{K}\right)\)for the acetic acid (HAc) dimer with an initial scan of intermolecular distances in the range from 3 to 16\(\text{\AA }\), in steps of 0.5\(\text{\AA }\). For each distance,\(144\times 144\times 16\)dimer configurations are calculated according to the scheme in [3] to determine each averaged\(\langle {\text{E}}_{\text{i}\text{j}}\rangle \left(\text{r},298\text{K}\right)\)value. The determined global averaged energy minimum at about r = 5\(\text{\AA }\)is refined using a two-stage minimization procedure (with initial step size of 0.1\(\text{\AA }\)and 0.01\(\text{\AA }\)in the second refinement stage). The determined approximation to the global minimum energy dimer configuration is shown at the top

For the detailed settings of the calculation process there are two text files available: In theMIPET.jobtext file, the OPLS-AA force field and the monomer molecules for mutual interaction calculation have to be specified. In theMIPET.propertiestext file, additional parameters related to the pipeline's execution can be set. Most of the settings are self-explanatory and described within the text file itself. The default parameters are based on extensive tests and do usually not need to be modified. Crucial parameter settings are the number of dimer configurations to be calculated for each distance (MIPETSphereNodeNumber\({N}_{sphere}\),MIPETRotationNumber\({N}_{rot}\)) and the number of CPU cores to be used in parallel (MIPETCPUCoreNumber), which determine the calculation speed. The calculation pipeline evaluates all dimer interaction energies according to the defined settings along the defined calculation scheme, and creates a subdirectory for each dimer interaction in its specified output path that contains all dimer-specific calculation results. These comprise general information about the intermolecular energies, intermolecular energy-distance plots, and the lowest-energy dimer configuration in PDB, xyz and tinker’s xyz format. The results may be further processed to obtain differential pair interaction energies or repulsion parameters for mesoscopic dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations. For the latter, each result directory already contains a text file with particle set data for the openMFsim/Jdpdsimulation environment [24,25,26,27]. The new variant of the calculation pipeline is openly available on GitHub [4].

A new local LigParGen-GUI application is provided (see Fig.2) as a supplementary, standalone tool that is not required for the calculation pipeline. It is currently only available for Windows 10 or later versions and facilitates the usage of the LigParGen v2.1 [11,12,13] and BOSS [14,15] software packages, where the BOSS software package can be requested as a compressed archive file via the William L. Jorgensen laboratory website [9]. The application is implemented in Python 3.11 [16] using the PyQt6 framework [17] and follows a Model-View-Controller (MVC) architecture. Since BOSS is compiled against 32-bit Linux libraries, it requires a 32-bit Linux system. Thus, calculations are executed within the Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL2), while the GUI itself runs natively on Windows. This architecture was specifically chosen to lower the entry barrier for Windows users, who would otherwise face a notoriously difficult manual setup process or require dedicated Linux hardware to run BOSS. The LigParGen-GUI exposes the same configuration options as the LigParGen web server [12,13,18], including settings for the number of molecular optimization iterations, the charge model, and the molecule charge. It supports all output formats available through the LigParGen command-line interface (CLI) and adds a built-in timeout mechanism to terminate calculations exceeding user-defined time limits. Communication between the Windows host and the WSL2 environment is managed by a microservice that uses ZeroMQ [19] in a push/pull messaging pattern. Since the GUI functions as a mere wrapper around the native LigParGen CLI, advanced Linux users can of course completely bypass the Windows GUI and feed native CLI outputs directly into the calculation pipeline.

Graphical user interface of the local LigParGen Windows application

A typical workflow with the local LigParGen-GUI application begins with specifying an input directory containing either the molecules’ PDB-files or a text file with their SMILES strings. The user then configures the LigParGen settings and selects the desired output file formats before choosing an output directory for storing calculation results transferred from WSL2. Once the job is submitted, the GUI transfers the job to the WSL2 microservice which invokes the LigParGen CLI with the appropriate arguments and communicates status updates back to the GUI. Progress is displayed in a dynamically updated dialog window, implemented with PyQt6’s signal-slot mechanism to ensure thread safety. Upon completion, the software notifies the user and offers the option to automatically open the output directory.

The local LigParGen calculations require the BOSS software package as a compressed archive file which can be installed directly through the LigParGen-GUI user interface: At first launch, the application prompts the user to provide the path to the BOSS ZIP-file.

The graphical user interface is distributed as a standalone executable generated with PyInstaller [20]. It includes a custom AlmaLinux distribution [21] that is automatically imported into WSL2 during installation and provides a preconfigured LigParGen environment. A convenient Windows installer executable built with Inno Setup 6 [22] is also provided. Documentation is available in PDF format through the Help menu. The complete LigParGen-GUI source code is openly accessible on GitHub [23].

The calculation results of the new pipeline variant can be directly compared to those of the dimer calculations provided in [3]: The analog Table1and corresponding Fig.3demonstrate that the new pipeline is on par with the established more complex approach. Since there is no final geometry optimization of the dimer, the new pipeline cannot calculate\({E}_{ij}^{min}\), but the results for the approximations\({E}_{ij}^{{C}^{*}}\left({r}_{\langle E\rangle ,min}\right)\)and the averages\({\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle }^{min}\)are in good agreement and close to\({E}_{ij}^{min}\). The use of LigParGen generated parameters also leads to comparable results to those of the original OPLS-AA force field (where original charges of TIP5P water are multiplied by a factor of 1.14, as is the case in the LigParGen calculations).

OPLS-AA intermolecular interaction energies (with the TIP5P model for water) in kcal/mole for different dimers and calculation pipelines at the corresponding minimum energy distances of the monomer molecules (see Table1). The solid lines refer to\({\langle {\text{E}}_{\text{i}\text{j}}\rangle }^{\text{m}\text{i}\text{n}}\), the dotted lines to\({\text{E}}_{\text{i}\text{j}}^{{\text{C}}^{*}}\left({\text{r}}_{\langle \text{E}\rangle ,\text{m}\text{i}\text{n}}\right)\)

The neglect of the final dimer geometry optimization to obtain\({E}_{ij}^{min}\)may cause significant deviations for larger monomer molecules, e.g., highly polar molecules with multiple polar atoms which form strong, highly directional electrostatic interactions, where small spatial misalignments could cause comparatively large artificial energy spikes, or molecules with a high degree of conformational freedom. The calculation pipeline automatically generates two diagnostic plots for each calculated dimer interaction in its specific output directory: These comprise detailed intermolecular energy-distance plots where unexpected fluctuations, artificial discontinuities, or incomplete convergence can be detected. The sketched unwanted deviations can be effectively mitigated by systematically increasing the configuration sampling size (by increasing\({N}_{sphere}\)and\({N}_{rot}\)correspondingly) to take more configurations into account.

Compared to the established calculation pipeline in [3], the exclusive in-memory calculations with comparable calculation results lead to a performance boost of more than two orders of magnitude–reducing computational “weeks and months” of the established approach to a mere “hours or days” for the new simplified in-memory variant. A direct comparison on an AMD Threadripper Pro 5995WX workstation with 64 calculation threads for calculating the mutual interaction energies of a set of 5 monomer molecules (H2O, Et, EtOH, Me, and Me2O, comprising 15 unique dimer interactions and 144 × 144x16 dimer configurations for each distance, compare Fig.1) yielded a computation time of 1080.0 s (18 min) until the original file-bound and Tinker-dependent pipeline (version 1.0.3) had completed the task, whilst the new in-memory variant (version 1.0.6) required only 6.1 s for the identical calculations – resulting in a speedup factor of 177 and illustrating the leap in performance achieved by eliminating disk I/O operations and external process overhead. Within a given time, the speed-up enables a significant increase of the number of calculated spatial dimer configurations to improve averages of non-bonded intermolecular interactions at different monomer distances as well as a considerably increased size of the monomer molecule set for calculating mutual interaction energies. While the established pipeline calculates with 144 × 144x16 (= 331,776) dimer configurations for each single average at each distance by default, the new variant routinely uses 1000 × 1000x60 (= 60 million) configurations. As a rule of thumb, the full calculation of a single dimer interaction energy scheme for obtaining\({r}_{\langle E\rangle ,min}\)and corresponding\({\langle {E}_{ij}\rangle }^{min}\)(see Fig.1and description above) takes less than 1 min with these 1000 × 1000x60 (60 million) dimer configurations using an AMD Threadripper 5995WX workstation processor with 64 calculation threads.

title: AI-guided De Novo design of DHPS inhibitors
author: Hongchul Shin; Kyuhyeon Bang; Ingyo Park; Hong-Rae Kim; Kwang Yeon Hwang
text:
Hypusine modification of eIF5A by Deoxyhypusine Synthase (DHPS) is essential for the replication of a broad range of viruses, making DHPS an attractive host-directed therapy (HDT) target for antiviral drug discovery. AI-based drug design methods spanning binding affinity prediction and de novo molecular generation are rapidly proliferating, yet systematic benchmarking of diverse algorithmic paradigms under identical conditions on a shared target, with experimental validation, remains scarce. Here, we present an integrated AI benchmarking pipeline targeting DHPS and evaluate the full process from computational prediction to experimental validation. We compared 13 MM-GBSA score estimation models and 10 de novo molecular generation methods under 5-seed repeated experiments. For the prediction task, we propose an Out-of-Fold stacking ensemble integrating gradient boosting, graph neural networks, and chemical language models, achieving the highest Spearman rank correlation of 0.861 among all compared models. For the generation task, we propose RL-Design, a reinforcement learning-based framework using the ensemble predictor as a scoring oracle. RL-Design achieved the highest hit rate of 92.02% and maintained drug-like physicochemical properties across generated molecules, outperforming all nine competing methods. Moreover, experimental dose–response assays confirmed inhibitory activity in all three predicted-active compounds, with two highly active compounds showing IC50values of 31.2 and 49.1 µM. Predicted and experimental activity showed complete concordance across all six tested compounds, providing oracle-independent validation of the pipeline. This pipeline provides a reproducible framework for AI-guided, target-specific inhibitor design and demonstrates the feasibility of HDT-focused antiviral drug discovery through systematic AI benchmarking.

Scientific contribution

This work proposes two methods for inhibitor discovery against DHPS, a host-directed antiviral target. A predictive model for MM-GBSA binding-score estimation and a generative model that designs candidate hit compounds both ranked first among previous prediction and generation models under identical benchmarking. The predicted activities were experimentally confirmed by dose–response enzymatic assays.

Viral infections continue to pose a major global health threat, causing substantial mortality and morbidity across diverse pathogen classes [1]. Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) are increasingly limited by the high mutation rates of viral genomes, which drive rapid resistance emergence and reduce long-term treatment efficacy [2]. Host-directed therapy (HDT) offers a complementary strategy by targeting host factors that are broadly co-opted by multiple viral pathogens, thereby providing a higher barrier to resistance and the potential for pan-viral activity [3]. The eukaryotic translation initiation factor eIF5A, activated through hypusine modification, has emerged as one such host dependency factor [4]. Hypusinated eIF5A supports the replication of a range of clinically important viruses, including HIV-1 and SARS-CoV-2, by facilitating the translation of viral frameshifting sequences and enabling the function of viral regulatory proteins [4]. Deoxyhypusine Synthase (DHPS), the enzyme catalyzing the committed step of hypusine biosynthesis, therefore represents an attractive HDT target for broad-spectrum antiviral drug discovery [5].

DHPS is the rate-limiting enzyme in hypusine biosynthesis, catalyzing the transfer of the 4-aminobutyl moiety of spermidine onto the Lys50 residue of the eIF5A precursor using NAD as a cofactor to generate a deoxyhypusine intermediate [6]. This intermediate is subsequently hydroxylated by Deoxyhypusine Hydroxylase (DOHH) to yield mature hypusinated eIF5A [7]. The most extensively characterized DHPS inhibitor to date is GC-7 (N1-guanyl-1, 7-diaminoheptane), a spermidine mimetic that occupies the spermidine binding site [8]. However, the structural similarity of GC-7 to spermidine confers a risk of nonselective binding and off-target toxicity, and its poor drug-likeness has precluded clinical development [9]. The discovery of structurally diverse, drug-like DHPS inhibitors targeting the NAD cofactor binding pocket is therefore warranted.

Recent years have seen a rapid influx of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) approaches across multiple stages of drug discovery [10,11,12]. Binding affinity prediction models enable large-scale virtual screening, while generative models based on reinforcement learning, variational autoencoders, and flow-based architectures have been applied to de novo molecular design [13]. However, each paradigm has inherent limitations. GNN-based prediction models are prone to overfitting on small target-specific datasets [14]. Latent space optimization-based generative models struggle to incorporate target-specific reward signals, resulting in low hit rates [15]. RL-based generation methods offer efficient exploration but often do not guarantee drug-likeness of generated molecules [16]. Despite these distinct strengths and weaknesses, direct comparison of these methods under identical conditions on a common target is rare [17]. End-to-end benchmarking of both prediction and generation models with experimental validation has seldom been reported.

In this study, we performed a systematic AI benchmarking study using DHPS as a shared target. We compared 13 MM-GBSA (Molecular Mechanics-Generalized Born Surface Area) score estimation models and 10 de novo molecular generation methods under 5-seed repeated experimental conditions. For the prediction task, we evaluated diverse architectures including gradient boosting, graph neural networks, and chemical language models, and propose an Out-of-Fold stacking (OOF-Stacking) ensemble as the optimal scoring oracle. For the generation task, our proposed RL-Design demonstrated superiority in hit rate, drug-likeness, and computational efficiency. SHAP analysis revealed that the top-ranked features are broadly consistent with the physicochemical properties expected for molecules engaging the active site of DHPS, supporting the chemical interpretability of the prediction model.

A target-specific dataset was constructed by docking 1920 fragment compounds into DHPS using Glide XP in Schrödinger Suite 2025-4 [18]. The 1920 fragments comprised the commercially available Enamine High Fidelity Fragment Library (HFF-1920), selected for its Rule-of-Three-compliant, structurally diverse, quality-controlled members and its amenability to commercial analog follow-up, with the library size matched to our experimental screening throughput. The crystal structure of human DHPS (PDB ID: 6PGR) was used as the receptor, and the docking grid was centered on the centroid of the co-crystallized ligand at the entrance of the NAD-binding pocket, which overlaps the spermidine-binding site. The receptor structure was prepared using the Protein Preparation Wizard, and fragment ligands were prepared using LigPrep [19]. To enhance sampling for fragment-sized ligands, docking was carried out using modified Glide XP settings recommended for fragment docking, with expanded sampling enabled, 50,000 initial poses retained per ligand, a scoring window of 500.0, and up to 1000 minimized poses per ligand. For each fragment, the top-ranked docked pose was selected and rescored using Prime MM-GBSA to obtain an estimated binding energy value [20,21]. These MM-GBSA-derived values were used as proxy scoring oracle labels for downstream machine learning model training and evaluation [20,22]. These values represent estimated relative binding affinities rather than ground truth binding free energies [23]. MM-GBSA was chosen for its favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost, being far less expensive than rigorous free-energy methods while more accurate than docking scores for rank-ordering, which makes it well suited to generating consistent labels across the full fragment library [24,25]. Physicochemical property distributions of the full training set are summarized in Fig. S1. The resulting MM-GBSA binding energy values ranged from − 48.0 to 11.3 kcal/mol, with a mean of − 27.8 ± 8.2 kcal/mol and a median of − 28.9 kcal/mol. The full distribution is shown in Fig. S1.

Representing molecules as numerical vectors is a prerequisite for machine learning models to learn structure–activity relationships. The choice of representation directly impacts prediction performance. We employed a hybrid molecular representation combining 2048-bit ECFP6 (Extended Connectivity Fingerprint 6) Morgan fingerprints and RDKit structural descriptors [26,27].

ECFP6 (radius = 3) encodes the local chemical environment within three bonds of each atom as a 2048-bit binary vector. It captures pharmacophore patterns, functional groups, and substructural similarities, and has been extensively validated in QSAR (Quantitative Structure–Activity Relationship) studies [28]. RDKit structural descriptors provide global physicochemical properties including molecular weight, logP, TPSA, and hydrogen bond donor and acceptor counts [26]. These complement the fingerprints by covering the continuous physicochemical space that binary fingerprints cannot capture. The combination of these two representations provides complementary structural and physicochemical information simultaneously. Multiple benchmarking studies have shown this hybrid approach yields better generalization than either representation alone. For a small-scale dataset of 1,920 molecules, the end-to-end representation learning of GNNs is susceptible to overfitting [29]. The domain knowledge-informed hybrid representation therefore provides a more reliable baseline. All continuous descriptors were Z-score normalized using training set statistics.

Prior MM-GBSA prediction studies have tended to focus on specific architectures. We systematically assembled 13 models to enable fair cross-family comparison and to derive a prediction model optimized for the DHPS target. All models underwent hyperparameter optimization using the Optuna framework (Bayesian optimization, TPE sampler, 100 trials), followed by evaluation via 5-seed fivefold cross-validation [30].

Twelve baseline models were optimized with the following configurations [30]. The first family comprises gradient boosting models: LightGBM was optimized to 960 trees with a learning rate of 0.0162 (num_leaves = 100, max_depth = 6) [31]; XGBoost converged to 853 trees at a learning rate of 0.0134 [32]; SVR (Support vector regression) was optimized to C = 996.7 and epsilon = 0.0184 with an RBF kernel [12]. Gradient boosting models are strong baselines for tabular data and have consistently demonstrated high performance in small-molecule QSAR studies [33]. The second family comprises six GNN architectures (GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, GIN, GPS, PNA) [14]. Molecules are naturally represented as graphs, and GNNs offer a natural inductive bias for end-to-end molecular representation learning. Hyperparameters were searched over hidden_dim ∈ (64, 128, 256), num_layers ∈ (2, 5), dropout ∈ (0.0, 0.3), and learning_rate ∈ (1 × 10⁻4, 5 × 10⁻3). Early stopping (patience = 20 epochs) was applied based on validation loss. The third family comprises three domain-specific models: ChemBERTa, a chemical language model pre-trained on a large SMILES corpus, was fine-tuned with lr = 7.59 × 10⁻5, dropout = 0.325, and head_hidden = 512 [34]; ChemProp, a directed message-passing neural network, was optimized with hidden_size = 512, depth = 3, and dropout = 0.015 [35]; AttentiveFP, an attention-based molecular representation model, used hidden_channels = 256, num_layers = 4, and dropout = 0.098.

The proposed OOF-Stacking ensemble integrates all three model families, gradient boosting, graph neural networks, and domain-specific models each with distinct inductive biases and error patterns, to achieve performance beyond any individual architecture [31,36]. Each base learner is trained via fivefold cross-validation to generate OOF prediction vectors across the full training set. These vectors are used as inputs to a Ridge regression meta-learner, avoiding data leakage from training data [37]. Final predictions are produced as a weighted average of all base learner outputs at test time. The regularization coefficient alpha of the meta-learner was optimized to 30.4 via Optuna, searched over the range (0.01, 100).

Numerous algorithmic paradigms have been proposed for de novo molecular generation, but systematic comparisons under identical conditions on a shared target remain rare. We benchmarked 10 representative methods spanning the major paradigms in molecular design to identify which algorithm is most suitable for DHPS inhibitor discovery. The comparison includes RL-Design (proposed in this study), VAE-BO (variational autoencoder with Bayesian optimization), Graph-GA (graph-based genetic algorithm), REINVENT (RNN-based reinforcement learning), CMA-ES (covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy), LIMO (latent space optimization), GFlowNet (flow-based generative model), and SELFIES-based string search methods (STONED, SA-SELFIES, HC-SELFIES) [38,39,40,41,42,43,44,45,46]. All methods were evaluated over 5 independent runs using the same seed compound and approximately 4,100 generated molecules per run. For RL-Design, each run used a different random seed for data splitting, oracle training, and population initialization, so the five runs learn independent oracles. Within each run, previously evaluated molecules were recorded and skipped to enforce exploration of new chemical space.

RL-Design is a reinforcement learning-based molecular generation framework proposed in this study, using the OOF-Stacking model as a scoring oracle. Its primary distinction from existing RL-based methods is the use of a target-specific ensemble predictor as the oracle. The reward function was defined as reward = 0.7 × activity + 0.2 × QED + 0.1 × SA score, a weighted sum of predicted activity, drug-likeness, and synthesizability, where the activity term is clipped as max(0, (− MM-GBSA − 10) / 40). Generated SELFIES strings were additionally validated using RDKit to ensure chemical correctness prior to scoring.

Generative hyperparameters were additionally optimized via Optuna (50 trials): population size 50 [searched over (20, 100)], number of generations 20 (searched over [10,40]), mutations per step 2 (searched over [1,4]), and activity weight 0.7 [searched over (0.5, 0.9)].

Baseline methods were configured with Optuna-optimized hyperparameters as follows: Graph-GA used a population of 100 molecules evolved over 80 generations with a mutation rate of 0.3 and crossover rate of 0.5. REINVENT used a 2-layer LSTM (hidden dim = 512) pre-trained for 30 epochs and fine-tuned via REINFORCE for 300 steps (batch size = 64). VAE-based methods (VAE-BO, LIMO, CMA-ES) shared a common VAE architecture (latent dim = 64, hidden dim = 256). VAE-BO performed 50 random initialization steps followed by 200 Bayesian optimization iterations with a Matérn-5/2 Gaussian process kernel. LIMO used 200 gradient ascent steps per molecule (lr = 0.05). CMA-ES ran for 100 generations (λ = 50, σ₀ = 1.0). GFlowNet was trained for 2,000 steps over 27 predefined fragment building blocks (lr = 1 × 10⁻3). STONED performed 5,000 SELFIES mutations (depth = 3). HC-SELFIES used greedy hill climbing with 30 restarts and 200 steps each. SA-SELFIES ran 20 simulated annealing chains of 500 steps with temperature annealed from 2.0 to 0.1.

Evaluation metrics were predefined for each stage to enable consistent performance comparison across prediction and generation models [47]. Prediction model performance was assessed using three regression metrics. Root mean squared error, Spearman rank correlation coefficient, and Pearson correlation coefficient [48,49]. Spearman rank correlation was adopted as the primary metric because rank accuracy is more directly relevant to the practical goal of active candidate identification in virtual screening than absolute numerical accuracy [50,51].

Generation model performance was assessed using three metrics [52]. Hit rate is the percentage of generated molecules with predicted MM-GBSA below −30.0 kcal/mol. High-QED rate is the percentage of top-10 molecules with QED above 0.6. Best MM-GBSA is the best predicted binding energy in kcal/mol. Hit rate was adopted as the primary metric because generating as many active candidates as efficiently as possible is the core objective at the discovery stage.

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values were computed for the LightGBM base learner of OOF-Stacking using the TreeExplainer from the SHAP library [53]. For each of the 5 seed experiments, a LightGBM model was trained on the combined training and validation set, and SHAP values were computed on the held-out test set and on RL-Design-generated molecules, respectively. SHAP values were averaged across all 5 seeds. Features were ranked by mean absolute SHAP value, and the top-20 features were identified independently for the training set and the RL-Design analysis.

To assess whether the generated molecules occupy chemical space distinct from the training set, we quantified their structural novelty [54]. For each RL-Design-generated molecule, the maximum Tanimoto similarity to the 1920 training fragments was computed using ECFP6 fingerprints (radius 3, 2048-bit) [54,55]. This maximum-similarity distribution measures how far the generated molecules lie from the training distribution and provides an out-of-distribution reference for interpreting the SHAP analysis of generated molecules [56,57].

Even molecules with high binding affinity are unlikely to progress as drug candidates without adequate drug-likeness profiles. To quantitatively compare drug-likeness across generation methods and to verify that RL-Design generates molecules within favorable drug-like chemical space, we assessed eight physicochemical properties: QED (Quantitative Estimate of Drug-likeness), molecular weight (MW), logP (octanol–water partition coefficient), TPSA (Topological Polar Surface Area), hydrogen bond donors (HBD), hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), rotatable bond count, and Lipinski Rule of Five violations (MW ≤ 500 Da, logP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10) [58,59]. All properties were computed using RDKit [60,61].

QED provides a continuous composite score (0–1) reflecting overall molecular drug-likeness, enabling quantitative comparison across methods [61]. Since a molecule may achieve a moderate QED while still violating one or more Lipinski criteria, Lipinski Rule of Five compliance was additionally assessed as a binary filter representing the minimum threshold for oral drug candidate suitability [62].

DHPS inhibitory activity was evaluated using the NADH-Glo Detection System (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) [63]. The standard reaction mixture (20 μl) contained 2 μg of DHPS, 20 μM spermidine, and 100 μM NAD in Glycine–NaOH buffer (pH 9.0), with each compound tested at 1, 10, 50, and 100 µM. For each compound and concentration, a parallel reaction lacking DHPS was prepared as a background control. Following a 2-h incubation at 37 °C to generate NADH, the mixtures were heated at 65 °C for 10 min to release all enzyme-bound NADH [63]. For luminescence detection, the samples were transferred in triplicate (5 μl/well) to a white 384-well plate and mixed with an equal volume (5 μl) of freshly prepared NADH-Glo reagent. The plate was incubated at room temperature for 30 min on a rocking platform, and luminescence was measured using a Hidex Sense microplate reader (Hidex, Turku, Finland). Percent inhibition was calculated as (1 − (signal − background)/(control − background)) × 100. IC50values were obtained by fitting a four-parameter logistic model to the dose–response data using the SciPy library in Python [22,64]. Differences between predicted-active and predicted-inactive compounds at 100 µM were assessed using Welch's t-test. The compounds prioritized for experimental validation, together with the positive control GC7, were obtained as commercially available samples (fragments from Enamine and GC7 from Sigma-Aldrich) and used without further purification. The co-crystal structure was determined in previous reports [9].

All pairwise model comparisons used a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test [65]. With n = 5 repeated seed experiments, the small sample size precludes normality verification, making a non-parametric test appropriate [66]. As all models were evaluated on the same five seeds, performance differences have a paired structure, which the Wilcoxon signed-rank test exploits for greater statistical power than an unpaired test [67,68]. Significance thresholds were defined as * p < 0.1, ** p < 0.05, and *** p < 0.001. Exact one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used, and at n = 5 the exact minimum attainable p-value is 1/25 = 0.0312. A p < 0.001 level therefore cannot be reached and no comparison is marked ***. OOF-Stacking served as the reference for prediction model comparisons and RL-Design for generation model comparisons.

Despite the widespread use of MM-GBSA score estimation in virtual screening and de novo molecular design, there is currently no clear consensus on which machine learning architecture is best suited for this task. Prior MM-GBSA prediction studies have tended to focus on deep learning-based models or GNNs. Whether such complex models offer a practical advantage over traditional boosting approaches on small, target-specific datasets remains unclear. We therefore systematically compared 13 machine learning models under identical conditions (5-seed fivefold cross-validation).

A notable finding is that gradient boosting models performed on par with or better than GNNs and domain-specific models including ChemProp and AttentiveFP. LightGBM achieved a Spearman rank correlation of 0.853 and an RMSE of 4.45 kcal/mol. This suggests that the advantages of end-to-end deep learning are limited in a small-scale dataset of 1,920 molecules. OOF-Stacking achieved the highest performance across all three metrics, with an RMSE of 4.38 ± 0.28 kcal/mol, a Spearman rank correlation of 0.861 ± 0.008, and a Pearson correlation of 0.847 ± 0.018 (Fig.1a–c). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirmed statistically significant superiority of OOF-Stacking over all baselines (p = 0.0312), except AttentiveFP on Spearman ρ (p = 0.0625). This reflects the ensemble's ability to realize performance beyond any single model family by integrating complementary predictions from gradient boosting, GNN, and domain-specific models.

Benchmarking of 13 MM-GBSA score estimation models.aRMSE (kcal/mol).bSpearman ρ.cPearson r.dEfficiency scatter: Spearman ρ vs. training time (log scale)

In terms of training efficiency, the mean training time of OOF-Stacking (211.6 s) was comparable to individual GNN models, and its performance-to-cost ratio was the best among all evaluated models (Fig.1d). The scatter plot of predicted versus actual MM-GBSA values for OOF-Stacking on the held-out test set is shown in Fig. S2. These results demonstrate that ensemble strategies consistently outperform individual architectures for MM-GBSA prediction, providing practical guidance for MM-GBSA estimation model selection with small molecular datasets. The learning-curve analysis confirmed that prediction performance approached saturation with increasing training-set size, with OOF-Stacking consistently matching or exceeding LightGBM across all training fractions (Fig. S3), indicating that the dataset is adequate for this target-specific task. OOF-Stacking was subsequently adopted as the evaluation oracle for de novo molecular generation experiments.

Directly comparing diverse algorithmic families under identical conditions on the same target is essential to determine which generative paradigm is genuinely superior. We compared 10 de novo molecular generation methods under the same conditions to identify the most suitable algorithm for DHPS inhibitor design. RL-Design, the method proposed in this study, ranked first on hit rate and high-QED rate within the benchmark defined by the OOF-Stacking oracle. Hit rate was 92.02 ± 0.80%, high-QED rate was 98.0 ± 4.0%, and best MM-GBSA was −47.94 ± 0.63 kcal/mol (Fig.2a-c). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirmed statistically significant superiority of RL-Design over all comparators for hit rate (p = 0.0312), and over all comparators except HC-SELFIES for high-QED rate.

By algorithm family, string-based search methods formed the second tier (STONED: 69.74%, HC-SELFIES: 64.09%), followed by REINVENT (55.04%). Latent space optimization (LIMO: 0.91%) and the flow-based model (GFlowNet: 0.00%) showed very low performance on the DHPS-specific dataset. This demonstrates the limitations of latent space interpolation without goal-directed search.

In terms of generation efficiency, RL-Design was the fastest at a mean of 72.7 s, achieving top performance 23 times faster than GFlowNet (1,682.1 s) (Fig.2d). RL-Design occupies a Pareto-optimal position across both performance and efficiency, demonstrating practical applicability even under limited computational resources. Notably, this efficiency gap was not closed by GPU acceleration. All methods were run on identical hardware, yet GFlowNet remained the slowest despite GPU acceleration, consistent with reports that GFlowNet-based molecular optimization is sample-inefficient and computationally demanding [69,70]. This indicates that algorithmic design, rather than hardware acceleration, dominates the overall computational effort. As RL-Design employs OOF-Stacking as its scoring oracle, these benchmark results reflect performance within the same scoring framework used for optimization. Oracle-independent validation through experimental enzymatic assay is reported in Sect. "Experimental validation", which partially mitigates this limitation. To investigate the structural basis of these results, we performed SHAP analysis in Sect. "SHAP feature importance and structural biology of the DHPS binding pocket".

To determine whether RL-Design's exploration of high-activity molecules reflects the chemical principles of DHPS binding rather than arbitrary score optimization, we performed SHAP analysis [53]. Because the meta-learner of OOF-Stacking (Ridge regression) takes OOF predictions of base learners as input, applying SHAP to the meta-learner reflects the importance of individual base learner predictions rather than original molecular features, precluding direct chemical interpretation [71]. LightGBM, which carries the highest weight in OOF-Stacking and takes original molecular descriptors directly as input, therefore provides the most representative and interpretable feature-level SHAP values. We calculated SHAP values on both the training set and RL-Design-generated molecules and interpreted the top features in the context of the DHPS active site (PDB: 6PGR) (Fig.3, Table S1).

The DHPS active site is located at the monomer–monomer interface and comprises the NAD binding pocket together with the spermidine-binding and catalytic region [72,73]. NAD functions as the electron acceptor for spermidine oxidation in the DHPS reaction [9]. The NAD binding pocket is characterized by aromatic stacking surfaces, a ribose hydroxyl hydrogen bonding network, and electrostatic stabilization of the phosphodiester linkage, while the adjacent spermidine-binding region provides the catalytic environment for deoxyhypusine formation [73].

The top SHAP features from the training set analysis are broadly consistent with the physicochemical properties expected for molecules interacting with the active site (Fig.3a, Table S1). Molar Refractivity reflects size and polarizability properties that may favor engagement with the aromatic surfaces of the active site. Structural Complexity, Connectivity Index, and Balaban J Index suggest a preference for heterocyclic scaffolds with topological properties compatible with the extended active site cavity [74]. Aliphatic OH Count, Ester Group Count, and Polar Surface Area are consistent with the hydrogen bonding capacity expected for interactions within a polar, cofactor-binding environment. Max and Min Partial Charge and Partial Charge VSA suggest electrostatic properties compatible with the basic residue microenvironment of active site [75]. The high importance of EState VSA and Min EState Index is consistent with a preference for aromatic ring systems with electron density distributions compatible with the active site environment [76]. Taken together, these results suggest that the top-ranked SHAP features reflect physicochemical patterns associated with the DHPS active site, including the NAD binding pocket. This interpretation was directly confirmed by an X-ray co-crystal structure of DHPS bound to 2-methyl-5, 6, 7, 8-tetrahydroquinazolin-6-amine. In this structure the compound occupies the entrance of the NAD-binding pocket, a site that overlaps the spermidine-binding region, and contacts His288, Asp316, Trp327, and Lys329 (Fig. S4) [73].

Before interpreting the SHAP analysis of generated molecules, we quantified how far these molecules lie from the training set. The maximum Tanimoto similarity of each generated molecule to the training fragments had a mean of 0.285 and a median of 0.257. A Tanimoto similarity below 0.4 is a commonly used threshold for considering two molecules structurally dissimilar [77], and has been applied to define structural novelty in drug discovery [78]. By this criterion, 88.0% of generated molecules fell below 0.4 and 96.9% below 0.6 (ECFP6, Fig. S5), indicating that the great majority of generated molecules are structurally dissimilar from any training compound.

Independent SHAP analysis of RL-Design-generated molecules revealed a top-20 feature set with substantial overlap with the training set analysis (14 of 20 features shared; Fig.3bold labels). Features shared across both panels include Molar Refractivity, Carboxylic Acid Count, Aliphatic OH Count, Polar Surface Area, Connectivity Index, Molecular Shape, and Stereocenters Count, consistent with the physicochemical requirements of the active site described above [79]. Six features appeared in the RL-Design top-20 are Molecular Shape, Norm. Connectivity, EState VSA, and non-tertiary aliphatic OH count [80]. These features collectively reflect a preference for more compact, topologically constrained scaffolds with specific hydroxyl accessibility, consistent with the drug-likeness component of the reward function optimizing toward reduced rotatable bonds and favorable hydrogen bonding geometry.

The high degree of feature overlap between the training set and RL-Design-generated molecules (14/20) suggests that RL-Design effectively preserves the structure–activity relationship learned from the DHPS dataset during reinforcement learning, rather than arbitrarily exploring chemical space. The subset of features unique to RL-Design reflects reward-driven refinement toward drug-like molecular geometry, consistent with the explicit QED term in the reward function. Together, these results indicate that RL-Design explores a chemical space that simultaneously satisfies the physicochemical requirements of the NAD binding pocket and drug-likeness constraints.

The SHAP analysis in Sect. "SHAP feature importance and structural biology of the DHPS binding pocket" showed that drug-likeness-related features including Molar Refractivity, Polar Surface Area, and logP carry high importance. Consistent with this, we assessed the eight drug-likeness properties defined in Sect. "Drug-likeness analysis" for molecules generated by five methods, compared against the training set (Fig.4).

Drug-likeness profiles of generated molecules vs. training set. Boxplots of QED, MW, logP, TPSA, HBD, HBA, rotatable bonds, and Lipinski violations for five generation methods and the training set

RL-Design generated molecules exhibited a higher median QED score (0.800 ± 0.067) compared to the training set (0.692 ± 0.081). This improvement reflects the design of the reward function: as described in Sect. "Generative model design setup", drug-likeness (QED) was explicitly incorporated as an optimization objective alongside binding energy. While the training set consists of compounds collected without drug-likeness filtering, RL-Design actively explored chemical space toward drug-like regions during reinforcement learning. The elevated QED of generated molecules therefore reflects reward-driven optimization rather than an intrinsic property of the target chemical space.

The distribution of hydrogen bond donor (HBD) count in RL-Design molecules was notably narrow, concentrated near zero. This pattern is consistent with the drug-likeness component of the reward function in that molecules with fewer polar hydrogen donors tend to have higher QED scores and greater membrane permeability, both of which are implicitly rewarded. The narrow HBD distribution thus reflects convergence toward a specific region of chemical space during reinforcement learning, rather than a failure of chemical diversity.

All RL-Design top-ranked molecules showed zero Lipinski Rule of Five violations, indicating full compliance with oral bioavailability criteria. This outcome is consistent with QED optimization, as QED integrates MW, logP, HBD, and HBA as component descriptors. Molecules with high QED scores are therefore expected to satisfy Lipinski criteria as a correlated consequence, even though Lipinski compliance was not explicitly encoded as a separate reward term. In contrast, Graph-GA showed only 2% Lipinski compliance, with markedly elevated MW and logP values, while REINVENT (56%) and HC-SELFIES (88%) also showed inferior compliance compared to RL-Design.

To provide an oracle-independent assessment of RL-Design's practical utility, six compounds were selected from its proposals (Fig. S6). Three were the highest-reward proposals forming the predicted-active set and three were the lowest-reward proposals forming the predicted-inactive set. Their DHPS inhibitory activity was measured by dose–response assay at 1, 10, 50, and 100 µM (Fig.5A). All three predicted-active compounds showed statistically significant inhibition relative to the predicted-inactive compounds at 100 µM (Welch’s t-test, p < 0.001). Among them, two yielded measurable IC50values, 2-(2-phenylethyl)morpholine at 31.2 µM and 5-methoxy-1,3-dimethyl-1H-pyrazol-4-amine at 49.1 µM. 2-methyl-5, 6, 7, 8-tetrahydroquinazolin-6-amine showed only weak inhibition with an IC50above the tested range (10.9% at 100 µM, IC50> 100 µM). Furthermore, the ligand-binding mode was directly validated by the 2Fo–Fc electron density map in the co-crystal structure (Fig.5B). The three predicted-inactive compounds showed no inhibition across the tested range. The predicted-active and predicted-inactive sets were thus clearly separated by experiment, showing that the OOF-Stacking oracle distinguishes active from inactive candidates beyond arbitrary score optimization. None of the tested compounds contained PAINS substructures and all showed low aggregation risk, indicating that the observed inhibition is not attributable to assay interference (Table S2).

Analysis of the two confirmed inhibitors reveals that both contain nitrogen-containing heterocyclic cores (morpholine and pyrazole), consistent with the SHAP-identified importance of nitrogen-containing heterocyclic frameworks, hydrogen bonding capacity, and polar surface area. To examine the structural basis of the experimental outcomes, the top-20 SHAP features were computed for all six tested compounds (Table S3). The weakly active 2-methyl-5, 6, 7, 8-tetrahydroquinazolin-6-amine shares the same nitrogen-containing heterocyclic feature, yet across the top-20 features it falls between the confirmed inhibitors and the inactive compounds, and no single SHAP feature distinguishes the active from the inactive compounds. Among the inactive compounds, 3-(butan-2-yl)-1, 2-oxazole-5-carboxylic acid and 1-(2, 2-difluoroethyl)-1H-pyrazole-3-carboxylic acid both contain carboxylate groups whose position or orientation may create geometric or electrostatic mismatch within the active site. This reflects an inherent limitation of SHAP rather than of the model. SHAP attributes an averaged contribution to each feature independently and does not expose the feature interactions or per-molecule combinations that govern binding. The OOF-Stacking oracle learns these interactions during prediction and RL-Design exploits them during generation. Nonetheless, the experimental confirmation of the predicted-active compounds provides oracle-independent validation beyond the computational prediction.

This study presented an integrated computational-experimental pipeline for the discovery of inhibitors targeting DHPS, a host enzyme essential for eIF5A hypusination and a validated HDT target against viral infections. The pipeline systematically benchmarked 13 MM-GBSA score estimation models and 10 de novo molecular generation methods, followed by SHAP-based mechanistic interpretation and experimental enzymatic validation, providing the first comprehensive AI benchmarking study for this antiviral target.

In the prediction stage, OOF-Stacking achieved best performance across all three metrics and the best performance-efficiency balance among 13 models evaluated. In the generation stage, RL-Design ranked first on hit rate and high-QED rate and achieved Pareto-optimal performance at 23 times lower computational cost than GFlowNet, the gap that persisted under identical GPU-accelerated hardware and reflects algorithmic rather than hardware factors. SHAP analysis revealed that the top-ranked features are broadly consistent with the physicochemical properties expected for molecules engaging the active site of DHPS, supporting the chemical interpretability of the prediction model. Experimental dose–response validation confirmed inhibitory activity in all three predicted-active compounds, two of them highly active, with complete concordance between predicted and experimental activity categories across six tested compounds. The active scaffolds are structurally distinct from GC-7, suggesting new chemical starting points for HDT-based antiviral development.

However, while dose–response assays over 1–100 µM established IC₅₀ values for the active compounds, Kidetermination, detailed kinetic characterization, and competitive inhibition assays with spermidine and NAD remain to be performed to elucidate the inhibition mechanism. Future directions include extension of this pipeline to additional RNA viruses such as influenza and dengue, for which eIF5A hypusination has also been implicated. As the present study targets the hit-discovery stage, toxicity endpoints such as AMES mutagenicity, hepatotoxicity, and hERG inhibition were not optimized; because the RL-Design reward is modular, these can be incorporated as additional reward terms in subsequent hit-to-lead optimization, alongside cellular eIF5A hypusination, target selectivity, and in vivo toxicity assessment. This study presents a reproducible framework for AI-guided antiviral drug discovery, integrating rigorous computational benchmarking with target-specific inhibitor design and experimental validation.

title: Train–test splits matter more for evaluation than for performance
author: Davide Crucitti; Adrián Mosquera Orgueira
text:
In machine learning for QSAR/QSPR, the choice of train–test splitting algorithm alters both a model’s realized performance and the accuracy with which that performance is estimated from the held-out test set. Prior work has established that structure-aware splits such as Kennard–Stone and SPXY produce optimistically biased internal estimates, but these characterizations typically examine one method family at a time. Here we quantify how fifteen splitting strategies from four method families differ across fifteen drug-discovery datasets on two criteria (realized external benchmark performance and performance-estimation bias), and further assess whether splitting strategy affects model-selection quality when multiple model classes are optimized simultaneously. A single, consistent pattern holds across all fifteen datasets and all eleven evaluation measures (RMSE, MAE, MedAE,\(\hbox {R}^{2}\), Spearman\(\rho\), Pearson r, Kendall\(\tau\), enrichment factor at 5/10/20%, and BEDROC): Kennard–Stone-type methods (KS, SPXY, MDKS, Morais) achieve the strongest external benchmark performance but produce the most optimistically biased internal estimates (median Spearman bias\(\Delta \rho\)\(\approx\)+0.17 to +0.22, SPXY most optimistic; median\(\hbox {R}^{2}\)bias\(\Delta \hbox {R}^{2}\)\(\approx\)+0.26 to +0.41), diversity-based methods (OptiSim, Maximum/Minimum Dissimilarity) achieve the weakest benchmark performance, and cluster-shuffle variants, particularly k-means- and k-medoids-shuffle, provide the best-calibrated internal estimates (near-zero bias) while remaining competitive on benchmark performance. For every measure the differences in estimation bias between splitters greatly exceed the differences in benchmark performance (for Spearman\(\rho\), a\(\approx\)0.20 bias gap versus a\(\approx\)0.02 benchmark gap), and the two criteria are inversely ranked (rank correlation\(\rho\)\(\approx\)−0.70 to −0.83). For model selection among competing model classes, in contrast, no method achieves statistical separation and effect sizes are small, indicating that splitter choice has no demonstrated impact on which model class is ultimately selected. Splitter choice in drug-discovery QSAR therefore primarily affects the reliability of performance evaluation rather than realized model generalization. Cluster-shuffle splitting provides near-zero estimation bias while maintaining competitive external performance, making it the recommended default for offline model evaluation, where calibration is the primary concern. Because no splitter separates on model-selection quality, it is a sound default for model selection as well. Practitioners who wish to explicitly optimize model selection may use KS-type splitting to identify the best model configuration, then re-split with cluster-shuffle to obtain a calibrated performance estimate.

Scientific contribution

We provide the first head-to-head comparison of fifteen train–test splitting algorithms from four method families on a common drug-discovery regression benchmark, showing that their effect on the credibility of internal performance estimates is roughly an order of magnitude larger than their effect on realized model performance. We further show that this optimism is general across all eleven evaluation measures, give it a geometric explanation in terms of train–test distributional distance, and separate the splitting problem into two tasks, performance estimation and model selection, that have different optimal choices. On this basis we recommend cluster-shuffle splitting as a calibrated default; whereas prior work described the overoptimism of a single method family (Kennard–Stone), our comparison spans four families and all eleven measures and turns this into a concrete recommendation.
