In supervised machine learning for QSAR/QSPR, reliable offline evaluation depends critically on how available data are partitioned into training and test subsets. Ideally, the test set should represent the compounds a deployed model will encounter: future, unseen molecules that may differ systematically from the training set. In practice, the test set is always drawn from the same corpus as the training data, making the split strategy a key determinant of whether internal evaluation is a faithful proxy for prospective performance.

Different splitting strategies impose different degrees of train–test dissimilarity, and this dissimilarity controls two distinct and often competing outcomes. First, it affects the training distribution and hence the model’s realized generalization: methods that concentrate structurally diverse or distant compounds in the test set tend to leave the model a less representative training set, potentially depressing external benchmark performance. Second, it affects evaluation credibility, the degree to which a measure computed on the internal test set accurately reflects the model’s performance on the real prospective challenge. Methods that create artificially easy test sets (i.e., sets that are internally similar to the training data) produce optimistic internal estimates that overstate prospective performance, while methods that create harder test sets tend to produce more conservative estimates.

The literature on these effects is substantial. Kennard–Stone (KS) [1] and its extensions (SPXY [2], MDKS [3], and Morais–Lima–Martin [4]) select test samples that span the descriptor space uniformly. This maximizes the training set’s coverage of the descriptor space but leaves the internal test set as a representative subsample of the development pool rather than a challenging hold-out. The consequences are well documented: KS and SPXY produce overoptimistic performance estimates, particularly when the test fraction is large [5,6,7,8,9]. Data-leakage effects from related methods have also been identified [10]. Diversity-based selection methods such as OptiSim [11], Minimum Dissimilarity, and Maximum Dissimilarity take the opposite approach, maximizing train–test separation; prior work suggests these produce more conservative estimates. Clustering-based splits [12] occupy an intermediate position.

The optimism of structure-aware splits is well established, but most quantitative characterizations come from spectroscopic and analytical-chemistry data and typically examine one method family at a time [5,13]. Less settled is how the major method families compare directly, on the same footing and across many evaluation measures, in the drug-discovery regression setting, and in particular how large the resulting differences in estimation error are relative to the accompanying differences in benchmark performance.

Two further aspects have received less systematic attention. First, internal test evaluation serves not only as a performance estimator but as a model-selection guide: practitioners use internal test scores to choose among competing configurations (algorithm class, hyperparameters), and it is unclear which splitting strategy produces internal rankings most correlated with external benchmark performance. Second, the applicability domain (AD) of a model determines whether a predicted value for a test compound is trustworthy; a training set whose AD barely covers the external benchmark means prospective performance is evaluated largely on out-of-domain compounds, reducing the interpretability of those measures regardless of their numerical value.

Using fifteen drug-discovery datasets with an externally defined temporal benchmark, we ask: (i) which splitting strategies yield higher external benchmark performance, (ii) which strategies most accurately estimate that performance using internal test data, (iii) which strategies produce models with higher applicability-domain coverage of the external benchmark, and (iv) which strategies best support model selection across competing model configurations.

We analyzed fifteen anonymized drug-discovery regression datasets from the publicly released Merck benchmark [14,15]. Table1summarizes the 15 datasets.

Dataset sizes span approximately 24-fold, from METAB (2,092 compounds) to LOGD (49,794 compounds), providing meaningful variation in the regime where splitting artifacts are known to scale with dataset size [13]. Molecular structures are not available in the public release; we use the provided precomputed atom-pair and donor–acceptor–pair descriptors. No additional preprocessing was performed.

Each dataset includes an externally defined temporal holdout provided by Merck. We treat this holdout as an immutable external benchmark: it is never used for model training or splitting-algorithm selection, only for final performance evaluation. All remaining data form the development pool.

Within the development pool, we apply 5 repeats\(\times\)5-fold outer cross-validation, producing 25 partially overlapping CV base sets per dataset (each comprising\(\approx\)80% of the development pool). This repeated structure reduces variance due to any single partition and provides 25 evaluation replicates per (dataset, splitter) pair. Because the repeated-CV base sets overlap (~80% shared compounds), these replicates are correlated rather than independent; accordingly, all across-method inference is performed at the level of the 15 datasets, with the per-replicate values only averaged to a single per-(dataset, splitter) score. Within each CV base set, each splitting algorithm partitions data into an internal train subset (\(\approx\)80% of the CV base set) and an internal test subset (\(\approx\)20%). A model is fitted on the internal train subset only and evaluated on both the internal test subset and the external benchmark.

To reduce dependence on any single descriptor subset, each fit is repeated with ten different feature-subsampling seeds controlling LightGBM’s internal feature subsampling (feature_fraction = 0.8, applied per boosting iteration), and the measures are averaged.

We compared fifteen splitting strategies across four families.

Kennard–Stone-type methodsselect the training set to span the descriptor space uniformly, leaving interior (low-dissimilarity) compounds in the test set. We include four variants: Kennard–Stone (KS) [1], SPXY [2] (which jointly maximizes dissimilarity in both descriptor and activity space), MDKS [3], and Morais–Lima–Martin [4]. Because the test set is composed of compounds close to the training set, these methods are known to generate optimistic performance estimates [5,6,7].

Diversity-based methodsmaximize train–test dissimilarity. OptiSim [11] selects test compounds from a pool of maximally diverse candidates; Maximum Dissimilarity (MaxDiss) greedily selects the test compound furthest from the training set; Minimum Dissimilarity (MinDiss) ensures every test compound exceeds a minimum distance from its nearest training neighbor. These methods create structurally remote test sets; prior work expects conservative internal estimates, although in our benchmark their estimates remain mildly optimistic.

Clustering-based methods[12] partition the descriptor space into clusters and assign compounds to train/test accordingly. Two assignment policies are compared: -Cluster-shuffle: entire clusters are assigned to either train or test, so no two compounds from the same cluster appear on opposite sides of the split. -Cluster-stratified: compounds are sampled proportionally from each cluster into both subsets, preserving the cluster distribution on both sides.

Three base clustering algorithms are used: hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC), k-means, and k-medoids, each with 10 clusters. These are combined with both policies, plus sphere-exclusion (Taylor–Butina) clustering [16] in shuffle mode only (variable cluster sizes make proportional stratification impractical), giving seven clustering splitters in total.

Random split:uniform random assignment without stratification, serving as the primary baseline.

For the splitting assessment experiment, all models use LightGBM with fixed hyperparameters:n_estimators = 500,learning_rate = 0.05,feature_fraction = 0.8[17]. We hold the model class and configuration constant to isolate splitting effects from modeling effects. For each (dataset, CV base set, splitting algorithm) combination, we train 10 independent LightGBM models on the internal train subset, each with a different random seed that controls the feature-fraction sampling. Reported measures are the average over these 10 runs, reducing Monte Carlo variance in the feature-fraction randomness. All 15 datasets are analyzed at full development-pool size.

The Mahalanobis Distribution Alignment Score (MDAS) [18] quantifies the distributional distance between each split’s internal test set (or external benchmark) and the training set. MDAS is a symmetric measure computed from the pooled train+test descriptor covariance, capturing both mean and covariance differences; the covariance is inverted via Cholesky decomposition with a ridge-regularized fallback for rank-deficient cases.

To probe robustness in the small-data regime, we conducted two subsampling experiments in which every outer CV base set was capped before splitting. The primary analysis caps at 150 compounds (“Sub-150 analysis”), chosen because datasets of this size are representative of real-world ADMET screening campaigns and early-stage drug-discovery assays, where experimental budgets are tight and splitting artefacts are most consequential for decision-making. A secondary analysis capping at 1,000 compounds (“Sub-1000 analysis”) is reported in Additional file 1 (Figs. S15–S17) for comparison across the size spectrum. All other aspects of the pipeline (splitting algorithms, modeling, evaluation measures, repeated CV structure) are identical to the main analysis.

To assess which splitting strategy most reliably identifies the best model when multiple model classes compete, we run a separate champion-selection experiment using the same CV base sets. For each (dataset, CV base set, splitting algorithm), we apply Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) hyperparameter optimization [19] with three-round successive halving across five model classes: LightGBM (gradient-boosted trees), Random Forest, KNN Regressor, Support Vector Regressor (\(\varepsilon\)-SVR, RBF kernel), and Elastic Net. Tuned hyperparameters for each class are listed in Additional file 1: Table S2.

The successive-halving schedule allocates up to 35 TPE trials to the eventual winner: Round 1 runs all five classes for 5 trials each with 2-fold inner CV (top 2 advance); Round 2 runs the two survivors for 15 trials each with 5-fold inner CV (top 1 advances); Round 3 runs the single survivor for the remaining 15 trials with 5-fold inner CV. When the training set contains more than 5,000 compounds, TPE trials are performed on a random subsample of 5,000 compounds to keep SVR computationally tractable; final retraining of the selected model always uses the full inner-train set.

All five model classes are retrained on the full internal train subset after model selection is complete, so that their predictions on the internal test and external benchmark are recorded.

We report eleven measures covering complementary aspects of regression and virtual-screening quality:

Error measures (lower is better): RMSE, MAE, MedAE (median absolute error, more robust to outliers than MAE)

Explained variance (higher is better):\(\hbox {R}^{2}\)

Correlation measures (higher is better): Spearman\(\rho\)and Kendall\(\tau\)(rank-based), and Pearson r (linear correlation)

Enrichment measures (higher is better): Enrichment factor at the top 5%, 10%, and 20% of the predicted ranking (EF-5%, EF-10%, EF-20%), and BEDROC. For each EF, “actives” are the true top-k% compounds by measured activity; EF = (hits/n_selected)/(n_actives/n), where EF = 1 indicates random ranking and EF = 1/kis the theoretical maximum. BEDROC [20] (\(\alpha\)= 20, active fraction = top 20% by measured activity) extends EF by weighting early-ranked hits exponentially more heavily, making it sensitive to recovery of the highest-scoring actives.

For each dataset\(\times\)algorithm\(\times\)CV base set, the benchmark gap is:

where\(S\)is computed on an oriented scale (higher always better).\(\Delta > 0\)indicates optimism (the internal estimate overstates the model’s true prospective performance);\(\Delta < 0\)indicates pessimism. We report mean\(\Delta\)(signed bias) and mean\(|\Delta |\)(estimation error, the unsigned magnitude) as measures of evaluation credibility: a split that yields a small\(|\Delta |\)provides credible, well-calibrated internal estimates of prospective performance.

We fit a k-nearest-neighbor distance-based applicability domain on the internal train subset (k = 5, threshold z = 1.5 standard deviations above the mean training-set NN distance) and compute the fraction of external benchmark compounds that fall within the AD (coverage). We further compare external benchmark performance on in-domain versus out-of-domain benchmark compounds, and report the internal test estimate as a reference. AD coverage bears on evaluation interpretability: predictions for in-domain compounds are more trustworthy than those for out-of-domain compounds, so scores computed on a benchmark with higher AD coverage are more interpretable.

For each CV base set, the model-selection experiment provides, for each splitting algorithm, a selected model and four runner-up models, each with their best-found hyperparameters, an inner-CV score, and an external benchmark score. We assess model-selection quality using two complementary measures:

Selection advantage: the external benchmark Spearman\(\rho\)of the internally selected model minus the external benchmark Spearman\(\rho\)of the best alternative model configuration. Positive values indicate that the internally selected model outperforms the best alternative externally; negative values indicate that a different model would have generalized better.

Selection hit rate: the fraction of folds in which the internally selected model is also the externally best-performing model. A higher hit rate means the splitting strategy more reliably identifies the best-generalizing model.

Across-dataset inference: For each dataset, algorithms are ranked on each target measure (average over 25 CV base sets); ranks are averaged over the 15 datasets. This rank-based aggregation is essential because several measures, in particular the error measures RMSE and MAE, are expressed in each dataset’s own activity units and are therefore not comparable across datasets as raw values. We use the Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc comparisons [21], following the approach recommended for benchmarking multiple algorithms across multiple datasets. A non-parametric rank-based procedure is preferred: measure distributions are heterogeneous across datasets, normality cannot be assumed, and the correlated CV replicates make parametric variance estimation unreliable. The Friedman test assesses whether mean ranks differ significantly across splitters; upon rejection (all cases, p < 0.001), the Nemenyi post-hoc test identifies statistically indistinguishable groups at\(\alpha\)= 0.05. The Nemenyi critical difference (CD) is the minimum rank difference required for two algorithms to be distinguished at the chosen\(\alpha\); pairs connected by a horizontal bar in CD diagrams [21] are statistically indistinguishable at this threshold. The Nemenyi test is appropriate for the complete block design of our benchmark (all 15 splitters\(\times\)all 15 datasets).

Effect sizes: We report median and interquartile range of per-dataset measure values alongside CD diagrams to convey practical magnitude independent of statistical significance thresholds.

To complement the two-objective (Pareto) analysis with a single overall ranking, we applied two established multicriteria decision-analysis (MCDA) methods, TOPSIS [22] and the ratio-system MOORA [23], via the JMcDM implementation [24]. Each takes a decision matrix of alternatives\(\times\)criteria with per-criterion weights and benefit/cost directions, applies vector normalization, and returns a scalar score per alternative (TOPSIS: closeness to the ideal solution, in [0, 1]; MOORA: a weighted benefit-minus-cost value). Because raw measure values are not comparable across datasets (above), we ran each MCDA within each dataset, taking the fifteen splitters as alternatives and the eleven measures as equally-weighted criteria (benefit or cost according to each measure’s direction), and averaged the per-dataset ranks across the fifteen datasets, as for the Nemenyi analysis. We evaluate three criterion sets: benchmark performance (the external-benchmark scores on the eleven measures), estimation credibility (the absolute estimation gaps |\(\Delta\)| on the eleven measures, all cost criteria), and their combination (all twenty-two criteria with equal weights). TOPSIS and MOORA agreed closely, so we report TOPSIS in the main text.

Figure1presents the complete picture: a heatmap of Nemenyi average ranks across all fifteen splitting strategies and eleven measures, for benchmark performance (left panel) and estimation gap |\(\Delta\)| (right panel). KS-type methods dominate the benchmark panel but rank last on calibration; k-means and k-medoids-shuffle lead on calibration while maintaining intermediate benchmark ranks. The following sections examine Spearman\(\rho\)as the primary worked example; RMSE,\(\hbox {R}^{2}\), and enrichment confirm the same pattern throughout.

Nemenyi average rank heatmap across all eleven measures. Each cell is a splitter’s average rank for that measure (ranked within each dataset, then averaged across the fifteen datasets). Left panel: benchmark performance (green = rank 1, best); right panel: estimation gap |\(\Delta\)| (green = rank 1, best calibrated)

Additional file 1: Figure S9 shows the family-level mean rank bar chart aggregated across all methods and measures, confirming that cluster-shuffle is the only family achieving competitive benchmark performance and the best calibration rank simultaneously.

Figure2shows the Nemenyi CD diagram for benchmark Spearman\(\rho\)(average rank across 15 datasets; lower rank = higher\(\rho\); CD = 5.538 at\(\alpha\)= 0.05). Three performance tiers are visible. KS-type methods (SPXY, KS, MDKS, Morais; ranks 1–4) form the top tier. Diversity-based methods (OptiSim, MinDiss, MaxDiss; ranks 12–15) form the bottom tier. An intermediate tier (Random, cluster-stratified variants, HAC-shuffle, Butina-shuffle, and the remaining cluster-shuffle methods) occupies ranks 5–12. KS-type methods are statistically distinguishable from the lowest-ranked diversity methods (rank gap exceeds the CD); adjacent tiers overlap under the CD bar, with no significant pairwise separation between neighboring groups.

Nemenyi CD diagram for external benchmark Spearman\(\rho\)(CD = 5.538,\(\alpha\)= 0.05; lower rank = better)

Spearman\(\rho\)medians differ by\(\Delta \rho\)\(\approx\)0.09 between the best and worst methods (Additional file 1: Fig. S1); within-method variance across datasets substantially exceeds between-method differences, confirming that dataset identity dominates over splitter choice for realized benchmark performance. The same three-tier ordering holds across all eleven measures (Additional file 1: Fig. S2; summarized in Fig.1): KS-type methods consistently rank highest, diversity-based methods lowest, and cluster-shuffle methods intermediate.

Figure3shows the CD diagram for absolute estimation error |\(\Delta\)Spearman|. The family ranking inverts relative to Fig.2. k-means-shuffle and k-medoids-shuffle are the best-calibrated methods (ranks 1–2), and together with diversity methods and the remaining cluster-shuffle variants (ranks 3–7) form the well-calibrated tier. SPXY and MDKS form the worst-calibrated tier (ranks 14–15) and are statistically distinguishable from the well-calibrated group (rank gap exceeds the CD). KS, Morais, cluster-stratified variants, and Random occupy an intermediate tier (ranks 8–13) indistinguishable from both extremes under the CD bar.

Nemenyi CD diagram for Spearman estimation error |\(\Delta\)Spearman| (CD = 5.538,\(\alpha\)= 0.05; lower rank = better calibrated)

Figure4shows the signed estimation bias for each splitter, sorted from best-calibrated (left) to worst (right). Every method is optimistic (\(\Delta\)> 0), but by very different amounts: k-means- and k-medoids-shuffle sit near zero (median\(\Delta\)\(\approx\)+0.02), while SPXY reaches median\(\Delta\)\(\approx\)+0.22, with a clear gradient across the remaining methods. The violin widths reflect substantial between-dataset variability: within-method spread often exceeds between-method differences, reinforcing that dataset identity is a stronger determinant of absolute bias magnitude than splitter choice.

Signed Spearman estimation bias\(\Delta\)=\(\rho\)_internal_test –\(\rho\)_benchmark across all (dataset, CV base set) combinations, sorted from best-calibrated (left) to worst (right). Dashed line:\(\Delta\)= 0 (perfect calibration)

Estimation-error differences far exceed benchmark-performance differences: the bias gap between SPXY (\(\Delta\)\(\approx\)+0.22) and k-means-shuffle (\(\Delta\)\(\approx\)+0.02) is approximately 0.20, roughly ten times the benchmark Spearman difference between the same two methods (\(\approx\)0.02). Across the full method set, the between-family bias spread (\(\approx\)0.22) exceeds the between-family benchmark-performance spread (\(\approx\)0.09) by approximately 2.5-fold.

Figure5shows this holds across datasets: SPXY and MDKS exceed\(\bar{\Delta }\)Spearman\(\bar{>}\)0.10 in 13 out of 15 datasets, while k-means- and k-medoids-shuffle do so in 7 out of 15, but with near-zero median bias (\(\Delta\)\(\approx\)+0.02), their exceedances reflect dataset-level variance rather than systematic optimism. Pessimistic bias (\(\Delta\)< 0) was rare for KS-type methods, confirming their optimism is nearly universal; cluster-shuffle methods have symmetric scatter around zero and no consistent direction. The same family ordering holds across all eleven measures (Additional file 1: Fig. S3; Figs. S18–S33 for individual per-measure CD diagrams; summarized in Fig.1), with\(\hbox {R}^{2}\)bias ranging from\(\Delta \hbox {R}^{2}\)\(\approx\)+0.41 for SPXY to\(\approx\)+0.03 for k-means/k-medoids-shuffle as an illustrative example. This finding directly confirms and quantifies the optimism of KS-type methods documented in the analytical chemistry and chemometrics literature [5,6,7,8].

Left: number of datasets (out of 15) in which |\(\Delta\)Spearman| exceeds 0.10, colored by method family. Right: fraction of datasets exceeding each threshold from 0 to 0.30

The benchmark-performance and calibration rankings are negatively correlated (rank correlation\(\rho\)= −0.73; Additional file 1: Fig. S4): methods that rank best on benchmark rank worst on calibration. Figure6makes this concrete: k-means- and k-medoids-shuffle occupy the Pareto-efficient position (high benchmark performance, near-zero bias); KS-type methods lead on benchmark at the cost of large bias; diversity methods score worst on benchmark performance but carry intermediate bias (~0.11); KS-type methods carry the largest bias (0.17–0.22). No single splitter wins on both criteria simultaneously; the\(\hbox {R}^{2}\)analogue of this trade-off is shown in Additional file 1: Fig. S5.

Median external benchmark Spearman\(\rho\)(x-axis) vs. median signed estimation bias\(\Delta\)(y-axis), one point per splitting method. Dashed line: zero bias. The ideal method sits bottom-right

Applying TOPSIS and MOORA with the eleven measures as criteria recovers the two-objective trade-off and condenses it into a single overall ranking (full per-criterion ranks for both methods in Additional file 1: Tables S4 and S5). Ranked on benchmark performance, the Kennard–Stone family is best (TOPSIS mean ranks: Morais 3.6, Kennard–Stone 3.8, SPXY 4.3) and diversity methods worst (11.9–13.1). Ranked on estimation credibility, the ordering inverts: cluster-shuffle methods lead (k-medoids-shuffle 3.8, k-means-shuffle 4.0), and the Kennard–Stone methods rank last (MDKS 13.9, SPXY 14.1). The combined ranking, which weights the two objectives equally, therefore rewards methods that are credible without being weak on performance: k-medoids-shuffle (3.8), k-means-shuffle (3.9) and Butina-shuffle (4.9) take the top three places, while SPXY (13.6) and MDKS (13.7) are last. This trade-off generalizes the single-measure inversion of Fig.6to all eleven measures: as Fig.7shows, no splitter ranks well on both performance and credibility. MOORA reproduces the combined ordering almost exactly (Spearman\(\rho\)= 0.98 between the two methods’ combined ranks). The ranking is also robust to the measures’ redundancy: weighting each construct (error, explained variance, correlation, enrichment) equally, rather than each of the correlated measures, leaves the combined ranking essentially unchanged (Spearman\(\rho\)= 0.97). The MCDA delivers a single overall ranking, but which method comes first depends on how performance and credibility are weighted; cluster-shuffle is the strategy that performs best when the two objectives are weighted equally.

Multicriteria trade-off between benchmark performance and estimation credibility (TOPSIS). Each rank is a single TOPSIS score that aggregates all eleven measures as criteria, with 1 best on each axis. The dashed line marks a perfect inversion between the two rankings

Figure8plots the MDAS from the internal test set to the training set (x-axis) against the MDAS from the external benchmark to the training set (y-axis), for each (splitter, dataset) combination (Spearman\(\rho\)= 0.71 across all pairs). KS-type methods sit above the diagonal with low internal MDAS: their internal test sets are much closer to training than the external benchmark, directly explaining their optimistic bias. Diversity methods also lie above the diagonal with similar or lower internal MDAS to KS (their diverse training sets cover internal chemical space broadly, keeping internal test performance moderate), but the external benchmark–train MDAS is substantially higher, placing them far above the diagonal. Cluster-shuffle methods are the rightmost group, sitting at or right of the diagonal: they create internal test sets as structurally remote from training as the external benchmark, or more so, which explains their near-zero bias.

Internal test–train MDAS (x-axis) vs. external benchmark–train MDAS (y-axis), one point per (splitter, dataset) combination. Points on the diagonal have equal distributional distance; above the diagonal indicates the internal test is closer to training than the external benchmark

Additional file 1: Figure S10 summarizes this relationship at the per-splitter level: methods whose external MDAS is close to their internal MDAS show smaller |\(\Delta\)Spearman|, confirming that geometric split quality is predictive of calibration quality. Full 15\(\times\)15 Nemenyi pairwise p-value matrices are provided as Additional file 1: Figs. S11 and S12, and the nearest-neighbor test–train distance distributions underlying this geometry as Additional file 1: Fig. S7.

Figure9stratifies external benchmark Spearman\(\rho\)by AD membership (in-domain vs. out-of-domain) for each splitter. For KS-type methods the in-domain benchmark half scores substantially higher than the out-of-domain half, yet the internal estimate (dashed) sits above even the in-domain score, confirming that KS inflates its internal estimates beyond what easy in-domain compounds alone can explain. Cluster-shuffle methods show a similar in-domain vs. out-of-domain gap to other families (~0.17), but their internal estimate (dashed) aligns with the overall benchmark level rather than sitting above it, consistent with their test sets being as structurally challenging as the temporal holdout. Diversity-based methods achieve the highest AD coverage; coverage fractions across splitters are shown in Additional file 1: Fig. S8.

Median external benchmark Spearman\(\rho\)by splitting method, stratified by applicability-domain membership (circles = in-domain; triangles = out-of-domain). Dashed line: internal test estimate

Figure10reveals an inversion: calibration quality and model-selection quality point in opposite directions. SPXY, the worst-calibrated splitter by estimation error, ranks among the top on both selection advantage and hit rate; k-means-shuffle, the best-calibrated splitter, ranks last on both. KS-type methods generally lead model selection while cluster-shuffle variants occupy the lower half of the table. The likely mechanism is that geometrically easy interior test sets (KS-type) preserve relative model rankings even while inflating absolute estimates: a model class that is superior on an easy test is still superior on the harder external benchmark. No method achieves statistical separation at the CD = 5.538 threshold, and effect sizes are small (Cohen’s d = 0.32/0.24 for SPXY vs k-means-shuffle; Additional file 1: Table S3), so these directional results should be treated as indicative. At Sub-150, selection advantage turns negative for all splitters, indicating that at\(\approx\)120 training compounds internal test evaluation does not reliably identify the externally best model regardless of splitting strategy.

Model-selection quality (CD = 5.538,\(\alpha\)= 0.05; lower rank = better). Left: selection advantage. Right: selection hit rate

The broad family-level pattern is preserved at Sub-150 (Figs.11,12): KS-type and diversity methods retain the highest estimation bias (KS-type\(\Delta \rho\)= +0.16-−0.27), cluster-shuffle the lowest, though individual method ranks within families shift more than at full scale. At this scale k-means-shuffle has a median\(\Delta \rho\)= -−0.03, marginally pessimistic. Benchmark performance is compressed into a narrow band (range\(\approx\)0.05 vs\(\approx\)0.09 at full scale) while bias spread remains large (\(\approx\)0.30), giving a bias-to-performance ratio of approximately 6\(\times\), up from 2.5\(\times\)at full scale, reflecting the dominance of noise at only 150 compounds (Fig.13). Model-selection results at Sub-150 show all methods clustered in a narrow rank band with no statistical separation whatsoever, further supporting the conclusion that splitting strategy does not affect which model class is selected (Additional file 1: Figs. S13–S14). Sub-1000 results are in agreement (Additional file 1: Figs. S15–S17).

Nemenyi CD diagram for Spearman benchmark performance, Sub-150 regime (CD = 5.538,\(\alpha\)= 0.05; lower rank = better)

Nemenyi CD diagram for Spearman estimation error |\(\Delta \rho\)|, Sub-150 regime (CD = 5.538,\(\alpha\)= 0.05; lower rank = better calibrated)

Signed Spearman estimation bias\(\Delta\)=\(\rho\)_internal_test –\(\rho\)_benchmark per splitter, Sub-150 regime, sorted from best-calibrated (left) to worst (right). Dashed line:\(\Delta\)= 0 (perfect calibration)

The direction of KS-type overoptimism is qualitatively established in spectroscopic and QSAR settings [5,6,7,8,9,10]. This work adds four elements. First, bias magnitude is shown to far exceed benchmark-performance differences across a drug-discovery regression benchmark, confirming that evaluation credibility is a more sensitive function of splitter choice than realized performance. Second, the effect is general across all eleven measures spanning error, explained variance, rank correlation, and enrichment, and cannot be dismissed as an artefact of a single scoring choice. Third, the MDAS analysis (Fig.8) provides a geometric mechanism grounding earlier qualitative arguments. Fourth, model-selection quality emerges as a distinct and opposing dimension: the worst-calibrated splitter (SPXY) numerically leads on selection advantage and hit rate, while the best-calibrated (k-means-shuffle) ranks last, though no method achieves statistical separation.

The dataset-size dependence documented in [13] is visible in our per-dataset spread (Additional file 1: Fig. S6), and the recently proposed XYOnion algorithm [25] corroborates our cluster-stratified results directionally.

KS’s uniformly spanning training set leaves interior, structurally easy compounds as the internal test set. This inflates internal scores while making the training set maximally representative, yielding the best benchmark performance. Diversity methods have similar or lower internal MDAS to KS, keeping internal performance at a moderate level, but the external benchmark is substantially harder still, so they remain mildly optimistic; cluster-shuffle holds out whole clusters as structurally remote from training as the external benchmark, yielding near-zero bias without sacrificing representative training.

The estimation bias is largely model-agnostic: recomputing the analysis using the per-split TPE-selected model (LightGBM, random forest, KNN, SVR, or elastic net) in place of the fixed LightGBM leaves per-splitter results essentially unchanged (benchmark Spearman\(\rho\)within\(\approx\)0.01, signed bias\(\Delta\)within\(\approx\)0.01; Additional file 1: Table S1). The optimism is a property of the test-set composition rather than of any particular learner.

The splitting problem divides cleanly into two tasks with different answers. The first task is estimating prospective performance. Here the evidence is statistically clear: cluster-shuffle and diversity-based methods achieve significantly better calibration across all measures. The second task is selecting the best model class when multiple classes compete: here no method achieves statistical separation and effect sizes are small (Cohen’s d\(\le\)0.32; Additional file 1: Table S3), meaning the choice of splitter has no demonstrated impact on which model class is ultimately selected.

Given this framing, the practical recommendation is straightforward: cluster-shuffle splitting is the preferred default, as it achieves the best calibration while remaining competitive on benchmark performance and is not demonstrably worse for model selection; diversity-based methods are similarly well-calibrated but rank worst on benchmark performance. Practitioners who prioritize model-selection quality may use a two-stage strategy: use KS-type splitting to select the model class and hyperparameters, then re-split with cluster-shuffle and retrain the selected model to obtain a calibrated estimate of prospective performance. The relative magnitude of estimation bias versus realized-performance differences will vary with dataset size and split ratio [5,13], and this disparity grows as datasets shrink, so the case for calibrated splitting is strongest in small-data regimes.

Dataset selection and benchmark: We analyze the publicly released Merck datasets, and we do not claim that the patterns described will necessarily hold for datasets outside drug-discovery regression. The Merck temporal split reflects compound testing order in a specific industrial organization and may not transfer to academic datasets or other prospective scenarios [26].

Molecular structures unavailable: Because structures are not provided, we cannot evaluate scaffold-aware or fingerprint-based splits in their native form, and whether results extend to explicit scaffold splits [27] remains an open question. More broadly, all methods here use a shared descriptor rather than the representations they would typically be deployed with; within-family rankings may therefore be descriptor-conditional.

Temporal benchmark: We treat the Merck temporal split as a proxy for prospective performance. This is a strong assumption.

Fixed model in the splitting-assessment experiment: The model-selection experiment confirms that the benchmark-performance and estimation-bias pattern is consistent across five algorithm classes under TPE optimization; whether it extends to model families not covered here remains to be verified.

Small-dataset generalizability: The Sub-150 sensitivity analysis is conducted across all 15 datasets uniformly capped at 150 development compounds; it is therefore not a direct observation of the full-data regime for any individual dataset but a controlled comparison at a fixed small-data size representative of real ADMET benchmarks. Whether findings extend to other small-data domains (e.g., non-drug-discovery regression) remains to be verified.

Fixed cluster count: All clustering-based methods use k = 10 clusters regardless of dataset size. For the largest datasets this is very coarse, making cluster-shuffle assignments closer to random. Results for the clustering family may therefore differ with other choices of k, and k-sensitivity is an open empirical question.

Nemenyi conservatism: The Nemenyi procedure is conservative; subtle real differences may not reach significance at\(\alpha\)= 0.05. Violin plots and spread charts are provided alongside CD diagrams to convey effect sizes independently of statistical thresholds.

Extensions that would strengthen generality include: (1) evaluation on non-drug-discovery datasets and datasets outside the Merck benchmark; (2) incorporation of structure-annotated datasets to include scaffold and pharmacophore splits; (3) validation with explicit temporal metadata within the development pool to enable comparison with temporal CV [28]; and (4) analysis of additional model classes.

Across fifteen drug-discovery datasets and eleven evaluation measures, train–test splitting strategy primarily affects the reliability of performance evaluation rather than realized model generalization. Kennard–Stone-type methods achieve modest benchmark-performance gains at the cost of substantially optimistic internal estimates, confirming and quantifying the overoptimism documented in prior literature, and confirmed here as general across error, explained-variance, rank-correlation, and early-enrichment scores.

The splitting problem is best understood as two distinct tasks. For performance estimation, the evidence is statistically clear: cluster-shuffle methods produce significantly better-calibrated estimates. For model selection among competing model classes, no splitting method achieves statistical separation and effect sizes are small, meaning the choice of splitter has no demonstrated impact on which model class is ultimately selected. Cluster-shuffle is therefore the recommended default: it wins decisively on calibration and is not demonstrably worse for model selection. Practitioners who wish to optimize model selection explicitly may use a two-stage strategy: KS-type splitting for model and hyperparameter selection, followed by re-splitting with cluster-shuffle and retraining to obtain a calibrated prospective performance estimate.

The molecular activity datasets analysed in this study are the publicly released portion of the Merck molecular activity benchmark and are available from the original publication (DOI: 10.1021/ci500747n). title: Explicitness in SMILES representation via ExACT: improved tokenization for aqueous solubility prediction
author: Domagoj Begušić; Damir Pintar; Zlatko Smole; Ernest Meštrović
text:
The representation of molecular structure in textual form plays a central role in data-driven cheminformatics, not just for deep learning models that often rely on sequence-based inputs, but also for classic machine learning pipelines which are still relevant in this field. The Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) representation and its explicit variants differ substantially, yet the implications of this difference for tokenization and downstream property prediction remain insufficiently characterized. This paper systematically investigates the role of explicitness in SMILES representation and its impact on aqueous solubility prediction. Four SMILES variations ranging from basic and canonical to explicit and explicit canonical are reviewed to illustrate how increasing explicit chemical detail alters the available information content. Building on this analysis, a novel tokenization approach termed ExACT (Explicit Atom level Context Tokenization) is introduced, which directly leverages atom level explicitness and local chemical context. In addition, a general strategy for enhancing existing tokenization methods through increased explicitness is proposed and demonstrated by upgrading the current state of the art atom-in-SMILES method to an explicit variant. All approaches are evaluated on the AqSolDB dataset using consistent machine learning pipelines and cross validation protocols. The results show that increased explicitness systematically improves predictive performance across tokenization strategies, yielding higher coefficients of determination, lower mean absolute and root mean squared errors, and reduced variance across folds. The proposed ExACT method achieves the best overall performance, largely outperforming traditional molecular fingerprint representations while remaining statistically comparable to the best competing tokenization methods. Furthermore, the efficiency analysis demonstrated that ExACT offers additional computational advantages, including lower dimensionality and the elimination of the decoding step, resulting in faster feature computation. These findings demonstrate that explicit SMILES representations encode chemically meaningful information that can be effectively exploited through context-aware tokenization, providing an interpretable and computationally efficient alternative representation for molecular property prediction.

Scientific contribution

This work investigates the role of explicitness in SMILES and its impact on aqueous solubility prediction, proposes a novel ExACT tokenization method and a general strategy for enhancing existing tokenization methods through increased explicitness.

Molecular representation underpins modern computational approaches in cheminformatics [1,2]. Textual representations in particular serve as the basis for both classical machine learning pipelines and contemporary sequence-based models [3]. Among textual formats, the Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) [4] has achieved near universal adoption due to its compactness and compatibility with standard cheminformatics toolkits. SMILES encodes molecular structure as a sequence of characters reflecting atoms, bonds, branches, and ring closures, thereby enabling straightforward storage, retrieval, and processing of chemical information. Despite its widespread use, SMILES suffers from inherent limitations related to representational ambiguity, token granularity, and insufficient encoding of local chemical context, all of which can influence downstream model performance [5].

Tokenization constitutes a critical preprocessing step in sequence based modeling. Although the term tokenization is most commonly associated with natural language processing and representation learning, it more generally denotes the process of transforming a sequential representation into a set of discrete symbolic units (tokens). In the present work, SMILES strings are decomposed into chemically meaningful units that serve as the fundamental elements of subsequent molecular representations. Within natural language processing, tokenization methods strongly affect model convergence, generalization, and the extraction of meaningful patterns from sequence inputs. Similarly, tokenization methods applied to SMILES significantly influence the information content available to models and the chemical interpretability of the learned features [6]. Conventional atom-wise or character-wise SMILES tokenization treats all occurrences of the same atomic symbol as identical tokens, thereby ignoring differences in chemical environment that are fundamental to molecular behavior. This approach, while straightforward, is limited by its lack of chemical context; atoms with identical atomic numbers but differing local environments are represented indistinguishably, which can obscure critical structural information during model training. Recent work has highlighted that such generic token representation can lead to token degeneration issues in language modeling tasks [7].

Research on SMILES tokenization methods has gained increasing attention with the rise of sequence-based machine learning models adapted from natural language processing [8]. Advanced tokenization strategies such as atom-in-SMILES (AIS) [9] enrich tokens with local chemical environment information derived from adjacent atom environments, demonstrating improved performance on translation and prediction tasks compared to traditional methods. Empirical evaluations show that AIS can outperform conventional tokenization approaches by generating more chemically informative token sequences and reducing repetitive token patterns that degrade model performance [7,10].

Additional tokenization strategies further emphasize the importance of capturing substructure patterns and data-driven token vocabularies. SMILES Pair Encoding (SPE) [11] learns frequent SMILES substrings as tokens from large chemical datasets, enhancing representation by including human-readable subunits extending beyond atom-level tokens. This method has been shown to improve performance for both molecular generation and quantitative structure-activity relationship prediction tasks relative to atom-level tokenization alone. Recent work has also focused on atomically complete tokenizers designed to better cover the complexity of the SMILES language under the OpenSMILES specification and address limitations in vocabularies used by molecular foundation models [12]. Comparative studies of SMILES and alternative string representations such as SELFIES further underscore the influence of representation and tokenization choice on predictive performance and structural fidelity in learned models [13].

Beyond tokenization itself, variations in SMILES representation including canonical, explicit, and explicit canonical forms further shape the distribution of tokens. Canonical SMILES enforces a deterministic ordering of atoms but retains an abstracted form of chemical detail. Explicit SMILES incorporates additional information such as explicit hydrogen atoms and bond specifications, increasing the granularity of the representation and potentially exposing models to deeper structural features. Explicit canonical forms combine deterministic atom ordering with full explicit specification, yielding representations that maximize explicit chemical detail. While representational richness is hypothesized to facilitate more informative tokenization, systematic analysis of how increasing explicitness impacts tokenization quality and predictive performance has not been comprehensively addressed.

In parallel with tokenization research, multiple studies have evaluated the use of SMILES and derived representations for molecular property prediction. Early work demonstrated that recurrent neural network models trained directly on SMILES strings can learn predictive patterns for chemical properties such as solubility and toxicity without explicit feature engineering, establishing SMILES-based deep learning models as viable alternatives to descriptor-based methods [14,15,16]. More recent explorations have combined SMILES representations with deep neural network architectures to predict diverse properties [17], while hybrid models integrating both SMILES and vector-based fingerprints indicate potential performance gains through multimodal feature integration [3,18,19,20]. Transformer-based architectures and attention mechanisms have further amplified the importance of tokenization design choices for downstream predictive performance [8,21,22].

Aqueous solubility is a fundamental physicochemical property that governs the applicability of chemical compounds across a broad range of domains, including pharmaceutical drug discovery and development, agrochemical design, and cosmetic formulation [23,24]. In drug development, solubility directly influences bioavailability, formulation strategy, and clinical efficacy, making it one of the earliest and most critical filters in compound selection [25]. Beyond pharmaceuticals, solubility also plays a decisive role in determining the environmental fate and biological activity of agrochemicals, as well as the stability and performance of active ingredients in cosmetics and related industries [26]. Reliable computational prediction of aqueous solubility therefore represents a high-value target in cheminformatics, with implications spanning early-stage virtual screening to the rational design of compounds with tailored physicochemical profiles [27,28].

Aqueous solubility prediction exemplifies a molecular property that is highly sensitive to structural subtleties including hydrogen bonding patterns and local chemical environments [29]. The development of benchmark datasets such as AqSolDB [28] which consolidates experimental solubility measurements with validated SMILES representations for thousands of compounds has enabled comparisons across descriptor-based, fingerprint-based, and sequence-based modeling approaches. Prior studies have used AqSolDB to train models incorporating SMILES randomization and descriptor augmentation to improve performance [30], while machine learning protocols have also been adapted to account for the inherent noise and variability in experimental solubility data [17,31]. Benchmark efforts in related computational property prediction challenges further emphasize the difficulty of accurately modeling physical properties from structural representations, motivating continued innovation in both representation and algorithmic design [32].

Despite these advancements, systematic investigation of how increasing explicit chemical detail in SMILES representations influences token quality and predictive performance remains underdeveloped. This paper addresses this gap by systematically exploring the role of explicitness in SMILES representations and its implications for tokenization and aqueous solubility prediction. We first review established tokenization methods across four SMILES formats spanning basic to explicit canonical representations, illustrating how increasing explicit chemical detail alters the information available for tokenization. Building on this analysis, we introduce ExACT (Explicit Atom level Context Tokenization), a novel tokenization method that leverages explicit representation to capture atom level context more effectively. Additionally, we present a strategy for enhancing existing tokenization methods through explicitness, demonstrated by upgrading the current state of the art atom-in-SMILES approach to an explicit variant. Finally, we evaluate the performance of all methods using consistent machine learning pipelines on the AqSolDB dataset. Results indicate that increased explicitness systematically improves predictive performance, yielding models with higher coefficients of determination, lower mean absolute and root mean squared errors, and reduced variance across cross validation folds. These findings underscore the importance of explicit chemical detail for tokenization in cheminformatics and provide a structured pathway for advancing sequence based property prediction without reliance on graph based neural architectures.

This section details the overall machine learning process implemented in this study and describes the specific methods used to evaluate the impact of explicit SMILES tokenization on aqueous solubility prediction. First, the general workflow of data preprocessing, representation, model training, and evaluation is outlined. Next, five methodological components are presented in dedicated subsections: (I) process overview, (II) used data characteristics and preprocessing, (III) the proposed explicit SMILES tokenization method ExACT, (IV) the approach of integrating explicitness in AIS tokenization method, and (V) the selection and rationale for the machine learning models employed.

The machine learning workflow employed in this study is structured to ensure consistent processing across datasets and tokenization variants. Two datasets were used: AqSolDB [28] and its new highly curated version that we will refer to as AqSolDBc [33] which was primarily used to extract the adjusted aqueous solubility values. The used datasets are described in detail in the next subsection. The input representation is SMILES strings from the AqSolDB dataset.

Molecular structures were represented using SMILES strings obtained from AqSolDB. The target variables extracted from AqSolDB included aqueous solubility, molecular weight, lipophilicity, and molar refractivity. Also, adjusted aqueous solubility values from AqSolDBc were incorporated as an additional target variable. The analysis presented in this paper focuses on aqueous solubility and molecular weight, while the results for lipophilicity, molar refractivity and adjusted aqueous solubility are provided in the supplementary materials (Appendix C).

The pipeline begins with preprocessing of the raw SMILES strings. First, invalid and duplicate SMILES strings were excluded. Then, all necessary SMILES representation formats were calculated for each molecule. Next, tokenization methods are applied to each appropriate SMILES representation variant to decompose the SMILES sequences into discrete tokens appropriate for encoding. The resulting token sequences are transformed into numerical feature vectors using term frequency inverse document frequency vectorization (TF-IDF). In this representation, each token is assigned a weight proportional to its frequency within a given sequence and inversely proportional to its occurrence across the full dataset, thereby reducing the influence of prevalent tokens. Using a simple, model-agnostic vectorization method allows the evaluation to focus on the impact of the proposed tokenization and explicitness strategies, without introducing additional variability from learned representation methods.

To obtain robust and statistically reliable performance estimates, model evaluation was conducted using a repeated 5-fold cross validation procedure with five repetitions. For each repetition, the dataset was randomly partitioned into five folds, with four folds used for training and one fold reserved for testing. This process was repeated until each fold had served as the test set once, resulting in a total of 25 evaluation runs for each experimental configuration. The study employed XGBoost Regressor and CatBoost Regressor models using their default hyperparameter settings. Fixed hyperparameters were intentionally retained throughout all experiments to reduce computational complexity and to avoid potential performance inflation associated with extensive hyperparameter optimization. This design choice ensures that observed differences in predictive performance can be more directly attributed to the investigated tokenization methods rather than to model-specific tuning procedures.

Model performance was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (\(R^2\)), mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean squared error (RMSE). In addition to predictive performance, the total computational time required to execute the complete machine learning pipeline, from feature generation based on the tokenized SMILES representations to model training and evaluation, was recorded. The dimensionality of each generated feature space (\(n_{features}\)) was also tracked to quantify the complexity of the resulting molecular representations.

The complete workflow is summarized in Fig.1. Throughout all experiments, identical data partitions, preprocessing procedures, model configurations, and evaluation protocols were maintained to ensure reproducibility and enable a fair comparison among the investigated tokenization methods.

The predictive evaluation conducted in this study utilizes the widely referenced AqSolDB dataset [28], which comprises experimentally measured aqueous solubility values paired with corresponding SMILES representations for a diverse set of organic molecules. To further characterize the chemical diversity of the filtered AqSolDB dataset, distributions of selected structural and physicochemical descriptors are provided in Appendix D. In addition to the original dataset, we also employed a highly curated variant recently published to assess robustness of tokenization methods [33] which we used as a source for adjusted aqueous solubility measurements. Both aqueous solubility and adjusted aqueous solubility measurements are expressed in consistentlog(S) units, enabling direct comparison across models. Aqueous solubility measurements encompasses a broad range of solubility values reflecting varying chemical classes, while the adjusted aqueous solubility measurements represent corrected and normalized records intended to mitigate measurement inconsistencies. Prior to model training, SMILES strings are validated for syntactic correctness, and molecules exhibiting invalid or ambiguous representations are excluded. During this validation step, only two SMILES samples in the original dataset were found to be syntactically invalid:CC1=CC=C[NH++]([O-])[CH-]1andOC(=O)C1=C[NH++]([O-])[CH-]C=C1. In both cases the nitrogen atom has an impossible valency of six, which is not allowed in SMILES grammar. As a result, no processing method that relies on correct SMILES grammar can work with these representations.

There is only one duplicate in AqSolDB: entries E-1289 and C-293 which both correspond to prostaglandin E2. While their stereochemical specifications differ, they represent the same molecular scaffold and have identical solubility values. To avoid duplicate sampling, we retained the stereochemically specified record (C-293) and removed E-1289.

For each retained molecule, four SMILES formats are generated: basic, canonical, explicit, and explicit canonical, to facilitate systematic comparison of tokenization methods across representational variants (Fig.2). SMILES variants beyond the basic SMILES were generated using RDKit [34] and all generated variants conform to valid SMILES grammar and are syntactically correct. The distributions of sequence lengths for all four used SMILES variations for the AqSolDB dataset are illustrated in Fig.3, providing a basic overview of representational complexity.

The central methodological contribution of this work is a novel tokenization approach termed Explicit Atom level Context Tokenization (ExACT). In contrast to traditional tokenization methods that treat identical atom symbols as equivalent regardless of local environment, ExACT constructs tokens that encode both atom identity and local explicit chemical context derived from the explicit SMILES representation. This representation includes all hydrogen atoms and bond specifications, thereby supplying richer structural information for token creation. The ExACT algorithm systematically incorporates atom neighborhoods and bond connectivity into token definitions, yielding tokens that uniquely reflect atom position and environment within each molecule. An example of ExACT tokenization for a representative molecule is provided in Fig.4, and the Algorithm 1 outlines the algorithmic steps for ExACT token generation. The proposed ExACT tokenization algorithm converts an explicit SMILES stringSinto a sequence of atom centered tokens while preserving structural information such as bonds, branching, and ring closures. The procedure first appliesSplitSMILESIntoParts(S), which segments the SMILES string into primitive components using a regular expression designed to identify atomic symbols, bracketed atoms, bond markers, digits representing ring indices, parentheses, and other SMILES control characters. The resulting sequence of parts is then processed sequentially to construct tokens. When a dot symbol is encountered, the current token is terminated and the dot is emitted as a separate token. When an atomic symbol or bracketed atom is encountered, a new token is created; if a previous token already exists, the operation MergeWithPreviousContext(current,p) is applied. This operation constructs the new token by combining the current atom symbol with the immediate structural context inherited from the preceding token, including bond symbols, branch delimiters, and ring-closure indicators that directly define the atom’s local connectivity. For example, a double bond (=), branch opening ((), or ring index (1) associated with the connection to the current atom is retained as part of the newly created token. In this way, ExACT preserves not only atom identity but also the explicit local bonding environment through which the atom participates in the molecular structure. After all parts have been processed, each token undergoes a normalization step usingNormalizeRingIndices(t), which adjusts the representation of ring closure indices by inserting explicit bond delimiters where required and removing redundant bond markers that may appear after closing parentheses. The final ordered list of tokens is then returned.

Figures3and6together show that canonicalization has little effect on the overall size of the molecular representation, but a noticeable impact on its token composition. As shown in Fig.3, canonical and non-canonical SMILES exhibit very similar sequence-length distributions, indicating that canonicalization largely preserves the amount of structural information encoded for each molecule. Consistent with this observation, Fig.6demonstrates that ExACT token counts remain nearly unchanged between explicit and explicit canonical SMILES, confirming that canonicalization does not alter the overall representation granularity. Additionally, Appendix A demonstrates that token length distributions are largely preserved between the explicit and explicit canonical SMILES representations. However, the distribution of unique ExACT tokens shifts slightly after canonicalization, reflecting changes in token identity and frequency caused by the deterministic atom-ordering procedure. By enforcing a consistent traversal of molecular structures, canonicalization reduces representational variability while preserving molecular identity and information content. Consequently, canonicalized explicit SMILES provide a more statistically consistent basis for ExACT token generation, leading to a more uniform and structured token vocabulary across molecules.
