The size of drug-like chemical space has been estimated to be on the order of\(10^{33}\)molecules [1], a size which is virtually impossible to explore with traditional workflows. Generative approaches [2] have emerged as promising ways forward for searching this vast space in a high throughput and systematic manner. A major challenge for generative approaches, however, is ideating truly novel molecules while ensuring their chemical validity and synthetic feasibility.

The Chemically Reasonable Mutations (CReM) framework [3] is a powerful and flexible generative approach that creates novel molecules from input structures using a database of interchangeable fragments. Given a small molecule, CReM generates new ideas by swapping substructures of the molecule with fragments which exist in a similar chemical context. The similarity of the context can be adjusted by setting a context radius: the larger the radius, the larger the context match that is required for a swap. In this way, chemically valid molecules are generated by design, and synthetic feasibility can be tuned by the size of the context radius. More recently, the CReM approach has been extended to enumerating molecular structures that conform to three dimensional pharmacophore models (CReM-pharm) [4].

The novelty and diversity of compounds generated by CReM is directly related to the novelty and diversity of the molecules in the fragment database. The original CReM release had a database based on ChEMBL22 [5], a manually curated collection of bioactive molecules with drug-like properties of approximately 1.56M molecules. The CReM repository (https://www.qsar4u.com/pages/crem.php) currently offers several fragment libraries, albeit of relatively modest size, derived from the ChEMBL22, ChEMBL23, and Enamine databases through the application of specific structural and property-based filters. In recent years, collections of synthetically accessible small molecules have continued to grow rapidly, with some like PubChem [6] and Enamine REAL [7] reaching 120M  and 10B molecules in size, respectively.

Creating fragment databases from these much larger libraries would significantly boost the generative power of CReM. Internally, for example, we have greatly expanded our fragment database by building an ultralarge CReM-compatible fragment library, TandemDB, assembled from five widely used chemical databases: ChEMBL (1.7 million molecules) [8], Enamine (48 million) [9], SureChEMBL (22.6 million) [10], PubChem (108 million) [11], and ZINC20 (897 million) [12]. In the case of Enamine, we considered a structurally diverse, drug-like subset of the entire library, and for ZINC20, we considered the “Wait Ok” dataset that contains all molecules that are likely to be purchasable within some reasonable timeframe. While TandemDB dramatically increased our coverage of chemical space, it also introduced a significant challenge to our computational infrastructure. The combined total of 988 million source molecules produced a database with more than 40 billion fragments and a storage footprint that exceeded 10 TB, making efficient querying difficult and impractical.

Here, we introduce a new framework for CReM fragment databases, oCReM (optimized CReM), that significantly reduces disk storage requirements and increases fragment query speed, making it feasible to use ultralarge libraries for generating novel molecules with unparalleled structural diversity. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: we begin by presenting the original CReM framework, and then detail our optimized oCReM framework, highlighting its key distinctions from the original implementation. We then provide a direct comparison of library sizes and enumeration capabilities between the optimized and original versions. Finally, we present case studies that demonstrate the benefits of accessing the vastly expanded chemical space enabled by this optimization.

In the original CReM framework, the fragment library is stored as a single table in an SQLite database with the following components (Table1):

core_smi: the SMILES representation of the fragment with its attachment point(s).

env: the chemical environment of the fragment, defined by the topological distance (i.e., the number of bonds) from its attachment point(s). Fragment environments are recorded for context radii ranging from 1 to 3.

core_sma: the SMARTS pattern that integrates core_smi with its environment.

core_num_atoms: the number of atoms in the fragment.

dist2: the topological distance between two attachment points in the fragment, and

freq: the frequency of occurrence of a given combination of  env and core_smi in the library

A given query molecule is first fragmented at the specified attachment point(s) to generate the fragment SMILES (query_smi) and the corresponding chemical environments (query_env) at those sites. The chemical environment captures the local molecular topology within a defined topological radius around each attachment point. Fragment SMARTS patterns are then constructed by combining each query_smi with its query_env, preserving fully the specified connectivity throughout the fragment except at the attachment site, while explicitly encoding the chemical environment of the attachment point(s). The CReM library is then searched for fragments with environments (env) that match query_env. For the matching fragments, a SMARTS-based transformation is carried out to replace query_sma with core_sma, producing new molecules (Algorithm  1).

SMARTS-based reaction in CReM to replace a query molecule fragment with a chemically compatible fragment

This framework supports both R-group enumeration using thegrow_molfunction when a single query_env is defined from the query_smi, and scaffold_hopping using themutate_molfunction, when multiple query_env are defined. In this way, the approach enables a systematic exploration of chemical space with flexible control over molecular diversity, novelty, and synthetic feasibility.

Major contributors to the fragment library size are the core_smi and core_sma fragment entries, each of which can be hundreds of characters. An alternative approach would be, for a given query molecule, to identify its core (query_smi), R-group(s), their chemical environment(s) (query_env), and attachment point(s). The query_env can then be used to find matching core_smi, which can be directly attached as R-groups to generate new molecules (Algorithm 2).

If the query molecule has multiple R-groups, its specific chemical environments can guide correct attachment placement. This strategy eliminates the need to store fragment SMARTS (core_sma), reducing by as much as 50%, the data that needs to be stored in the tables, excluding the table indices.

Strategy for directly attaching fragments to a query molecule core, without using a query or replacement fragment SMARTS

In CReM, a single fragment may correspond to multiple chemical environments, and each environment can, in turn, match several fragments. In the original fragment library format, all such combinations are stored as a flattened list, leading to redundancy in both the env and core_smi columns. This redundancy becomes more pronounced when the libraries are built from multiple chemical databases. A more efficient approach would be to maintain separate, de-duplicated, and indexed tables of unique env and core_smi, along with a mapping table that defines their relationships (Fig.1). This new database schema would further reduce the overall size of the fragment library. Together, these optimizations significantly reduce the size of the fragment library while also improving the efficiency of library queries.

Schema of the oCReM fragment libraries. Indexed fields are denoted with a # sign. Symbols1andnindicate a one-to-many relationship between a primary key and a foreign key in the env_fragment table

To demonstrate the advantages of this optimized implementation of CReM, we consider fragment libraries derived from ChEMBL22 that were available as part of the original CReM distribution (https://www.qsar4u.com/pages/crem.php). CheMBL22 contains 1.7 million molecules and the CReM-compatible fragment library for ChEMBL22, in its original (SQLite DB) form, contains 110 million items and has a size of 30 GB. Our optimized version of this library has a size of 15.1 GB, a reduction of 51% (Table2).

We note that we chose PostgreSQL over SQLite internally to support our ultralarge fragment libraries due to PostgreSQL’s superior scalability, advanced indexing capabilities, and robust concurrent access support. Unlike SQLite, which is limited by its single-writer model and file-based architecture, PostgreSQL offers a client–server model that can efficiently handle complex queries and large volumes of data. Its extensible design, support for parallelism, and rich feature set make it better suited for managing the scale and performance demands of our optimized fragment enumeration framework. The ChemBL22 fragment library, in its optimized form in PostgreSQL, has a similarly reduced, 14.6 GB footprint (Table2).

To demonstrate the efficiency gains enabled by oCReM in a practical drug discovery setting, we carried out two molecular enumeration case studies: an R-group enumeration on the purine-based CDK2 inhibitor NU6094 [13] using thegrow_molfunction, and a core hop enumeration on MRTX0902, an inhibitor of the protein-protein interaction (PPI) of SOS1:KRAS [14], using themutate_molfunction (Fig.2). The enumeration statistics are summarized in Table3. In both cases, oCReM reproduced the same set of molecules as CReM, confirming functional equivalence. The optimized version, however, outperformed the original in speed, achieving a 30–67% improvement in the R-group enumeration speed and similarly large speed-ups in the core hop enumeration.

Molecules selected for enumeration using CReM and oCReM. PanelsAandDshow the CDK2 inhibitor NU6094 scaffold,Bshows the SOS1:KRAS PPI inhibitor MRTX0902, andCshows a TYK2 inhibitor scaffold. R-group enumeration is performed forAandC, whereas core hop enumeration is applied toBandD. In each structure, the enumeration site or core is highlighted in gold

The advantages of oCReM become more pronounced with increasing size of the fragment library. As mentioned earlier, we assembled a large fragment library in house, TandemDB, from multiple chemical databases, comprising a total of 988 million molecules. In the original CReM framework, this fragment library consisted of over 40 billion fragments and exceeds 10 TB. In oCReM, the overall size is reduced by 85% to 1.5 TB.

This large reduction in fragment library size is crucial for molecular enumerations with such large fragment libraries, enabling CReM to explore ultralarge chemical spaces. We illustrate this point by (a) comparing the number of molecules enumerated for R-group and a core hop enumerations using ChEMBL22 and TandemDB, and (b) comparing the computational cost associated with such an R-group and core hop enumerations on a library as large as TandemDB using the original CReM framework and oCReM. The R-group enumeration is performed on a well-known Tyk2 inhibitor scaffold (Fig.2C) [15], and the core hop enumeration is performed on the CDK2 inhibitor NU6094 (Fig.2D) [13]. In the case of R-group enumeration, we observed approximately 50–100 times more molecules with varying R-groups and 20–80 times more molecules with different cores from using TandemDB compared to ChEMBL22, emphasizing the impact of large fragment libraries (Table4).

A direct comparison of computational costs between CReM and oCReM reveals speed-ups of up to 85–95%, highlighting the impact of fragment library optimization on enumeration efficiency. We note that in this comparison, oCReM uses the Postgres format for the fragment libraries, whereas CReM uses SQLite. Given the comparable performance of CReM enumerations across both SQLite and Postgres formats for ChEMBL22, we anticipate similar behavior for the two formats of TandemDB as well.

The significance of the expanded, accessible chemical space afforded by TandemDB for the R-group enumeration on the TYK2 inhibitor scaffold is further illustrated in Fig.3. For the enumeration with a context radius of 3, tSNE embeddings of compatible R-groups obtained from the ChEMBL22 and TandemDB libraries are shown in Fig.3A and B, respectively. For ChEMBL22, all 38,788 molecules were included. For TandemDB, due to its large size, a structurally diverse subset of 30,000 R-groups, determined based on all-to-all Tanimoto similarity to the ChEMBL22 molecules, was selected from the 1.78M enumerated compounds (Table4). As seen in the tSNE plots, TandemDB, which by design encompasses all R groups obtained from ChEMBL22, covers a significantly broader chemical space.

To evaluate the quality of the enumerated molecules, we went a step further and estimated their binding affinities using LigUnity, a foundation model for protein–ligand affinity prediction [16,17,18]. LigUnity is trained on a multi-task framework, leveraging both coarse virtual screening data and high-resolution binding affinity measurements, and can be fine-tuned with target-specific datasets. The predictive accuracy of LigUnity was demonstrated on a broad set of systems containing eight different benchmark datasets, where the model was shown to achieve state-of-the-art predictive performance across split-by-time, split-by-scaffold, and split-by-unit settings [18]. In this study, we employed the LigUnity model fine-tuned on internal binding affinity data derived from free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations of Tyk2 and CDK2 inhibitors [19].

The binding affinity predictions for TYK2 and CDK2 analogs generated from ChEMBL22 and TandemDB, as evaluated using the fine-tuned LigUnity model, are summarized in the “N mol (Good binders)” columns of Table4, with the corresponding affinity distributions for TYK2 analogs shown in Fig.3C and D. For the ChEMBL fragment libraries, when the number of generated molecules exceeded 50,000 (e.g., TYK2 radius 1 and 2 enumerations), a structurally diverse subset of 30,000 R-groups was selected based on all-to-all Tanimoto similarity. Predictions were performed using three independent random selections to ensure reproducibility. For TandemDB, in cases where more than 50,000 molecules were generated, a similarly diverse subset of 30,000 R-groups (for TYK2) or scaffolds(for CDK2) was selected based on all-to-all Tanimoto similarity relative to the ChEMBL molecules. Additionally, since FEP predictions, and consequently LigUnity’s performance, are most reliable for modeling smaller structural perturbations, affinity estimation was restricted to analogs differing by eight or fewer heavy atoms.

Given that the lead compounds from the inhibitor series based on the scaffolds shown in Fig.2C and D, Compound 37 in Ref. [20] for TYK2 and Compound NU6102 in Ref. [21] for CDK2, are already highly potent, with single-digit nanomolar affinities (\(\Delta G \sim -12\)kcal/mol), we defined “good binders” as analogs within a 10-fold range (1.4 kcal/mol) of the respective lead compound. Using this criterion, TandemDB libraries yield substantially more good binders than ChEMBL22. For example, in the TYK2 case with a context radius of 3, TandemDB produced 593 good binders compared to 76 from ChEMBL22, corresponding to nearly an eight-fold increase. The distribution of these compounds in t-SNE space further suggests that many of the good binders occupy regions of chemical space that are not accessible through ChEMBL22.

The docked 3D poses of the top five molecules with the highest predicted binding affinities are shown in Fig.4and summarized in Table S1. The docked poses of the enumerated molecules were generated using a constrained embedding approach, with the crystal structure of NU6094 serving as the reference. Notably, two of these molecules correspond to previously reported compounds from the same lead optimization series [20]. Specifically, Compound 1 and Compound 5 identified in our study are Compounds 30 and 39 in Ref. [20]. As shown in Fig.4, these compounds establish novel interactions with the protein binding site residues that are likely the basis for their high predicted affinity.

In both cases, only analogs containing R-groups with eight or fewer heavy atoms were retained, resulting in filtered datasets comprising 2,301 molecules for ChEMBL22 and 18,789 molecules for TandemDB. Analogs that were predicted to have\(\Delta\)Gs less than −10.6 kcal/mol (within 10-fold of lead compound 36 in this series [20]) were classified as good binders and are shown in darker colors in both the distribution and t-SNE plots

Panels A-E illustrate 3D poses of the top five CReM-enumerated molecules on a TYK2 inhibitor scaffold, with their predicted affinities and novel interactions from the added R-groups highlighted. All compounds form hydrogen bonds with the active-site valine (VAL981), while Compound 3 additionally exhibits a hydrophobic interaction with a nearby tyrosine (TYR980)

We have introduced an optimized version of the CReM method, oCReM, that significantly reduces the size of the molecular fragment database and increases the speed of molecular generation, enabling the use of ultralarge fragment libraries on the scale of tens of billions of fragments. This optimization focuses on the architecture of the fragment database and the manner in which fragments are combined, while preserving all capabilities of the original CReM framework. We demonstrated how access to this expanded space afforded better small molecule compounds along multiple dimensions, especially that of protein-ligand potency as assessed by a machine learning model. oCReM extends the powerful CReM approach, allowing the incorporation of fragments from the rapidly growing chemical space of accessible molecules while retaining the power and flexibility of the original CReM approach to ideate novel molecules that are chemically valid and synthetically feasible.

title: Transformer-based molecular fragment prediction using SMILES and DeepSMILES representations in a fragment-based drug discovery pipeline
author: Aayush Kothari; Amish Gupta; Nisarg Shah; Thomas Reed; Anvita Nattuva; Rahima Nazirudeen; Harman Brah; Marx Akl
text:
Fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD) uses small molecular fragments as starting points for drug development, and machine-learning models that operate on molecular string representations are increasingly applied to fragment-related tasks. SMILES is the dominant such representation, but its paired ring closures and balanced parentheses introduce syntactic complexity that can affect model behavior. We present a controlled study of how molecular string representation influences transformer-based fragment recovery, using an FBDD-motivated label pipeline: reference fragments are derived from known drugs via RECAP fragmentation and docking-based ranking, and the model is scored on recovering them. We introduce DeepBERTa, a ChemBERTa-derived transformer pretrained on DeepSMILES, and evaluate it against a matched SMILES baseline under identical architecture, data splits, and optimization (approximately 34,000 drug–fragment pairs). DeepSMILES produces syntactically valid predictions more often than SMILES (54.2% vs. 43.5%) and a higher full test-set mean Tanimoto similarity (0.36 vs. 0.29). A per-sample selection between the two representations raises mean Tanimoto to 0.43, and a deployable variant that selects on model confidence rather than the reference recovers most of this gain. Among molecules where one representation strictly wins, DeepSMILES wins more often than SMILES (27.8% vs. 16.3% of test molecules). These results show that string representation meaningfully influences transformer fragment recovery and that representation-aware selection outperforms either representation alone.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of SMILES and DeepSMILES under matched conditions for transformer-based molecular fragment recovery. We introduce DeepBERTa, a ChemBERTa-derived transformer pretrained on DeepSMILES, and show that string representation measurably affects both syntactic validity and recovery similarity.

Fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD) is a paradigm in which small molecular fragments (typically < 300 Da) are used as starting points for drug development [1], as shown in Fig.1. Unlike high-throughput screening (HTS) of large drug-like molecules, FBDD involves screening a relatively small library of fragments to identify weak binders, which are then optimized or linked to yield lead compounds. This approach has gained traction for targets that challenge conventional screening approaches, as fragment hits can be grown or linked to produce high-affinity inhibitors, enabling more effective exploration of the chemical space [2]. Recent advances in artificial intelligence are accelerating FBDD by enablingin silicoprediction of fragment binding and automated design of fragment-derived candidates [3,4]. In particular, machine learning models that operate on chemical representations can help identify which substructures of a complex molecule are critical for activity, guiding medicinal chemists in fragmentation and elaboration [5].

Overview of the Fragment-Based Drug Discovery (FBDD) workflow in relation to the broader Drug Development pipeline

One of the most widely used representations for encoding molecular structures is SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System). This linear notation treats molecules as sequences of characters, while critically retaining essential stereochemical information [6]. SMILES is supported by numerous programming libraries and integrated into widely used molecular databases such as PubChem and ZINC [7,8]. This linear chemical language has allowed natural language processing (NLP) models to be applied to chemistry [9], where they have shown great promise for molecular property prediction and generation tasks [10,11,12].

One notable example is ChemBERTa, a RoBERTa-based transformer model explicitly fine-tuned for SMILES representations in chemical applications [9]. Transformer models are particularly suitable for processing such chemical representations due to their self-attention mechanism [13], which captures both local bonding patterns and long-range dependencies across molecular substructures, even when relevant atoms are separated by multiple tokens [11]. This combination enables transformers to learn robust and context-aware representations, which are vital for accuracy in molecular tasks [9].

Multiple state-of-the-art transformer models have been developed for both masked language modeling (MLM) and multitask regression (MTR) paradigms and have achieved strong performance on molecular benchmarks such as MoleculeNet [14,15]. In addition to ChemBERTa, other notable transformer models include MolBERT [16], SMILES-BERT [11], and MolGPT [17], each pretrained on increasingly larger dataset sizes. For example, MolBERT was trained on approximately 1.6 million compounds [16], SMILES-BERT on 18.7 million compounds [11], and the latest ChemBERTa-2 on 77 million compounds [14]. More recent efforts, such as MoLFormer [18] and ChemBERTa-3 [19], have scaled pretraining to more than a billion molecules, combining PubChem [7] and ZINC [8]. This progression reflects a broader trend in molecular deep learning: increasing pretraining size leads to better generalization and chemical understanding [20].

Despite these advances, the universal adoption of SMILES has significant drawbacks. Although SMILES-based methods have been more widely adopted and tested than other chemical representations, they still face challenges in downstream tasks [21]. Furthermore, the use of paired ring closure digits and nested brackets makes SMILES strings prone to parsing errors during molecule prediction paradigms [22]. SMILES strings, while representative, can be slow to process and consume valuable computational resources [23]. These challenges lead to lower performance during molecule generation tasks by increasing syntactic errors and meaningless outputs [23].

Our work builds on the ChemBERTa paradigm of MLM on SMILES, but uses DeepSMILES as an alternative encoding to investigate whether addressing SMILES syntax issues can lead to better outcomes. DeepSMILES, introduced by O’Boyle and Dalke in 2018 [24], uses a single ring closure number instead of a pair and replaces balanced parentheses with multiple closing parentheses to indicate branch length. For example, a branch of length N is closed by N right parentheses in a row, rather than matching each opening parenthesis individually. This postfix notation has been shown to increase validity during generation and enhance computational speed [24]. Although multiple studies have explored the benefits of DeepSMILES in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [24] and variational autoencoders (VAEs) [25], limited analysis has been done on the performance of DeepSMILES on transformers.

In this study, we examine how SMILES and DeepSMILES influence transformer-based fragment prediction under controlled conditions. We introduce DeepBERTa, a ChemBERTa-derived transformer trained on DeepSMILES, and evaluate it alongside a SMILES-based ChemBERTa model using identical architectures, data splits, and optimization. FBDD is used as a motivating setting, with fragment prediction defined as the recovery of docking-ranked retrosynthetic fragments derived from known molecules. We emphasize at the outset that this is a controlled representation-learning study using an FBDD-motivated label-generation pipeline; recovering a docking-ranked RECAP leaf fragment of a known molecule is a surrogate for fragment prioritization, not a deployable substitute for prospective fragment screening.

There is a rich history of computational methods that utilize molecular fragments, aligning with the principles of FBDD [26]. Traditional methods include algorithms like RECAP for fragmenting molecules [27] and fragment-linking strategies [28], while recent AI models incorporate fragments to improve generation. For instance, junction-tree neural networks construct molecules by joining fragment subgraphs, ensuring chemical validity by design [5]. In sequence-based models,MolMiner, an auto-regressive transformer, generates molecules as sequences of fragment building steps (“molecular stories”). By adding fragments one by one and applying chemical rules at each step, their approach guarantees that intermediate and final molecules are valid and enhances interpretability, since each generation step corresponds to a meaningful modification [29]. This trend of injecting domain knowledge (fragment libraries or chemical rules) into generative models addresses challenges of validity and transparency. Our work shares a similar spirit: rather than assembling molecules fragment by fragment, we focus on fragment prediction using a molecular language model.

SMILES is not the only representation for string-based molecule encoding. SELFIES (Self-Referencing Embedded Strings) is another representation that guarantees 100% syntactic validity—every SELFIES string maps to a valid molecule [22]. SELFIES employs a grammar of tokens that encode chemical valence rules, allowing even random token sequences to produce valid structures. However, the ChemBERTa team found that SELFIES did not yield significant improvements, and that training with SELFIES was substantially slower while offering minimal gain. This inefficiency is a result of SELFIES producing longer token sequences and requiring larger vocabularies, which increases training time and memory consumption [9].

DeepSMILES is a recent alternative to SMILES. It does not guarantee the validity of every string, but it simplifies the syntax to reduce parsing errors and increase processing speeds [24]. Designed to address the issue of paired symbols, DeepSMILES uses a number to indicate the ring size, reducing the complexity and length of the string. Because DeepSMILES was designed with machine-learning compatibility in mind, we selected DeepSMILES over SELFIES for this study to examine representation-level differences under transformer-based modeling. Indeed, prior studies have reported differences in behavior between DeepSMILES- and SMILES-based models in generative tasks [25,30,31]. Examples of how representative fragments are encoded in SMILES and DeepSMILES are shown in Table1.

We focus on DeepSMILES rather than SELFIES because SELFIES’ core advantage – guaranteed validity – does not address our task’s bottleneck. We score predictions by structural similarity to a specific reference fragment, where a valid but incorrect molecule is penalized as heavily as an invalid one, and our invalid predictions are mostly near-misses rather than syntactic noise. Recent work further suggests that enforcing validity can impair a chemical language model’s learning [32], and that the best representation is strongly task-dependent rather than universal [33]. DeepSMILES also preserves SMILES-like tokenization, keeping the comparison to our SMILES baseline controlled. A direct SELFIES baseline remains a natural extension.

Approximately 34,000 drug molecules were selected and fragmented, with fragments subsequently ranked using a docking-based scoring procedure against the mTOR protein kinase. We chose mTOR as the target for this study because of its pharmacological importance and the atypical scaffolds of its known inhibitors (e.g., the macrocyclic rapamycin), making it a challenging and illustrative test case. To generate the dataset, we first fragmented all drugs using the RECAP fragmentation algorithm [27]. We then assigned each fragment a numerical score according to a heuristic scoring function, and for every drug, selected the highest-scoring fragment and wrote the corresponding drug–fragment pair to the output training dataset. If all fragments received the lowest possible score, no pair was written for that drug. Our scoring function uses configurable weights and minimum/maximum bounds for various criteria, meant to reflect differing opinions regarding what constitutes a promising fragment candidate, as well as basic filtering. The scoring function evaluates each fragment according to the following rules:

Hard filtering (automatic rejection).A fragment is immediately assigned the lowest possible score if any of the following conditions are met:

It is “trivial,” defined as having fewer than 5 non-hydrogen atoms, or having fewer than 8 non-hydrogen atoms and containing only carbon and hydrogen.

Its molecular weight exceeds 300 Da, or its predicted logP exceeds 3 (Rule of Three) [34].

Its predicted logS (ESOL) [35] is less than\(-3\).

Score initialization.If the fragment passes all hard filters, it is assigned an initial score of 0.

Soft penalties and adjustments.

The Rule of Three suggests that good fragments contain no more than three hydrogen bond donors and no more than three hydrogen bond acceptors (Lipinski definitions) [34]. Therefore, the score is decreased by 1 for each donor or acceptor individually exceeding three.

The fragment’s synthetic accessibility (SAscore) [36] is multiplied by 0.5 and subtracted from the score, penalizing synthetically complex fragments.

Docking-based contribution.The fragment is docked against the target’s active site to estimate its binding affinity and ligand efficiency (binding affinity normalized by the number of non-hydrogen atoms). This contribution is added to the fragment’s score.

To ensure reproducibility and promote future development, we made all code and datasets publicly available. In this work, “fragment prediction” refers to generating a chemically meaningful fragment that resembles the reference fragment obtained from RECAP and docking. Our comparisons evaluate structural similarity, not fragment-contribution analysis or identification of which substructures drive binding affinity.

Our objective was to examine how SMILES and DeepSMILES representations influence transformer-based fragment prediction and to assess whether a simple hybrid selection strategy reveals complementary behavior between the two molecular encodings. To this end, we developed two parallel modeling pipelines—one based on ChemBERTa, trained on SMILES strings, and the other based on DeepBERTa, trained on DeepSMILES representations—as illustrated in Fig.2. Each pipeline begins with pretraining on the ZINC molecular database, followed by RECAP-based fragmentation of the mTOR dataset to generate paired drug–fragment data. The resulting fragment prediction models independently output candidate fragments, which are then compared and validated. In the final stage, both outputs are evaluated, and the one with the higher Tanimoto similarity is chosen.

Overview of the SMILES and DeepSMILES fragment prediction pipeline. The model is trained using both SMILES and DeepSMILES molecules and predicts fragments that are decoded back to SMILES for evaluation

For the SMILES-based model, we experimented with several publicly available ChemBERTa checkpoints and found that the zinc-base-100k-v1 model hosted on Hugging Face provided the best performance in terms of fragment prediction. Even though other models were trained on larger datasets (ChemBERTa-77M-MLM), the distribution of molecules in ZINC was similar to that in our target domain [8]. After training, the predicted fragments were assessed via Tanimoto similarity to the true fragments and processed further. Post-processing was outside the scope of this study, as our goal was to evaluate raw model predictions.

The DeepSMILES-based pipeline mirrored the SMILES pipeline, but required additional pretraining from scratch. Building on the insight that zinc-base-100k-v1 performed best for SMILES, we adopted the same 100k molecule ZINC subset for pretraining. Notably, all molecules were successfully converted to DeepSMILES [8]. Using an identical RoBERTa-base architecture and the open-source ChemBERTa training framework, we trained a DeepSMILES model (DeepBERTa) that closely matches the SMILES model architecture, preserving the same number of attention heads, transformer layers, vocabulary size, and tokenizer-related parameters.

Although the DeepSMILES-based model was trained using the ChemBERTa framework [9], certain differences arose when compared with the original ChemBERTa model. Due to the partial availability of original hyperparameters, we approximated certain values [37]. We list the key hyperparameters and their values in Table2. Nevertheless, our model—designed to imitateChemBERTa-zinc-base-100k-v1(henceforth referred to as DeepBERTa)—remains architecturally comparable, preserving the same number of attention heads, transformer layers, vocabulary size, and tokenizer-related parameters.

We fine-tuned the ChemBERTa and DeepBERTa models on a fragment prediction task, where each training example consisted of a drug molecule (as SMILES or DeepSMILES) as input and its corresponding fragment string as the target output.

To ensure that both SMILES and DeepSMILES models were trained and evaluated on the same data, we split the dataset, which consisted of approximately 34,000 molecules, into training, validation, and test sets. The same random train-val-test split (80–15–5) was used for both SMILES and DeepSMILES to ensure comparability. We verified that all examples were distinct and that no data leakage occurred between the training, validation, and test sets. The test set contained 1,689 examples. Fragment predictions were evaluated using Tanimoto similarity [38], a widely used metric that measures structural overlap between two molecules. We utilized Morgan fingerprints [39] with a radius of 2 and a length of 2048 bits.

We trained our models using the AdamW optimizer [40] with weight decay regularization. To curb early training instability, we applied a linear learning-rate scheduler with warmup [41] over 10% of the total training steps. Furthermore, because Tanimoto similarity is not directly optimized by the model’s cross-entropy (CE) loss, we incorporated a sequence penalty term that scales the CE loss based on the predicted sequence’s Tanimoto similarity, encouraging the model to produce outputs closer to the reference fragments.

To discourage the model from producing syntactically invalid predictions, we added a penalty that scales the per-batch loss according to the fraction of invalid predictions. For a batch size ofB, we compute

where\(v_n\)is either 0 or 1 if it passes or fails an RDKit [42] validity check. Then, we multiply it by our CE loss and regularization term to get the final loss function.

where\(\alpha _{\text {invalid}}\)represents the weight applied to\(f_{\text {invalid}}\)after being scaled by the batch size. When a specific batch contains a large number of invalid outputs, this loss is amplified. During backpropagation, this yields larger gradient updates, steering the model to reduce invalid outputs. Since any invalid output automatically yields a Tanimoto similarity of 0, we included L1 regularization with the CE loss before scaling, penalizing batches with high proportions of invalid predictions. Throughout the training process, we aimed for the model to learn to prioritize syntactically valid SMILES and DeepSMILES.

Hyperparameters, including maximum sequence length, batch size, learning rate, weight decay, and penalty coefficients, were tuned using Optuna [43] with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) sampler and median pruning. The best configuration was selected based on the mean Tanimoto similarity over 40 optimization trials.

Furthermore, we performed statistical comparisons of per-sample Tanimoto similarities across representations using a two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test [44].

ChatGPT 5.0 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 were used only for formatting support (e.g., LaTeX tables, figure captions, and minor wording adjustments). They were not used to generate, analyze, or interpret scientific content. All material was reviewed and verified by the authors.

For each test example, we computed the Tanimoto similarity between the predicted and reference fragment: if a predicted string was invalid (could not be parsed into a molecule), it was assigned a Tanimoto similarity of 0. We also calculated the average string similarity for the best-performing models using the Sequence Matcher Library [45].

Loss (left) and mean Tanimoto similarity (right) for the best-performing SMILES-based model

Loss (left) and mean Tanimoto similarity (right) for the best-performing DeepSMILES-based model

The loss and Tanimoto similarity plots for representative SMILES and DeepSMILES based models are shown in Figs.3and4, respectively. Differences in chemical validity were observed between the two representations:

DeepSMILES-based models yielded a higher fraction of syntactically valid predictions (54.2%) than SMILES-based models (43.5%). When considering only valid predictions, the two representations yield nearly identical performance (mean Tanimoto similarity of 0.67 for SMILES vs. 0.66 for DeepSMILES). However, this conditional metric does not capture the primary representation effect. The key difference lies in the frequency with which each representation produces a syntactically valid, scorable output. This is best reflected in the full test-set mean Tanimoto similarity (where invalid predictions are scored as 0), which we therefore adopt as the headline metric (Table3).

Validity here reflects a strict conditional-recovery task (reproducing a specific reference fragment), and is not comparable to the high validity reported for unconditioned de novo generators. We note that invalid predictions are predominantly near-misses rather than noise: their mean string similarity to the reference is\(\sim\)0.60 (vs.\(\sim\)0.83 for valid predictions), indicating the models usually capture most of the target and fail on a local syntactic error, the failure mode DeepSMILES is designed to reduce. The hybrid raises validity to 65.3% because a valid prediction from either representation can be selected.

When evaluated on the test set, the mean Tanimoto similarity differed between representations as well, with DeepSMILES-based models yielding a mean value of 0.36 and SMILES-based models yielding a mean value of 0.29. Examination of the similarity distribution showed that 31% of DeepSMILES predictions and 24% of SMILES predictions exceeded a Tanimoto similarity of 0.8, suggesting that high-similarity predictions are distributed differently across the two representations rather than uniformly improved across all samples.

Paired comparisons of per-sample Tanimoto (two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank; n = 1,689; zeros dropped) with rank-biserial effect sizes, exact p-values, bootstrap 95% CIs, and a Holm correction are given in Table4. A McNemar test on paired validity outcomes confirms DeepSMILES is valid significantly more often than SMILES: it is valid where SMILES fails in 369 cases versus the reverse in 188 (p = 1.4\(\times\)10–14).

SMILES predictions achieved a higher mean string similarity (0.71) than DeepSMILES (0.61), while the hybrid was intermediate (0.66). SMILES-based models preserve greater character-level similarity, whereas DeepSMILES-based models more often produce predictions that are structurally closer at the molecular level, despite lower string-level similarity; the two metrics capture different aspects of prediction quality.

As reported, drug-level overlap across train/test is low (1.6%), but fragment-level overlap is high (exact-fragment overlap 88.8%, Murcko-scaffold match 76.4%), reflecting the prevalence of frequently observed fragments. As direct evidence of the effect’s magnitude, we stratified test performance by reference-fragment frequency: on fragments that recur in the test set, mean Tanimoto is 0.41/0.48/0.58 (SMILES/DeepSMILES/hybrid), whereas on fragments appearing only once, it falls to 0.07/0.12/0.15; only 47% of reference fragments are distinct. Thus, the aggregate numbers are carried by frequently recurring fragments, and performance on rare (more plausibly novel) fragments is substantially weaker. The task, as constructed, primarily measures the model’s ability to contextualize known substructures rather than to generate entirely novel chemistry.

As shown in Table5, mean Tanimoto on seen fragments was 0.33, 0.40, and 0.48 for SMILES, DeepSMILES, and the hybrid model, respectively, whereas performance on novel fragments dropped substantially to 0.04, 0.05, and 0.08. The model, therefore, largely recalls training fragments and, as currently trained, does not generalize to novel chemistry. Crucially, the relative ordering (DeepSMILES> SMILES, hybrid> both) is preserved in both strata: the overlap inflates absolute similarity for both representations approximately equally and does not overturn the representation comparison that is this paper’s central claim.

Selecting the higher-Tanimoto prediction per molecule (oracle hybrid) raised the mean Tanimoto to 0.43, with 39% of selected predictions exceeding 0.8. Among decisive molecules, DeepSMILES wins more often than SMILES (469 vs. 275; Table6), and the average gain when each representation wins is comparable, so the two are genuinely complementary rather than one contributing rare-but-large gains.

The oracle hybrid requires the reference fragment and is therefore an upper bound. We tested a deployable selector that, for each molecule, chooses the representation with the lower per-prediction loss (the model’s own confidence, logged at inference; no reference used). This recovers most of the oracle gain (Table7): mean Tanimoto 0.427 vs. the oracle’s 0.432, i.e., 93% of the gain over the best single representation, agreeing with the oracle on 94% of molecules where the representations differ. The improvement over the best single model is significant (Wilcoxon Z = − 17.738, p< 10–70; rank-biserial + 0.95), and the residual gap to the oracle is small but significant (Z = − 5.841, p = 5×10−9), indicating headroom for a better selector. The effect is robust to confidence normalization across the two tokenizers: length-normalized loss recovers 92.6% of the gain (94% agreement), per-model percentile-rank 86.3% (93%), and even a conservative per-model z-score 64.5%. A decoding-time ensemble that merges token probabilities from both representations is a natural next step.

Furthermore, we examined two representative examples from the test set. For each parent molecule, we compared fragments generated by the SMILES and DeepSMILES models across multiple analytical dimensions: structural similarity to reference fragments, chemical space context via nearest-neighbor analysis, and scaffold preservation assessment (Supporting Information).

Top panel (Case 1): parent molecule with reference fragment highlighted, perfect SMILES prediction, and DeepSMILES alternative showing minor structural perturbations. Bottom panel (Case 2): parent molecule with sulfonamide–nitrile pharmacophore highlighted, incomplete SMILES prediction missing key groups, and corrected DeepSMILES prediction restoring critical binding elements

In the first scenario, Fig.5, the parent molecule contains a substituted phenyl–alcohol scaffold with clear fragmentation points. While the DeepSMILES component of the framework produces a structurally similar analogue (Tanimoto similarity = 0.62) with minor differences in the substitution pattern, the hybrid selection logic identifies the SMILES-based output, which achieves an exact recovery of the reference fragment (Tanimoto similarity = 1.00). This case highlights the framework’s ability to preserve exact matches by leveraging the syntactic precision of standard SMILES when appropriate.

Here, the framework compensates for the limitations of the SMILES-based model, which retains the aromatic ring and trifluoromethyl group but omits both the sulfonyl and nitrile groups present in the reference fragment (Tanimoto similarity = 0.22). The hybrid system utilizes the DeepSMILES component, which successfully recovers the nitrile group while preserving the aromatic core and trifluoromethyl substituent, improving structural relevance (Tanimoto similarity = 0.46). Although neither model fully captures the sulfonyl group, the DeepSMILES prediction restores a greater proportion of the reference pharmacophore. By selecting the DeepSMILES prediction, the framework preserves key pharmacophoric elements that would otherwise be lost in a single-representation system.

Our experiments underscored the importance of pretraining on a sufficiently large and relevant dataset [9,20,46]. DeepBERTa models without robust pretraining (e.g., starting from only 1k molecules) failed to learn the fragment task, essentially producing random fragments. Once we scaled pretraining to hundreds of thousands of molecules, performance markedly improved [11]. We suspect that both the choice of molecules—fragment-oriented or not—and the pretraining corpus can play a significant role in overall model performance [9,11,47].

In addition, the size of the fine-tuning dataset remains a fundamental limiting factor. With only 34,000 molecule–fragment pairs (all for the same target, mTOR), the model had a limited basis for generalization [5]. In a practical setting, one would ideally experiment on multiple targets to assess the generality of the results. Our focus on mTOR, while a useful case study, means the model may exploit idiosyncrasies of that particular protein. Notably, mTOR’s primary inhibitor, rapamycin, is a large, non-traditional drug molecule. Testing the method on more “drug-like” targets in the future would help validate its generality.

In both SMILES and DeepSMILES, a key drawback is that a molecule can often be broken into multiple meaningful fragments, and the model has no way of knowing which fragment was optimal. Our choice of metric, Tanimoto similarity, was appropriate in most cases, but exceptions arose when high-performing fragments were structurally dissimilar to the top-ranked reference. It is possible that a model predicted the second- or third-best fragment, but because our methodology had no way of identifying this, the prediction was penalized as if it were irrelevant. In future work, we plan to compare predictions with the second- and third-best fragments to mitigate this issue.

We acknowledge that Tanimoto similarity is a strict metric that penalizes any mismatch. However, this strictness is necessary for establishing a baseline [30]. In future work, we might consider alternative metrics or manual evaluation to better assess the usefulness of the predictions. For instance, a prediction that recovers the correct scaffold but is missing a substituent is arguably a success in terms of identifying the critical part of the molecule, even if the Tanimoto score is not high [48].

Beyond choosing a robust notation, there are other ways to enforce validity and robustness in fragment prediction. One approach is to use an encoder–decoder model that generates the fragment string from the molecule (rather than our single-model MLM approach) [10,49,50]. Another approach is constrained decoding: for SMILES, one can incorporate grammar rules during generation to prevent invalid outputs [51].

In terms of generative modeling, one could envision a fragment prediction approach that is more akin to a retrieval or classification problem: selecting the most likely fragment from a predefined library [52]. This would guarantee valid outputs (since all library fragments are valid) and could be easier for a model to learn (multi-class classification). However, it limits predictions to known fragments and cannot suggest novel ones [53]. Our free-form generation allows novel fragment suggestions, which could be valuable in discovering new scaffolds, albeit with the occasional risk of structurally implausible predictions [54].

This work opens several avenues for future improvement. First, expanding the training data—both pretraining and fine-tuning—would likely boost performance for both SMILES and DeepSMILES. A model like DeepBERTa, trained on tens of millions of molecules, is expected to capture a broader range of chemical patterns, which may further improve fragment prediction behavior. On the fine-tuning side, incorporating fragment data for multiple targets (not just mTOR) or utilizing semi-supervised approaches (e.g., treating any high-scoring fragment from docking as a training example) could be beneficial.

Moreover, retrosynthetic fragmentation, which pairs the entire molecule with its most anchoring fragment (without the full ligand context), can introduce additional hydrogen bonds or bare polar groups that increase binding affinity. These artifacts can amplify biases in the results. Additionally, separating the fragment can modify the orientation or binding pocket engagement, since separated fragments may attach to different sites.

We recognize that retrosynthetic fragmentation can occasionally yield fragments with additional hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, potentially inflating their docking scores and, by extension, the apparent predictive performance of models trained on such data. However, this inflation would apply uniformly to all models because both SMILES- and DeepSMILES-based pipelines were trained and evaluated on the exact same fragment set. As a result, while the absolute Tanimoto similarities reported here may be slightly optimistic, the relative differences between representations—and the consistent improvement observed in the hybrid approach—remain valid indicators of model capability. A sensitivity analysis confirms that fragment selection is robust to the weight of the docking term and is not systematically biased toward polar or charged fragments. As is common in retrosynthetic fragmentation over finite drug datasets, the same fragment scaffolds frequently recur across structurally distinct drugs, resulting in overlap between the fragment vocabularies of the training and test splits [55].

This affects absolute Tanimoto values across both representations. The Tanimoto scores reported reflect the model’s ability and do not distort the relative comparison between SMILES and DeepSMILES. Overall, the conclusions from this study are more relevant from a machine-learning and representation-learning perspective, whereas their direct biophysical interpretability is limited by the assumptions of the fragmentation algorithm.

Future work incorporating interaction-preserving fragmentation will allow us to reassess absolute performance under more physically rigorous conditions and techniques. One notable example of such an approach is MedChemFrag [56], one of the few methods designed specifically for interaction-preserving fragmentation, which performs ligand fragmentation explicitly in the context of a protein–ligand complex, thereby preserving key binding interactions. In addition, Receptor-based Reverse Fragment-Based Drug Design (R-FBDD) [57] or Fragment Molecular Orbital methods (specifically used for protein–ligand complexes) [58] can reduce predispositions by beginning with the ligand docked to the receptor and properly assessing the separated fragment’s energy with respect to the whole ligand–receptor complex.

We present a study of transformer-based fragment prediction comparing SMILES and DeepSMILES representations and examining their complementarity through a per-sample hybrid selection analysis. We introduce DeepBERTa, a ChemBERTa-like transformer pretrained on DeepSMILES, and evaluate it alongside a SMILES-based counterpart under matched experimental conditions. Our results show that representation choice meaningfully influences prediction behavior: DeepSMILES yields higher syntactic validity and higher aggregate similarity when invalid outputs are included, whereas SMILES more closely preserves character-level similarity to reference fragments. Apost hocselection of the higher-similarity prediction across representations increases the aggregate similarity beyond either representation alone, indicating complementary strengths across different molecular contexts. Taken together, these findings motivate further investigation of representation-aware modeling and selection strategies in cheminformatics.

All training, evaluation, and preprocessing code, as well as pretrained models, are available athttps://github.com/AayushK-othari/FBDD_ChemBERTaand on Hugging Face under the usernameaakothari. The datasets used for model training and validation are derived from publicly available ZINC20 resources. Selection and preprocessing scripts are included in the repository to ensure reproducibility.

title: How well can off-the-shelf LLMs elucidate molecular structures from mass spectra using chain-of-thought reasoning?
author: Yufeng Wang; Lu Wei; Lin Liu; Hao Xu; Haibin Ling
text:
Mass spectrometry (MS) is a powerful analytical technique for identifying small molecules, yet determining complete molecular structures directly from tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) remains a long-standing challenge due to complex fragmentation patterns and the vast diversity of chemical space. Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has shown promise for reasoning-intensive scientific tasks, but their capability for chemical interpretation is still unclear. We present a zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) benchmark for evaluating how well off-the-shelf general-purpose LLMs can infer molecular structure from text-serialized MS/MS peak lists and a known molecular formula, without fine-tuning, retrieval, external chemistry tools, or constrained search. Rather than proposing a new spectrum-trained model, our goal is diagnostic: to isolate what the evaluated off-the-shelf LLMs can and cannot do in a direct MS/MS-to-SMILES generation setting when only textualized spectral evidence and prompting are available. This distinction is important because our benchmark targets a deliberately constrained regime: direct structure generation from text-formatted spectral evidence alone, rather than multimodal reasoning with spectral images, candidate reranking over structures generated by specialized chemistry systems, or knowledge and search-augmented LLM workflows. We formalize expert chemists’ reasoning steps (such as double bond equivalent (DBE) analysis, neutral loss identification, and fragment assembly) into structured prompts and assess multiple state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama-3 series) using the MassSpecGym dataset. Our evaluation across metrics of SMILES validity, formula consistency, and structural similarity reveals that while LLMs can produce syntactically valid and partially plausible structures, they fail to achieve chemical accuracy or link reasoning to correct molecular predictions. These findings highlight both the interpretive potential and the current limitations of LLM-based reasoning for molecular elucidation, providing a foundation for future work that combines domain knowledge and reinforcement learning to achieve chemically grounded AI reasoning.

Scientific contribution

We introduce a zero-shot chain-of-thought benchmark for direct MS/MS-to-SMILES prediction with off-the-shelf general-purpose LLMs, providing a controlled test of text-only, no-tools molecular structure elucidation. In contrast to prior approaches based on spectrum-trained models, multimodal reasoning, or tool-augmented candidate pipelines, our study isolates the capabilities and limitations of prompting alone. We show that fluent chain-of-thought reasoning does not translate into chemically grounded structure recovery, establishing a reproducible baseline and a clear target for future method development.

Mass spectrometry (MS) is a fundamental analytical technique for small-molecule identification, widely used in natural product discovery, metabolomics, and drug development [1]. Its high sensitivity, fast throughput, and ability to resolve complex mixtures make it suitable for analyzing the chemical composition of biological and environmental samples [2]. By providing accurate mass measurements and fragmentation patterns through tandem MS (MS/MS), this technique enables determination of molecular formulas and substructures, supporting both the identification of known compounds and the partial characterization of unknowns [3]. Despite these advantages, determining complete molecular structures from MS data alone remains a long-standing challenge due to the ambiguity of fragmentation spectra and the vast diversity of chemical space [4]. Consequently, expert chemists rely on domain knowledge, careful interpretation of fragment ions, and iterative hypothesis refinement to infer plausible molecular structures.

Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) methods, especially deep generative and discriminative models, have been increasingly explored for molecular structure elucidation from mass spectrometry data [5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12]. Early systems such as SIRIUS formulate identification as a fragmentation-tree optimization problem, using Bayesian scoring over putative fragment trees to infer molecular formulas and rank candidate structures from spectral libraries [5]. MSNovelist combines spectrum-derived molecular fingerprints with an encoder-decoder network that generates SMILES (Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System) strings de novo from MS/MS data, enabling open-set structure prediction beyond database lookup [6,13,14]. MassGenie trains a large Transformer (around 400 M parameters) directly on collections of simulated spectra and SMILES strings to learn mappings from fragmentation patterns to structures [7]. End-to-end encoder-decoder models such as Spec2Mol [8,15] similarly process spectra with a neural encoder and decode candidate SMILES sequences. These approaches perform well when spectra contain rich fragmentation information, but their performance often degrades on experimental MS/MS data due to weak generalization to unseen chemotypes and the lack of explicit domain constraints (e.g., atom valency or molecular formulas). In addition, sequence-based models are sensitive to peak order, can produce inconsistent results under minor spectral perturbations, and are generally difficult to interpret because they output structures without exposing intermediate chemical reasoning or substructure relationships. To overcome some of these limitations, more recent work has integrated domain-specific priors and structured chemical representations into spectrum-to-structure models [9,10,11,16,17,18]. MIST [9] proposes a spectrum-to-fingerprint Transformer that leverages peak annotations, neutral losses, and a progressive fingerprint decoding process, improving interpretability and downstream reconstruction. DiffMS [10] extends this idea with a formula-constrained graph diffusion model that generates molecular graphs directly from spectra while respecting atom-composition constraints; the diffusion mechanism also supports permutation invariance in both molecular and spectral representations. MADGEN [11] introduces a two-stage approach that first retrieves a scaffold via contrastive learning and then generates full structures around it, narrowing the search space and improving robustness for sparse spectra. While these methods emphasize structural constraints and inductive biases, they remain primarily model-centric: they focus on learning accurate mappings from spectra to structures but still provide limited visibility into the reasoning process by which spectral evidence is translated into molecular hypotheses.

In parallel, LLMs have demonstrated strong general-purpose reasoning capabilities. CoT prompting, where a model is instructed to generate intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at a final answer, has been shown to substantially improve performance on tasks that require multi-step logic, arithmetic, and symbolic manipulation [19]. Beyond pure prompting, reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful tool for sharpening these reasoning abilities. InstructGPT and related reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) systems fine-tune LLMs with human preference feedback, yielding models that follow instructions more faithfully, provide more truthful explanations, and better align their step-by-step reasoning with user intent [20,21,22,23,24]. ReAct-style agents interleave natural-language reasoning with external actions, generating thought-action trajectories that query tools or environments and update plans based on observations [25], and more recent work uses RL to improve multi-step reasoning by exposing models to progressively more challenging reasoning tasks [26,27]. Together, these CoT and RL advances move beyond static pattern matching toward models that can iteratively plan, reflect, and adapt, suggesting a promising yet largely unexplored direction for applying LLM-style reasoning to physically grounded scientific domains such as mass spectral structure elucidation.

Interpreting MS/MS spectra to determine molecular structures is inherently a multi-step analytical process: chemists start from the precursor formula and DBE, identify key peaks and neutral losses, group fragments into substructures, and finally assemble a globally consistent molecular graph [28,29]. These characteristics make the MS-to-molecule problem naturally suitable for CoT-style reasoning. However, it is not yet clear to what extent general-purpose LLMs can perform such structured analysis or whether their explanations meaningfully reflect underlying chemical constraints [30]. An overview of our CoT guided MS-to-SMILES benchmarking framework is shown in Figure2.

A key scope clarification is necessary. In this work, we donotevaluate multimodal LLMs operating over raw spectral images, tool-augmented agents that call external chemistry software, retrieval-based systems, or fine-tuned spectrum-specialized models. Instead, we study a narrower but important diagnostic setting: off-the-shelf general-purpose LLMs, prompted in a strictly zero-shot manner, given text-formatted MS/MS peak lists and a molecular formula, and asked to directly generate a SMILES string without external tools or task-specific adaptation. We intentionally isolate this setting to test whether fluent CoT reasoning alone is sufficient for chemically grounded mass spectral structure elucidation.

Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce a zero-shot CoT benchmark for direct MS/MS-to-SMILES prediction using off-the-shelf general-purpose LLMs, where the model receives text-serialized peak lists and a molecular formula and must generate a structure without any model updates or external chemistry tools.

We provide a diagnostic evaluation protocol that measures not only structural correctness and similarity, but also the consistency between the model’s intermediate CoT reasoning and its final predicted structure.

We show that, in this constrained no-tools setting, the four evaluated off-the-shelf LLMs can produce fluent and expert-like chemical explanations while failing to recover chemically correct structures, revealing a substantial gap between linguistic plausibility and mechanistic grounding.

Classical and learning-based molecular structure elucidation. Molecular structure elucidation has a long history in computational chemistry, including computer-assisted structure elucidation (CASE) systems and spectrum-aware pipelines that combine expert rules, database matching, and specialized predictive models. More recent machine learning methods have approached spectrum-to-structure prediction directly, including mass-spectrometry-specific generative and retrieval-oriented systems. These methods are typically designed around spectral inductive bias, chemistry-aware constraints, or task-specific training, which distinguishes them from the off-the-shelf prompted LLM setting studied here.

LLMs and benchmark-style evaluation for structure elucidation. Recent work has begun to examine structure elucidation as a challenging reasoning problem for LLMs. Most closely related isMolPuzzle[31], which formulates molecular structure elucidation as a multimodal puzzle-solving benchmark involving molecular formulas together with IR, mass,\(^{1}\)H-NMR, and\(^{13}\)C-NMR evidence. MolPuzzle decomposes the task into molecule understanding, spectrum interpretation, and molecule construction, and shows that even strong LLMs remain far below human performance, with the best exact-match rate reported as only 1.4%. These results are highly relevant to our study because they likewise suggest that structure elucidation remains difficult for general-purpose LLMs, especially in the stages requiring deep spectral interpretation and consistent molecule construction. However, our setting is different: instead of a multimodal puzzle benchmark with multiple spectroscopy modalities and staged sub-tasks, we focus specifically on direct MS/MS-to-SMILES generation from text-serialized peak lists and a known formula, and we explicitly analyze the consistency between CoT traces and final structural predictions.

LLMs for spectroscopy-based chemical reasoning benchmarks. Recent work has also shown that LLM performance in chemistry can be substantially stronger on certain structured spectroscopy reasoning tasks than on full direct structure reconstruction. For example,NMR-Challenge for LLMs[32] evaluates multiple LLMs on text-formatted NMR structure-determination problems derived from educational and experimental settings, and reports that newer reasoning-focused models can outperform undergraduate students on that benchmark. Importantly, this study emphasizes reasoning over raw-spectrum perception by converting spectral information into a textual representation, and shows that model performance depends strongly on the problem format and available formula information. We view these findings as complementary rather than contradictory to ours: they suggest that LLMs can succeed on some spectroscopy-centered reasoning tasks, while our results show thatdirectzero-shot MS/MS-to-SMILES generation without external chemistry scaffolding remains substantially more difficult.

LLMs as components in tool-augmented elucidation workflows. Another important line of work uses LLMs not as standalone inverse solvers, but as reasoning modules embedded inside broader chemistry pipelines. For example, Priessner et al. [33] integrate reasoning-capable LLMs into a candidate-based NMR structure elucidation workflow in which specialized systems first generate molecular candidates, spectral-analysis modules quantitatively compare those candidates to experimental data, and the LLM then performs evidence-aware analysis and reranking. In that setting, the LLM improves top-ranked identification substantially, demonstrating that language models can add value when placed in the role of interpretable evaluator over candidate sets. This is complementary to our benchmark rather than contradictory to it: in contrast to their workflow, our models receive no pre-generated candidate structures, no dedicated spectral matching module, and no chemistry-specific evaluation tool during inference.

Knowledge- and search-augmented LLM reasoning for elucidation. A third line of work improves LLM performance by adding explicit domain scaffolding during inference. The recent K-MSE framework [34] augments a base LLM with a molecular substructure knowledge base, a molecule-spectrum scoring model, and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-style reasoning and self-refinement. On the MolPuzzle benchmark, this knowledge-enhanced search procedure substantially improves over the underlying base models. Importantly, this paper attributes the weakness of plain LLMs to limited chemistry-specific knowledge and poor self-evaluation, which aligns closely with our observation that free-form CoT can appear chemically plausible while remaining weakly grounded in the spectrum. K-MSE therefore does not invalidate our negative result; instead, it suggests a concrete path forward: meaningful gains may require retrieval, explicit search, and chemistry-specific reward signals rather than prompting alone.

Position of this work. Relative to these prior studies, our paper addresses a deliberately narrower diagnostic question: How well do off-the-shelf general-purpose LLMs perform in a zero-shot, text-only, no-tools setting when asked to directly infer a molecular structure from MS/MS evidence and a known formula? This setting differs from multimodal structure-elucidation benchmarks, candidate-reranking systems, and knowledge/search-augmented reasoning frameworks. Our contribution is therefore not a claim that LLMs have never been studied for structure elucidation, but rather a targeted evaluation showing that, in the absence of chemistry-specific scaffolding, fluent CoT reasoning does not yield chemically reliable direct MS/MS-to-SMILES prediction.

All experiments in this study use the MassSpecGym benchmark [35], a large-scale, well-established resource published at NeurIPS 2024 (Track on Datasets and Benchmarks). MassSpecGym is the largest publicly available collection of quality-controlled, expert-validated MS/MS spectra paired with confirmed molecular structures, comprising 231,104 spectra representing approximately 29,000 unique molecules. Critically, the benchmark annotations were subjected to a rigorous, multi-stage quality-control pipeline: (1) a SIRIUS-based formula-decomposition filter removing spectra where less than 50% of total intensity could be explained by chemically valid fragment sub-formulae; (2) cross-validation against the commercial NIST20 spectral library, removing spectra with no shared peaks or cosine similarity below 0.2; and (3) pairwise intra-dataset outlier removal [35]. A manual audit confirmed that discarded entries were “at least suspicious, with many clearly being wrongly annotated.” The resulting dataset draws from the established public repositories GNPS, MoNA, and MassBank, as well as in-house authentic-standard measurements. Each data instance consists of: (i) a tandem MS/MS spectrum given as a list of (m/z, relative-intensity) peak pairs acquired in positive-ion mode on Orbitrap-type instruments at a range of collision energies; (ii) the molecular formula of the precursor compound, provided as an oracle input (i.e., assumed known); (iii) the canonical SMILES string of the ground-truth structure, used as the evaluation target; and (iv) acquisition metadata including instrument type, adduct, and collision energy. The molecular formula is not predicted by the models; it is given as part of the input, reflecting a common real-world scenario in metabolomics where the formula is determined from the high-resolution precursor mass before structural elucidation.

The number of peaksNvaries by spectrum; in practice, each instance contains a variable-length peak list from positive-ion MS/MS acquisition, together with instrument metadata such as Orbitrap, adduct type, and collision energy when available. Each spectrum is paired with exactly one ground-truth molecular formula (provided as oracle input; the model is not asked to search over multiple candidate formulas) and one canonical SMILES. MassSpecGym does not expose a per-pair confidence score or provenance rationale for each individual spectrum-structure link beyond the source-database curation pipeline; our benchmark therefore treats the released annotations as ground truth, following prior work [10,35]. The train/test split used in this work follows the protocol of DiffMS [10], enforcing a minimum common edge subgraph (MCES) dissimilarity of\(\ge 10\)between all training and test molecules to prevent graph-level overlap and ensure generalization to structurally novel chemotypes.
