The filtered POI–E3 ligase conformational ensembles provided initial docking samples with a wide range of physically realistic binding orientations ready for downstream analyses of POI–E3 conformational clustering.

Following attachment atom distance-based filtering, the remaining POI–E3 ligase conformational ensembles were clustered to identify distinct and representative protein–protein geometries. Clustering was performed using a Cα RMSD threshold of 7.5 Å, whereby conformations with RMSD ≤ 7.5 Å were considered structurally similar and grouped into the same cluster, while conformations differing by more than 7.5 Å were treated as distinct binding modes.

From each cluster, a single representative conformation was selected based on the MOE S docking score, with more negative values indicating more favorable protein–protein interactions. This procedure ensured that the retained representatives captured both geometric diversity and energetically favorable binding modes. As shown in Figure3B, clustering resulted in a dramatic reduction of the conformational space for all modeled systems. Whereas the initial docking generated hundreds to thousands of POI–E3 ligase poses per system, clustering condensed these ensembles into a small number of representative conformations. Number of clusters ranged between 3 and 13 per system, with PTPN2-CRBN displaying the highest number, reflecting a comparatively diverse set of physically plausible POI–E3 orientations. These representative states captured the dominant binding geometries of each system and formed the basis for subsequent evaluation of ubiquitination competence.

The representative POI–E3 ligase conformations identified through clustering were subsequently evaluated for ubiquitination accessibility to determine which geometries are compatible with productive ubiquitin transfer. For each system, the representative POI–E3 ligase conformations were aligned onto their corresponding CRL4CRBN or CRL2VHL ubiquitination assemblies by superposition of the shared E3 ligase subunits, thereby positioning the POI relative to the full ubiquitination machinery in a biologically relevant architecture.

As summarized in Fig.3C, this analysis revealed ubiquitination competence across several representative conformations within the same POI–E3 ligase system. First, representative poses in which the POI sterically clashed with components of the ubiquitination machinery were excluded, retaining only geometrically feasible (non-clashing) POI–E3 ligase conformations. The number of feasible conformations varied across systems, ranging from as few as one to three (e.g., BRD4BD2-VHL, KRas-VHL and WEE1-VHL systems) to eight to ten in systems including PTPN2-CRBN, SMARCA2-VHL, SMARCA4-VHL and BRD4BD1-VHL. Among the retained feasible assemblies, multiple distinct conformations satisfied the productive ubiquitin transfer geometries by the presence of at least one solvent-exposed POI lysine residue within 50 Å of the catalytic E2 residue Cys111. Conversely, a small subset of non-clashing POI–E3 ligase conformations displayed POI lysine residues positioned beyond the 50 Å distance threshold from the E2 Cys111, rendering them non-ubiquitinable despite satisfying steric and linker-length criteria. Most systems retained multiple ubiquitinable conformations, with PTPN2-CRBN and BRD4BD1-VHL exhibiting the highest number (six conformations each), indicating that productive ubiquitination can arise from multiple distinct POI–E3 ligase geometries. In contrast, other systems exhibited a more limited number of ubiquitinable conformations or, in some cases, only a single productive geometry as in the cases of BRD4BD2-VHL, KRas-VHL and WEE1-VHL systems.

All geometrically feasible cluster representatives identified through static ubiquitination assessment, irrespective of the lysine positions, were subsequently advanced to 100 ns MD simulations. These simulations were used to validate the sustained attachment-atom connectivity and ubiquitination accessibility over time, ensuring that only models maintaining productive conformations were retained for PROTAC ternary complex design.

The representative POI–E3 ligase conformations identified through the conformational clustering and ubiquitinability assessment were subsequently advanced to MD simulations to evaluate their dynamics and sustained productivity. All feasible (non-clashing) conformations were simulated, regardless of the observed static ubiquitination accessibility, to capture potential conformational rearrangements that could affect lysine positions. For each conformation, 100 ns MD simulations were performed in triplicate using different random seeds to ensure robustness and reproducibility. Trajectory analyses primarily focused on Cα RMSD, warhead attachment atom distances and ubiquitination competence of solvent-exposed POI lysine residues. As summarized in Fig.4A, the majority of POI–E3 ligase conformations exhibited RMSD distributions typically centered between 2 and 6 Å over the 100 ns simulations. These values reflect moderate flexibility while preserving the overall protein–protein geometries required for productive ternary complex formation. Two notable exceptions were observed. The BCL2-VHL–M4 model exhibited elevated RMSD values of approximately 8 Å and stabilized in a conformation different from the initial static structure. Similarly, the BRD4BD1-VHL–M8 complex showed pronounced RMSD fluctuations, reaching values above 10 Å, and underwent substantial conformational rearrangements.

Ubiquitination accessibility was then assessed by monitoring the distances between solvent-exposed POI lysine residues and the E2 catalytic Cys111. All non-clashing conformations in which POI lysine residues were outside the ubiquitinability range (>50 Å from E2 Cys111) remained highly stable; consequently, no conformational rearrangements were observed to reposition these lysine residues to be within the ubiquitination range. These models were considered non-productive and were excluded from further analysis. However, with the exception of BRD4BD1-VHL–M8, all other models retained the same solvent-exposed lysine residue observed in the static assessment within 50 Å of Cys111 for a substantial fraction of the simulation time and were therefore considered productive. Visual inspection of the BRD4BD1-VHL–M8 trajectories revealed significant conformational rearrangements that led to steric clashes between BRD4BD1 and components of the ubiquitination machinery leading to its classification as non-feasible. The sustained ubiquitinability of productive geometries is further illustrated in the ubiquitination accessibility heatmap (Fig.4B), which summarizes the percentage of simulation time during which individual solvent-exposed POI lysine residues remained within 50 Å of E2 Cys111. Across systems, productive models typically maintained POI lysine residues within this distance threshold for a large fraction of the trajectory, often exceeding 50-75% of the simulation time.

Finally, the ability of the productive modeled conformations to recover experimentally observed POI–E3 ligase geometries of ternary complexes was evaluated by computing Cα RMSD values relative to the experimental structures (Fig.4C). In all systems except KRas-VHL, at least one modeled productive conformation exhibited close structural similarity with the experimental reference, typically within 1-4 Å RMSD. In the case of KRas-VHL system, the only identified productive model (M4) showed Cα RMSD of 12.00 and 11.70 Å relative to the experimental conformations of PDB IDs 8QW6 and 8QW7, respectively. The recovery of 33 out of the 34 experimental structures confirms that the computational workflow not only captures physically feasible and ubiquitination-competent assemblies but also ensures sampling of experimentally identified POI–E3 ligase conformations. However, additional sampling may identify further ubiquitination-competent conformations and potentially improve structural recovery, particularly for the KRas-VHL system. Detailed modeling analyses of each individual system are provided in the Supplementary Information for in-depth inspection of Cα RMSD behavior, warhead attachment atom distances and ubiquitination accessibility trends across all productive models (Figures S9-S38 and Tables S3-S16, Supplement).

On the basis of the robustness and consistency of this workflow, it was subsequently applied to model WEE1-CRBN and PKMYT1-CRBN conformations. The aim of this step was to rationalize the activity of published and in-house WEE1- and PKMYT1-targeting CRBN-mediated PROTACs, to inform the future design of degraders targeting these kinases and to assess the generalizability of our computational workflow for modeling POI–E3 ligase conformations in the absence of experimental structural data.

Following validation of our computational workflow on experimentally characterized structures, the same pipeline was applied to model productive protein–protein conformations for the WEE1- and PKMYT1-CRBN systems. These two kinases were selected as case studies since corresponding experimental ternary complex structures are unavailable. For the WEE1 system, WEE1 bound to AZD1775 (PDB ID: 5V5Y) was docked to CRBN prepared from PDB ID 8OIZ while for the PKMYT1 system, PKMYT1 in complex with compound 41 (PDB ID: 8D6F) was docked to CRBN derived from PDB ID 8RQA. The 2D structures of AZD1775 and compound 41 are depicted in Fig.5A and B. This docking step yielded 701 WEE1-CRBN and 472 PKMYT1-CRBN initial protein–protein conformations, respectively (Fig.5C–F). The resulting conformational ensembles were filtered using the same criteria established earlier. Docking poses exceeding the 15 Å attachment atom distance limit were excluded, and the remaining conformations with feasible warhead connectivity were clustered using the 7.5 Å Cα RMSD threshold to identify structurally distinct protein–protein arrangements.

Attachment atoms were selected based on their solvent-exposed positions, allowing appropriate connectivity for PROTAC design. For CRBN, the selected attachment atom was the C15 atom of the phenyl ring of the CRBN ligand (pomalidomide or lenalidomide). The attachment atom for the WEE1 ligand AZD1775 was defined as the N2 atom of the piperazine ring, whereas two potential attachment atoms were considered for the PKMYT1 ligand (compound 41), namely the N23 atom of the amide group and the C8 atom of the phenyl ring. This filtering step yielded 156 WEE1-CRBN and 78 PKMYT1-CRBN geometrically feasible conformations suitable for linker design, corresponding to approximately 22% and 16.5% of the initially generated ensembles, respectively. The PKMYT1-CRBN count was combined for filtering based on both attachment atom pairs. Subsequent clustering of these filtered ensembles resulted in nine WEE1-CRBN and eight PKMYT1-CRBN distinct representative conformations. The clustering statistics and protein–protein docking energy scores of the representative WEE1-CRBN and PKMYT1-CRBN conformations are summarized in Tables2and3, respectively. For the WEE1-CRBN system, cluster 9 was the most populated, comprising 71 members and exhibited average pairwise Cα RMSD value of 5.35 Å. For the PKMYT1-CRBN system, clustering was performed independently for the two selected attachment atom pairs (N23–C15 and C8–C15). Filtering based on the N23–C15 distance resulted in four clusters, whereas filtering based on the C8–C15 distance yielded six clusters. In both cases, the largest clusters contained 30 and 31 conformations, exhibiting average pairwise RMSD values of 4.61 Å and 4.81 Å, respectively. Across clusters, representative docking energies spanned a broad range (− 35.07 to − 64.19 kcal/mol for WEE1-CRBN and − 34.05 to − 69.59 kcal/mol for PKMYT1-CRBN), indicating no clear correlation between docking energy and conformational sampling population, as energetically favorable representatives were identified across clusters irrespective of cluster size.

The ubiquitination competence of the selected representative WEE1-CRBN and PKMYT1-CRBN models was next evaluated under static conditions by positioning each conformation within the CRL4CRBN ubiquitination assembly. Representative poses in which WEE1 or PKMYT1 exhibited steric clashes with components of the ubiquitination machinery were excluded, retaining only geometrically feasible, non-clashing conformations. This step resulted in the exclusion of two WEE1-CRBN models (WEE1-CRBN–M2 and WEE1-CRBN–M9) and two PKMYT1-CRBN models (PKMYT1-CRBN–M1 and PKMYT1-CRBN–M7). The remaining seven WEE1-CRBN and six PKMYT1-CRBN models were subsequently subjected to three independent 100 ns MD simulation runs to assess their dynamics and time-dependent ubiquitinability. As shown in Fig.6, the retained representative models for both systems exhibited consistent and reproducible behavior across all three simulations. For the majority of models, the POI–E3 ligase conformations were well-maintained over the simulation timescale with Cα RMSD values stabilizing around 2-4 Å. Only WEE1-CRBN–M6 and M7, as well as PKMYT1-CRBN–M8 displayed moderate flexibility, with RMSD values fluctuating between 4 and 6 Å, yet without any large-scale conformational destabilization. In parallel, ubiquitination accessibility was evaluated dynamically by monitoring the distances between solvent-exposed lysine residues and the E2 Cys111 throughout the 100 ns simulations. As summarized in Fig.7, all simulated models exhibited consistent and reproducible ubiquitination accessibility profiles across the three simulation runs, with at least one lysine residue remaining within 50 Å of E2 Cys111 for the whole duration of the simulations. In the WEE1-CRBN system, Lys304, Lys331 and Lys332 were ubiquitinable in five of the seven models, defining dominant and recurrent ubiquitination hotspots. WEE1-CRBN–M5 and WEE1-CRBN–M8 exhibited distinct accessibility patterns, demonstrated by the ubiquitinability of alternative lysine sets. In contrast, PKMYT1-CRBN models displayed greater variability and redundancy in accessible lysines, with most conformations exhibiting ubiquitinability through multiple distinct residues. Only PKMYT1-CRBN–M2 exhibited a single ubiquitination accessible lysine residue, Lys126. These ubiquitinable conformations were subsequently advanced to induced-fit docking of active PROTACs to assess their capacity to accommodate active PROTACs and form sustained, productive ternary complexes.

To evaluate whether the productive conformations can accommodate active degraders, induced-fit docking was performed on the identified WEE1-CRBN and PKMYT1-CRBN models. Six reported CRBN-mediated WEE1 PROTACs (MA071, ZNL-02-012, ZNL-02-040, ZNL-02-047, ZNL-02-096, and TL12-186) and one CRBN-mediated PKMYT1 PROTAC (D16-M1P2, evaluated in bothR- andS-oxa-azaspirodecane linker configurations) were included in this analysis (Table4). Docked poses were required to satisfy the pharmacophoric features defined for the corresponding warheads in the modeled POI–CRBN conformations (Section 6.1; Figure S39, Supplement). Despite conformational diversity among the WEE1-CRBN models, all were capable of accommodating MA071, ZNL-02-012, ZNL-02-040 and ZNL-02-047, with the most favorable docking scores consistently observed in the WEE1-CRBN–M3 conformation (− 16.27, − 16.40, − 15.29 and − 15.63 kcal/mol, respectively). In contrast, ZNL-02-096 was exclusively accommodated in the WEE1-CRBN–M5 model with a docking score of -14.01 kcal/mol while docking of TL12-186 was only successful in WEE1-CRBN–M5 and WEE1-CRBN–M8 models with the superior docking score being in M5 (− 14.29 kcal/mol). WEE1-CRBN models accessibility to PROTACs and energy scores of successfully docked poses are summarized in Table5. For the PKMYT1 system, ternary complex formation was more restrictive as docking of D16-M1P2 was only achieved in PKMYT1-CRBN–M4 conformation, irrespective of linker stereochemistry. The top-ranked pose of D16-M1P2, in both stereochemical forms of the oxa-azaspirodecane linker motif, showed docking scores of − 10.85 kcal/mol for theRconfiguration and − 10.70 kcal/mol for theSconfiguration.

The top-ranked poses—MA071, ZNL-02-012, ZNL-02-040 and ZNL-02-047 in WEE1-CRBN–M3; ZNL-02-096 and TL12-186 in WEE1-CRBN–M5; and both stereochemical forms of D16-M1P2 in PKMYT1-CRBN–M4—showed successful alignment with the defined pharmacophores. In all cases, the PROTAC linkers adopted conformations embedded at the POI–CRBN interface, while preserving the key interactions of each warhead within its respective binding pocket (Figure8). Subsequently, these successfully generated ternary complexes were advanced to extended 1µs MD simulations to assess their long-timescale dynamic behavior. Across all systems, the ternary complexes remained moderately stable throughout the simulations, with Cα RMSD values generally ranging between 4 and 6 Å and PROTAC RMSD values between 3 and 5 Å (Fig.9). Notably, the ZNL-02-096–mediated WEE1-CRBN–M5 ternary complex exhibited the lowest overall structural deviations, stabilizing at 4 Å for Cα atoms and 3 Å for PROTAC atoms. In the TL12-186–mediated WEE1-CRBN–M5 ternary complex, three transient RMSD excursions reaching ~7-8 Å were observed; however, each persisted for less than 10 ns. Throughout all simulations, PROTAC-POI and PROTAC-CRBN interactions were well maintained, displaying moderate to high occupancy rates over time (Figures S40-S42, Supplement). Moreover, all ternary complexes exhibited sustained ubiquitination accessibility throughout the 1 µs simulations, fully consistent with the trends observed previously in the 100 ns MD runs, thereby confirming the long-timescale productivity of their geometries (Figures S43-S45, Supplement).

To assess whether the attachment-atom distance windows derived from productive POI–E3 ligase conformations could rationalize PROTAC activity and inform linker design, we analyzed the conformational sampling of linkers from the studied active WEE1- and PKMYT1-targeting PROTACs, together with four in-house PKMYT1 PROTACs that were found to be inactive degraders. 2D structures of PKMYT1 PROTACs (H100-103) are shown in Table6(Synthesis and analytical characterization of the four compounds are given in the Supplement, Schemes 1 and 2). For each compound, linker conformers were generated using the ConfGen tool implemented in the Schrödinger Suite (v2025), and their end-to-end distances were measured and directly compared with the attachment-atom distances observed during 100 ns MD simulations of the corresponding productive POI–E3 ligase models. Prior to this analysis, the warheads employed in the PKMYT1 PROTACs (Compound 4 and D6) were docked into the PKMYT1-CRBN models and subjected to triplicate 100 ns MD simulations to confirm their compatibility with the D16-M1P2 employed warheads. This step ensured that the attachment-atom distance windows extracted from POI–E3 simulations could be meaningfully applied to linker screening and rational PROTAC design based on Compound 4 and D6 structures.

For the WEE1-CRBN–M3 model, the attachment-atom distance defined by the AZD1775 N2- Pomalidomide C14 pair, corresponding to the link points in ZNL-02-012, ZNL-02-040, and ZNL-02-047, remained between approximately 8.5 and 10.5 Å throughout the simulations (Fig.10A). In the WEE1-CRBN–M5 model, two distinct attachment-atom pairs were considered, reflecting the link points of ZNL-02-096 (N2-C14) and TL12-186 (N2-C15). In this case, the N2-C14 distance fluctuated between 5 and 7 Å, whereas the N2-C15 distance exhibited a range of 7 to 9 Å (Fig.10B). For the PKMYT1-CRBN–M4 model, simulations performed with Compound 4 and D6 revealed attachment-atom distances (Compound 4 N1- D6 C13) ranging from approximately 8 to 11 Å (Fig.10C). Simulations of the same model with Compound 41 and lenalidomide exhibited a longer attachment-atom distance (Compound 41 C8- Lenalidomid C13), fluctuating between 13 and 15 Å (Fig.10D).

Analysis of the linker conformer length distributions demonstrated a strong correspondence between PROTAC activity and compatibility with the attachment-atom distance windows derived from productive POI–E3 models. All active WEE1 PROTACs displayed linker conformations whose lengths aligned with the monitored attachment-atom distances of their respective productive models (Figure10E). Specifically, linker conformers of ZNL-02-012, ZNL-02-040, and ZNL-02-047 were compatible with the 8.5–10.5 Å distance window of WEE1-CRBN–M3. Notably, ZNL-02-096 linker conformers exhibited lengths that matched exclusively the N2–C14 distance window (5–7 Å) of WEE1-CRBN–M5, consistent with the observation that this was the only model capable of accommodating ZNL-02-096. Similarly, TL12-186 linker conformers aligned uniquely with the N2–C15 distance window (7–9 Å) of WEE1-CRBN–M5, and were also compatible with the WEE1-CRBN–M8 distance range (see Supplementary Material for a comprehensive comparison across models, Figures S46-S48). In the PKMYT1 system, D16-M1P2 linkers, in both stereochemical configurations, exhibited highly similar length distributions, each aligning well with the attachment-atom distance window observed for PKMYT1-CRBN–M4 (Fig.10F). In contrast, the linkers of the inactive in-house PKMYT1 PROTACs (H100-H103), which connect C8 of Compound 41 to C13 of lenalidomide or pomalidomide, did not sample linker lengths compatible with any productive PKMYT1-CRBN C8–C13 attachment-distance window. These inactive linkers adopted lengths between 2 and 12 Å, whereas the shortest C8–C13 distance observed across all PKMYT1-CRBN models was approximately 13 Å, observed by the PKMYT1-CRBN–M4 model. Induced-fit docking of these inactive PROTACs was consistent with the observed linker lengths, as none of the models successfully accommodated them.

Recent advances in computational modeling have substantially improved our ability to characterize PROTAC-mediated ternary complexes, enabling structure-based exploration of degrader-induced protein–protein interactions [55,56,57]. Ensemble-based docking and MD simulations allow sampling of diverse POI–E3 conformational states beyond static experimental structures [58,59,60]. However, successful modeling of productive ternary complexes requires deeper incorporation of mechanistic constraints. In particular, physically feasible warhead connectivity, functional discrimination between conformational states, and ubiquitination accessibility are fundamental determinants of productive degradation that remain underrepresented in many current modeling workflows. Integrating these mechanistic insights is therefore essential for improving the predictive power of PROTAC ternary complex modeling and for guiding rational degrader design. In this study, we performed an integrated static and dynamic structural analysis of experimentally resolved ternary complexes to elucidate key geometric determinants underlying productive PROTAC-mediated ubiquitination and degradation. By monitoring linker connectivity, POI–E3 ligase conformational variation, ternary complex dynamics and ubiquitination accessibility, we derive quantitative structural thresholds that inform de novo degrader design.

Analysis of experimental ternary structures revealed that physically feasible warhead connectivity is tightly constrained, with lengths not exceeding 15 Å. This observation supports the use of a conservative 15 Å distance threshold to filter docking-derived POI–E3 conformations and exclude geometries unlikely to be realizable by a PROTAC molecule. MD simulations further showed that overall linker lengths fluctuate within a window of approximately 2 Å, indicating balanced conformational plasticity. Consistent with these observations, Yang et al. reported that degradation efficiency depends on the formation and maintenance of specific hydrophobic patches at the POI–E3 interface, which are sensitive to linker length and flexibility. Both insufficient and excessive linker flexibility were shown to reduce degradation efficiency by disrupting key interfacial hydrophobic interactions [61]. Our assessment of linker lengths further supports and extends the conclusion that physically feasible warhead connectivity and constrained linker flexibility dictate whether functionally relevant interfacial contacts can form, thereby controlling degradation outcomes [62,63]. One notable exception was observed for WDR5-VHL–mediated PROTACs, which exhibited substantial linker conformational sampling. This pronounced linker flexibility observed in MD simulations is consistent with experimental structures, in which WDR5-VHL PROTACs display static linker lengths ranging from 6.9 to 13.8 Å, despite connecting the same attachment atoms within identical WDR5-VHL conformations [64].

Ubiquitination accessibility assessment further showed that experimental ternary geometries are productive, consistently position one or more solvent-exposed POI lysine residues within 50 Å of the E2 catalytic Cys111, and providing a mechanistically meaningful criterion for ubiquitination competence of modeled structures. Consistent with recent cryo-EM and ubiquitinomics analyses of the MZ1-induced BRD4BD2-VHL complex, our modeled CRL2VHL ubiquitination machinery correctly identified experimentally observed ubiquitination-competent lysines including Lys362, Lys368, Lys445 and Lys456 [10]. Although Lys368 was positioned within the ubiquitinable range, it was excluded in our analysis due to limited solvent accessibility. Notably, experimental ternary complexes displayed substantially different dynamics, with subsets showing high stability, moderate flexibility or pronounced instability. However, all complexes maintained the architecture required for sustained ubiquitination accessibility, indicating that high stability alone is insufficient to assess degradation outcomes. In light of these structural insights, we mapped productive POI–E3 ligase conformations of 34 experimental PROTAC ternary structures. The multiple productive POI–E3 ligase conformations we identified per system corroborate Ma et al.’s observation that the SMARCA2 domain occupies a broader range of productive positions relative to VHL than crystal structures alone suggest [65]. Furthermore, modeling of the CDK2-CRBN system yielded model M7_P-P197, which reproduces the conformation observed in the cryo-EM structure PDB 9D0W, and model M6_P-P103, which matches the recently resolved cryo-EM structure PDB 9NYR [66,67]. Given that the two experimental structures exhibit substantial structural divergence (Cα RMSD ~10 Å), these findings underscore the predictive strength of our approach and suggest that multiple productive conformations per system could be experimentally confirmed. On the other hand, modeled conformations in which POI lysines were positioned >50 Å from E2 Cys111 exhibited high stability and showed no conformational rearrangements capable of repositioning these residues into the ubiquitination range. This finding aligns with the possibility that rigid POI–E3 ligase conformations can arise in which solvent-accessible lysine residues are not positioned for ubiquitination, resulting in unsuccessful POI degradation [18].

After analyzing the experimental benchmark dataset, we applied our computational workflow to model WEE1-CRBN and PKMYT1-CRBN PROTACs, selected to assess workflow generalizability in the absence of experimental ternary complex structures. Seven WEE1-CRBN and six PKMYT1-CRBN representative conformations exhibiting feasible warhead connectivity and sustained ubiquitination accessibility were identified. These conformations span a diverse set of geometrically plausible assemblies suitable for further evaluation of linker design and assessment of PROTAC-induced degradation potential. Docking energies of representative conformations were independent of conformational sampling populations or ubiquitinability, indicating that POI–E3 binding affinity is inadequate to predict degradation outcome and that multiple conformations must be considered in modeling efforts. However, induced-fit docking of active PROTACs showed that, despite conformational diversity among the WEE1-CRBN models, all conformations were capable of accommodating four of the six WEE1 PROTACs examined, whereas the remaining two PROTACs were exclusively accommodated either in a single model (WEE1-CRBN–M5 in the case of ZNL-02-096) or in two models (WEE1-CRBN–M5 and M8 in the case of TL12-186). In this context, PROTAC docking scores were used to prioritize the generated PROTAC ternary complexes for further evaluation, while accounting for the possibility that the same PROTAC may engage distinct productive POI–E3 conformations. Induced-fit docking of the PKMYT1 PROTAC D16-M1P2 was successful only in PKMYT1-CRBN–M4 irrespective of linker stereochemistry, consistent with the developers’ claim that variations in linker stereochemistry do not impact PROTAC activity [50]. Analysis of linker conformations revealed a strong correlation between PROTAC activity and linker compatibility with attachment-atom distance windows derived from productive POI–E3 models. Active WEE1 and PKMYT1 PROTACs adopted linker lengths matching these windows, whereas linkers of inactive PKMYT1 PROTACs were too short to bridge productive PKMYT1-CRBN geometries. These results highlight that appropriate linker length is critical for ternary complex formation and provide a rational framework for designing linkers with optimal degradation potential. Recently, Kumar and Sophia addressed the principle that degradation competence depends on ubiquitination accessibility, conformational diversity, and linker-dependent geometry by employing an integrative computational framework with an application to PTP1B-VHL system [68]. Our work extends this approach by introducing quantitative, transferable design rules with explicit numerical thresholds and by validating generalizability across additional POI–E3 ligase systems (WEE1- and PKMYT1-CRBN). Together, these modeling efforts provide a more comprehensive understanding of target protein degradation beyond static experimental snapshots and offer mechanistically grounded strategies for future degrader design.

This study demonstrates that productive degradation arises from a balance of conformational diversity and preserved ubiquitination competence, rather than from ternary complex stability or binding affinity alone. By integrating structural benchmarking, connectivity constraints, conformational clustering, ubiquitination accessibility metrics and MD simulations, we establish a generalizable computational framework for identifying productive POI–E3 ligase models. Quantitative thresholds for warhead attachment distances, Cα RMSD-based conformational divergence and lysine proximity to the E2 catalytic site provide mechanistically interpretable design rules that can be applied prospectively. Application to WEE1-CRBN and PKMYT1-CRBN systems reveals that multiple productive conformations must be considered during PROTAC design and that linker length compatibility with the attachment atom distance windows is a critical determinant of activity. Importantly, the decoupling of POI–E3 binding affinity from degradation potential highlights the need to move beyond static or single-structure paradigms. Future impact lies in accelerating this workflow (e.g., through fast AI-assisted conformational sampling beyond the limited set of dominant cofolding predictions), incorporating enhanced sampling strategies to identify additional ubiquitination-competent conformations and in extending it to additional degraders and E3 ligases. Together, these advances will enable more predictive, mechanism-driven design of next-generation targeted protein degraders.

title: AlphaDTA: integrating AlphaFold3 embeddings and 3D complex structures for drug–target binding affinity prediction
author: Minjae Chung; Sejin Park; Hyunju Lee
text:
Accurate prediction of drug–target binding affinity plays an important role in structure-based drug discovery, yet existing approaches are constrained by their reliance on scarce experimentally determined protein–ligand complex structures. In this context, recent advances in biomolecular structure prediction models, such as AlphaFold3, have emerged as a promising approach to alleviate the scarcity of experimentally determined protein–ligand complex structures. In this study, we introduce AlphaDTA, a framework that integrates AlphaFold3-predicted structures and embeddings for drug–target binding affinity prediction. AlphaDTA processes two types of AlphaFold3 embeddings, single and pair embeddings. We utilized the single embeddings at both fine-grained and coarse-grained levels to capture local interaction patterns and global binding context, and used the pair embeddings to encode cross-molecular relational features. The AlphaFold3-predicted structures are further processed by a three-dimensional structure-based geometric encoder to produce corresponding structural embedding representations. The resulting single, pair, and structural embeddings are then integrated through adaptive fusion for affinity prediction. When we evaluated AlphaDTA using recently proposed PDBbind data splits designed to reduce train–test structural overlap, AlphaDTA achieved state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multiple independent benchmarks. In a case study on the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, AlphaDTA correctly identifies a clinically approved potentiator and suggests a potential repurposing candidate among FDA-approved drugs.

Scientific contribution

AlphaDTA enables accurate drug–target binding affinity prediction without relying on experimentally determined protein–ligand complex structures. By integrating AlphaFold3-derived single, pair, and structure-based embeddings through adaptive fusion, AlphaDTA improves generalization on structurally nonredundant benchmarks and demonstrates utility for target-specific drug repurposing.

Identifying small molecules (ligands) that bind effectively to disease-relevant target proteins is a central challenge in drug discovery, making a thorough understanding of protein–ligand interactions (PLIs) essential for therapeutic development [1,2]. However, the vast chemical space of potential ligands makes it impractical to characterize all candidate protein–ligand pairs using experimental methods, given the technical complexity and substantial resources involved [2,3,4]. Computational approaches therefore offer a scalable alternative for predicting PLIs across large compound libraries [5,6]. Among these tasks, drug–target affinity (DTA) prediction plays a crucial role in computational drug discovery, as it quantifies binding strength to systematically rank and prioritize candidate ligands for a given target protein [7,8].

Existing methods for binding affinity prediction can be broadly divided into free-energy–based approaches and scoring-function–based approaches [9,10]. Free-energy–based approaches estimate binding affinity by computing the binding free energy (\(\Delta G\)) using explicit physical models together with conformational sampling, but remain computationally expensive and impractical for large-scale screening [9,10,11]. Scoring-function–based methods approximate affinity using predefined interaction terms and are commonly formulated as force-field–based, empirical, or knowledge-based scoring functions [9,10,12], yet their fixed functional forms constrain their capacity to capture complex or atypical interaction patterns [10]. More recently, deep learning-based scoring models have gained considerable attention for their ability to learn data-driven representations that capture complex binding patterns from data [5,9,13,14]. These deep learning approaches can be further categorized into sequence-based and complex-based methods depending on their use of three-dimensional (3D) structural information [15,16].

Sequence-based methods [17,18,19] take proteins as amino acid sequences and ligands as SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) [20] strings as input, enabling scalable learning from large datasets without requiring 3D structural information [15,17,18,19]. However, because binding affinity is governed by spatial interactions within the binding site, the lack of explicit 3D structural context can limit predictive accuracy [5,14,21,22,23]. In contrast, complex-based methods [16,24,25,26] leverage 3D protein–ligand complex structures to directly model binding geometry. However, their applicability is constrained by the limited availability of high-quality 3D structural data [16,27,28].

Recently, significant advances in 3D biomolecular complex structure prediction models such as NeuralPLexer [29], RoseTTAFold All-Atom [30], UMol [31], and AlphaFold3 [32] have alleviated these limitations. Among these, AlphaFold3 has achieved unprecedented performance in predicting biological complex structures including protein–ligand, protein–nucleic acid, and other molecular interactions, establishing a new standard in this domain [33,34]. These advances now enable complex-based binding affinity prediction methods to access high-quality complex structures without relying on experimental determination.

In parallel, large-scale foundation models pretrained with self-supervised objectives such as ChemBERTa-2 [35], MolFormer [36], ProtTrans [37], and ESM2 [38] have demonstrated strong transfer across biochemical domains. Consequently, recent approaches for protein–ligand binding prediction, including both drug–target interaction and binding affinity prediction tasks, increasingly leverage contextual embeddings extracted from pretrained encoders [39,40,41,42,43]. These approaches primarily employ protein language models trained on protein sequences and molecular language models trained on SMILES strings to extract rich biochemical representations from sequence-level inputs, thereby enhancing generalization under limited labeled data. Recent studies have further extended this paradigm to complex-based methods by additionally incorporating pretrained sequence-level protein and ligand representations, demonstrating improved binding affinity prediction accuracy [44,45,46]. However, in these approaches, the protein and ligand encoders are pretrained independently on their respective modalities, without exposure to joint protein–ligand interaction context.

In this regard, beyond its role as a structure predictor, AlphaFold3 also generates two types of embeddings during the structure prediction process: single embeddings, which capture per-atom and per-residue features, and pair embeddings, which encode pairwise relational information. In the protein–ligand setting considered here, these representations are produced while modeling the protein and ligand together. Thus, AlphaFold3 embeddings differ from representations obtained from independently pretrained protein language models and molecular language models. Specifically, AlphaFold3 embeddings can represent proteins and ligands in a shared interaction-aware structural context, providing rich structural and interaction information learned from large-scale molecular data. However, despite their quality and potential relevance, such embeddings have not been effectively leveraged for binding affinity prediction.

In this work, we propose AlphaDTA, a framework for drug–target affinity prediction that integrates AlphaFold3-predicted complex structures and embeddings. AlphaDTA consists of two complementary encoders: a Multi-Granularity Encoder and a Geometric Encoder. The Multi-Granularity Encoder processes two types of AlphaFold3 embeddings—single and pair embeddings. Specifically, single embeddings are utilized at both fine-grained and coarse-grained levels to capture local interaction patterns and global binding context, while pair embeddings encode cross-molecular relational features between atoms and residues. The Geometric Encoder operates directly on the predicted 3D complex structure to extract structure-aware interaction features that explicitly model spatial binding geometry. For affinity prediction, the representations learned by the two encoders are adaptively fused to form a unified feature representation. AlphaDTA achieves competitive or superior performance across multiple benchmark datasets compared to existing methods. In addition, a case study on the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator highlights its practical applicability, where the model suggests a clinically approved potentiator and a potential repurposing candidate among FDA-approved drugs.

AlphaDTA is a deep learning framework for drug–target binding affinity prediction that leverages predicted complex structures and two types of embeddings generated by AlphaFold3 from protein sequences and ligand SMILES strings (Fig.1). From the full AlphaFold3-generated embeddings, pocket-level representations are constructed by retaining protein residues within 10 Å of any ligand heavy atom together with all ligand tokens, forming the input to the subsequent encoders. AlphaDTA is composed of two main encoders: a Multi-Granularity Encoder and a Geometric Encoder. The Multi-Granularity Encoder derives fine-grained and coarse-grained feature vectors from AlphaFold3 single and pair embeddings, capturing interaction patterns at multiple levels of resolution. In parallel, the Geometric Encoder extracts structure-aware geometric feature vectors from the predicted 3D protein–ligand complex. The resulting representations are then integrated through a Triple Adaptive Fusion module to produce the final binding affinity prediction. Detailed descriptions of AlphaFold3 inference and data preprocessing are provided in Additional file 1: Sections S1 and S2, respectively.

Overview of the AlphaDTA framework. Given a protein sequence and ligand SMILES, AlphaFold3 (AF3) generates a predicted complex structure and embeddings (single and pair). Pocket-level embeddings are extracted based on residues within 10 Å of the ligand. The Multi-Granularity Encoder processes these embeddings through Fine-grained, Coarse-grained, and Pair Extractors, while the Geometric Encoder extracts structural features via InteractionGraphNet (IGN). The resulting representations are integrated through Triple Adaptive Fusion to predict binding affinity (pK)

Multi-Granularity Encoder (MGE) extracts features from AlphaFold3 embeddings at multiple levels of granularity to capture both detailed molecular interactions and global binding context. The AlphaFold3 embeddings consist of a single embedding\(S \in \mathbb {R}^{N \times 384}\)and a pair embedding\(Z \in \mathbb {R}^{N \times N \times 128}\), where\(N = N_p + N_l\), with\(N_p\)protein residues and\(N_l\)ligand heavy atoms. The single embedding encodes individual characteristics of each token, including local structural and chemical properties, while the pair embedding captures relational information between token pairs, representing potential interactions and spatial dependencies across the complex. To process these two embeddings, MGE consists of four components: a Residual Token Projection (RTP) that adapts the single embedding, a Single Extractor that encodes it at fine-grained and coarse-grained levels, a Pair Extractor that extracts interaction-specific features from the pair embedding, and a Fusion layer that combines these representations.

Residual Token Projection

The residual formulation allows the model to refine the pretrained embeddings while maintaining the original representation as a stable reference. We adopt a pre-normalization design, applying layer normalization\(\textrm{LN}(\cdot )\)prior to the MLP to improve optimization stability.

The PDBbind database [27] is a widely used benchmark for protein–ligand binding affinity prediction, providing experimentally measured binding affinities paired with 3D complex structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) [49]. In this study, we use PDBbind v2020, which is organized into three hierarchical subsets: theGeneral Set, theRefined Set, and theCore Set.

TheGeneral Setis the largest subset, containing 19,443 protein–ligand complexes with experimentally reported binding affinities expressed as\(pK_d\)(\(-\log K_d\)),\(pK_i\)(\(-\log K_i\)), or\(pIC_{50}\)(\(-\log IC_{50}\)), collectively denoted aspKin this work. TheRefined Setis a high-quality subset derived from the General Set through stringent filtering criteria. It comprises 5,316 complexes with crystal structure resolution better than 2.5 Å and reliable\(K_d\)or\(K_i\)measurements, excluding\(IC_{50}\)values. TheCore Setis a carefully selected, non-redundant subset of 285 complexes drawn from the Refined Set via cluster analysis. This subset forms the CASF2016 (Comparative Assessment of Scoring Functions) benchmark [50], which evaluates the generalization of scoring functions across diverse protein families. CASF2016 consists of 57 target-based clusters, each containing five complexes sharing the same protein target but different ligands and binding affinities.

Three additional external benchmark datasets from Li et al. [51]—BDB2020+ (a BindingDB-derived dataset), Mpro (SARS-CoV-2 main protease complexes), and EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor complexes)—are employed to assess generalization across varying similarity profiles. Detailed descriptions are provided in theExperimental Setupsection.

A common practice is to use the PDBbind General Set (excluding CASF2016) for training and validation and to evaluate performance on CASF2016 as an independent test set [16,21,24,25,26]. However, recent studies [26,45,51,52] have reported a critical data leakage issue in this conventional split. High structural and sequence similarities between training and test complexes may lead to overly optimistic performance estimates, as models can rely on memorization rather than learning generalizable binding principles.

To mitigate data leakage and enable a more rigorous evaluation of generalization, we construct our experiments using two reorganized versions of PDBbind v2020: Leak-Proof PDBbind [51] and PDBbind CleanSplit [45]. Although both are derived from the same PDBbind release, they differ in their splitting strategies. Leak-Proof PDBbind controls protein sequence similarity across subsets, whereas PDBbind CleanSplit removes structurally similar complexes based on 3D protein–ligand alignment to prevent overlap with CASF2016. Together, these datasets enable evaluation under sequence-level and structure-level dissimilarity.

In addition, we evaluate performance using both experimentally determined crystal structures and AlphaFold3-predicted structures, allowing assessment under validated geometries as well as robustness to structural prediction uncertainty. In all experiments, model performance is evaluated in terms of the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) and root mean squared error (RMSE) (Additional file 1: Section S3).

During preprocessing and AlphaFold3-based structure generation, a subset of complexes could not be processed due to molecule-parsing or graph-construction errors. These failures were excluded from the corresponding analyses, and all performance comparisons were conducted on the intersection of complexes successfully processed by all compared methods. A detailed analysis of the failure types, excluded complexes, and potential mitigation strategies is provided in Additional file 1: Section S6.

We first evaluate AlphaDTA on the Leak-Proof PDBbind (LP-PDBbind) dataset [51], which is designed to mitigate data leakage through two approaches: quality-based filtering and similarity-controlled splitting. For quality-based filtering, LP-PDBbind defines two cleaning levels: Clean Level 1 (CL1) and Clean Level 2 (CL2). CL1 removes covalent binders, complexes with structural defects (e.g., steric clashes or distant ligands), and ligands with uncommon elements or poor drug-likeness, whereas CL2 further restricts affinity measurements to high-confidence\(K_d\)or\(K_i\)values, excluding\(IC_{50}\). For similarity-controlled splitting, a maximum protein sequence similarity of 50% and ligand similarity of 99% are enforced between training and validation/test sets. Based on these criteria, LP-PDBbind provides an independent train–validation–test split comprising 7,393 non-covalent CL1 complexes for training, 958 CL2 complexes for validation, and 2,171 CL2 complexes for testing.

To further assess generalization under different similarity regimes, we additionally evaluate on three external benchmarks provided by Li et al. [51]:

BDB2020+ (115 complexes): A benchmark dataset compiled from BindingDB [53] entries deposited after 2020 and matched with PDB crystal structures, providing temporal separation from PDBbind v2020. The same similarity thresholds used in LP-PDBbind splitting are applied to ensure no overlap with the train set.

Mpro (40 complexes): A moderate-similarity benchmark dataset targeting the SARS-CoV-2 main protease. The train set contains a related SARS-CoV-1 main protease (PDB ID: 3V3M), yielding partial protein and ligand similarity to the training data.

EGFR (23 complexes): A challenging low-similarity benchmark dataset in which both the target protein and ligands exhibit minimal similarity to the train set, testing generalization to new protein–ligand systems.

Prediction models are trained using the LP-PDBbind training and validation sets and evaluated on the LP-PDBbind test set as well as the three external benchmarks (BDB2020+, Mpro, and EGFR). All experiments are repeated with five random seeds to ensure generalization across varying similarity profiles.

Experiments are additionally conducted using the PDBbind CleanSplit dataset proposed by Graber et al. [45]. Whereas LP-PDBbind constructs an independent train–validation–test split with sequence-based similarity control across subsets, PDBbind CleanSplit fixes CASF2016 as the external test set and systematically removes training complexes that structurally resemble any CASF2016 entry.

Similarity is assessed using three complementary metrics: protein structural alignment via TM-align scores, ligand chemical similarity via Tanimoto scores, and binding conformation similarity via pocket-aligned ligand RMSD (root mean squared deviation). Training complexes with high combined similarity across these dimensions are excluded to eliminate train–test overlap. Beyond mitigating external leakage, PDBbind CleanSplit also reduces internal redundancies by removing similarity clusters within the training data, ensuring learning from a diverse, non-redundant set.

Prediction models are trained on PDBbind CleanSplit using five-fold cross-validation and evaluated on the fixed CASF2016 benchmark, providing a stringent assessment of generalization to structurally dissimilar complexes.

To further evaluate generalization under strict data separation, we constructed an additional cluster-based PDBbind split inspired by recent cluster-based evaluation protocols for drug–target interaction prediction [43,54]. Unlike random or pair-level splitting, this setting separates complexes at both ligand- and protein-cluster levels, thereby reducing overlap in chemical and protein sequence spaces across training, validation, and test sets.

For ligand clustering, compounds were represented using ECFP4 (4-bond extended-connectivity fingerprint) [55] fingerprints, and pairwise ligand distances were computed using the Jaccard distance. For protein clustering, target sequences were represented using pseudo-amino acid composition (PSC) [56] descriptors, and pairwise protein distances were computed using the cosine distance. Ligands and proteins were then independently clustered using single-linkage hierarchical clustering, resulting in 5,649 ligand clusters and 3,761 protein clusters.

For each random seed, ligand clusters and protein clusters were independently partitioned into training, validation, and test groups at a ratio of 60:20:20. A complex was assigned to a split only when both its ligand cluster and protein cluster belonged to the corresponding partition; complexes spanning different partitions were excluded. This procedure ensured that the training, validation, and test sets shared no ligand clusters or protein clusters.

We generated five independent cluster-based splits using different random seeds. For each split, models were trained on the training set, selected using the cluster-disjoint validation set, and evaluated on the held-out test set. Final performance was reported as the mean and standard deviation across the five test sets.

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of AlphaDTA, we compare against ten established benchmark methods with diverse architectures and input modalities:

Sequence-based methods

These methods use only protein sequences and ligand SMILES as input:

DeepDTA [17]: Encodes protein amino acid sequences and ligand SMILES using separate 1D-CNNs and combining the representations via fully connected layers.

BAPULM [39]: Encodes protein amino acid sequences and ligand SMILES using pretrained language models (ProtT5-XL-U50 [37] for proteins; MolFormer [36] for ligands), then applies a prediction head to the concatenated embeddings.

PMMR [40]: Fuses pretrained sequence embeddings (ESM2 [38] for proteins; ChemBERTa-2 [35] for ligands) with 2D ligand graph features, integrating sequence semantics and graph topology in a unified predictor.

Complex-based methods

These methods leverage 3D protein–ligand complex structures:

RF-Score [10]: A Random Forest that uses predefined atom-pair interaction features based on occurrence counts of nine atomic types within a 12 Å distance cutoff.

IGN [26]: Utilizes 3D molecular interaction graphs using two stacked graph convolution modules to sequentially capture intra-molecular and inter-molecular interactions.

Search top-5 complexes [45]: A nearest-neighbor baseline that retrieves the five most similar training complexes and predicts affinity by averaging their labels.

GenScore [57]: Combines graph-based geometric modeling with a probabilistic scoring formulation to estimate interaction strength.

Pafnucy [25]: Converts 3D protein–ligand structures into voxel grids and learns spatial interaction patterns with 3D-CNNs.

GEMS [45]: Constructs spatial interaction graphs by integrating 3D proximity-based interactions with pretrained protein/ligand language-model embeddings to capture sequence-level semantics.

AutoDock Vina [58]: A traditional empirical scoring function widely used for protein–ligand docking and scoring. In this study, AutoDock Vina was used in a scoring-only setting, where complex structures were directly scored without docking or model training (Additional file 1: Section S4.7).

To determine whether the performance gains of AlphaDTA arise solely from the use of AlphaFold3 embeddings or from the proposed MGE, we introduce a simplified variant:

AlphaDTA (Simplified MGE): A simplified version of AlphaDTA where the MGE is replaced by a simplified embedding processing module (Additional file 1: Section S5.1).

The baseline comparisons followed the benchmark sets used in the original studies that introduced each evaluation setting. For the LP-PDBbind setting, we followed Li et al. [51], including DeepDTA, RF-Score, IGN, and AutoDock Vina, and additionally included AlphaDTA (Simplified MGE) as our model variant. For the PDBbind CleanSplit/CASF2016 setting, we followed Graber et al. [45], including Search top-5 complexes, GenScore, Pafnucy, and GEMS. BAPULM and PMMR were included separately for the pretrained-representation comparison. For the cluster-based PDBbind split, we included all baselines evaluated across both settings: DeepDTA, RF-Score, IGN, AutoDock Vina, Search top-5 complexes, GenScore, Pafnucy, and GEMS. Detailed hyperparameter configurations and search procedures are provided in Additional file 1: Section S4.

All models except AutoDock Vina were trained on the LP-PDBbind training and validation sets across five random seeds. AutoDock Vina was instead used as a scoring-only baseline by directly scoring the corresponding complex structures without docking. All models were evaluated on the LP-PDBbind test set and three external benchmarks (BDB2020+, Mpro, and EGFR). Complex-based models were evaluated using either experimentally determined crystal or AF3-predicted structures; sequence-based baselines are included in both blocks for reference.

On the LP-PDBbind test set with crystal structures, AlphaDTA achieved the best performance (RMSE\(=1.529\), PCC\(=0.578\)), outperforming all baselines (Table1, Crystal). Similar trends were observed on external benchmarks, including BDB2020+ (RMSE\(=0.981\), PCC\(=0.604\)) and EGFR (RMSE\(=0.613\), PCC\(=0.714\)), where AlphaDTA achieved the best performance in both metrics. On Mpro, RF-Score achieved the lowest RMSE (RMSE\(=0.756\)), followed by AlphaDTA with the second-lowest RMSE (RMSE\(=0.808\)); notably, AlphaDTA obtained the highest PCC (PCC\(=0.721\)). AlphaDTA also consistently outperformed AlphaDTA (Simplified MGE) across all benchmarks in both RMSE and PCC. Overall, AlphaDTA demonstrated robust generalization across diverse benchmarks with varying protein sequence similarity profiles, achieving the best results on LP-PDBbind, BDB2020+, and EGFR, while remaining competitive on Mpro.

On the LP-PDBbind test set with AlphaFold3-predicted structures, AlphaDTA achieved the lowest RMSE (RMSE\(=\)1.561) and second-best PCC (PCC\(=0.555\)) comparable to RF-Score (PCC\(=0.562\)) (Table1, AF3). AlphaDTA achieved the best performance on both BDB2020+ (RMSE\(=0.996\), PCC\(=0.574\)) and EGFR (RMSE\(=0.586\), PCC\(=0.729\)). On Mpro, AlphaDTA achieved the highest PCC (PCC\(=\)0.715), while its RMSE (RMSE\(=\)0.800) was comparable to AutoDock Vina (RMSE\(=\)0.799) and remained close to the best RMSE achieved by RF-Score (RMSE\(=\)0.770). AlphaDTA also outperformed AlphaDTA (Simplified MGE) across all benchmarks in both RMSE and PCC.

Compared with the crystal structure setting, the performance gap between AlphaDTA with AlphaFold3-predicted structures and AlphaDTA with crystal structures was small across most benchmarks. On LP-PDBbind, the difference was\(\Delta\)RMSE\(=+0.032\)and\(\Delta\)PCC\(=-0.023\). On BDB2020+, the gap was similarly modest (\(\Delta\)RMSE\(=+0.015\),\(\Delta\)PCC\(=-0.030\)). On EGFR, AlphaDTA with AlphaFold3-predicted structures even outperformed the crystal structure counterpart, suggesting that AlphaFold3-predicted structures can provide complementary structural information in some settings. On Mpro, the gap remained marginal (\(\Delta\)RMSE\(=-0.008\),\(\Delta\)PCC\(=-0.006\)). Overall, these results indicate that AlphaDTA with AlphaFold3-predicted structures achieves performance closely comparable to its crystal structure counterpart, supporting the practical utility of the framework when experimentally determined complex structures are unavailable.

All models were trained on the PDBbind CleanSplit via 5-fold cross-validation and evaluated on the fixed CASF2016 test set using either experimentally determined crystal structures or AlphaFold3-predicted structures.

On CASF2016, AlphaDTA achieved the best overall performance with an average RMSE of 1.289 and PCC of 0.816 across five independently trained models from 5-fold cross-validation (\(n=284\); one complex was excluded due to ligand sanitization failure during IGN graph construction), outperforming GEMS (RMSE\(=1.308\), PCC\(=0.803\)) and the remaining baselines (Table2). Overall, AlphaDTA demonstrated robust generalization to structurally dissimilar protein–ligand complexes across protein structure, ligand chemistry, and binding conformation.

For the CASF2016 evaluation using AlphaFold3-predicted structures, we focused on GEMS as the primary comparator because it was the strongest baseline in the CleanSplit/CASF2016 benchmark using crystal structures (Fig.2). Figure2a shows that AlphaDTA achieved lower RMSE and higher PCC than GEMS (AlphaDTA: RMSE\(=1.306\), PCC\(=0.824\); GEMS: RMSE\(=1.350\), PCC\(=0.803\)) on CASF2016 using AlphaFold3-predicted structures, with ensemble predictions averaged over the five cross-validation models. Figure2b compares per-cluster PCC on the subset of CASF2016 clusters for which all five complexes were successfully processed under AlphaFold3 (\(n=44\)clusters). The remaining 13 clusters were excluded from the per-cluster analysis because at least one complex in each cluster failed during IGN graph construction for AlphaFold3-predicted structures (Additional file 1: Section S6), preventing complete five-complex cluster-level PCC calculation. AlphaDTA achieved higher PCC than GEMS in 32 clusters, whereas GEMS achieved higher PCC than AlphaDTA in 12 clusters. These results demonstrate that AlphaDTA maintains robust performance even under the structural noise in AlphaFold3-predicted structures, outperforming GEMS, the best-performing baseline. Furthermore, the cluster-level comparison shows that AlphaDTA’s gains are broadly distributed across diverse target families (32 out of 44 clusters), rather than being driven by a small number of favorable cases.

We further evaluated AlphaDTA using the cluster-based PDBbind split, where training, validation, and test complexes were separated at both ligand- and protein-cluster levels. This setting provides a strict assessment of generalization because model selection is also performed on a validation set composed of clusters unseen during training. All complex-based models in this comparison were evaluated using experimentally determined crystal structures, while AlphaDTA was additionally evaluated using AlphaFold3-predicted structures to assess its applicability when crystal complex structures are unavailable. The results are summarized in Table3.

Under experimentally determined crystal structures, AlphaDTA achieved the best overall performance among the evaluated models (RMSE\(=1.487\), PCC\(=0.579\)). AlphaDTA outperformed the second-best model, Pafnucy, in both RMSE (RMSE\(=1.499\)) and PCC (PCC\(=0.557\)), indicating that AlphaDTA remains robust even under cluster-disjoint train–validation–test separation. While AlphaDTA using AlphaFold3-predicted structures showed slightly lower performance than its crystal-structure counterpart, it still achieved competitive performance (RMSE\(=1.506\), PCC\(=0.565\)). Notably, AlphaDTA with AlphaFold3-predicted structures achieved a higher PCC than all non-AlphaDTA baseline models, including Pafnucy, IGN, GEMS, GenScore, RF-Score, DeepDTA, AutoDock Vina, and Search top-5 complexes. These results suggest that AlphaDTA can retain strong ranking performance even when experimentally determined complex structures are unavailable, supporting the practical advantage of integrating AlphaFold3-derived structures and embeddings for binding affinity prediction.

AlphaFold3 embeddings encode structural and relational information learned from diverse biomolecular complexes, unlike independently pretrained language models that process protein sequences and ligand SMILES separately. To assess whether this distinction translates to improved binding affinity prediction, AlphaDTA (w/o GE)—a variant of AlphaDTA that relies solely on AlphaFold3’s embeddings without the Geometric Encoder—is compared against BAPULM and PMMR, which employ independently pretrained language models (ProtT5, ESM2 for proteins; MolFormer, ChemBERTa-2 for ligands).

Across benchmarks, AlphaDTA (w/o GE) consistently showed strong performance (Table4). On the LP-PDBbind test set, it achieved the best overall results (RMSE\(=1.573\), PCC\(=0.559\)), outperforming BAPULM (RMSE\(=1.580\), PCC\(=0.530\)) and PMMR (RMSE\(=1.650\), PCC\(=0.494\)). On BDB2020+, AlphaDTA (w/o GE) achieved a competitive PCC (0.467) relative to BAPULM (0.504). However, AlphaDTA (w/o GE) demonstrated superior predictive accuracy with a significantly lower RMSE (1.131) compared to BAPULM (1.261). Moreover, on EGFR, BAPULM failed to generalize (PCC\(=-0.051\)), whereas AlphaDTA (w/o GE) showed best performance (RMSE\(=0.896\), PCC\(=0.270\)). On Mpro, AlphaDTA (w/o GE) achieved the highest PCC (PCC\(=0.586\)), outperforming BAPULM (PCC\(=0.388\)) and PMMR (PCC\(=0.421\)), with a competitive RMSE that ranked second (RMSE\(=0.970\)). Overall, AlphaDTA (w/o GE) demonstrated competitive or superior performance relative to BAPULM and PMMR across benchmarks, suggesting that AlphaFold3’s embeddings provide effective representations for binding affinity prediction.

To systematically evaluate the contributions of each component, we designed an ablation study to examine (i) the complementarity between AlphaFold3 embeddings and geometric representations, (ii) the relative contributions of single and pair embeddings, and (iii) the effectiveness of the Fine-grained and Coarse-grained components. As shown in Table5, all variants are evaluated using experimentally determined crystal structures and averaged over five independent runs. Since removing individual components changes model capacity and optimization behavior, each ablation variant was independently tuned using the same predefined hyperparameter search space to avoid penalizing any variant due to hyperparameter mismatch. In addition, to examine whether the simultaneous use of attention, max, and mean pooling in Eq. (12) is necessary, we conducted additional ablation studies on pooling strategies. These results are reported in Additional file 1: Section S5.2.

Removing AlphaFold3 single and pair embeddings consistently reduces performance. Compared to the full model, the w/o Single&Pair variant shows degraded RMSE (1.505\(\rightarrow\)1.524) and PCC (0.584\(\rightarrow\)0.569) on LP-PDBbind, as well as across all external benchmarks (BDB2020+: RMSE 1.003\(\rightarrow\)1.055, PCC 0.574\(\rightarrow\)0.507; Mpro: RMSE 0.808\(\rightarrow\)0.881, PCC 0.721\(\rightarrow\)0.680). On EGFR, the variant also exhibits degraded RMSE (0.716\(\rightarrow\)0.848) with a slight decrease in PCC (0.530\(\rightarrow\)0.526). These findings indicate that AlphaFold3 embeddings provide complementary information beyond geometric features.

Across benchmarks, removing pair embeddings (w/o Pair) generally led to larger degradations than removing single embeddings (w/o Single). Compared to the full model, the performance changes were as follows: LP-PDBbind test set (\(\Delta\)RMSE\(=+0.078\)(w/o Pair),\(+0.011\)(w/o Single);\(\Delta\)PCC\(= -0.036\)(w/o Pair),\(-0.001\)(w/o Single)), BDB2020+ (\(\Delta\)RMSE\(= +0.058\)(w/o Pair),\(+0.099\)(w/o Single);\(\Delta\)PCC\(= -0.093\)(w/o Pair),\(-0.092\)(w/o Single)), EGFR (\(\Delta\)RMSE\(= +0.060\)(w/o Pair),\(-0.006\)(w/o Single);\(\Delta\)PCC\(= -0.003\)(w/o Pair),\(+0.044\)(w/o Single)), and Mpro (\(\Delta\)RMSE\(= +0.142\)(w/o Pair),\(+0.108\)(w/o Single);\(\Delta\)PCC\(= -0.032\)(w/o Pair),\(-0.033\)(w/o Single)). This suggests a stronger contribution from pair embeddings in most settings. Furthermore, the full model outperformed both w/o Pair and w/o Single on LP-PDBbind, BDB2020+, and Mpro, indicating that combining pair and single embeddings is typically beneficial. EGFR represents a target-specific exception, where w/o Single marginally outperformed the full model in PCC.

Removing the Fine-grained component (w/o Fine-grained) consistently degraded performance on LP-PDBbind test set (RMSE 1.505\(\rightarrow\)1.556; PCC 0.584\(\rightarrow\)0.570), BDB2020+ (RMSE 1.003\(\rightarrow\)1.151; PCC 0.574\(\rightarrow\)0.465), and Mpro (RMSE 0.808\(\rightarrow\)1.010; PCC 0.721\(\rightarrow\)0.587), and also increased RMSE on EGFR (0.716\(\rightarrow\)0.748), with no change in PCC. Removing the Coarse-grained component (w/o Coarse-grained) likewise reduced performance on LP-PDBbind test set (RMSE 1.505\(\rightarrow\)1.570; PCC 0.584\(\rightarrow\)0.557) and BDB2020+ (RMSE 1.003\(\rightarrow\)1.190; PCC 0.574\(\rightarrow\)0.508), and also degraded EGFR performance (RMSE 0.716\(\rightarrow\)0.763; PCC 0.530\(\rightarrow\)0.505). On Mpro, w/o Coarse-grained showed a lower RMSE (RMSE\(=0.752\)vs. 0.808) but a lower PCC (PCC\(=0.594\)vs. 0.721). Overall, both the Fine-grained and Coarse-grained components of MGE are essential to AlphaDTA, with the Fine-grained component capturing detailed protein–ligand cross-interaction patterns and the Coarse-grained component capturing global binding context.

To demonstrate the practical applicability of AlphaDTA, we conducted a case study targeting cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) to identify candidate potentiators among FDA-approved drugs. A total of 979 FDA-approved drugs (excluding cancer drugs) were screened. Ivacaftor, a clinically approved CFTR potentiator with well-characterized binding interactions [61], was included as a benchmark compound to validate our computational pipeline.

For each drug, AlphaFold3 was used to generate drug–target complex structures and embeddings from the CFTR amino acid sequence and drug SMILES. The resulting outputs served as input for AlphaDTA (trained on the PDBbind CleanSplit) to predict ensemblepKvalues. Binding affinity prediction was successfully completed for 904 of the 979 FDA-approved drugs considered; the remaining 75 drugs were excluded because ligand sanitization failed during IGN graph construction from AlphaFold3-predicted structures (Additional file 1: Section S6). To prioritize candidates binding to the therapeutically relevant site, we established the CFTR–ivacaftor crystal structure (PDB ID: 6O2P) as our reference. The binding site is composed of ten residues: A309, G930, L233, F236, F305, F312, F931, F932, S308, and Y304. Drugs were selected as candidates if their AlphaFold3-predicted binding sites overlapped with the reference binding site by at least five residues. Among 904 drugs for which binding affinity prediction was successfully completed, 50 drugs met this criterion (Additional file 1: Section S7).

For ivacaftor, the AlphaFold3-predicted binding site overlapped with the reference site at nine residues and achieved a predictedpKof 7.1, the highest value among all candidates. This demonstrates that AlphaDTA successfully identified ivacaftor, a clinically validated potentiator, as the top-ranked candidate within the FDA-approved drug library without relying on experimentally determined complex structures.

Among the 50 candidates, closantel emerged as the most promising compound, achieving the highest predictedpK(6.736) after ivacaftor while exhibiting eight common residues with the reference binding site. Analysis of protein–ligand interactions using PLIP (Protein–Ligand Interaction Profiler) [59] revealed that ivacaftor formed hydrogen bonds with S308,\(\pi\)–\(\pi\)stacking with F312, and hydrophobic contacts with Y304, F305, F236, and F931 (Fig.3a). Closantel similarly interacted with multiple binding site residues critical for potentiator function (Fig.3b), forming hydrophobic interactions with F316, F305, and F931,\(\pi\)–\(\pi\)stacking with F312, and hydrogen bonds with S308 and Y304. The importance of these interactions is supported by experimental evidence. Crystallographic investigations of CFTR–potentiator complexes demonstrated that S308 forms hydrogen bonds with bound potentiators, while F312 forms critical\(\pi\)–\(\pi\)stacking interactions [61]. Experimental studies using site-directed mutagenesis showed that disrupting these interactions by replacing S308 or Y304 with alanine dramatically reduced potentiator efficacy, confirming these residues as critical determinants of drug binding [61].

Protein–ligand interaction profiles ofaivacaftor,bclosantel, andcxipamide with CFTR. Grey dashed lines indicate hydrophobic contacts, blue dashed lines indicate hydrogen bonds, and green dashed lines indicate\(\pi\)–\(\pi\)stacking interactions. 2D interaction diagrams were generated using PLIP [59] and plip-to-2D [60] software. 3D binding poses of the three compounds are shown in Additional file 1: Figure S2

Not all candidates with high common residue counts exhibited favorable binding profiles. For instance, xipamide shared eight common residues with the reference site (equal to closantel), yet its predictedpK(6.003) was substantially lower than closantel’s. PLIP analysis revealed that xipamide formed hydrophobic interactions,\(\pi\)–\(\pi\)stacking, and hydrogen bonds centered on F931, along with additional hydrophobic contacts involving F312, F316, and L233 (Fig.3c). Notably, xipamide lacked the critical hydrogen bonding interactions with residues experimentally shown to be essential for potentiator binding (S308 and Y304) [61].

Within this computational screening of FDA-approved drugs, closantel was identified as a potential CFTR potentiator candidate. This assessment was based on its relatively high predicted binding affinity and predicted interactions with multiple residues previously implicated in potentiator activity [61], suggesting that closantel could be considered for experimental validation.

Under leakage-controlled configurations derived from PDBbind v2020, AlphaDTA achieved state-of-the-art or competitive performance across all benchmarks, including external test sets with varying similarity profiles to the training data, using both experimentally determined crystal structures and AlphaFold3-predicted structures. Under a strict cluster-based split, where training, validation, and test sets were separated at both ligand- and protein-cluster levels, AlphaDTA continued to achieve the best overall performance among all evaluated models. This consistency across leakage-controlled, cluster-disjoint, and external evaluation settings suggests that AlphaDTA learns representations that generalize beyond sequence or structural overlap with the training data.

Beyond prediction accuracy, the consistent performance on AlphaFold3-predicted structures has practical implications for drug discovery. By leveraging AlphaFold3-predicted complex structures and their single and pair embeddings, AlphaDTA enables binding affinity prediction using only protein sequences and ligand SMILES, without requiring experimentally resolved complex structures. Additionally, the CFTR case study demonstrates the practical utility of the pipeline. Using only sequence-derived inputs, the model ranked ivacaftor—a clinically approved CFTR potentiator—as the top candidate among FDA-approved drugs and suggested closantel as a potential drug repurposing candidate.

The performance of AlphaDTA critically depends on how representations derived from AlphaFold3 are utilized. A variant relying solely on AlphaFold3 embeddings (without GE) achieved superior or competitive performance compared to methods based on independently pretrained protein and ligand encoders (BAPULM and PMMR), suggesting that AlphaFold3 embeddings provide sufficient representational capacity for affinity prediction. Ablation studies further suggest that pair embeddings are more informative than single embeddings, as their removal leads to greater performance degradation across benchmarks. Comparisons with the simplified MGE variant suggest that these gains cannot be attributed to the embeddings alone. Instead, they arise from how MGE decomposes and integrates these representations across multiple levels of granularity, together with how Triple Adaptive Fusion leverages geometric features from predicted structures. Specifically, the Fine-grained component captures detailed protein–ligand interaction patterns through bidirectional cross-attention, whereas the Coarse-grained component provides global binding context through joint sequence encoding. Therefore, ablation experiments show that removing either component consistently degrades performance, highlighting the benefit of multi-granularity processing.

Despite these strengths, several limitations exist. A central limitation of AlphaDTA is its dependence on AlphaFold3 for protein–ligand complex prediction and representation extraction. First, this dependence introduces substantial computational cost, making AlphaDTA unsuitable for initial screening of ultra-large compound libraries containing millions of molecules. Because AlphaDTA requires AlphaFold3 inference for each protein–ligand pair, the main computational overhead arises from MSA search and template retrieval. Therefore, AlphaDTA is better suited for later-stage affinity prediction and re-ranking after the initial library has been reduced to a smaller candidate set, such as hundreds to a few thousand compounds. Second, limitations in AlphaFold3-derived representations can propagate to downstream affinity predictions. Subtle mutation-induced structural effects, local binding-site rearrangements, or alternative conformational states may not be fully captured by a single AlphaFold3-predicted complex representation. Consistent with this limitation, our additional mutation-response evaluation showed reduced sensitivity to fine-grained affinity changes between closely related protein variants (Additional file 1: Section S8).

In future work, AlphaDTA could be further improved through architectural extensions. The current architecture processes AlphaFold3 embeddings and geometric features through separate encoders before fusion. Integrating AlphaFold3 embeddings more directly into the graph construction process could enable richer interactions between structural and embedding information. In addition, the Geometric Encoder may benefit from recent advances in geometric deep learning, such as equivariant graph neural networks, which are designed to better capture the symmetries of molecular systems. We anticipate that early embedding–geometry integration, modern geometric architectures, and continued advances in protein–ligand structure prediction will further strengthen AlphaDTA and related affinity prediction frameworks.

AlphaDTA provides a framework for drug–target binding affinity prediction that leverages AlphaFold3-predicted complex structures and embeddings, reducing dependence on experimentally resolved protein–ligand complex structures. Across leakage-controlled evaluation settings derived from PDBbind, AlphaDTA achieved state-of-the-art or competitive performance on benchmarks designed to reduce sequence- and structure-level train–test overlap, using both crystal and AlphaFold3-predicted structures. The CFTR case study further demonstrated the practical utility of the framework by prioritizing ivacaftor, a clinically approved potentiator, and identifying closantel as a promising repurposing candidate among FDA-approved drugs. Together, these results support AlphaDTA as an effective approach for affinity prediction and structure-guided drug discovery when experimentally determined complex structures are unavailable.
