Given the restricted accessibility of the dataset used in this study, we conducted an ablation study on an additional publicly available dataset and corresponding task to improve reproducibility and verify that the observed trends in predictive performance are not dataset-specific.

The Tox24 Challenge is an international computational toxicology competition designed to evaluate the predictive performance of modern machine learning approaches in predicting the in vitro activity of chemicals  [28]. Specifically, building upon the earlier Tox21 initiative [29], the Tox24 Challenge focuses on predicting the binding activity of chemical compounds to transthyretin (TTR) [30], a transport protein associated with thyroid hormone regulation. The released benchmark comprises 1,512 compounds with TTR binding measurements, split into training (1,012), leaderboard (LD, 200), and blind (300) sets. The chemical structures are represented as SMILES, primarily derived from the ToxCast libraries, and encompass heterogeneous entities such as mixtures, salts, and metal-containing compounds. During the challenge, the leaderboard subset supported preliminary evaluation; in a later phase, organizers released leaderboard labels and allowed participants to merge those compounds (with labels) into the training pool for refinement, whereas the blind subset remained undisclosed until the challenge ended and defined the official RMSE-based ranking. In our ablation study, the released leaderboard labels were merged into the training pool following this protocol. Therefore, all configurations were trained on the combined 1,212 compounds (training and leaderboard sets), and the blind set served as the sole held-out evaluation set.

Table6reports the Tox24 ablation following the same (A) to (D) progression as in the main study. This experiment was not designed as a fully optimized Tox24 submission. Rather, we applied the workflow with minimal challenge-specific modification to assess whether the staged improvements observed in the ASK1 study also appear on an independently accessible benchmark. Because Tox24 differs from ASK1 in target biology, assay characteristics, data composition, and challenge design, the absolute predictive performance level and the optimal regressor are not expected to transfer directly. Consistently, whereas SVR paired best with MLM embeddings in the ASK1 study, LightGBM performed best among the regressors evaluated under the same protocol for Tox24.

Under this constrained verification setting, blind-set RMSE improved progressively from configuration (A) to (D). Adding mix-up augmentation in (C) produced the largest blind-set gain in this ladder, and tuning the regressor in (D) further reduced the blind RMSE. The 5-fold CV RMSE followed the same downward trend, decreasing from 26.9 in (A) to 25.7 in (D), providing a held-out estimate consistent with the blind-set progression. Therefore, the Tox24 experiment should be interpreted as a transparency and reproducibility check rather than as a claim of Tox24-specific optimization or state-of-the-art predictive performance. Despite this limitation, the consistent improvement across the ablation sequence supports the main methodological claim that the proposed combination of molecular representation learning, augmentation, and regressor tuning can improve external-set performance beyond the restricted ASK1 dataset.

This study highlights how SMILES preprocessing, feature extraction, model selection, and data augmentation collectively influence model performance in the prediction of IC50values for ASK1 inhibitors. Among all tested molecular representations, the combination of ChemBERTa-77 M-MLM embeddings with SVR achieved the highest predictive performance on the external test set. Because predictive performance varied substantially across both molecular encoders and regressors, the choice of encoder-regressor pair appears to play a decisive role in determining predictive accuracy.

In Tables1and5, discrepancies were observed between the cross-validation and test-set results. This discrepancy should be interpreted cautiously because the test set was not generated by splitting the full dataset, but was instead provided as an external set fromYuhan Corporationbased on in-house experiments. In terms of representation geometry, the PCA-based chemical-space analysis (Fig.2) indicates that the test compounds are largely embedded within the training-set manifold, suggesting that the test set is not entirely outside the training chemical space. However, this apparent overlap should be interpreted cautiously, because PCA provides a low-dimensional global projection and does not necessarily reflect local compound-level structural similarity between individual training and test compounds. To further examine this point, we calculated pairwise Tanimoto similarities between the test and training compounds as described in Table S3. The average similarity across the full test-training similarity matrix was 0.23, indicating that most test-training pairs were structurally dissimilar. In addition, the average nearest-neighbor similarity for each test compound was 0.53, with the highest nearest-neighbor similarity reaching 0.88. These results suggest that, although some test compounds had close analogues in the training set, the overall local structural similarity between the two sets was limited. Therefore, the PCA overlap may reflect global embedding-level similarity rather than strong compound-level similarity across the two splits.

Because the individual test-set labels were not disclosed, we could not directly assess whether label shift occurred. Therefore, the discrepancy between cross-validation and test-set performance should not be attributed to covariate shift alone. A plausible hypothesis is that the test compounds occupy a partially overlapping chemical space while exhibiting different pIC50distributions due to differences in assay conditions, experimental protocols, or measurement contexts. Accordingly, we interpret the gap in predictive performance as a possible consequence of both limited local structural similarity and potential label shift, rather than as definitive evidence of covariate shift alone.

Furthermore, although ChemBERTa-77 M-MTR has been shown to outperform ChemBERTa-77 M-MLM across multiple downstream fine-tuning tasks [22], the pretrained MLM embeddings yielded superior predictive performance in our IC50prediction setting. This suggests that ASK1 inhibitor potency prediction is less dependent on the task-specific molecular descriptors incorporated into the MTR training objectives and may instead benefit more from the structural and contextual patterns captured by MLM-based representations.

Notably, MolCLR-based embeddings (GCN/GIN) exhibited a larger fraction of explained variance in the first principal components (PC1 and PC1+PC2), implying a more compressed low-dimensional structure. However, this variance concentration did not translate into improved predictive performance (Table1), underscoring that PCA compactness is not necessarily aligned with task-relevant information for potency prediction. This is plausible because PCA is unsupervised and emphasizes directions of maximum variance, which may be driven by variance-dominant factors, such as molecular size or frequent structural motifs, rather than potency-relevant signals. Consequently, task-informative features may reside in lower-variance directions that are not captured by PC1/PC2.

In this study, we selected these molecular representation models to reflect three widely adopted paradigms [31]: a fingerprint-based approach (ECFP4), a SMILES-based transformer approach (ChemBERTa-2), and a graph-based approach (MolCLR). This selection was intended to cover conceptually distinct and commonly used representation strategies. We acknowledge that other molecular representation models, such as MolFormer [32] and MolEncoder [33], are also relevant and may offer complementary strengths. However, due to the constraints of the competitive setting and the substantial improvement of ChemBERTa-2 MLM over baseline ECFP4, we prioritized the initially selected representation models instead of conducting additional exhaustive comparison. Future work will focus on evaluating a broader range of molecular representation models to better assess their predictive performance and generalizability in SMILES-based IC50prediction tasks.

For the PubChem dataset, most data points were filtered out during the preprocessing steps. In particular, the “Unlabeled” category contains SMILES strings without associated experimental values, which limited its direct use in supervised learning. Nonetheless, these unlabeled molecules may still have considerable value. Instead of merely using them to recover missing labels and enlarge the supervised dataset, future research could explore their relationship to the synthetic samples generated through mix-up augmentation. Because those augmented samples were obtained by interpolating embedding vectors from a large pretrained model, the unlabeled molecules may help reveal whether the generated samples occupy chemically meaningful regions of the latent space.

In addition to the choice of pretrained embeddings, the mix-up-based data augmentation strategy contributed notably to improvements in predictive performance [27]. Although previous studies have shown that SMILES enumeration can expand the explored chemical space [26], it cannot populate empty regions between existing samples. Moreover, applying mix-up directly at the SMILES string level can generate chemically invalid molecules due to violations of SMILES grammar. To address these limitations, we applied mix-up in the embedding space, which avoids syntactic issues and enables smooth interpolation within the learned latent chemical manifold. This embedding-level augmentation produced more robust representations and improved generalization on the external test set.

This improved generalization is particularly relevant in regions where the original data distribution is sparse. In our dataset, no compounds were observed in the pIC50range between 10 and 13, resulting in an apparent gap in the activity distribution. Such a pattern may suggest the presence of an activity cliff, where small structural differences lead to large changes in biological activity [34]. In this context, mix-up augmentation in the embedding space can partially alleviate this issue by introducing intermediate representations (e.g., around pIC50\(\sim\)11), thereby improving the continuity of the pIC50distribution. However, these interpolated samples are synthetic and may not correspond to real molecular structures, and should therefore be interpreted with caution.

Apart from mix-up augmentation, hyperparameter optimization of the SVR model further mitigated biases arising from imbalance in the original dataset, particularly the scarcity of samples in the pIC50range of 10-12 [35]. This, in turn, improved the ability of the model to generalize across the augmented label space.

Because the proprietary CAS-derived fraction of the training data and the held-out competition test labels are not publicly redistributable, independent replication using the full Jump AI(.py) 2025 dataset is constrained. To provide verifiable evidence for the proposed workflow despite this limitation, we repeated the (A) to (D) ablation on the Tox24 challenge (Table6), which uses a publicly available dataset. The blind-set labels were released after the challenge closed, and the official ranking was based on blind RMSE. Predictive performance improved from configuration (A) to configuration (D), although the best-performing regressor differed from that used in the ASK1 study.

On Tox24, the absolute predictive performance remains modest relative to the challenge front-runners. The final configuration (D) achieved a blind RMSE of 22.7 (Table6), whereas the published leaderboard reported top blind RMSE values near 20.5 - 20.8 [36]. In terms of cross-validation performance (Table6), our 5-fold CV RMSE decreased from configuration (A) to configuration (D), consistent with the blind-set improvement. For reference, the nine individual teams analyzed by Cirino et al. [37] reported train-set CV RMSEs ranging from 20.8 to 26.5; our configuration (D) at 25.7 falls within this range, near the lower tier. Although our blind RMSE of 22.74 does not match the strongest reported results, published accounts of the challenge indicate that the top-performing entries typically relied on consensus or ensemble predictors combining multiple models, rather than on a single regressor. In contrast, our goal was not to construct a Tox24-specific optimized submission, but to retain a single explicit pipeline for ablation and external validation. Closing the remaining gap in predictive would likely require analogous ensemble, consensus, or multi-representation strategies, which we consider beyond the scope of this study.

In summary, careful data preprocessing and appropriate selection of representation are critical for accurate IC50prediction, a key component of early-stage drug discovery. This work provides a concise yet comprehensive methodology for SMILES-based potency prediction that integrates data preprocessing, molecular representation, data augmentation and regression modeling. Future work will explore additional molecular representation strategies and explore mix-up augmentation more thoroughly to further extend the proposed methodology.

title: MINERVA: a public XAI-powered platform advancing multi-target discovery in Alzheimer’s disease
author: Nicola Gambacorta; Daniela Trisciuzzi; Fabrizio Mastrolorito; Francesco Leonetti; Cosimo D. Altomare; Modesto de Candia; Marco Catto; Nicola Amoroso; Fulvio Ciriaco; Orazio Nicolotti
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder involving a complex interplay of interconnected pharmacological targets, a feature that limits the success of traditional single-target medicinal chemistry approaches. Here, we present MINERVA (Multi-target Interactive Network for Explainable Research and Visualization in Alzheimer’s disease), a public web-based platform designed to support multi-target drug discovery assisted by eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) strategies. MINERVA integrates large-scale disease-focused high-quality data comprising as many as 70,960 small molecules annotated across 33ADrelevant targets, taken from ChEMBL and CADRO databases. To capture different levels of pharmacological relevance, four distinct pharmacological thresholds (i.e., 10 μM, 1 μM, 100 nM, and 10 nM) were set to enable the parallel exploration of weak to high-affinity ligand spaces. Independent Balanced Random Forest (BRF) classifiers were trained for each AD target threshold combination using an extended core-substituent fingerprint, which ensures robustness against class imbalance and chemical heterogeneity. MINERVA incorporates a probability binning based domain of applicability (DoA) to quantify prediction reliability and a SHAP-based explainability framework to fairly map fragment-level contributions directly onto chemical structures. MINERVA is freely accessible athttps://prometheus.farmacia.uniba.it/minerva/.

Scientific contribution

Herein we introduce MINERVA, the first freely accessible platform that combines large-scale AD-related data curation, multi-target prediction, and multi-threshold bioactivity modeling within a fully explainable and user-friendly environment. By enabling transparent, ligand-based exploration of chemical space across multiple AD pathways, MINERVA provides a unique and practical resource for accelerating multi-target drug discovery in the neurodegenerative research area.

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia and a pressing global health concern, affecting more than 55 million people worldwide. By 2050, this number is expected to rise to 130 million, with significant socioeconomic and medical burdens on individuals and healthcare systems [1,2].ADmanifests clinically through progressive memory loss, cognitive decline, language impairment, and behavioral disturbances [3]. The pathology is characterized by a complex interplay of neurodegenerative mechanisms, including extracellular accumulation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques, intracellular aggregation of hyperphosphorylated tau protein forming neurofibrillary tangles, mitochondrial dysfunction, cholinergic deficits, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress [3,4,5,6]. Over the last two decades, substantial efforts have been devoted to unraveling the molecular bases of AD [7,8]. Nonetheless, therapeutic development has been met with repeated clinical failures, with more than 90% of drug candidate compounds failing during phase II and III clinical trials. Among the primary reasons for this attrition there are the limited understanding of disease heterogeneity, poor target validation, and insufficient predictability of preclinical models [9,10]. These shortcomings have fueled interest in developing predictive approaches that can properly guide early stage drug discovery by integrating bioinformatics, cheminformatics, and systems biology data [11,12,13,14]. Recent advances based on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have facilitated the derivation of highly reliable predictive models for pharmacological profiling, target engagement, toxicity prediction, and multi-target design [15,16,17,18,19,20,21,22]. While such approaches have been widely applied in oncology [23], cardiology [24], and infectious diseases [25,26], their application to neurodegenerative disorders remains relatively underexplored. In particular, existing predictive strategies often focus on single or a limited number of targets (e.g., AChE, BACE1) [27,28,29,30], thereby overlooking the multifactorial and polypharmacological nature of AD, which involves a wide network of tightly interconnected biological pathways and molecular targets. To the best of our knowledge AD involves a broad spectrum of functional classes, contributing to the onset and progression of the disorder: these span cholinergic modulation, amyloidogenic enzymes, tau-associated regulators, neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress mediators, neurotransmitter transporters and receptors, hormonal and nuclear signaling pathways, growth factor and stem cell receptors, intracellular kinases, matrix remodeling enzymes, and proteins involved in lipid and glucose metabolism [31].

In the present study, we identified 33AD-related targets based on their functional classifications and the availability of high-quality data. Experimental data for these targets were collected from two main sources: (i) the ChEMBL database [32], one of the most comprehensive repositories of chemical and pharmacological information on about three million of bioactive compounds, by employing a Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) ID driven retrieval strategy to systematically extract AD associated bioactivity data; and (ii) the Common Alzheimer's and Related Dementias Research Ontology (CADRO) database [33], a specialized resource for neurodegeneration related targets. Leveraging this comprehensive body of solid pharmacological data, we introduce MINERVA (Multi-target Interactive Network for Explainable Research and Visualization in Alzheimer's Disease), a free web-based predictive technological platform to drive the multi-target design of AD therapeutic small molecules by predicting a comprehensive interaction profile. MINERVA employs independent Balanced Random Forest classifiers trained on the entire pool of AD targets defined on the basis of their functional categories. MINERVA employs the extended core substituent fingerprint (CSFP) [34], which is optimized for medicinal chemistry purposes and provides a robust representation of fragment-level features. Noteworthy, to improve the understanding and transparency of the results, MINERVA is also empowered with an eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) framework, based on SHAP [35] (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to give users the chance of visualizing the bioactivity contribution of single molecular fragments across the 33 explored AD-related targets. This level of interpretability is essential for rational drug design, as it allows medicinal chemists to pinpoint chemotypes and pharmacophores that may drive AD target engagement. To further enhance the reliability of predictions, MINERVA incorporates an innovative domain of applicability (DoA) strategy based on probability binning. By integrating disease-specific target curation, robust ensemble modeling, fragment-based explainability, and a stringent DoA, MINERVA fills a significant gap in the neurodegenerative drug discovery landscape by allowing hypothesis-driven exploration of chemical space for multi-target AD drug candidates. It is freely accessible via an intuitive web interface available athttps://prometheus.farmacia.uniba.it/minerva/, thereby allowing access to cutting-edge predictive tools for researchers in academia and industry.

MINERVA comprises a large volume of high-quality experimental data on 70,960 small molecules with associated bioactivity values across 33 well-established AD-related targets. Specifically, ChEMBL database was employed to retrieve data, while CADRO was used exclusively as a curated source for AD target identification. AD targets have been selected on the basis of their documented involvement in AD pathology. Nevertheless, some among them (e.g., sigma 1 and sigma 2 receptors) [36,37] have not been enrolled in MINERVA due to the paucity of quantitative data currently available. With respect to ChEMBL, a MeSH ID driven approach was employed to associate specific AD ontologies with protein targets. The MeSH IDs are unique identifiers corresponding to standardized biomedical terms within the MeSH vocabulary maintained by the U.S. National Library of Medicine (https://www.nlm.nih.gov/mesh) and are extremely effective in data mining by avoiding ambiguity while ensuring consistency. The MeSH ID for AD is D000544. Within ChEMBL, the corresponding AD-related target identifiers (the so called TIDs) were thus selected by first intersecting “drug mechanism” and “drug indication” tables and then filtering the entries labeled with D000544 as MeSH ID (details are provided athttps://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/chembl/ChEMBLdb/releases/chembl_35/schema_documentation.html). Overall, this explorative analysis yielded 29AD-related targets from ChEMBL while other four were taken from CADRO, as detailed in Table1. [38,39,40,41]. To ensure homogeneous and consistent data retrieval, ChEMBL was used as the sole source for mining chemical and pharmacological information related to the 33ADassociated targets, as shown in Fig.1.

MINERVA data gathering scheme

For the sake of clarity, we grouped all the retrieved AD-related targets within their specific functional categories, as reported in Table1.

Experimental IC₅₀ values were generally used to pharmacologically flag AD-related targeting compounds. The only exception was PPARγ, for which EC₅₀ values were employed, as only agonists are relevant to AD-related therapeutic mechanisms. Bioactivity data were encoded as binary variables using four thresholds, thereby enabling users to explore varying and more stringent classification levels. More specifically, four bioactivity cutoffs were set: 10 μM, 1 μM, 100 nM, and 10 nM. For each AD-related target, compounds with bioactivity data equal to or below each given threshold were thus labeled as active, the counterpart as inactive. However, the number of classification levels also depends on the number of compounds available for each AD-related target. In this respect, a number of at least 100 active and inactive compounds was required at each bioactivity threshold to ensure statistical validity. Consequently, models were successfully derived for all bioactivity cutoffs for 20 of the 33AD-related targets. For those remaining, complete model derivation across all cutoffs was not carried out because of limited data availability. For the sake of completeness, additional information is reported in Table S1 of the Supporting Information.

The compounds reported for the AD-related targets were represented by using their canonical SMILES, target names, and associated bioactivity data. To ensure data consistency and standardization, only entries explicitly reported with IC₅₀ (or EC₅₀ in the case of PPARγ) as the standard_type were retained. Our multiple classification strategy enabled exploration of a broader range of bioactivity definitions across 33AD-related targets, thereby providing a more robust foundation for training and validating structure–activity relationship (SAR) models. In total, 70,960 compounds were collected across 33AD-related targets. The activity distribution for each targetperbioactivity cutoff is detailed in Fig.2, while the distributions of active and inactive compounds for each AD-related target at each bioactivity threshold are detailed in Table S1 of the Supporting Information.

Activity distribution of the 33AD-related targets calculated as pIC50and pEC50values and represented as purple bins. Black, yellow, cyan and red dashed lines show the employed bioactivity thresholds equal to 10 μM, 1 μM, 100 nM and 10 nM, respectively

To minimize discrepancies during the data collection from ChEMBL, a set of filtering criteria was employed as described elsewhere [15,72]: (i) target filter: “target_type: Single protein”; (ii) ligand filter: “molecule_type: Small_molecule”; “prodrug: not 1”; (iii) activity record filters: “confidence_score: > 5”; “standard_relation: = ”; “standard_type: IC50|EC50”; “standard_units: nM”; (iv) when multiple activity experimental values were available for the same compound, values in the upper and lower quintiles were discarded to mitigate the influence of outliers when estimating the average.

We employed an extended version of the CSFP, a fragment-based molecular representation specifically tailored for medicinal chemistry applications, for representing AD-related targeting compounds. The original CSFP framework was developed through the systematic decomposition of over 67,000 biologically active compounds from ChEMBL, yielding a comprehensive library of molecular cores and substituents. From this collection, the most frequent 250 single-ring fragments, 250 fused-ring fragments, and 500 common substituents were selected based on their prevalence in known bioactive scaffolds, resulting in a 1000-bit fingerprint encoding system. For the present investigation, the fingerprint dictionary was further expanded by incorporating 13 additional fragments to better reflect the structural diversity present in AD-related chemical space. These supplemental bits were specifically designed to encode functional groups and ring systems frequently encountered in drug-like molecules but underrepresented in the original CSFP. The additions include several heterocyclic and saturated ring motifs (e.g., tetrahydropyridine, hexahydropyrimidine, 2H-pyrrole, aziridine), conjugated systems such as 1,4-cyclohexadiene, and macrocyclic or large-ring features with heteroatoms (e.g., > 8-membered rings containing oxygen or nitrogen). Additional descriptors were also added for key functional moieties like carbonyls and oxepane, as well as for atoms embedded within medium- to large-sized heterocycles (e.g., sulfur, nitrogen, or oxygen in 7- to 8-membered rings) [24]. This fingerprint enhancement allowed for a more representative and chemically diverse encoding, ultimately improving the ability of ML models to discern SAR across many AD-related targets.

To mitigate informational redundancy and improve computational efficiency, a two-step feature selection strategy was carried out. Initially, pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients were computed between all feature pairs. For each pair with a correlation coefficient > 0.9, one of the two features was removed to reduce multicollinearity, thereby limiting noise in the predictive models and bias in downstream interpretability analyses. In the subsequent step, Balanced Random Forest (BRF) based feature importance was computed on the remaining variables, retaining only those with an importance score exceeding 0.001. This approach allowed us to focus on features with substantial predictive values, effectively reducing dimensionality without compromising model performance. Importantly, the removal of redundant features also plays a critical role in the context of model explainability: high feature correlation can alter SHAP value distributions, leading to misleading attributions. By implementing this stringent reduction pipeline, we enhanced both the efficiency and the interpretive clarity of our models, facilitating more reliable chemical insight in the multi-target drug discovery framework for AD. Table S2 summarizes the final number of features usedpertarget at each bioactivity threshold after applying the described filters.

The BRF algorithm was employed to develop all the predictive models. This ensemble method extends the traditional Random Forest by performing random undersampling of the majority class within each bootstrap iteration, thereby mitigating class imbalance and improving predictive performance for minority classes. To assess model performance, ten independent random splits were performed, each allocating 20% of the experimental data to external test sets. The remaining 80% of the data served as the training set and was subjected to fivefold stratified cross-validation (CV), maintaining the ration of actives and inactive unchanged in each fold. This was iterated ten times to ensure statistical robustness. The overall summary concerning the training and derivation of the models is detailed in Fig.3.

Comprehensive pipeline of model training and derivation

Model performances were evaluated using several metrics, including accuracy, balanced accuracy (BA), F1-score, sensitivity, specificity, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), computed as follows:

For reasons of completeness, additional metrics (e.g. AUC, NPV, PPV, BA, F1-score) were enclosed (File_S1.csv, File_S2.csv, File_S3.csv and File_S4.csv) as Supporting Information.

To ensure optimal model configuration, we explored a hyperparameter grid search including the number of estimators (100, 200, 500), maximum features (sqrt, log2), and minimum samplesperleaf (1, 2, 4) for the most populated bioactivity threshold (1 μM). As reported in the File_S6.csv of the Supporting Information, the MCC showed no significant changes over the baseline models.

The reliability prediction of thein silicostrategies represents a critical aspect of drug discovery, especially when employing multiple level classifiers across heterogeneous biological mechanisms as those involved in AD. To evaluate the predictive reliability, we analyzed the distribution of correctly and incorrectly classified samples across probability bins ranging from 0 to 1, with a bin width of 0.1. For each AD-related target, the ratio between correct and total predictions was computed within each bin as an estimate of predictive reliability. Because the different AD datasets were very often highly imbalanced, a balancing correction was applied to adjust the relative contribution of low- and high-probability bins. The balancing coefficients\({c}_{0}\)and\({c}_{1}\), were equal to the total number of true active and true inactive compounds, respectively, across the entire bin range.

The ratio between these coefficients was used to assess the degree of imbalance:

If the ratio deviated significantly from 1, the counts within each bin were rescaled proportionally to\({c}_{0}\)and\({c}_{1}\)to achieve a more uniform contribution across the probability spectrum. The final balanced reliability ratio was then computed as:

wherekdenotes the probability bin index (k= 1,…,10), corresponding to the ten sub-intervals of the [0,1] prediction range defined by a bin width of 0.1. For each bink,\({n}_{corr,k}^{\left(bal\right)}\)and\({n}_{incorr,k}^{\left(bal\right)}\)represent the balanced counts of correctly and incorrectly classified samples after applying the rescaling factors derived fromc0andc1.This manual correction procedure ensured a more consistent estimation of prediction reliability across bins, particularly for those targets affected by strong class imbalance. This analysis shows that model confidence is highest at the boundaries of the predicted score range. Predictions associated with high scores (e.g., > 0.9) consistently exhibit high reliability and are therefore considered within the DoA, whereas predictions with scores close to 0.5 display near-random reliability and should be regarded as outside the DoA and interpreted with caution. This approach allows us to evaluate the prediction accuracy within each bin using CV. The resulting DoA histograms provide users with an intuitive, probabilistically anchored assessment of confidence, by improving traditional distance-to-model or leverage-based DoA techniques.

In this study, model interpretability was addressed through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, which are grounded in cooperative game theory and quantify the individual contribution of each feature to a given prediction. For each of the 33AD-related targets, explainability analysis was performed using a tree-based SHAP explainer implemented via the SHAP Python package (v0.44.0). This allowed for both global and local interpretation of model behavior across structurally diverse compounds. To facilitate chemical insight, the SHAP derived fragment importance scores were mapped directly onto molecular structures, where each bit of the extended CSFP contributed to the final classification output. These fragments were flagged with color-coded highlights identifying molecular substructures associated with predicted activity. This fragment-level transparency enhances the interpretability of predictions, enabling researchers to identify molecular moieties likely to drive or prevent bioactivity across many AD-related targets.

Following the data curation protocol outlined in the Methods section, a total of 70,960 compounds were collected across the 33AD-related targets, each fulfilling the criteria for IC₅₀ (or EC50) based classification. The final dataset encompassed many protein targets with sufficient bioactivity data to support robust SAR analyses. For each retained AD-related target, compound distributions were evaluated across the four bioactivity thresholds (10 μM, 1 μM, 100 nM, and 10 nM), thereby providing multiple level classifications. Within each bioactivity threshold, we observed heterogeneous yet informative distributions: some AD-related targets exhibited relatively balanced ratios between active and inactive compounds, whereas others displayed strong imbalances, possibly reflecting the biological relevance or assay coverage. This variability underscores the importance of adopting target- and threshold-specific modeling strategies in conceiving ML workflows.

Multiple level classifiers based on BRF were successfully trained at each bioactivity threshold considering all the AD-related targets. Performance evaluation across the ten independent data splits demonstrated consistent and reliable predictive behaviors. For each split, the external test sets, comprising 20% of the initial data, provided an unbiased measure of generalization performance, while the 5-fold stratified CV iterated ten times on the remaining 80% offered insights into model stability and robustness. Across all AD-related targets, the models achieved generally fair to high balanced accuracy (with mean values in the range from 0.65 to 0.91 irrespective of the bioactivity cutoffs), with particularly strong performance observed on AD-related targets with more balanced distributions. Sensitivity and specificity values varied (with mean values in the range from 0.64 to 0.91 and from 0.59 to 0.91 respectively, irrespective of the bioactivity cutoffs) depending on class imbalance, yet remained within acceptable ranges, indicating that the models were capable of correctly identifying both active and inactive compounds. Overall metrics obtained from CV analyses are reported in Table2.

Notably, as detailed in Table S3 of the Supporting Information, MCC values ranging from 0.26 to 0.82 further confirmed the model predictive power, especially for those AD-related targets with highly unbalanced datasets. In this respect, we also compared our BRF models against alternative imbalanced-learning strategies, such as SMOTE and cost-sensitive methods [73,74]. As shown in File_S5.csv of the Supporting Information, the results are consistent with those returned by using BRF, thus further supporting the robustness of our modeling framework.

Overall, the ten-fold repetition of both CV and data splitting allowed for a thorough statistical characterization of model performance, mitigating the impact of data partitioning bias. For clarity, the CV and test set MCC values for each AD-related target, computed at each bioactivity threshold, are shown in Table S3 of the Supporting Information. To provide a complete picture, all computed metrics for each cutoff were attached to the Supporting Information as File S1, S2, S3 and S4 for 10 ﻿μM, 1 ﻿μM, 100 nM and 10 nM thresholds, respectively.

To better challenge the reliability of our models, a scaffold split-based validation was performed at each bioactivity threshold. Specifically, compounds were clustered according to their Bemis-Murcko scaffolds [75], and a group-fivefold cross-validation scheme was applied. This analysis showed a slight deterioration of the average MCC values due to the structural diversity of the scaffolds held out in each validation fold but without compromising the robustness of the predictive power across all models at each cut-off, as shown in Table S5 of the Supporting Information.

The CSFP was preferred as fingerprint as it is acknowledged to ensure a straight link between model performance and unequivocal chemical patterns, thereby enhancing model transparency [76,77]. Consequently, SHAP based interpretability analyses provided a comprehensive overview of the fragment-level determinants driving model predictions across the 33AD-related targets. For each AD model, global SHAP summary plots were generated with the aim of ranking the CSFP encoded fragments according to their overall contribution to the classification result. As representative examples, we show here a pair of AD-related targets taken from distinct functional categories (Figs.4,5), by reporting the global SHAP summary plot corresponding to the most stringent bioactivity threshold. For the remaining AD-related targets, all global SHAP visualizations are freely available for download in the Data section of the MINERVA website.

Each point represents a compound in the training set, where positive or negative SHAP values indicate the fragment contribution toward predicting the active or inactive class, respectively. As far as AChE is concerned, the two most influential features driving the predicted activity class were the 1,2,3,4-tetrahydroacridine and piperidine rings. Notably, the 1,2,3,4-tetrahydroacridine scaffold constitutes the core of tacrine, a well-established AChE inhibitor and the structural core of several highly potent analogues [78,79,80,81]. Similarly, the piperidine ring is a moiety of the approved drug donepezil, where it plays a key role in mediating π–π and cation–π interactions with the critical Trp86 residue within anionic subsite of the catalytic site (CAS) [82]. For BACE1, the pyridine ring emerged as the most informative fragment, in line with structural and computational evidence showing that its nitrogen atom often forms hydrogen bond or electrostatic interactions with Trp76 in the S2′ subsite and can also engage in stabilizing contacts with Arg235 [83,84]. Moreover, extensive fluorine scan studies have demonstrated that strategic fluorination of aromatic rings can affect both binding affinity and ADME properties across many BACE1 inhibitors, highlighting its relevance in the optimization of drug-like profiles [85]. Interestingly, similar patterns of features for AChE and BACE- are consistently observed across all bioactivity cutoffs, further highlighting the importance of these features in distinguishing active compounds.

For PPARγ, two structural features emerged as the most relevant drivers of the active class prediction: the oxazole ring and the methoxy/ethoxy substituted benzene moiety. The oxazole heterocycle is a well-established scaffold in PPARγ ligand design, largely due to its dual capability to act as a hydrogen bond acceptor and to engage in aromatic interactions within the ligand binding pocket. The combination of methoxy and ethoxy groups increases the electron density of the aromatic ring, important for high affinity binding in the predominantly hydrophobic cavity of PPARγ [86,87].

With regard to HDAC1, the most informative fragment was the long aliphatic chain, which is specifically designed to occupy the narrow hydrophobic slot leading to the catalytic Zn2⁺ ion, a region naturally engaged by the acetylated lysine side chain of histone substrates. In addition, the thienyl group frequently appears in potent HDAC inhibitors because of its ability to accommodate within the so called foot pocket, reinforcing hydrophobic interactions and contributing to optimal positioning of the zinc binding group [88,89,90]. In line with the previous case study, the recurrence of specific and discussed feature patterns for PPARγ and HDAC1 across all activity thresholds further supports and strengthens the explainability analysis performed by MINERVA. Satisfactorily, across all examined targets, the features highlighted by the SHAP analysis strongly align with their experimentally known interaction patterns. For transparency, Figures S1-S6 show the global SHAP analysis for 10 ﻿μM, 1 ﻿μM and 100 nM cutoffs, respectively.

The MINERVA platform provides a free, browser-based environment for real timein silicomulti-target prediction of small molecules against 33 targets implicated in AD. The web interface allows users to input a query compound either by drawing its 2D structure through an embedded JSME editor or by pasting its SMILES notation, as shown in Fig.6.

MINERVA input page. For the sake of clarity, the 2D structure of XYY-CP1106 is reported on the white board

Upon submission, MINERVA executes a standardized prediction workflow, with each query typically completing within a few seconds depending on server load and molecular complexity. The platform returns a report structured of three main sections and made available as HyperText Markup Language (HTML) links.

(i) The first panel indicates whether the query molecule is present in the training datasets of MINERVA. When available, a summary table containing the corresponding TID, target name, and experimental activity (nM) is provided; otherwise, a notice explicitly states that the query compound does not have any computed experimental value.

(ii) The second panel consists of a summary table listing all 33AD-related targets. For each AD-related target, MINERVA reports a binary prediction (active/inactive) in which are included:

The Pred_score, indicating the prediction score of each model.

The DoA_score, reflecting the domain of applicability analysis, expressing the reliability of the prediction whose value corresponds to the\({R}_{k}^{\left(bal\right)}\)described in Method section.

(iii) When the query compound is predicted as active toward a given AD-related target, MINERVA generates additional levels of visualization. These include:

A SHAP-based local explanation plot, highlighting fragment-level contributions to the predicted activity.

A reliability plot evaluating the robustness of the individual model prediction.

To illustrate the complete prediction workflow, we evaluated MINERVA using XYY-CP1106, an investigational drug candidate for AD treatment exhibiting an inhibitory activity (IC50) of 14.7 nM against Monoamine Oxidase B (MAO-B) [91]. Results are summarized in Fig.7.

Target-level MINERVA output page for predicted active compounds towards MAO-B target, including color map based SHAP explanation and reliability assessment

As shown in Fig.7, MINERVA correctly identified XYY-CP1106 as an active compound across all four bioactivity thresholds for MAO-B, with DoA scores of 0.94, 0.71, 0.61, and 0.61 at the 10 µM, 1 µM, 100 nM, and 10 nM thresholds, respectively. The explainability analysis further highlighted the coumarin core as chemotype widely occurring in potent MAO-B inhibitors, as a key contributor to activity [92]. In particular, the combination of the coumarin ring with an ethoxy linker connecting to a second aromatic moiety was consistently ranked among the most influential structural elements. This arrangement aligns with established SARs for MAO-B ligands, where planar aromatic systems favor π–π stacking interactions within the aromatic cage (e.g., residues Tyr398 , Tyr435 and FAD cofactor), while flexible linkers help position substituents toward the hydrophobic binding cavity. For the sake of clarity, only the 10 nM model, the most informative threshold due to its ability to capture the highest affinity ligand subset, was included in the figure. In line with MINERVA multi-target design framework, XYY-CP1106 was also predicted to display reliable activity against additional AD relevant targets, including AChE and BACE1, supporting its potential suitability as a multi-target agent. As described in Fig.8, the explainability maps for AChE again emphasized the coumarin core linked to an additional aromatic moiety, in agreement with structural features frequently observed in dual AChE and MAO-B inhibitors, as reported elsewhere [92]. Conversely, the model for BACE1 assigned elevated importance to the fluorine atoms linked to aromatic ring and to the dihydropyridine fragment, both of which are consistent with known medicinal chemistry determinants for BACE1 binding.

Additional target-level output returned from XYY-CP1106 prediction

In agreement with this multi-target profile, XYY-CP1106 was also predicted to be active against COX-2 and MMP-13. In this context, the presence of a the hydroxypyridone moiety (i.e., the pharmacophore of the iron-chelator drug deferiprone) introduces an additional disease-oriented mechanism through its well-established Fe3⁺-chelating capability. While this fragment is not expected to directly interact with enzymatic metal centers, metal chelation may modulate redox- and inflammation-driven pathways implicated in AD. This aspect is particularly relevant for the heme-dependent COX-2 and for inflammation-associated metalloproteinases such as MMP-13, whose expression and functional regulation are influenced by oxidative stress. Altogether, the predicted activity on these targets, combined with the deferiprone fragment, further supports a multi-mechanistic and system-level mode of action. For completeness, Figure S7 of Supporting Information reports the corresponding results.

In this work, we present MINERVA, a dedicated predictive platform for AD that integrates high quality bioactivity data, robust machine learning models, and fragment-level explainability. By collecting 70,960 compounds across 33ADrelevant targets and applying an enhanced CSFP fingerprint, BRF classifiers, and a probability-binning DoA, we conceived a framework capable of reliable activity prediction across heterogeneous and imbalanced datasets. Furthermore, the ability to explore four different bioactivity thresholds provides a customizable level of analysis, making MINERVA suitable for both expert and non-expert users according to their specific goals. Moreover, a key strength of MINERVA is the use of SHAP-based interpretability, which maps molecular fragments directly to their contributions in target specific predictions with the aim of better driving the rational design of multi-target ligands. The MINERVA web-based interface also demonstrates its ability to recognize known patterns and provide transparent target-level explanations. Overall, MINERVA fills a critical gap in computational resources for neurodegenerative drug discovery. By combining disease-specific target curation, high performance predictive modeling, and interpretable output within an accessible framework, it offers a practical and free-to-use tool to guide the exploration of chemical space in AD. Future extensions may incorporate additional targets, endpoints, and modeling strategies, further expanding the platform purpose in accelerating multi-target AD drug design. Last not least, MINERVA can screen large volumes of data on demand, ensuring both scalability and flexibility in its application. title: P2MAT: A machine learning (ML) driven software for Property Prediction of MATerial
author: Methun Kamruzzaman; Alexander Landera; Nalini Menon; Mark D. Allendorf; Kunal Poorey
text:
Accurate prediction of melting points for pure molecules remains a significant challenge in predictive chemistry, with implications across various scientific fields, including materials science, drug discovery, and separations chemistry. Traditional methods, such as group contribution (GC) techniques, have shown limited success due to the complex relationship between molecular structure and melting point. In this study, we present a data-driven machine learning (ML) approach to predict the melting points of organic compounds, leveraging both 2D and 3D molecular descriptors. Our results indicate that ML models can significantly improve melting-point predictions, providing a robust tool for the scientific community.

Scientific contribution

Our detailed analysis on melting point prediction, along with SHAP explainability, reveals the top influencing features for the prediction. The P2MAT application we developed as part of this study can predict both melting and boiling points from a SMILES string. P2MAT is available as an easy-to-install, user-friendly GUI for maximum outreach to the scientific community. Our benchmark analysis demonstrates the excellence of our method for predicting melting points.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

An important and long-standing goal in predictive chemistry is the development of an accurate melting point model that is generally applicable to a wide range of molecules. Many decades of work have been invested in this endeavor, but thus far, none are sufficiently accurate to make useful and confident predictions for compounds without a measured melting point. Indeed, an improved understanding of melting point would be useful across large areas of science, including, but not limited to, materials for energy applications [1,2,3], drug discovery [4,5], organic hydrogen getters [6,7], ionic liquids [8,9], and separations chemistry [10,11] as well as the prediction of properties such as viscosity [12]. Accurate predictions of melting points are difficult because large differences in melting points can arise from small changes to molecular structure. Existing melting point models fall broadly into two categories: those that leverage group contribution (GC) theory and those that use machine learning (ML) techniques. Krzyzaniak et al. [13] used the solid–liquid phase transition equation,\(T_m = \frac{\Delta H_m}{\Delta S_m}\), to develop a melting point model. The enthalpy of melting (\(\Delta H_m\)) was estimated using GC methods, and the entropy of melting (\(\Delta S_m\)) was estimated using an equation that depends on the rotational symmetry number and the molecular flexibility number of the target molecule. Using a database of 596 melting points containing only aliphatic non-hydrogen-bonding molecules, their method was found to have a root mean square error (RMSE) of\(34.3\,^\circ\)C. Subsequent papers from this group have suggested that the largest source of error comes from the estimate of\(\Delta S_m\). The model was later expanded to include aromatic and aliphatic rings using a modified expression for the molecular flexibility number, yielding a comparable average absolute error (AAE) of\(33.2\,^\circ\)C [14]. Estimating\(\Delta S_m\)is challenging and limits the utility of methods that make use of the phase transition equation. Marrero and Gani [15] developed a different GC method that accounts for the chemical environment around a chemical group via the use of second-order and third-order group contributions. Second and third-order group contributions are corrections to the original, first-order contribution. Special emphasis was given to improving the prediction of cyclic groups (both aliphatic and aromatic). When both second and third-order groups were used, the AAE was reduced to\(20.22\,^\circ\)C (down from\(24.9\,^\circ\)C when only first-order corrections were used). ML methods that incorporate molecular descriptors can serve as an alternative to GC-based methods. For example [16], used a series of ML methods incorporating 2D and 3D features. 2D features are chemical descriptors that encode topological information, whereas 3D features encode 3-dimensional shape and functionality information. Several approaches were used, in which different sets of databases, different ML methods, and different sets of features were used. These approaches achieved an MAE of 25–\(29\,^\circ\)C. [17] used the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Center (CCDC) database, which contains 58, 810 unique crystal structures with associated melting points (Zhu 2023). Some of these crystal structures are duplicates, but are considered unique by the authors because they are different enough. The authors argue that because their goal is to generate 3D descriptors from the crystal structures, these duplicates are worth keeping in the dataset. The authors went on to train their melting point model by using Deep learning [18], XGBoost [19], and Random forest methods [20], using 2D, 3D, and 2D + 3D descriptors. The best-performing model was trained using XGBoost with only 2D descriptors. This model achieved an MAE of\(28.1\,^\circ\)C.

Here, we report the development of several melting point ML models trained using a database of 19, 811 data points [21]. The models differ based on the ML technique (linear regression [22], deep learning, etc.), the use of 2D structural Padel features vs. 2D + 3D structural Padel features, and the degree of feature engineering used. Errors are quantified using 5-fold validation. Explainability is incorporated into the best-performing model via the SHAP algorithm [23], and a discussion of the accuracy of the best-performing melting point model on subsets of chemically relevant molecules (molecules containing onlyC,H, andO, for example) is given.

P2MAT is a desktop application that works on multiple platforms. It predicts the thermophysical properties of chemical compounds using SMILES input strings. This section explains the third-party packages that support the software, the technical setup that connects these components, the installation, the license, and the known limitations of the current version. Table1lists the main third-party libraries used in P2MAT. The software needs Python 3.12 and operates within a specificcondaenvironment [24] (qsai), as defined inQSAI.yml. Figure1provides a schematic overview of how the different parts of P2MAT work together.

High-level system architecture of P2MAT. The application has a multi-threaded design. A PyQt5-based GUI manages user interactions. A dedicated background worker handles the four-step structural property prediction pipeline. This includes molecule validation, batch descriptor computation, and domain-specific stacking ensemble prediction

Graphical user interface

The application window (GUI Layer), shown in Fig.1, is built using PyQt5 [25]. To keep the Qt event loop responsive during predictions, all blocking tasks are handled in aQThreadsubclass calledPredictionWorker. This worker communicates with the main thread using four specific Qt signals:progress(int),result(object),invalid_smiles(list), anderror(str). When the application starts, it loads the visible properties and the enabled state of each checkbox from a singleconfig.jsonfile. This setup allows users to change properties without needing to recompile or repackage the application.

Molecular descriptor computation

Molecular features are computed using PaDEL-Descriptor [26], a Java-based cheminformatics tool that generates both 2D and 3D descriptors from SMILES strings. ThepadelpyPython wrapper calls PaDEL through the system’s Java runtime, producing up to about 1,240 numerical descriptors per molecule. To process large query sets efficiently, SMILES strings are submitted to PaDEL in batches of 128 molecules by default. A divide-and-conquer fallback strategy ensures that if a batch call fails, the batch is split in half until individual molecules are processed. This way, one problematic structure does not stop the analysis of the remaining molecules. The temporary.smiinput and.csvoutput files created during each PaDEL call are stored in the operating system’s temporary directory and are deleted right after they are read, whether the call succeeds or fails.

Input SMILES strings are checked for structure using RDKit [27] before calculating any descriptors. Specifically,Chem.MolFromSmilesprocesses each candidate string. A return value ofNoneor any exception indicates an invalid structure. Invalid SMILES strings are sent back to the caller and shown to the user without interrupting predictions for the other molecules.

Path resolution and packaging

Resource paths for models, feature lists, CSS, and images are managed by thehelper.resource_pathutility. This tool checks during runtime whether the application is running as a standard Python script or as a PyInstaller-frozen binary (sys._MEIPASS). This method provides consistent and dependable access to assets in both deployment modes.

P2MAT is open-source software available for download athttps://doi.org/10.11578/ dc.20260318.3. Detailed instructions for setting up and using this software are available on the GitHub readme page, along with a visual representation that should help users get started directly.

P2MAT is distributed as a platform-specific installer that automates all prerequisite setup. Three platforms are currently supported: macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows (x64), and Linux (x86_64 / aarch64). Table2summarises the installer type, distribution format, install location, and approximate disk footprint for each platform.

All three installers follow the same six-stage sequence: (1) verify the system and architecture, (2) install Java, (3) install Miniconda3, (4) create theqsaiConda environment fromQSAI.yml, (5) copy application files, and (6) create a launcher or shortcut. It requires an active internet connection for the initial installation; all subsequent launches can be done offline. The macOS installer requires Homebrew as the package manager. The Linux installer automatically detects the distribution from/etc/os-releaseand selects the right package manager (apt,dnf,zypper, orpacman) to install OpenJDK,17. On Windows, Java can be obtained throughwingetor by direct MSI download ifwingetis not available. An optional Inno Setup wizard installer (P2MAT-v1.0.0-Windows-x64-Setup.exe) is provided for users who want a guided graphical installation experience. For advanced users who already havecondaand Java installed, the application can be launched directly from the repository without running the specific installer.

conda env create -f QSAI.yml

cd P2MAT && python p2mat.py
