The current release of P2MAT has the following known technical and usability limitations.

Technical limitations

Platform support: The macOS distribution has been compiled and tested only on Apple Silicon (M-series) hardware. An Intel Mac build is unavailable because the melting-point DNN was trained with PyTorch’s Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend. Running the same artifact on an x86 CPU would need retraining on that hardware.

Java dependency: PaDEL-Descriptor requires a Java runtime environment, specifically OpenJDK 11 or later. If Java is not installed or not in the systemPATH, descriptor computation may fail due to a timeout or subprocess error. The installers take care of this requirement automatically. However, for manual installations, users must ensure that Java is properly installed and configured.

PaDEL timeout and complex molecules: Each molecule has a 10-second timeout in PaDEL. Very large, highly branched, or structurally unusual molecules might exceed this limit, causing them to be skipped without notice after the divide-and-conquer method has been exhausted. Processing these molecules one at a time or increasing the timeout value may help with this problem.

Applicability domain: All machine learning models for predicting melting and boiling points were trained on limited, curated datasets made mostly of organic molecules. As a result, predictions for structures outside the chemical space covered by the training data, such as inorganic salts, organometallic compounds, or molecules with very rare functional groups, might be unreliable. Since there is no automatic filter for applicability domains, users must carefully interpret results for unusual inputs.

Internet requirement: An active internet connection is needed during the first installation to download Miniconda, the package dependencies, and OpenJDK. Offline installation is not supported.

Usability limitations

Input format: P2MAT accepts only SMILES strings as input. Other common molecular representations, like InChI, MOL/SDF files, and CAS registry numbers, are not supported. They must be converted to SMILES externally before use.

Batched descriptor computation: Molecular descriptors are created in batches of 128 SMILES strings using PaDEL-Descriptor, a Java-based application that runs as a subprocess. PaDEL starts once per batch instead of once for the entire dataset, causing the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) startup time to occur repeatedly, about\(\lceil \frac{N}{128}\rceil\)times for N molecules. Since each JVM initialization usually takes several seconds, this cumulative time becomes significant for large datasets. This is the main reason processing hundreds of molecules can take several minutes.

Single-session results: Prediction results are kept in memory only for the session. The system does not have history tracking or session persistence. Any results that are not exported to a CSV file before closing the window will be lost permanently.

Minimum one property constraint: The graphical user interface requires users to select at least one property checkbox at all times. If all checkboxes are unchecked, the melting point option is automatically turned back on as a fallback. This design stops prediction runs from happening with no properties selected, even though it may be surprising for users who only want to check SMILES input without running a model.

Schematic of the full modeling pipeline, from data preprocessing and feature selection to model training and evaluation

The modeling pipeline (Fig.2) was created as a clear and fully reproducible framework. It included preprocessing methods, feature selection techniques, and machine learning algorithms across three chemically defined datasets: CHO, CHON, and FULL. Each dataset went through three input transformation methods: no transformation, StandardScaler, and Quantile Transformer. Four feature selection approaches were applied: Whole (no feature removal), Boruta [28], Pearson correlation [29] filtering, and principal component analysis (PCA) [30]. The resulting feature sets trained six regression models: Ridge [31], ElasticNet [32], Extra Trees [33], LightGBM [34], XGBoost [19], and a deep neural network (DNN) [35], resulting in a total of 216 distinct model configurations. For each configuration, we optimized hyperparameters independently using Bayesian search [36] to ensure fair comparison. The best-performing base learners were then combined into a two-level stacking ensemble [37]. Out-of-fold predictions served as meta-features for a Ridge regression meta-learner. This approach created a final model with lower generalization error than any individual model. We also conducted an applicability domain analysis using the Williams plot [38]. This analysis identified response outliers and high-leverage compounds, assessed the structural coverage of the training set, and evaluated the reliability of predictions on the test set. Finally, to understand the predictions of the top-performing tree-based models and identify the molecular descriptors that mainly drive changes in property prediction, we calculated Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) [23] using the TreeExplainer algorithm. This analysis provided precise feature attributions for each compound while meeting the key game-theoretic principles of efficiency, symmetry, and additivity.

In this pipeline, StandardScaler was employed as one of three input transformation methods, together with no transformation and QuantileTransformer. To prevent data leakage, it was fitted exclusively to the training set. This approach centers each molecular descriptor to a mean of zero and scales it to unit variance. Consequently, models that are sensitive to feature gradients, such as Ridge, Elastic Net, and deep neural networks (DNNs), are less likely to be disproportionately affected by descriptors with large numerical ranges.

The Quantile Transformer was adopted as an alternative to the Standard Scaler to better accommodate the skewed, heavy-tailed distributions frequently present in computed molecular descriptors, including topological indices and connectivity counts. Instead of scaling features to unit variance, this method transforms each feature’s marginal distribution into a uniform or approximately normal distribution. Consequently, it offers increased robustness to outliers, which might otherwise distort variance estimates and negatively influence the performance of distance-based or gradient-based machine learning algorithms.

Boruta feature selection approach [28] was designed to identify all features that provide meaningful information about the target variable, rather than stopping once a minimal sufficient subset had been found. In the current pipeline, XGBoost was used as the base estimator, configured with 100 estimators and tree_method=“hist” on the CPU. The algorithm was allowed to run for up to 100 iterations. In each iteration, shadow versions of all features were generated by permuting their values, and the model was trained on the combined set of original and shadow features. A feature was considered confirmed if its importance exceeded the maximum importance of the shadow features at the 100th percentile, which served as a stringent selection criterion. To reduce unnecessary computation, early stopping was applied after 20 consecutive rounds without change. Both confirmed and tentatively confirmed (weakly confirmed) features were retained according to the support criterion. This procedure yielded compact feature subsets ranging from 78 to 127 features, depending on the dataset (e.g., 101 for CHO and 127 for FULL). Overall, this represented approximately a\(90\%\)reduction from the original\(\sim 1,100\)to 1, 200 descriptors while preserving the most informative variables.

Feature selection was performed using a two-stage Pearson correlation [29] filter applied exclusively to the training set. In the first stage (termed relevance filtering), features (X) were retained only when the absolute Pearson correlation between each feature and the target variable (Y) exceeded 0.05. This step eliminated descriptors with little linear association withY. In the second stage (referred to as redundancy reduction), the remaining features were ranked in descending order according to their correlation with the target and then pruned greedily. A feature was removed if its correlation with any previously accepted feature was greater than or equal to 0.85. This procedure reduced multicollinearity while preserving the most informative representative from each related feature cluster. The final subset was of moderate size and low redundancy, comprising approximately 306–389 features across the datasets.

Principal component analysis (PCA) [30] was used as a feature selection strategy to transform the scaled molecular descriptor space into an orthogonal, lower-dimensional representation. The method was configured to retain the smallest number of principal components (PCs) required to explain at least\(90\%\)of the total variance in the training set, while also enforcing a minimum of 10 components to prevent cases in which only a few PCs captured nearly all of the variance. As a result, between 84 and 113 PCs were retained, depending on the dataset, representing a substantial reduction from the original 1,100–1,200 descriptors. Although PCA reduces collinearity and noise by discarding low-variance directions, it also decreases interpretability because each component represents a combination of the original descriptors. More importantly, because PCA is an unsupervised method that maximizes variance rather than predictive relevance, it can weaken the relationship between features and target variables. This limitation was reflected in the observed model performance.

To minimize structural overlap between training and test sets and reduce the risk of information leakage in model evaluation, a chemistry-aware cluster-based split was employed in place of a simple random partition. Morgan circular fingerprints [39,40] (radius 2,2048 bits) were computed for all valid compounds using RDKit’s MorganGenerator. Pairwise Tanimoto distances [41,42] were then computed in parallel across all compound pairs, and the Butina algorithm [43] was applied to cluster compounds at a similarity threshold of 0.8 (distance cutoff 0.2). The resulting clusters were randomly shuffled and greedily assigned to the test set until approximately\(20\%\)of the dataset was reached, ensuring that structurally similar compounds always reside in the same partition. The quality of the split was assessed by computing three Tanimoto similarity distributions: pairwise within-train, pairwise within-test, and the maximum cross-set similarity of each test compound to its nearest training neighbor. A low mean cross-set similarity and a small fraction of test compounds with nearest-neighbor similarity\(\ge 0.8\)confirm that the cluster-based partition effectively separates the chemical spaces of the training and test sets. Figure3illustrates the train-test splitting strategy used to minimize information leakage.

Butina clustering was used to split the data, as shown here. The full dataset was grouped based on Tanimoto similarity of molecular fingerprints. Clusters were then assigned to the training and test sets to minimize structural overlap. Table3presents the resulting distributions of pairwise similarities within and between the sets

Ridge regression [31] is a regularized extension of ordinary least squares (OLS). It is designed to reduce multicollinearity and limit overfitting by adding an\(L_2\)penalty to the loss function. It aims to minimize the residual sum of squares while enforcing a constraint on the squared Euclidean norm of the coefficient vector:

where\(\alpha \ge 0\)is the regularization hyperparameter. The closed-form solution,\(\hat{\textbf{w}} = (\textbf{X}^\top \textbf{X} + \alpha \textbf{I})^{-1}\textbf{X}^\top \textbf{y}\), always exists. This holds true even when\(\textbf{X}^\top \textbf{X}\)is singular, which improves numerical stability in high-dimensional descriptor spaces. As\(\alpha\)increases, the coefficient magnitudes shrink toward zero. This reduces model variance, but it also increases bias. Unlike Lasso, Ridge keeps all features and applies the penalty evenly across correlated predictors instead of selecting one variable arbitrarily. In this study, Ridge Regression is the linear baseline for comparing the nonlinear models. We optimized the regularization strength,\(\alpha\), using Bayesian hyperparameter optimization over the range\([10^{-4},10^3]\)with a log-uniform prior. This approach reflects the wide dynamic range usually seen for this parameter in high-dimensional QSAR settings.

Elastic Net regression [32] combines the\(L_1\)penalty from Lasso and the\(L_2\)penalty from Ridge regression within a single optimization framework. This allows for variable selection and coefficient shrinkage to happen at the same time.

where\(\alpha\)controls the overall regularization strength and\(\rho \in [0,1]\)(the l1_ratio) determines the balance between the two penalties. When\(\rho =1\), Elastic Net becomes Lasso. When\(\rho = 0\), it becomes Ridge. The\(L_1\)component encourages sparsity by shrinking irrelevant coefficients to exactly zero, which provides implicit feature selection. The\(L_2\)component stabilizes the solution when there are groups of highly correlated descriptors. This is common in molecular fingerprint spaces, where similar fragments create correlated binary bits. Elastic Net was chosen over Support Vector Regression (SVR) [44] because it has a much lower computational cost on large datasets, training in seconds instead of minutes. It also fits well with high-dimensional, sparse descriptor matrices. Both\(\alpha\)and\(\rho\)were optimized together using Bayesian search.

The Extra Trees (Extremely Randomized Trees) [33] algorithm is an ensemble learning method that builds a large number of unpruned decision trees and averages their predictions. It expands on the Random Forest framework [20] by adding another layer of randomness. In Random Forest, the optimal split threshold for each candidate feature is chosen. In contrast, Extra Trees randomly selects thresholds from the range of each feature. Specifically, at each node,Kfeatures are picked at random, and for each feature (\(f_k\)), a threshold (\(t_k\)) is sampled uniformly from (\([\min (f_k), \max (f_k)]\)). The split (\((\hat{f}, \hat{t})\)) that maximizes variance reduction is selected from this random set. This dual randomization of both features and thresholds further reduces the correlation among trees compared to Random Forest. It reduces ensemble variance while only slightly increasing bias. In practice, Extra Trees usually trains two to four times faster than Random Forest, as it avoids the computationally heavy threshold search during node splitting. In high-dimensional molecular descriptor datasets, this random splitting method acts as an effective form of implicit regularization. It helps prevent individual trees from overfitting to correlated fingerprint features. The main hyperparameters, such as the number of estimators, maximum tree depth, minimum samples needed for splitting and for leaf nodes, and the proportion of features considered at each split, were optimized using Bayesian search.

LightGBM [34] is a gradient boosting framework created by Microsoft. It delivers top performance on tabular data through two main innovations compared to traditional gradient boosting machines (GBMs) [45]. The first innovation is Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS). It keeps all instances with large gradients or high errors, while randomly selecting instances with small gradients. This approach reduces data volume while maintaining the most important training signals. The second innovation is Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB). This method finds sparse features that rarely take on nonzero values at the same time and merges them into a single bundle, which decreases the effective number of features.

Tree construction uses a histogram-based method. This bin’s continuous feature values into discrete buckets. As a result, the computational cost of finding splits drops from the expensive\(O(n \log n)\)needed by traditional GBMs toO(B), whereBis the number of bins. Importantly, LightGBM uses a leaf-wise growth strategy. At each step, it splits the leaf that offers the greatest reduction in loss, no matter the tree’s depth. This approach usually leads to deeper, uneven trees that achieve lower training errors with fewer trees compared to the level-wise growth used by XGBoost and scikit-learn’s GBM. However, it needs careful regularization with parameters such as min_child_samples, num_leaves, and max_depth to avoid overfitting.

The model trains using the gradient and Hessian of the loss function, which is Mean Absolute Error in this study. It also supports parallel split finding across CPU cores through OpenMP.

XGBoost (eXtreme Gradient Boosting) [19] is a scalable, regularized gradient-boosting implementation that builds on the classical GBM framework by adding\(L_1\)and\(L_2\)regularization terms directly into the tree-building goal. At iterationt, the regularized objective function is defined as:

whereTdenotes the number of leaves,\(\textbf{w}\)represents the leaf weights,\(\gamma\)is the minimum loss-reduction threshold needed for splitting, and\(\lambda\)and\(\alpha\)correspond to the\(L_2\)and\(L_1\)regularization penalties, respectively. XGBoost finds the optimal split by using a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss function, which includes both the gradient\(g_i\)and the Hessian\(h_i\). In this study, we use the histogram-based tree method. This method employs the same histogram binning strategy as LightGBM and improves the efficiency of finding splits in large datasets. Unlike LightGBM’s leaf-wise growth approach, XGBoost uses level-wise tree growth. It builds each tree to a fixed depth before going further, which usually leads to more balanced trees. This more cautious exploration of the hypothesis space may help with generalization on smaller datasets.

The deep neural network (DNN) [35] used in this study is a fully connected feed-forward regression model. It is implemented in PyTorch and wrapped in a scikit-learn compatible interface to help integrate with the Bayesian hyperparameter optimization pipeline. The network architecture (shown in Fig.4) includes\(n_{layers}\)repeated blocks. Each block consists of a linear projection, batch normalization, a nonlinear activation function, and dropout regularization. This is followed by a single linear output neuron.

Deep Neural Network architecture diagram. The network consists of\(n_{layers}\)fully-connected blocks, each containing a linear layer, Batch Normalization, a non-linear activation function, and dropout regularisation, followed by a single linear output neuron for regression

Batch normalization is applied to each pre-activation in the mini-batch to reduce internal covariate shift and allow for higher learning rates. The activation function, (\(\sigma\)), is chosen through hyperparameter optimization from (\(\text {ReLU}\)), (\(\text {Leaky ReLU}\)), and (\(\tanh\)). The network is trained using the Huber loss, which acts quadratically for small residuals and linearly for large residuals. This improves robustness to outliers caused by polymorphism or measurement inconsistencies in the dataset. Optimization is performed with Adam, using a learning rate sampled from\([10^{-4}, 10^{-2}]\)under a log-uniform prior. Learning rate annealing is carried out with ReduceLROnPlateau. Early stopping with a set patience helps prevent overfitting. To take advantage of Apple hardware, the model is assigned to the Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend when available. If MPS is not available, it falls back to CUDA and then to the CPU. To make Bayesian hyperparameter optimization more manageable, a two-stage training strategy is used. First, candidate configurations are evaluated with a lower budget of 50 epochs and a patience of 10 during the search phase. Then, the best-performing configuration is retrained from scratch using the full budget of 200 epochs and a patience of 20.

The stacking ensemble (shown in Fig.5) is a two-level meta-learning architecture designed to combine the strengths of LightGBM, XGBoost, Extra Trees, and a deep neural network (DNN) into a single model that has a lower generalization error than any individual component. In the first level, each base learner is trained separately using its own tuned hyperparameters, feature selection method, and data transformation strategy. This results in four unique predictors with different error profiles. To give the meta-learner an unbiased training signal and avoid data leakage, out-of-fold (OOF) predictions are created through five-fold cross-validation. Each base model is re-instantiated with its best saved hyperparameters and trained on four folds of the training data. It then generates predictions for the remaining held-out fold. This method results in a prediction matrix\(\textbf{Z}\in \mathbb {R}^{n_\text {train} \times 4}\), where each column\(\textbf{z}_k =[\hat{y}_1^{(k)},\ldots ,\hat{y}_n^{(k)}]^\top\)holds the OOF predictions from base modelk. In the second level, a Ridge regression meta-learner is trained on\(\textbf{Z}\).

Stacking ensemble architecture diagram. The ensemble consists of four base learners (LightGBM, XGBoost, Extra Trees, DNN) that generate out-of-fold predictions on the training set to train a Ridge regression meta-learner. At inference time, the base learners produce predictions on the test set, which the meta-learner combines to produce the final output

\(L_2\)regularization in the ridge meta-learner prevents the model weights from leaning toward a single base learner. This helps use complementary information from all four contributors. During inference, the four fully trained base models make predictions for the test set. These predictions are then arranged into a matrix,\(\textbf{Z}_{\textrm{test}} \in \mathbb {R}^{n_{\textrm{test}} \times 4}\), and passed through the fitted meta-learner to get the final prediction. To avoid unnecessary computation when adding new base models or retuning the meta-learner, the out-of-fold and test predictions for each base model are saved to disk as NumPy arrays and reloaded in future runs. Only predictions from new models are recalculated. The stacking framework does not depend on the feature spaces used by the individual base models. Each model applies its own fitted scaler and feature selector internally. This makes the approach strong when different feature-selection methods create descriptor subsets of varying sizes.

Outlier detection used the Williams plot method, a common applicability domain analysis technique recommended by the OECD [46] guidelines for QSAR model validation [38]. In this study, the Williams plot was created in the meta-feature space of the stacking ensemble. This four-dimensional space is defined by the out-of-fold predictions from the base models, which include LightGBM, XGBoost, Extra Trees, and DNN. It was not built in the raw descriptor space.

For each compound, two values were calculated: leverage (h) and standardized residuals. Leverage measures how much a compound impacts the centroid of the training set. It was determined using the formula\(h_i = x_i^T(X^TX)^{-1}x_i\), whereXis the OOF meta-feature matrix. The leverage threshold,\(h^* =\frac{3(k+1)}{n}\), sets the boundary for the applicability domain, wherekis the number of base models, andnis the training set size.

Standardized residuals were calculated by scaling the prediction errors of both training and test compounds with the standard deviation of the training residuals. This step ensures a uniform scale across data splits. Three types of outliers were identified: (i) response outliers, for which\(|\text {standardized residual}|> 3\), indicating possible measurement errors or incorrect SMILES; (ii) leverage outliers, for which\(h > h^*\), representing compounds outside the structural applicability domain; and (iii) bad leverage points, which meet both criteria, indicating the most questionable compounds.

Model explainability was evaluated using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) [23], a framework for understanding machine learning model predictions. Based on cooperative game theory, SHAP values quantify how much each feature contributes to an individual prediction. In this study, we calculated SHAP values for the top-performing base learners, LightGBM and XGBoost, as well as for the Ridge meta-learner in the stacking ensemble. We used TreeExplainer for the tree-based models and LinearExplainer for the Ridge model. We determined global feature importance by averaging the absolute SHAP values across the test set. The SHAP beeswarm plot provided a comprehensive summary of the ensemble model’s behavior. In this visualization, each row represents a feature, ranked by mean absolute SHAP value from most to least important. Each dot corresponds to a single compound in the test set. The horizontal position of each dot shows the SHAP value: points to the right of zero indicate that the feature increased the predicted values, while points to the left indicate a decrease. Dot color indicates the raw feature value, with red for high values and blue for low values. This reveals whether a feature has a direct effect or a varying impact across compounds. This analysis identified the molecular descriptors that most significantly influenced prediction and showed how their effects differed among compounds.

Two complementary measures of uncertainty were calculated for the stacking ensemble on each test set. First, we measured disagreement among the base models by computing the standard deviation of predictions from the four base learners (LightGBM, XGBoost, ExtraTrees, and DNN) for each test compound [47]. This metric acts as a per-sample indicator of uncertainty since compounds with greater disagreement between the base models are expected to have larger absolute prediction errors. We checked this relationship by calculating the Spearman rank correlation (\(\rho\)) [48] between the standard deviation of the base models and the absolute test error.

Second, we generated split-conformal prediction intervals using the out-of-fold (OOF) training residuals as the calibration set [49,50]. The nonconformity score for each training compound was defined as\(s_i = |y_i - \hat{y}i^{\textrm{OOF}}|\). We calculated the conformal quantile at a desired coverage level\(\alpha\)as\(q_\alpha = \textrm{quantile}(s, \lceil (n+1)\alpha \rceil / n)\), wherenis the number of training compounds. We defined the prediction interval for a test compound as\([\hat{y} - q_\alpha , \hat{y} + q_\alpha ]\). This method offers a distribution-free coverage guarantee: if the calibration set is properly specified, the proportion of test compounds whose true melting points fall within the interval approaches\(\alpha\)asnincreases. We evaluated empirical coverage at nominal levels of\(50\%, 60\%, 70\%, 80\%, 90\%, 95\%\), and\(99\%\)to check interval calibration across the entire confidence spectrum.

A variety of methods are available for estimating boiling points, each with its own set of pros and cons. Coefficient-based methods, such as DIPPR-based methods, rely on experimental data to regress and determine a set of coefficients that can then be used to calculate vapor pressure via a governing equation (“Design Institute for Physical Properties" 1996). Those coefficients can then be used to determine the temperature at which the vapor pressure equals 1 Atm, yielding the boiling point. When available, coefficient-based methods provide high-quality estimates of the boiling point. However, not all molecules have associated coefficients, and if experimental data is not available, those coefficients cannot be determined. Group contribution methods offer an alternative to coefficient-based methods. Group contribution methods assign a value to each chemical group. These values are obtained by regression from a wide range of boiling-point data. By applying these values to a working equation, boiling-point estimates within a few degrees of experimental measurements are often possible. The Joback method is a popular method for estimating boiling points. Based on a set of 438 molecules, the Joback method has an average absolute error of 12.9 °C [51]. Brown and Stein improve on the Joback method by adding a correction term [52]. Based on a dataset of 6, 584 boiling points, the Brown-Stein method has an absolute average error of 20.4 °C. Group-contribution methods are easy to implement and can provide reasonable boiling-point estimates. They work best for molecules similar to those found in the database used in regression. Group contribution methods do not have values for every possible group and cannot be applied to molecules that lack a represented chemical group. If the desired group is unavailable, other methods must be used. More rigorous, physics-based methods, such as the Equation of State (EoS), have been proven to provide very accurate vapor pressures while often running on just a laptop’s resources. Examples here include the Saft-gamme Mie, SAFT-VR, Peng Robinson, and Cubic Plus Association (CPA) [53]. Like coefficient-based methods, EoS methods require experimental data to estimate parameters. However, this is not an impediment, as experimental data using a variety of different physical properties are usually available.

This section provides a detailed overview of the QSAR melting-point prediction pipeline (considering 2D features) across three chemical-space datasets: CHO, CHON, and Full. Similar analyses of the melting point (considering 3D features) and the boiling point are presented in the supplementary document.

Three separate datasets were created from the curated experimental melting-point database to evaluate model performance across chemical spaces with increasing diversity. The CHO subset includes compounds made only of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. It represents aliphatic and aromatic oxygenates, such as alcohols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids. The CHON subset builds on the CHO set by adding nitrogen-containing compounds, which include amines, amides, imines, nitro groups, and heterocyclic structures. The Full dataset includes all compounds, regardless of their elemental makeup. This dataset contains halogenated, sulfur, phosphorus, and metal-containing molecules, along with CHO and CHON compounds.

The complete dataset was divided into 15, 428 training compounds and 3, 860 test compounds using Butina clustering with a Tanimoto similarity threshold of 0.7. In the training set, the mean pairwise Tanimoto similarity was 0.142, and the median was 0.107. In the test set, the corresponding values were 0.139 and 0.105. Across both sets, the mean maximum similarity between each test compound and its nearest training neighbor was 0.121, with a median of 0.094 and a maximum of 0.698. No test compound showed a nearest-neighbor similarity that met or exceeded the 0.7 threshold. These results (shown in Table3) indicate that the cluster-based split effectively reduced structural overlap between the training and test sets, which helps prevent information leakage during model evaluation.

Table4summarizes the resulting sample sizes after partitioning the data. The full dataset is about 2.4 times larger than the CHO and CHON datasets. This highlights the wider range of the complete experimental collection. Since the CHO and CHON subsets have overlapping compounds, the differences in model performance between these two sets mainly show the effect of including nitrogen-containing chemistry. They do not reflect differences attributable solely to dataset size.

Before stacking, six base learners were trained independently using every combination of the three datasets and four feature-selection methods: the full feature set, Boruta, correlation-based selection, and principal component analysis (PCA). This process led to 72 individual training experiments. Table6summarizes the mean absolute error (MAE, in K) for each combination.

Across all three datasets, several consistent patterns appear. Gradient-boosted tree ensembles, specifically LightGBM (LGBM) and XGBoost, have the lowest mean absolute errors (MAEs) among the individual models in every instance. For the Full dataset, LGBM with correlation-based feature selection produced a test MAE of 28.29 K. For the CHO dataset, LGBM using the complete feature set achieved 26.46 K. For the CHON dataset, XGBoost with the complete feature set reached 29.45 K. In contrast, the linear models, Ridge Regression and ElasticNet, perform about 3 to 5 K worse under every feature-selection strategy. This reinforces the idea that melting-point variation across chemical space is inherently nonlinear.

Although ExtraTrees does not match the performance of LGBM or XGBoost, it consistently outperforms all linear regressors. The deep neural network (DNN) shows the most variability across feature-selection strategies. It performs poorly when trained on the full raw feature set, with MAE values as high as 43.57 K on the Full dataset. However, it becomes competitive with ExtraTrees when using Boruta-selected features, achieving 29.41 K on Full and 30.70 K on CHO. This pattern likely reflects the DNN’s need for a more compact and less collinear input space. Lastly, PCA-based feature selection consistently yields the highest MAE across all models. This indicates that the principal components explaining the greatest variance in the descriptor matrix are not the most informative for predicting the target property.

A stacking ensemble was created by training a Ridge meta-learner on the out-of-fold predictions from the four best-performing base models: LightGBM, XGBoost, ExtraTrees, and a deep neural network (DNN). Table5shows the training and test performance of the stacking ensemble for each dataset, using the full feature set without removing outliers. The results show that the stacking ensemble achieved better generalization, as evidenced by reduced overfitting on the training data. Table6further expands this comparison by including all feature-selection strategies.

Across all datasets, the stacking ensemble reduced test MAE compared to the best individual model. For the CHO dataset, test MAE decreased from 26.46 to 25.29 K, a\(4.4\%\)reduction. For CHON, the MAE declined from 29.45 to 28.73 K, a\(2.4\%\)improvement. Similarly, for the Full dataset, the MAE dropped from 28.29 to 27.07 K, showing a\(4.3\%\)reduction (see Table6for the best stacking setup for each dataset). Although these improvements are modest, they are consistent. This suggests that the four base learners capture different sources of variance, and the meta-learner adjusts each model’s contribution based on the chemical subspace where it performs best. Among the datasets, CHO had the highest test-set\(R^2\)of 0.829, likely due to its narrower, more uniform chemical space. In contrast, CHON had a lower\(R^2\)of 0.701, likely due to the greater structural diversity associated with nitrogen-containing functional groups and more complex interactions, such as intramolecular hydrogen bonding and amide resonance stabilization. These interactions are more difficult to characterize with PaDEL descriptors alone. The Full dataset showed an intermediate\(R^2\)of 0.818, benefiting from a larger training set and greater chemical diversity. Finally, the small difference between training and test performance–for instance, 24.12 K versus 25.29 K for CHO–suggests that the stacking ensemble generalizes well without significant overfitting.

The stacking ensemble shows its biggest improvement over the individual models with PCA-based feature selection. For instance, XGBoost performs 29.08 K compared to 39.21 K with the full feature set. This indicates that the meta-learner is particularly good at finding predictive signals when the base models work in a compressed input space that loses some information. Throughout all 12 datasets and feature selection combinations, the stacking ensemble consistently ranks first, highlighting the strength of the meta-learning approach.

Figure6A, B shows scatter plots comparing stacking-ensemble predictions with experimental melting points for the training and test sets of each dataset. The close grouping of the points along the diagonal indicates a strong agreement between predicted and observed values. As expected, the training scatter (panel A) is more tightly clustered than the test scatter (panel B), showing a slight advantage in performance for the training set. Noticeable deviations from the diagonal occur at the extremes of the melting-point range. Compounds with experimental melting points below approximately 200 K tend to be overpredicted, while those above 550 K tend to be underpredicted. This compression toward the mean is a known issue in QSAR models trained on right-skewed target distributions and likely reflects the limited number of compounds with extreme melting points in the training data.

Figure6C, D shows the Williams plots for train and test data. In each plot, the horizontal axis represents the leverage,\(h_i\), of a training compound. This reflects its structural distance from the training centroid in descriptor space. The vertical axis displays the standardized residual,\(\varepsilon _i = (y_i - \hat{y}_i)/s\), wheresis the standard deviation of the training residuals. The dashed vertical line at\(h = h^*\)marks the boundary of the applicability domain. The horizontal dashed lines at\(\varepsilon = \pm 3\)indicate the threshold for response outliers. Compounds in the upper-left quadrant (\(|\varepsilon | > 3\),\(h \le h^*\)) are response outliers without structural issues and likely show incorrect experimental values. Those in the lower-right quadrant (\(h > h^*\),\(|\varepsilon | \le 3\)) are leverage points that the model predicts well. Compounds in the upper-right quadrant are bad leverage points that raise both types of concerns. To assess whether removing response outliers from the training set improves model generalization, the entire stacking pipeline was retrained from scratch after excluding the identified outliers (\(|\varepsilon | > 3\)and bad leverage points). Pure leverage outliers (\(h > h*\)only) were kept because, while they are structurally unusual, not having a large prediction error does not suggest measurement error.

Table7summarises the AD statistics for all three datasets. Data cleaning after removing outliers from the training data resulted in noticeably tighter fit sets across all three datasets. Training MAE improved (not shown in the table for space limitation) from 24.12 to 22.28 K for CHO, from 27.89 to 26.50 K for CHON, and from 25.86 to 24.03 K for the Full dataset. This confirms that the removed compounds were true high-residual observations that distorted the meta-learner’s fit. However, the effect on test-set generalization was inconsistent. For the Full dataset, removing 204 compounds (\(1.3\%\)of the training data) led to a slight improvement of 0.09 K in test MAE (27.32–27.23 K;\(+0.3\%\)). In contrast, the cleaned models performed slightly worse for CHO and CHON, with test MAE increased by 0.64 K (\(+2.5\%\)) for CHO and by 0.28 K (\(+0.97\%\)) for CHON. This decline suggests that the flagged compounds in the smaller datasets were not erroneous measurements but valid compounds located at the structural extremes. Removing these compounds reduced the model’s coverage of the melting-point distribution. Therefore, the original, uncleaned models were retained as the primary models across all three datasets.

Figure6E shows the importance of each feature and how they influence the predicted melting point based on SHAP analysis. The results reveal patterns that make sense both chemically and physically. In each plot, features are listed from top to bottom according to their mean absolute SHAP values, and each dot represents an individual compound. The horizontal position of a dot reflects its SHAP contribution to the predicted melting point. Positive values increase the prediction, while negative values decrease it. The color of the dot indicates the raw feature value, with red signifying high values and blue indicating low values.

In the CHO dataset, the top features, especially the molecular distance edge descriptor MDEO-11 [54] and the average simple path index ASP-1 [55], shows the key role of global molecular structure and specific atomic connections in determining activity. Next in importance, van der Waals volume-weighted spatial autocorrelation descriptors like ATSC1v and AATS2v suggest that the arrangement of steric bulk significantly affects target interactions [55]. The model’s predictive ability is also strongly influenced by thermodynamic solvation parameters from Abraham’s Molecular Linear Free Energy Relationship descriptors, including MLFER_E, MLFER_A, and MLFER_S, which capture polarizability and hydrogen-bond acidity [56]. Additionally, local electronic environments, as indicated by electrotopological state indices such as SHBint2 and SsOH  [57], along with molecular flexibility, as characterized by the fraction of rotatable bonds (RotBFrac) [55], provide a clearer picture of ligand-binding potential. Overall, the SHAP profile for the CHO dataset shows that model predictions mainly rely on large-scale structural connectivity, then steric distribution and solvation thermodynamics.

In the CHON dataset (Fig. S1 (E) in the supplementary document), which includes nitrogen in the chemical space, the feature ranking shifts significantly toward descriptors associated with hydrogen bonding and electronic effects. MLFER_E moves to the top position, while maxHBint2, defined as the highest intramolecular hydrogen bond at a two-bond distance (r = +0.92), and SHBd, the total of hydrogen-bond donor E-state values [57], ranked second and third, respectively. This trend highlights the strong role of nitrogen-mediated donor-acceptor interactions in crystal cohesion. In the Full dataset (Fig. S2 (E) in the supplementary document), MLFER_S, which reflects Abraham’s dipolarity/polarizability, outshines all other features, with an average SHAP value of 11.4 K and a range from −42 to +22 K. This prominence mostly comes from the large polarity differences between ionic and zwitterionic compounds, like sulfonates and phosphates, compared to nonpolar hydrocarbons that define this broader chemical space.

Across all three datasets, MLFER_E, MLFER_S, and MLFER_A consistently rank among the most important predictors, reinforcing the theoretical importance of linear free-energy relationships in melting-point prediction [56]. In contrast, the fraction of rotatable bonds (RotBFrac [55]) is the only descriptor that consistently shows a negative SHAP direction, ranking 10th, 5th, and 6th in the CHO, CHON, and Full datasets, respectively. Increased flexibility affects the entropic penalty during crystallization, lowering the melting temperature regardless of elemental makeup. Overall, this SHAP-based profile supports the models’ physical interpretability, showing a shift from macro-structural connectivity to steric distribution and solvation thermodynamics, and finally to local electronic environments. It also offers molecular-level insight for designing compounds with specific melting points. Section 1.3 of the supplementary document describes each feature presented in the three datasets using our SHAP analysis.

Prediction uncertainty was characterized through two complementary approaches: base-model disagreement and split-conformal prediction intervals. Figure7presents the four-panel uncertainty diagnostic for each dataset.

A four-panel uncertainty analysis was carried out for theCHOdataset stacking ensemble using the complete feature set with StandardScaler (\(n_\text {test}=1{,}374\)). PanelAillustrates the relationship between base-model disagreement and absolute error. It features a scatter plot showing the standard deviation of predictions from the four base models (LightGBM, XGBoost, ExtraTrees, and DNN) against the absolute prediction error\(|y - \hat{y}|\)for each test compound. Points are colored based on the stack prediction value (plasma scale). The Spearman rank correlation (\(\rho = 0.227\),\(p < 0.0001\)) suggests that greater disagreement among models is a statistically significant, though modest, sign of increased prediction error. PanelBshows conformal prediction intervals for the test set, with compounds arranged by increasing stack prediction value along the x-axis. Blue shaded bands indicate the symmetric\(80\%\)and\(90\%\)split-conformal prediction intervals. The solid line represents the stack prediction, while red dots show the true experimental melting points. The empirical\(90\%\)coverage (\(89.2\%\)) is close to the nominal\(90\%\)target (\(\pm 1.2\)percentage points), which supports calibration. The conformal quantile is\(q_{90} = \pm 53.3\)K. Panelcpresents the coverage calibration curve, plotting nominal coverage against empirical coverage across seven levels (\(50\%\)–\(99\%\)). The dashed gray diagonal indicates perfect calibration. The conformal curve closely follows it across all levels, indicating no systematic over- or under-coverage. Panelddisplays the distribution of base-model disagreement as a density histogram of the base-model standard deviation across all test compounds (mean\(= 9.18\)K, with the median marked by dashed lines). The inset horizontal bar chart shows the individual test MAE of each base model (LightGBM, XGBoost, ExtraTrees, and DNN), providing context for interpreting the level of disagreement

Base-model disagreement: For each test compound, the standard deviation of the four base-learners predictions (LightGBM, XGBoost, ExtraTrees, DNN) were computed as a per-sample epistemic uncertainty proxy. The Spearman rank correlation between this standard deviation and the absolute prediction error was\(\rho = 0.227\)(\(p < 0.0001\)) for CHO,\(\rho = 0.175\)(\(p < 0.0001\)) for CHON, and\(\rho = 0.201\)(\(p < 0.0001\)) for Full, confirming that higher inter-model disagreement is a statistically significant, though modest, signal of elevated prediction error. The mean base-model standard deviation across test compounds was 9.18 K (CHO), 9.95 K (CHON), and 10.08 K (Full), indicating a broadly similar level of base-learner diversity across all three chemical spaces.

Conformal prediction intervals: Split-conformal intervals were constructed using the out-of-fold (OOF) training residuals as a calibration set. The non-conformity score for each training compound was defined as\(s_i = |y_i - \hat{y}_i^\text {OOF}|\), and the conformal quantile at coverage level\(\alpha\)was computed as\(q_\alpha = \text {quantile}(s,\, \lceil (n+1)\alpha \rceil /n)\). The resulting symmetric prediction interval for each test compound is\([\hat{y} - q_\alpha ,\; \hat{y} + q_\alpha ]\). At a nominal 90% coverage level, the conformal quantiles were ±53.3 K (CHO), ±59.6 K (CHON), and ±56.5 K (Full), with empirical test-set coverages of 89.2%, 89.2%, and 88.8%, respectively — all within 1.2 percentage points of the nominal target. The close agreement between nominal and empirical coverage across all seven evaluated levels (50%–99%) confirms that the conformal intervals are well-calibrated and reliably bound the true melting point without systematic over- or under-coverage. The wide 90% interval widths reflect the intrinsic scatter of the melting-point distribution rather than a deficiency of the model: the distribution-free guarantee holds regardless of the underlying data distribution, and the intervals correctly widen for compounds in sparsely populated regions of chemical space where individual base-model errors are larger.

To put P2MAT’s predictive performance into context, we compared our top stacking model (MAE = 25.29 K, RMSE = 36.28 K, and\(R^2\)= 0.83 on the internal test set) with seven melting-point prediction models reported over the last two decades, as shown in Table8. For each benchmark study, we applied P2MAT directly to the authors’ original compound set and provided MAE, RMSE, and\(R^2\)alongside the published values. Lower error values and higher\(R^2\)indicate better performance.

To better understand the performance differences, given the overlap in training data, we measured structural similarity between our training set and each external dataset using two metrics derived from Morgan circular fingerprints (ECFP4; radius = 2, 2048 bits) implemented in RDKit [27]. For each compound in one dataset, we identified the highest Tanimoto coefficient with any compound in the other dataset using bulk similarity search. We defined the mean maximum Tanimoto similarity (MMTS) as the average of these maximum values per compound. This serves as a continuous measure of chemical space overlap that does not depend on a threshold. We defined the leakage fraction (LF) as the percentage of compounds whose nearest-neighbor Tanimoto similarity was at least 0.8, which is the near-duplicate threshold used for scaffold-based clustering [43]. Both metrics were calculated in both directions and summarized as symmetric scores:\(\text {MMTS}\text {sym} = (\text {MMTS}{A\rightarrow B} + \text {MMTS}{B\rightarrow A})/2\)and\(\text {LF}\text {sym} = (\text {LF}{A\rightarrow B} + \text {LF}{B\rightarrow A})/2\). Higher values for either metric indicate greater structural overlap, suggesting a higher likelihood of information leakage.

Overall, P2MAT surpassed the published model in six out of seven external comparisons, and the MMTS and LF values help clarify the observed results. On the dataset from McDonagh et al. [14] (MMTS = 0.623,  LF =\(34.05\%\)), P2MAT lowered the reported MLR error from 33.20 to 22.20 K, marking an improvement of roughly\(23\%\). For the large MDPI dataset from Karthikeyan et al. [58] (4, 173 compounds; MMTS = 0.685, LF =\(45.13\%\)), the MAE decreased from 32.60 to 22.20 K and the RMSE from 49.30 to 35.65 K, while\(R^2\)stayed similar at 0.68. On the drug-compound dataset from Modarresi et al. [59] (MMTS = 0.574, LF =\(34.94\%\)), the RMSE dropped from 42.00 to 32.08 K, and\(R^2\)increased from 0.66 to 0.80. When tested on the large OCHEM dataset used by both Tetko et al. [60] and Sivaraman et al. [16] (21, 840compounds; MMTS = 0.842, LF =\(66.01\%\)), P2MAT achieved an RMSE of 35.10 K, compared to Tetko’s 38.00 K, and an\(R^2\)of 0.83, compared to Sivaraman’s 0.77. The strong performance likely stems from the high overlap with our training set. P2MAT performed best on the dataset from McDonagh et al. [61] (1, 100 compounds; MMTS = 0.665, LF =\(42.21\%\)), where the RMSE improved from 41.30 to 27.43 K and\(R^2\)rose from 0.75 to 0.90. Notably, this dataset is a subset of the compounds used to train P2MAT, which suggests that the high LF reflects direct overlap with the training set rather than genuine external generalization. The only exception was the dataset from Bergström et al. [62] (277 compounds; MMTS = 0.415, LF =\(10.26\%\)), which includes structurally constrained, drug-like molecules and had the least overlap among the benchmark sets. On this out-of-distribution dataset, P2MAT produced an RMSE of 48.86 K and an\(R^2\)of 0.03, consistent with its limited structural similarity to our training data. Together, these results indicate that P2MAT generalizes well across chemically diverse external datasets, while instances of poorer performance relate closely to lower structural overlap with the training set.

The stacking ensembles achieved test MAEs of 25.3–28.7 K and\(R^2\)values of 0.70–0.83. This performance puts them within the 2–35 K range reported for similar QSAR and deep-learning models predicting melting points in the literature [58,62,63]. Across all 12 dataset and feature-selection combinations, the stack consistently improved MAE by 2–4% compared to the best individual base model. This confirms that the Ridge meta-learner effectively uses the complementary strengths of the four base learners. The significantly lower\(R^2\)for CHON (0.701) compared to CHO (0.829) indicates that nitrogen-containing compounds introduce extra structural variability. This variability includes intramolecular hydrogen bonding, tautomerism, and resonance delocalization in heterocycles that fixed 2D PaDEL descriptors cannot fully capture. Incorporating graph neural network embeddings that respond to electronic structure represents a logical way to improve further.

Together, the SHAP and applicability-domain analyses create a physically sound and practically useful uncertainty framework. SHAP rankings show that the Abraham LFER descriptors (MLFER_E,MLFER_S, andMLFER_A) are the most influential predictors across all three datasets. This supports the theoretical basis of linear free-energy relationships for melting-point prediction. In contrast,RotBFracis the most consistent negative predictor. This indicates that molecular flexibility generally lowers the melting point by increasing the crystallization entropy penalty, regardless of elemental composition. For deployment, the Williams-plot applicability-domain boundary (\(h_i > h^*\)) and conformal prediction intervals provide two complementary levels of uncertainty communication. In-domain predictions are linked to a well-calibrated\(90\%\)interval of ±53 to 60 K and have an expected MAE of 23–27 K. However, out-of-domain queries (\(3.9\%\)of test compounds in each dataset) must be interpreted carefully because structural extrapolation introduces an additional systematic error of about 2–3 K.

title: Multimodal feature fusion for molecular property classification
author: Jing Liu; Li Xue; Yin Wang; Qiaorong Wu; Wenwei Tao; Yiwei Wang; Jianming Wu; Jiesi Luo
text:
Accurate molecular property prediction is a cornerstone of modern chemical science, driving progress in drug discovery, materials design, and environmental research. Yet, most existing models remain unimodal, while multimodal approaches often rely on simple aggregation, leaving much of the complementary chemical information underexploited. In this work, we present a multimodal feature fusion framework that unites the strengths of deep chemical language processing (CLP) models and molecular fingerprints, integrating sequential and structural representations for more comprehensive molecular characterization. Unlike previous heuristic combinations, our framework systematically investigates the principles of effective cross-modal fusion. We benchmark ten CLP architectures and eight fingerprint types through exhaustive combinatorial search to identify the most synergistic configurations. This exploration shows that aggregating multiple models does not necessarily improve performance; instead, successful fusion requires data-aware design guided by feature integration and complementarity. The proposed strategy effectively couples sequential features learned from SMILES with structural information captured by molecular fingerprints, resulting in a coherent and chemically interpretable molecular representation. Evaluated across 60 datasets from MoleculeNet and TOXRIC, our fusion models deliver consistent and substantial gains over state-of-the-art baselines. Beyond outperforming existing architectures, this work provides conceptual insights and practical guidelines for multimodal fusion in molecular property prediction, highlighting the importance of efficient fusion strategies in building robust and generalizable molecular models.

Scientific contribution

This study provides a large-scale empirical evaluation of multimodal feature fusion for molecular property classification by systematically integrating SMILES-based chemical language representations with fingerprint-based structural descriptors across 60 benchmark datasets. The framework introduces a data-aware combinatorial fusion strategy to identify task-specific complementary feature combinations, improving robustness and interpretability compared with unimodal models and baseline approaches. The results clarify how sequence-based and structure-based molecular representations complement each other, providing practical guidance for designing multimodal models in cheminformatics.

Drug discovery is an inherently complex and resource-intensive process characterized by long development cycles and high failure rates [1]. The vastness of chemical space and the high cost of experimental validation have made it increasingly difficult to identify compounds with desirable pharmacological and physicochemical properties [2]. Over the past decade, Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach to address these challenges by enabling data-driven strategies that can predict molecular behavior prior to synthesis or testing [3]. By learning from accumulated chemical and biological data, AI systems can guide compound selection, structural refinement, and risk assessment across different stages of discovery [4]. Among the diverse applications of AI in this field, molecular property prediction remains a central task. It focuses on learning the quantitative relationship between molecular structure and properties such as potency, selectivity, solubility, and toxicity, which largely determine a compound’s potential as a viable drug candidate [5,6]. Reliable property prediction not only accelerates early screening but also enhances our understanding of how structural variations influence molecular function.

In parallel with these developments, advances in molecular representation have played a crucial role in the evolution of predictive models [7]. Early computational approaches typically relied on a single representation, such as handcrafted descriptors, structural fingerprints, or SMILES strings, to encode chemical information [8,9]. While these unimodal strategies laid the foundation for data-driven modeling, each captures only specific aspects of molecular structure, providing an incomplete view of chemical space. As molecular datasets have grown more diverse and prediction tasks more complex, this limitation has become more pronounced, prompting increased interest in integrating multiple sources of molecular information [10].

Motivated by this need, recent studies have explored multimodal learning to construct more comprehensive molecular representations. By combining sequence-based SMILES encodings with structural, physicochemical, or graph-based features, multimodal models have shown improved performance across various tasks. For instance, Lu et al. demonstrated that integrating SMILES-encoded vectors, ECFP fingerprints, and molecular graphs using Transformer-Encoder, BiGRU, and GCN significantly enhanced molecular property prediction [11]. Rollins et al. proposed MolPROP, combining the pretrained ChemBERTa-2 language model with graph neural networks, showing significant improvement in regression tasks such as hydration free energy, water solubility, lipophilicity, and clinical toxicity [12]. Zhou et al. introduced MMFRL, combining relational learning with multimodal fusion, which enhanced molecular property prediction by improving embedding initialization during pre-training [13]. Gong et al. presented MDFCL, a framework that integrates multimodal data fusion and graph contrastive learning, addressing data scarcity and outperformed conventional models on 13 benchmark datasets [14]. Chen et al. proposed DrugDAGT, a dual-attention graph transformer with contrastive learning, which improves drug-drug interaction prediction by capturing both local and global relationships between drugs [15]. Fang et al. introduced GEM, a geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning method that integrates three-dimensional molecular geometry, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in molecular property prediction tasks [16]. Zang et al. developed MolMFD, a self-supervised framework that fuses 2D and 3D molecular structural information, significantly improving molecular prediction accuracy [17]. These efforts highlight a shift toward leveraging complementary molecular views instead of relying on a single representation. However, despite the promise of multimodal approaches, effective integration of diverse modalities remains a significant challenge. Many models use basic fusion techniques, such as feature concatenation, which often fail to capture meaningful interactions between different data types [18,19]. Furthermore, the relevance of each modality can vary across datasets, making it difficult to design generalizable fusion strategies [20]. These challenges underscore the need for more sophisticated multimodal frameworks that can integrate diverse data types effectively while maintaining flexibility across prediction tasks.

To address the aforementioned challenges, this study introduces a multimodal fusion framework that integrates molecular fingerprints with CLP models under a unified and data-aware design. The framework tackles the difficulty of multimodal representation learning by systematically combining sequential and structural features, enabling complementary chemical information to be captured and leveraged more effectively. Through an extensive evaluation of 10 distinct unimodal CLP models and 255 potential multimodal combinations, the most effective modality configurations were identified across 60 molecular property prediction tasks. This analysis demonstrates that successful multimodal fusion relies not on simple model aggregation, but on task-specific feature integration and modality complementarity. The resulting models consistently outperform unimodal approaches, establishing multimodal fusion as a powerful tool for predicting molecular properties. In addition, interpretability and quantitative analyses reveal meaningful patterns within and across modalities, providing mechanistic insights into how sequential and structural features jointly contribute to predictive performance. Collectively, this framework offers a methodological foundation for advancing robust and interpretable multimodal learning, fostering a deeper integration of data-driven and chemical insights in molecular property prediction.

A comprehensive evaluation was carried out on 60 classification tasks spanning the MoleculeNet [21] and TOXRIC [22] datasets, which collectively represent a diverse and challenging benchmark for molecular property prediction. MoleculeNet comprises 30 well-established tasks, including BACE, BBBP, ClinTox, and the 27-task SIDER suite, representing a wide spectrum of biochemical and pharmacological challenges. The BBBP dataset contains 2,039 compounds annotated according to their ability to penetrate the blood–brain barrier, a property essential for central nervous system drug development. ClinTox includes 1,478 molecules with information on both clinical efficacy and toxicity outcomes, enabling a reliable evaluation of compound safety. The BACE dataset consists of 1,513 SMILES-encoded molecules curated for β-secretase 1 inhibition classification, providing insights into structural determinants of inhibitory potency. SIDER includes 1,427 compounds distributed across 27 adverse drug reaction categories, including hepatobiliary, immune, vascular, and nervous system disorders, thereby facilitating the systematic analysis of molecular features associated with side effects. Complementing MoleculeNet, TOXRIC contributes 30 additional toxicity-related tasks and approximately 150,000 experimental measurements spanning five toxicity domains, namely genetic, organic, clinical, developmental and reproductive, and reactive toxicity. Its acute toxicity subset contains 59 endpoints, 80,081 compounds, and 122,594 records covering multiple species, administration routes, and toxicity indicators such as LD₅₀, LDLo, and TDLo. Characterized by data sparsity (approximately 97.4% missing entries) and pronounced class imbalance, TOXRIC provides a challenging yet realistic environment for evaluating model robustness and generalization.

In this study, the datasets were randomly partitioned into training, validation, and test sets following a 70:10:20 ratio. To ensure statistical robustness, the random splitting procedure was independently repeated five times with different random seeds, generating five distinct data partitions. This process, which shuffles molecular entries prior to each split, enables estimation of the uncertainty associated with model performance on the test set. The same predefined splits were consistently applied across all experiments to guarantee fair and unbiased model comparisons.

Molecular string representations, such as SMILES and SELFIES, are widely used to encode molecular structures into textual formats for cheminformatics applications [23]. By treating molecular strings as a chemical language, CLP models can directly learn structure–property relationships from sequential data, extending deep learning architectures originally developed for text analysis to molecular representations [24,25,26,27]. These models have shown strong predictive performance across a variety of molecular tasks, providing both efficiency and interpretability advantages.

In this study, ten representative CLP architectures, covering a spectrum of model complexities and structural designs, were systematically evaluated [28,29,30,31,32,33]. Each model used a unified embedding configuration (128-dimensional vectors, maximum sequence length 250) to ensure comparability while highlighting differences in network structure, feature representation, and computational strategies. The architectures and their key implementation details are summarized below.

BiLSTM. Recurrent neural network (RNN) is designed to capture sequential dependencies, and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) extends this capability by processing input sequences in both forward and backward directions. Input SMILES sequences were first tokenized and embedded into 128-dimensional vectors, followed by SpatialDropout1D (rate = 0.2) for regularization. A BiLSTM with 128 hidden units encoded contextual dependencies across the molecular sequence. Global max pooling aggregated hidden states into a fixed-length representation, followed by a 256-unit ReLU dense layer and a sigmoid output layer.

CNN_RNN hybrid. Convolutional neural network (CNN) and RNN capture complementary aspects of sequential data: CNN extracts local features, while RNN captures long-range dependencies. In the CNN_RNN hybrid, embedded SMILES sequences are first processed through a 1D convolutional layer (filters = 300, kernel size = 3, ReLU), followed by max pooling (pool size = 2) to extract local chemical motifs. The resulting features are then processed by a bidirectional gated recurrent unit (BiGRU) with 128 units to capture sequential context. Global max pooling aggregates the features into a fixed-length representation, which is subsequently passed through a 256-unit ReLU dense layer and a sigmoid output layer.

DPCNN. The deep pyramid CNN (DPCNN) extends conventional CNN with hierarchical feature abstraction through stacked residual convolutional blocks. Embedded SMILES sequences are first regularized with SpatialDropout1D (rate = 0.2) and processed by an initial region embedding block consisting of three 1D convolutional layers (filters = 250, kernel size = 3, ReLU), each with residual connections. Three pyramid stages are applied, each combining max pooling (pool size = 3, stride = 2) with two convolutional layers and skip connections, progressively reducing the sequence resolution while increasing representational depth. The output is aggregated via global max pooling, followed by a 256-unit ReLU dense layer and a sigmoid output layer.

FastText. FastText is a lightweight embedding-based model that represents each SMILES sequence by averaging the embeddings of all tokens to produce a compact vector representation. The resulting sequence embedding is directly connected to a sigmoid output layer for binary classification. Despite its simplicity, FastText provides a strong baseline by capturing coarse-grained statistical patterns in molecular sequences.

FNet. FNet replaces the self-attention mechanism of Transformers with Fourier transformations, providing an efficient approach to capture global dependencies. Token and positional embeddings of SMILES sequences are processed through three stacked FNetEncoder layers (intermediate dimension = 512), which apply Fourier mixing operations to exchange information across sequence positions. The encoded representations are aggregated by global average pooling, regularized with dropout (rate = 0.1), and passed to a sigmoid output layer.

Multi_Text_CNN. Building upon the Text_CNN paradigm, Multi_Text_CNN employs a deeper and more expressive multi-channel convolutional framework. Embedded SMILES sequences are regularized by SpatialDropout1D (rate = 0.2) and processed through four convolutional branches with kernel sizes of 2, 3, 4, and 5. Each branch contains two stacked 1D convolutional layers (filters = 300, ReLU activation, with batch normalization), followed by global max pooling. The pooled outputs are concatenated and passed through a 256-unit ReLU dense layer and a sigmoid output layer.

RCNN. Recurrent CNN (RCNN) combines recurrent and convolutional operations to simultaneously capture contextual and local features. Embedded SMILES sequences are processed by forward and backward SimpleRNN layers (128 units each) to generate contextual embeddings. The outputs are concatenated with the original embeddings and passed through a 1D convolutional layer (filters = 64, kernel size = 1, tanh activation). Global max pooling aggregates semantic features into a single vector, followed by a sigmoid output layer for binary prediction.

RNN_CNN hybrid. The RNN_CNN hybrid processes embedded SMILES sequences through a BiGRU (128 units) to capture long-range dependencies, followed by a 1D convolutional layer (filters = 64, kernel size = 2) to extract localized n-gram features. Global average and max pooling are jointly applied to aggregate features, followed by a 256-unit ReLU dense layer and a sigmoid output layer.

Text_CNN. The Text_CNN employs multiple convolutional filters to capture local compositional patterns in SMILES sequences. Embedded inputs are processed through four parallel 1D convolutional layers (kernel sizes = 2,3,4,5; filters = 300, ReLU), each followed by global max pooling. The pooled outputs are concatenated, passed through a 256-unit ReLU dense layer, and a sigmoid output layer.

Transformer. The Transformer architecture leverages multi-head self-attention to model relationships among all tokens in a sequence simultaneously. Embedded and positional-encoded SMILES sequences are processed through a Transformer encoder layer with two attention heads and an intermediate dimension of 512. Global average pooling and dropout (rate = 0.1) are applied before a sigmoid output layer.

Molecular fingerprints are fixed-length vectorized representations that encode the structural and physicochemical characteristics of molecules [34]. Unlike chemical language models, which operate on sequential SMILES strings, fingerprint-based representations are derived directly from molecular graphs, capturing information about atomic environments, bonding patterns, and substructural occurrences. These representations have been widely adopted in cheminformatics for similarity search, virtual screening, and quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modeling [35,36]. Since different fingerprinting algorithms emphasize distinct aspects of molecular topology, electronic distribution, and structural patterns, the use of multiple fingerprint types enables a more comprehensive characterization of molecular structure.

In this study, eight widely used molecular fingerprinting methods were employed to capture complementary structural and electronic features [37].

Atom Pair 2D (AP2D): a 780-bit fingerprint encoding atom pairs across various topological distances, effectively representing molecular connectivity patterns.

E-State Fingerprint (EStateFP): a 79-bit fingerprint derived from electrotopological state fragments that quantify the intrinsic electronic state of each atom, modulated by its chemical environment and molecular topology.

CDK Extended Fingerprint (ExtFP): a 1,024-bit fingerprint from the Chemistry Development Kit that extends the traditional substructure fingerprint with additional descriptors for ring structures and isotopic masses.

CDK Graph-only Fingerprint (GraphFP): a specialized 1,024-bit variant that encodes atomic graph topology while excluding bond order information.

Klekota-Roth Fingerprint (KRFP): a high-dimensional 4,860-bit fingerprint capturing a comprehensive library of predefined functional fragments, providing detailed coverage of molecular substructures.

MACCS Keys Fingerprint (MACCSFP): a 166-bit binary fingerprint encoding the presence of key structural fragments and heavy-atom-based substructure patterns.

PubChem Fingerprint (PubChemFP): an 881-bit substructure fingerprint designed by the PubChem database, encompassing atom counts, bond connectivity, and ring systems.

Substructure Fingerprint (SubFP): a 307-bit SMARTS-based fingerprint capturing the presence of functional groups and ring features, as defined in the Christian Laggner fragment library.

Each molecular fingerprint was used as the input feature to an identical fully connected deep neural network (DNN) model. The DNN architecture consisted of two hidden layers, where the number of neurons was progressively halved in each layer to encourage hierarchical feature compression. Dropout regularization (rate = 0.2) was applied between layers to mitigate overfitting, and the final sigmoid output unit performed binary classification. This standardized modeling design enabled a consistent comparison across fingerprint representations, allowing assessment of how different molecular encoding strategies influence predictive performance.

MFM was developed to integrate the complementary strengths of CLP and FCM. CLP generates sequence-based molecular representations from SMILES strings, capturing token-level dependencies, whereas FCM encodes structural features such as atomic connectivity and electronic properties. However, establishing a direct correspondence between SMILES tokens and fingerprint elements is non-trivial, as there is no inherent one-to-one mapping between sequential representations and structural descriptors.

To address this challenge, a combinatorial strategy was employed to explore potential multimodal configurations across different CLP models and FCM fingerprint types. The top-performing CLP models were paired with eight distinct fingerprint models, generating all possible combinations of the two modalities. In terms of model structure, the early fusion components from the selected models were initially used to process the multi-modal data, converting them into 2D tensors for each modality. These tensors were then concatenated along the feature dimension in the hidden space. All neural network models were trained for 25 epochs on a single NVIDIA T600 GPU. During training, the validation accuracy and loss were continuously monitored to select the optimal checkpoint for final evaluation on the test set. The batch size was set to 12 for most experiments; however, for larger datasets with higher computational demands, it was increased to 256 to improve training efficiency. Model optimization was performed using the Adam optimizer with a fixed learning rate of 0.001, and the binary cross-entropy loss function was minimized between the predicted probabilities and the corresponding ground-truth labels. For comparative analyses with the corresponding single-modality counterparts and alternative multimodal fusion strategies, all models were trained independently under identical hyperparameter settings and loss functions to ensure fairness. The entire experimental framework was implemented using the autoBioSeqpy toolkit [39].

The performance of the multimodal fusion model was evaluated against several state-of-the-art supervised unimodal machine learning methods. For conventional baselines, LightGBM (LGBM) was used, with molecular descriptors generated by RDKit as input features. The directed message passing neural network (D-MPNN) [40], implemented using the kgcnn framework [41], served as the graph neural network (GNN)-based baseline. Additionally, pre-trained models such as ChemBERTa [42] and RoBERTa [43] were considered. Molecular embeddings were extracted from these models and fed into LGBM for final prediction. The LGBM model was trained on these embeddings, with hyperparameters optimized through grid search to ensure optimal performance.

For molecular property classification tasks, model performance was evaluated using three widely adopted metrics: accuracy (ACC), Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). In binary classification tasks, each molecule was assigned a predicted probability of belonging to the positive class, representing either active or toxic compounds. Molecules with probabilities exceeding the default threshold of 0.5 were classified as positive, while those below this threshold were assigned to the negative class, corresponding to inactive or non-toxic samples. This classification process produces four possible outcomes: true positive (TP), false positive (FP), true negative (TN), and false negative (FN).
