Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the deadliest infectious diseases worldwide and is caused by the intracellular pathogenMycobacterium tuberculosis(Mtb) [1]. Despite notable progress in diagnostics and treatment strategies, TB continues to pose a substantial global health burden. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately 10.8 million new TB cases and 1.25 million TB-related deaths were reported in 2023. These finding highlight the persistent challenges in disease control and emphasize the urgent need for more effective and durable therapeutic interventions. A major contributor to the success of Mtb as a pathogen is its remarkable ability to survive and persist within host macrophages. Mtb employs a range of immune evasion strategies, including suppression of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, modulation of host lipid metabolism, inhibition of antigen presentation, and induction of macrophage necrosis [2]. Together, these mechanisms enable long-term intracellular survival, promote chronic infection, and allow the bacterium to withstand host-induced stress, ultimately contributing to treatment failure and disease transmission.

Pyrazinamide (PZA) is a cornerstone of first-line TB chemotherapy and plays a critical role in shortening treatment duration [3]. When administered alongside rifampicin, isoniazid, and ethambutol, PZA reduces therapy length from 9 to 12 months to approximately 6 months [4]. PZA acts as a prodrug that is converted by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase (PZase), encoded by pncA, into its active form, pyrazinoic acid (POA) [5]. Although the molecular mechanism of PZA action remained controversial for decades, accumulating evidence has established ribosomal protein S1 (RpsA) as a key POA target [6,7,8,9]. POA binding disrupts trans-translation, leading to accumulation of incomplete polypeptides and, ultimately, bacterial death [10]. RpsA plays a central role in the bacterial trans-translation rescue pathway by coordinating with small protein B (SmpB), elongation factor EF-Tu, and transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA) to resolve stalled ribosomes and tag aberrant proteins for degradation [11]. This quality-control system is essential for bacterial survival under stress conditions such as nutrient limitation, oxidative damage, and immune pressure [12].

Structural studies have shown that POA interacts with key residues in RpsA, including Lys303, Phe307, Phe310, Glu318 and Arg357, through hydrogen bonding and π–π interactions [13]. These interactions competitively block tmRNA binding, impair protein homeostasis, and suppress bacterial viability. The clinical utility of PZA, however, has been increasingly compromised by the emergence of drug-resistant TB. While mutations in pncA represent a major resistance mechanism, resistance can also arise from structural alterations in RpsA itself. A clinically relevant mutation involving deletion of alanine at residue 438 (RpsAΔ438) induces pronounced changes in the C-terminal binding pocket [13]. This deletion enhances the flexibility of key residues, weakens critical hydrogen bonding and aromatic stacking interactions with POA, and substantially reduces binding affinity. As a result, POA fails to stably engage the mutated pocket, conferring resistance to PZA.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful paradigm in modern drug discovery, offering solutions to the limitations of traditional screening approaches, including long development timelines, high attrition rates, and escalating costs [14]. Transformer-based deep learning models, originally developed for natural language processing, have demonstrated exceptional performance in molecular representation learning and virtual screening [15]. By encoding chemical structures as SMILES strings and leveraging self-attention mechanisms, Transformers capture complex structural patterns and long-range dependencies that are difficult to model using conventional methods [16,17]. This enables efficient extraction of structure–activity relationships and rapid identification of bioactive compounds with high predictive accuracy. For antimicrobial-resistant pathogens such as Mtb, Transformer-driven screening provides a scalable and cost-effective strategy for identifying chemically diverse compounds with anti-mycobacterial activity. To complement these AI-based, target-agnostic predictions, the identified compounds are further screened against the RpsAΔ438mutant using structure-based computational techniques, including molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, to prioritize candidates with favorable target-specific interactions. Docking approaches predict binding poses and estimate affinities while identifying key intermolecular interactions [18]. However, docking inherently treats proteins as largely rigid entities and cannot fully account for conformational flexibility, solvent effects, or mutation-induced energetic changes [19]. MD simulations address these limitations by modeling atomic motions over time under near-physiological conditions, enabling detailed analysis of binding stability, conformational rearrangements, and resistance mechanisms [20]. Enhanced sampling methods such as Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) are particularly valuable for studying RpsAΔ438, where deletion-induced flexibility cannot be adequately captured by conventional MD alone [21].

In this study, we integrate Transformer-based virtual screening with molecular docking and Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics simulations to identify novel inhibitors targeting the RpsAΔ438mutant. By combining deep learning with dynamic structural validation, we aim to discover compounds capable of stabilizing the altered binding pocket and overcoming PZA resistance. This computationally accelerated framework provides a rational and scalable strategy for the discovery of next-generation anti-tuberculosis agents against drug-resistant Mtb.

Biological activity data forMycobacterium tuberculosis-related compounds were retrieved from the ChEMBL database (Target ID: CHEMBL360) [22], which collect experimentally validated bioactivity records for compounds tested againstMycobacterium tuberculosis. The initial dataset comprised 208,233 compounds associated with diverse activity measurements, including minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values derived from in vitro assays. To ensure data consistency, reliability, and suitability for machine learning model development, a rigorous preprocessing pipeline was implemented. Compounds with missing or ambiguous bioactivity information were first excluded. Only records reporting MIC values expressed explicitly in μg/mL were retained to maintain uniformity in activity type and measurement units. Duplicate entries arising from repeated assays or redundant compound annotations were subsequently removed to avoid data leakage and bias during model training. Chemical structures were then standardized using the RDKit cheminformatics toolkit [23]. This step involved canonicalization of SMILES representations, removal of salts, inorganic ions, and other disconnected molecular fragments, and normalization of chemical structures to ensure consistency across the dataset. Such standardization is essential for minimizing noise and enabling accurate learning of Transformer models. Following these filtering and standardization procedures, a rigorously curated, high-quality dataset ofMycobacterium tuberculosis-active compounds was established to support transformer-based model development, virtual screening, and structure-guided computational analyses.

Compound diversity is a fundamental prerequisite for building robust machine learning models with strong generalization capability. MACCS molecular fingerprints consisting of 166 binary bits [24] were generated for each compound using the RDKit toolkit, and pairwise Tanimoto values [25] were calculated to evaluate structural diversity among compounds. The Tanimoto coefficient is one of the most widely used metrics for assessing molecular similarity and is defined as:

wherearepresents the number of features present in the fingerprint of compound A, but absent in compound B,brepresents the number of features present in compound B, but absent in compound A, andcrepresents the number of features shared by both compounds. A higher Tanimoto values indicates greater structural similarity between two compounds, whereas a lower value reflects higher structural diversity. In addition, to assess the diversity of physicochemical properties, molecular weight (MT), lipophilicity (LogP), the number of hydrogen bond donors (HBD), and the number of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA) were calculated for each compound using RDKit toolkit. By jointly considering structural and physicochemical features, the overall chemical diversity of the dataset can be comprehensively characterized, providing a solid data foundation for subsequent model training.

To construct a biologically meaningful and statistically robust classification dataset, the distribution of minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values was systematically analyzed. Descriptive statistical measures, including extreme values, mean, and median, were examined to evaluate distribution skewness and identify potential outlier effects. Based on these analyses, a classification threshold was selected that minimizes sensitivity to extreme values while maintaining biological relevance. Compounds exhibiting MIC values below the selected threshold were classified as sensitive and assigned a label of 1, whereas compounds with MIC values greater than or equal to the threshold were classified as resistant and assigned a label of 0. This labeling strategy enabled balanced discrimination between active and less active compounds and provided a consistent foundation for subsequent transformer-based classification modeling.

The curated dataset was randomly divided into training, validation, and test sets using a stratified sampling strategy at an approximate ratio of 8:1:1. Stratification was performed based on compound labels to ensure that the relative proportions of sensitive and resistant compounds were preserved across all subsets, thereby minimizing potential bias arising from class imbalance during model training and evaluation. To reduce the influence of randomness associated with a single data split and to enhance the robustness of performance assessment, the splitting procedure was independently repeated six times. Each repetition employed a distinct random seed (8, 16, 24, 32, 48, and 64), resulting in six independent sets of training, validation, and test partitions. This multi-split strategy enabled more reliable estimation of model performance and improved reproducibility of the results. In addition, 166-bit MACCS fingerprints were generated for all compounds across the training, validation, and test sets, and t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) [26] was applied to project the high-dimensional fingerprint space into two dimensions. This chemical space analysis was conducted to confirm consistent distribution patterns among the subsets, ensuring that model evaluation was not confounded by systematic chemical space discrepancies.

To enable effective molecular representation learning, a SMILES tokenizer was developed to decompose chemical structures into discrete tokens suitable for Transformer-based modeling. The tokenizer was implemented using regular expressions [27] and was designed to preserve the syntactic and semantic integrity of SMILES strings. Specifically, the tokenizer first identifies atoms enclosed in square brackets, such as [Na+], and [OH−], which often denote charged or non-standard atomic states. It also recognizes multi-character halogen symbols, including Br and Cl, as single tokens to prevent erroneous fragmentation. Common organic element symbols, such as C, N, O, S, and P, are subsequently matched. In addition to atomic symbols, the tokenizer captures structural symbols essential for molecular connectivity and stereochemistry, including bond types (= , #), stereochemical annotations (@, @@), branch delimiters ((,)), and two-digit ring closure markers (e.g., 10%). Single-digit numerals are treated as independent tokens to represent ring closures and branching positions. This tokenizer effectively preserves the semantic integrity of SMILES strings and returns valid chemical tokens in their original character order.

The regular expression-based SMILES tokenizer was applied to tokenize the SMILES strings of all compounds in the curated dataset. The resulting tokens were aggregated across the dataset, deduplicated, and their occurrence frequencies were computed. Tokens were then sorted according to frequency to construct the final vocabulary. To support robust sequence modeling, four special tokens were prepended to the vocabulary: <PAD> for sequence length alignment, <UNK> for handling out-of-vocabulary tokens, <BOS> to denote the beginning of a sequence, and <EOS> to indicate sequence termination. These tokens enable consistent handling of variable-length SMILES sequences during model training and inference. Each token in the vocabulary was subsequently assigned a unique integer index based on its position in the vocabulary, allowing SMILES sequences to be converted into discrete numerical representations suitable for Transformer model input.

The proposed model was implemented using PyTorch (version 2.7.1) and comprises two primary components: a Transformer encoder for molecular feature extraction and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for binary classification. The Transformer encoder learns high-level representations of molecular structures, while the MLP predicts compound sensitivity or resistance toMycobacterium tuberculosis. SMILES strings were used as model inputs and were first tokenized and mapped to integer indices based on the constructed vocabulary. Special tokens <BOS> and <EOS> were appended to the beginning and end of each sequence, respectively, to explicitly define sequence boundaries. To ensure uniform sequence lengths within each batch, padding tokens <PAD> were added after the <EOS> oken as required. Any token not present in the vocabulary was mapped to the <UNK> index. The resulting discrete SMILES sequences were transformed into continuous vector representations using a trainable embedding layer. Positional encoding was added to the embeddings to incorporate information about token order, which is essential for capturing sequential dependencies in SMILES strings. The combined embeddings were subsequently processed through layer normalization and dropout to improve training stability and reduce overfitting. A learnable classification token (CLS) embedding, with the same dimensionality as the token embeddings, was prepended to each sequence to serve as a global molecular representation. The augmented embedding matrix was then passed through multiple stacked Transformer encoder layers, each consisting of multi-head self-attention mechanisms followed by position-wise feed-forward neural networks. Following Transformer encoding, the CLS representation and the mean-pooled representation of the token embeddings were combined using learnable weights to form a unified molecular feature vector. This combined representation was subsequently fed into the MLP classifier, which comprised layer normalization, fully connected layers, GELU activation functions, and dropout regularization. A final linear layer with a single output neuron produced classification logits, which were converted into probability scores using a sigmoid function. Compounds with predicted probabilities greater than 0.5 were classified as sensitive, enabling binary prediction of drug response inMycobacterium tuberculosis.

Hyperparameter optimization was performed using Optuna [28] with 100 optimization trials to improve model fitting on the training set while minimizing validation error. The search space encompassed key architectural and regularization parameters, including the number of attention heads (2, 4, 8), embedding dimension (64, 128, 256), feed-forward network dimension (256, 512, 1024), dropout rate (0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4), number of Transformer encoder layers (2, 3, 4, 6), and layer drop rate (0.1, 0.2, 0.3). Each hyperparameter configuration was evaluated using fivefold cross-validation on the training set. The mean MCC across the fivefolds was used as the objective metric to reduce variance introduced by a single split and to provide a balanced assessment of classification performance. Duplicate hyperparameter combinations were automatically excluded during optimization to improve sampling efficiency. To balance computational cost with performance stability, the top three hyperparameter configurations ranked by cross-validated MCC were selected for final model training. This strategy reduced sensitivity to random hyperparameter selection and ensured robust and reliable predictive performance across independent dataset splits.

Model training was conducted using a batch size of 32 for the training, validation, and test sets. Binary cross-entropy with logits loss (BCEWithLogitsLoss) was employed as the objective function to support stable optimization in binary classification. Model parameters were optimized using the AdamW optimizer, with both the learning rate and weight decay set to 1 × 10−4. A cosine annealing learning rate scheduler (CosineAnnealingLR) was applied to dynamically adjust the learning rate throughout training, facilitating smoother convergence and improved optimization stability. To enhance model generalization, a layer drop (LayerDrop) strategy was incorporated, in which Transformer encoder layers were randomly skipped during training. The maximum number of training epochs was set to 100, and an early stopping criterion was applied such that training was terminated if the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) on the validation set did not improve for 10 consecutive epochs. The model checkpoint achieving the highest validation MCC was retained for final evaluation. To prevent gradient explosion and improve numerical stability, gradient clipping was applied after each training epoch by constraining the L2 norm of all parameter gradients to a maximum value of 1.

Following training, model performance was evaluated on the independent test set using a comprehensive set of classification metrics. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was used to assess the model’s overall discriminative capability between sensitive and resistant compounds. Accuracy (Acc) quantified the proportion of correctly classified samples. The Matthews correlation coefficient was employed as a primary metric to account for class imbalance and prediction bias, providing a robust measure of classification quality. Additional performance metrics included the F1 score (F1), which balances precision and recall; precision (Pre), representing the proportion of correctly predicted positive samples; sensitivity (Se), measuring the ability to correctly identify resistant compounds; and specificity (Sp), reflecting the ability to correctly identify sensitive compounds. The Youden index was calculated to provide an integrated measure of diagnostic effectiveness, summarizing the model’s ability to discriminate between sensitive and resistant compounds.

To compare performance with traditional machine learning methods, Random Forest (RF) and XGBoost models based on ECFP4 fingerprints were trained on each training set using the Scikit-learn machine learning toolkit. RF is a decision‑tree‑based ensemble algorithm that improves model stability and generalization by constructing multiple independent decision trees and aggregating their predictions via voting [29]. During training, random seeds were set to 6, 18, 24, 32, 48 and 64. A grid search strategy with fivefold cross‑validation was employed to explore combinations of three hyperparameters: the number of trees (10, 30, 50, 70, 90), the maximum number of leaf nodes (20, 30, 50), and the maximum number of features considered for each split (1, 10, 20). XGBoost is an ensemble learning method based on the gradient boosting framework that sequentially builds additive decision trees and incorporates regularization to enhance predictive accuracy and robustness [30]. For XGBoost, the random seeds were set to 6, 18, 24, 32, 48 and 64, and a grid search with fivefold cross‑validation was performed over the following hyperparameter combinations: learning rate (0.1, 0.01), number of boosting rounds (10, 30, 50, 70, 90), maximum tree depth (2, 3, 4), subsample ratio of training instances (0.3, 0.5), and subsample ratio of features per tree (0.3, 0.5). After training, the performance of both traditional machine learning models was evaluated on the test sets generated using the same random seeds as the corresponding training sets, with exactly the same set of metrics applied. Subsequently, the best-performing model from each of the two model types was selected for systematic comparison with the Transformer model.

Based on the combined assessment of generalization ability and classification performance, the optimal model was selected for downstream virtual screening. To maximize chemical space coverage and enhance hit diversity, two complementary compound libraries were screened including FDA-approved drug database containing 20,000 [31] and the Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) database containing ~61,966 unique herbal ingredients [32]. The FDA-approved drug library comprises clinically validated molecules with established safety and pharmacokinetic profiles, offering strong potential for drug repurposing. In contrast, the TCM database provides structurally diverse natural products and herbal-derived compounds, which are well recognized as rich sources of bioactive chemical scaffolds. The combined use of these two libraries enabled comprehensive exploration of chemically and biologically relevant space for identifying potential inhibitors targetingMycobacterium tuberculosis.

Molecular docking was performed to predict the binding conformations and interaction profiles of screened compounds against the RpsAΔ438mutant. The crystal structure ofMycobacterium tuberculosisRpsA (PDB ID: 4NNI) [33] was downloaded from the Protein Data Bank and processed in PyMOL [34]. The alanine residue at position 438 was deleted to generate the RpsAΔ438mutant, followed by structural refinement and optimization using energy minimization to relieve local steric clashes. Protein preparation included the removal of crystallographic water molecules beyond 5 Å from the binding pocket, addition of polar hydrogens, optimization of protonation states at pH 7.4, and assignment of partial charges. Ligand structures were prepared using RDKit, where salts were removed, tautomer standardized, and MMFF94 charges [35] assigned. Ligand conformers were generated using ETKDG sampling [36] to ensure optimal exploration of conformational space. Docking was conducted using AutoDock Vina 1.2.3 [37], which incorporates expanded scoring function terms, AutoDock4 atom types, and improved local search performance compared with earlier versions. The docking grid was centered on the known POA-binding region of RpsA, covering key residues Lys303, Phe307, and Phe310. Exhaustiveness was set to 32, and the top-ranked binding conformations were selected based on binding affinity and interaction plausibility. All docking poses were visually inspected to confirm hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, π–π stacking, and salt bridges relevant to the biological mechanism.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out to evaluate dynamic behavior of RpsAΔ438–ligand complexes. All simulations were performed using Amber v.24 with the GPU-accelerated PMEMD engine [38]. The ff19SB force field [39] was used for protein parameters, while ligand parameters were generated using the General Amber Force Field 2 (GAFF2) with AM1-BCC charges assigned using Antechamber [40]. Each system was solvated in an OPC water box with a minimum buffer distance of 14 Å from the solute. Appropriate counterions (Na+/Cl−) were added to ensure system neutrality. Energy minimization was performed in two stages: initially, the protein–ligand complex was restrained to relax solvent molecules and ions, followed by an unrestrained minimization of the entire system to remove residual steric clashes. The systems were gradually heated from 0 to 310 K over 200 ps under the NVT ensemble. This was followed by 500 ps of density equilibration under NPT conditions at 1 atm. Positional restraints were progressively reduced during equilibration to allow controlled relaxation of the system. Subsequently, 400 ns production MD simulations were carried out under NPT conditions using a 2-fs integration timestep. Long-range electrostatic interactions were treated using the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method [41], and trajectory coordinates were recorded every 10 ps. Temperature was maintained using Langevin dynamics, while pressure was controlled using the Berendsen barostat. To enhance conformational sampling of the flexible RpsAΔ438binding pocket, Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) simulations [42], were performed following conventional MD equilibration. GaMD improves sampling efficiency by applying a harmonic boost potential to smooth the system’s potential energy surface, thereby facilitating the exploration of otherwise inaccessible conformational states while allowing recovery of the free-energy landscape through reweighting. Dual-boost GaMD (igamd = 3) was employed, applying boost potentials to both the dihedral and total potential energy terms. The threshold energy for both boosts was set to the lower bound (E = Vmax), and harmonic force constants were adaptively determined with upper limits of σ0P = 6.0 kcal/mol and σ0D = 6.0 kcal/mol for the total and dihedral boosts, respectively, following established protocols for protein–ligand systems [43]. The averaging interval for potential statistics was set to ntave = 50,000 steps. All trajectories were processed using CPPTRAJ. Structural and dynamic analyses included root mean square deviation (RMSD), root mean square fluctuation (RMSF), radius of gyration (Rg), hydrogen bond analysis, solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), and principal component analysis (PCA). Binding free energies were calculated using the MM/GBSA method [44] across 500 snapshots extracted from the equilibrated portions of the trajectories.

The drug-likeness properties of the compounds were assessed using the SwissADME server (http://www.swissadme.ch/index.php), based on Lipinski’s rule of five (RO5). Key parameters including the number of hydrogen-bond donors, hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the Lead likeness score were extracted. Subsequently, comprehensive ADME/T (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) properties, including physicochemical descriptors, cardiac safety, hepatotoxicity, genotoxicity, skin sensitization, carcinogenicity, organ-specific toxicities, and cell-based cytotoxicity, were predicted using ADMETlab 3.0 (https://admetlab3.scbdd.com/). These evaluations provide critical insights into the drug-likeness and ADME/T of the top compounds, essential for ensuring that the identified candidates possess genuine clinical potential.

A computational workflow was designed to identify potential RpsAΔ438inhibitors by integrating Transformer model, virtual screening, molecular docking, and Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) simulations. Transformer model was carried out using transparent and reproducible strategies, with binary classification labels unambiguously defined based on the MIC values of compounds againstMycobacterium tuberculosis. Transformer-based models were trained using SMILES representations of the compounds as input, with repeated stratified splits of 80/10/10 allocated to the training, validation, and testing sets, respectively. Model robustness and generalization were evaluated using multiple performance metrics. The best-performing model was subsequently applied to virtually screen compounds from FDA-approved drugs and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) databases. Top-ranked candidates were then subjected to molecular docking, and their binding stability and conformational dynamics were further assessed using GaMD simulations. The overall workflow of the study is depicted in Fig.1.

Overall workflow for screening RpsAΔ438inhibitors

After preprocessing, a total of 12,756Mycobacterium tuberculosis-related compounds were obtained. The distribution of structural similarity among these compounds is shown in Fig.2a. The Tanimoto similarity coefficients span a wide range, with the main peak located in the low-similarity region (below 0.5). Most compound pairs exhibit similarity values between 0.1 and 0.6, with a mean of 0.3641 and a median of 0.3623. Notably, 61.68% of compound pairs have Tanimoto similarity values below 0.4. These results indicate that the compounds in the dataset exhibit low structural similarity and encompass a rich variety of chemical scaffolds, without bias toward a limited set of scaffolds or structural motifs, thereby achieving effective coverage of a broad chemical space.

Chemical diversity and bioactivity distribution ofMycobacterium tuberculosis-related compounds.aDistribution of pairwise Tanimoto similarity scores.bViolin plots of key physicochemical properties.cHistogram of −log10MIC values.dViolin plot of −log10MIC values showing the overall activity distribution

In addition, the distributions of physicochemical properties are shown in Fig.2b. For visualization purposes, molecular weight (MW) values were scaled by a factor of 0.01, resulting in a range from 0.4509 to 20.9443 (corresponding to actual molecular weights of 45.09–2094.43 Da), with a mean of 4.1107 and a standard deviation of 1.4534. This indicates that the dataset covers a broad spectrum ranging from low-molecular-weight small molecules to high-molecular-weight complex compounds, reflecting substantial diversity in molecular size and structural complexity. Such diversity is beneficial for enhancing the model’s adaptability and generalization across compounds with varying molecular weights and structural features. The LogP values range from −10.3369 to 17.8956, with a mean of 3.8830 and a standard deviation of 2.0734, indicating that the dataset includes both highly hydrophilic (low LogP) and highly lipophilic (high LogP) compounds. This hydrophilic–lipophilic balance ensures that the model is not biased toward compounds with a single solubility profile but can instead learn from diverse solubility patterns. The numbers of hydrogen bond donors (nHBDon) and hydrogen bond acceptors (nHBAcc) range from 0 to 22 and 0 to 45, with means of 1.3282 and 5.5659, and standard deviations of 1.5784 and 2.9278, respectively. These distributions demonstrate substantial variability in hydrogen-bonding capacity and the number of polar interaction sites, reflecting rich diversity in molecular polarity and noncovalent interaction patterns. Overall, the broad ranges and high variability of MW, LogP, HBD, and HBA collectively indicate extensive coverage of physicochemical property space. Combined with the observed structural diversity, these characteristics provide a robust data foundation for constructing Transformer-based models with strong generalization capabilities.

The MIC values of the 12,756Mycobacterium tuberculosis-related compounds ranged from 0.0002 to 3125 μg/mL, with a median of 12.50 μg/mL and a mean of 40.81 μg/mL. Due to the presence of extreme values, constructing a regression model would make the training process highly sensitive to outliers, potentially causing predictions to deviate from the general trends of most samples. In contrast, a binary classification model, which only determines whether a compound is sensitive or resistant, is less affected by such extremes. Therefore, a binary classification strategy was deemed more suitable for this dataset. The MIC distribution exhibits a pronounced right skew, as indicated by the mean being greater than the median. Consequently, the median MIC value was selected as the classification threshold to distinguish sensitive and resistant compounds. The median provides robustness against outliers and skewed distributions while maintaining clear biological interpretability based on experimentally measured activity. Compounds with MIC values ≥12.50 μg/mL were defined as resistant (label = 0), totaling 6645 compounds, whereas those with MIC values <12.50 μg/mL were defined as sensitive (label = 1), totaling 6111 compounds. This thresholding approach yielded a balanced dataset suitable for supervised learning. For visualization, MIC values were transformed to the –log10scale (−log1012.50 ≈ −1.10; −log1040.81 ≈ −1.61). As shown in Fig.2c and d, using the median MIC value as the classification threshold effectively partitions the compounds into balanced sensitive and resistant classes.

Following compound labeling, the dataset was partitioned into training, validation, and test subsets using stratified sampling with an approximate ratio of 8:1:1. Stratification was performed based on compound labels to preserve class proportions across all subsets. To mitigate potential bias introduced by a single random split and to assess the stability of data partitioning, this procedure was independently repeated six times using different random seeds (8, 16, 24, 32, 48, and 64). Across all six repetitions, each training set contained 10,332 compounds (4950 sensitive and 5382 resistant), each validation set comprised 1148 compounds (550 sensitive and 598 resistant), and each test set included 1276 compounds (611 sensitive and 665 resistant).

To examine whether the different subsets maintained comparable chemical characteristics, chemical space analysis was performed using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE). High-dimensional 166-bit MACCS fingerprints were projected into a two-dimensional space, and the resulting distributions for the training, validation, and test sets corresponding to each random split are shown in Fig.3a–f. In all six projections, the training sets (blue points) form a broad and continuous distribution, reflecting the overall chemical diversity of the curated dataset. Importantly, the validation (orange points) and test (green points) compounds are consistently interspersed within the same regions of chemical space, rather than forming isolated clusters or occupying distinct regions. The close spatial overlap observed across all splits indicates that the validation and test subsets are chemically representative of the corresponding training sets. This consistency suggests that differences in model performance across splits are not driven by systematic chemical space mismatches but instead reflect genuine variations arising from model training and optimization. Moreover, the reproducibility of these patterns across six independent random seeds demonstrates that the stratified splitting strategy yields stable and well-balanced partitions, reducing the likelihood of split-dependent artifacts. Overall, the t-SNE analysis confirms that the adopted dataset splitting protocol preserves chemical space continuity between training, validation, and test subsets across multiple independent partitions. This provides a sound basis for subsequent model training, performance comparison, and downstream virtual screening, ensuring that evaluation results are derived from chemically consistent and representative data subsets.

t-SNE projections of MACCS fingerprint-based chemical space for training (blue), validation (orange), and test (green) sets across six independent stratified data splits generated using different random seeds (a–f), showing consistent overlap and representative distribution among subsets

The top three hyperparameter configurations identified for each of the six random seeds are summarized in Table1. All selected configurations achieved a mean Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) above 0.380 based on fivefold cross-validation on the training set, indicating stable and reproducible performance across different architectural settings. The relatively narrow MCC range across configurations suggests that the Transformer model exhibits consistent behavior under moderate variations in hyperparameters.

Across all optimal configurations, an embedding dimension (Embed Dim) of 256 was consistently selected, indicating that this representation size provides sufficient capacity to encode SMILES token information without introducing unnecessary model complexity. Similarly, the Dropout rate was uniformly fixed at 0.1, suggesting that mild regularization is adequate to stabilize training for the current dataset size and class distribution. In addition, the majority of configurations (15 out of 18, 83.33%) adopted a LayerDrop rate of 0.1, reflecting a preference for low-probability stochastic layer skipping to improve training robustness while preserving model depth. In contrast, greater variability was observed in the number of attention heads (NHead), feed-forward network dimension (FFN Dim), and the number of Transformer encoder layers (Layers). Attention heads ranged from 2 to 8, FFN dimensions varied between 256 and 1024, and the number of layers spanned from 2 to 6. This variability indicates that multiple architectural combinations can yield comparable performance, and that no single dominant configuration exists for these parameters under the current experimental setting. Overall, the hyperparameter optimization results demonstrate that the Transformer framework maintains stable performance across diverse configurations, providing flexibility in model design while ensuring reliable training outcomes.

To rigorously assess model stability and generalization, the curated dataset was partitioned into training, validation, and test sets using six independent stratified splits. For each split, the top three hyperparameter configurations identified through Optuna optimization based on mean cross-validated Matthew’s correlation coefficient (MCC) was selected for model training. This strategy resulted in a total of 18 independently trained Transformer models (6 data splits × 3 hyperparameter ranks), enabling a comprehensive evaluation of performance variability arising from both data partitioning and architectural differences. Model performance was evaluated on the independent test sets using multiple complementary metrics, including the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy (Acc), Matthew’s correlation coefficient (MCC), F1 score (F1), precision (Pre), sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), and the Youden index. To facilitate clear comparison, models were denoted using the notation Seed_x_Rank_y, where Seed_x indicates the random seed used for dataset partitioning and Rank_y corresponds to the ranking of the hyperparameter configuration within that split based on cross-validated MCC. For example, Seed_8_Rank_1 represents the model trained using the best-performing hyperparameter configuration for the data split generated with random seed 8.

As summarized in Fig.4, all 18 Transformer models demonstrated strong discriminative capability, with test-set AUC values exceeding 0.720. This consistently high AUC indicates reliable separation between sensitive and resistant compounds across all data splits and hyperparameter configurations. The highest AUC values were observed for Seed_8_Rank_1 (0.844), Seed_24_Rank_2 (0.834), and Seed_8_Rank_2 (0.832), reflecting particularly effective ranking of compounds by predicted sensitivity. Accuracy values further supported the robustness of the models, with all but one configuration (Seed_32_Rank_1, 0.659) achieving accuracies above 0.710. The best-performing models in terms of accuracy were Seed_8_Rank_1 (0.772), Seed_24_Rank_2 (0.763), and Seed_16_Rank_1 (0.762), indicating close agreement between predicted and true class labels. Importantly, MCC values, which provide a balanced assessment of classification quality under potential class imbalance, exceeded 0.410 for all models except Seed_32_Rank_1 (0.316). The highest MCC values were obtained for Seed_8_Rank_1 (0.543), Seed_24_Rank_2 (0.524), and Seed_16_Rank_1 (0.522), confirming strong correlation between predicted and true labels. F1 scores, which reflect the harmonic balance between precision and sensitivity, were consistently high across models, exceeding 0.680 for all configurations except Seed_32_Rank_1 (0.613). The highest F1 scores were achieved by Seed_8_Rank_1 (0.759), Seed_24_Rank_2 (0.753), Seed_16_Rank_1 (0.743), and Seed_32_Rank_3 (0.743), indicating effective trade-offs between false positives and false negatives. Precision values were generally above 0.710, with Seed_8_Rank_1, Seed_16_Rank_1, and Seed_24_Rank_1 achieving the highest precision (up to 0.768), demonstrating high reliability in identifying sensitive compounds. Sensitivity values, which measure the ability to correctly identify sensitive compounds (positive class), exceeded 0.600 for all models except Seed_32_Rank_1 (0.563). The highest sensitivity was observed for Seed_24_Rank_2 (0.755), followed by Seed_8_Rank_1 (0.750) and Seed_32_Rank_3 (0.730). In contrast, specificity values, reflecting the ability to correctly identify resistant compounds (negative class), were consistently high across all models, exceeding 0.730. The strongest specificity was achieved by Seed_64_Rank_2 (0.844), Seed_24_Rank_3 (0.814), and Seed_24_Rank_1 (0.806). These results indicate that while some models favored sensitivity, others emphasized specificity, underscoring the importance of balanced metric consideration during model selection. The Youden index, which integrates sensitivity and specificity into a single measure of diagnostic effectiveness, exceeded 0.371 for all models. The highest Youden index values were observed for Seed_8_Rank_3 (0.585), Seed_48_Rank_3 (0.558), and Seed_48_Rank_1 (0.540), further highlighting metric-dependent performance differences among models.

Performance comparison of 18 Transformer models across six independent stratified data splits (a-f), showing test-set AUC, accuracy, MCC, F1 score, precision, sensitivity, specificity, and Youden index for the top three hyperparameter configurations per split

Taken together, no single model simultaneously maximized all evaluation metrics. However, because MCC was used as the primary optimization objectives during hyperparameter selection, Seed_8_Rank_1 was identified as the optimal model. This configuration consistently ranked among the top performers across AUC, MCC, accuracy, F1 score, and precision, indicating well-balanced and robust classification behavior. Consequently, Seed_8_Rank_1 was selected for subsequent virtual screening analyses. Training dynamics for the selected model further supported its stability. As shown in Supplementary Figure1a, MCC values on both the training and validation sets increased steadily during training, indicating progressive improvement in classification performance. Early stopping terminated training at the 69th epoch, effectively preventing excessive fitting. To further assess generalization, AUC values on the training and test sets were compared after training (Supplementary Figure1b). Although a moderate train-test AUC gap (0.115) was observed, the top-tier rankings achieved across multiple performance metrics on test set, combined with early stopping, stochastic layer dropping, and regularization, indicates acceptable generalization for large-scale virtual screening applications.

To further compare performance with machine learning models, 18 random forest (RF) and 18 XGBoost models were trained respectively (6 data splits × 3 hyperparameter ranks) using the scikit-learn package [45]. These models were named using the convention Seed_x_Rank_y, where Seed_x indicates the random seed used for dataset partitioning and Rank_y corresponds to the ranking of the hyperparameter configuration. The performance of these two types of models on the test set is presented in Supplementary Figures2and3, respectively. For the RF models, Seed_16_Rank_1 achieved the best overall performance among all RF models, yielding an AUC of 0.822, accuracy of 0.747, MCC of 0.501, F1 score of 0.701, sensitivity of 0.619 and Youden index of 0.506, all of which were the highest among all RF models. Its precision (0.808) was moderate relative to other RF models, while its specificity (0.865) was slightly lower than most models. For the XGBoost models, Seed_16_Rank_1 achieved the best overall performance among all XGBoost models, yielding an AUC of 0.832, accuracy of 0.762, MCC of 0.524, F1 score of 0.734, sensitivity of 0.686 and Youden index of 0.530, all of which were the highest among all XGBoost models. Its precision (0.789) ranked third among all XGBoost models, while its specificity (0.832) was moderate.

In summary, the Seed_16_Rank_1 were selected to represent the RF and XGBoost models, respectively, and were systematically compared with the Seed_8_Rank_1 of the Transformer model to validate its performance. The performance comparison of the three models is shown in Table2. The Transformer model outperformed both RF and XGBoost on five key metrics: AUC, accuracy, MCC, F1 score and sensitivity. Although RF and XGBoost achieved slightly higher precision, specificity and Youden index than the Transformer, AUC and MCC are robust metrics that are insensitive to class imbalance and threshold selection, thus better reflecting the true discriminative ability of a model. The Transformer achieved the highest values on both of these metrics (AUC 0.844, MCC 0.543), and also showed superior performance in accuracy, F1 score and sensitivity, indicating its better overall capability in distinguishing between resistant and sensitive compounds.

A representative molecule, CHEMBL523618, was randomly selected from the independent test set, and its chemical structure is shown in Supplementary Figure4. To interpret how the Transformer model processes molecular information, the average self-attention weight matrices across the six encoder layers of the selected model (Seed_8_Rank_1) were visualized and are presented in Fig.5.

Average attention heatmaps of the six Transformer encoder layers (a-f) of Seed_8_Rank_1 for a representative test-set molecule (CHEMBL523618). Color intensity represents the relative attention weights between query and key tokens

In the first encoder layer (Fig.5a), attention weights were broadly distributed across atoms, indicating an initial exploratory encoding stage. Nevertheless, distinct patterns were already evident. Elevated attention was observed between negatively charged oxygen atoms (O−) and aliphatic carbon atoms (C), suggesting that the model began capturing relationships between charged functional groups and the molecular backbone. In addition, increased attention among fluorine (F) and chlorine (Cl) atoms indicated early recognition of halogen substitution patterns, reflecting sensitivity to chemically similar atom types even in the absence of direct bonding relationships. In the second encoder layer (Fig.5b), attention became more structured while retaining key interactions observed in the first layer. In particular, positively charged aromatic nitrogen atoms (n+) exhibited increased attention with aliphatic nitrogen atoms (N) and chlorine atoms, indicating that the model could distinguish nitrogen atoms across different charge states and chemical environments. Concurrently, interactions involving aliphatic carbon and nitrogen atoms became more prominent, reflecting a gradual shift toward chemically meaningful grouping of heteroatoms and backbone features.

By the third encoder layer (Fig.5c), the attention distribution exhibited clear structural organization. Stronger attention was allocated between the molecular backbone and neutral oxygen atoms (O), suggesting integration of backbone connectivity with polar functional groups. Notably, a pronounced increase in attention toward negatively charged oxygen atoms (O−) was observed across nearly all query positions, indicating that these atoms had begun to function as central reference points in the learned molecular representation. This trend intensified in the fourth encoder layer (Fig.5d), where attention became more concentrated and globally coherent. Nearly all atoms showed increased attention toward O−atoms compared with previous layers, indicating that negatively charged oxygen atoms had emerged as dominant attention centers. Through this consistent weighting, the model effectively integrated information related to molecular charge distribution and polarity, which are critical determinants of intermolecular interactions and biological activity.

In the fifth and sixth encoder layers (Fig.5e, f), attention toward O−atoms reached its maximum and became highly uniform across the molecule. All atoms exhibited strongly enhanced attention weights directed toward these charged oxygen atoms, forming a stable and coherent global attention pattern. This behavior indicates that the deeper encoder layers consolidate chemically salient features, enabling fine-grained integration of global electronic and structural properties rather than focusing on isolated local interactions.

Overall, the attention analysis reveals a stable and hierarchical feature-learning process within the Seed_8_Rank_1 Transformer model. Early encoder layers primarily capture local atomic relationships and chemically similar atom types, intermediate layers integrate multi-atom structural information with increasing emphasis on polar functional groups, and deeper layers establish global attention centered on charged oxygen atoms. This progressive abstraction demonstrates that the model does not rely on incidental or spurious features, but instead learns chemically meaningful representations that reflect both local structure and global electronic characteristics. Such hierarchical attention behavior supports the reliability of the learned molecular embeddings and provides mechanistic confidence in the model’s suitability for downstream virtual screening and structure-guided analyses.

The optimal Transformer model identified from hyperparameter optimization (Seed_8_Rank_1) was selected for large-scale virtual screening based on its stable performance and favorable balance between training and validation metrics. This model was applied to two chemically and biologically complementary compound libraries: the FDA-approved drug database and the Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) compound database. The FDA database offers compounds with established clinical safety profiles, while the TCM database provides structurally diverse natural products and herbal-derived molecules. Using model-predicted sensitivity probabilities, 317 compounds from the FDA database and 1757 compounds from the TCM database were classified as potentially active againstMycobacterium tuberculosis. Compounds within each database were subsequently ranked according to their predicted probabilities, and the top 50 FDA compounds and top 100 TCM compounds were selected for structure-based molecular docking against the RpsAΔ438mutant.

Molecular docking was performed to evaluate binding orientations, interaction patterns, and relative binding affinities within the POA-binding pocket of RpsAΔ438. The 2D structures of the screened compounds and their interaction with target protein are shown in Supplementary Figures5and6. Representative binding modes of the reference ligand and selected top-ranked compounds, highlighting their interactions with key residues implicated in PZA resistance (including Lys303, Arg356, Arg357, Glu318, Tyr280, and Ile358), together with the wild-type RpsA reference complex as a structural baseline, are presented in Fig.6. Notably, the reference ligand contacts identical key residues Arg357, Lys303, and Glu318 in both wild-type and RpsAΔ438, confirming that the A438 deletion preserves the binding site identity while fundamentally destabilizing its dynamic character, consistent with Zhi et al. [13].

Representative docking poses of the reference ligand (pyrazinoic acid, POA) and selected top-ranked compounds within the RpsAΔ438binding pocket, highlighting key hydrogen-bonding, ionic, and π-related interactions with functionally important residues

To quantitatively characterize these interactions, detailed docking interaction profiles were extracted and summarized in Table3. In parallel, attention heatmaps derived from the Transformer model were generated for the top-ranked compounds to visualize the learned inter-atomic attention patterns (Supplementary Figure7). The screened compounds generally displayed more favorable docking scores than the reference ligand, accompanied by shorter interaction distances and stronger interaction energies. Notably, multiple compounds formed simultaneous hydrogen-bonding and ionic interactions with Lys303, Arg357, and Glu318, residues that play a central role in ligand recognition and binding stability.

Specifically, in TCM26045, the oxygen atoms at positions 5, 8, 11, and 20 formed hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions with Gly316, Glu318, Glu318, and Arg357, respectively, while the nitrogen at position 34 donated hydrogen bonds to Arg356 and Arg375. The attention heatmap (Supplementary Figure7a) identified the nitrogen at position 34 as a critical atom, receiving dominant attention from all other atoms during representation updates. In TCM36252, the oxygen atoms at positions 24 and 33 and the nitrogen at position 30 formed hydrogen bonds with Glu318, Tyr280, and Arg357, and a C–H\(\cdots\)π interaction was observed between the carbon at position 23 and Phe310, the heatmap (Supplementary Figure7b), highlighted the oxygen at position 24 and 33 and the nitrogen at position 30 as key nodes with high inter-atomic attention. For TCM46589, the nitrogens at positions 26 and 37 and the oxygen at position 29 established hydrogen bonds with Glu318, Arg356, Arg357, and Lys303, in agreement with the attention heatmap (Supplementary Figure7c) where these atoms were identified as major attention sinks. In Z1511483977, the oxygens at positions 2, 3, 4, 7, and 18 formed hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions with Arg357, Arg357, Lys303, Lys303, and Glu318, while the nitrogen at position 22 formed a hydrogen bond with Arg356, the heatmap (Supplementary Figure7d) identified the nitrogen at position 22 as the principal focus of inter-atomic attention. For Z2235802088, the nitrogens at positions 6, 22, and 23 interacted with Glu318 and Lys303 via hydrogen bonds, and the oxygens at positions 33 and 36 formed hydrogen bonds with Arg357 and Ile358, additionally, the nitrogens at positions 6 and 9 participated in ionic interactions. The attention heatmap (Supplementary Figure7e) highlighted the nitrogens at positions 6, 9, 22, and 23 and the oxygens at positions 33 and 36 as atoms that attracted high attention from all other atoms. In Z2568748600, the oxygens at positions 1 and 3 and the nitrogen at position 12 formed hydrogen bonds with Lys303, Arg357, and Glu318, with the oxygens also involved in ionic interactions, a C–H\(\cdots\)π interaction was formed between the carbon at position 32 and Tyr280. The attention heatmap (Supplementary Figure7f) pinpointed the oxygens at positions 1 and 3 and the nitrogen at position 12 as critical atoms that dominated the attention patterns. Finally, for the reference molecule (pyrazinoic acid), the oxygen atoms at positions 1 and 3 and the nitrogen atom at position 6 formed hydrogen bonds with Arg357, Lys303, and Arg357, respectively. The attention heatmap (Supplementary Figure7g) for this molecule showed that the model identified the nitrogen at position 6 and the oxygens at positions 1 and 3 as important atoms, and that every atom, when updating its own representation, focused heavily on these atoms.

These interaction patterns indicate that the identified compounds are capable of compensating for the structural perturbations caused by the A438 deletion, thereby maintaining stable engagement with the RpsAΔ438binding pocket. Importantly, the wild-type structural comparison confirms that screened compounds engage the same pharmacophoric space as POA but with substantially expanded interaction networks, directly addressing the conformational instability introduced by the deletion. Overall, the combined virtual screening and docking results identify a subset of FDA and TCM compounds with favorable binding characteristics and interaction profiles, providing a rational basis for subsequent molecular dynamics simulations and dynamic stability assessment.

To evaluate the dynamic stability of the RpsAΔ438protein in different binding states, 400 ns molecular dynamics simulations were performed for the apo form (4NNI-APO), the reference complex (4NNI-reference), wild-type RpsA, and selected ligand-bound complexes identified from virtual screening and docking. The backbone RMSD profiles of all systems are shown in Fig.7. The wild-type RpsA system maintains stable RMSD values fluctuating between ~1.5 and 3.0 Å throughout the entire 400 ns trajectory, reflecting the structural integrity of the intact C-terminal pocket and establishing a dynamic baseline for evaluating the conformational consequences of the A438 deletion. The apo RpsAΔ438system exhibits relatively stable behavior throughout the simulation, with RMSD values fluctuating predominantly between ~1.5 and 2.5 Å, indicating that the deletion mutant maintains overall structural integrity in the absence of ligand binding. In contrast, the reference complex displays noticeably higher RMSD fluctuations, with values rising to ~4.0–5.0 Å during the mid-simulation period (150–250 ns), followed by partial stabilization at ~3.0 Å. This elevated deviation relative to both the wild-type and apo systems directly reflects deletion-induced pocket destabilization, confirming that the A438 deletion compromises stable ligand engagement rather than abolishing the binding site. This elevated deviation suggests reduced structural stability of the reference ligand within the mutated binding pocket.

Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) profiles of the RpsAΔ438apo form (4NNI-APO), reference complex (4NNI-reference), selected ligand-bound complexes and wild-type RpsA, over 400 ns molecular dynamics simulations, indicate the comparative structural stability and dynamic behavior of the protein in the absence and presence of screened compounds

Among the screened compounds, distinct stability patterns were observed. The TCM26045-bound complex maintained RMSD values mostly below ~3.0 Å, with moderate fluctuations emerging after ~250 ns, indicating stable but dynamically adaptive binding. TCM36252 exhibited larger RMSD excursions, reaching ~4.5–5.0 Å, particularly during the latter half of the simulation, suggesting increased conformational rearrangements within the complex. Similarly, the TCM46589 system showed pronounced fluctuations between ~2.0 and 3.5 Å, reflecting intermediate stability relative to the reference complex. Notably, several compounds demonstrated enhanced stabilization of the RpsAΔ438structure. The Z1511483977-bound system maintained RMSD values primarily within the ~1.5–2.5 Å range for most of the simulation, with only transient increases observed after ~250 ns. The Z2235802088 complex showed a gradual RMSD increase toward ~3.5–4.0 Å at later stages, indicating delayed but measurable structural adjustments. In contrast, Z2568748600 displayed the most stable RMSD profile among all ligand-bound systems, remaining consistently around ~1.2–2.0 Å throughout the 400 ns trajectory, with minimal long-term drift. Notably, the RMSD behavior of Z2568748600 most closely approximates that of the wild-type system, suggesting that this compound effectively restores the dynamic stability compromised by the A438 deletion.

Overall, the RMSD analysis demonstrates that several screened compounds confer improved structural stability to the RpsAΔ438protein compared with the reference ligand. In particular, Z2568748600 and Z1511483977 exhibit reduced backbone deviations and sustained stability over extended simulation timescales, supporting their favorable binding behavior observed in docking analyses. These results provide a dynamic validation of the virtual screening and docking outcomes and justify further investigation of these compounds using additional trajectory-based analyses.

To further characterize the local flexibility of the RpsAΔ438protein and to identify ligand-induced effects at the residue level, root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) analysis was performed for all systems over the 400 ns molecular dynamics trajectories. RMSF profiles for residues spanning the C-terminal region (residues ~280–440), which includes the POA-binding site and the Δ438 deletion region, are shown in Fig.8a–i, together with the corresponding secondary structure map (Fig.8j).

In the apo RpsAΔ438system (Fig.8a), moderate fluctuations are observed across the C-terminal domain, with RMSF values generally ranging between ~0.8 and 2.5 Å. Pronounced flexibility is evident near loop regions and terminal segments, particularly around residues 385–405, consistent with the loss of structural constraints caused by the A438 deletion. This intrinsic flexibility provides a baseline for evaluating ligand-induced stabilization effects. For structural context, the wild-type RpsA system (Fig.8i) exhibits well-constrained residue-level fluctuations generally between ~1.0 and 2.0 Å across the C-terminal domain, with only a localized peak near residue ~280, reflecting the inherent stability of the intact C-terminal pocket and establishing a reference for the degree of stabilization achievable upon restoration of pocket integrity.

The reference complex (Fig.8b) exhibits elevated fluctuations across multiple regions, with RMSF peaks exceeding ~3.0 Å in segments encompassing residues ~385–405. These regions correspond to β–loop–β motifs  shown in the secondary structure map. This elevated flexibility relative to wild-type directly confirms that the reference ligand fails to restore the conformational restraint lost upon A438 deletion, consistent with its near-unbinding behavior observed in RMSD and PCA analyses. The increased mobility indicates that the reference ligand does not sufficiently restrain the flexible C-terminal architecture of RpsAΔ438, in agreement with the higher RMSD values observed for this complex.

Among the screened compounds, distinct modulation of residue-level flexibility was observed. The TCM26045-bound system (Fig.8c) shows reduced RMSF values across most regions compared with the reference complex, with fluctuations largely confined below ~2.5 Å, except for transient peaks near residue ~280. This suggests partial stabilization of the binding region while retaining local flexibility. In contrast, the TCM36252 system (Fig.8d) displays higher RMSF peaks, reaching ~4.0–5.0 Å at the terminal region and loop segments near residues ~385–405, indicating persistent flexibility consistent with its elevated RMSD behavior. The TCM46589 complex (Fig.8e) exhibits intermediate flexibility, with RMSF values generally between ~1.0 and 3.0 Å. Although reduced relative to the reference complex, localized peaks remain around β-rich regions  proximal to the deletion site, suggesting incomplete structural restraint. The Z1511483977-bound system (Fig.8f) demonstrates more pronounced suppression of residue-level fluctuations, with RMSF values mostly below ~2.0 Å across the binding pocket and surrounding secondary structural elements, indicating effective stabilization of flexible regions. Notably, the Z2235802088 complex (Fig.8g) shows moderate RMSF increases toward the C-terminal end, particularly around residues ~385–405, consistent with the delayed RMSD rise observed in this system. In contrast, Z2568748600 (Fig.8h) exhibits the lowest overall RMSF values among all ligand-bound systems, with fluctuations largely constrained below ~1.5–2.0 Å throughout the analyzed region. This pronounced reduction in flexibility spans  β-strands adjacent to helices H6-H7, highlighting strong ligand-induced stabilization of the mutation-affected domain. Notably, the RMSF profile of Z2568748600 most closely recapitulates the constrained flexibility pattern of wild-type RpsA, providing strong evidence that this compound effectively restores the residue-level stability compromised by the A438 deletion. Overall, the RMSF analysis reveals that several screened compounds effectively reduce local flexibility within the C-terminal region of RpsAΔ438compared with the reference ligand. In particular, Z2568748600 and Z1511483977 demonstrate substantial suppression of residue-level fluctuations in structurally and functionally critical regions, corroborating the RMSD results and docking interaction profiles. These findings provide mechanistic insight into how selected compounds stabilize the deletion-altered binding pocket and support their prioritization for further dynamic and energetic analyses.

To assess the effect of ligand binding on the global compactness of the RpsAΔ438protein, the radius of gyration (Rg) was calculated for all systems over the 400 ns molecular dynamics trajectories. The time evolution of Rg values for the reference complex and selected ligand-bound systems is shown in Fig.9. The reference complex (4NNI-reference) exhibits a pronounced increase in Rg during the simulation, rising from approximately ~18.0 Å in the early stages to values exceeding ~23.0–24.0 Å after ~200 ns. This progressive expansion indicates a loss of structural compactness and suggests that the reference ligand fails to restrain large-scale conformational rearrangements induced by the A438 deletion. Notably, the wild-type RpsA system displays a strikingly similar Rg expansion profile, rising from ~18.0 to ~22–23 Å after ~250 ns. This unexpected parallel between the wild-type apo protein and the RpsAΔ438reference complex suggests that in the absence of effective ligand stabilization, both systems undergo comparable large-scale structural expansion further confirming that the reference ligand fails to provide sufficient conformational restraint within the deletion-altered pocket, behaving effectively as an unbound system. The TCM26045-bound system maintains Rg values tightly clustered around ~18.0–18.5 Å throughout the entire simulation, indicating preserved global compactness. Similar behavior is observed for TCM36252 and TCM46589, which fluctuate narrowly around ~18.0–19.0 Å with no evidence of long-term expansion. Among the ZINC-derived compounds, Z1511483977 and Z2235802088 show stable Rg distributions centered near ~18.0–18.8 Å, with only minor fluctuations at later time points. Notably, the Z2568748600 complex exhibits the most compact and stable Rg profile, remaining close to ~18.0 Å across the full 400 ns trajectory. This behavior is consistent with its low RMSD and RMSF values and indicates strong stabilization of the overall protein fold. Collectively, the Rg analysis demonstrates that ligand binding substantially suppresses global expansion of the RpsAΔ438protein relative to the reference complex. In particular, Z2568748600 and Z1511483977 maintain compact protein conformations over extended simulation timescales, reinforcing their favorable dynamic behavior observed in previous structural stability analyses.

To further elucidate the stability and persistence of protein–ligand interactions, hydrogen-bond (H-bond) lifetime analysis was performed for the reference complex, wild-type RpsA, and selected ligand-bound RpsAΔ438systems over the equilibrated portions of the 400 ns molecular dynamics trajectories. The maximum H-bond lifetimes for key interacting residues are summarized in Fig.10a–h, providing residue-level insight into interaction persistence and binding stability.

The longest-lived interactions were observed for ARG356-NH1 and ASN278-ND2, with maximum lifetimes exceeding 3.0 frames, indicating intermittent but relatively persistent hydrogen bonding. In contrast, the TCM46589-bound system (Fig.10d) displayed a more structured H-bonding pattern. Notably, ARG355-NH1 exhibited a maximum lifetime of approximately 3.0 frames, while ASN401-ND2 and ASN278-ND2 also showed elevated persistence. These longer-lived interactions suggest improved stabilization of the binding pocket relative to TCM36252, consistent with its intermediate dynamic behavior. The Z1511483977 complex (Fig.10e) demonstrated a dense and persistent hydrogen-bond network involving multiple key residues. Several interactions, including ARG285-NH2, ARG356-NH1, ARG289-NH2, and ARG356-NH2, exhibited lifetimes exceeding 3.0–4.0 frames. The presence of multiple long-lived H-bonds distributed across the binding pocket indicates strong and cooperative ligand anchoring, which correlates with the reduced RMSD and RMSF observed for this system. Similarly, the Z2235802088-bound complex (Fig.10f) showed enhanced H-bond persistence compared with the reference ligand. While the reference ligand and weaker binders rely on transient hydrogen bonds, the top-performing compounds particularly Z2568748600 and Z1511483977 form multiple long-lived hydrogen bonds with functionally important residues such as Lys303, Arg356, Arg357, ASN278, and Glu318. The direct comparison with wild-type RpsA confirms that these persistent interactions most closely recapitulate the stable H-bond framework of the intact pocket, providing a mechanistic rationale for their superior dynamic stability and establishing their potential to overcome deletion-induced resistance.

To characterize the dominant collective motions and conformational landscapes of RpsAΔ438in different binding states, principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the equilibrated portions of the 400 ns molecular dynamics trajectories. Two-dimensional projections along the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) for the apo protein, the reference complex, wild-type RpsA, and selected ligand-bound systems are shown in Fig.11. The apo RpsAΔ438system exhibits a broad and dispersed distribution in PC space, indicating substantial conformational heterogeneity and high intrinsic flexibility of the C-terminal region following the A438 deletion. This wide sampling reflects the absence of stabilizing ligand interactions and is consistent with the moderate RMSD and elevated RMSF observed for the apo state. The wild-type RpsA system occupies the most compact and constrained PC space among all systems (±30 units, single dominant basin), establishing a clear structural baseline that highlights the conformational consequences of the A438 deletion.

In contrast, the reference complex displays an expanded and fragmented conformational distribution, spanning a much larger PC space of approximately ±200–400 units 5–10 times larger than all ligand-bound systems and markedly larger than the wild-type distribution with multiple disconnected regions. This dramatic expansion relative to wild-type is diagnostic of near-unbinding behavior, wherein the reference ligand undergoes large-scale positional excursions within the destabilized pocket without achieving stable thermodynamic anchoring, confirming that the A438 deletion operates through conformational destabilization rather than steric disruption of the binding site. This behavior indicates unstable binding and frequent transitions between distinct conformational states, consistent with the reduced structural stability of the reference ligand in the mutated pocket.

Among the screened compounds, distinct ligand-dependent modulation of conformational dynamics was observed. The TCM26045- and TCM46589-bound systems show partial compaction of the conformational landscape compared with the reference complex, with trajectories populating fewer dominant regions in PC space. However, these systems still sample multiple basins, indicating residual flexibility and incomplete stabilization of the binding pocket. In contrast, the TCM36252 system exhibits elongated and anisotropic distributions along PC2, suggesting directional collective motions and persistent conformational rearrangements, consistent with its higher RMSD and RMSF values. Notably, the Z1511483977 and Z2568748600-bound systems demonstrate markedly more compact and well-defined conformational distributions. These systems populate one or two dominant basins with high point density, indicating restricted conformational sampling and enhanced structural stability. Among all systems, Z2568748600 shows the most localized conformational ensemble most closely approaching the compactness of the wild-type distribution reflecting strong suppression of large-scale motions and effective stabilization of the deletion-affected C-terminal domain. The Z2235802088 complex displays intermediate behavior, with partial compaction relative to the reference ligand but retaining moderate flexibility at the periphery of the sampled conformational space.

The eigenvalue contribution analysis further supports these observations and provides quantitative confirmation of the conformational hierarchy observed in the PC projections. The wild-type RpsA system shows a moderate first eigenvector contribution (~35%) with steep and smooth decay, reflecting well-distributed but constrained collective motions characteristic of a stable, geometrically defined binding pocket. The reference complex retains the highest variance in the first eigenvector (~45%) with a notably slow decay across multiple eigenvectors remaining elevated at eigenvector 3 (~20%) relative to all other systems confirming broadly distributed large-amplitude motions consistent with near-unbinding behavior in the deletion-destabilized pocket. In contrast, Z2568748600 and Z1511483977 exhibit among the steepest eigenvalue decay profiles, with variance dropping sharply after the first eigenvector and approaching zero by eigenvector 4, indicating highly constrained near-equilibrium dynamics and effective suppression of deletion-induced large-scale motions. The remaining systems TCM36252, TCM46589, and Z2235802088 display intermediate decay profiles, consistent with their partial stabilization observed in the PC projections.

To visually assess the time-dependent structural behavior of RpsAΔ438and ligand binding stability, representative snapshots were extracted at 0, 100, 250, and 400 ns from the molecular dynamics trajectories of the reference complex, wild-type RpsA, and selected ligand-bound systems, as shown in Supplementary Figure8. These snapshots provide a qualitative complement to the quantitative RMSD, RMSF, hydrogen-bond lifetime, and PCA analyses. The wild-type RpsA system maintains consistent ligand positioning and well-preserved secondary structure elements throughout the entire 0–400 ns trajectory, with no visible displacement of the ligand or deformation of surrounding helices and loops. This structural persistence establishes a visual baseline reflecting the stable binding achievable within the intact C-terminal pocket and provides a direct reference for evaluating the degree of stabilization conferred by screened compounds in the mutant context.

In the reference complex (4NNI-reference), the ligand exhibits noticeable positional drift relative to the POA-binding pocket over time. While initial contacts with key residues such as Lys303, Phe307, and Phe310 are maintained at early stages, progressive displacement of the ligand and reorientation of surrounding loop regions are evident at later time points. This structural deterioration stands in stark contrast to the wild-type system, visually confirming that the A438 deletion compromises stable ligand engagement despite preservation of the binding site residues. This loss of stable pocket engagement is consistent with the elevated RMSD, increased residue-level flexibility, and fragmented conformational landscape observed for the reference system.

Among the screened compounds, distinct ligand-dependent stabilization patterns were observed. TCM26045 maintains overall binding within the pocket across the simulation; however, gradual reorientation of the ligand and local rearrangements of secondary structural elements are evident at later stages, indicating dynamically adaptive but not fully constrained binding. In contrast, TCM36252 displays pronounced ligand mobility and pocket deformation over time, with visible changes in ligand orientation and surrounding helices, supporting its higher RMSD, RMSF, and broader PCA distribution. The TCM46589-bound system shows intermediate behavior, with the ligand remaining pocket-associated but exhibiting moderate positional fluctuations and local conformational adjustments. Notably, the Z1511483977 and Z2568748600 complexes demonstrate markedly enhanced structural stability throughout the simulation. In these systems, the ligands remain tightly anchored within the binding pocket from 0 to 400 ns, with minimal displacement and sustained alignment relative to key interacting residues. The surrounding secondary structure elements, particularly helices and loops adjacent to the C-terminal region, exhibit limited deformation over time. Among all systems, Z2568748600 shows the most persistent binding and minimal structural drift, consistent with its lowest RMSD and RMSF values, dense hydrogen-bonding network, and highly compact PCA conformational ensemble. The structural behavior of Z2568748600 most closely recapitulates the visual stability observed for the wild-type system, providing direct structural evidence that this compound effectively restores the binding persistence compromised by the A438 deletion.

To quantitatively compare the binding affinities of the reference ligand and selected screened compounds toward RpsAΔ438, MM/GBSA total binding free energies (ΔG_TOTAL) were calculated using snapshots extracted from the equilibrated regions of the 400 ns molecular dynamics trajectories. The resulting ΔG_TOTAL values are summarized in Table4and illustrated in Fig.13. To provide a structural energetic baseline, the MM/GBSA binding free energy of the reference ligand bound to wild-type RpsA was also calculated, yielding a ΔG_TOTAL of −23.85 ± 3.00 kJ/mol. This value reflects the energetic stabilization achievable within the intact C-terminal pocket and serves as a direct reference for quantifying the energetic consequence of the A438 deletion. The reference complex (4NNI-reference) exhibited a relatively weak binding affinity, with a ΔG_TOTAL of −13.03 ± 2.66 kJ/mol, indicating limited energetic stabilization within the deletion-altered binding pocket. The marked reduction in binding free energy relative to the wild-type complex (ΔΔG = ~10.82 kJ/mol) directly quantifies the energetic penalty imposed by the A438 deletion, confirming that deletion-induced conformational destabilization substantially compromises ligand binding thermodynamics. In contrast, all screened compounds demonstrated substantially more favorable total binding free energies, confirming improved binding strength compared with the reference ligand in the mutant.
