Drug development is a complex, time-consuming, and expensive process. Traditional drug development methods often require years and substantial financial investment to bring a new drug to market [1]. The pivotal success of clinical trials significantly shapes the course of drug development, holding paramount importance for pharmaceutical investors and patients alike. Nevertheless, about 40–60% of drug candidates succumb to unfavorable ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) characteristics during clinical trials [2]. By anticipating these ADMET properties, researchers can pinpoint and eradicate unfavorable pharmacokinetic traits in prospective compounds, expediting the developmental process while curbing time and financial expenses. This proactive strategy also facilitates the early recognition of potentially efficacious compounds during screening, prioritizing them for subsequent advancements and refining the selection of candidates with the highest likelihood of success as novel medications. Furthermore, it underpins the determination of optimal dosing, optimal routes of administration, and minimizes the threat of adverse reactions, enhancing both the safety and efficacy of drug candidates [3,4].

In recent years, the landscape of computational simulation software for ADMET property prediction has undergone remarkable advancements, achieving notable strides in enhancing prediction accuracy [5]. To further refine this intricate endeavor, artificial intelligence technologies have emerged as pivotal players in diverse ADMET computational frameworks, yielding an array of outstanding prediction tools, including ADMETlab, admetSAR, Interpretable-ADMET, HelixADMET, among others [6,7,8,9,10]. Nevertheless, the application of current models confronts myriad challenges, encompassing poor data quality, limited generalization capabilities, interpretability gaps, data scarcity and uncertainties, thereby restricting model accuracy and reliability. These hurdles underscore the urgency for continued research and optimization.

The algorithmic evolution in drug ADMET prediction has witnessed profound transitions, evolving from traditional machine learning through deep learning to the advent of pre-trained models. Initially, researchers harnessed traditional methods like linear regression, support vector machines, and random forests, relying on manual feature engineering to capture molecular attributes [11]. However, these approaches often grappled with the intricacies of ADMET prediction. As computational prowess and data availability soared, deep learning techniques emerged, automating feature learning and demonstrating exceptional performance in ADMET prediction tasks [12]. Nevertheless, their hunger for massive datasets and challenges in generalization amidst data scarcity remain obstacles. Recently, pre-trained models have emerged as promising avenues for ADMET prediction. By pre-training on extensive datasets, these models acquire rich feature representations that are subsequently fine-tuned for specific ADMET tasks, significantly bolstering generalization and prediction precision. They not only adapt seamlessly to diverse ADMET prediction scenarios but also address data scarcity and uncertainty more adeptly, marking the cutting edge of algorithmic developments in this field [13].

In the present work, the model underwent an extensive unsupervised pre-training regimen utilizing a vast small molecule dataset. The pre-training employs a dual-component architecture to discern intricate and abstract feature representations from different aspects, which we refer to as the Dual-component Pre-trained Model (DCPM). One component, based on the XLNet architecture, is used to learn the semantic differences in molecular sequences, while the other, utilizing an RNN-based architecture, captures complex representations at the level of molecular properties. Subsequently, DCPM was trained and evaluated across a broad spectrum of downstream tasks, encompassing various challenges within the MoleculeNet benchmark dataset, such as predicting Caco-2 Permeability, BBB Penetration, and identifying CYP450 1A2 Inhibitors. Its competitive performance and robust generalization capabilities across these tasks validated its accuracy and reliability. Building upon this success, we further extended DCPM's reach by subjecting it to rigorous training and testing within 97 downstream ADMET tasks. We conducted a comparison with the traditional molecular fingerprint ECFP and our method demonstrated superiority in nearly 69.07% of the tasks. In addition, compared with existing tools, our model covers the largest number of ADMET regression tasks, which are designed to provide more accurate prediction results. Simultaneously, our overall dataset is also the largest, containing over 460,000 entries, thereby laying a solid foundation for a more holistic and comprehensive approach to drug ADMET prediction.

The DCPM-ADMET training process incorporates diverse datasets, encompassing chemical molecule collections for pre-training and targeted ADMET datasets for constructing predictive models. The pre-training phase leverages PubChem [14], a comprehensive bioactivity database housing millions of compound records spanning pharmaceuticals, natural products, and chemicals. From this repository, we extracted SMILES and InChI representations of chemical molecules, subjecting them to a rigorous data preparation pipeline:

Data standardization: utilizing RDKit (version 2023.9.6), SMILES strings underwent standardization procedures, including bond order canonicalization and removal of redundant hydrogen atoms.

Missing & duplicate value filtering: molecules that failed standardization were deemed missing values, the missing and duplicate values were removed to ensure data uniqueness and validity.

Property descriptor calculation: based on the standardized SMILES, we employed RDKit to compute nine crucial physicochemical properties for each molecule, serving as molecular property descriptors. These encompassed logP, maximal and minimal partial charges, valence electron count, hydrogen bond donor and acceptor numbers, Balaban's J value, molar refractivity, and topological polar surface area.

These processes yielded 111,295,885 data points for pre-training.

For the ADMET property datasets, we aggregated resources from multiple experimental compound databases, notably PubChem, ChEMBL [15] and TDC [16], and implemented a meticulous data processing strategy:

Data standardization: SMILES representations were standardized using RDKit, and harmonizing data across datasets into consistent units like pEC50 and mol/L.

Data cleaning & merging: a rigorous comparison of entries across similar datasets from different sources led to the removal of conflicting samples in classification sets and unreliable samples in regression sets exhibiting discrepancies exceeding an order of magnitude. Subsequently, datasets were merged and further cleaned.

Duplicate data elimination: following cleaning and merging, duplicate entries were purged, resulting in a refined ADMET dataset.

This final dataset comprises 97 ADMET sets, segmented into 43 regression and 54 classification datasets, totaling 465,470 data entries.

The DCPM-ADMET molecular property prediction framework encapsulates two essential components: a feature extraction module and a downstream task prediction module. The feature extraction module meticulously crafts deep and versatile vector representations from SMILES molecular sequences. These representations then underpin tailored modeling for diverse downstream tasks.

Inspired by Transformer-based models' exceptional performance, DCPM embraces pre-trained architectures to refine SMILES sequences. However, prevalent methods like MoLFormer [17] and KPGT [18], which adopt the Transformer encoder during pre-training with masked token recovery akin to BERT [19], confront a pre-training-fine-tuning disparity when real-world inputs lack mask tokens [20].

1. XLNet [21], which combines autoregressive and permutation strategies, resolves this inconsistency while enabling bidirectional context analysis, a feat previously unattainable by autoregressive models. By leveraging XLNet's permutation technique and dual-stream attention, DCPM captures global SMILES sequence patterns through self-attention and distills chemical insights from bidirectionally permuted contexts, enriching feature representation.

2. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), XLNet leverages the Transformer-XL architecture to enhance its capability in managing extremely long texts. Nevertheless, the SMILES sequences of chemical molecules, characterized by their relatively shorter lengths and smaller vocabularies, are more susceptible to overfitting challenges. To mitigate this, we have omitted the long text processing feature and incorporated an additional RNN structure, drawing inspiration from the approach of Robin Winter [12]. This RNN conducts a Seq2Seq SMILES-to-InChI translation while regressing nine physicochemical descriptors. By integrating InChI's fundamental physicochemical insights and descriptor regression into the pre-training objectives, we augment task complexity, mitigating overfitting, and fostering deeper molecular knowledge extraction beyond mere sequence reconstruction.

3. Considering that tokenized SMILES sequences mainly consist of atomic tokens, lacking substructure fragment information of chemical molecules, we added a feature fusion layer to DCPM. This layer amalgamates XLNet and RNN hidden layers with Extended Connectivity Fingerprints (ECFP) [22], an atomic connectivity graph-based descriptor rich in topological and substructure information, augmenting the model's substructural comprehension.

To verify the effectiveness of each component, we conducted a series of ablation experiments on benchmark datasets. The results confirmed that the multimodal fused features of XLNet_RNN_ECFP represent the optimal combination. Detailed results are provided in the Supplementary Information (SI): “Ablation Experiments on Components of DCPM-ADMET”.

In Fig.1a, the pre-training workflow is outlined: SMILES are tokenized, embedded, and processed by an Encoder amalgamating GRU cells and XLNet layers. Extracted features are fed into three decoders, optimizing across InChI reconstruction, property prediction, and masked structure tasks. To enhance reproducibility, the optimal hyperparameter settings of the pre-training model are explicitly reported in the Supplementary Data Table S1.

Schematic workflow of the DCPM-ADMET framework.aPre-training phase: The model captures comprehensive molecular representations by simultaneously learning to reconstruct InChI tokens, property descriptors, and masked molecular structures.bFine-tuning phase: The pre-trained encoders are frozen and integrated with ECFP features through a fusion layer to perform downstream molecular property predictions

For fine-tuning, depicted in Fig.1b, the feature extraction layer is frozen, while the downstream prediction layer is trained. In this phase, the 512-dimensional structural embedding from XLNet, the 512-dimensional property embedding from the RNN, and the 512-dimensional ECFP fingerprints are concatenated into a final 1536-dimensional feature vector. For binary classification and regression tasks, we employ Random Forest to predict properties. The deep neural network applied in multi-task uses three hidden layers, optimizing key hyperparameters such as L2 regularization, dropout, and the number of neurons in each hidden layer. The Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) algorithm is used to identify the best hyperparameters across 50 evaluations. We employed early stopping and an 8:1:1 Bemis–Murcko scaffold-based train-validation-test split. Multiple evaluation metrics were utilized, with AUC as the primary indicator, and five independent runs were conducted to guarantee model robustness. Here, we systematically evaluated various fine-tuning strategies-specifically full-parameter fine-tuning versus parameter freezing (feature extraction)-alongside the selection of downstream models, including Random Forest (RF) and DNN (Deep Neural Network). For the DNN architecture, we further explored the differences between single-task and multi-task learning schemes. Our results indicate that parameter freezing (feature extraction) integrated with RF for single-task and DNN for multi-task learning achieves the best performance, aligning with the methodological strategies employed in prior research [23,24,25,26]. This optimized framework was adopted for all subsequent analyses, with full details provided in the Supplementary Information (SI): “Selection of Fine-Tuning Strategies and Model Architectures”.

DCPM's prowess is validated against ECFP on MoleculeNet, demonstrating superiority across 10 subsets (7 classification and 3 regression tasks). Among the seven classification datasets, ClinTox, SIDER, Tox21, and ToxCast are multi-label classification tasks, while the other three classification datasets (BACE, BBBP, and HIV) and the regression datasets (ESOL, Lipophilicity and FreeSolv) are single-task. Ultimately, DCPM-ADMET is trained on a comprehensive ADMET dataset, encompassing 54 classification and 43 regression tasks, solidifying its standing as a useful tool for ADMET property prediction.

For enhanced usability, we have integrated 36 additional directly computable endpoints (see the Supplementary Data Table S2 for detailed values), encompassing the calculation of physicochemical properties, medicinal chemistry principles, and toxicophore rules using the RDKit and Scopy packages [27].

First, when compared with traditional fingerprint features, ECFP, across 10 benchmark datasets, DCPM outperformed traditional fingerprints in 7 out of 10 tasks (Tables1-2, and Supplementary Data Tables S3-S5), demonstrating a clear advantage. This generalization is further confirmed by benchmarking against state-of-the-art pre-trained models, including KPGT [28]、KERMT [29]、MoleculeSTM-Graph [30]、MPG [31] and Mole-BERT [32] (Tables1-2, and Supplementary Data Tables S3-S5). The results demonstrate that DCPM achieved the highest number of optimal performances across the benchmarks, securing top results in 5 out of 10 tasks (BBBP, HIV, ToxCast, ESOL, and FreeSolv). In comparison, KPGT, MPG, and Mole-BERT reached optimal performance in 3 (BACE, SIDER, and Tox21), 1 (ClinTox), and 1 (Lipophilicity) tasks, respectively.

To validate the practical utility of our approach, we developed a comprehensive modeling framework covering 97 ADMET property prediction tasks, enabling a holistic characterization of molecular ADMET profiles. Comparative analysis demonstrates that our proposed scheme outperforms traditional fingerprint-based methods in 67 tasks (comprising 39 classification and 28 regression tasks), achieving an overall success rate of 69.07%. Specifically, the average AUC for classification tasks improved from 0.812 to 0.831, while the average Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) for regression tasks increased significantly from 0.661 to 0.701. Detailed performance metrics for all tasks are provided in Tables S6–S7 of the Supplementary Data.

We conducted a comparative analysis of endpoint information and data size across several prominent ADMET prediction platforms, namely ADMETlab 3.0 [33], admetSAR 3.0 [34], ProTox3.0 [35], ADMETboost [36], toxCSM [37] and Interpretable-ADMET [9]. The comprehensive details of this comparison are outlined in Table3. The results indicate that our platform encompasses the highest number of ADMET regression tasks. Furthermore, we possess the largest dataset, which serves as a robust foundation for model development. Overall, DCPM-ADMET provides more options for ADMET prediction.

DCPM-ADMET presents a user-centric web application that seamlessly integrates pre-trained and 97 specialized ADMET models and 36 directly computable properties in the cloud. This platform enables users to effortlessly engage with ADMET prediction outcomes through a highly intuitive graphical interface, as exemplified in Fig.2.

DCPM-ADMET Web Application Prediction Workflow. The platform features a user-friendly interface for seamless interaction: (Left) User Input: Molecular structures can be submitted via SMILES strings. (Middle) Cloud Computing: Input data is processed in the background. (Right) Results Display: Prediction outcomes are presented through a comprehensive dashboard, featuring 2D/3D molecular visualizations, basic physicochemical properties (e.g., Molecular Weight, LogP), and detailed ADMET classification/regression results with visual indicators (green/red dots) to highlight potential toxicity or metabolic risks. A more detailed introduction is available through the Documents component

In the DCPM-ADMET prediction module, users input molecular representations in SMILES format, and the system processes them via cloud-based RDKit to generate key molecular attributes, including molecular structure, molecular weight and other properties. ADMET predictions are provided for both regression and classification tasks.

Regression results include predictions for critical aspects: basic properties, as well as absorption, distribution, metabolism, and toxicity. Drug-likeness is assessed based on thresholds derived from pharmacological research, marked as “√” (acceptable), “ × ” (unacceptable), or “warning” for intermediate values. For instance (Fig.3b), Apixaban’s bioavailability is predicted at 46.48%, marked as “√”, indicating good bioavailability, while its plasma protein binding is 89.02%, marked as “warning”, suggesting reduced efficacy.

Molecular structure and ADMET profile of apixaban.a2D structure and SMILES.bAbsorption and distribution predictions.cCYP450 metabolism predictions

In classification tasks, probabilities for various ADMET categories are displayed, with values between 0–35% labeled as negative (“−”), 65–100% as positive (“ + ”), and 35–65% as “warning”. For example (Fig.3c), Apixaban’s predictions for CYP450 2C9 inhibitor, CYP450 3A4 inhibitor, and CYP450 3A4 substrate are marked as “ + ”, indicating metabolism via these enzymes, consistent with its known metabolic pathways.

We analyzed 45 withdrawn drugs from DrugBank [39] (version 5.1.12) and predicted their ADMET properties using DCPM-ADMET. These drugs were withdrawn due to potential toxicity, with hERG toxicity [40] and hepatotoxicity [41] being the main causes. Among the 45 drugs, 24 were withdrawn due to hERG toxicity, 16 due to hepatotoxicity, 2 due to carcinogenicity and genotoxicity, and 1 due to skin irritation.

DCPM-ADMET accurately predicted potential toxicity in 36 out of 45 drugs, marking a success rate of approximately 80.0% (see Supplementary Data Table S8). To ensure unbiased results, we ensured no overlap between DrugBank molecules used in these tasks and our training sets. Molecular fingerprint similarity analysis using Tanimoto coefficients revealed low average similarities (0.06–0.164) between the 45 drugs and their training set counterparts, further validating the model's generalization. Among drugs with maximum similarity below 0.4, prediction accuracy remained consistent with the overall accuracy (87.5%), reinforcing DCPM-ADMET's robust generalization capabilities (see Supplementary Data Table S8).

Furthermore, we compared our tool with the current mainstream ADMET web tools (ADMETlab 3.0 and admetSAR 3.0), and the results showed that we have certain advantages in hERG prediction. This demonstrated the necessity and practicality of DCPM-ADMET as another ADMET tool available for online use (see Supplementary Data Table S8).

Thalidomide, initially synthesized by CIBA (predecessor of Novartis), was marketed in Europe in 1957 as an antiemetic for pregnant women, tragically leading to numerous birth defects. Our tool foresaw its genotoxicity (Fig.4a), emphasizing the potential to avert such disasters with early predictions.

Thalidomide & Nefazodone Prediction Insights

For hERG inhibition and hepatotoxicity, DCPM-ADMET boasted prediction accuracies of 91.7% and 75.0%, respectively, underscoring its robust predictive capabilities. Specifically, Nefazodone has demonstrated the trustworthiness of DCPM-ADMET’s prediction. According to its description, Nefazodone has a very low incidence of liver damage, with a serious liver injury occurrence rate of 1 in 250,000 to 300,000 users annually. However, DCPM-ADMET is still capable of predicting its hepatotoxicity (Fig.4b). On the other hand, Nefazodone was predicted as high risk for DILI (drug-induced liver injury) with DCPM-ADMET, prompting further investigation. Reports suggest that Nefazodone is oxidized by CYP3A4 (our prediction also shows it as a substrate for CYP3A4), and its active metabolites can bind with GSH to produce toxicity, potentially explaining the high DILI risk and the discrepancy in its hepatotoxicity prediction. This demonstrates the tool’s ability to accurately predict ADMET properties and guide our understanding of the intrinsic factors underlying drug properties.

DCPM-ADMET predicted that Fexofenadine (0.826) has a lower risk of side effects compared to Terfenadine (0.868) (Fig.5a), aligning with its safer profile and reduced risk of QT prolongation. In the case of IAP antagonists, DCPM-ADMET accurately predicted the impact of structural modifications on the ADMET properties of tolinapant (Fig.5b). By incorporating a hydroxymethyl group, tolinapant's lipophilicity decreased (LogD: 2.12 vs. 2.58; LogP: 4.17 vs. 4.32), and its probability of being a CYP3A4 substrate (60.56%) was lower than that of AT-IAP (67.09%). These predictions were consistent with experimental data [42], validating DCPM-ADMET's effectiveness in drug optimization.

Comparative ADMET prediction results of multiple drugs.aComparison of side effect risks between fexofenadine and terfenadine;bEffects of structural modification on the ADMET properties of tolinapant

To assess DCPM-ADMET's performance further, we analyzed 71 drugs with Caco-2 permeability data from DrugBank. Caco-2 permeability gauges a drug's intestinal absorption, serving as the gold standard for in vitro predictions [43]. Our model achieved an RMSE of 0.47 and a PCC of 0.83 on these data (Fig.6), signifying minimal error and strong correlation between predictions and experimental values. Molecules in the test set exhibited low mean similarity to the training set (0.045–0.16), highlighting the model's generalization ability (all data and prediction values see Supplementary Data Table S9).

Prediction results for 71 drugs with Caco-2 values

In this study, we present DCPM-ADMET, an advanced tool for predicting drug ADMET properties using a novel pre-trained model architecture that combines the strengths of both RNN and Transformer models. By incorporating molecular substructure information through ECFP fingerprints, DCPM outperforms traditional molecular fingerprint methods and most pre-trained models, offering accurate and reliable predictions across a wide range of molecular properties.

DCPM-ADMET is capable of predicting 133 ADMET endpoints, covering 54 classification tasks and 43 regression tasks. The model is trained on a high-quality dataset consisting of 465,470 entries associated with diverse ADMET profiles. Additionally, it integrates 36 computational descriptors linked to physicochemical characteristics, medicinal chemistry guidelines, and toxicophore rules. Benefiting from such comprehensive functionalities, DCPM-ADMET serves as a complementary online ADMET prediction platform and delivers a set of unique predictive endpoints. This tool enables the early recognition of drug candidates with poor pharmacokinetic behaviors, facilitating the structural optimization of molecules to further improve drug efficacy and safety.

Looking forward, the methodologies employed in DCPM can be extended to other areas of drug discovery, such as predicting drug-drug interactions and optimizing molecular bioactivities. With the continuous availability of more data, the model's accuracy and generalizability can be further refined.

title: DICL: a manually curated database of ion channels and ligands as a useful platform for drug discovery targeting ion channels
author: Wei Zhao; Xiaoqing Gong; Yanan Tian; Lingling Wang; Chenggong Fu; Xiaojun Yao; Huanxiang Liu
text:
Ion channels represent a crucial class of drug targets. Currently, with the structural elucidation of more and more ion channels and the rapid development of artificial intelligence in drug discovery, unprecedented opportunities have emerged for designing and discovering drugs that target ion channels. However, both traditional computer-aided drug design and artificial intelligence drug design rely heavily on a large amount of effective data, particularly high-quality data. Yet, data pertaining to relevant ion channels and their ligands are notably scarce. Therefore, constructing a comprehensive and reliable database encompassing ion channels and their ligands is paramount for drug discovery efforts centered around ion channels. To address this gap, we developed database (DICL, Database of Ion Channels and Ligands) including 464,225 data records with the manually curated structure and activity information of ligands from over 6,000 peer-reviewed publications, patents and other databases. As far as we know, it represents the largest and most detailed online database dedicated to ion channels and their ligands. Additionally, the database integrates information regarding the binding sites of ligands, channelopathies, and specific experimental conditions related to biological activities for the first time. Furthermore, it features a user-friendly interface that facilitates querying, browsing, and utilization of this resource. DICL is freely available and can be accessed at https://fca_icdb.mpu.edu.mo/ICHDB/public/.

DICL comprises 464,225 data records, including 7,122 related to peptides, 150,208 related to compounds from peer-reviewed publications or patents, and 306,895 compounds from the hERGCentral database, as well as 1,750 subtypes of ion channels from 165 species, which represents the most comprehensive and most detailed online database of ion channels and their ligands.

The database integrates information regarding the binding sites of ligands, channelopathies, and specific experimental conditions related to biological activities for the first time.

This database not only addresses a crucial gap in the comprehensive database of ion channels and their ligands but also serves as a foundation for pioneering drug development strategies targeting ion channels.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

Ion channels are crucial for the regulation of key physiological and pathophysiological processes, which positions them as highly promising therapeutic targets [1,2,3,4]. To date, more than 60 channelopathies have been identified [5,6], and the DisGeNET knowledge platform has cataloged 196 distinct subtypes of ion channels that are related to human diseases [7], including diabetes [8,9], epilepsy [10,11], hypertension [12], cancer [13,14], and chronic pain [15]. As a result, ion channels have emerged as highly attractive targets for drug development. Statistical data reveal that 18% of small molecule drugs listed in the ChEMBL database are modulators of ion channels [16,17], with approximately 170 drugs available on the market and over 60 undergoing clinical trials [18,19]. Noteworthy examples include the cAMP-dependent chloride channel corrector lumacaftor for the treatment of cystic fibrosis [20,21], calcium channel blocker isoptin for the treatment of hypertension and angina [22], and transient receptor potential channel (TRPV1) modulators, such as capsaicin, used to relieve muscle and joint pain as well as neuralgia [23]. Despite the considerable number of existing drugs and ongoing clinical trials, ion channels remain relatively underexploited for therapeutic interventions [24]. Furthermore, some ion channels—including the Voltage-dependent L-type calcium channel subunit alpha-1C (Cav1.2), the human ether-à-go-go-related gene (hERG), and the Sodium channel protein type 5 subunit alpha (Nav1.5)—are associated with cardiotoxicity [25,26,27]. Consequently, the development of effective and selective modulators targeting ion channels has long been a focal point of research.

The limited availability of ion channel structures and the incomplete understanding of their corresponding functions significantly constrain the development of ion channel drugs. The advancement of cryo-electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) [28,29], coupled with the introduction of AlphaFold Protein Structure Database [30], presents significant opportunities for structure-based drug design. For instance, Jiang et al. performed virtual screening (VS) of an 8-million-compound library with computed fragment maps to discover two PIEZO1 activators [31]. The advent of deep learning provides enough speed to deal with VS of billions of molecules, such as Deep Docking [32], RosettaVS [33], GENTRL [34]. Concurrently, molecular generation utilizing deep learning methodologies has introduced innovative approaches for the design of hit compounds with novel structural frameworks [35,36]. Notably, both computer-aided drug design (CADD) and artificial intelligence-driven drug design (AIDD) rely heavily on large amounts of precise and effective data, especially AIDD, a data-driven drug design method [37,38,39]. Xu posited that high-quality data facilitates artificial intelligence models in recognizing significant patterns and producing corresponding predictions [40]. Therefore, the quantity and quality of data are very important factors affecting drug design based on artificial intelligence. Nevertheless, there remains a significant deficiency in comprehensive and reliable data pertaining to ion channels and their modulators.

To provide the valuable information for drug design targeting ion channels, researchers have tried to collect various information related to ion channels. For instance, Gallin et al. compiled VKCDB (voltage-gated K+channel database) consisting of 2,063 unique channel sequences derived from Bacteria (477), Archaea (18) and Eukaryotes (1568), which were used for phylogenetic and comparative analysis [41]. But in this dataset, only sequence information of ion channels was included. In 2023, Nikolay et al.released the Kalium3.0, which consolidates information of polypeptide ligands associated with potassium channels [42]. The cardiotoxicity associated with hERG has garnered significant attention, leading to the publication of extensive data, with hERGCentral being one of the most widely utilized resources [43]. This database, which offered information on the chemical structures and biological activities over 300,000 compounds identified through high throughput screening [43], is currently no longer maintained and its original web interface is currently inaccessible. Furthermore, Wang et al.developed the Voltage-Gated Sodium Channels Database, which provides 6,055 data records of 3,396 compounds from 173 references [44]. Additionally, allosteric modulators represent a significant class of ion channel drug design. The ASD database includes 153 allosteric proteins of ion channels and 15,177 modulators in 2023 [45]. Users can retrieve chemical structure, biological activity (IC50/EC50), various chemical and physical properties from these databases. Some comprehensive databases, such as, BindingDB [46], PubChem database [47], ChEMBL [17], therapeutic target database (TTD) [48], also contain relevant information. Although these works can provide some useful information about some ion channels and their ligands, a multifaceted and integrated ion channel-related dataset with curated activity and structural data is still lacking [49]. Additionally, it has been brought to our attention that there are inaccuracies concerning the stereochemical assignment of specific compounds, as detailed in the supplementary information (13321_2026_1246_MOESM1_ESM.docx), although such inconsistencies are not widespread. Notably, existing databases lack detailed information on binding sites, channelopathies, and the specific experimental conditions under which biological activities were determined. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a professional and comprehensive database to integrate ion channel-related information.

In this work, we developed the database of ion channels and ligands (DICL), a comprehensive database that encompasses data resources for ligands (compounds and peptides) targeting ion channels, and functional data for ion channels (Fig.1). This database catalogues 1,750 ion channel protein subtypes across 27 major types as listed in Table1, including Voltage-gated potassium channels (VGKCs), Transient receptor potential channels (TRP), and Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs). Furthermore, the DICL database includes 150,208 compound entries and 7,122 peptide records from over 6,000 peer-reviewed articles and patents, along with 306,895 compound records from the hERGCentral database. Each data record comprises over 30 distinct items of information, including biological activity or affinity metrics (IC50, EC50, Ki, Kd), experimental conditions, target information, channelopathy, binding sites of ligands, etc. These data have been manually validated and are supported by corresponding references. In summary, this database offers accurate and comprehensive information on ion channels and ligands, serving as a valuable resource for ion channel drug design. As far as we know, it represents the largest and most detailed online database dedicated to ion channels and their ligands, serving as a foundational tool for innovative drug development strategies aimed at ion channel modulation.

Overview of the database of ion channels and ligands (DICL): construction process, data types, and functions

The data for DICL were sourced from both literature and publicly accessible databases, as illustrated in Fig.1. A comprehensive literature search was performed using PubMed, Google Patents, and Web of Science databases. Keywords such as ‘compound’, ‘peptide’, ‘modulator’, ‘molecule’, ‘agonist’, ‘antagonist’, ‘inhibitor’, and ‘blocker’, in conjunction with ‘Voltage-dependent calcium channel’ and other specific ion channel names, were employed to query these resources. The search in Google Patents followed a similar keyword-based strategy to identify relevant patent documents. The scope of the search included both article titles and abstracts. Candidate compounds and peptides retrieved through search were initially identified based on functional and structural information in the literature. To extract ion channel sequences and UniProt accession numbers, targeted keyword searches were conducted using terms such as “Voltage-gated potassium channels”, “Aquaporins”, “Voltage-dependent calcium channels”, “γ-Aminobutyric acid type A receptors”, “ionotropic glutamate receptors”, “Chloride channels”, et al.across UniProt [50], Protein Data Bank (PDB) [51] and GenBank [52]. Each UniProt accession number corresponds to a unique ion channel sequence from a specific organism and all retrieved data were individually checked to ensure accuracy. Subsequently, molecular information from the literature was collated and curated using DrugFlow [53] and StoneMind Collector [54]. This included data such as IC50/EC50/Ki/Kdvalues, compound structures, target receptors, binding sites, and experimental conditions. The data in DICL were collected not only from peer-reviewed literature but also from patents to ensure comprehensive information. Additionally, we compiled the information of ion channels and ligands from several reputable databases (Fig.2), including BindingDB [46], ChEMBL [17], Protein Data Bank [55], UniProt, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database [30], VGSC-DB [44], PubChem [56], and TTD [48]. In accordance with our data inclusion policy, every compound must be traceable to a primary empirical source. Therefore, entries sourced from external databases (e.g., ChEMBL, BindingDB) that are not grounded in verifiable literature are omitted from our collection. Additionally, over 300,000 compounds from hERGCentral [43] were also integrated into DICL. As the original hERGCentral database is no longer maintained and is currently inaccessible, the relevant data was sourced from a third-party repository [57].

Data sources integrated in DICL. The database integrates data from ten public resources: BindingDB, ChEMBL, Protein Data Bank (PDB), UniProt, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, VGSC-DB, PubChem, ASD, Kalium 3.0, and TTD. (Detailed information is provided in 13321_2026_1246_MOESM6_ESM.xlsx of the Supplementary Information.)

In the context of compounds’ information, each record identified by a unique DICL ID comprises 35 distinct items of information. The two-dimensional structures of the compounds were generated utilizing SMILES Drawer [58]. Biological activity or binding affinity were quantitatively assessed using established biochemical and biophysical metrics, including IC50, EC50, Kiand Kd, with nanomolar (nM) as the standard unit of measurement. Binding sites were first categorized as either agonists or antagonists. Given the distinct pharmacological implications, the antagonist sites were further classified into "Inhibitor" and "Blocker" subtypes based on their precise location and mode of action. Additionally, "Allosteric" sites were separately highlighted due to their significant and distinct role in modulating ion channel function. The determination of binding site residues required corroboration by at least two independent lines of evidence. These included mutagenesis data demonstrating significant functional impact, high-resolution structural data (from X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM), or computational validation via molecular dynamics simulations or docking studies. Data on biological activity, binding affinity, targets, binding sites, and organisms were compiled from the literature. The process of data integration and standardization is shown in Fig.3. The compound information was initially obtained from public databases, including BindingDB, ChEMBL, and TTD. For each database, we downloaded all available molecular representations—such as SMILES, SDF, and InChI—to ensure data completeness. Canonical SMILES strings served uniformly as the primary input for our standardization pipeline, while the corresponding 2D structures were employed for initial validation. All SMILES strings were subsequently verified manually using ChemDraw 19.0 (PerkinElmer Informatics, Inc.) [59]. A rigorous standardization protocol was applied, including neutralization, salt and solvent stripping, and normalization of specific functional groups. Using RDKit [60], we generated corresponding InChI, InChIKey, and 2D SDF files from the standardized SMILES. Functional classifications (e.g., antagonist, inhibitor, blocker, agonist, activator) were assigned based on the roles explicitly stated in the originating primary literature or patents. While data from curated sources like ChEMBL were considered, they did not supersede direct annotations from primary sources. Crucially, our inclusion criteria required every compound entry to be supported by a citation to a primary empirical study. Consequently, any database entries lacking such verifiable references were excluded from the final collection. The classification of each peptide was further verified by cross-referencing its sequence or identifier with the UniProt database (using UniProt Accession Numbers where available). Article DOI and PMID information were gathered from PubMed. Furthermore, eight critical properties associated with drug-likeness were predicted and incorporated into DICL. Properties including the number of heavy atoms counts (HAC), hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), rotatable bonds (RB), topological polar surface area (TPSA), complexity, ring count and hydrogen bond donors (HBD) were calculated utilizing RDKit, whereas logP values were determined using ADMETlab 3.0 software [61]. Consequently, two separate tables were used to document the information for compounds and peptides, respectively, due to their significant differences in features. Detailed information on small molecules is available in CSV files.

Data standardization and integration workflow. The process involved standardizing, harmonizing, and manually verifying the data collected from diverse sources, including original databases and published literature

The DICL_Pro ID serves as a unique identifier within the database that is associated with ion channels. The UniProt accession number, name, synonyms, and target descriptions are sourced from UniProt, with certain modifications applied to the original descriptions. To optimize the functional annotations, the following modifications were undertaken: (1) removal of internal cross-reference identifiers (e.g., [EC:1.1.1.1], [GO:0005634]) for readability; (2) condensation of redundant or overly technical phrasing into core functional statements for clarity; and (3) supplementation with literature-curated, clinically relevant protein-disease relationships to enhance biological context. The target structures are sourced from the PDB database or AlphaFold Protein Structure Database [30], while the corresponding binding site data are collected from peer-reviewed literature. All files in DICL are available for free download. The DICL accommodates the complexity of compound-target interactions by systematically organizing the data. Since a single compound may interact with multiple targets under varied experimental conditions, each compound’s data is categorized into distinct, method-specific records based on the experimental methodology, target, organism, and other relevant parameters. Users can access the details page of each record to find more information. Additionally, the activity value serves as the foundation for both qualitative and quantitative analyses. It is important to note that research findings from various groups may sometimes conflict, leading to discrepancies that can pose challenges for users. Therefore, we meticulously verified and amended these data entries based on the reliability and recency of the supporting research. Our evaluation criteria included the completeness of methodological descriptions, the use of orthogonal validation assays, the presence of appropriate controls, and the rigor of statistical analyses. In essence, we refined and standardized the data according to the factual information to improve user engagement.

The website was built using the CodeIgniter 4.6 framework, with CSS and JavaScript for front-end development, and PHP 8.1.2 and MySQL for back-end functionality, all hosted on Apache2.The three-dimensional structures of ion channels were visualized using 3Dmol.js for online protein visualization. The two-dimensional structures of compounds were displayed using the SMILES Drawer. All technical operations of DICL adhered to the established standards.

To highlight the novel information in our database, we conducted a comparison between the DICL database and other related databases (as shown in Table2). Firstly, ChEMBL encompasses a broad range of small molecule activities assessed in phenotypic and biological assays, totally including approximately 111,890 records related to ion channels [17]. BindingDB primarily focuses on experimentally measured protein-small molecule binding affinities, comprising approximately 148,570 records related to ion channels sourced from peer-reviewed publications and patents [46]. Kalium 3.0 integrates data on polypeptide ligands associated with potassium channels, encompassing a total of 4,108 records [42]. Unlike the databases mentioned above, the hERGCentral database provides information on the biological activities of 318,941 compounds related to hERG, identified through high-throughput screening [43]. However, it is currently inaccessible. To construct a more comprehensive and reliable database encompassing ion channels and their ligands, here, we integrated these databases and other scattered data from peer-reviewed publications and patents to construct the DICL database. The DICL database comprises 150,208 compound entries and 7,122 peptide records sourced from more than 6,000 peer-reviewed articles and patents, in addition to 306,895 activity data (hERGCentral database) points obtained from the third part source [57]. DICL is an integrated resource encompassing ion channels and their associated binding ligands (including peptides and small molecules), covering not only potassium channels but also Voltage-dependent calcium channels (VGCCs), Voltage-gated sodium channels (VGSCs), and Chloride channels. Due to this broad scope, DICL currently represents the most comprehensive publicly available database dedicated to ion channels and their ligands. Secondly, the DICL database incorporates 1,750 subtypes of 27 different types of ion channel proteins and their related information from 165 species. Additionally, beyond compiling bioactivity, affinity, and molecular property data, DICL also incorporates key functional annotations—including ligand binding sites, associated channelopathies, and detailed experimental conditions. Therefore, DICL represents the most comprehensive and detailed online database of ion channels and their ligands.

To present detailed information from DICL, we conducted statistical analyses of the data. It should be noted that the biological activity values from hERGCentral are reported exclusively as percentage inhibition rates, rather than standardized quantitative measures (e.g., IC50, EC50, or Ki). Due to this unit incompatibility with the other datasets, direct comparative analysis was not methodologically sound. Consequently, these data were excluded from further analysis.

The DICL includes a curated collection of approximately 1,750 ion channel protein subtypes from 165 species (Supplementary Information [13321_2026_1246_MOESM4_ESM.xlsx]). These subtypes are systematically classified into 27 major ion channel types based on the authoritative framework provided by the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology [64]. As depicted in Fig.4, over 200 unique sequences of VGKCs and Aquaporins (AQPs) are included. Furthermore, more than 100 unique sequences have been collected for the following channel types: VGCC, γ-Aminobutyric acid type A receptors (γ-GABA-ARs), Ionotropic glutamate receptors (i-GluRs), Chloride channels, and Gap junction channel (GJ channel). Additionally, the database contains more than 50 unique sequences for several key ion channel families, including VGSCs, Inwardly rectifying potassium channels (Kir), Calcium-activated potassium channels (KCa), TRP, and nAChRs. Moreover, Fig.4illustrates that the types of ion channels found in humans, rats, and mice collectively represent nearly 50% of the total identified sequences. It is noteworthy that the types of VGKCs, VDCCs, γ-GABA-ARs, i-GluRs, KCa, Kir, and TRP identified are relatively abundant, with VGKCs being particularly prominent, encompassing nearly 50 subtypes.

Except the data from hERGCentral database, this current version of DICL comprises 150,208 data entries related to 72,420 compounds gathered from 5,960 peer-reviewed publications or patents. Figure5A illustrates the distribution of binding affinity or biological activity for compounds in the database across ion channels. There are over 10,000 records for VGKCs, VGSCs, nAChRs, i-GluRs, and TRP. Notably, the records for VGKCs exceed 20,000, accounting for more than 20% of the total data. This prevalence may be attributed to the increased focus on the cardiotoxicity issues associated with hERG. In contrast, there are only a few dozen records for Cyclic nucleotide-gated channel (CNG), Voltage-gated proton channel (VGHC), Two-pore channel (TPC), Piezo channels, and Epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). A statistically significant divergence in modulator efficacy was observed across ion channel families. Over 70% of compounds exhibited antagonistic effects on VGKCs, VGSCs, i-GluRs, and TRP channels. In contrast, more than 50% of compounds acted as agonists on γ-GABA-ARs and nAChRs. The observed target-class bias likely stems from a combination of factors. This includes practical aspects such as the composition of screening libraries and historical pharmaceutical focus (e.g., the high number of TRP channel antagonists related to analgesic development). At the same time, the bias may also reflect the inherent physiological and pharmacological characteristics of different ion channel families, such as variations in the accessibility or druggability of key regulatory sites. The uneven distribution of reported compounds across different subtypes of ion channels indicates that the function of some ion channels needs to be explored and underscores the urgent need for innovative drug development targeting the unexploited targets. In Fig.5B, we can clearly observe that the data in database is more concentrated on high and moderate bioactivity (the value of IC50< 100 nM and IC50from 100 nM to 10,000 nM) for ion channels. One contributing factor is that high-throughput screening (HTS) studies frequently generate large compound libraries, however, the resulting publications often omit inactive or weakly active compounds (the value of IC50> 100,000 nM and from 10,000 nM to 100,000 nM) from their reported datasets. It is noteworthy that extensively studied targets—including VGKCs, VGSCs, VGCCs, i-GluRs, and TRP channels, each with over 5,000 activity records—constitute a major focus of pharmacological research and are therefore particularly well-represented in the database (the detailed data and 2D figure shown in the 13321_2026_1246_MOESM2_ESM.xlsx of Supplementary Information). This pattern reflects both sustained research interest and comprehensive functional characterization.

DICL offers users a search (Fig.8A) function for retrieving information on compounds and peptides. Users can select the search category from the "All Categories" drop-down menu for quick searches (Fig.8B). For compound retrieval, available search options include "SMILES", "Organism", "IUPAC Name", "Ion Channel Name", "References", "PubChem CID", "InChIKey", "Function", "Value", and "DICL ID". The "DICL ID" serves as a unique identifier within the database for ligands targeting ion channels. The "Value" field includes numerical data such as Ki, EC50, IC50, and Kd. The "SMILES" search pattern is text-based, and users may input an isomeric SMILES string either obtained from PubChem or derived from the molecular structure. When a SMILES query is submitted, the system invokes RDKit to parse the input string into a molecular graph, determine aromaticity and bond orders, and generate a canonical isomeric SMILES representation. This normalized form is then directly compared to the canonical SMILES strings stored in the database, guaranteeing accurate structure-based retrieval irrespective of variations in the original input. For peptide retrieval, the available options differ and include "Sequence", "Organism", "Ion Channel Name", "References", "Function", "Value", and "DICL ID". Currently, sequence searching relies on SQL substring matching, which retrieves entries containing the input fragment anywhere in the text fields. Specifically, this approach performs an exact match query on the sequence column using the SQL equality operator ("=") with search keyword, returning only records that exactly match the search keyword. Additionally, users can select one or more keywords from options such as ion channel name, organism, function, Ki, EC50, IC50and Kdto perform an advanced search (Fig.8C). Upon completion of the search, users are redirected to a results page that displays the DICL ID, Ion Channel, Compound function, Species, Compound Activity, and References (Fig.8D).

This page is organized into three distinct sections: Summary, Binding Sites, and Target List. The three-dimensional structure of the protein is displayed in an interactive window, enabling users to rotate and zoom the model. The Binding Sites section is categorized into four classifications according to the function of ligands, namely inhibitor, agonist, blocker, and allosteric modulator. In this study, we developed the DICL, a comprehensive database that integrates data resources for ion channels and their ligands (compounds and peptides). DICL encompasses more than 1,750 subtypes ion channel proteins, categorized into 27 different types of ion channels. Meanwhile, it contains 464,225 data records, including 150,208 data records of compounds sourced from 5,960 peer-reviewed publications and patents, 306,895 data records of compounds sourced from the hERGCentral database, as well as 7,122 data records of peptides from 708 peer-reviewed publications and patents. To the best of our knowledge, DICL is the most comprehensive and detailed online database dedicated to ion channels and their corresponding ligands. Serving as a foundational resource for innovative drug development, the database provides a user-friendly interface and extensive information to support querying, browsing, and in-depth analysis of ion channels, their ligand interactions, and associated functions. The constructed platform provides a valuable contribution to the development of effective drug design strategies targeting ion channels and the drug discovery related to ion channels.

DICL serves as a valuable platform offering extensive information on ion channels and their ligands, providing a solid foundation for the development of AI-based drug design methods specifically tailored to ion channels and advancing target-based drug discovery. The accurate and comprehensive data on ion channels and their ligands can be leveraged to develop machine learning and AI-based models for identifying binding sites, discovering agonists and antagonists, and elucidating selective mechanisms of ion modulation as well as toxicology prediction models since cardiotoxicity is closely related with some ion channels [66,67,68]. DICL contains 18,823, 2,481, and 1,045 raw data entries for hERG, Nav1.5, and Cav1.2, respectively. These data can provide strong support for the development and evaluation of cardiotoxicity prediction models. Moreover, it also serves as a reference for the design of experimental methodologies.

However, several issues remain to be addressed. Firstly, some compounds have been excluded from the database due to the unavailability of precise biological activity values. Secondly, while we strive to minimize potential errors throughout this process, we acknowledge that some mistakes due to oversight may still occur. Additionally, although the current version of the platform provides full access to all core database content and supports essential search and download functions, several aspects can be further optimized to better serve advanced research needs and enhance usability. Future improvements will focus on the following areas: (1) System Performance and Scalability. While basic queries perform adequately, complex searches or bulk data operations can experience delays. We are optimizing backend query processing and implementing advanced caching mechanisms to significantly accelerate data retrieval and support larger-scale user interactions. (2) User Workflow and Customization Features. The site currently does not support user-specific features such as saving search conditions, storing personal molecule sets, or annotating records. We are developing user management capabilities that will allow researchers to track their query history, create custom compound lists, and share results with collaborators. (3) Enhanced Visualization and Interactive Tools. Although the platform includes a structure viewer, its functionality remains limited to basic visualization. (4) Development of Chemical Search Functionality. Implementing a true chemical search system—capable of substructure or similarity queries based on molecular fingerprints—would represent a highly valuable addition. However, robust deployment of such functionality requires substantial computational backend development and integration. Establishing a comprehensive chemical search system, including both substructure and similarity capabilities, is therefore an important objective for future versions of the database. In summary, we are working to integrate more advanced and interactive tools for exploring protein–ligand interactions, analyzing binding poses, and visualizing structure–activity relationships.

In the future, we plan to maintain and expand DICL by periodically incorporating additional ion channels and their corresponding ligands, sourced from newly published research. We anticipate that DICL will serve as a significant resource and a robust tool for the study of ion channels, as well as for the innovative design of ion channel modulators. We also encourage users to provide feedback to help us improve the platform.

title: Learning a chemistry-aware latent space for molecular encoding and generation with a large-scale transformer variational autoencoder
author: Hugo Talibart; Dimitri Gilis
text:
Searching for molecules optimizing certain properties remains a key challenge due to the vastness of the chemical space, its discrete nature, and the limited availability of bioactivity data. One way to address these issues is to build a mapping from the chemical space to a continuous latent embedding space where efficient exploration and smooth interpolations become possible. Existing methods suffer from several limitations: failure to accurately reconstruct molecules, poorly structured latent space where whole regions cannot be decoded to valid molecular graphs or where distances fail to reflect chemical similarities, not to mention the unavailability of ready-to-use code or models trained on sufficiently large datasets, limiting their practical application. In this work, we provide a large-scale pre-trained Variational Autoencoder based on the Transformer architecture to convert small organic molecules to continuous fixed-size embeddings in a chemistry-aware structured latent space and back. With a\(97\%\)reconstruction rate and a\(100\%\)validity rate, the model provides a reliable mapping and is able to generate a high diversity of novel molecules. We introduce a training objective with a novel loss term explicitly enforcing embedding distances to reflect Tanimoto similarities between molecular fingerprints, leading to a smooth and well-structured latent space enabling seamless exploration and interpolation. We show that our model achieves solid performances on molecular optimization tasks compared to other generative models. We release an open-source, user-friendly implementation as a pip package and at github.com/3BioCompBio/chembed, along with pre-trained models, that can be readily used or fine-tuned for downstream drug design applications.

We introduce a large-scale SELFIES Transformer VAE with a novel loss aligning latent space distances with chemical similarity. This yields a highly structured, chemistry-aware latent space, alongside high reconstruction accuracy. Our open-source release with pre-trained weights makes the model directly usable and adaptable for molecular design applications.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

Drug design is a time-consuming and expensive process: it is estimated that developing a single drug may take 10 to 20 years and cost around 2 billion dollars [1,2]. Candidate molecules must be identified within the vast chemical space, where the number of theoretically synthesizable drug-like compounds was estimated to be in the order of\(10^{60}\)[3]. The virtually unlimited size and inherently discrete nature of this chemical space make it difficult to explore, to design molecules with desired features, targeting specific receptors or optimizing certain properties. Furthermore, in contrast with the vastness of the chemical space, the amount of available annotated data on molecular properties and bioactivity is astronomically small. Hence, while deep learning models have achieved spectacular breakthroughs in areas such as computer vision and natural language processing and their application to drug design related tasks is compelling, their effectiveness in real-life scenarios may be hindered by the scarcity and quality of available data for the task at hand. Training a model from scratch on each dataset risks overfitting, poor generalization, or low diversity among proposed molecules. In light of the scarcity of annotated data relative to the vastness of the search space, there is a need for unsupervised computational methods to make use of unlabelled molecular datasets to map the molecular space to a latent embedding space, to provide versatile representations for downstream tasks and enable smooth exploration. To these aims, the learned embeddings should capture essential and meaningful patterns in the original data, their structure should reflect their underlying relationships, and the mapping between original molecules and their embeddings should be reversible.

In the field of molecular design, different methods were proposed over the years to map the chemical space to a latent embedding space. Early work on this matter was mainly based on variational autoencoders [4] trained to reconstruct molecular graphs [5] or string representations such as SMILES [6]. In contrast with regular autoencoders, variational autoencoders learn a probabilistic distribution over the latent space, enabling sampling and interpolation by enforcing continuity and structure in the latent representations. The choice of which molecular representation to be reconstructed comes with trade-offs: graph-based representations may offer more faithful and unique representations of the molecular structures but are more computationally demanding, while string-based representations such as SMILES [7] are more efficient. As models may struggle to learn the specific syntax of SMILES and produce strings that cannot be translated to semantically valid molecules, potentially leading to large "dead areas" in latent spaces [6], SELFIES [8] emerged as a promising alternative, ensuring that all token sequences correspond to semantically valid molecular graphs, while retaining the efficiency of linear notation approaches. Representing molecules as token sequences made it possible to capitalize on deep learning advances in Natural Language Processing. In particular, following the success of Transformers [9], their architecture and training strategies [10] were soon adopted in the field of drug design for tasks such as property prediction [11,12,13] and molecular generation [14]. The attention mechanism in Transformers enables them to focus on relevant parts of the inputs and capture long-range dependencies between tokens, which is of particular relevance in the context of molecules, where tokens represent atoms, rings and branches that interact with each other. Despite the success of pretrained models and their generative capacities, their latent space lacks regularization and structure, making them less suitable for controlled molecular optimization and chemical space navigation, as they cannot produce fixed-size, self-contained embeddings that are directly decodable, nor do they support smooth interpolations and transitions in their latent space.

The question of latent space semantic consistency remains largely underexplored in the field of small molecules design. Most models rely at most on a Kullback–Leibler divergence loss term alone to regularize latent space structure. Although this strategy encourages some continuity between input representations, it does not enforce any semantic continuity between the initial objects that are represented. Indeed, two sequences of tokens may differ by only a few token edits but represent significantly different molecules, and conversely, two molecules that are closely related may be represented by significantly different linear notations, as SMILES or SELFIES canonicalization only addresses the question of unicity. A few strategies were proposed to actively steer models to build a semantically meaningful latent space. Some strategies common in Bayesian Optimization consist in jointly training models with predictive tasks and/or periodically retrain them with new samples evaluated by the black-box objective functions to be optimized during the process [15,16]. However, on top of a risk of overfitting [17], models may end up embedding linearly the target properties into few dimensions of the latent vectors [18]. Alternatively, a handful of methods have begun incorporating ideas from metric learning, a concept introduced in [19] which aims at learning mappings where distances in latent space are consistent with input class labels, and which was shown to improve generalization in predictive tasks. Grosnit et al. [20] introduced a molecular VAE trained with a triplet loss to enforce a discriminative latent space where "positive" and "negative" samples according to a threshold in the objective function to be optimized are clustered separately. A similar idea was also proposed by Koge et al. [18], with a log-ratio loss. In both cases, the structure imposed on the latent space depends on the task-specific labels, limiting their use as general-purpose molecular encoders. More recently, Sellner et al. [21] trained SMILES Transformers with an additional loss termL(A,B) defined, for one anchor moleculeAand all other samplesBin the batch, as:

whereais a hyperparameter,fis the encoding function – here defined as a Transformer Encoder followed by a pooling operation—andsimcan be any similarity measure between two molecules, which in practice they set to the Tanimoto similarity between molecular fingerprints [22]. Their method avoids the need to define positive and negative samples and showed substantial search space reduction in virtual screening tasks. Independently, in a recent preprint, Lžičař et al. [23] trained a differentiable encoder similar to Siamese networks with a contrastive loss function reducing the squared error between Euclidean distances in latent space and distance in chemical space:

where in practice the dissimilaritydis based on 3D shape similarity or electrostatic similarity. An efficient approximate nearest neighbor search implementation allowed them to achieve significant speed improvements in virtual screening benchmarks. However, embeddings obtained by these approaches cannot be decoded back to the original molecules: Sellner et al. [21] obtain latent representations by average pooling over the encoder output, which cannot be directly decoded by their Transformer decoder, while Lžičař et al. [23] train an encoder-only model with no decoder at all. This prevents their use in downstream molecular generation or optimization tasks.

In this paper, we introduce a SELFIES variational autoencoder with a Transformer-derived architecture trained on a large molecular dataset with a novel training objective focusing on reconstruction and latent space semantic consistency. This architecture leverages both the attention mechanism of Transformers and the capacity of the variational autoencoder framework to produce a smooth latent space. We address latent space structure with an auxiliary molecular prediction task and a novel loss term which explicitly enforces Euclidean distances between embeddings in latent space to be consistent with Tanimoto similarities between molecular fingerprints of encoded molecules. We show that this loss term induces a highly structured latent space that allows for smooth interpolations and exploration: applying small perturbations to an embedding produces structurally similar molecules, while larger perturbations lead to more dissimilar ones, enabling smooth interpolations and exploration of the chemical space. The use of SELFIES representations enables computational efficiency and ensures that all vectors in latent space can be decoded to semantically valid molecular structures. Aware of the reconstruction issues reported in several widely cited models [24], we reduce the regularization as recommended in [25] to obtain high reconstruction rates. We show that, even with a naive search strategy, the model is able to propose relevant molecule candidates in molecular optimization tasks. Beyond the mere proof-of-concept, we prioritize usability by releasing a user-friendly implementation with complete code, environment and pre-trained models. We trained it on a large dataset derived from PubChem [26] with a focus on small organic molecules within the typical bioactive range. While graph-based models typically treat molecules as undirected 2D graphs, limiting their ability to represent stereochemistry information, and string-based models, though in principle capable of handling stereochemistry, are in practice distributed with restricted vocabularies excluding stereochemistry-related tokens, requiring adaptations and retraining, our model is built on a stereochemistry-aware vocabulary, making it immediately applicable to stereochemistry-sensitive tasks without any adaptation. The model provided is ready to use or fine-tune for tasks like molecular generation, optimization, and representation learning, sparing users the time and computational cost to train a large model from scratch.

This section outlines the key components of our approach. First, we describe how molecular structures are converted into standardized token sequences to provide as input to our model. Then, we detail the architecture of our model, which embeds the Transformer architecture into a variational framework to leverage attention mechanisms to map molecules to meaningful fixed-size latent vectors, enabling both reconstruction and generation of novel molecules. To ensure that this mapping is reliable and relevant for practical and efficient chemical space exploration, we designed a composite training objective which emphasizes reconstruction and latent space organization thanks to an auxiliary molecular prediction task and a novel loss term explicitly aligning latent embedding distances to Tanimoto similarities between molecular fingerprints. We specify the pre-processing steps used to construct the large dataset of small organic molecules on which our model was trained, and how token imbalance was handled. Then, we describe the simple algorithm for molecular optimization search used to validate our model. An overview of the model is depicted Fig.1. Comprehensive implementation details including the full architecture, training setup and hyperparameters are provided in Additional file 1, section 1.

Overview of the model. Molecules are represented by SELFIES strings and fed to the encoder, which outputs an embedding vector following a Gaussian distribution. The decoder is able to decode any embedding vector into a SELFIES string, which in turn can be decoded to a valid molecular graph. A property regressor is jointly trained to predict chosen properties of the initial molecules from their latent embeddings alone, thereby encouraging more meaningful embeddings. By integrating an additional loss term explicitly aligning embedding distances to chemical similarities into the variational framework (see sectionTraining objective), the latent space is structured so that neighboring vectors represent similar molecules

To avoid the computational cost associated with molecular graph matching which would make it prohibitively expensive to train it on large datasets, we adopted string-based representations. Since SMILES [7] representations often lead to large "dead areas" in latent space [6] as models struggle to learn the specific SMILES syntax, we used SELFIES representations instead [8], ensuring that all vectors in latent space can be decoded to semantically valid molecules. To ensure canonicity, molecules are standardized using the ChEMBL standardization procedure described in Bento et al. [27] and RDKit [28] before conversion to SELFIES. These SELFIES strings are tokenized using a vocabulary derived from the large dataset described in sectionDataset and pre-processing. Though this vocabulary is large, occasionally some SELFIES strings may contain unseen tokens, in which case they may be replaced with the semantically closest tokens according to a specifically crafted distance metric. Details on how this SELFIES token semantic distance is defined are provided in Additional file 1, section 2.

The autoencoder consists in two modules: an encoder that maps SELFIES tokens to latent vectors of dimension (1,d) with\(d=256\)and a decoder that maps latent vectors back to SELFIES tokens. Both modules are based on the Transformer architecture [9], allowing them to capture long-range interactions between tokens. Tokens are embedded via an embedding layer initialized using an MDS projection based on the SELFIES token semantic distance (as described in sectionToken imbalance handling strategies), combined with positional encoding, before being fed to a Transformer encoder stacking 6 layers with multi-head attention and feedforward. To embed the Transformer into a variational autoencoder framework [4], a bottleneck is introduced by using only the first position of the Transformer encoder output to derive mean and standard deviation vectors parameterizing the Gaussian distribution from which the latent vector is then sampled (see Fig.2). To decode a latent vector, it is provided as memory input to a 6-layer Transformer decoder. During training (Fig.3), the decoder inputs the target tokens shifted by one position, while at inference time (Fig.4), it autoregressively generates tokens by conditioning on previously decoded outputs using a greedy decoding strategy. Target tokens are embedded the same way as in the encoder module, and the output logits, which represent unnormalized likelihood scores for each token in the vocabulary, are produced by applying the transpose of the embedding layer.

The output of the Transformer Encoder is split horizontally and only the first position of each vector is retained to derive the mean\(\mu\)and standard deviation\(\sigma\)defining the Gaussian distribution from which the latent embedding vectorzis sampled. Target tokens are shifted and fed to an Embedding layer and a Positional Encoding module in the same way as in the Encoder to obtain a (L,d) tensor which is fed to a Transformer Decoder module consisting of 6 stacked Transformer Decoder layers along with the embedding vectorz. The training objective seeks to balance accurate reconstruction of input molecules with the enforcement of a smooth and semantically meaningful latent space. To this end, we include a reconstruction loss,\(\mathcal {L}_{rec}\), penalizing discrepancies between the input and the output of the decoder, defined for a single sample of lengthLas the cross-entropy between one-hot encoded input tokensyand the predicted token distributions\(\widehat{y}\):

Acting as a regularizer, a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence loss term,\(\mathcal {L}_{KL}\), pushes the latent embeddings distribution towards a normal prior:

where\(\mu\)and\(\sigma\)are respectively the mean and standard deviation of the distribution from which the latent vector is sampled.

While the KL divergence alone may be sufficient in certain datasets to provide an acceptable smoothness and structure of latent space, it should be noted that representing molecules with strings such as SELFIES implies an additional layer of abstraction between the target molecules and their representations. Indeed, two sequences of SELFIES tokens may differ by only a few token edits but represent significantly different molecules, particularly when substitutions affect topological tokens. Conversely, despite efforts towards canonicalization, very similar molecules may sometimes be represented by dissimilar SELFIES strings. To address this and improve latent space structure, we introduce a novel loss term, termedTanimoto loss, to explicitly enforce Euclidean distances between vectors in latent space to be consistent with similarities between the molecules they represent, measured as the Tanimoto similarities [22] between Morgan fingerprints [29] computed by RDKit (with radius 2 and 1024 bits). Given a batch ofNmolecules, letTdenote the\(N \times N\)Tanimoto similarity matrix where\(T_{ij} = Tanimoto(mol_i, mol_j)\)andDdenote the\(N \times N\)Euclidean distance matrix where\(D_{ij} = \Vert z_i - z_j \Vert\)where\(z_i\)is the latent embedding of moleculei, then the Tanimoto loss\(\mathcal {L}_{Tanimoto}\)is defined as the correlation between the upper triangular values of the two matrices, shifted by 1 to be positive:

where\(\bar{T}\)and\(\bar{D}\)are the means over the upper-triangular entries.

Finally, to further improve the semantic meaningfulness of latent embeddings, we incorporate an auxiliary molecular prediction task alongside the autoencoding objective by jointly training a regressor – a simple multi-layer perceptron with two hidden layers with respectively 32 and 16 neurons and ReLU activations – to predict selected properties from latent vectors. By default, predicted properties include molecular weight, logP and polar surface area, as well as four graph topological descriptors: the Bertz CT index [30] which reflects molecular complexity, and the Kappa 1, 2, 3 indexes [31] which capture, respectively, the "cyclicity" of molecules, the "spatial density of atoms" and the "centrality of branching", leading to a total of\(N_{prop}=7\)properties. The regressor is trained to minimize the average mean squared error (MSE),\(\mathcal {L}_{prop}\), between its output\(\widehat{p}\)and (normalized) target propertiesp:
