title: Determination of bonding radii from small-molecule crystal structures
author: Eglė Šidlauskaitė; Andrius Merkys; Antanas Vaitkus; Algirdas Grybauskas; Saulius Gražulis
text:
X-ray crystallography rarely captures chemical bonding between atoms of a structure in question. Most of the time distance-based heuristics are applied to establish the pairs of bonded atoms. One class of such heuristics depends on a set of bonding radii that estimate the idealised size of each chemical element in a bond. This publication describes an unsupervised workflow for deriving a bonding radii set from crystal structure data in the Crystallography Open Database.

An atomic bonding radii set is derived from the Crystallography Open Database using a novel, unsupervised and fully automated workflow. The method does not use any prior knowledge about the connectivity in input crystal structures, relying solely on their Voronoi tesselations.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

Chemical connectivity in crystal structures is of interest to many derivative studies. Connectivity is an unavoidable prerequisite for, to name a few, the identification of chemical substances [1,2], analysis of molecular geometry [3] and crystal properties [4]. X-ray crystallography – a well-established technique for the determination of 3D atom coordinates in crystal structures – is in practice rarely used to detect chemical connectivity, which, although possible using charge density analysis, is very demanding for data quality and the expertise of the researcher [5]. Thus heuristics are often applied to derive the connectivity, usually based either on per-element contribution called abonding radiusor maximal bonding distance defined per each pair of elements [6]. The former is an often used bond determination heuristic which states that the distance between two chemically bonded atoms has to be smaller than or equal to the sum of their bonding radii [7,8,9,10,11]. Thus two atoms of chemical elementsiandjseparated by distance\(d_{i,j}\)are treated as bonded if the following inequality holds:

Here\(r_i\)is the bonding radius of chemical elementiand\(\epsilon\)is a sensitivity constant, usually ranging between 0.35 Å and 0.45 Å [12]. Such radii are not constant intrinsic properties of atoms as their sizes are highly dependent on the environment [13]. Nevertheless bonding radii are approximated well enough and used in the distance-based connectivity criterion.

Although there are a number of published bonding radii sets [7,13,14,15,16], a univocal method for bonding radii derivation has not been established. A widely used bonding radii set published as a part of the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD) [17] has received critique for manual adjustments of radii aimed to fit specific molecules as well as default values being used in place of unknown radii [13]. In many other studies [7,13] bonding radii sets are derived from the CSD crystal structures that are annotated with expert-curated connectivity information. Connectivity as derived by experienced chemists is usually of high quality, however, manual marking of connectivity is a slow and expensive process. Moreover, the CSD operates under a proprietary license, restricting the spread of the derivative datasets and preventing the replicability of study results. In addition, values in bonding radii sets can differ quite significantly, in some cases exhibiting differences of over 1 Å, as evident from Fig.1. The need for an automated bonding radii derivation approach is addressed in recent studies published by Nikolaienko and coworkers [18,19]. However, the main limitation of these studies is that the derived datasets involve only a few select elements thus reducing their applicability. For a more detailed review of currently available bonding radii sets see [20].

Bonding radii sets are usually interaction-type-specific. In this study we aim to determine radii encompassing all of the intramolecular interactions (covalent, ionic, metallic bonding, etc.) because such radii could be used to determine bonding in crystallographic structures. In the study published by Alvarez [21] an interatomic distance distribution is used to determine the typical distance between atoms that interact mainly by the van der Waals forces. In a typical interatomic distance distribution intramolecular and intermolecular interactions are separated by thevan der Waals gapdue to a significant difference in the interaction strength. Identification of the van der Waals gap should be sufficient to determine the longest possible interatomic distance for each pair of elements that would still allow an intramolecular bond, at the same time rejecting longer intermolecular interactions. Throughout our study we maintain the view of interatomic distance distributions as postulated by Alvarez, on the other hand acknowledging departures from it due to the vast variability of chemical environments.

In this study we have developed an automated and unsupervised workflow for the derivation of bonding radii sets from any small-molecule crystallographic data, expressed in CIF files using the IUCr coreCIF dictionary data items. The set derived from the data in the Crystallography Open Database (COD) [22] is validated and compared to other similar bonding radii sets.

We used all 519 021 crystal structure records from the COD revision 295629 as input for our study. In the COD, crystal structures are stored as the Crystallographic Information File (CIF) format [23] files and are therefore directly suitable for the workflow described here. While the coreCIF dictionary defines data names for bond lengths (GEOM_BONDcategory), this information mostly concerns bonded interactions and is not guaranteed to be complete or free from mistakes [3], thus we analysed the atomic positions only.

We imposed several criteria to select only complete, experimentally measured structures and reject various biases and outliers. We strove to use only the structures having 3D coordinates for all of their sites, including the solvent molecules. This criterion stems from the need to correctly identify direct intramolecular and intermolecular interactions. Due to the difficulties in addressing disordered structures, we have decided to exclude them altogether. We employed several heuristics to exclude theoretical structures and the ones having one or more atoms which were not backed by experimental evidence. Outlier rejection also removes structures solved under unusual conditions such as high pressure.

We have excluded the following kinds of structures from our calculations:

Disordered structures. We exclude structures that are either explicitly marked as disordered in their CIF files or that are detected as disordered by thecif_mark_disorderprogram from thecod-toolsv3.10.0 package [24]. This is done because disordered structures are difficult to accommodate in the present analysis. Such structures provide either alternative sites for a set of atoms (positional disorder), alternative chemical elements occupying the same site (compositional disorder), or a combination of both. There is no clear solution for handling such structures as input for geometric analysis. One possible method would be to generate all possible combinations of disordered fragments and exclude the repetitive measurements from the stable part of the structure. However, alternative atom positions may affect the whole Voronoi partition rather than just the immediate environment of the disordered fragment. Moreover, Voronoi partition may depend on disorder in neighbouring crystal cells. Supercell modelling approach might offset the former problem for the price of increased computation complexity. Due to this complexity we decided to exclude disordered structures altogether.

Structures with partially occupied atom sites. Partially occupied sites appear in structures with vacancy defects, crystallographically disordered structures as well as improperly modelled structures. All these cases are difficult to accommodate in the current statistical analysis, thus the corresponding structures are excluded.

Structures with different declared and calculated formulae. The difference in heavy atom numbers between formulae usually means that the described structure is incomplete.

Structures having attached hydrogen atoms. When the 3D coordinates of hydrogen atoms cannot be determined, their presence near a specific heavy atom is sometimes instead indicated as the number of attached hydrogen atoms (also known as virtual hydrogen atoms) using the_atom_site_attached_hydrogensCIF data item. Since in this case the 3D coordinates of the hydrogen sites are unknown, we cannot precisely identify contacts involving them. While it would be possible to ignore only the interactions of the atoms having attached hydrogen atoms, we have decided to exclude such structures altogether since they comprise less than 1% of the COD.

Structures having dummy sites. Dummy sites in CIF files do not pertain to actual atom positions, but they may signal that certain atoms are missing from the structure. Therefore it is safer to exclude such structures. There are 420 such entries in the COD in total.

Duplicate entries. The COD contains a couple thousand of duplicated entries, marked as such by its maintainers. These entries are excluded to avoid overrepresentation of certain observations.

Structures with calculated heavy atom sites. We exclude structures with explicitly marked calculated sites to retain only experimentally located atoms.

Structures solved in superspace groups. Superspace group structures are difficult to accommodate in our current analysis due to interatomic distances in them being dependent on modulation waves spanning many crystal cells.

Theoretical structures. We base our insights on experimentally determined structures, thus we filter out COD entries that were marked as theoretical by the curators of the database.

Structures with unmodelled solvent. Solvent is rarely interesting in structural analysis, moreover, disordered or mobile molecules may be difficult to represent in CIF files. Non-modelled solvent molecules are sometimes reported using the_platon_squeeze_void_count_electronsor_smtbx_masks_void_count_electronsCIF data items, thus we have excluded all structures containing these data items (27 189 in total). However, these data items are often absent, thus we also rely on other filters (formulae mismatch, unrealistic densities, etc.) to identify such structures.

Unusual crystal densities. We have excluded crystals with density lower than 0.17\(\frac{\text {g}}{\text {cm}^3}\)(density of extremely low density structures as reported in [25]) or higher than 22.59\(\frac{\text {g}}{\text {cm}^3}\)(density of osmium as reported in [26]), both declared and calculated from formula and cell parameters. To ensure consistency between the declared crystal density and the calculated one, we exclude structures with the ratios of said densities outside the range of [0.75, 1.25].

Structures with large absolute density differences between original and relaxed form. To exclude incomplete or otherwise unrealistic crystal structures we have removed from consideration the ones which significantly diverge when relaxed using the M3GNet [27] graph deep learning interatomic potential (Justinas Šlepavičius, personal communication). It should be noted, however, that the relaxation appropriately preserves naturally porous structures such as metal-organic frameworks, as their framework structure is strong enough to be kept in place. Since the relaxation process can considerably alter both the cell parameters and atom coordinate values without actually changing the structure (this usually happens when there is a change in the unit cell basis), we based our exclusion criterion on the difference of crystal structure densities. Thus we exclude structures undergoing absolute density change of\(0.5\frac{\text {g}}{\text {cm}^3}\)or more.

Structures with high R factor values. We require the crystallographic R factor to be known and be\(\le 0.1\), per the IUCr validation guidelines [28]. Requirement for R factor to be known is ignored for neutron diffraction structures in order to retain as many such structures as possible.

Structures with high weighted R factor values. We require the weighted crystallographic R factor (wR) to be known and be\(\le 0.25\), per the IUCr validation guidelines [29]. Requirement for wR factor to be known is ignored for neutron diffraction structures in order to retain as many such structures as possible.

Structures measured under extreme temperature. Extreme temperatures (higher than 320 K) may affect the crystal geometry.

Structures measured under extreme pressure. Extreme pressures (lower than 80 kPa or higher than 120 kPa) may affect crystal geometry.

Most of the filters are constructed using the output produced by theCOD::CIF::Data::CIF2CODandCOD::CIF::Data::CODFlagsmodules fromcod-tools. All filters were applied sequentially on the input data. In total, 249 032 entries were used for further analysis.

The COD contains crystal structures described by their asymmetric units plus their space group. This description is enough to reconstruct all atom positions in the unit cell. We reconstruct the symmetrically equivalent positions with thecif_fill cellscript fromcod-tools[30]. The same tool constructs a\(3 \times 3 \times 3\)supercell to represent all interactions where atoms from the central unit cell participate.

We have harnessed Voronoi tessellation to detect the pairs of possibly interacting atoms. To perform the tessellation, we have chosen an algorithm implemented invoronotav1.18.1877 [31]. For each pair of directly contacting atomsvoronotacalculates both the contact distance and the contact area which is later used as a weight of a contact. Invoronota, which is mainly used to locate and describe contacts in protein structures, a probe is used to cut off distant pairwise interactions. We have disabled the probe feature in our calculations by setting it to the longest diagonal of the supercell, as we are interested in all pairwise interactions regardless of their distance. To usevoronotain our calculations, we have wrapped it into a tool namedcif_contactsof thecrystal-contactspackage [32], revision 56.

Due to the abundance and relatively low precision of their site 3D coordinates determined by X-ray diffraction, hydrogen atoms require special treatment. While hydrogen coordinates in neutron diffraction structures can usually be trusted, explicit hydrogen sites in X-ray structures usually are imprecise and/or derived using geometric constraints. Thus taking their contacts into consideration is unlikely to result in meaningful radii values. Nevertheless, however imprecise, hydrogen sites act as natural “barriers” separating heavier atoms with distant interactions. Therefore we use all hydrogen atom sites in the input for Voronoi tessellation, but for non-neutron diffraction structures we afterwards discard all the observed contacts involving hydrogen atoms. Neutron diffraction structures, on the other hand, are processed differently: in them, hydrogen atoms are treated just as any other atoms and their contacts are preserved. This is done to obtain a bonding radius for hydrogen. After filtering the COD structures as described inStructure selection criteria, 489 neutron diffraction structures remain in the filtered dataset.

After finding and calculating all the contacts from the\(3 \times 3 \times 3\)supercell withcif_contacts, we retain only those contacts that involve at least one atom from the asymmetric unit. This is done bycif_bonds_anglesfrom theatomclassespackage [3]. By removing interactions between symmetric equivalents we prevent overrepresentation of contacts.

From the total pool of calculated interatomic distances we exclude unusually short and unusually long observations. Distances involving hydrogen (from neutron diffraction structures only) are limited to the inclusive range of [0.5, 6] Å, the other distances being limited to the inclusive range of [1, 6] Å. Cutoff on the lower end is imposed to filter out steric clashes, possibly arising due to unmarked and undetected disorder. Cutoff on the upper end is supposed to reduce the influence of very distant interactions, for example, in MOFs or other porous crystals. The upper limit is derived based on the longest possible covalent bond permitted by the covalent radii set of Cordero et al. [13] (5.2 Å for Fr–Fr).

Having processed all pairs of directly interacting atoms in the input data, we weigh each observation by the area of its contact [33] to reduce the influence of long distances, group them by chemical elements and for each pair of elements (we call it aclass) fit a density model and identify thebond peak, which we deem to contain the longest intramolecular interactions. Each of these steps is described in more detail in the following paragraphs.

To facilitate the analysis of the density of a class, we fit a Gaussian mixture model on the sample composed of the class distances (Fig.2). Fitting is done using the expectation maximisation algorithm with a modification to accept weights. In order to reduce the influence of long nonbonded interactions we use the following weighting scheme for interaction observed between atomsiandj:

Here\(S_i\)is the total sum of all the contact areas for atomi, and\(S_{i,j}\)is the contact area between atomsiandj. To find the best fitting Gaussian mixture model for each class, we use the expectation maximisation method to determine parameters for mixtures with the number of normal components ranging from 1 to 10. Classes larger than 200 000 observations are reduced by randomly picking 200 000 observations from them. On the other end, we require a minimal 1:30 ratio of model parameters to observations. This means that for a mixture ofNGaussian components to be considered, a sample needs at least\(30 \times (3N-1)\)observations. Component centres for the initial steps are taken from sample quantiles. From the fitted mixtures, all components accounting for less than 10 observations are removed to avoid fitting to the possible outliers. From these ten mixtures we select the one with an optimal Bayesian information criterion (BIC [34]) value. Both the fitting and the BIC computation is performed usingMixtureFittingv0.7.0 [35] package written inR.

We have tailored the method for bond peak selection based on the chemical elements participating in the class:

For classes involving at least one alkali or alkaline earth metal, the first mixture component is deemed to be the bond peak, as these elements very rarely form higher order bonds.

For interactions between halogens and non-organogenic elements (not C, N, O, P, S, Se), the first mixture component is deemed to be the bond peak.

For interactions between oxygen and U, Np and Pu, the last mixture component is deemed to be the bond peak.

For the rest, the component preceding the lowest-density antimode (supposedly corresponding to the van der Waals gap) is deemed to be the bond peak.

Different treatment of classes based on the types of elements participating in them is necessary to accommodate the variability of chemical interactions.

To select the lowest-density antimode, we inspect the density zones between each pair of neighbouring component centres. As a midpoint between the component centres might fall on a slope of the density function, we employ the Nelder–Mead method [36] to locate the actual minimum. If the Nelder–Mead method locates the density minimum outside the range limited by neighbouring component centres, it is held that these components are inseparable.

More rules dictated by the common chemical sense could be further applied to select the correct bond peaks. In one instance, the F–F class, we have decided to completely remove the class from consideration due to its negative influence on the overall bonding radii derivation (described in sectionBonding radii). Proper F–F bonds are too rare in the COD to form a detectable bond peak (Fig.3), thus a peak formed by non-bonded interaction distances is chosen as the bond peak; no van der Waals gap is visible. While such aberrations are possible under our methodology, we expect them to be dominated by correctly determined bond peaks. Unfortunately, F–F class is the most populated among all F-involving classes, thus the overly long bonding distance is assigned the largest weight. In order to offset the influence of F–F class we have decided to remove this class altogether.

We have derived the bonding radii by approximately solving an overdetermined equation system via the least squares method:

Where\(r_{i}\)is the bonding radii for chemical elementi,\(d_{i,j}\)is the bond peak centre in class of chemical elementsiandj(including\(i = j\)), and\(W_{i,j}\)is the weight of the equation equal to the number of observations in the class. Weights are used to increase the influence of larger classes in the least squares calculation, as their models should be more accurate.RpackageRlinsolvev0.3.2 [37] was used to approximately solve the system of equations.

Since both the mixture model fitting and the antimode selection could be affected by peculiarities of certain classes, we have applied an iterative outlier removal procedure to arrive to self-consistent radii set. During each iteration, Eq.3is approximately solved and the largest class having the difference between its bond peak and radii sum greater than 0.35 Å is selected. Then the selected class is excluded from Eq.3and the next iteration commences. This is repeated until no classes with\(d_\text {i,j} - (r_\text {i} + r_\text {j}) > 0.35\)Å are found. It is important to note that the difference in this criterion is not absolute, that is, only classes with bond peak position larger than radii sum are excluded. This is done in order to eliminate classes where the bond peak centres might be detected incorrectly due to the relative abundance of long intermolecular distances.

We have also attempted to use the iterative reweighting approach for the least squares calculation (IRLS) [38], which iteratively decreases the weights of equations producing the largest errors in least squares calculation. However, IRLS did not perform better than our iterative outlier removal approach, which is specifically tailored to alleviate the shortcomings of our methods.

In total, 3107 contact classes were observed, consisting of 97 unique chemical elements (Fig.5). Mixture models were derived for 954 classes. This number excludes classes with too few observations to reliably fit even a one-component Gaussian mixture model. Correspondingly, coverage of the periodic table decreased to 84 chemical elements. Although BIC was applied as a measure to prefer simpler mixture models, there is a tendency of larger classes to be approximated with mixtures containing greater number of components, as seen in Fig.4.

The resulting radii set (Table1) is close to the one derived by Pyykkö and Atsumi [14], especially in treatment of organogenic, alkali and alkaline earth metals where the absolute differences for most elements do not exceed 0.075 Å. With the exception of considerably different radii for Kr, Pr, Tl and Pb, the largest deviations between these two radii sets are observed in the d-block elements. A comparison with published bonding radii sets is provided in Fig.1

The derived bonding radii set was evaluated for its suitability for interatomic bonding determination in crystallographic data. For this purpose, we analysed the bonding presented in a collection of chemically annotated crystallographic structures in SDF format that were previously derived from the COD data using a chemical perception pipeline [2]. The chemical perception pipeline establishes the bonding based on the bonding radii set compiled by Pyykkö and Atsumi paired with the followingad hocrules as implemented in thecif-perceive-chemistryprogram version 0.4.0 [39], therefore it can be viewed as a completely independent approach.

Removal of incorrectly assigned intraring bonds. Due to short interatomic distances in flat 4-membered rings, an extra covalent bond is sometimes placed between the diagonal atoms. Since non-flat rings may contain legitimate diagonal bonds (e.g., bicyclobutane, tetrahedrane derivates), such bonds are removed, but only if the absolute dihedral angle between the atoms of the ring is smaller than 20° (see Fig.6).

Removal of incorrectly assigned metal-ligand bonds. Short interatomic distances can also result in spurious bonding between a metal centre and atoms in its second coordination sphere, i.e., atoms covalently bound to directly coordinated ligands. Such bonds are therefore removed.

Addition of bonds to aromatic\(\pi\)-ligands. Steric effects and bulky substituents may increase metal-ligand distances thus leading to underestimation of ligand hapticity (e.g., a cyclopentadienyl ligand may be marked as connected only by 3 atoms instead of the expected 5). Therefore, if an atom ring is flat and more than half of the ring atoms have connections to the same metal atom, the ring is treated as being fully coordinated by that metal atom and metal-ligand bonds are assigned to all ring atoms.

Only the structures which passed all of the data quality checks imposed by the pipeline (data consistency, chemical validity, etc.) are used in the analysis to ensure that the presented connectivity reflects proper intramolecular bonds.

We subjected the coordinates-only part of chemically annotated structures to connectivity detection using Eq.1(\(\epsilon = 0.45\)Å) looking for two types of bonding differences: missing bonds (input structure lacks an explicit bond between atoms) and overlong bonds (input structure contains an explicit bond which is deemed to be too long by our new criteria). The connectivity detection also reproduces the flat 4-membered ring diagonal bond removal employed by the chemical perception pipeline This is done by identifying pairs of triangles sharing an edge and having sums of their angles within [340, 380]°. Every such pair is treated as constituting a flat 4-membered ring and their shared bond is removed.

In over 365,000 input structures 80,487 mismatches were detected. Around 92% of them are due to the new bonds assigned by our radii set, with the rest being missing (i.e. unreproduced) bonds. Classes with the most differences of both kinds are shown in Table2, with classes involving carbon and other organogenic elements provided for reference. In both the newly assigned and unreproduced bonds, certain bond classes led to improved bonding accuracy while others introduced errors.

The majority of the newly detected bonds are between the same metal atoms, highlighting the fact that our radii for these elements are longer than the ones derived by Pyykkö and Atsumi. For Mo and V elements, the elongation of bonding radii is influenced by metal-OH contacts in polyoxometalates shifting the van der Waals gap to the longer side. In turn, longer Mo and V bonding radii treat as bonded the indirect contacts between metal atoms inMO\(_6\)or, more generally,MX\(_6\)coordination clusters (M\(\in\){Mo, V},X– any element). Clearly, these contacts are recognised as bonds incorrectly, which showcases a limitation of distance-based connectivity heuristic, as distance alone is not enough to determine connectivity in such cases. Nevertheless,Jmol3D viewer [40] recognises the same indirect Mo–Mo and V–V contacts as bonds. In practical applications, such indirect contacts could possibly be filtered out by employing the Voronoi tessellation. On the other hand, the newly assigned Cu–O bonds mostly represent proper coordination interactions between Cu and axial water or ketone ligands that were not detected by the chemical perception pipeline.

Most of the unreproduced bonds can be attributed to the significantly shorter bonding radii for Ce and Pr. This is caused by a small component present in both Ce–O and O–Pr classes, which primarily consist of interactions involving CeO\(_6\)and PrN\(_2\)O\(_4\). While such radii effectively identify smaller coordination spheres, they fail to capture connectivity in complexes with the coordination number of 7 or higher.

Outside the d-block the largest increases in radii lengths with regards to Pyykkö and Atsumi are Kr, Tl and Pb. While increases in Kr and Tl radii do not affect the validation outcomes much, number of new O–Pb bonds exceed 1000 observations. Most of them appear to be proper coordination sphere contacts between Pb and oxygen in ketones or carboxyl groups that were not detected by the chemical perception pipeline.

We have attempted validation by plugging in our radii set toMaterialsCoordbenchmark [12] (Git commitd9158f3[41]) which evaluates the performance of several bonding heuristics as implemented in thepymatgenv2022.11.7 package [42] for the task of predicting coordination numbers in inorganic structures.MaterialsCoordhas theJmolNNclass which implements the criterion described in Eq.1with\(\epsilon = 0.45\)Å. Due to the similarity of theJmolNNclass to our method, we inheritedJmolNNclass to allow for easier plugging in of other radii sets, naming the derived classCovalentRadiiTableNeighbours.MaterialsCoorduses a set of 116 diverse experimentally determined structures, notably excluding organic compounds.

The comparison results are plotted in Fig.7. AlthoughMaterialsCoorddoes not encompass organic structures, we can see that the bonding radii set presented in this paper fares better than the earlier radii sets. Our radii set fared consistently better thanJmol’sautoBondalgorithm, the only radii sum based method described in [12]. It should be noted thatMaterialsCoorddoes not perform diagonal bond removal from 4-membered rings, but that places our method on a par with the other compared methods.

We have evaluated the usability of the determined bond peaks (described in sectionDetermination of the bond peak) in element-pair-specific distance-based connectivity detection. To do so, we have repeated the comparison with the chemical perception pipeline (as described in sectionComparison with a chemical perception pipeline) by replacing radii sum in Eq.1with bond peak distance and using\(\epsilon = 0.45\)Å. For classes where bond peak distances were unavailable due to the lack of observations, the original radii sum approach was retained using radii from Table1.

In over 365 000 input structures 109,178 mismatches were detected, a substantial increase from 80,487 which were observed using radii sum criterion in sectionComparison with a chemical perception pipeline. Classes with the most new and missing bonds are shown in Table3, with classes involving carbon and other organogenic elements provided for reference.

Out of the classes with the most of newly detected bonds, only the new bonds in C–K class are proper bonds not detected by the chemical perception pipeline. Newly detected C–K bonds occur mostly in half-sandwich compounds between potassium atoms bound to benzene rings, thus longer C–K bonding distance might be useful in detecting such compounds. New bonds in other classes, C–Zn, Cu–Cu, Ag–Ag and C–Na, correspond to clearly nonbonded interactions between an atom and its second coordination sphere neighbours. For the class of C–Zn, a single component model is selected as the best, which results in the bond peak being placed at 2.49 Å.

The most populous classes of unreproduced bonds contain nitrogens in coordination interactions. In these cases the selected bonding distances are too short and miss proper coordination bonds.

Thus while the bonding distance-based connectivity criterion allows much more control over which interactions should be regarded as bonds, it is more difficult to derive in an unsupervised manner. Lack of data, problems associated with outliers or model selection strongly affect the derived bonding distances, whereas bonding radii are much less sensitive to problematic classes due to them being averaged out by the less problematic ones. Therefore, with the current methodology, we recommend using bonding radii criterion over the one based on the bonding distances. Nevertheless we provide both the bonding radii and distance sets [43].

To better assess and compare the different algorithms and the derived sets, we have developed an interactive website [44]. The website facilitates browsing of calculated radii sets, comparing between different sets and reviewing the details of radii derivation. Radii are presented in the form of a periodic table, and a drop-down menu presents the option of switching between our radii sets and those published by other authors [7,13,14].

Clicking on a chemical element in the table opens a list of diagrams showing all the classes where the selected element participates in. Each diagram shows a class histogram, fitted Gaussian mixture model, detected van der Waals gap and the sum of radii of the participating elements. We have intensively used this website during the development of our methods.

We have created a website [45] exposing our connectivity validator which we have described in sectionComparison with a chemical perception pipeline. This website accepts uploads in structural data file (SDF) and chemical markup language (CML) formats, and highlights the differences between connectivity described in the input file and the one determined using our radii set.

The derived radii set is greatly skewed towards organic environments due to the abundance of organic and metalorganic compounds in the COD. Weights of organogenic elements dominate the other elements in approximate least squares matrix solution, some of the rarer elements have contacts with organogenic elements only. Class sizes are shown in Fig.5.

Classes are not free from outlier observations, warranting stricter structure selection criteria, which could result in exclusion of valid observations. In particular, it has been observed that relaxation-based criterion does not identify structures having insignificant amounts of atoms with significant displacements from their equilibrium positions. Moving such atoms to their equilibrium positions does not affect the unit cell, therefore no changes in crystal density are observed. A more sensitive approach would be to identify atoms with high potential energies.

Our method of approximating the distribution of interatomic distances with a Gaussian mixture and then selecting an antimode as a limit between bonded and non-bonded interactions has several limitations. All of them are related to the inability of our method to generalise over the variety of chemical interactions.

Many interaction classes do not contain pronounced gaps in their densities. In some cases even antimodes are not present at all (as in unimodal mixtures, mixtures with components having very low proportions, or substantially overlapping components), or are not pronounced. Cu–O class has a pair of antimodes, but both of them are still populated. Interestingly, first of the pronounced antimodes lands in between components of equatorial and axial interactions in complexes affected by the Jahn-Teller effect, both of which we would like to detect as bonds. Cu–Cu distance distribution is highly skewed towards longer distances and does not contain a gap; even the detected antimodes are not evident. A special case of this problem is the unimodal distribution where it is impossible to say whether the mode contains bonded or non-bonded interactions. Currently we treat this mode as containing bonded interactions, but this is clearly incorrect for element pairs which do not form bonds or of which bonded interactions are not observed in the COD.

Our method is sensitive to the absence and overrepresentation of certain chemical environments. For example, F–F class (Fig.3) is dominated by nonbonded F–F interactions, therefore identification of the van der Waals gap there is unreliable While this is a correct representation of F–F interactions, it needsad hochandling.

We have attempted to group classes by the shape of their distributions in an attempt to identify common traits and use them to apply different methods for separation of bonded and non-bonded interactions. We have used both two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test and our own method of mixture model difference integral:

WhereAandBare classes and\(p_X(x)\)is a mixture model density function for classX. Both methods resulted in similar distance matrices, however, neither of them highlighted sensible clusters. Most likely neither of the methods is sensitive enough to detect the similarities evident to the human eye without being penalised for differences, usually in location and scale. We have attempted aligning the distributions and models using normalisation and matching of the components surrounding the perceived van der Waals gap, but none of them yielded better outcomes.

Radii for some of the elements in our set are missing due to the lack of observations in the COD (inert gases, most of the elements with\(Z > 83\)). Some sources suggest replacing missing radii from the other radii sets or using fixed reasonable values [46]. We recommend taking the missing radii values from Pyykkö and Atsumi set.

Some of the other elements have unusually short or long radii, as evident from Fig.1. Again, replacing them with values from other radii sets is a possibility. Another solution would be to average over all radii, or fitting a smoothing spline to each of the periods. We suggest a conservative approach of averaging over the outlying radii values, however care should be taken to maintain the periodic trends.

While the described radii sum heuristic is very widely used in practice, there are many ongoing efforts to improve it or present alternatives to them, summarised and evaluated in, for example, Pan et al. [12], which measures the performance of various heuristics in the task of predicting coordination numbers in crystal structures. Some of the methods already incorporate Voronoi tessellation [42,47,48].

In this publication we present a method for unsupervised derivation of sets of bonding radii from crystallographic small molecule datasets. The devised method allows for fully automated bonding radii derivation, making the method suitable for periodic analysis of large crystallographic resources. This property is especially useful for deriving bonding radii from crystallographic databases, such as the COD.

In addition, we present a bonding radii set derived from the COD. The presented set follows the trends also visible in other widely used bonding radii sets. We have evaluated our bonding radii set by applying it on structures with known connectivities to find the apriori and derived connectivities to be in a good agreement.

It is clear that the bonding radii sum based methods will not supersede more precise methods which pay more respect to chemical environments. However, they have their place in the computational chemist’s toolbox as an indispensable approach for the derivation of connectivity when only the coordinates of atoms are known.

title: Integrating multimodal features with deep learning for protein solubility prediction
author: Zechen Wang; Lai Heng Tan; Liangzhen Zheng; Jagath C. Rajapakse; Yuguang Mu
text:
Protein solubility prediction holds significant importance in the fields of biotechnology and medicine. With the continual advancements of computational and experimental techniques such as protein design, enzyme mining, and directed evolution, accurate prediction of native and mutant protein solubility has become a key step in accelerating the development of functional proteins. In this study, we extracted physicochemical properties and co-evolutionary features from protein sequences, and further incorporated graph-based protein representations along with surface features as inputs for solubility prediction. Building upon these features, we developed two models, ProSolNet and ProSolNetMut. ProSolNet predicts whether a protein is soluble, while ProSolNetMutpredicts solubility changes induced by mutations. Compared with state-of-the-art models, both models achieved higher accuracy in their respective tasks. In addition, we investigated the underlying mechanisms and application potential of the models through interpretability analysis.

In this work, we present ProSolNet and ProSolNetMutto predict protein solubility and mutation-induced solubility changes by leveraging multimodal protein features, including sequence-based global descriptors, structure-based graph representations, and protein surface features. The proposed models achieve improved performance compared with representative existing models.

Obtaining proteins with desired functions is a crucial task in protein engineering [1,2,3]. However, obtaining adequate amounts of proteins directly from natural sources is often limited by low yields and various technical constraints, making it challenging to meet practical application requirements [4]. To overcome these challenges, expressing recombinant proteins in heterologous hosts has become a widely used strategy. Among available systems,Escherichia coli(E. coli) remains the most popular host [5] due to its ease of genetic manipulation [6,7], the availability of diverse molecular tools [8], and its capacity for rapid, large-scale cultivation [7]. However, during heterologous overexpression, many proteins tend to aggregate into inclusion bodies composed of misfolded or unfolded species, posing a major challenge in protein engineering [9]. This phenomenon is closely associated with the limited solubility of recombinant proteins.

Previous studies have demonstrated that, for certain proteins, activity and solubility are closely correlated [10]. For instance, some insoluble enzymes in the deoxyxylulose phosphate pathway exhibit significantly lower enzymatic activity compared with an equivalent amount of their soluble enzymes [3]. These findings suggest that solubility may serve as a critical criterion for screening and selecting promising enzyme candidates and their mutants. Therefore, accurately evaluating solubility is essential for guiding protein selection, expression, purification, and downstream applications in both protein and enzyme engineering [3,4,5,6]. However, since experimental determination of solubility is often time-consuming and resource-intensive, computational prediction offers an efficient alternative.

In recent years, machine learning and deep learning have been successfully applied to various bioinformatics tasks, including protein structure prediction [11], protein-ligand interaction prediction [12,13,14,15,16], enzyme kinetic parameter prediction [17,18], and so on. This trend is also evident in the field of protein solubility prediction [10,19,20,21,22,23], where most models are trained using data derived from public protein repositories such as TargetTrack [24] and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) [25]. A common labeling strategy assigns proteins as soluble if they are experimentally annotated as “soluble” inE. coli, or if they possess downstream indicators consistent with soluble expression [21]. Conversely, proteins that fail during expression or purification are labeled as insoluble [19,21]. This strategy enables the construction of large-scale solubility datasets and allows predictive models to estimate the likelihood that a target protein can be obtained in a soluble form upon overexpression inE. coli.

Early models primarily relied on features extracted directly from protein sequences. For instance, SoluProt utilized sequence-derived features such as amino acid composition, dipeptide frequency, and physicochemical properties, and trained a gradient boosting classifier for solubility prediction [19]. DeepSoluE employed similar descriptors but adopted a long short-term memory (LSTM) network as the modeling architecture [20]. Unlike SoluProt and DeepSoluE, which relied solely on sequence information, GraphSol constructed protein graphs from predicted contact maps, integrated physicochemical properties and evolutionary information, and employed a graph neural network to predict protein solubility [22]. Recently, significant advances in protein structure prediction have enabled the acquisition of high-quality 3D protein structures through computational approaches [11,26,27]. Building on these advances, Tan et al. proposed PROTSOLM, a graph neural network that leverages ESMFold-predicted 3D structures [27] together with fine-tuning strategies, achieving competitive performance on both internal and external test sets for protein solubility predictions [21].

Another challenge in protein and enzyme engineering is assessing the impact of mutations on protein solubility, as even a single-point mutation can lead to a substantial change in solubility [28]. Therefore, developing predictive models for mutation-induced solubility changes is crucial for guiding rational mutation design. To address this need, Yang et al. developed PON-Sol2, a gradient boosting tree-based model that utilizes amino acid composition, conservation, mutation type, neighborhood, and protein type features to characterize mutation-induced solubility changes [29]. More recently, Wang et al. proposed DeepMutSol, a graph neural network that integrates AlphaFold2-predicted 3D structures with embeddings derived from a protein language model as inputs [30]. Although DeepMutSol outperforms PON-Sol2 across multiple evaluation metrics, the model still has room for improvement in distinguishing mutants with different effects on solubility. In particular, it shows limited ability to assign high scores to beneficial mutations, likely due to the scarcity of such samples in the training set.

We speculate that, in addition to data scarcity, limitations in feature modeling represent another key factor constraining the performance of current solubility prediction models. To address these challenges, we extract multimodal features from both the primary and tertiary structures of proteins, including embedding representations from the protein language model Prot_t5_xl_uniref50 (ProtT5) [31], molecular physicochemical properties, protein graph structures, and surface features. Based on these representations and graph neural networks, we developed two models, ProSolNet and ProSolNetMut. ProSolNet predicts whether a protein is soluble, while ProSolNetMutpredicts mutation-induced changes in solubility. Compared with baseline models, our proposed models achieve consistently superior performance, improving accuracy (ACC) from 0.794 to 0.827 and from 0.618 to 0.636 on the two corresponding test sets. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of different features to solubility prediction. Finally, we discuss the strengths and limitations of current methods and provide perspectives for future research in this field.

Overview of ProSolNet, including the feature extraction process and model architecture

Protein solubility is fundamentally influenced by factors such as the distribution of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues, surface charge patterns, and local structural packing [1]. Early solubility prediction models relied solely on amino acid sequences, whereas recent advances in protein structure prediction have given rise to structure-based approaches. However, these models have not fully explored the contributions of physicochemical features to solubility prediction.

In this study, global protein features at the sequence level were first extracted, as these features have proven effective in previous works [19,20]. For structural representation, each protein was encoded as a graph derived from its 3D structure predicted by ESMFold [27], where residues were treated as nodes and edges were constructed between residue pairs whose C\(_{\alpha }\)atoms were within 8 Å. The node features were initialized using ProtT5 embeddings. To further explore the structural features closely related to protein solubility and to enrich the representation of protein features, we incorporated protein surface descriptors generated by MaSIF [32]. MaSIF computes a set of biophysical properties for each vertex of the protein surface mesh, including electrostatic potential, hydrogen bond potential, and hydropathy index. To obtain residue-level surface features, each surface mesh vertex was assigned to its nearest residue based on Euclidean distance, and the surface descriptors were averaged over all vertices mapped to the same residue. The resulting residue-level surface features were then concatenated with the corresponding node features learned from the protein structure graph. To aggregate residue-level features into a global protein representation, we employed an attention-based pooling mechanism that learns adaptive weights for different residues during training. This aggregation allows the model to flexibly combine information from residues with varying contributions to solubility prediction. Finally, the three types of features described above were concatenated to form the overall protein representation, which was then fed into a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to predict the solubility. The overall workflow of ProSolNet is illustrated in Fig.1.

Comparison of ProSolNet with baseline models.a,c,e, andgshow the AUC, ACC, MCC, and F1 score on the test set, respectively, whileb,d,f, andhpresent the corresponding metrics on the external test set

We used the training, validation, and test sets of the PDBSol dataset to train and evaluate ProSolNet. Since the model outputs probabilities ranging from 0 to 1, a threshold is required to distinguish between soluble and insoluble proteins. To this end, we evaluated the F1 score at different threshold values on the validation set, as shown in Supplementary Figure S1. When the threshold is set to 0.42, the model achieves the highest F1 score on the validation set. Therefore, 0.42 was selected as the final classification threshold.

We first compared ProSolNet with baseline models [19,20,21,33,34,35,36,37] on the test set. ProSolNet attained an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.920, an accuracy (ACC) of 0.827, a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.655, and an F1 score of 0.840, outperforming PROTSOLM, which reached an AUC of 0.794, an ACC of 0.794, an MCC of 0.588, and an F1 score of 0.801 (Fig.2a, c, e and g). To further assess the generalization capability of ProSolNet, we conducted evaluations on an external test set. On this dataset, ProSolNet achieved AUC, ACC, and MCC of 0.679, 0.632, and 0.266, respectively, outperforming the baseline models (Fig.2b, d, and f). However, we observed that ProSolNet achieves a slightly lower F1 score on the external test set compared to PLM_Sol, NetSolP, SoluProt, and DeepSoluE (Fig.2h). This may be partly explained by the higher sequence identity between the proteins in their training sets and those in the external test set, with some proteins even reaching 100% sequence identity. Such high sequence identity may introduce redundancy between training and test data, potentially contributing to relatively optimistic performance. In contrast, the sequence identity between the training set of ProSolNet and the external test set is strictly below 25%, indicating a more challenging and realistic evaluation setting.

To further evaluate the robustness of ProSolNet, we performed five-fold cross-validation. Specifically, the original training and validation sets were combined, and cross-validation was conducted on the merged dataset. The threshold of 0.42, determined on the validation set, was consistently applied across all folds and evaluation datasets. As shown in Supplementary Table S1, ProSolNet exhibits consistently low standard deviations across folds. In addition, the ensemble model achieves performance comparable to that obtained using the original training and validation split (Supplementary Table S2). These results indicate that ProSolNet is stable under different data splits and produces consistent results across training configurations.

To further assess the practical applicability of ProSolNet, we evaluated the model on the eSOL [38,39] dataset, which provides experimentally measured solubility values forE. coliproteins. Unlike the PDBSol dataset, eSOL reports continuous solubility percentages derived from in vitro expression experiments, thereby enabling direct comparison between model predictions and experimentally observed solubility. To evaluate classification performance on high-confidence samples, we followed previous studies and adopted commonly used thresholds to define binary labels. Specifically, proteins with solubility greater than 70% were labeled as soluble, while those with solubility lower than 30% were labeled as insoluble [38]. On this subset, ProSolNet achieved an accuracy of 0.693, an AUROC of 0.763, and an MCC of 0.405, demonstrating its ability to distinguish soluble proteins from aggregation-prone ones based on experimental data. In addition, proteins were grouped into bins according to predicted solubility probabilities, and the distribution of experimental solubility values was analyzed across bins (Supplementary Figure S2). As the predicted probability increases, the median experimental solubility shows a clear upward trend, indicating that higher predicted scores are generally associated with higher experimentally measured solubility. Despite the spread within each bin, the overall monotonic trend further supports the ability of ProSolNet to capture solubility-related patterns. These results demonstrate that ProSolNet is not only effective on curated benchmark datasets, but also exhibits meaningful consistency with experimentally measured solubility, highlighting its potential utility in prioritizing candidate proteins for recombinant expression experiments.

Feature importance analysis and visualization.aanddshow the integrated gradients attribution (IGA) of graph residue features and protein surface features, respectively, obtained using the Integrated Gradients method. Within each panel, larger IGA values indicate greater relative contributions to the model output.b,c,e, andfpresent the t-SNE visualization of processed sequence features, structural features, surface features, and final merged features

To investigate the contribution of different feature types to solubility prediction, we conducted ablation experiments. As shown in Table1, structural features were more effective than protein-level sequence features, highlighting the advantage of structure-based graph representations for this task. In addition, the contribution of surface features was less pronounced compared with the other feature modalities. This may be because the protein graph representation implicitly captures certain aspects of residue exposure and local surface-related information, thereby reducing the additional benefit provided by explicitly computed surface descriptors.

To investigate the contribution of individual components within each feature modality, we employed the Integrated Gradients (IG) method to quantify their relative importance. Specifically, for the protein graph, we assessed per-residue-type importance using two complementary aggregation strategies. First, we averaged normalized node-level IG attributions (IGA) within each protein and then aggregated them across all proteins in the test set, thereby capturing the typical contribution of each residue type to the model predictions when it occurs in a protein. As shown in Figure3a, Methionine (M) and Leucine (L) exhibit the strongest influence under this per-protein normalized analysis. Second, we computed a global residue-type importance by accumulating normalized node-level IGA over all proteins, reflecting the overall contribution of each residue type across the entire dataset. Under this global aggregation, Leucine (L) shows the largest overall contribution (Supplementary Figure 3a). However, it should be noted that the second strategy does not normalize for residue frequency, and thus the resulting importance scores may be influenced by the occurrence frequency of specific residues in protein sequences.

Similarly, we also analyzed the importance of individual components within the protein surface features and the sequence-based global features. For protein surface features, we computed normalized per-feature importance scores and observed that hydropathy-related features receive the highest attribution values, indicating that the model relies more strongly on hydropathy information of surface regions in making predictions (Figure3d). Among the sequence-based global features, the maximum identity to theE. coliPDB subset exhibits the highest importance, likely because it implicitly captures evolutionary and experimental biases associated with proteins that have been successfully expressed and structurally characterized inE. coli(Supplementary Figure 3b).

To provide an intuitive visualization of the learned representations from different feature modalities in ProSolNet, we extracted intermediate embeddings from hidden layers and visualized their distributions using t-SNE. The sequence-based, structural, surface, and final integrated embeddings are shown in Figs.3b,3c,3e, and3f, respectively. As illustrated, the embeddings derived from structural and surface features appear to exhibit a clearer clustering tendency between soluble and insoluble proteins compared with sequence-based representations, while the final integrated embeddings show the most visually distinct grouping. This qualitative visualization is consistent with the ablation results and suggests that structural features are associated with more separable embedding patterns, while multimodal fusion corresponds to more organized latent representations.

The protein IDs corresponding toaande,bandf,candg, anddandhare 32319, 64302, 64509, and 27604, respectively. Each panel includes a color bar, where a redder color indicates higher attention. For clearer representation, the original attention scores were scaled by a factor of 100

We also visualized the attention distribution learned by the model on several proteins, as shown in Fig.4. After global aggregation across nodes in the protein graph, we observed that the model sometimes assigns relatively higher attention weights to residues located near the N- and C-termini. This pattern reflects how the model internally weights different regions when forming the protein representation. Notably, terminal regions have been reported in previous studies to be associated with solubility-related properties, and the observed attention pattern appears to be consistent with these reports [40,41].

Another important question is whether using protein structures from different sources during inference affects the prediction performance. To investigate this, we randomly selected 100 soluble and 100 insoluble proteins from the external test set, generated their structures using the AlphaFold server, and used them as inputs to ProSolNet for solubility prediction. We then compared these predictions with those obtained using ESMFold-generated structures. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 4, the use of protein structures from these two different sources has a minor effect on the model’s predictions. Among the 200 samples, only 4 exhibited inconsistent prediction results.

Architecture of ProSolNetMut.aOverview of the ProSolNetMutframework.bThe details of protein encoder module

Protein mutation is a primary strategy for protein modification in protein engineering [42,43]. In some cases, even a single amino acid substitution can lead to substantial changes in solubility. To address this challenge, we developed ProSolNetMut, a model designed to predict mutation-induced effects on protein solubility using structural and surface features. We adopted the dataset employed in previous works [30], which includes a 10-fold cross-validation set and an independent test set. These datasets were used for training and evaluation of ProSolNetMut. The dataset defines three labels, – 1 (decreased solubility), 0 (no change), and 1 (increased solubility), making it a three-class classification task. Given the limited availability of mutation–solubility data, we applied a symmetry-based data augmentation strategy to enlarge the effective size of the training set. Specifically, if a mutantMis derived from a wild-type sequence, the wild-type sequence can be regarded as the reverse mutant ofM. This operation effectively doubles the size of the training set.

The overall framework of ProSolNetMutis illustrated in Fig.5a. The 3D structures of both the mutant and the wild-type were first fed into a protein encoder (Fig.5b) to obtain their corresponding embeddings. A difference vector was then computed by subtracting the wild-type embedding from the mutant embedding, and subsequently passed through an MLP to generate the final output.

The goal of this task is to predict whether a mutation results in decreased, unchanged, or increased protein solubility, corresponding to labels of – 1, 0, and 1, respectively. These labels follow an inherent ordinal relationship, reflecting a progressive increase in solubility from – 1 to 1. However, conventional classification approaches based on cross-entropy loss treat these classes as independent and fail to capture this ordered relationship. To address this limitation, ProSolNetMutoutputs a continuous value ranging from – 1 to 1, where values closer to 1 indicate increased solubility, whereas values closer to – 1 indicate decreased solubility. To convert the continuous outputs into three discrete classes, two thresholds need to be introduced to separate decrease, no change, and increase in solubility. To determine the optimal thresholds, we collected the predictions from the validation set of each fold in the 10-fold cross-validation and combined them into a unified validation prediction set. Based on this combined set, the threshold combination that maximizes the normalized ACC was selected. As shown in Fig.6a, the highest normalized ACC is achieved when the two thresholds are set to −0.40 and 0.34. Accordingly, predicted values in the range of – 1 to −0.40 are classified as decreased solubility, values between −0.40 and 0.34 are classified as unchanged solubility, and values between 0.34 and 1 are classified as increased solubility.

Compared with ProSolNet, ProSolNetMutemploys a new protein encoder to represent protein structures. In addition, a new GNN module was introduced to replace the original global sequence feature module, thereby enhancing the model’s sensitivity to mutations, as shown in Fig.5b. This GNN incorporates customized node features, including one-hot encodings of residue type, polarity, aromaticity, hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity, and secondary structure, further improving the model’s ability to capture mutation effects.

Since the number of samples across different classes varies substantially, directly evaluating the raw predictions could introduce bias. To ensure a fair comparison with baseline models, we adopted the same normalization strategy as previous studies to mitigate the impact of class imbalance. Details of the normalization are described in the Methods section.

Performance of ProSolNetMuton the test set.aHeatmap of normalized validation accuracy across different threshold combinations. The cutoff combination yielding the maximum accuracy was selected and is highlighted in red.bComparison of ProSolNetMutand DeepMutSol on the ten-fold cross-validation set. The y-axis represents the average normalized ACC achieved by the models on the ten validation sets during ten-fold cross-validation.cPrediction distributions of ProSolNetMutacross three categories of mutation effects on solubility.dComparison of ProSolNetMutwith baseline models in terms of normalized ACC

Because the number of solubility-increasing mutants is much smaller than that of the other two classes, deep learning models such as DeepMutSol often struggle to assign high scores to samples that increase solubility. To address this issue, we assigned larger weights to solubility-increasing samples in the loss function to encourage the model to better learn this minority class. On the ten-fold cross-validation set, ProSolNetMutachieved a normalized ACC of 0.688, outperforming DeepMutSol, which achieved 0.654 (Fig.6b). As shown in Fig.6c, we visualized the distribution of ProSolNetMutpredictions across the three categories on the test set. The results clearly show that the predicted values exhibit distinct separations among the three groups, with median values of −0.791, −0.031, and 0.267, respectively.

On the overall test set, ProSolNetMutachieved the highest normalized ACC of 0.636, followed by DeepMutSol with an ACC of 0.618 (Fig.6d). The positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), sensitivity, and specificity achieved by the baseline models and the two ablation models across different categories are summarized in Table2. As shown, ProSolNetMutoutperforms most baseline models, including DeepMutSol, on the majority of metrics. The ablation experiments indicate that the contribution of surface features to ProSolNetMutis limited compared with that of the GNN incorporating customized features. This may be because the mutation sites in the dataset are not always located on the protein surface, leading the model to regard surface features as less reliable indicators.

Given the vast mutation space of proteins, where each residue can mutate into any of the other 19 amino acids, we selected a protein containing 276 mutants across 28 mutation sites from the test set to evaluate the performance of ProSolNetMuton this protein with diverse mutation patterns. Figure7a and b illustrate the proportions of beneficial mutations and the ACC predicted by ProSolNetMutat each mutation site, respectively. Redder colors indicate higher proportions and ACC values. The 3D structure reveals that these mutation sites are spatially dispersed, with some residues participating in the formation of secondary structures such as helices, while others are located in loop regions. The model appears capable of delivering accurate predictions, irrespective of the secondary structure context of the mutation site. Figure7c and d show the prediction distributions across the three categories and the confusion matrix, respectively. As shown, ProSolNetMutachieves an ACC of 76.0% in identifying deleterious mutations and 56.5% in recognizing solubility-increasing mutations. These results may indicate that our model can maintain reasonable predictive performance even when mutations are widely distributed across the entire protein.
