Macromolecules such as peptides [5], oligonucleotides [22], and hybrid constructs [23] play a central role in modern biology and drug discovery. These molecules include peptides that act as hormones and signaling agents [3], oligonucleotides that regulate gene expression [1], and conjugates that combine small molecules, linkers, and biopolymers into multifunctional therapeutics [7]. Collectively, they span a continuum between small molecules and large biologics, offering tunable specificity, potency, and pharmacokinetic properties [25]. Their expanding use across oncology, metabolic disorders, and infectious diseases highlights the growing need for computational tools capable of handling their structural diversity.

With the increasing sophistication of designed macromolecules, including non-natural residues, cyclic topologies, chemical linkers, and hybrid architectures, manual analysis and representation have become unfeasible. Computational tools are essential for virtual screening, property prediction, structure generation, and synthetic planning. Central to these applications is the ability to accurately represent and manipulate macromolecular structuresin silico[2]. However, existing cheminformatics tools are typically tailored to either linear biopolymers or small molecules, making them ill-suited for hierarchical structures that combine both [9].

Biopolymers can be represented in a variety of ways. Sequence-based formats such as FASTA [15] encode peptides or nucleic acids as strings of monomer symbols, providing a compact and human-readable representation. However, they cannot describe non-linear architectures, chemical linkers, or modified monomers. Conversely, atom-level formats such as SMILES [26], InChI [6], or MDL [4] describe molecules as arbitrary chemical graphs, allowing full flexibility but losing the hierarchical, monomer-based organization that facilitates sequence-level operations. Tasks such as identifying termini, counting residues, or mapping modifications become nontrivial graph traversal problems.

The Hierarchical Editing Language for Macromolecules (HELM) [28] was developed to bridge this gap. HELM combines the clarity of sequence-based notation with the expressiveness of chemical graph representations. It encodes macromolecules as sets of named monomers connected through explicitly defined attachment points. Each monomer’s chemical structure and bonding information are defined in a monomer database, enabling the representation of peptides, RNA, DNA, chemical linkers, and hybrid constructs within a unified framework.

While several open-source tools can parse HELM, they often suffer from limited functionality and poor scalability. For example, the widely used RDKit [10] provides only basic parsing and cannot handle extended monomer definitions or nested polymer structures. The more recentpyPeptlibrary [14] supports custom monomers but focuses exclusively on peptides, lacks support for inline monomers, and struggles with datasets where monomer names contain special characters, which are issues common in public resources such as PubChem [8] or CycPeptMPDB [11]. Furthermore, its performance constraints, typically processing only a few molecules per second, limit its suitability for high-throughput workflows.

To overcome these limitations, we introducehelmkit, a dedicated Python library for converting HELM strings into RDKit molecular objects. Unlike peptide-specific tools,helmkitis designed for general hierarchical structures, supporting peptides, nucleic acids, chemical linkers, and hybrid combinations thereof. It natively handles inline monomers, custom monomer definitions, and special character encodings, ensuring compatibility with real-world datasets. The implementation emphasizes efficiency and robustness, with built-in parallelization and optimized data structures enabling throughput approaching 5,000 HELM entities per second on standard hardware.helmkithas been validated across large-scale datasets from PubChem and CycPeptMPDB, demonstrating both correctness and scalability for modern macromolecular informatics.

The development of tools for handling macromolecular structures has evolved alongside the increasing complexity of biotherapeutic design. Several open-source software packages support the parsing, manipulation, and conversion of HELM notation, reflecting its adoption as a standard for representing diverse biomolecules. These tools vary in scope, from general-purpose cheminformatics libraries to specialized parsers, but often exhibit limitations in scalability, flexibility, or integration with popular Python ecosystems such as RDKit. Below, we survey key existing approaches, highlighting their strengths and gaps thathelmkitaddresses.

Prominent open-source cheminformatics toolkits provide partial support for HELM, primarily focusing on basic parsing and conversion to molecular objects.

The RDKit library itself offers native HELM parsing through theMolFromHELMfunction, which converts HELM strings directly intoChem.Molobjects. This functionality is efficient for standard monomers, such as natural amino acids and nucleotides, and integrates seamlessly with RDKit’s extensive suite of molecular manipulation tools. However, RDKit’s HELM support is constrained to a predefined set of monomers; user-supplied custom monomers are not natively supported. As a result, it is unsuitable for diverse real-world datasets without significant preprocessing.

Other general libraries, such as the Chemistry Development Kit (CDK) [24] in Java, indirectly support HELM through integrations with specialized toolkits (discussed below). CDK excels in graph-based molecular representations and can generate SMILES or other formats from parsed structures, but it does not natively parse HELM, requiring additional layers for macromolecular handling.

The Pistoia Alliance, the organization behind the HELM standard, maintains a suite of open-source tools under the PistoiaHELM project on GitHub [17]. These are primarily implemented in Java and serve as reference implementations for HELM parsing and manipulation.

The HELM2 Notation Toolkit [19] is the core reference implementation for HELM version 2.0. It provides robust parsing of HELM strings, creation of HELM notation objects, validation, and basic calculations (e.g., molecular weight). Leveraging CDK for chemistry operations, it supports ambiguous structures and can be configured for external monomer databases via web services. While it enables conversion to atom-level representations such as SMILES through CDK, it does not directly output RDKit-compatible molecules and is not designed for Python workflows. An earlier HELM Notation Toolkit exists for version 1.0, with similar features but without ambiguity support.

Complementing the toolkit are graphical editors: the HELM Web-editor [20], a web-based tool for drawing and editing biomolecules, and the HELM Antibody Editor (HAbE) [18] for specialized antibody notations. These tools facilitate visual structure creation and export to HELM strings but are not optimized for batch processing or programmatic conversion. A.NET implementation of the HELM Toolkit is also available, offering similar parsing capabilities for Windows-centric environments, although it lacks the CDK integration for advanced conversions.

Overall, the Pistoia tools provide comprehensive HELM compliance and are ideal for validation or standalone Java/.NET applications. However, their language-specific nature limits their adoption in Python-dominated cheminformatics pipelines, and their performance in high-throughput scenarios is not emphasized.

In the Python ecosystem, options for HELM handling are more limited, with a focus on domain-specific applications.

The pyPept library [14] is a notable Python tool for peptide structures, supporting HELM parsing and conversion to RDKit molecules. To the best of our knowledge, it is the only Python library capable of handling HELM with custom monomer libraries. It handles custom monomers via SDF files and includes features for 2D/3D conformer generation. However, as detailed in Sect.Differences with pyPept, pyPept is restricted to peptides, employs inefficient intermediate representations (e.g., BILN to sequence), requires multiple dependencies (e.g., pandas, Biopython, igraph), and struggles with monomer names containing special characters. Its performance, at a few molecules per second, hinders large-scale use, and error handling via process termination (exit()) is suboptimal for robust applications.

Existing tools demonstrate HELM’s maturity but reveal key shortcomings: general libraries such as RDKit lack extensibility for custom macromolecules, Pistoia tools are not Python-native, and specialized options such as pyPept are narrow in scope and inefficient. None emphasize parallel processing, inline monomer support, or automatic R-group inference for underspecified datasets such as PubChem.helmkitfills these voids by offering a lightweight, Python-centric library with direct HELM-to-RDKit conversion, broad macromolecular compatibility, and high-throughput capabilities, making it a valuable addition to the ecosystem.

The Hierarchical Editing Language for Macromolecules (HELM) [28] is a line notation developed to represent complex biomolecular structures in a concise, hierarchical, and computationally accessible format. It overcomes the limitations of sequence-based or atom-only representations by organizing structural information across four levels: complex polymer, simple polymer, monomer, and atom. This hierarchy enables the accurate encoding of large, chemically modified biomolecules, including peptides, oligonucleotides, antibody–drug conjugates, and crosslinked systems, while remaining convertible to both atomic-level formats (e.g., SMILES, InChI) and biological sequences.

Thehelmkitlibrary is designed for compatibility with modern Python environments and depends only on Python version 3.11 or higher, along with the RDKit cheminformatics library. No additional third-party packages are required for core functionality. The package is officially distributed through PyPI and can be installed usingpip install helmkit. Further instructions, including guidance on the development environment setup and custom monomer library configuration, are provided in the repository’sREADME.mdfile.

Thehelmkitlibrary is engineered with a focus on modularity, efficiency, and extensibility to facilitate seamless integration into cheminformatics pipelines. The primary entry point is theMoleculeclass constructor, which accepts a single HELM string as input. This class encapsulates all necessary methods for parsing the HELM notation and converting it directly to an RDKitChem.Molobject. Internally, the class maintains state for the RDKit molecule, inter-monomer bonds, individual monomers, and polymer chains.

The parsing process begins by dissecting the HELM string into its constituent sections: simple polymers, connections, hydrogen bonds (if present), and attributes. For each simple polymer, the monomers are parsed sequentially. In peptide chains, connections are formed by linking the R2 attachment point of one monomer to the R1 of the next. For RNA polymers, the logic accommodates branched structures: bases enclosed in parentheses are attached via their R1 to the R3 of the preceding sugar monomer, whereas the backbone continues from the R2 of the sugar to the next monomer (e.g., a phosphate). Unutilized R-groups are capped with appropriate substituents, such as hydrogens or hydroxyls, based on the monomer definitions.

Connections between polymers are applied post-parsing, and the specified attachment points are used to form covalent bonds. Hydrogen bonds in HELM are specified at the monomer level usingpairannotations, which represent non-covalent interactions such as Watson–Crick base pairing in nucleic acids. Due to potential ambiguities in mapping these to specific atoms (e.g., multiple hydrogen bonds per pair),helmkitparses and stores them as metadata attributes on theMoleculeobject but does not integrate them into the covalent RDKit graph, due to their non-covalent nature and the ambiguity in atom-level mapping. Future extensions may include optional atom-level resolution based on standard pairing schemes.

Error handling is robust, with descriptive exceptions raised for invalid HELM syntax, undefined monomers, or incompatible attachments. These exceptions include contextual information such as the problematic HELM substring and the specific parsing stage where the error occurred, facilitating debugging. This design ensures that the library fails gracefully without terminating the parent process, enabling batch processing workflows where individual failures should not halt the entire operation.

ThepyPeptlibrary is a Python tool designed for parsing and manipulating peptide structures, supporting conversion from HELM to RDKit molecules via intermediate representations such as Boehringer Ingelheim Line Notation (BILN) and sequence objects. WhilepyPeptis effective for its intended domain,helmkitaddresses several limitations and design choices that impact both performance and usability. A comprehensive comparison of key differences is presented in Table1.

The most fundamental architectural difference lies in the conversion pathway. WhereaspyPeptemploys a multi-step pipeline (HELM\(\rightarrow\)BILN\(\rightarrow\)Sequence\(\rightarrow\)RDKit),helmkitperforms direct conversion from HELM to RDKit, eliminating intermediate representations. This design choice reduces computational overhead, minimizes potential error sources, and simplifies the codebase. The streamlined approach contributes significantly to the performance improvements demonstrated in Sect.Performance, wherehelmkitachieves speedups of over 300\(\times\)compared withpyPept.

In addition to architectural differences,helmkitextends support to a broader range of biomolecules. WhilepyPeptis restricted to peptides,helmkitnatively handles nucleic acids, chemical linkers, and hybrid macromolecules, making it suitable for a wider variety of HELM-encoded structures. This expanded scope is particularly valuable for applications involving RNA therapeutics, peptide–nucleic acid conjugates, and other complex biomolecular systems.

Operational differences also distinguish the two libraries.helmkitloads the monomer library once per session and reuses it across multiple parsing operations, whereaspyPeptreloads the library for every peptide. This design, combined with the simpler dependency footprint (RDKit only, versus five dependencies forpyPept), reduces both the initialization overhead and the installation complexity. Additionally,helmkitrequires only a file path to the monomer library, whereaspyPeptdemands a directory structure organized as a Python module with__init__.py.

Robustness is another key differentiator.helmkittolerates monomer names containing special characters such as whitespaces, hyphens, and parentheses, provided that they do not disrupt bracket or parenthesis balancing. In contrast,pyPeptenforces strict naming conventions and fails on such inputs. This flexibility is crucial for processing real-world datasets such as CycPeptMPDB, wherepyPeptoften encounters parsing failures due to non-standard monomer names.

Finally, error handling approaches differ substantially.helmkitraises Python exceptions that can be caught and handled programmatically, enabling graceful error recovery and integration into larger workflows.pyPept, however, callsexit()upon encountering errors, which abruptly terminates the entire process. This design choice makespyPeptunsuitable for batch processing scenarios where individual failures should not halt the entire operation.

To accommodate diverse macromolecular datasets,helmkitallows loading custom monomer libraries via theload_monomer_libraryutility function, which accepts a path to an SDF file. This function employs a least-recently-used (LRU) cache to prevent redundant loading of the same library, optimizing memory and time in batch processing scenarios.

The loaded library is structured as a dictionary, with top-level keys representing monomer types (e.g.,aafor amino acids,rnafor nucleic acid components, andchemfor chemical linkers). Each type maps to a sub-dictionary where keys are monomer names and values are dictionaries containing the RDKit molecule, R-group indices, substituents, and attachment points. These details must be annotated in the SDF file using tags compatible withpyPept:symbol(monomer ID),m_Rgroups(substituent specifications),m_RgroupIdx(R-group atom indices), andm_type(monomer category).

UnlikepyPept,helmkitinfers attachment points automatically from the R-group indices, eliminating the need for explicit definitions. Additionally, the SDF file can reside at any filesystem path, without requiring encapsulation in a Python module.

Public repositories such as PubChem frequently embed monomer definitions directly within HELM strings using SMILES notation augmented with R-group placeholders. These inline definitions typically omit unused substituents, including only attachment-relevant R-groups. For instance:

helmkitnatively parses such inline monomers by extracting the SMILES, identifying R-group labels (e.g.,_R2), and integrating them into the molecule assembly. This feature ensures compatibility with real-world data sources without requiring external monomer databases.

In cases where inline or custom monomers lack explicit R-group definitions, which occurs in PubChem for several in-line amino acids,helmkitemploys heuristic substructure matching to infer attachment points. This is activated only for peptide monomers to maintain specificity.

The matching is performed using SMARTS (SMiles ARbitrary Target Specification) patterns, a cheminformatics language that extends SMILES to describe molecular substructures with precise atom and bond constraints. SMARTS allows specification of atom types, hybridization states, hydrogen counts, and bond orders, enabling robust pattern matching against molecular graphs.

For the N-terminal R1 (amine group), the library searches for patterns such as[#6][NX3H][#6](alpha-amino carbon) or[NX3H2][#6](primary amine). If exactly one match is found, a placeholder atom is appended as the R1 group, with the attachment indexed accordingly.

For the C-terminal R2 (carboxyl group), patterns such as[CX3H1]=O(aldehyde) orCX3[OH](carboxylic acid) are matched. A similar placeholder is added if exactly one match exists.

This inference prevents parsing failures and enables the processing of underspecified monomers, with the placeholders later replaced during chain assembly.

For high-throughput applications,helmkitprovides theload_in_parallelfunction. This accepts a list of HELM strings and an optional custom monomer library path, returning a list of RDKit molecules. Leveraging Python’s multiprocessing module, it distributes parsing across available CPU cores, potentially achieving linear speedups on multicore systems.

Key attributes are available to inspect the resulting structure:

molecule.monomers: A list of dictionaries, each describing a single monomer (chain identifier, name, type, abbreviation, etc.).

molecule.monomer_indices: An array mapping each atom in the molecule to its parent monomer. For example,[0, 0, 0, 1, 1]means that the first 3 atoms belong to monomer 0 and the next 2 to monomer 1.

molecule.bond_indices: The list of 0-based indices of all inter-monomer bonds in the atomistic structure.

molecule.hydrogen_bonds: A list of tuples, each describing a single hydrogen bond (source chain, source monomer, target chain, target monomer).

Validation flow for HELM parsing withhelmkit

The validation ofhelmkitemployed a multi-tiered approach combining systematic random generation and large-scale dataset validation to ensure both correctness and robustness across diverse macromolecular structures. The testing strategy addresses the inherent complexity of HELM parsing, where errors in monomer connection, R-group handling, or attachment point resolution can propagate to produce incorrect molecular graphs that may still be chemically valid but structurally distinct from the intended representation.

Integration tests were implemented using Python’spytestframework, exercising core parsing functionality, monomer library loading, R-group inference, and connection handling. To validate end-to-end correctness, tests compared HELM-derived RDKit molecules against equivalent structures parsed from alternative representations using well-established tools. The International Chemical Identifier (InChI) served as the primary validation metric, providing a canonical representation that is sensitive to structural differences while remaining invariant to the representation format. For each test case, InChI strings computed from HELM-parsed molecules were compared against reference InChI values derived from equivalent input formats. Figure6illustrates this process.

Systematic validation employed randomly generated macromolecules to exercise the parser across a broad parameter space. Monomers were sampled from standard biological sets: the 20 canonical amino acids for peptides, and the four standard RNA bases (A, C, G, U) along with ribose sugar and phosphate linker for nucleic acids. Peptides were constructed as linear chains spanning 2–50 residues, while RNA structures tested both common monomer orderings:[sugar](base)[linker]and[linker][sugar](base)formats, with chain lengths ranging from 5–40 nucleotides. For each set, 1,000 random HELM strings were generated, parsed, converted to an RDKit molecule, and cross-validated by parsing the equivalent sequence representation (FASTA) using RDKit’s native parsers and comparing the resulting InChI identifiers.

Large-scale validation leveraged real-world datasets to assess the performance on structures encountered in production environments. The PubChem database provided 878,442 entries containing HELM notations for peptides and RNA, including 867,922 peptide entries as of August 11, 2025 and 10,520 RNA records. Prior to validation, double-bond stereochemistry and isotopic specifications were intentionally stripped, as these features cannot be consistently or unambiguously represented within the constraints of HELM. The CycPeptMPDB dataset (version 1.2) comprised 7,298 cyclic and lariat peptides, including complex topologies and non-standard modifications that challenge parsing robustness. For each entry with available monomer definitions, the HELM string was parsed, converted to an RDKit molecule, and the computed InChI was compared against reference values. Discrepancies underwent manual inspection to distinguish library errors from database inconsistencies, leading to iterative refinements in R-group inference algorithms and connection-handling logic.

Table2summarizes the full set of validation results, which demonstrate thathelmkitperforms accurately across all datasets. For PubChem,pyPeptwas evaluated only on the peptide subset because of its limited domain support. Among the 867,922 peptide HELM entries, 90,095 (\(\approx 10.38\%\)) were successfully parsed, with most errors stemming from its inability to handle inline monomers. In contrast,helmkitachieved over\(99\%\)concordance across the full PubChem HELM dataset. All RNA-related failures were manually inspected, and every case was traced back to incorrect structures embedded in the in-line monomers, with the vast majority caused by a missing oxygen atom in diphosphate or triphosphate groups. Peptide discrepancies were also examined on a sampled basis, and all checked cases were confirmed to have originated from database errors, although the full set was too large to review exhaustively.

We have introducedhelmkit, a Python library that addresses fundamental limitations in existing HELM parsing tools through architectural innovation and comprehensive biomolecule support. The library’s direct HELM-to-RDKit conversion pathway, which eliminates intermediate representations used by tools such aspyPept, achieves speedups exceeding 300\(\times\)in standard configurations and over 700\(\times\)with parallelization, enabling a throughput of nearly 5000 HELM entities per second on commodity hardware.

In addition to performance,helmkitextends functionality to nucleic acids, chemical linkers, and hybrid macromolecules, addressing a critical gap where existing tools are restricted to peptides. The implementation’s robustness is demonstrated through successful processing of real-world datasets that challenge other parsers:helmkitachieves\(100\%\)concordance on CycPeptMPDB and\(>99\%\)on PubChem’s HELM entries, handling monomer names with special characters, inline SMILES definitions, and missing R-groups that cause failures in alternative tools.

Key design decisions contribute to both performance and usability. The single-dependency architecture (RDKit only) simplifies deployment, whereas session-level monomer library caching eliminates redundant I/O operations. Programmatic error handling via exceptions enables batch processing workflows that are impractical with tools that terminate the process on errors. These features, combined with support for arbitrary monomer naming conventions, makehelmkitsuitable for production cheminformatics pipelines that process diverse macromolecular datasets.

Validation across thousands of structures from public repositories confirms both correctness and scalability. The library’s ability to process datasets like CycPeptMPDB that are partially incompatible with existing tools demonstrates its practical value for modern macromolecular informatics. As the field increasingly relies on hierarchical representations for complex therapeutics,helmkitprovides a foundation for high-throughput analysis of peptides, oligonucleotides, and hybrid constructs within unified computational workflows.

Potential extensions tohelmkitinclude atom-level resolution of hydrogen bonds based on standard pairing schemes, which would enable explicit representation of non-covalent interactions in the molecular graph. Support for more HELM notation features, integration with conformer generation tools, and export formats that preserve hierarchical information represent additional directions for expansion. The development of formalized benchmark suites and enhanced monomer curator tooling could facilitate broader community adoption and contributions to monomer libraries.

title: Towards the design of artificial sensing materials via quantum-informed explainable AI
author: Li Chen; Leonardo Medrano Sandonas; Shirong Huang; Alexander Croy; Gianaurelio Cuniberti
text:
Computational design of sensing materials remains fundamentally challenging due to the vast configurational landscape and the absence of robust property correlations that enable efficient molecular representation. These challenges become particularly critical in healthcare applications, where reliable and interpretable molecular recognition is essential for non-invasive diagnostics. To address these challenges, we developed MORE-ML, a quantum-informed AI framework that combines electronic-structure-derived properties of e-nose molecular building blocks with machine learning (ML) methods to uncover sensing mechanisms and guide the design of new systems. Within this framework, we expanded our previous dataset, MORE-Q, to MORE-QX by sampling a larger conformational space of interactions between body odor volatilomes (BOV) molecules and mucin-derived receptors, both in the gas phase and when deposited on graphene. MORE-QX provides extensive electronic binding features (BFs) computed upon BOV adsorption. Analysis of the property space revealed weak correlations between quantum-mechanical (QM) properties of building blocks and resulting BFs. Leveraging this observation, we defined electronic descriptors of building blocks as inputs for tree-based ML models to predict BFs. Benchmarking showed CatBoost models outperform alternatives, especially in transferability to unseen compounds. Through explainable AI, we reduced the high-dimensional QM property space to a compact and physically interpretable set of descriptors, revealing the properties that most influence BF predictions. Collectively, MORE-ML combines QM insights with ML to provide mechanistic understanding and rational design principles for artificial sensing materials in BOV sensing. This approach establishes a foundation for advancing materials capable of analyzing complex odor mixtures, bridging the gap between molecular-level computations and practical e-nose applications.

We developed the MORE-ML framework, which integrates electronic-structure-derived molecular descriptors with interpretable tree-based modeling and SHAP analysis to uncover physically and chemically grounded design principles for artificial sensing materials. In this context, we introduced the MORE-QX dataset, an extensive collection of electronic binding features characterizing the selectivity and sensitivity of a broad range of odorant–receptor conformations. Our work establishes an AI-assisted strategy for rational receptor engineering and identifies the key quantum-mechanical features governing binding behavior, thereby providing a more transparent and navigable pathway through the largely unexplored receptor design space.

The rapid advancement in artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly accelerated the development of AI-driven technologies, enabling precise recognition of objects, faces, voices, and tactile sensations [1,2]. Despite these advancements, a considerable technological gap persists in effectively interpreting and predicting the chemical environment surrounding humans. To bridge this gap, customized electronic noses have emerged, demonstrating notable proficiency in detecting volatile organic compounds (VOCs) [3,4,5,6]. Specifically, VOCs emitted from the human body (referred to as body odor volatilome (BOV)) act as unique chemical fingerprints and hold great promise for healthcare applications [7], e.g., serving as biomarkers for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases [8,9]. However, there remains a strong and persistent need for rapid and reliable sensing materials capable of detecting biomarkers [10] e.g., BOV molecules within digital olfactory systems, particularly for medical diagnostics.

Inspired by the sensitivity [11] and the discriminative power of the human olfactory system [12], diverse molecular olfactory receptors have recently been synthesized (e.g., mucin-derived receptors [13,14,15]). This progress has driven the development of experimental protocols aimed at controlling receptor affinity toward BOV molecules in gas sensing by incorporating specific functional groups with varying chemical characteristics on glaco-conjugated [16]. However, obtaining detailed information on BOV–receptor interactions—and thus guidance for receptor optimization—remains both costly and time-consuming when relying on empirical trial-and-error screening. This indicates that a key limitation of current prototype receptors lies in the lack of mechanistic insight into their sensitivity and selectivity across the vast chemical space of BOV–receptor systems. This bottleneck underscores the need for sustainable strategies to rationally design high-performance receptor-based biomimetic sensors. Similar to the transformative impact of molecular electronics a few decades ago [17], quantum-mechanical (QM) methodologies could revolutionize the field of chemical sensing by providing a deeper understanding of the physical and chemical interactions that govern key performance metrics such as recovery time, charge transfer, and Schottky barrier potential [18]. Furthermore, integrating QM-derived property data with AI techniques has the potential to yield reliable and efficient computational frameworks for guiding the design of materials for sensors with high sensitivity and selectivity—an approach that has recently proven successful in drug discovery studies [19,20,21,22].

Within this context, we have recently introduced the MORE-Q dataset [23], providing, for the first time, an extensive set of QM property data corresponding to the atomistic building blocks of artificial olfactory molecular sensors: BOV molecules, mucin-derived olfactorial receptors, and BOV-receptor dimer systems. MORE-Q also contains electronic structure data describing the intermolecular interactions between the most stable dimer systems and a graphene surface. All together, this dataset enables the exploration of key binding features (BFs) induced by BOV adsorption such as adsorption energy [24,25], charge transfer [26], and work function change [27]. This collection of BFs represent a big step towards the rational design and optimization of BOV–receptor systems due to the comprehensive electronic description of sensing performance; however, there are still some additional challenges to address before developing a sustainable framework for BOV–receptor design. For instance, analogous to ligand-pocket motifs [28,29], the sensing process is inherently dynamic and governed by weak non-covalent interactions (electrostatics and hydrogen bonding), indicating a structural flexibility that yield a rugged energy landscape with myriad local minima and versatile binding configurations [30]. On the other hand, current theoretical models lack the quantitative rigor required to quantitatively delineate property–property and structure–property relationships, hindering a clear understanding of the role of sensing building blocks in BF behavior.

A promising approach to elucidate the complex mappings between atomic structures and BFs is the sustainable use of machine learning (ML) methods [31]. For instance, Ulissi et al. recently introduced the AdsorbML framework [32], which integrates heuristic search with ML potentials to accelerate gas–metal adsorption energy calculations, achieving both high predictive accuracy and substantial computational speedups compared to conventional density functional theory (DFT). Similarly, GAME-Net [33], a graph neural network model, was developed to predict adsorption energies of organic molecules on catalytic surfaces with near-DFT accuracy, reaching errors of 0.18 eV (0.016 eV per atom) for large biomass and plastic fragments. More recently, Chen et al. introduced AdsMT [34], a multimodal Transformer that combines catalyst surface graph representations with adsorbate feature vectors through a cross-attention mechanism to predict global minimum adsorption energies without enumerating adsorption sites. While various ML-based studies [35,36,37,38,39] have focused on the adsorption of small and simple adsorbates (e.g.,\({\hbox {O}_2}\),\({\hbox {CO}_2}\), and\({\hbox {H}_2}\)) on flat metal surfaces, other electronic BFs, such as charge transfer and work function change, have been less explored. In addition, for large interacting molecules like the BOV-receptor systems, the concepts of binding site and adsorption distance become ill-defined owing to complex interaction morphologies and configurational polymorphism, which makes the development of predictive models more challenging. Furthermore, most of these works prioritize achieving high predictive accuracy, often at the expense of model interpretability, thereby limiting the physical and chemical insights that can be derived from these complex mappings. This lack of explainability also affects the exploration of the binding features space, where the optimization of one feature offers no guarantee of concurrent improvements in others, complicating further the rational design of sensing materials.

To address these challenges, we develop the MORE-ML framework, which integrates QM-derived molecular properties with ML methods to investigate how structural, global, and atomic-level features of electronic-nose building blocks influence BOV adsorption. By doing so, we seek to clarify the sensing mechanism and formulate design principles for BOV–receptor systems in artificial sensing materials. To approximate the thermodynamic ensemble, we expanded the MORE-Q dataset [23] into MORE-QX by sampling multiple low-energy BOV–receptor dimer (DM) conformers adsorbed on graphene. This process increased the number of BOV–receptor–graphene complexes from 1,836 to 10,441 (see Fig.1). A comprehensive analysis of MORE-QX reveals that DM conformers with similar binding energies can nevertheless show markedly different BFs such as charge transfer and work function change. Furthermore, DM properties and BFs exhibit only weak to moderate correlations, even though these properties were chosen following fundamental physical and chemical principles. Despite particularly weak correlations among BFs, we retain flexibility in identifying systems that share a similar set of electronic binding characteristics—clear evidence for the existence of “Freedom of design” in the MORE-QX property space [40]. To enable rapid and accurate navigation of the binding feature space–and thereby support practical design of BOV–receptor complexes for sensing–we develop tree-based regression models that map QM-derived property data of building blocks to their associated BFs. Within MORE-ML, we further exploit the interpretability of these models using SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) [41] to extract mechanistic insights into the sensing process. Overall, this work provides quantum-informed understanding of adsorption mechanisms and BOV–receptor-graphene interactions, paving the way for controlled and robust discovery of artificial sensing materials.

The intrinsic flexibility of large molecular receptors (REC) brings a crucial factor to consider in the understanding of the sensing mechanism in artificial olfactory sensors. Analogous to the binding process of ligands into protein pockets [28,29], the interaction between odorant molecules (OM) and molecular receptors is inherently dynamic. Indeed, DM systems (refer to as dimer system) continually interconvert among multiple conformations, i.e., jumping between minima on the potential energy surface (PES). Previous studies have shown that conformations of large molecules in both gas-phase [42] and deposited on graphene nanoribbon [43] can exhibit comparable quantum-mechanical (QM) properties, raising the question of whether such effects also occur in these DM systems. Therefore, instead of considering only the most stable conformer for each DM configuration, as is common in many DFT studies, we sampled a broader ensemble of low-energy conformers and adsorbed them onto graphene. This procedure expands the MORE-Q dataset [23] into MORE-QX and increases the number of CPLX systems from 1, 836 to 10, 441 (see Figs.1a–c). Accordingly, the same set of QM properties computed for the CPLX systems in MORE-Q was also calculated for the additional DM conformations. Note that the number of sampled conformers is adaptively adjusted to the morphological complexity of the DM system to ensure robust sampling. This means that systems with more flexible morphologies will yield a larger number of sampled conformers. On average, we considered six conformers per DM system. The initial set of 83,916 dimer configurations (50 per combination) was generated using the automated Interaction Site Screening (aISS) package [44]. Previous benchmarking on representative intermolecular complexes showed that aISS produces structures comparable in quality to those obtained with the widely used CREST code [44,45], while requiring substantially lower computational cost. This improvement in efficiency mainly arises from the demanding metadynamics-based conformational search employed in the CREST workflow, which makes it less practical for the efficient exploration of a large number of non-covalent complexes. After generating dimer configurations with aISS, we then remove redundant conformers within each BOV–receptor combination by clustering the structures by hierarchical clustering based on the user-defined pairwise root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) similarity distance. A larger cutoff distance leads to fewer clusters and vice versa. To balance computational cost and configurational diversity, we examined the number of clusters obtained for each combination as a function of the similarity cutoff and ultimately selected a value of 1.5 Å. This strategy enables flexible conformer selection: combinations with more complex configurational landscapes retain more conformers, whereas simpler combinations retain fewer. As a result, 10,411 conformers were obtained for subsequent deposition on the graphene surface.

Similar to the MORE-Q dataset [23], the quantum-mechanical (QM) properties of BOVs, molecular receptors, and their dimer conformations contained in MORE-QX dataset were obtained both at GFN2-xTB+D4 level and PBE+D3 with def2-TZVPP basis set using xTB (version 6.6.0) [46] and ORCA (version 5.0.3) [47] packages, respectively. The BOV-receptor-graphene complex (CPLX) systems underwent geometry optimization using the DFTB+ [48] package, employing the GFN2-xTB Hamiltonian with D4 dispersion correction. While optimizing the structures, we fixed the atomic positions in the graphene layer, as the adsorption of the OM molecules will not significantly affect the geometry of graphene, and the electrode is restricting the deformation degree of the graphene for a chemiresistive sensing device. To create the SUB system (or REC-graphene system), we removed the BOV molecule from the CPLX system and did not optimize the structures in order to investigate the pure electronic effect of the binding features.

MORE-QX provides extensive sets of QM global and local properties (up to 39) for single BOV/receptor molecules (MORE-QX-G1), BOV-receptor molecular dimers (MORE-QX-G2), and complex systems (MORE-QX-G3). The MORE-QX-G1 subset contains QM property data for 102 BOV molecules and 18 molecular receptors. Among the 39 molecular and atomic properties, we computed the D3 energy, dipole moment, polarizability, and Mulliken charges. The MORE-QX-G2 subset is built on the geometries from MORE-QX-G1 via the search for molecular docking conformations using BOV molecules and receptors. Accordingly, MORE-QX-G2 contains QM property data for 23,838 dimer conformations at the GFN2-xTB+D4 level and for 10,411 dimers with the lowest binding energies at the PBE+D3 level (see the property list in Tables S2 and S3 of the SI). The MORE-QX-G3 subset contains 10,411 selected dimers from MORE-QX-G2 on graphene surface. Consequently, MORE-Q-G3 includes QM property data at the PBE+D3 level for both the CPLX and SUB systems, as well as binding features that account for property changes in single systems induced by BOV molecule adsorption. The expansion including GFN-xTB+D4 geometry relaxation and DFT calculation took\(\sim 25\)Mio CPUhs.

Spearman is chosen owing to its robustness against outliers and the enhanced non-linear capturing ability compared to the counterpart Pearson correlation.

As stated above, the combination of GFN2-xTB for molecular structure generation and PBE+D3 for property calculations provides a suitable and balanced strategy for generating a comprehensive dataset of molecule-substrate systems. The reliability of GFN2-xTB for generating molecular structures has already been demonstrated in several dataset-generation workflows (e.g., QCML [49], QMugs [50]). Similarly, the PBE functional, as implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP [51,52], version 6.3.1), has been extensively used to generate benchmark materials datasets such as Alexandria [53], OMat24 [54], and MPtrj [55]. The PBE functional has also been employed to investigate diverse surface-induced properties in inorganic and organic–inorganic systems, such as work-function changes [56,57,58]. This widespread use indicates that PBE remains a good compromise between accuracy and computational efficiency for calculating properties across a large number of material systems. We further include the D3 van der Waals dispersion correction with PBE to improve the description of long-range interactions, which are particularly important when molecular dimers are deposited on substrates. A comparison with the more accurate PBE0+D3 functional shows that PBE+D3 and PBE0+D3 produce similar trends for most electronic properties (see Fig. S11 of the SI). However, the main difference lies in the computational cost, which increases significantly for complex systems containing approximately 300 atoms. Under the same computational setup, the average PBE0+D3 calculation time was approximately twelve times longer than that of PBE+D3 when using 256 cores of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8470 processor. This would represent a substantial increase in computational resources for calculating the binding features of the 10,411 complex systems considered in MORE-QX. Therefore, electronic-structure calculations of the SUB and CPLX systems were conducted at tightly converged PBE+D3 theory level by VASP package. The energy cutoff for the plane-wave basis set and the SCF convergence threshold were set to 600 and\(1\cdot 10^{-4}\)eV, respectively. And all simulations were conducted at Gamma point. The dipole correction along the slab direction (50.68Å) was switched on to obtain flat electrostatic potential.

We designed theMolecularOlfactorialReceptorEngineering byMachineLearning (MORE-ML) framework to simultaneously perform binding feature regression and model explanation tasks, as illustrated in Fig.3a. Among the spectrum of ML algorithms, linear models offer the highest explainability but lack sufficient capacity, whereas neural networks provide exceptional representational power yet suffer from nascent explainability [60]. To strike a balance between predictive performance and transparency, we employ tree-based models, which deliver both robust accuracy and an inherently interpretable decision process via hierarchical splitting [61]. Moreover, when integrated with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) tools–e.g.,SHapleyAdditive exPlanations (SHAP) [41]–these models not only yield precise predictions of binding features but also facilitate the extraction of underlying physical insights [62].

Building on the defined ML tasks, we now describe the training procedure for a single ML model, as depicted in Fig.3b. In our initial training loops, we identified some systems in which the dominant interactions occurred between the OM and the graphene surface rather than with the receptor. By projecting the data into UMAP space and clustering based on SHAP values (for better cluster forming [63,64]), we uncovered a distinct cluster corresponding to these outliers. We subsequently removed all 932 systems, as they lie outside the scope of DM pair design and would otherwise impair the effectiveness of our model (see more details in Fig. S4 of the SI).

The remaining data points are then split into training and test sets via farthest-point sampling (FPS) in the binding-feature t-SNE space, since t-SNE captures nonlinear relationships and clusters systems with similar binding mechanisms—preserving local consistency better than alternatives such as PCA or UMAP and homogeneous sampling in this space minimizes distributional divergence between the two sets. The dataset was partitioned into training and test sets at a fixed ratio of\(9\!:\!1\). The corresponding learning curves are shown in Fig. S5. This fixed test set is used to benchmark both intermediate models and the final model throughout the entire training process. Then we conducted 100 iterations of Bayesian optimization (BO) to identify optimal hyperparameters, using the mean root-mean-square error (mRMSE) from 10-fold cross-validation at each BO iteration as the objective. The best-found hyperparameters were then applied to retrain the models on the training set, and final performance was evaluated on the fixed test set.

In this work, we employSHapleyAdditive exPlanations (SHAP) to interpret ML regression models developed for predicting binding features in a post-hoc manner. SHAP is a game-theoretic framework for explaining ML model outputs, grounded in cooperative game theory and based on Shapley values, which quantify how each input feature influences the deviation of an individual prediction from the expected/average output of the model. Consequently, this method allows for a more transparent interpretation of the learned correlations, highlighting the relative importance of features and how they interact to affect the predicted outcomes. SHAP converts the value of featurejto the SHAP value\(\phi _j\)by considering its margin contribution towards the modelfoutput, and hence the SHAP value of featurejis defined as:

whereSstands for feature subset without featurej,Nis the total feature set, andfis the ML model. This equation defines the SHAP value as the sum of featurej’s marginal contributions across every subsetS, each term weighted by the probability that exactly those features inSappear beforejin all ordering combinations of all features.

In the same context, we also use the intrinsic explainability of decision-tree–based models, which formulate predictions as a nested rule structure. Starting from the root node, the model recursively subdivides the feature space by applying feature-dependent thresholding conditions (e.g., border values in CatBoost), producing a hierarchy of progressively constrained decision subspaces. The partitioning process terminates at leaf nodes, each associated with a fixed prediction value or a set of distributional parameters. The prediction mechanism for any leaf can be explicitly recovered by back-tracking along its unique partition path, yielding an interpretable representation of the model as a piecewise-constant function over disjoint regions of the input space. Therefore, we further analyze two complementary intrinsic metrics of the tree-based models to support and validate the findings obtained through the SHAP method: (1) node splitting frequency and (2) split threshold values. Specifically, we quantify how often each feature is used for node splitting across different tree depths to assess its global importance. In addition, we examine the range of threshold values associated with each feature to better understand how variations in feature values influence the model’s decision-making process and overall importance.

We first analyze two-dimensional (2D) projections of the high-dimensional property space spanned by CPLX systems in MORE-QX. In Fig.1d, we illustrate the property space defined by the work function change (\(\Delta \phi\)) and the dimer interaction energy (\(E_{\text{int}}\)), i.e.,\(\left( \Delta \phi , E_{\text{int}} \right)\). Overall, one can see a lack of correlation between both properties, which indicates a degree of flexibility when searching for dimer conformations with a given pair of\(\left( \Delta \phi , E_{\text{int}} \right)\)values. To understand better the influence of conformational sampling, two example configurations were selected, see rectangles in Fig.1d. In the red rectangle,\(\Delta \phi\)is also uncorrelated with\(E_{\text{int}}\)and displays a large variation in magnitude with respect to the value corresponding to the most stable conformation, from 0.0 to 0.4\(\text{eV}\). This change is also much larger compared to\(E_{\text{int}}\)that only decreases from\(-0.8\)to\(-0.75\)\(\text{eV}\)(i.e.,\(\sim 0.05\,\text{eV}\)). Similarly, in the second set of studied conformations (enclosed by the rectangle blue),\(E_{\text{int}}\)is reduced because the OM molecule is changed by a smaller one, but\(\Delta \phi\)still covers a larger property range (\(\sim 0.25\,\text{eV}\)) This flexibility persists across the entire\(\left( \Delta \phi , E_{\text{int}} \right)\)property space, independent of the chosen DM configuration, underscoring the complexity of inferring binding features from QM properties of DM conformations. Moreover, this result already indicates the challenge in determining simple physical and chemical rules for the simultaneous optimization of properties in the MORE-QX property space (vide infra). Nevertheless, Fig.1d conveys another important message for designing artificial olfactory systems: given a fixed\(E_{\text{int}}\), we might be able to find multiple CPLX systems with a desired\(\Delta \phi\)value within a large range. Inversely, it is also possible to find different DM configurations with a desired\(E_{\text{int}}\)value in a large\(\Delta \phi\)range. These initial observations provide the first evidence of an intrinsic “Freedom of design” in the MORE-QX property space [40], which will be discussed in the context of the binding feature space in the next section (see Fig.2). Additional property distributions representing the effect of conformational sampling can be found in Fig. S1 of the Supplementary Information (SI).

To gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between the QM properties of the building blocks and the resulting binding features (BFs), we examined selected pairwise correlations within the high-dimensional property space spanned by MORE-QX. Specifically, we analyzed correlations between the properties of DM systems and the associated BFs (see the full property list in Table1). DM properties were selected because of their strong involvement in physicochemical effects arising from molecule–surface interactions, such as orbital hybridization, polarization effects, charge density redistribution, and charge transfer, which ultimately influence the binding features [65]. Overall, Fig.2a shows that nearly all of the 45 unique pairwise projections (i.e., 2D correlation plots) resemble structureless “blobs”, indicating that most of these QM properties are effectively uncorrelated. To quantify the degree of correlation, we computed the absolute value of the Spearman correlation coefficient,\(|\rho _s|\)(see Eq.2). The distributions of\(|\rho _s|\)for DM properties and BFs are shown in the upper and lower panels of Fig.2b, respectively, where the pairwise correlations are categorized according to their\(|\rho _s|\)values. Properties are considered strongly correlated if\(|\rho _s| > 0.8\), moderately correlated if\(0.5 < |\rho _s| \le 0.8\), and weakly correlated if\(|\rho _s| \le 0.5\). Accordingly, among the DM properties, 1 out of 21 pairwise correlations (\(\approx 4.8\%\)) is strongly correlated, 4 out of 21 (\(\approx 19\%\)) are moderately correlated, and the remaining 16 (\(\approx 76\%\)) are weakly correlated. In contrast, none of the 24 correlations associated with BFs are strongly correlated; 2 out of 24 (\(\approx 8\%\)) exhibit moderate correlation, while the remaining 22 (\(\approx 92\%\)) are weakly correlated. This comparison demonstrates that correlations are generally weak for both DM properties and BFs, with correlations among BFs being even weaker than those among DM properties. This behavior reflects a more intricate and nontrivial interplay of interatomic interactions in OM–REC–graphene (CPLX) systems compared to single dimers (OM-REC systems).

Among the 2D property spaces analyzed, a few cases of interest exhibit moderate to strong correlations (highlighted by yellow frames in Fig.2a). For example, the HOMO-LUMO gap (\(\epsilon _{\text{gap,DM}}\)) of DM systems shows a more linear correlation with the LUMO energy (\(\epsilon _{\text{L,DM}}\)) than with the HOMO energy (\(\epsilon _{\text{H,DM}}\)). This observation implies that\(\epsilon _{\text{H,DM}}\)can be used to distinguish DM systems with similar\(\epsilon _{\text{gap,DM}}\), which is an important requirement for constructing efficient electronic descriptors. Regarding correlations with BFs, the interaction energy (\(E_{\text{int}}\)) of DM systems and the corresponding adsorption energy (\(E_{\text{ads}}\)) exhibit a strong correlation, with\(|\rho _s| = 0.86\). This result suggests that the interaction mechanism between OM and REC systems can be transferred to CPLX systems to describe trends in\(E_{\text{ads}}\). However, the correlation is not fully linear, indicating that fluctuations arise from geometry and charge-distribution changes induced by surface interactions. Another relevant BF is the adsorbate-induced charge transfer (\(\Delta Q\)), which is commonly interpreted within the orbital-mixing theory that describes the alignment between the substrate Fermi level (the DM system in this work) and the frontier orbital energies of the adsorbate [66]. By computing\(|\rho _s|\)between\(\Delta Q\)and the orbital energies of DM systems, we find that both HOMO and LUMO energies are only weakly correlated with\(\Delta Q\), with\(|\rho _s| = 0.02\)and\(|\rho _s| = 0.11\), respectively. Similarly, orbital energies associated to OM systems are also uncorrelated with\(\Delta Q\), yielding\(|\rho _s| < 0.3\). This lack of correlation reveals the complexity of using orbital energies alone to define design principles for tuning\(\Delta Q\). At the same time, it reflects a certain “freedom of design” within the binding feature space, enabling the identification of DM systems with targeted orbital energies that can serve as components of electronic descriptors for BF prediction (vide infra).

In our correlation analysis with the work function change (\(\Delta \phi\)), we found that the z-component of the dipole moment in the DM (\(\mu _{\text{z,DM}}\)) and OM (\(\mu _{\text{z,OM}}\)) systems shows a moderate correlation with\(\Delta \phi\), with\(|\rho _s| = 0.51\)and\(|\rho _s| = 0.68\), respectively. where the components\(\Delta p_{\text{cplx}}\),\(p_{\text{a}}\), and\(p_{\text{s}} - p_0\)denote the adsorbate-induced surface dipole moment change by spatial charge redistribution, adsorbate dipole moment, and surface deformation, respectively.\(\mu _{\text{z,DM}}\)inherently contains information related to\(\mu _{\text{z,OM}}\), which is tightly associated with the\(p_a\)term and yields a moderate correlation (\(|\rho _s| = 0.51\)). However, other contributions—particularly\(\Delta p_{\text{cplx}}\), which describes spatial charge redistribution—are poorly captured by\(\mu _{\text{z,DM}}\)or by any other DM property e.g., polarizability\(\alpha _\text{S,DM}\), as evidenced by the very low correlation (\(|\rho _s| = 0.07\)between\(\Delta \phi\)and\(\alpha _\text{S,DM}\)). These findings highlight both the intrinsic complexity of\(\Delta \phi\)and the insufficiency of current physicochemical heuristics for tailoring it. While the weak-to-moderate correlations between DM properties and BFs provide some theoretical guidance based on physicochemical intuition, no clear patterns emerge to navigate the binding feature space. Moreover, there is little correlation among the BFs themselves. For example,\(E_\text{ads}\)is only weakly correlated with\(\Delta \phi\)(\(|\rho _s| = 0.14\)). Likewise,\(\Delta Q\)shows a weak correlation with\(E_\text{ads}\)(\(|\rho _s| = 0.05\)) and a moderate correlation with\(\Delta \phi\)(\(|\rho _s| = 0.40\)), the latter arising from spatial charge redistribution upon adsorption [67,69]. Collectively, these observations indicate that only few constraints limit a DM system from simultaneously exhibiting any given pair of DM and BF properties considered in Fig.2a, providing compelling evidence for the existence of a “freedom of design” in the binding feature space. Building on this concept, we also analyzed how the weak correlations among BFs enable the identification of DM conformations tailored to specific target properties (see the SI for details). Consequently, a large number of electronic features may serve as efficient molecular descriptors for BF prediction; however, owing to differences in correlation strength and underlying physicochemical insight, some descriptors are likely to be more relevant than others.

Notice that, even though Boltzmann-weighted properties could in principle be used to construct more accurate ensembles [70], we treat each low-energy dimer conformer equally in order to probe conformer-specific effects and to explore the potential energy surface more comprehensively than a static Boltzmann average would allow. Because the low-energy conformers have similar Boltzmann weights, weighting or direct averaging would obscure subtle inter-conformer differences. Since our primary goal is to examine how BFs vary across individual surface-bound dimers, we therefore do not apply Boltzmann weighting.

Although the lack of correlation among BFs provides a flexibility in designing CPLX systems with desired sensing-related properties, determining the relationship between BFs and electronic properties of molecular building blocks (OM, REC, and DM systems) is still challenging. To address this issue, we have implemented the machine learning (ML) framework MORE-ML (see Fig.3), which aims at establishing a quantitative and explainable mapping between these property spaces by using ML regression techniques and explainable AI methods (see Methods). To identify the most suitable regression models for BF prediction, we benchmark the performance of several tree-based methods: random forest (RF) [71], gradient boosting decision trees (GB), XGBoost (XGB) [72], CatBoost (CAT) [73], and LightGBM (LGBM) [74]. The best-performing models will be subsequently analyzed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) [41], an efficient explainable AI framework well suited to tree-based models. As a training strategy, we prioritized electronic-structure–derived descriptors (\(D_\text{ele}\)), composed of QM properties of OM, REC, and DM systems, owing to their lightweight nature and clear physicochemical interpretability (see Table S3 in the SI). Moreover, inspired by the development of the QUED framework [21], we investigated whether model performance could be further improved by combining\(D_\text{ele}\)with geometrical descriptors\(D_\text{geo}\)(e.g., Bag-of-Bonds [75], SOAP [76], and MACE [77]) and the corresponding Mulliken atomic chargesq(\(D_q\)). However, as shown in Figs. S7 and S8 of the SI, the inclusion of these additional descriptors did not improve the performance of the ML models. This effect may be attributed to the fact that certain electronic features of DM systems already encode relevant geometric information. For example, the dipole moment,\(\mu _\text{DM}\), is the most sensitive to structural variations across different conformations, with changes of up to 80% (see Fig. S12 of the SI). The HOMO–LUMO gap,\(\epsilon _{gap}\), exhibits fluctuations of up to 20%, whereas the HOMO energy,\(\epsilon _{H, DM}\), shows smaller variations of up to 8% across different DM configurations. Consequently, explicit geometric descriptors provide limited additional predictive value, as geometry-dependent information is already implicitly captured by the electronic descriptors. Regarding the\(D_q\)descriptor, its limited predictive power may stem from the accuracy of Mulliken charges. However, addressing this limitation would require adopting more robust charge partitioning schemes (e.g., CM5 or Hirshfeld) implemented in alternative DFT packages, or developing dedicated ML models for charge prediction, which is beyond the scope of the present work. Accordingly, we performed a more in-depth analysis of ML model accuracy using only\(D_\text{ele}\).

Fig.4a shows the coefficient of determination (\(R^2\)) and mean absolute error (MAE) for predicting the adsorption energy,\(E_{\text{ads}}\), using the full\(D_\text{ele}\)descriptor (130 features). The MORE-QX dataset was partitioned into training (TR) and test (TE) sets using a fixed 9:1 ratio. Additional details on the dataset splitting procedure and the selection of training samples are provided in the Methods section. By comparing the results obtained for\(E_{\text{ads}}\)with those corresponding to other binding features (see Fig. S7 in the SI), we find that all benchmarked methods exhibit similar performance trends across features. Consequently,\(E_{\text{ads}}\)is used here as a representative case. Among the tree-based methods, RF performs the worst in the TE set, yielding an\(R^2\)of 0.818 and an MAE of 0.062 eV. This suggests that gradient-boosting approaches outperform RF’s bagging strategy in capturing latent correlations between\(D_\text{ele}\)and the binding features. A likely explanation is that, in boosting, each successive tree corrects the residuals of its predecessor, whereas RF relies on an ensemble of independent trees. Within the gradient-boosting family, CAT achieves the best performance, with an\(R^2\)of 0.86 and an MAE of 0.058 eV. This advantage likely arises from the use of oblivious (symmetric) trees, in which all nodes at a given depth split on the same feature. Such a structure imposes strong regularization on tree complexity, thereby improving generalization in binding feature prediction. As a result, we adopt CAT as the final ML regression model for subsequent analyses.

Then, we focus on selecting the most informative subset of QM properties within\(D_\text{ele}\)to mitigate high dimensionality and reduce model noise. By identifying and removing redundant and highly correlated features, we aim to prevent overfitting and improve the generalizability of the ML model. To this end, we employed an iterative SHAP-driven feature selection procedure using the CAT models. At each iteration, the model is retrained with a reduced subset of the full\(D_\text{ele}\), consisting of the top-ranked features according to SHAP importance. The number of selected features was gradually increased from 5 to 105 in increments of 5, and model performance was evaluated at each stage. The resulting learning curves for the\(R^2\)and MAE metrics are shown in Fig.4b. Based on the results for the TR and TE sets, the feature learning behavior can be divided into growing and saturated regimes. In the small-\(D_\text{ele}\)regime, performance improves gradually but remains inferior to that achieved with the full descriptor set (see dashed lines), indicating that an insufficient number of QM properties is available to accurately capture the adsorption mechanism. Once the size of\(D_\text{ele}\)exceeds a critical threshold, the performance curves begin to plateau: the TE scores no longer improve, while the TR scores show only minor fluctuations. This behavior indicates that additional features do not further enhance the model’s understanding of the adsorption mechanism, suggesting the existence of an optimal QM subset that balances accuracy and efficiency. Based on this exhaustive analysis, we selected the top 50 electronic features (star-labeled) as the effective descriptor set for\(E_{\text{ads}}\). Using the same procedure, the top 60 and top 80 features were selected for\(\Delta \phi\)and\(\Delta Q\), respectively (see Fig. S7 in the SI).

Indeed, the final ML regression models for predicting\(E_\text{ads}\),\(\Delta \phi\)and\(\Delta Q\)were developed using the optimized subset of QM features and CAT method (see Fig.5). To assess their overall learning capability, we first examine the\(\mathrm R^2\)metric, which quantifies the variance between DFT-calculated and ML-predicted values. For TR set,\(\mathrm R^2\)reaches 0.99 for both\(E_\text{ads}\)and\(\Delta Q\), whereas a slightly lower value of 0.93 is obtained for\(\Delta \phi\). This difference is reflected in the larger dispersion of the orange data points around the\(y=x\)reference line (dashed). Considering the MAE metric, the corresponding values for TR set of\(E_\text{ads}\)and\(\Delta Q\)are\(0.017\,\mathrm eV\), and\(0.001\,\mathrm e\), respectively, while\(\Delta \phi\)exhibits a higher MAE of\(0.026\,\mathrm eV\). Given the discrete nature of the binding feature space and the limited coverage of MORE-QX dataset, we further evaluate model performance using the relative error\(\epsilon = \dfrac{|y_\text{ML} -y_\text{DFT}|}{\Delta y}\times 100\)with\(y_\text{ML}\)and\(y_\text{DFT}\)as the ML and DFT values of the propertyy.\(\Delta y\)represents the extent of the property spectrum across the entire dataset. The resulting relative errors for\(E_\text{ads}\),\(\Delta \phi\)and\(\Delta Q\)are\(1.7\%\),\(2.6\%\)and\(1\%\), respectively. These small values indicate that the models accurately reproduce the training data.

We next examine the generalization capability of the ML models by evaluating their performance on unseen systems considered in the TE set. As expected, model accuracy decreases relative to the TR set, yielding\(\mathrm R^2\)values of 0.86, 0.76, and 0.81 for\(E_\text{ads}\),\(\Delta \phi\), and\(\Delta Q\), respectively. The relative errors also increases, but remain below\(6\%\):\(5.4\%\)for\(E_\text{ads}\),\(4.8\%\)for\(\Delta \phi\), and\(5.6\%\)for\(\Delta Q\). The moderate performance gap between the TR and TE sets indicates that the models retain high predictive accuracy for novel systems, underscoring their potential to generalize across a much larger configuration and conformational space. This conclusion is further supported by the close agreement between the distributions of predicted binding features for the TR and TE sets (see right panels in Figs.5a–c). The complete set of evaluation metrics for each model is summarized in Table S6. To elucidate the slightly reduced accuracy of the model predicting\(\Delta \phi\), we separately predicted\(\phi\)values for both the complex (\(\phi _\text{CPLX}\)) and the substrate (\(\phi _\text{SUB}\)) systems using the same TR and TE sets. As shown in Fig. S10, the predictions for\(\phi _\text{CPLX}\)yield\(\mathrm R^2 = 0.87\)and\(\text{MAE} = 0.045\, \mathrm eV\); while those for\(\phi _\text{SUB}\)achieve\(\mathrm R^2 = 0.89\)and\(\text{MAE} = 0.029\, \mathrm eV\). Despite these favorable metrics, the parity plot for\(\phi _\text{SUB}\)exhibits an unexpected zigzag pattern in both the TR and TE sets, and the model fails to reproduce the bimodal distribution of\(\phi _\text{SUB}\). This shortcoming likely stems from the limited diversity of\(\phi _\text{SUB}\)values in the dataset: the QM descriptors of the building blocks, particularly those derived from the 18 REC structures, are insufficient to capture the subtle conformational variations that govern\(\phi _\text{SUB}\). Consequently, noise is introduced into the prediction of\(\phi _\text{SUB}\), even though\(\phi _\text{CPLX}\)is modeled accurately.

To better interpret the tree-based ML models developed for BF prediction, we performed an explainability analysis using both their intrinsic interpretability and SHAP method (see Methods). The beeswarm plots in Figs.5d–f summarize the distribution of SHAP values for the most influential features in each prediction task. In these plots, features are ranked by importance from top to bottom, and their corresponding SHAP values are shown along thex-axis. Positive SHAP values indicate that a feature increases the predicted outcome, whereas negative values indicate a decrease. The color gradient encodes the feature magnitude, with red representing high values and blue representing low values.

The SHAP value distribution in Fig.5d clearly shows that the dimer (DM) interaction energy,\(E_\text{int}\), plays the most dominant role in determining\(E_\text{ads}\). The color gradient indicates that smaller\(E_\text{int}\)values lead to smaller\(E_\text{ads}\)values and vice versa, since both quantities are negatives. This strong coupling between\(E_\text{int}\)and its SHAP value is reflected in the high Spearman correlation coefficient,\(|\rho _s| = 0.86\), indicating that\(E_\text{int}\)serves as an effective descriptor for\(E_\text{ads}\)on the graphene surface. Although\(E_\text{int}\)contains the majority of the predictive information for\(E_\text{ads}\), the model still needs to account for a small residual difference between these two energetics to achieve higher accuracy. This difference is captured by morphological descriptors, such as the components of the inertia tensor (I) of the DM systems and the radius of gyration (\(R_g\)) of the OM system, highlighting that molecular structure also plays a critical role. Furthermore, the dipole moments (\(\mu\)) of OM and REC systems rank among the top ten features, indicating that charge redistribution is relevant for describing non-covalent interactions during adsorption. The SHAP values of these additional features are distributed much more narrowly than those of\(E_\text{int}\), which explains their lower overall importance. Consequently, these features-together with the remaining descriptors, primarily act as fine-tuning factors, capturing a small number of outliers and subtle corrections compared to the dominant contribution of\(E_\text{int}\).
