A similar trend can be observed in the SHAP analysis for predicting\(\Delta Q\)(see Fig.5f). In contrast to the morphology-correlated binding feature\(E_\text{ads}\),\(\Delta Q\)is primarily correlated with charge-related properties. In particular, the dipole and quadrupole moments emerge as the most relevant features, whereas molecular orbital energies appear lower in the ranking; e.g.,\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm OM}\)and\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm REC}\)occupy the\(4^\text{th}\)and\(6^\text{th}\)positions, respectively. This indicates that several properties contribute synergistically to the prediction of\(\Delta Q\), with no single dominant feature. Moreover, the SHAP analysis highlights the limited capability of a purely qualitative orbital-mixing description of charge transfer [66], as the frontier orbital energies are not among the dominant predictors. Unlike\(E_\text{ads}\)and\(\Delta Q\), the prediction of\(\Delta \phi\)is governed by two dominant features: the vertical dipole moment of the OM,\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\), and the HOMO energy of the DM system,\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\), which exhibit a wide distribution in Fig.5e. The importance of\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\)is readily explained by Eq.10, since it directly contributes to the total change in the surface dipole moment. Interestingly, the SHAP distribution of\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm OM}\)(ranked\(5^\text{th}\)) shows a trend similar to that of\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\), which is the second most important feature. A qualitative explanation for the high ranking of frontier orbital energies (HOMO/LUMO) is that\(\Delta \phi\)partially originates from spatial charge redistribution. In this context, the HOMO and LUMO energies represent the primary donor and acceptor orbitals, respectively, thereby inducing charge-density changes on and near the associated atoms.

To gain further physical insight into the prediction of\(\Delta \phi\), we first analyzed the Spearman correlation coefficient,\(|\rho _s|\), between the top 10 QM features and\(\Delta \phi\)(see Fig.6a). Among these features, only a few properties exhibit clear correlations. For example,\(\mu _{z,\text{OM}}\)and\(\mu _{z,\text{DM}}\)are strongly correlated, as\(\mu _{z,\text{DM}}\)contains information from\(\mu _{z,\text{OM}}\). These features are also correlated with\(\Delta \phi\)because they partially enter Eq.10. In contrast, the majority of the top 10 features show weak correlations (\(|\rho _s| < 0.05\)), indicating that SHAP-based feature ranking effectively mitigates multicollinearity among the QM descriptors. This procedure filters out highly correlated and thus noisy features, ultimately leading to improved generalization by leveraging a diverse set of non-redundant descriptors. Moreover, the counterpart\(\epsilon _{\text{L,DM}}\)of\(\epsilon _{\text{H,DM}}\)does not appear among the top 10 features, whereas\(\epsilon _{\text{H,DM}}\)ranks second. This suggests that the surface Fermi level predominantly interacts with\(\epsilon _{\text{H,DM}}\), consistent with orbital mixing theory [66]. Consequently,\(\epsilon _{\text{H,DM}}\)tends to align with the surface Fermi level, and the resulting Fermi level of the complex system,\(E_{\text{f,CPLX}}\), is more strongly associated with\(\epsilon _{\text{H,DM}}\)than with\(\epsilon _{\text{L,DM}}\), with\(\rho _s = 0.8\)and\(\rho _s = -0.35\), respectively (see Fig.6b). To further investigate the synergistic mechanisms of the most important QM features, e.g.,\(u_{z,\mathrm OM}\)and\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\), in tuning\(\Delta \phi\), we analyze their contribution behavior by correlating SHAP values with property distributions (see Fig.6(c)). In the left panel, the SHAP values of\(\mu _\mathrm{z,\mathrm OM}\)exhibit a clear linear correlation with the feature itself: negative\(\mu _\mathrm{z,\mathrm OM}\)values yield positive contributions to\(\Delta \phi\), and vice versa, with the sign determined by the direction of the surface dipole moment. In general, larger absolute values of\(\mu _\mathrm{z,\mathrm OM}\)lead to stronger contributions to\(\Delta \phi\), consistent with its\(\rho _s\)value. In contrast, the SHAP values of\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\)in the right panel remain nearly constant as\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\)increases from its minimum up to approximately\(-5.25\,\mathrm eV\). Beyond this turning point, a linear correlation between SHAP values and\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\)emerges as the feature value increases further.

These behaviors can be understood through the intrinsic interpretability of tree-based models. Owing to the hierarchical splitting process, features used at shallower tree depths acquire greater importance than those applied deeper in the tree, since early splits typically yield larger information gains by partitioning a larger fraction of the dataset. As shown in Fig.6d, we quantify the frequency with which\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\),\(\epsilon _\text{H, DM}\)and\(\epsilon _\text{H, REC}\)(ranked\(4^\text{th}\)in Fig.5) participate in splits at each tree depth. At the first tree level, the bars corresponding to\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\)and\(\epsilon _\text{H, DM}\)are markedly higher than that of\(\epsilon _\text{H, REC}\), with\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\)also significantly exceeding\(\epsilon _\text{H, DM}\). At greater depths,\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\)and\(\epsilon _\text{H, DM}\)continue to participate frequently in splits, albeit with reduced information gain due to the smaller number of remaining data points. Notably,\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\)slightly surpasses\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\)in splitting frequency at deeper levels, corresponding to splits that isolate a small number of exceptional outliers. This compensates for the stronger early contribution of\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\), resulting in comparable total SHAP contributions for the two features, as reflected in the importance ranking in Fig.5. Overall, these observations confirm the dominant and widespread importance of\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\)and\(\epsilon _\text{H, DM}\), with\(\mu _{z,\mathrm OM}\)retaining a slightly higher overall ranking. The shorter bar heights of\(\epsilon _\text{H,REC}\)are also consistent with its narrowly distributed SHAP values and, consequently, its lower importance. Moreovero, the turning point at\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM} \approx -5.25\,\mathrm eV\)can be illustrated by the participation of the property values (corresponding to decision borders in tree-based models) at the splitting nodes (see Fig.6e). The number of borders with values\(> -5.25 \, \mathrm eV\)is significantly higher than those\(\le -5.25 \, \mathrm eV\), indicating that the values above this threshold appear more frequently in the split decisions. In this regime, the property values are more continuous and lead to a broader range of contribution values, whereas borders\(\le -5.25 \, \mathrm eV\)participate much less frequently in the splitting process. Indeed, the cumulative information gain from borders\(\le -5.25 \, \mathrm eV\)results in only minor contributions, fluctuating between 0 and\(0.1\, \mathrm eV\)to\(\Delta \phi\). Contrarily, border\(> -5.25 \, \mathrm eV\)yield large contribution with a broad distribution, consistent with the threshold effect shown in the left panel of Fig.6c. This behavior can be attributed to the energetic alignment between the molecular frontier orbitals and the surface Fermi level in the CPLX system. In particular,\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\)plays a critical role, as evidenced by its stronger correlation with\(E_\text{f,CPLX}\)(see Fig.6b). We therefore hypothesize that when\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\)lies well below the surface Fermi level, the HOMO is energetically inaccessible and induces negligible charge redistribution at the surface, resulting in a minimal impact on work-function modulation. Conversely, when\(\epsilon _\mathrm{H,\mathrm DM}\)exceeds the surface Fermi level, substantial charge redistribution can occur, and\(\Delta \phi\)is governed by the energetic separation between the HOMO and the surface Fermi level. Finally, this threshold effect may also be influenced by the spatial localization of the frontier orbitals on the molecule [78], which affects their coupling to the surface.

In the present work, we have introduced MORE-ML, a computational framework that integrates quantum-mechanical (QM) property data of electronic-nose molecular building blocks with machine-learning (ML) methods to predict and interpret the physicochemical mechanisms governing sensing-related properties. This challenging task is addressed by expanding our previously generated MORE-Q dataset into MORE-QX, which spans a significantly larger conformational and property space for interacting systems composed of combinations of body-odor volatilomes (BOVs) and mucin-derived receptors (REC). Based on MORE-QX, we construct a set of binding features (BFs) by computing the adsorption energy (\(E_\text{ads}\)), work-function change (\(\Delta \phi\)), and charge transfer (\(\Delta Q\)). These quantities quantify the impact of BOV–REC interactions on the energy, work function (\(\phi\)), and charge distribution of the REC–graphene systems. Analysis of the property space spanned by MORE-QX reveals clear evidence of “Freedom of design” in the BF space, i.e., the ability to identify chemically diverse OM–REC–graphene (CPLX) conformations that exhibit a targeted set of BFs. This flexibility arises from the weak correlations observed among most QM properties. Furthermore, property–property correlation analysis highlights the potential of several electronic features to discriminate between similar DM and CPLX conformations, a key requirement for constructing efficient molecular descriptors. Most electronic features included in MORE-QX are invariant with respect to translations, rotations, and atom permutations, thereby satisfying a central requirement for a complete molecular representation suitable for ML-based predictive modeling.

Leveraging these insights within the MORE-ML framework, we define deterministic mappings between the electronic features of molecular building blocks (e.g., OM, REC, and DM systems) and the BFs. These mappings are designed to reduce the computational cost of determining sensing-related properties, as computing QM properties for individual building blocks is significantly less expensive than direct BF calculations. To this end, we performed feature engineering and benchmarked multiple ML regression techniques to identify the optimal set of electronic features for developing accurate and reliable regression models for each BF. In contrast to previous ML studies that primarily emphasize predictive performance, we place strong emphasis on model explainability by combining the intrinsic interpretability of tree-based models with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. Indeed, we find that\(E_\text{ads}\)is largely governed by the interaction energy between the OM and REC systems, whereas\(\Delta Q\)is primarily influenced by charge-related properties, such as dipole and quadrupole moments. In the case of\(\Delta \phi\), an interplay emerges between the vertical dipole moment of OM and the HOMO energy of the DM system, reflecting the physical mechanisms underlying the determination of the work function\(\phi\). This in-depth investigation reveals the key physicochemical factors governing each BF and thereby establishes a more transparent and navigable pathway through the largely unexplored binding feature space.

From the e-nose sensing materials design perspective, the demonstrated “Freedom of design” in the binding feature space is particularly valuable, as it suggests that sensor sensitivity, baseline stability, and selectivity can be tuned semi-independently through receptor engineering rather than relying on trial-and-error material screening. The finding that adsorption energy, charge transfer, and work function modulation are governed by distinct and weakly correlated electronic descriptors aligns well with practical observations in sensor arrays, where signal amplitude, recovery behavior, and device-to-device variability often decouple. Importantly, the interpretability of the MORE-ML framework provides experimentally actionable guidelines for selecting or synthesizing receptor molecules that target specific transduction mechanisms, thereby reducing empirical optimization cycles. The accuracy and interpretability of our ML models could be further improved by adopting\(\Delta\)-ML strategies for predicting BFs, as has been successfully demonstrated for other relevant physicochemical properties of complex molecular systems [79,80,81]. In principle, two possible\(\Delta\)-ML strategies could be considered for developing a robust baseline model. First, a linear relationship could be established between the most relevant descriptors, identified through SHAP analysis, and the BFs. Second, a mathematical expression involving these descriptors could be constructed using the sure independence screening and sparsifying operator (SISSO) method [82].

Based on the findings presented in this work, we successfully demonstrate a sustainable AI-based framework that reveals multiple sensing mechanisms from a computational perspective [31]. Although MORE-QX is limited to sensing-related properties on graphene surfaces, this comprehensive analysis elucidates the fundamental mechanisms controlling BFs—properties that are strongly linked to sensing performance—through the manipulation of DM properties. However, to extend the applicability and improve the reliability of our regression models to other relevant 2D sensing material substrates, such as two-dimensional MXenes [83,84] and transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) [85,86], electronic features describing receptor–substrate interactions must be incorporated into the MORE-ML framework. These augmented descriptors may provide a more appropriate mapping between the property space of e-nose molecular building blocks and the binding-feature space. This, in turn, enables the definition of novel design principles for high-performance, sensitive, and selective molecular receptors, which can subsequently be validated using generative AI approaches or experimental measurements. We note that achieving a full understanding of sensing mechanisms in electronic-nose devices also requires investigating the contact potential between the electrode and the sensing surface (i.e., the Schottky barrier effect [27]), as it may play a dominant role in sensing performance. Therefore, we expect this work to motivate future research aimed at advancing sensing materials by leveraging physical and chemical insights together with deterministic property mappings enabled by the integration of quantum science and interpretable ML regression models.

All datasets, source code, running examples, and trained ML models presented in this work are available in the MORE-Q GitHub repository (https://github.com/LiC1117/MORE-Q) and are also publicly available on Zenodo under the DOIhttps://zenodo.org/records/14720508.

title: Efficient fine-tuning of vision-language adapters in chemical VLMs for molecular image-text tasks
author: Hyukjun Choi; Donghyeon Lee; Juyoung Kang
text:
Vision–language models (VLMs) have recently shown strong potential for multimodal scientific applications, yet their direct application to molecular structure images remains challenging due to the need for precise visual–textual alignment. In this study, we investigate efficient fine-tuning strategies for adapting a large-scale VLM to molecular image captioning tasks. Our approach is built upon the Qwen3.5—9B architecture and focuses on lightweight parameter-efficient adaptation.

Specifically, we apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to the language-side MLP layers and explore selective tuning of the visual merger module that bridges the vision encoder and the language model. This module compresses visual features and projects them into the language embedding space, making it a critical component for cross-modal alignment. Experimental results on molecular image captioning tasks show that the combined L-MLP + Visual Merger tuning strategy achieves the best performance while maintaining low computational overhead.

In addition, we evaluate multiple decoding strategies, including greedy decoding and stochastic sampling methods, to identify the most suitable inference configuration for molecular image captioning. The results demonstrate that selective fine-tuning of the visual–language interface significantly improves caption accuracy while preserving efficiency. These findings highlight the importance of adapting cross-modal projection modules when deploying general-purpose VLMs in specialized scientific domains such as cheminformatics.

Scientific contribution

We provide a systematic analysis of layer-wise fine-tuning strategies in large-scale vision–language models(VLMs), identifying which components are most critical for adapting general-purpose models to molecular image captioning tasks.

We identify the cross-modal projection module (visual merger) as a key factor in visual–textual alignment, demonstrating that its selective adaptation plays a central role in improving caption quality.

We propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy that combines light weight language-side adaptation with targeted tuning of the visual–language interface, achieving an effective balance between performance and computational cost.

We provide practical insights into efficient adaptation of VLMs in scientific domains, highlighting key considerations for achieving performance under computational constraints.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a wide range of tasks, including those within scientific domains such as biology, medicine, and chemistry. Artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning have emerged as powerful tools in molecular science, enhancing the speed, accuracy, and scalability of molecular discovery and understanding. Among these, models like MolT5 support text-based molecular generation and captioning, helping researchers describe molecules in natural language or generate molecular structures from text [1]. However, despite such progress, most studies applying LLMs to chemistry, including property prediction, retrosynthesis, and molecule captioning, have relied on general-purpose models and remained limited to isolated case studies without extensive domain adaptation [2]. Recent research has begun to incorporate visual modalities, particularly molecular structure images, into multimodal models. For example, ChemVLM combines a 6B image encoder with a 20B chemical language model and applies Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) based fine-tuning to improve molecular captioning performance [3]. However, such large-scale models often require significant computational resources, limiting their practical deployment in resource-constrained environments.

Existing pipelines for converting images to chemical structures, such as Image2SMILES and MolNexTR, focus primarily on format conversion (pixels to structural representations or strings). These methods often fall short in providing human-interpretable, contextual, and explanatory information, such as a molecule's meaning, purpose, or notable features [4,5]. In contrast, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) combine image and text modalities to generate natural language captions, creating explanations that are directly useful to humans.

To enable meaningful text–structure associations in the chemical domain, a clear understanding of chemical representations is essential. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) has established a systematic nomenclature based on the structure and substructures of chemical compounds, enabling consistent and interpretable naming across the scientific community [6]. In parallel, the Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) has become a widely adopted standard format in cheminformatics and molecular datasets. SMILES encodes molecular structures as text strings using grammatical rules to represent atoms and bonds, allowing straightforward generation from 2D chemical graphs. Unlike coordinate-based representations, SMILES offers a compact and flexible alternative for representing molecular systems and is extensively used in machine learning applications such as de novo drug design, data augmentation, and structural fingerprinting [7].

Despite these promising advances, fine-tuning vision-language models such as CLIP poses challenges, particularly the risk of catastrophic forgetting, which can degrade zero-shot performance and multimodal alignment [8]. Indiscriminate fine-tuning may cause the model to lose valuable pre-trained knowledge, underscoring the necessity for selective fine-tuning strategies. By updating only a subset of critical layers, these strategies strive to balance effective domain adaptation with preservation of prior knowledge.

Numerous fine-tuning strategies have been proposed in prior research, necessitating careful selection to achieve optimal performance. As pre-trained language models scale up, fine-tuning all parameters becomes prohibitively expensive and practically infeasible [9]. Furthermore, inappropriate selection of fine-tuning strategies may degrade zero-shot performance on unseen tasks [10] and incur unnecessary computational overhead. Moreover, growing environmental concerns regarding the energy demands of AI training, combined with the scarcity of domain-specific chemical datasets, underscore the importance of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for the sustainable adaptation of vision-language models (VLMs) to specialized scientific domains [11]. Accordingly, the AI research community increasingly advocates for sustainable AI practices, with an emphasis on both efficiency and scalability [12]. The increasing demand for lightweight and domain-specialized models has highlighted the importance of fine-tuning strategies that are both memory-efficient and performance-effective, enabling cost-efficient deployment and faster inference in constrained environments. In the chemistry domain specifically, compact and specialized models can help overcome the limitations of general-purpose models, such as linguistic inaccuracies and a lack of domain-specific knowledge [13]. Therefore, fine-tuning methods must be not only accurate but also modular, cost-effective, and deployable on limited computational infrastructure.

LayerNorm stabilizes and accelerates training by normalizing intermediate representations within each layer, improving generalization and robustness across tasks [14]. Recent findings show that output LayerNorm parameters change more than any other component during fine-tuning and that tuning only LayerNorm can achieve comparable—or even superior—performance to full fine-tuning or other parameter-efficient strategies [15].

While existing work like ChemVLM has explored LoRA-based fine-tuning on large-scale models, there remains a need to investigate alternative parameter-efficient approaches and their effectiveness on smaller, more deployable models. Specifically, examining how selective fine-tuning of key components such as visual merger and LayerNorm can enhance performance in chemical tasks while maintaining computational efficiency represents an underexplored research direction in the chemistry domain.

To overcome these challenges, we present a fine-tuning approach for VLMs specifically adapted for chemical tasks. By leveraging both molecular structure images and their corresponding textual descriptions, our method aims to enhance the model's ability to interpret, reason, and generate domain-specific chemical knowledge. Specifically, we focus on tasks such as predicting the IUPAC name and generating the SMILES representation from a given molecular structure image. This approach not only expands the capabilities of multimodal LLMs within scientific applications but also offers practical insights into how such models can support chemists in tasks that require integration of visual and textual information. Moreover, generative AI has shown promising potential in science and chemistry education by enabling personalized learning and providing immediate feedback, thereby enhancing students' understanding and problem-solving skills [16,17,18,19,20].

To address these limitations, we present a specialized approach for fine-tuning Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in the chemistry domain. Our key contributions are as follows:

Efficient fine-tuning strategy for chemical VLMs: We propose a domain-specific fine-tuning method that selectively updates key components (e.g., visual merger and LayerNorm) to achieve high performance with reduced computational cost, enabling practical adaptation of VLMs for chemistry-related tasks.

Generative AI-assisted data pipeline: We develop a workflow that leverages generative AI to automate dataset construction and evaluation, facilitating scalable training and assessment of multimodal models specialized in chemical understanding.

We developed a small model capable of natural language and image-based chemical captioning, usable for educational and research support.

In this section, building on recent deep learning approaches for chemical structure recognition, we discuss efficient fine-tuning strategies for language models, focusing on strategies for selecting parameters to optimize memory efficiency during the tuning process, as well as methods to enhance generalization performance.

Recent developments in general image recognition have shifted toward efficient one-stage Transformer architectures. For instance, the Low-Rank Spatial Channel Transformer (LrSC-T) introduces a novel attention mechanism that combines cosine similarity and bilinear outer product projections. This approach effectively captures higher-order feature interactions by utilizing features directly from a pre-trained Swin Transformer, eliminating the need for separate region-based processing [21]. However, such models primarily optimized for general objects may not be fully suitable for specialized domains like molecular image recognition that require precise structural interpretation.

Another significant advancement is the Cross-Modal Spatial-Channel (CM-SC) attention network, which addresses the limitations of conventional first-order attention by capturing higher-order interactions across different modalities. By utilizing a flexible variant of cross-variance, the CM-SC mechanism effectively models intricate spatial and channel-wise relationships between visual and textual information without increasing the parameter count. This approach has demonstrated a 20.74% reduction in average computation time while maintaining competitive performance on standard datasets like MSCOCO and Flickr30K [22]. Despite these improvements in cross-modal efficiency, such models are primarily optimized for general-purpose captioning and may not fully account for the specific structural constraints and naming conventions inherent in chemical informatics.

Furthermore, the Geometric Information-driven Network (IGINet) enhances image captioning by incorporating spatial and positional relationships among visual objects through a novel attention mechanism called GeoAtt. By utilizing low-rank bilinear pooling, GeoAtt enables more effective multimodal reasoning and selectively harnesses visual features to capture intricate inter-modal interactions. A key contribution of IGINet is the integration of normalized geometric features directly into the attention mechanism, allowing the model to focus on the most relevant image regions [23]. While this approach achieved a state-of-the-art BLEU-4 score of 39.9 on the MSCOCO benchmark, its focus on geometric and positional relationships in general scenes may not directly translate to the specialized structural and hierarchical naming logic required for molecular informatics.

The extraction of chemical formulas from images has long posed significant challenges due to the diverse graphical representations of molecules, shifting the problem from simple classification to complex formula generation [24]. Recent studies in chemical structure recognition have employed various deep learning techniques with notable success. One approach utilizes a Visual geometry group-based segmentation model to accurately detect chemical structure regions within images, achieving a segmentation accuracy of 99.8%. This crucial step isolates relevant chemical diagrams from complex backgrounds [25]. Another prominent method, DECIMER 1.0, combines convolutional neural networks (InceptionV3 or EfficientNet-B3) as image encoders with a Transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture. It outputs molecular representations in the SELFIES format, enhancing chemical validity and achieving an average Tanimoto similarity of 85.38% between predicted and true molecular structures [26].

Expanding on these methods, other research has focused on improving the robustness of models to different image qualities and graphical styles. For example, a study on Atom-Level Optical Chemical Structure Recognition proposes reframing the task as an object detection problem, first identifying individual atoms and bonds, and then reconstructing the full molecular graph [27]. This approach addresses a key limitation of sequence-to-sequence models, which can sometimes produce invalid or chemically implausible outputs, by directly generating a graph representation that is inherently more structured and chemically sound. In a similar vein, Chemception adapts the Inception architecture, a widely used convolutional neural network, for the specific task of recognizing chemical structures [28]. By pre-training the model on a large dataset of chemical images and then fine-tuning it, Chemception achieves high accuracy, particularly in identifying common substructures and functional groups, which are critical for accurate formula generation. More recently, the MolScribe model has been introduced as an image-to-graph model that directly predicts a molecular graph from an image [29]. These diverse approaches reflect the vibrant and ongoing research in applying deep learning to chemical structure recognition.

When training a Vision-Language model with a small amount of data, overfitting can occur. One of the representative approaches to mitigate this issue is data augmentation. By artificially expanding visual data through various methods such as image rotation, translation, and blur processing, the model's generalization ability can be improved [30]. Several prior studies have reported that these image data augmentation techniques increase visual diversity and enhance image classification performance [31,32,33].

High-quality, large-scale datasets are a critical component in the development of powerful natural language processing (NLP) models. However, collecting such datasets through manual annotation is often costly, labor-intensive, and constrained by issues such as data scarcity and privacy concerns. Moreover, human-generated data can introduce biases and inconsistencies, potentially undermining the robustness and fairness of the resulting models.

To overcome these limitations, synthetic data generated by large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising alternative. LLMs, trained on vast corpora, possess strong language understanding capabilities and can follow instructions with high fidelity, allowing for flexible and targeted data generation. As a result, LLM-generated synthetic data is increasingly being regarded as a reliable resource for training and fine-tuning NLP models [34].

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of multimodal data augmentation approaches that leverage large language models for generating synthetic training data across image, text, and speech modalities. This multi-step process is designed to significantly enhance machine learning models by diversifying training datasets, particularly in scenarios where data scarcity is a limiting factor [35]. The integration of LLMs in data augmentation has shown promising results in healthcare applications, including patient-trial matching and privacy-preserving synthetic data generation, though challenges remain in balancing data quality with privacy constraints [36].

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that introduces trainable low-rank matrices into the weights of pre-trained models while keeping the original weights frozen. Instead of updating full weight matrices, LoRA decomposes the weight update into two smaller matrices, significantly reducing trainable parameters and memory usage. This approach enables efficient adaptation without compromising performance and incurs no additional inference latency, making it particularly suitable for fine-tuning large-scale models such as GPT-3 [37].

Recent studies on visual Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) have focused on reducing the number of trainable parameters by freezing most of the pre-trained model while adapting it to downstream tasks. To address the limitations of heuristic-based parameter allocation, a sensitivity-aware approach, SPT (Sensitivity-aware visual Parameter-efficient fine-Tuning), was introduced. SPT identifies task-specific sensitive parameters in a data-driven manner and selectively applies structured tuning methods such as LoRA or Adapters when sensitivity exceeds a predefined threshold. Experimental results demonstrate that SPT significantly improves the performance of existing PEFT techniques, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like FGVC and VTAB-1 k [38].

CLIPFit is another parameter-efficient tuning method designed for vision-language models. It updates only the bias terms in the projection layers of the text encoder and the LayerNorm components of the image encoder in CLIP. Unlike prompt tuning or adapter-based methods, CLIPFit introduces no external parameters. Experiments conducted on 11 benchmark datasets confirm its effectiveness, supported by analyses of internal parameter changes and representation shifts [39].

Finally, partial fine-tuning strategies focusing on the later layers of Vision Transformers (ViTs) have shown superior performance compared to tuning earlier layers. Specifically, fine-tuning the MLP and attention modules in the later stages was more effective than modifying those in the initial layers. These observations suggest that the depth of layer selection plays a critical role in the efficiency and effectiveness of fine-tuning [40]. To evaluate the quality of the generated molecular captions, we employ both traditional automatic metrics and LLM-based evaluation methods. Among the commonly used automatic metrics for text generation tasks, BLEU and ROUGE measure the similarity between generated text and reference descriptions by comparing n-gram overlaps. BLEU evaluates the precision of n-gram matches between generated outputs and reference texts, while ROUGE focuses on recall-oriented overlap and is widely used in summarization and captioning tasks.

In addition to these traditional metrics, recent studies have increasingly explored the use of large language models (LLMs) as evaluators of generated outputs. In this paradigm, often referred to asLLM-as-judge, powerful LLMs are used to assess the quality of generated text by providing scores or qualitative judgments. For example, G-Eval employs GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 with chain-of-thought prompting to evaluate outputs in tasks such as summarization and dialogue generation [41]. Similarly, GEMBA introduces a GPT-based evaluation framework for machine translation quality assessment using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 [41].

LLM-based evaluation approaches have also begun to appear in scientific and technical domains. Recent work proposes combining human feedback with LLM-generated judgments through a control-variate framework, enabling efficient and scalable evaluation while maintaining consistency with human ratings [42]. Motivated by these developments, our study adopts an LLM-based evaluation framework alongside traditional metrics to comprehensively assess the quality of generated captions in the molecular image captioning task.

In this section, we describe the comprehensive research pipeline, encompassing the systematic construction of a chemical dataset, the fine-tuning process of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), and our dual-task evaluation framework. The overall workflow is designed to enhance the model's capability in both basic molecular identification and the interpretation of complex chemical naming principles. Sects. "Model Architecture" to "Fine-tuning Configurations" describe the model architecture, dataset preparation, data augmentation, decoding strategies, and fine-tuning configurations in detail. An example of model inference

Our model is built upon the Qwen3.5—9B architecture. The framework consists of a vision encoder, a vision–language merger, and a large language model (LLM). The vision encoder extracts visual representations from the input molecular structure images, while the vision–language merger projects the visual features into the hidden embedding space of the language model. Specifically, the merger compresses spatial visual features in a 2 × 2 grouping and maps them into visual tokens aligned with the LLM’s hidden dimension through a two-layer MLP. These visual tokens are then processed by the language model to generate textual descriptions of the molecular structures [43]. Figure3illustrates a simplified overview of the Qwen3.5—9B architecture used in this study.

Simplified architecture of the Qwen3.5—9B Vision Model

We constructed a specialized dataset of organic compounds sourced from the PubChem database, specifically targeting the Literature, Safety and Hazards, and Use and Manufacturing categories to ensure a diverse representation of chemical properties. A total of 8822 unique compounds were collected. To ensure dataset integrity, we implemented a Python-based verification pipeline to confirm that there were no duplicate or missing entries across the train, validation, and test splits. As a secondary validation step, each compound’s IUPAC name was converted into a SMILES representation, and we verified that no duplicate SMILES strings existed across the dataset. Additionally, molecular validity was checked using RDKit to ensure that all compounds corresponded to chemically valid structures.

To evaluate the model's depth of understanding, we categorized the dataset into two distinct task types:

Task 1 (Simple IUPAC Naming): Focused on generating the standard IUPAC name from a molecular image.

Task 2 (Detailed Nomenclature Logic): Focused on explaining the systematic principles of IUPAC nomenclature. These detailed annotations (4.75% of the training set and 5.10% of the test set) were generated using the GPT-4o-mini model and underwent manual expert verification to ensure chemical accuracy and logical consistency.

The collected dataset was partitioned into 7176 samples for training, and 823 samples each for validation and testing. To improve the model's generalization and prevent overfitting, we performed data augmentation on the training set. By applying an n = 1 augmentation strategy, the final training pool was expanded to 14,352 instances.

Instead of simple pixel-level noise, we employed Random Affine Transformations to simulate various orientations and scales of molecular structures found in real-world literature. The specific augmentation parameters were configured as follows:

Rotation: The images were subjected to random rotations within a range of plus or minus 10 degrees to account for various tilted structural orientations often found in chemical diagrams

Translation: Horizontal and vertical shifts restricted to 2% (0.02) of the image dimensions to keep the molecule centered.

Scaling: Slight scaling variations between 0.97 × times and 1.03 × times to simulate different drawing sizes.

Padding: To maintain the integrity of the chemical diagrams, any void spaces created by transformations were filled with a value of 255 (white), consistent with the background color of the original dataset.

To investigate the effect of decoding strategies on molecular image captioning, we evaluate several token generation methods during inference using the best-performing fine-tuned model. Specifically, we compare deterministic and stochastic decoding approaches to identify which strategy is most suitable for generating accurate textual descriptions of molecular structures.

Greedy search is a deterministic decoding method that selects the token with the highest probability at each generation step. This approach produces consistent outputs because it always chooses the most likely token according to the model’s predicted distribution [44].

In contrast, stochastic decoding methods introduce randomness by sampling tokens from the predicted probability distribution. Temperature sampling controls the sharpness of this distribution using a temperature parameter τ. Lower temperature values make the distribution more concentrated on high-probability tokens, leading to more deterministic outputs, while higher values increase randomness and diversity in the generated text [44].

In addition, we employ min-p sampling, a dynamic token filtering method that adjusts the candidate token set based on the probability of the most likely token. Specifically, tokens whose probability is lower than a threshold determined by the base probability multiplied by the probability of the most probable token are filtered out before sampling. This strategy allows the model to maintain generation diversity while preventing extremely low-probability tokens from being selected [45].

Based on these methods, we evaluate three decoding configurations: (1) greedy search, (2) temperature sampling with (τ = 0.5) and min_p = 0.1, and (3) temperature sampling with (τ = 0.1) and min_p = 0.05. Through this comparison, we aim to identify the decoding strategy that produces the most accurate descriptions for the molecular image captioning task.

To design an effective and computationally efficient fine-tuning strategy, we selected Qwen3.5—9B as our base Vision-Language Model. This model was prioritized due to its state-of-the-art performance in the MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding) benchmark, where it recorded a score of 78.4 Table2. This exceptional capability in STEM-related tasks makes it highly suitable for the complex structural and logical reasoning required in chemical nomenclature.

In this architecture, LayerNorm plays a crucial role beyond simple activation stabilization; it enhances the expressivity of attention layers by projecting inputs to a balanced hyperplane, ensuring that attention queries treat keys more equally and preventing certain features from being ignored [44]. Recent research has demonstrated that tuning only the LayerNorm modules in multimodal LLMs can effectively reduce cross-layer similarity, fostering richer representations and often outperforming full-model fine-tuning on downstream tasks [45].

Furthermore, we focus on the MLP layers within the vision encoder, which are critical for progressively projecting high-dimensional visual features into the shared embedding space. This process facilitates the precise alignment between the visual representations of molecular structures and their corresponding linguistic descriptors [47].

By building upon these insights—specifically the strategic importance of LayerNorm and vision-language alignment components—we explore efficient fine-tuning strategies for adapting Qwen3.5—9B to the chemical domain. Our approach aims to minimize computational overhead while maintaining the model’s robust STEM reasoning capabilities, ensuring high performance in both molecular image recognition and detailed IUPAC nomenclature tasks.

We evaluate the performance of the model under the following fine-tuning configurations, all based on the Qwen3.5—9B architecture:

L-MLP Only: LoRA is applied solely to the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) modules in the language model. All other parameters are frozen.

L-MLP + V-MLP: In addition to applying LoRA to the language MLP modules, we fine-tune the later-stage MLP layers of the vision encoder. The rest of the model remains frozen.

L-MLP + VM: LoRA is applied to the language MLP modules, and we simultaneously fine-tune the visual merger (the projection module responsible for bridging the vision encoder and the language model). All other layers are kept frozen.

L-MLP + L-LN: LoRA is applied to the language MLP modules, and all LayerNorm layers throughout the entire language model are selected for fine-tuning. All other parameters are frozen.

Efficient fine-tuning strategies on Qwen3.5 -9B Vision

We fine-tuned the Qwen3.5—9B model, which demonstrates strong multimodal capabilities and serves as a robust alternative to self-attention-only architectures [46]. The fine-tuning was performed using a lightweight training configuration optimized for environments with limited GPU memory, specifically on an NVIDIA RTX5090 with 32 GB of VRAM. The LoRA technique was applied selectively to the language model’s MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron) modules, while other layers were fine-tuned using standard parameter updates where appropriate.

For LoRA, we set the rank parameter to 32, with a scaling factor (LoRA alpha) of 64, and applied a dropout rate of 0.1 to prevent overfitting during adaptation. The base learning rate was set to 5e-5 and scheduled to follow a cosine decay policy, which smoothly reduces the learning rate over time and has been shown to enhance training stability and final performance [47,48]. We used a batch size of 4 per device with gradient accumulation over 8 steps, yielding an effective batch size of 32, and trained the model for a total of 2 epochs. The random seed in the SFTConfig was set to 3407 to ensure reproducibility. The full training configuration is summarized in Table3.

To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned vision–language model, we employed a hybrid evaluation strategy combining traditional automatic metrics and an LLM-based assessment using OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini. Conventional text generation metrics, including BLEU and ROUGE, were used to measure lexical overlap between the generated outputs and the reference answers.

Because our dataset contains two distinct task types, we adopted different evaluation strategies depending on the task characteristics. For Task 1 (Simple IUPAC Naming), which requires the generation of an exact chemical name, we applied a Python-based string exact match evaluation to determine correctness. For Task 2 (Detailed Nomenclature Logic), which involves explanatory descriptions of IUPAC naming principles, we employed BLEU-1 F1 and ROUGE-1 F1 metrics to capture lexical similarity between the generated explanations and the reference annotations.

In addition to these automated metrics, we introduced an LLM-based evaluation to assess semantic correctness. GPT-4o-mini was prompted to compare each generated answer with the corresponding ground truth and determine whether their meanings were equivalent. Based on this judgment, we assigned a binary accuracy score: 1 for semantically correct outputs and 0 for incorrect ones. The final accuracy was computed as the proportion of correct outputs across the evaluation set. To ensure reliability, the GPT-based evaluations were further manually verified by the researchers.

Furthermore, incorrect model outputs were qualitatively analyzed by the researchers, and common error patterns were categorized to better understand the limitations of the model and the types of mistakes occurring in molecular image interpretation.

This hybrid evaluation framework allows traditional n-gram-based metrics to capture surface-level similarity, while the LLM-based judge provides an additional semantic verification layer. By combining these approaches, we aim to obtain a more reliable and context-aware assessment of model performance for the molecular image captioning task. Notably, the baseline zero-shot performance of the pre-trained model for Task 1 (Simple IUPAC Naming) was merely 15.88%. Applying LoRA solely to the language-side MLPs (L-MLP Only) yielded an accuracy of 68.89%, representing a massive absolute increase of over 50 percentage points. Among the evaluated strategies, L-MLP + VM (Visual Merger) achieved the highest performance for Task 1, reaching 70.42%. This demonstrates that selectively tuning the visual merger—the critical module responsible for projecting vision outputs into the language space—is highly effective for precise cross-modal alignment.

Furthermore, this study evaluated the model's ability to explain detailed IUPAC naming principles (Task 2). In terms of lexical overlap, the L-MLP + VM strategy consistently outperformed the others, recording the highest scores in both ROUGE-1 F1 and BLEU-1 F1 metrics. To rigorously assess the logical correctness beyond.

Surface-level text matching, an LLM-based evaluator was employed to measure the semantic equivalence between the predicted explanations and the ground truth. Interestingly, this semantic evaluation revealed that L-MLP Only, L-MLP + VM, and L-MLP + L-LN all achieved an identical score of 57.14%. While the L-MLP + L-LN strategy (tuning all language LayerNorms) slightly dropped to 68.50% in Task 1, it maintained baseline semantic reasoning capabilities in Task 2, indicating that additional LayerNorm tuning provided no substantial advantage for this specific domain adaptation.

Conversely, the L-MLP + V-LMLP strategy—which fine-tuned the later-stage MLPs of the vision encoder—exhibited a severe performance drop, achieving an accuracy of only 29.07% in Task 1. This significant degradation provides a critical insight: modifying the parameters of a well-trained vision encoder can disrupt its established, robust visual representations. Rather than adapting to chemical structures, altering the vision encoder hinders the learning process for highly fine-grained visual recognition tasks.

To better understand the remaining limitations, a qualitative error analysis was conducted on the predictions of the best-performing L-MLP + VM configuration. The distribution of the identified error categories is summarized in Table6. The analysis revealed that locant (positional) errors were the most frequent, accounting for 56.3% of the incorrect outputs. This was followed by partial naming errors, which constituted 22.9%. These findings suggest that while the model successfully captures the main structural framework and functional groups of the molecules, precisely mapping the positional numbers of these components remains a primary challenge.

Overall, the results indicate that the L-MLP + VM strategy offers the most favorable parameter-to-performance ratio. By leaving the foundational vision encoder frozen and focusing strictly on the language model and the bridging visual merger, this approach achieves top-tier accuracy in both simple structural identification and complex logical reasoning tasks with minimal computational overhead.

To further optimize the generation process, this study investigated the impact of different decoding strategies during inference. Table7presents the performance variations across three distinct configurations: Greedy search, a highly conservative sampling strategy (Temperature = 0.1, min_p = 0.05), and a moderately relaxed sampling strategy (Temperature = 0.5, min_p = 0.1).

While the overall performance differences across the strategies were relatively marginal, distinct trends emerged depending on the nature of the task:

Task 1 (Exact Match) and Lexical Similarity: For the simple IUPAC naming task (Task 1), the conservative sampling configuration (Temperature: 0.1, min_p: 0.05) achieved the highest Exact Match score of 70.42%. This configuration also recorded the highest lexical overlap in Task 2, with a ROUGE-1 F1 of 0.7778 and a BLEU-1 of 0.7388. This indicates that introducing a very slight degree of flexibility, constrained by a strict probability filter, is optimal for generating the precise character sequences required for chemical strings, effectively suppressing hallucinations while outperforming pure greedy decoding.

Task 2 (Semantic Accuracy): Interestingly, the results for the LLM-based semantic evaluation in Task 2 showed a different pattern. Both the Greedy approach and the moderately relaxed configuration (Temperature: 0.5, min_p: 0.1) achieved the highest accuracy of 59.52%, slightly outperforming the conservative sampling strategy (57.14%). This suggests a subtle trade-off: while highly restricted decoding improves surface-level text matching, either strict determinism (Greedy) or slightly more diverse phrasing (Temp: 0.5) may be slightly more advantageous for formulating the underlying logic and reasoning steps required for nomenclature explanations.

In summary, the conservative sampling strategy (Temperature: 0.1, min_p: 0.05) offers the best balance for tasks demanding strict structural identification, whereas purely deterministic or moderately diverse strategies maintain a slight edge in capturing semantic equivalence in explanatory contexts.

This study proposes an efficient fine-tuning strategy for vision-language models that significantly reduces memory usage and training time, enabling faster model development and deployment with lower infrastructure requirements. The research contributes to the field of multimodal learning in chemical domains by demonstrating that effective fine-tuning can be achieved even under limited computing resources. By developing a selective fine-tuning approach tailored to the fine-grained nature of chemical image recognition, the model achieved improved performance with significantly fewer trainable parameters. This makes the methodology accessible to researchers working with constrained computational budgets.

In addition, the integration of generative AI to create synthetic datasets provides a practical advancement for automating both data preparation and quality assurance. This approach helps address data scarcity in specialized domains such as chemistry and pharmaceuticals and offers a scalable framework for dataset augmentation that may be extended to various scientific fields.

Unlike many previous studies that focus primarily on CLIP-based architectures, this research explores fine-tuning strategies for the Qwen3.5—9B model. This demonstrates that efficient fine-tuning strategies can be successfully adapted to smaller and more accessible models, broadening the range of applicable architectures. Furthermore, a specialized evaluation method is introduced to overcome the limitations of conventional metrics such as BLEU when applied to chemical nomenclature tasks, offering a more accurate assessment framework for chemical structure recognition and description.

By extending vision-language learning to the domain of chemical structure images, this study expands the application scope of multimodal models beyond general-purpose image tasks. The proposed methods have the potential to support a wide range of scientific applications, particularly in chemistry and related fields.

The effectiveness of this approach, combined with its lower computational requirements, has important implications for democratizing access to advanced AI tools in scientific research. The use of synthetic data generation and augmentation is especially promising for automating data preparation in domains where such tasks are traditionally labor-intensive and require specialized expertise.

While our results are promising, the model's generalization performance can still be improved. To further enhance robustness, increasing the diversity and size of the dataset remains essential. A larger and more varied dataset would enable the model to learn more comprehensive chemical knowledge, improving its ability to handle unseen molecular structures and generate more accurate predictions.

Future work will focus on improving the scalability and robustness of the proposed framework, exploring further domain adaptation strategies, and expanding the model's capabilities to address more complex chemical tasks. The integration of additional data modalities and enhanced fine-tuning techniques could lead to even more powerful tools for advancing scientific research in chemistry and beyond.

title: Integrating chemical structure and high-throughput transcriptomics for mechanistically interpretable Tox21 bioactivity prediction
author: Guillaume Cattebeke; Anne-Sofie Vermeersch; Davie Cappoen; Dieter Deforce; Filip Van Nieuwerburgh
text:
Predictive toxicology increasingly emphasizes methods that combine scalable chemical screening with biologically interpretable mechanistic information. Existing computational approaches, however, rely largely on chemical structure alone and often fail to capture the cellular programs underlying compound-induced cellular responses. Herein, we describe a multimodal modeling framework that integrates chemical fingerprints with high-throughput transcriptomic (HTTr) dose–response profiles to predict activity for 41 curated Tox21 assay endpoints. HTTr data were obtained from TempO-Seq screens in MCF-7, U-2 OS, and HepaRG cells following exposure to ToxCast compounds across an eight-point concentration series ranging from 0.03 to 100 µM. Using gradient-boosted decision trees and nested compound-aware cross-validation, 13 assays achieved robust performance (mean area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC) > 0.75), spanning nuclear receptor signaling, stress-response pathways, and xenobiotic metabolism. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based feature attribution analysis showed that predictions depend on both structural motifs and transcriptional programs, in a manner consistent with established mechanistic relationships between chemical structure, nuclear receptor biology, and adaptive cellular responses. These findings illustrate how structure and high-throughput transcriptomic dose–response signature integration enables models that are accurate and mechanistically grounded, shifting computational toxicology toward transparent and biologically informed mechanistic bioactivity prediction.

We introduce a scalable multimodal framework for mechanistically interpretable Tox21 bioactivity prediction that jointly leverages chemical structure and multi-dose HTTr response profiles across three human cell lines to model 41 curated assay endpoints under compound-aware validation. Unlike prior work that is typically structure-only or limited to single-dose and/or single-cell-line transcriptomic designs, our approach integrates dose–response–derived biological summaries with interpretable structural keys and demonstrates robust generalization. We further differentiate the framework by providing model interpretability via SHAP, explicitly linking predictive performance to endpoint-relevant structural motifs and transcriptional programs.

The assessment of chemical toxicity and safety has traditionally relied heavily on animal testing. Yet, despite several significant contributions, animal models often remain poor predictors of human outcomes [1]. Translating their findings to human health has proven challenging, as inter-species differences in physiology, metabolism, and molecular signaling often result in poor concordance rates between animal test results and actual human responses. Moreover, traditional in vivo studies are increasingly criticized for their ethical implications, substantial costs, and poor reproducibility, limiting their relevance in modern-day toxicology [2]. At the same time, the expanding chemical landscape presents a different challenge, as humans are exposed to a wide range of compounds, characterized by distinct physicochemical properties, biological targets, and unique mechanisms of toxicity. Taken together, this creates a level of complexity that traditional testing methods struggle to address, making comprehensive evaluation both resource-intensive and often ineffective.

In light of this, alternative testing methods have progressed considerably [3,4]. Modern in vitro systems now enable the evaluation of large amounts of chemicals on biologically relevant mechanisms without relying on whole-animal models, and instead contribute to a growing framework of innovative strategies collectively named New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). Defined as any in vitro, in silico, or alternative testing method used to inform chemical hazard and risk assessment without the use of animals, NAMs have gained traction in recent years, with regulatory agencies beginning to incorporate them into established evaluation frameworks [5]. Within this context, high-throughput screening (HTS) platforms enable the evaluation of large and diverse sets of chemicals at an unprecedented scale. Likewise, high-throughput transcriptomics (HTTr) comprehensively profiles gene expression changes in response to a wide variety of chemical perturbations. As such, large-scale collaborative initiatives have begun to systematically generate, organize, and share high-quality toxicity data. Prominent examples include the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Toxicity Forecaster (ToxCast) program, which compiles results from hundreds of high-throughput assays [6], as well as the Tox21 program, which applies HTS to evaluate thousands of chemicals across nuclear receptor and stress-response pathways [7,8]. More recently, efforts at the EPA’s Center for Computational Toxicology and Exposure (CCTE) have focused on systematically cataloging chemical-induced gene expression changes through the adoption of a TempO-Seq–based targeted RNA-Seq platform, which enables cost-effective transcriptomic screening at scale [9,10,11]. Through large HTTr screenings, over 1,000 chemicals from the ToxCast collection have now been profiled across multiple human cell lines, effectively expanding the chemical screening landscape with complementary transcriptome-wide gene expression data.

Although transcriptomic approaches have shown promise in specific case studies, their application to chemical toxicity assessment has generally been limited to specific biological domains or small chemical sets, often relying on reduced gene panels that capture only a subset of the transcriptional response [12,13]. In parallel, traditional computational toxicology has relied heavily on chemical descriptors and quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models, which capture intrinsic molecular features but lack direct biological context [14]. Although QSAR models can perform well within specific chemical domains, their reliance on structural descriptors limits mechanistic interpretability, highlighting the need for biological measurements that reflect the consequences of chemical exposure. Large-scale HTS and HTTr platforms now address this by enabling the systematic profiling of thousands of chemical–dose–cell line combinations, generating complementary information on both chemical activities and downstream cellular responses. Despite advances in modeling and rapid progress in generating these datasets, current approaches remain limited to narrow transcriptomic profiles, single-dose designs, or single-cell-line systems, leaving no general framework for integrating full transcriptome dose–response information with chemical structure at scale. Advancing beyond these limitations will require integrative approaches that extend biological coverage, uncover conserved mechanisms across diverse assays, and enable models that are both predictive and mechanistically informative.

In this study, we introduce a modeling framework that integrates these modalities and predicts bioactivity across Tox21 assay endpoints. The framework combines chemical fingerprints with transcriptomic dose–response summaries from multiple human cell lines to generate scalable, mechanistically interpretable predictions across a diverse panel of nuclear receptor, stress-response, and xenobiotic-metabolism assays. It demonstrates how large-scale data integration can enhance chemical safety assessment and shift predictive toxicology toward human-relevant, mechanism-based evaluation frameworks.

To enable robust and generalizable predictive modeling, we first curated a high-confidence subset of endpoints from the Tox21 assay collection. Starting from 290 assay components, stepwise filtering based on sample size, class distribution, data completeness, and viability metrics retained 41 endpoints suitable for model development, collectively spanning key toxicological mechanisms such as nuclear receptor signaling (e.g., estrogen and androgen receptor activity), stress-response pathways (e.g., DNA damage and oxidative stress), and xenobiotic metabolism (e.g., cytochrome P450 inhibition) (Additional file 1: Table S1). Most exclusions resulted from initial data-quality filtering, which removed well over half of the original assay components as formats or readouts not suitable for primary activity modeling. Subsequent viability and class-balance criteria further narrowed the remaining set to those with sufficiently reliable and well-distributed activity data. Collectively, this curated panel offers coverage of toxicological mechanisms relevant to human chemical safety assessment.

Across the 41 endpoints, the integrated dataset covered 1,985 unique chemicals representing the union of DTXSIDs with usable HTTr-derived features from at least one of the three cell-line datasets. This corresponds to a subset of the broader chemical space covered by the curated Tox21 assay panel, which comprised 8,948 unique DTXSIDs across all assays. While some endpoints exhibited nearly complete activity coverage, others displayed substantial data sparsity with an overall missingness ranging from 10 to 60%. This uneven coverage coincided with substantial variation in both the fraction of actives (class balance) and the absolute number of active compounds across assays (Fig.1). For example, CYP450 antagonist assays (e.g., P450 CYP2C9 antagonist assay) contained comparatively large positive classes, consistent with their broad substrate specificity and central role in xenobiotic metabolism [15]. In contrast, nuclear receptor and transcription factor assays (e.g., ERa antagonist assay) typically had fewer active compounds, which is expected given that only structurally specific molecules can modulate these pathways [16]. The number of active compounds varied across endpoints, corresponding to class balances between 3 and 60%. Such imbalance has important implications for predictive modeling, as highly imbalanced datasets can lead to models that disproportionately favor the majority (inactive) class, resulting in inflated accuracy and diminished sensitivity toward minority (active) compounds. These rare actives are often of greatest toxicological concern, as they reveal specific molecular interactions capable of disrupting key signaling or metabolic pathways, and therefore highlight why sensitivity, rather than accuracy, is the more meaningful performance metric in this context.

To identify the transcriptomic features most informative for predicting bioactivity, we applied the Boruta feature-selection algorithm to the transcriptomic dose–response summary features for each endpoint. Boruta was chosen to address both the high dimensionality and the strong correlations inherent in these data. Unlike embedded or sparsity-based feature-selection approaches which typically yield a minimal subset of predictors optimized primarily for model performance, Boruta performs feature selection by retaining all predictors that demonstrate consistent importance, rather than restricting the model to the smallest set that maximizes predictive accuracy [17]. From an initial set of 16,821 dose–response summaries, the number of stably retained features varied across assays, with an average of 83 ± 50 per endpoint (Fig.1). Consensus-retained transcriptomic features for each modeled endpoint are provided in Additional file 1: Table S2. This represents a reduction of more than two orders of magnitude in feature space, underscoring that only a small fraction of transcriptomic responses consistently carry predictive signal. Because the feature space consisted exclusively of pathway- and regulator-level summaries (originating from Hallmark, DoRothEA and PROGENy), the retained features reflected higher-order biological processes rather than individual gene responses. Retained features were distributed across these different summary layers, indicating that predictive signal arises from multiple pathways rather than a single dominant biological process. In parallel, chemical structure was encoded using the 166-bit MACCS fingerprints (Additional file 1: Table S3). Notably, the dimensionality of the Boruta-selected features was of the same order of magnitude as that of the MACCS fingerprints, which prevented one modality from dominating the feature space and facilitated more equal integration of chemical and biological descriptors during model training. In practice, this ensured that predictions were not biased toward structural similarity alone, but instead reflected both intrinsic chemical properties and observed cellular consequences. This balance is important, as prior multimodal profiling work has shown that structure- and biology-based descriptors tend to capture complementary signals and generally yield stronger and more mechanistically informative models when used together than when applied in isolation [18]. Consequently, the integrated feature space used here supports predictions shaped by both molecular scaffolds and the transcriptional programs they induce.

Model performance was evaluated on held-out test folds using a nested, group-aware cross-validation workflow to avoid information leakage. Overall, the integrated models achieved strong predictive performance across the 41 retained endpoints, although performance varied among assays (Table1). Due to the pronounced class imbalance, metrics such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) can overestimate predictive ability, as high ROC AUC values may still correspond to poor sensitivity for the minority (active) class (e.g., GR Agonist assay). In contrast, the area under precision-recall curve (AUPRC) is more informative under class imbalance, as it explicitly quantifies the tradeoff between precision and recall for the positive class (i.e. active compounds). Accordingly, AUPRC was adopted as the primary metric for comparing model performance across endpoints. Sensitivity, specificity, and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) were also evaluated to further characterize classifier behavior.

The mean AUPRC values per assay ranged from near-random (AUPRC ≈ 0.3–0.5) for the most challenging nuclear receptor endpoints, to very high accuracies for the best-performing assays (AUPRC ≈ 0.8–0.9). As expected, predictive performance was strongly associated with the number of positive cases (i.e. active compounds) (Fig.2). This relationship is also reflected in the threshold-dependent sensitivity, as endpoints with higher AUPRC values typically achieved sensitivities above 0.8 at their F1-optimal thresholds. Consistent with this pattern, all of the CYP450 antagonism endpoints ranked among the most accurately predicted and had comparatively large numbers of positive classes. For instance, the CYP2C9 antagonist assay achieved an AUROC of 0.896 ± 0.019 and an AUPRC of 0.908 ± 0.016, and had the highest number of active compounds (n = 1,596), while assays such as the GR agonist (n = 105) and HDAC antagonist assay (n = 124) with one of the fewest active compounds, exhibited substantially lower performance.

To delineate which endpoints can be considered reliably predictable, we applied an empirical cutoff of mean AUPRC > 0.75. This threshold reflects a clear separation from random performance and denotes models with a practically meaningful precision–recall trade-off (high recall at manageable false-positive rates) for identifying active compounds. From a toxicological perspective, emphasizing AUPRC is particularly appropriate, since positive (active/toxic) compounds are typically rare yet carry the greatest regulatory and health relevance. Using this criterion, 13 of the 41 endpoints were classified as predictive, representing assays with sufficiently balanced activity and mechanistic signal to support robust, generalizable insights.

A modality-ablation analysis further showed that the full multimodal model outperformed structure-only and HTTr-only models in 38/41 and 39/41 assays, respectively, supporting complementary predictive value of the two feature modalities (Additional file 1: Fig. S15). Direct comparison of the two unimodal models showed that their relative performance was endpoint-dependent. Structure-only models outperformed HTTr-only models for 15/41 endpoints, with the strongest advantage observed for the CYP antagonist assays, including all five CYP endpoints. This pattern is consistent with CYP inhibition being strongly influenced by scaffold- and substructure-level properties represented in the MACCS fingerprint. In contrast, HTTr-only models performed better for 26/41 endpoints, including several receptor- and stress-response endpoints, where activity may be more closely reflected in downstream transcriptional programs. To assess whether the multimodal signal depended on the inclusion of all three HTTr cell lines, cell-line-restricted sensitivity analyses were also performed. Performance changes were assay-dependent, with MCF-7-containing subsets generally retaining performance most effectively, whereas HepaRG-only and U-2 OS-only settings more often fell below the full-model baseline. For the predictive endpoints, however, these effects were generally limited, with several settings showing little or no deviation from baseline (Additional file 1: Fig. S16). Applicability domain (AD) was also assessed in both structural and transcriptomic feature space using fold-specific nearest-neighbor similarity to the training set. Compounds inside the AD generally showed higher predictive performance than outside-AD compounds, with this pattern observed in 32/41 assays for the structural AD and 26/41 assays for the transcriptomic AD (Additional file 1: Tables S5–S6).

To identify which features most strongly contributed to model predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values were computed on the held-out test set within each cross-validation fold and were aggregated across folds. The resulting feature importance patterns indicated that model predictions were not driven by structural information alone, as the top contributors repeatedly combined MACCS fragments with dose–response summary features (Additional file 1: Fig. S1–S13). Within the 13 selected assays, consistent patterns emerged: on the structural side, recurrent MACCS keys highlighted common molecular scaffolds and substituents across endpoints. The most influential fragments included six-membered ring motifs and oxygen-rich substituents, such as hydroxyl, ether-like, and other polar oxygen-containing groups (MACCS_145, MACCS_146, MACCS_140, MACCS_159, MACCS_126, MACCS_113), as well as amine- and heteroatom-containing features (MACCS_151, MACCS_124), and exhibited largely consistent predictive contributions. Together, these patterns are consistent with established principles of ligand–protein recognition: ring scaffolds often provide hydrophobic anchoring elements within binding pockets, while polar substituents enable hydrogen bonding and modulate the electronic properties of the molecular framework, enhancing both affinity and selectivity. Likewise, heteroatoms and amine functionalities introduce polarity and electrostatic complementarity that stabilize interactions within protein binding sites [19]. Beyond structural determinants, SHAP analysis also highlighted contributions from transcriptomic features derived from dose–response profiles. These features frequently captured conserved programs of stress adaptation and growth regulation, including hypoxia and ATF4-mediated integrated stress responses, IGF/ERK-driven survival signaling, and amino acid–sensing pathways. The recurrence of these modules across most assays suggests that the models capture central stress- and growth-regulatory circuits engaged during xenobiotic exposure [20,21]. At the same time, these signatures may also reflect more general cellular stress responses to xenobiotic exposure, and therefore may not always correspond to assay-specific mechanisms. Nonetheless, several assays showed transcriptomic signatures that were unique to their specific biological mechanisms. A cross-assay summary heatmap of the top SHAP-ranked features for the 13 predictive endpoints further illustrated that feature overlap was only partial, with some predictive features recurring across multiple assays whereas others remained endpoint-specific (Additional file 1: Fig. S14).

To illustrate these trends, the progesterone receptor (PR) beta-lactamase (BLA) antagonist assay model was selected as a representative case for SHAP-based interpretation (Fig.3). Although not the top-performing assay based on AUPRC, it highlights a well-characterized nuclear receptor pathway for which structural determinants and transcriptomic profiles are well understood, making it easier to contextualize SHAP values in terms of mechanistic relevance and biological interpretability. Within this model, several structural features stood out as consistent with known pharmacology of antiprogestins. For instance, MACCS keys capturing oxygen-rich and heteroatom-containing fragments, including multiple oxygen atoms and ether-like linkages (MACCS_146, MACCS_126, MACCS_113) and amine or ring-nitrogen features (MACCS_151, MACCS_161, MACCS_137), were positive contributors toward antagonism, likely reflecting the 11β-aryl and heteroatom substitutions that distinguish antagonists such as mifepristone from receptor agonists [22]. SHAP analysis also identified transcriptomic programs closely linked to PR biology. The most direct PR-relevant feature was the late estrogen response module (LI_ESTROGENE_LATE_E2_RESPONSE_max), which contributed positively towards antagonism, a result that likely reflects compensatory activation of estrogen-associated pathways through ER–PR crosstalk [23]. Additional features captured compensatory growth factor signaling, most notably the upregulation of IGF1/2 targets (PACHER_TARGETS_OF_IGF1_AND_IGF2_UP_max) and modulation of ERK-related programs (FURUKAWA_DUSP6_TARGETS_PC3S_dose_at_max). Compounds that activated ERK/DUSP6 modules only at higher concentrations were more likely to be classified as PR antagonists, suggesting that MAPK engagement represents a secondary adaptive response rather than a direct effect. This interpretation aligns with mechanistic studies showing that while PR antagonists act directly at the receptor, ERK/DUSP6 feedback emerges later as a compensatory mechanism to sustain cell survival [24]. Collectively, the PR model exemplifies how structural motifs, generic stress-adaptation pathways, and receptor-specific transcriptomic signatures converge to produce mechanistically interpretable predictions that align with established principles of receptor pharmacology.
