Catalysts accelerate chemical transformations by lowering activation barriers through alternative reaction pathways. Consequently, catalyst innovation is pivotal for advancing the energy transition, green chemistry, and pollution control. Despite this significance, the development process remains prohibitively resource-intensive. Conventional discovery relies heavily on empirical trial-and-error methodologies. For instance, the optimization of precious metal catalysts frequently necessitates extensive experimental screening spanning months to years and is further constrained by reliance on researcher intuition and stochastic factors [1].

To transcend the limitations of traditional empirical experimentation, quantum chemical methods such as Density Functional Theory (DFT) [2,3] facilitate rational design by simulating atomic-scale descriptors, including surface adsorption energies and transition states. Parallel to this, expert systems utilize established knowledge bases to model structure–activity relationships. Nevertheless, the application of DFT to complex heterogeneous systems is severely limited by computational cost, as a single high-fidelity simulation can require weeks to complete. Similarly, expert systems [4,5,6] offer rapid screening capabilities but fail to encompass the vast chemical space due to the inherent constraints of their knowledge bases and the limited generalizability of rule-based logic. Consequently, a critical challenge in intelligent catalyst design is the development of a data-driven prediction framework that effectively exploits existing reaction data to reconcile the computational inefficiency of quantum chemistry with the rigid generalization of expert systems.

The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced transformative paradigms to catalyst prediction. Within cheminformatics, AI has proven effective in tasks ranging from retrosynthetic planning [7,8,9,10,11,12] and molecular property prediction [13,14,15,16,17,18] to de novo material design [19,20,21]. The primary advantage of these approaches lies in their ability to leverage machine learning algorithms, such as Random Forests [22,23,24,25] and Support Vector Machines [26,27,28,29,30,31], alongside deep learning architectures like Convolutional Neural Networks [32,33] and Graph Attention Networks [34,35,36], to uncover latent correlations within extensive datasets. This capability facilitates the construction of robust quantitative structure–property relationship models. Deep learning frameworks [37,38,39,40,41,42] capture underlying data distributions to generate predictions solely based on historical data, thereby circumventing the need for physical reagents or immediate experimental instrumentation. Compared to quantum chemical calculations, this data-driven strategy significantly reduces computational overhead and resource expenditure. Furthermore, deep learning models operate independently of human heuristics and expert knowledge. By transcending the limitations of researcher intuition, they enable the unbiased and efficient exploration of vast chemical spaces. This capacity facilitates the rapid identification of high-quality candidate molecules with superior physicochemical properties, significantly accelerating the catalyst discovery lifecycle.

Recently, several sophisticated computational frameworks have been developed to capture the intricate logic of chemical transformations. Early advancements in this area saw the introduction of Parrot [43], which utilized a sequence-to-sequence transformer architecture to achieve interpretable reaction condition predictions by leveraging unsupervised learning of reaction centers. Building on the need for broader chemical context, TextReact [44] subsequently enhanced predictive performance by adopting a retrieval-augmented approach, integrating external chemical knowledge from literature directly with molecular representations. More recently, traditional descriptors combined with multi-task learning strategies have been systematically evaluated; notably, Morgan MTNN was highlighted as a representative model configuration in a 2025 data-driven perspective on reaction condition prediction [45], where multi-task neural networks are employed to process standard molecular fingerprints. While these methodologies have demonstrated significant progress in general reaction-related tasks over the years, their specialized application and effectiveness in the rigorous multi-class catalyst prediction domain remain to be fully established, particularly when structural complexity and class imbalance are prevalent.

Despite their promise, traditional computer-aided catalyst design methods frequently exhibit inefficiencies and limited generalizability. A critical bottleneck in existing research is the reliance on simplistic representations, such as one-hot encoding, for catalysts, while focusing primarily on reactant and product information. This oversimplification neglects the intrinsic structural complexity of catalyst molecules, including atomic composition and bond topology, which severely constrains the model's ability to uncover and exploit the latent dependencies governing the interactions between reactants, products, and catalysts.

We propose CataCon, a contrastive learning-based deep neural network designed to predict optimal catalyst types by leveraging detailed molecular information. The framework initially employs GraphSAGE [46] to generate feature embeddings for the molecular graphs of reactants, products, and catalysts, thereby ensuring the comprehensive extraction of structural attributes and physicochemical properties. This approach preserves critical topological information across the reaction coordinate and specifically addresses the representational deficiencies of traditional one-hot encoding by enabling dense feature extraction for catalyst structures. Subsequently, CataCon integrates a contrastive learning module that mines intrinsic correlations between reactant-product pairs and catalysts by constructing positive and negative sample pairs. During training, this mechanism aligns feature distributions across diverse views, which enhances the model's capacity to capture latent interactions between reaction dynamics and catalyst molecular architecture. Experimental evaluations on public catalytic reaction datasets demonstrate that CataCon significantly outperforms baseline methods in catalyst classification tasks. Ablation studies confirm the specific contributions of each module, validating the efficacy of synergizing graph representation learning with contrastive strategies for multi-view feature integration. Furthermore, t-SNE visualization and interpretability analyses elucidate the model's decision-making processes, providing novel insights into the complex dependencies governing the relationships among reactants, products, and catalysts.

Given a catalyst dataset denoted as\({D=\{\left({x}_{i}, {y}_{i}\right)\}}_{i=1}^{n},\), let\({x}_{i}\)represent the\(i\)catalytic reaction sample comprising SMILES strings for the reactant and product entities, and let\({y}_{i}\in \{1,...,C\}\)denote the corresponding ground-truth catalyst category from a set of\(C\)distinct classes. The objective of this study is to develop a contrastive learning-based framework that learns a mapping function\(f: \mathcal{X}\to \mathcal{Y}\)to accurately classify reaction samples into their respective catalyst categories, thereby transforming the input reactant-product molecular representations into multi-class predictive outputs.

The catalytic reaction dataset employed in this study is the USPTO-Catalyst benchmark, a publicly available collection curated and released by the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC). Derived from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) chemical reaction archive, the dataset focuses on reactions containing explicit catalyst information, specifically retaining high-frequency catalysts with over 100 occurrences. Each entry includes identifiers and SMILES strings for reactants, products, and catalyst categories.

However, the raw dataset presents significant challenges for high-fidelity modeling. The prevalence of non-canonical SMILES representations introduces structural ambiguity and hinders the model’s ability to quantify molecular similarities accurately. Furthermore, an analysis of the 888 initial catalyst categories reveals that many annotations functionally serve as solvents rather than true catalysts. Such mislabeling can confound the model's understanding of catalytic roles, ultimately degrading predictive precision.

To ensure robustness and reproducibility, we implemented a deterministic preprocessing pipeline to transform the raw USPTO-Catalyst collection into a curated benchmark. The process began with SMILES standardization and canonicalization. For each reactant, product, and catalyst field, multi-component SMILES strings were partitioned into individual molecular entities using the dot delimiter. Each component was parsed via RDKit; invalid entries were discarded, while valid molecules were standardized and converted into their unique canonical SMILES forms. To guarantee representation uniqueness, canonicalized components within each field were sorted lexicographically before being recombined.

Following canonicalization, we performed multi-level redundancy mitigation to address duplicate samples at two hierarchical levels. First, entries sharing identical canonicalized reactant, product, and catalyst strings were treated as duplicate triplets and removed. Subsequently, the remaining entries with identical reactant-product pairs were merged to eliminate residual redundancy stemming from the repeated reporting of the same chemical transformation.

Finally, to resolve the issue of mislabeled categories, we executed a catalyst refinement and label remapping protocol. We curated a comprehensive reference library of common solvents and evaluated each dataset entry. A catalyst entry was excluded only if all its constituent molecules matched the solvent library. Entries containing at least one non-solvent component were retained as valid catalyst-solvent mixtures to preserve the essential chemical context. The filtered catalyst categories were then remapped onto a contiguous label space to facilitate efficient model training.

The stage-wise statistics of this curation process are summarized in Table1. To further support reproducibility, the exact preprocessing scripts and the final catalyst label mappings are provided in our code repository.

CataCon comprises four distinct modules: data preprocessing, graph encoding, contrastive learning, and predictive classification (As shown in Fig.1). In the data preprocessing module, SMILES strings are transformed into molecular graphs wherein atoms function as nodes and chemical bonds as edges. This module extracts atomic and bond-level information from the SMILES input, encoding them into atomic tensors and bond tensors, respectively. The atomic tensor encapsulates the physicochemical properties of each atom, while the bond tensor characterizes the specific bonding interactions between atoms. Additionally, an adjacency matrix, referred to as the link index, records the connectivity between atoms to construct a comprehensive molecular graph data structure. This graph-based representation effectively captures the topological architecture and intrinsic chemical attributes of the molecules, thereby providing a standardized input for the deep learning framework and augmenting its capacity to learn molecular representations.

Discrete atomic features are mapped into a continuous vector space via the atom encoder, respectively.CGraphSAGE executes multi-layer message passing and neighbor aggregation to update the feature representation of each atomic node. Following this, a global mean pooling operation aggregates the nodal representations within each molecule into a fixed-dimensional molecular vector. The primary objective of the contrastive learning module is to compute the contrastive loss. This module accepts feature embeddings for reactions and catalysts, which are generated from the reactant, product, and catalyst subsets by the feature extraction module. These embeddings are subsequently fed into a contrastive loss function that evaluates the loss based on the cosine similarity between representations. The design of this loss function aims to minimize the feature distance between positive pairs while maximizing the distance between negative pairs. By optimizing this objective, the model learns highly discriminative feature representations, thereby enhancing its robustness in distinguishing between distinct sample categories.

The classification module functions to map the learned high-level feature representations to predictive outcomes. This module is composed primarily of stacked linear layers that perform linear transformations within the feature space, ultimately yielding probability distributions for classification. The predicted outputs are compared against ground truth labels to compute the cross-entropy loss. This loss function serves as a direct metric of classification performance. Its optimization drives the adjustment of model parameters to minimize prediction error, thereby facilitating more precise final classification results.

In chemoinformatics, molecular graphs transcend the limitations of sequence-based data by preserving topological connectivity and preventing the loss of structural information associated with flattening. Consequently, they are extensively utilized in molecular representation, property prediction, and reaction analysis. To leverage molecular information more effectively for deep learning applications, this chapter details the conversion of SMILES strings into attribute-rich molecular graphs. A molecular graph is formalized as a quadruple\(\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{A})\), defined as follows:

(1)\(\mathcal{V}=\{{v}_{i}{\}}_{i=1}^{n}\)denotes the set of atomic nodes, where\(n\)represents the total number of non-hydrogen atoms in the molecule.

(2)\(\mathcal{E}\subseteq \mathcal{V}\times \mathcal{V}\)denotes the set of directed edges representing chemical bonds between atoms. For every chemical bond, both the forward edge\((i,j)\in \mathcal{E}\)and its reverse counterpart\((j,i)\in \mathcal{E}\)are included to ensure the symmetry of the graph structure.

(3)\(\mathbf{X}\in {\mathbb{Z}}^{n\times {d}_{x}}\)is the node feature matrix encoding atomic-level physicochemical properties. The dimension\({d}_{x}=9\)corresponds to nine specific attributes: atomic number, chirality, total valence, formal charge, hydrogen count, radical electron count, hybridization state, aromaticity, and ring membership.

(4)\(\mathbf{A}\in {\mathbb{Z}}^{2\mid \mathcal{B}\mid \times {d}_{e}}\)is the edge property matrix describing bond characteristics, where the dimension\({d}_{e}=3\)encompasses three bond attributes: bond type, stereochemistry, and conjugation status. For each chemical bond\({b}_{ij}\in \mathcal{B}\), its bidirectional edge properties are defined via the mapping function:

Here,\({\phi}_{e}({b}_{ij})\)denotes the intrinsic attributes of the bond\({b}_{ij}\), and\({e}_{\text{map}}\)represents the bond attribute dictionary. Through these procedures, the data preprocessing module transforms SMILES strings into standardized molecular graph representations. The resulting graphs serve as input for graph neural networks to facilitate molecular feature extraction, thereby providing high-fidelity structural representations for downstream tasks.

Previous approaches focused exclusively on the molecular features of reactants and products while reducing catalysts to simplistic one-hot vectors, a practice that neglects the rich structural information inherent in catalyst molecules. To address this limitation, this work integrates catalyst molecular information into the feature extraction pipeline and enables the model to learn the intrinsic correlations between catalytic reaction dynamics and catalyst properties. This section first delineates the molecular graph feature extraction process for reactants, products, and catalysts, and subsequently describes the fusion mechanism used to derive composite catalytic reaction features.

Molecular graph feature extraction is grounded in the previously defined formalism\(\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{A})\). In the final GraphSAGE based CataCon model, molecular feature extraction consists of four main steps: atomic feature encoding, graph structural feature extraction, global pooling, and a fully connected transformation. Bond attributes are retained as part of the molecular graph representation, but they are not explicitly injected into the GraphSAGE message passing update. They are only used in the edge aware GAT based backbone variants included in the comparison experiments.

In the atomic feature representation learning phase, each column of the atomic feature matrix, which corresponds to a discrete attribute, is mapped to a continuous vector space via a dedicated embedding layer. These embeddings are then aggregated to construct the initial atomic representation. Specifically, for each atom\({v}_{i}\)with feature vector\({\mathbf{X}}_{i,:}\), its\(f\)-th attribute\({X}_{i,f}\)is transformed into a dense vector via the corresponding embedding matrix\({\mathbf{E}}_{f}\in {\mathbb{R}}^{\mid {\mathcal{C}}_{f}\mid \times {d}_{m}}\), where\(\mid {\mathcal{C}}_{f}\mid\)denotes the cardinality of the value set for that attribute. The initial representation of the atom is computed by summing the embedding vectors across all attributes:

Bond attributes are retained in the molecular graph as edge descriptors. However, in the final GraphSAGE based CataCon model, these edge attributes are not explicitly incorporated into the message passing update. Instead, GraphSAGE operates on node representations together with graph connectivity. For completeness, we note that edge attributes are used in the edge aware GAT and GATv2 variants included in the backbone comparison experiments, where bond descriptors are embedded and passed as edge features.

In the implemented GraphSAGE backbone, message passing depends on node representations and adjacency structure only, without an explicit edge attribute term. The graph structural feature extraction module leverages the GraphSAGE architecture, which facilitates information propagation across nodes and aggregates neighborhood features via the edge set\(\mathcal{E}\). This process incrementally updates the representation of each atomic node in a layer-wise manner. Here,\({h}_{i}^{(k-1)}\)denotes the feature representation of node\({v}_{i}\)from the preceding layer;\(\mathcal{N}(i)\)represents the set of immediate neighbors of node\({v}_{i}\);\({\mathbf{W}}^{(k)}\)signifies the learnable weight matrix for the\(k\)-th layer; and\(\sigma (\cdot )\)denotes a non-linear activation function, such as ReLU.

Given that the graph neural network yields feature representations for individual atomic nodes, an aggregation operation is required to derive a molecular-level feature vector from the constituent atoms. To this end, a global mean pooling strategy is employed:

Here,\({\mathcal{V}}_{\text{mol}}\)denotes the set of atomic nodes constituting a specific molecule, and\({h}_{i}^{(L)}\)represents the final node embedding of atom\({v}_{i}\)after propagation through an\(L\)-layer graph neural network.

The resulting output\({\mathbf{H}}_{final}\in {\mathbb{R}}^{{d}_{model}}\)serves as the definitive embedding representation for each molecule.

In the preceding stage, the feature extraction modules derived representations\({h}_{r}\)and\({h}_{p}\)for reactants and products, respectively. These representations are subsequently fused to construct the composite catalytic reaction features. Initially, a sequence dimension is expanded for both the reactant and product features, which are then concatenated to form the sequence\(\mathbf{X}=[{h}_{r},{h}_{p}]\in {\mathbb{R}}^{2\times {d}_{model}}\). This sequence is then processed by a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) model.

The GRU is a variant of recurrent neural network architecture incorporating a gating mechanism designed to capture sequential dependencies. In this context, the GRU is utilized to integrate feature information across the reactant and product stages. The GRU processes the input sequence\(\mathbf{X}\)and generates a hidden state trajectory for the entire sequence. The hidden state at the final time step is extracted as the definitive fused feature vector. This vector provides a comprehensive representation of both reactants and products, supplying high-fidelity reaction features for downstream tasks. This strategy effectively synergizes the strengths of graph neural networks in capturing molecular topology with the sequential modeling capabilities of GRUs, thereby achieving a robust fusion of reactant and product information.

Contrastive learning is a self-supervised paradigm primarily utilized to discern similarity relationships among samples. Its fundamental principle involves the construction of positive and negative pairs to train models that minimize the latent distance between similar representations while maximizing the distance between dissimilar ones. This methodology has been extensively applied across computer vision, natural language processing, and graph representation learning, demonstrating exceptional efficacy in feature extraction tasks. The essence of contrastive learning lies in compressing the feature space for semantically related samples and expanding it for unrelated ones, thereby yielding highly discriminative embeddings. theoretically, this approach is grounded in the maximization of mutual information, ensuring that the learned features possess sufficient entropy to distinguish data across distinct categories.

In this study, a contrastive learning module is introduced to implicitly capture the latent associations between catalytic reactions and catalysts directly from molecular graph features. Leveraging the core mechanism of contrastive learning, we integrate detailed catalyst structural information into the global feature learning pipeline, marking a departure from traditional one-hot encoding strategies. This integration facilitates the acquisition of more nuanced and discriminative representations. Specifically, we designed a specialized loss function governed by the following workflow. Samples belonging to the same catalyst category are designated as positive pairs, whereas those from disparate categories are treated as negative pairs. By incorporating the structural features of catalysts, the module learns to cluster representations of similar samples while separating those of dissimilar ones within a high-dimensional feature space. This process enhances the model's capacity to discern the intrinsic correlations between catalysts and catalytic reactions. In contrast to traditional methods that rely solely on one-hot encoding, our approach provides a richer information representation by integrating these structural features, leading to improved model robustness and generalization performance.

The prediction and classification module is designed to classify catalysts based on the feature representations generated by the contrastive learning module. This classification task is optimized using the cross-entropy loss function. The process begins with the features for both catalytic reactions and catalyst structures. Analogous to the procedure in the contrastive learning module, these features first undergo L2 normalization to mitigate scale differences. Subsequently, feature similarity logits are computed. To maintain numerical stability, these logits are normalized by subtracting their maximum value. A final softmax operation is then applied to the adjusted logits to yield the prediction probabilities\({p}_{ij}\)for each category:

The top-k accuracy is a standard metric for evaluating a model's classification performance. For a given integer\(k\), a prediction is considered correct if the ground truth label is among the\(k\)categories with the highest predicted probabilities.

The multi-class cross-entropy loss function for the classification task is defined as:

Here,\(N\)represents the batch size, and\({s}_{i,{y}_{i}}\)is the logit for the\(i\)-th sample corresponding to its ground truth category\({y}_{i}\). This loss function assigns a small penalty when the model predicts a high probability for the correct category. Conversely, it imposes a large penalty if the predicted probability for the correct category is low, which signifies an inaccurate prediction.

The total loss function is a weighted sum of the two loss components, where the hyperparameter\(\alpha\)balances their relative contributions. Adjusting\(\alpha\)during training allows for the optimization of the model's performance. This composite loss structure enables the model to simultaneously learn discriminative representations by clustering similar samples and separating dissimilar ones, while also improving the accuracy of catalyst classification. Consequently, this approach enhances the model's overall generalization capability.

To rigorously evaluate the generalization performance of CataCon, we employed two distinct data partition protocols: the original 8:1:1 random split and a chemically more stringent scaffold split, designed specifically to test the model's adaptability to unseen chemistry. The comparative results are summarized in Tables2and3and visualized in Fig.2for the random and scaffold splits, respectively. All reported values represent the mean across three random seeds, with corresponding standard deviations detailed in the tables.

The bars report the mean values of Top 1, Top 3, Top 5, Top 10, F1, Balanced Accuracy, and AUPRC for CataCon and the compared baselines, including graph based variants, the strong non graph Fingerprint MLP baseline, and adapted external baselines

Under the random split, CataCon consistently outperformed all competing methods across all Top-k ranking metrics (k = 1, 3, 5, 10). Notably, it achieved a Top-1 accuracy of 0.4371, surpassing the strongest non-graph internal baseline, Fingerprint MLP (0.4184). CataCon's superiority extends beyond simple ranking accuracy; it also excelled in macro-level metrics that are highly sensitive to class imbalance. Specifically, the model recorded the highest Macro F1 (0.3535), Balanced Accuracy (0.3528), and AUPRC (0.3853). These results demonstrate CataCon's robust overall performance when compared against both strong fingerprint-based baselines and other adapted external models.

As expected, the chemically demanding scaffold split led to an overall performance degradation across all models, confirming the increased difficulty of this evaluation protocol. Nevertheless, CataCon maintained its clear competitive edge. It achieved a Top-1 accuracy of 0.3827, significantly outperforming Fingerprint MLP (0.3536), the Parrot adaptation (0.2374), and the Morgan MTNN adaptation (0.2729). Furthermore, CataCon retained the highest scores for Macro F1 (0.3046), Balanced Accuracy (0.3060), and AUPRC (0.3235) in this rigorous setting. This sustained advantage indicates that CataCon's performance gains are not merely artifacts of preprocessing or graph backbone selection, but stem from genuine improvements in handling complex, out-of-distribution chemical scenarios.

Taken together, the results from both partition protocols confirm that CataCon's strengths are not restricted to memorizing familiar reaction patterns from random splits. Its resilient performance under the rigorous scaffold split strongly validates its enhanced generalization capabilities.

To quantify the specific contribution of each architectural component within CataCon, we conducted comprehensive ablation experiments under both the random and scaffold splits. As summarized in Tables4and5and visualized in Fig.3, the complete CataCon model delivered the optimal performance across primary ranking metrics, Macro F1, Balanced Accuracy, and AUPRC in both settings, verifying the necessity of each integrated module.

Ablation analysis of CataCon under the scaffold split and the random split.a. Ablation results under the scaffold split.b. Ablation results under the random split. The bars report the mean values of Top 1, Top 3, Top 5, Top 10, F1, Balanced Accuracy, and AUPRC for the full model and the ablated variants, including removal of contrastive learning, GRU based fusion, reactant information, and product information

In the random split, the removal of the contrastive learning module led to notable performance penalties: Top-1 accuracy dropped from 0.4371 to 0.3982, Macro F1 from 0.3535 to 0.2931, Balanced Accuracy from 0.3528 to 0.3032, and AUPRC from 0.3853 to 0.3387. Removing either the GRU-based fusion module or the product information resulted in similar declines in Top-1 accuracy (yielding 0.3648 and 0.3643, respectively). The most drastic deterioration occurred when reactant information was excluded, which plummeted the Top-1 accuracy to 0.2394 and Macro F1 to 0.1484. These findings highlight that contrastive alignment, GRU-based feature fusion, and the synergistic utilization of both reactant and product data are all indispensable to the model's predictive success.

This dependency pattern held remarkably true under the harder scaffold split. Compared to the intact model's Top-1 accuracy of 0.3827, removing contrastive learning (0.3441), the GRU module (0.3309), product data (0.3217), or reactant data (0.1880) all resulted in marked performance drops. The full architecture also preserved its lead in Macro F1 (0.3046), Balanced Accuracy (0.3060), and AUPRC (0.3235). While certain ablated variants occasionally edged higher on specific auxiliary metrics, the complete model consistently dominated the most critical evaluation criteria, proving its robustness even under chemically stringent conditions.

In conclusion, the ablation analysis establishes two key points: first, the comprehensive CataCon architecture consistently yields the best overall performance regardless of data partitioning; second, the model's superiority is not driven by any single component, but rather emerges from the synergistic integration of contrastive alignment, GRU-based fusion, and comprehensive reaction data.

To evaluate the feature representation capability of the CataCon model and enhance its interpretability, this study employs t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) for visualization analysis. t-SNE is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction method commonly used in high-dimensional data analysis, effectively preserving the local structure of data to clearly reveal the distribution patterns of high-dimensional features in a low-dimensional space. This method is particularly well-suited for analyzing sample clustering in complex feature spaces, providing an intuitive means to understand the feature information learned by the model.

In this study, t-SNE was applied to visualize the dimensionality reduction of outputs from the CataCon model's molecular feature extraction module. The objective was to explore the distribution of features learned by the model and analyze similarities and differences among samples [47,48,49]. This approach reveals clustering patterns of different feature categories in the embedded space, thereby evaluating the model's discriminative capability and generalization performance. Additionally, t-SNE can be used to detect whether the features extracted by the model possess reasonable separability, providing important references for model optimization.

As shown in Fig.4, samples from 10 categories were randomly selected from the test set, with 10 data points per category, and input into the trained model to obtain feature representations. Subsequently, t-SNE was applied to reduce the dimensionality and visualize the extracted high-dimensional feature matrix, enabling more intuitive observation of the data distribution characteristics and the latent patterns learned by the model. The t-SNE visualization reveals the overall distribution of the catalyst prediction model based on contrastive learning after dimensionality reduction. This model forms a high-dimensional representation by concatenating catalytic reaction features (derived from the fusion of reactant and product features) with catalyst features. t-SNE is then applied for dimensionality reduction to explore its intrinsic clustering structure. The visualization reveals distinct cluster distributions for different categories within the t-SNE space, indicating the model's learned features possess strong discriminative power. The compactness of intra-category clustering reflects the model's consistency in handling similar samples, while the pronounced separation between categories further validates the model's ability to distinguish different catalyst types. This distinct clustering structure indicates that the model's contrastive learning strategy effectively enhances feature discriminability, causing catalytically similar reactions to cluster more tightly in the low-dimensional space while maintaining good separation between samples of different categories. Notably, some categories exhibit relatively compact point distributions, potentially indicating higher consistency among catalysts within that category in the feature space. Conversely, certain categories show significant internal dispersion, which may correlate with the diversity of catalysts across different reaction systems. These distribution characteristics not only provide a basis for further analyzing the clustering quality of specific categories but also aid in evaluating the model's generalization capability across different catalyst types.

t-SNE visualization of learned feature representations for 10 randomly selected catalyst categories

In summary, the t-SNE analysis provides strong qualitative evidence of the model's learning capabilities and offers valuable insights for its further optimization. This visualization confirms CataCon's effectiveness in both feature extraction and classification, establishing it as a promising tool for future catalyst design and screening.

To illustrate the model's practical application, we conducted a case study on a randomly selected reaction from the test set, as depicted in Fig.5. The SMILES strings of the reactant and product were first preprocessed and converted into molecular graph representations to capture their topological and chemical features. This graph-based input was then fed into the trained CataCon model, which in turn generated a ranked list of predicted catalyst candidates for the given reaction.

Case study of a randomly selected catalytic reaction

As detailed in Table6, the model's top-10 predictions for the selected reaction were led by CCO.[Pd], which precisely matched the ground truth catalyst. This successful identification underscores the model's accuracy in pinpointing suitable catalyst classes.

A deeper analysis of the ranked list reveals that the model has learned chemically meaningful structural relationships. The majority of the high-ranking candidates, including CCO.[C].[Pd] and CCO.O.[Pd], retained the core [Pd] center while exhibiting variations in their ligand structures, often involving functional groups similar to CCO. This pattern suggests that the model not only recognizes the essential catalytic core but also explores a chemically relevant space of ligand modifications that modulate electronic and steric properties.

In conclusion, this case study demonstrates that the CataCon model functions beyond simple classification. It accurately identifies known catalysts and, more importantly, generates a ranked list of structurally similar and potentially viable alternatives. This capability to produce a rational set of candidates highlights the model's practical utility in guiding catalyst design and optimization, thereby providing a solid foundation for subsequent experimental validation.

To gain deeper insights into the predictive boundaries of CataCon and understand the specific scenarios where the model excels or struggles, we conducted a granular error analysis. This analysis was performed on the rigorous product-scaffold split to reflect true out-of-distribution generalization behavior. We systematically investigated the best- and worst-performing catalyst classes, the most frequent confusion pairs, and the sensitivity of the model to specific product scaffolds.

First, an examination of class-level performance (Supplementary Table S1) reveals that CataCon performs exceptionally well on several catalyst classes characterized by distinctive structural signatures and adequate training support. However, the model struggles with certain catalyst categories where the Top-1 recall drops to zero. A closer inspection indicates that many of these worst-performing classes belong to highly structurally similar families, particularly Palladium-based (Pd-based) catalysts with minor ligand variations.

To understand the underlying mechanism of these misclassifications, we analyzed the most frequent confusion pairs (Supplementary Table S2). The results highlight a clear pattern: the vast majority of residual errors are concentrated among closely related Pd-based catalyst choices. For example, frequent errors involve predicting CO.[Pd] when the true catalyst is CCO.[Pd], CCOC(C) = O.[Pd], or simply [Pd]. This phenomenon suggests that while the contrastive learning framework successfully identifies the essential catalytic active center (the [Pd] core), it occasionally exhibits a tendency to collapse similar, less frequent catalyst variants toward the most statistically common Pd prototype in the training distribution. This indicates that distinguishing minor electronic or steric differences in ligands remains a frontier challenge.

Finally, we evaluated the model's performance across different product scaffolds (Supplementary Table S3). The analysis demonstrates that while CataCon accurately solves transformations for many complex backbones, certain specific scaffolds consistently yield poor predictions, even when they possess reasonable representation in the training set. This suggests that the inherent chemical difficulty of the transformation plays a significant role in predictive accuracy alongside data sparsity. In summary, while CataCon achieves state-of-the-art performance in overall catalyst prediction, its primary limitation lies in the occasional inability to perfectly discriminate between highly homologous ligand structures within the same metal family. Future optimizations could incorporate 3D conformational features or quantum chemical descriptors to further enhance the model's resolution for fine-grained ligand distinctions.

This study provides a detailed exploration of the design, experimental evaluation, and practical application of the CataCon catalyst prediction framework. To rigorously validate the model's effectiveness and generalization capacity, comparative experiments were conducted under both standard random splits and chemically stringent product-scaffold splits. Results demonstrate that CataCon achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple Top-k and macro-level evaluation metrics, consistently outperforming not only alternative graph backbones (e.g., GCN, GIN, GAT variants) but also strong non-graph baselines (Fingerprint MLP) and adapted modern reaction encoders (Parrot, Morgan MTNN, and TextReact). Furthermore, the proposed contrastive loss function significantly enhances the distinction between positive and negative samples, strengthening the model's overarching predictive capability.

Ablation experiments further confirmed the necessity of each architectural component. Complete reactant and product information proved crucial for accurate catalyst prediction, while the GRU module effectively integrated cross-side feature dependencies. Synergistically, the contrastive learning mechanism empowered the model's discriminative capacity, preventing performance collapse under out-of-distribution scenarios.

To enhance model interpretability, t-SNE visualization revealed distinct clustering distributions of catalyst categories in the embedding space. In specific case studies, CataCon not only accurately predicted the ground-truth catalysts but also generated rational lists of structurally homologous candidates. Finally, a granular error analysis provided transparent insights into the model's boundaries, highlighting the ongoing challenge of perfectly discriminating between highly similar ligand variations within the same metal family. Overall, this study systematically validates CataCon as a robust and highly effective tool for catalyst prediction, offering a powerful data-driven foundation for future intelligent chemical synthesis and material discovery.

title: Revisiting ADMET prediction reliability under real-world challenges in the foundation model era
author: Donghai Zhao; Yuchen Zhu; Zhenxing Wu; Yue Wan; Xiaonan Liu; Shuaiyan Li; Hongxia Xu; Tingjun Hou; Chang-Yu Hsieh
text:
As AI-driven drug discovery fully enters the era of foundation models, druggability prediction is undergoing a profound transformation from being experience-driven to “data-driven.” While numerous molecular foundation models with diverse representation capabilities have emerged, there remains a lack of systematic empirical mapping regarding their frontier boundaries and intrinsic limitations when faced with real-world drug discovery challenges. To this end, this study establishes a testing benchmark encompassing four major challenges—data scarcity and Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization, class imbalance, “beyond Rule of 5” (bRo5) chemical space generalization, and activity cliffs—to perform large-scale benchmarking on cutting-edge architectures such as molecular foundation models (KPGT, Uni-Mol) and tabular foundation models (TabPFNv2). Our analysis reveals the current frontiers and limitations of the molecular AI field: in few-shot and OOD scenarios, the tabular foundation model TabPFNv2 demonstrates superior generalization capabilities that often outperform those of the evaluated customized molecular foundation models; to address extreme class imbalance, ensemble strategies based on undersampling provide a robust mitigation approach with a reasonable trade-off between recall and precision; and within complex bRo5 chemical spaces, the pre-trained Graph Neural Network (GNN) KPGT achieves higher predictive accuracy compared to other tested architectures in predicting cyclic peptide permeability when provided with sufficient samples. However, all model categories consistently struggle to effectively identify activity cliffs, highlighting a persistent challenge for the AI architectures evaluated in this study to capture the phenomenon where minute structural variations lead to dramatic shifts in properties. To tackle these complex real-world challenges, this study confirms that ensembling high-performance models of different modalities is an effective strategy for improving predictive robustness. Furthermore, to facilitate the low-cost screening and construction of the high-quality base models needed for such ensembles, we validated that the molecular property landscape roughness index can serve as a lightweight diagnostic tool. Taken together, these insights provide practical guidance for the evaluation and selection of contemporary druggability prediction models.

Scientific contribution

This study establishes a systematic benchmark framework for druggability prediction, simulating four key real-world drug discovery scenarios—including the underexplored generalization challenge in the bRo5 chemical space—and comprehensively evaluating molecular foundation models, the tabular foundation model TabPFNv2, GNNs, Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) framework, and classical machine learning approaches, thereby overcoming limitations of prior benchmarks in task diversity and model coverage. Through large-scale train–evaluation cycles, the study reveals both scenario-specific strengths of different models and their persistent shared weaknesses. Beyond benchmarking, it demonstrates that ensembling different types of models improves predictive performance and that the molecular property landscape roughness index serves as a low-cost tool for selecting high-quality models, offering more actionable insights than previous comparison studies.

In drug research, the absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties of candidates are critical determinants of clinical success [1]. Despite substantial annual investments [2,3], the success rate of new drug development remains low [4], with up to 50% of clinical trial failures attributed to poor ADMET profiles [1]. This highlights an urgent need for predictive models that not only achieve high accuracy but also remain reliable under the complex, data-limited, and chemically diverse conditions encountered in real-world drug discovery [5]. In recent years, machine learning has emerged as a key enabler in this space [6,7], evolving from classic algorithms [8,9] using expert-designed features to end-to-end deep learning architectures like Graph Neural Networks [10,11] (GNNs), which learn directly from molecular structures. The field has since entered the era of molecular foundation models, where large-scale pretraining yields representations capable of generalizing across endpoints and chemical classes [12,13,14,15,16]. Pretrained GNNs such as KPGT [17], MOLMCL [18], and Uni-Mol [19] have reported strong performance on widely used benchmarks [20,21]. At the same time, advanced tabular models—most notably TabPFNv2 [23]—have achieved remarkable success in structured data domains and present an underexplored but promising direction for molecular property prediction. Yet, despite this progress, fundamental questions remain unanswered. How well do these modern architectures perform under the real-world constraints of drug discovery, including (i) data scarcity and Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization [24,25]; (ii) pervasive class imbalance [26]; (iii) activity cliffs, where small structural perturbations yield ≥ 100-fold changes in biological activity, violating smoothness assumptions in standard learning algorithms [27,28]; and (iv) the increasing shift toward “beyond Rule of 5” (bRo5) molecules, such as macrocycles and peptide-like compounds [29,30]. While a number of valuable studies on the potentials and limitations of deep molecular learning models exist [27,31,32,33,34,35], most have not evaluated foundation models under a unified framework that simultaneously incorporates OOD shifts, activity cliffs, and the bRo5 chemical space. Furthermore, prior studies often freeze pretrained embeddings without task-specific fine-tuning and evaluate only a narrow set of endpoints or architectures. In addition, models like TabPFNv2, which adapt techniques from the large language modeling to structured tabular inputs, have not yet been systematically evaluated in the realm of molecular science. In short, we still lack an actionable guidance on the model selection and evaluation of this fast-evolving landscape of molecular property predictions. To identify reliable modeling methods for real-world drug discovery scenarios and to enhance the understanding of the progress made by advanced deep learning techniques (such as the pre-trained GNN KPGT and TabPFNv2) at the frontiers of AI4Science, we conducted a systematic and thorough benchmarking study, the overall framework of which is illustrated in Fig.1.

Protocol for the systematic evaluation of ADMET models

To this end, we established a comprehensive evaluation benchmark encompassing data scarcity, class imbalance, activity cliffs, and the bRo5 chemical space (cyclic and linear peptides), systematically evaluating representative architectures including molecular/tabular foundation models, GNNs, Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) framework, and classical algorithms. Based on the robust evaluation of extensive model weights, this study clearly delineates the ADMET prediction landscape in the era of foundation models: (1) in small-sample scenarios characterized by data scarcity, the tabular foundation model TabPFNv2 demonstrates superior generalization capabilities that surpass those of customized deep learning models; (2) to address the challenge of class imbalance, ensemble strategies based on undersampling prove to be a robust and effective mitigation solution; (3) within the bRo5 space, pre-trained graph models (e.g., KPGT) exhibit leading performance on handling complex macrocyclic topologies, whereas expert features combined with tabular models remain highly competitive and advantageous for linear peptide tasks with limited data; and (4) accurately capturing activity cliffs remains a persistent challenge for the AI architectures evaluated in this study. To tackle these challenges, we not only confirm that ensembling algorithms with orthogonal advantages can significantly enhance predictive robustness but also validate that molecular property landscape roughness indices can serve as a lightweight diagnostic tool for the low-cost screening of high-quality pre-trained representations.

Together, these contributions provide both practical guidance for selecting and combining AI models in drug discovery and conceptual insights into the next-generation challenges that must be addressed to advance molecular machine learning.

To rigorously and comprehensively evaluate the performance of various druggability prediction models in real-world drug discovery scenarios, we meticulously constructed a benchmarking test set covering ADMET properties (the types, scales, and core biological descriptions of each dataset are summarized in Table1). This benchmark is designed to recapitulate the core challenges inherent in real-world drug discovery. Regarding data scarcity and OOD generalization, as shown in Fig.2a, we selected eight representative ADMET datasets, including hERG, Mutagenicity, BBBP, HLM Metabolic Stability, Oral Bioavailability, Caco2 cell permeability, Half-Life, and VDss. Among these, the latter four datasets—each with a sample size of fewer than 2000—centrally reflect the typical extreme data scarcity bottlenecks in drug development. On these datasets, we designed three data-splitting strategies of increasing difficulty—Random Split, Scaffold Split, and Perimeter Split (based on maximum distance pair selection)—to simulate escalating OOD extrapolation challenges. Taking BBBP as an example (Fig.2b; for chemical space distributions of other datasets, see Supplementary Fig. 1), a distinct chemical space distribution shift between the test and training sets emerges as we move from Random Split to Scaffold Split and finally to Perimeter Split. To address the challenge of class imbalance, as shown in Fig.2c, the benchmark includes the Tox21 NR ER dataset, with a positive-to-negative ratio as high as 1:7, as well as the CYP2C9 substrate and CYP2D6 inhibitor datasets characterized by significant class imbalance, aiming to strictly test the predictive robustness of models under such conditions. Furthermore, in terms of generalizing across complex chemical spaces that break the bRo5, we specifically introduced a cyclic peptide permeability dataset (CycPept-PAMPA) and linear peptide datasets (LinPept-NonFouling and LinPept-CellPen). The extremely high molecular weight (Fig.2d) and conformational flexibility of these molecules present unprecedented challenges to the structural perception capabilities of existing models.

Molecules were represented using Morgan fingerprints and reduced to two dimensions via multidimensional scaling (MDS), with the third dimension indicating the respective molecular property. The landscapes were generated using the code provided by Coley et al. [36]

Although the aforementioned ADMET datasets can examine a model’s generalization ability within the macro-chemical space, in actual lead optimization processes, key ADMET attributes—much like biological activity—often face a microscopic pain point that violates the “similar structure, similar property” assumption: “activity cliffs.” In these regions, minor modifications to the molecular scaffold lead to unpredictable and drastic mutations in pharmacokinetic or toxicological profiles. To rigorously test whether models possess the capability to accurately capture these local microscopic mutations, we introduced the MoleculeACE benchmark [27], which contains 30 highly non-linear activity prediction tasks, to complete a comprehensive assessment of the models’ integrated capabilities. Additionally, we utilized Multi-Dimensional Scaling (MDS) to plot 3D molecular property landscapes for four representative regression tasks (Fig.2e), intuitively demonstrating the intrinsic modeling difficulty of these benchmark datasets. It is clearly visible from these plots that the property landscapes for Half-Life, VDss, and the ChEMBL218_EC50 dataset in MoleculeACE are extremely rugged and rough. This widespread non-linear mutation (i.e., activity cliffs) indicates that building highly robust predictive models on these benchmarks will face significant challenges.

After establishing the evaluation benchmarks described above, we conducted a systematic assessment of mainstream druggability prediction models to re-examine and delineate the frontier boundaries and real-world limitations of prediction in the era of foundation models. In the field of end-to-end deep learning, we focused on evaluating large-scale pre-trained molecular foundation models represented by KPGT, Uni-Mol, and GEM, alongside various other advanced GNN architectures. Within the expert-descriptor-based modeling pathway, we not only examined classical machine learning algorithms such as Random Forest and XGBoost but also introduced TabPFNv2, a pre-trained tabular foundation model optimized for small-sample scenarios, and AutoGluon, an AutoML framework that integrates multiple classical algorithms. To ensure the scientific validity of the performance comparisons, we adopted unified evaluation metrics: classification tasks utilize the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (ROC AUC), which is independent of prediction thresholds; for regression tasks, we discarded the Pearson correlation coefficient, which is insufficiently sensitive to systematic bias, and consistently adopted the R2to more accurately reflect the true predictive bias and variance explanation power of the models under extreme challenges.

In addressing the dual real-world challenges of data scarcity and structural distribution shift (OOD), our evaluation reveals a critical performance divergence: large-scale pre-trained molecular foundation models, represented by KPGT, exhibit leading performance on tasks with relatively sufficient data, whereas the general-purpose tabular foundation model (TabPFNv2) demonstrates exceptional performance in few-shot OOD scenarios, surpassing various end-to-end molecular deep learning models. Given the myriad of complex combinations between classical machine learning algorithms and molecular representations, we conducted rigorous preliminary screening to ensure a clear and focused presentation in subsequent evaluations, specifically selecting high-performing and highly representative combinations for the final comparison (see Supplementary Fig. 2 for screening performance evidence). First, when cross-comparing various predictors using a unified feature set (RDKit 2D) (Supplementary Fig. 2a), XGBoost and CatBoost exhibited excellent and highly robust performance among classical algorithms, in addition to the advanced pre-trained tabular foundation model (TabPFNv2) and the AutoML framework (AutoGluon). Considering that XGBoost maintains a predictive accuracy similar to CatBoost while offering higher computational and operational efficiency at equivalent parameter scales (Supplementary Table 8), we ultimately selected XGBoost as the unified downstream predictor to comprehensively test 13 different molecular representations (Supplementary Fig. 2b). The results indicate that Mordred and RDKit 2D are the top-performing expert descriptors, KPGT Repr is the most informative feature extracted from pre-trained models, and MorganCount is a superior classical topological fingerprint. Consequently, we integrated the combinations of these four representative representations with XGBoost into the final evaluation framework as baseline models for the classical machine learning pathway. Furthermore, given the input feature dimensionality constraints of the general tabular foundation model TabPFNv2 (which requires fewer than 500 dimensions) and the computational cost associated with high-dimensional features in AutoGluon, we consistently utilized RDKit 2D—which performed exceptionally well in the aforementioned tests—as the core input for both TabPFNv2 and AutoGluon to ensure fairness and feasibility in our comparisons.

Following the establishment of this evaluation framework centered on XGBoost, TabPFNv2, AutoGluon, and representative deep learning algorithms, we conducted a comprehensive assessment across eight representative ADMET datasets (results in Fig.3; detailed results in Supplementary Fig. 3). Notably, as the evaluation benchmark shifts from the identically distributed Random Split to the Perimeter Split, all models inevitably experienced a decline in overall predictive performance due to the significant increase in structural distribution shift difficulty (Fig.3a–f). Nevertheless, among the end-to-end deep learning models, pre-trained models such as KPGT and MOLMCL maintained relatively robust resistance to these shifts. In contrast, standard GNNs, along with GNNAK—designed to enhance local topological expression—and the recently introduced Kolmogorov-Arnold Network-based KA-GNN, showed more significant performance drops in OOD scenarios despite acceptable performance under identical distributions, primarily due to a lack of macro-level prior knowledge provided by large-scale pre-training.

Furthermore, the model ranking heatmap in Fig.3g, arranged by dataset size (from largest to smallest), clearly illustrates that as sample sizes decrease significantly (e.g., Oral Bioavailability, Half-Life, VDss, and Caco2 at the bottom of the heatmap), the predictive performance of most end-to-end deep learning models deteriorates markedly. In these instances, the general tabular foundation model TabPFNv2 exhibits a prominent performance advantage, ranking first across multiple few-shot datasets. This foundation model, pre-trained on synthetic tabular data, effectively mitigates the risk of overfitting in few-shot scenarios without requiring molecular-specific fine-tuning. Conversely, although AutoGluon performs well under Random and Scaffold Splits, it exhibits a tendency toward overfitting in the Perimeter Split—where structural shifts are more pronounced—likely due to its complex internal greedy ensemble strategy.

In addition to data scarcity and structural distribution shift, class imbalance is another prevalent and severe challenge in druggability modeling. Our assessment reveals that an undersampling-based ensemble strategy is a robust solution for addressing class imbalance, significantly enhancing the recognition capability (recall) of various foundation models and classical algorithms for the minority class, while effectively maintaining a controllable False Positive Rate (FPR). To systematically and extensively validate this conclusion, we selected three datasets with typical imbalance ratios: the CYP2C9 substrate dataset and CYP2D6 inhibitor dataset (positive-to-negative ratio approximately 1:4), and the Tox21 NR ER dataset (positive-to-negative ratio approximately 1:7). To evaluate the effectiveness of different strategies, we selected five representative models: the pre-trained model (KPGT) and GNN (RGCN) representing end-to-end learning, the classical machine learning algorithm (RF), the tabular foundation model (TabPFNv2) which performed excellently in the previous small-sample scenarios, and the AutoML framework (AutoGluon). For these base models, we systematically tested five strategies—unweighted (Unweighted), category weight adjustment (Weighted), oversampling (Oversample), undersampling (Downsample), and undersampling-based ensemble (Ensemble)—and additionally introduced a specific balanced sub-sampling (Subsample) strategy for the RF algorithm (results shown in Fig.4).

The evaluation results (Fig.4) demonstrate a performance divergence among different strategies for addressing class imbalance. In the default state (Unweighted), models tend to be extremely conservative in predicting the minority class due to the severe lack of minority samples, resulting in very low recall for the positive samples. However, when the undersampling-based ensemble strategy is employed, the minority class recall for all model architectures is significantly improved. In contrast, using category weight adjustment alone provides only a limited improvement in recall, while the oversampling strategy exhibits substantial volatility and instability in several experiments. Considering that pursuing improved recall alone might lead models to over-predict positive samples, thereby causing a higher FPR, we further evaluated the practical reliability of each strategy in conjunction with the FPR heatmap in Fig.4d. The results indicate that the ensemble strategy does not blindly sacrifice specificity for recall; instead, it successfully maintains the FPR within a reasonable and controllable range. When comparing different base models, KPGT often yields the highest F1 score (Fig.4c) and demonstrates prominent performance potential when combined with the ensemble strategy. Specifically, in the CYP2C9 and CYP2D6 tasks, the KPGT-ensemble combination not only achieved leading recall (0.64 and 0.80, respectively) but also suppressed the FPR to the lowest level among all evaluated models (0.38 and 0.16, respectively). In the Tox21 NR ER task, its recall jumped significantly from 0.22 to 0.60, while the FPR was maintained at 0.27. This suggests that the macro-level chemical prior knowledge embedded within KPGT allows it to reshape decision boundaries more accurately than standard GNNs or tabular models after receiving balanced class signals, effectively suppressing false positive warnings while enhancing the identification rate of the minority class. Considering all metrics comprehensively, the ensemble strategy demonstrates excellent robustness, achieving a balance between predictive precision and recall. In early drug discovery tasks where the cost of “missing a hit” is high, it is a rational choice that meets real-world industrial needs to accept a moderate decrease in precision in exchange for a higher identification rate of minority classes, such as toxic molecules.

Modern drug discovery is increasingly expanding into the bRo5 chemical space. These molecules typically possess higher molecular weights, more complex topologies, and greater conformational flexibility, posing significant challenges to traditional modeling methods. To systematically evaluate the structural generalization capabilities of representative models in complex chemical spaces, we selected the cyclic peptide permeability dataset (CycPept-PAMPA) [37], the linear peptide anti-fouling dataset (LinPept-NonFouling) [38], and the linear peptide cell permeability dataset (LinPept-CellPen) [39] as evaluation benchmarks. Our evaluation results reveal that in scenarios with sufficient data and complex cyclic topologies, pre-trained GNNs exhibit leading performance due to their global perception capabilities. Conversely, in data-scarce linear peptide tasks, the combination of high-quality expert features and tabular foundation models continues to demonstrate a competitive advantage.

The evaluation results (Fig.5) intuitively display the performance of each model under rigorous splitting strategies. In tasks with relatively sufficient sample sizes, end-to-end deep learning models show significant advantages. Specifically, in the CycPept-PAMPA task containing 6637 samples, the pre-trained model KPGT achieved the best performance (R2= 0.627), followed closely by GNNAK (R2= 0.605), indicating that the topological priors of graph models can be effectively transferred to cyclic peptide modeling. On the linear peptide dataset LinPept-NonFouling (7239 samples), the hybrid architecture D-MPNN & RDKit 2D, which merges expert descriptors, performed best (ROC AUC = 0.770), while KPGT (0.769) and GEM (0.768) performed comparably. Overall, models based on 2D molecular graphs generally outperform 1D sequence models (such as K-BERT, which ranked last in this task). Whether through the introduction of physicochemical descriptors or via large-scale self-supervised pre-training, the representation capability of models in specific complex chemical spaces can be effectively enhanced. Furthermore, on the smaller-scale linear peptide permeability task (LinPept-CellPen, 1960 samples), the tabular foundation model TabPFNv2 and the AutoML framework AutoGluon, combined with RDKit 2D descriptors, achieved leading predictive performance (both reaching ROC AUC = 0.972), with the classical machine learning algorithm XGBoost (0.970) also performing excellently. This not only proves that in peptide chemical spaces with clear features, high-quality expert features combined with tabular predictors remain highly competitive, but also further corroborates the findings in section "The dual challenge of small dataset and structural distribution shift"—that advanced tabular models possess a prominent generalization advantage in low-data scenarios. Notably, the two representative models incorporating 3D conformational information (GEM and Uni-Mol) showed significant differences on bRo5 molecules. GEM, a GNN based on local geometric structures (such as bond lengths and angles), performed well on the two linear peptide tasks (ranking 3rd and 6th, respectively), suggesting that the introduction of local 3D information helps capture the spatial features of linear molecules. However, the pre-trained model Uni-Mol, which relies heavily on global static 3D coordinates, lagged overall across all bRo5 tasks (e.g., ranking last at 19th in LinPept-CellPen and only 11th in CycPept-PAMPA). In fact, even the better-performing GEM saw its performance drop significantly to 9th place when facing cyclic peptides with complex macrocyclic folding states (CycPept-PAMPA). This phenomenon reflects an intrinsic limitation of current mainstream 3D modeling methods: bRo5 molecules (especially macrocycles and peptides) typically exist as highly dynamic multi-conformational ensembles in real biological environments. If a model relies solely on a single static low-energy conformation as input, it is often difficult to accurately characterize their complex structure–activity relationships. Therefore, developing algorithmic architectures that can effectively represent dynamic conformational flexibility is an urgent priority for future complex molecule modeling.

While the aforementioned ADMET datasets effectively evaluate the generalization capabilities of models in the macro-chemical space, the actual lead optimization process often reveals a microscopic “Achilles’ heel”—activity cliffs—where pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiles, much like biological activity, violate the “similar structure, similar property” principle. In these localized regions of the chemical space, minor modifications to the molecular scaffold trigger unpredictable and dramatic shifts in biological properties. To rigorously test the ability of existing models to capture these local microscopic mutations, we introduced the MoleculeACE benchmark, which includes 30 highly non-linear activity prediction tasks, aiming to conduct a comprehensive assessment of various representative models. Our benchmarking results highlight a widespread and severe limitation: current mainstream druggability prediction models struggle to effectively and robustly capture these sharp, localized transitions in the structure–activity relationship (SAR).

From the perspective of overall predictive performance (Fig.6a), the pre-trained model KPGT achieved the highest overall performance (R2= 0.678). Meanwhile, classical machine learning models using expert features (XGBoost & MorganCount, R2= 0.668) and the tabular foundation model (TabPFNv2 & RDKit 2D, R2= 0.649) also demonstrated highly competitive predictive levels. In contrast, GNNs that require training from scratch, such as RGCN, AttentiveFP, and GNNAK, performed poorly, further underscoring the vital importance of pre-training for end-to-end deep learning models. Although some models performed well on aggregate metrics, they all revealed consistent limitations when distinguishing between activity cliff and non-activity-cliff molecules (definition in MethodAlgorithm selection). As shown in Fig.6b, predictive accuracy for all models was generally high for non-activity-cliff molecules but plummeted for activity cliff molecules. For instance, although XGBoost & MorganCount achieved the highest R2on activity cliff molecules (0.51), this was still significantly lower than its performance on non-activity-cliff molecules (0.69); KPGT’s R2on activity cliff molecules similarly dropped to 0.46.

To conduct an even more rigorous test, we further evaluated the recall of activity cliff pairs (defined as structure similarity ≥ 0.7 and activity difference ≥ 100, with success defined as predicting a difference of at least two orders of magnitude), as shown in Fig.6c. The results show that no model achieved satisfactory recall. Aside from the top two performers, MOLMCL (0.130) and KPGT (0.128), all other models had recall rates below 10%. Notably, pre-trained models incorporating 3D conformational information, such as Uni-Mol and GEM, underperformed in this task (recalls of 0.098 and 0.026, respectively). This again reflects a major flaw in current 3D modeling paradigms: they typically rely on a single, static low-energy conformation generated by tools like RDKit as input. Such static conformations, lacking molecular dynamics optimization, often fail to accurately reflect the dynamic binding states and subtle conformational differences that trigger activity mutations in real biological environments. The slight advantage shown by MOLMCL may be attributed to its unique “molecule-scaffold” contrastive pre-training strategy and a fine-tuning mechanism based on landscape roughness indices, which prompts the model to pay more attention to minor structural changes. However, objectively speaking, neither end-to-end deep learning nor advanced tabular foundation models have fundamentally solved the challenge of activity cliff identification. This universal failure highlights a core limitation in the current field of molecular property prediction: the lack of a mechanism to effectively capture sharp local discontinuities in the structure–activity space. This remains a critical blind spot that next-generation molecular representation algorithms must break through.

In the era of foundation models, to mitigate the severe challenges of druggability prediction in real-world scenarios, we validated a simple yet effective strategy at the model-building level: ensembling models that possess different modal representation capabilities and strong performance. As shown in Fig.7a, for challenges involving data scarcity, OOD generalization, and the structurally complex bRo5 space, we ensembled the pre-trained model KPGT, which captures 2D topological features, with the 3D geometric model GEM to achieve complementary advantages between topological and spatial information. For the MoleculeACE benchmark, we integrated KPGT with the expert-feature-based XGBoost & MorganCount to fuse data-driven deep representations with precise human-prior substructure matching. Experimental results demonstrate that this ensemble strategy, which merges orthogonal advantages, robustly outperforms the single best model in various challenge scenarios. Specifically, this strategy achieved a performance gain of approximately 5% on the Caco2 permeability task and improved the average R2across the 30 MoleculeACE datasets from 0.68 to 0.70. The only exception was the CycPept-PAMPA task, where the ensemble model’s R2decreased slightly from 0.63 to 0.61. This minor discrepancy is attributed to GEM’s inherent limitations in handling highly flexible macrocyclic molecules. Furthermore, it is important to note that while this cross-modal ensemble excels in addressing structural representation and generalization difficulties, its direct performance gain in mitigating extreme class imbalance challenges is marginal (see Supplementary Fig. 6.4). This phenomenon further corroborates our conclusion in section "The challenge of class imbalance": the core of addressing data distribution imbalance lies in reshaping the decision boundary, making the data-level undersampling-based ensemble strategy a much more targeted solution. Taken together, the overall performance enhancement proves that strategic ensembling of algorithmic architectures or sampling mechanisms with complementary strengths is a reliable path for alleviating performance bottlenecks and enhancing model robustness in druggability prediction.
