In drug discovery, computational screening is commonly used to identify known compounds as potential drugs or lead compounds for further development [1,2,3]. This process, known as virtual screening (VS), is broadly classified into two main approaches: ligand-based virtual screening (LBVS) and structure-based virtual screening (SBVS). LBVS identifies ligands in a library that have some similarity to known template active molecules [4,5], whereas SBVS selects ligands that are compatible with a target receptor pocket in terms of the geometry or energetics [6,7,8]. Unlike LBVS, SBVS leverages receptor structures and does not require prior knowledge of known drugs. Consequently, SBVS tends to identify a more diverse set of compounds compared to LBVS.

Most SBVS methods, particularly docking programs, rely on force field-based scoring functions to calculate binding energy. In this approach, the Gibbs binding free energy (ΔGbind) of a protein–ligand complex is determined as the sum of atomic pair interaction energies, which depend on interatomic distances. While widely used, this method has notable limitations, particularly its sensitivity to receptor conformational changes. As a result, even minor receptor structure variations can significantly impact predictions, often leading to failures, especially when a predicted receptor protein structure or apo structure is used [9,10,11,12]. Guterres et al. [11] employed AutoDock Vina to assess the efficacy of docking and virtual screening on apo and holo structure pairs. The mean ligand root-mean-square-distance (RMSD) increased from 1.34 Å to 3.65 Å, while the enrichment factor at 1% (EF1%) decreased from 10.0 to 3.5 when the receptor structure was changed from holo to apo form. In a similar vein, AlphaFold predicted models exhibited an estimated 40% of holo structures EF1% (20.5 to 8.8) [12]. Despite these limitations, SBVS is increasingly utilized because it provides an atomic-level view of compound-receptor interactions, offering direct insights for downstream lead optimization. Additionally, the growing availability of receptor structures, through cryo-electron microscopy and structure prediction methods, further supports its adoption.

Previously, we introduced PL-PatchSurfer2 (PL-PS2) [10], a novel SBVS program designed to overcome the limitations of traditional methods. Instead of relying on atomic details, this program captures protein–ligand complementarity using a surface patch description. The receptor’s binding pocket and the ligand are segmented into overlapping patches, each assigned four physicochemical properties: shape, electrostatic potential, hydrogen bonding, and hydrophobicity. These properties are then encoded using the three-dimensional Zernike descriptor (3DZD) [13,14], representing coefficients from a series expansion of Zernike basis functions. The rotational invariance of 3DZD allows for shape comparisons without requiring structural alignment. 3DZD has been successfully applied to various biological problems, including protein–protein docking [15,16,17], protein–protein interface comparison [18], ligand-ligand comparison [19], pocket-pocket comparison [20,21,22], electron density maps from electron microscopy [23,24], and protein structure similarity search [25,26]. By incorporating 3DZD, PL-PS2 offers advantages in both tolerance to receptor conformational changes and computational efficiency. Benchmarking results demonstrate that our program maintains ~ 80% of the EFs achieved on holo structures when applied to homology-modeled and apo structures, whereas other SBVS programs show significant performance deterioration under these conditions [10]. These findings highlight the effectiveness and robustness of PL-PS2 in VS applications.

Here, we introduce PL-PatchSurfer3 (PL-PS3), an enhanced version of our SBVS program that builds upon PL-PS2 while incorporating key updates. One major improvement is the refinement of the hydrogen bonding term, which can now capture hydrogen bonds more accurately. Additionally, PL-PS3 introduces a new feature called visibility, which enhances the characterization of molecular surfaces by accounting for surface curvature, an aspect not adequately captured by the shape feature alone. By incorporating both, PL-PS3 provides a more comprehensive representation of molecular surface characteristics, improving its ability to capture key molecular interactions and enhance virtual screening performance.

PL-PS3 was benchmarked on the DUD dataset [27], which includes 40 pharmaceutically important targets, active molecules (binders), and decoy compounds (non-binders), demonstrating higher accuracy than existing SBVS methods. We primarily used DUD to be able to compare with benchmark results of PL-PS2, AutoDock Vina, and DOCK6 in our earlier work [10]. The improvement was particularly evident when apo forms of target receptors were used as queries. We further evaluated the method using predicted receptor structures generated by MODELLER [28], AlphaFold2 [29], and AlphaFold3 [30], where PL-PS3 showed higher values in many metrics than PL-PS2, AutoDock Vina, and DOCK6, while showing comparable performance to recent deep learning (DL)-based methods [31,32]. In addition, PL-PS3 was benchmarked against the LIT-PCBA dataset [33], showing a comparable performance to other screening methods including the deep learning-based methods.

The framework of the PL-PS algorithm was described in our previous publications [10,34]. In this section, we briefly introduce the algorithm, focusing on the new features in PL-PS3. The overall workflow of the program is illustrated in Fig.1.

To account for ligand flexibility, a pre-generated set of up to 50 3D conformers was produced using OMEGA [35]. The primary innovation of PL-PS3 lies in its evaluation of surface complementarity between a binding pocket and a ligand. Its surface-based representation is tolerant to minor conformational changes in both the binding pocket and ligands. By employing 3D Zernike descriptors (3DZD), PL-PS3 efficiently compares both the shape and physicochemical properties of the interacting surfaces. The molecular surfaces and their associated electrostatic potentials for both the binding pocket and ligand conformers are computed using the Adaptive Poisson-Boltzmann Solver (APBS) [37]. After generating the molecular surfaces, PL-PS3 calculates surface hydrophobicity, hydrogen bonding potential, and the surface visibility (Fig.1).

PL-PS3 introduces a new feature calledpocket visibility, which quantifies the local curvature of surface points [21,22,38]. Visibility is measured by casting 512 rays from a point of interest (e.g., the bottom of a pocket) and counting the number of rays that are not obstructed by the molecular surface. The visibility is then defined as the fraction of unblocked rays. Lower visibility values indicate that the point lies within a concave region or cavity, whereas higher values suggest that the point is located on a protruding surface.

The concept of visibility was initially introduced for pocket identification in the VisGrid program [38] and was subsequently applied to quantify similarity between binding pockets [21,22]. Similar ray-casting concepts have been applied in other SBVS programs. VolSite [39,40] defines cavities and evaluates buriedness by counting intersections among 120 rays. DARC [41] assesses shape complementarity by computing the ratio of blocked to total rays cast within the binding pocket. The visibility concept introduced in PL-PS3 differs from previous ray-casting approaches in several aspects. First, visibility is defined as the fraction of unblocked rays, providing a continuous descriptor of local surface curvature. Second, PL-PS3 casts rays from surface voxel points rather than all grid points in a 3D lattice, resulting in a surface-centric formulation that naturally aligns with the PL-PS framework, which represents protein–ligand interactions using surface patch descriptors rather than volumetric cavities. Third, the downstream usage differs: in VolSite, ray-casting-derived buriedness is used as a binary criterion for cavity detection or pharmacophore filtering and is not propagated as a scoring feature for virtual screening. In contrast, PL-PS3 encodes visibility values of all surface points within a patch into a 3DZD representation, which is directly used to compute patch complementarity.

Furthermore, we revised the representation of hydrogen bonding complementarity between two surfaces. In PL-PS2, voxels close to a hydrogen donor or acceptor atom are assigned a value of 1 or -1, respectively, and 0 otherwise, and assigned values on a surface are converted into a 3DZD. In PL-PS3, we simply compare the number of hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor voxels of local surface patches to capture a global compatibility of two surface patches to form hydrogen bonds. We revised it because the previous representation occasionally imposed overly strict constraints on the positions of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors. Additionally, we found that the Euclidean distance used for comparing hydrogen bonding 3DZD descriptors penalized cases too severely when a patch lacking hydrogen bonding character was matched with one that possessed it.

After assigning all characteristics, electrostatic potential, hydrophobicity, visibility, and hydrogen bonding, to the surface points, the molecular surface of each conformation is divided into overlapping patches. This process begins by selecting seed points, which serve as the centers of the patches. A minimum distance of 3 Å is maintained between seed points to ensure even coverage. Around each seed point, a sphere with a radius of 5 Å is defined, establishing the boundary of each surface patch.

The dimension of 3DZD is determined by the order n. By setting n = 15, PL-PS3 has a 72-dimensional vector.

The performance of PL-PS3 was primarily evaluated on the DUD dataset [27]. The DUD dataset consists of 40 proteins, each with a ligand library composed of active compounds that have been experimentally validated and decoy compounds that possess similar chemical features. From the DUD dataset, the same benchmark set as PL-PS2 [10] was employed. The same compound libraries for each target from the PL-PS2 benchmark [10] were employed to compare. The ratio between active compounds and decoy compounds in the dataset was set to 1:29, selecting the decoy compounds randomly from the original DUD set. The ratio is kept uniform across the targets. The average number of actives and decoys for a receptor was 51 and 1486, respectively. We used the holo structures that were provided in the DUD dataset.

In addition to holo receptor structures included in the DUD dataset, we also evaluated PL-PS3 on apo structures, which are usually more difficult for virtual screening, as the conformation of the pocket may exhibit differences from the holo form. Eighteen apo protein structures tested in the PL-PS2 paper, collected from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) [43,44], were used for evaluation. When multiple apo receptor structures were available, the structure with the lowest resolution was selected. For the same 18 receptors, we also generated homology models using MODELLER [28]. Furthermore, a benchmarking analysis was conducted on AlphaFold2 (AF2) models extracted from EBI-AlphaFold database [45]. Three targets originating from viruses, HIVPR, HIVRT, and NA, are not available in the AlphaFold2 model database, so they were excluded from our AF2 benchmark. PDGFrb was also removed because the holo crystal structure was not provided in the original DUD set, making the number of targets in the AF2 benchmark set 21. We also benchmarked on Alphafold3 (AF3) [30] models for the same targets.

Finally, in addition to DUD, LIT-PCBA [33] was also included for benchmarking, which has a larger ratio of inactives relative to actives.

First, we report the benchmark results on the 25 holo structure targets from the DUD dataset. This dataset excludes 15 targets from DUD containing cofactors with atoms that cannot be processed by APBS, as it lacks the parameters required to assign atomic properties and accurately compute electrostatic potentials for these molecules. We performed a two-fold cross-validation as follows: The 25 targets were divided into two sets as performed in our previous work [10]. The list of proteins for each set is listed in Supplementary Information Table S1. Then, the weights for the conformer score (Eq.8), which balance the distance of patch features and locations of patches in the binding pocket and a ligand, were optimized on one of the sets. The resulting conformer score was applied to the other set. This was repeated two times by altering the training and the test sets. A grid search was performed by varying the weights from 0.1 to 1.5 with an increment of 0.1, which results in 50,625 parameter combinations. The weights were optimized to achieve a high Boltzmann-enhanced discrimination of receiver operating characteristic (BEDROC) score [46,47]. The optimized weights for the two sets were (kP= 0.2, kG= 0.4, kA= 1.0, kS= 0.7) and (kP= 0.4, kG= 0.8, kA= 0.7, kS= 1.0), respectively, for sets 1 and 2. Although the parameter values look somewhat different, the top parameter combinations for each protein set performed very similarly. Indeed, the difference of BEDROC score between the top parameter set and the 50th parameter set was only 0.0018 (0.2666 to 0.2684) for protein set 1, and 0.0012 (0.3112 to 0.3124) for protein set 2, respectively. Also, the trends are similar to each other. kGis twice as high as kP, and kSis 2.5 or 3.5 times as high as kp. For practical use of PL-PS3, we recommend to use the parameters trained on protein set 2 because that parameters set has the highest BEDROC when applied to all the targets from both set 1 and set 2. Results of the 25 targets were computed when they were in the test set and summarized in Table1. Results of individual targets are provided in Supplementary Information Table S2.

The virtual screening performance was evaluated in three metrics: enrichment factor (EF), area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and BEDROC. The EF measures the fraction of active compounds within the top x% relative to the overall fraction of active compounds in the compound dataset [48]. In Table1, we computed EF at three cutoffs, 1%, 5%, and 10%. The AUC evaluates the rate of retrieving active compounds in higher ranks relative to the accumulation of false positives [46]. BEDROC is similar to AUC but incorporates a Boltzmann weight factor that assigns higher weights to early-ranked actives, giving more importance to early recognition of actives.

The results of PL-PS3 represent the average performance over the 25 targets when each was used as the test set. The highest value for each metric is highlighted in bold. Binding pockets were defined using the co-crystallized ligands present in the crystal structures of the receptors. For apo and modeled structures (discussed later), the binding pockets were defined based on the holo structures after structural alignment using TM- align [49] and transferring the ligands accordingly. Protonation states and atomic charges were assigned using UCSF Chimera [50]. For AutoDock Vina [51], the docking box was defined as a cube with 25 Å sides. For DOCK6 [52], the docking box was constructed with a 5 Å margin around the space occupied by the cognate ligand. All other parameters for the three programs were set to their default values. For Interformer [31] and SurfDock [32], the pre-trained weights and virtual screening pipeline made available by the authors were used without parameter modifications. Interformer generates 21 conformers for each ligand, from which the conformer of the highest score was used to rank ligands. SurfDock outputs 40 conformers for a ligand, and from which the one with the highest score was used to rank different ligands.

PL-PS3 was compared against PL-PS2, two widely used SBVS methods, AutoDock Vina [51] and DOCK6 [52], and two recent deep learning-based methods, Interformer and SurfDock. First, we compared two ligand ranking schemes, BWS (Eq.9) and LCS. BWS consistently yielded higher values across all evaluation metrics for both PL-PS3 and PL-PS2. This is consistent with our previous study on PL-PS2 [10].

When PL-PS3 was compared with PL-PS2, the new version demonstrated improved performance across all metrics with both BWS and LCS schemes except EF1% with the BWS scheme. In order to ascertain statistical significance, Wilcoxon signed-rank test was employed to calculate p-values. Utilizing a threshold of p < 0.1, EF10% (0.081) and AUC (0.014) demonstrated that PL-PS3 has exhibited a statistically significant enhancement in performance in the BWS scoring scheme. In this holo form dataset, PL-PS2 showed a higher value in EF1% but that is not significant (p-value = 0.717).

Notable improvements by PL-PS3 include the EF1% for ERα agonists and antagonists, which increased from 9.0 to 13.50 and from 0.0 to 8.18, respectively, under the LCS scheme. Additionally, for the nuclear hormone receptor family, EF1% using the BWS scheme improved from 11.6 to 12.4 with PL-PS3. Similarly, BEDROC also increased from 0.288 to 0.328. These receptors commonly feature binding pockets with hydrogen-bonding groups located at peripheral regions, forming hydrogen-bonding networks with water and ligand molecules [53]. The compatibility between the hydrogen-bonding donors and acceptors was more accurately captured by the updated hydrogen-bonding feature implementation in PL-PS3. To systematically analyze the effect of the change in hydrogen-bonding definition, we calculated, for each target, the ratio of pocket patches containing hydrogen-bonding terms in PL-PS2 and PL-PS3 (Supplementary Table S3). Among the 25 targets, 14 exhibited a substantial increase in the ratio of patches with hydrogen-bonding terms in PL-PS3, with a ratio difference greater than 0.75. We call these targets as HB-term enriched targets by PL-PS3. With the BWS scoring scheme, EF1% was improved from 13.95 to 15.13, (p= 0.091), which also reflected in a significant AUC improvement from 0.558 to 0.598 (p= 0.005).

When comparing PL-PS3 (BWS) with AutoDock Vina, PL-PS3 outperformed in EF1%, EF5%, and BEDROC, with a particularly notable improvement in EF1%, where PL-PS3 achieved a score of 14.35 compared to 7.92 for AutoDock Vina. On the other hand, PL-PS3 was only slightly lower in EF10% and AUC, which indicates that PL-PS3 has superior performance in early active ligand detection. When compared with DOCK6, PL-PS3 demonstrated consistently better performance across all evaluation metrics. The performance difference of PL-PS3 against AutoDock Vina and DOCK6 have p-values of 0.002 and 0.066, respectively, showing significance.

PL-PS3 was also compared with Interformer [31] and SurfDock [32]. SurfDock showed the highest values across all metrics and all programs except for EF1%, where PL-PS3 had the highest value with a p-value of 0.196. PL-PS3 had a significantly higher EF1% value than Interformer (p= 0.002).

Regarding computational time for scoring a single molecule on a single CPU, PL-PS3 completes the task in 3.9 s, while AutoDock Vina and DOCK6 require 101.6 and 58.4 s, respectively. Conversely, when utilizing a single GPU, Interformer and SurfDock achieve completion times of 8.5 and 3.8 s, respectively.

Next, in Table2, we investigated how the structural similarity between active compounds and the co-crystallized ligand of the receptor protein affects screening performance. More detailed results are shown in Supplementary Information Table S4. Since we used the binding pocket from the holo form for screening, active compounds that are more similar to the co-crystallized ligand are expected to be easier to identify. To assess this effect, we divided the 25 targets into four classes based on the average structural similarity of the active compounds in each ligand pool to the co-crystallized molecule. Similarity was measured using SIMCOMP [54], which quantifies two-dimensional (2D) chemical structure similarity on a scale from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating identical molecules.

The results in Table2reveal a clear pattern. When the active compounds are structurally similar, SurfDock recorded the highest EF1% value of 22.73, and other methods had an EF1% in a similar range, between 11 and 13. However, when the similarity of active compounds drops below 0.4, AutoDock Vina and Interformer’s EF1% decreases by more than half. DOCK6 also shows a decline in EF1%, though to a lesser extent. In contrast, PL-PS3 maintains consistent EF1% values and even shows improved performance in the three lower ligand similarity classes. This trend aligns with the compound ranking scores BWS and LCS. To assess the effect of similarity to the co-crystallized ligand, we reselected receptor structures from the high-similarity set (similarity > 0.4) and replaced them with structures bound to dissimilar compounds (similarity < 0.2; bottom row). The performance of each method and the selected receptor PDB IDs are listed in Supplementary Table S4. Notably, the EF1% of all methods except PL-PS3 decreased by more than 29%, whereas PL-PS3 retained 92% of its performance (from 10.78 to 9.91), demonstrating its robustness.

Apo structures were available for 18 targets in PDB. The overall results are summarized in Table3, and detailed results for each target are provided in Supplementary Information Table S5.

Statistical comparisons of EF1% across the 18 apo-structure targets, using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, showed that PL-PS3 (BWS) significantly outperformed AutoDock Vina (p= 0.001), DOCK6 (p= 0.020), and Interformer (p= 0.003). When the target of interest does not have an experimental structure, structure prediction is widely used for SBVS. Similar to the apo structure, it is reported that the modeled structure also deteriorates the performance of SBVS [10,12]. Thus, we tested PL-PS3 with the traditional methods to investigate whether our program can also retain the performance or not. The 18 receptor structures were modelled using MODELLER [28]. The sequence identity between the template structure used to the target receptor ranges from 30 to 78% (Supplementary Table S1). We ensured that the identity is at least 30%, because in general proteins with about 30% sequence identity share the same fold [55]. RMSD of the homology model and the target ranged from 0.32 to 3.73 Å (Supplementary Information Table S6). The results are summarized in the bottom rows in Table3.

In the homology model dataset, PL-PS3 showed higher values than PL-PS2 in EF10% and AUC and PL-PS2 had higher values in EF1% and EF5%. BEDROC values were similar. The increase of EF10% by PL-PS3 over PL-PS2 (BWS) was significant (p= 0.07) and all other differences did not reach to a significance level. AutoDock Vina and DOCK6 dropped their performance substantially when homology models were used. Particularly, EF1% performance of AutoDock Vina dropped from 7.34 (holo structure) to 1.86, a decrease of 74.7%. On the other hand, the decrease observed for PL-PS3 (BWS) was minimum, 20.9% (from 13.71 to 11.31). In recent years, deep-learning-based protein prediction methods have caused a major paradigm shift, achieving remarkably high accuracy. Thus, we tested our program against the AlphaFold-predicted structures. The EBI-AlphaFold database [45] contains 21 protein structures out of the DUD holo benchmark set. The models were downloaded and prepared in the same manner as the apo and the homology model set. For the same targets, AlphaFold3 (AF3) models were also predicted and prepared. The result is summarized in Table4. Data for the individual targets are provided in the supplementary material (Supplementary Information Table S7 and Table S8).

Similar to apo and homology modeled structures, PL-PS3 showed the highest values across all metrics except AUC on AF2 models when compared to the classical docking programs. For AF2 models, PL-PS3 performed better than PL-PS2, in all metrics with both BWS and LCS schemes. With Wilcoxon’s signed rank test, AUC of PL-PS3 (BWS) was significantly improved from PL-PS2 (0.012), while difference in other metrics did not show significance withp< 0.1. (EF1%: 0.632, EF5%: 0.139, EF10%: 0.181). Considering 12 HB-term enriched targets included among the 21 targets, the increase of AUC of PL-PS3 (BWS) over PL-PS2 (BWS) is significant (p-value = 0.022).

When compared to the DL-based methods, PL-PS3 showed a higher value in EF1% than Interformer (p-value: 0.018). SurfDock had higher values than PL-PS3 for all the metrics.

Similar to Fig.3, in Fig.5we showed the decrease in performance of each target when the AF2 model was used. For both AutoDock Vina (blue dots) and DOCK6 (purple triangle), EF1% decreased to zero for seven targets while PL-PS3 maintained close to 0 difference even when the AF2 model’s RMSD was as worse as 2.5 Å (Fig.5A). However, PL-PS3 exhibited a smaller degree of sensitivity to this effect compared to conventional approaches. Taken together, the statistical comparisons across all structure categories consistently support the conclusion that PL-PS3 maintains significantly superior early enrichment performance relative to conventional docking methods, regardless of the source or generation method of the predicted receptor structure.

Similar to many docking and virtual screening workflows [58,59,60], which omit cofactors during receptor preparation. PL-PS3 does not explicitly account for cofactors in the binding pocket. This limitation arises because APBS, which is used to calculate electrostatic potentials, lacks appropriate parameters for some heteroatoms, such as metal ions and molecules like ATP. For this reason, 15 targets in DUD that contain cofactors were excluded from Table1and subsequent analyses. However, here, following the common receptor-preparation practice in docking studies [61,62], we performed screening for these 15 targets by removing the cofactors from the binding pockets. For PL-PS3, we implemented a new option where surface patches that only interacting with a cofactor (within 3 Å) are excluded in the compound matching process. To run the other programs, we defined the center of the binding pocket as the geometrical center of the co-crystalized ligand. Table5summarizes the results. Results for individual targets are provided in Supplementary Information Table S9.

Consistent with results for targets without cofactors, PL-PS3 achieved the highest EF1% among all benchmarked methods, including deep learning–based approaches. Among conventional screening methods, PL-PS3 showed higher values against AutoDock Vina and DOCK6 across all evaluated metrics. Statistical significance was assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test; for EF1%, the improvement over AutoDock Vina was significant (p= 0.002), while the p-value versus DOCK6 was 0.138. Compared with deep learning–based methods, PL-PS3 showed a significant advantage over Interformer (p= 0.014), indicating consistent early enrichment in cofactor-containing binding sites, and comparable performance to SurfDock (p= 0.365).

We further tested PL-PS3 on the LIT-PCBA dataset with 15 targets, which reflects more realistic screening scenarios by ruling out frequent hitters, nonspecific binders, promiscuous aggregators, and considering mid-potency active molecules from PubChem BioAssay [33]. The overall performance of all methods on this dataset was lower than on the DUD benchmark, which is consistent with prior observations [33,63]. To reduce computational overhead and to make computation feasible on our computer system, we limited the number of inactive compounds to a maximum of 10,000 per target by random downsampling for targets that have a larger number of inactives. All active compounds were retained. For each receptor, the lowest-resolution holo structure was selected for screening. The same downsampled dataset and the receptor structure were used across all methods to ensure a fair comparison. The results are summarized in Table6.

AutoDock Vina recorded the highest EF1% (2.69), while PL-PS3 (BWS) showed a lower value of 0.87. However, EF1% can be sensitive to the small absolute number of actives at the top of a ranked list, particularly in low-hit-rate settings, and may not fully reflect the overall discriminative ability of a method. Ten targets have a hit ratio lower than 1% out of 15 LIT-PCBA targets. PL-PS3 (BWS) showed the highest values across EF5% (1.58), EF10% (1.54), AUC (0.568), and BEDROC (0.084), which provide a more stable assessment of enrichment across a broader fraction of the compound library. The DL-based methods, Interformer and SurfDock, showed notably lower AUC (0.454 and 0.507, respectively) and BEDROC (0.054 and 0.052, respectively) values on this dataset. In terms ofp-values of EF1%, none of the methods showed superior performance with statistical significance withp-value cutoff of 0.1. Thus, PL-PS3 retains competitive discriminative performance in a more realistic virtual screening scenario.

At last, we discussed two cases where PL-PS3 exhibited worse performance: AmpC in the DUD dataset and TP53 in the LIT-PCBA. AmpC, in particular, features a shallow, solvent-exposed active-site groove rather than a well-enclosed binding pocket. This shallow groove provides access to the catalytic Ser64 from multiple solvent directions. The highly solvent-exposed active site of AmpC requires careful treatment of water-mediated interactions to achieve accurate docking and screening results [64,65]. PL-PS3 failed to identify active molecules for AmpC, yielding EF1% values of zero. In contrast, DOCK6 and SurfDock achieved substantially higher enrichment factors, implying that the observed failure may be specific to the surface patch representation.

TP53 represents a similar failure case in a different biological context. The binding site targeted by small molecules is located at the interface formed with MDM. Such protein–protein interaction (PPI) interfaces are inherently flat and lack the concave geometry typical of conventional ligand-binding pockets [66,67]. As a result, PPIs are generally more challenging targets for virtual screening, due to their large and shallow binding surfaces. The limited depth and enclosure of these sites further reduce their druggability by conventional small-molecule screening approaches [68]. PL-PatchSurfer3 fails to enrich active compounds for this target in the LIT-PCBA benchmark (EF1%: 0.00), whereas AutoDock Vina and SurfDock are able to identify hits within the top 1% (EF1%: 6.33). Taken together with the results for AmpC, these findings suggest that PL-PatchSurfer3 is best suited for targets with enclosed, well-defined binding pockets, and that caution is warranted when applying it to targets with flat grooves or PPI interfaces.

Structural flexibility poses a key challenge in SBVS. As demonstrated in this study, SBVS methods are sensitive to deviations of the receptor structure from its holo form. Therefore, it is crucial to develop SBVS methods that maintain high performance even when using apo structures or computationally modeled receptors. This need is further underscored by the observation that homology models and even AlphaFold-predicted structures often exhibit significantly reduced screening performance.

The proposed PL-PatchSurfer3 reduces the decline in screening performance by using a local surface patch representation instead of an atomic-level representation. This is because surface patches are more tolerant to structural variations in both ligands and receptor binding pockets. PL-PatchSurfer3 compares favorably with existing docking methods across a broad range of receptor structures, including apo and predicted models. In recent years, numerous deep learning–based approaches have been developed in structural bioinformatics and cheminformatics. Although such methods are expected to become mainstream in SBVS, our results demonstrate that a surface-based approach remains competitive with current state-of-the-art deep learning methods. These findings suggest that integrating surface representations, such as 3D Zernike descriptors, which are more tolerant to conformational variability, into deep learning frameworks may be a promising direction for future development.

title: Bridging predictive reliability and explainability: a multi-representation deep learning framework for chemical space analysis of immune bioassays
author: V. A. Jyothy; Maya L. Pai; E. PA. Sandesh; U. C. A. Jaleel
text:
Convergence of chemical and biological space into a unified decision space requires coordinated interactions across the triad- molecular representations, learning algorithms, and explainability. This study establishes a benchmarking framework for Virtual Screening (VS) that integrates this triad to enable consistent, predictive, and interpretable modelling of complex immune-related bioassays. The study employed a wide range of Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models across three molecular input modalities—descriptors, images, and graphs—while prioritizing predictive reliability and model interpretability. Among classical ML models, Support Vector Machines (SVM) demonstrated the strongest overall performance, while the AttentiveFP architecture outperformed other DL models. Beyond identifying context-specific optimal VS networks, this study derives latent learned concepts that support subsequent hypothesis generation and experimental validation of the interaction between immune targets and ligands.

Scientific contribution

This study establishes a benchmarking framework for virtual screening of immune targets by curating representative bioassay datasets, systematically evaluating multiple molecular representations and learning algorithms, and integrating explainability into the best-performing models. By combining Concept Whitening with the AttentiveFP architecture, we introduce an integrated explainable DL framework that maintains predictive reliability while enabling alignment and separation of domain-specific concepts for immune-target virtual screening. In addition, the study highlights the potential for decision- and logical-level model ensembling, identifies target-specific concept relevance in decision-making, and demonstrates the relationship between data characteristics and model behaviour.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

The immune system is a highly complex, multilayered and context-dependent network, which limits the effectiveness of standardized datasets, general-purpose algorithms and direct analytical pipelines for elucidating ligand–target interactions. Owing to their inherently dynamic and nonlinear behavior, single-scale datasets and generic modeling approaches rarely capture the full spectrum of functional states, thereby masking mechanistically relevant patterns in traditional data-mining workflows. Therefore, immune-focused modeling necessitates target-specific datasets, adaptive molecular representations and explainability-driven algorithms capable of capturing complex, non-linear relationships and biologically conditioned variability.

The effectiveness of virtual classification critically depends on data quality, structural diversity, and class imbalance [28], and the crucial factor influencing model performance is the choice of molecular representation [41]. Descriptor-based representations encode molecules as structured numerical descriptors, emphasizing computational efficiency [12,22]. Image-based encodings represent rich structural and chemical features in visual formats, enabling the extraction of spatial patterns from molecular structures, whereas graph-based representations preserve stereochemical and topological relationships [22,26,30].

The predictive reliability of a model is critically influenced by selecting an architecture whose inductive biases align with the intrinsic structure of the chosen molecular representation [9,24]. Descriptor-based vectors can be processed using Feed Forward Neural Networks (FFNNs), which can capture non-linear relationships in low-dimensional structured data [48]. Image-based molecular representations are encoded using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for their ability to extract spatially coherent motifs and localized structural features [16]. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can be used to model graph-based molecular representations that effectively capture atomic connectivity and bonding topology, thereby capturing stereochemical features necessary for reliably predicting bioactivity [14,47,51]. Despite the rise of DL, classical ML models, such as SVMs, remain highly effective for virtual classification tasks in settings with limited sample sizes of molecular data [43]. The prevalence of ensemble learning in classification tasks necessitates a systematic investigation of the optimal ensemble strategies [11,13,33,37].

Although DL has advanced rapidly and is widely adopted, in safety–critical domains like Drug Discovery, it is frequently regarded as a black-box system, limiting mechanistic interpretability and decision transparency [17,19,23,31,34]. Consequently, Explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as an essential architectural component for enabling trust-centric and regulatory-compliant deployment of AI systems within the drug discovery pipeline [6,39]. The existing XAI methodologies can be systematically classified into three categories based on their underlying logic: post-hoc attribution methods, attention-based interpretability approaches, and concept-based interpretability frameworks that aim to bridge the gap between model outputs and their biological relevance [2,45]. The post-hoc attribution methods, such as Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) [27], Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) [36], and Integrated Gradients (IG) [44] are widely adopted for their feature-level or atom-level contributions in model predictions. However, these approaches can exhibit stochastic instability, high sensitivity to input perturbations and limited alignment with chemically meaningful concepts, as the resulting explanations are derived from latent representations and are not explicitly optimized for interpretability, which restricts the derivation of meaningful insights [3,38,42]. Attention-based interpretability, prevalent in GNNs and transformer-based molecular models, enables structural transparency by highlighting salient atoms, bonds, or molecular substructures, and offers intuitive visualisations of focus regions in molecular graphs and their target interactions [21]. However, the empirical evidence suggests that attention weights do not correlate with causal feature importance, which cannot account for mechanistic decision pathways [21,40]. Concept-aligned interpretability approaches address the limitations of post-hoc methods, which integrate transparency into training by aligning latent axes with predefined, domain-relevant concepts via orthogonal rotations, enabling disentangled feature learning, stable concept-level traceability and improved mechanistic alignment [1,7,8,25,34].

In drug discovery, in silico Virtual Screening (VS) enables systematic interrogation of large chemical libraries, thereby prioritizing potential lead candidates by computationally predicting the interactions, binding affinity, biological activity, and pharmacophoric profiles, however lack mechanistic understanding and regulatory acceptance [10,52]. By elucidating descriptors, pharmacophoric features, and spatial interaction motifs, XAI mitigates this issue, thereby shifting VS from purely statistical correlation to mechanism-informed drug discovery. Recent advancements in XAI-enabled VS include GNN explainability methods, which identify the molecular subgraphs with concept-level explainability and a unified benchmarking platform facilitating visualization, quantitative evaluation and comparison of multiple XAI methods for drug screening [4,50].

This study investigates how different molecular representation paradigms- descriptor-based, image-based and graph-based approaches- affect the learning pipeline using bioassay outcomes as the benchmark. The study also evaluates how different algorithms, ranging from classical ML models to DL architectures, perform with varying choices of molecular representation. The study further investigates whether ensemble-based integration of multiple models can enhance predictive reliability, particularly in bioactivity prediction, in which maintaining a trade-off between sensitivity and specificity is crucial. To strengthen interpretability across state-of-the-art deep classification frameworks, we integrate CW into the best-performing DL model AttentiveFP, providing transparent attribution of predictions to chemically relevant concepts while retaining the predictive power of latent graph embeddings, thereby bridging reliability and interpretability. The graphical abstract summarizing the conceptual framework of the study is presented in Fig.1.

Graphical abstract depicting the proposed representation-learning-explainability triad and optimization for virtual screening of bioassay molecules

In essence, the study makes the following key contributions to the field:

The study developed a biologically relevant immune-target benchmark integrating both activation and inhibition bioassays, making context-aware evaluation of models under complex immunological signaling.

By systematically benchmarking classical ML models, DL models and hybrid ensemble architectures against descriptor-based, image-based and graph-based molecular representations, the study identified graphs as the principal direction of immune-target virtual screening. Following systematic experimentation, benchmarking, and comparative analysis, the study identified SVM and AttentiveFP as the best-performing ML and DL architectures, respectively, for virtual classification of immune-related targets.

The study developed an AttentiveFP–Concept Whitening framework that provides domain-aligned, concept-level interpretability and enables the identification of target-specific subsets of the most relevant chemical concepts.

For virtual classification of bioassays, the study identified Majority Voting as the most effective ensembling approach for DL architectures.

Identified target-specific and cross-target molecular descriptors, reinforcing model learning and interpretation, are relevant to immune-target virtual screening.

The datasets employed in the study comprise four bioassays, namely AID932, AID1239, AID1578, and AID1259354, sourced from the publicly available PubChem database, which modulate key immune response pathways to classify molecules by their molecular bioactivity. The target variables examined in the study include four proteins: STAT1-alpha/beta isoform alpha (activation), NF-Kappa-B p105 subunit isoform1 (activation), NOD1isoform 1 (inhibition), and ST2 (IL1RL1) (inhibition), which play a vital role in signalling pathways that regulate immune and inflammatory response, as shown in Table1.

The dataset composition of the selected bioassays is provided in Table1. The dataset AID932, focused on the immune target STAT1-alpha/beta isoform alpha of activity type ‘activation’, contained 196012 compounds, of which 5134 were active and 190878 were inactive. The datasets were selectively designed to obtain a balanced distribution of active and inactive molecules, enabling robust algorithm evaluation to mitigate class imbalance. For each molecule in the balanced datasets, the corresponding SMILES strings were retrieved from the PubChem database, and RDKit-based molecular descriptors were extracted through the Online Chemical Modeling Environment (OChem) database.

The data is preprocessed to prepare the datasets for subsequent analysis, ensuring compatibility with the input representations required by descriptor-based, image-based and graph-based modeling techniques. Descriptor columns containing more than 50% missing or zero values were discarded, and remaining missing entries were assigned with zero. Details of data preprocessing are provided in Additional File 1: Table 1. Descriptor-based and image-based models were standardised using z-score normalization, whereas graph-based models (Vanilla GNN, GCN, AttentiveFP) were constructed from SMILES using PyTorch Geometric, with atoms encoded as node features and bond types represented as edge attributes.

Across all datasets, a stratified 80:20 train–test split was applied; descriptor-based models used scikit-learn utilities for splitting and scaling; and graph-based data were mini-batched using the PyTorch Geometric DataLoader. Activity labels were binarized (active = 1, inactive = 0), and residual NaN or infinite values were sanitised to prevent computational instability.

To systematically decode immune-relevant chemical space, this study derives an optimal triad comprising the most informative molecular representation, the best-performing learning framework, and an enhanced concept-level interpretability approach. As a result, we propose a unified analytical framework for exploring chemical space and classifying virtual bioassays, as illustrated in Fig.2.

Framework for analyzing the chemical space of molecules by classification

The chemical space analysis incorporates four distinct bioassay datasets, evaluated using a range of algorithms spanning both conventional ML and advanced DL approaches. The processing was initiated with classical ML models, including SVM and Gaussian Naive Bayes classifiers, which were used as baseline methods for predictive analysis. To qualitatively assess the feature-space topology and facilitate interpretation of class separability and the underlying structural organization, t-SNE visualisation was implemented. The DL analysis was based on three types of molecular input representations: descriptor-based, image-based and graph-based. Molecular features were first represented as descriptor vectors, and used FFNN to capture the non-linear relationships among the molecules. Then, as two-dimensional images, which allows CNN to extract spatial and topological features. Finally, molecules were represented as graphs. As a base model, VanillaGNN was adopted to define a benchmark for graph learning. Next, GCN was applied to learn structure-informed representations that capture atomic connectivity and bonding patterns in molecular graphs. AttentiveFP was employed to embed molecular properties using attention mechanisms, allowing the model to selectively focus on substructures most relevant to predicting target properties. Model performance strongly depends on hyperparameters, making optimization essential for interpretable benchmarking across models and datasets.

Table2lists the specific setup for all ML and DL models used in the study.

Optuna is a framework for optimizing hyperparameters designed to identify the set of parameters that deliver the best performance [5]. The main aim of the optimization process is to maximize the ROC-AUC score or to improve the test accuracy on the test set [5]. The hyperparameter tuning process defined a search space consisting of the number of hidden layers, the number of neurons, the learning rate on a logarithmic scale from 10–5to 10–1, dropout ranging from 0.0 to 0.6, and weight decay ranging from 10–7to 10–3.

The parameter set that produced the best performance after 20 iterations of hyperparameter tuning was selected for the final model training. Hyperparameter optimization was employed on every DL model trained on each dataset. The specific configurations used for hyperparameter tuning of each model are described in Table3.

Model training after Optuna optimization

All five models were trained for 75 epochs, employing binary cross-entropy loss as the objective function for the binary classification problem. Adam optimizer was used by incorporating weight decay for regularisation to train the models. To address overfitting, early stopping was employed by monitoring the validation loss and halting training when performance levelled off.

Model evaluation metrics

To assess the performance of each model, a set of evaluation metrics was used, including accuracy, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Area Under Curve (AUC), F1- score, Cohen’s Kappa (κ), precision and recall [35,46].

As a methodological extension beyond the previously described representation-specific models, an ensemble-based framework was devised to integrate the aforementioned predictive DL models and synthesize their outputs through logic-based networks, including Logical AND, Logical OR, and Majority Voting [32]. Ensemble learning is well-established for improving predictive accuracy, robustness, and generalization in molecular classification tasks [15,18,20]. In this study, predictions from FFNN, CNN, VanillaGNN, GCN, and AttentiveFP models were combined, and the efficacy of the ensemble-combination: Logical AND, Logical OR, and Majority Voting was systematically evaluated, as detailed in Fig.3.

Ensemble learning for virtual classification of molecules

Only upon unanimous agreement among all constituent models did the Logical AND ensemble approach classify a molecule as ‘active’, thus prioritising high precision at the cost of recall. Therefore, the approach minimizes false positives by compromising the identification of true positives, thereby reducing type I errors. Logical AND voting is most effective during late-stage validation, where high-confidence predictions are crucial to minimizing experimental costs [15]. Conversely, the Logical OR ensemble strategy classified a molecule as Active if ‘any’ constituent model predicted it as such, prioritizing high recall, potentially at the expense of precision. The Logical OR approach is ideal when the goal is to identify the maximum number of true positives. Though the approach prioritizes sensitivity (true positive rate), which maximizes the identification of active compounds, it may lead to a higher occurrence of false positives. The third technique, Majority Voting, determines the final classification label based on the most common prediction among the ensemble of five constituent models. In the study, a given compound is assigned the 'Active' classification if a minimum of three of the five individual models yield a positive prediction. In contrast to the Logical OR and Logical AND techniques that employed row-wise filtering based on label agreement across models, the Majority Voting technique utilized the entire test dataset, assuming consistent ground truth labels across datasets [29].

To support interpretable molecular activity prediction, the AttentiveFP architecture [49] was extended with CW, enabling latent dimensions to align with predefined physicochemical descriptors. A high-level schematic of the integrated framework is presented in Fig.4.

Graphical abstract of Concept Whitening integrated in AttentiveFP framework

Molecular graphs were generated from SMILES using RDKit. Atom-level features encoded element type, valency, hybridization, formal charge, aromaticity, total hydrogen count and chirality. Bond-level features captured bond order (single, double, triple, aromatic), conjugation, ring membership and stereo configuration. Graphs were processed with an AttentiveFP backbone comprised of four graph attention layers (hidden dimension = 64, diffusion steps = 4, dropout = 0.2), followed by attentive pooling and a feed-forward classifier (64 → 32 → 2). The network was trained for 50 epochs with Adam (learning rate 3 × 10⁻4, weight decay 1 × 10⁻5, batch size 64) using cross-entropy loss.

To obtain interpretable latent dimensions, we applied CW to the pooled AttentiveFP embeddings. A curated set of fifty RDKit-derived descriptors was used as target concepts, grouped into six chemically distinct families: (A) constitutional size and composition, (B) polarity, lipophilicity and surface area, (C) hydrogen-bonding and ionisation capacity, (D) aromaticity, conjugation and ring topology, (E) charge distribution and electrotopological state, and (F) topological shape and molecular complexity. For each molecule in the training set, we computed a 64-dimensional pooled embedding\(z\)and a 50-dimensional descriptor vector\({y}_{c}\). Let\(Z\)denote the matrix of pooled embeddings. ZCA whitening was applied by centring with the empirical mean\(\mu\)and applying the inverse square root of the covariance as shown in Eq.1.

Each standardized concept\({y}_{c,i}\)are then regressed on\({Z}_{w}\)using linear regression, and the resulting coefficient vectors are orthonormalised (QR decomposition) and extended to a full orthonormal rotation matrix\(R\in {\mathbb{R}}^{64\times 64}\). The Concept Whitening transform is defined as in Eq.2.

where the first\(k=50\)coordinates are constrained to be maximally correlated with the predefined descriptors, and the remaining coordinates span an orthogonal residual subspace. A Hungarian assignment on the absolute correlation between CW axes and descriptors was used to obtain a one-to-one axis–concept mapping, followed by sign flips to ensure that the correlation was positive. After fitting CW on the warm-up model, the AttentiveFP backbone and classifier were fine-tuned end-to-end with CW integrated into the forward pass (learning rate\(1\times {10}^{-4}\), up to 200 epochs, early stopping with patience 20). At inference time, each pooled embedding is centred, whitened and rotated using the learned\(\mu\),\({\Sigma }^{-1/2}\)and\(R\), yielding a representation\([{z}_{concept},{z}_{residual}]\)in which the leading dimensions are aligned to specific physicochemical descriptors and the remaining dimensions capture task-relevant residual variation.

This section analyses the performance of each model trained on four bioassay datasets.

Figures5,6,7,8show t-SNE embeddings of the training and test sets for each bioassay dataset, derived from the SVM classifier outputs, providing a visual complement to the chemical space analysis.

SVM model trained on the AID932 dataset

SVM model trained on the AID1239 dataset

SVM model trained on the AID1578 dataset

SVM model trained on the AID1259354 dataset

The T-SNE projections provide qualitative evidence that the topology of chemical space differs substantially across datasets. It is evident from the Figures that, by employing SVM, the T-SNE projections of dataset AID932 reveal two highly distinct, compact clusters corresponding to the active and inactive classes, indicating that the underlying chemical space is governed by well-defined structural or physicochemical features that strongly discriminate biological activity. The t-SNE visualizations for the dataset AID1239 are given in Fig.6. AID1239 exhibits a clear class separation, with a limited but noticeable margin overlap. That means, while the actives and inactives largely occupy different areas of chemical space, specific subsets with shared features overlap at the margins. The t-SNE embeddings for AID1578, as shown in Fig.7, indicate diverse features with overlapping physicochemical properties between active and inactive compounds. This suggests heterogeneous chemotypes with subtle or context-dependent activity signals. AID1259354 exhibits the highest overlap between active and inactive classes, with unclear cluster boundaries among the analyzed datasets. As shown in Fig.8, the dataset exhibits widespread intermixing of molecules, suggesting weak distinguishing attributes, and their high inter-class variability influences the chemical space. Hence, it can be concluded that while AID932 and AID1239 show clear class separations, indicating strong structure–activity relationships, the greater overlap in datasets AID1578 and AID1259354 implies weaker relationships and increased chemical diversity. These insights reveal that classification performance depends on the underlying structure of chemical space, necessitating dataset-specific model selection and evaluation.

Tables4and5report how SVM and NB models performed across the four datasets.

SVM outperformed the NB model across all datasets, indicating that bioactivity depends on correlated, partially non-linear interactions among descriptors that violate the feature-independence assumption. Table4shows that AID932 exhibited exceptional class discrimination (test accuracy = 99.75%, ROC-AUC = 0.9988, κ = 0.9950), whereas it showed only moderate performance on AID1239 and AID1259354, which are more complex or noisy. These findings indicate that the SVM outperformed the NB classifier and is therefore well-suited to capturing the intrinsic structure–activity relationships across the datasets.

A major drawback of the SVM model is its inability to capture intrinsic structural relationships in chemically heterogeneous datasets. This shortcoming necessitates exploring computational methodologies, such as DL architectures and GNNs, to achieve better classification performance. The following sections present the performance of the DL models classified into descriptor-based (FFNN), image-based (CNN) and graph-based (VanillaGNN, GCN, and AttentiveFP).

The FFNN model employed for the descriptor-based analysis exhibited strong performance on AID932 and AID1239, indicating clear structure-activity relationships as shown in Table6. Conversely, the performance declined, with reduced accuracy and a moderate Cohen’s Kappa value indicating weaker descriptor-activity associations on AID1578 and AID1259354. These results suggest that descriptor-based models are highly dataset-dependent, act as benchmarks for structured bioassays, and emphasize the need for advanced hybrid methods in noisy chemical datasets.

The image-based CNN showed only moderate generalisation on AID932 and AID1239 (test accuracy of 68.50–70%, ROC-AUC ranging from 0.76 to 0.88, F1≈0.68) with limited reliability as evident from Table7. For AID1578 and AID1259354, pronounced overfitting was observed, with high training accuracy (> 89%) collapsing to 56–57% test accuracy, low ROC-AUC (0.59–0.62), and minimal agreement beyond chance with Cohen’s Kappa less than 0.15.

These results indicate that while CNNs are capable of capturing discriminative image-derived features in relatively less heterogeneous datasets. However, their robustness and reliability deteriorate significantly when applied to complex molecular data, highlighting the need for more rigorous regularisation strategies and domain-guided design optimization.

The VanillaGNN model showed moderate, yet dataset-dependent, predictive performance as detailed in Table8. AID932 showed high recall (0.965) but reduced precision, reflecting sensitivity bias, whereas AID1239 achieved a more balanced profile with Cohen’s Kappa of 0.495. In AID1578, the degraded performance, with an accuracy of 69.63% and a Cohen's Kappa of 0.3925, can be attributed to noisy structure–activity relationships. However, the most consistent performance of AID1259354 achieved an accuracy of 76.16% and a Cohen's Kappa of 0.5233, indicating stronger graph-activity correlations. These results indicate that while VanillaGNN learns key graph-level representations, its recall bias and moderate discrimination limit its effectiveness as a base model. Therefore, to improve performance on chemical heterogeneous datasets underscores the need for more advanced GNN variants.

The GCN model exhibited moderate predictive performance, which depends on the dataset used, with test accuracies ranging from 66.75% (AID1578) to 74.62% (AID1239), as shown in Table9. For datasets AID932 and AID1259354, the model achieved recall rates of 0.9225 and 0.9260, but lower precision rates of 0.77 and 0.78, indicating a recall-oriented bias with more false positives (Table9). In contrast, AID1239 achieved balanced outcomes with a precision of 0.7729 and a recall of 0.89, resulting in a stable F1-score of 0.7577 and a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.4925, indicating that the structural–activity relationships in the dataset aligned well with the GCN’s feature aggregation. In contrast, AID1578 displayed the lowest performance, with an accuracy of 66.75%, a Cohen’s kappa of 0.34, moderate recall of 0.79, but lower precision of 0.71 and an ROC-AUC of 0.70, indicating limited generalisability to noisy or diffuse graph-activity relationships. From these results, it can be concluded that, although GCN captures relevant graph-level representations, predictive accuracy is constrained by a recall-oriented bias and reduced robustness across datasets. This variability emphasizes need for attention-based or hierarchical GNN variants to improve generalizability and reliability in virtual classification and activity prediction.

The AttentiveFP model exhibited strong predictive capability on datasets with well-defined structure–activity relationships, as shown in Table10. The balanced precision-recall, substantial agreement and test accuracies exceeding 81% on datasets AID932 and AID1239 indicate that AttentiveFP effectively captures structural dependencies resulting in robust classification. AID1578 showed the weakest performance, indicating a sensitivity bias and over-prediction of actives in noisy or weakly correlated patterns. With an accuracy of 78.2% and a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.56, AID1259354 showed moderate performance, characterised by strong recall but reduced discriminative ability with chemically diverse molecules.

The comparative evaluation of DL architectures, including FFNN, CNN, Vanilla GNN, GCN, and AttentiveFP, across the datasets reveals distinct patterns in predictive accuracy, error tendencies, and dataset-specific sensitivity. FFNN and AttentiveFP demonstrated stable performance with higher test accuracy and ROC-AUC on AID932 and AID1239, indicating effective feature learning and generalisation on moderately complex datasets. CNN exhibited severe overfitting, with high training accuracy and sharp drops in test accuracy, along with very low Cohen’s Kappa. This indicates their limited suitability for chemically heterogeneous datasets. Considering the graph-based models, VanillaGNN and GCN achieved test accuracies between 70 and 76% across all datasets, outperforming CNN in recall and reliability, though slightly lower than FFNN and AttentiveFP on less complex datasets. These findings suggest that graph-based models maintain stability across heterogeneous molecular spaces; FFNN remains competitive when descriptors are chemically informative, and AttentiveFP achieves the most generalizable performance across diverse molecular spaces.

To rigorously evaluate model generalization under chemically realistic conditions, all models were assessed using Murcko scaffold-based splitting, enforcing strict structural disjointness between training, validation, and test sets. Results across all models and datasets are presented in Tables 2–5 of Additional File 1, (see Additional File 1), enabling direct comparison with baseline methods. Under this setting, most models exhibit marginally reduced performance relative to random splits, indicating the influence of structural overlap on prior estimates.

Despite this, AttentiveFP consistently demonstrates superior or competitive performance across datasets, consistent with its performance under random-split evaluation; achieving the highest or near-highest ROC–AUC, PR–AUC, and F1-score, indicating robust generalization and effective learning of transferable structure–activity relationships beyond scaffold-specific patterns. Among baseline methods, FFNN exhibits relatively strong and stable performance under scaffold-based constraints, underscoring the continued relevance of descriptor-based representations. Notably, GCN achieves the highest F1-score in the AID1259354 dataset, likely reflecting dataset-specific structural characteristics rather than consistent generalization.

Overall, AttentiveFP exhibits superior generalization and predictive stability under scaffold-based validation, identifying it as the most reliable model and highlighting the effectiveness of attention-driven graph representations in capturing transferable structure–activity relationships.

Given the results of comparative performance analysis and scaffold-based evaluation, in which the AttentiveFP model exhibited the most reliable performance across diverse datasets, it is necessary to verify whether this performance arises from true structure–activity learning rather than from dataset-specific bias or split-dependent effects. Therefore, the AttentiveFP model was selected for rigorous robustness evaluation, using all datasets with adequate active and inactive molecules, employing four orthogonal validation strategies namely, scaffold generalization, multi-seed stability, y-randomization and imbalance sensitivity analysis, to ensure reliability in realistic screening and deployment settings. The results are provided in Table 6-Additional File 1.

Murcko scaffold-based splitting was employed, and the model performance was evaluated using ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, F1-score, and Cohen’s Kappa to quantify discriminative ability, early retrieval capability, and predictive agreement under strict structural separation. The model maintained strong predictive performance across all datasets, achieving ROC-AUC values of approximately 0.79–0.86 and PR-AUC consistently exceeding 0.90, with Cohen’s Kappa indicating moderate to substantial agreement. These results confirm that the predictive signal arises from learned structure–activity relationships rather than scaffold-level memorization, thereby demonstrating robust generalization under chemically realistic validation conditions.

All experiments were repeated across five fixed random seeds (0–4), and performance metrics were reported as mean ± standard deviation (see Additional File 1). The consistently low dispersion (ROC-AUC σ typically < 0.04; accuracy σ typically < 0.03) indicates stable convergence and high reproducibility across data permutations, confirming that model performance is not driven by stochastic variability.

To verify that predictive performance was not driven by data leakage, scaffold overlap, or spurious dataset correlations, Y-randomization was performed. Training labels were randomly permuted while preserving the Murcko scaffold-based train/validation/test splits, model architecture, and fixed hyperparameters; validation and test labels were kept unchanged to maintain a valid external evaluation reference. Collapse of ROC-AUC to near-random levels (≈0.48–0.57) and κ ≈ 0 confirmed the absence of data leakage, scaffold memorization, or hyperparameter-induced artifacts.

To simulate realistic high-throughput screening conditions, datasets were restructured to a negative-dominant distribution (1:5 active: inactive) by retaining all active compounds and randomly subsampling inactive compounds. Class imbalance was addressed using class-weighted Binary Cross-Entropy loss. Hyperparameters were fixed without retuning to ensure that performance differences reflected data distribution shifts rather than optimization effects, and all experiments were repeated across five independent random seeds. Under this imbalance regime, the model maintained stable discriminatory performance (ROC-AUC ≈ 0.80–0.86; PR-AUC ≈ 0.90–0.93), substantially exceeding the random baseline PR-AUC (≈ 0.17, equal to positive class prevalence). These results confirm that predictive performance is not dependent on artificially balanced datasets and remains robust under screening-relevant negative-dominant conditions.

Additionally, AttentiveFP, the best-performing DL model, was combined with the top classical ML model, SVM, and compared to the baseline end-to-end DL configuration. That means, an SVM classifier trained on AttentiveFP-derived molecular embeddings was tested against a fully end-to-end AttentiveFP-Multi-Layer Perceptron (AttentiveFP-MLP) model. The AttentiveFP-SVM approach achieved the best ROC-AUC results across the four datasets, but it showed lower F1 score, accuracy, precision, recall, and Cohen’s kappa than the end-to-end AttentiveFP-MLP model. This shows a clear trade-off between ranking performance and reliable classification accuracy.

To evaluate whether ensembling enhances predictive performance, outputs from five DL models- FFNN, CNN, VanillaGNN, GCN and AttentiveFP- were integrated using three ensemble schemes: Logical AND, Logical OR and Majority Voting. The findings are outlined in Table11. With a highest precision of 0.9462, the Logical AND approach indicates that the ‘active’ predictions were highly reliable. But the recall dropped to 0.4681, resulting in an F1 score of 0.6263 and a Cohen’s kappa of 0.4563. This approach is well-suited when minimizing false positives is the priority. The Logical OR ensemble achieved high recall (0.9840), identifying almost all active compounds, but with lower precision (0.6446), leading to a higher false-positive rate. While maintaining high ROC-AUC (0.7491) and F1-score (0.7789), the ensemble prioritized sensitivity over balance, making it ideal for screening tasks, where avoiding false negatives is the priority. The Majority Voting ensemble attained the most balanced classification performance with the highest accuracy of 74.88%, and Cohen’s Kappa of 0.4935, supported by precision (0.7584) and recall (0.73), yielded strong F1-score (0.7439) as shown in Table11. The ROC-AUC (0.7488) of Majority Voting was comparable to the Logical OR scheme, but this ensemble approach delivered more stable and reliable discrimination. By leveraging complementary error patterns across the five models, Majority Voting mitigated the extreme conservatism of Logical AND and the permissiveness of Logical OR, making it the most adaptable ensemble method for chemically diverse datasets.

Post-training analysis focused on the CW-aligned latent space to evaluate whether the resulting axes captured underlying physicochemical determinants of biological activity. For each bioassay dataset, the influence of individual physicochemical descriptors was quantified from the first 50 concept-aligned coordinates using three metrics: axis–descriptor correlation, permutation-induced accuracy drop (∆Acc), and classifier weight-based importance. A composite importance index was subsequently computed by combining the ΔAcc and weight-based importance scores.

Descriptor-axis correlations

Figures9,10,11,12summarise the ten most strongly correlated axes for each dataset. Across all four datasets, FractionCSP3 consistently emerged as the dominant aligned concept, while ExactMolWt and MolWt recurred among the top axes in three datasets, and LabuteASA, Chi1n, NumHeteroatoms, HeavyAtomCount and AromaticAtomProportion did so in two. These patterns indicate that CW aligns the latent space with chemically interpretable dimensions rather than arbitrary embeddings, and the consistency of descriptor alignment across assays supports the robustness of the approach.

A global ranking across all datasets was computed, with the top 25 descriptors summarised in Fig.25. The top-ranked descriptors resolved into three chemical domains—(i) electronic properties (MinEStateIndex, MinAbsPartialCharge, NumValenceElectrons), (ii) aromaticity and scaffold complexity (AromaticAtomProportion, Aromaticity_VSA, HallKierAlpha), and (iii) steric/topological factors (MolMR, Chi indices, HeavyAtomMolWt), delineating chemically interpretable structure–activity axes rather than opaque latent features.

To assess the stability of the CW alignment, an intersection analysis was performed to evaluate how frequently descriptors appeared across datasets and evaluation metrics. Results are summarized in Table12. The top 10 descriptors were identified for each metric category, and the descriptors AromaticAtomProportion, MolMR, HallKierAlpha, and Aromaticity_VSA were found to recur across three datasets.

These findings collectively indicate that descriptor–axis alignment is globally stable under correlation analysis, whereas predictive importance is strongly dataset-dependent, as reflected by ΔAcc. At the same time, the weight and composite metrics reveal a conserved chemical subspace that the model exploits consistently across datasets.

To derive a stable and biologically meaningful feature subset, a two-stage Composite–Stability Feature Selection method was employed. Initially, features were ranked using a composite score computed as the mean of the permutation-based accuracy drop and the weight-based importance across datasets, and only descriptors above the 75th percentile were retained as high-impact candidates. Second, robustness was assessed via cross-dataset recurrence, retaining only features that appeared in the top 10-ranked set across at least three of the four activity datasets, thereby reducing dataset-specific bias and enforcing cross-domain generalizability.

The process yielded a compact, consistently relevant set of features across all experiments. MinEStateIndex and AromaticAtomProportion were identified as the most prominent descriptors. The selected descriptors align strongly with the model's decision boundaries and generalise across chemical space, validating their role as reliable and interpretable factors for bioactivity classification. Therefore, these results indicate that CW serves both as an interpretability mechanism and as a data-driven framework for feature selection, while also enabling model refinement, making it well-suited for downstream applications such as interpretable generative modeling.

The application of the triads-algorithm, representation, and explainability-together with their downstream variants, enables their effective convergence of chemical and biological spaces into a unified decision space for meaningful results. The study established graphs as the principal direction for the virtual screening pipeline, with molecules represented as graphs, deep graph associations for learning, with the intricacies of ligand-target interactions, attention applied both to edge-atom bonds and to atoms themselves during the final pooling stage, and aligning graph latent embeddings to explainable concepts. Across different stages of the experimental workflow, datasets such as AID932 were identified as exhibiting predominantly linear behaviour with clear class separability, making them analytically simpler. In contrast, more challenging datasets could be effectively distinguished only through subtle substructural patterns captured within both chemical and algorithmic spaces. Among traditional ML approaches, SVM consistently demonstrated strong performance, reflecting its effectiveness in modeling structural-activity relationships. Although the best-performing model varied across individual datasets, the AttentiveFP network achieved the highest overall predictive accuracy, establishing itself as the most effective DL architecture in this study. Among the ensemble strategies evaluated, Majority Voting achieved superior performance with high precision, recall and ROC-AUC values, confirming its suitability for hybrid DL frameworks. In the best-performing AttentiveFP model, the application of Concept Whitening enabled the identification of chemically meaningful concepts driving classification and revealed clear target-specific differences. Notably, MinEStateIndex and AromaticAtomProportion consistently emerged as influential features across immune-related targets.

The study is limited by the evaluation on four immunity-related bioassays, including datasets with a relatively small number of active compounds, and by restricting the Concept Whitening framework to fifty predefined domain-specific descriptors. Despite these limitations, integrating AttentiveFP embeddings with SVM classifiers shows that deep feature learning and classical machine learning can together provide reliable, interpretable, and generalizable predictive performance. These results indicate the potential for future ensemble approaches at both decision and architectural levels.

Future studies should focus on improving dataset diversity using generative AI methods to address data scarcity in DL models. Incorporating protein structural information from experimental studies or predictive models such as AlphaFold, along with binding affinity measurements and molecular dynamics data, into graph-based virtual screening frameworks represents an important research direction. In addition, systematic evaluation of XAI methods beyond CW and investigation of hybrid approaches combining multiple explainability techniques are required to further improve model interpretability and reliability. The development of target-specific virtual screening architectures guided by concept-aligned representations is expected to enhance predictive reliability and support dependable deployment of AI-driven drug discovery systems.

title: De novo design of anticancer 4-thiazolidinone derivatives: a generative framework shaped by activity cliffs
author: Tomasz Szostek; Maciej Wiśniewski; Davide Ballabio; Viviana Consonni; Dariusz Plewczyński; Daniel Szulczyk
text:
Activity cliffs (AC) correspond to large potency differences between highly similar compounds and pose a persistent challenge for both predictive modeling and de novo molecular design, particularly in small and underexplored areas of the chemical space. In this study, we introduce an AC-aware generative framework for the de novo design of anticancer thiazolidinone derivatives relevant to non-small cell lung cancer. We identify difficult regions of structure–activity landscape and extract chemical pattern signals hidden in its discontinuities directly from AC pairs using a dedicated algorithm. These signals are incorporated into a fragment-based generative pipeline to guide molecular construction and candidate selection. Compared with a standard QSAR-guided approach, the proposed framework yields a higher fraction of candidates with favorable docking profiles across multiple cancer-relevant targets and produces ligands with more stable binding modes in molecular dynamics simulations. Among the top five candidates selected by a molecular dynamics, multi-metric consensus combining docking affinity, binding stability (ligand and pocket RMSD/RMSF), and energetic criteria, four were generated using the AC-aware CAFE LATE strategy. The two highest-ranked hits exhibited binding energies of − 7.78 and − 7.70 kcal/mol, markedly more favorable than the native reference (− 4.09 kcal/mol), and consistently outperformed native ligands across all evaluated stability metrics. Those results suggest that explicit use of AC information can improve the quality of de novo generated small-molecule candidates in data-limited settings.

This study introduces a new AC-informed small-molecule design framework that explicitly exposes crucial structure–activity information hidden in steep regions of the SAR landscape and uses it as an operationalized design signal. Our algorithm converts AC knowledge into reverse QSAR and generation leverage, enabling exploration of unknown areas of the chemical space, and discovery of the best performing candidates supported in molecular dynamics simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reverse QSAR and fragment-based generative framework to operationalize AC information at the fragment level within a unified machine learning workflow.
