title: Predictive machine learning models for rational permeability design in de novo macrocycle engineering: a review
author: M. Taleb Albrijawi; Reda Alhajj
text:
Small molecule drug discovery has been highly successful across many therapeutic areas over decades of progress; however, many disease-relevant proteins remain difficult to target. In particular, intracellular proteins with large, shallow, or flexible interaction surfaces are poorly addressed by classical drug-like compounds. For these reasons, drug discovery efforts have shifted toward alternative molecular classes. This has led to growing interest in macrocyclic compounds in recent years, which have emerged as an important class of therapeutic molecules, particularly for targets that are out of reach for conventional small molecules. These compounds operate within the chemical space beyond Lipinski’s Rule of Five (bRo5) and offer new opportunities for modulating difficult intracellular targets. At the same time, their size, flexibility, and structural complexity introduce significant challenges, among which the accurate prediction of membrane permeability remains one of the persistent limitations in their rational design, particularly for orally bioavailable candidates.  This review examines 11 published studies, specifically those focusing on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) driven methodologies for predicting macrocycle permeability. Contemporary ML models utilize a diverse array of molecular representations, including two-dimensional descriptors, three-dimensional conformational features, molecular graphs, and Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) sequences, all aimed at accelerating prediction pipelines. The architectural range of these models spans from classical Quantitative Structure-Permeability Relationship (QSPR) algorithms to advanced deep learning frameworks, including Transformer-based models, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and vision-based approaches. Significant progress in this domain has been largely powered by the establishment of the CycPeptMPDB (Cyclic Peptide Membrane Permeability Database), which provides standardized permeability annotations for thousands of cyclic peptides and has facilitated progress in predictive modeling. Nevertheless, several substantial challenges remain, such as issues of poor generalizability across different chemical scaffolds, the inherent limitations in interpretability characteristic of deep learning models, and biases frequently introduced by dataset imbalance or the particular details of permeability assays. Non-peptidic macrocycles are of growing relevance in drug discovery, but there are remarkably few proposed models that have been developed for this particular subclass. The recent introduction of NPMMPD, a curated dataset focusing on non-peptidic scaffolds offers a promising path toward further advances. This database will allow the development of ML models for the early-stage screening and rational design of orally available non-peptidic macrocycles. Ultimately, these advancements highlight the critical importance of integrating mechanistic biophysical insights with data-driven learning paradigms to accelerate the discovery of the oral therapeutic potential of macrocycles within the bRo5 chemical space.

Today, modern drug discovery represents a paradox of abundance and absence. We possess more data, more tools, and more computational algorithms than ever before, but many of the world’s most devastating diseases remain without effective therapies. Macrocyclic molecules sit at the heart of this challenge. These molecules occupy a rare intersection of promise and challenge, a chemical space rich in potential but also extremely difficult to control. Macrocycles are typically defined as organic compounds containing a ring of 12 or more non-hydrogen (heavy) atoms [15]. At this scale, their conformational flexibility and intricate intramolecular interactions features set them apart from both traditional small molecules and larger biologics [45,53]. Macrocycles are structurally rich and conformationally dynamic, which makes them particularly ideal for engaging molecular targets that are inaccessible to traditional small molecule ligands. Their architectures allow them to wrap around shallow grooves, engage flat or extended protein interfaces, and mimic secondary structural motifs to unlock pharmacological interactions long considered inaccessible [12]. The traditional approach of small molecule drug discovery, while enormously successful, is now approaching its practical limits, particularly when dealing with the growing complexity of therapeutic targets and the expanding patient populations with unmet medical needs[32]. It is estimated that 75% of disease-associated proteins remain inaccessible by current small molecules or biologics, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic modalities [14]. Therefore, the path to next-generation therapies lies in moving past traditional design rules and learning to work with much more complex molecular structures.

Macrocycles occupy a distinctive niche in drug discovery by bridging the gap between small molecules and biologics, as illustrated in Fig.1. By combining the high target specificity typically associated with larger biomolecules with the conformational adaptability of smaller compounds, macrocycles are uniquely positioned to address targets that have long been considered inaccessible. This balance has made them particularly valuable across therapeutic areas such as oncology, infectious diseases, and immunology [21]. Structurally, macrocycles are broadly categorized into peptidic and non-peptidic subclasses. While peptide-based macrocycles effectively replicate natural amino acid sequences, their clinical utility is often limited by metabolic instability in the body. In particular, the rapid proteolytic cleavage of amide bonds often results in unfavorable pharmacokinetic profiles and reduced systemic bioavailability. In contrast, non-peptidic macrocycles utilize a variety of chemical building blocks that provide greater structural diversity and more direct control over their physicochemical properties. Both peptidic and non-peptidic macrocycles possess substantial therapeutic potential for pushing drug discovery efforts beyond the traditional “Rule of 5” small-molecule space [23]. They represent a promising chemical space, particularly for modulating disease-relevant protein–protein interactions (PPIs) that remain inaccessible to classical small-molecule approaches [15,38,39].

Molecular weight and permeability ranges for different drug classes. Small molecules, macrocycles, and biologics, reflecting differences in size and membrane crossing potential. Cell permeability decreases as molecular weight increases across these classes

Macrocycles in drug development have been regarded with cautious admiration from the sidelines. To date, only 67 macrocycles have been approved by the FDA [21]. Figure2presents some randomly selected FDA-approved macrocycles, including Clarithromycin, Lurbinectedin, Setmelanotide[16], Cyclosporine[28], Eptifibatide [25], and Simeprevir [26]. While oral administration is preferred, only 39% of approved macrocycles are given orally, reflecting ongoing challenges in achieving good bioavailability; the remaining 61% are delivered parenterally. The vast majority of these drugs 88% are natural products or their derivatives. Therapeutically, infectious diseases represent the largest category, accounting for 44.4% of macrocyclic drug approvals, mainly antibacterials but also antivirals and antifungals. Oncology is the next most common indication 20.8%, with an increasing number of macrocycles targeting diverse proteins such as kinases and hormone receptors. Other notable uses include autoimmune diseases and immunosuppression.

Selected FDA-approved macrocyclic drugs and their clinical applications. Shown are examples of clinically used macrocyclic drugs, including cyclosporine A (immunosuppression), eptifibatide (antiplatelet therapy), simeprevir (antiviral), setmelanotide (metabolic regulation), and lurbinectedin (oncology)

The construction of the macrocyclic ring itself is often the most critical and demanding step, frequently plagued by low yields [44,55]. Achieving the desired ring closure requires overcoming the inherent strain of bringing distant molecular ends together. This often necessitates highly diluted reaction conditions, particularly for methods like macrolactonization, or certain ring closing metathesis approaches, to favour intramolecular cyclization over intermolecular polymerisation [56]. Beyond ring formation, controlling the precise stereochemistry and conformation of these complex molecules adds further layers of difficulty. Traditional synthetic approaches often involve lengthy, multi-step routes that demand significant labour, time, and highly specialised expertise, with extensive and time-intensive purification steps. [44,55,56]. This collective synthetic intractability has been a primary reason why macrocycles remain a sparsely exploited structural class in many drug design projects[56]. Despite these challenges, macrocycles have carved out a significant niche in medicine, giving rise to highly successful drugs across diverse therapeutic areas [21,38,39].

Many clinically used macrocycles originated as natural products or their derivatives, relying on complex biosynthetic machinery that chemists have sought to mimic or adapt through painstaking total synthesis [23]. Examples span potent antibiotics like Vancomycin, the Rifamycin family (including Rifampin), daptomycin, and the polymyxins; immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine and Tacrolimus; and anticancer agents like Romidepsin and Epothilone B derivatives like Ixabepilone. The complex structures of these molecules, often featuring multiple stereocentres, diverse functional groups, and challenging macrocyclic linkages (such as lactones, lactams, or thioethers), stand as testament to the synthetic prowess required for their realization. The success of macrocycles like Lorlatinib and Pacritinib, derived through macrocyclic modification of simpler acyclic precursors, further underscores the value in finding efficient routes to incorporate macrocyclic scaffolds. The sheer difficulty and resource intensity of macrocycle synthesis have driven the search for ways to streamline the process. Increasingly, the pharmaceutical industry is turning towards artificial intelligence (AI) and computational tools to help navigate this complex landscape. The vision is that AI can serve not just as a design aid, but also as a powerful tool for accelerating the path to synthesizable macrocycles. By leveraging computational power, we might move from relying solely on empirical knowledge and opaque procedures towards optimising synthetic routes, predicting reaction outcomes, reducing the risk associated with low yielding steps, and ultimately expanding the realm of "synthetically accessible" macrocycles. Recent years have seen exciting developments in this direction. While traditional computational approaches to macrocyclization often rely on searching pre-built databases of linkers and applying geometric constraints to linear precursors, cutting edge

AI models offer new possibilities. Methods based on deep learning, such as Macformer [9], demonstrate the potential to move beyond these limitations. By treating macrocyclization as a sequence to sequence translation task, Macformer can learn complex implicit relationships and generate diverse and novel macrocyclic structures from linear inputs, exploring the vast chemical space more effectively. Such tools represent early, yet significant, steps in applying AI to the macrocycle challenge, primarily focusing on the critical upfront design of novel macrocyclic scaffolds that are amenable to synthesis. These advancements signal a paradigm shift, promising to transform how we approach the synthesis of this valuable drug class.

While a handful of macrocyclic drugs have reached the market, the field remains circumspect. Not because macrocycles lack therapeutic value, but because they defy our conventional frameworks. Their size, flexibility, and polarity violate medicinal chemistry’s golden heuristics. Lipinski’s Rule of Five, which once served as a guiding compass, becomes more of a constraint than a tool [35]. Devised in the late 1990s by Christopher Lipinski and his colleagues, these rules emerged from a systematic analysis of molecular properties shared by successful oral drugs. The physicochemical parameters that an orally active drug should have no more than 5 hydrogen bond donors (HBD), 10 hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), a molecular weight (MW) under 500 Da (daltons), and a lipophilicity (LogP) below 5 emerged from a systematic analysis of molecular properties shared by successful oral drugs. While instrumental in shaping early drug discovery paradigms, their rigid application can limit exploration of promising chemical spaces, many compounds that violate the rule of five (Ro5) are effective drug candidates, and it is accepted that drug development efforts should not be restricted to the Ro5 chemical space. By setting thresholds on molecular weight, lipophilicity, and hydrogen bonding capacity, it shaped the design of drug candidates within a “drug-like” chemical space favoring molecules that are small, moderately lipophilic, and chemically restrained.

While Lipinski’s rule of 5 (Ro5) has undeniably served as a crucial filter, guiding early drug discovery efforts towards molecules amenable to oral administration and reducing attrition, its widespread adoption, sometimes through rigid application, has also sparked debate and a perceived reluctance to explore chemical space that lies outside these guidelines [13,40]. Yet, the evolving landscape of drug discovery, continually presenting novel, often ’difficult to drug,’ targets identified through advances in genomics and proteomics, necessitates venturing into this uncharted territory [11,40]. These challenging targets frequently possess binding sites that are large, flat, flexible, or featureless, making them difficult to modulate with smaller, Ro5-compliant molecules; examples include protein-protein interactions (PPIs), certain kinases, proteases, and isomerases. Modulating such targets often requires larger, more complex ligands. This growing need has catalyzed the exploration of chemical space ’beyond the rule of 5’ (bRo5).

Although no single, universally agreed upon definition of bRo5 exists, comprehensive analyses of approved drugs and clinical candidates with molecular weights exceeding 500 Da have begun to map this territory, demonstrating that oral drugs and candidates do exist significantly beyond strict Ro5 boundaries. These studies suggest that the boundaries of this oral druggable space extend considerably, approximating outer limits where a reasonable chance of cell permeability and oral bioavailability exists, typically delineated by thresholds like MWle1000 Da, an expanded calculated LogP (cLogP) window of approximately -2 to 10 (though still centered around 4), HBDle6 (strictly controlled), HBAle15, polar surface area (PSA)le250 ø\(\hbox {A}^2\), and number of rotatable bonds (NRotB)le20. The pharmaceutical industry is increasingly capitalizing on this expanded space, with a steady increase in the fraction of approved drugs exceeding 500 Da. Prominent oral bRo5 drug classes often originate from natural products and include macrolide antibacterials, immunosuppressants, taxane anticancer agents, and cardiac glycosides, alongside more recently de novo designed drugs like certain HCV and HIV inhibitors.

But how do these larger, more complex molecules achieve oral bioavailability and cellular permeability? Success often hinges on specific structural features and properties that mitigate the inherent risks associated with increased size and polarity. Crucially, successful oral administration depends on a delicate balance between aqueous solubility and the capacity to permeate biological membranes, as clearly illustrated in Fig.3. Key tactics include conformational shielding of polar groups by lipophilic substituents, covalent modifications like N-methylation of amide bonds, the strategic induction and stabilization of intramolecular hydrogen bonds (IMHB), and macrocyclization, all of which improve permeability by effectively reducing the exposed polar surface area or masking polar groups. Furthermore, the emerging concept of molecular flexibility playing a critical role is proving key; for a macrocyclic compound to be permeable, it needs to be conformationally flexible meaning it can twist and rearrange between different shapes, stretched out and polar when floating in water, tight and greasy when squeezing through a membrane. This chameleonic property allows compounds to adopt different conformations tailored to varying environments, balancing the opposing requirements of high permeability (favoring a compact, less polar conformation) and good solubility (requiring exposed polar groups).

The critical balance between aqueous solubility and lipophilicity required for successful passive intestinal absorption and oral bioavailability. A molecule must possess sufficient solubility in the aqueous environment of the gut and an optimal degree of lipophilicity to partition into and traverse the lipid bilayer of the intestinal membrane without becoming sequestered

Chameleonic properties refer to a molecule’s ability to conceal its polarity in non-polar settings while revealing it in aqueous environments, enabling optimal permeability and solubility for high molecular weight drug compounds [7]. This adaptability, often facilitated by dynamic IMHBs, is observed in several oral bRo5 drugs like Cyclosporin A [31] and certain de novo designed macrocycles, explaining how compounds significantly exceeding traditional PSA limits can still be orally bioavailable. Beyond molecular design, strategies such as achieving high local intestinal concentrations through moderate to high dosing, or using specialized formulations, can also help overcome permeability or efflux challenges. Adding another layer, recent work suggests that bRo5 ligands are advantageous for certain target binding sites, not just simple ones; for targets with complex binding sites, larger ligands can engage more hot spots, leading to increased binding affinity that can be traded for improved pharmaceutical properties (Complex I targets), or primarily enhance selectivity by binding to regions beyond conserved sites (Complex II targets, e.g., kinases) [18]. Despite these opportunities and strategies, navigating bRo5 chemical space remains challenging and is associated with increased risks, particularly related to solubility, passive permeability, efflux, metabolism, and synthetic complexity. However, some risks like promiscuity might decrease with increasing MW. A direct comparison of the classical Rule of 5 and the broader bRo5 criteria is shown in Table1, highlighting the physicochemical differences that shape permeability challenges in larger molecules. This complex picture underscores the need for a nuanced understanding of structure property relationships, setting the stage for exploring how advanced tools might aid in designing compounds, particularly macrocycles, within this space.

A critical determinant of success for orally administered drugs particularly those beyond the Rule of Five (bRo5) is sufficient cellular permeability. This property is essential for overcoming biological barriers, such as the intestinal epithelium, to achieve systemic exposure [43]. In vitro permeability assays remain indispensable tools for evaluating this capability, with widely adopted methods including cell based models (e.g., Caco-2 monolayers [24]) and artificial membrane systems like the Parallel Artificial Membrane Permeability Assay (PAMPA) [29]. The Caco-2 assay provides insights into both passive diffusion and active transporter effects (e.g., efflux by P-glycoprotein) through bidirectional transport measurements, correlating well with human intestinal absorption. In contrast, PAMPA is primarily used to assess passive permeability, offering a high-throughput alternative.

For orally bioavailable drugs, a permeability threshold is often considered typically a\(\hbox {P}_{\text {app}}\)(apparent permeability) value of\(>1 \times 10^{-6}\)cm/s in Caco-2 assays suggests high absorption potential, while values below\(0.1 \times 10^{-6}\)cm/s indicate poor permeability [?]. However, bRo5 compounds frequently fall into a gray zone, where marginal structural modifications (e.g., introduction of a hydrogen bond donor or slight lipophilicity change) can drastically alter permeability. This sensitivity underscores the need for robust experimental data to guide optimization. Beyond serving as screening tools, these assays generate datasets that fuel predictive modeling, especially in machine learning driven drug discovery [54]. For bRo5 molecules where traditional design rules often fail high quality permeability data becomes even more critical to navigate their complex structure property relationships. While in vitro permeability assays have limitations such as the absence of full in vivo physiological context and variability in data reproducibility, they remain foundational for generating empirical permeability profiles. These assays enable rational optimization of challenging chemotypes by providing critical, experimentally derived permeability data [50].

The central question motivating this review is thus one of both necessity and opportunity: Can the burgeoning capabilities of machine learning (ML), when thoughtfully applied to the nuanced biophysics of macrocyclic permeability, bridge this translational gap and furnish predictive tools that are proven in peptidic macrocycles and potentially extendable to non-peptidic scaffolds? The inherent complexity of MC behavior their conformational dynamism, the subtle interplay of desolvation penalties, polarity masking, and topological shifts lends itself, at least hypothetically, to the pattern recognition strengths of advanced computational algorithms. Therefore, the principal goals of this review are articulated as follows:

To critically survey and synthesize the landscape of existing predictive models and seminal studies focused on the cell permeability of macrocycles, with an initial emphasis on peptide-based systems where the bulk of empirical and computational efforts has historically resided. To dissect and illuminate the fundamental physicochemical and structural principles such as conformational flexibility, the strategic deployment of IMHB, polarity surface area modulation, and dynamic topological adaptation that govern the membrane transit of these fascinating molecular architectures.

To rigorously interrogate the parallels between peptide-based and non-peptidic macrocycles, leveraging their shared characteristics (e.g., conformational adaptability, potential for polarity masking) to justify and guide the extrapolation of insights from the former to inform the design of predictive models applicable to the latter, particularly in the context of high throughput virtual screening. To candidly address the extant limitations in predicting non-peptidic macrocycle permeability and, more importantly, to propose forward-looking, mechanistically grounded strategies that synergize advanced computational methodologies with a deeper structural and biophysical understanding, thereby charting a course toward more reliable in silico permeability assessment. By navigating these objectives, this review aims not merely to collate existing knowledge, but to foster a deeper, more integrated understanding of macrocyclic permeability. We aspire to catalyze a shift from predominantly empirical approaches towards a more predictive, design-driven paradigm, ultimately empowering the scientific community to more effectively harness the therapeutic potential of both peptidic and, crucially, non-peptidic macrocycles for oral drug development. The promise lies in transforming the art of macrocycle design into a more robust science, with machine learning acting as a central tool, especially given the rapid advancements in the power and capabilities of newly proposed models.

To identify key trends and significant advancements in the field of permeability prediction for macrocyclic drugs, we initiated a targeted search strategy across three academic databases: Web of Science, Scopus, and PubMed. Our aim was to curate a comprehensive collection of peer-reviewed articles specifically addressing the use of computational methods, including ML and AI, in this critical area of research.

Our search strategy combined three conceptual domains using Boolean operators. We searched for terms related to macrocyclic compounds (macrocycles, cyclic peptides, macrocyclic molecules), permeability assessment (cell permeability, membrane permeability, PAMPA, Caco-2), and computational approaches (machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, predictive modeling). To maximize coverage of relevant studies, no time restrictions were imposed on the search. This yielded 152 articles: 109 from Web of Science, 32 from Scopus, and 11 from PubMed. Notably, most identified studies were published within the last two years, with the most recent included study from August 2025, reflecting the recent growth of this field. After removing 21 duplicates, 131 unique articles underwent title and abstract screening, where 108 were excluded for being reviews, published datasets, lacking macrocycle focus, or not applying machine learning methods. The remaining 23 articles advanced to full-text evaluation.

During full-text screening, we assessed whether each study explicitly addressed permeability or related membrane transport phenomena in macrocyclic compounds, utilized machine learning or computational techniques, and included experimental validation or benchmarking. We prioritized works offering insights from peptide-based models that might inform non-peptidic macrocycles, and gave particular attention to research employing ML-driven strategies with external test sets or introducing novel methodologies such as unsupervised pretraining or multimodal approaches. From the 23 full-text articles, 12 were excluded for being out of scope, inaccessible, or lacking computational modeling of permeability. This evaluation process resulted in 11 studies meeting all inclusion criteria and forming the analytical core of this review. To extract meaningful insights and ensure a coherent narrative across the diverse set of studies reviewed, we adopted a structured analytical framework that allowed for consistent comparison and critical evaluation. Rather than merely describing each study in isolation, we sought to identify underlying patterns, methodological trends, and points of divergence that reveal the current state and future potential of permeability prediction in macrocyclic drug discovery. A central goal was to uncover what works, why it works, and can these approaches be expected to generalize. To achieve this, each study was examined along several intersecting dimensions ranging from the molecular types and descriptor sets used, to the computational strategies adopted, and the experimental contexts in which models were trained and validated. This approach enabled us to assess not only the predictive accuracy of the models, but also the soundness of their design and the rigor of their evaluation pipelines. We paid particular attention to whether models were grounded in peptide-based systems, how features were engineered or learned, and whether model generalization was supported through external benchmarking.

Equally important was our consideration of methodological transparency, including the availability of datasets and source code, as this often serves as a proxy for reproducibility and scientific utility. In building a comparative table focused exclusively on machine learning (ML) methods to synthesize our findings, we emphasized variables that are critical to modeling success yet often underreported such as the nature of the permeability data used, the extent of cross-validation, and the presence of mechanistic insights beyond statistical fit. This table, which anchors the discussion in the following sections, serves not only as a map of existing work, but as a diagnostic tool that reveals both the strengths of current approaches and the limitations that may constrain their broader adoption. Through this categorization process, we aim to offer a nuanced perspective that is both reflective and forwardlooking, providing clarity on how computational methods have been deployed to overcome this complex prediction task and where innovation is still most needed. The prediction of membrane permeability for macrocyclic peptides remains a central challenge in translating these molecules into viable therapeutics, particularly for intracellular targets. As we have demonstrated in previous sections, the structural complexity and dynamic nature of these molecules often violate traditional rules and occupy the beyond-Rule-of-5 chemical space, thus necessitating more sophisticated computational frameworks. Conformational adaptability, solvent shielding, and membrane partitioning are now recognized as central determinants of permeability. Although physics-based simulations have clarified many of these mechanistic contributors, their routine application is constrained by computational expense, methodological sensitivity to force-field and membrane choices, and limited scalability. Machine learning approaches have therefore emerged not as replacements for physics-based models, but as complementary tools capable of encoding these mechanistic insights into rapid predictive frameworks. The current landscape of ML-driven permeability prediction for macrocycles is still relatively sparse; the available studies collectively reveal a clear methodological evolution from descriptor-driven QSPR models toward multimodal and self-supervised representation learning, while simultaneously highlighting persistent challenges related to data quality, assay heterogeneity, and chemical space coverage.

Early investigations established the physicochemical basis that continues to support modern models. Classical QSPR analyses such as Digiesi et al. [10] demonstrated that relatively simple descriptor sets including lipophilicity-related features could already explain substantial variance in PAMPA permeability, consistent with traditional regression frameworks including PLS [5]. Complementing this statistical perspective, the structural analysis of Over et al. [47], based on structurally diverse macrocycles derived from the Broad Institute DOS library [49], revealed that permeability depends critically on a molecule’s ability to reorganize between solvent-exposed conformations and internally shielded states compatible with membrane partitioning. Together, these studies established a dual conceptual foundation for permeability. On one hand, it is strongly correlated with polarity distribution and lipophilicity. On the other, it is mechanistically governed by conformational adaptability. This apparent contradiction, where static descriptors predict a fundamentally dynamic phenomenon, remains central to how later machine learning models interpret structural information (Fig.5).

The transition to modern data-driven modeling was enabled primarily by the introduction of the CycPeptMPDB dataset [34], which consolidated roughly seven thousand cyclic peptides with experimentally measured permeability values aggregated from literature and patent sources, including PAMPA, Caco-2, RRCK, and MDCK assays. The associated CycPeptMP framework [33] demonstrated that hierarchical multi-level encodings integrating atom-, residue-, and peptide-scale representations substantially improved predictive accuracy, achieving correlations approaching 0.88 and MAE values near 0.35, outperforming conventional machine learning baselines such as SVM [46] and RF [3]. This work established two main characteristics of the field. First, multi-scale structural encoding enhances predictive power. Second, most subsequent studies rely on essentially the same aggregated dataset, often supplemented by entries originating from repositories such as PubChem [30] or SureChEMBL [48]. While this shared resource has enabled systematic benchmarking, it also concentrates dataset-specific biases and assay variability across nearly all models.

Subsequent methodological advances varied primarily in how molecular structure is represented and learned. Multimodal architectures exemplified by Multi_CycGT [4] combine complementary encoding pathways, typically integrating SMILES-based transformer models, often benefiting from augmentation strategies such as SMILES enumeration [2], with graph neural networks capturing connectivity patterns and additional physicochemical descriptors. On curated PAMPA-derived datasets of approximately 6,900 peptides, such models achieve classification accuracies around 0.82 and AUC values near 0.86-−0.87, consistently outperforming single-representation baselines.

Further developments in multimodal learning expanded this idea by incorporating additional representation views and alignment strategies. The MuCoCP framework [57] introduced a multi-scale contrastive learning strategy that jointly aligns graph-based molecular encodings with sequence-level contextual embeddings, demonstrating that coupling structural connectivity with sequence-aware representations improves robustness in the low-data bRo5 regime. Evaluated on CycPeptMPDB partitions, MuCoCP achieved correlations around 0.82-−0.85 with MAE near 0.31-−0.34, outperforming standalone GNN or transformer baselines and confirming that coordinated multi-view representation learning contributes materially to predictive stability.

Multimodal integration was pushed further by MultiCycPermea [51], which introduced molecular images as an additional representation modality. Using a Swin Transformer image encoder alongside a SMILES-based transformer and a substructure-constrained feature alignment module, the model achieved strong performance across random, scaffold-based, and permeability-cliff evaluation settings, reducing mean squared error substantially relative to earlier multimodal systems such as Multi_CycGT and reaching Pearson correlations up to approximately 0.85 in-distribution. The ability to detect permeability cliffs and identify low-permeability candidates in external design tasks highlights the practical utility of cross-modal representation alignment, even though image-based inputs remain limited by their inability to capture stereochemistry or conformational flexibility.

Transformer-based architectures incorporating explicit structural priors represent another major direction. The CPMP model [27] extends the Molecular Attention Transformer framework [41], conceptually related to BERT-style attention architectures [8], by integrating molecular topology and interatomic distance matrices into the attention mechanism. When trained on CycPeptMPDB splits, the model achieves\(\hbox {R}^2\)values spanning roughly 0.62 to 0.75 depending on the assay subset, with weaker performance in smaller datasets such as RRCK and MDCK. This assay-dependent variability highlights a broader limitation. Predictive accuracy is usually constrained more by data availability and measurement consistency than by model design. Nonetheless, most studies continue to treat different assays as if they measure the same thing.

Efforts to improve extrapolation beyond training distributions have motivated architectures emphasizing representation robustness and pretraining. CyclePermea [52] employs a RoBERTa-style peptide encoder combined with Morgan fingerprint descriptors [42] and a multi-task objective including permeability regression and supporting structural prediction. Leveraging large-scale molecular collections, including datasets related to PubChem [30] and pretrained chemical language models such as ChemBERTa variants [1,6], the model achieves strong performance on random splits, with MSE around 0.22, MAE around 0.33, and Pearson correlation near 0.80. Under scaffold-based partitioning, correlation drops to roughly 0.52, quantitatively illustrating the persistent generalization gap that remains obscured by conventional random-split benchmarking.

Contrastive learning strategies attempt to address this limitation by structuring embedding spaces according to permeability similarity. PeptideCLM [19] uses a transformer-based peptide encoder combined with contrastive objectives aligning representations of peptides with similar permeability profiles, achieving correlations near 0.80 and MAE values around 0.33-−0.36. These results are consistent with the improvements observed in MuCoCP, reinforcing that relational supervision can provide robust signal even when absolute permeability measurements are sparse or noisy. Nevertheless, these models still rely primarily on static structural representations, leaving conformational dynamics implicitly inferred rather than explicitly modeled.

At the same time, not all progress has depended on increasingly complex architectures. The CYCLOPS study [17] systematically compared representation strategies, data augmentation methods, and architectural variations using LSTM-based predictors trained on CycPeptMPDB derived datasets. The combination of amino acid level sequential descriptors with global peptide physicochemical features achieved the strongest performance, with accuracy around 0.82 and F1-score near 0.87, while SMILES-only models consistently underperformed. These findings demonstrate that carefully selected physicochemical representations within relatively simple neural architectures can rival more complex multimodal systems, emphasizing again that representation relevance and dataset structure often dominate model complexity.

Questions of reliability and deployment extend beyond predictive accuracy alone. The methodological analysis by Geylan et al. [22] directly addressed the issue of applicability domains by evaluating classical fingerprint-based models under source-separated validation scenarios. Models that performed well under conventional validation showed near-random performance when tested on peptides originating from different literature sources, with balanced accuracy falling toward 0.5-−0.6. The study demonstrated that conformal prediction and recalibration using small representative samples from the target domain can substantially restore predictive reliability without retraining. This work highlights that uncertainty quantification and domain-awareness are not optional refinements but necessary components for real-world deployment of permeability predictors.

These collective observations clarify several consistent mechanistic and methodological insights. Lipophilicity emerges as a dominant determinant of macrocycle permeability, a relationship established in early QSPR analyses and now implicitly recapitulated across modern deep-learning architectures. Permeability is not governed by any single descriptor in isolation. Hydrogen-bonding capacity, polar surface area, and specific substructural motifs influence transport primarily through nonlinear and context-dependent interactions, reinforcing the need for models capable of capturing higher-order feature coupling rather than relying on additive descriptor effects. Conformational flexibility remains the most persistent unresolved variable. Experimental studies and molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that macrocycles dynamically reorganize between solvent-exposed and polarity-shielded states, directly modulating membrane compatibility. Most current machine learning models still operate on static two-dimensional representations or simplified minimized energy 3D conformations, implicitly inferring flexibility rather than modeling it explicitly. Incorporating ensemble-based descriptors, MD-derived structural features, in hybrid physics-informed learning frameworks therefore represents a logical direction for improving both mechanistic fidelity and predictive generalization.

A second structural limitation concerns data composition and chemical-space representation. Many reviewed models ultimately depend on overlapping peptide-centric datasets enriched in particular ring sizes, sequence motifs, or experimental sources, which constrains external validity even when internal benchmark performance appears strong. The carefully curated experimental framework established by Over et al. [47] illustrates how thoughtfully designed libraries can simultaneously provide mechanistic clarity and predictive robustness. Extending comparable experimental rigor to broader macrocycle collections, including structurally diverse non-peptidic scaffolds, will be essential for training models that generalize beyond peptide-focused domains. Equally important is the treatment of permeability assays themselves. PAMPA, Caco-2, RRCK, and MDCK measurements are frequently aggregated as interchangeable endpoints, despite capturing partially distinct biological processes involving passive diffusion, transporter effects, and cellular context. Modeling these assays within unified but explicitly differentiated frameworks, rather than collapsing them into a single target, may help disentangle intrinsic permeability from confounding influences such as efflux, solubility, or metabolic stability.

The literature therefore reflects a clear conceptual transition. Descriptor-driven QSPR studies established the physicochemical principles governing permeability and provided interpretable design guidelines. Contemporary deep-learning systems increasingly attempt to incorporate those principles through multimodal encodings, large-scale pretraining, and representation learning, enabling prediction across thousands of candidates and supporting generative design workflows. The next stage of progress will likely depend less on further architectural complexity and more on integrating complementary strengths. These include the mechanistic transparency of physics-based and descriptor-centered approaches, the scalability and pattern-recognition capacity of modern deep learning, and the statistical robustness afforded by richer, better-curated experimental datasets. Emerging meta-learning paradigms reinforce this perspective. Methods such as Meta-GAT [36] demonstrate that transferring meta-knowledge across related molecular prediction tasks can improve performance when labeled data are limited, while initiatives such as Meta-MolNet [37] emphasize standardized evaluation of domain generalization and predictive uncertainty across chemically distinct scaffolds. Embedding these principles into macrocycle permeability prediction may help shift the field from retrospective benchmarking toward adaptive, prospectively reliable modeling.

Ultimately, the central question is no longer whether permeability can be predicted within familiar chemical space, but whether predictive systems remain reliable when chemotypes, conformational regimes, or experimental contexts diverge from training distributions. Addressing this challenge, through improved data diversity, explicit incorporation of conformational dynamics, assay-aware modeling strategies, and principled uncertainty estimation, will determine whether current machine learning approaches evolve from analytical research tools into dependable engines for rational permeability optimization in macrocycle drug discovery.

The next generation of permeability prediction models for macrocyclic scaffolds must go beyond monolithic architectures and embrace truly hybrid and multimodal frameworks. One promising avenue is the integration of differnt data types sequence-based notations, graph topologies, 3D conformational ensembles, and physicochemical descriptors within unified transformer based backbones. These models have shown exceptional capacity to infer permeability related patterns directly from sequence representations, even recovering cyclization constraints and conformational priors without explicit structural input. Graph-based encodings, in particular, offer a complementary perspective by capturing localized electronic, topological, and substructural features often invisible to sequence only models. The convergence of GNNs with transformer-based attention layers suggests that interleaving graph and sequence views can provide superior generalization. However, model complexity must be critically balanced against interpretability and practical deployability. Over parameterized networks trained on limited data often yield high apparent performance but lack robustness. Conversely, recent evidence suggests that simpler, well-regularized models when coupled with rigorous calibration (e.g., conformal prediction, dropout-based uncertainty quantification) can match or exceed the predictive utility of deep black box models. Thus, simplicity with accountability should not be mistaken for methodological conservatism, it is a design strength. The quality, structure, and documentation of datasets will increasingly define the ceiling of model performance.

CycPeptMDB database has been instrumental in advancing peptide based modeling, future efforts must focus on curating domain specific, chemically diverse, and experimentally annotated datasets with rich metadata (e.g., permeability assay protocols, membrane types, solvent systems), enabling fair benchmarking and transfer learning. Indeed, transfer learning stands out as a critical enabler of progress. Pretraining large scale transformers on linear peptides, or even small molecules, has proven effective in capturing transferable chemical rules. These pretrained models can be fine-tuned to the macrocyclic domain particularly the non-linear, and aslsoe the non-peptidic space achieving strong performance with limited labeled samples. Such cross-domain adaptation will be vital for navigating the sparsity inherent in macrocycle pharmacology.

The recent establishment of NPMMPD [20] (https://swemacrocycledb.com/) , a structured foundation for modeling non-peptidic macrocycles at a level of granularity comparable to what CycPeptMPDB enabled for cyclic peptides. Its significance lies not merely in data accumulation, but in the possibility of moving beyond subclass-specific predictors toward integrative frameworks that operate across the broader macrocycle landscape. Any such model must encode the shared physicochemical drivers of passive permeability chameleonic behavior, intramolecular hydrogen-bonding networks, and conformational plasticity while remaining sensitive to the fundamental architectural differences between sequence-defined peptide backbones and chemically diverse non-peptidic scaffolds. In this context, cross-domain transfer learning offers a pragmatic strategy to leverage information from the more data-rich subclass, whereas multimodal architectures that combine sequence-aware representations with graph- or structure-based encodings provide a more principled route to capturing complementary structural abstractions. The central challenge is not merely technical generalization, but the faithful representation of permeability-relevant conformational ensembles across chemically heterogeneous macrocyclic systems.

Macrocyclic compounds are increasingly expanding the landscape of drug discovery by enabling engagement of challenging intracellular targets, although permeability still represents the main barrier to their broader therapeutic translation. Across the 11 machine learning studies examined in this review, a consistent methodological progression can be seen. Early QSPR models clarified the central roles of lipophilicity, hydrogen-bonding capacity, and polarity in governing permeability, whereas more recent approaches including graph neural networks, transformer-based language models, and multimodal fusion frameworks show that learned molecular representations can capture these determinants with improving predictive performance and scalability. These findings indicate that machine learning has moved from being a purely supportive analytical role and is becoming a practical predictive tool for macrocycle permeability, with accuracy approaching that of physics-based simulations while remaining compatible with the speed requirements of modern discovery pipelines.

Despite this progress, the analysis also reveals persistent structural limitations that constrain the field. The most significant challenge remains data availability and quality, as most available datasets are dominated by cyclic peptides, frequently derived from PAMPA and Caco-2 measurements and often limited in size, chemical diversity, or assay consistency. As Caco-2 permeability reflects a composite of passive diffusion and transporter mediated effects, models trained on such data may learn mixed transport signals rather than permeability alone, further complicating interpretation and transferability. These issues are amplified when attempting to generalize predictions beyond the chemical space represented in training sets. Non-peptidic macrocycles account for a large number of clinically approved drugs, but this class remains poorly represented in available datasets, which limits progress in building models that can meaningfully support their development. Expanding experimentally validated permeability resources for structurally diverse macrocycles, including initiatives similar to CycPeptMPDB and the proposed NPMMPD, will therefore be important for enabling more reliable and broadly applicable prediction frameworks.

Methodologically, a second recurring concerns the treatment of molecular conformation. Many current models rely on static 2D representations, simplified conformers, or force field optimized geometries that may not adequately capture the dynamic “chameleonic” behavior central to beyond-Rule-of-5 permeability. Generating conformational ensembles from short molecular dynamics simulations offers a practical compromise, providing more realistic structural descriptors while remaining computationally tractable. When available, comparison of such ensembles with experimental structural data could further improve confidence in feature extraction and model reliability. Incorporating these physically grounded representations into learning pipelines represents a concrete opportunity to bridge the long standing divide between mechanistic simulation and data-driven prediction.

The most promising future direction therefore lies not in choosing between physics-based and machine learning approaches, but in integrating them. Hybrid strategies that embed experimentally informed descriptors such as intramolecular hydrogen-bond shielding, conformational adaptability, solvent exposure, and polarity modulation into modern representation learning frameworks could deliver models that are simultaneously accurate, interpretable, and chemically meaningful. Transfer learning across macrocycle subclasses, self-supervised pretraining on extensive chemical libraries, and multimodal architectures capable of combining sequence, graph, and structural information further strengthen this integrative vision. Such approaches will be particularly important for extending predictive capability to non-peptidic macrocycles, where purely data-driven models currently lack sufficient training coverage.

In this context, the central question is no longer whether macrocycle permeability can be predicted, but how reliably such predictions can guide molecular design across diverse macrocyclic chemotypes. Achieving this goal will require coordinated advances in dataset quality, conformational modeling, and hybrid approach development. With continued progress along these directions, predictive modeling is positioned to evolve from a retrospective screening tool into a proactive design framework supporting the rational engineering of permeable macrocycles and accelerating the discovery of therapeutics capable of reaching targets beyond the reach of conventional small molecules.

title: Generalizable deep-learning-based mRNA-protein interaction prediction strongly depends on protein diversity
author: Yu-Huai Yu; Han-Ting Hong; Tzu-Hsien Yang
text:
Proteins regulate diverse biological processes through interactions with other molecules, including RNAs. RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are essential regulators of gene expression, forming specific mRNA-protein interactions (mRPIs) that influence mRNA processing, translation, and stability. Recently, deep-learning models have been proposed to predict mRPIs using only sequence information, with some reporting near-perfect accuracy. However, such performance appears inconsistent with the biological complexity of RNA recognition by proteins, which is often influenced by protein tertiary structures that are computationally challenging to predict. In related fields such as protein-protein interaction prediction, data leakage, particularly caused by overlapping proteins between training and test sets, has been shown to substantially inflate performance metrics. Nevertheless, whether similar issues affect mRPI prediction has not yet been systematically investigated.

We constructed an mRPI benchmark dataset from CLIP experiments and implemented two data partitioning schemes: a random interaction-level split and an RBP-aware split in which pairs of all test RBPs were excluded from training. Three RBP sequence encoding strategies were evaluated within an attention-based deep-learning framework under both partitioning settings: sequence-based one-hot encoding, language model-derived encoding, and structure-aware encoding. Across all models, performance remained high only when test RBPs were also present in the training data. When predicting interactions for unseen RBPs, performance dropped substantially, indicating limited generalization. Even replacing RBPs with their most similar counterparts from the training set did not meaningfully improve generalization. These results suggest that additional protein features beyond sequence information are required to achieve robust mRPI prediction. Overall, our study demonstrated that existing mRPI prediction models are largely overfitted to their original training RBPs and fail to generalize to unseen proteins.

Overall, we provided a curated benchmark dataset, a rigorous evaluation framework, and an attention-based model that achieves the best generalization performance among currently available methods, with an approximately 8.5% auROC improvement over existing tools. These resources will facilitate the development of more reliable and broadly applicable mRPI prediction tools.

This work presented the first systematic investigation of data leakage and generalization in mRNA-protein interaction prediction, demonstrating that most reported near-perfect performance is largely driven by RBP overlap between training and test sets. By introducing an RBP-aware evaluation framework and a benchmark dataset, we revealed that most sequence-based models fail to generalize to unseen RBPs, even when enhanced with protein language model-derived and structure-aware encodings. Our study established a more rigorous evaluation standard for mRNA-protein interaction prediction, highlighting the critical need for protein diversity and beyond-sequence features to advance reliable mRNA-protein interaction prediction.

Proteins are the primary molecular machines that drive diverse cellular functions. Among them, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) interact with RNAs to form RNA-protein interactions (RPIs) that play critical roles in post-transcriptional regulation, including mRNA stability, localization, and translation efficiency [1,2]. Disruptions in RPIs have recently been associated with various human diseases [3], underscoring the biological and clinical importance of understanding RBP-targeting mechanisms. Despite their significance, the principles governing the selective binding of RBPs to their RNA targets remain largely elusive, highlighting the need for deeper investigation into RPI mechanisms.

To address this, experimental approaches such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and X-ray crystallography can reveal structural details of RPIs [4]. High-throughput methods such as cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP) sequencing and photoactivatable-ribonucleoside enhanced cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (PAR-CLIP) sequencing enable transcriptome-wide identification of RBP targets [5]. However, these approaches are costly and labor-intensive. Currently, only around 200–300 human RBPs have publicly available CLIP-seq data [6], despite more than 2,000 RBPs being known in humans [1]. This data bottleneck has motivated the development of numerous computational tools for RPI prediction. In particular, several deep-learning-based methods have been proposed to model RPIs using protein and RNA sequence information, including IPMiner [7], RPI-SAN [8], RPIFSE [9], and ELM [10]. Notably, most of these tools reported near-perfect performance (approximately 90–99%) on their prepared benchmark datasets.

Nonetheless, the reported performance of these deep-learning models appears inconsistent with the intrinsic complexity of RBP-RNA interaction recognition. RPI formation is highly dependent on the tertiary structures of proteins and contextual cues beyond primary sequence information [11], suggesting potential caveats in the near-perfect performance reported by simple sequence-based models. Recent breakthroughs in protein structure prediction, such as the AlphaFold suite [12], have demonstrated that accurate inference of 3D structures from amino acid sequences requires sophisticated model architectures as well as the integration of multiple sequence alignments and docking-related information [13]. These developments raise concerns regarding the near-perfect accuracy reported by existing RPI prediction tools that rely solely on primary sequence features.

Indeed, recent studies in protein-protein interaction prediction have revealed that many deep-learning-based predictors suffer from serious data leakage, particularly due to overlapping proteins between the training and test sets, which can artificially inflate performance [14,15,16,17]. However, this critical issue has not yet been thoroughly investigated in the context of RPI prediction, despite the substantial complexity implied by the more than 2,000 known human RBPs. These observations suggest that the reported accuracies may reflect overfitting rather than true generalization in existing RPI prediction tools, highlighting the urgent need for more rigorous evaluation strategies and deeper examination of model limitations in RPI prediction. Furthermore, it remains unclear whether alternative protein encoding schemes, including pre-trained protein large language models [18] and homologous structure prediction results [19], can mitigate this overfitting issue.

In this study, we systematically investigated the key methodological issues in applying deep learning and machine learning approaches to mRNA-RBP interaction (mRPI) prediction. We first prepared an mRPI ground-truth dataset from CLIP experiments and implemented a modern attention-based deep-learning model to demonstrate that random partitioning of mRPI pairs substantially inflates prediction performance compared with RBP-aware partitioning. An alternative test set partitioning scheme, termed RBP-aware partitioning, reserves all RNA-protein pairs associated with held-out RBPs during evaluation, thereby better reflecting real-world generalization scenarios. To further examine the role of input representations, we evaluated various protein encoding strategies beyond one-hot encoding, including ProteinBERT embeddings [18] and AlphaFold-based structural features [19], and showed that richer encodings do not adequately resolve the generalization gap caused by limited RBP diversity. We also benchmarked existing RPI prediction tools under controlled conditions, revealing that many were overfitted to specific RBPs and failed to generalize when tested on unseen proteins. Finally, we demonstrate that our attention-based deep-learning model [20,21], trained on RBP-disjoint datasets, outperforms existing tools by approximately 8.5% in auROC. Overall, our work introduced a high-quality benchmark dataset and a systematic evaluation framework to guide the development of next-generation mRPI prediction models with improved robustness and practical utility.

In this study, we designed a comprehensive evaluation workflow to investigate the generalizability of deep-learning-based mRNA-protein interaction (mRPI) prediction (see Fig.1). First, we constructed a ground-truth mRPI dataset from CLIP-seq experiments, in which experimentally supported RBP-binding peak regions were processed and merged to generate reliable mRNA-RBP interaction pairs. Second, to systematically examine potential data leakage and generalization issues, we implemented an RBP-aware partitioning strategy that explicitly accounts for RBP identities during dataset splitting. Specifically, interaction pairs were divided into a training set and two different types of test sets: (i) a random test set generated by random pair sampling, allowing RBPs to completely overlap between the training and test sets, and (ii) an RBP-aware test set in which all RBPs in the test set are entirely absent from the training set, enabling evaluation on previously unseen RBPs. Third, we evaluated an attention-based deep-learning model under these partitioning schemes using three different protein encoding strategies, including one-hot sequence encoding, ProteinBERT-based protein language (LLM) model encoding, and structure-aware encoding. Finally, by comparing model performance across the random and RBP-aware test settings, we assessed whether improved protein encoding could mitigate the generalization gap. Detailed descriptions of these steps are provided in the following subsections.

Overview of the evaluation workflow for mRNA-protein interaction prediction generalizability. Ground-truth mRPI pairs were prepared from CLIP-seq data and split into one training and two test sets (random vs. RBP-aware). An attention-based model was evaluated using three protein encoding schemes (one-hot, ProteinBERT/Protein-LLM, and structure-aware) to assess generalization, particularly on unseen RBPs in the RBP-aware test set. The structure image was downloaded from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database [22]

In this research, we focused on evaluating sequence-based models for mRNA-protein interaction (mRPI) prediction. To this end, we prepared an mRPI ground-truth dataset from collected cross-linking immunoprecipitation sequencing (CLIP-seq) experiment results. Several data processing steps were designed to construct this dataset (Fig.2). First, we downloaded pre-processed CLIP-seq binding segment results from CLIPdb [6]. In total, 38,361,545 genomic binding regions from 220 human RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were collected. These genomic binding peak regions were then aligned to the human transcriptome (hg38 [23]) to obtain the corresponding mRNA binding site regions, yielding 41,876,769 mRNA binding site segments for these 220 RBPs. The list of the 220 RBPs can be downloaded via the link provided in the “Data and Tool Availability” section. To reduce redundancy, overlapping mRNA binding site segments associated with the same RBP were merged, producing 20,285,684 non-overlapping mRNA segments. Since alternatively spliced transcripts from the same gene may share similar binding site regions recognized by an RBP, we further applied CD-HIT [24] clustering with a 70% sequence identity threshold to remove duplicate binding fragments for each RBP. The choice of a 70% identity threshold reflected a balance between eliminating highly similar sequences and retaining sufficient data for model training. After CD-HIT processing, 494,616 unique mRPI binding pairs were obtained, each linked to its corresponding RBP as a confirmed positive interaction pair (Fig.2a).

The steps for preparing the mRNA-protein interaction ground-truth dataset.aIdentification of the binding pairs.bPreparation of the non-binding pairs

To construct negative samples, we performed RBP permutation on the positive binding pairs (Fig.2b). Specifically, for each mRNA segment-RBP binding pair, the associated RBP label was replaced with that of another RBP for which no binding event had been observed on the transcript from which the mRNA segment originated. The resulting mRNA fragment-permuted RBP pairs were then de-duplicated using CD-HIT with a 70% sequence identity threshold. In addition, we ensured that no CLIP-identified mRNA binding segments for a given RBP were included in its corresponding negative pairs. This process yielded 477,249 unique negative samples. In total, the complete mRPI dataset comprised 971,865 mRNA fragment-RBP pairs, including 494,616 positive and 477,249 negative pairs that cover 220 RBPs.

In the above data processing steps, we did not adopt an abritrary window to center on CLIP read peaks to get windowed, peak-centered segments. As detailed in previous paragraphs, the mRNA segments used in the ground-truth dataset were derived from processed CLIP-seq peaks. These mRNA segments included in our ground-truth dataset correspond directly to these CLIP-seq peak regions, together with their associated flanking sequences. Overlapping peak intervals were further merged during preprocessing to avoid redundant entries. Therefore, the input mRNA segment sequences represent merged experimentally supported binding regions rather than arbitrary windows centered on peak signals. Notably, whether the peak signal is precisely centered within the final sequence segment is not critical for the deep-learning models adopted in this study, as convolutional layers and attention mechanisms used in the models are designed to capture local binding motifs and contextual patterns regardless of their absolute position within the input sequence.

In these mRPI pairs, we used the full-length amino acid sequences of RBPs rather than restricting the representation to annotated RNA-binding domains. Although domain-level representations, which can be obtained from resources such as Pfam or InterPro [25], could potentially improve feature specificity, CLIP-seq experiments do not provide domain-resolved interaction annotations. This makes it difficult to reliably associate observed binding peaks with specific protein domains. Therefore, we adopted full-length sequence processing to ensure methodological consistency and to avoid introducing additional assumptions regarding domain-level binding mechanisms.

In this research, we emphasized the necessity of preparing the test set in an RBP-aware manner, in contrast to conventional random partitioning. To evaluate model performance under different partitioning conditions, the processed mRPI ground-truth dataset was divided into multiple subsets. In total, the dataset includes pairs from 220 RBPs. First, we selected 180 RBPs from the full dataset, resulting in 781,603 pairs. These 781,603 pairs consist of 398,944 positive mRPI pairs and 382,659 negative random pairings. Next, two distinct test sets were prepared. The random test set contained 35,349 pairs derived from the selected 180 RBPs by randomly sampling 5% of the pairs associated with these RBPs (Fig.3a). The remaining mRPI pairs and random pairings from these 180 RBPs were used as the training-validation set. This random test set evaluates a model’s performance on RBPs it has already seen during training, but with new RBP-mRNA fragment pairs. Finally, the remaining 40 RBPs were further divided into two subsets, each containing 20 RBPs.

The data partitioning for evaluating sequence-based models in mRPI prediction.aThe random test set prepared by random selection of pairs associated with the same pool of RBPs in the training-validation set.bThe RBP-aware test set obtained by first reserving 20 RBPs and then choosing all pairs of these reserved RBPs into an independent test set. Pairs from the remaining 20 RBPs were saved for future benchmark usage

The second test set was termed the RBP-aware test set (Fig.3b). This RBP-aware test set consisted of pairs from the reserved 20 RBPs that are completely distinct from the previously selected 180 RBPs, resulting in 42,818 binding pairs and 40,561 non-binding pairs. The RBP-aware test set enables the assessment of model generalization to mRPI pairs involving entirely unseen RBPs, thereby providing a more unbiased and realistic performance estimate. In addition, we reserved another subset from the remaining 20 RBPs as an independent benchmark set, containing 40,645 binding pairs and 42,355 non-binding pairs. This benchmark set was not used in the evaluations conducted in this study and is intended for future fair benchmarking. The final partitioned datasets can be downloaded via the link provided in the “Data and Tool Availability” section.

In the aforementioned setting, a total of 220 RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were included and divided into three subsets following an approximately 80%: 10%: 10% split, corresponding to 180 RBPs for model development, 20 RBPs for evaluation, and 20 RBPs reserved as an independent benchmark set. This ratio was chosen to balance effective model training with leakage-aware evaluation while preserving a strictly held-out benchmark for future use. The reservation of an independent benchmark RBP set was motivated by concerns regarding data torturing, a phenomenon in which repeated evaluations on the same test set can lead to overly optimistic and non-generalizable performance estimates [26]. In the context of mRPI prediction, where available datasets are limited, and test RBPs are frequently reused across studies, such repeated exposure may unintentionally bias model evaluation. By isolating a completely clean and untouched mRPI benchmark set, a more reliable reference point for future comparisons is established, reducing the risk of performance inflation caused by test set overuse.

Sequence-based deep-learning models require appropriate encoding schemes for both RBP and mRNA sequences. Therefore, three different protein-encoding strategies were investigated in this study, each capturing distinct levels of sequence and structural information of RBPs. After encoding, the encoding tensors of RBPs and mRNAs were padded to their respective maximum sequence lengths observed in the dataset. Zero-padding was applied when sequences were shorter than the predefined maximum length. Protein sequences were padded to 2,804, while mRNA segment sequences were padded to 1,024. In this study, mRNA fragments were consistently encoded using one-hot encoding. In contrast, RBPs were encoded using one of three strategies: one-hot encoding, large language model (LLM)-derived encoding, or structure-aware encoding. By employing these three protein-encoding approaches, we enabled a direct comparison of how different levels of protein representation influence mRPI prediction performance. The details of these encoding schemes are described in the following three subsections.

In the one-hot encoding scheme, each amino acid in a protein sequence was mapped to a unique binary vector of dimension 20, corresponding to the 20 standard amino acids. A value of 1 indicates the presence of a specific amino acid at that position, and 0 otherwise. Protein sequences shorter than 2,804 residues were zero-padded, resulting in an RBP encoding tensor\(E_{P}\)of size\(2804 \times 20\). This representation preserves exact residue identity and positional information without incorporating additional prior biological knowledge. Similarly, mRNA fragments were one-hot encoded using a 4-dimensional vector representing the four nucleotide types at each position, and sequences shorter than 1,024 nucleotides were zero-padded. This process produced an mRNA encoding tensor\(E_{m}\)of size\(1024 \times 4\).

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising achievements in biological research [18,27,28]. Therefore, we sought to incorporate contextual and evolutionary information extracted from protein amino acid sequences using a pre-trained protein LLM. Specifically, we adopted the LLM-based encoding provided by ProteinBERT [18]. ProteinBERT is a transformer-based model pre-trained on millions of protein sequences, enabling it to learn local sequence motif patterns, conservation signals, and potential long-range dependencies relevant to protein functions. Such LLM-derived embeddings have been shown to capture inferred protein biochemical, structural, and evolutionary information [18]. In ProteinBERT, each RBP is represented by an encoding tensor\(E_{P}\)of size\(l \times 1562\), where 1,562 denotes the embedding dimension assigned to each amino acid residue. RBP sequences shorter than 2,804 residues were zero-padded, resulting in\(l = 2804\). Compared with one-hot encoding, this LLM-based representation is substantially richer, as it incorporates contextual knowledge learned from diverse protein families rather than treating each residue independently. In this study, we evaluated whether such additional contextual information could mitigate the generalization issue in mRPI prediction under limited RBP diversity.

Previous studies have shown that structural information plays a critical role in RBP function [1]. Based on this premise, we further integrated LLM-based sequence embeddings with AlphaFold-predicted structural features [22] to construct a structure-aware encoding scheme for RBPs. This combined representation enables evaluation of how contextual sequence information and predicted three-dimensional structural features jointly influence model generalization in mRPI prediction.

In the structure-aware encoding scheme, we first downloaded the AlphaFold-predicted.pdbstructure file for each RBP from UniProt [29]. For each RBP, the atoms of every amino acid residue were mapped to their corresponding Cartesian coordinates (X, Y, Z) recorded in the.pdbfile. The average coordinate value of all atoms within each residue was then computed, resulting in a single representative spatial point per amino acid. Next, the three-dimensional space occupied by the RBP was transformed into a discretized spatial grid of size\(16 \times 16 \times 16\). Because residue coordinates are continuous rather than integer values, each transformed coordinatedwas mapped to points ranging between\(\lfloor d \rfloor\)and\(\lceil d \rceil\). The corresponding ProteinBERT embedding of each amino acid was then assigned to its associated voxel locations, producing a structure-aware input tensor\(E_{P}\)of shape\(16 \times 16 \times 16 \times 1562\)for each RBP. Under this encoding scheme, 3D convolutional operations were applied in the deep-learning model to capture spatial structural features.

To evaluate the effects of the two data partitioning schemes on sequence-based deep learning models, we adopted a modern attention-based architecture that has been shown to be effective for molecular interaction prediction [20,21]. Using this framework, we systematically investigated the potential limitations of sequence-based mRPI prediction under different RBP encodings. As illustrated in Fig.4, the attention-based deep network consists of three main components: (1) local feature extraction, (2) binding feature integration, and (3) feature aggregation and classification. These three components are elucidated in the following subsections.

The implemented modern attention-based model used to evaluate the issues of sequence-based mRPI prediction. The network consists of three parts. The local feature extraction part tries to learn the patterns from the encoding; the binding feature integration part learns the binding patterns for RBPs and mRNA segments; and the feature aggregation part helps complete the final binding pair classification.
