Three independent attention-based deep networks were constructed, each corresponding to a distinct RBP encoding strategy: (1) the one-hot encoding model, (2) the LLM-encoding model, and (3) the structure-aware encoding model. To ensure a robust and fair comparison, all models were trained using consistent optimization strategies. Through 5-fold cross-validation on the training-validation set, the following hyperparameters were selected for all three models: (1) training batch size: 64; (2) number of training epochs: 20; (3) learning rate schedule: linear warm-up to 1e-4, followed by exponential decay with a rate of 0.95 to a final learning rate of 1e-10; (4) dropout: dropout layers with a rate of 0.3 applied after each dense layer; and (5) loss function: binary categorical cross-entropy. All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

In this research, the mRPI prediction task is formulated as a binary classification problem, where each mRNA-protein pair is labeled as either a binding pair (positive) or a non-binding pair (negative). Model performance is therefore evaluated by comparing predicted labels with ground-truth labels to form the confusion matrix. Based on this matrix, the following evaluation metrics [30] were adopted in this study:

In mRPI prediction, a true positive (TP) occurs when the model correctly predicts a binding pair; a false positive (FP) occurs when the model predicts a binding pair that is actually non-binding; a true negative (TN) refers to correctly predicting a non-binding pair; and a false negative (FN) arises when the model fails to detect a true binding pair. The above metrics were calculated using a predefined fair decision threshold of 0.5 in this study. To enable threshold-independent comparisons, we evaluated the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and precision-recall (PR) curves. The ROC curve plots sensitivity against the false positive rate (FPR) across different decision thresholds. The area under the ROC curve (auROC) summarizes this relationship into a single score, where higher values indicate better discrimination between binding and non-binding pairs. The PR curve can be used to better account for the prevalence of the positive class. It plots precision against recall at varying thresholds, and the area under the PR curve (auPRC) reflects the model’s ability to maintain high precision while capturing a large fraction of true binding pairs, making it particularly informative for imbalanced classification tasks [34,35]. Since our dataset is nearly balanced, we primarily focused on auROC as a threshold-independent metric for model evaluation. Nevertheless, all metrics were reported to provide a comprehensive assessment of the performance of the proposed attention-based models.

To investigate the influence of dataset partitioning strategies on model generalization, we first evaluated mRPI prediction using simple one-hot encoding for both RBP and mRNA segment sequences within the aforementioned attention-based framework (referred to as the one-hot encoding model in this study). Two distinct test set designs were implemented, as described in the “The Evaluated Data Partitioning Schemes” section. In the random test setting, pairs associated with the same RBPs in the training set were randomly sampled and reserved for testing, allowing identical RBPs to appear in both the training-validation and test sets. In contrast, the RBP-aware test set ensured that all RBPs in the test set were completely absent from the training-validation set, thereby simulating a realistic scenario in which interactions must be predicted for entirely unseen RBPs.

The training and evaluation results of the model based on the sequence one-hot encoding.aThe learning curves of the one-hot-encoding model.bThe ROC curves of the 5-fold validation results, the results on the random test set, and the results on the RBP-aware test set

The parameters of the attention-based model using RBP one-hot encoding were first optimized on the training-validation set. Model fitness was monitored using learning curves (Fig.5a). The average training and validation F1 curves converged closely, indicating that the model did not exhibit obvious overfitting. The corresponding training and validation loss learning curves are shown in Fig. S1-a of the Supplementary File. However, the test results revealed a sharp contrast between the two partitioning strategies. On the random test set, the model achieved high predictive performance (test auROC = 90.5%, F1 = 82.1%), comparable to the average 5-fold cross-validation results (See Fig.5b and Table1). In contrast, performance dropped substantially on the RBP-aware test set, with a 22.3% decrease in auROC and a 34.2% decrease in F1 (test auROC = 68.2%, F1 = 47.9%; see Fig.5b and Table1). These findings demonstrated a pronounced generalization gap when predicting interactions involving unseen RBPs. The results suggested that random partitioning can lead to overly optimistic performance estimates due to protein identity leakage between training and test sets, causing models to rely on RBP-specific sequence patterns rather than general principles of mRPI recognition. In contrast, RBP-aware evaluation provides a more stringent and biologically realistic assessment of model capability, revealing the true limitations of current deep-learning approaches in mRPI prediction. Overall, these results indicated that for mRPI prediction to be practically useful, particularly for pairs involving uncharacterized RBPs, models must be evaluated under RBP-disjoint settings.

The training and evaluation results of the model based on the sequence LLM (ProteinBERT) encoding.aThe learning curves of the LLM-encoding model.bThe ROC curves of the 5-fold validation results, the results on the random test set, and the results on the RBP-aware test set

We next evaluated whether protein LLM-derived embeddings for RBPs could help mitigate the generalization gap observed with one-hot encoding. Specifically, the RBP sequence representation was replaced with embeddings generated by ProteinBERT [18]. ProteinBERT is a transformer-based model trained on millions of protein sequences and is designed to capture local motif patterns, global contextual relationships, and evolutionary information that are difficult to represent using simple one-hot encodings. These LLM embeddings were then used as input to the same attention-based architecture described above (referred to as the LLM-encoding model in this study), ensuring that any observed performance differences were attributable solely to the protein encoding strategy.

We also used learning curves to verify that the LLM-encoding model converged properly and achieved stable fitting (see Fig.6a). The corresponding training and validation loss learning curves are shown in Fig. S1-b of the Supplementary File. The model was then evaluated on both the random test set and the RBP-aware test set. On the random test set, the LLM-encoding model achieved similar performance (random test auROC = 90.7% and F1 = 82.4%; see Fig.6b and Table2) to the training-validation results. However, on the RBP-aware test set, performance dropped substantially (RBP-aware test auROC = 71.5% and F1 = 52.0%; see Fig.6b and Table2), corresponding to decreases of approximately 19.2% in auROC and 30.4% in F1 compared with the random test setting. These results indicated that although LLM-derived features may provide more informative and potentially transferable protein representations, they do not fully resolve the fundamental limitation of poor generalization to unseen RBPs. Overall, the findings suggested that strategies beyond sequence-context enrichment are required to substantially improve generalizability in mRPI prediction.

To further examine whether structural context can enhance model generalization, we combined ProteinBERT sequence embeddings with 3D structural information predicted by AlphaFold [22]. The.pdbfiles of the AlphaFold-predicted structural information for RBPs were downloaded from UniProt [29], enabling extraction of residue-level spatial coordinate features that capture the spatial organization of each RBP. These structural descriptors were integrated with ProteinBERT embeddings to construct a hybrid representation that combines contextual sequence information and predicted tertiary structural properties. Detailed procedures for this hybrid embedding can be referred to in the “Structure-aware Encoding of RBPs” subsection.

The training and evaluation results of the model based on the sequence-predicted structure information along with the LLM encoding.aThe learning curves of the structure-aware-encoding model.bThe ROC curves of the 5-fold validation results, the results on the random test set, and the results on the RBP-aware test set

We adopted a similarly designed attention-based architecture for the structure-aware encoding of RBPs (referred to as the structure-aware-encoding model in this study), with the only modification being the replacement of 1D convolutions with 3D convolutions for RBP representations. This adjustment enables the model to better incorporate three-dimensional structural information. When trained on the training-validation set, the average cross-validation F1 learning curves showed smooth and stable convergence (Fig.7a), indicating that the inclusion of structural features did not destabilize optimization. The corresponding training and validation loss learning curves are presented in Fig. S1-c of the Supplementary File. On the random test set, the combination of ProteinBERT embeddings with AlphaFold-derived structural information achieved performance comparable to the 5-fold cross-validation results (random test auROC = 90.8%, F1 = 82.4%; see Fig.7b and Table3). However, on the RBP-aware test set, the auROC performance dropped substantially (auROC = 59.7%), remaining approximately 30% lower than that on the random test set. Similar trends were observed for other evaluation metrics (Table3). These findings indicated that although predicted 3D structural features increase RBP representational richness, they do not compensate for the limited protein diversity in the training-validation dataset and still lead to overfitting to RBPs present during training. In summary, incorporating sequence-based structural predictions into LLM-derived embeddings is insufficient to eliminate the pronounced performance decline when predicting interactions for unseen RBPs. Collectively, the results from the three encoding schemes suggested that additional information beyond sequence-derived features may be required to achieve robust cross-RBP generalization in mRPI prediction.

Note that the number of training epochs was carefully selected based on extensive preliminary cross-validation experiments to ensure stable convergence while avoiding overfitting. As shown in Figs.5a,6a, and7a, both the training and validation F1-scores plateaued well before 20 epochs, with no evidence of divergence or validation degradation in later epochs. This behavior suggested that the models reached a well-fitted regime rather than continuing to over-optimize the training data. Although an explicit early stopping criterion was not implemented, our learning rate schedule served a similar regularization function. Specifically, after an initial warm-up phase, the learning rate decays exponentially to an extremely small value (1e-10), resulting in negligible parameter updates during the final training epochs. In practice, the last several epochs function similarly to early stopping, as model weights effectively stabilize and the risk of further overfitting is minimal. Training and validation results were continuously monitored across all folds during 5-fold cross-validation, and the selected hyperparameters consistently produced stable validation results across different folds. This strategy ensured fair control of overfitting for subsequent comparisons among different RBP encoding schemes.

From the above evaluations, we observed that the three RBP encoding schemes (one-hot encoding, LLM encoding, and structure-aware encoding) exhibited similar performance trends. Therefore, all three models were included in the subsequent computational analyses. We next examined whether considering the most similar RBP sequence from the training-validation set for an unseen RBP could mitigate the observed generalization gap in mRPI prediction. To this end, each RBP in the RBP-aware test set was searched against RBPs in the training-validation set using BLASTP [36] with default parameters. For RBPs with identified homologs in the training-validation set, we replaced the original RBP in the query pairs with its most similar counterpart from the training-validation set. If no similar protein was identified, the original RBP was retained. Using this replacement strategy, predictions were performed on the RBP-aware test set using the three aforementioned models. As summarized in Tables1,2, and3, the auROC values on the RBP-aware test set with BLASTP replacement were 68.6%, 69.5%, and 70.3% for the one-hot encoding model, the LLM encoding model, and the structure-aware encoding model, respectively. All three models still exhibited substantial performance degradation compared with predictions on the random test set. These results indicated that protein sequence similarity matching alone is insufficient to close the generalization gap for sequence-based models. These observations also suggested that the learned representations were largely driven by protein-specific binding patterns rather than genuinely transferable interaction principles. In other words, the models might rely on direct or indirect memorization of RBP-dependent features. Consequently, the strong performance observed under random partitioning likely reflected the presence of overlapping RBPs in the training data. Overall, this BLASTP analysis further supports the conclusion that insufficient RBP diversity in current datasets is a key factor limiting generalizable mRPI prediction. In summary, sequence-based models are prone to overfitting through memorization of protein-specific features rather than achieving true generalization across structurally or functionally related proteins, further underscoring the importance of increasing RBP diversity in mRPI ground-truth datasets.

Because CLIP-seq detection sensitivity depends on transcript abundance, certain highly expressed mRNAs may be overrepresented in the interaction dataset, raising the concern that mRNA selection bias could potentially influence model performance. To examine this possibility, we conducted two baseline evaluations. First, we constructed an mRNA frequency baseline, in which the prediction score was determined solely by the occurrence frequency of each mRNA in the training-validation set. Second, we evaluated the mRNA-only baselines by setting the RBP representation to an all-zero vector in all three RBP-encoding models, allowing the attention-based models to generate predictions based exclusively on mRNA features. On the RBP-aware test set (See Fig.8a), the mRNA frequency baseline achieved near random-guessing performance (auROC = 45.5%), and the mRNA-only models (auROC = 61.9%, 58.5%, 57.9%, when setting RBPs as zero vectors in the one-hot encoding, LLM-encoding, and structure-aware encoding models) performed approximately 10% worse than their corresponding settings where RBP information were provided. On the random test set, similar performance trend for the three models when setting the RBPs as zero vectors (auROC = 61.7%, 53.5%, 58.5%, when setting RBPs as zero vectors in the one-hot encoding, LLM-encoding, and structure-aware encoding models) were also observed (See Fig.8b). These results indicated that mRPI prediction in the prepared dataset cannot be explained solely by mRNA occurrence bias and that meaningful RBP-dependent information is essential for accurate prediction.

We note that CLIP-seq can also be used to investigate RBP interactions with non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), and several previous studies have explored RBP-ncRNA binding prediction. However, ncRNA-related datasets are typically more heterogeneous and may involve additional complexities, such as transcript annotation ambiguity, diverse RNA structural properties, and more context-dependent binding behaviors [37,38]. Although similar generalization challenges are expected to arise in RBP-ncRNA interaction prediction, extending our evaluation framework to systematically assess generalization in RBP-ncRNA interaction prediction remains an important direction for future research.

To further characterize the impact of data leakage, we additionally performed an RBP-aware 5-fold cross-validation in which all interaction pairs associated with the same RBPs were strictly assigned to the same data fold. This setting provided an additional RBP-aware evaluation of generalization to previously unseen RBPs. The models were optimized using the same learning curve method and training strategy described above. Under RBP-aware 5-fold cross-validation, consistent performance trends were observed across all three encoding schemes evaluated in this study. Specifically, the average validation performance (auROC = 83.8%, 87.6%, and 84.4% for the one-hot, protein LLM-derived, and structure-aware encoding models, respectively; see Table4) was consistently lower than that obtained under conventional random 5-fold cross-validation listed in Tables1,2, and3, reflecting a more stringent evaluation setting.

Regarding test performance of the RBP-aware cross-validated models, the random test set results (auROC = 71.8%, 71.3%, and 70.0% for the one-hot, protein LLM-derived, and structure-aware encoding models, respectively; also see Table4) already showed at least a 12% decrease compared with the average validation performance, partly because some RBPs in the random test set were not seen during training. Under the RBP-aware test setting, pronounced performance degradation was also observed (auROC = 70.1%, 71.3%, and 54.5% for the one-hot, protein LLM-derived, and structure-aware encoding models, respectively; see Table4) for these RBP-aware cross-validated models. Similar trends were observed for other evaluation metrics (Table4). These results further demonstrated that simply preventing direct RBP overlap does not fully resolve the generalization problem. While RBP-aware cross-validation reduces explicit data leakage across validation folds, it does not eliminate the fundamental limitation imposed by restricted RBP diversity in current datasets. Taken together, these analyses indicated that the observed generalization gap is consistent across different cross-validation strategies and is not an artifact of a single test set. More importantly, they highlighted that insufficient RBP diversity, rather than the cross-validation strategy alone, constitutes a major bottleneck in developing truly generalizable mRPI prediction models.

We next evaluated the RBP generalization issue of existing mRPI identification tools using the random test set and the RBP-aware test set. In total, nine currently available mRPI-related prediction tools were considered. These methods can be categorized into two types according to their input requirements. Type 1 tools take both RNA and RBP sequences as input, including RPISeq-SVM [39], RPISeq-RF [39], IPMiner [7], and iDeepC [40]. RPISeq-SVM and RPISeq-RF use k-mer frequency features and apply a support vector machine or random forest classifier, respectively. IPMiner uses stacked autoencoders to jointly learn hidden representations from RNA and protein sequences. iDeepC integrates convolutional neural networks to extract sequence features from circular RNAs (circRNAs). However, since iDeepC can only handle relatively short input sequences, it was excluded from the following comparison. Type 2 tools take only RNA sequences as input and are typically trained in a protein-specific manner, including MultiRBP [41], deepCLIP [42], Pysster [43], GraphProt [44], and deepRAM [45]. Among these methods, MultiRBP predicts binding events for hundreds of RBPs on a given RNA sequence, deepCLIP combines convolutional layers with bidirectional LSTMs for RNA motif learning, Pysster applies convolutional operations to sequences and sequenced-based predicted structures, GraphProt encodes RNA sequences and secondary structure predictions as graphs and identifies motifs using graph kernels, and deepRAM integrates deep recurrent and convolutional architectures for RNA sequence modeling. All tools were evaluated on the random test set and the RBP-aware test set. In order to have fair comparison, tools were retrained using our prepared training set with default parameter settings if possible. For methods with available retraining pipelines (deepRAM, DeepCLIP, and GraphProt), we retrained them using the same training-validation set adopted in our study. For tools without publicly available retraining code (PRIseq, IPMiner, MultiRBP, and pysster), we evaluated their provided pre-trained models under both partitioning schemes when applicable. As reviewed above, all existing tools were developed primarily based on sequence-derived information.

Evaluation of the generalization performance of existing mRPI identification tools onathe RBP-aware test set andbthe random test set

We compared these currently available tools with the attention-based models described in the "Random partitioning can inflate the mRPI identification performance" section. On the RBP-aware test set, most existing tools performed only slightly better than random guessing (theoretical auROC for random guessing: 50%), in contrast to their originally reported results (Fig.9a). Since existing tools were developed and optimized for specific RBPs, this substantial performance drop indicated pronounced RBP overfitting to RBP-specific patterns and limited ability to generalize to unseen proteins. Among the three attention-based models using different RBP encoding schemes, the LLM-encoded model achieved the best overall performance (auROC = 71.5%), outperforming all other evaluated tools by at least 8.5% in auROC (the second-best method: GraphProt, auROC = 63.0%) on the RBP-aware test set. Although LLM-derived protein embeddings combined with an attention-based architecture provide clear advantages over existing methods, fully overcoming the generalization gap in mRPI identification will likely require further methodological innovations and the incorporation of more diverse and representative training datasets.

We then evaluated these currently available RPI prediction tools under the random partitioning setting (Fig.9b). A direct comparison of performance under the random test set and the RBP-aware test set allows explicit quantification of the performance gap for each tool. However, the results showed that most sequence-based methods performed close to random guessing under both test settings, and none of them demonstrated substantially improved robustness under the RBP-aware evaluation. This near-random performance on both test sets further supports the conclusion that most existing tools are overfitted to specific RBPs and lack general cross-RBP predictive capability. The consistent degradation pattern across existing tools further highlights that the generalization issue is not specific to our attention-based framework, but instead reflects a broader limitation of current mRPI prediction approaches when evaluated on unseen RBPs.

To achieve a more rigorous assessment of the model generalization issue highlighted in this study, we independently constructed an additional external test set by collecting CLIP-seq experiments performed by Van Nostrand et al. [46] for RBPs that were not included in our training-validation set and the original test sets. This external dataset was designed to provide a strictly unseen evaluation scenario for independent confirmation of our findings. The additional RBPs are summarized in the Supplementary File. Raw CLIP-seq reads were mapped to the transcriptome using STAR [47], and transcript redundancy was reduced by selecting the longest transcript per gene. The STAR command used for CLIP read alignment can be also found in the Supplementary File. For each RBP in this independent test set, a region was defined as its confident binding site region if all its bases had a read depth larger than 50 (see Fig. S2 in the Supplementary File for threshold selection). Confident negative samples were constructed from consecutive regions with zero read depth. In total, 151,518 confident mRPI pairs and 2,994,237 confident non-binding pairs from 27 RBPs were included in this independent test set. These data are also available via the link provided in the “Availability of Data and Materials” subsection.

Using this independent test set, we evaluated the models using the three RBP encoding schemes investigated in the "Random partitioning can inflate the mRPI identification performance" section. As summarized in Table5, on this external dataset, the three encoding schemes achieved similar degraded performance (auROC = 62.3%/62.3%/64.6% for the one-hot encoding model, the LLM encoding model, and the structure-aware encoding model, respectively), consistent with the degraded results observed on the RBP-aware test set. Note that the low auPRC and F1 values shown in Table5reflect the low prevalence of positive samples in this independently prepared test set. Importantly, the auROC values remain substantially lower than those on the random test set, indicating that performance degradation persists when models are evaluated on independently prepared mRPI pairs involving unseen RBPs. Therefore, this evaluation further confirms our main conclusion that current deep-learning-based mRPI prediction models are strongly limited by insufficient protein diversity and exhibit restricted generalization capability on unseen RBPs.

In this research, we comprehensively evaluated key issues associated with sequence-based mRPI modeling. We found that most existing tools were developed and optimized using a relatively small set of RBPs. Consequently, these models tend to learn RBP-specific sequence signatures rather than generalizable principles of mRPIs. When evaluated on interactions involving completely unseen RBPs, their predictive performance declines substantially, indicating a strong dependence on protein identity overlap between the training and test datasets.

Due to the limited availability of RBP CLIP datasets, several existing RBP binding prediction tools were designed in a protein-specific manner [11]. In these approaches, models were trained and evaluated using binding site data from the same target RBP, enabling them to learn RBP-specific binding preferences. However, such protein-specific settings inherently cannot address the broader challenge of generalizing to unseen RBPs. For RBP-specific prediction, evaluation based on random interaction-level splits may not necessarily constitute data leakage. Nevertheless, this evaluation strategy can also lead to overly optimistic conclusions if the models were misused as general-purpose tools or claimed to be transferable across different RBPs. This situation, therefore, underscores the need to assess whether mRPI predictors truly generalize beyond the RBPs observed during training.

In our study, the attention-based model using protein LLM embeddings achieved the highest performance (auROC = 71.5% on the RBP-aware test set) among the evaluated RBP encoding schemes. However, even this model exhibited limited performance when applied to unseen RBPs, indicating that the overfitting issue is not unique to traditional approaches but also affects modern deep-learning frameworks. These findings suggested that results obtained from sequence-based models should be interpreted with caution, particularly when evaluation is conducted under random partitioning schemes that do not control for protein identity leakage between training and test sets.

Previous studies have shown that although human RBPs exhibit unexpectedly low diversity in RNA-binding motifs, with many proteins converging on a relatively small set of often low-complexity motifs (e.g., U-rich or G-rich patterns), they frequently display preferences for specific surrounding sequence contexts, leading to preferred motif patterns across different RBPs [48]. To achieve functional specificity, RBPs can rely heavily on contextual features such as surrounding nucleotide composition, the presence of bipartite motifs (two specific sequences separated by a gap), and RNA secondary structures (the physical folding of the molecule) [49]. These biological characteristics further complicate the learning of RBP targeting rules. This motif-family effect therefore provides an additional biological explanation for the observed overfitting issue and further motivates the use of an RBP-aware test set to reduce implicit overfitting of simple motif-related signals. More broadly, our findings integrated this motif family and contextual feature concept to suggest that increasing and carefully controlling RBP diversity, not only in terms of protein identity but also with respect to motif families and contextual classes, will be critical for developing mRPI prediction models with robust generalization.

Similar issues have been reported in related domains, such as miRNA-mRNA binding prediction, where high performance on standard benchmarks often fails to translate into robust predictions for new novel sequences [50]. In both contexts, the fundamental limitation stems from heavy reliance on sequence similarity to drive predictions, which constrains the ability to extrapolate to molecules with distinct sequence profiles. Addressing this limitation in future model designs may also require integrating additional sources of information beyond primary sequence features. The generalization issue highlighted here is also a relevant topic that could be further investigated in other domains, such as microbial protein function classification [51] and disease-compound interaction identification [52], where robust cross-molecule generalization is expected to be a critical challenge.

Taken together, the evaluation results in this study, along with prior findings in miRNA-mRNA binding prediction [50] and protein-protein interaction prediction [14,15,16,17], suggest that the performance of sequence-based models can be easily overestimated under conventional evaluation schemes. These observations warrant careful consideration in future computational biology research.

In this research, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of sequence-based models for mRPI prediction. Our results showed that existing sequence-based deep learning models for mPRI prediction often reported inflated performance due to data leakage caused by random partitioning of pairs obtained from the same training set RBPs. In contrast, their actual prediction accuracies dropped sharply when they were evaluated on mRNA-protein pairs from previously unseen RBPs. Although the ProteinBERT LLM-derived encoding achieved the best performance among the evaluated representations, it did not fully resolve the generalization gap, and incorporating AlphaFold-based structural information provided only limited improvement. These results highlighted the importance of adopting RBP-aware evaluation strategies, expanding protein diversity in ground-truth datasets, and integrating richer biological information beyond primary protein sequences to develop more robust and generalizable mRPI prediction tools.

title: ChemScreener: an active learning enabled hit discovery workflow with WDR5 inhibitor case study
author: Lingling Shen; Jian Fang; Lulu Liu; Rena Wang; Jeremy L. Jenkins; He Wang
text:
Active deep learning offers a promising approach for hit discovery starting from limited data by iteratively updating and improving models during screening by applying new data and adapting decisions. Key open questions include how best to explore chemical space, how it compares to non-iterative methods, and how to use it under data scarcity. We present ChemScreener, a multi-task active learning workflow for early drug discovery across large, diverse libraries or chemical spaces. Its Balanced-Ranking acquisition strategy leverages ensemble uncertainty to explore novel chemistry while maintaining hit rate enrichment by prioritizing predicted activity. In five iterative single-dose HTRF screens on WDR5 protein, ChemScreener increased hit rates from 0.49% (primary HTS screen) to 3–10% (average 5.91%; 104 hits from 1760 compounds). Hits were consolidated, retested with close analogs together in the 269 compounds set and clustered; 44 hit compounds from 81 clusters of 269 compounds set advanced to dose–response and filtered by counter HTRF assays. Over 50% of those with IC50 < 45 μM were validated as WDR5 binders by DSF. We de novo identified three scaffold series and three singleton scaffolds as the hits. Overall, we demonstrated that ChemScreener can accelerate early hit discovery and yield more diverse chemotypes.

Scientific contribution

Hit identification is a costly, time-intensive stage in drug discovery. We developed ChemScreener, a scalable active learning workflow for early hit discovery that improves hit rate enrichment through iterative screening of small number of compounds and expands chemical diversity by de novo hit scaffolds identified. ChemScreener offers a generalizable, target-specific, ligand-based virtual screening framework that accelerates early discovery and enhances effectiveness across large, diverse chemical libraries.

Get related insights from Springer Nature content.

Deep learning is widely used for hit identification in drug discovery, especially for virtual screening across large proprietary collections and commercial libraries spanning millions to billions of compounds. However, reliably prioritizing compounds for experimental testing typically requires substantial training data, ideally thousands of validated examples. In practice, virtual screening relies on two complementary strategies: ligand-based and structure-based approaches [1], which can synergistically and orthogonally prioritize compounds. Yet, in early hit discovery, accurate pocket structures are often unavailable, limiting structure-based methods. Meanwhile, target-specific ligand robust experimental data (e.g., dose–response curve) are small and with narrow chemical space, constraining model predictive accuracy, and practical application. Additionally, library chemical space often differs from that of training data, further reducing prediction accuracy and reliability.

Active learning can help address early hit discovery challenges in virtual screens, such as low amounts of available data and chemotype-shift in model training, by iteratively coupling model-guided selection with rapid experimental feedback. A typical workflow starts with a small, structurally diverse compound subset from the library, trains a baseline model, and scores the remaining compounds. An acquisition function such as uncertainty sampling, diversity-aware selection, or hybrid exploitation–exploration can select a small batch of compounds for wet-lab biological assays [2]. New experimental data are analyzed and merged with all previous experimental data, the model is retrained, and the cycle repeats, progressively uncovering de novo hit chemotypes while minimizing assay size in terms of compound number to test. Thus, active learning seeks to find more bioactive molecules with fewer resources than one-shot virtual screening.

Despite several early pioneering applications of active learning to hit finding, key technical and practical questions remain [3,4]. Screening efficiency relative to traditional methods has not been systematically quantified in real drug discovery settings, and prior work has focused more on methodology benchmarking and model variability than on hit enrichment [5]. Low-data scenarios are common in hit identification stage, with small experimental datasets used to prioritize large libraries in virtual screening. The impact of initial compound diversity on screening campaign outcomes is also unclear. As active learning becomes more relevant, including in automated discovery and self-driving lab contexts, the lack of computational guidelines may hinder its practical adoption.

To demonstrate active learning in a drug discovery use case, we developed ChemScreener and applied it to WDR5 protein. WDR5 is a cofactor of MLL1, a SET-domain histone methyltransferase originally identified as frequently rearranged in poor-prognosis leukemia (MLL-r) [6]. MLL often forms fusion proteins that assemble super complexes, drive aberrant transcription, and cause aggressive disease [7,8]. Targeting MLL1 through essential co-factors in this complex offers therapeutic opportunities, including WDR5, a conserved WD40 β-propeller protein with WIN and WBM pockets illustrated in Fig.1a [9,10]. MLL1 binds to the WIN pocket, and this interaction sustains MLL1’s methyltransferase activity [11,12]. Disrupting WDR5–MLL1 interaction impairs the core enzyme and is a promising anti-MLL-r strategy. Peptidomimetics and small molecules that bind to WDR5 WIN site and block this interaction inhibit MLL1 activity and MLL-r cell proliferation and are progressing toward the clinic [13,14,15]. Thus, WDR5 is a suitable candidate target for an active learning–enabled hit-finding approach, supported by established, validated assays and benchmark reference inhibitors like Compound 19 [15] in Fig.1b. The objective is to expand the structural diversity of hits, thereby advancing WDR5 drug discovery efforts while validating the ChemScreener active learning workflow.

Overview of the WDR5 structure and the reference inhibitor Compound 19.aIllustration of WIN (blue) and WBM (red) pockets on WDR5 protein. MLL binds to WIN pocket of WDR5. (PDB: 8F1G),bChemical structure of published WDR5 inhibitor used in ChemScreener study as the reference compound. Compound 19 is from Novartis

In our study, we built ChemScreener, a multi-task active learning workflow to accelerate early hit finding across large, diverse chemical spaces and lay a foundation for practical industrial screening drug discovery applications. We explore multiple options for active-learning-based screening, including hit discovery across deep learning architectures and acquisition functions, the effects of initial training set size and structural diversity, and the benefits of active versus non-iterative approaches. We also introduce Balanced-Ranking, an enhanced acquisition strategy that leverages ensemble uncertainty to explore novel chemistry while prioritizing top prediction for enrichment. Fine-tuned and optimized with WDR5 iterative screens and supported by the de novo hits we identified for WDR5 inhibitors successfully, ChemScreener offers a practical tool to guide adoption of active deep learning for early hit finding.

We developed an iterative active learning framework for multi-task, binary molecular classification that couples Chemprop ensembles with a principled acquisition strategy to guide experimental testing (Fig.2) [16,17]. At each iteration, we train a Chemprop model ensemble on the labeled assay results and scored an unlabeled SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) compound library to nominate hit candidates, while excluding close analogs of the identified hit chemotype in the next round of experiments to allow other potential novel hits to emerge. After assays are completed, new hit chemotypes are identified, new measurements are merged into the labeled training set, and the corresponding compounds are removed from the unlabeled pool to prevent re-selection. This cycle repeats, enabling progressively refined models and more informative acquisitions over time. Our main methodological contribution is a Balanced-Ranking acquisition strategy that integrates predicted activity and model uncertainty in a scale-robust manner, improving the trade-off between exploitation and exploration without the need for additional hyperparameters.

ChemScreener workflow overview. The workflow begins with an initial assay screen using single- or multi-assay data. A Chemprop multi-task ensemble model is then trained and applied to search the available library using the Balanced-Ranking acquisition strategy. In each iteration, 100–500 diverse compounds are selected for experimental testing, and newly identified hits are added to the training set for subsequent rounds. This iterative process progressively explores unscreened chemical space to identify de novo hit scaffolds and diverse chemotypes for a given target

Models were implemented using Chemprop’s message-passing neural network (MPNN) backend for multi-task binary classification. The backbone consists of a bond-centered message passing network with mean aggregation, paired with a multi-task feed-forward classification head. Training was conducted with PyTorch Lightning using mini-batches (typically 256–512 compound data points) [18]. To mitigate overfitting in low-data regimes, we fixed the number of epochs at 50–100 and maintained a focus on graph-learned representations. We did not incorporate auxiliary descriptors (e.g., Morgan fingerprints) in the reported experiments [19].

For each active learning iteration, we trained an ensemble of K independently initialized Chemprop models (typically K = 10) on the same training set. For the unlabeled library, each ensemble member produced per-task positive-class probabilities, forming a 3D prediction tensor with shape [K, N, C], where K indexes ensemble members, N indexes molecules in the library, and C indexes tasks; an entry [k, n, c] is the positive-class probability from model k for molecule n on task c [20,21,22].

We examined three acquisition strategies operating on ensemble outputs. The exploitative strategy ranks molecules by the mean predicted probability of the positive class, favoring high-confidence actives. The mutual information (MI) strategy ranks molecules by the sum of mutual information across tasks, prioritizing ensemble disagreement, and thus potential information gain [2]. Our primary contribution, Balanced-Ranking, combines exploitation and uncertainty in a rank-based aggregation that is robust to scale differences across tasks. For each molecule and task, we compute a prediction rank based on the mean ensemble probability (higher is better) and an uncertainty rank based on ensemble variance (higher is better). These ranks are summed across tasks to produce a molecule-level score, and molecules are ordered by the summed ranks to select the top n candidates. This procedure provides a simple, parameter-free balance between exploration and exploitation and is well suited for multi-task settings where absolute score scales may differ across tasks.

To assess performance in a fully observed setting, we conducted a retrospective evaluation in which ground-truth assay outcomes were available for all compounds. We first performed a scaffold-based split to construct an initial training set while holding out the remaining compounds as the candidate library, ensuring scaffold-level separation between training and selection pools. The active learning loop was then simulated for five iterations. In each iteration, the ensemble was trained on the current labeled set, the library was scored, and the acquisition function selected 300 compounds. Rather than executing physical experiments, we revealed the known labels for the selected compounds, counted the number of hits identified in that round. The primary metric was the number of hits acquired per iteration, which quantifies practical enrichment of actives over time. For completeness, we also tracked cumulative hit count and, when relevant, enrichment relative to non-iterative selection baselines matched by batch size. This protocol isolates the contribution of the acquisition strategy and model updates under a realistic, scaffold-split regime.

Starting from the iteration 0 (Iter0) (compounds tested in both WDR5 HTRF and FP assays, we executed five prospective iterations (Iter1-Iter5). For hit calling, we used 3std-dev (threefold standard deviations) criteria with an HTRF activity threshold of ≤ 0.7 (DMSO = 1). In each iteration, we applied Balanced-Ranking and selected 352 compounds (to efficiently fit into one 384-well plate along assay controls) for single dose testing in HTRF and FP assays, and enforced novelty and quality filters: removal of known WDR5 binders and close SAR analogs, compound availability constraints, and drug‑like property filters. The full loop (train, score, select, assay, merge) required 4 h approximately per iteration on a single GPU (Graphics Processing Units).

All experiments were conducted in Python with chemoinformatics library RDKit [23]. Hardware acceleration was configured via PyTorch Lightning’s accelerator [24].

The assay was adapted [15] and performed in 384-well white OptiPlate plate (PerkinElmer) for compound single dose (26.7 μM) or the dose response assay as indicated. The compounds from ChemScreener were serially diluted in DMSO to obtain a total of 14-dose, twofold dilution scheme with the top concentration of 80 μM or 12-dose, threefold dilution scheme with the top concentration of 10 μM particularly for the reference Compound 19 [15] or as the dose dilution indicated in the graph, and added to the wells. The assay mixture containing 4 nM WDR5 and 15 nM MLL WIN-Biotin peptide (3762–3773 a.a.) in the assay buffer (25 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 0.05% Tween 20, 2 mM DTT, 100 mM NaCl, 0.1% BSA) was added to the wells as the final concentration. After 20 min of incubation at room temperature (RT), detection reagents of 6 nM Eu-W1024-anti-6xHis (Revvity AD0402) and 40 nM Streptavidin-Surelight APC (Revvity AD02021), incubate at RT for 1 h. After 1 h of incubation, the plates were read on Envision (PerkinElmer). For the counter assay, the protein pair of WDR5 and MLL was replaced with a 10 nM Biotin-miniPEG-6His peptide (GenScript), to evaluate if the compound interferes with elements of the HTRF assay. This helps to characterize the specific activity of the compound against the PPI of WDR5 and MLL in HTRF. HTRF signals were normalized based on the DMSO (activity as 1) to give the percentage of activity left. Dose–response curves were generated by GraphPad Prism, and half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) was calculated. The representative curves are based on the mean values from at least two independent experiments in triplicates.

The FP assay was performed in a 384‑well black plate (Greiner Bio‑One #784,076) using 2 µM WDR5 protein (N‑His tagged, residues 1–334) and 10 nM FITC‑conjugated MLL1 WIN peptide tracer (FITC‑Ahx‑GSARAEVHLRKS‑NH2, reconstituted in DMSO and protected from light) in assay buffer (20 mM Tris·HCl pH 8.0, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.01% Tween‑20). Controls included buffer‑only for background subtraction, tracer‑only for the free baseline, WDR5 plus tracer without compound for maximal binding, DMSO normalization for tested compounds, and reference Compound 19 in a 12‑dose, threefold dilution series with a top concentration of 10 μM to generate IC50 values and confirm run‑to‑run consistency. ChemScreener compounds were evaluated at a single 20 µM dose in duplicate, and signals were acquired on an Envision instrument (PerkinElmer) using an FITC FP protocol (excitation 485 nm, emission 535 nm, parallel/perpendicular channels, reported in mP). Data were processed by subtracting buffer‑only background and normalizing percent inhibition/displacement to DMSO and QC metrics using reference Compound 19.

The compound was dissolved in DMSO at a concentration of 10 mM before mixing with WDR5. 2 µM full-length WDR5 protein was mixed with 5 × SYPRO Orange (Thermo Fisher Scientific, S6650) in DSF assay buffer (20 mM HEPES pH = 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) and then mixed with 100 or 200 µM compound in a 384-well PCR plate. The mixture solution was then incubated with shaking for 5 min before running the thermal melting experiments on the CFX384 Touch™Real-Time PCR detection system (Bio-Rad). The samples were heated from 20 to 95 °C at a rate of 0.5 °C/30 s. The melting curve and peak data were analyzed by a modified Boltzmann equation using a Novartis in-house program. The reported Tm (melting temperature) values are based on the mean values from two independent experiments in triplicates.

Compound 19: We recently reported WDR5 inhibitor Compound 19 and its close analogs [15], including their biological activities and structure (also shown in Fig.1b). Across multiple ChemScreener hit‑finding iterations, it consistently exhibited HTRF IC50 values of 3.0–7.2 nM and FP IC50 values of 1.6–2.8 μM. Representative curves are presented in the Results section. Its Tm shift in DSF is over 22 °C at 5 μM.

Purification of the compounds was carried out either using pre-packed silica gel cartridges (Biotage or ISCO) or reverse-phase HPLC (High-performance liquid chromatography) with C18 columns, > 95% purity for all the active compounds tested in the biological assay has been confirmed by analytical HPLC.1H NMR (proton nuclear magnetic resonance) spectra were recorded in acetonitrile-d3or methanol-d4, on Bruker NMR spectrometer with 400 or 500 MHz 1H Larmor frequency. NMR chemical shifts (δ) were quoted in parts per million (ppm) and are reported relative to residual nondeuterated solvent signals. Coupling constants are reported in Hertz (Hz). As we introduced, ChemScreener is a multi-task active learning workflow that accelerates early hit identification across large, diverse chemical libraries. It couples Chemprop ensemble models with a Balanced-Ranking acquisition strategy that is exploration focused and integrates ensemble uncertainty and predicted activity via rank-based scoring. This approach balances exploration and exploitation across multiple assay endpoints without additional hyperparameters, supporting scalable application in drug discovery process for early hit discovery. We selected WDR5, a conserved WD40 scaffold protein central to complexes such as MLL that drives leukemogenesis, as the exploration target for ChemScreener use case. In a retrospective evaluation, we analyzed an existing enriched single-point WDR5 inhibitor primary HTS screening dataset of 78,241 compounds assayed by HTRF (26.7 μM) and FP (20 μM) from Novartis (HTRF screen activity distribution in Supplementary Table 1S). Using a 3std-dev hit-calling criterion, the observed hit rates were 0.49% for HTRF (Fig.3).

To contextualize acquisition choices and workflow, we performed retrospective validations. ChemScreener’s retrospective validation evaluates a Chemprop multi-task model with scaffold-split of FP and HTRF WDR5 assay data, using 10% of data for training (7826 compounds), 10% for validation (7825 compounds), and reserving 80% as the screening library (62,598 compounds). The main endpoint is HTRF, and the auxiliary endpoint is FP results empirically based on the assay robustness. In here, FP data are used solely to enhance the active learning model’s predictive strength for identifying HTRF hits and are not used for hit calling or data analysis, so FP results are not shown separately. Three acquisition criteria are evaluated: Balanced-Ranking, Exploitation (selecting top model predictions) [26], and Mutual Information (BALD-based, choosing compounds with lowest mutual information) [27]. The study is run across 5 repeats (run0–run4), with 5 active learning iterations per repeat. Each active learning iteration selects 300 compounds from the screening library (80% of HTRF and FP WDR5 assay data), with a total of 1500 compounds selected. In addition, one-shot non-iterative baseline screen is conducted by selecting 1500 compounds using the same acquisition criteria. Finally for each acquisition function, ChemScreener yields 15,000 compounds overall across all runs. Computationally, the retrospective workflow is completed in approximately one day on an HPC (high-performance computing) node with a single GPU, indicating the approach’s tractability for larger-scale studies.

One objective of the ChemScreener workflow is to quantify hit rate improvements by reporting hit rates for each acquisition method and comparing active learning against the baseline. As shown in Fig.4for HTRF results, across all repeats, Balanced-Ranking and Exploitation consistently achieve higher hit rates than Mutual Information for WDR5 case (Fig.4a), and their aggregated hit rates across active learning iterations exceed the baseline (Fig.4b), indicating clear gains from active learning under these strategies.

Another key objective is to assess hit chemotype novelty and diversity. As shown in Fig.5, Balanced-Ranking consistently delivers strong hit rate enrichment while improving the diversity of de novo hits relative to purely exploitative selection, with t-SNE visualizations indicating broader chemical space coverage [28]. Mutual Information sampling attains the widest diversity but sacrifices hit-rate enrichment, consistent with its BALD-driven emphasis on exploration. In principle, adjusting the Balanced-Ranking weights between prediction rank and uncertainty rank (currently 1:1) could steer the workflow toward greater diversity or stronger hit rate enrichment.

Moreover, for each repeat, we computed the correlation between HTRF and FP data across the 1500 compounds selected by each acquisition method to assess whether active learning, via multitask modeling, enhances assay synergy and yields more consensus hits, even when HTRF is the primary modeling endpoint. The results are encouraging. As shown in Fig.6, both Balanced-Ranking and Exploitation achieve higher linear regression R2(up to 0.24, corresponding to r ≈ 0.49, statistically significant at p < 0.05 with n = 1500, Bevington df = 1498) than Mutual Information (R2= 0.06 at most) and the initial training set from diverse screening (around 0), with consensus hits accumulating over active learning iterations. This suggests the workflow is effective for consensus hit finding across orthogonal assays.

Building on the retrospective findings, we conducted a prospective ChemScreener active-learning campaign for WDR5 hit findings. Starting from Iter0, in which 55,292 compounds were tested in both HTRF and FP assays, we executed five iterations (Iter1-Iter5) and applied hit calling at 3std-dev with an HTRF activity threshold of ≤ 0.7 (DMSO = 1). Each iteration used the Balanced-Ranking acquisition criterion, scored the library with multi-task Chemprop ensembles, and selected 352 compounds for single-point HTRF and FP. HTRF was the primary endpoint, with FP as an auxiliary endpoint. To maintain novelty and practical relevance, selection criteria included the Balanced-Ranking score, compound ordering availability, removal of known binders and close analogs via Murcko ring clustering [29], and a drug-like filter (MW 250–800, SlogP − 1–7, PSA ≤ 125, rotatable bonds 3–12) [30,31]. As shown in Fig.7, the iterative loop—training ensembles, scoring, selecting, assaying, and merging new labels—ran efficiently, requiring approximately four hours per iteration on a single GPU.

WDR5 perspective ChemScreener screening process. In Iteration 0, 55,292 compounds from legacy HTRF and FP screens were used to train the initial Chemprop multi-task ensemble, and Balanced-Ranking selected the top 352 compounds for follow-up testing. In Iterations 1–5, single-dose HTRF and FP assays were performed on 352 model-selected compounds per iteration, while close analogs of confirmed hit chemotypes were excluded from subsequent selection rounds to promote chemical novelty. During hit consolidation and confirmation, 269 compounds across all iterations were retested in HTRF and counter assays. The 44 confirmed hits were then profiled in HTRF dose–response and counter assays to determine IC50 values, followed by validation using the biophysical DSF assay. The final steps included chemical space analysis of the hits and docking into the WIN pocket of the WDR5 protein

Across the five prospective iterations, ChemScreener markedly increased the HTRF hit rate relative to the original single-point diversity set primary screen. As shown in Table1, per-iteration HTRF hit rates ranged from 3.13% to 9.94%, yielding 104 hits from 1760 tested compounds and an overall hit rate of 5.91%—more than a tenfold improvement over the 0.49% baseline. Several de novo hit series (CS1, CS2, and CS3) emerged across different iterations, as indicated in the final column. Iteration 5 also identified additional de novo series, which were deprioritized due to frequent-hitter activity in unrelated assays, suboptimal drug-like properties, or lack of DSF validation in further study.

To further confirm these potential hits, we conducted an additional round assessing consolidated candidates from iterations 1–5 at a single HTRF dose of 26.7 μM. We tested 269 compounds, comprising Iter1–5 hits and the close analogs that had high Balanced-Ranking score but not previously evaluated in HTRF or the counter assay. Using the criteria HTRF activity ≤ 0.7 (DMSO = 1) with Counter activity ≥ 0.9, or HTRF activity ≤ 0.5 with counter assay activity ≥ 0.5, 62 compounds were confirmed, yielding a 23% hit rate. Murcko ring clustering across all 269 compounds produced 81 clusters: 5 hit‑enriched clusters were retained, 2 non‑drug‑like hit‑enriched clusters were removed, and 11 promising unique scaffolds were selected for further analysis. In total, 44 of the 62 confirmed hits were advanced to the next step HTRF dose‑response testing with the counter assay.

We next performed WDR5–MLL HTRF dose–response (DRC) studies to quantify activity from the primary hits screen in the prospective study as the biochemical assay diagram in Fig.8a. DRC testing confirmed many single‑dose HTRF hits and yielded IC50 values for the best compounds in the single digit µM range (Fig.8b, c), although weaker than Compound 19 in the same assay (Fig.8d). These compounds, with one exception, showed no activity in the HTRF counter assay, as indicated in the Fig.8b summary or by the blue dots in Fig.8c, suggesting specificity for disrupting the WDR5–MLL interaction.

Differential Scanning Fluorimetry (DSF) results demonstrated direct binding by thermal shift analysis showing that adding these compounds at 100 μM to WDR5 induced Tm shifts of 1.2–7.6 °C compared with DMSO control (which Tm is 61.9 °C and the 3std-dev is 0.21 °C). From HTRF DRC and DSF profiling, validated hit rates are notably high when using the potency threshold from either Tier 1 or Tier 1 + 2 in Table2. Among the 44 advanced compounds, 9 achieved Tier 1 confirmation (HTRF dose–response IC50 ≤ 20 μM with DSF validation), and 24 met the broader Tier 1 + 2 threshold (IC50 ≤ 45 μM but still with DSF validation), corresponding to a validated hit rate of 20.45% or 54.55%, exceeding the screen-level hit confirmation alone. These results highlight ChemScreener’s ability to generate diverse, validated binders—true hits from low-data starting points via iterative, model-guided selection.

Additionally, the single-point hits from Iter1–5 and the HTRF hit repeat with counter (orange dots), along with the confirmed hits, occupy distinct regions of the map relative to the original diversity-screen single-point hits, indicating that the specific DRC hits represent structurally distinct chemotypes.

We further examined prospective hit chemotypes through docking to the WDR5 binding site using Glide [25] with a template based on PDB entry 6E1Y, followed by MMGBSA rescoring [32,33]. Ligand preparation included desalting, tautomer generation, and ionization with Epik, using the OPLS4 force field and enumerating up to 32 stereoisomers per ligand. The top confirmed hits, when docked into the WDR5 ternary complex (PDB 6E1Y) [34] in Fig.12, consistently localize to the intended MLL binding pocket, indicating good pocket fidelity, and reinforcing the validity of the docking setup and constraints. Closer inspection of individual poses shows that CS6 (rendered in yellow) closely overlaps the reference ligand (C2) from 6E1Y (in cyan), with comparable orientation and key contact geometry, which is expected given that CS6 and the 6E1Y ligand C2 share the same chemotype and thus similar pharmacophore features. This convergence supports the notion that the scoring and placement are capturing the key interaction pattern for this scaffold rather than overfitting to noise. In parallel, compared with reference ligand C2, the docked poses for CS1.1 and CS1.2 within the 6E1Y pocket share some of key interactions and shape complementarity, while introducing additional interactions consistent with their modified substituents and distinct chemotypes. These added contacts explain differences in predicted binding mode and may influence shifts in selectivity or affinity, collectively suggesting that the docking outcomes are chemically reasonable across both scaffold-matched and scaffold-divergent compounds.

Together, these findings on WDR5 de novo hits demonstrate that multi-task active learning with exploration-focused acquisition can substantially improve early hit discovery outcomes. The rank-based Balanced-Ranking strategy offers a pragmatic solution to multi-endpoint selection under differing score scales and limited data, navigating the trade-off between discovering novel chemical matter and maintaining hit-rate enrichment. In WDR5, ChemScreener’s iterative loop yielded substantially higher hit rates than legacy screening, delivered confirmed binders across multiple chemotypes, and validated binding through orthogonal DSF measurements, all with relatively modest computational resources per iteration. Limitations remain, including modest potency ranges characteristic of early hits, the need to guard against assay artifacts and frequent hitters, and the requirement for medicinal chemistry optimization to translate micromolar activity into lead compound like potency profiles. Future directions include expanding to additional targets and endpoints, exploring adaptive acquisition that dynamically weights exploration versus exploitation, and integrating complementary features, such as structure-based descriptors or physicochemical fingerprints, to improve calibration and generalization.

ChemScreener is a practical and effective active learning workflow tailored for early hit finding across large, diverse libraries. By combining Chemprop ensembles with rank-aggregated activity and uncertainty, it balances exploration of novel chemistry with enrichment of likely actives, enabling faster, more effective discovery from low-data beginnings. Applied prospectively to WDR5, ChemScreener achieved a tenfold improvement in hit rate over legacy single-point screening and a 54.55% hit rate after validation among advanced compounds, identifying three de novo confirmed series and three confirmed singletons for further investigation. These results provide evidence that multi-task active learning can accelerate hit identification while broadening chemical diversity, offering a foundation for scalable, iterative screening in drug discovery.

This study focuses on a single prospective target (WDR5), its associated assays, and our in-house library, the results demonstrate that ChemScreener can be effectively deployed in a real-world discovery setting. Also, ChemScreener currently implements the Chemprop ensemble models combined with the customized Balanced-Ranking acquisition strategy, providing a flexible and effective foundation for active learning–driven virtual screening. While this study focuses on a specific target (WDR5) and assay conditions, the modular design of the workflow readily allows extension to other use cases. Additional modeling choices such as alternative uncertainty estimation methods, molecular representations, and acquisition objectives (e.g., diversity or efficacy aware selection), were not explored here but can be naturally incorporated as needed for different scientific contexts. Our future work will extend ChemScreener to a broader range of targets and assay formats, explore alternative model architectures and acquisition strategies, and evaluate performance across diverse compound libraries. These efforts will help further characterize the applicability of the framework and support its use in more drug discovery settings.

The screening data used in this study are proprietary to Novartis and therefore cannot be made publicly available due to intellectual property restrictions. To support transparency and methodological reproducibility of the ChemScreener workflow within these constraints, we provide the following resources. title: CheMLT-F: multitask learning in biochemistry through transformer fusion
author: Vladislav Mun; Siamac Fazli
text:
Drug discovery remains a slow and costly process, in part because efficacy, toxicity, and physicochemical liabilities must be screened across a vast chemical space. Stand-alone, single-task predictors can help, but they lead to fragmented workflows and make it hard to reuse learned representations, data processing, and infrastructure across endpoints (i.e., prediction tasks). Here we presentCheMLT-F, a compact multitask transformer that fuses encoders for molecular and protein sequences to learn a unified representation spanning680+ endpoints, including diverse toxicities, physicochemical properties, and drug–target interactions. Across 13 public benchmarks, CheMLT-F matches state-of-the-art toxicity classifiers and sets new performance marks for physicochemical property prediction, while remaining competitive for drug–target affinity (KIBA and Davis). Moreover, CheMLT-F demonstrates competitive performance on an external protein-family benchmark spanning seven target superfamilies, indicating broad generalizability in bioactivity prediction. Multitask parameter sharing keeps the model lightweight and inference-efficient, and its modular heads make extensions to new endpoints straightforward. By replacing many individual models with a single, extensible backbone, CheMLT-F streamlines in silico screening and lowers the barrier to broad, data-driven decision-making in early drug discovery.

Scientific contribution

We introduce a unified transformer architecture that jointly models molecular and protein sequences across hundreds of pharmacologically relevant endpoints spanning toxicity, physicochemical properties, and drug–target interactions. A tailored training strategy that combines partial encoder freezing, global–local loss balancing, and weighted task sampling reduces trainable parameters and deployment complexity while preserving strong cross-domain generalization. Comprehensive evaluation across 13 public datasets, including scaffold-aware and random data splits, demonstrates competitive accuracy with substantially lower operational overhead than maintaining numerous single-task models, establishing a scalable foundation for extensible and holistic predictive modeling in computational drug discovery.
