title: Comparative genomics of zooxanthellate and azooxanthellate Palythoa (Cnidaria: Zoantharia) provides insights into symbiosis evolution and the origin of palytoxin
author: Yoshioka, Y.; Shoguchi, E.; Chiu, Y.-L.; Kawamitsu, M.; Reimer, J. D.; Yamashita, H.
text: BackgroundZoantharians (Cnidaria) are globally distributed from shallow reefs to the deep sea, yet their genomic resources remain scarce. Within the zoantharian genusPalythoa, most species harbor photosymbiotic dinoflagellates, whereas some have secondarily lost this symbiosis, allowing genomic changes associated with symbiotic status to be examined.Palythoais also the original source of palytoxin, one of the most potent marine toxins known, but whether it is produced by the host or by associated microorganisms remains unresolved. Here we generated high-quality genome assemblies of two zooxanthellatePalythoaspecies and compared fivePalythoagenomes spanning both symbiotic states with those of other anthozoans. ResultsAcross anthozoans, genome size scaled with transposable element content, particularly retrotransposons. The azooxanthellate lineage carries substitutions in conserved domains of the symbiosis-related proteins LePin and NPC2 and shows rapid evolution of the lectin geneCLEC4A, whereas NF-κB and V-type H+-ATPase remain conserved.Palythoagenomes showed no lineage-specific expansion of polyketide synthase (PKS) genes; cnidarian PKS genes were restricted toP. caribaeorumandP.sp. sakurajimensis (clade III). In contrast, 27 bacterial PKS sequences were recovered from metatranscriptomes and a metagenome-assembled genome across species, including an azooxanthellate species, indicating that they derive from associated bacterial rather than Symbiodiniaceae. ConclusionsThese genomes provide a comparative framework for zoantharians and reveal genomic changes associated with symbiotic status. We propose that palytoxin originates from associated bacteria rather than from the host, a hypothesis that can be tested by identifying the producing bacteria and their biosynthetic gene clusters. Zoantharians (Cnidaria: Anthozoa: Hexacorallia) are globally distributed and occupy diverse habitats ranging from shallow coastal reefs to the deep sea [1,2]. Most zoantharian species incorporate sand grains and detrital particles into their tissues, a distinctive trait thought to reinforce their body structure [3,4]. Zoantharians are divided into two suborders. Macrocnemina species span a broad depth range and frequently engage in symbioses with a variety of marine organisms [5], whereas Brachycnemina are predominantly shallow-water taxa, most of which harbor photosynthetic dinoflagellates of the family Symbiodiniaceae [6]. Within Brachycnemina,PalythoaandZoanthusare among the most abundant and conspicuous genera on coral reefs, wherePalythoaspecies can exert strong ecological influences [7,8] and, in some cases, produce palytoxin and/or palytoxin-like molecules (42-hydroxy-palytoxin) [9–12]. Although genome assemblies are now available for multiple actiniarian and scleractinian species [13], greatly advancing our understanding of anthozoan genome evolution [14–17], high-quality genomic resources and genomic studies for zoantharians remain comparatively sparse [18–20], limiting broader evolutionary inferences across Hexacorallia. WithinPalythoa, most species harbor Symbiodiniaceae, whereasP. mizigamaandP. umbrosainhabit low-light reef caves and lack Symbiodiniaceae symbionts, making them azooxanthellate [7]. Because symbiosis with Symbiodiniaceae likely originated in the common ancestor of Brachycnemina [21,22], these species are thought to have secondarily lost algal symbiosis, makingPalythoaa valuable system for comparing closely related zooxanthellate and azooxanthellate species. Our previous study using draft genomes of these two species revealed genomic features potentially associated with life in reef caves and the loss of algal symbiosis [20]. However, without genomes of zooxanthellate congeners, it remains unclear which of these features are shared acrossPalythoaand which are specific to azooxanthellate lineages. Palytoxin, first isolated fromPalythoa toxica[23], is one of the most potent marine toxins known, with a reported median lethal dose (LD50) of 25–450 ng/kg in several animal models [24]. Its exceptionally large and complex structure [25,26] suggests biosynthesis by polyketide synthases (PKSs), in which ketosynthase (KS) domains serve as the core catalytic components [27,28]. Complex polyketides in marine animals can be synthesized either by the animals themselves via PKS and animal fatty acid synthase-like PKS (AFPK) genes [29–31] or by bacterial symbionts [32–34]. Whether palytoxin inPalythoais synthesized by the host or by associated bacteria therefore remains unresolved. Although some KS domain-containing genes were identified in draft genomes ofP. mizigamaandP. umbrosa[20], PKS genes have received little attention in other cnidarians, and no comparative survey within cnidarians has been conducted. Here we present high-quality whole-genome assemblies and gene models for two zooxanthellatePalythoaspecies,Palythoacf.toxica(Ptox) andPalythoasp. sakurajimensis (Psak), together with curated genomes of the azooxanthellateP. mizigama(Pmiz) andP. umbrosa(Pumb) (Fig. 1a–c). Combined with a chromosome-level genome assembly ofPalythoa caribaeorum(Pcar) from the Wellcome Sanger Institute, we performed comparative genomic analyses to (i) characterize genome evolution in zoantharians, (ii) identify genomic changes associated with symbiotic status by comparing zooxanthellate and azooxanthellate species, and (iii) evaluate the origin of palytoxin by surveying KS domain-containing genes in host genomes and associated microbes. This study provides genomic resources and candidate genes that establish a framework for future studies of symbiosis evolution and the origin of palytoxin inPalythoa. (a–c)Colonies of(a)Palythoacf.toxica,(b)Palythoa umbrosa, and(c)Palythoasp. sakurajimensis (Photo credits: JDR). White scale bars indicate approximately 1 cm, 1 cm, and 2 cm, respectively.(d)Maximum-likelihood molecular phylogeny of anthozoans inferred from 1,887 single-copy orthologs (942,596 amino acid positions), with octocorals as the outgroup. All nodes received 100% bootstrap support (1,000 replicates). The scale bar indicates expected substitutions per site. Boxes indicate symbiotic status ofPalythoaspecies with Symbiodiniaceae (filled, symbiotic; dashed, non-symbiotic), and clade numbers follow the main text. Symbiotic status is not shown for other species because it could not be confirmed for the sequenced samples. We generated 50 Gb and 66 Gb of PacBio HiFi reads for Psak and Ptox, with mean read lengths of 5,433 bp and 5,599 bp, respectively (Table S1). The resulting draft genome assemblies spanned 880 Mb for Psak and 649 Mb for Ptox, with N50 values of 12.2 Mb and 0.82 Mb, respectively (Table 1; Fig. S1). Genome size estimates based on read depth were 819.3 Mb for Psak and 624.8 Mb for Ptox, indicating that the assemblies closely approximated the expected genome sizes [18]. In addition to these newly assembled genomes, we curated previously published genome assemblies of the azooxanthellatePalythoaspecies Pmiz and Pumb by removing contigs likely derived from contaminants (Fig. S2). BUSCO completeness scores for Psak, Ptox, and Pcar exceeded 90%, with low duplication rates (≤ 3%) (Table 1). Based on transcriptomic evidence and homology with metazoan orthologs, we predicted 20,594 protein-coding genes in Psak, 44,006 in Ptox, and 18,823 in Pcar (Table 1). Gene models for Pumb were re-predicted with transcriptomic evidence (22,498 genes), and those for Pmiz were re-predicted with metazoan protein evidence only because no RNA-seq data were available (27,878 genes) (Table 1). BUSCO completeness of the gene models was 86.2% (1.6% duplicates) for Psak, 75.0% (2.2% duplicates) for Ptox, 86.2% (1.8% duplicates) for Pcar, 77.8% (1.2% duplicates) for Pumb, and 78.9% (1.8% duplicates) for Pmiz (Table 1). Complete mitochondrial genomes were also assembled for Psak (21,100 bp) and Ptox (21,227 bp), each encoding 13 protein-coding genes (Fig. S3). A previously reported novel mitochondrial ORF inPalythoa tuberculosa(Ptub) [35] was not detected in either species, supporting the hypothesis that the ORF was inserted in the common ancestor of Ptub and Pcar, rather than in the common ancestor ofPalythoaclade III [35]. Using 1,887 single-copy orthologs, we reconstructed a maximum likelihood phylogeny of anthozoans (Fig. 1d). Consistent with analyses based on ultra-conserved elements [36], zoantharians were recovered as the sister group to a clade comprising Actiniaria, Antipatharia, Corallimorpharia, and Scleractinia. WithinPalythoa, phylogenetic relationships inferred from nuclear single-copy orthologs were identical to those obtained using the mitochondrialrrnLmarker, resolving three distinct clades: clade I (Ptox), clade II (azooxanthellate Pmiz and Pumb), and clade III (Psak and Pcar) (Fig. S4). This topology is congruent with previous phylogenetic reconstructions of zoantharians (e.g., Swain [22]). Genome size varied substantially among anthozoans, including withinPalythoa(Tables 1and S2). Although more than 100 anthozoan genome assemblies are now publicly available [13], comparative analyses of genome-wide features across anthozoans remain limited. To place zoantharian genomes in this broader context, we examined how assembly size relates to genomic features across selected anthozoan species. A previous study suggested a correlation between assembly size and transposable element (TE) content in zoantharians [18], and we found that this relationship holds across anthozoans (Fig. 2). Assembly size was strongly correlated with total length of interspersed repeats (r= 0.968,P< 0.01) and moderately correlated with mean gene length (r= 0.700,P< 0.01) (Fig. 2). In contrast, neither protein-coding gene number nor mean CDS length showed a significant correlation with genome size. Non-TE sequence length (assembly size minus interspersed repeats) was also associated with assembly size, as was TE length, after phylogenetic correction (PGLS, λ = 0,r= 0.943–0.968,P< 0.01; Fig. S5a, b), indicating that genome expansion involved non-TE as well as TE sequences. Moreover, the TE proportion increased with assembly size (r= 0.617,P< 0.05), with a significant contribution from class I elements (retrotransposons;r= 0.593,P< 0.05) and a marginal contribution from unclassified elements (r= 0.498,P= 0.050), but not from class II elements (Fig. S5c–f). Thus, genome size variation in anthozoans is driven by the expansion of non-coding sequences, mainly retrotransposons together with introns and intergenic regions, as observed in other animals [37,38]. (a)Total length of transposable elements (Mb),(b)mean gene length,(c)number of protein-coding genes, and(d)mean CDS length, each plotted against assembly size. Each point represents one species, colored by order as indicated in (b). Lines indicate linear regressions, andrandPindicate Pearson’s correlation coefficients and their significance. PGLS results are shown in Fig. S5, and the underlying values are listed in Table S15. To infer the history of TE activity, Kimura substitution levels were calculated for all TE copies in each genome (Fig. S6). Lower Kimura distances indicate more recent transposition, whereas higher values reflect ancient transposition events. Clade I species (Ptox) displayed three pronounced peaks in Kimura distances, clade II species (Pmiz and Pumb) showed a diffuse pattern without clear peaks, and clade III (Psak and Pcar) exhibited a gradual decline with a peak at low divergence levels. Relatively high numbers of recent TE copies were commonly detected in allPalythoaclades, suggesting that genome size increases with TE amplification occurred relatively recently. TE-driven genome expansion has been shown to generate genomic diversity inHydra[39], and a similar process may contribute to genomic diversity inPalythoaand perhaps other zoantharians. Gene duplication also contributed to genome expansion, although to a lesser extent than TE insertion. With the exception of Ptox, protein-coding gene numbers were relatively uniform among anthozoans (Table S3). Psak, Pumb, Pmiz, and Pcar harbored 22,448 genes on average, whereas Ptox encoded 44,006 genes—nearly twice the average (Table 1). Furthermore, the proportion of intron-containing genes was markedly lower in Ptox (53.2%) than in otherPalythoaspecies (69.8–78.9%;Table 1), suggesting extensive duplication of intron-less genes. Analysis of duplication mode revealed that dispersed duplications predominated (49–60%) in allPalythoagenomes, with Ptox exhibiting approximately twice as many dispersed duplications as other species (Fig. 3a). The wide spread of dispersed duplicates has been considered to be due to mechanisms mediated by transposons [40]. Most duplicated gene pairs showedKsvalues below the medianKsof single-copy orthologs betweenPalythoaspecies, calculated from orthologs that are single-copy across hexacorals (Fig. 3b), indicating that the majority of duplication events occurred afterPalythoadiversification. (a)Number of genes in each duplication mode (dispersed, proximal, tandem, WGD/segmental, and singleton) classified by MCScanX. Numbers in parentheses indicate the percentage of all genes, andnindicates the number of predicted genes in each genome. (b)Ksdistributions of paralogous gene pairs in each duplication mode. Dashed lines indicate the medianKsbetweenPalythoaspecies, calculated from orthologs that are single-copy across hexacorals, and the number of gene pairs is shown in each panel. Colors indicate species as in (a). To investigate the molecular basis of zoantharian evolution, we examined gene family evolution across anthozoans. From 366,162 protein-coding genes, 93.6% were assigned to 26,532 orthogroups (OGs) (Table S4). Among these, 5,441 OGs were conserved across hexacorals, 342 OGs were specific toPalythoa, and 16 OGs were absent fromPalythoa(Table S5). Of the shared OGs, we analyzed the 4,944 OGs present in at least one octocoral. Using CAFE5, we identified 193 OGs that were significantly expanded in the common ancestor ofPalythoa(FDR < 0.05;Fig. 4a; Table S6). These families were enriched in functions related to ion transport, including calcium channel activity, and to extracellular matrix (ECM) interactions, including glycosaminoglycan and heparin binding and metallopeptidase activity (Fig. 4b). These functions may be linked to a distinctive trait of zoantharians. Most zoantharians, particularlyPalythoa, incorporate sand and detritus into their tissues to reinforce structural integrity [3]. As other anthozoans either secrete skeletons or maintain soft tissue without persistent foreign inclusions, incorporation of those particles likely requires specialized cellular processes. InHydra, the mesoglea is an ECM containing collagens, laminin, and proteoglycans, and both its remodeling by matrix metalloproteinases and its interactions with cells, mediated in part by integrins, are required for morphogenesis and the maintenance of differentiated cells [41,42]. The expansion of ECM-related gene families inPalythoamay therefore reflect the evolution of cellular machinery that actively integrates sediment into the mesoglea. (a)Numbers of orthogroups (OGs) that significantly expanded (red) or contracted (blue) on each branch, inferred with CAFE5 (FDR < 0.05). (b)GO enrichment (Molecular Function) of the 193 OGs that expanded in the common ancestor ofPalythoa. The top 20 terms are shown. The x-axis indicates the number of OGs, and circle size indicates fold enrichment. GO terms were assigned toP. caribaeorumproteins with eggNOG-mapper. The 4,944 OGs tested by CAFE5 served as the background, and enrichment was assessed using the weight01 algorithm with Fisher’s exact test, considering only GO terms annotated to at least five OGs. Among the 342Palythoa-restricted OGs, 289 (85%) were present as single copies or fewer than two copies per species (Fig. S7), suggesting that duplication ofPalythoa-specific genes has been largely suppressed following lineage divergence. Functional annotation revealed that the most abundant categories among these OGs were “signal transduction mechanisms”, “post translational modification, protein turnover, chaperones”, and “transcription”, although “poorly characterized proteins” predominated (Fig. S8; Table S7). This pattern is consistent with taxonomically restricted genes (TRGs), which often lack annotated homologs but can play important roles in development and lineage-specific adaptations [43]. Sixteen OGs were inferred to be lost inPalythoa; of these, 11 were poorly characterized (Table S8). The remaining OGs included genes involved in chemoreception, sterol desaturation, and amide metabolism. Importantly, genes essential for amino acid biosynthesis were retained, indicating thatPalythoaspecies likely retain the amino acid biosynthetic pathways present in other anthozoans. Compared with our previous study based on fragmented genomes and uncurated transcriptomes [20], the present results differ in some details. Nevertheless, the loss of a gene homologous to spermatogenesis-associated protein 7 (SPATA7), involved in photoreceptor ciliary function in mammals [44], was consistently detected, supporting its genuine absence inPalythoa. In addition, the visual pigment-like receptor peropsin (RRH) was also inferred to be lost, suggesting partial loss of photoreceptor-related functions acrossPalythoa, irrespective of symbiotic status. We identified 890, 484, and 107 OGs exclusive to clade I (Ptox), clade II (Pmiz and Pumb), and clade III (Pcar and Psak), respectively, containing 3,006 (Ptox), 586 (Pumb), and 143 (Pcar) genes in the representative genomes, respectively (Table S9). The majority of these genes lacked functional annotation (i.e., no COG category assigned or assigned to category S, “function unknown”): 84.1% (2,529 genes) in clade I, 75.1% (440 genes) in clade II, and 83.9% (120 genes) in clade III. Notably, 9.4% of clade I-specific genes encoded proteins with a reverse transcriptase (RVT) domain (Fig. S9; Table S9), suggesting lineage-specific expansion, particularly in Ptox. Although OGs exclusive to each clade arose independently, they often shared homologous Pfam domains. In particular, genes containing reverse transcriptase (RVT_1; PF00078) and integrase (rve; PF00665) domains, both characteristic of retrotransposons, were recurrently detected in clades I and II (Fig. S9; Table S9). This pattern likely reflects the independent proliferation of retrotransposon-derived genes in each lineage, some of which may represent TE-derived open reading frames that escaped repeat masking. Such retrotransposon activity may also have increased gene numbers through RNA-mediated duplication [45], consistent with the high proportion of intron-less genes in Ptox. We also identified paralogous gene pairs showing signatures of rapid evolution (Ka/Ks> 1). Ptox exhibited a high number of rapidly evolving paralogous gene pairs (20 pairs), whereas other species showed fewer (5 pairs each) (Fig. S10; Table S10). Notably, tumor protein translationally-controlled 1 (TPT1: OG0001769) showed rapid evolution in clade III species, while C-type lectin domain family 4 member A (CLEC4A: OG0002049) evolved rapidly in clade II.TPT1is involved in cell growth and proliferation [46] and its rapid evolution might therefore be related to the rapid growth and ecological dominance of clade III species, such as Pcar, on coral reefs [47–50].CLEC4Abinds carbohydrates abundant on cell surfaces, such as mannose and N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) [51], and shows broad glycan-binding specificity in humans [52]. Because even a few substitutions in the carbohydrate-recognition domain can shift sugar-binding specificity [53], rapid evolution ofCLEC4Acould either narrow its recognition to particular glycans or further broaden it. Such changes might facilitate association with specific bacteria in azooxanthellate clade II and contribute to adaptation to reef caves. Both hypotheses remain to be tested by functional analyses. Amplicon sequencing of symbiotic algae revealed distinct Symbiodiniaceae associations: Psak was dominated byDurusdinium(74.2%), whereas Ptox predominantly harboredCladocopium(98.3%) (Table S11). Although extensive examination of symbiotic algae across host clades was not performed, given that symbiosis with Symbiodiniaceae likely originated in the common ancestor of Brachycnemina [21,22], transitions of algal partners likely occurred duringPalythoaevolution. Alternatively, species inPalythoaclade III may exhibit greater flexibility in their symbiotic associations [54–56]. Genes encoding fluorescent protein homologs (OG0000497) were absent from clade II (Pmiz and Pumb). To trace the evolutionary history of this gene family, we examined microsynteny around the eight fluorescent protein homologs in the chromosome-level Pcar genome, which are distributed across three chromosomes and include two tandem clusters (g726–g727 and g742–g745) (Fig. S11). Around g496 and g726–g727, flanking genes were retained on single contigs in both Pmiz and Pumb, but no fluorescent protein homolog was present between them, and none was detected by BLASTN or HMM searches of six-frame translations of either assembly. For the other regions, the corresponding loci were interrupted by contig ends in the azooxanthellate assemblies. Although Ptox possesses 10 homologs, none was located at the corresponding loci (Fig. S11a, b). These results suggest that fluorescent protein homologs inPalythoahave undergone repeated duplication and loss rather than being stably inherited at fixed genomic positions. The absence of fluorescent protein homologs in Pmiz and Pumb is consistent with the lack of detectable autofluorescence in these species [7]. Autofluorescence, mostly due to green fluorescent protein, is widespread in cnidarians and has been proposed to function in prey attraction [57,58], algal symbiont attraction [59,60], and fine-tuning of light microclimate [61,62]. These functions depend on ambient light, and some of them also depend on algal symbionts, so they are likely to be of limited value for azooxanthellate species inhabiting low-light reef caves. Relaxed selection associated with low-light habitats and the loss of algal symbionts may have allowed the gene family to be lost entirely in the lineage leading to Pmiz and Pumb. These findings suggest a reorganization of light-dependent and feeding-related functions in azooxanthellate zoantharians, although targeted ecological and physiological studies will be required to clarify the underlying mechanisms. A recent study demonstrated that LePin (lectin and Kazal protease inhibitor domains) is involved in the initiation of endosymbiosis in the octocoralXeniasp. [63]. Although this gene is widely conserved among anthozoans, structural divergence has been suggested in the azooxanthellate sea anemoneNematostella vectensis[63]. InPalythoaspecies, some LePin homologs were identified in OG0000224 (Table S5). Some homologs retained the conserved domain architecture observed inXenia(i.e., C-type lectin, H-type lectin, EGF-like, and Kazal domains), whereas others exhibited more diverse protein domain architectures (Fig. 5). Comparison of amino acid sequences that retained conserved domain architecture revealed five sites with substitutions specific to azooxanthellate lineages, four of which were located within annotated functional domains (H-type lectin, C-type lectin, and EGF-like domains) and were conserved among zooxanthellatePalythoaandXenia. Although the functional consequences of these substitutions remain unclear, their localization within key domains suggests potential functional modification or reduction of LePin in azooxanthellatePalythoa. (a)Domain architectures of LePin homologs inPalythoaandXeniasp. (Xe_002591). Colors indicate protein domains, with InterPro or Pfam entries in parentheses. Genes that retain the domain architecture of Xenia LePin are shown in bold. (b)Amino acid alignment of the homologs with the conserved domain architecture. Domain regions are colored as in (a). Arrowheads and red letters indicate substitutions specific to azooxanthellatePalythoa. We further examined three proteins central to cnidarian-dinoflagellate symbiosis: the transcription factor NF-κB, which regulates host immune responses during symbiosis [64,65], a proton pump V-type H+-ATPase (VHA), which is present in the host membrane surrounding the algal symbionts and acidifies the symbiosome to promote algal photosynthesis [66], and the sterol transporter Niemann-Pick type C2 (NPC2), which mediates sterol transfer between symbionts and hosts [67–69]. No azooxanthellate-specific substitutions were found in NF-κB (Fig. S12) or VHA (Fig. S13), consistent with their broad roles in immunity and cellular homeostasis across animals. In contrast, azooxanthellate-specific substitutions were found within conserved domain regions in two of the four NPC2 paralog groups (Fig. S14). Thus, lineage-specific changes in azooxanthellatePalythoawere detected in genes involved in symbiont recognition (LePin) and nutrient exchange (NPC2), whereas the broadly acting NF-κB and VHA remained conserved. These substitutions may reflect functional modification or relaxed selective constraint. However, because both azooxanthellate species belong to a single clade (clade II), we cannot determine whether they contributed to or resulted from the loss of symbiosis, or arose in the clade II ancestor for unrelated reasons; addressing this will require comparison with independently derived azooxanthellate lineages and experimental validation. We identified 166 KS domain-containing gene candidates, of which 95 passed the score threshold of AFPK-Finder (Fig. 6). Molecular phylogenetic analysis grouped these into four clades: FAS, FAS II, cnidarian PKS, and bacterial PKS (Fig. 6). FAS genes, which are highly conserved among animals and are responsible for synthesizing saturated fatty acids from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA, were present in all examined hexacorals except actiniarians, including all fivePalythoaspecies. Most cnidarian PKS proteins contained a patched domain (IPR003392) in addition to the canonical KS, AT, DH, KR, and TE domains (Fig. S15). WithinPalythoa, cnidarian PKS genes were detected only in the genomes of Pcar and Psak (Fig. 6). Microsynteny analysis showed that, in Ptox, the genes flanking the PKS locus were retained on a single contig but no PKS gene was present between them (Fig. S16a). In Pmiz and Pumb, the corresponding region was interrupted by contig end; however, no cnidarian PKS gene was detected anywhere in these assemblies by BLSATN or HMM searches of six-frame translations, indicating that this locus is restricted to Pcar and Psak among the species examined. Pcar carried two copies, and microsynteny suggested that the ancestral copy became a pseudogene, containing two premature stop codons, after duplication (Fig. S16). Notably, no lineage-specific PKS expansion was observed in anyPalythoagenome. (a)t-SNE plot generated by AFPK-Finder. Colors indicate clades defined by Lin et al. [31], and candidates identified in this study are shown in yellow. (b)Maximum likelihood tree of KS domains. KS sequences from non-anthozoan organisms were retrieved from the AFPK-Finder dataset. Colors indicate clades as in (a), and branches containing cnidarian sequences are shown in yellow. Bootstrap values (1,000 replicates) are shown for major nodes. (c–e)Enlarged views of the clades containing (c) bacterial PKSs,(d)cnidarian PKSs, and(e)FASs.Palythoasequences are shown in red. “meta” and “bin” indicate sequences from metatranscriptome and metagenome-assembled genomes, respectively. Red circles indicate bootstrap values ≥ 90. Scale bars indicate substitutions per site. The alignment file is available in Zenodo, and domain architectures of cnidarian genes are shown in Fig. S15. PKS, polyketide synthase; FAS, fatty-acid synthase; AFPK, animal fatty-acid synthase-like polyketide synthase. In contrast, bacterial PKS sequences were recurrently detected in the microbial fraction ofPalythoasamples. We recovered 25 such sequences from metatranscriptomes of Pcar and Psak and two from a MAG assigned to Campylobacterota, reconstructed from Pumb reads (Fig. 6; Tables S12–S14). Their recurrent detection in three independent Pcar datasets and in Psak, together with the bacterial MAG from the azooxanthellate Pumb, indicates that PKS-bearing bacteria are consistently associated withPalythoaand that these genes are not derived from Symbiodiniaceae. No bacterial PKS sequences were recovered from Ptox and Pumb metatranscriptomes; however, these yielded far fewer predicted proteins that those of Pcar and Psak (approximately 24,000 vs. 83,000–288,000; Table S13), and Ptox RNA was partially degraded (Table S1), so this absence likely reflects limited sequencing depth. Only one bacterial-like PKS gene (pmiz_c2019.g002) was found in aPalythoagenome assembly. This gene contained three introns, indicating that it is integrated into the host genome rather than derived from bacterial contamination, and suggesting acquisition through horizontal gene transfer. Together, the absence of host PKS expansion, the absence of cnidarian PKS from Ptox, and the recurrent detection of expressed bacterial PKS genes inPalythoa-associated microbes suggest that associated bacteria, rather than host-encoded PKSs, are the most likely source of palytoxin. We present new genome assemblies of two zooxanthellatePalythoaspecies and curated assemblies of two azooxanthellate species, which, together with the chromosome-level genome ofP. caribaeorum, provide a comparative genomic framework for zoantharians. Across anthozoans, genome size variation was closely associated with TE content, particularly retrotransposons. Gene families related to ion transport and extracellular matrix interactions expanded in the common ancestor ofPalythoa, possibly in association with the incorporation of sand into the mesoglea. Comparisons between zooxanthellate and azooxanthellate species revealed genomic changes associated with symbiotic status. The azooxanthellate lineage has lost a fluorescent protein gene family that otherwise undergoes repeated duplication and loss, and shows lineage-specific substitutions in the symbiosis-related proteins LePin and NPC2 and rapid evolution of the lectin geneCLEC4A, whereas NF-κB and VHA remain conserved. Regarding the origin of palytoxin,Palythoagenomes showed no lineage-specific expansion of PKS genes, whereas bacterial PKS genes were recurrently detected and expressed inPalythoa-associated microbial communities. Based on these findings, we propose that palytoxin originates from associated bacteria rather than from the host. Testing this hypothesis will require identifying the producing bacteria and their biosynthetic gene clusters, relating their abundance and expression to palytoxin content across species and colonies, and experimental approaches such as antibiotic treatment of host colonies or cultivation of candidate bacteria. Ptox and Psak were collected between September 16-17, 2023 from reefs around Iriomote Island, Okinawa, Japan, at depths of ∼20 m and 5 m, respectively, and maintained for approximately twenty months in aquaria at the Yaeyama Station, Fisheries Technology Institute (Okinawa, Japan). For DNA extraction, a single polyp was collected from each colony, cut into small pieces using a razor blade, and briefly dissociated with Trypsin/EDTA (T4049, Sigma-Aldrich) for 5 min at room temperature. After digestion, the suspension was centrifuged at 500 ×gfor 5 min, and the resulting pellet was washed with artificial seawater filtered through 0.22 µm membranes (FSW). High molecular weight DNA was extracted from the pellet using the MagAttract HMW DNA kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Sequencing libraries were prepared using the HiFi DNA protocol (Pacific Biosciences) for Psak and the HiFi ultra-low input DNA protocol for Ptox. Libraries were sequenced on the PacBio Revio system (Pacific Biosciences). In addition, to improve previously reported gene models of Pumb, polyps of the species were also collected and processed in the same manner as the other two species from a specimen collected on September 16, 2023 from Nakano Beach, Iriomote Island at 5 m depth. Polyps from thePalythoacolonies used for this work have been deposited in the University of the Ryukyus Fujukan Museum under specimen numbers XXXXX. Fresh polyps of Psak, Ptox, and Pumb were individually homogenized in TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Total RNA was extracted according to the manufacturer’s protocol and its quantity and quality were assessed using Qubit RNA Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a TapeStation (Agilent). RNA-seq libraries were constructed using the NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X with 150-bp paired-end mode (Table S1). HiFi reads potentially originating from non-cnidarian organisms were identified with FCS-GX v0.5.4 [70] and were removed from further steps. Mitochondrial genomes were first assembled from the filtered HiFi reads using the MitoHiFi pipeline v3.2.1 [71]. Reads mapping to mitochondrial genomes were subsequently removed prior to nuclear genome assembly. Contaminant- and mitochondria-free HiFi reads were assembled using Hifiasm v0.23.0-r691 [72]. Primary contigs generated by Hifiasm were used for downstream analyses. Haplotigs were removed using a combination of the kmerDedup pipeline (https://github.com/xiekunwhy/kmerDedup) and purge_dups v1.2.5 [73]. Assembly polishing was performed using Inspector v1.3 [74] with filtered HiFi reads. Assemblies were evaluated using BlobTools v1.1.1 [75]. Contigs classified as taxa other than “Cnidaria” or “no-hit” were considered as non-Palythoasequences and excluded from further analyses. Genome completeness was assessed using BUSCO v6.0.0 [76] with the “metazoa_odb12” dataset (n= 672). Genome size was estimated using the backmap.pl v0.6 pipeline [77], in which filtered HiFi reads were mapped back to the draft assembly using minimap2 v2.26-r1175 [78] with the option (-ax map-hifi). For comparative analyses, the genome assembly ofPalythoa caribaeorum(Pcar; chromosome-level, GCA_965234985) was retrieved from NCBI. Genome assemblies of Pumb and Pmiz (contig-level), previously reported in Yoshioka et al. [20], were also included and curated using BlobTools, with non-cnidarian contigs removed. In addition, genome assemblies generated using long-read sequencing (PacBio or Oxford Nanopore) from representative species across six anthozoan orders were included for comparative analyses (Tables S2 and S3). Repetitive elements were identifiedde novousing RepeatModeler v2.0.4 [79] with the option (-LTRStruct). Repeats identifiedde novoand known repeats from RepeatMasker database were combined and soft-masked using RepeatMasker v4.1.5 [80]. Transposable elements’ (TE) divergence and landscape analyses were performed using the RepeatMasker scripts “calcDivergenceFromAlign.pl” and “createRepeatLandscape.pl”. TEs were classified into nine categories: DNA transposons, LINEs, LTRs, PLEs, rolling circle (RC)/Helitrons, Retroposons, Satellites, SINEs, and unclassified elements. When we performed correlation analysis with genome size, interspersed repeats were further grouped into three: class I Retroelements (LINEs, SINEs, LTR, PLE and retroposons), class II DNA transposons (DNA transposons and RC/Helitrons) or Unclassified. RNA-seq reads were quality trimmed using fastp v1.0.1 [81] with a minimum read length of 50 bp. Filtered reads were assembledde novousing TRINITY v2.15.1 [82] with default parameters. To remove low-abundance transcripts, reads were mapped back to the transcriptome assembly, and only concordantly mapped reads were retained as in [83]. These reads were aligned to the genome assembly using HISAT2 v2.2.1 [84]. Gene prediction was performed using BRAKER pipeline v3.0.8 [85–87], with soft-masked genomes, RNA-seq alignments, and Metazoa OrthoDB v12 as input. Gene models were further refined using PASA v2.5.2 [88] with genome-guided transcriptome assemblies generated by TRINITY. Genes with CDS length greater than 99 bp were retained. Gene identifiers were assigned sequentially based on contig position (e.g., c0001.g001 is the first gene of contig c0001). Gene model completeness was assessed using BUSCO v6.0.0 with the “metazoa_odb12” dataset. RNA-seq data used for gene prediction are listed in Table S1. For each species, the longest CDS per gene was selected and translated into protein sequences using TransDecoder v5.7.1 (https://github.com/TransDecoder/), following Yoshioka et al. [89]. Orthogroups (OGs) were inferred using OrthoFinder v2.5.5 [90]. Duplicated genes were classified as dispersed, proximal, singleton, tandem, or whole genome duplication (WGD)/segmental using MCScanX v1.0.0 [40]. For gene family expansion and contraction analysis, we used Computational Analysis of gene Family Evolution (CAFE5) v5.1.0 [91]. Orthogroups in which any single species had more than 100 gene copies were removed, because such families cause CAFE’s parameter estimates to be non-informative. The maximum-likelihood species tree inferred from 1,887 concatenated single-copy orthologs was rooted with the octocorals using ape v5.8-1 [92] in R. The tree was then made ultrametric by penalized likelihood with “chronos()” (correlated-rate model, smoothing parameter λ = 1). A single error rate (ε) for gene counts was first estimated to allow for assembly and annotation errors, which could differ among genomes of different completeness. The base model was then refitted with this error distribution fixed. For each orthogroup, CAFE5 computes a family-widePvalue for deviation from the fitted birth–death model. We corrected thesePvalues for multiple testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg method. For each branch, we counted the significant orthogroups that expanded or contracted between the ancestral and descendant nodes reconstructed by CAFE5. To examine gene duplication history, paralogous gene pairs were identified within each genome, and pairwise nonsynonymous (Ka) and synonymous (Ks) substitution rates were calculated following Mathers et al. [93]. All-against-all BLASTP searches were performed among genes within each duplication category. Paralog pairs were retained if they aligned over ≥150 amino acids with ≥30% identity, and for each gene only its closest paralog was kept. Because each pair was detected in both directions (e.g., A–B and B–A), only one of the two was retained. Finally, to avoid ambiguous assignments, pairs whose genes were not assigned to the same OG were excluded. Protein alignments were generated using MAFFT [94] with the E-INS-i strategy, and corresponding codon alignments were obtained using PAL2NAL [95].KaandKsvalues were calculated using KaKs_Calculator 2.0 [96] under the Yang-Nielsen model. Paralog pairs withKs□<□0.01 orKs>□2 were excluded. MedianKsvalues of single-copy orthologs among hexacorals were used to classify duplications as pre- or post-speciation events. Multiple testing corrections were applied using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. Gene pairs withKa/Ks□>□1 and adjustedP< 0.05 were considered to be under positive selection. Nucleotide or protein sequences were aligned using MAFFT v7.525 with the option (--auto), and poorly aligned regions were trimmed using ClipKIT v2.2.4 [97]. Concatenated alignments were generated using PhyKIT v2.0.1 [98]. Maximum likelihood phylogenies were inferred using IQ-TREE v2.2.2.6 [99] with ModelFinder [100] (-m MFP or -m MFP+MERGE) and UFBoot [101] (-B 1000). We reconstructed metatranscriptome assemblies and MAGs using raw sequencing data. For metatranscriptome assembly, raw RNA-seq reads were treated with fastp as described above and assembled using rnaSPAdes v4.3.0 [102] with default settings. Amino acid sequences were obtained from resulting transcripts translated using TransDecoder with the option “-m 100”. For MAG reconstruction, raw HiFi reads were mapped to the host draft genomes, and unmapped HiFi reads were extracted. The extracted HiFi reads were assembled using metaMDBG v1.3.1 [103]. The metagenomic contigs were classified with Kraken2 v2.17.1 [104] against the standard database (v2026-06-26). Contigs assigned to Bacteria or Archaea (NCBI taxonomy IDs 2 and 2157) were extracted with KrakenTools v1.2.1 [105]. The contigs were binned with COMEBin v1.1.0 [106] using contig sequences and coverage. CheckM2 v1.1.0 [107] was used to estimate the quality of each bin. MAGs meeting at least the MIMAG medium-quality criteria (≥50% completeness and <10% contamination) [108] were retained. All retained MAGs were screened for biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) with antiSMASH v8.0.4 [109] with the option “--genefinding-tool prodigal”. To screen PKS-like genes, we built a profile hidden Markov model (HMM) of the ketosynthase (KS) domain with hmmbuild of HMMER v3.4 [110] from the KS alignment [31]. We searched two sets of sequences with this HMM using hmmsearch (E-value cutoff: 1e-5). All hits at this E-value were treated as KS-domain sequences. (i) Genome assemblies of the fivePalythoaspecies were translated in six frames with esl-translate (-l 100), so that genes missing from the gene annotations could also be found. (ii) The gene models and metatranscriptomes of each species were searched directly. For the metatranscriptome hits, we extracted the region of each protein aligned to the HMM. Redundant sequences, such as isoforms and the same transcript assembled in different runs, were removed with CD-HIT v4.8.1 [111] with options (“-c 0.99” and “-aS 0.9”). We classified the candidate sequences with AFPK-Finder [31]. AFPK-Finder scores each sequence against 30 KS-related profile HMMs. A sequence is retained only if its full-sequence bit score exceeds 300 for at least one profile. The retained sequences are then embedded together with training KS sequences by t-SNE, at two perplexities. For molecular phylogenetic analysis of PKS genes, as PKS/FAS are multidomain enzymes that are difficult to align, only ketosynthase (KS) domain (Beta-ketoacyl synthase-like, N-terminal domain, InterPro IPR014030; Beta-ketoacyl synthase, C-terminal domain, IPR014031) sequences were aligned as in Lin et al. [31], and molecular phylogenetic analyses were performed as described above. To reduce computational cost, we subsampled 30 genes from each clade using “sample” command of SeqKit v2.10.0 [112]. The polyps from each colony were collected using clean scissors, rinsed in FSW, and placed in a 1.5-mL tube containing FSW. The polyp tissues were gently disrupted and squeezed against the tube wall with a pipette tip to release Symbiodiniaceae cells into FSW. The suspension was briefly centrifuged at low speed using a manual centrifuge (1011/1025, Hettich) to remove large tissue debris. The resulting supernatant containing Symbiodiniaceae cells was transferred to a new 1.5-mL tube and centrifuged (6000 ×gfor 5 min) to obtain Symbiodiniaceae cell pellets. Total DNA was extracted from the pellets using MightyPrep reagent for DNA (TaKaRa) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The nuclear ITS2 region was amplified using Tks Gflex DNA Polymerase Low DNA (TaKaRa) with primers “SYM_VAR_5.8S” and “SYM_VAR_REV” [113]. The PCR conditions were as follows: an initial denaturation at 94 °C for 1 min, followed by 25 cycles of 98 °C for 10 s, 56 °C for 30 s, and 68 °C for 30 s, and a final extension step of 68 °C for 5 min. PCR products were pooled together in an equimolar concentration and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform. Sequencing data were analyzed using the SymPortal pipeline [114] under default settings. Genome and gene statistics were calculated using SeqKit v2.10.0. Introns were defined as genomic regions between CDSs within genes. Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated using the “smplot2” package [115] and visualized with the “ggplot2” package [116] in R v4.5.1 [117]. For PGLS analyses, assembly size was regressed on each of the following predictors in separate models: TE length, non-TE length, class I length, class II length and unclassified repeat length. Models were fitted by maximum likelihood with “gls()” in the nlme v3.1-170 package [117]. The residual covariance structure followed Pagel’s λ model (“corPagel()”) [118,119]. In this model, λ scales the phylogenetic covariances among species: λ = 0 corresponds to independent residuals (ordinary least squares) and λ = 1 to Brownian motion along the tree. The estimated λ was tested against λ = 0 and λ = 1 by likelihood-ratio tests (one degree of freedom), which assess, respectively, whether the residuals contain detectable phylogenetic signal and whether they depart from Brownian-motion expectations. Functional annotation was performed using eggNOG-mapper v2.1.12 [120] based on the eggNOG v5.0 database [121]. Pcar was used as the representative zoantharian genome for clade III, and Pumb for clade II, based on genome BUSCO completeness. The actiniarianNematostella vectensiswas used as the anthozoan representative. Gene family enrichment analyses were conducted using topGO package [122], based on GO terms assigned by EggNOG-mapper. For survey of PKS genes, protein domain search using InterProScan [123] v5.69-97.0 was performed. Raw sequencing data are deposited in the DRA under the accession numbers DRR932003–DRR932009 and DRR1213993-DRR1213994, and the genome assemblies ofP. cf.toxicaandP. sp. sakurajimensis are available in DDBJ/ENA/GenBank under accession numbers BAAKIW010000000 and BAAKIX010000000, respectively (BioProject PRJDB18008). The gene models for all species used in this study, metatranscriptome assemblies, and MAGs generated in this study are available in Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23311753). title: From Arm to Leg: A Shared Primitive Framework for Solving Inverse Kinematics in Human Movement
author: Koren, Y.; Flash, T.
text: In motor control, the idea of a modular control architecture has been repeatedly discussed. This framework has been widely applied to kinematic and kinetic data, primarily to examine how the central nervous system (CNS) controls multiple elements simultaneously and how it handles redundant or excessive degrees of freedom. However, the inverse kinematics problem—traditionally defined as the mapping from a desired task-space outcome to the corresponding joint-space solution—has usually been treated separately from this framework. Recent work from our laboratory suggests that modular control may directly address all these problems by relying on a shared low-dimensional primitive space common to internal and external movement representations, as supported by recent studies of human hand-drawing kinematics. In the present study, we extended this framework from upper-limb drawing to lower-limb gait kinematics. We also used it to explore how different CNS pathologies may alter the organization of movement within this shared space. Overall, this study investigates whether walking, like other forms of movement, can be understood as arising from a small number of underlying primitives that are flexibly combined across coordinate systems. From the simple act of reaching for an external object to the complex dynamics of bipedal locomotion, the central nervous system (CNS) must constantly plan, control, and execute a vast repertoire of movements. Generating each movement may seem effortless, but it requires solving several non-trivial computational problems. These problems arise because the CNS must translate a high-level goal (e.g., “reach toward this object”) into precise, time-varying patterns of joint rotations and muscle activations, while accounting for mechanical and neural constraints. Consider, for example, a simple reaching movement. At the behavioural level, this movement can be described by specifying the trajectory of the hand in three-dimensional space, from its initial to its final position (task space, i.e., three-dimensional Euclidean space; see [1]). However, the motor commands that generate the movement are defined at the level of joint rotations and muscle activations. Thus, at some stage, the CNS must transform a desired hand trajectory in task space into a corresponding trajectory in joint space. This transformation is known as inverse kinematics (IK): given a desired end-effector position or trajectory, it determines the joint angles that will produce the task-level solution. Because this mapping is generally nonlinear, it may admit multiple solutions and can be computationally quite demanding [2]. The IK problem is further complicated by the fact that the human musculoskeletal system is highly redundant. Redundancy means that the system possesses more degrees of freedom (DOF) than are strictly required to accomplish a given task. In the human arm, for example, there are more joint DOF than spatial DOF of the hand. Consequently, many different joint configurations can yield the same end-effector position. The existence of an excess of degrees-of-freedom [2] is beneficial because it allows greater flexibility and robustness. For instance, it enables the system to avoid obstacles or compensate for weakness or fatigue. However, it also implies that the IK problem does not have a unique solution (is ill-posed [3]). The CNS must therefore select a specific joint-space solution from among a very large number of solutions that satisfy the same task-space goal. Even after a particular joint trajectory has been selected, another layer of complexity remains. Each joint is actuated by multiple muscles, each comprised of many motor units, the activation of which is orchestrated by a vast population of up-stream central neurons. In principle, the CNS could specify separate commands to each controlled element, but this would impose an enormous computational burden. Instead, a widely accepted view in motor control research is that the CNS simplifies control by using a modular architecture [4–7]. In such an architecture, groups of elements (e.g., muscles, joints, or even task variables) are controlled together as functional units or “modules.” Depending on the level of analysis, these modules have been referred to as synergies— i.e., coordinated patterns of activation across multiple elements [8,9] —or as primitives/source functions, which denote more elementary building blocks whose appropriate combination gives rise to those synergies and the resulting movements [10,11]. Mathematically, modularity is typically inferred using dimensionality-reduction techniques. These methods seek a small set of structured patterns that can account for most of the variance in high-dimensional data sets. For example, principal component analysis or non-negative matrix factorization, when applied to kinematic or electromyographic signals, often reveals a limited number of components that can be linearly combined to reconstruct the original signals (e.g., [5,6,8–10,12]). From this perspective, movement is planned and controlled within a low-dimensional “synergy space,” rather than directly within the full joint or muscle space. This strategy effectively reduces the number of DOF the CNS must regulate, thereby simplifying both the redundancy and control problems: instead of selecting from all possible joint trajectories, the CNS selects combinations of a small number of modules. Importantly, this modular control hypothesis also provides a principled framework for probing alterations in motor coordination associated with CNS pathologies (e.g., [12,13]). Changes in the number, structure, or recruitment of modules can reveal how neurological disorders reshape the organization of motor control, offering quantitative markers for characterizing disease mechanisms and tracking functional recovery. Recently, modularity has been proposed not only as a solution to the motor control problem but also as a mechanism for simplifying the IK problem itself. Barliya et al. [11] suggested that the CNS may rely on a shared, lower-dimensional set of kinematic primitives common to both internal and external representations. Within this framework, internal variables (e.g., joint angles) and external variables (e.g., hand position) are both expressed as combinations of a small number of time-varying basis functions (primitives). These shared primitives function as intermediaries between representational spaces. Rather than directly transforming a complete task-space trajectory into a corresponding joint-space trajectory, the CNS could map task-space goals onto a low-dimensional primitive space and map the resulting primitive representation to joint space. If the same primitives underlie both task and joint spaces, the transformation reduces to adjusting a limited set of weight parameters and temporal offsets (for mathematical proof, see [11]). In this way, the dimensionality and computational complexity of the IK transformation are substantially reduced. A critical aspect of this framework concerns the choice of coordinate frames for internal (and external) representations. Joint space can be described either in terms of anatomical (relative) joint angles or in terms of elevation angles (absolute segment orientations with respect to gravity). Barliya et al. [11] analysed upper-limb drawing movements and found that the time-varying primitives extracted from joint space showed greater similarity to those derived from task space when joint space was represented using elevation angles rather than anatomical angles. This finding is consistent with earlier work on human locomotion demonstrating that the elevation angles of the thigh, shank, and foot covary within a plane—a phenomenon known as the “intersegmental coordination law” [8,9,12]. It also aligns with psychophysical studies, indicating that elevation angles based representations support more accurate position matching than representations based on anatomical joint angles [14,15]. Taken together, these results suggest that an absolute, gravity-referenced frame of reference may constitute a preferred internal representation for movement planning. In this report, the shared-primitive framework is extended from upper-limb drawing to lower-limb locomotion. Specifically, a subset of gait kinematic data from healthy adults and individuals with Parkinson’s disease (PD) and cerebellar ataxia (AX) is reanalysed. For each participant, four coordinate frames are examined: two internal representations (anatomical joint angles and elevation angles) and two external representations (end-effector position expressed in Cartesian and Polar coordinates). We hypothesized that (1) internal and external representations of walking share a common, low-dimensional primitive structure, as suggested in [11]; and (2) elevation angles as the internal representation and polar coordinates as the external representation would best satisfy the shared primitive hypothesis and, therefore, would constitute the most plausible candidates for CNS computations. This prediction is based on previous work in human locomotion [9], which suggests that the absolute angles of the limb segments are rotated synergistically and that each kinematic synergy is used to control foot position, that is, task-space position, in a polar coordinate frame. In addition, we sought to demonstrate the utility of this approach for motor-control research by examining whether and how neurological pathologies alter this shared primitive space and the associated patterns of temporal delays and weights, which have been proposed to covary within and between DOF and to reflect coordinated actions [11]. By addressing these questions, the study aims to test whether the shared primitive framework provides a unified account of the DOF, IK and control problems in gait, and to explore how different neurological pathologies alter the underlying modular organization of human locomotion. The shared primitive framework assumes that high-dimensional movement signals decompose as linear superpositions of a low number of source functions (primitives) with trial-varying weights and temporal delays:where(t) represents the m-thDOF at time t in triall,s(t) are invariant basis functions,are time-varying mixing weights, andare temporal delays. Critically, if both internal (joint space) and external (task space) representations can be reconstructed from the same set of basis functions (sp), the transformation between spaces can be expressed in terms of the corresponding primitive parameters (c and τ) rather than as a time-varying transformation between individual coordinates. Thus, rather than solving the inverse-kinematics problem independently at each time point (t), the CNS could, in principle, transform between the two representations by operating on the low-dimensional set of shared primitives and their associated weights and delays. This provides a potential mechanism by which the redundancy and nonlinear complexity of conventional inverse kinematics can be substantially reduced, without requiring an explicit solution of the conventional joint-level inverse-kinematics equations1. To identify kinematic primitives, we used the Fourier-based Anechoic Demixing Algorithm (FADA), a source-separation method that models each observed signal as a linear combination of a few smooth temporal sources with DOF- and trial-specific weights and time delays. In this framework, the sources are assumed invariant across strides, while the weights and delays capture stride-to-stride and DOF-specific variabilities [16]. FADA belongs to the family of anechoic mixture models and has two key advantages for gait analysis. First, by representing sources in a truncated Fourier basis, it exploits the smooth, band-limited nature of kinematic signals, which greatly reduces the number of parameters to estimate and improves robustness to noise and local minima. Second, it naturally accommodates delayed activations of primitives, allowing to quantify both spatial (weight) structure and temporal (delay) structure within a single unified framework, and to compare these patterns across groups and coordinate representations [16]. The MATLAB implementation of the FADA is availableHere. In this report, we analyse a subset of the data reported in [12,17]. Specifically, walking kinematic data were obtained from healthy controls and patients with PD and AX. Controls were matched to patients by age, sex, weight, and height. Within each matched control–patient pair, the control participant was instructed to walk at the same speed as the corresponding patient. The participants’ characteristics can be found in [12,17]. All participants were free of any neurologic (other than PD or AX) or musculoskeletal conditions that can affect their gait. All participants ambulated without an assistive device during the test. Participants were instrumented with reflective markers that were positioned according to the standard convention. The 3-D walking kinematic data were captured by an eight-camera video system (Hi-Res, Motion Analysis System, Santa Rosa, CA) at a 60Hz sampling frequency. In the subset of data used here, participants were instructed to walk several times on a ∼10-14m long straight course, with their eyes open. During walking, participants were instructed to look straight ahead with their arm crossed to avoid obscuring the reflective markers on the legs. Healthy participants were instructed to walk at approximately the same pace as their designated matched patient. All other walking conditions reported in [12,17] were discarded from the present analysis. Initial marker processing yielded a series of complete strides per participant. Specifically, we extracted four 2-D sagittal-plane representations for each stride: Anatomical angles (AA): hip, knee, ankle joint angles Elevation angles (EA): thigh, shank, foot angles relative to gravity End-Effector (EE): mid-sole X,Y Cartesian positions Polar (Pl): limb length (R, hip-to-mid-sole), orientation (Phi, relative to vertical) Each stride and representation were time-normalized to 200 samples via spline interpolation, low-pass filtered at 6 Hz, and demeaned. For consistency, we selected 10 random strides per participant, excluding participants with <10 strides available (and their matched controls). Mean stride velocity differences within matched pairs were <2 cm/s and non-significant (p=0.08, Wilcoxon signed-rank). For each of the 4 representations, the 10 strides were decomposed using FADA, assuming 1-4 kinematic primitives. The source separation procedure resulted ins(for the most part,s=2) number of primitives, with each primitive having 10-time delays and 10 weight coefficients (one for each stride). The total kinematic variance explained was determined by using the above variables to reconstruct each stride and calculating the amount of variance explained by the reconstructed strides. All subsequent analyses were based on these data. To investigate lower-limb walking kinematics within the shared-primitive framework, we evaluated the similarity of primitives extracted from different representations. For each pair of internal (AA/EA) and external (EE/Pl) representations, we computed the maximum circular cross-correlation between corresponding primitives. Unlike PCA, in which the first principal component explains the largest proportion of variance, the order of FADA decomposition primitives is not meaningful. Therefore, to match primitives between the two spaces, we tested all four possible combinations of the two Internal primitives and the two External primitives: I1 –E1, I1 –E2,I2 –E1,and I2 –E2, whereIandEdenote primitives extracted from the internal and external representations, respectively. The combination yielding the highest value was assigned as ‘first’, and the reciprocal pair was assigned as ‘second’. For example, if the pair I1 –E2 yielded the highest correlation coefficient from among all possible pairs, this pair was assigned the value ‘first’ and its reciprocal pair, I2 –E1 was assigned the value ‘second’. Under the proposed framework, different gait kinematic profiles can be achieved by varying the weight coefficients and time delays. Therefore, this variance holds important information about the consistency and flexibility of the system [5]. Furthermore, it is not only the amount of variance that is important. In fact, Barliya et al. [11] suggested that time delays may vary in a coordinated manner within and between DOF, indicating that while primitives are independent, they may still be activated in a synergistic manner. Therefore, to quantify the amount of stride-to-stride delay variance, we used the circular statistic Rho [18], whose values lie within the range 0-1, with high values indicating low variance. To investigate whether time delays covary within- and between-DOF, as an indication of coordinated activation patterns, we used the correlation coefficient derived from a circular cross-correlation procedure (between the series of corresponding delays). Ifτ11andτ12covary, this might indicate within DOF coordination. Ifτ11andτ31covary, this might indicate between-DOF coordination. Note that time delays are assumed to be directional (circular) data. We reason that due to the periodic nature of gait kinematics, primitives are also periodic, and therefore time delays represent directional data. Thus, time delays (τ) were converted to angular data usingfor the above computations. As a measure of stride-to-stride variance of the weight coefficients, the range of observed values was used. I.e., max(α)-min(α). We performed all statistical analyses in SPSS (Version 31, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). The significance level was set a priori to α<0.05, and sequential Bonferroni correction was applied where appropriate to control for multiple comparisons. Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were used for all inferential tests. Preliminary analyses showed that includingPair(matched control–patient pairs) as a random effect did not improve model fit, so onlyParticipantwas retained as a random effect. To analyse the effect of participant groups, we structured the data using one of two equivalent frameworks. We either treated the participants as four distinct groups (PD controls, AX controls, PD patients, and AX patients) or organized them by two overarching factors: Pathology (PD vs. AX) and Health Status (control vs. patient). The choice of framework for any given analysis was dictated solely by the simplicity and interpretability of the resulting model. Residuals distributions were inspected for all models. Because many dependent measures were correlation coefficients or otherwise bounded, most variables of interest were Fisher Z-transformed [19] prior to analysis to address distributional and range constraints. To determine how many primitives to use, we tested the effects of Primitive number and Group on the percentage of kinematic variance explained. The dependent variable was variance explained, with Primitive number, Group (four levels), and their interaction entered as fixed effects. To quantify similarity between primitives extracted from different coordinate frames, we modelled Z-transformed correlation coefficients between primitives as the dependent variable. Fixed effects were Internal frame (AA, EA), External frame (EE, Pl), and their interaction. To test whether PD and/or AX altered primitive similarity, we used a separate model with Z-transformed correlation coefficients as the dependent variable and Pathology (PD, AX), Health Status (control, patient), and their interaction as fixed effects. Each matched control– patient pair was assigned to a pathology category, and Health Status captured differences within each pair. To examine the effects of pathology on the amount of variability in temporal delays, we first computed delay variance for each DOF across all controls and identified the two DOFs with the highest and the two with the lowest variances. We then tested the effects of DOF, Group (four levels), and their interaction on delay variance, with variance as the dependent variable. An analogous model (same fixed effects) was used to analyse stride-to-stride variance of the weight coefficients. The a-priori assumption was that low variance indicates tightly controlled DOF. 5. Coordination patterns (within and between DOFs). To quantify the coordination between primitives, we used the delay structure illustrated above as a guide: covariation between delays within a DOF (e.g. τ₁₁ and τ₁₂) was interpreted as within-DOF coordination, whereas covariation between delays of the same primitive across DOF (e.g. τ₁₁ and τ₃₁) was interpreted as between-DOF coordination. We first computed circular cross-correlations between the relevant delays for all DOF (within-DOF) and for all DOF combinations (between-DOF) in the control group. We then selected a subset of DOF pairs for formal testing (see Results). For these selected pairs, Z-transformed coefficients served as the dependent variable in LMMs with DOF and Group as fixed effects. Comparing the variance explained by the number of primitives and by group revealed two effects. First, each additional primitive significantly increased the explained variance (p< 0.003;Figure 1a). Second, the explained variance differed incrementally across groups, from lowest to highest: AX patients, AX controls, PD controls, and PD patients (Figure 1b). Nonetheless, the difference between AX and PD controls was non-significant (p = 0.1), and neither was the difference between PD patients and controls (p = 0.1). Two kinematic primitives explained ∼99% of gait variance in controls and PD patients, and ∼98% in AX patients (Figure 1c). Therefore, for the remainder of the analysis, we utilized the data extracted using two kinematic primitives. Variance explained as a function of the number of primitives (a) and by group (b). On the level of the individual DOF, this was only true for the X-coordinate and Phi DOF (p<0.03). However, after correcting for multiple comparisons, none of these differences were significant (p>=0.051). For PD, the variance observed in patients was lower than that of controls, a difference that did not reach statistical significance (p>0.13). Importantly, the variance observed in PD patients and controls was lower than that of both AX patients and AX controls (p<0.03). AX patients also exhibited significantly greater variance in the mixing weights than all other groups (p<0.003), supporting the interpretation that AX impairs both the timing and scaling of primitives. Next, we quantified the within-DOF correlation of delays in control subjects (seeFigure 4a) and found that the greatest values were observed in the shank EA, followed by the X-coordinate and Phi DOF. For consistency with the previous section, we also included the R DOF in the analysis to test the effect of different pathologies. Testing this effect within each DOF (Figure 4b) revealed that, after correction for multiple comparisons, this was true for the X-coordinate and shank EA DOF (p=0.034 and p=0.002, respectively) in the AX group, and only for the shank EA DOF (p<0.001) in the PD group. Results revealed that the greatest correlations were between the shank EA and Phi and X-coordinate DOFs, both indicating a between-coordinate-frame coordination. Within coordinate frames, the correlations between shank and foot EA, and between Phi and R, were the greatest. Testing the effect of pathologies on these patterns (Figure 5b) revealed lower values for AX patients compared with controls (p = 0.04), but there was no difference between PD patients and controls (p = 0.82). Exploring this effect within each pair revealed that this was true only for the correlation between delays from the shank EA and the X-coordinate (p=0.03). However, the interaction term in this model was non-significant (i.e., DOF by Group, p = 0.77), making it unclear whether this was a meaningful finding. This study has extended the shared primitive framework proposed by Barliya et al. [11] from upper limb drawing to lower limb locomotion and asked whether the same principles can explain how gait is organized. In doing so, it linked three classic problems in motor control—the DOF problem, the IK problem and the control problem—to a single, low-dimensional description of walking. Barliya et al. [11] suggested that the CNS may address the DOF, IK and control problems by representing movement in a shared, low-dimensional primitive space that is common to both internal (joint) and external (task) variables. In this framework, primitives are not synergies in the usual sense, but elementary temporal building blocks whose scaled and time-shifted combinations generate the observed kinematics [16]. Rather than computing a full nonlinear mapping between joint and task space, the CNS could operate on a small set of such building blocks and then apply simple gain and delay operations to express them in different coordinate frames. Our results support and extend this framework to human walking. Two kinematic primitives were sufficient to explain about 99% of gait variance in controls (and 98% in AX), slightly exceeding the variance captured by PCA on the same dataset [12], consistent with a compact modular description of gait. Primitives extracted from internal and external representations were highly similar (median r≈0.93), and this similarity was significantly greater when elevation angles were used as the internal coordinate frame (p<0.001). Similarity was largely preserved in both PD and AX, although AX patients showed lower values than PD (p=0.01), indicating that the underlying primitive space is preserved but somewhat degraded in cerebellar pathology. Together with Barliya et al.’s upper-limb results, these findings support a general principle: instead of explicitly solving IK in a high-dimensional space, the CNS may embed movements in a common primitive space and map between representations by adjusting a limited set of weight parameters and temporal offsets of a few building blocks. A central finding was that primitives extracted from the elevation angles data were more similar to external-space primitives than those extracted from anatomical joint angles data (p<0.001). This confirms and extends previous reports in both locomotion and upper-limb control, showing that elevation-angle representations support a low-dimensional structure that is less apparent in anatomical angle representation [8,9,11]. Psychophysical evidence further supports the superiority of elevation angles for internal computations: several studies have shown smaller position-matching errors when limb orientation is represented relative to gravity than when it is represented in terms of anatomical joint angles [14,15]. This in turn predicts that changes in gravitational context, such as microgravity, will alter proprioceptive acuity—a prediction repeatedly confirmed in the proprioception literature [20]. When combined with the present results, these findings point to elevation angles as plausible internal representation variables used by the CNS for lower-limb control during walking. A primitive-based description simplifies control but inherently limits flexibility: if movement is constructed from a few building blocks, adaptability must arise from how these blocks are timed and scaled. Within this framework, variability in delays and weights is therefore informative, as it reflects how flexibly the system can deploy primitives [5]. We found that PD and AX show opposite trends in delay variance. AX patients exhibited significantly increased delay variance relative to controls (p=0.03), particularly in task-space coordinates (X-coordinate and Phi), whereas PD patients showed a non-significant trend toward reduced delay variance (p>0.13). This pattern is compatible with the known pathophysiology: cerebellar damage is closely associated with impaired timing and prediction, while basal ganglia dysfunction in PD is linked to rigidity and difficulty in initiating or modulating actions. The higher variance of weight coefficients in AX (p<0.003) further suggests that cerebellar pathology disrupts both the timing at which primitives are activated and how strongly they contribute to the movement. At the same time, the AX sample was small (n=5), and several DOF-specific effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. These results should therefore be regarded as preliminary, highlighting plausible mechanistic differences between PD and AX that require confirmation in larger, prospectively designed cohorts. Variance alone cannot distinguish poor control from adaptive flexibility. To probe coordination more directly, we examined how delays covaried within and between DOF, following the simple system outlined in the Methods. In this system, covariation between the delays of the two primitives within a DOF (e.g. τ₁₁ and τ₁₂) indicates that those primitives tend to be activated in a fixed temporal relationship for that DOF (within-DOF coordination), whereas covariation between delays of the same primitive across DOF (e.g. τ₁₁ and τ₃₁) reflects coupling between segments or between internal and external variables (between-DOF coordination). An important observation is that coordination was generally stronger within DOF than between DOFs: correlations between the delays of the two primitives within a given DOF were higher than those between DOF for the same primitive. This suggests that, although primitives themselves are defined as independent temporal building blocks, their activation within each DOF tends to be synergistic—their delays are not arbitrary but are coordinated to produce stable local patterns. Between DOF, by contrast, coordination is weaker, indicating a more flexible coupling across segments and between internal and external spaces. Both PD and AX reduced this within-DOF temporal coordination: delay correlations between the two primitives within the same DOF were lower in patients compared with controls (p=0.026 for PD, p=0.001 for AX), particularly for shank elevation and X-coordinate. For between-DOF coordination, only AX patients showed clear reductions in their temporal correlation, especially for coupling between shank elevation and X-coordinate (p=0.04), whereas PD patients did not differ significantly from controls (p=0.82). These results suggest a layered organization: primitives remain the basic temporal building blocks, but their activation patterns form coordinated “activation synergies” within each DOF, and AX, in particular, disrupts both this local coordination and the weaker coupling across DOF. This interpretation is consistent with PCA-based work showing opposite rotations of the intersegmental covariation plane in PD and AX patients [12], which has been linked to distinct roles of basal ganglia (rhythm regulation) and cerebellum (fine-tuning coordination) during gait. Methodologically, this work highlights several strengths of combining the shared primitive framework with FADA. FADA generalizes beyond PCA by allowing both weights and temporal delays to vary across strides, a critical feature for rhythmic behaviours such as walking where timing variability is crucial [16,21]. On the same dataset, FADA captured slightly more variance with two primitives than PCA did with two components [12], likely because it explicitly models the periodic structure and phase shifts inherent in cyclic movements. The framework also provides a principled way to evaluate candidate internal and external representations by asking which combinations can be expressed via a common primitive set and how pathologies alter that shared space and its activation patterns. Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, primitives in this context are statistical building blocks of the kinematics; demonstrating that they correspond to specific neural processes will require converging evidence from neurophysiology, imaging or behavioural studies [4]. Second, the sample size, especially for AX, was modest; the analysis focused on straight-line overground walking; and this FADA-based re-analysis was not pre-planned, all of which constrain generalizability, particularly for pathology-specific conclusions. Future work should include larger, prospectively recruited cohorts, richer locomotor tasks and explicit modelling of disease severity and medication state. Finally, the analysis was restricted to the sagittal plane in line with the law of intersegmental coordination [8,9,12], omitting frontal and transverse plane dynamics that are important for balance and complex gait adaptations. Overall, the present results show that a shared primitive framework can account for the structure of normal gait and characteristic changes in PD and AX. They support the idea that the CNS solves the DOF, IK and control problems in locomotion by operating on a small set of temporal building blocks, and that while these primitives remain largely intact in pathology, their activation patterns and coordination—especially within and between DOFs—are selectively altered.
