The m6A Cap-1 structure of mammalian messenger RNA was discovered in the 1970’s (6–8,43) but the biological role of the modification has only begun to unfold due to the recent advances in analytical methods such as LC-MS (44) and RNA sequencing technologies (11,45), and the discovery of PCIF1 as the sole enzyme responsible for the modification in mammalian cells (11–13,15). While still under investigation, the biological role of m6A Cap-1 modification appears to be diverse in different cell types and may provide the cell with tunable mechanisms to regulate transcription and translation. Nonetheless, reports that synthetic mRNA containing m6A Cap-1 modification increase the duration and level of protein expressionin vivo(36,46,47) suggest that the modification can be a means to improve the performance of mRNA therapeutics. In addition to enzymatic capping, trinucleotide cap analogs are commonly used to synthesize Cap-1 RNA in IVT (48). Trinucleotide cap analogs refer to a class of synthetic cap analogs consisting of the first two nucleosides connected by a canonical 3’ to 5’ phosphate diester bond and a m7G structure connected to the first nucleotide via a 5’ to 5’ triphosphate linkage. Early kinetics studies of T7 RNA polymerase suggest that nucleotide triphosphate binding at the +2-nucleotide site of transcription precedes that at +1 site (49,50). It has also been reported that dinucleotides pppGpA and pppGpG are potent initiators for T7 RNA polymerasein vitro(51,52). It was therefore conceivable that trinucleotide cap analogs such as CleanCap®AG support T7 RNA polymerase transcription initiation efficiently (48,53). m6A-modified trinucleotide cap analogs such as CleanCap®Reagent M6 (Trilink) have been used to synthesize m6A Cap-1 RNAin vitro. However, addition of a methyl group to the N6 position of the initiating adenosine of these trinucleotide cap analogs requires modifications of reaction conditions such as high cap analog and T7 RNA polymerase concentrations (36,54) or mutations in T7 RNA polymerase to facilitate efficient transcription (55). Evidence suggests that the Hoogsteen edge of guanosine and adenosine at the +1-nucleotide position is an important factor in T7 RNA polymerase transcription initiation (56,57). For adenosine, the Hoogsteen edge consists of the N6 and N7 groups. The methyl group at the N6 position of trinucleotide Cap-1 analogs may therefore disrupt the formation of a productive initiation complex and lead to low IVT yield under standard conditions. To overcome the mechanistic shortfall in IVT initiation, millimolar concentrations of N6A-methylated trinucleotide cap analog are needed to drive the incorporation of the cap analog into the IVT products, while only one molecule of the cap analog is required per RNA transcript. Since IVT yields oftentimes culminate in high nanomolar to low micromolar concentrations, a large majority of the cap analogs added to IVT reactions are not incorporated into the RNA transcript and discarded (57). RNA capping and cap modifying enzymes, on the other hand, turnover multiple times within the reactions using commodity co-substrates (GTP, which is already present in IVT reactions, and SAM) and are therefore a more efficient means for large scale synthesis. Using bioinformatics and functional screening, we selected and characterized two robust homologs of human PCIF1 as a means to domesticate the cap-specific N6A methyltransferase activity and created economical and adaptable solutions to synthesize m6A Cap-1 RNAin vitro. The two enzymes methylate the initiating adenosine of 5′-m7G-capped RNA at nanomolar concentrations and are compatible with conditions commonly used forin vitrotranscription and RNA capping reactions. Robust methylation activity was observed for RNA oligos, IVT transcripts containing m1Ψ, and trinucleotide cap analogs. PC04 and PC05 can be incorporated into existing IVT workflows to synthesize m6A Cap-1 RNA efficiently (FIG 8). IVT transcripts produced using trinucleotide Cap-1 analogs or enzymatic capping can be methylated to form m6A Cap-1 after a purification step (Route 1). PC04 and PC05 can be added to FCE/VCE and Vaccinia cap 2′-O methyltransferase reactions to facilitate one-pot post-transcriptional capping and cap modification (Route 2). Taking advantage of the methylation activity on trinucleotide cap analogs, we showed that PC05 can be used to convert trinucleotide Cap-1 analogs to their m6A counterparts that can be directly used in IVT (Route 3). Ultimately, one-pot one-step m6A Cap-1 synthesis can be achieved by including PC05 in enzymatic co-transcriptional capping IVT reactions using an FCE::T7RNAP fusion protein and Vaccinia cap 2′OMTase (Route 4). Route 1: Cap-1 IVT transcripts produced using trinucleotide Cap-1 analogs or post-transcriptional enzymatic capping can be methylated to form m6A Cap-1 post-transcriptionally after a purification step. Route 2: One-pot post-transcriptional 5’ capping and cap modification using PC04 or PC05 in addition to FCE/VCE and Vaccinia cap 2′-O methyltransferase. Route 3: An one-pot, two steps workflow where PC05 is used to convert millimolar concentrations of a trinucleotide Cap-1 analog to its m6A form that can be directly used in IVT reactions. Route 4: All enzymatic one-pot one-step m6A Cap-1 RNA synthesis using an FCE::T7RNAP fusion protein, Vaccinia cap 2′OMTase and PC05. The availability of an efficient cap N6-adenosine methyltransferase such as PC04 and PC05 can enable more research on the biological role of the m6A Cap-1 modification, the establishment of more potent mRNA therapeutics and novel applications. For example, m6A Cap-1 RNA can be readily synthesized and transfected different cell types under different growth conditions to decipher their biological effects via transcriptomic analyses (63). Recombinant human PCIF1 has been used to introduce cap-adjacent adenosine with N6’-propargyl groups that allow functionalization of synthetic RNA through click-chemistry (45,64). In summary, we identified two RNA 5’ cap N6-adenosine methyltransferases that are highly active and can readily be incorporated into IVT workflows to produce m6A Cap-1 RNAin vitro. These enzymes present additional tools for research on the biological roles of the m6A Cap-1 modification and development of therapeutic mRNA. PCIF1-like sequences were collected from the Joint Genome Institute Integrated Microbial Genomes & Microbiomes (65, 66). AlphaFold2 Structural predictions (39) of sequences using the Colab web server (38) were visualized using PyMol (67). Fifty-five PCIF1-like amino acids sequences were selected for functional screening. Expression plasmids (pET-29b(+)) with inserts containingE. colicodon-optimized genes were purchased from Twist Bioscience. A total of 250 ng of plasmid DNA was used for 30 µLin vitrotranscription-translation reactions (IVTT) (PURExpress ΔRF123In vitroProtein Synthesis Kit; New England Biolabs; E6850S) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After a 3-hour incubation at 37°C, the solutions were added to a screening reaction mixture containing substrate RNA oligos with a 3′-desthiobiotin modification and a 5′ Cap-0 (Oligo 5, Cap0 1A 25mer[dsbtn]) or Cap-1 (Oligo 14, Cap0 1A 25mer[dsbtn]) structure. The 50 µL reactions containing 5% (v/v) IVTT solution, 0.6 µM RNA, 1 U/µL Murine RNase Inhibiter and 0.2 mM SAM in 1x capping buffer (New England Biolabs, B2080AAVIAL) were incubated at 37°C for 1 hour. The RNA oligo was then purified using hydrophilic streptavidin-coated magnetic beads (New England Biolabs; S1421S). Reactions were mixed with the beads at a 1:1 ratio and incubatedfor 30 min at room temperature before being washed thrice with a wash buffer (5 mM Tris, pH 7.5, 60 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA). RNA was eluted in 30 µL nuclease-free water by heating to 65°C for 4 minutes. Samples were filtered in 0.22 µm centrifugal filters (Millipore; UFC30GV0S) and methylation status was analyzed by intact oligo LC-MS/MS. Plasmids encoding Vaccinia VP39 (a Cap-0 2′OMTase) served as a positive control for IVTT and cap modification assay. IVT templates were designed to encode two 2.1 kb RNA molecules each containing the first 50 bases of a 5′UTR, the consensus mammalian Kozak sequence, a firefly luciferase coding sequence, a 3′UTR derived from the publicly available sequence of BNT162b2, a 60-adenosine tail, and a BspQI restriction site. Transcription of the RNA is driven by the T7 Phi2.5 promoter. The 5’UTRs were a derivation of pRNA21 with a 5’-AGGA extension (pRNA21_AGGA) or the human ETS1 mRNA (ETS1; NCBI ID NM_001143820.2). The DNA sequences of the T7 transcription template are available in Supplementary Table S2. The cloning of the inserts into pUC57, preparation and linearization of the plasmid DNA were done commercially (Genscript). Supplementary Table S3 shows the expected RNA transcript sequences based on the DNA templates. Protein expression and purification for data presented here was performed commercially (Genscript). Expression constructs containing the PC04 and PC05 ORFs with a C-term 6x His-Tag were inserted into pET29b(+) and used to transformE. coliT7ExpresslysY/Iq(New England Biolabs, C3013I). Recombinant protein expression was induced by 0.5 mM IPTG once cell density reached OD600nm=0.6-0.8 and incubation at 15°C for 16 hrs. The proteins were purified from cell lysate supernatant in two steps using a Ni-NTA column and size exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200). Protein purity was >90% by Comassie blue-stained SDS-polyacrylamide gel. Stocks of each enzyme were prepared by dialyzing into a storage buffer containing 50% glycerol. Working stocks of 10 µM enzyme, quantified using the Bradford colorimetric assay (Bio-Rad), were stored at -20°C for over 6 months with no observable loss of activity. Nucleoside analysis was performed to verify the identity of the methylation products of the PCIF1-like enzymes (FIG 2D). Oligo 14, a synthetic 25mer with the Cap-1 structure (m7GpppAm-) containing a single cap-adjacent 2’-O-methyl-adenosine was used such that the presence of the N6,2′-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) is indicative of cap-specific N6-adenosine methyltransferase activity after decapping. The methylation reaction containing 2 µM of enzyme and 1.5 µM of substrate was incubated at 37°C for 2.5 hours. Since no validated m6A Cap-1 dinucleotide (m7Gpppm6Am) standard substance is commercially available, the methylation reaction products were decapped before subjecting the RNA to nucleoside digestion such that the presence of 2’-O,N6-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) is indicative of the formation of m6A Cap-1. Ten micrograms of reaction products were decapped using mRNA decapping enzyme (New England Biolabs; M0608S) and purified using hydrophilic streptavidin-coated magnetic beads (New England Biolabs; S1421S) yielding RNA with monophosphate (p-) 5′ ends. The oligos were converted to nucleosides using Nucleoside Digestion Mix (New England Biolabs; M0649S) and filtered using 0.22 µM spin column (Millipore; UFC30GV25). The modified nucleotide species present in each sample was resolved using UHPLC-MS/MS analysis with dynamic multiple reaction monitoring with technical duplicates (dMRM). Enzyme activity assays were conducted in 1x capping buffer (New England Biolabs, B2080AAVIAL) containing 400 µM SAM, 1 U/uL Murine RNase Inhibiter and indicated concentrations of RNA oligos in duplicate unless specified otherwise. Reactions at 30 µL final volume were incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes and stopped by heating to 75°C for 5 minutes in a thermocycler. Enzymes stocks were diluted in 1x capping buffer for assays unless specified. A 3′-desthiobiotin TEG modification ([dsbtn]) is present in indicated RNA substrates to enable purification of the oligos from the reaction mixtures for compatibility with LC-MS/MS. Percent composition of methylated oligos was determined for each sample by mass signal intensity of the corresponding species. The mean ± 1 standard deviation of duplicate experiments are reported. A table of oligo substrates is found in Supplementary Table 1. Substrate specificity experiments presented in FIG 2C were performed on RNA oligos with different 5′ chemical groups (oligos2-10in Supplementary Table S1) using 10 nM enzyme and 1.5 µM substrate. Oligo 3, which contains a 5’ diphosphate group was generated by incubating oligo 2 (containing a 5’ triphosphate group) with FCE (NEB) in the absence of co-substrates GTP or SAM. Oligo 4 contains an unmethylated G-cap generated by incubating oligo 2 with FCE in the presence of GTP. Oligo 5 contains a Cap-0 structure generated by incubating Oligo 2 with FCE, GTP and SAM. The reacted oligos were purified using hydrophilic streptavidin-coated magnetic beads (New England Biolabs; S1421S). Enzyme titration assays (FIG 3A, D) were performed by incubating serial dilutions of PC04 or PC05 with 1µM of Cap-1 RNA oligo substrates in 1x reaction buffer at 37°C for 30 minutes, followed by heating to 75°C for 5 minutes. Oligo 1 (Cap-1 1A 12mer[dsbtn]) is a 12mer with a single Cap-adjacent 2′-O-methyladenosine. Oligo 6 (Cap-1 8A 25mer[dsbtn]) is a 25mer containing 8 internal adenosines. Oligos 12 (Cap-1 AU 12mer) and 13 (Cap-1 Am1Ψ 12mer) are 12mers designed specifically to place a uridine or N1-methylpseudouridine at position 2, adjacent to the methyl acceptor 2′-O-methyladenosine. To investigate the temperature range of the enzymes (FIG 3B), reaction mixtures were set up in pre-chilled tubes in 4°C cold blocks to ensure synchronized initiation. Reaction mixture (270 µL) containing 2 nM of enzyme and 1 µM oligo 1 (Cap-1 1A 12mer[dsbtn]) were aliquoted and placed at temperatures ranging from 15-65°C in a thermocycler with variable heating zones (Applied Biosystems VeritiPro) to initiate the reactions. To investigate the pH range of the enzymes (FIG 3C,Supplementary FIG S4), a final concentration of 50 mM Tris, HEPES, Bis-Tris, or Bis-Tris Propane solutions (Hampton Research) at the indicated pHs were added to a minimal reaction buffer (400 µM SAM, 2.5 mM Tris pH 7.0, 5 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 1 U/uL Murine RNase Inhibiter, pH 7.0 at 25°C) and 1 µM of oligo 1 (Cap-1 1A 12mer[dsbtn]). Reactions were initiated with the addition of enzyme diluted in minimal reaction buffer at a final concentration of 2.5 nM. For RNA methylation activity assays in the presence of NTPs or Cap-1 analogs (FIG 5B, C), 0.2-10 mM of each of the individual NTPs or CleanCap®Reagent AG (Trilink; N-7113) or CleanCap®Reagent AU (Trilink; N-7114) were incubated with 5 nM enzyme and 1 µM oligo 1 (Cap-1 1A 12mer[dsbtn]) substrate at 37°C for 30 min, followed by heat inactivation and LC-MS/MS analysis as indicated above. Substrate RNA was made by IVT using HiScribe T7 High Yield RNA Synthesis Kits (New England Biolabs; E2040S) with or without trinucleotide Cap-1 analogs following manufacturer’s recommended protocols. N1-methylpseudouridine modified RNA was made by substituting UTP with m1ΨTP. After IVT, the DNA template was removed by adding 1 µL of DNase I-XT (New England Biolabs; M0570S) per 20 µL of IVT and incubating at 37°C for 20 min. The RNA was purified using Monarch RNA Cleanup kits (New England Biolabs; T2040S) according to the recommended protocol. For enzymatically capped RNA, purified uncapped IVT RNA was capped to Cap-1 using FCE with Vaccinia 2’OMTase (New England Biolabs; M0366S) according to recommended protocol and purified. RNA quantification was done using a NanoDrop instrument (Thermo Fisher). Size and integrity were assessed by RNA Tapestation and RNA ScreenTapes (Agilent). For each duplicated experiment, a 5′ cap composition analysis was performed using the RNase 4-LC-MS/MS method detailed in (41) and described below. Reaction volumes varied from 50 to 80 µL to ensure a minimum of 40 µg of mRNA for cap analysis. The percent composition of methylated oligos was determined for each sample by MS signal intensity of annotated fragments. The mean ±1 standard deviation of replicated experiments are reported. Purified Cap-1 RNA at a concentration of 0.75 µg/µL (∼1 µM) that had been enzymatically capped or co-transcriptionally capped with a Cap-1 analog was allowed to react with 120 nM of PC04 or PC05 in 1x capping buffer (New England Biolabs, B2080AAVIAL) with 1 U/µL Murine RNase Inhibiter) containing 400 µM SAM at 37°C for 60 min. One-pot, three-enzyme m6A Cap-1 capping on purified uncapped IVT RNA was performed in reactions containing 400 µM SAM, 500 µM GTP, 120 nM PC04 or PC05, 5 U/µL Vac 2’OMTase and 1 U/µL VCE or FCE in 1x capping buffer (New England Biolabs, B2080AAVIAL) containing 1 U/uL Murine RNase Inhibiter. The VCE reactions contained 0.5 µg/µL substrate RNA. The FCE reactions contained 0.75 µg/µL substrate. The composition of mRNA 5′ end was determined by RNase 4 endonuclease protection assay published previously (41). Briefly, an antisense DNA oligo probe containing a desthiobiotin modification is annealed to the 5′ 18-25 bases of an mRNA and digested with RNase 4 (New England Biolabs; M1284S) using 1 µL of 50U/µL RNase 4 in 1x NEB Buffer r1.1 (New England Biolabs; B6001SVIAL). Hybrid duplexes containing the DNA probe and the protected 5′ mRNA fragments are then purified and enriched using hydrophilic streptavidin-coated magnetic beads (New England Biolabs; S1421S). The fragments are subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis. The mass of RNase 4 cleavage fragments matching the relevant 5′ structures (pppA-, ppA-, GpppA- and GpppA-with 1, 2 or 3 methyl groups) were assigned to the appropriate 5′ structures. Specifically, masses that are consistent with GpppA-plus one, two and three methyl groups are assigned Cap-0, Cap-1 and m6A Cap-1 respectively. The mass intensities of the assigned RNase 4 cleavage fragments were used to estimate the percentage of the corresponding 5’ structure in the mRNA preparations. To verify the identity of m6A Cap-1 on RNA, the methylation reaction product RNA was decapped using mRNA decapping enzyme (New England Biolabs) according to manufacturer’s instructions. The decapped mRNA was purified using Monarch RNA Cleanup kit (New England Biolabs; T2040S). The purified decapped mRNA was incubated overnight with nucleoside digestion mix (New England Biolabs; M0649S) and subjected to nucleoside analysis using LC-MS/MS with dynamic multiple reaction monitoring (dMRM). With decapping, m6Am detected in LC-MS/MS is attributed to the N6-adenosine methyltransferase activity of the PCIF1 enzymes and 2’-O-methyltransferase activity of vaccinia cap 2’-O-methyltransferase activity. The mass intensity of the detected m6Am, m6A and Am was used to estimate the level of m6A Cap-1 incorporation. For activity assays using Cap-1 analog as substrates, 1 µM CleanCap®Reagent AG (Trilink; N-7113) or CleanCap®Reagent AU (Trilink; N-7114) was incubated with 0.6 to 40 nM of PC04 or PC05 in 1x capping buffer (New England Biolabs, B2080AAVIAL) at 37°C for 30 min in duplicate. The reactions were stopped by heating at 80°C for 5 min and the mass composition of methylated CleanCap®Reagent AG was determined by LC-MS/MS. High trinucleotide cap analog concentration reactions (FIG 6A) combined 4 or 8 mM of CleanCap®Reagent AG (Trilink; N-7113) with 5 µM PC04 or PC05 enzyme in a reaction buffer (50 mM Bis-Tris, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, 5% DMSO, pH 6.8 at 25°C). Methyl doner and MgCl2concentrations were adjusted according to the substrate concentration. Reactions containing 4 mM substrate had 8 mM SAM and 4 mM MgCl2while 8 mM substrate reactions had 12 mM SAM and 8 mM MgCl2. Reactions were incubated at 37°C for 18 hours and stopped by heating at 80°C for 5 min. Composition of the methylated CleanCap®Reagent AG was determined by LC-MS/MS. The mean ±1 standard deviation of quadruplicate experiments is reported. For reactions combining enzymatic methylation activity on Cap-1 analog with IVT (FIG 6B-F), 100 µL reaction mixtures of 9 mM CleanCap®Reagent AG (Trilink; N-7113) and 5 µM PC04 or PC05 in a reaction buffer (50 mM Bis-Tris, 5 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, 5% DMSO, pH 6.8 at 25°C) containing 13 mM SAM and 9 mM MgCl2were incubated for 18 hours at 37°C. The reaction was stopped by heating to 80°C for 5 min and an aliquot was removed for product analysis by LC-MS/MS. The overnight reactions were mixed with a solution containing IVT reagents at a 3:1 ratio to achieve final conditions of 6 mM Cap analog and 3 mM NTPs. The 120 µL IVT reaction conditions were as follows: 50 mM Bis-Tris pH 6.8, 5 mM DTT, 15 mM MgCl2, 2.12 mM spermidine, 1 U/µL Murine RNase Inhibitor, 3 mM NTP mix, 1 U/mLE. coliInorganic Pyrophosphatase, 0.05 µg/µL DNA template (pRNA21_AGGA), and 9375 U/mL T7 RNA Polymerase (New England Biolabs; M0251S). A solution of 9 mM CleanCap®Reagent M6 (CleanCap®Reagent m6AG (3’Ome); Trilink; N-7453), 50 mM Bis-Tris pH 6.8, 5 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, 9 mM MgCl2, and 5% DMSO was used in place of the PCIF1 reactions as a positive control for IVT with co-transcriptional capping using an m6A modified Cap-1 analog. The solutions were incubated at 37°C for 3 hours with gentle inversion at 30 min intervals. DNA template was removed by adding 6 µL of DNase I-XT (New England Biolabs; M0570S) for 37°C for 20 min. The RNA was purified by mixing with RNACleanXP magnetic beads (Beckman Coulter; A63987) at a 1:1.8 volume ratio, washed three times with 70% ethanol, and eluted in 1 mM sodium citrate, pH 6.5. The size and integrity of the purified RNA was assessed by Tapestation and RNA ScreenTape (Agilient) (Supplementary FIG S6A). RNA 5′ analysis was performed using the RNase 4-LC-MS/MS method. The identity of the added m6A Cap-1 structure was verified using the nucleoside analysis workflow described above. For one-pot m6A Cap-1 synthesis using the FCE::T7RNAP fusion enzyme (FIG 7), 100 µL IVT reactions containing 200 nM PC04 or 100 nM PC05 were mixed with 0.05 µg/uL DNA template, 100 nM FCE::T7RNAP, 5 U/µL Vac 2′OMTase, 5 mM of each NTP, 400 µM SAM, 1U/µL Murine RNase Inhibitor, 5 U/µLE. colipyrophosphatase, 5 mM DTT, an additional 14 mM MgCl2, in 1x T7 RNAP Polymerase Reaction Buffer (40 mM Tris-HCl, 6 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, 2 mM spermidine, pH 7.9 at 25°C). Reactions were incubated at 37°C for 90 minutes. DNA template was removed by adding 5 µL DNase I-XT (NEB) and incubating at 37°C for 20 min. The IVT products were purified using Monarch RNA Cleanup kits (New England Biolabs; T2040S) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The IVT yield was assessed using a NanoDrop instrument (Thermo Fisher). RNA 5′ analysis was performed using the RNase 4-LC-MS/MS method. Decapping-nucleoside analysis was used to confirm the identity of modified nucleosides. title: Methyl-TROSY NMR at 1.2 GHz: exploiting resolution and magnetic field alignment for structure and dynamics of large biomolecular assemblies
author: Lobbia, V. R.; Orsetti, A.; van Ingen, H.
text: The range of protein assemblies that can be studied by NMR has greatly expanded both by increases in magnetic field strength and by development of new NMR approaches, such as methyl-group specific transverse relaxation optimized spectroscopy (methyl-TROSY). Recently, a new generation of NMR magnets operating at 1.2 GHz have become available, offering the highest resolution for biomolecular NMR. Here, we investigated the performance of methyl-TROSY NMR at 1.2 GHz in the characterization of the structure and dynamics of large biomolecular assemblies, using the nucleosome, a 200 kDa protein-DNA complex, as a test sample. We find that the increased resolution of the 1.2 GHz system allowed to resolve small asymmetries in sidechain conformations that remained hidden at lower magnetic field strengths. Increased CSA relaxation effectively increased13C transverse relaxation rates by 20% at 1200 compared to 900 MHz, negatively impacting sensitivity. We further observed significant magnetic field alignment of the nucleosome at 1.2 GHz, giving rise to methyl1H-13C residual dipolar couplings (RDCs). We show that these histone methyl group RDCs can be used to aid stereo-specific assignment and to determine the overall conformation of the nucleosomal DNA, revealing a significant unwrapping of the DNA from the histone core in solution. We expect that 1.2 GHz NMR will be very advantageous for studies of large biomolecular assemblies, and in particular for protein-DNA complexes. With availability of higher magnetic fields, the increased resolution and sensitivity have enabled NMR spectroscopists to study more complex systems. Next to these instrumental factors, the development of new labeling approaches and transverse-relaxation optimized spectroscopy (TROSY), and in particular methyl-TROSY, have greatly expanded the size limit of the system that can be studied using solution NMR1–10. Thanks to development of high-temperature superconducting materials, the leading commercial manufacturer in NMR spectrometers has been able to build a high-resolution NMR machine operating at 28.2 T or 1H resonance frequency of 1.2 GHz. The performance of solution NMR at this ultra-high field has been discussed in a few recent papers11,12. As anticipated early on65, the increased magnetic field will also increase the effects of magnetic field alignment. When molecules with an anisotropic magnetic susceptibility are placed in a magnetic field, the induced magnetic moment will depend on their orientation with respect to the field, causing them to align in such a way that the induced magnetic moments are minimal13,14. Nucleic acids are well known to have a large magnetic susceptibility anisotropy (χa) due to the nearly colinear arrangement of the aromatic bases, and thus show pronounced magnetic field alignment13,15,16. The net alignment of the molecule causes incomplete averaging of the dipolar interactions and hence result in residual dipolar couplings (RDCs) which can be used to determine structure17–20. Proteins show less magnetic field alignment compared to nucleic acids as they in general have few aromatic residues which will be not colinear. Yet, even for ubiquitin at moderate magnetic field strength of 750 MHz small magnetic field induced RDCs (fiRDCs) have been measured.21As the alignment depends on the square of the magnetic field, significant fiRDCs for both proteins and nucleic acids can be expected at 1.2 GHz. These fiRDCs will add to the regular J-coupling splitting and “traditional” RDC splittings when using anisotropic solutions, as has been evaluated in detail for nucleic acids22. Importantly, as magnetic susceptibility anisotropy can be predicted quite accurately from the structure of a molecule23, fiRDCs can be used for structure determination17–20,24. Fo large biomolecular assemblies, the symmetric stacking of subunits can increase the magnetic susceptibility anisotropy of the assembly, increasing the field-induced alignment. Thus, methyl-TROSY NMR at 1.2 GHz also offers exciting new potential for structure determination of large biomolecular assemblies, in particular for large complexes involving nucleic acids, such as the nucleosome. Here, we compared methyl-TROSY spectra recorded at 600, 900 and 1200 MHz in terms of sensitivity, resolution and extracted fiRDCs. We found that methyl-TROSY spectra at the 1200 MHz system were ∼20% less sensitive than at 900 MHz system, likely due to a combination of increased transverse relaxation and hardware and sample factors. At 1200 MHz, resonances for several isoleucine, leucine and valine (ILV) methyl groups show clearly resolved splittings that correlate with asymmetric rotamer states in many nucleosome crystal structures. Further, we observe large fiRDCs of up to 8 Hz at 1200 MHz. We show that these can be used to obtain stereospecific assignments of nearly all methyl groups. Importantly, the experimental fiRDCs can be used to determine the conformation of the linker DNA in the nucleosome, revealing significant unwrapping of the nucleosomal DNA from the histone core. The histones, H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, fromXenopus laevis(Xl.)were transformed into BL21(DE3) pLysS cells using pET3a derived plasmids encoding histones (Uniprot P06897, P02281, P84233, P62799). Histones were perdeuterated using an adapted protocol of Marley et al30. In short, cells were grown at 37 °C in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium to optical density (OD) 1.5, then spun down and washed twice in D2O-based M9 medium without glucose and NH4Cl. Cell pellets were resuspended in D2O M9 with deuterated glucose, and15NH4Cl for labeled histones or14NH4Cl for fully deuterated histones to an OD of ∼0.6 and incubated for 1–2 hours at 37 °C. To obtain perdeuterated15N,{1H-13C}-ILV labeled H2B, 60 mL/L α-ketobutyric acid (4-13C,3,3-2d) and 80 mg/L α-ketoisovalerate (3-(methyl-d3),4-13C,3-d) sodium salt (Sigma-Aldrich) were added to the culture and incubated for another hour, while for H2B with {1H-13C}-labeling of both LV methyl groups (2MeLV), 80 mg/L 2-Keto-(3-methyl-13C)-butyric-4-13C,3d acid (Sigma-Aldrich) was added. All histones were expressed overnight with 1 mM IPTG at 37 °C. Histones were purified as described previously in Klinker et al.31. Briefly, cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris, 100 mM NaCl, 1% triton, pH 7.5) with lysozyme, then lysed using one freeze-thaw cycle and sonication. The inclusion bodies were collected and unfolded using unfolding buffer (6 M Guanidinium-HCl, 50 mM Tris, 100 mM NaCl, pH 7.5). Unfolded histones were purified using first size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) over a superdex 75 column (GE Healthcare) in denaturing buffer (7 M urea, 50 mM KPi, 1 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.5) and then using ion-exchange chromatography (IEX) over a combined HiTrap Q and HiTrap SP column (Cytiva) in denaturing buffer, where the HiTrap Q column was removed before eluting the histones from the SP column using a salt gradient (0.15 – 1 M NaCl in denaturing buffer). Fractions were analyzed using SDS-PAGE, histone containing fractions were pooled and concentrated to 3 mg/mL, supplemented with 1 mM lysine, and stored at -20°C for further use. A pUC19 plasmid containing 12 x 167 base pair repeats was used to produce 167 base pair 601 Widom DNA32. Plasmids were produced using DH5alpha in 2xYT medium with an overnight culture at 37 °C. Plasmids were isolated using alkaline lysis33followed by isopropanol and ethanol precipitation and redissolved in TE buffer (10 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA, pH 8.0). Plasmids were purified using IEX over HiTrap Q column (Cytiva) with a 0-1 M NaCl gradient in TE buffer. Purified plasmids were digested in TE buffer supplemented with 10x Cutsmart buffer (New England Biolabs) to 1x final concentration using 700U ScaI-HF (New England Biolabs) per 10 mg plasmid DNA for 72 hours at 1mg/mL plasmid concentration. Completion of the restriction was monitored using PAGE. Then 167 bp DNA fragments were purified using anion exchange (HiTrap Q column 5 mL), ethanol precipitated and resuspended in TE buffer to a concentration of ∼2.4 mg/mL before storage at -20 °C. The histone octamer was refolded as described in Dyer et al33. In brief, histones were mixed in equimolar ratio in denaturing buffer (7 M urea, 50 mM Tris, 100 mM NaCl, pH 7.5) at 1 mg/mL protein concentration, using absorbance at 280 nm to determine their concentrations. The histone octamer mixture was dialyzed in three steps for 16, 8, and 16 hours to high salt buffer (2 M NaCl, 10 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA) at 4 °C using 3 kDa MWCO membrane and then purified using SEC over a superdex 200 column (120 mL, GE Healthcare) in high salt buffer. Peak fractions were analyzed using SDS PAGE. The histone octamer eluted at 64 mL, with a yield of ∼70%. Fractions containing pure octamers were pooled and concentrated to ∼4 mg/mL and stored at 4 °C before immediate use. Nucleosomes were reconstituted from 601 DNA and perdeuterated histones and ILV-labeled H2B according to the protocol described by Dyer et al.33. Briefly, stock-solution of 601 DNA was adjusted with 4 M NaCl to a final salt concentration 2 M and ∼3 mg/mL DNA. Equimolar amounts of histone octamer (in high salt buffer) and 601 DNA were mixed at 4 °C and diluted to 0.7 mg/mL protein concentration using high salt buffer, incubated for 2 hours, and then dialyzed using a 16-hour gradient to low salt buffer (0.25 M KCl, 10 mM Tris, pH 7.5, 1 mM EDTA). The soluble fractions containing nucleosomes (ca. 70% yield based on DNA absorbance) was then buffer exchanged to NMR buffer (20 mM KPi, pH 6.2, 0.01% NaN3, 100% D2O) and concentrated to ∼13.6 mg/mL over a 30kDa MWCO centrifugal concentration device. Analysis by SDS-PAGE and native PAGE confirmed that the obtained nucleosomes are free of significant amounts of free DNA (Supplementary Figure S1). Nucleosomes were stored at 4 °C before use. All NMR experiments were recorded on Bruker Avance spectrometers, using either an Avance III 600 MHz spectrometer with 5 mm room-temperature probe, an Avance III 900 MHz spectrometer with a 5 mm cryo-probe, or an Avance NEO 1200 MHz spectrometer with a 3 mm cryo-probe. Samples were measured in a 5 mm Shigemi tube (600, 900 MHz) or a 3 mm tube (1200 MHz), in all cases containing 64.3 μM nucleosomes in 300 μL NMR buffer (20 mM KPi, pH 6.2, 0.01% NaN3, 100% D2O). All experiments were recorded at 45 °C. NMR data were processed using Bruker Topspin using forward linear prediction in the indirect dimension(s) and cosine-squared window functions, and subsequently analyzed using NMRFAM-SPARKY34, except where noted otherwise. To compare resolution and sensitivity, methyl-TROSY HMQC experiments were recorded at 600, 900 and 1200 MHz. Experiments used the SOFAST fast-pulsing method29with a PC9-shaped methyl selective pulse with 120° flip angle and Reburp 180° pulse (both with 6 ppm band width), a recycle delay of 0.5 s, and acquisition times of 66.5 ms (1H) and 42.4 ms (13C), and 3.3 kHz WALTZ64 decoupling during acquisition. Total measurement time was 2 hours for all three spectra. Peak intensities and noise levels were determined using the built-in functions of NMRFAM-SPARKY using data processed without linear prediction. Sucrose measurements showed that the 1.2 GHz offers same or up to 30% more sensitivity compared to the 900 MHz system, depending on the ionic strength of the sample. Extrapolating from these measurements, one would expect ca. 10% sensitivity increase at 1.2 GHz at the low ionic strength (I= 25 mM) of the nucleosome sample. Accounting for differences in the inner diameter of the tubes used for the sucrose measurements and our nucleosome sample, which result in relative number of active spins of 33% for sucrose and 28% for the nucleosome at 1.2 GHz, we expected a relative sensitivity at 1.2 GHz of ∼93% (0.28/0.33*1.1). Initial assignments of the ILV methyl group resonances inXenopus leaevis (Xl.)H2B were based on assignment transfer from the availableDrosophila melanogaster(Dm.) chemical shifts35. As the methyl-TROSY effect relies on relaxation interference between intra-methyl1H-13C dipolar interactions it is purely dipolar in nature and field independent6,25. However, the13C spin in a methyl group has a small, but non negligible chemical shift anisotropy (CSA)26, causing a field-dependent increase to the transverse relaxation rate27. Spectral comparison shows clearly that peak overlap that is present at 600 or 900 MHz is resolved at 1200 MHz (Fig. 1aandS2). More detailed analysis shows that when expressed in ppm, the line widths at 1200 MHz are decreased by 23% in the1H and 7% in the13C dimension compared to the line widths at 900 MHz. To compare the sensitivity of the methyl-TROSY spectra, we focused on the 900 and 1200 MHz spectra as these were both recorded using cryo-probes. Notably, the 1.2 GHz system is equipped with a 3 mm probe, whereas the 900 MHz system has a 5 mm probe. As we used the nucleosome sample at the same concentration, the number of spins in the active volume of the 1.2 GHz is ca. 28% of that for the 900 MHz. Despite this, the sensitivity at 1200 MHz is close to that of the 900 MHz system, albeit on average 20% lower (Fig. 1b). To explain this reduction in sensitivity, we measured1H and1H-13C multiple-quantum (MQ)R2relaxation rates. On average, the1H-13C MQR2rates are 1.2 times higher at 1200 vs. 900 MHz (Fig. 1c), while there was no notable change in1H R2(Fig. S3). This is in-line with the expected impact of the CSA contribution to the transverse relaxation of methyl groups27. Studies on ubiquitin have shown that the1H CSA is very small, on the order of 1 ppm, while the13C CSA is sizable, with average value of 18 ppm for Leu/Val and 25 ppm for Ile methyl groups26. The increased13C CSA relaxation at 1.2 GHz thus explains most of the observed sensitivity loss. The reduction in sensitivity could additionally be caused by differences in steady-state1H magnetization as we recorded these experiments using the SOFAST fast-pulsing approach28,29. In this approach the sensitivity gain depends on the longitudinal relaxation rate of the1H spins, which will decrease slightly with increased magnetic field. To investigate this we measured methyl group1H longitudinal relaxation times (R1) rates of the H2B ILV methyl groups in the nucleosome. We used both a methyl-selective (R1,sel) and a non-selective1H excitation pulse (R1,uni) at 900 MHz and then compared the R1,seldifferent magnetic field strengths (Fig. 2a-c). Overall, the1H R1relaxation is more efficient when using the selective pulse, indicating a significant ‘spin cooling’ effect by keeping non-methyl protons in equilibrium (Fig. 2a, b). The I36 methyl group experiences the largest increase in relaxation rate which can be explained by its proximity to the protonated DNA. The other H2B methyl groups are however far from the DNA. For instance, V63 and V66 experience a large increase in relaxation rate but are in the core of the nucleosome at considerable distance from the DNA (12.5 and 19 Å, respectively). This indicates that enhancement of R1relaxation for the nucleosome core methyl groups is likely due to the presence of non-methyl1H spins within the histone and/or very efficient spin-diffusion throughout the histone1H-1H network to the protonated DNA. At this point we cannot tell the origin of this process and how it is related to asymmetry in sidechain conformations seen in the crystal and cyro-EM structures. A recent solid-state NMR study suggested that the histone octamer contains several dynamic hotspots in H3 and H4 that could be connected in a dynamic network that extends from the DNA binding surface into the octamer interior52. The data here suggest that such dynamic network may also be present within the H2A-H2B dimer, or at least within H2B, as the identified residues are similarly distributed from the DNA binding site to the interior. We next examined the degree of magnetic field induced alignment of the nucleosomes. The expected molecular magnetic susceptibility anisotropy Δχmolwas calculated for various model structures using residue-specific values of Δχ for the nucleobases, aromatic groups and the carbonyl backbone groups. To understand the alignment of the nucleosome, we first compared the Δχmoltensor for linear DNA and DNA arranged in a super-helix, as in the archaeal hyper-nucleosome53,54(Fig. 4). For linear DNA where the bases are stacked colinearly, the individual Δχ tensors add up almost perfectly, resulting in Δχmoltensor with a main axis along the helical axis and thus a preferred molecular orientation orthogonal to the external magnetic field. When DNA is arranged in a super-helix, the main axis will be aligned with super helical axis (Fig. 4). As nucleosome core particle, which has 147 bp of DNA, has its DNA arranged in superhelix, we thus expect similar alignment with preferred orientation such that the superhelical axis is orthogonal to external magnetic field. Using the crystal structure of the nucleosome core particle (1KX5) and considering both DNA and protein contributions, the predicted Δχmoltensor has a main axial component of 105 10−27J T−2and low rhombicity (R= 0.07), resulting a significant degree of alignment (1.3 10−3). This would subsequently result in1H-13C fiRDCs of up to 18 Hz for a completely rigid methyl group. For linear DNA the largest tensor is predicted along the helix of the DNA. For a superhelix of DNA, the largest tensor aligns along the superhelical axis of the DNA. Both nucleosomes with and without linker DNA have the largest tensor along the superhelical axis, like the superhelix (histone proteins not shown). Linker DNA of 2x 10bp have only a minor influence on the size of the Xzz tensor but have a large influence on the Xxx and Xyy tensor components. To experimentally determine the extent of magnetic field induced alignment of the nucleosome we recorded IPAP methyl-TROSY experiments43at 600, 900 and 1200 MHz. While at 600 MHz already small deviations from the expected 125 Hz1JCHsplitting are observed, this becomes particularly clear at 1200 MHz where the splitting ranges between 118.4 and 135.0 Hz (Fig. 5a). This indicates that there is a substantial contribution of fiRDC to the peak splitting, and thus magnetic field induced alignment of the nucleosome. For 33 out of 36 methyl group signals, peak splittings could reliable be measured at all three fields and fitted to extract the1H-13C methyl fiRDC at 1200 MHz (Fig. 5b, c). These fiRDCs range from -7.8 to +7.9 Hz. These values are ca. 44% of the predicted maximum fiRDC for the nucleosome core particle. The prediction did however not consider the presence of the additional linker DNA in our system, nor the presence of methyl group dynamics which will downscale the RDC by the order parameterS. From the distribution of the fiRDCs, we can estimate that the alignment tensor has high rhombicity (Fig. 5d), which is in sharp contrast with predicted tensor based on the nucleosome core particle structure. Having established that the experimental fiRDCs agree well to the H2B structure, we next wondered whether the fiRDCs could also be used to determine the linker DNA conformation. Linker DNA has been observed with DNA ends bound to the core, detached from the core, or transiently wrap and unwrap from the nucleosome core56–60. Additionally, opening of the linkers has been described to occur symmetrically and non-symmetrically61–63. The (average) linker DNA conformation in solution can be derived from the fiRDCs, as the extracted alignment tensor can be directly converted into the magnetic susceptibility tensor, which is turn determined mostly by the DNA conformation in the nucleosome. We constructed models of nucleosome with linker DNA in closed or various open states and calculated the Δχmolfrom these structures. While the anisotropy of the Δχmoltensor is not much affected by the conformation of the linker DNA, it is clear from the models that there is strong impact on the rhombicity of the tensor (Fig. 7aandTable S6). The rhombicity is predicted to be highest when the linker DNA extend parallel in the same direction from the nucleosome core particle and decreases upon opening or closing the DNA (Fig. 7a). Thus, comparison of experimental and calculated rhombicity should give a good indication of the average linker DNA conformation. To determine the Δχmoltensor from the experimental fiRDCs we first extended our analysis from using a single H2B copy to both H2B copies in the nucleosome. Fits to either copy are of similar quality and result in similar orientation of the alignment tensor principal axis frame (PAS) with respect to the molecular frame (Fig. 7b). Indeed, the observation of a single fiRDC for each H2B methyl indicates that the PAS is oriented along the symmetry axis of the nucleosome, as also predicted from the calculated Δχmolbased on the structure (Fig. 7a). Fitting the experimental fiRDCs to both symmetry related H2B copies simultaneously results in a good correlation between observed and predicted RDCs, although Q factor is slightly higher than for the single chain fit (Q= 0.233 vs. 0.217). The alignment tensor from this fit was converted into the magnetic susceptibility tensor to compare against the structure predicted Δχmoltensors (Fig. 7c). The PAS of the experimental tensor is oriented along the dyad, with the Δχzzcomponent along the super helical axis and the Δχxxcomponent perpendicular, in good agreement with orientation of the predicted tensors. The fitted tensor anisotropy is about 60% of the calculated value, reflecting the impact of methyl groups dynamics. While DNA dynamics (transient wrapping and unwrapping of the DNA from the histone core) could also scale the alignment tensor and reduce the fiRDCs, this is less likely to be responsible as the different nucleosome models have all similar anisotropies. As the lowest rhombicity for a compacted linker DNA conformation was predicted to be 0.48, the experimental data suggest that the linker DNA confirmation is rather open. A model with 20 bp unwrapped on both sides from the core particle result in the same rhombicity as experimental (Fig. 7a), indicating that this opened nucleosome represents the time averaged conformation under our conditions. The data on the nucleosome indicate that magnetic field induced alignment at 1200 MHz can make fiRDCs will be an extremely useful tool to study structure and dynamics of large nucleic acid complexes. For protein-only assemblies, or complexes involving shorter nucleic acid fragments, the alignment will likely be significantly smaller. To test the application range of fiRDCs, we finally examined a small protein-DNA complex, formed by the DNA binding domain of pioneer transcription factor Sox2 and a 13 bp double-strand DNA fragment containing its cognate binding site. For a linear B-form DNA of 13 bp, a maximum methyl group RDC of 3.5 Hz is predicted for a bound protein. As Sox2 bends the DNA upon binding, the anisotropies of the nuclesobases will not add up as effectively and a smaller alignment and smaller fiRDCs can be expected. For 8 out 18 LV methyl groups, a fiRDC magnitude larger than 0.2 Hz was obtained, with maximum magnitude of 1.0 Hz, at 1200 MHz (Fig. S6). Overall, the experimental values show reasonable correlation with the structure-based predicted values, albeit that slight differences in DNA and protein conformation give considerable spread in predicted fiRDCs (Fig. S6). Of note, L100 in Sox2 has different side chain conformations in the available structures, resulting in predicted fiRDCs of opposite sign. Experimentally, L100 methyls have close to 0 fiRDCs, suggesting that these different conformations are dynamically averaged in solution (Fig. S6). We here analyzed the performance of methyl-TROSY NMR at 1.2 GHz with particular attention to use of high resolution and magnetic field induced alignment for the characterization of biomolecular assemblies. We found that for our particular system, the nucleosome, and particular hardware, the methyl-TROSY experiment at 1.2 GHz had on average 20% reduced sensitivity compared to the 900 MHz. It should be noted that the sample had the same concentration at both fields, thus when the same number of spins would be fitted into the active volume of the probe at both fields (3 mm probe and sample at 1200 MHz vs. 5mm probe and sample at 900 MHz), the sensitivity would be increased ∼2.8x at 1200 MHz compared to 900 MHz. The reduced sensitivity is at least in part explained by the increased CSA contribution to the13C transverse relaxation. Our data further indicate that the relative sensitivity of the 1.2 GHz experiment could have been increased somewhat by using slightly longer recycle delays in the fast-pulsing implementation of the methyl-TROSY experiment. Additionally, the use of tailored pulse shapes may increase the relative performance of the 1.2 GHz instrument66,67,68. The increased resolution at 1200 MHz permitted the unambiguous detection of NMR signal duplicities for several histone methyl groups, pointing to a subtle conformational heterogeneity that had been unresolved before. Strikingly, the affected residues correlate with histone side chains that have different conformations between symmetry-related copies in various nucleosome structures. This suggests that the detected conformational heterogeneity may be related to structural differences between symmetry-related histone pairs within the same nucleosome particle. As a large protein-nucleic acid complex, its DNA component results in a large overall anisotropy in the magnetic susceptibility of the nucleosome, and thus substantial magnetic field induced alignment. Due to the squared dependence on the magnetic field strength, the resulting RDCs are amplified at 1200 MHz. In many cases, such as the Sox2-DNA complex demonstrated here, the field induced RDCs may only become observable at the ultra-high field. For protein-only assemblies, the degree of alignment largely depends on the distribution of aromatic rings in the structure. For symmetric assemblies, the alignment tensors of individual subunits in elongated structures such as the proteasome will add up. For nearly spherical assemblies, such as a viral capsid, the vector-sum will largely cancel out. The fiRDCs observed for the nucleosome strongly correlated with those predicted for known nucleosome structures and could be used to stereospecifically assign nearly all methyl resonances which were not assignable using conventional NOESY experiments. In cases where a divide-and-conquer approach is not possible or sufficient, assignment of methyl groups in large assemblies is a major challenge, requiring a combination of mutation and NOESY-based strategies. Field-induced alignment is thus a useful addition to obtain stereo-specific assignments and in favorable cases, aid assignment. Furthermore, the fiRDCs could be used to refine nucleosome structure at both local and global level. At the local level, out of rotamer conformations observed in nucleosome structures, the fiRDCs were used to select the best fitting rotamer for I58. At the global level, we used the fiRDCs to derive that the nucleosome adopts an open conformation of the linker DNA under our conditions. The data indicate that on average not the textbook 1.7, but rather 1.4 superhelical turns of DNA are wrapped around the histone octamer. Single molecule FRET measurements have shown that presence of linker DNA increases opening of nucleosomes, in particular under low ionic strength conditions such as those used here, suggesting that electrostatic repulsion between the linkers is a dominant factor64. Furthermore, the data also indicate that the average linker DNA conformation is symmetric as any asymmetry in linker DNA unwrapping would result in a very different orientation of the PAS (seeFig. 7a). This is in contrast to recent MD study that indicated that linker DNA in 601-nucleosome has intrinsically asymmetric dynamics63. It could be that at the longer time scales sampled by the experimental fiRDCs the linkers behave symmetrical, but not at shorter time scale probed by the MD simulations. Alternatively, the asymmetries in DNA dynamics could be too subtle to significantly affect the magnetic susceptibility tensor and thus to be picked up in our experiment. Together, our results highlight how ultra-high field methyl-TROSY solution NMR at 1.2 GHz offers greatly improved resolving power and strongly amplified magnetic field induced alignment. Thanks to the ultra-high field data we found evidence for subtle conformational heterogeneities in the nucleosome core and could determine an overall opened structure of the nucleosome in which the DNA is less wrapped compared to crystal or cryo-EM structures. Recently methyltransferases were applied to methylate nucleosomal DNA and used as NMR probes39. As nucleosomal DNA is challenging to study by NMR, combination of these type of labeling approaches and fiRDCs can be used to give structural insights in the orientations and dynamics of nucleosomal DNA during critical processes such as nucleosome remodeling and transcription factor binding. Since field induced alignment is unavoidable as soon as the sample is in the magnet, the combination of ultra-high field and methyl-TROSY solution NMR make field-induced RDCs into a practical tool for the characterization of structural and dynamical features of biomolecular assemblies.
