title: Targeted HPLC-MS/MS Profiling of Diacylglycerols for Krill Oil Authentication and Adulteration Detection
author: Makeeva, D.; Michaelson, L. V.
text: A rapid HPLC-MS/MS method based on multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) was developed for comprehensive analysis of diacylglycerol (DAG) molecular species in plant and marine oils. The method enabled the determination of 75 DAG molecular species within 5 min, with a 6-fold linear range and 0.02-0.2 µg/mL limits of detection. The method was successfully applied to the detection of krill oil (KO) adulteration with fish oil (FO), soybean oil (SBO), and sunflower oil (SFO). Principal component analysis (PCA) provided clear discrimination between pure and adulterated KO samples. Potential adulteration markers were identified using combined PLS-DA and random forest analysis. For FO adulteration, DAG 16:0_18:0, 20:1_20:5, 18:0_20:1, 18:0_20:0, and 20:2_22:6 were identified. For SBO and SFO adulteration DAG 18:0_18:2, 18:2_18:2, 20:2_22:6, 18:3_18:3, and 16:0_18:2 were identified as markers. The method establishes DAG profiling for quick and sensitive oil adulteration detection. A rapid 5-min HPLC-MS/MS-MRM method was developed for DAG profiling. Seventy-five DAG molecular species were quantified in plant and marine oils. The method enabled discrimination of pure and adulterated krill oil samples. DAG markers of krill oil adulteration were identified. Krill oil (KO) is a valuable marine-derived oil known for its high content of omega-3 fatty acids, particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), which are present in both triacylglycerol and phospholipid classes. DHA and EPA from krill and are associated with enhanced bioavailability (Ramprasath et al., 2015). Owing to its reported health benefits, including cardiovascular, cognitive, and anti-inflammatory effects, krill oil has become an increasingly important ingredient in nutritional supplements and functional foods (Kwantes & Grundmann, 2015). Because of the rapid growth of the global KO supplement market and the substantially higher price of krill oil compared with conventional fish oil, there is a strong economic incentive for product adulteration. KO may be diluted or substituted with fish oil while maintaining comparable EPA and DHA levels, making the fraud difficult to detect. It can also be adulterated with cheap plant oils such as soybean oil (SBO) or sunflower oil (SFO) (Lee et al., 2024a). Such adulteration can change the lipid profiles of triacylglycerols (TAG), diacylglycerols (DAG), free fatty acids (FFA), or phospholipids (PL), many of which may escape detection by conventional lipid analytical techniques (Araujo et al., 2013;Cui et al., 2021a;Zailer et al., 2018). Various analytical approaches have been developed for the detection of KO adulteration, including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) (Monakhova et al., 2018), Raman and infrared (IR) spectroscopy (Ahmmed et al., 2023), fluorescence spectroscopy (Ke et al., 2025), gas chromatography coupled with flame ionization detection (GC-FID) (Araujo et al., 2013;Fuller et al., 2020), thin-layer chromatography coupled with flame ionization detection (TLC-FID) (Akanbi & Barrow, 2017), and HPLC-MS/MS (Castro-Gómez et al., 2015). HPLC–MS/MS represents a powerful analytical approach for the detection and assessment of oil adulteration, owing to its ability to provide structural characterization of individual lipid species. Since oils derived from different sources exhibit distinct fatty acyl compositions, these differences are directly reflected in the molecular profiles of their constituent lipid classes. Therefore, HPLC–MS/MS analysis offers exceptional sensitivity for detecting compositional variations and subtle modifications in lipid profiles, ensuring the authenticity of oil-based products. Existing HPLC–MS methods are predominantly focused on the analysis of major lipid classes, including TAG (Araujo et al., 2018) and PL (Cui et al., 2021b). This is unsurprising, as these lipid classes are generally the most abundant and are highly studied. However, the lipid composition of KO is very complex, with TAG and PL fractions exhibiting extensive molecular diversity due to the presence of numerous fatty acyl chains, including 14:0, 16:0, 16:1n7, 18:0, 18:1n9, 18:1n7, 18:2n6, 18:4n3, 20:5n3, and 22:6n3 (Akanbi & Barrow, 2017b). Consequently, the comprehensive characterization of lipid molecular species within these major lipid classes often requires lengthy chromatographic separations, high-resolution instrumentation, and optimized methods capable of resolving closely related lipid species. In krill, as in other organisms, diacylglycerol (DAG) represents a central intermediate in glycerolipid metabolism, serving as a key precursor for the biosynthesis of both TAG and PL via the Kennedy pathway(Gibellini & Smith, 2010). TAG biosynthesis occurs through the enzymatic acylation of DAG resulting in the formation of storage lipids. Similarly, DAG contributes to PL biosynthesis, where it undergoes head-group modification to generate major membrane lipids such as phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE). DAG connects membrane synthesis and energy storage and occupies a central position in glycerolipid metabolism. DAG profiling for the detection of oil adulteration has received considerably less attention than TAG-(Akanbi & Barrow, 2017b) and PL-based approaches (Cui et al., 2021c). DAGs represent a promising and potentially underexploited lipid class for oil authentication. Compared with TAG, the number of possible DAG molecular species is substantially lower owing to the presence of only two fatty acid moieties rather than three. This enables a more focused and comprehensive characterization of the DAG fraction with reduced analytical complexity and significantly shorter analysis times. Importantly, DAGs occupy a central position in glycerolipid metabolism and can retain compositional characteristics associated with both membrane phospholipids and storage triacylglycerols. Consequently, DAG profiling has the potential to capture complementary information on lipid composition while providing a simpler and more cost-effective analytical strategy for oil authentication and adulteration detection. In this study, we developed a rapid and sensitive DAG-based method for the detection of KO adulteration with FO and other plant-derived oils, including SBO and SFO. The method combines targeted MRM analysis with response factor-based quantitation, enabling accurate profiling of DAG species within a 5 min HPLC-MS/MS run. The approach proved effective for the detection and quantification of oil adulteration. LC-MS grade acetonitrile, isopropanol, formic acid, methanol, and HPLC-grade hexane, chloroform, and formic acid were acquired from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, United States). A 10 M ammonium formate solution was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (Buchs, Switzerland). All DAG standards were obtained from Nu-Chek Prep (Elysian, Minnesota, USA). The following abbreviations, which indicate the length of each acyl chain and the number of double bonds per chain, were used in this study: dipalmitin (DAG 16:0_16:0), distearin (DAG 18:0_18:0), diarachidin (TAG 20:0_20:0), diolein (DAG 18:1_18:1Δ9), dilinolein (DAG 18:2_18:2Δ9,12), dilinolenin (DAG 18:3_18:3Δ9,12,15), dieicosenoin (DAG 20:1_20:1Δ11), dieicosadienoin (DAG 20:2_20:2Δ11,14), dieicosatrienoin (DAG 20:3_20:3Δ11,14,17), diarachidonin (DAG 20:4_20:4Δ5,8,11,14), didocosahexaenoin (DAG 22:6_22:6 Δ4,7,10,13,16,19). Fish oil (FO), soybean oil (SBO), and sunflower oil (SFO) pharmaceutical secondary standards (Supelco), together with a krill oil United States Pharmacopeia (USP) reference standard, were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (Buchs, Switzerland). Artificial adulterated samples were prepared by gravimetrically mixing the USP krill oil reference standard with pharmaceutical secondary standards of fish, soybean, and sunflower oils at predefined proportions. LC-MS/MS analyses were performed using a SCIEX ExionLC AD UHPLC system (SCIEX, USA) coupled to a SCIEX 6500+ triple quad liquid MS system. DAGs were ionized using electrospray ionization (ESI) and detected in positive ion mode using MRM. Chromatographic separations were performed on an Zorbax Eclipse Plus C18 RRHD column (50 × 2.1 mm, 1.8 µm, Agilent). Mobile phase A consisted of acetonitrile:water (50:50, v/v) with 10 mM ammonium formate and 0.1% formic acid, while mobile phase B consisted of isopropanol:acetonitrile:water (88:10:2, v/v/v) with 2 mM ammonium formate and 0.02% formic acid. The flow rate was 0.6 mL/min. The injection volume was 1 µL, the column oven was maintained at 40 °C, and the autosampler was set at 10 °C. A needle wash with isopropanol was performed before each injection, using a wash time of 2 seconds and a wash speed of 10 µL/s. The total run time was 5.0 minutes with the following solvent gradient: 0.0 min, 70% B; 0.1 min, 70% B; 3.5 min, 95% B; 3.6 min, 99% B; 4.0 min, 99% B; 4.1 min, 70% B; 5.0 min, stop run. The ESI parameters curtain gas (CUR), gas 1 (GS1), and gas 2 (GS2) were set to 35, 50, and 50 psi, respectively. Optimal parameters for Ion Spray Voltage (IS), Collision gas (CAD), and Temperature (TEM) were 4500 V, low and 200°C, respectively. Mass spectra was acquired using scheduled MRM with a cycling time of one second and an MRM window of 60 seconds. MRM values for individual lipid species are shown inTable 1. Declustering (DP), entrance (EP), cell exit potentials (CXP), and collision energy (CE) were optimising using standards and were 100, 10, 30 and 10, respectively. Calibration curves were built for each of the DAG standards listed above (Chemical reagents). These were dissolved in a CHCl3/MeOH (2:1, v/v) mixture to prepare three 10 mg/mL stock solutions for each DAG standard. The stock solutions were stored at −20 °C. Prior to use, the solutions were thawed to room temperature, and three sets of standard mixtures were prepared by combining stock solutions and diluting them with mobile phase B, yielding working solutions with the following concentrations of each lipid: 0.0001, 0.010, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50, 1.00, 2.50, 5.00 and 10.00 µg/mL. The average peak areas were used to generate the final calibration curves. The calibration curves were used to calculate response factors (RFs) by the approach described by (Holčapek et al., 2005). Briefly, the slope of each individual calibration curve was used to estimate response factors for single fatty acids DAGs in relation to DAG 18:1_18:1, the response factor of which was set to 1:The RFs of mixed fatty acid DAGs were calculated as the average of the corresponding RFs of individual fatty acid DAGs: Standard oil samples for DAG profile analysis of the pure oils were subjected to a 100-fold dilution prior to analysis using CHCl3/MeOH (2:1, v/v), resulting in an approximate concentration of 10 mg/mL. Adulterated samples were prepared by mixing 10 mg/mL oil solutions at appropriate volume ratios to obtain final adulterant concentrations of 2.5, 4, 5, 10, and 15% (w/w). Prior to analysis, samples were diluted by mixing 10 µL of the oil sample (pure or adulterated) with 10 µL of a 2 µg/mL DAG 20:3/20:3 internal standard solution and 80 µL of mobile phase A. The resulting mixtures were subsequently subjected to DAG analysis. Data processing was performed usingSkyline(Adams et al., 2020) software, which provided good visualization of the MS/MS results. For each target DAG molecule, product ion lists were generated using anin silicolibrary created withLipidCreator(Peng et al., 2020a). Comparative study of DAG composition of oils was carried out using partial least squares discriminate analysis (PLS−DA), and variable importance in projection (VIP) scores and heat map visualization, in MetaboAnalyst 6.0 (Pang et al., 2024). Log transformation (base 10) and data scaling (mean-centering and division by the square root of each variable’s standard deviation) were performed prior to statistical analysis. To identify molecular markers associated with adulteration, PLS-DA and random forest classification models were applied. The top 10 discriminating compounds ranked according to VIP scores from PLS-DA and variable importance values from random forest were compared. Five compounds identified by both complementary approaches were selected as robust candidate markers. These markers were subsequently validated using one-way ANOVA to confirm significant differences among the sample groups. In positive-ion MS/MS, DAG is preferentially ionized as [M+NH₄]⁺ or [M+Na]⁺ precursor ions and typically fragment through cleavage of the ester bonds, resulting in characteristic neutral losses of fatty acids (Figure 1). These neutral losses generate monoacylglycerol (MAG)-type fragment ions that enable identification of the fatty acyl chains present in the DAG species. Intact DAG precursor ions also undergo dehydration, producing [M+NH3−H₂O]⁺ fragment ions, which are typically the most abundant product ions under mild collision-induced dissociation (CID) conditions. However, different DAG species with distinct fatty acyl compositions can produce identical dehydration fragments, increasing the risk of misidentification and fragment overlap. Therefore, only MAG-type fragment ions were used for DAG identification (Table 1). In this approach, the detection of two MAG-type fragment ions originating from the same precursor ion [M+NH4]+was considered evidence for the presence of the corresponding DAG species in the sample. Separation was performed using mobile phase A (acetonitrile:water, 50:50, v/v, containing 10 mM ammonium formate and 0.1% formic acid) and mobile phase B (isopropanol:acetonitrile:water, 88:10:2, v/v/v, containing 2 mM ammonium formate and 0.02% formic acid) at a flow rate of 0.6 mL min⁻¹. The gradient program was: 0.0-0.1 min, 70% B; 3.5 min, 95% B; 3.6-4.0 min, 99% B; 4.1 min, 70% B; and 5.0 min, end of run. The list of DAG targets was generated using anin silicolibrary created withLipidCreator(Peng et al., 2020b). All predicted precursor and product ions, except for the dehydration [M+H−H₂O]⁺ fragments, were screened in pooled sample containing equal amounts of KO, FO, SBO, and SFO. Only targets yielding both expected MAG-type product ions were retained for subsequent analysis. The ESI parameters were optimized for ionization, with final IS, CAD, and TEM values set to 4500 V, low, and 200 °C, respectively. DP, EP, CXP, and CE were optimized using standards to achieve the highest signal intensity and were set to 100, 10, 30, and 10, respectively. Different chromatographic parameters, including column temperature, mobile phase composition, and gradient profile, were evaluated to achieve optimal separation while maintaining the shortest possible analysis time. The final chromatographic conditions are described in Section 2.2. A column temperature of 40°C resulted in lower backpressure, allowing an increased flow rate and consequently reducing the overall analysis time. For each identified DAG species, retention time (RT) evaluation was used to support structural assignment. Similar to TAG (Makeeva et al., 2026), the RT of DAG in reverse-phase chromatography depends on the total carbon number (CN) and the number of double bonds (DB) in the fatty acyl chains. An increase in the total carbon number results in a positive shift in RT, whereas each additional double bond contributes to a decrease in RT. Therefore, when DAG species identified based on MS/MS fragment alignment are arranged according to the same total carbon number and ordered by DB increase, a gradual decrease in retention time should be observed (Figure 2). The position of each DAG species within this retention time trend provides an additional confirmation of the assigned structure. RT of DAG, grouped by total carbon number and increasing desaturation. (i) Heatmap of selected DAG molecular species identified and quantified in KO and FO. Simplified for visual clarity. (ii) Fatty acyl composition of the DAG fraction of the analysed pure oils. (iii) Heatmap of DAG molecular species detected across KO, FO, SFO, and SBO. (iv) PCA biplot of the pure oils based on DAG profiles. Thus, a method for the HPLC-MS/MS determination of 75 DAG species within 5 minutes was developed, comprehensively covering the DAG molecular species present in KO and its most common adulterants and providing profiling of the oils (Figure 1). The different MS responses of DAG species, which depend on their fatty acyl compositions (Holčapek et al., 2005), (Makeeva et al., 2026), require the application of response factors (RFs) for accurate quantitation, particularly when detecting adulterated samples. To account for the influence of fatty acyl composition, RFs were calculated using authentic standards of DAG species containing single fatty acids. Subsequently, individual RFs for mixed fatty acid DAG species were calculated by averaging the corresponding RFs of the single fatty acid DAG standards, as described inSection 2.3. For each sample analysed the RFs were used to produce the quantitative data (Suppl. Materials 1,Table 1-4). The method was validated using authentic standards of DAG species containing identical fatty acyl chains. Calibration curves were constructed for these standards (Section 2.2), and the linear range, LOD, and LOQ were determined. The method exhibited a 6-fold linear range, with correlation coefficients over 0.98 and LOQ values ranging from 0.06 to 0.3 µg/mL (Table 2). The aim of this study was to determine whether DAG profiles of marine and plant oils can be used for the detection of adulteration with a performance comparable to TAG or PL-based analyses. Due to the simplicity of DAG profiling and the relatively short analysis time, this approach may provide a more accessible and cost-effective alternative for oil authentication. To evaluate the differences in DAG profiles among oils of different origins, quantitative DAG analysis was performed on pure oil standards, including FO, KO, SFO, and SBO (Suppl. Materials 1,Table 1). PCA score plots (Figure 2iv.) demonstrated clear separation among all four oil groups, indicating distinct DAG composition profiles. The first principal component (PC1) explained 98.2% of the total variance and primarily separated plant-derived oils from marine-derived oils. The second principal component (PC2), accounting for 1.1% of the variance, contributed to further discrimination among the different oil groups. The observed separation reflects differences in fatty acid composition between marine and plant oils, particularly the presence of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, such as EPA and DHA, in marine oils, which are absent or present at very low levels in plant oils. Replicates within each group clustered closely together, demonstrating strong intra-group consistency and high analytical reproducibility. The fatty acyl composition of the DAG fraction was calculated from the quantitative DAG data. The molar content of each fatty acyl species was determined by summing the concentrations of all DAG molecular species containing the corresponding fatty acyl chain, multiplied by the number of occurrences of that fatty acyl chain within each DAG molecule by the following formula:where m – number of fatty acyls occurrences, n – is molar concentration. The molar percentage of each fatty acyl species was subsequently calculated to determine the relative fatty acyl composition of the oils.Figure 2ii demonstrated the fatty acyls composition of DAG fraction from KO, FO, SFO and SBO. In KO, the most abundant fatty acyl species in DAG were 16:0 (22.3 ± 0.6%), 18:1 (15.2 ± 0.8%), 20:5 (23.6 ± 0.7%), and 22:6 (17.2 ± 1.2%). The fatty acyl composition of the DAG fraction showed characteristics intermediate between those reported for the PL and TAG fractions byXie et al., 2019. The PL fraction was dominated by 20:5, which accounted for approximately 30% of the total fatty acyl content, followed by 16:0 and 22:6 at approximately 23% and 15%, respectively. In contrast, the TAG fraction contained relatively higher proportions of 18:1 and 16:1 fatty acids. A similar fatty acyl profile was observed for FO, although FO differed from KO by exhibiting a lower proportion of 18:1 and higher proportions of 14:0 and 16:1 fatty acyls. Overall, KO and FO exhibited highly similar fatty acyl compositions in their DAG fractions, suggesting that adulteration of KO with FO may be more challenging to detect compared to plant oils. The plant-derived oils, SFO and SBO, predominantly consists of 18:1, 16:0, 18:2, and 18:3 fatty acyl species, but differ in their relative abundances of these fatty acyls. SFO contained a higher proportion of 18:1, whereas SBO was characterised by higher proportions of 16:0 and 18:3. These differences in fatty acyl composition contributed to the distinct DAG profiles observed between the two plant-derived oils. The DAG profiles also exhibited distinct signatures among the pure oils analysed. Figure 2iii. shows a heatmap of the DAG species commonly detected across all oils, based on their absolute concentrations. In contrast,Figure 2i. shows the DAG composition of KO and FO, including all DAG species identified in the pooled marine oil samples. The heatmap inFigure 2reveals that the oils are distinguished by differences in the relative abundances of individual DAG molecular species. As shown by the fatty acyl profiles and DAG heatmaps, FO and KO exhibit highly similar DAG compositions. Therefore, the detection of FO adulteration in KO is expected to be challenging, particularly at low levels of adulteration. KO samples adulterated with 0, 4, 10, and 20% FO were analysed (Suppl. Materials 1,Table 2) in terms of their DAG profiles using the developed method, and the resulting data were subjected to PCA (Figure 4i.). The pure KO samples (0% FO) were clearly separated from the adulterated samples and formed a distinct cluster. The adulterated samples were also grouped according to the level of FO addition, with the 4, 10, and 20% FO-adulterated samples showing progressive separation from one another. This clustering pattern indicates that the DAG profile was sensitive to the level of FO adulteration and that the developed method could discriminate KO samples according to the extent of adulteration. The increasing separation of the samples with increasing FO content suggests that the compositional changes in the DAG profile become more pronounced as the proportion of FO increases. (i) PCA score plot showing the separation of pure KO and KO samples adulterated with different percentages of FO. (ii) Fatty acyl composition of the DAG fraction in KO and FO samples calculated from DAG molecular species data. (iii) Box plots showing the distribution of DAG species selected by both PLS-DA and random forest analyses. Statistical significance was evaluated using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test. To identify molecular features capable of discriminating FO-adulterated KO samples, the dataset containing was analysed using two complementary supervised approaches: partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) and random forest classification (Schwarz et al., 2025). Random forest set up were as follows: number of trees to grow – 500, number of predictors to try – 7, randomness – on. Random forest classification achieved an out-of-bag error rate of 5%, corresponding to an overall classification accuracy of 95%. All KO, KO+10% FO, and KO+20% FO samples were correctly classified, while one KO+4% FO sample was misclassified as KO+10% FO. These results demonstrate the discriminative ability of the selected lipid features for detecting FO adulteration in KO samples. Variables contributing most strongly to sample discrimination were ranked based on their variable importance in projection (VIP) scores from the PLS-DA model and variable importance values from the random forest model (Suppl. Materials 2,Tables 1-2). The 15 highest-ranked features from each model were compared, and only molecules consistently selected by both approaches were considered robust candidate markers of FO adulteration. This combined strategy was applied to minimize the influence of model-specific feature selection and to identify molecular markers with the greatest potential for reliable discrimination of adulterated KO samples. The discriminatory potential of the selected markers was further evaluated by one-way ANOVA followed by false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The following DAG species were found in both lists: DAG 16:0_18:0, DAG 20:1_20:5, DAG 18:0_20:1, DAG 18:0_20:0, DAG 20:2_22:6 (Figure 4iii.). All selected markers showed significant differences among the sample groups after multiple-testing correction. Tukey’s post-hoc analysis was subsequently performed to identify the specific group differences responsible for the observed variation. As shown in (Figure 4iii.), the abundance of the selected markers directly correlated with increasing FO adulteration levels, with significant differences observed between KO and FO-adulterated samples. These results confirm the ability of the identified markers to discriminate KO samples adulterated with FO. A separate experiment was conducted in which KO samples were adulterated with different levels (2.5, 5.0, 10.0, and 15.0%) of two plant oils, SFO and SBO. Figure 5ii. presents the PCA score plots obtained from the analysis of pure and adulterated KO samples, separately for SFO and SBO adulteration. In both cases, the pure KO samples were clearly separated from the adulterated samples, demonstrating that the DAG profile was sensitive to the presence of the added plant oils. Furthermore, a concentration-dependent separation pattern was observed, with the samples progressively shifting away from the pure KO cluster as the level of adulteration increased. The distinct clustering of samples according to the adulteration level indicates that the changes in the DAG profile were related to the proportion of added SFO or SBO. These results demonstrate that the developed method has the potential not only to discriminate pure KO from adulterated samples but also to differentiate samples according to the extent of adulteration. When the pure KO and KO samples adulterated with either SBO or SFO were analysed together, the pure KO samples formed a distinct and closely grouped cluster, clearly separated from the adulterated samples (Figure 5i.). To further investigate the discrimination of adulterated samples and identify potential markers of adulteration, the data were subjected to random forest and PLS-DA analyses (Suppl. Materials 2, Tables 3-4), following a similar approach to that used for the FO adulteration study. The variables identified by both approaches are presented in Figure 5iii. The identified markers included DAG species originating from the added plant oils, as well as endogenous KO DAG species whose relative abundance decreased with increasing levels of adulteration. One example is DAG 20:2_22:6, which showed a progressive decrease with increasing adulterant concentration. The complementary changes in DAG species, including the increase in plant-oil-derived DAGs and the decrease in characteristic KO DAGs, provided a clear molecular signature of adulteration and contributed to the discrimination of pure and adulterated KO samples. (i) PCA score plot showing the separation of pure KO and KO samples adulterated with different percentages of SBO and SFO. (ii) PCA score plot showing a separate analysis of KO samples adulterated with SBO and SFO. (iii) Box plots showing the distribution of DAG species selected by both PLS-DA and random forest analyses. Statistical significance was evaluated using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test. A rapid and comprehensive HPLC-MS/MS method based on multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) was successfully developed for the analysis of DAG molecular species in plant and marine oils. The method enabled the determination of 75 DAG molecular species within 5 min, with a six-fold linear range and low limits of detection and quantification, providing an efficient approach for DAG profiling. Its applicability was demonstrated through the detection and discrimination of KO adulterated with FO, SBO, and SFO. PCA showed clear separation between pure and adulterated KO samples, as well as concentration-dependent changes associated with increasing adulterant levels. Furthermore, the combined use of PLS-DA and random forest analysis enabled the identification of potential DAG markers characteristic of FO, SBO, and SFO adulteration. Overall, the developed method provides a rapid, sensitive, and informative analytical approach for DAG profiling and supports the detection and characterisation of adulteration in marine and plant oils. title: Tuning inhibitor susceptibility of human 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase to rescue tyrosine catabolism in the presence of β-triketones
author: Neuckermans, J.; Mertens, A.; Lequeue, S.; Salvi, N. S.; Desmet, L.; Del'Haye, G. G.; Tretowicz, K.; Vanhaecke, T.; Schwaneberg, U.; De Kock, J.
text: Human 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD) catalyses a key step in tyrosine degradation via homogentisate in liver and kidney cells. Pharmacological inhibition of HPD with nitisinone (NTBC) is standard treatment for tyrosinemia type 1 (HT1) and alkaptonuria (AKU). Although life-changing, continuous NTBC treatment limits metabolic flexibility and complicates emerging gene- and cell-based therapeutic approaches. Engineering HPD variants that retain catalytic activity during NTBC exposure could facilitate restoration of tyrosine metabolism, yet the molecular determinants of inhibitor tolerance remain poorly understood. Here, we applied Knowledge Gaining Directed Evolution (KnowVolution) to enhance NTBC tolerance while considering enzyme activity, predicted stability, and MHC-II peptide binding. Random mutagenesis, site-saturation mutagenesis, and computational analyses identified beneficial substitutions that improved enzyme activity in the presence of NTBC. These substitutions are predominantly located outside the catalytic cavity, suggesting that NTBC tolerance may involve distal structural effects rather than direct modification of inhibitor-binding residues. Recombination of selected substitutions, guided by activity and computational predictions of stability and MHC-II binding, yielded multi-substitution HPD variants with markedly increased NTBC tolerance. The leading variant, HPD-M8, exhibited up to 40-fold greater NTBC tolerance than wild-type HPD and increased tolerance to structurally related β-triketone inhibitors, without an overall increase in predicted MHC-II binder burden. Computational analyses suggested altered catalytic access-pathway energetics without major perturbation of the conserved catalytic machinery, consistent with a possible contribution of distal substitutions to inhibitor tolerance. Together, these findings provide insight into HPD inhibitor tolerance and establish a foundation for future HT1 and AKU therapeutic strategies. Human 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD; EC 1.13.11.27) is a non-heme iron (II)-dependent oxygenase that catalyses the second step in tyrosine degradation: the conversion of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (HPP) to homogentisate (HGA) (Fig. 1a), with concomitant CO2release. This complex reaction, involving oxidative decarboxylation, aromatic hydroxylation, and side-chain migration within a single catalytic cycle, is essential for funnelling tyrosine toward fumarate and acetoacetate[1–4]. (a) Chemical conversion of HPP to HGA, catalysed by HPD (structures obtained from ChemSpider-Created in BioRender. Lequeue, S. (2026)https://BioRender.com/ujgkc2c). (b) Homodimeric structure of human HPD shown as cartoon representation with chain A in grey and chain B in blue. The catalytic Fe² ion (purple sphere) is coordinated by the conserved 2-His-1-carboxylate motif consisting of His183, His266, and Glu349 (red). (c) Close-up view of the catalytic cavity showing key residues involved in substrate coordination and catalysis. HPP is shown in pink and the catalytic Fe² ion in purple. Residues (His183, His266, Glu349) coordinating the Fe² ion are shown in dark blue as ball-and-stick representations. The carboxyl group of HPP forms a hydrogen bond with Gln334, Asn363 (shown in orange) and Glu349 (shown in cyan blue), the 4-hydroxyl group on the aromatic ring interacts with Gln251 and Gln265 (shown in orange), π-π interactions essential for the positioning of the benzene ring of the HPP for oxidation involve Phe364 (shown in red). Gln272, Gln286, and Gln358 (shown in green) play a central role in HPP binding and the first nucleophilic attack. Asn261 and Ser246 (shown in yellow) play a key role in the electrophilic attack of the aromatic C1 for hydroxylation and the final ortho-rearrangement [8]. (d) Binding mode of the inhibitor NTBC (pink) within the catalytic cavity. Two carbonyl groups of NTBC are conjugated with the Fe2+, which is also chelated by the conservative triad of His183, His266, and Glu349 (shown in dark blue as ball and sticks). The cyclohexanedione is surrounded by Val185, Pro239, Asn241, Ser226, and Phe 259 (shown in orange), the phenyl moiety of NTBC forms π-π interactions with Phe336 and Phe364 (shown in red), and the trifluoromethyl group is bound to Phe336, Phe364 (shown in red), and Leu323, Asn362, and Leu367 (shown in green) [7]. Structural figures were generated using UCSF ChimeraX. Structurally, human HPD is a 393-residue homodimer with a conserved C-terminal β-barrel that houses the catalytic Fe(II), coordinated by the canonical 2-His-1-carboxylate motif (His183, His266, Glu349) (Fig. 1b-c). Access to this buried catalytic core is regulated by a C-terminal α-helix that functions as a gating element [2,5,6]. Recent structural and computational studies further demonstrated that ligand binding induces pronounced conformational rearrangements of the C-terminal gating helix and adjacent loop regions, stabilizing an open state of the catalytic cavity and facilitating substrate or inhibitor accommodation [7–9]. Despite limited sequence identity across species, the structural fold is highly conserved, and mutagenesis studies have highlighted the contribution of residues throughout both N- and C-termini for catalysis and stability [2,3,5,6,10]. Loss of HPD function leads to upstream metabolite accumulation and causes the metabolic disorder hereditary tyrosinemia type 3, characterized by neurocognitive impairment, while specific dominant HPD mutations, e.g. c.722A>G (p.N241S) and c.97G>A (p.A33T), exist that cause hawkinsinuria, an ultra-rare disorder characterized by renal excretion of the unusual tyrosine metabolites hawkinsin and 4-hydroxycyclohexylacetic acid [1,11–14]. However, HPD is the main therapeutic target in hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (HT1) and alkaptonuria (AKU). In both diseases, pharmacological HPD inhibition reduces HGA formation and prevents accumulation of downstream toxic intermediates [4,15,16]. The only approved HPD inhibitor, nitisinone or 2-(2-nitro-4-trifluoromethylbenzoyl)-1,3-cyclohexanedione (NTBC), is a potent β-triketone originally developed as a herbicide [17,18]. Structurally mimicking HPP, NTBC forms a tight, slowly dissociating enzyme–inhibitor complex through reversible π-stacking interactions with active-site phenylalanine residues (Phe336 and Phe364) in the C-terminal domain, bidentate Fe(II) coordination, and deprotonation of the enol form. Recent crystal structures of the human HPD–NTBC complex further revealed extensive hydrophobic interactions within the catalytic cavity and ligand-induced rearrangements surrounding the C-terminal gating helix that stabilize inhibitor binding [7]. The resulting highly stable enzyme-inhibitor complex leads to near-irreversible enzyme inactivation with extremely slow recovery of HPD activity (Fig. 1d) [3,4,19–24]. Although NTBC dramatically improves survival in HT1, it neither corrects the underlying FAH deficiency [25] nor eliminates the risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma [26–28]. NTBC withdrawal remains necessary in most gene- or cell-based therapies to create selective pressure for corrected hepatocytes, yet this exposes uncorrected cells to toxicity and facilitates malignant transformation. Because complete hepatocyte correction is unrealistic, NTBC remains indispensable while simultaneously limiting advanced therapeutic strategies [29,30]. To bypass the limitations of NTBC-dependent therapy, metabolic pathway reprogramming has emerged as an alternative strategy. Upstream inactivation of HPD via CRISPR-mediated disruption orin uterocytosine base editing can rescue the lethal HT1 phenotype in mice and pigs following NTBC withdrawal. However, this permanently introduces a secondary genetic lesion, producing an HT3-like metabolic state without correcting the underlying HT1-causing FAH mutation [31–34]. To overcome the drawbacks of both NTBC-dependent therapy and irreversible HPD inactivation, we aimed to engineer HPD variants capable of maintaining catalytic activity in the presence of NTBC. Using directed protein evolution (DPE) through the Knowledge Gaining Directed Evolution (KnowVolution) strategy, we generated NTBC-resistant HPD variants. KnowVolution integrates random mutagenesis, targeted saturation mutagenesis, computational modelling, and combinatorial recombination to efficiently identify and exploit positions contributing to a desired protein property [35]. Through iterative rounds of mutagenesis and high-throughput selection in our bacterial screening system[36], we identified eight substitutions that increased resistance to NTBC and related β-triketone inhibitors without compromising catalytic activity. The best-performing variant retained catalytic activity at NTBC concentrations far exceeding those tolerated by wild-type (wt) HPDin vitro. By showing the feasibility of engineering NTBC-tolerant human HPD variants, this study tackles the main hurdle in the development of future gene- and cell-based therapies for HT1 that seek to maintain tyrosine catabolism. This strategy could eliminate the need for NTBC withdrawal and hereby reduces hepatotoxic risk. Such an advancement is particularly relevant given that residual FAH-deficient hepatocytes remain intrinsically prone to malignant transformation when exposed to accumulated toxic intermediates. All chemicals were of analytical-reagent grade or higher quality and were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Chemie GmbH (Schnelldorf, Germany), AppliChem (Darmstadt, Germany), or Carl Roth GmbH (Karlsruhe, Germany). All enzymes were purchased from New England Biolabs (Beverly, USA), Sigma Aldrich (Hamburg, Germany), or ThermoFisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA). NTBC was purchased from Yecuris (Tualatin, OR, USA). Oligonucleotides were purchased from Eurofins MWG Operon (Ebersberg, Germany) or ThermoFisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA) in salt-free form. A thermal cycler (Mastercycler gradient; Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany) and thin-wall PCR tubes (Multi ultra-tubes; 0.2 mL; Carl Roth, Germany) were used in all PCRs. Plasmid extraction and PCR purification kits were purchased from Macherey-Nagel GmbH & Co. (Düren, Germany), Sigma Aldrich (Hamburg, Germany), and Qiagen (Hilden, Germany). DNA concentrations were quantified using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Wilmington, USA). Microtiter plates for protein expression (96-wells; V-shaped) and for absorbance measurements (96-wells, flat-bottom) (Greiner Bio-One GmbH, Frickenhausen, Germany) were incubated in a Multitron II Infors shaker (Infors AG, Bottmingen, Switzerland) or InnovaTM42R Incubator Shaker (Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany). For detection of absorbance, Tecan Sunrise®or Tecan Infinite®M200 pro (Tecan Group Ltd, Männedorf, Switzerland) plate readers or Victor3 multilabel plate reader (Perkin Elmer, Waltham, MA, USA) were used. Escherichia coli(E. coli) DH5α (Stratagene, La Jolla, CA, USA) was used for DNA propagation, andE. coliC43 (DE3) (Lucigen Corporation, Middleton, WI, USA) for expression of recombinant enzymes and library screening. The expression vector pET42b(+) (Novagen, Darmstadt, Germany) carried a kanamycin resistance gene. As a negative control, empty pET42b(+) (EV) was transformed intoE. coli[36]. cDNA of WT human HPD (NM_002150.2) was obtained from Geneart in a pMA-T-based cloning plasmid (Thermo Scientific), optimized forE. colicodon usage (see supplementary information 1). The HPD gene was subcloned as an NdeI-XhoI fragment into pET42b(+), transformed intoE. coliDH5α and sequenced. Lysogeny Broth (LB) medium supplemented with kanamycin (50 μg/mL) was used for selection [36]. Sanger sequencing was performed by GATC Biotech AG (Cologne, Germany) using T7 FW (5’-TAA TAC GAC TCA CTA TAG GG -3’; Tm 53.2°C, GC 40%) and T7 RV (5’-GCT AGT TAT TGC TCA GCG GT - 3’; Tm 54.5°C, GC 47%). Alignments were performed using BioEdit 7.2. Random mutagenesis was performed using epPCR [37] in tandem with phosphorothioate-based ligase-independent gene cloning[38] (PLICing; list of PTO-primers in supplementary data table S1). MnCl2concentration (0–0.5mM) was optimized to achieve ∼50% active clones. PCR conditions for the HPD insert in the presence of Taq DNA polymerase to generate a mutant library were 94°C for 3 min; 30 cycles of 94°C 30 s, 48.5°C 30 s, 72°C 1 min; final elongation 72°C 10 min. Vector backbone amplification was performed in the presence of Phusion High-Fidelity DNA polymerase with the following cycling conditions: 98°C 3 min; 25 cycles of 98°C 30 s, 58.3°C 30 s, 72°C 2 min; final elongation 72°C 5 min. PCR products were verified by agarose gel electrophoresis [39], digested with DpnI (20 U, NEB), purified, quantified, and used in PLICing reactions with a 0.05 pmol/µL insert to 0.03 pmol/µL vector ratio. Products were transformed into chemically competentE. coliC43 (DE3) and plated on LBKANA. Religation and DpnI controls were included to monitor background colony formation. Nine positions (118, 137, 151, 153, 166, 177, 278, 302, and 307) identified from epPCR were subjected to SSM using 22c-trick primers [40] (NDT : VHG : TGG = 12:9:1, see supplementary data table S2 for primer sequences). A modified QuikChange two-step PCR protocol was applied with Phusion High- fidelity Polymerase[41]. PCR conditions for the first step: 98°C for 1 min; 3 cycles of 98°C 30 s, 60°C 30 s, 72°C 3 min. For the second step: 98°C 1 min; 18 cycles of 98°C 30 s, 60°C 30 s, 72°C 3 min; final elongation 72°C 8 min. After PCR, DpnI digestion removed template DNA. Libraries were transformed intoE. coliC43 (DE3) and screened in 96-well plates using the previously described high-throughput assay [36]. An oversampling factor of three was applied to achieve ∼95% coverage of the theoretical variant space, requiring screening of ∼66 colonies per position [40]. The crystal structure of human HPD was obtained from the Protein Data Bank (PDB ID: 3ISQ)[42]. Structural visualization, residue mapping, and figure preparation were performed using UCSF ChimeraX (version 1.11.1) [43]. The HPD-M8 structural model was generated byin silicomutagenesis of the HPD-WT structure using Rowan Scientific Boltz-2 based co-folding (https://www.rowansci.comaccessed 2026) and subsequently visualized in ChimeraX. Experimentally identified substitutions from phase I of KnowVolution were mapped onto chain A of the HPD structure and classified according to their spatial localization relative to the catalytic cavity. Catalytic pocket residues were defined as residues located within 5 Å of either the Fe(II) cofactor or the substrate/inhibitor binding region. Surface residues were identified based on solvent exposure following visualization of the molecular surface in ChimeraX. Protein stability effects of individual substitutions were assessed on the (i) Boltz-2 generated monomer, (ii) the crystal structure of human HPD-WT complexed with NTBC (8IM2) and (iii) a Boltz-2 generated model of HPD-WT homodimer complexed with TTC36 and Fe2+, using the DynaMut2 web server (https://biosig.lab.uq.edu.au/dynamut2/), which predicts mutation-induced changes in folding stability (ΔΔG, kcal/mol) from protein structural information [44]. Averaged positive ΔΔG values from all three models were interpreted as stabilizing and negative values as destabilizing. The predicted folding stability of HPD-WT and the final eight-substitution variant HPD-M8 was evaluated using IFUM (in silicoevaluation of unfolding Free energy with Unfolded state ensemble Modeling), a deep-learning method that estimates absolute unfolding free energy (ΔG) by jointly considering sequence and structural representations of the folded and unfolded states [45] Predicted ΔG values were obtained for the complete wild-type and M8 sequences, and the stability difference (ΔΔG) was calculated as ΔGM8− ΔGWT, with positive values indicating increased predicted stability of the variant. Potential changes in MHC class II peptide presentation were evaluated using NetMHCIIpan 4.1 BA mode (https://tools.iedb.org/mhcii/) across representative HLA-DR, HLA-DP, and HLA-DQ alleles [46]. For each variant, the number of predicted MHC-II binders was compared with that of HPD-WT. Substitutions were classified according to the net gain or loss of predicted binders. Docking analyses of the native substrate HPP and the inhibitor NTBC were performed using the DiffDock/SMINA [47] pipeline implemented through the NeuroSnap platform (NeuroSnap Inc., 2022). Docking calculations were carried out for both HPD-WT and the engineered HPD-M8 variant. For each ligand-protein combination, multiple docking poses were generated and ranked according to docking rank and SMINA affinity score, where lower affinity scores indicate more favourable predicted binding interactions. Docking analyses were interpreted qualitatively to compare substrate and inhibitor accommodation patterns between HPD-WT and HPD-M8. Structural interface analyses of the HPD biological assembly were performed using the PDBePISA server (v.1.52 10/20/2014) [48,49] to evaluate solvent accessibility surface area (ASA), buried surface area (BSA), and potential contributions of experimentally identified residues to the HPD dimer interface. Tunnel and catalytic access pathway analyses were performed using CAVER Web[50] to investigate ligand accessibility of the buried catalytic cavity. HPD-WT and HPD-M8 structural models were co-folded with TTC36 [51] as molecular chaperone using Boltz-2 and analysed using both HPP, NTBC and HGA as ligands. The catalytic Fe(II) centre was used as the starting point for tunnel calculations. Resulting transport-energy profiles and energetic barriers along the catalytic access pathway were compared between HPD-WT and HPD-M8 to assess potential effects of the experimentally identified substitutions on substrate and inhibitor passage. Evolutionary conservation analysis was performed using the ConSurf server [52]. Homologous sequences were identified with HMMER [53] (E-value ≤ 0.0001), filtered with CD-HIT [54] (≤ 95% sequence identity), and aligned using MAFFT [55]. A phylogenetic tree was generated using the Neighbor-Joining method with maximum-likelihood distance estimation [56], and site-specific conservation scores were calculated with Rate4Site [57]. Conservation scores of experimentally identified residues were compared with those of residues forming the catalytic centre and inhibitor-binding cavity of HPD. Six positions (239, 241, 334, 363, 364, and 367) identified after molecular modelling (in the catalytic centre) were subjected to SSM using 22c-trick primers [40] (NDT : VHG : TGG = 12:9:1, see supplementary data table S3). A modified QuikChange two-step PCR protocol was applied [41]. PCR conditions for the first step: 98°C for 1 min; 3 cycles of 98°C 30 s, 60°C 30 s, 72°C 3 min. For the second step: 98°C 1 min; 18 cycles of 98°C 30 s, 60°C 30 s, 72°C 3 min; final elongation 72°C 8 min. After PCR, DpnI digestion removed template DNA. Libraries were transformed intoE. coliC43 (DE3) and screened in 96-well plates using the previously described high-throughput assay [36]. Beneficial substitutions were combined to create triple (M3), quintuple (M5), and octuple (M8) HPD variants using a two-step PCR protocol with Phusion High-fidelity polymerase [41]. Primer mixes were designed for region 1 (positions 118, 138, 151, 153, 177) and region 2 (278, 302, 307) (see supplementary data table S4). PCR conditions for the first step: 98°C for 1 min; 3 cycles of 98°C 30 s, 60°C 30 s, 72°C 3 min. For the second step: 98°C 1 min; 18 cycles of 98°C 30 s, 60°C 30 s, 72°C 3 min; final elongation 72°C 8 min. After PCR, DpnI digestion removed template DNA. Libraries were transformed intoE. coliC43 (DE3) and screened in 96-well plates using the previously described high-throughput assay [36]. PCR products were digested with DpnI and transformed intoE. coliC43 (DE3) for expression. The basics of the HTS assay have been previously described [36]. Briefly, colonies were inoculated in 96-well plates with 100 µL LB + 1% glucose and incubated at 30°C, 900rpm, 70% RH for 16 h. Cultures were transferred to expression plates with 1mM isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) and 0.75 mg/mL Tyr, in the absence or presence of NTBC. After 24 h at 37°C, 900rpm, 70% RH, cultures were centrifuged, and OD405was measured to quantify pyomelanin formation. Variants of interest were rescreened with increasing NTBC concentrations. Overnight cultures were diluted to OD6000.1, grown to OD6000.6– 0.8, induced with 1mM IPTG, and challenged with NTBC with four replicates of each variant per concentration in 96-well plates. Absorbance at OD405was measured after 24 h [36]. HPD-WT and HPD-M8 were assayed against mesotrione (0 – 15µM), NTBC (0 – 20µM), sulcotrione (0 – 20µM), and tembotrione (0 – 40µM) with 4 replicates per concentration (n = 20). The normalized OD405(OD405-N) was calculated according to OD405-N= OD405– OD405-EV(Eq. 1) where OD405-EV= measured OD405of the EV. The activity percentage (Act. %) was calculated with GraphPad Prism 7 software according to the equation Act.% = (OD405-N/OD405-M) * 100 (Eq. 2), where OD405-Mis the mean of OD405measured at 0µM (i.e. 100% activity)[36]. The HPD-M8 enzyme variant and the HPD-WT enzyme were challenged with different concentrations of tyrosine (0 – 10mM) with 4 replicates per concentration to assess substrate responsiveness. The same reaction was also set up, but with the addition of 2µM NTBC, i.e., the concentration where the HPD-WT is completely blocked and HPD-M8 is 100% active. The assay and measurements were performed as previously described [36]. Plasmids from overnight cultures were purified using the Nucleospin® Plasmid DNA Purification kit from Macherey-Nagel GmbH & Co. (Düren, Germany). The isolated plasmid DNA was quantified at 260nm and sequenced using T7 primers. Alignments were performed in BioEdit 7.2. OD405values were blank-corrected using EV+NTBC and normalized to WT or HPD-M8 without NTBC. Data are expressed as mean ± 95% CI. One-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni post hoc test was applied (α = 0.05) using GraphPad Prism 11.0.1. The aim of this study was to engineer human HPD variants with improved tolerance to NTBC and related β-triketones while preserving their native catalytic function. Despite extensive structural analysis and multiple rational design attempts [2,3,5,6,10], the contribution of individual residues to NTBC binding or tolerance remains poorly understood. To address this, we applied the KnowVolution strategy, which integrates random mutagenesis, site-saturation mutagenesis, computational analysis, and recombination (Fig 2). This workflow efficiently identifies beneficial substitutions while reducing screening effort and often outperforms classical multi-round directed evolution campaigns [35]. Schematic overview of the KnowVolution strategy applied to engineer NTBC-tolerant human HPD variants. In Phase I, random mutant libraries were generated by epPCR and screened using the previously described high-throughput assay [36] in the presence of NTBC, resulting in the identification of nine beneficial positions associated with increased inhibitor tolerance. In Phase II, site-saturation mutagenesis (SSM) was performed on the preselected positions, together with selected catalytic-site residues involved in NTBC accommodation, to identify beneficial amino acid substitutions while assessing tolerance of active-site modifications. In Phase III, computational structural analyses including PDBePISA, DiffDock/SMINA docking, DynaMut2, NetMHCIIpan, CAVER Web transport analyses, and ConSurf conservation analysis were used to investigate the mechanistic basis of NTBC tolerance. These analyses revealed that beneficial substitutions predominantly localize to solvent-exposed surface regions and indirectly modulate catalytic cavity accessibility and inhibitor transport energetics without disrupting the conserved catalytic machinery. In Phase IV, beneficial substitutions identified in Phases I and II were recombined by multi-site directed mutagenesis (MSDM), resulting in the HPD-M8 variant, which retained full catalytic activity at NTBC concentrations approximately 40-fold higher than those inhibiting HPD-WT. (Created in BioRender. Lequeue, S. (2026)https://BioRender.com/ad1l3q5). Random mutant libraries were generated using 0.1mM MnCl2, low-fidelity DNA polymerase, and balanced dNTPs, and screened using a whole-cell colorimetric assay based on pyomelanin formation (Fig.3a – b) [36]. As pyomelanin production reflects HPD activity and is strongly inhibited by NTBC, pigment formation in its presence served as a proxy for inhibitor tolerance. Screening ∼1700 clones simultaneously without NTBC and at 0.25 – 0.50µM NTBC yielded nine variants with reproducible improvements in tolerance. A secondary rescreen across 0 – 1µM confirmed these observations. Sequencing identified several recurrent positions (i.e. 151 and 302), though with distinct amino-acid substitutions. The identified substitutions included M118I/N, Q137R, N151D, I153N, M166T, S177G, I278V, K302R, and K307N. Furthermore, comparison of variant activities in the absence and presence of NTBC revealed distinct effects on basal activity and inhibitor tolerance. I278V and N151D exhibited increased basal activity (∼115 – 120% of WT) and improved NTBC tolerance, retaining ∼71% and ∼45% of their respective uninhibited activities at 0.50µM NTBC, compared with ∼3% for WT. M118I also showed increased inhibitor tolerance despite reduced basal activity, whereas I153N, S177G, K302R, and K307N displayed increased basal activity and varying degrees of tolerance, particularly at 0.25µM NTBC. In contrast, M166T showed a modest increase in basal activity, but remained susceptible to inhibition at higher NTBC concentrations, while Q137R showed no apparent improvement in either property (Fig. 3c – f). High-throughput screening of human HPD variant libraries in the (a) absence and (b) presence of 0.25µM NTBC resulting in inactive and active (improved) variants. Overall, I278V and N151D exhibited the most pronounced combined improvements in activity and NTBC tolerance, with I278V retaining 6.8 ± 2.2% residual activity at 1µM NTBC, although all variants were strongly inhibited at 1µM NTBC (Fig. 3c – f). To gain structural and mechanistic insight, the identified positions were mapped onto the 3D monomeric structure of HPD. All identified residues were solvent-exposed and spatially separated from the catalytic pocket. Notably, none of the identified positions were located within the catalytic pocket (Fig. 3g). Targeted saturation mutagenesis was performed at the nine positions identified in phase 1. Substitutions at positions 153 (I153E) and 307 (K307P) generated the largest increases in NTBC tolerance, and T138S emerged as an additional beneficial substitution. Positions 118, 151, 166, 177, or 302 did not yield enhanced tolerance upon systematic substitution (Fig. 4). To ensure ∼95% coverage of the variant space, at least 66 clones per position were required [40]. In practice, 88 SSM clones per position were screened across 0–2µM NTBC. This confirmed the phase 1 findings and narrowed the key positions and substitutions for further combinatorial optimization. Positive ΔΔG values indicate stabilizing substitutions, whereas negative values indicate destabilizing substitutions. Statistical significance between substitutions at the same amino-acid position is indicated as ns, not significant; *p < 0.05; and ***p < 0.001. (b) Changes in the number of predicted MHC-II binders determined using NetMHCIIpan for HLA-DR, HLA-DP, and HLA-DQ alleles. Values represent the net change in predicted binders relative to HPD-WT, with green indicating a loss and red indicating a gain of predicted MHC-II binders. M8 represents the lead variant containing eight accumulated substitutions. Individual substitutions identified in the preceding two phases were evaluated computationally with respect to their predicted effects on protein stability and MHC-II peptide presentation to guide subsequent recombination. DynaMut2 analysis predicted that N151D, I153D/E/N, M166S/T, and K307N/P were to be stabilizing or near-neutral, with the largest favourable stability changes observed for M166S (+0.72 ± 0.06 kcal/mol), I153E (+0.70 ± 0.04 kcal/mol), and M166T (+0.67 ± 0.11 kcal/mol). In contrast, M118I/L, Q137R, T138S, S177G/Q, I278V, and K302R were predicted to be destabilizing, with I278V showing the largest predicted stability penalty (−1.45 ± 0.48 kcal/mol) (Fig.5a; Table S5). NetMHCIIpan analysis further revealed mutation-specific changes in the predicted HLA-II binder profile. I153D/E/N and S177G did not alter the total number of predicted binders, whereas M118I, I278V, and K307N reduced the predicted binder burden by 3, 3, and 6 binders, respectively. Conversely, Q137R and K302R produced the largest increases, with net gains of 11 and 5 predicted binders across the HLA-DR, -DP, and -DQ panels (Fig.5b; Fig.S1). Based on the knowledge gained within the previous three phases of KnowVolution, multi-site directed mutagenesis (MSDM) was performed to combine all beneficial substitutions into a single HPD variant with high NTBC tolerance. The positions were grouped into two regions: R1 (positions 118, 138, 151, 153, 177 – M5) and R2 (positions 278, 302, 307 – M3). Using HPD-M3 as a template, all R1 positions were combined to generate the final variant HPD-M8, containing all beneficial changes. The resulting clones (M5, M3, and M8) were assayed across 1–6µM NTBC. HPD-WT was fully inhibited at 1µM NTBC. M5 retained 100% activity at 1–2µM and 30–40% at 3µM, whereas M3 showed 75% activity at 1µM and was fully blocked at 2–3µM. HPD-M8 retained full activity at 4µM NTBC, ∼50% activity at 5µM, and ∼5% at 6µM, corresponding to an approximate 40-fold improvement relative to WT (Fig. 6). Computational analyses were performed to investigate how surface substitutions improve NTBC tolerance without compromising catalytic activity. Human HPD functions as a homodimer (PDB ID: 3ISQ)[42] and contains a highly conserved catalytic centre coordinating Fe(II) via His183, His266, and Glu349. Molecular docking confirmed that both HPP and NTBC interact within the same Fe(II) centred pocket (Fig. 1c-d). Consistent with previous structural studies, HPP formed interactions with residues including N241, G360, and Q334, whereas NTBC additionally interacted with residues lining the hydrophobic catalytic cavity, including P239, N241, Q334, N363, F364, and L367. Whole-protein docking analyses using DiffDock/SMINA showed that HPP retained favourable low-rank docking poses in both HPD-WT and HPD-M8, consistent with preserved substrate accommodation. NTBC docking produced a broader and more dispersed distribution of docking poses, particularly in HPD-M8 (Fig. 7), indicating greater variability in predicted inhibitor-binding conformations. However, as these docking analyses do not account for ligand transport, catalytic gating, or slow-binding kinetics, they were interpreted as supportive rather than definitive mechanistic evidence. DiffDock/SMINA whole-protein docking analyses of the native substrate 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (HPP) and the inhibitor nitisinone (NTBC) in human HPD-WT and the engineered HPD-M8 variant. (a) Docking distribution of HPP in HPD-WT. (b) Docking distribution of NTBC in HPD-WT. (c) Docking distribution of HPP in HPD-M8. (d) Docking distribution of NTBC in HPD-M8. Each point represents an individual docking pose generated by the DiffDock/SMINA pipeline. Docking poses are plotted according to DiffDock docking rank and corresponding SMINA affinity score, where lower docking ranks and lower affinity scores indicate more favourable predicted ligand accommodation. HPP retained favourable low-rank docking poses in both HPD-WT and HPD-M8, consistent with preservation of productive substrate accommodation. In contrast, NTBC docking profiles appeared more dispersed and less consistently favourable, particularly in HPD-M8, indicating increased sensitivity of inhibitor accommodation to the engineered substitutions relative to substrate positioning. Because these docking analyses do not account for ligand transport, catalytic gating, or slow-binding kinetics, they were interpreted as supportive rather than definitive mechanistic evidence. Structural mapping revealed that beneficial substitutions cluster on the protein surface and remain spatially separated from the catalytic pocket (Fig 3g). None of the substitutions directly contacted either the substrate or inhibitor, indicating that NTBC tolerance is not mediated through direct perturbation of catalytic-site interactions. Most identified positions localized to flexible loop regions (Met118, Asn151, Ile153, Met166, Ser177, and Lys307), α-helices (Ile278 and Lys302), or β-sheet-associated surface regions (Gln137 and Thr138), suggesting a potential role in modulating protein dynamics or catalytic cavity accessibility. PDBePISA analysis demonstrated that all beneficial substitutions are solvent-exposed and do not contribute to the dimer interface (BSA ∼ 0), suggesting that NTBC tolerance is unlikely to arise from direct perturbation of inhibitor-binding residues or altered dimerization. To further investigate whether distal surface substitutions indirectly influence ligand accessibility, transport analyses were performed using CAVER Web and its docking module CaverDock (Fig. 8). Not surprisingly, the ligand transport tunnel, connecting the surface to the catalytic pocket, was significantly altered. Compared to HPD-WT, the bottleneck radius of HPD-M8’s ligand transport tunnel increased from 1.4 Å to 1.5 Å corresponding to an increase in throughput from 0.46 to 0.55 (Fig. 8a-g). The entrance region of the tunnel was energetically favourable in both proteins. Within the first 5 Å from the protein surface, HPD-WT and HPD-M8 showed comparable binding energy values, suggesting that the surface-proximal tunnel opening does not account for the major difference between the two systems (Fig. 8h-i). The main difference occurred in the central part of the tunnel. In HPD-WT, NTBC encountered a pronounced transport barrier, with binding energy reaching 31.5 kcal/mol at 11.39 Å from the tunnel entrance. This high-energy region extended across a broad central segment of the pathway, with binding energy remaining above 20 kcal/mol between approximately 9.69 Å and 15.46 Å (Fig. 8h-i). This central barrier coincided with tunnel narrowing, and the narrowest point of the HPD-WT trajectory was observed at 14.48 Å, where the tunnel radius decreased to 1.4 Å (Fig. 8g). In contrast, HPD-M8 displayed a substantially lower maximum binding energy of 9.9 kcal/mol at 11.83 Å from the tunnel entrance. Although the mutant tunnel also contained constricted regions, its energy profile did not reproduce the high central barrier observed in HPD-WT (Fig. 8h-i). The narrowest point in HPD-M8 occurred earlier along the transport pathway, at 7.91 Å, with a minimum radius of 1.5 Å (Fig. 8g). In addition, HPD-M8 showed a later moderate-energy region around 18 Å to 19.5 Å, suggesting redistribution of transport constraints rather than simple occlusion of the tunnel (Fig. 8h-i). CAVER Web ligand transport tunnel analyses using Boltz-2 prediction models of human wild-type HPD homodimer or HPD-M8 (gold) co-folded with the molecular chaperone TTC36 (green). Visualization of the ligand transport tunnel connecting the surface and the buried active site of (a, b) HPD-WT, (c, d) HPD-M8 and (e, f) their superposition (g). Tunnel geometry significantly differs between HPD-WT and M8 from 11 Å to 22 Å distal from the surface (h-i). CaverDock analyses and (j) pose visualization of NTBC, HPP, and HGA transport through the predicted access tunnel of HPD-WT and HPD-M8. Transport-energy profiles were calculated along this catalytic access and egress pathway. Transport profiles of HPP and HGA were predicted to be positively enhanced in HPD-M8versusHPD-WT. (k) HPD-WT displayed a pronounced central NTBC transport barrier, with binding energy reaching 31.5 kcal/mol at 11.39 Å and remained elevated across the central tunnel segment. This region coincided with tunnel narrowing and a major NTBC pose inversion between approximately 11.39 and 11.59 Å. (l) In contrast, HPD-M8 showed a shorter transport trajectory and a lower maximum binding energy of 9.9 kcal/mol at 11.83 Å. (m) The M8 mutant profile lacked the dominant WT-like central barrier, but showed redistributed moderate-energy regions, including a later constraint around 18 to 19.5 Å. Representative NTBC, HPP and HGA poses illustrate mutation-dependent differences in ligand orientation and accommodation along the tunnel pathway. In addition, the maximal energy barriers for HPP decreased in HPD-M8 from 11.8 kcal/mol to 3.4 kcal/mol compared to HPD-WT and for HGA from 12.5 kcal/mol to 5.4 kcal/mol while binding energies near the surface and active site remained relatively unchanged (Fig. 8h-i). This suggests that the mutant tunnel remains competent for normal substrate entry and product passage, and that the M8 mutations are unlikely to impair the native catalytic cycle at the level of ligand transport. Analysis of the NTBC poses along the tunnel further supported distinct ligand-accommodation patterns in the two proteins. In HPD-WT, the major NTBC reorientation occurred within the high-energy central barrier, between approximately 11.39 Å and 11.59 Å from the tunnel entrance. Across this transition, NTBC underwent an almost complete inversion of its aromatic-to-dione molecular axis, indicating that passage through this region requires a substantial pose rearrangement (Fig. 8k). This inversion was accompanied by changes in the relative positioning of the NTBC dione, nitro, trifluoromethyl and aromatic groups with respect to tunnel-lining residues, including Leu289, Phe336, Lys338, Pro339, Phe347, Ala370, Phe371, Glu374, and Arg378 (Fig.8k). HPD-M8 also exhibited NTBC reorientation near the central part of the tunnel, between approximately 11.83 Å and 11.99 Å (Fig. 8l). However, this transition occurred at a markedly lower energy than in HPD-WT. Additional pose rearrangements were observed in the later tunnel segment, particularly between 18.9 Å and 19.5 Å, where NTBC passed through a secondary moderate-energy region and shifted poses two times. These later rearrangements involved residues located deeper in the transport pathway, including Asn187, Leu224, Asn241, Ile252, Glu254, Tyr255, Gln265, Pro344, Phe347 and Phe371 (Fig. 8m). The M8 substitutions were not predicted to contact NTBC directly along the sampled transport trajectory. Instead, the observed differences are most consistent with an indirect structural effect, in which the M8 variant remodels the tunnel geometry and alters the sequence of NTBC poses adopted during transport. As such, HPD-M8 appears to shorten and reshape the access pathway, reduce the dominant WT-like central energy barrier and redistribute ligand-accommodation constraints toward additional tunnel regions. These findings suggest that the M8 substitutions alter NTBC access and positioning through long-range effects on tunnel architecture rather than through direct mutation/inhibitor contacts. Such changes may reduce the efficiency of NTBC accommodation and contribute to the observed inhibitor tolerance while maintaining substrate accessibility. Evolutionary conservation analysis using ConSurf further demonstrated that most experimentally identified positions are weakly conserved among HPD homologues, with Lys302 representing the main exception. In contrast, residues forming the catalytic centre and inhibitor-binding cavity remained highly conserved. These observations support a model in which NTBC tolerance arises through substitutions at evolutionarily permissive surface regions that modulate structural dynamics without disrupting the conserved catalytic machinery. The folding stability of the final HPD-M8 variant was further evaluated using IFUM [45]. HPD-WT showed a predicted unfolding free energy (ΔG) of 28.144 kcal/mol, whereas HPD-M8 displayed a higher predicted ΔG of 30.153 kcal/mol, corresponding to a ΔΔG of +2.009 kcal/mol. The higher IFUM-predicted unfolding free energy of HPD-M8 compared with wild-type HPD suggests that accumulation of the eight beneficial substitutions did not compromise overall protein stability and may instead confer a modest stabilizing effect. This is particularly relevant, because DynaMut2 predicted both stabilizing and destabilizing effects for the individual substitutions, indicating that their combined effect in HPD-M8 cannot be inferred solely from single-mutation predictions. The predicted MHC-II presentation profile was additionally assessed for the final lead variant HPD-M8, which contained eight accumulated substitutions (Fig.5b) [46]. NetMHCIIpan predicted a net reduction of eight MHC-II binders relative to HPD-WT, comprising losses of seven HLA-DR and three HLA-DQ binders that were partially offset by the gain of two HLA-DP binders. The strongest reductions were associated with HLA-DRB112:01, HLA-DQA101:02/DQB106:02, and HLA-DRB501:01, whereas only limited allele-specific increases were observed (Fig.S1). Consequently, accumulation of the eight beneficial substitutions did not increase the overall predicted MHC-II binder burden, indicating that the enhanced functional properties of HPD-M8 were retained without a concomitant increase in predicted HLA-II peptide presentation across the investigated allele panel. To determine whether direct perturbation of NTBC-contacting residues could similarly improve inhibitor tolerance, saturation mutagenesis was additionally performed on active-site residues involved in NTBC accommodation (Pro239, Asn241, Gln334, Asn363, Phe364, and Leu367). However, most substitutions resulted in inactive enzymes or variants indistinguishable from HPD-WT, indicating that direct modification of the catalytic pocket is poorly tolerated. Similar observations have previously been reported for homologous HPD enzymes, where active-site substitutions disrupt substrate positioning and reduce catalytic activity [5,58,59]. Collectively, these findings indicate that NTBC tolerance in HPD is mediated through long-range modulation of catalytic cavity accessibility rather than direct disruption of inhibitor-binding interactions. Inhibition of HPD-WT and HPD-M8 by triketones was evaluated in IPTG-inducedE. coliexpressing the enzyme [36]. Although NTBC is the only clinically relevant inhibitor, mesotrione, sulcotrione, and tembotrione were included to assess the broader tolerance of HPD-M8 [4]. Inhibitors were applied at 0–15µM (mesotrione), 0–20µM (NTBC, sulcotrione), and 0–40µM (tembotrione), with four replicates per concentration (Fig. 9a–d). Pyomelanin formation, reflecting HPD activity, decreased with increasing inhibitor concentration; bacterial cells were centrifuged prior to colorimetric quantification to prevent interference. IC50values were determined using four-parameter logistic fits. HPD-WT IC50s were 0.363 ± 0.013µM (mesotrione), 0.195 ± 0.003µM (NTBC), 0.164 ± 0.015µM (sulcotrione), and 0.611 ± 0.015µM (tembotrione). HPD-M8 IC50s increased substantially to 5.103 ± 0.092µM, 3.933 ± 0.499µM, 3.249 ± 0.397µM, and 5.504 ± 0.174µM (Fig. 9e), respectively, corresponding to fold changes of 14–20 for mesotrione, NTBC, and sulcotrione, and ∼9 for tembotrione. Thus, HPD-M8 is broadly β-triketone tolerant, not NTBC-specific. Dose-response inhibition curves of the prototypical β-triketone inhibitors (a) mesotrione (0 – 15µM), (b) nitisinone (0 – 20µM), (c) sulcotrione (0 – 20µM), and (d) tembotrione (0 – 40µM) for HPD-WT and HPD-M8. (e) The calculated IC50values for each of the HPD inhibitors (n = 4). The data are represented as mean ± 95% CI. Statistical significance was determined by a two-way ANOVA with Holm-Sidak correction (P < 0.05). (f) Comparative activity analysis of HPD-WT and the engineered HPD-M8 variant at increasing tyrosine concentrations in the presence of a fixed NTBC concentration (2µM). Residual HPD activity was assessed using the whole-cell pyomelanin-based bio-assay [36] to evaluate whether the engineered substitutions altered the response of HPD-M8 to increasing substrate availability under inhibitory conditions. While HPD-WT activity remained strongly inhibited by NTBC, HPD-M8 retained substantially higher activity across increasing tyrosine concentrations, consistent with enhanced NTBC tolerance while preserving catalytic function. Data are represented as mean ± 95% CI from four biological replicates. To assess whether HPD-M8 exhibited altered substrate responsiveness, HPD-WT and M8 were exposed to 0 – 10mM tyrosine. Since tyrosine availability determines HPP formation upstream, deviations could indicate altered substrate affinity. Both WT and M8 produced comparable pyomelanin levels across all conditions, in the presence or absence of 2µM NTBC (Fig. 9f). These findings indicate that HPD-M8 retains WT-like responsiveness to tyrosine and does not show obvious changes consistent with a modified Km. A key limitation is the lack of direct kinetic characterization (Km, kcat, kcat/Km). Subtle effects on catalytic efficiency therefore cannot yet be excluded, especially given the complex multi-step inhibition of HPD by NTBC [1,4]. Although IC50measurements provide comparative insights, more detailed kinetic analysis,viacoupled-enzyme assays [10,58,60,61], oxygen consumption, HPLC methods [2,6], or composite kinetic metrics such as ON/OFF rate ratios, are required to definitively confirm that catalytic properties were unaltered [62]. The use of a bacterial evolution platform is another consideration. Although prokaryotic and yeast platforms are standard in directed evolution due to rapid growth and efficiency [63–66], they lack the native mammalian folding, degradation, localization machinery, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) [63,66]. Human HPD contains several PTMs, three phosphoserines (211, 226, 250), one N6-succinyllysine (132), and an N-acetyl-threonine (2) [1,4], none of which occur at the mutated positions, suggesting minimal risk of PTM interference. Structural differences between bacterial and mammalian HPD homologs, including tetrameric assembly inP. fluorescens versusdimeric organization in mammals [4,23,67–69], may also contribute to system-specific behaviour. Nonetheless, bacterial platforms remain effective for enzyme engineering when coupled to a robust, phenotype-linked assay [63–67], as demonstrated by the successful evolution of HPD-M8. Another limitation is that the NetMHCIIpan analysis only predicts peptide–MHC-II binding and therefore does not account for antigen processing, peptide abundance, T-cell receptor recognition or other factors that ultimately determine immunogenicityin vivo. Finally, the CAVER/CaverDock data should be interpreted as a predicted transport model, not as direct evidence of ligand diffusion dynamics, in support of a structural explanation for the reduced sensitivity of HPD-M8 to triketone inhibitors. In this study, human HPD was successfully engineered using the KnowVolution strategy, yielding variants with markedly increased tolerance to NTBC and other β-triketone inhibitors. The final HPD-M8 variant retained fullin vitrocatalytic activity at NTBC concentrations at least 40-fold higher than those that completely inhibit HPD-WT. These results demonstrate that directed evolution can be applied to human metabolic enzymes to overcome clinically relevant inhibitor sensitivity, thereby opening new possibilities for designing gene-and cell-based therapeutic strategies for monogenic metabolic diseases.
