title: Conformational Reorganization of a Processive Cellulase on Crystalline Cellulose
author: Pingali, S. V.; He, J.; Petridis, L.; Evans, B. R.; Heller, W. T.; Alekozai, E.; Cheng, X.; Lindner, B.; Smith, J.; Urban, V. S.; Davison, B. H.; Langan, P.; O'Neill, H.
text: Enzymes that degrade insoluble polymers must couple catalytic chemistry to productive engagement with heterogeneous substrate interfaces, yet direct structural information on these interfacial states remains limited. We investigated the conformational organization of the processive cellulaseTrichoderma reeseiCel7A both free in solution and bound to an insoluble cellulose substrate using small-angle neutron scattering (SANS). Use of biosynthetically deuterated bacterial cellulose allowed the scattering contribution of the cellulose-associated Cel7A holoenzyme to be selectively highlighted using SANS with contrast matching. SANS measurements performed under conditions supporting high or low catalytic activity revealed distinct differences between the free and cellulose-bound enzyme. Under poorly active conditions, the conformational distributions of free and bound Cel7A were similar. In contrast, catalytically favorable conditions produced an additional interdomain correlation in the bound enzyme, consistent with redistribution toward a substrate-selected conformational ensemble. Molecular dynamics simulations showed that free Cel7A samples can assume compact, intermediate, and extended conformations, but these solution-state ensembles did not reproduce the structural features of cellulose-bound Cel7A. These results identify productive cellulose engagement as a structurally distinct state of the Cel7A holoenzyme and support a dynamic model in which the linker and carbohydrate-binding module modulate interfacial positioning of the catalytic domain rather than functioning as a rigid mechanical unit during processive hydrolysis. More broadly, the findings suggest that heterogeneous biocatalysis depends not only on substrate binding and active-site chemistry, but also on interface-selected conformational states that determine whether binding becomes productive. The study further demonstrates how deuteration and neutron contrast variation can reveal functional macromolecular conformations directly within complex interfacial environments. Enzymes that degrade insoluble polymers operate under fundamentally different constraints from enzymes acting on soluble substrates. In addition to catalyzing bond cleavage, these enzymes must first interact with a heterogeneous solid–liquid interface, identify accessible polymer segments or chain ends, and form a catalytically competent complex. Depending on the system, efficient turnover may then require processive movement along the polymer, repeated cycles of dissociation and rebinding, or sustained surface association. Consequently, the overall efficiency of polymer degradation reflects not only active-site chemistry but also substrate accessibility, productive and nonproductive adsorption, polymer-chain engagement, processive motion, and eventual dissociation1,2. These features are evident across enzymes acting on crystalline polysaccharides such as cellulose, chitin, and starch, as well as in emerging studies of enzymes that depolymerize synthetic polymers such as polyethylene terephthalate (PET)2–7. Bacteria and fungi secrete a variety of enzymes that act synergistically to degrade the crystalline fibrous cellulosic component of plant cell walls into soluble sugars. One of the most extensively studied cellulases is the family 7 cellobiohydrolase Cel7A fromTrichoderma reesei, which represents a major component of the extracellular cellulase system of this fungus8. Cel7A is a processive enzyme that acts predominantly on free reducing ends of individual cellulose chains exposed at the surface of cellulose fibrils and cleaves cellobiose units as it proceeds9,10. It consists of an N-terminal glycoside hydrolase family 7 catalytic domain (CD) and a C-terminal family 1 carbohydrate-binding module (CBM1), connected by a short, flexible, O-glycosylated, proline/serine/threonine-rich linker. High-resolution structures of the catalytic domain and CBM have been determined independently by crystallography and NMR, respectively, and identified an approximately 50Å long tunnel in the catalytic domain capable of accommodating a single cellulose chain11–13. Direct high-speed atomic force microscopy subsequently demonstrated unidirectional processive movement of Cel7A on crystalline cellulose at approximately 3.5 nm s⁻¹. Notably, the isolated catalytic domain moved at a similar velocity, indicating that the catalytic domain itself contains the essential machinery for processive translocation, whereas the CBM and linker modulate interactions of the holoenzyme with the cellulose interface14. Despite intensive study, the binding mechanism ofT. reeseiCel7A to cellulose by both the CD and CDM is not understood fully and cannot be described simply as formation of a single enzyme– substrate complex. Recent single-molecule measurements have shown that cellulose-bound Cel7A molecules populate kinetically distinct states. Haviland et al. tracked more than 11,000 individual quantum dot labeled Cel7A molecules and found that most surface-associated molecules remained static during the observation period, whereas a smaller population underwent processive motion; individual enzymes could also transition between static and moving states15. These observations support a mechanistic distinction between adsorption to the cellulose surface, productive complexation of a cellulose chain within the catalytic tunnel, processive hydrolysis, and stalled or nonproductive binding. The individual steps can also be perturbed independently. For example, single-molecule analysis of product inhibition showed that cellobiose both decreases the initial association of Cel7A with cellulose and reduces the velocity and run length of enzymes that have already entered a processive state16. Thus, an important unresolved question is how productive engagement with cellulose is reflected in the structure and interdomain organization of the intact Cel7A holoenzyme. The flexible linker and CBM are likely to be important in defining this interfacial conformational landscape. Early models proposed that the linker coordinates the catalytic domain and CBM through compression–extension motions that allow the two domains to advance along cellulose in a “caterpillar-like” manner, with the CBM helping to localize or extract cellulose chains while the catalytic domain performs processive hydrolysis17–19. Deletion or removal of the linker and CBM can reduce binding and activity on crystalline cellulose, demonstrating that these regions make important contributions to holoenzyme function20. However, the observation that the isolated catalytic domain is itself capable of processive motion argues against a requirement for the CBM to act as a mechanical motor during every catalytic step14. Instead, subsequent computational and experimental work has emphasized the dynamic nature of the multidomain enzyme. Simulations of full-length Cel7A indicate that O-glycosylation of the linker restricts its conformational ensemble, favors more extended conformations, and promotes coordinated motion between the catalytic domain and CBM21. These findings suggest that the linker and CBM may regulate the probability and geometry of productive interfacial engagement rather than functioning simply as a mechanical spring. Although atomic level crystallographic information on the holoenzyme has so far been elusive, its solution conformation has been studied with SAXS and SANS revealing insights into pH dependent conformational changes that can be correlated to its catalytic activity and the effect of O-glycosylation on the linker domain on the interaction of the CD and CBM22–24. Nevertheless, direct experimental structural information on the intact Cel7A holoenzyme while associated with insoluble cellulose remains limited. A major technical challenge in investigating enzyme action at heterogeneous biological interfaces is the difficulty in obtaining molecular-level information when the enzyme is bound to an insoluble substrate. Small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) provides a means of overcoming this limitation because isotopic substitution can generate contrast between enzyme and the insoluble substrates. This was demonstrated in a recent study that investigated a deuterium-labeled multidomain lytic polysaccharide monooxygenase binding to a chitin substrate25. In the present study, bacterial cellulose was biosynthetically deuterated26,27so that its scattering contribution could be strongly attenuated by contrast matching, allowing the scattering from cellulose-associatedT. reeseiCel7A to be examined independently. We used contrast-variation SANS together with molecular dynamics simulations to compare the conformational ensembles of Cel7A free in solution and bound to cellulose under conditions that support either high or low catalytic activity. Specifically, we asked whether cellulose association alters the interdomain organization of the intact enzyme, whether catalytically active and poorly active binding conditions produce distinguishable conformational ensembles, and whether the resulting structures are consistent with models in which the catalytic domain and CBM remain coordinately engaged with the same cellulose chain during processive hydrolysis. In this study, we used contrast-variation SANS in combination with molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the conformational organization ofT. reeseiCel7A both free in solution and associated with an insoluble cellulose substrate. The ability to selectively attenuate the scattering contribution from deuterated bacterial cellulose provides structural information on the intact holoenzyme while it is bound to cellulose, a state that remains difficult to access using conventional high-resolution structural methods. Analysis of the SANS curves shows significant differences between free and bound Cel7A that provide insight into the relative organization of the catalytic domain (CD), linker, and carbohydrate-binding module (CBM) during cellulose hydrolysis. In particular, the conformational distributions of free and cellulose-bound Cel7A are similar at pD 7.0, where the enzyme binds cellulose but has low catalytic activity, whereas marked differences emerge at pD 4.2 and 5.3, conditions that support cellulose hydrolysis. Under these catalytically favorable conditions, the bound enzyme exhibits an enhanced correlation at approximately 46 Å that is not apparent for either free Cel7A or cellulose-bound Cel7A at pD 7.0. Together with the persistence of longer-distance correlations and similar overall maximum dimensions, these observations suggest that cellulose-bound Cel7A does not adopt a single compact structure but instead populates an ensemble containing both compact and more extended interdomain configurations. The distinction between the conformational behavior observed under active and poorly active conditions is particularly relevant in light of recent evidence that cellulose-bound Cel7A exists in multiple kinetically distinct states. Single-molecule fluorescence measurements have shown that the majority of surface-associated Cel7A molecules remain static over the period of observation, whereas a smaller population undergoes processive motion; individual enzymes can also reversibly transition between static and processive states before dissociation15,57. Haviland et al. therefore proposed that the transition from a static surface-bound state into a processive state represents an important kinetic limitation in cellulose degradation. More recently, single-molecule measurements of product inhibition demonstrated that cellobiose can inhibit both the initial interaction of Cel7A with cellulose and the velocity and run length of molecules that have already entered a processive state, further emphasizing that adsorption, productive complexation, processive hydrolysis, stalling, and dissociation represent mechanistically distinguishable steps16. The present SANS measurements do not distinguish individual productive and nonproductive molecules, and a heterogeneous population is expected even under conditions that support catalysis. Nevertheless, the emergence of a distinct interdomain correlation specifically under catalytically favorable conditions suggests that productive engagement with cellulose is associated with a redistribution of the conformational ensemble of the intact holoenzyme. We therefore interpret the active cellulose-bound state not as a single structure, but as a substrate-selected conformational ensemble that is enriched under conditions favorable for catalysis. The SANS data further indicate that this substrate-selected ensemble involves the relative organization of the CD, linker, and CBM rather than a simple global collapse of the protein. The principal peak in thep(R)distribution at approximately 24 Å is present under all conditions and is largely attributable to intradomain correlations within the catalytic domain, whereas the longer-distance features report on correlations involving the linker and CBM. At pD 4.2 and 5.3, the appearance of the additional correlation at approximately 46 Å is consistent with an increased population in which part of the linker/CBM region occupies a more defined position relative to the catalytic domain. At the same time, the longer-distance component of thep(R)distribution remains evident, indicating that extended conformations continue to be populated. Earlier molecular dynamics simulations of an isolated Cel7A linker identified free-energy minima corresponding to compressed and extended linker configurations of approximately 25 and 55 Å, respectively19. The approximately 22–24 Å separation between the principal and secondary peaks observed here under catalytically favorable conditions is therefore comparable to the length predicted for a compressed linker configuration. However, rather than implying interconversion between two rigid conformations, the present data are better interpreted as a shift in the relative populations of a heterogeneous conformational ensemble. This ensemble-based interpretation is also consistent with recent work on the Cel7A linker and its extensive glycosylation. The linker has traditionally been viewed primarily as a flexible tether connecting the CD and CBM, and deletion or removal of the linker reduces both cellulose binding and catalytic activity20. However, the glycosylated linker itself can interact dynamically with cellulose. Payne et al. showed that addition of the native glycosylated Cel7A linker to CBM1 increased its affinity for crystalline cellulose by approximately an order of magnitude compared with the isolated CBM, while molecular simulations indicated transient association of linker glycans with the cellulose surface58. Integrative modeling and molecular dynamics of full-length Cel7A subsequently demonstrated that O-glycosylation restricts the conformational ensemble of the linker, favors more elongated structures, and results in more coordinated interdomain motion. Whereas in the absence of glycosylation, substantially greater conformational plasticity and frequent compression of the CD and CBM were observed21. These studies support the view that the linker is not simply a passive tether or mechanical spring. Instead, linker flexibility and glycosylation appear to define the range and probability of interdomain configurations available to the holoenzyme and may thereby influence its interaction with the cellulose interface. The substrate-dependent changes observed in the present SANS measurements are consistent with this more dynamic role and suggest that the cellulose surface selectively stabilizes or enriches particular interdomain arrangements from the broader conformational landscape of Cel7A. The results also provide an opportunity to reconsider the classical “caterpillar” model proposed for Cel7A processivity. In the original model, both the CD and CBM remain associated with the same cellulose chain and coordinated compression and extension of the linker allow the domains to advance alternately along the substrate17–19. Such a model is attractive because it provides a mechanical role for the multidomain architecture of the enzyme. However, subsequent experiments have demonstrated that the essential processive movement is intrinsic to the catalytic domain. High-speed atomic force microscopy directly visualized Cel7A moving unidirectionally along crystalline cellulose at approximately 3.5 nm s⁻¹ and showed that removal of the CBM did not eliminate processive movement, indicating that the catalytic domain contains the principal machinery required for chain engagement and translocation14. Current models of processive glycoside hydrolases likewise emphasize the energetic coupling among polymer-chain complexation, decrystallization, movement through the catalytic tunnel, hydrolysis, product release, and decomplexation rather than requiring a mechanically stepping CBM1. Our SANS-constrained simulations are consistent with this revised view. None of the conformations sampled in simulations of Cel7A free in solution accurately reproduced the secondary correlation observed experimentally for cellulose-bound Cel7A under active conditions, suggesting that interaction with the cellulose interface stabilizes or enriches conformations that are poorly sampled in solution. Furthermore, simulations in which the catalytic cleft faced the cellulose surface and the CD and CBM were constrained to the same cellulose strand, while their separation was varied over a broad range, did not reproduce the secondary feature of the experimentalp(R)distributions. Thus, the data are not readily explained by a simple configuration in which the CD and CBM remain simultaneously constrained to a single cellulose chain throughout the catalytic cycle. Importantly, this result does not exclude coordinated motions of the two domains or transient simultaneous surface contact, nor does it establish a unique alternative geometry. Rather, it argues against the most restrictive interpretation of the caterpillar mechanism in which the CBM that mechanically advances with the catalytic domain along the same cellulose strand. A more flexible model is consistent with both the present results and the recent literature. The CBM may primarily increase the probability that Cel7A remains localized at the cellulose interface, while the glycosylated linker permits the catalytic domain to explore different positions and orientations relative to the surface. This arrangement would allow the CD to engage accessible reducing chain ends or chain breaks while the CBM remains associated elsewhere on the fibril. Earlier biochemical studies showing that the linker and CBM increase cellulose affinity and affect catalytic efficiency are compatible with such a role20,58. At the single-molecule level, the existence of static, processive, and stalled surface-bound populations further suggests that productive engagement is not determined simply by whether Cel7A is adsorbed to cellulose, but by whether the catalytic domain can adopt a geometry that permits chain complexation and entry into the catalytic tunnel15,16. The enhanced interdomain correlation observed here may therefore reflect a substrate-selected configuration, or family of configurations, associated with this transition. Some of the MD conformations consistent with the additionalp(R)feature contain a pronounced bend in the linker, raising the possibility that the CD can transiently move away from direct contact with the cellulose surface while the CBM remains associated. Our data do not require such detachment, however, the low spatial resolution and ensemble nature of SANS preclude assignment of a unique trajectory. We therefore regard transient CD repositioning or detachment as a mechanistic model consistent with the observations rather than as a direct structural conclusion. The substrate-dependent conformational selection observed here may reflect a more general requirement for enzymes acting on recalcitrant polymers to reorganize upon productive engagement with a solid interface. Processive chitinases provide a particularly close mechanistic comparison. Like Cel7A,Serratia marcescenschitinase A acts processively on a crystalline polysaccharide using an extended substrate-binding cleft. Single-molecule measurements showed approximately 1-nm forward and backward steps during processive movement and demonstrated that extraction, or decrystallization, of a single chitin chain from the crystal surface is considerably slower than the glycosidic-bond cleavage reaction itself2. Thus, for both cellulose and chitin degradation, productive catalysis requires coupling active-site chemistry to the physical problems of polymer-chain capture, decrystallization, translocation, and maintenance of a catalytically competent interfacial complex. In this context, the structural redistribution observed for Cel7A may represent one manifestation of a broader mechanistic principle: interaction with a heterogeneous polymer surface selects among multiple enzyme conformations, only a subset of which are compatible with productive substrate engagement. A similar distinction between adsorption and productive engagement is emerging for enzymes that degrade synthetic insoluble polymers. Fluorescence measurements of PET hydrolases have revealed slow adsorption/desorption dynamics and long-lived surface-associated populations, highlighting that strong or persistent surface association is not necessarily equivalent to productive catalysis59. Although PET hydrolases are not generally considered processive like Cel7A, they face the same requirement to transition from nonspecific or weakly productive surface association into a geometry that permits polymer-chain engagement and bond cleavage. These systems therefore reinforce the broader relevance of distinguishing among solution, adsorbed, productively engaged, stalled or nonproductive, and dissociated states when considering enzymes that act at insoluble polymer interfaces. Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the present results. First, SANS measures a population-averaged conformational ensemble and cannot identify the catalytic state of individual surface-bound molecules. The samples therefore almost certainly contain mixtures of adsorbed, productively engaged, processive, stalled, and nonproductive Cel7A, even at pD values that favor cellulose hydrolysis. Second, alteration of pD changes the conformational equilibrium of Cel7A in solution as well as its catalytic activity, making it difficult to assign every structural difference exclusively to catalysis. Third, the structural information obtained from SANS is low resolution, so individual domain orientations and transient contacts cannot be uniquely assigned. Finally, the constrained MD simulations test defined classes of surface-bound configurations, so failure of a particular configuration to reproduce the experimental scattering excludes that model under the imposed constraints but does not uniquely specify the geometry of the productive complex. These limitations argue for an ensemble-level interpretation of the data and against assigning the scattering observations to a single molecular trajectory. The combined contrast-variation SANS and molecular dynamics results show that productive engagement ofT. reeseiCel7A with cellulose is accompanied by its reorganization into a substrate-selected ensemble that is distinct from the conformations sampled in solution. Under catalytically favorable conditions, cellulose-bound Cel7A exhibits structural correlations not observed for the free enzyme or for the poorly active bound state, indicating that adsorption alone is insufficient to define the catalytically relevant configuration. The inability of models in which the catalytic domain and CBM are constrained to the same cellulose strand, to reproduce the bound-state scattering argues against a simple rigid caterpillar-like mechanism and instead supports a more dynamic model in which the CBM maintains interfacial localization while the glycosylated linker allows the catalytic domain to explore positions and orientations compatible with productive chain engagement, processive hydrolysis, and release. More broadly, these findings support the view that heterogeneous biocatalysis is governed not only by active-site chemistry and substrate affinity, but also by interface-selected conformational states that determine whether binding becomes productive. The study also demonstrates the advantage of neutron scattering using biosynthetic deuteration and contrast matching. Nanoscale structural information can be obtained for proteins operating at complex interfaces under functionally relevant conditions. This approach should be broadly applicable to other enzymes and biomolecules that function at insoluble polymer surfaces and in heterogeneous biological environments, where the conformational states most relevant to activity may be inaccessible to conventional structural methods. title: Parvalbumin interneuron maturation reorganizes cortical population activity structure during development
author: Wu, M. W.; Mariani, M.; Suresh, A.; Kourdougli, N.; Jiang, G.; Kothari, A. J.; Jain, T. S.; Dipoppa, M.; Portera-Cailliau, C.
text: During brain development, spontaneous cortical activity undergoes a dramatic transformation from highly synchronous network events to less correlated and sparse neuronal firing that is thought to underlie more flexible neural coding. However, how the structure of population activity changes across this transition, what circuit mechanisms drive this reorganization, and the implications for information encoding have not been fully established. Using longitudinal in vivo calcium imaging in early postnatal mice, we demonstrate that cortical network desynchronization during the second postnatal week is accompanied by a redistribution of fractional variance from dominant, low-dimensional modes into many weaker dimensions, and a growing influence of GABAergic interneurons (INs) on the network. All-optical circuit interrogation revealed that parvalbumin (PV) INs, but not somatostatin (SST) INs, are sufficient to desynchronize the network and shift the distribution of population variance. Through targeted ablation of a fraction of PV INs, we show dimensionality is highly correlated with stimulus decoding accuracy. Furthermore, PV INs undergo a sharp increase in transcriptional maturation between postnatal day (P) 8 and 11, during which they preferentially enrich for synaptic genes. Lastly, a novel, biologically plausible, multi-cell-type computational model reproduced the developmental desynchronization and rise in dimensionality. Strikingly, without being constrained by perturbation data, the model accurately predicted the effects of each IN class on the network that we observed empirically. Spontaneous network activity in the cerebral cortex undergoes a dramatic transformation during development from an initial pattern that is dominated by intermittent, highly synchronous bursts of neuronal firing to a sparse and continuous pattern that is typical of the mature brain1–4. In rodents, this transition occurs during the second postnatal week and is characterized by reduced pairwise correlations between neurons, an increased frequency of population events, and a decreased neuronal participation in those events5–9. This developmental transformation of cortical network dynamics is thought to be of fundamental importance because of its implications for neural computation4,5,10,11. However, although the phenomenology of this network transition and the contributions of sensory input in generating synchronous bursts have been well characterized12–15, neither the circuit mechanisms that underlie this transition nor its consequences for neural population coding have been elucidated. One influential framework for cortical computation proposes that primary sensory cortices implement sparse and distributed population codes16–18, which are predicted to support a high-dimensional representational space with large coding capacity19. In the adult cortex, neural population activity occupies a high-dimensional state space, with both sensory-evoked and spontaneous activity exhibiting variance distributed across many dimensions20,21. Although pairwise correlations decrease during development, it remains unclear how this transition gives rise to the high-dimensional population activity characteristic of the mature cortex. Recent work has shown that spontaneous cortical activity becomes higher-dimensional across the second postnatal week22, suggesting that this developmental transition involves a reorganization of the structure of population activity. How this reorganization emerges mechanistically, and its consequences for the cortex’s coding capacity, remain unknown. A leading candidate mechanism for this developmental reorganization is the maturation of cortical inhibitory circuits. In particular, GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) born in the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE) undergo a prolonged maturation process that extends postnatally23–25, coinciding with the developmental window during which cortical population activity decorrelates. The MGE gives rise to two major classes of IN, parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SST), which express an overlapping sequence of transcription factors throughout their embryonic and early postnatal development in mice26–28. Despite this shared lineage, PV and SST INs target different compartments of excitatory (Exc) neurons to differentially shape cortical network activity29. Recent studies have begun to uncover how manipulating inhibitory activity affects network synchrony, such that broad optogenetic activation of GABAergic INs decorrelates spontaneous cortical activity30while chemogenetic activation of SST INs increases spontaneous correlations31. However, whether specific IN subtypes drive the developmental expansion of population dimensionality has never been explored. Here, we investigate how the structure of population activity reorganizes across development and identify the circuit and cellular mechanisms that drive the emergence of high-dimensional cortical activity. Because interneuron (IN) subtypes act within recurrent circuitry, a computational model is crucial to establish how each subtype contributes to developmental desynchronization. However, no existing mechanistic model combines all the features needed to address this problem: recurrent connectivity, single-neuron resolution, IN-subtype specificity, and slow population fluctuations at the correlation levels measured over the second postnatal week. In fact, several existing models of developmental changes in that time period are feedforward and thus lack recurrent connectivity32–34or single-cell resolution35,36. Meanwhile, population models with single-neuron resolution did not differentiate between IN subtypes30,37or, in their mechanistic versions, did not consider a sufficiently long span of developmental age and fluctuations generated intrinsically by the network38. Existing recurrent multi-cell-type models of intrinsic neural synchrony with single-neuron resolution39,40focus on the adult mouse brain and consistently show faster fluctuations than those observed in development. Conversely, models with emergent slow fluctuations in neural activity either lack the single-neuron resolution needed to study dimensionality of neural activity41or they require synchronous events to be driven exogenously42. Finally, single-neuron resolution models capable of generating slow-rate fluctuations exhibit average neuronal correlations that are much weaker than those observed experimentally43. Together, these limitations motivate us to develop a recurrent, multi-cell-type circuit framework that can simultaneously capture the slow dynamics of SNEs, the structure of population activity, and the experimentally observed levels of correlation, enabling us to investigate which circuit mechanisms drive the reorganization of cortical dynamics. By leveraging longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of excitatory and MGE INs, we found that population activity increases its dimensionality during the second postnatal week through a redistribution of fractional variance (the proportion of population activity patterns explained by each dimension) from a few dominant dimensions to many weaker ones. Optogenetic activation of PV but not SST INs at P10 partially recapitulated the restructuring of population activity. Through single-nucleus RNA-sequencing analyses, we identified P8-P11 as a major transition period for the transcriptional maturation of MGE INs, during which PV and SST INs manifest unique gene-level implementations within shared pathways. We also link population dimensionality to stimulus encoding. Finally, we developed a multi-cell-type recurrent circuit model of early postnatal cortical network activity that recapitulates major experimentally observed features of developmental network reorganization, predicts qualitatively the effects of PV IN activation observed in the data, and identifies circuit mechanisms that can account for coordinated changes in network dynamics. To record the activity of excitatory (Exc) and inhibitory (Inh) neurons in S1, we performed longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging (GCaMP8s, 15.1 Hz) from P9 to P14 in head-fixed Nkx2.1-Cre;Ai14 mice that express tdTom in MGE-derived INs44(Figures 1AandS1A). At P9, network activity appeared as episodic bursts of activity involving large numbers of both Exc and Inh neurons, whereas at P14 activity was continuous and sparse (Figure 1B). Quantification of the properties of synchronous network events (SNEs), defined as periods in which a higher-than-chance proportion of neurons are simultaneously active, showed that their frequency significantly increased from P9 to P13 (Figure 1C), while their duration decreased (Figure S1B). During this period, the fraction of Exc neurons recruited per SNE was reduced by half, from ∼40% at P9 to ∼20% at P13 (Figure 1D). In contrast, Inh neurons were more globally and stably recruited across the second postnatal week, with 60-80% of the population participating in SNEs regardless of age (Figure 1D). Both the Exc population, despite its decline in recruitment, and the Inh population become more heterogeneous in their participation across SNEs at older ages, as reflected by an increasing coefficient of variation (Figure S1C), suggesting that the neurons being recruited are increasingly variable across SNEs. Consistent with previous work, we observed a decline in Exc-Exc pairwise correlations between P9 and P135,22. This trajectory was significantly different than that of Inh-Inh pairwise correlations, which remained elevated after P10 (Figure 1E). Analyzing pairwise correlations as a function of distance between neurons revealed that the distance-dependence of Exc-Exc correlations decays more than that of the Inh-Inh correlations (Figure S1D), in accordance with previous findings5,45. Furthermore, Exc-Exc and Inh-Inh correlations were significantly greater than chance at both P9 and P14, although for Exc-Exc pairs the difference was much smaller at P14 than for Inh-Inh pairs (Figure S1E). To characterize how spontaneous population activity is organized during development, we applied principal component analysis (PCA), which decomposes population activity into orthogonal modes (principal components, PC) that can be ordered by the fraction of variance they explain (fractional variance; eigenvalues normalized by total variance, i.e., the sum of all eigenvalues) (Figure 1F). From this decomposition we derived the participation ratio (PR), a summary statistic that estimates the effective dimensionality of a population by quantifying how evenly fractional variance is distributed across PCs46. The previously described age-dependent increase in SNE frequency and decrease in Exc-Exc correlations were accompanied by a dramatic increase in PR for the excitatory population (Figure 1G), indicating a developmental shift toward higher-dimensional activity. To examine this shift across the full dimensionality of the data, rather than the single value captured by PR, we next inspected the eigenspectrum, the normalized eigenvalues ranked in descending order, which describes how fractional variance is distributed across all dimensions of population activity (Figure 1F; see Methods). The increase in participation ratio (Figure 1G) indicates that the distribution of eigenvalues becomes less concentrated across development, but this could be consistent with different spectrum shapes. To further investigate different possibilities, we first examined how the eigenspectrum of population activity changes between P9 and P14 using random subsamples of neurons (see Methods). At P9, fractional variance was concentrated in the leading dimensions, with a relatively steep decay across dimensions. In contrast, at P14, the fractional variance spectrum was less concentrated in the leading dimensions and more evenly distributed across dimensions, leading to a shallower eigenspectrum than at P9 (Figure 1H). Thus, fractional variance is redistributed from the leading dimensions into the later dimensions, producing a crossover in the eigenspectrum. To confirm that our subsample size was sufficient to capture spectral shape, we repeated this analysis across a range of subsample sizes (Figure S2A; see Methods). Although fractional variance showed more spread across subsampling levels at P14, spectra that were rescaled relative to the mean variance of the top 5 PCs (to enable shape comparison by aligning the spectra to the top components, which are most stable across subsampling levels) aligned well at early and intermediate ranks down to subsamples of just 180 neurons, indicating that subsamples of 180 neurons or larger reliably capture spectral shape. At both ages, spectra were unstable at the tail, reflecting proximity to the noise floor. While PCA captures all variance, it does not distinguish between variance that is reproducible across time and variance that reflects transient or noisy neural activity. Therefore, we next applied a variation of shared variance component analysis (SVCA, modified from Stringer et al.21; see Methods) to estimate temporally reliable variance, defined as the variance shared across non-overlapping time windows (i.e., shared variance). Fractional shared variance was more evenly distributed across dimensions at P14 compared to at P9 (Figure 1I), reflecting the redistribution of fractional variance seen in the PCA eigenspectrum. In the adult cortex, the eigenspectrum and shared variance spectrum follow an approximate power law20,21. During the second postnatal week, the spectra are not linear on a log-log scale, suggesting that this organizational principle of mature population activity has not yet emerged. However, to quantify the difference in spectral shape between ages, we estimated the decay exponent (α) over an intermediate range of dimensions. The decay exponent was significantly smaller at P14 than at P9 for both PCA and SVCA (Figure 1J), indicating a shallower spectral decay and a progression towards a more distributed spectrum. Additionally, we found that the reliable variance fraction, defined as the ratio of SVCA to PCA fractional variance at matched ranks, increased broadly across all dimensions at P14 compared to P9 (Figure S2B), indicating that a larger fraction of overall population activity is temporally reliable across the spectrum. Thus, the circuit at P14 reorganizes how fractional shared variance is distributed across dimensions, resulting in a population that explores more dimensions and does so more consistently. Overall, these findings demonstrate that cortical network activity undergoes a profound transformation over just a few days during the second postnatal week, achieving a higher dimensionality consistent with the more distributed population geometry reported in the adult cortex21. Whereas the eigenspectrum describes how much variance each PC explains, the PC loadings describe which neuron types, Exc or Inh, contribute (Figure 1K). Our recordings in Nkx2.1-Cre;Ai14 mice allowed us to examine the contributions of Exc and Inh neurons to each dimension. At P9, Exc and Inh neurons contributed to each PC in proportion to their numeric representation, consistent with the population variance having no cell type-specific organization (Figure 1L). In contrast, at P14, Inh neurons were overrepresented in the leading components. Both z-scored and mean-centered (Figure S2C; see Methods) analyses concur, suggesting that the dominant modes of population activity become preferentially shaped by inhibitory circuits across development regardless of variance in activity. This aligns with the timing of when MGE INs are integrated into cortical circuits during this postnatal period3,23,27. However, even though inhibition becomes more dominant in the leading PCs, this does not establish whether the redistribution of fractional variance is causally driven by inhibition, or which inhibitory subtype is responsible. Previous studies had hinted at a role for GABAergic INs in mediating the desynchronization of network activity30,31,47,48. However, none of these prior studies examined the impact of such manipulations on population structure and dimensionality. To address this important question, we used acute cell type-specific optogenetic perturbations to determine whether transient activation of either of the MGE IN classes – PV or SST – is sufficient to reproduce the redistribution of variance observed between P9 and P14. To selectively target PV INs, we generated Nkx2.1-Cre;Sst-FlpO mice and injected rAAV8-nEF1-Con/Foff-ChRmine-oScarlet into S1 at P1 (see Methods, adapted from Kourdougli et al.47). We then acutely activated the excitatory opsin ChRmine in vivo by scanning a 1,040 nm laser across the field of view (6 trials, 10s on / 20s off) while simultaneously recording Exc and PV neurons at P10, P12, and P14 (Figures 2Aand2B). ChRmine expression was already robust at P10, as indicated by oScarlet expression (Figure S3A). Acute activation of PV INs robustly suppressed network activity, significantly reducing SNE frequency during stimulation, an effect that became stronger across development (Figure 2C). Pairwise correlations were also significantly reduced during PV IN activation at all ages (Figure 2D). This reduction was largest at P10, even after controlling for the reduced firing rate of Exc neurons49(Figures 2EandS3D). Additionally, at P10, but not at the older ages, the decrease in correlation was strongest for nearby neuron pairs, revealing a spatially localized effect of PV IN activation (Figure 2F). Differences in PV IN recruitment by optogenetic stimulation could not account for the effect on pairwise correlations, as activating even a small number of PV INs was sufficient to drive network desynchronization, and the percentage of stimulus responsive neurons did not predict the magnitude of the change in correlation (Figure S3E). Of note, the PV INs that we identified as being responsive to optogenetic activation likely represent only a subset of the true responsive population, since our assessment was restricted to cells that co-expressed ChRmine and GCaMP8s. The observed effects on SNE frequency and pairwise correlations were also robust to the choice of protocol, as delivering optogenetic stimulation across 20 shorter trials (1s on / 3s off) produced similar reductions in SNE frequency and pairwise correlations (Figures S4A-S4C). Control experiments in animals expressing mCherry alone (no opsin) produced no change in SNE frequency or correlations during laser stimulation (Figures S4D-S4F), confirming that the observed effects are due to optogenetic activation of PV INs and not to optical artifacts. Given that PV IN activation acutely desynchronizes cortical activity at P10, we next tested whether this manipulation is sufficient to reshape the structure of population activity similar to normal development. At P10, PV IN activation produced a significant increase in fractional variance in the intermediate-rank components, with no significant change in the leading components (Figure 2G). More strongly, PV IN activation significantly reduced the leading components and increased the intermediate-rank components of fractional shared variance (Figure 2H), in essence shifting its distribution in the direction of development. For both PCA and SVCA eigenspectra, the estimated decay exponent (α) over an intermediate range of dimensions was significantly smaller during PV IN activation (Figure 2I), indicating a more evenly distributed variance, just as we had observed during development (Figure 1J). Together, these results show that optogenetically engaging PV INs is sufficient to shift the distribution of fractional shared variance in the direction of the developmental transition during the second postnatal week. The effect of PV IN activation on the distribution of fractional variance was greatest at P10, before the network desynchronizes, and was absent from the fractional variance eigenspectrum by P14, when cortical desynchronization is largely complete (Figure S3F). However, PV IN activation did produce a significant shift in fractional shared variance at P14, suggesting that PV IN activation at P14 modulates the reliability of activity within an already-redistributed framework, rather than further reorganizing the population structure itself. We next tested whether activation of SST INs produces similar effects on population activity, using Sst-FlpO mice and injecting a rAAV8-nEF1-Coff/Fon-ChRmine-oScarlet virus (Figures 3A, 3B, S5A,andS5B). Putative SST INs were identified by their reliable responses to optogenetic stimulation and were excluded from subsequent analyses. Similar to PV IN experiments, optogenetic activation of SST INs significantly reduced the frequency of SNEs across development, with larger effects at later ages (Figure 3C). However, SST IN activation did not consistently reduce pairwise correlations at any age (Figures 3D, S5C,andS5D). At P10, there was a modest increase in pairwise correlations at higher firing rates and for nearby neurons (Figures 3Eand3F). Therefore, while SST IN activation suppressed network activity, it failed to desynchronize the population, underscoring the unique role of PV INs in shaping network synchrony during development. We next tested whether SST IN activation would alter the structure of population activity. SST IN activation did not significantly alter the fractional variance eigenspectrum at either early or intermediate dimensions (Figure 3G), and only minimally altered the fractional shared variance spectrum (Figure 3H) at P10. Consistent with this, the estimated decay exponent (α) over an intermediate range of dimensions for both PCA and SVCA eigenspectra did not significantly change between baseline and SST activation at P10 (Figure 3I). Interestingly, SST IN activation did produce a significant shift in fractional variance at P14, with a significant reduction in early dimensions in the PCA eigenspectrum and significant effects at both early and intermediate dimensions in the SVCA spectrum (Figure S5E). The emergence of this effect at P14 but not P10 suggests a dependence on circuit maturation state. Thus, at P10, before the network desynchronizes, SST INs can suppress SNEs without producing a detectable shift in population structure, consistent with the idea that reducing network activity alone is insufficient to shift the distribution of variance across dimensions, and that this ability is specific to PV INs. We next investigated the molecular pathways underlying MGE IN maturation during the few days of postnatal development when network activity undergoes its dramatic transformation to better understand why PV INs might play a more protagonist role than SST INs and to explore whether cell type-specific changes in gene expression across relevant pathways might explain the circuit level functional differences. To address this, we performed single nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) in S1 at P9 and P11 (Figures S6A-S6E). We also reanalyzed a rich snRNA-seq dataset of primary visual cortex (V1) from Gao et al.28to compare the transcriptional programs of PV and SST INs at this critical age (Figure 4A). We first compared the maturation trajectories of PV and SST INs using pseudobulk gene expression profiles across developmental timepoints relative to mature (P56) reference profiles (see Methods). Maturation was quantified as convergence towards the adult transcriptional state using two complementary metrics, Spearman correlation and Euclidean distance. These metrics measure, respectively, how close the relative ordering of genes is to the mature state at P56 (gene expression hierarchy), and how far expression levels are from the same mature state (gene expression magnitude), which we can use to infer maturational state. Across both metrics, both PV and SST INs exhibited a gradual developmental maturation toward the P56 state (Figure 4B). The most pronounced change, however, occurred between P8 and P11, identifying this window as a major transition for transcriptional maturation. Spearman correlation increased sharply over this interval, with the P8-P11 transition accounting for 36.0% of the total increase in transcriptional similarity between P2 and P56 in PV INs and 39.6% of the total increase in SST INs, indicating rapid alignment of gene expression hierarchy with the mature state. Euclidean distance decreased in parallel during the P8-P11 interval, accounting for 36.0% of the total reduction in transcriptional distance from P2 to P56 in PV INs and 46.5% of the total reduction in SST INs, reflecting substantial convergence in gene expression magnitude (Figure 4B). Thus, both classes of MGE INs experience a remarkable degree of transcriptional maturation during a narrow developmental window that coincides with the postnatal period in which we observed dramatic changes in network synchrony and population geometry. We next investigated whether PV and SST INs differ in their transcriptional regulatory mechanisms. We performed gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis on each cell type and assessed changes in transcription factor (TF) regulon activity between P8 and P11, focusing on TFs showing significant up- or downregulation. The majority of significant regulons were shared between PV and SST INs (Figure 4C). The shared transcriptional regulatory programs identified by GRN analysis might suggest that PV and SST INs experience similar functional changes during this period. To probe the functional significance of the transcriptomic changes at P8-P11, we performed pathway enrichment analysis. Genes were classified based on their contribution to changes in gene expression hierarchy (gene program) or expression magnitude (magnitude). Consistent with the convergent regulatory programs, PV and SST INs showed similar pathway-level changes (Figure 4D). In both cell types, maturation was characterized by upregulation of pathways associated with neuronal signaling and synapse organization, alongside downregulation of pathways associated with protein translation, RNA processing, and genome maintenance (Figure S7A). Fewer pathways were driven by changes in gene expression hierarchy alone (Figure S7A), suggesting that while large-scale reorganization of gene expression contributes to maturation, it is not the dominant driver at the pathway level; rather, maturation reflects quantitative scaling of gene expression within established programs. Given this pathway-level similarity, we next asked whether differences between PV and SST INs might emerge at the level of individual genes within shared pathways. Because theNeuronal Systempathway exhibited both the strongest enrichment and the largest gene set for both PV and SST INs among the pathways commonly upregulated during the transcriptional maturation window, we focused on gene-level contributions within this pathway. PV INs preferentially enriched for genes associated with fast synaptic transmission, including ion channels, synaptic vesicle components, and ligand-gated receptors. In contrast, SST-biased genes were predominantly associated with postsynaptic signaling and dendritic integration, including glutamate receptors, metabotropic receptors, and synaptic scaffolding proteins (Figure 4E), a profile consistent with the preferential upregulation of theGPCR Signalingpathway in SST INs (Figure 4D). To assess whether these cell type-specific gene expression patterns generalize across sensory cortical regions, we examined PV and SST INs in our own snRNA-seq dataset obtained from S1 and spanning a similar developmental window (P9-P11) (Figures S6A-S6D). We discovered that PV INs in S1 showed the same preferential expression of genes associated with synaptic transmission relative to SST INs (Figure 4E), indicating that the differential implementation of molecular programs across MGE subtypes is conserved across primary sensory cortical areas. Thus, we describe a two-tiered organization of MGE IN maturation during the P8-P11 transition. At the regulatory and pathway level, PV and SST INs execute a largely shared transcriptional program, engaging overlapping GRNs and converging on the same broad functional categories. However, within these shared pathways, the two cell types diverge in their specific gene-level implementations, with PV INs elaborating the machinery for fast, precise synaptic output and SST INs focusing on modulatory signaling. This pattern, which is conserved across primary sensory cortical areas, describes a common maturation framework that is differentially tuned, allowing for progressive specialization of each IN subtype. The rapid developmental transformation of the cortical network to a higher-dimensional regime is thought to result in a sparse and distributed coding scheme16,17,20. Given that PV INs are critical for this transition, we next sought to disrupt PV INs to test whether perturbations in the network impact how the S1 population represents sensory information. Instead of brief optogenetic silencing, we triggered programmed cell death in a small fraction of PV INs to permanently remove them from the network after P9. This manipulation is clinically relevant, as a reduced density of PV INs has been reported in human brain tissue from cases diagnosed with Fragile X syndrome50and in several mouse models of autism spectrum disorder (ASD)51, and is likely caused by excess developmental cell death47. We selectively expressed the cell death protein Caspase-3 in PV INs by injecting the Cre-dependent rAAV5-Flex-taCasp3 into S1 at P9 (Figure 5A). This resulted in a ∼20% decrease in the density of PV INs in S1 of the injected hemisphere relative to contralateral S1 (Figures S8AandS8B), which matches the reduced PV IN density reported inFmr1andShank3mutant mice47,50,52–54. This modest reduction in PV IN density resulted in a trend toward elevated pairwise correlations in the Caspase-3 group at P14 (Figure 5B), although the mean PCA eigenspectrum did not show a clear change (Figure 5C). To assess whether PV cell loss affects sensory encoding, we performed a whisker stimulation assay consisting of 100 trials of brief (50 ms) single-whisker deflections with two different stimulus amplitudes presented in random order (see Methods) (Figure 5D). We trained a linear decoder to classify stimulus identity from population activity in S1 using the most stimulus-selective neurons (top 20% by d’). Decoding accuracy was similar between control and Caspase-3 groups (Figure S8C), indicating that stimulus information is preserved with a modest reduction in PV IN density. Importantly, we observed a much stronger correlation between population dimensionality during the stimulation period and decoding accuracy in the Caspase-3 group (Figure 5E), though not in the control group (Figure 5F). Although population dimensionality spanned a similar range across groups, decoding accuracy in the Caspase-3 group covaried more strongly with dimensionality, suggesting that PV IN ablation alters stimulus encoding in proportion to the degree of dimensionality reduction. We sought to reproduce the slow, second-scale dynamics of SNEs while generating these events intrinsically within a recurrent, single-neuron-resolution, multi-cell-type circuit model. Existing models of developmental desynchronization30,32–35,37,38incorporate only a subset of these network properties while recurrent, single-neuron-resolution, multi-cell-type circuit models that focus on the adult mouse brain and support intrinsically generated fluctuations39,40do not reproduce the second timescales observed in the data. Our model successfully reproduced the key features of network activity observed in calcium imaging data: at P9, neural dynamics exhibit pronounced population-wide fluctuations, characterized by alternating low- and high-activity periods with intermediate PCCs (Figure 6D); while at P14 the dynamics exhibit a more desynchronized activity pattern with heterogeneous firing across neurons and lower PCCs (Figure 6E). Synaptic connections were structured in a way that supported clustered patterns of activity43,62, in which only a subset of neurons would have elevated firing rate (local SNEs). Absent other features, such as periods of silence, this dynamic structure would exhibit unrealistically low firing rates during development43, while the simple alternation between periods of silence and global SNEs would exhibit unrealistically high correlations (Figure S9K). Our network solves this conundrum by alternating periods of silence with periods of local SNEs, which induces low but non-negligible correlations (PCC ∼0.1) compatible with the experimental data. Clustering in the excitatory connections results in clustered activity bursts and, consequently, in low PCC (Figure S9K), even in the presence of strong fluctuations in the average population rate (as measured by a bimodality index; see Methods). We sought parameter sets such that the solutions would reproduce key neural statistics63,64and developmental trajectories. Specifically, we required the model to reproduce developmental changes in average PCCs, SNE frequency, participation ratio, and strong fluctuations in the average rate. Additionally, we required the parameters to align as closely as possible with known developmental changes (Figure 6C). Although the existence of solutions exhibiting the observed changes in structure and neural dynamics was not guaranteeda priori, our network simulations revealed that such solutions exist across a broad range of parameter values. Averaging across the top 100 biologically aligned solutions confirmed that the circuit model exhibited during development: a progressive decrease in pairwise correlations between excitatory neurons (Figure 6F); an increase in the frequency of SNEs (Figure 6G); and an increase in participation ratio (Figure 6H). Finally, the model’s average excitatory firing rate exhibited a bimodal distribution at early developmental stages, corresponding to alternating low- and high-activity states, and this bimodality progressively weakened from P9 to P14 (Figure S9L). These results show that a recurrent Exc–PV–SST circuit in which excitatory and PV parameters progressively strengthen during development can reproduce the experimentally observed changes. We then asked whether our circuit model could predict changes in PCCs caused by cell-type-specific optogenetic stimulation. We considered the top biologically aligned model solutions (Figure 6), which were not specifically selected to reproduce responses to optogenetic perturbations. At P9, the prediction matches our data, as PV, but not SST, stimulation reduced spontaneous pairwise correlations (Figure 7Aand7B), as observed experimentally (Figures 2and3). By P14, both model and data show only weak effects of either manipulation (Figures 7Aand2). At P10, the distribution of PCC induced by PV stimulation was shifted toward negative values (Figure 7C), whereas the distribution for SST stimulation remained centered near zero (Figure 7D). By P14, both distributions were concentrated around zero, indicating that the effect of optogenetic perturbations on network correlations diminished with development (Figures 7Eand7F). These results were unchanged as the number of retained parameter sets increased (Figures S10AandS10B). Across the top 100 parameter sets, the optogenetically induced changes in PCC covaried with changes in network properties in the participation ratio and in SNE occupancy, defined as the fraction of time spent in synchronous network events (Figures S10C). Together, these results suggest that PV IN modulation influences network correlations by reshaping the temporal organization of collective activity. The remarkable transformation of cortical network activity that takes place during the second postnatal week in rodents (corresponding to the time of birth in humans), has been extensively characterized phenomenologically2,4,65,66. Over a period of just a few days, from P9 to P13, population activity becomes more continuous, with neurons firing sparsely, a regime that has been predicted to enable a greater coding capacity. The goals of this study were three-fold: first, to investigate the circuit and molecular mechanisms that bring about this critical developmental milestone; second, to better understand the relationship between population dynamics and information encoding; and finally, to develop a biologically plausible computational model of developmental network activity that could assist in future studies (e.g., by making predictions about potential mechanisms, etc.). Our longitudinal recordings of spontaneous activity between P9 and P14, combined with IN perturbations and single-cell transcriptomics, reveal five key findings: 1) The developmental expansion of dimensionality reflects a redistribution of fractional variance from a few leading dimensions toward a broader, more uniform distribution across the population. 2) Acute optogenetic activation of PV INs but not SST INs at P10 shifts fractional variance towards a more uniform distribution, implicating PV IN activity as a driver of the redistribution of fractional variance that accompanies dimensionality expansion during development. 3) Between P8 and P11, PV and SST INs undergo rapid transcriptional maturation but diverge in the regulation of genes associated with fast synaptic transmission, which are selectively enriched in PV INs, providing a molecular basis for their distinct functional role. 4) Networks with higher dimensionality support greater stimulus encoding capacity, linking developmental circuit-level reorganization to the cortex’s ability to represent sensory information. 5) A new computational model reproduces developmental trajectories of population activity and predicts the privileged role of PV INs in driving network desynchronization. The developmental reorganization we describe suggests that circuit maturation does not merely reflect the elaboration of existing structures or the loss of coordination but instead arises from a fundamental redistribution of fractional variance from a few dominant, synchronous modes into many weaker dimensions. The shift towards a more distributed eigenspectrum and fractional shared variance spectrum across postnatal development is a progression toward the higher-dimensional, structured spontaneous activity reported in adult primary sensory cortex21. Our optogenetics results extend previous observations using activation of a broad IN population driven by pan-GABAergic promoters such asGad2orGad6730,48by demonstrating the protagonist role of PV INs over SST INs. The acute activation of PV INs significantly decorrelated activity at P10 in a distance-dependent manner, consistent with previous work30,31. Although acute optogenetic activation of PV INs drove decorrelation, it did not completely recapitulate the redistribution of fractional variance observed in development. This could be attributed to limitations in our experimental approach, such as the fact that ChRmine was only expressed in a subset of PV INs (likely ∼30%47) or that our laser scanning was restricted to only a small volume of S1. Another possibility is that because PV INs are not fully mature, their synaptic connections, both to other PV INs and to the Exc population, have not yet reached full strength, further limiting the effect of acute PV IN activation at the early timepoint of P10. Indeed, although PV INs are functionally connected to Exc neurons at P1047, the peak of PV synaptogenesis occurs around P10-P1229. It is likely that other maturational factors are necessary as PV activation did not fully recapitulate the developmental reorganization of network activity. Besides PV INs, the significant reduction in the intrinsic excitability of the Exc population in the network may play a role. Indeed, the resting membrane potential of cortical pyramidal neurons decreases between P6-8 and P13-1667, presumably because of changes in the expression of leak conductances, including Ih, as previously proposed5. The comparatively depolarized state of the P10 network could limit how far acute PV IN activation alone can push dimensionality. Other developmental changes, such as the transition from transient excitatory corticothalamic amplification to corticothalamic recruitment of inhibition15, could also contribute. Interestingly, PV IN activation also significantly increased fractional shared variance in the intermediate dimensions at P14, though with a smaller effect size than at P10 (Figure S3F), despite no significant change in the PCA eigenspectrum. This is consistent with acute PV IN activation having a reduced capacity to further reorganize an already-redistributed population structure, while retaining a residual capacity to modulate the reliability of activity within the existing framework. Likewise, the increased ability of SST INs to shift fractional shared variance at P14 (Figure S5F) could reflect a dependence on circuit maturation; SST INs’ modulatory action may require a mature dimensional structure that is not present until later in development, potentially as a consequence of PV-mediated redistribution. Our findings add to a proposed framework in which GABAergic INs sequentially control network activity during development4,48,68. SST-expressing hub cells orchestrate network synchrony early in postnatal development69,70while PV INs become the dominant influence during the second postnatal week, undergoing a period of transcriptional maturation that gives them the ability to drive an expansion of dimensionality. This is consistent with prior studies demonstrating a role for SST INs in PV circuit maturation during the first postnatal week in both deep and superficial layers31,61. A protagonist role for PV INs in desynchronization is consistent with the timing of their maturation. They assume their chemical and electrophysiological identity at P9-P1024,60,71, as they begin to expressPvalbandKv3.1b, the potassium channel that allows them to be fast-spiking58,72,73. There is also a strengthening of reciprocal glutamatergic drive onto PV INs themselves throughout this time window74. The differential effects of PV and SST INs on correlated activity and dimensional structure may reflect cell type-specific implementation of shared maturational programs acting on already established circuit architecture. PV INs, which target the perisomatic region of pyramidal cells75,76, preferentially express genes supporting fast synaptic transmission during the P8-P11 transition window, while SST INs, which preferentially make synapses onto apical dendrites77,78, exhibit a bias towards modulatory signaling components. The covariation between stimulus encoding and network dimensionality in the Caspase-3 mice, whose degree of PV IN loss was variable, may have clinical relevance for neurodevelopmental disorders associated with PV IN deficits. For example, the overall ∼20% reduction in PV IN numbers we achieved with Caspase-3 expression is similar to that reported in theFmr1knockout mouse model of Fragile X syndrome47,52,53, which demonstrates a delayed desynchronization of network activity79,80. As in models of Fragile X syndrome47,53, the degree of reduction in PV IN density in the Caspase-3 group was variable across animals. This variability and its corresponding relationship with decoding accuracy suggests that a spectrum of PV IN density loss may produce correspondingly graded reductions in network dimensionality and stimulus encoding capacity, providing a potential link between the degree of PV IN deficit and the variability of behavioral symptoms such as sensory hypersensitivity and cognitive impairment. Future work examining how dimensionality evolves during postnatal development across neurodevelopmental disorders, both during spontaneous activity and during sensory stimulation, could directly test this hypothesis. It is difficult for the data alone to isolate which of the maturational changes drives the reorganization of activity: Exc, PV, and SST populations are embedded in recurrent loops, so the effect of strengthening a synapse or shifting an excitability threshold depends on every other concurrent change. To disentangle these interacting factors and establish a mechanistic link between the developmental reorganization of cortical activity and maturation of the underlying circuitry, we introduced a biologically realistic multi-cell-type recurrent circuit model. Our model was designed to overcome limitations of previous models of developmental desynchronization30,32–35,37,38, as described in the Introduction. It is, to our knowledge, the first to combine recurrent connectivity, single-neuron resolution, and three neuronal cell types, while generating seconds-scale synchronous events intrinsically that match pairwise correlations measured in vivo. A broad range of model solutions satisfying biologically motivated developmental constraints reproduced the principal features of this transition, including reduced Exc-Exc pairwise correlations, increased SNE frequency, and increased activity dimensionality. These results suggest that the developmental reorganization of recurrent Exc and PV circuitry can generate a transition from a network dominated by large, population-wide fluctuations to one characterized by more frequent but spatially restricted events. Importantly, the model does not require external inputs to drive synchronous events, suggesting that the slow, seconds-scale fluctuations observed experimentally can emerge intrinsically from recurrent interactions among distinct neuronal populations. The model also provides a mechanistic explanation for why relatively weak average pairwise correlations, typically associated with stationary global population activity81,82, here coexist with strong fluctuations83,84: clustered excitatory connectivity promotes local synchronous events while preventing global synchronization. Finally, we recapitulated the developmental specificity of PV-mediated modulation observed experimentally, predicting that PV activation reduces excitatory correlations early in development while having little effect at later stages. This modulation was associated with changes in SNE occupancy, suggesting that PV neurons regulate correlations by reshaping the temporal organization of the collective network. Our model provides a mechanistic link between circuit maturation, the emergence of higher-dimensional activity, and the developmental loss of global synchrony, and it opens new avenues for hypothesis generation that will undoubtedly motivate future in vivo experiments. Briefly, a quiet baseline period was identified and used to Z-score the neuropil-subtracted fluorescence to normalize while preserving neuronal activity variance: Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated using deconvolved, non-binarized traces. The entire trace was used. For distance analysis, neurons pairs were binned by their physical distance in 100 μm increments for pairwise correlations. For correlations versus chance, a subset of 10,000 neuron pairs per recording was used. 50 chance distributions were generated by randomly circularly shifting the trace of 1 randomly chosen neuron and computing the correlation to the other neurons. Traces were binned (to 1s) and z-scored for this calculation. For mean firing-rate correction, the mean firing-rate proxy (derived from deconvolved activity) was calculated for each neuron pair. Neuron pairs were grouped into bins according to their mean firing rate (bin width = 0.02; maximum = 0.10, based on the firing-rate distribution). To balance observations across recordings, periods, and firing-rate bins, 1000 neuron pairs were randomly sampled without replacement from each recording session, experimental period (Baseline or Stimulus), and firing-rate bin. Pairwise correlations from these sampled neuron pairs were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) with Firing-Rate Bin, Period, and their interaction as fixed effects and Subject (mouse ID) as a random intercept. When the omnibus Wald test identified a significant Firing-Rate Bin × Period interaction, post hoc LMMs were fit separately within each firing-rate bin to compare Condition (Baseline or Stimulus), with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons. For visualization, pairwise correlations were averaged within each mouse for each firing-rate bin and period, and data are presented as mean ± SEM across mice. To detect synchronous network events, we used binarized activity vectors. These were constructed from the deconvolved traces with a threshold of 2 standard deviations above the mean. Binarized activity vectors were randomly circularly shifted to create 1,000 surrogate distributions, and a sum of active cells vector was created for each frame. The 97.5thpercentile was used as a statistical threshold. Peaks that were at least 3 frames long were considered SNEs. The onset and offset of a SNE are defined as the first frame above threshold and the first frame below threshold respectively. Coefficient of variation was defined as the ratio of the standard deviation of the fraction active to the mean of the fraction active, where the fraction active is the percent of cells active in each SNE. The participation ratio was computed from deconvolved, non-binarized neural activity traces. It was defined as the ratio between the second and the first moments of the spectral density, obtained via eigen decomposition of the covariance matrix of neural activity46,87.
