title: OP-GLX: A MATLAB toolbox for online processing and plotting of Neuropixels data acquired with SpikeGLX
author: Slack, J. C.; Rutledge, G.; Doss, M. D.; Yadav, A. P.
text: Online processing and visualization of large-scale neural data is critical for neuroscientific discovery and advancements in neural engineering. However, with the development of technologies like Neuropixels (NP) probes, which enable simultaneous streaming from hundreds of recording electrodes, handling such data in real-time has become an ongoing challenge. Moreover, keeping pace with recording hardware has required most existing software, such as SpikeGLX for NP probes, to prioritize acquisition stability, leaving data processing and visualization to primarily be performed offline. Thus, we created OP-GLX, a MATLAB-based toolbox designed to operate in tandem with SpikeGLX to enhance the fetching, processing, and visualization of incoming neural data. The OP-GLX toolbox features several processing capabilities, including spike detection, computing time-binned firing rates, plotting spike waveforms, and conducting principal component analysis (PCA). The processed neural data is displayed on a native graphical user interface (GUI) for intuitive and customizable interaction with the experiment. The performance testing of OP-GLX showed that it supports real-time operation, confirmed by the absence of SpikeGLX stream buffer fetch errors across multiple acquisition settings. By complementing current neural data acquisition methods and providing stable online functionality, we envision that OP-GLX will enable researchers to visualize and interpret their data more effectively during ongoing neuroscience experiments. Recent hardware advancements in semiconductor technology have promoted the creation of high-density recording devices with high spatial and temporal resolution. Such advancements include the Neuropixels (NP) probes, which are capable of simultaneously recording large populations of neurons across a linear, one-centimeter path [1]. These probes have become a standard tool for neuroscientists and are increasingly attractive for neural engineering and brain-computer interface (BCI) applications requiring large-scale recordings [2], [3]. The high spatial and temporal resolution of these probes has facilitated numerous scientific discoveries from both chronic [4], [5] and acute [6] studies. However, the data acquired from such probes is inherently high-dimensional and frequently generates data on the order of Gigabytes/minute [7], making visualization of incoming neural signals a challenge. The ability to visualize high-dimensional neural datasets during data acquisition is crucial for neurological discovery, as it can facilitate a deeper understanding of the collected data. Visualization tools also provide researchers with feedback on incoming data, enabling insights into variables such as probe placement, noise levels and stimulus features during data collection. Moreover, high-dimensional neural data streams are spatially [8] and temporally [9] complex, as features of interest can occur on sub-second timescales and across a multitude of neurological structures. The current standard for NP data acquisition (DAQ) necessitates the use of either SpikeGLX [10] or Open Ephys [11] hardware/software platforms. While Open Ephys offers increased modularity and visualization of DAQ workflows, SpikeGLX was explicitly designed for stable, low-latency acquisition and recordings of high channel-count NP probes. Although widely adopted and robust, online data processing and visualization capabilities of SpikeGLX are largely limited to raw or filtered voltage traces and manual thresholding of single channels for spike detection with more complex analysis methods, such as spike-sorting, performed offline (Fig. 1A). Additionally, spike detection across all channels involves a single threshold value and is viewed on a heatmap of the probe, limiting the ability to visualize the relationships of activity among multiple spatial recording regions. Presently, few systems exist that provide advanced real-time processing methods or are highly specific to perform one task, such as spike-sorting [12]. Because of the increasingly widespread adoption of high-density NP probes for neuroscientific research and their relevance in BCI applications, there is an urgent need for ubiquitous systems that provide online data processing and visualization of large-scale neural recording streams. a) Standard workflow of Neuropixels data acquisition via SpikeGLX. Priority is given to maintaining stable, low-latency, high-throughput acquisition where online analysis is limited and primarily performed offline.b) OP-GLX toolbox runs alongside SpikeGLX providing advanced functionality without impeding acquisition. OP-GLX utilizes asynchronous and parallel functionality to fetch data from SpikeGLX enabling complex processing methods (green text) to be performed online. Here, we present OP-GLX: a MATLAB toolbox for online processing and plotting (OP) of NP data acquired by SpikeGLX. The primary purpose of OP-GLX is to neatly package incoming chunks of data from the 30kHz action potential (AP)-band streams utilizing the SpikeGLX MATLAB software development kit (SDK) [13] to allow for real-time data processing and visualization (Fig. 1B, Supplementary Video 1). Designed as a MATLAB toolbox, OP-GLX can be easily installed and incorporated within SpikeGLX acquisition workflows, where fetched data is processed and subsequently plotted in a separate MATLAB graphical user interface (GUI). Additionally, OP-GLX design philosophy prioritizes both ease of implementation for non-technical users while offering the ability to integrate custom scripts and functions for advanced users. Source code, toolbox installation and instructions can be found on the GitHub repository:https://github.com/yadavlabs/OP-GLX. Development and testing of OP-GLX was performed in MATLAB versions R2024b and R2025b on a Windows 11 laptop with 16GB of RAM and a Windows 11 desktop with 128GB of RAM. SpikeGLX versions v20241215-phase30 (now removed) andv20250325-phase30were used alongside the precompiled application programming interface (API) from the SpikeGLX-MATLAB-SDK (commit 26ae92d). SpikeGLX and OP-GLX instances were run on the same device with the SpikeGLX remote command server set to the default loopback address (127.0.0.1) and port (4142). OP-GLX is a MATLAB toolbox built around theSpikeGLAPI class provided by the SpikeGLX-MATLAB-SDK. The toolbox structures and extends API calls enabling real-time fetching, processing, and visualization of NP acquisition streams during ongoing experiments. To avoid ambiguity, functions and methods originating from the SpikeGLX-MATLAB-SDK are referred to throughout the paper as the “API” or “API calls”; OP-GLX-originating functionality will be referred to explicitly by class, method, or function name. The precompiledSpikeGLAPI is packaged with the toolbox and can be found in/toolbox/external/directory of the repository. The OP-GLX toolbox is organized using MATLAB namespaces (e.g., +packageName) to group functions and classes by functionality while preventing name collisions with user code or third-party packages (Table 1). Core components include data fetching and buffering, parallel processing, spike detection and feature extraction, and GUI-based control and visualization. SpikeGLX maintains first in, first out (FIFO) buffers to store the most recent samples from acquisition streams. For a given NP probe, two AP-band stream buffers are available for sampling: 1) an 8-second raw data buffer, and 2) a configurable bandpass filtered, demultiplexed, global common average referenced (CAR) buffer of up to two seconds in length that runs in parallel with the raw stream. TheSpikeGLAPI exposes functions to query the current sample count of a chosen stream (GetStreamSampleCount) and to retrieve data from a specified sample index (Fetch) or from the most recently available samples (FetchLatest). Online processing of continuous data streams imposes the two primary constraints for a system utilizing theSpikeGLAPI: For these reasons, OP-GLX exclusively utilizesFetchrather thanFetchLatest. BecauseFetchLatestdoes not allow for a current stream sample count to be directly specified, its use can result in overlapping samples (if time between consecutive calls is too short or the requested number of samples is too large) or missed samples (if time between consecutive calls is too long). In contrast,Fetchenables explicit sample count querying, provided that additional constraints are met: Fetchcalls must reference samples still present in the SpikeGLX buffer, and Fetchcalls must be adequately spaced to avoid saturation of the SpikeGLX command server. For a given sample counts0returned byGetStreamSampleCount, aFetchcall requesting samples ats0must occur within the length of time thats0is present in the stream buffer (e.g. within 8 seconds for raw streams or up to two seconds for the filtered streams). CallingFetchwith ans0that is no longer present in the buffer results in a “FETCH: Too late” error. Conversely, extremely high-frequencyFetchcalls can result in freezing of the SpikeGLX console and stream viewer windows potentially leading to the acquisition crashing. Attempting to reestablish a connection will result in a “Receive timed out” error. To operate within these constraints, OP-GLX implements theSpikeFetcherclass, which serves as the core data fetching and scheduling component of the toolbox. ASpikeFetcherinstance can be run in two modes: 1)Continuous, in which data are fetched and processed indefinitely until user termination, and 2)Event, in which data are fetched and processed around externally defined experimental events. In this section, theContinuousmode is described as this mode encompasses the core fetching and processing mechanisms used by OP-GLX.Eventmode builds directly on this infrastructure and is detailed separately below. A sequence diagram illustrating theContinuousmode workflow along with GUI integration (detailed in a later section) can be seen inFigure 2. Through GUI interaction, a researcher can start and stop data fetching from SpikeGLX via the OP-GLXSpikeFetcherclass. Upon start, a MATLAB-side first-in, first-out (FIFO) buffer is initialized and the current SpikeGLX acquisition stream sample count is queried by API callGetStreamSampleCount(…)to set the initial fetch index (s0). A MATLAB timer is then started to periodically callfetchChunk(…)which requests available samples from SpikeGLX stream buffers starting froms0via API callFetch(…), updatess0based on the number of returned samples, and writes the data to the FIFO buffer. Once the buffer accumulates a user-specified window of data,sendToWorker(…)is called where the data is extracted and passed to a parallel worker for processing to allow data fetching to continue uninterrupted. When processing completes, results are returned to the main MATLAB session and the GUI plots are updated. This loop continues until the researcher presses the stop button which stops the periodic timer, halting data fetching and online processing. To initiateContinuousmode operation, theSpikeFetchermethodstart(fetchType)is called withfetchTypeset to “Continuous”. Upon initiation,SpikeFetcherqueries the current stream sample count with the API callGetStreamSampleCountand stores the returned value as the initial fetch index,s0. Rather than continuously polling SpikeGLX in a loop,SpikeFetcheruses a MATLAB timer to schedule periodic calls to its methodfetchChunk()at a user-specified fetch interval. This interval is expressed as a fraction of the processing window length which is defined as the amount of data processed as a single unit. Each call tofetchChunk()does the following: requests available samples from the SpikeGLX buffer starting ats0viaFetchAPI call, writes the returned data to a MATLAB-side FIFO buffer, and checks if the buffer has filled to the user-specified processing window length Through explicit control of fetch frequency and decoupling of fetch scheduling from processing, this approach prevents excessive API calls that could degrade SpikeGLX performance while ensuring retrieval of new samples occurs in a timely manner. To minimize blocking ofFetchAPI calls, which could lead to ans0falling outside of the SpikeGLX stream buffer, data processing is performed using parallel workers. Specifically, OP-GLX utilizes MATLAB’s thread-based environment viaparpool(‘Threads’)which allows workers to share memory with the main MATLAB session, avoiding the potential overhead associated with copying large data arrays to other processes. When the number of samples accumulated in the MATLAB-side buffer reaches the user-specified processing window length, theSpikeFetchermethodsendToWorker()is called at the end of the currentfetchChunk()execution. Because of the limited precision and variability of MATLAB timers, there is no guarantee that the nextFetchAPI call will return the same number of samples as the previous call. Explicitly setting a window length ensures that data is processed with a static size allowing other variables, such as time arrays and plotting objects, to be pre-allocated. Once filled, data is extracted from the buffer based on the window length and a processing function is assigned based on the type of analysis or plot the user has selected. The data and function are then passed to a parallel worker for processing using the MATLABparfevalfunction. Finally, a plotting function is assigned to update plots in the main MATLAB session once the worker finishes processing. Presently, OP-GLX provides four processing functions (found in the +spikes namespace) that support GUI visualization (detailed in a later section): rasterSpikes, which returns rasterized spike times from all channels getSpikeWaveforms, which returns AP-band traces and aligned spike waveforms getSpikeFiringRates, which computes time-binned firing rates across channels pcaSpikes, which computes PCA on time-binned firing rates and returns the first three principal components over time. All four functions rely on an underlying spike detection function which identifies threshold crossing events across all channels of a NP probe. OP-GLX includes two functions:detectSpikesanddetectSpikesLW, a lightweight version of the former. Spike detection is implemented with the following general procedure: Noise standard deviation (SD) is estimated per channel via user-selectable estimation method. Candidate spikes are identified via threshold crossing using a user-specified multiple of the noise estimate. Removal of artifacts not eliminated via CAR by blanking candidate “spikes” that occur on more than a user-specified fraction of channels simultaneously (a simplified approach to the-gfixoption from the offline CatGT tool[14]). Candidates are confirmed as spikes if threshold is crossed for a specified number of consecutive samples (stay-below criteria). At present, the supported noise SD estimation methods are median absolute deviation (MAD) [15], [16] which is located in the+thresholdnamespace and MATLAB’s built-in SD functionstd. MAD implementationmadEstimationuses MATLAB’smadfunction multiplied by the standard normal scaling factor (1.4826). When fetching from the filtered stream buffers, CAR-applied data is returned zero-median. In this case,madEstimationZeroMediancan be used to avoid redundant median calculations. Additionally, custom estimation functions can be written following the format of the existing functions and placed in the+thresholdnamespace. Importantly, the implementation of step 4 returns spike times corresponding to the first sample which meets the stay-below criteria and does not guarantee a local minimum. IndetectSpikes, a final step is performed to search for and adjust spike times to the local minimum of each threshold crossing. The search is conducted using a look-ahead window which can be adjusted by the user. Additionally, small above-threshold gaps may be present between below-threshold samples resulting in either two “spikes” being detected or a spike being missed. To handle this,detectSpikesfills in one-sample gaps by default or set by the user. In cases where it is not critical that spike times reflect the minimum of an action potential,detectSpikesLWcan be used which returns spike times as the first sample meeting the stay-below criteria. Detected spike times and corresponding channel indices are returned for further processing. The detection algorithm is fully vectorized and, along with the four processing functions and noise estimation methods, fully supported in MATLAB’s thread-based environment. During recordings involving experimental events, such as somatic [17], visual [18], [19], or electrical stimuli [20], [21], [22], it can be helpful to analyze and visualize brain responses while the experiment is ongoing. TheEventmode ofSpikerFetcherprovides this functionality when used with the toolbox’sStimulationInterfaceclass (toolbox/+stim). StimulationInterface is an abstract class with properties, methods, and events that can be used by aSpikeFetcherinstance or within the GUI. A custom class is written which inherits and defines the properties and methods to be used with a specific stimulator. An example stimulator class is provided, theArduinoStimulatorinterfaces an Arduino microcontroller to control a vibration motor for delivering vibrotactile stimuli. In this example setup, a pin on the Arduino is connected to a digital input of a National Instruments (NI) board configured for SpikeGLX acquisition. The duration and amplitude of the vibrotactile stimulus can be set byupdateParameters()and delivered viadeliverStimulus(). When delivered, the Arduino pin goes high for the duration of the stimulus and is acquired on one bit of the digital input channel. Once the stimulator is setup, a MATLAB event listener is attached to calldeliverStimulus()when aSpikeFetchernotifies “DeliverStimulus”.SpikeFetchercan now be run inEventmode, which starts a MATLAB timer to call thefindEvent()method and notifies the stimulator to deliver the stimulus. InfindEvent(), the NI acquisition stream is queried with theSpikeGLAPI to scan for, in this example, the rising edge of the stimulus event, and is called periodically by a user-specified frequency until an event is found. Once the event is found, thefetchEvent()method is called which: Stops and reassigns the timer to callfetchChunk()as inContinuousmode. Maps the identified event sample count of the NI stream to the NP data stream using the API callMapSample Set the runnings0counter to the mapped sample minus a user-specified pre-stimulus window Starts the timer which callsfecthChunk()until the MATLAB-side buffer is filled to the user-specified pre-stimulus, stimulus, and post-stimulus windows length When all samples around the event are fetched from SpikeGLX, the MATLAB timer is stopped, and the data is processed and displayed in a figure window or GUI with vertical lines marking the start and stop of the event. WhileSpikeFetchercan be run independently in the MATLAB command window or via scripts, OP-GLX is packaged with a GUI that provides integrated control of data fetching, processing, and visualization (Fig. 3a). After beginning a SpikeGLX acquisition (Fig. 3b), a user can open the GUI (toolbox/apps/opglx.mlapp) and press theInitializationbutton which queries parameters of the run. Once initialized, a user can select to start aContinuousorEvent(if a stimulator is enabled) run. Most parameters can be changed while inContinuousmode and are applied immediately via theParamaterManagerhandle class. Switching the plot tabs at the top of the app similarly switches the type of analysis to be performed and takes effect at the nextsendToWorker()call. a) The OP-GLX toolbox is packaged with a MATLAB-based GUI that utilizesSpikeFetcherfor online processing and visualization of SpikeGLX NP data streams. The GUI provides controls for initialization, data fetching, setting parameters, and selection of plot tabs to switch between raster display, waveform display, PCA trajectory, and firing-rate estimates. When set toContinuousmode, data fetching, processing, and plotting will continue until the stop button is pressed.b) SpikeGLX graph viewer (top) and console (bottom) running on the same system showing conventional AP-band displays and command server/API logging. SpikeGLX remains responsible for data acquisition while OP-GLX interfaces with SpikeGLX via the MATLAB API to enable online, probe-wide analysis and visualization during experiments. A critical feature of OP-GLX is to reliably schedule fetching, processing, and plotting of data while remaining within and at the front of the SpikeGLX buffers. To measure and quantify the performance and stability of the toolbox in a real-time setting, a sample NP recording was simulated in SpikeGLX and aSpikeFetcherinstance was set to fetch from the filtered stream inContinuousmode for multiple fetch lengths and processing window lengths. For each fetch length and processing window length combination,SpikeFetchercollected performance metrics for 60 seconds. Fetch lengths equal to or below a given window length were tested. In all cases, online processing was set to compute and plot rasterized spike times usingrasterSpikeswhich callsdetectSpikes(Fig. 4) ordetectSpikesLW(Supp.Fig. 1). a) Acquisition lag as a function of acquisition time across 60-second runs for multiple fetch lengths and processing window lengths. Black text arrows indicate a significant positive correlation between acquisition time and acquisition lag (Pearson’s correlation coefficient).b) Acquisition lag deviation from nominal fetch length (y==0) for each fetch length averaged across window lengths. Dark bars indicate performance runs where fetch length is less than the window length. Light bars indicate performance runs with positive correlation from (a) where fetch length is equal to window length as represented by * in the legend. Error bars indicate SEM.c) Real-time factor (RTF) computed for processing (Work), plotting (Plot), and total (End-to-End) times. Dashed red line indicates RTF of 1, when the processing time (PT) equals the processing length (PL). Boxes extend from 25th to 75th percentiles with horizontal lines indicating median. Filled circles indicate outliers identified as values 1.5x(interquartile range) away from 25th and 75th percentiles. Whiskers correspond to the maximum and minimum non-outlier values. Columns indicate window lengths as in (a).d) Mean Work and Plot RTF averaged across all fetch length and window lengths combinations (n=17 runs). Error bars indicate SEM. ****: p<0.0001 (two-tailed paired t-test). The data used for assessing the toolbox consisted of NP recordings from follow-up experiments of a previous study [23]. In that study, the data were collected during an acute implantation of an NP probe (Neuropixels 1.0, IMEC, Belgium) in a urethane-anesthetized (1.2 g/kg, IP) rat (Long-Evans, male, 2–3-month-old). During the experiment, the rat was stabilized in a stereotaxic frame with ear bars, and probe trajectory and craniotomy location were planned using the Pinpoint trajectory planning software [24] with the Waxholm rat atlas to target the somatosensory cortex (S1) and ventral posterolateral thalamic nucleus (VPL). The probe insertion coordinates were (AP: -0.92 mm; ML: -2.68 mm; azimuth: -169°; elevation: 65°) relative to bregma. After dura removal and securing a ground screw near the craniotomy, a stereotaxic micromanipulator (M3-LS-3.4-15-XYZ-MPM-Inverted, New Scale Technologies) was used to insert the NP probe 7.81 mm into the brain before initiating neural recordings. To quantify the delay between afetchChunk()call and the current acquisition time, acquisition lag is measured. Acquisition lag is defined as the difference between the current acquisition time and the currents0to request samples from with theFetchAPI call. At the top offetchChunk(),GetStreamSampleCountis queried directly before theFetchAPI call to provide a value of the current acquisition time. As the MATLAB timer schedulesfetchChunk()calls periodically based on the fetch length, it would be expected that the acquisition lag should be approximately equal to the set fetch length. Additionally, the acquisition lag should remain constant (zero slope) over the course of the acquisition. An increase in acquisition lag over time indicates thatSpikeFetcheris falling behind the SpikeGLX stream buffers which will eventually lead tos0requests that are no longer in the buffers. Over the course of 60 second runs, acquisition lag remained stable when fetch length was not equal to window length (Fig. 4a, Supp.Fig. 1a). In these cases, across different window lengths, acquisition lag was less than the nominal fetch length by 1.29 ± 0.04%, 1.06 ± 0.06%, 0.67 ± 0.14%, 0.71 ± 0.74%, and 0.87 ± 0.74% for fetch lengths of 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, and 0.5 sec, respectively (Fig. 4b, dark bars). Similar acquisition lag trends were found whendetectSpikesLWwas used (Supp.Fig. 1b). This indicates that fetching remained stable over time, remaining well within the SpikeGLX stream buffers. When fetch length was equal to the window length, a steady increase in acquisition lag was observed, with significant positive correlation for bothdetectSpikesanddetectSpikesLW(Fig. 4a, Supp.Fig. 1a, text arrows). When runningdetectSpikes, for fetch lengths of 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, and 1 sec, acquisition lag was observed to be greater than the nominal fetch length by 166.29 ± 3.67%, 27.00 ± 1.11%, 5.44 ± 0.8%, and 0.26 ± 1.61%, respectively (Fig. 4b, light bars). FordetectSpikesLW, three of the four cases (0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 sec) found acquisition lag to be greater than the nominal fetch length with the fourth case (1 sec) marginally below the nominal value (Supp.Fig. 1b, light blue bar). While fetch errors did not occur during the 60-second acquisition tests in these four cases, it is expected that lag will continue to accumulate until reaching the stream buffer length and will eventually fail with a “FETCH: Too late” error. We calculated real-time factor (RTF) to quantify the processing performance of the parallel workers. RTF was computed as the ratio of processing time (PT), defined as the elapsed wall-clock time required for a parallel worker to complete computation, to processing length (PL), defined as the duration of neural data being processed. An RTF of 1 indicates that processing time keeps pace with the incoming data, while values below 1 indicate real-time capability with available computational margin. Timestamps were recorded immediately before data were dispatched to a parallel worker, upon worker completion, and after plot updates in the main MATLAB session. Using these timestamps, RTF was computed separately for the time spent performing data processing (“Work”), updating the visualization object (“Plot”) and total end-to-end latency from dispatch to plot completion (“End-to-End”). For all tested combinations of fetch length and processing window length, RTF values for all three PT stages remained below 1 (Fig. 4c, Supp.Fig. 1c). This indicated that probe-wide spike detection and rasterization consistently completed faster than the duration of the processed data window, confirming that OP-GLX was able to sustain real-time operation under the tested conditions. Across window and fetch lengths, Work RTF was significantly greater than Plot RTF (mean ± SD: 0.1820 ± 0.0142; 95% CI [0.1747, 0.1893], p < 0.0001,Fig. 4d), indicative of the computational cost of spike detection and rasterization relative to the graphical updates. Similar RTF trends were observed whendetectSpikesLWwas utilized (Supp.Fig. 1d). Plotting, while faster on average, exhibited greater variance across fetch lengths and trials, likely reflecting variability in MATLAB’s graphics rendering and event queue scheduling. Across conditions, End- to-End RTF remained well below 1 (mean ± SD: 0.2326 ± 0.0584; 95% CI [0.2025, 0.2626]; p < 0.0001, two-tailed one-sample t-test against µ = 1) indicating that combined processing and visualization latency does not accumulate over time. Notably, as the PT measurements were not taken in reference to the current acquisition time, the lag accumulation observed inFig. 4awas not present in RTF. Together, these results demonstrate that OP-GLX provides sufficient computational performance for real-time analysis and visualization of NP data across a range of processing window sizes and fetch lengths, while maintaining stable end-to-end latency necessary for online experimental monitoring. Finally, to assess the ability of OP-GLX to capture meaningful information about the neural acquisition, online processing methods were compared to offline spike-sorting using Kilosort [25]. Using a 30-second recording,detectSpikeswas run using a threshold of 4x (and default values for all other parameters) on 0.5-second chunks of data to return channel-based spikes times across the entire recording. Spike-sorting was performed on the same recording and, to provide a direct comparison to the channel-based method, spike times from identified single-units were labelled based on the peak channel of the given single-unit (Fig. 5a). Across the recording,detectSpikesdetected 157,807 spikes originating from 376 channels and Kilosort extracted 48,680 from 156 single-units mapped to 152 channels. a) Raster plot of spike times detected via channel-baseddetectSpikesfunction (black) and from offline spike-sorting with Kilosort (orange). Kilosort spikes from single-units were labelled corresponding to the peak channel of each spike’s unit.b) Visualization of the spike-matching method used to match OP-GLX spikes to Kilosort spikes for channel radius of 80 µm and time window of 1 msec. Thick, colored ticks indicate Kilosort spikes that were matched by at least onedetectSpikesspike. Thin, colored ticks representdetectSpikesspikes that were matched to a Kilosort spike. Black ticks indicate Kilosort spikes that were not matched with adetectSpikesspike.c) Heatmaps of recall (fraction of Kilosort spikes detected viadetectSpikes) and precision (fraction of OP-GLX spikes matched to Kilosort spikes) for multiple time window lengths and channel radii.d) Biadjacency matrix of spike matching for channel radius of 80µm and time window of 1ms. Blue squares indicate that at least onedetectSpikesspike from a given channel (y-axis) matched with a Kilosort spike at its unit’s peak channel (x-axis). Bar plot represents the number of channels with at least one spike that matched a given Kilosort peak channel. For a radius of 80µm, a maximum of 9 channels around a Kilosort channel could contain matches based on probe mapping and geometry.e) PCA trajectories during the time-course in (a) of firing rates estimated fromdetectSpikesor Kilosort spikes. The first three principal components ofdetectSpikes-derived trajectories were transformed into Kilosort-derived trajectories following Procrustes analysis. Two key metrics were calculated: 1) The fraction of Kilosort spikes that were detected bydetectSpikes(recall), and 2) the fraction ofdetectSpikesspikes that matched with a Kilosort spike (precision). Matches were considered when adetectSpikesspike from a channel within a specified radius around each Kilosort peak channel fell within a specified time window (match window) around a Kilosort spike (Fig. 5b). Recall and precision, measured across multiple radii (20, 30, 60, 80, 120 µm) and match window lengths (0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, and 1.5 msec) were found to increase with increasing radius and match window length (Fig. 5c). Highest values were found to be 0.8039 and 0.8091 for recall and precision, respectively at a radius of 120 µm and match window of 1.5 ms. However, as the radius and match window are relatively large, a radius of 80 µm and match window of 1 ms were used in the remaining analyses (recall - 0.7707; precision – 0.7582). Matching was further characterized by measuring the number of channels with at least one spike that matched to a Kilosort spike per Kilosort peak channel (Fig. 5d). Averaged across all combinations of radii and match windows, a given Kilosort peak channel matched withdetectSpikesspikes from 5 ± 3 channels. While spike-sorting may not be considered a true “ground-truth”, these results indicate thatdetectSpikesreliably detects “ground-truth” spikes based on offline analysis. Lastly, population activity representations using principal component analysis (PCA) were examined. Specifically, PCA was performed on z-scored firing rates estimated from time-binned spikes and smoothed using a gaussian kernel. Trajectory similarity of the first three principal components derived fromdetectSpikesspikes or Kilosort spikes was next assessed using Procrustes analysis without reflection (Fig. 5e, Supp.Fig. 2a). Procrustes squared distance between PCA trajectories across firing rate estimation parameters was found to be low, within a range of 0.08-0.15 (Supp.Fig. 2b) indicating lower dimensional representations of neural activity is preserved by OP-GLX processing methods. The widespread adoption of high-density NP probes has generated a growing demand for software systems that can operate on high-bandwidth neural data streams in real time. While SpikeGLX provides a robust, low-latency platform for data acquisition, its online processing and plotting capabilities are intentionally limited to prioritize acquisition stability. OP-GLX was developed to address this gap by providing a flexible, MATLAB-based toolbox for enabling real-time fetching, processing, and visualization of NP data that seamlessly integrates with existing SpikeGLX workflows. A central design challenge addressed by OP-GLX was to maintain reliable, online performance within the constraints imposed by the SpikeGLX ecosystem. These constraints required that API data requests must be carefully scheduled to avoid both 1) falling behind the SpikeGLX stream buffers when calls are too infrequent (“FETCH: Too late”) and 2) saturating the command server when calls are too rapid. OP-GLX addressed these constraints by decoupling data request scheduling from data processing using MATLAB timers and buffers, fixed-sized processing windows for deterministic downstream computation, and parallel processing to prevent blocking of data requests. Performance testing confirmed that when fetch lengths were chosen to be shorter than the processing window length, acquisition lag remained stable and bounded over time. This confirms that OP-GLX can remain reliably synchronized with the SpikeGLX stream buffers during sustained operation. A critical architectural decision that enabled real-time performance was the use of parallel processing with MATLAB’s thread-based workers. By offloading spike detection and signal processing to shared-memory worker threads, OP-GLX minimized blocking ofFetchAPI calls and avoided the overhead involved with inter-process data copying. RTF measurements indicated that probe-wide spike detection and visualization consistently completed faster than the duration of the processing window, demonstrating that OP-GLX can sustain real-time operation when analyzing all channels of an NP probe simultaneously. This performance margin can allow users to trade computational headroom for more sophisticated analyses or shorter processing windows when lower latency is desired. Despite these demonstrated capabilities, OP-GLX has important limitations. Primarily, OP-GLX performsindirectstreaming of neural data, relying on the SpikeGLX MATLAB API rather than directly accessing the acquisition buffers. Due to this indirect streaming, the minimum achievable end-to-end latency of OP-GLX is ∼6.5ms [13], which is defined by the measured round-trip latency of the SpikeGLX API. The < 10 milliseconds latency is acceptable for most purposes such as online monitoring of neural data during experimental events or behavioral tasks [17], [18], [19], [22], [26], [27], [28], and closed-loop experiments which necessitate data binning on the order of tens of milliseconds [20], [21], [29], [30]. However, OP-GLX may not be ideal for applications requiring precise millisecond to sub-millisecond feedback such as circuit-level investigations of synaptic plasticity [31], [32], [33]. Additional limitations arise from the design choice of prioritizing performance and usability over computationally intensive processing methods. The implemented spike detection algorithm in OP-GLX was intentionally lightweight and performed at the channel-level. Although sufficient for online firing-rate estimation and population-level analyses, this approach did not employ spike-sorting methods for resolving single- and/or multi-units in real-time. Furthermore, the current implementation was designed around single-probe operation. While adding probe selection functionality may be relatively straightforward, simultaneously fetching from multiple NP probes will require additional coordination and optimization of fetch scheduling, parallel worker allocation, and memory management to maintain real-time performance. Several future directions could substantially extend the utility of the OP-GLX toolbox. Incorporating online spike sorting would enable single- and multi-unit identification during experiments. Extending our architecture to support multiple probes would broaden its use in large-scale recording paradigms that are increasingly common in systems neuroscience [4], [34], [35]. Finally, translating or reimplementing core components in Python or C/C++, either by the SpikeGLX-CPP-SDK [36] or a lightweight server-client architecture, could reduce latency, remove MATLAB-specific overhead and dependencies, and enable tighter integration with the SpikeGLX control systems. At present, OP-GLX provides a practical and customizable toolbox for online processing and visualization of NP data acquired by SpikeGLX. By explicitly addressing the timing and buffering constraints of SpikeGLX and its MATLAB API, and by enabling parallel computation in MATLAB, OP-GLX provides stable, online analyses across all channels of a Neuropixel probe during ongoing experiments. As high-density neural recording technologies continue to be adopted, tools such as OP-GLX will play an important role in bridging the gap between data acquisition and analysis, facilitating more informed experimental control, and furthering progress in systems neuroscience and neural engineering. title: Micro-C-TALE: BAC-based targeted high-resolution measurement of 3D chromatin interactions
author: Golberg, A.; Golov, A. K.; Shemer, R.; Kaplan, N.
text: Chromosome conformation capture methods have greatly advanced our understanding of genome organization, but obtaining high-resolution interaction maps of selected genomic regions remains costly due to the sequencing requirements. Here, we introduce Micro-C-TALE, a new chromosome conformation capture method that combines Micro-C, which uses micrococcal nuclease to improve the resolution and sensitivity of chromatin interaction measurements, and C-TALE, which uses probes generated from bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs) for targeted enrichment. This combination enables the generation of high-resolution interaction maps without requiring custom synthesis of capture oligonucleotides. We applied Micro-C-TALE to a 214 kb region in human HAP1 cells, obtaining detailed interaction maps with approximately 5-6 million sequenced read pairs. Compared with published genome-wide Micro-C data, Micro-C-TALE yielded a higher amount of informative interactions within the targeted region despite ∼550-fold lower sequencing depth. To evaluate the sensitivity of the method to fine-scale changes in genome organization, we introduced a heterozygous CTCF binding site into the targeted region using CRISPR-Cas9. Comparing Micro-C-TALE to the restriction enzyme-based C-TALE, we found Micro-C-TALE yielded a ∼5-fold higher fraction of informative reads and detected novel CTCF-mediated point interactions associated with the inserted CTCF site, which were barely discernible using C-TALE. Our results demonstrate that Micro-C-TALE provides a flexible and cost-effective approach for targeted high-resolution measurement of chromatin interactions, facilitating the investigation of fine-scale genome organization and its response to genetic perturbations. The spatial organization of the genome is closely linked to various nuclear processes, including transcription, DNA replication, DNA repair and cell division1–3. Over the past two decades, chromosome conformation capture (3C)-based methods have greatly advanced our understanding of genome organization by allowing high-throughput measurement of spatial interactions between genomic loci4–7, and have also been leveraged for genome assembly applications8–11. In particular, Hi-C enables genome-wide measurement of pairwise chromatin interactions, revealing organizational features at different genomic scales, including genomic compartments, Topologically Associating Domains (TADs), and point interactions5,6,12–15. Some of these structural features have been linked to specific molecular mechanisms, such as the role of cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and CTCF in the formation of TADs and point interactions in vertebrates16–19. However, despite important methodological improvements, obtaining cost-effective highly-detailed chromatin interaction maps remains challenging, particularly when studying fine-scale interactions between individual genomic elements. The resolution of Hi-C interaction maps is limited both by the size of restriction fragments and by sequencing depth6,7. Thus, obtaining detailed interaction maps of specific genomic loci in mammalian genomes may require extensive genome-wide sequencing, making such experiments costly and inefficient. To address this limitation, several targeted chromosome conformation capture methods have been developed, allowing deeper sampling of selected genomic regions while reducing sequencing requirements. Early approaches such as 4C and 5C enabled high-throughput measurement of interactions involving selected viewpoints or multiple predefined genomic fragments20–22. Subsequently, hybridization-based enrichment approaches were developed, using biotinylated probes to capture selected proximity-ligation products. These include Capture-C, NG Capture-C, Capture Hi-C and promoter Capture Hi-C, which enable detailed analysis of interactions involving selected genomic viewpoints, such as gene promoters23–26. Other approaches, including Targeted Chromatin Capture (T2C), Hi-C² and Tiled-C, use capture probes spanning extended genomic regions to generate high-resolution interaction maps27–29. C-TALE (Chromatin TArget Ligation Enrichment) provides an alternative regional targeting strategy using probes generated from bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs), avoiding the need for custom oligonucleotide synthesis and providing a flexible and cost-effective approach for targeted enrichment30. An important advance in chromosome conformation capture was the development of Micro-C, which substitutes restriction enzyme digestion with micrococcal nuclease (MNase) digestion31–34. MNase preferentially digests linker DNA between nucleosomes, allowing chromatin fragmentation at approximately nucleosome-scale resolution. Unlike restriction enzyme-based approaches, MNase digestion is not constrained by the distribution of specific recognition sequences, enabling the measurement of chromatin interactions at substantially finer genomic scales. Initially developed in yeast, Micro-C was subsequently adapted to mammalian genomes, revealing fine-scale chromatin organization and point interactions that are difficult to resolve using conventional Hi-C33,34. Importantly, beyond its improved fragmentation resolution, Micro-C and some of its variants have been shown to provide a higher signal-to-noise ratio and increased sensitivity to point interactions compared with Hi-C, enabling significantly improved detection of interactions involving CTCF binding sites, enhancers and promoters33–36. These capabilities have facilitated high-resolution investigation of enhancer-promoter communication and the relationship between transcriptional regulation and chromatin interactions36,37. However, achieving these higher resolutions still requires massive sequencing depth, as the space of possible interactions grows quadratically with the number of interrogated loci. Thus, obtaining sufficiently sampled interaction maps at nucleosome-scale resolution remains challenging, particularly when studying individual genomic regions within large mammalian genomes. To overcome the sequencing depth limitations of genome-wide Micro-C, several approaches have recently been developed combining MNase-based fragmentation with targeted enrichment of chromatin interactions. Micro-Capture-C (MCC) uses hybridization-based capture of selected genomic viewpoints, enabling the measurement of interactions between regulatory elements at near base-pair resolution38,39. Tiled Micro-Capture-C (TMCC) extends this approach by using densely tiled capture probes across extended genomic regions, allowing the generation of high-resolution contact maps and the investigation of fine-scale chromatin structures and their dependence on cohesin and CTCF40. Similarly, Region Capture Micro-C (RCMC) combines Micro-C with targeted enrichment of extended genomic regions, enabling exceptionally deep sequencing and revealing previously unresolved interactions between enhancers and promoters, including highly nested structures termed microcompartments41. Other MNase-based approaches, including MChIP-C and Micro-C-ChIP, use chromatin immunoprecipitation to enrich interactions associated with specific chromatin proteins or histone modifications, enabling high-resolution characterization of chromatin interactions without restricting the analysis to predefined genomic regions36,42. Together, these methods demonstrate the utility of combining MNase-based fragmentation with targeted enrichment for studying fine-scale genome organization. However, methods based on hybridization capture of extended genomic regions generally require custom-designed and synthesized oligonucleotide probes, motivating the development of alternative targeting strategies. Here, we present Micro-C-TALE, a targeted chromosome conformation capture method combining the nucleosome-scale fragmentation of Micro-C with the cost-effective BAC-based enrichment strategy of C-TALE. We apply Micro-C-TALE to a selected genomic region in human HAP1 cells and characterize the resulting interaction maps and sequencing efficiency. Finally, to evaluate the ability of Micro-C-TALE to detect fine-scale changes in chromatin organization, we use CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce a CTCF binding site into the targeted region and compare the resulting interaction maps with those obtained using C-TALE. Our results demonstrate the applicability of BAC-based enrichment to Micro-C and provide an alternative approach for high-resolution analysis of chromatin interactions in selected genomic regions. To enable high-resolution measurement of chromatin interactions in selected genomic regions, we developed Micro-C-TALE, combining the MNase-based chromatin fragmentation of Micro-C with the BAC-based targeting strategy of C-TALE (Figure 1; step-by-step protocol provided in Supplementary Methods). The protocol consists of three main stages: Micro-C library preparation, production of BAC-derived capture probes, and targeted enrichment of Micro-C libraries. Schematic representation of the three main stages of the Micro-C-TALE protocol.(a)Micro-C library preparation, including chromatin crosslinking, MNase digestion, end repair and proximity ligation, DNA purification and bead-based size selection, and library amplification using indexed primers.(b)Production of biotinylated capture probes from bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) DNA by sonication, end repair, adapter ligation and PCR amplification using biotinylated primers.(c)Two rounds of targeted enrichment by hybridization with BAC-derived probes, streptavidin pull-down and PCR amplification, followed by next-generation sequencing. For Micro-C library preparation, cells are first crosslinked with formaldehyde, followed by cell lysis and chromatin digestion using micrococcal nuclease (MNase). The amount of MNase is calibrated to obtain predominantly mononucleosomal fragments while avoiding excessive digestion. Following MNase digestion, DNA ends are repaired and subjected to proximity ligation. In contrast to conventional Micro-C, we omit biotin labeling and streptavidin pull-down of ligation junctions, aiming to minimize potential loss of library complexity, as previously suggested for C-TALE30. Following reversal of crosslinking and DNA purification, we use AMPURE XP bead-based size selection to enrich for ligated fragments and remove unligated mononucleosomal DNA. The resulting DNA is converted into an indexed Illumina sequencing library. In parallel, BAC-derived capture probes are prepared according to the general strategy of C-TALE30. BAC clones covering the genomic region of interest are isolated and fragmented by sonication. The fragments are ligated to custom adapters and amplified using biotinylated primers, producing a pool of double-stranded DNA probes covering the targeted genomic region. This strategy avoids the need for custom synthesis of capture oligonucleotides and allows the production of additional probes by PCR amplification. Finally, the Micro-C libraries are subjected to two rounds of hybridization-based enrichment using the BAC-derived probes. Following each round of hybridization, probe-bound DNA fragments are recovered using streptavidin beads, washed and PCR-amplified. The resulting enriched libraries are sequenced to produce high-resolution interaction maps of the targeted genomic region. To evaluate the performance of Micro-C-TALE, we applied the method to human HAP1 cells, targeting a 214 kb region on chromosome 1 (Chr1:30,754,221–30,968,290, hg38) using BAC-derived capture probes. We generated Micro-C libraries from wild-type HAP1 cells, followed by two rounds of targeted enrichment and paired-end sequencing. We obtained approximately 5.8 million sequenced read pairs, of which ∼2.3 million represented uniquely mapped interactions. Of these, approximately 873,000 unique read pairs mapped on both sides to the targeted region, corresponding to 38% of all unique read pairs. As expected for MNase-based chromatin fragmentation without biotin enrichment of ligation fragments, a large proportion of these interactions occurred at short genomic distances. Restricting the analysis to interactions spanning at least 1 kb or 5 kb, we obtained approximately 107,000 and 60,000 unique on-target interactions, respectively. These favorably compare to a recent genome-wide Micro-C experiment in which ∼3,186 million read pairs were sequenced (550x more than Micro-C-TALE), resulting in a lower amount of informative reads for the same target region (∼82,000 unique on target >1kb; ∼26,000 unique on target >5kb). Thus, despite the relatively modest sequencing depth, these results indicate substantial enrichment of interactions involving the targeted region. We next examined the resulting interaction map at 2Kb resolution and compared it with a HAP1 Hi-C map18of the same region (Figure 2). While the Hi-C map appears extremely noisy at this resolution, the Micro-C-TALE map shows clearly outlined structures including TADs and point interactions. Specifically, CTCF-CTCF point interactions anchored at the TAD boundaries are clearly observable and accurately positioned in the Micro-C-TALE map, but barely observable in the Hi-C map. These results demonstrate that Micro-C-TALE can generate targeted chromatin interaction maps from relatively modest sequencing depths, allowing the detection of fine-scale features of genomic organization that may be missed by standard Hi-C. Micro-C-TALE and Hi-C 2kb resolution interaction maps of target region in HAP1 cells. Hi-C was taken from Sanborn et al.18. HAP1 wildtype CTCF ChIP-Seq from Haarhuis et al.43is shown below in blue. Dashed squares indicate regions which are enlarged on the right, containing CTCF-associated point interactions. Next, we asked whether Micro-C-TALE is sensitive enough to detect subtle small-scale changes in 3D genome organization. To this end, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to introduce a single CTCF binding site into the target region. Sanger sequencing showed a combination of the wildtype and mutant alleles, suggesting that the HAP1 cells underwent diploidization prior to the insertion44. We reasoned that the insertion of a single heterozygous CTCF binding site might create CTCF-CTCF point interactions that would require a highly-sensitive assay to detect. We performed Micro-C-TALE on the heterozygous CTCF insertion clone, resulting in 5.3 million read pairs which yielded ∼85,000 and ∼47,000 uniquely mapped on-target reads with genomic distances >1kb and >5kb respectively. We then compared the interaction maps visually (Figure 3a). Both maps showed TAD structures and point interactions. Reassuringly, the interaction map of the CTCF insertion clone showed new point interactions emerging at the intersection of the CTCF insertion site with other established CTCF interacting sites. To further examine this change, we used a virtual 4C to plot the interactions of the target insertion locus with its downstream genomic vicinity. We observe the appearance of two interacting peaks at the locations of known HAP1 CTCF sites, consistent with the formation of new CTCF-CTCF point interactions (Figure 3b). Importantly, these new interactions are apparent despite their signal intensity being reduced by approximately half due to heterozygosity (effectively averaging with the non-interacting wildtype allele). These results indicate that Micro-C-TALE can be sensitive enough to detect subtle structural changes in localized regulatory genomic features. (a)Micro-C-TALE 1kb resolution interaction maps of target region for wildtype and CTCF insert clone. HAP1 wildtype CTCF ChIP-Seq from Haarhuis et al.43is shown in blue below and on the side of interaction maps. Dashed squares indicate regions which are enlarged on the right. The green cross indicates the CTCF insertion site, and the arrow indicates an emerging CTCF-associated point interaction.(b)Virtual 4C plot showing the interactions of the insertion locus (Chr1:30,817,713) with its downstream genomic vicinity. Wildtype is shown in magenta and the CTCF insertion clone in blue. HAP1 wildtype CTCF ChIP-Seq is shown above. To further dissect whether the improved interaction map quality of Micro-C-TALE is due to sequencing depth or MNase usage, we generated a C-TALE interaction map for the same target region, using the same HAP1 CTCF-insertion clone. We sequenced ∼16 million read pairs from the C-TALE library, ultimately yielding ∼49,000 and ∼36,000 uniquely mapped on-target reads with genomic distances >1kb and >5kb respectively. Comparatively, this gives 0.3%/0.2% (>1kb/>5kb) uniquely mapped on-target reads out of total sequenced reads for C-TALE, relative to 1.6%/0.9% and 1.9%/1.0% for the Micro-C-TALE libraries. This suggests that Micro-C-TALE is also more efficient than C-TALE in capturing informative DNA fragments, in spite of these protocols sharing the probe preparation and capture steps. We then compared the C-TALE and Micro-C-TALE interaction maps of the HAP1 CTCF-insertion clone (Figure 4). Interestingly, despite its targeted nature, the C-TALE map did not show obvious CTCF-CTCF point interactions, consistent with previous observations regarding the improved sensitivity of MNase-based assay in detecting such interactions. Thus, our results suggest that Micro-C-TALE may provide higher resolution, better sensitivity and increased efficiency than C-TALE. Interaction frequency maps of the targeted region in the HAP1 CTCF insertion clone, generated using Micro-C-TALE and C-TALE at 1 kb resolution. HAP1 wildtype CTCF ChIP-Seq from Haarhuis et al.43is shown below in blue. Dashed squares indicate regions which are enlarged on the right. The green cross indicates the CTCF insertion site, and the arrow indicates a CTCF-associated point interaction that is clearly detected by Micro-C-TALE but is barely discernible by C-TALE. In this work we developed Micro-C-TALE, a targeted chromosome conformation capture method combining the nucleosome-scale fragmentation of Micro-C with the BAC-based enrichment strategy of C-TALE. We demonstrate that Micro-C-TALE enables the generation of detailed chromatin interaction maps of selected genomic regions of interest using modest sequencing depth. An important advantage of Micro-C-TALE is the use of BAC-derived probes for targeted enrichment. In contrast to methods relying on custom-designed oligonucleotide panels, BAC-based probes can be generated using standard molecular biology procedures without requiring custom oligonucleotide synthesis. Once prepared, the BAC-derived probe libraries can be amplified to produce additional material for subsequent experiments. This provides a flexible and cost-effective approach, particularly for studies focusing on extended genomic regions or requiring comparisons across multiple experimental conditions. Micro-C-TALE thus complements existing targeted Micro-C approaches, including MCC, TMCC and RCMC, by providing an alternative strategy for targeted enrichment. The increased fragmentation resolution and sensitivity of Micro-C-TALE provide important advantages over restriction enzyme-based approaches such as Hi-C and C-TALE. Unlike restriction enzyme digestion, MNase digestion is not constrained by the distribution of specific recognition sequences, enabling more detailed characterization of fine-scale chromatin interactions, including point interactions involving regulatory elements. In addition, previous studies have demonstrated that Micro-C provides increased sensitivity to point interactions compared with Hi-C33,34,36,37. We demonstrate this advantage experimentally by introducing a CTCF binding site into the targeted genomic region and directly comparing the resulting interaction maps generated using Micro-C-TALE and C-TALE. The point interaction associated with the inserted CTCF site is clearly detected using Micro-C-TALE - despite it being heterozygous - but is barely discernible using C-TALE, demonstrating the improved sensitivity of Micro-C-TALE to fine-scale changes in chromatin organization. Another characteristic of Micro-C-TALE is the omission of biotin labeling and streptavidin pull-down of proximity-ligation junctions during library preparation. This choice was motivated by the possibility of preserving library complexity, as previously suggested for C-TALE30. However, omitting this junction pull-down step also results in the retention of DNA fragments that do not contain ligation junctions, potentially reducing the fraction of informative sequencing reads. We partially address this limitation by size selection to enrich for ligated fragments. Since targeted enrichment substantially reduces the sequencing depth required to obtain detailed maps of selected regions, this trade-off is often acceptable in applications where library complexity is particularly important. Nevertheless, further optimization and direct comparisons would be necessary to determine the effects of this choice on library complexity and sequencing efficiency. Micro-C-TALE retains some limitations inherent to hybridization-based capture, including variation in enrichment efficiency across genomic regions and dependence on the availability and coverage of suitable BAC clones. Furthermore, the relatively extensive hybridization and enrichment procedure adds experimental time and complexity compared with standard genome-wide approaches. As with other chromosome conformation capture methods, the resulting interaction maps represent population-averaged interaction frequencies rather than direct measurements of three-dimensional distances. In summary, Micro-C-TALE provides a cost-effective strategy for targeted, high-resolution measurement of chromatin interactions. By combining MNase-based fragmentation with BAC-derived regional enrichment, the method enables detailed investigation of chromatin organization in selected genomic regions and facilitates the detection of fine-scale structural changes following genetic or other experimental perturbations. Complete step-by-step Micro-C-TALE protocols are provided in the Supplementary Methods. HAP1 cells were cultured in IMDM medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Cells were harvested using trypsin, counted, and centrifuged at 500 × g for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were resuspended in 950 µl PBS and 55 µl 37% Formaldehyde for every 10⁷ cells. The cells were then crosslinked for 10 min at room temperature with gentle agitation. Crosslinking was quenched by dropwise addition of 600 µl of 2 M Tris-HCl (pH 7.4) per 10⁷ cells, followed by 5 min of rocking and 10 min on ice. Cells were centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 5 min at 4 °C, washed with PBS containing 0.1 M Tris-HCl, and divided into aliquots of 5 × 10⁶ cells. Following centrifugation, cell pellets were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. A total of 1.3 µg of BAC DNA (CH17-219E19; chr1:30,754,221–30,968,290) was fragmented by sonication using a Covaris system to obtain fragments of 200–300 bp. Fragmented DNA was subjected to end repair and A-tailing using NEBNext Ultra II End Prep reagents (30 min at 20 °C followed by 30 min at 65 °C), followed by ligation of BAC-specific forked adapters for 30 min at 20 °C. The adapters were prepared by annealing complementary oligonucleotides at 98 °C followed by gradual cooling to 4 °C (1 °C per 15 s). Adapter and primer sequences are provided in the Supplementary Methods. Adapter-ligated DNA was purified using AMPure XP beads at a 1:1 bead-to-sample volume ratio and quantified. A calibration PCR was performed using KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix and 5′-biotinylated BAC-specific primers (see Supplementary Methods). Aliquots were collected after 6, 8, 10 and 12 PCR cycles and analyzed by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis to determine the optimal number of amplification cycles (1-2 cycles before reaching gel smear saturation). BAC-derived capture probes were then produced by three 50 µl PCR reactions using the conditions established during calibration. PCR products were pooled, purified using AMPure XP beads at a 1.7:1 bead-to-sample volume ratio, and quantified before use with DeNovix high-sensitivity assay. Frozen cell pellets containing 5 × 10⁶ cells were thawed on ice and lysed in ice-cold buffer containing 20 mM HEPES, 2 mM MgCl₂, 0.5× protease inhibitor cocktail, and 0.5× PMSF. Following 5 min on ice, 1% digitonin stock solution was added to a final concentration of 0.01%, followed by an additional 5 min on ice. Cell membranes were disrupted by repeated pipetting (10×) against the bottom of the microcentrifuge tube using a 1 mL pipette tip. Nuclei were centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 4 min at 4 °C and resuspended in MNase digestion buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 1 mM CaCl₂). Chromatin was digested with micrococcal nuclease (MNase) for 1 h at 37 °C with agitation at 1,000 rpm. The MNase amount was calibrated on the wildtype sample to obtain predominantly mononucleosomal fragments, as assessed by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis. Calibration reactions tested 5–35 U of MNase per 110 µl reaction (see Supplementary Methods). Based on these results, we chose 70U for 450 µl reaction. Digestion was terminated by addition of EGTA to a final concentration of 5 mM. Following MNase digestion, nuclei were washed with PBS and resuspended in ligation buffer containing dNTPs and ATP. DNA ends were repaired using 100 U of T4 polynucleotide kinase and 50 U of Klenow fragment, added simultaneously and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C with agitation at 1,000 rpm. Proximity ligation was initiated by adding 5,000 U of T4 DNA ligase and incubating for 1 h at 37 °C with agitation at 1,000 rpm, followed by addition of another 5,000 U of ligase and overnight incubation at 20 °C. Crosslinks were reversed by incubation with proteinase K at 65 °C for 2–3 h. DNA was purified by phenol–chloroform extraction and ethanol precipitation, followed by RNase A treatment. To reduce the proportion of unligated mononucleosomal fragments, DNA was subjected to size selection using AMPure XP beads at a 0.7:1 bead-to-sample volume ratio, retaining the bead-bound DNA. DNA concentration was measured using a high-sensitivity DeNovix assay. Sequencing libraries were prepared from 500 ng of size-selected DNA using the NEBNext Ultra II DNA Library Prep Kit. End repair and A-tailing were performed for 30 min at 20 °C followed by 30 min at 65 °C. Illumina adapters were ligated for 30 min at 20 °C, followed by USER enzyme treatment for 15 min at 37 °C. DNA was purified using AMPure XP beads at a 0.9:1 bead-to-sample volume ratio and resuspended in 27 µl 10 mM Tris-HCl. Libraries were amplified using KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix and indexed primers from the NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina kit. The number of PCR cycles was determined by 25 µl calibration PCR with 5 µL of adapter ligated library as template, testing 4, 6, 8 and 10 cycles and selecting the minimal number of cycles producing detectable DNA product smear on a 1% agarose gel. Libraries were amplified in two 50 µl reactions per sample, pooled, purified using AMPure XP beads at a 1.7:1 bead-to-sample volume ratio, and quantified using a high-sensitivity DeNovix assay. Libraries from individual samples were subsequently pooled to a total amount of 1 µg DNA per one capture reaction. Targeted enrichment was performed using two successive rounds of hybridization with biotinylated BAC-derived probes. For the first round, a library mixture containing up to 1 µg of pooled Micro-C libraries, 3 µg of sheared salmon sperm DNA, and blocking oligonucleotides complementary to the library adapter sequences (20 pmol each) was prepared. Separately, a probe mixture containing 500 ng of biotinylated BAC-derived probes, 1.5 µg of Cot-1 DNA to block repetitive sequences, and blocking oligonucleotides complementary to the probe adapter sequences (10 pmol each) was prepared. Oligonucleotide sequences are provided in the Supplementary Methods. The two mixtures were denatured separately at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by incubation at 65 °C for 10 min. Pre-warmed hybridization buffer was added to each mixture, followed by incubation at 65 °C for 1 h. The library and probe mixtures were then combined and incubated at 65 °C for 20–24 h. The final hybridization conditions were 5× SSPE, 5× Denhardt’s solution, 5 mM EDTA and 0.1% SDS. Following hybridization, the samples were incubated for 30 min at room temperature with 15 µl of streptavidin-coated magnetic beads, pre-washed in high salt buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 1 mM EDTA), with occasional mixing. The beads with pooled down library fragments were washed once with low stringency wash buffer (1× SSC, 0.1% SDS) for 15 min at room temperature, then three times with high stringency wash buffer (0.1× SSC, 0.1% SDS) for 10 min each at 65 °C with shaking at 800 rpm, and three times with low salt wash buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 10 mM NaCl). After the last wash, beads were resuspended in 26 µl of 10 mM Tris-HCl. The captured libraries were amplified directly from the beads (5 µl of bead suspension per reaction) using KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix and Illumina PCR primers in four 50 µl reactions. To determine the optimal number of PCR cycles, one calibration PCR reaction of 25 µl was performed with aliquots of PCR products taken after 16, 18, 20, and 22 cycles. The final amplification was then carried out using 1-2 cycles fewer than the number required for the DNA product smear on the gel to reach saturation. Amplified products were pooled, purified using AMPure XP beads at a 1.7:1 bead-to-sample volume ratio and quantified using a high-sensitivity DeNovix assay. The amplified library was subjected to a second round of hybridization using 1 µg of the first-capture library, fresh BAC-derived probes (500 ng) and the same hybridization and washing conditions; after the final wash beads were resuspended in 26 µl of 10 mM Tris-HCl. Following the second capture, the optimal number of PCR cycles was determined by 25 µl calibration PCR with 5 µl of bead suspension testing 8, 10, 12 and 14 cycles; final amplification was then carried out in 2 50 µl PCR reactions using 1-2 cycles fewer than the number required for the smear on the gel to reach saturation. Amplified products were pooled, purified using AMPure XP beads at a 1.7:1 bead-to-sample volume ratio, and quantified using a high-sensitivity DeNovix assay. The final libraries were sequenced 2×150 bp by paired-end sequencing. The C-TALE experiment was conducted as previously described30, but following Hi-C45rather than 3C-Seq. Briefly, HAP1 cells were crosslinked, permeabilized, and digested with DpnII. In contrast to the published C-TALE protocol, which does not include biotin fill-in and streptavidin pull-down during this stage, DNA ends were filled in with biotin-14-dATP using DNA polymerase I Klenow fragment, followed by blunt-end ligation with T4 DNA ligase. Crosslinking was reversed by incubation with Proteinase K and heating, and DNA was purified by phenol–chloroform extraction and ethanol precipitation. Biotin was removed from unligated DNA ends using T4 DNA polymerase. DNA was then sonicated to a fragment size of 200–300 bp using a Covaris sonicator. Biotinylated ligation products were enriched using streptavidin-coated magnetic beads. The enriched DNA was subjected to end repair and A-tailing using the NEBNext Ultra II DNA Library Prep Kit, followed by Illumina adaptors ligation. Libraries were amplified by PCR using indexed primers, purified with AMPure XP beads, and quantified. Subsequent BAC-based probe preparation and target enrichment were performed as described for Micro-C libraries. To introduce a CTCF binding site into the targeted genomic region, HAP1 cells were edited using CRISPR-Cas9. Cells were cultured in Iscove’s Modified Dulbecco’s Medium (IMDM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin–streptomycin, and transfected at approximately 60% confluence. Cells were co-transfected with 2.5 µg of a pSpCas9(BB)-2A-GFP (PX458) plasmid expressing Cas9 and guide RNA 313, targeting the insertion site (Chr1:30,817,713), and 2.5 µg of a double-stranded DNA repair template containing the CTCF binding site flanked by 200 bp homology arms. The inserted sequence was taken from Chr2:43,056,093-43,056,234. The repair template was excised from a custom pUC57-based plasmid (GenScript) using EcoRI and HindIII, and purified before transfection. Transfection was performed using jetOPTIMUS reagent (Polyplus) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Guide RNA and PCR primer sequences are provided in the Supplementary Methods. At 24 h after transfection, cells were harvested, passed through a 40 µm strainer, and subjected to fluorescence-activated cell sorting. Individual GFP-positive cells were sorted into 96-well plates containing 200 µl IMDM per well, and clonal outgrowth was monitored for two weeks. Genomic DNA was extracted from expanded clones using either alkaline lysis or the Norgen Cells and Tissue DNA Isolation Kit. Clones were screened by PCR using primers flanking the insertion site (CRM 1A F/R or CRM 2C F/R). The expected amplicon sizes were 624 bp for the knock-in allele and 409 bp for the wildtype allele. One clone yielded both the wildtype and knock-in PCR products, consistent with the presence of both alleles (HAP1 cells often go through diploidization44). Sanger sequencing of the knock-in PCR product using primer CRM 1A F confirmed integration of the donor sequence at the targeted locus, without additional sequence alterations in the sequenced amplicon. Micro-C-TALE, C-TALE and Micro-C data libraries were processed using distiller-nf (https://github.com/open2c/distiller-nf) and cooler46to generate interaction maps in mcool format. Briefly, paired-end reads were aligned to the human genome (hg38), uniquely mapping non-duplicate read pairs were retained, reads were binned into specified resolutions and interaction maps were filtered and balanced. For Micro-C-TALE and C-TALE, balancing was performed only on the submatrix containing the target region. Micro-C data was taken from Barshad et al.37and Hi-C data was taken from Guetta et al.45. CTCF ChIP-Seq was taken from Haarhuis et al.43using Cistrome Data Browser47. On target read pairs were defined as read pairs in which both sides map to the target region. Raw and processed Micro-C-TALE and C-TALE data files have been submitted to GEO and are available at GSEXXXXX.
