title: Structure and antigenicity of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein
author: Addetia, A.; Uriu, K.; Stewart, C.; Sprouse, K. R.; Kaku, Y.; Kibria, M. G.; Putri, O.; Shah, S. T.; Fukushima, Y.; Kawakubo, S.; Park, Y.-J.; Saito, A.; Sato, K.; Veesler, D.
text: An outbreak of ebolavirus disease caused by a new zoonotic spillover of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) is currently spreading at an unprecedented pace in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. The outbreak has resulted in 7,733 cases with a case-fatality ratio of 48%, yet no BDBV-specific vaccines or therapeutics are available. The ebolavirus glycoprotein (GP) promotes viral entry and is the target of neutralizing antibodies and vaccine development. Here, we engineered a soluble, prefusion-stabilized GP trimer from a contemporary BDBV isolate and determined its cryo-electron microscopy structure bound to the broadly neutralizing antibody EBOV-515. It reveals the molecular basis for EBOV-515 cross-reactivity and suggests that the antibody inhibits viral entry by interfering with NPC1 engagement in addition to trapping GP in the prefusion conformation and hindering glycan cap cleavage. Mapping lineage-defining substitutions identified changes in GP1 and GP2, including R506S within an antigenic site targeted by multiple broadly neutralizing antibodies recognizing the fusion loop. Nevertheless, we found that several glycan cap-, GP base-, and HR2-directed antibodies cross-reacted and neutralized BDBV DRC/2026 GP pseudovirus with potency comparable or greater to that observed against earlier BDBV isolates and the Zaire ebolavirus Makona/2024 isolate. These findings define the antigenic properties of contemporary BDBV GP and delineate conserved epitopes as ideal targets for antibody therapeutics and for the development of pan-ebolavirus vaccines. Filoviruses are highly lethal pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever and organ failure with fatality rates ranging from 25 to 90%1. They are divided in two genera, designated Ebolavirus and Marburgvirus, and typically spillover to humans from bats2–4. The Ebolavirus genus comprises six viral species, namely Zaire (ZEBV), Sudan (SUDV), Bundibugyo (BDBV), Tai Forest (TAFV), Reston (RESTV), and Bombali (BOMV) with the first three species causing fatal disease in humans. The 2013-2016 EBOV outbreak in West Africa is the largest documented outbreak thus far with 28,616 infections and 11,310 deaths. An outbreak of ebolavirus disease caused by BDBV is currently ongoing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and in Uganda with cases exported to Germany and France. Although this outbreak was only recognized by the WHO in May, genomic sequencing indicates that the virus has been circulating since February. To date, the ongoing outbreak has led to greater than 7,279 confirmed cases and 3,512 deaths(Fig 1a). It is the second-largest outbreak in history and is currently spreading more rapidly than the 2013-2016 EBOV outbreak in West Africa. It is therefore predicted to become the largest outbreak of ebolavirus disease ever documented which is particularly concerning as no BDBV-specific or pan-ebolavirus vaccines or treatments are approved. As a result, the WHO declared this outbreak a public health emergency of international concern. a, Cumulative numbers of confirmed cases and deaths of BDBV disease. Data were obtained from WHO AFRO Weekly External Situation Reports Reports 01–18 (data as of 2026-Sep-13).b,Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree based on whole genome nucleotide sequences of BDBV.c,Phylogenetic tree based on GP coding region nucleotide sequences of BDBV.d,Schematic of BDBV GP domain organization and mutations found in the BDBV DRC/2026 GP sequence relative to GP sequences from the prior outbreaks of BDBV-induced disease (BDBV Uganda/2007 and BDBV DRC/2012). CD, cytoplasmic domain; FCS, furin cleavage site; GC, glycan cap; MLD, mucin-like domain; TM, transmembrane domain. SP, signal peptide. Filoviruses enter cells using glycoprotein (GP) homotrimers, which mediate host receptor engagement and fusion of the endosomal and viral membranes to initiate infection5–10. GP is cleaved by furin during biogenesis, yielding GP1 and GP2 that remain covalently linked via a disulfide bond at the base of the prefusion GP trimer. Upon viral internalization, cathepsin-mediated GP cleavage enables shedding of the glycan cap and mucin-like domain, enabling engagement of the NPC1 host receptor before further cleavage promotes the large-scale conformational changes leading to membrane fusion11–13. GP is the target of neutralizing antibodies which correlate with protection in small animal and non-human primate challenge models14–26. A live-attenuated vaccine based on a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) encoding EBOV GP was developed and licensed under the commercial name Ervebo27–29. Ebolavirus species exhibit considerable evolutionary divergence with GPs from two species typically sharing only 55-65% amino acid sequence identity. As a result, GP-elicited antibody responses against vaccine-mismatched GP species are reduced and vaccine-induced protection is dampened in animal models, relative to vaccine-matched immunity30–33. A clinical trial run during the 2018 EBOV outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo showed that the mAb114 monotherapy and the Inmazeb (REGN-EB3) cocktail therapy outperformed the previously developed Zmapp cocktail to reduce EBOV-induced mortality and they are now both approved by the FDA for treatment of EBOV infections34,35. However, these licensed mAbs are specific for EBOV GP and not for use against other ebolavirus species. Analysis of genome and GP sequences obtained from individuals infected during the ongoing outbreak indicate that BDBV DRC/2026 isolates form a distinct phylogenetic cluster from BDBV isolates associated with the 2007 and 2012 outbreaks, consistent with a new zoonotic spillover event36(Fig 1b-d). To characterize the GP architecture of the circulating BDBV strain and map lineage-defining mutations, we sought to recombinantly produce a soluble, prefusion-stabilized ectodomain GP trimer. We first evaluated a construct encoding for a mucin domain-deleted GP, obtained from a genome sequence collected on May 7th 2026 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (https://pathoplexus.org/seq/PP_006XHL9.2), with a C-terminally fused foldon trimerization domain(Fig 2a). Given the instability and poor recombinant expression yield observed for this ectodomain trimer construct (GPΔMuc), we opted to introduce two prefusion-stabilizing mutations previously described for EBOV and SUDV GPs (L579P and K588F)37and one prefusion-stabilizing mutation that is broadly portable to all ebolavirus GPs (W615L)38. We thus compared the aforementioned construct to three designed GP mutant constructs harboring the L579P/W615L (termed BDBV GPΔMuc WL2P4), L579P/K588F (termed BDBV GPΔMuc F-P4), or L579P/K588F/W615L (termed BDBV GPΔMuc F-WL2P4) residue substitutions with or without co-transfection of furin. GP constructs co-expressed with furin led to complete cleavage of the GP into GP1 and GP2, while those expressed without furin resulted in incomplete GP cleavage(Fig 2b). In presence of furin, all three stabilized BDBV GP constructs expressed to markedly greater levels than the unmutated construct with BDBV GPΔMuc F-WL2P4yielding the greatest expression yields and monodispersity, as analyzed by size-exclusion chromatography and electron microscopy imaging of negatively stained samples(Fig 2c-d). All ectodomains bound to immobilized EBOV-515 IgG(Fig 2e), confirming the GPs are antigenetically intact, although the lower binding response observed for BDBV GPΔMuc, relative to the other three constructs, concurred with the heterogeneity observed by EM imaging (Fig 2d-e). These data enabled identification of an optimal prefusion-stabilization strategy for 2026 BDBV GP which will facilitate functional and immunological studies of this circulating virus. a, Schematic of BDBV GP domain organization and mutations included in GPΔMuc ectodomain constructs. CD, cytoplasmic domain; FCS, furin cleavage site; GC, glycan cap; MLD, mucin-like domain; TM, transmembrane domain. SP, signal peptide. The designed BDBV GPΔMuc constructs contain the following stabilizing mutations: WL2P4: L579P/W615L; F-P4: L579P/K588F; F-WL2P4: L579P/W615L/K588F.b,Western blot analysis of GP cleavage for the four designed BDBV GPΔMuc constructs using an anti-his tag primary antibody.c,Recombinant production yields for the BDBV GPΔMuc constructs after purification by affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography. Each point represents an independently expressed biological replicate and the bar indicates the mean yield across the biological replicates. Fold-change in yields relative to BDBV GPΔMuc are indicated above each bar.d,Size-exclusion chromatograms for the BDBV GPΔMuc constructs.e,30 Å low-pass filtered electron micrographs of negatively stained BDBV GPΔMuc ectodomains. Scale bar, 50 nm.f,Analysis of BDBV GPΔMuc constructs at a concentration of 0.03 mg/mL binding to immobilized EBOV-515 IgG assessed by BLI. We used single particle cryo-electron microscopy to determine a structure of BDBV GPΔMuc F-WL2P4in complex with the EBOV-515 antibody Fab fragment at 3.2 Å resolution (Fig 3a-b, Extended Data Fig 1 and Extended Data Table 1). We selected EBOV-515 as this GP base-directed antibody is endowed with broadly neutralizing activity against EBOV, SUDV and historical BDBV isolates. Furthermore, EBOV-515 was shown to synergize with glycan cap-directed antibodies and to protect animals challenged with all three ebolavirus species prominently causing disease in humans18,39. The structure shows that GP adopts the prefusion state22,23, validating the design strategy, and resolves GP1, including part of the glycan cap, GP2 up to residue G598, and three bound EBOV-515 Fab fragments. Two out of the three introduced prefusion-stabilizing mutations are resolved in the cryoEM map, enabling visualization of their contribution in the context of BDBV GP. L579P introduces a proline residue that disfavors HR1 refolding to form a central 3-helix bundle (characteristic of postfusion GP) whereas K588F strengthens interactions with the GP1 N-terminal region, ultimately promoting prefusion BDBV GP stability(Fig 3c). a, CryoEM structure of the prefusion-stabilized (L579P/K588F/W615L) BDBV ectodomain trimer (PP_006XHL9.2) bound to three EBOV-515 Fab fragments. GP1 and GP2 are shown in shades of purple and gold, respectively. The EBOV-515 heavy chain is shown in orange and the light chain is shown in light orange (only the Fab variable domains were modelled into the density). N-linked glycans are rendered as light blue surfaces. The GP heptad repeat 2 and membrane-proximal region are not resolved in the cryoEM map and are schematically shown connecting to the viral membrane.b,A single BDBV GP protomer is shown bound to EBOV-515 in two distinct orientations with domains annotated.c,The BDBV ectodomain trimer is shown with zoomed-in views of the two prefusion-stabilized mutations resolved in the cryoEM density (L579P and K588F).d,Mapping of the 2026 lineage-defining GP mutations relative to 2007/2012 BDBV GPs on the cryoEM structure shown as a surface (GP1: light gray, GP2: dark grey) in two orthogonal orientations.e,Analysis of amino acid residue conservation within the EBOV-515 epitope among ebolavirus GPs colored according to the key (conserved: orange, variable: green) and mapped on the BDBV GP surface.f,Binding modes of the NPC1 receptor (yellow) and EBOV-515 (orange/light orange) to the BDBV GP. The position of NPC1 was determined by superimposing the EBOV GP–NPC1 (PBD:5JNX) and BDBV-EBOV-515 Fab structures. The EBOV GP trimer and the region of the BDBV GP glycan cap resolved in our structure (residues 191-310) are not shown for clarity. The red star denotes steric clashes. The structure further resolves GP mutations distinguishing BDBV 2026 isolates from 2012 isolates (L310F and R506S) and from 2007 isolates (Y151F, E188K and R506S)(Fig 3d). Residue 506 maps to the GP2 N-terminal region, and participates in antigenic sites targeted by several monoclonal antibodies, such as EBOV-515, EBOV-520 and ADI-15946 (recognizing the base of the fusion loop) as well as ADI-15878 and REGN-3479 (binding to the tip of the fusion loop). The Y151F GP1 residue substitution maps to the GP1 head and is solvent-exposed without obvious predicted impact on function, concurring with its occurrence in BDBV 2012 and EBOV GPs. The BDBV L310F mutation is in the glycan cap region that is targeted by a set of antibodies that use their CDRH2 or CDRH3 to displace the segment harboring residue 310, including BDBV289 (PDB 7KEJ) and BDBV-43 (PDB 7KEW)39. It is likely that the BDBV E188K mutation has a similar impact to the Q188R mutation, which was previously described to reduce binding of the BDBV91 mAb to EBOV soluble GP (sGP)25. sGP accounts for ∼80% of GP produced upon infection, forms homodimers and is believed to act as a decoy for antibodies40–42. However, BDBV91 does not bind to the prefusion GP trimer and is therefore non-neutralizing. Only three additional mutations (K299R, P344S, and I486T) have arisen in more than 10 of the 810 BDBV genomes sequenced in the current outbreak. K299R is in the glycan cap, but not resolved in our structure, P344S is in the mucin-like domain which was not included in the construct used here (given that it is unresolved in experimental structures), and I486T is in the region of GP1 preceding the furin cleavage, which is not resolved in our structure. Our structural data reveal the molecular basis for EBOV-515 mediated broad neutralization of BDBV along with shared and unique features relative to complexes with EBOV GP, which shares ∼65% amino acid sequence identity with BDBV GP. EBOV-515 recognizes a glycan-free epitope involving contacts with both GP1 and GP2, including the base of the fusion loop(Fig 3e). Most of the epitope residues are conserved across GPs from distinct ebolavirus species(Fig 3e), explaining its broadly neutralizing activity of EBOV, SUDV and BDBV. S506 makes tenuous contacts with EBOV-515 in our structure(Fig 3d), as is possibly the case for residue N506 in an EBOV-515-bound EBOV GP structure (PDB 7M8L)18. Moreover, EBOV GP N506 was modeled in the vicinity of the ADI-15946 heavy chain (PDB 6MAM)43and of the REGN-3479 light chain whereas it does not appear to contact EBOV-520 (PDB 6OZ9)44(PDB7TN9)24in the respective complex structures. Therefore, our data suggest that amino acid mutations at position 506, such as the 2026 BDBV GP R506S substitution, may modulate binding and neutralization of some monoclonal antibodies recognizing this antigenic site in addition to modulating entry into cells. Besides trapping GP in the prefusion state and reducing GP processing, as previously reported17, our data indicate that EBOV-515 would inhibit viral entry via steric hindrance with the NPC1 N-terminal domain(Fig 3f), as previously described for the broadly neutralizing marburgvirus antibody MARV1645. To determine if monoclonal antibodies differentially recognize ebolavirus GPs, we assessed binding of a panel of immobilized antibodies to the BDBV DRC/2026 GPΔMuc F-WL2P4, EBOV Makona/2014 GPΔMuc, and SUDV Gulu/2000 GPΔMuc ectodomains by surface plasmon resonance(Figure 4). Antibodies targeting the GP2 base and GP2 stalk exhibited comparable apparent binding affinities across the three GP ectodomains. Only 2 out of 6 antibodies targeting the GP1 glycan cap bound similarly to all three GPΔMuc ectodomains whereas the other 4 antibodies had marked variability across ebolavirus species. These results indicate that glycan cap antibodies are more sensitive to GP sequence variation, concurring with the more rapid evolutionary divergence of the glycan cap and mucin-like domain relative to other parts of GP. Comparison of cross-reactivity with the the wildtype BDBV DRC/2026 GPΔMuc F-WL2P4ectodomain and the S506R BDBV DRC/2026 GPΔMuc F-WL2P4ectodomain showed comparable binding for all antibodies tested despite the fact that residue 506 maps within the epitope of several GP2 base antibodies(Figure 4). We further found that GP2 base and stalk-directed antibodies recognized the BDBV DRC/2026 GPΔMuc F-WL2P4and SUDV Gulu/2000 GPΔMuc ectodomains cleaved by thermolysin, to remove the GP1 glycan cap as mediated by endosomal cathepsins during viral entry. However, no binding of glycan cap-directed antibodies was observed, as expected due to shedding of this domain upon cleavage. Three of the GP2 base antibodies, ADI-23744, ADI-15946, and EBOV-520, displayed markedly increased affinities towards the thermolysin-cleaved GP ectodomains compared to the uncleaved ectodomains, consistent with the glycan cap partially shielding the epitopes of these antibodies. Overall, our data show that numerous neutralizing antibodies retain strong binding to the currently circulating BDBV DRC/2026 GP. Apparent binding affinity and neutralization potency of monoclonal antibodies targeting ebolavirus GPs. Binding affinity was assessed by surface plasma resonance using the BDBV DRC/2026 GPΔMuc F-WL2P4, BDBV DRC/2026 GPΔMuc F-WL2P4harboring the S506R mutation, EBOV Makona/2014 GPΔMuc, SUDV Gulu/2000 GPΔMuc, thermolysin cleaved BDBV DRC/2026 GPΔMuc F-WL2P4, or thermolysin cleaved SUDV Gulu/2000 GPΔMuc ectodomain. One to two technical replicates were performed to determine the binding affinity (KD; nM) Neutralization assays were performed using pseudoviruses harboring the GP proteins of BDBV DRC/2026, BDBV Uganda/2007, BDBV DRC/2012, and EBOV Makona/2014. The assay was performed in quadruplicate for each antibody at each concentration to determine the 50% inhibitory concentration (IC50; ng/ml), and the assay was independently repeated three times. The average of IC50 values from three independent assays is shown. FL: fusion loop; GC: glycan cap; sGP: soluble glycoprotein. To assess whether sequence variation in the 2026 BDBV GP alters sensitivity to monoclonal neutralizing antibodies, we compared neutralization of contemporary and historical BDBV GP pseudoviruses using a lentiviral pseusotyping platform (Table 1 and Extended Data Fig 2). We observed that the BDBV DRC/2026 isolate remained susceptible to all antibodies that neutralized earlier BDBV isolates. Among the therapeutic antibodies tested, both ADI-15878 (a component of MBP134) and REGN3479 (also known as maftivimab and a component of Inmazeb) potently neutralized BDBV DRC/2026 pseudovirus. These findings indicate that the 2026 BDBV GP retains susceptibility to the broadly neutralizing antibodies tested, including components of the clinical stage MBP134 cocktail and of the Inmazeb cocktail approved for EBOV. Although the licensed Ervebo vaccine has proven highly effective during the pivotal Ebola Ça Suffit! Clinical trial in Guinea in 201529, it is based on EBOV GP, which is considerably divergent from BDBV GP and even more so from SUDV GP. Consequently, the protective efficacy of this vaccine against disease caused by BDBV and SUDV in humans remains uncertain and the World Health Organization announced it will be supporting its clinical evaluation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo where the ongoing outbreak of BDBV-induced disease is spreading rapidly (https://www.who.int/news/item/20-08-2026-who-and-africa-cdc-welcome-the-allocation-of-ebola-vaccines-to-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo). The marked genetic and antigenic distance between GP trimers of various ebolavirus species, however, indicates that species-matched vaccines will need to be developed for providing optimal protection against BDBV, as has been initiated for SUDV46,47. Prefusion-stabilization has enabled recombinant production of ectodomain constructs faithfully recapitulating the native architecture and antigenicity of numerous viral surface glycoproteins. A combination of disulfide engineering and cavity filling mutations yielded several approved respiratory syncytial vaccines48–53whereas introduction of proline residues incompatible with the large-scale fusogenic conformational changes led to several efficacious COVID-19 vaccines54–59. We identify here an optimal prefusion GP stabilization strategy by introducing mutations ported from other ebolavirus GPs to BDBV GP37,38. A minimum of two mutations were needed to enhance recombinant expression yields by greater than 10-fold, relative to an unmutated ectodomain construct. Specifically, substitution of GP2 residue 579 for a proline, to disfavor formation of the postfusion HR1 central 3-helix bundle, and of GP2 residue 588 for a phenylalanine, to strengthen interactions with GP1, acted in concert to promote prefusion BDBV GP stability. We anticipate that the stabilized BDBV GP ectodomain trimer described here will accelerate the design of BDBV vaccines and immunological studies of infected or vaccinated individuals or animals to assist with the identification of potent BDBV GP monoclonal antibody therapeutics. Naturally occurring GP mutations have been documented by sequencing isolates found in humans infected with the various ebolavirus species associated with epidemics60,61. The glycan cap and the mucin-like domain are prime targets of serum antibodies and the vast majority of GP mutations accumulate in these domains, as is the case with recently sequenced 2026 BDBV genomes. Mutations in other GP regions, such as the GP1 head or the GP1/GP2 base have also been observed and it is therefore key to map these mutations and characterize them experimentally. The data presented here provide a molecular blueprint and a functional framework to understand present and future GP mutations and their impact on immune responses and pathogenicity. The development of mAbs that are neutralizing and protective against other ebolavirus species than EBOV, particularly BDBV and SUDV, inclusive of all their variants, is a priority to identify therapeutic solutions for the repeated spillovers of these latter two viruses. The identification and preclinical evaluation of several mAbs with broad activity against EBOV, BDBV and SUDV, based on direct viral neutralization and Fc-mediated effector functions, is a key step forward toward achieving this goal14–18,20,22–24,26. Several mAbs targeting the GP base are endowed with potent and broad neutralizing activity and provide effective post-exposure protection in animal models whereas many mAbs targeting the glycan cap have limitedin vitroneutralizing activity and modest therapeutic efficacy although they can synergize with other mAbs. The most advanced candidate is a broadly protective mAb cocktail (designated MBP134) which comprises derivatives of ADI-15878 and ADI-15946. Several other mAb cocktails have yielded promising results for post-exposure treatment of animals experimentally infected with EBOV, BDBV and SUDV and warrant clinical evaluation. The observed binding andin vitroneutralizing activity against 2026 BDBV for the panel of mAbs evaluated here provides encouraging results as to the expected retention ofin vivoefficacy of these therapeutic candidates. Specifically, the equivalent 2026 BDBV pseudovirus neutralization potency of of ADI-15878 to that observed against prior BDBV isolates and 2014 EBOV provides support to the recent decision of the World Health Organization to evaluate if administration of MBP134 and remdesivir improves survival among patients diagnosed with BDBV infection in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (https://www.who.int/news/item/02-07-2026-patient-enrolment-begins-in-a-scientific-trial-to-identify-the-first-effective-treatments-for-bundibugyo-virus-disease). Weekly counts of confirmed BDBV disease cases and deaths were obtained from the Weekly External Situation Reports on the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak, published by the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa (WHO AFRO:https://www.afro.who.int). Cumulative numbers of confirmed cases and confirmed deaths were manually extracted from Situation Reports 01–18. Suspected and probable cases were excluded. Data were visualized in R v.4.4.1 using the ggplot2 package v.4.0.1. BDBV sequence data were downloaded from Pathoplexus (https://pathoplexus.org) on 28 August 2026. All entries released under the OPEN data use terms were retrieved, together with one sequence released under RESTRICTED terms (Pathoplexus accession no. PP_006XXY5.1), which was included with permission from the data submitters (Prof. Dr. Christian, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany). In total, n = 46 sequences were analyzed. Sequences were aligned with MAFFT v7.52662using the ––localpair option. Maximum-likelihood phylogenies were reconstructed from the whole-genome and GP coding region nucleotide alignments using IQ-TREE v3.0.163. For each alignment, the best-fitting nucleotide substitution model was selected with ModelFinder as implemented in IQ-TREE based on the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), with FreeRate models included to account for among-site rate heterogeneity (-m TEST-mrate R). TIM+F+R2 and TN+F+R2 were selected for the whole-genome and GP trees, respectively. Branch support was assessed with 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates. Trees were visualised in PearTree v1.2.0 (https://github.com/artic-network/peartree), and amino acid substitutions were plotted with snipit v1.7 (https://github.com/aineniamh/snipit). HEK293T cells (a human embryonic kidney cell line; ATCC, Cat# CRL-1573) and Lenti-X 293T cells (Takara, Cat# 632180) were cultured in high glucose Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (Wako, Cat# 044-29765) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Nichirei, Cat# 175012) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (P/S) All cells were maintained at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. Expi293 cells (ThermoFisher) were grown in Expi293 medium at 37°C at 5% CO2. Cell lines were not authenticated or tested for mycoplasma contamination. The construct encoding the wild-type BDBV GPΔMuc ectodomain (residues 1-312 and 471-649) with a C-terminal T4 foldon trimerization sequence followed by an 8x His tag was codon-optimized, synthesized, and inserted into pcDNA3.4 by Genscript. The stabilized constructs containing the L579P and K588F, L579P and W615L, or L579P, K588F, and W615L mutations were generated through mutagenesis of the wild-type BDBV GPΔMuc by Genscript. The construct encoding the EBOV Makona/2014 GPΔMuc, SUDV Gulu/2000 GPΔMuc, furin, the EBOV-515 heavy chain, and the EBOV-515 light chain was previously described45. A plasmid expressing the Ebola virus GP protein of the Makona strain (EBOV Makona/2014) was prepared in the previous study64. Plasmids expressing the BDBV GP proteins of the Uganda/2007 strain (Accession no.FJ217161.1), DRC/2012 strain (Accession no.MT680262.1) , and DRC/2026 strain (Pathoplexus accessions no. PP_006XXY5.1) were artificially synthesized by the Fasmac Gene Synthesis service (Fasmac Co., Ltd.). Permission to use the 2026 GP sequence in this study was obtained from the data submitters, Prof. Dr. Christian Drosten (Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany) Plasmids expressing the BDBV GP proteins of the 2026 strain derivative were generated by site-directed overlap extension PCR using the primers listed inExtended Data Table 2. The resulting PCR fragment was digested with KpnI and NotI and inserted into the corresponding site of the pCAGGS vector65. For monoclonal antibodies used in the neutralization assays, plasmids expressing the heavy chain (HC), kappa chain (KC), or lambda chain (LC) were constructed as follows. The sequences of the variable regions were obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank (https://www.rcsb.org/) for REGN-3479 (PDB: 7TN9), BDBV43 (PDB: 7KEW), and BDBV91 (PDB: 5KEM); from IEDB (https://www.iedb.org/) for ADI-15742 and EBOV-515; and from EBOV-AbDab (https://zenodo.org/records/10564972) for BDBV223, BDBV289, and BDBV329. The variable regions of REGN-3479 were generated by overlap PCR using the primers listed inExtended Data Table 2. The variable regions of the HC and KC of the other antibodies, and the open reading frame of the BDBV289 LC, were artificially synthesized together with the corresponding leader sequences (MEFGLSWLFLVAILTGVQC for HC and MDMRVPAQLLGLLLLWFPGARC for KC) (Fasmac). The resulting coding sequences of the variable regions of the heavy and light chains were cloned into the pCAGGS vector together65with the sequence encoding the human immunoglobulin γ1 constant region (Accession no. QRG33624.1) or the kappa constant region (Accession no. AAA59000.1). Nucleotide sequences were determined by DNA sequencing services (Eurofins Genomics), and the sequence data were analyzed by SnapGene v8.2.2 software (MDF Co., Ltd.). For monoclonal antibodies used for surface plasmon resonance, the variable regions of heavy and light chain sequences were synthesized and inserted into the pTT5 vector containing the constant regions for the respective heavy, lambda, or kappa chain by Genscript. The recombinant BDBV, EBOV, and SUDV GPΔMuc ectodomains were expressed and purified as previously described45. In brief, Expi293 cells were grown to 3 million cells per mL and transfected with the BDBV GPΔMuc construct with or without furin (at a 3:1 mass ratio, if co-transfected furin) using Expifectamine293 (ThermoFisher) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After 5 days, the supernatant was collected, clarified by centrifugation, and incubated with Ni Sepharose Excel Resin (Cytiva) for 1 hour at room temperature. The resin was collected in a gravity-flow column and washed with wash buffer (25 mM Na2PO4, 300 mM NaCl, 50 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). The GPΔMuc was eluted from the resin using elution buffer (25 mM Na2PO4, 300 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, pH 8.0) and further purified and exchanged in TBS (20 mM Tris-HCl, 100 mM NaCl, pH 7.4) using a Superose6 Increase 10/300 GL column. The purified proteins were flash frozen and stored at –80°C until use. Thermolysin cleavage of the BDBV and SUDV GPΔMuc ectodomains was completed as previously described45. In brief, the ectodomains were expressed and purified as described above. The GPΔMuc ectodomains were diluted to 1 mg/mL in TBS and incubated thermolysin (Sigma-Aldrich) diluted to 0.2 mg/mL at 37°C for 1 hr. Next, phosphoramidon (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to a final concentration of 500 µM to inhibit the thermolysin. The cleaved GPΔMuc ectodomains were purified using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column into TBS. EBOV-515 and ADI-15878 IgGs were expressed and purified as previously described45. Briefly, Expi293 cells at a density of 3 million cells per mL were co-transfected with the EBOV-515 heavy and light chain constructs at a 1:1 mass ratio using Expifectamine293 (ThermoFisher) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After 4 days, the supernatant was collected, clarified by centrifugation, and flowed over a HiTrap Protein A column (Cytiva) for 1 hour at room temperature. The column was washed with 20 mM Na2PO, pH 8.0 and the recombinant IgG was eluted using 0.1 M citric acid, pH 3.0 directly into 1 M Tris-HCl, pH 9.0. The IgG was exchanged into TBS (20 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, pH 8.0) using a 100-kDa Amicon Ultra centrifugal filter. To generate EBOV-515 Fab, the IgG was digested with LysC (NEB), resuspended in TBS, at a 4,000:1 mass ratio at 37°C for 18 hours. Undigested IgG and free Fc fragments were collected by incubating the digestion product with MabSelect resin (Cytiva) for 1 hour at room temperature. The resin was captured with a gravity-flow column and the flow-through was collected. To further purify the Fab, the flow-through was run over a Superdex75 Increase 10/300 GL column equilibrated with TBS. The IgG and Fab were stored at 4°C until use. The additional monoclonal antibodies used for surface plasmon resonance were expressed and purified from CHO-K1 cells into a sodium acetate buffer with 0.2 M L-Arginine, pH5.5 by Genscript. To assess the binding affinity between the monoclonal antibodies and the GPΔMuc ectodomains, the monoclonal antibodies were diluted in HEPES buffered saline with Tween-20 (HBST; Carterra) to 1, 0.2, 0.04 µg/mL and spotted onto a pre-conditioned Protein A-coated biosensor chip (PAHC200M; Carterra). Next, a non-regenerative kinetics capture experiment was performed by injecting the GPΔMuc ectodomain serially diluted in HBST with 0.5% BSA from 0.411 to 900 nM over the surface of the mAb-coated biosensor chip with an association time of 300 s and a dissociation time of 900 s for each concentration of GPΔMuc ectodomain. All injections were completed at 25°C. The chip was regenerated with 10 mM glycine, pH 2.0 and re-spotted with monoclonal antibodies before proceeding with the next GPΔMuc ectodomain kinetics capture cycle. The resulting data was analyzed using the Kinetics software (Carterra). The data were corrected using a reference spot and leading buffer blank, y-aligned to the baseline before the first GPΔMuc ectodomain injection, and fit using a 1:1 binding model using float T0to account for the non-regenerative kinetics cycle. BDBV GPΔMuc-EBOV-515 Fab complexes were formed by incubating 100 µg of BDBV GPΔMuc with 150 µg of EBOV-515 at 4°C for 18 hours. Excess Fab was removed by washing the complexes 5 times with TBS in a 100-kDa Amicon Ultra centrifugal filter. Immediately prior to freezing, either CHAPSO at a final concentration of 6 mM was added to the GP-Fab complexes concentrated to 4 mg/mL or a surfactant mixture (0.0048% FOM, 0.06% Bril-35, 0.05% CHAPSO and 0.25% Amphipol 8-35)66was added to the GP-Fab complexes concentrated to 1 mg/mL. The complexes were added to the freshly glow-discharged UltrAuFoil R 2.0/2.0 grids (200 mesh) and the grids were then plunge frozen using a Vitrobot MarkIV (ThermoFisher) with a 10 second wait time, a –2 blot force, and a 4 second blotting time at 100% humidity and 23°C. Data were acquired on an FEI Glacios operated at 100 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 Summit. Automated data collection was carried out using a Leginon at a nominal magnification of 45,000x with a pixel size of 0.89 Å, a defocus range of –0.1 to –4.0 µm, and a stage tilt of 0° or 30°. Patch motion correction. and estimation of microscope CTF parameters were completed using cryoSPARC (v5.0.6)67. Particle picking was carried out using 20 Å low-pass filtered templates generated from a prior EBOV GP-EBOV515 Fab model (PBD: 7KF9)39followed by extraction of particles downsampled to a pixel size of 1.78 Å using a box size of 200 pixels2were performed in cryoSPARC. Two rounds of reference-free 2D classification followed by ab-initio 3D and heterogenous refinement were performed to select well-defined particles using cryoSPARC. The pixel size was adjusted to 0.89 Å and box size was adjusted to 400 pixels, after which 3D refinement was carried out using non-uniform refinement with C3 symmetry and global and per-particle defocus in cryoSPARC68. Next, reference-based motion correction followed by another round of nonuniform refinement with C3 symmetry and global and per-particle defocus were performed with cryoSPARC. Local refinement with a mask encompassing the BDBV GP excluding the HR2 stalk (residues 612-649) and the variable regions of the EBOV-515 and enforcing C3 symmetry was conducted using cryoSPARC. A previously determined BDBV GP (PDB 7KEW)39was docked into the cryoEM reconstruction using ChimeraX69before manual rebuilding using Coot70and refinement using Phenix71using sharpened and unsharpened maps. Validation was carried out with Phenix, Molprobity72and Privateer73. Among the anti-EBOV monoclonal antibodies, ADI-15878 was purchased from MedChemExpress (Cat# HY-P991450), and the others were constructed in-house. Recombinant immunoglobulin G (IgG) was produced and purified as previously described74. Briefly, pairs of heavy– and light-chain plasmids were co-transfected into 293T cells using PEI MAX (Polysciences, Inc.). The culture medium was replaced with fresh D-MEM (High Glucose; Wako) the next day of the transfection, and the supernatant was harvested 3 days post-transfection. IgGs were purified using MonoSpin ProA Spin columns (GL Sciences). Pseudoviruses were prepared as previously described75–79with minor modifications. Briefly, lentivirus (HIV-1)-based, luciferase-expressing reporter viruses were pseudotyped with the EBOV/BDBV GPs. LentiX-293T cells (1,000,000 cells) were cotransfected with 1 μg psPAX2-IN/HiBiT80, 1 μg pWPI-Luc280, and 500 ng plasmids expressing parental GPs using TransIT-293 transfection reagent (Mirus, Cat# MIR2704) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Two days post transfection, the culture supernatants were harvested and filtrated. The pseudoviruses were stored at –80°C until use. Neutralization assay was prepared as previously described75–79. Briefly, the EBOV/BDBV GPs pseudoviruses (counting ∼20,000 relative light units) were incubated with serially diluted monoclonal antibodies in a range from 50 µg/ml to 5.0 × 10-9 µg/ml at the final concentration at 37°C for 1 h. Pseudoviruses without sera were included as controls. Then, a mixture of pseudovirus and antibody was added to HEK293T cells (10,000 cells) in a 96-well white plate. At 2 d.p.i., the infected cells were lysed with a Bright-Glo™ Luciferase Assay System (Promega, Cat# E2650), and the luminescent signal was measured using a GloMax explorer multimode microplate reader 3500 (Promega). The assay of each serum sample was performed in quadruplicate, and the half maximal Inhibitory Concentration (IC50) was calculated using Prism 9 (GraphPad Software). a-b, Representative cryo-EM micrograph (a) and 2D class averages (b) for the BDBV GPΔMuc F-WL2P4-EBOV-515 Fab complex. Scale bar: 100 nm.c,Cryo-EM data processing workflow. NUR: non-uniform refinement.d,Gold-standard fourier shell correlation curves for the locally refined BDBV GPΔMuc F-WL2P4-EBOV-515 Fab complex Fab complex (using a mask comprising the GP trimer, excluding the HR2 stalk, and EBOV-515 Fab variable domains).e,Local resolution calculated with cryoSPARC for the locally refined BDBV GPΔMuc F-WL2P4-EBOV-515 complex.f,Heat map of angular distribution for the particles contributing to the final reconstruction.g,Conical fourier shell correlation plot. a-d, Representative neutralization dose-response curves for ADI-15472, ADI-15878, BDBV43, BDBV91, BDBV223, BDBV289, BDBV329, EBOV-515, and REGN3479 against HIV-based pseudovirus displaying the EBOV Makona/2014 (a), BDBV DRC/2007 (b), BDBV Uganda/2012 (c), or BDBV DRC/2026 (d) GP. title: A coordinated and reproducible multicellular response to AD pathology
author: Vilkaite, G.; Volcov, E.; An, L.; Xiao, Y.; Hristovska, I.; Rosat Consiglio, C.; Pichet-Binette, A.; Mattsson-Carlgren, N.; Gaiteri, C.; Vogel, J. W.
text: While single-cell measurements of the Alzheimer’s disease (AD) brain allow investigation of vulnerable cells in unprecedented depth, reported findings are heterogeneous, mostly descriptive and often ignore interdependence of cellular responses. Operationalization of these findings requires a multi-cellular model of AD that is robust and reproducible. Here, we utilize a coordinated multicellular community approach across 2.3 million nuclei from 427 ROSMAP donors to identify robust multicellular axes associated with AD pathology and sex. The AD signature comprised profound alteration to RORB-GABRG excitatory neurons and disrupted oligodendrocyte precursor cell signaling. A separate set of AD-related cell-type specific molecular processes with strong sexual dimorphism also emerged. Importantly, these signatures developed and ROSMAP predicted neuropathology and sex, respectively, in a completely independent dataset (SEA-AD). These findings altogether summarize a highly consistent multi-cellular response to AD pathology in the human brain, creating a baseline cellular model to which perturbation and treatment experiments can be compared. Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, characterized by the progressive accumulation of β-amyloid plaques, and neurofibrillary tau tangles. However these hallmark pathologies do not by themselves explain the broader cellular and molecular changes accompanying the disease progression or the variability in cognitive impairment. Recent human transcriptomics atlas studies increasingly support a view where amyloid and tau unfold alongside broader disruptions in synaptic function, neuroinflammation and glial dysfunctions, suggesting that AD reflects a failure of a brain ecosystem as a whole rather than a purely cell-autonomous pathology accumulation1–4. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing studies have further shown that these changes are highly cell type-and cell subtype-specific, affecting excitatory and inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, OPCs, and vascular-associated cells in distinct ways4–6. Selective vulnerability and resilience also vary across cellular populations, for example, RORB-expressing excitatory neurons and specific inhibitory neuron subtypes showing distinct patterns of disease-associated alteration across AD stages7–9. At the same time, increasing evidence suggests that the distinct cellular and molecular changes identified across studies may represent components of a broader coordinated multicellular response to AD pathology. In aged human cortex, neuronal, glial and endothelial populations have been shown to co-vary as coordinated multicellular communities associated with AD pathology and cognitive decline10. Trajectory-based analyses have similarly identified coordinated cellular changes across disease progression, particularly among glial support cells8,11. These coordinated responses may also be shaped by communication between neighboring neuronal and glial cells within the same tissue environment10,12–14. To provide clear and robust summarization of single cell AD data, we therefore utilise a coordinated multicellular community (CMC) approach to single cell Alzheimer’s data, emphasizing coherent transcriptional changes across multiple cell types. However, comparing multicellular structures across studies remains technically difficult. Differences in cohorts, brain regions, disease and pathology measures, and analytical frameworks limit direct comparison of the multicellular patterns reported across studies. Although these studies identify broadly related disease processes, they often emphasize different cellular populations and capture different components of the wider multicellular response. Additionally, benchmarking studies have shown that analytical choices across single-cell RNA-sequencing workflows, such as normalization, filtering and clustering, can alter detected expression differences and cell type assignments, substantially influencing downstream findings and biological interpretation15,16. These sources of variation make it difficult to determine whether differences between studies reflect genuine biological heterogeneity or analytical instability. Identifying coordinated changes that remain robust and reproducible across independent cohorts is therefore important for moving beyond individual descriptions towards a more integrated model of cellular response to AD pathology. There has also been limited exploration as to how these multicellular signatures vary in association with demographic and genetic factors. Sex is particularly relevant, as women are more frequently affected by AD, have been reported to show greater tau burden and faster tau accumulation than men17,18, sex-associated immune and glial differences in AD19,20. To address these gaps, we applied the CMC framework to single-nucleus transcriptomic data from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of 427 donors from the Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP) to identify a robust and reproducible multicellular representation of AD-associated transcriptional variation and determine whether the resulting gene modules formed coordinated axes associated with neuropathology. To ensure robustness, we systematically evaluated 432 preprocessing and clustering parameter combinations to identify a reproducible and biologically interpretable representation of disease-associated transcriptional variation, and tested its reproducibility in the independent SEA-AD cohort. We next examined how these coordinated multicellular responses change across increasing pathology, relate to cognitive decline, and are connected through predicted cell-cell communication. Results from these approaches support a multicellular model of AD, in which disease progression reflects coordinated changes across interacting brain cell populations rather than isolated alterations within individual cell types. We developed a modular analytical pipeline and applied it to approximately 2.3 million nuclei from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of 427 ROSMAP donors, including 146 cognitively unimpaired individuals, 110 with mild cognitive impairment, and 171 with dementia4to identify coordinated multicellular transcriptional changes robustly associated with AD-related phenotypes (Fig. 1A). We first preprocessed the data at the single-cell level and constructed donor-and cell subtype-specific metacells, groups of transcriptionally similar cells aggregated to reduce data sparsity and technical noise. Metacells were then split into training, validation and test sets, whilst ensuring that metacells from the same donor were assigned to the same set. Within each cell subtype, genes were clustered into co-expression modules, and linear mixed-effects modelling was used to identify modules associated with AD-related pathological and clinical phenotypes, including global AD pathology burden, amyloid and tau burden, neuropathological staging, vascular and co-pathology measures, APOE genotype and clinical diagnosis. Modules that showed robust associations across training and validation datasets were retained as AD-associated gene modules (AGMs). These AGMs were used in partial least squares (PLS) regression to identify multivariate AGM-phenotype relationships, and were further characterized through other downstream analyses. Findings were replicated in the independent SEA-AD snRNA-seq cohort8. Single-nuclei RNA-seq data from dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (427 donors, ∼2.3 million nuclei) was preprocessed, and cells were clustered into metacells via k-means. Data was split into three parts: train set, validation set and test set. The train set was used for gene clustering into networks and used in the LMER model to select AD-associated gene co-expression clusters. The validation set was used for replication to identify and robust AD-associated gene co-expression modules to be used in Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression analysis and other downstream analyses.(B) Top 10 parameter sets rankedby PLS cross-validated model’s adjusted-R2 performance.(C) Barplot comparison of optimized parameters (Set 363 and Set 309) versus default settings (Set 1),showing cross-validated adjusted-R2 value in training set and predictive adjusted-R2 value in test sets.(D) Effects of individual preprocessing parameterson model performance of all runs, including gene dispersion threshold, gene clustering range, gene expression range, metacell granularity, and sparsity filtering. Preprocessing and clustering parameter choices can strongly influence the detection of AD-associated gene modules, including how cells are aggregated, which genes are retained, and how co-expression modules are defined. Since our goal was to develop a robust cellular signature of AD, we systematically optimised key preprocessing and clustering parameters using a grid search of 432 predefined parameter combinations. The parameter grid included metacell granularity, gene expression thresholds, gene dispersion thresholds, sparsity filters, and gene clustering ranges (Table 1), with the model performance evaluated using adjusted cross-validated R2 (Fig. 1A). Parameter combinations were evaluated using R2 values of the downstream PLS model. The set with the highest training set R2 value was chosen. Next, we ranked all pipeline runs by the adjusted cross-validated R2 of the resulting PLS models, evaluating how well they summarised the main relationships between AD-associated gene module expression and phenotypes. The two best performing parameter sets, Set363 and Set309, achieved similar model performance, (Fig. 1B; Supplementary Table 1). However, Set309 provided a more parsimonious and biologically interpretable model using two PLS latent components. In contrast, Set363 required five components to explain a similar amount of variance, making the model more difficult to interpret. To assess whether optimisation improved performance beyond standard preprocessing choices, we compared the two best-performing parameter sets, Set 309 and Set 363, with the default parameter set, Set 1, which represented Scanpy package’s default preprocessing parameters and the reference clustering configuration defined prior to optimisation (Fig. 1C). In the training dataset, optimisation increased adjusted cross-validated R2 from 0.066 in Set 1 to 0.089 in Set 309 and 0.091 in Set 363, corresponding to an approximately 33% improvement. This improvement generalised to the independent ROSMAP test set, where adjusted R2 increased from-0.005 in Set 1 to 0.036 in Set 309 and 0.026 in Set 363. To further evaluate external generalisability, we applied the same analytical framework to the SEA-AD prefrontal cortex cohort by reconstructing ROSMAP-derived AD-associated gene modules in SEA-AD. Consistent with the ROSMAP results, Set 309 showed improved performance in both train and test sets compared with the default parameter set. Overall, Set 309 provided the best balance between predictive performance, generalisability, and interpretability, and was therefore selected for downstream analyses. Notably, many of the top performing parameter sets had similar R2 values and converged on similar parameter ranges. Aggregating performance across all runs revealed systematic effects of preprocessing choices (Fig. 1D). Higher gene clustering ranges, and thus smaller, finer gene co-expression modules, were associated with improved R2 value of PLS models (Fig. 1D). Higher gene dispersion thresholds, which restrict highly variable genes (HVG) selection to only the most variable genes, also improved model performance. This suggests that focusing on only the strongest and most variable transcriptional signals enhances the stability and predictive power of the downstream models. Similarly, more granular metacells tended to increase performance, whereas extreme settings such as pseudobulk aggregation of each cell subtype per each donor slightly reduced it. To identify gene modules robustly associated with AD-related phenotypes, we next performed linear mixed-effects regression (LMER) analyses across all gene modules and neuropathological and clinical phenotypes (Fig. 2A). Module-phenotype associations were first tested in the training subset, and significant module-phenotype associations (FDR < 0.05) were further re-tested in a validation subset using nominal (p<0.05) significance thresholds (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Table 2). To prioritize reproducible associations and reduce false-positive findings from high-dimensional testing, we retained only modules that were significant in both datasets and showed consistent effect directionality. We identified 24 AGMs out of 533 tested gene modules, corresponding to approximately 4.5% of all modules evaluated, indicating that only a restricted subset of transcriptional programs demonstrated reproducible associations with AD-related phenotypes. The 24 AGMs were distributed across multiple major cell classes, but they were not evenly represented across cell types. Eleven AGMs mapped to excitatory neuronal populations, including seven distinct AGMs from the Exc L4-5 RORB GABRG1 subtype alone. Six AGMs mapped to inhibitory neurons, including four from the Inh LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) population and two from Inh PVALB-like interneurons. The remaining AGMs comprised one astrocytic module, one OPC module, two oligodendrocyte modules, and three microglial modules. Replicated associations were primarily found among neuropathological traits such as Braak score, which had 15 replicable AGMs associated with it, global AD pathology burden (See Methods) (11 AGMs), NIA-Reagan score (13 AGMs), amyloid plaques (10 AGMs) and tau tangles (8 AGMs associated). Notably, AGMs were found almost exclusively for AD-associated phenotypes. The lone exception was Inhibitory PVALB-like gene cluster 12, which was associated only with CAA. To interpret the biological functions represented by the AGMs, we next annotated the modules using complementary enrichment strategies (Fig. 2B, Supplementary Table 3-4). First, each full AGM gene list was tested for over-representation of GO Biological Processes and KEGG terms, identifying significant functional enrichment for 12 AGMs (FDR < 0.05). To more thoroughly characterize AGMs, we additionally used STRING network analysis to identify connected gene subnetworks within each AGM and tested them for functional enrichment (FDR<0.05). This allowed us to detect biologically coherent gene groups embedded within larger AGMs, even when the full module did not show significant enrichment. Finally, exploratory annotations were added for modules with recurrent genes or recognizable functional themes that did not reach statistical significance in the enrichment analyses. These three annotation levels are shown separately inFig. 2B. Together, these approaches provided functional annotations for 20 of the 24 AGMs, whereas four modules showed no clear enrichment and could not be readily interpreted. Annotated AGMs captured a wide range of biological processes, including synaptic signaling, neuronal plasticity and axonogenesis, extracellular matrix (ECM) organisation as well as cellular stress and protein-folding pathways. We also tested the AGMs for enrichment in long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and unannotated transcripts using Fisher’s exact test. While none of the AGMs were significantly enriched for lncRNAs (FDR<0.05), several modules were significantly enriched for unannotated transcripts. The limited functional information available for these transcripts may partly explain why some AGMs were more difficult to annotate. Beyond the presence of these broad functional categories, their distribution across cell types was informative. Axonogenesis, neuronal projection and plasticity-related annotations were present in AGMs from several excitatory, glial and microglial populations, including Exc L6 CT, Exc L3-4 RORB PLCH1, Exc L3-4 RORB CUX2, OPCs, oligodendrocytes and microglia. In contrast, these annotations were absent from the AGMs belonging to Excitatory L4-5 RORB GABRG1 and Inhibitory LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) neurons, two neuronal populations previously implicated to be vulnerable in AD. Instead, AGMs from these vulnerable populations were mainly associated with synaptic receptor activity, ECM organisation, transcriptional regulation, cellular stress, protein folding and mitochondrial respiration, suggesting a stronger association with synaptic dysfunction and cellular stress rather than axonal or structural plasticity. Exc L4-5 RORB GABRG1 neurons showed several diverse AGMs, with C0 and C7 negatively associated with AD pathology, whereas C8, C13 and C5 were positively associated with at least one AD hallmark pathology (Fig 2B, right panel). C0 contained a 53-gene STRING subnetwork linked to neuroimmune signalling (Fig 2B; Supplementary Fig. 1A). C7, while harder to characterise due to enrichment in unannotated transcripts, included several known synaptic and stress-related genes, includingGRIN3A,SNCG,LAMP5,CRYAB,CIRBP,ROMO1andSH3BGRL3. In contrast, C8 showed a clear glutamatergic profile, with enrichment in terms associated to modulation of synaptic transmission and G protein-coupled glutamate receptor signaling, and contained genes includingGRIK2,CNTNAP,CNTNandCDH12/18and GRM family members (Fig 2B; Supplementary Fig. 1B). The positive association of this glutamatergic receptor and synaptic signalling module with pathology suggests that increase in AD pathology is also associated with a shift in excitatory synaptic signaling within Exc L4-5 RORB GABRG1 neurons. Some AGMs also pointed to more pathology-specific cellular states. Inhibitory PVALB-like C12 was selectively associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, rather than broader AD pathology measures. It showed significant enrichment for neuromodulatory/neuropeptide activity, including genes such asNPY,PNOCandVIP, while also containing vascular-associated genes such asTIMP1,MET,RASIP1andMFSD2A. Together, its CAA-specific association and neuromodulatory/vascular profile suggest that C12 may capture a PVALB-like interneuron state linking neurovascular coupling with vascular amyloid pathology. OPC C16 was negatively associated with global AD pathology and enriched for axonogenesis and synaptic signalling terms, including chemical synaptic transmission and voltage-gated cation channel activity, with genes such asGABRA4,GABRG2andGABRG3(Fig 2B; Supplementary Fig. 1D). This suggests that increasing pathology is accompanied by loss of OPC functions related to neuronal and synapse sensing and circuit maintenance. Additionally, the three microglial AGMs also showed distinct functional profiles. Microglia C0 and C11 were negatively associated with pathology and contained annotations related to neuronal maintenance, including axonogenesis, neuromodulation, neuronal plasticity, and, within specific subnetworks, myelination-related processes. Their negative associations with pathology suggest that these supportive transcriptional programs become less prominent with increasing pathological burden, consistent with the negatively associated neuroimmune-signalling module in Exc L4-5 RORB GABRG1 neurons C0. Overall, the functional diversity and contrasting pathology associations of the AGMs indicate that AD is accompanied not by a single uniform transcriptional response, but by multiple distinct neuronal and glial biological processes that are differentially altered across disease pathology. After identifying disease-associated transcriptional changes, we next sought to understand whether or not these changes were independently associated with AD pathology. To do this, we applied Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression to model the multivariate relationship between donor-level gene module expression of these 24 AGMs and AD-associated neuropathological and clinical phenotypes. Adjusted cross-validated model performance was highest for a two-component model (total multi-dataset covariance R2=0.09;Fig. 3A). Permutation testing confirmed that both components captured non-random structure (both PLS Component 1 and Component 2 empirical p=0.001;Fig. 3B), supporting the selection of a two-component solution. PLS Component 1 (PLS-C1) was associated with a broad pathology-linked latent axis, accounting for 24.7% of the shared covariance between the AGM expression and the phenotypes, and was driven by contributions from all selected AGMs (Fig. 3C, Supplementary Table 5). On the phenotype side, this component loaded positively with higher global AD pathology, more amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tau tangles, higher TDP-43 load stages, more severe arteriolosclerosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and chronic microinfarcts, and more advanced clinical diagnosis. APOE E2 loaded negatively, with APOE E2 carriage associated with lower component scores (Fig. 3D). To further characterize the pathology-associated PLS-C1 axis, we evaluated associations between this multicellular transcriptional signature and AD-associated phenotypes. Consistent with the phenotype loadings, higher PLS-C1 gene scores were associated with greater neuropathological burden, including higher global AD pathology burden, amyloid, and tau tangles (Fig. 3F; Supplementary Fig. 2). Similar positive associations were also observed across regional measures of amyloid, neuritic and dense plaques, and neurofibrillary tangles, indicating that the PLS-C1 association was not driven by pathology in a single brain region, but reflected a more broad AD pathology signature (Supplementary Fig. 3A-D). PLS-C1 gene scores were also higher in donors with dementia than in cognitively normal donors or those with mild cognitive impairment, and showed opposing associations with APOE genotype, lower scores in APOE E2 carriers and higher scores in APOE E4 carriers. Together, these findings support PLS-C1 as a coordinated multicellular transcriptional axis associated with increasing AD pathology and more advanced clinical disease. Component 2 (PLS-C2), on the other hand, captured a distinct sex-associated axis. Although it explained 53.8% of leftover covariance after PLS-C1, only four AGMs loaded significantly onto this component (Fig. 3C, Supplementary Table 5). The dominant phenotype loading on Component 2 was sex, showing positive associations with men and a weaker negative loading for APOE E2. Component 2 gene scores were also strongly separated by sex, with men showing much higher gene scores than women (Fig. 3E). Thus, the two-component PLS solution separated a broadly distributed pathology-associated multicellular program from a more focused sex-linked transcriptional signal. We next tested whether the pathology and sex-associated PLS components identified in the ROSMAP cohort could be reproduced in SEA-AD, an independent snRNA-seq prefrontal cortex dataset with similar AD-related phenotypes. AGMs, previously defined in ROSMAP, were reconstructed using the corresponding genes available in SEA-AD (Supplementary Fig. 4C-D). We first fit a de novo PLS model using the reconstructed SEA-AD AGMs. Cross-validation supported a two-component solution, and permutation testing indicated that the selected components captured non-random structure (Supplementary Fig. 4A). As in ROSMAP, SEA-AD PLS Component 1 was primarily associated with pathology-related phenotypes, whereas Component 2 was aligned with sex (Fig. 3G; Supplementary Fig. 4B). Consistent with the phenotype loadings, higher PLS-C1 gene scores were associated with greater pathology burden measures (Fig. 3I) and PLS-C2 gene scores were higher in men than in women (Fig. 3K). We next compared the loadings of matched AGMs between the ROSMAP and SEA-AD PLS models. AGM loadings showed strong concordance between cohorts for both components (PLS-C1 r=0.94; PLS-C2 r=0.84), with most significantly loading AGMs matching loading directions and indicating that modules contributing most strongly to the component were largely preserved across cohorts (Fig. 3H). Moreover, projecting the ROSMAP-trained PLS model directly onto SEA-AD AGM matrix without retraining reproduced the expected relationships between latent scores, pathology, and sex (Fig. 3J, L). Together, these results indicate that the AGM loading patterns underlying both pathology and sex-associated components are highly consistent between ROSMAP and SEA-AD. This cross-cohort replication indicates that PLS-C1 captures a highly reproducible, shared, dataset-independent transcriptomic trend that robustly tracks AD pathological progression, and PLS-C2 captured consistent, similarly reproducible and pronounced sex-associated differences across both datasets. Having established a reproducible, multicellular signature associated with AD pathology, we next sought to characterize the dynamics of this cell network. First, we asked whether the AD-associated modules change in parallel or whether they follow different temporal patterns across the disease continuum. To test this, we modeled AGMs expression as a function of global AD pathology using generalized additive models (GAMs), and grouped the fitted trajectories by spectral clustering. This identified two linked pseudoprogression trajectories (Fig. 5A). One group, comprising 14 AGMs, showed progressive increase in gene expression with increasing global AD pathology, whereas the second group, comprising 10 AGMs, showed a constant decrease in gene expression. Interestingly, modules within each group followed nearly identical trajectories (Supplementary Fig. 5), either rising or falling at similar rates, indicating that their expression changes are likely coordinated in time. Given that PLS-C1 was strongly associated with pathology burden, we next tested whether its relationship with longitudinal cognitive decline differed across levels of global AD pathology. Moderation analysis showed that the association between higher PLS-C1 gene scores and faster decline became stronger as global AD pathology increased for both episodic memory (β=−0.015, 95%CI [−0.025, −0.006], t=−3.16, FDR-p=0.011) and global cognition (β=−0.013, 95%CI [−0.022, −0.003], t=−2.58; FDR-adj p = 0.021;Fig. 5B). At low levels of global AD pathology, PLS-C1 scores showed little association with cognitive change. In contrast, among individuals with high pathology burden, higher PLS-C1 scores were associated with faster antemortem decline in episodic memory and global cognition. The pathology-dependent association between PLS-C1 and cognitive decline raised the possibility that these multicellular transcriptional changes might mediate the established relationship between AD pathology and cognition. We therefore first tested whether PLS-C1 gene scores mediated the association between global AD pathology and cognitive decline. This model showed no evidence of an indirect effect through PLS-C1 (Supplementary Fig. 6A). We next tested the complementary model, in which global AD pathology mediated the association between PLS-C1 gene scores and cognition. Higher PLS-C1 scores were associated with greater global AD pathology, which in turn was associated with faster decline in episodic memory and global cognition (Fig. 5C, Supplementary Fig. 6B). Significant indirect effects were observed for episodic memory (indirect effect = −0.006, 95%CI[-0.009,-0.004], p<0.001) and global cognition (indirect effect = −0.005, 95%CI[-0.008,-0.003], p<0.001). Global AD pathology accounted for an estimated 66% of the total association between PLS-C1 and episodic memory decline and 58% of the association between PLS-C1 and global cognitive decline (Supplementary Fig. 6C). Together, these results suggest that the multicellular transcriptional process captured by PLS-C1 are at least partially independent of AD neuropathology, but affect cognition mainly through its interaction with neuropathology. The PLS model identified a shared transcriptional pattern across multiple cell populations, and so we next aimed to examine what intercellular crosstalk between different cell types might coordinate the changes identified by the PLS model. To address this, we constructed a predictive cell-cell communications network inferring ligand-receptor, adhesion-adhesion, and gap-junction interactions between AGMs using CellPhoneDb v5.0.0. The results revealed a dense network of communication including all major cell classes, with predicted ligand-receptor interactions arising from AGMs that increase or decrease with AD pathology, capturing communication changes across disease progression, rather than treating the network as a static disease-state architecture (Fig. 6A, top panel). The observed network contained 125 predicted molecular interactions, including 111 ligand-receptor (LR) interactions distributed across 94 directed AGM-AGM edges, 13 adhesion-adhesion interactions distributed across 12 AGM-AGM edges, and one gap-junction interaction. Because the analysis was restricted to AD-associated AGMs, both genes in each predicted LR pair originated from modules whose expression change was associated with pathology. The amount of cell-cell communication (expressed here as the number of LR pairs) significantly exceeded what would be expected from a similar sized network of random cell subtypes, whereas adhesion-adhesion connectivity remained within the null range (Fig. 6B, Supplementary Table 6). We used the null modeling procedure as a conservative measure to prune cell-cell connections that do not exceed chance levels (in terms of number of connections expected between two cell subtypes of similar size and composition;Fig. 6Abottom). The pruned network highlighted several features that were not immediately apparent from the full network. Most notably, OPCs retained reciprocal connections with two excitatory neuronal subtypes, Exc L3-4 RORB CUX2 and Exc L3-5 RORB GABRG1, as well as PVALB-like inhibitory interneurons, and microglia. This indicated that OPC communication remained prominent even after controlling for random network structure. This was also reflected in the sender/receiver summary, where OPCs retained nearly all detected ligand-receptor connections after null modelling, with 10/10 incoming and 11/14 outgoing LR connections passing the null threshold (Fig. 6D). In contrast, several highly connected subtypes in the full network, such as LAMP5 NRG1 Rosehip interneurons, did not retain these connections after null modeling, indicating that high overall connectivity did not necessarily correspond to high-confidence communication. At the AGM level, OPCs were represented by a single AGM which was negatively associated with AD pathology (Fig. 6C). In the retained network, OPC C16 had reciprocal connections to several neuronal AGMs, many of which were positively associated with pathology. OPC C16 mainly received signals through the receptorsROBO2,ADGRL2, andEPHA4. These interactions were primarily associated with Teneurin, Ephrin, and SLIT/NTRK-like signalling. In the opposite direction, the most frequently detected OPC-expressed ligands wereEFNA5andTENM2, which predominantly interacted with EPHA-family receptors andADGRL2expressed by neuronal, microglial, and OPC AGMs. The predominance of Ephrin-, Teneurin-, and SLIT-related interactions suggests that OPC C16 may contribute to adhesion-and guidance-related communication with neighbouring neuronal and glial populations. This communication profile is consistent with the functional annotation of OPC C16, which also pointed toward neuronal and circuit-associated processes; AGM negative associations thus suggest reduced representation of this OPC-centered communication network as pathology increases. Worth noting, Exc L4-5 RORB GABRG1 emerged as one of the most connected excitatory subtypes in the retained ligand-receptor network (Fig. 6A, D). However, most significant LR pairs involving this subtype reflected within-subtype communication, out of 13 sent and 12 received LR pairs, 8 originated from within the same subtype, including fibroblast growth factor (FGF), opioid, SLIT and pleiotrophin signaling. The remaining incoming interactions came from Exc L3-5 RORB PLCH1, involving pleiotrophin, opioid, and retinoic-acid-associated signalling, and from OPCs through somatostatin, SLIT and Teneurin signalling (Supplementary Table 6). This suggests that the Exc L4-5 RORB GABRG1 network is dominated by recurrent module-to-module communication, with additional input from neighbouring excitatory and OPC-associated signalling axes. These findings together suggest that AD-associated AGMs are linked by a non-random ligand-receptor network with prominent recurrent excitatory communication and retained OPC-mediated crosstalk.
