Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is increasingly understood as a multicellular disorder, in which amyloid and tau pathology accumulate alongside coordinated changes in various brain cells. Yet, it remains difficult to distinguish which transcriptional changes reflect causal disease-driving mechanisms, compensatory responses, or downstream consequences of neurodegeneration. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing makes it possible to reconstruct the natural history of these changes in human AD, moving toward models of how cellular and molecular responses emerge, interact, and change with pathology3,4,8,11. These studies reveal widespread changes across diverse brain cell types, suggesting that AD-associated transcriptional variation is likely organised into complex, multicellular programs, rather than several populations changing separately. Modeling these programs will be essential for testing which cellular responses, if any, contribute causally to disease progression, how cells respond to drug treatments, and whether those changes mediate pathological or cognitive outcomes. These endeavors will not be possible without robust models of disease associated cellular changes that are reproducible across different cohorts. We identified a robust network of transcriptomic modules, distributed across multiple cell types, that emerged in response to advancing AD pathology consistently across datasets. In contrast to some previous studies6,11,21, the signature we identified was predominantly neuronal, with only a few modules stemming from glia. However, consistent with several previous studies identifying RORB-expressing excitatory neurons as selectively vulnerable in AD, including in entorhinal and neocortical excitatory populations affected by tau pathology4,7,22, we too have detected AGMs from 3 different RORB-expressing subtypes, including RORB CUX2, RORB PLCH1 and RORB GABRG1. In particular, we found Exc L4-5 RORB GABRG1 neurons to contribute substantially more independent transcriptional modifications than other cell subtypes, suggesting these neuronal types have a particularly strong response to AD in the dlPFC. One of the positively-associated gene modules from this subtype was enriched for chemical synaptic transmission and G protein-coupled glutamate receptor signalling, and contained metabotropic glutamate receptor modulatory subunitsGRM3/4/8, kainate receptorGRIK2, presynaptic genesRIMS1andSYN3, and several synaptic adhesion and guidance genes fromCDH,CNTNandCNTNAPfamilies. Together, these changes point to substantial synaptic dysregulation involving glutamatergic receptor signalling, synaptic remodelling, neurotransmitter release and neuronal excitability, all of which have been widely implicated in AD, including in neurons bearing neurofibrillary tangles22,23. Similarly, previous studies have described an upregulated glutamatergic-neuron module in human AD enriched for voltage-gated calcium channels, GPCRs and increased predicted intracellular communication24. However, RORB-associated vulnerability and transcriptional responses appear to vary by subtype and brain region. Mathys et al. identified a vulnerable RORB-expressing L5 AGBL1/GPC5 population in the entorhinal cortex, while Leng et al. found two vulnerable RORB-expressing EC subtypes and noted that the vulnerable RORB+ populations in the SFG were those most similar to their EC counterparts3,7. In contrast, Dharshini et al. identified a distinct, relatively preserved RORB/CUX2/EYA4 layer 4 population with increased expression of genes involved in synaptic maintenance, plasticity and calcium homeostasis, which they interpreted as a compensatory response to hyperexcitability25. Altered expression ofGRIK2,GRM5/7,NRXN1andCDH12has also been linked to disturbed calcium signalling and firing homeostasis in human-induced glutamatergic neurons, with overlapping glutamate-receptor and channel alterations observed in glutamatergic neurons from human AD brains26. Therefore, it is difficult to define whether mechanisms captured in RORB GARBG1 excitatory neurons represent compensatory maintenance of remaining connections, maladaptive excitatory signalling, or both. This RORB GABRG1 signature was accompanied by transcriptomic changes in LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) interneurons, which was another major source of transcriptomic variation observed in our analyses. LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) interneurons had a module enriched in mitochondrial respiration and oxidative phosphorylation, driven by electron transport chain genes fromNDUF,UQCR, andCOXfamilies, alongside superoxide-response and cell-death pathways involvingPRDX1,SOD1,GPX4,FTH1,CLUandHSP90AA1. This module was negatively associated with AD pathology, suggesting reduced interneuron activity and stress-response capacity as pathology increases. Importantly, our CCC analysis predicted ligand-receptor interactions between RORB GABRG1 excitatory neuron and LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) interneuron gene modules, including guidance, remodelling and neuromodulatory signals. Similar AD-associated excitatory-inhibitory communication changes involving synaptic signalling have recently been reported24. An elevated synaptic excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratio has previously been observed in human AD parietal cortex across anatomical, electrophysiological and transcriptomic measurements, with the transcriptional and cellular shifts driven largely by reduced inhibitory components27. LAMP5-expressing interneurons have been shown to suppress neuronal network hyperexcitation, while their loss contributes to AD-and tauopathy-related circuit dysfunction9. The coupled RORB GABRG1 and LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) signatures may therefore reflect a local E/I imbalance in which declining interneuron function permits or amplifies hyperexcitability-related changes in vulnerable RORB GABRG1 excitatory neurons. Other neuronal and glial cell types, less central to this coordinated response, consistently showed strong enrichment for genes involved in axonogenesis and neuronal plasticity. A consistent observation across other neuronal and glial cells less prominent in this coordinated response, was a strong enrichment in transcription of genes involved in axonogenesis and neuronal plasticity. Mathys et al. also reported synapse-and cell projection related changes across multiple cell types4, indicating broad pathology-associated changes in synaptic organisation and maintenance. Similar changes in axon-guidance and synaptic pathways have been observed in excitatory neurons during early amyloid pathology28, while perturbed axonogenesis accompanied by impaired neurite outgrowth has been reported in iPSC-derived AD neurons29. These recurring axonogenesis-related changes across several neuronal subtypes may reflect attempts to remodel or maintain neuronal connections as pathology progresses, but may also include maladaptive responses associated with impaired neurite growth. One interesting example of this in our dataset came from oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), which receive synaptic input from neurons, respond to neuronal activity, and contribute to circuit remodelling and activity-dependent myelination30–32. Our CCC analysis revealed robust reciprocal communication between one prominent OPC module and several neuronal modules. This suggests that these OPCs may help maintain neuronal plasticity and circuit stability, with its pathology-associated decline contributing to the loss of neuronal support in AD. Similarly, Gabitto et al. reported early upregulation of OPC differentiation and remyelination factors, which they interpreted as a potentially compensatory response, followed by a decrease later8. SMOC1, an OPC-expressed extracellular matrix protein, is also altered early with Aβ plaque accumulation and repeatedly emerges across CSF and brain proteomic studies of AD33–35. In parallel, Aβ plaque-associated OPCs have been shown to adopt senescence-like inflammatory states and lose differentiation capacity36, suggesting that the negative association of OPC C16 may reflect erosion of an OPC-mediated neuronal maintenance or plasticity state as pathology increases. Microglia in AD are often associated with neuroinflammatory signatures37,38. Whilst we didn’t detect any robust neuroinflammatory signatures in our results, we found two microglial gene modules that were negatively associated with AD and contained networks associated with axonogenesis, neuronal plasticity, and myelination. Previous literature has also shown that microglia are known to participate in synaptic remodelling and maintenance39,40, and promote learning-dependent synapse formation through BDNF41. It is worth noting that our use of cell-type specific background sets in our enrichment analyses may have attenuated our power to detect very common microglial signals, such as those related to neuroinflammation. Similarly, our null modeling approach seemed to disproportionately prune microglial CCC connections. We therefore cannot rule out the lack of expected neuroinflammation signals, due to our conservative approach resulting in type II error. Nevertheless, the negative association of synaptic maintenance microglial gene modules may reflect reduced homeostatic microglial support for neuronal processes along the pathology axis. In all, increased AD pathology was associated with a strong transcriptomic response selectively in RORB GABRG excitatory neurons and LAMP5 inhibitory neurons, perhaps reflecting an E/I imbalance, and accompanied by reduced homeostatic functions in glial support cells, and increased synaptic reorganization in other neuronal types. Determining the biological role of this multicellular signature is inherently challenging. Observational transcriptomic data cannot establish whether it represents a compensatory response, a disease-driving mechanism, or a downstream consequence of accumulating pathology, and these possibilities are not mutually exclusive. Nevertheless, several features of our results provide clues to the biological significance of this cellular signature of AD. The signature appears organised, involving multiple different cell types and spanning across the pathology continuum. Together with the observed cell-cell communication network, this shows a reproducible tissue-level response that evolves throughout disease progression. This interpretation is consistent with recent transcriptomic, spatial, and proteomic studies showing that coordinated molecular networks emerge early in AD and continue to change across the pathological continuum8,10,11,33,42. The signature also appears to contain both potentially adaptive and maladaptive components. Several positively associated AGMs were enriched for axonogenesis, neurite guidance, extracellular matrix remodelling and neuronal plasticity, while oligodendrocyte-associated modules furthermore showed enrichment for processes including ion homeostasis, intracellular signalling, lipid metabolism, extracellular remodelling and stress adaptation. These changes could represent attempts to preserve neuronal connectivity and tissue homeostasis in the face of accumulating pathology. Conversely, negatively associated AGMs suggest progressive loss of supportive cellular functions, including the decline of OPC modules enriched for axonogenesis and synaptic support, together with the reduction of LAMP5 rosehip interneuron modules enriched for mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation pathways. At the same time, multiple RORB GABRG1 excitatory neuron AGMs showed increased expression of synaptic signalling pathways, raising the possibility that selective loss of inhibitory restraint alongside enhanced excitatory signalling contributes to a gradual shift in cortical E/I balance, rather than simply widespread neuronal dysfunction. Taken together, these observations suggest that the signature reflects a structured change of the cortical cellular ecosystem, in which adaptive and maladaptive responses coexist throughout disease progression. Finally, the pathology-related PLS axis was associated with clinical disease severity, while the mediation and moderation analyses indicated a more complex relationship between the multicellular signature, neuropathological burden and cognition. The signature did not mediate the effect of global AD pathology on cognition, arguing against a simple model in which pathology induces the multicellular response, which then drives cognitive decline. Instead, global AD pathology mediated the association between the signature and cognition, while the relationship between the signature and cognitive decline became stronger as pathology increased. This suggests that the signature may not be inherently detrimental, but that the cellular changes it captures become increasingly maladaptive as pathology accumulates. Similar transcriptomic studies have identified molecular states associated with both AD pathology and cognitive decline, while showing that their relationships with cognition are not fully accounted for by amyloid and tau burden alone4,43. Rather than representing either successful compensation or inevitable degeneration, this coordinated multicellular signature may therefore capture how the brain reorganises as AD pathology accumulates, with different components contributing to tissue adaptation, cellular dysfunction and the clinical expression of disease. One of the strengths of this study is the focus on optimizing data preprocessing in advance of data-analysis. Benchmarking studies have shown that parameter choices and workflow structure in snRNA and scRNA data contexts substantially affect downstream performance, and that optimal settings depend on the dataset, method, and analytical task, rather than being universal15,16,44–48. Although much of this work has focused on clustering, dimensionality reduction, cell-type annotation, or tool comparison, the same principle is relevant for disease-focused modelling. This is also important for robustness, as single-cell studies can be vulnerable to false discoveries when replicate structure and technical variability are not handled carefully49,50. In line with this, we did not treat default preprocessing settings as inherently best, but optimised parameters for the specific aim of identifying reproducible cell-subtype-specific gene modules that improved PLS model performance. Importantly, we did this in a manner that avoided data leakage and minimized overfitting. Thus, the selected parameter set should be interpreted as the best-performing configuration for this downstream task, and not as a generally superior preprocessing strategy for all snRNA-seq analyses. This optimisation improved not only apparent model performance but also generalisability. Concordant AGM loadings and successful projection of the ROSMAP-trained model into SEA-AD suggest that the workflow captured a reproducible biological structure rather than cohort-specific one. What was not necessarily expected was that the parameter set optimized in ROSMAP also performed substantially better than default settings in the SEA-AD dataset. While we cannot extrapolate whether this optimized parameter set is superior beyond the study of AD-associated changes in these two datasets, it does suggest that parameter optimization may generalize to additional datasets as long as the data and analytic goals remain similar. The best-performing parameter sets converged on biologically interpretable features. Higher dispersion thresholds reduced the number of highly variable genes entering downstream analysis, suggesting that stricter feature selection helped limit noisy or weakly informative signals. In addition, higher gene-clustering ranges produced smaller and more specific AGMs, which may have helped separate AD-associated processes, such as stress responses, axonogenesis, and extracellular matrix remodelling, that would otherwise be collapsed into broader transcriptional aggregates. Subtype-specific metacells provided a compromise between robustness and biological resolution, sitting between noisy individual nuclei and coarse donor-level pseudobulking. This reduced dropout and sampling noise while retaining finer within-subtype variation51,52. However, this robustness may come at the cost of sensitivity to rare or transient cell states, such as reactive microglial populations outnumbered by more abundant homeostatic microglia. Constructing metacells within predefined subtypes limited the risk of merging biologically distinct populations, although heterogeneous metacells can still distort downstream signals if not carefully tuned53. Sexual dimorphism in the prevalence of AD has been consistently reported and well described, with women more frequently affected than men54. Women have also been reported to show faster cognitive decline and greater brain atrophy55,56, more rapid tau accumulation in the presence of elevated amyloid burden57, and differences in cognitive and neuropsychiatric presentation across the AD continuum55,56. We were interested in characterizing a universal cellular response to AD, and so we initially included sex primarily as a covariate of no interest when defining AGMs. Despite this analytical choice, sex emerged as a strong and reproducible source of multicellular transcriptional variation. After the primary AD-related cellular response, the strongest source of covariance among AGMs related almost exclusively to sex, a finding that was replicated in the external SEA-AD cohort. While we detected no significant sex-by-pathology interactions among individual AGMs, several modules were independently associated with both sex and global AD pathology and showed sexually dimorphic baseline expression. Previous single-cell studies have primarily linked sex differences in AD to immune and glial transcriptional states, including alterations in microglial lysosomal activity58, an increased abundance of disease-associated microglia in females19, and astrocytic inflammatory responses59. Our findings extend these observations by identifying sex-associated modules in oligodendrocytes and selected neuronal types, suggesting that sexual dimorphism may span a broad range of AD-relevant cellular processes. Some of these AGMs also contained sex-chromosome genes, suggesting that dimorphic expression may be influenced by differences in X and Y-linked gene expression as well as hormone-dependent regulation. However, these effects cannot be clearly disentangled using postmortem transcriptomic data alone. One such example was oligodendrocytes cluster 12, which was positively associated with pathology and showed higher baseline expression in women. Although the module was not significantly enriched, several genes and a small subnetwork pointed to lipid and fatty-acid handling, and oxidative-stress responses. Its higher expression in women may reflect a more disease-associated or stress-responsive oligodendrocyte state at baseline, consistent with experimental evidence that sex-biased oligodendrocyte responses can emerge before myelin loss and vary with age and pathological context60. Given the large number of poorly annotated transcripts in this AGM, it may also capture sex-related oligodendrocyte mechanisms that are relevant to AD but remain incompletely understood. Sexual dimorphism was also evident in the previously discussed LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) response. Cluster 6 contained a subnetwork related to the unfolded-protein response, chaperone-mediated protein refolding, MAPK regulation and activity-dependent transcription, suggesting a stress-adaptive neuronal state61. Its lower expression in women may therefore indicate reduced capacity to mount these responses, potentially increasing the susceptibility of LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) interneurons to dysfunction as pathology accumulates. These observations raise the possibility that sex influences AD not only by modifying disease-associated responses, but also through inherent differences in the expression of gene networks that later participate in the disease process. Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, our analysis is based on postmortem single-nucleus transcriptomic data and therefore captures RNA abundance within surviving nuclei at a single terminal time point, rather than dynamic molecular changes in living tissue. Postmortem interval and other events surrounding death may further influence the measured expression profiles, despite statistical adjustment and quality control62. Second, nuclear RNA represents only part of the cellular transcriptome and doesn’t reflect cytoplasmic or locally translated synaptic processes. Moreover, the most vulnerable cell populations may already have been depleted by the time of tissue collection, thus potentially biasing the observed signatures towards surviving cellular states. Our analyses were also limited to the dlPFC, a region affected relatively late in AD, which may limit detection of earlier disease-associated cellular changes. Our deliberately conservative discovery and validation framework prioritised robustness and replication over sensitivity. Although this reduced the likelihood of false-positive findings, it may also have excluded weaker, heterogeneous, or less well-powered disease-associated responses, particularly in rare cell populations. This may also partially explain why reproducible associations were concentrated among pathology measures, while APOE genotype and vascular measures showed few or none. This lack of robust associations likely reflects limited power, given the small number of E2 and E4 carriers, or weaker, more heterogeneous transcriptional effects, rather than a true absence of transcriptional associations. Biological interpretation was further limited by incomplete annotation resources, as many detected transcripts remain poorly characterised, while cell-cell communication analyses rely on ever evolving ligand-receptor databases that may still be missing relevant interactions. Since our snRNA-seq data lack spatial information, we cannot establish whether the predicted ligand-receptor pairs reflect direct interactions between cells in the tissue. Finally, generating sufficiently large donor-by-subtype groups for metacell and AGM construction required merging some related cellular states, preventing separate analysis of potentially distinct reactive populations, particularly among microglia. In summary, we identified a reproducible multicellular transcriptional signature associated with AD pathology and replicated its major pathology-and sex-related axes in an independent cohort. The signature linked vulnerable neuronal populations with glial states involved in cellular stress, circuit regulation and neuronal support, suggesting that AD progression involves both adaptive and dysfunctional tissue-level responses. Future work should determine how specific this signature is to AD by examining aging and other neurodegenerative disease datasets, and assess how consistently the response is observed across different brain regions. Developing animal or cellular models that reproduce this multicellular response could help establish its temporal sequence, while analysis of tissue from patients treated with AD-targeting therapies may reveal whether modifying pathology alters the signature. Spatial and multi-omic approaches could be used to test the predicted cellular interactions and determine how the identified modules relate to protein-level changes, while experimental perturbation will be needed to establish which responses contribute to pathology and which reflect compensation. Overall, this framework provides a basis for studying AD as a coordinated multicellular process and for identifying cellular responses that may influence vulnerability, progression and clinical outcomes. We developed a multi-step computational pipeline to identify robust gene expression modules associated with Alzheimer’s disease pathology from single-nucleus RNA-seq data (Fig. 1A). Before running the main pipeline, a preliminary preprocessing and clustering step was used to consolidate low-abundance cell subtypes that contained too few nuclei to support stable downstream preprocessing. Following subtype consolidation, raw count matrices were reprocessed separately for each major cell type using the parameter settings evaluated in the optimization framework. Then the data was grouped by cell subtypes and donors, and transcriptionally similar nuclei were aggregated into metacells to reduce single-cell sparsity and generate more stable expression profiles. Donors were then split into three equal parts: train, validate and test sets, and gene co-expression modules were constructed within each subtype and tested for associations with disease-related phenotypes using linear mixed effects models. Modules that replicated across training and validation datasets were retained as AD-associated gene modules for downstream multivariate Partial Least Squares (PLS) and other downstream analyses. These steps are outlined in detail below. Dataset donors were assigned into three equal sets, stratified by sex and dementia diagnosis, with all nuclei and derived metacells from the same donor assigned to the same dataset. Training and validation sets were used to identify robust AD-associated gene modules, and the test set was used for PLS evaluation. Before running the main analysis pipeline, we performed a preliminary preprocessing step to identify low-abundance subtypes requiring consolidation. ROSMAP single-nucleus RNA-seq count matrices were processed at each major cell type level using Scanpy v1.10.164. Nuclei with fewer than 100 detected genes were removed, and genes detected in fewer than three nuclei were excluded. Counts were then library-size normalized to 10,000 counts per nucleus and log-transformed. Highly variable genes were identified separately within each major cell type initially using minimum and maximum mean-expression thresholds of 0.0125 and 3.0, and a minimum dispersion threshold of 0.5. We then calculated cell subtype-averaged HVG expression profiles and performed hierarchical clustering using Ward linkage and Euclidean distance. Cell subtypes represented by fewer than 20,000 nuclei across all donors were merged with their nearest transcriptional neighbor. The complete mapping from original annotations to merged subtypes can be found in Supplementary Table 7. This preliminary preprocessing step was used only to determine the final subtype groupings. The normalized expression values and highly variable genes generated during this step were not carried forward into the main analysis pipeline. Cell subtype naming conventions differed between the ROSMAP and SEA-AD datasets. However, because the underlying transcriptional subtype structure showed high concordance across cohorts, SEA-AD subtype labels were harmonized to match the ROSMAP nomenclature before downstream replication analyses. Cell subtype matching was performed separately within each major cell type. For both datasets, nuclei with fewer than 100 detected genes were removed, and genes detected in fewer than three nuclei were removed. Genes shared between ROSMAP and SEA-AD were then retained. Expression values were library-size normalized to a target sum of 10,000 counts per nucleus and log-transformed. For each dataset, mean gene expression was then calculated for each subtype using the shared gene set. Subtype-level expression profiles were standardized by z-scoring, and pairwise correlations were computed between ROSMAP and SEA-AD subtype profiles. The resulting correlation matrices were visualized as heatmaps and manually inspected to identify the best-matching SEA-AD subtype for each ROSMAP subtype. These matches were then used to rename SEA-AD subtypes according to the ROSMAP annotation scheme (Supplementary Fig. 7; Supplementary Table 7). Following subtype consolidation, the raw count matrices were reprocessed from the beginning separately for each major cell type, since downstream analyses compared gene networks within specific cell subtypes rather than across the entire dataset. Nuclei and lowly detected genes were removed, after which counts were library-size normalized to 10,000 counts per nucleus and log-transformed. Highly variable genes (HVGs) were identified using the functionscanpy.pp.highly_variable_genes()at the major cell type level. HVG selection served as a feature selection step, restricting analyses to the most informative genes while reducing noise from invariant ones. Additionally, identifying HVGs at the cell type (rather than subtype) level ensured that gene lists were specific to each major lineage but remained comparable across its constituent subtypes. Parameter optimization for HVG selection is described below, in sectionParameter optimization). Because snRNA-seq data is known to be noisy and highly sparse, largely due to stochastic dropout65,66, we aggregated cells into metacells to reduce this noise and sparsity (Fig. 1A). This pooling strategy differs from pseudobulking, which groups all cells of a subtype within a donor into one profile. Metacells instead group a predefined number of similar cells, preserving within-donor cell heterogeneity while still producing more stable expression profiles that are better suited for downstream analyses52. To achieve this, metacells were constructed within each donor and cell subtype group using a k-nearest neighbour (kNN) graph. The parameterk(number of neighbors) controlled granularity, with smaller values retaining fine-grained variation and vice versa.kwas defined via parameter optimization, described below. For each donor-by-subtype group, metacells were generated iteratively. At each iteration, PCA was performed on the remaining cells to identify a seed cell, defined as the cell with the largest absolute PC1 score. The seed cell and its nearest neighbors, for a total of k cells, were grouped into one metacell and then removed from the remaining cell pool. This procedure was repeated until no further metacells could be formed. After metacell clustering, each metacell was assigned to the training, validation, or test set according to the donor-level split described earlier. Metacell sparsity was calculated as the proportion of genes with zero detected expression, and metacells exceeding the predefined sparsity level (an optimised parameter) were removed. Individual gene expression is noisy and expression changes rarely happen in isolation. Therefore, after clustering the cells into metacells, we then clustered the genes into gene co-expression modules viak-means to derive co-expression networks that may reflect independent intracellular processes, pathways or components (Fig. 1A). The optimal number of gene co-expression modules was determined by scanning across a defined range ofkvalues (an optimized parameter), calculating silhouette scores for each solution, and selecting the peak with the highest score. Module assignments defined in the training set were then propagated to the validation and test sets. Gene clustering across all subtypes produced a large number of modules, many of which were unlikely to be relevant to AD. To reduce dimensionality and focus on biologically meaningful signals, we tested each module for association with AD-associated phenotypes using linear mixed-effects regression (LMER), implemented in the lme4 and lmerTest R packages (Fig. 1A). The model included phenotype, sex, and sparsity as fixed effects and donor as a random effect: Gene co-expression module ∼ phenotype + sex + sparsity + (1|donor) Phenotypes included APOE E2 and E4 allele status, cognitive diagnosis, age at death, Braak stage, CERAD score, global AD pathology (gpath), NIA-Reagan score, amyloid load, neurofibrillary tangles, arteriolosclerosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), presence of microinfarcts, and cerebral atherosclerosis. Gene expression modules significantly associated with any phenotypes after FDR correction (FDR <0.05) in the training set were taken forward to the validation set, where replication was defined as passing a nominal p-value < 0.05. Only modules replicating in both datasets were retained as AD-associated gene modules (AGMs). Rather than investigating AGMs individually, we applied partial least squares (PLS) regression to jointly analyze all AGMs and AD phenotypes using a multivariate approach (Fig. 1). PLS derives latent components that maximize the covariance between two data matrices, allowing us to identify coordinated patterns of AGMs that covary with multiple disease traits simultaneously. In our case, we sought to estimate covariance between AGMs (X) and AD-related phenotypes (Y). AGMs (PLS X) from all cell types were combined across the training and validation sets. For each AGM, metacell-level expression values were averaged per donor to generate a donor-level AGM expression matrix. Donors and AGMs with more than 30% missing values were excluded. Remaining missing values were imputed using k-nearest-neighbor imputation (k= 5), and AGM expression values were scaled using MinMax scaling. Phenotype data were processed using the same imputation and scaling approach. Amyloid, tangle, and global AD pathology scores were log-transformed before scaling. The phenotype data (PLS Y) was restricted to a focused panel of age-and AD-relevant variables, including age at death, global AD pathology, amyloid load, neurofibrillary tangles, TDP-43 stages, arteriolosclerosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), cerebral atherosclerosis, chronic microinfarcts, APOE E2 and E4 allele status, and the final consensus cognitive diagnosis at the time of death (CU, MCI, or dementia). To determine the optimal number of components in PLS model selection, models with one to ten components were trained and evaluated using five-fold cross-validation, repeated ten times. Adjusted cross-validated R2 and mean absolute error (MAE) were computed, and the model with the highest adjusted cross-validated R2 was selected. Statistical significance of the PLS components was assessed using permutation testing with 1,000 iterations. Stability of PLS component loadings was assessed using bootstrap resampling with replacement across 10,000 iterations. Because upstream preprocessing choices influence the AGM features used in the final PLS model, and there is no single universally optimal setting for these steps in single-nucleus RNA-seq data, we systematically tested several pipeline parameters and ranked parameter sets by downstream (cross-validated) PLS performance. Pipeline parameters were varied across HVG selection, metacell construction, sparsity filtering, and gene-module clustering. For HVG selection, several dispersion thresholds and minimum and maximum expression cutoffs were tested. For metacell construction, differentkvalues and clustering resolutions were tested, including pseudobulking as a non-metacell comparison. We also varied the threshold used to exclude sparse metacells. For gene-module clustering, multiplekranges were assessed to determine the optimal number of modules (Table 1). The full parameter grid was run in parallel on a high-performance computing cluster, testing 432 parameter combinations in total. Parameter sets were ranked by mean repeated adjusted cross-validated PLS R² within the merged training and validation set. The independent test set was withheld from parameter tuning and used only for final model assessment. For final model evaluation, the PLS model was fitted on the merged training-validation dataset using the selected number of components. The independent test set was processed using the same selected AGMs and transformed using the imputation and scaling parameters fitted on the merged training-validation data. The trained PLS model was then applied to the transformed test set to evaluate generalizability. After subtype harmonization, the SEA-AD snRNA-seq dataset was processed using the default and optimized pipeline parameters selected in ROSMAP. Because SEA-AD was used as an external replication cohort, gene modules were not independently rediscovered in SEA-AD. Instead, the AD-associated gene modules (AGMs) previously defined in ROSMAP were reconstructed in SEA-AD using the same module gene assignments. This allowed us to test whether the transcriptional programs identified in ROSMAP could be recovered in an independent cohort. To assess whether similar multivariate transcriptomic–phenotypic structure could be identified directly within SEA-AD, we trained a de novo partial least squares (PLS) regression model using SEA-AD donor-level AGM expression profiles as predictor variables. The phenotype matrix included age at death, sex, overall AD neuropathologic change, Braak stage, Thal phase, and CERAD score. Donor-level AGM expression values were derived as described for ROSMAP by averaging AGM expression across metacells belonging to the same donor. Model preprocessing, component selection, and evaluation followed the same procedure used for the ROSMAP PLS analysis. To directly assess the replicability of the ROSMAP-derived transcriptional structure, the fitted ROSMAP PLS model was applied to the SEA-AD donor-level AGM matrix using thePLSRegression.transform()function. This projects new observations into the latent space defined by the original ROSMAP model without refitting the model in SEA-AD. Before projection, the SEA-AD predictor matrix was aligned to the ROSMAP AGM feature matrix to ensure that module columns matched the features used to train the original ROSMAP model. Missing values in the SEA-AD matrix were imputed using the gene imputer fitted to the ROSMAP training data, after which the matrix was transformed using the MinMax scaler fitted to the ROSMAP training data. Neither the imputer nor the scaler was refitted using SEA-AD data. One ROSMAP-derived module, Exc NRGN Cluster 15, was not present in the SEA-AD reconstructed AGM matrix. To preserve feature alignment, a placeholder column was added for this module. Because MinMax scaling was used during preprocessing, all values in this placeholder column were assigned a value of 0.5, corresponding to the midpoint of the scaled feature range. The resulting SEA-AD matrix was then transformed using the fitted ROSMAP PLS model to derive SEA-AD PLS X scores. These projected scores were used to evaluate whether the donor-level transcriptional axis identified in ROSMAP generalized to the independent SEA-AD cohort. To capture the trajectories of transcriptional changes across disease progression, we treated global AD pathology burden as a cross-sectional proxy for disease progression and fit each AGM as a smooth function of log-transformed global AD pathology using generalized additive models (GAMs) with the pyGAM package v0.12.067. AGM expression values were z-scored to put them on a comparable scale, and models were fitted with penalized spline terms (splines = 5). P-values for the global AD pathology term were corrected across AGMs using false discovery rate (FDR) correction. To compare dynamic patterns across AGMs, fitted curves were predicted over a common global AD pathology grid and independently z-scored to remove differences in baseline expression and response amplitude, thereby emphasizing trajectory shape. Similarity between the standardized curves was quantified using cosine similarity, and AGMs were grouped into trajectory classes using spectral clustering. Because these data are cross-sectional rather than longitudinal, we refer to these curves as pseudoprogression trajectories. To characterize how these transcriptional trajectories differ between men and women, we extended the GAM model by adding a sex term and an interaction term between globa lAD pathology burden and sex. For each AGM, we applied false discovery rate (FDR) correction for the p-values to identify modules with sex-global AD pathology interactions and independent associations with each variable. To infer putative intercellular signaling involving AGMs, we used the curated interaction annotations from the CellPhoneDB v5.0.0 database (accessed via:https://github.com/ventolab/CellphoneDB-data)68. We did not use the CellPhoneDB analysis software; instead, we implemented custom code to identify CellPhoneDB-supported ligand-receptor, adhesion, and gap-junction interactions between genes contained in AGMs and their corresponding cell subtypes. We performed two complementary permutation analyses to assess whether the observed AGM interaction network showed greater connectivity than expected by chance. For both analyses, we generated 10,000 null module sets in which each null module was matched to an observed AGM by module size and sampled from the same subtype-specific highly variable gene background. First, we tested overall network connectivity by counting the number of edges formed between modules in each null network and comparing this null distribution with the number of edges observed in the AGM network. In this analysis, edges were treated as binary: two AGMs were considered connected if at least one CellPhoneDB-supported interaction was identified between them, regardless of how many individual ligand-receptor, adhesion, or gap-junction interactions supported that connection. The observed AGM network was considered more connected than expected when its number of edges exceeded the upper bound of the 95% null interval. Second, we assessed edge strength by comparing the observed weight of each AGM-AGM connection, defined by the number of interactions, with the corresponding null distribution generated from matched null module pairs. Here we considered the edge significant when its weight exceeded the null 95% interval. The same framework was also applied at the parent cell-subtype level by aggregating module-level interactions according to their assigned subtypes, allowing us to identify subtype-subtype connections with greater interaction strength than expected by chance. These analyses were used to prioritize putative sender-receiver relationships associated with AD-linked transcriptional programs. Gene set annotation analyses were performed to assign biological interpretations to the AGMs. First, each AGM was tested for functional and pathway enrichment using over-representation analysis (ORA). Analysis was performed usinggseapy.enrichr()function from the Python gseapy v1.1.13 package69. For each AGM, the gene input list consisted of genes assigned to that AGM and the background gene set was defined as the highly variable genes from the corresponding cell type from which the AGM was derived. For the enrichment, we queried KEGG and Gene Ontology Biological Process databases, and the terms were considered significantly enriched if the adjusted p-value was < 0.05 (FDR correction). Additionally, since the AGMs were derived using a purely data driven approach, we additionally used STRING DB to see whether genes within each AGM formed smaller functionally connected subgroups. Networks were queried using the functional network type with a required interaction confidence score of 400. The STRING evidence channels retained for network construction were co-expression, experimental evidence, and text mining, while neighbourhood, fusion, co-occurrence, and database evidence channels were excluded. The resulting STRING edge tables contained pairwise gene associations and channel-specific evidence scores. Using NetworkX, we then grouped genes connected by STRING edges into groups, and using STRING gene set description API, the group functional descriptions were annotated based on STRING internal enrichment. For STRING-connected groups that remained unannotated, we performed an additional ORA analysis, using the same gseapy.enrichr() approach as described above. Finally, AGM or STRING-connected subgroups that remained without statistically significant enrichment were assessed descriptively by looking at the gene composition. Known functional gene groups were used to provide qualitative labels where possible. AGMs without clear enrichment or interpretable gene-level themes were left unannotated. These approaches were considered to represent three decreasing levels of evidence: AGM-level enrichment, enrichment within STRING-connected subgroups, and descriptive interpretation based on gene composition. Exploratory mediation and moderation analyses were performed to examine relationships among donor-level PLS component 1 (PLS C1) gene scores, global AD pathology burden, and retrospective longitudinal cognitive decline before death. For cognitive outcomes, we used estimated person-specific slopes for working memory, episodic memory, semantic memory, perceptual speed, perceptual orientation, and global cognition, as previously described70. These slope measures represent the rate of change in cognition over time, and were previously adjusted for age at baseline, sex, and years of education. The underlying cognitive measures were composite scores derived from a battery of 19 neuropsychological tests. The tests contributing to each cognitive measure are provided in Supplementary Table 8. Mediation analyses were performed using Pingouin v0.6.071. Two complementary mediation models were tested for each cognitive domain. In the first model, global AD pathology was specified as the predictor, PLSX1 gene score as the mediator, and cognitive slope as the outcome. In the second model, PLSX1 gene score was specified as the predictor, global AD pathology as the mediator, and cognitive slope as the outcome. Moderation analyses tested whether the association between PLSX1 scores and cognitive slopes varied at different levels of global AD pathology burden. Linear models were fitted with an interaction term between PLSX1 and global AD pathology, adjusting for age at death and sex. For visualization purposes, donors were stratified into low, medium, and high global AD pathology groups. To determine whether the DLPFC-derived PLSX1 gene score was associated specifically with pathology in the prefrontal cortex or reflected a broader brain-wide neurodegenerative process, we examined its associations with regional pathology measures. Here we’ve used linear regression models to associate PLSX1 gene scores with pathology whilst covarying for age at death and sex. Regional tau-related measures included neurofibrillary tangle burden and tau tangle measures across multiple brain regions: the angular gyrus, entorhinal cortex, hippocampus, midfrontal cortex, midtemporal cortex, calcarine cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, inferior temporal cortex, and superior frontal gyrus. Amyloid-related measures included amyloid burden, neuritic plaques, and diffuse plaques measured across the same available brain regions. title: Opposing plasticity mechanisms enhance visual inputs that violate their context
author: Seignette, K.; de Kraker, L.; Halak, M.; Papale, P.; Petro, L. S.; Montijn, J. S.; Self, M. W.; Wilmes, K. A.; Larkum, M. E.; Roelfsema, P. R.; Muckli, L.; Levelt, C. N.
text:
To navigate complex environments, the mammalian visual system prioritizes informative inputs by comparing incoming sensory signals with learned contextual information. While this process is often conceptualized as a difference computation, cortical circuitry poses fundamental challenges: visual contextual feedback is predominantly amplifying, and whether inhibitory circuits support selective subtraction is unknown. Here, we show how layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in mouse primary visual cortex can implement this comparison through plasticity that acts in opposite directions on responses to direct visual stimulation and contextual signals. To dissociate these components, we presented full images to mice or images where one quadrant was occluded, removing direct visual stimulation while preserving surrounding contextual information, and measured pyramidal cell responses to these stimuli before and after visual familiarization. After familiarization to non-occluded images, responses to direct visual inputs were selectively reduced, whereas contextual responses to occluded images strengthened. This strengthening generalized across natural scenes, allowing contextual inputs to also drive responses to novel occluded images and amplify responses to novel non-occluded images. A computational model reproduced these changes by weakening feedforward inputs and strengthening both feedforward-driven inhibition and contextual feedback in response to repeated pyramidal cell activity. This context-contrasting mechanism produced a conserved structure of responses to occluded and non-occluded images across mice and previously acquired monkey and human data. Together, these results suggest a mechanism for saliency assignment that exploits the compartmental organization of cortical pyramidal neurons: they learn the generalized statistical structure of familiar contexts, allowing selective amplification of improbable inputs or omissions. Visual scenes contain far more information than can be processed rapidly. The visual system must therefore prioritize the most informative elements – features that deviate from their surroundings and learned contextual expectations1–4. How cortical circuits implement such comparisons remains a central challenge in neuroscience research5–7. Theoretical accounts often propose that deviations are detected through subtractive or difference-like computations between feedforward input and contextual feedback8–13. This mechanism may indeed account for attenuation of self-motion related responses14. However, how such selective subtraction could be implemented by cortical circuits remains unclear. Visual feedback is predominantly amplifying, and although feedback can recruit inhibitory circuits15, it is not known whether these provide the feature-specific inhibition required to subtract complex contextual inputs from incoming sensory signals. This raises a fundamental question: how does the cortex compare feedforward visual input with complex contextual signals within the constraints of cortical circuitry? Addressing this question requires experimentally dissociating direct sensory drive from contextual influences. In primary visual cortex (V1), neurons respond not only to stimuli within their classical receptive fields (cRFs), but also to contextual signals conveyed by recurrent and feedback connections16, giving rise to extraclassical receptive field (ecRF) responses17–20. Partially occluded visual stimuli provide a powerful approach to disentangle these inputs as they eliminate feedforward input to a retinotopic region of V1 while preserving surrounding visual context21. Human fMRI studies22–26and electrophysiological recordings in non-human primates27have shown that occluded regions can evoke robust, image-specific responses in V1, driven by information from beyond the classical receptive field. These responses reflect contextual inputs rather than modulation of direct sensory input, making occlusion paradigms well suited for isolating contextual signals and studying their experience-dependent modulation. Here, we used two-photon calcium imaging to record the activity of layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (PyCs) in mouse V1 during presentation of non-occluded and partially occluded natural images, before and after visual familiarization. This approach allowed us to ask whether experience alters direct and contextual inputs differently at the level of individual neurons, and whether such changes can account for experience-dependent assignment of saliency to sensory inputs. Our results support a mechanism for saliency assignment that aligns with cortical circuitry, in which PyC connectivity is dynamically optimized to emphasize contrast between feedforward and contextual inputs. To assess neural responses to non-occluded and occluded scenes, we recorded calcium signals from L2/3 PyCs in V1 of awake mice using wide-field (WF) and two-photon (2P) imaging while presenting six different natural images in both conditions (Fig. 1A–C). The luminance of the occluded area was equal to that of the gray screen during the intertrial interval, ensuring that neurons with cRFs within the occluded area did not experience any change in feedforward drive when the contextual stimuli were presented (Fig. 1A). Mice were naive to visual input other than normal visual experience within the animal facility. A) Schematic of experimental setup. Mice were head-fixed on a running wheel centered in front of a screen displaying non-occluded and occluded natural scenes. B) Imaging approach showing wide-field (WF) and two-photon (2P) calcium imaging in L2/3 PyCs in V1 of TIT2L-GCaMP6f x G35-3 mice. Scale bar, 100 µm. C) Schematic of calcium imaging and behavioral training steps. ‘Naive’ mice were subjected to a WF population RF mapping session followed by retinotopically targeted WF and 2P occlusion experiments. 2P sessions were performed before (naive) and after (expert) a behavioral training phase to familiarize mice with the natural scenes. For behavioral training we used a subset (4/6) of the images, without occlusion. One additional 2P imaging session with familiar images was performed while the mice were engaged in the task (during task). To test the effect of visual experience on these responses, we familiarized the mice to a subset of the images in a simple stimulus detection task, allowing us to compare neural responses in naive and experienced animals. During this familiarization process, which lasted 2-4 weeks, we presented only four out of the six images to the mice, and only their non-occluded versions. To ensure engagement, mice received a small water reward if they licked within the time window 1–2 s after disappearance of any image. Mice learned to associate the stimuli with a reward, leading to anticipatory-licking and high hit rates (Fig. S1A-B). After the familiarization procedure, we again assessed visual responses to the non-occluded images. During these passive imaging sessions before (“naive mice”) and after (“expert mice”) familiarization, mice were not performing the task but passively viewed the stimuli and no reward was given. Excluding two out of six images during familiarization allowed us to compare experience-dependent changes in neuronal responses to “familiar” (i.e. used for training) and “novel” (i.e. not used for training) images. To test the influence of engagement, we also recorded responses in one extra 2P session during task performance (“during task”). During this session, occluded and non-occluded images were shown, but the “novel” images were not included. We performed calcium imaging in L2/3 PyCs by recording in TIT2L-GCaMP6f x G35-3-Cre mice, in which Cre is expressed in cortical excitatory neurons28(Fig. 1B). We targeted our recordings to the region of V1 that retinotopically represented the occluded quadrant of the natural scenes. To achieve this, we first used WF calcium imaging to perform a population receptive field (pRF) mapping29session immediately followed by the occlusion experiment (S1C). We used 2P calcium imaging to record the responses of individual L2/3 PyCs. We studied how these responses depended on visual experience by recording the activity of neurons before and after familiarization with the non-occluded versions of the natural scenes, and during task performance. Using the WF pRF map, we targeted our 2P imaging to the region of V1 representing the occluder (Fig. 2A). We then mapped the cRF locations of all recorded neurons using sparse noise stimuli and applied strict criteria to only include neurons in all subsequent analyses with high quality cRFs within the occluded region (see Materials and Methods andFigs. 2BandS2). Within this population, both non-occluded and occluded scenes elicited robust responses (Figs. 2A–E). Thus, as previously observed in humans23,25and monkeys27, a subset of PyCs in mouse V1 respond to the occluded natural scenes while receiving no feedforward input from the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN), demonstrating that these responses are driven by visual context. A) WF field-sign map showing V1 (blue) and higher visual areas (red) as obtained by population receptive field mapping for an example mouse (same asFigure 1D). Green areas represent regions for which the sign could not be determined. The yellow outline indicates the area in V1 that represents the occluded quadrant on the screen. 2P imaging was targeted in the center of this region (red dot). B) Visual field representation of the stimulus screen showing single cell RF centers. Gray dots are excluded RFs and black dots included RFs. C) Heatmap of z-scored ΔF/F responses for individual neurons across conditions and stimuli. Neurons are sorted within each condition (Naive/Expert/Task) based on their average response (t = 0.2-1 s) to the non-occluded stimuli. N = 841 neurons (Naive), 884 neurons (Expert) and 300 neurons (Task) from 6 mice. NO: non-occluded, O: occluded. D) Z-scored ΔF/F traces averaged across neurons and stimuli for all conditions. Traces represent mean ± SEM over neurons. Brown bars indicate stimulus epoch. E) Mean response strength across stimuli and conditions (mean ± SEM, averaged between t = 0.2-1 s). LMEM with post hoc Tukey HSD for all comparisons, ***: p<0.001, ns: not significant. F) Scatter plot showing average z-scored ΔF/F responses (t = 0.2-1 s) to the non-occluded (x-axis) and occluded (y-axis) stimulus across conditions. N = 841 neurons (Naive), 884 neurons (Expert) and 300 neurons (Task) from 6 mice. R, correlation coefficient; SI, separation index. G) Left: zoom of mean response to NO and O images across neurons during task performance (mean ± SEM). Dotted lines represent mean onset times. Right: quantification of onset times (NO: n = 142 neurons, O: n = 174 neurons). LMEM for all comparisons, ***: p<0.001. H) Stimulus selectivity (lifetime sparseness) for responses to NO and O stimuli. NO: N = 382 neurons (Naive), 223 neurons (Expert) and 79 neurons (Task) from 6 mice. O: N = 79 neurons (Naive), 182 neurons (Expert) and 79 neurons (Task) from 6 mice. LMEM with post hoc Tukey HSD for all comparisons, ***: p<0.001, ns: not significant. I) Scatter plots showing average z-scored ΔF/F responses (t = 0.2-1 s) to the non-occluded (x-axis) and occluded (y-axis) stimulus of chronically matched neurons in naive mice and mice performing the task, color coded for the dominant direction in which their responses transitioned between the naive and the task condition (yellow=reduced NO, blue=increased NO, green=decreased O, red=increased O response, gray=stable). N = 110 neurons from 6 mice. Numbers of the indicated neurons correspond to the neurons in J. The colored disc displays the percentages of the neurons transitioning in each direction. J) Neuronal responses of individual, chronically matched example neurons in naive mice (left) and mice performing the task (right). NO, non-occluded; O, occluded. Scale bar,z 1 z-scored ΔF/F. Traces represent mean ± SEM over trials. The shaded bars indicate stimulus epochs. We first examined PyC responses to familiar images repeatedly presented during training (Fig. 2C–E). Statistical comparisons were performed using a linear mixed-effects model (LMEM), which accounts for dependencies in the data and variability across mice. In naive mice, a subset of neurons responded reliably to occluded stimuli (4% with z-scored responses > 0.5;Fig. 2C), whereas responses to non-occluded stimuli were more widespread (30% responsive neurons). Although population-averaged responses measured with two-photon calcium imaging were relatively small (Fig. 2D), this primarily reflected the relatively small fractions of neurons responding to each image rather than weak responses in individual responsive neurons. Among responsive neurons (>0.5 z-scored response), mean response amplitudes were 0.95 z-score (ΔF/F ≈ 9%) for non-occluded images and 0.97 z-score (ΔF/F ≈ 9.5%) for occluded images (Fig. 2C, F), comparable to natural-image responses reported previously Visual experience had profound effects on PyC responses to non-occluded and occluded stimuli. In expert mice, the magnitude of responses to occluded stimuli was strongly increased (Fig. 2D-E), as was the percentage of responsive neurons (from 4% to 10%). In contrast, responses to non-occluded stimuli showed the opposite pattern. They weakened in expert mice, and fewer neurons were responsive (from 30% to 14%). During task performance, the percentage of neurons responsive to occluded stimuli was even higher (18%), while the decrease in the percentage of neurons responsive to non-occluded was less pronounced (21%). As locomotion is known to modulate visual responses in mouse V118,30, we assessed whether changes in locomotion influenced the observed plasticity of responses to non-occluded and occluded stimuli but found that this was not the case (Fig. S3A-B). We also ruled out the possibility that mice made eye movements in response to stimulus presentations, which might otherwise have positioned non-occluded image regions in the cRFs (Fig. S3C-D). We conclude that visual experience decreased responses of L2/3 PyCs to non-occluded images, while it increased responses to the visual context provided by occluded images. Task engagement further enhanced responses to occluded images, suggesting that it strengthens responses to the visual contextual inputs. The observation that locomotion and task engagement did not significantly change the reduction of non-occluded image responses suggests that it is not caused by diminished attention. We next analyzed how responses to non-occluded and occluded images were distributed across neurons. Interestingly, many PyCs appeared to respond to either the non-occluded stimuli or the occluded stimuli but not to both. This separation strengthened after familiarization with the images (“expert”) and was most pronounced in the condition under which the mice had been familiarized (“task”) (Fig. 2C, F, forresponses to pairs of individual occluded and/or non-occluded images seeFigs. S4andS5). To quantify the extent of this unexpected separation of PyCs into two non-overlapping populations, we computed a separation index (SI) ranging from –1 to 1 (see Materials and Methods). The SI is positive when the degree of separation is higher than expected under the assumption that activity elicited by non-occluded and occluded stimuli is uncorrelated across PyCs. The SI is negative when both categories of stimuli activate the same neurons. The SI increased with experience and task engagement (Fig. 2F, SI: 0.040 for naive, 0.426 for expert and 0.874 for task). In parallel, the correlation coefficient (R) between population responses to non-occluded and occluded stimuli (averaged across images per neuron) decreased (R: 0.139 for naive, –0.036 for expert, –0.111 for task), affirming the separation in responses to the two types of stimuli. The responses of PyCs to occluded images were reminiscent of inverse receptive field responses, which have been shown to depend on feedback inputs from higher order visual areas31,32. As responses to feedback inputs are characterized by a delay in response onset27,31,32, the onset latency of calcium responses to occluded images is expected to be longer than to non-occluded images if they are driven by feedback inputs. We determined latencies by fitting a curve to the activity time course and taking the time point at which the curve reached 33% of its maximum32. We only included neurons with high quality fits (see Materials and Methods). Although calcium activity rises slower than spiking activity, the responses elicited by occluded stimuli were indeed delayed compared to responses elicited by non-occluded images (Fig. 2G, 189 ± 5.6 ms for non-occluded and 253 ± 8.0 ms for occluded,P< 0.001, LMEM). This delayed response is in line with the interpretation that they were predominantly driven by feedback inputs, but does not rule out a contribution of lateral connections within V1. We tested whether the responses to occluded stimuli could be explained by responsiveness to the nearby edge of the occluded region, in which case the responsiveness would depend on proximity to this edge. However, the correlation between response strength and cRF distance from the edge of the occluded region was weak and statistically non-significant (Fig. S6, R = – 0.005,P= 0.876), consistent with findings from human fMRI and monkey recordings23,27. After familiarization with non-occluded natural images, PyCs became more selective for individual images (Fig. 2H; lifetime sparseness). This increase in selectivity was associated with preferential suppression of neurons that responded to multiple images, as stimulus selectivity in naive mice was negatively correlated with the change in response amplitude after familiarization (R = −0.299, P = 0.001;Fig. S7). Selectivity for occluded images was much lower and did not increase with experience (Fig. 2H). Taken together, our results indicate that responses to feedforward and contextual inputs predominantly occur in separate populations of L2/3 PyCs. Moreover, familiarization weakens responses to stimuli that included feedforward inputs, mostly affecting PyCs responding to multiple images. In contrast, responses to contextual inputs increase upon familiarization, in line with previous work33. To understand how these changes at the population level were caused by changes in response properties of individual neurons, we matched neurons recorded at the different stages of the experiment and assessed how their responses to non-occluded and occluded images changed. This confirmed that PyCs responding to non-occluded images in naive mice mostly became less responsive in expert mice (Fig. S8) and when engaged in the task (Fig. 2I: yellow cells;Fig. 2J&S9: cells 1 & 5). In contrast, a subset of PyCs that were initially unresponsive became responsive to occluded images after familiarization (Fig. 2I: red cells;Fig. 2J&S9: cells 2 & 3). This was also true for some PyCs that were initially responsive to non-occluded images (Fig. 2J&S9, cell 7). A small subset of neurons moved in the opposite direction of the majority of neurons (Fig. 2I&Fig. S8: blue and green cells;Fig. 2J&S9: cell 4). Interestingly, cells that increased their responsiveness to non-occluded images were highly selective for the individual familiarized images (lifetime sparseness of 0.48 in task, 0.69 in expert). We conclude that also at the level of individual L2/3 PyCs, repeated visual stimulation drives plasticity of responses to contextual inputs alone in the opposite direction of those to stimuli that include feedforward inputs. This reorganization can shift cells from unresponsive or non-occluded image-driven toward strongly occluded image-driven. In a small subset of PyCs, however, changes occurred in the opposite directions. We sought to determine why neurons responsive to occluded images do not respond strongly to non-occluded images, despite the presence of identical contextual stimuli. One explanation for this separation of responses could be that neurons responding to occluded images preferred large stimuli and responded to the occluder or its high-contrast edge, despite the absence of any change in the cRF input. However, the cRF sizes of PyCs responding to occluded or non-occluded images were similar (non-occluded: 17.16 ± 0.54°, occluded: 17.01 ± 0.67°, P=0.98, LMEM), which does not support this hypothesis. Moreover, as described above, responses were also not explained by proximity to the occluder edge (Fig. S6). As a more direct test for selectivity for the occluder or its high contrast borders, we repeated the experiment with additional stimuli, including black and white noise stimuli – lacking the structure of natural images – with or without a gray or white occluder. To accelerate learning, we slightly changed the paradigm. The mice were now familiarized only by passive viewing of 4 of the 6 non-occluded images during 6 sessions across 3 days without rewards or lick training (Figure 3A). After familiarization, we again observed that distinct L2/3 PyC populations responded to occluded and non-occluded images (Figure 3B). Familiarization weakened responses to non-occluded images, while responses to occluded images were increased, albeit less strongly than after reward-assisted training (Figure 3C). B) Scatter plot showing average z-scored ΔF/F responses (t = 0.2-1 s) to the non-occluded (x-axis) and occluded (y-axis) stimulus across conditions. N = 1820 neurons (Naive) and 2106 neurons (Passive Expert) from 7 mice. C) Mean response strength across stimuli and conditions (mean ± SEM, averaged between t = 0.2-1 s). LMEM for all comparisons, ***: p<0.001. D) Example stimuli used for this experiment. Image + gray occl: familiar natural images with a gray occluder. Noise + gray occl: images consisting of black and white random noise with a gray occluder. Noise + white occl: images consisting of black and white random noise with a white occluder. E) Responses of all neurons in passive expert mice to the different stimuli in D), color coded by their response strength to familiar natural images with a gray occluder (image + gray occl response strength). F) Response strengths elicited by the different occluded stimuli, of neurons responsive to the “image + gray occl” condition (defined by response > 0.5 in E)). N = 99 neurons. LMEM for all comparisons, ***: p<0.001, ns: not significant. G) Surround suppression stimuli. The size in visual degrees has been indicated. H) Normalized responses of neurons responding to NO or O stimuli (defined by a response > 0.5). Note the stronger surround suppression for neurons responding to O stimuli. Tuning curves of each neuron were normalized to their maximum responses. Traces represent mean ± SEM over neurons. I) Mean surround suppression index for NO vs O responders in Naive and Passive Expert mice (mean ± SEM, calculated as (Rmax– Rlarge) / Rmax). NO neurons Naive: N = 691, O neurons Naive: N = 61. NO neurons Passive Expert: N = 392, O neurons Passive Expert: N = 100, from 7 mice. J) Annulus stimuli with their respective sizes in visual degrees as used in this experiment. The inner circle of the annulus matched the diameter of the surround suppression stimuli as shown in G). K) Normalized annulus response curves for neurons responding to NO or O stimuli (defined by response > 0.5). Note the stronger annulus responses at larger sizes for neurons responding to O stimuli. Tuning curves of each neuron were normalized to their maximum responses. Traces represent mean ± SEM over neurons. L) Mean annulus index for NO vs O responders in Naive and Passive Expert mice (mean ± SEM, calculated as Rsmall– Rlarge). NO neurons Naive: N = 691, O neurons Naive: N = 61. NO neurons Passive Expert: N = 392, O neurons Passive Expert: N = 100, from 7 mice. M) Accuracy of population decoding of stimulus identity. We then assessed whether L2/3 PyCs responsive to occluded natural images also responded to noise stimuli with gray or white occluders (Figure 3D). While some L2/3 PyCs responded to both occluded natural images and occluded noise stimuli, most L2/3 PyCs that responded to occluded natural images responded weakly to noise stimuli with a gray occluder and even less to those with a white occluder (Figure 3E). As a result, the average responses of L2/3 PyCs that were responsive to occluded natural images were markedly lower when stimulated with noise containing gray or white occluders (Figure 3F). While these results do not rule out that a subset of PyCs responsive to occluded images are tuned to the grey occluder itself, they indicate that most of these neurons respond to ecRF inputs originating beyond the occluded region. We then tested another explanation for the separation of PyCs responding to non-occluded and occluded images. We reasoned that PyCs responding to occluded images may receive strong ecRF inputs, while being suppressed during presentation of non-occluded images. Such suppression could arise from local inhibitory mechanisms engaged when nearby PyCs with overlapping or adjacent cRF are co-activated, a phenomenon known as surround suppression (Fig. S10). Importantly, this form of suppression would be minimal for occluded images, as well as for the sparse noise stimuli used to map cRFs. To test this hypothesis, we presented gratings in the form of discs and annuli of varying sizes to assess surround suppression and responses to stimuli beyond their cRFs, respectively, both before and after familiarizing mice with the non-occluded natural images. We found that after familiarization, neurons responsive to occluded images showed significantly stronger surround suppression than those responsive to non-occluded images (Fig. 3G-I). Moreover, occluded-image responders showed weaker absolute responses to larger discs compared to non-occluded-image responders, both before familiarization (0.30 ± 0.044 vs. 0.41 ± 0.012) and even more prominently after familiarization (0.21 ± 0.025 vs. 0.45 ± 0.018). These results support the idea that neurons responsive to occluded images are more strongly suppressed by large stimuli. Furthermore, neurons responsive to occluded images preferred larger annuli than those responsive to non-occluded images, and unlike the latter, they also responded to annuli positioned entirely outside the occluded quadrant (92°;Fig. 3J-L). This suggests that although occluded image-responders also received ecRF input from within the upper left quadrant, inputs from outside this region were sufficient to drive their responses to occluded images. To assess whether responses to occluded images carried stimulus-specific information, we performed a population classification analysis using all neurons with cRFs within the occluded region, averaging responses for each neuron and each trial (between 0.2-1 s after stimulus onset). We used 50% of the trials to train a linear classifier (linear discriminant analysis; LDA) and the 50% remaining trials for testing. Training and testing the classifier on either non-occluded (Train-Test, i.e. NO-NO) or occluded (O-O) responses allowed us to examine whether these signals contain stimulus-specific information (Fig. 3M). We found that the identity of non-occluded images could be decoded with 100% accuracy. Decoding accuracy of occluded images was lower (64%), but well above chance level (25%), confirming a limited degree of specificity of L2/3 PyCs responses to occluded images. Together, these results support the hypothesis that responses to occluded images arise from a combination of weakly selective contextual inputs from beyond the occluder in combination with release from surround suppression, possibly signaling a salient omission of a probable feedforward input. We also asked whether the salient presence of an improbable feedforward input would also evoke enhanced responses. Given that responses to non-occluded images were more selective than responses to occluded images (Figs. 2H,3J,S5B), we hypothesized that plasticity of these responses would follow the same pattern: repeated feedforward inputs would undergo selective weakening, whereas repeated ecRF inputs would be strengthened in a correspondingly broader, more generalized way. This scenario yields three testable predictions. First, because novel images were not presented during training, responses selective for non-occluded novel images should not decrease. Second, if ecRF inputs strengthen in a way that generalizes across stimuli, the contextual inputs recruited by novel images should overlap with those recruited by familiar images. Such overlap could account for the enhanced responses to occluded novel images. Finally, because feedforward responses selective for non-occluded novel images remain intact, they could be further amplified by the strengthened contextual inputs, resulting in the increased responses observed for non-occluded novel images. We found experimental support for all three predictions. First, we assessed the overlap in contextual inputs for familiar and novel images, by correlating the responses of PyCs to occluded versions of the familiar and novel images. PyCs that responded strongly to occluded novel images in expert mice indeed also responded to occluded familiar images (Fig. 4E, R=0.789, P<0.001). Moreover, neurons that increased their responses to the occluded novel images also increased their responses to occluded familiar images (Fig. 4F, R=0.791, P<0.001). One could argue that enhanced responses to occluded images reflect nonspecific surprise-driven amplification to any deviation from the familiarized stimulus. However, the occluded white noise stimuli in the second (passive familiarization) dataset did not show such enhancement after familiarization (Fig. 4G), despite the fact that they strongly deviate from the familiarized images. As the occluded white noise stimuli lack the structure of natural images, this finding instead supports the interpretation that ecRF responses strengthen and generalize across natural images sharing contextual information. Second, we tested whether familiarization left responses to non-occluded novel images selectively intact. This is expected to increase selectivity for novel versus familiar images after familiarization. Indeed, we observed a significant experience-dependent increase in selectivity for novel over familiar images (Fig. 4H), consistent with a selective weakening of feedforward inputs. Finally, if strengthened ecRF inputs amplify responses to novel images, PyCs responding to novel images should be more strongly influenced by these ecRF inputs. To test this, we quantified the relative contribution of visual input from inside versus outside the compound receptive field area (RFs of all neurons together) of the recorded neurons. We presented 3,600 non-occluded natural images to the mice that had been previously familiarized with four non-occluded images through passive exposure. For each neuron, we computed reverse correlations between local image structure and neural responses across this image set. As a measure of local image structure, we used Shannon entropy, which captures the spatial complexity of pixel intensities within a region. This approach allowed us to weight each image location by how strongly its local structure elicited neuronal responses. Using these weights, we generated entropy-based activation maps for each neuron, indicating the spatial distribution of image features driving its responses. We then averaged these maps across neurons grouped by response type (occluded vs. non-occluded; familiar vs. novel). Each resulting map therefore reflects, for a given neuronal population, the spatial locations whose local image entropy most strongly contributed to their responses (Fig. S12A). By comparing the ratio of activity elicited by inputs outside versus within the compound cRF region across neuronal categories, we found that PyCs responding to novel non-occluded images received stronger ecRF inputs than those responding to familiar images (Fig. S12B). Together, these findings support the idea that enhanced novelty responses in L2/3 PyCs arise from non-adapted selective responses to visual stimuli within the cRF, amplified by strengthened ecRF inputs that generalize across different natural scenes. This mechanism is consistent with the idea that interactions between feedforward and feedback inputs can generate mismatch-like responses34but adds that opposing plasticity of these pathways is required to tune their interactions towards selective experience-based amplification of mismatched inputs.
