Decoding performance across conditions in mice was strikingly similar to that obtained by applying the same analysis to previously acquired data in humans and non-human primates (Fig. 5B-D), despite differences in species and recording techniques. Across all species and recording modalities, decoding accuracy was highest within stimulus conditions and lower for cross-condition decoding. We observed high (>80%) and significant decoding of responses to non-occluded stimuli (NO-NO). O-O decoding accuracy was lower but significant, just like in humans and non-human primates (Fig. 5B). Moreover, across all species and conditions, classifiers trained on non-occluded responses and tested on occluded responses (NO-O) were less accurate than the other way around. This asymmetry may reflect that classifiers trained on non-occluded images rely more strongly on feedforward responses, which are absent for occluded images, whereas classifiers trained on occluded images exploit contextual responses that also weakly contribute to non-occluded responses. Interestingly, the (O-NO) cross-decoding in mice only became significantly higher than chance during task (Fig. S13), suggesting that experience and task-engagement influenced the decoding efficiency. The overall weaker cross-decoding in both directions, compared to O-O and NO-NO decoding, is not surprising given that responses to direct and contextual inputs arose predominantly from distinct neuronal populations. This limited cross-decoding may reflect a subset of neurons that responded to both full and occluded images – either weakly under both conditions, or strongly under one and weakly under the other. Such neurons may act as a bridge between direct and contextual representations, enabling partial generalization across these stimulus types. Based on these data, we hypothesized that two plasticity mechanisms with opposite directionality in individual PyCs enhance cortical responses to salient visual stimuli: selective weakening of responses to feedforward inputs and strengthening of contextual inputs that generalize across scenes. This strengthening amplifies responses of PyCs responsive to novel, non-adapted feedforward inputs and, if strong enough, enables responses by contextual inputs alone, when feedforward drive that recruits inhibition is absent (Fig. 6). Before familiarization (left), PyCs integrate feedforward (FF) visual input within their classical receptive fields and contextual input from surrounding regions. Non-occluded training– and novel images (neurons 1&2) evoke responses driven through FF inputs and modulated by context. Occluded images elicit little activity due to weak contextual drive and absence of FF input (neuron 1). Upon familiarization (right), FF input from the training image selectively adapts and recruits stronger surround suppression (neuron 1), while contextual inputs strengthen in a generalizing way (neurons 1&2). As a result, responses to the non-occluded training image are reduced. In contrast, the occluded training image engages the strengthened contextual input in the absence of FF-driven inhibition, driving neural activity (neuron 1). The novel image also recruits this strengthened generalized context that enhances responses in PyCs that receive selective, non-adapted FF inputs from this image (neuron 2). Together, these opposing plasticity processes selectively amplify improbable inputs or omissions by maximizing the contrast between feedforward and contextual signals in individual neurons. We simulated familiarization with two non-occluded images and measured responses to familiar and novel images, with and without occlusion (Fig. 7A). Non-occluded images provided feedforward inputs to inhibitory cells and PyCs and contextual inputs to PyCs, while occluded images only provided contextual inputs to PyCs. We modeled the three dominant transition types separately using the same model, varying a small number of parameters controlling feedforward and feedback input strengths, PV-mediated inhibition, and apical gain (Table S2): reduced responses to non-occluded images (−NO), enhanced responses to occluded images (+O), and enhanced responses to non-occluded images (+NO). To match the data, we modeled the −NO transition as stronger for familiar images and the +NO transition as stronger for novel images, while +O transition models were similar across conditions. Weighting the modeled transitions by their observed proportions in the data, with more −NO transitions for familiar and more +NO transitions for novel images, closely reproduced the population-average responses (Fig. 7B). The same model thus reproduced reduced responses to familiar non-occluded images and enhanced responses to familiar occluded images, as well as enhanced responses to occluded and non-occluded novel images, depending on the initial conditions (Fig. 7C, D). To also account for the small population of highly selective PyCs whose responses to familiar non-occluded images increased (Fig. 2I, S8), we gated the rate of basal plasticity by a current slowly accumulating with repeated basal activity, resulting in weaker feedforward depression in cells responding to only one image (in line withFig. S7). This allowed strengthened contextual inputs to outweigh mild feedforward adaptation, reproducing the +NO transition for familiar images (Fig. 7C, D). The −NO, +O and +NO transitions were robust to variation in individual model parameters. For most parameters, transition direction and magnitude were largely preserved across the full tested range, from 0.05 to 5 times the fitted value, although some parameters showed narrower ranges of robustness (Fig. S14A-C). While the model thus reliably captured the most frequent transitions, it did not address the less common reduction in responses to occluded images (−O). Accounting for this transition may require extending the model to include lateral inhibition or plasticity in cortical areas providing contextual feedback. Ablating contextual inputs after familiarization reduced responses to familiar and novel occluded images (Fig. 7E, S15), and reversed the +NO transitions in both conditions, indicating that these response increases depended on strengthened contextual inputs. Conversely, removing inhibition caused +O PyCs to respond strongly to non-occluded images, supporting a role for feedforward-driven inhibition in separating this response population from PyC responding to non-occluded images after familiarization (Fig. 7E, S15). Interestingly, −NO transitions persisted after either ablation for familiar images, consistent with depression of feedforward inputs, whereas −NO transitions for novel images reversed upon removing inhibition, suggesting a stronger contribution of inhibitory plasticity. Together, these simulations support the idea that opposing plasticity of inputs onto individual PyCs, combined with feedforward-driven inhibition, provide a possible explanation for the principal familiarization-induced response changes. Our results show that familiarization to natural images induces a striking rebalancing of L2/3 PyCs responses in V1 to non-occluded and occluded images. Repeated responses to non-occluded images providing direct sensory inputs are selectively weakened, whereas contextual responses to occluded images strengthen and generalize across images. Acting together within individual neurons, these opposing plasticity mechanisms may enable PyCs to extract salient signals and omissions from predictable visual backgrounds, without requiring a difference computation. Several mechanisms may contribute to the selective downscaling of neural responses to direct visual inputs after familiarization. These include synaptic depression36,37and reduced intrinsic excitability that both occur in relatively short time spans38,39, and synaptic scaling via decreased postsynaptic AMPA receptor conductance over longer periods40,41. Additionally, repeated activation can strengthen inhibition, suppressing highly active excitatory neurons42,43and contributing to surround suppression. Acting across different timescales and levels of organization, these mechanisms may synergistically reduce responses to familiar stimuli, while contextual influence is increasing. Repeated presentation of natural visual scenes particularly reduced responses of less selective PyCs that responded to multiple images during familiarization. This disproportionate reduction of broadly-tuned neuron responses increased the relative contribution of more selective neurons, leading to a sharpening of visual responses, in accordance with previous work44–46. The observed sharpening is consistent with an adaptive normalization mechanism, in which gain reductions scale with a neuron’s cumulative activity during repeated stimulus exposure47. This sharpening is not expected in classical formulations of hierarchical predictive coding that emphasize feedback-driven inhibition ‘explaining away’ expected inputs, resulting in dampening44,48–52. A subset of PyCs responded to occluded natural scenes despite the absence of cRF input, reminiscent of inverse receptive field responses driven by feedback inputs in the absence of feedforward drive31. This population of occluded image responders increased following familiarization with non-occluded scenes. Most of these neurons did not respond to the non-occluded familiar images, suggesting that strengthening of ecRF inputs does not require somatic spiking activity. This observation aligns with evidence that potentiation of feedback inputs onto L2/3 PyC dendrites can occur independently of somatic firing53but may require dendritic NMDA spikes54. Disinhibition may have also supported the strengthening of ecRF inputs32,55. However, since most PyCs that responded to occluded images in expert mice did not at all respond to them before familiarization, disinhibition alone is unlikely to explain the observed changes. Possibly, disinhibition may have facilitated plasticity of ecRF inputs onto L2/3 pyramidal cells56,57. While PyC responses to different occluded images generalized across scenes, they nevertheless carried image-specific information, as stimulus identity could be decoded from these responses. This observation is consistent with a recent report showing that responses to occluded regions generalize across scenes while still retaining stimulus-specific information58. Moreover, because PyCs responding to occluded images also received input from more proximal visual locations, as revealed by annulus stimuli, they appear to integrate spatially distributed contextual signals across the surround. Synaptic strengthening in apical dendrites depends on the co-activation of nearby synapses⁵⁰, suggesting that this form of plasticity could support the learning of structured contextual regularities rather than merely reinforcing frequently occurring features. Such contextual learning at the level of individual neurons may therefore enable selective amplification of inputs that violate these learned regularities. Future experiments will be needed to characterize the statistical structure of these contextual signals and to determine how it depends on stimulus proximity and spatial arrangement. Occlusion-responsive neurons exhibited more surround suppression and received more distal ecRF inputs than those responding to non-occluded images. This combination of response properties may explain responses to occluded images, but also inverse receptive field responses31,32. In this scenario, weakly selective inhibition from local interneurons59, driven when neighboring neurons are activated by the non-occluded stimulus, suppresses occluded image responders. When feedforward input near the cRF is absent, inhibition is reduced, allowing input from the surrounding visual context to drive the PyC’s response (Fig. S10). This mechanism, requiring feedforward-driven inhibition, would also explain why responses to occluded and non-occluded images occur in separate neuronal population. These responses to occluded regions may highlight regions where visible input is missing from a scene, contributing to the perception of such areas as figures32,58. Whether such responses can also support contextual completion60when parts of familiar scenes are blurred or ambiguous is currently unclear. Strengthening of ecRF inputs may also explain enhanced responses elicited by novel images presented after familiarization. Because these contextual inputs generalized across familiarized and novel images, PyCs selective for these novel images likely receive stronger visual contextual inputs after familiarization. However, unlike PyCs responsive to familiar images, they did not undergo adaptation during familiarization. Consequently, the coincidence of non-adapted feedforward and strengthened contextual input may enhance feedforward drive in a context-dependent way61. This could involve apical amplification, consistent with models in which apical dendrites integrate contextual input and modulate somatic gain62–65. Supporting this idea, we observed that PyCs responding to novel images were more strongly influenced by inputs outside their cRFs than those responding to familiar images. It is well possible that additional novelty related inputs, such a thalamic or neuromodulatory inputs, further enhance responses to occluded or novel images4. While most PyCs reduced their responses to familiar images, a small subset showed increased responsiveness and strong selectivity for familiarized stimuli. One explanation for this observation is that selective neurons may adapt less as they respond less frequently, and actually become more responsive due to the enhanced contextual inputs. We can indeed simulate this response strengthening of selective neurons by making them adapt more slowly. Alternatively, these neurons may not compute how feedforward inputs relate to context, but instead encode learned, behaviorally relevant signals. If so, they could represent a distinct subtype of L2/3 PyCs shaped by Hebbian plasticity, potentially enabled by a different source of feedback aligned with their cRF inputs. Consistent with this idea, it was found that L2/3 feedback aligns with cRF responses, whereas feedback from L5 PyCs in the lateromedial area originates from more distal ecRF regions and is not anatomically aligned with postsynaptic orientation preference68. Recent work showed that the emergence of such mismatched feedback during development can be modeled by Hebbian plasticity of feedforward inputs combined with anti-Hebbian plasticity of feedback inputs67. While this developmental plasticity also wires PyCs to enhance responses to deviations between feedforward and feedback signals, its functional outcome differs from what we observe in adult V1: the model predicts that experienced feedforward responses are strengthened, whereas matching feedback connections become disconnected. Notably, decoding of non-occluded and occluded images, as well as cross-decoding between them, was similarly efficient across humans, monkeys, and mice, despite being measured with fMRI, electrophysiology, and 2P calcium imaging, respectively. This convergence across species and recording modalities suggests that common neural mechanisms underlie contextual processing, consistent with the circuit principles described above. The above-chance decoding of occluded natural images in naive mice suggests that contextual inputs are already structured before familiarization with these images, potentially reflecting connectivity shaped during development or by natural vision during adulthood. Ongoing plasticity would then allow this connectivity to be continuously refined, tuning the system to the statistical regularities of the animal’s current environment and ensuring that saliency is assigned relative to what is presently familiar. A simple circuit-level explanation consistent with our findings, is one in which two plasticity mechanisms with opposite directionality in individual PyCs dynamically optimize cortical responses to salient visual stimuli (Fig. 6). One mechanism selectively weakens responses to frequently active feedforward inputs36,40,41,44,48,68–71, while the other strengthens regularly active contextual inputs33,53,54,56that generalize across scenes. This strengthening has two major consequences: 1) it amplifies responses to novel, non-adapted feedforward inputs that violate the statistical structure of familiarized contexts and 2) when local feedforward drive recruiting inhibition is absent, it enables contextual signals to drive responses that may signal the absence of expected inputs. By maximizing the contrast between feedforward and contextual influences within individual L2/3 PyCs, this circuitry provides a plausible cellular mechanism for detecting and enhancing salient information. When we explored this circuit mechanism in a computational model, we found that simple plasticity rules operating exclusively at the cellular level were sufficient to reproduce the dominant response transitions, including the counterintuitive strengthening of image-selective responses to familiarized images. Feedback-driven inhibition was not required. Importantly, the model demonstrates how a single mechanism – strengthened contextual inputs – can account for enhanced responses to both novel and occluded images, through dendritic amplification and dendritic drive, respectively. This context-contrasting mechanism fits well with Helmholtz’s classic idea of unconscious inference, in which perception reflects experience-based interpretation rather than passive sensory reception72. By amplifying responses to deviations from learned contextual structures, this circuitry may support rapid detection of behaviorally relevant stimuli within familiar scenes. When feedforward input is missing, strengthened context-driven responses may highlight such occluded regions, contributing to their perception as coherent shapes. These responses may also support contextual completion when inputs are degraded or ambiguous. Importantly, this concept may also help shed light on psychiatric symptoms such as psychosis: if the processes underlying context-contrasting plasticity are disrupted, the brain may assign saliency to inappropriate inputs, potentially contributing to hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized thinking73. By identifying a potential cellular mechanism for disrupted saliency processing within individual neurons, context-contrasting circuitry may offer new mechanistic approaches for understanding these conditions. We used 4 female and 2 male G35-3Dtl28crossed to AI93 TITL-GCaMP6f mice (Jackson Laboratories,www.jaxmice.jax.org, strain 024107). Mice were group housed under a 12 h reversed day/night cycle and provided with ad libitum access to food and water. Experiments were performed in the dark phase. Experimental animals were adult at surgery (>40 days) and both males and females were used. Mice had access to a running wheel in their home cage throughout the experiment. For the cranial window surgery, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane (4% induction, 1.6% maintenance in oxygen). During the surgeries, temperature was maintained at 37°C with euthermic pads and eyes were protected from light and drying using Cavasan eye ointment. Mice were implanted with a double (3+4 mm diameter) glass window and a custom metal head-ring on the center of V1 to allow head-fixation. The glass window and head-ring were fixed to the skull using dental cement. At least one week after the window surgery, mice were handled and trained to be head immobilized in our setup until they sat comfortably and started running regularly on their own. Two-photon experiments were performed on a two-photon microscope (Neurolabware) equipped with a Ti-sapphire laser (Mai-Tai ‘Deepsee’, Spectraphysics; wavelength, 920 nm) and a 16x, 0.8 NA water immersion objective (Nikon) at a zoom of 1.6x. The microscope was controlled by Scanbox (Neurolabware) running on MATLAB (Mathworks). Images were acquired at a frame rate of 15.5 (RF mapping) or 31 Hz (occlusion experiments) in V1 L2/3 at a depth of 150-250 µm from the cortical surface. For all behavioral training and imaging sessions, mice were head restrained and free to run on a 3D-printed running wheel (8.5 cm diameter). Locomotion speed was measured with a rotary encoder and processed using Arduino and MATLAB. All visual stimuli for two-photon imaging were presented on a 24-inch gamma-corrected non-occluded HD LED monitor (1920×1080 pixels) using OpenGL and Psychophysics Toolbox 3 running on MATLAB. The monitor was positioned centered at 15 cm away from the mouse, yielding a field-of-view of 120° x 90°. For RF mapping, we used eccentricity-corrected sparse noise stimuli with squares of 7.5 visual degrees at different locations covering the entire screen. Each trial consisted of 3 black and 3 white randomly positioned squares on a gray background. Stimuli were presented for 0.5 s with a gray screen ITI of 1.5 s. For occlusion experiments, we presented 6 natural images that were part of a dataset used for similar experiments before23,27. The images were presented in gray scale and were corrected for overall luminance across images. We modeled the three most common response transitions observedin vivo, separately for familiar and novel images, yielding six separate mean-field transition models. –NO transition was defined as a decrease in NO response greater than the change in O response; +O transition as an increase in O response greater than the change in NO response, and +NO transition as an increase in NO response greater than the change in O response. To verify the robustness of our model to the exact parameter values and ratios between parameters, we conducted a robustness analysis, where we varied one continuous parameter at a time around each of the six mean-field models’ parameter initializations. Concretely, every scalar model parameter was multiplied by factors ranging from 0.05x to 5x. The leak ratesαyandαp, which are fractions, were capped at one. To check whether the model was sensitive to the magnitude of the fitted weights while preserving the fitted proportions, each complete set of weights (wwFF,wwFB,wwPV, andwLAT) was scaled simultaneously by the same factors, and the scaled weights were clipped to the allowed weight interval [0,1] enforced throughout modeling. Furthermore, every individual [0-1] weight coordinate was also independently set to the absolute values between 0.01 and 1.0, spanning the full allowed weight range independently of each fitted weight’s initial magnitude. With each robustness check, all unperturbed parameters remained at their fitted mean-field transition values. This robustness validation design contained 1,965 perturbations across the six mean-field transition models. To evaluate the outcomes of the robustness analysis, we measured the effects of each perturbation on 1) the magnitude of the perturbed transition vectors for each transition relative to the unperturbed case, and 2) whether the new perturbed transition vector ended up in the same transition quadrant as the unperturbed transition (+NO / –NO / +O). We considered a transition-parameter combination robust if the perturbed transition vector showed at least 25% magnitude of the original transition vector in the same transition sector as the original average transition. title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
author: Prius Mengual, J.; Hoerder-Suabedissen, A.; Mao, R.; Taylor, L.; Chakrabarty, A.; Newey, S.; Jagannath, A.; Akerman, C.; Vyazovskiy, V. V.
text: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep-wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure. Sleep is essential for normal cognitive function, including attention, memory, and behavioural performance. Prolonged wakefulness impairs cognition and alters cortical activity in both humans and animals (Andrillon et al., 2021;Huber et al., 2004;Nir et al., 2017;Van Dongen, 2025;Vyazovskiy et al., 2011). However, the biological role of sleep in general and the specific physiological characteristics defining sleep largely remain elusive. One of the electrophysiological markers of sleep homeostasis is electroencephalographic (EEG) slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.5–4 Hz) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, which increases as a function of prior wake duration and declines during subsequent sleep (Borbély et al., 2016). Moreover, slow waves can emerge during wakefulness following sleep deprivation (SD), leading to the idea that sleep is an activity-dependent process (Alfonsa et al., 2023;Andrillon et al., 2021;Krueger et al., 2019;Thomas et al., 2020a;Vyazovskiy et al., 2011). The cellular and network counterpart of EEG slow waves is the alternation of neuronal activity and silence, often referred to as ON/OFF periods (Vyazovskiy et al., 2009). The incidence and duration of OFF-periods were shown to reflect sleep-wake history (Thomas et al., 2020b), and their experimental induction may lead to a decrease in electrophysiological and molecular signatures of sleep pressure (Driessen et al., 2026). Sleep-dependent homeostatic processes have also been linked to cellular maintenance and macromolecule biosynthesis, both essential for a broad range of brain functions. For example, extended wakefulness is associated with widespread transcriptional and translational changes, including the altered expression of genes involved in synaptic plasticity, protein synthesis, and cellular stress pathways (Abdalla et al., 2026a;Lyons et al., 2023;Mackiewicz et al., 2007,2008;Mignot, 2008;Vanrobaeys et al., 2023). Earlier studies have posited that wakefulness is associated with heightened neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity and neurotransmission in local neuronal circuits and the whole brain (Cirelli et al., 2004;Cirelli & Tononi, 2000), all functions requiring protein synthesis and changes in gene expression (Cirelli et al., 2004;Ma et al., 2023;Tononi & Cirelli, 2014). Protein synthesis is a tightly regulated process, of which the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is an essential regulator (Walter & Ron, 2011). The UPR is an evolutionarily conserved signalling pathway activated by the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER lumen, observed in all species studied to date (Cirelli et al., 2004;Hetz et al., 2020;Maret et al., 2007;Naidoo et al., 2005,2007;Walter & Ron, 2011). Activation of the UPR is initiated through three major signalling branches mediated by inositol requiring enzyme-1 (IRE1), PKR-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), and activating transcription factor-6 (ATF6). These ER stress sensors are regulated in part through their association with the ER ATP-dependent chaperone binding immunoglobulin protein (BiP). During ER stress, altered interactions with BiP and unfolded proteins promotes activation of the UPR sensors, triggering signalling cascades that regulate protein synthesis, chaperone production and protein degradation. These responses initially act to restore ER proteostasis, whereas prolonged or unresolved ER stress can engage apoptotic pathways (H. P.Harding et al., 2009;Shen & Prywes, 2005;Walter & Ron, 2011;Ye et al., 2000) (Figure 1). Previous studies have shown that SD increases the expression of UPR-related genes in the brain of several vertebrate and invertebrate species (Abdalla et al., 2026b;Cirelli et al., 2004,2005;Ford et al., 2024;Mongrain et al., 2025a;Naidoo et al., 2005,2007;Terao et al., 2006), consistent with the view that neuronal activity during wakefulness imposes increased biosynthetic demand on neuronal networks. Although SD leads to changes in both cortical activity and ER stress, it is not known whether and to what extent the altered neuronal activity contributes to the observed molecular changes. Misfolded proteins in the lumen of the ER activate the stress sensors IRE1, PERK and ATF6. Early response of the UPR generates active transcription factors to increase the protein-folding capacity of the ER while decreasing the load of proteins entering the ER. All three branches of the UPR are activated by dissociation of the ATP-chaperone protein BiP and its membrane receptor. Both IRE1 and PERK undergo phosphorylation and dimerization to reach an active configuration: IRE1 acts upon splicing transcription factor XBP1 to generate an active form capable of entering the nucleus, promoting the protein degradation machinery while increasing the synthesis of new chaperones. PERK phosphorylates eiF2α, which inhibits protein translation in the ER. If ER stress persists, eiF2α will induce transcription factor ATF4, which would lead to the activation of the cell apoptotic program. ATF6 is spliced, and the excised portion acts as a transcription factor that promotes chaperone production in the lumen of the ER. Here, we tested how changes in cortical neuronal activity and prior sleep-wake history interact to regulate cortical gene expression and electrophysiological signatures of sleep homeostasis. To this end, we combined SD with monocular flickering light stimulation (FLS) at 8 Hz, a physiological sensory manipulation previously shown to modulate cortical activity in the visual cortex (Manning et al., 2007;Manning & Uhlrich, 2009;Uhlrich et al., 2005). Using electrophysiological recordings and cortical region-specific molecular analyses, we found that SD alone increased both activity-dependent and UPR-related gene expression together with SWA during subsequent sleep. In contrast, combining SD with FLS produced increased neuronal OFF periods during waking and further enhanced SWA during subsequent sleep, but prevented the widespread increase in both activity-dependent and UPR-related gene expression. Our findings identify physiological manipulation of neuronal activity as a potent modulator of ER-stress-associated gene expression in the cortex. Experiments were carried out in adult male C57BL/6 mice. We designed and performed three different series of experiments. In the first experimental series, we recorded EEG and EMG data to evaluate regional and state-dependent differences in brain activity. Two cohorts of n=8 animals, (n=16 animals total) were implanted with EEG screws bilaterally in frontal and occipital cortices and nuchal EMG wires and were subjected to 4h sleep-deprivation (SD) with or without monocular flickering light stimulation (FLS). All these animals were subsequently used to collect tissue for molecular biology analysis. EEG and EMG signals of sufficiently high quality for subsequent analyses were acquired in n=12 animals. In the second experimental series, we recorded local field potentials (LFPs) and multi-unit activity (MUA) from the visual cortex. Two cohorts of mice (n=4 and n=8, total of n=12 animals) were implanted with LFP electrodes unilaterally in the occipital cortex, EEG screws in contralateral occipital cortex and both frontal cortices, nuchal EMG and a head-mounted device for the FLS delivery to one eye. Good quality EEG, EMG, LFP and MUA signals were acquired in n=8 animals. A third cohort (n=4) of mice were implanted with EEG screws, LFP electrodes bilaterally in occipital cortex, nuchal EMG wires and had a head-mounted device for the monocular FLS device. In all cases, mice were subjected to 4h sleep-deprivation (SD) with and without FLS. For a subset of n=4, monocular FLS to the eye ipsilateral to the LFP electrode was performed instead of SD alone. The brains of these animals were subsequently processed histologically to confirm laminar probe location in cortex. In the third experimental series, animals were intended exclusively for molecular biology analysis such as quantitative Polymerase Chain Reactions (qPCRs). It included a group of unimplanted animals (n=20 total) some of which were subjected to 4h SD (n=12) and some were left undisturbed for the duration of the experiment and served as controls (n=8). N=4 animals underwent surgery to attach the head-mounted monocular FLS device on top of the skull but had no EEG electrodes implanted. Further animals were EEG-screw implanted (but no EEG recordings were made) and either allowed to sleep (n=4; data not used) or underwent SD alone (n=12) or SD with FLS (n=4). All animals used were between 7 and 10 weeks old at the start of the experiment. Mice were group housed until they underwent surgeries and singly housed subsequently. Following surgery, animals had a recovery period of at least seven days before being transferred into custom made Plexiglas cages (20.3 x 32 x 35 cm (W, D, H)) placed inside ventilated, sound attenuated Faraday cambers (Campden Instruments, Loughborough, UK) under standard 12h:12h light-dark cycle. Mice were habituated to the recording chambers and the tethering for 3 days before the start of recordings. Similarly, unimplanted mice for tissue collection were singly housed and habituated to the recording chambers for three days prior to the tissue collection day. Animals always had ad libitum access to food and water. Room temperature and relative humidity were maintained at 22±1°C and 50±20%, respectively. All procedures conformed to the Animal (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 and were performed under UK Home Office Project and Personal Licenses in accordance with institutional guidelines. To study the effects of SD and FLS on brain activity, we performed surgical procedures for implantation of EEG screws, LFP electrodes, EMG wires and/or skull-mounted attachment of the screw for the monocular FLS device under aseptic conditions using isoflurane anaesthesia (3-5% for induction and 1-2% for maintenance). Three days before surgeries, mice started receiving plain jelly and mash daily for habituation to post-operative care. The day of the surgeries, Metacam (1–2 mg kg, subcutaneous (s.c)), and vetergesic (0.08 mg/kg, s.c.) were administered preoperatively. EEG/EMG mounts were composed of stainless-steel screws (shaft diameter,0.86 mm; InterFocus Ltd., UK) soldered to custom-made headmount connectors (8415-SM, PinnacleTechnology Inc., USA) and bilaterally implanted into frontal (motor area, anteroposterior (AP) 2 mm, mediolateral (ML) ±2 mm) and occipital cortical areas (visual area, V1, AP 3.5–4 mm, ML ±2.5 mm). A reference electrode was implanted above the cerebellum and two single stranded stainless-steel wires were inserted either side of the nuchal muscle to record electromyography (EMG) activity. All screws and wires were secured to the skull using dental cement (Super Bond Bulk mix kit, Sun Medical Co., LTD). The small attachment for the LED headstage was mounted during the surgery on the anterior portion of the acrylic head mount. To study neuronal responses to the FLS, laminar probes were implanted in one or both primary visual cortices (visual area, V1, AP 3.5 mm, ML ± 2.5 mm). All laminar recordings were performed using 16-channel silicon probes (NeuroNexus Technologies Inc., Ann Arbor, MI, USA; model: A1×16-3mm-100-703-Z16) with a spacing of 100 μm between individual channels. The tips of laminar implants were stained before surgery with the orange-red fluorescent membrane stain Dil ® (1,1′-Dioctadecyl-3,3,3′,3′-Tetramethylindocarbocyanine Perchlorate; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) by immersion of the electrode shank into a 20 mg/ml solution (in 50/50% acetone/methanol) for later histological assessment of the electrode position (Krone et al., 2021;Magill et al., 2006). After completion of the experiments, microlesions of selected channels on the laminar probe were performed under terminal pentobarbital anaesthesia using the electroplating device NanoZ™ (White Matter LLC, Seattle, WA, USA) applying 10 mA direct current for 25 s to each respective channel. Immediately following microlesioning, mice were perfused with 0.01M phosphate buffered saline (PBS; P4417, Sigma-Aldrich) followed by 4 % formaldehyde (F4775, Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS. A vibrating microtome (Leica VT1000S) was used to section the brains into 50 μm coronal slices. Slices in the appropriate region were stained with DAPI (4’,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole; D3571, Sigma-Aldrich, at 5μg/ml in PBS) at room temperature for one hour before being mounted and coverslipped. Slices were imaged using a Leica epifluorescence microscope (DMR) equipped with a Leica DC500 CCD camera. Images of implantation sites were aligned to the Paxinos and Franklin mouse brain atlas (Keith B.J. Franklin & George Paxinos, 2019) and the depth of the laminar implant was assessed measuring the distance between cortical surface and the electrical current induced tissue microlesions. The histological assessment of the insertion tract was performed in all animals, which were implanted with laminar probes. To enable a direct comparison of electrophysiological and molecular markers of neuronal activity and ER stress, we performed two types of complementary experiments. Firstly, to confirm regional variation in brain activity and assess the effect of monocular FLS, we used mice implanted with bilateral frontal and occipital EEG screws, a subset of which were also implanted with LFP electrodes. Secondly, to assess cellular activity at the molecular level and the unfolded protein response (UPR), brains of EEG implanted mice were used for regional tissue collection and qPCR after electrophysiological recordings, together with brains from unimplanted animals. Brain tissue samples were collected around ZT4 both for implanted and unimplanted animals, as well as for undisturbed and sleep-deprived mice. EEG implanted animals typically underwent chronic EEG recordings combined with SD and/or SD+FLS on 1-3 occasions prior to the day of tissue collection (n=16), except for two groups (n=12) that received single SD+FLS on the day of tissue collection and were not used for chronic EEG recordings. Animals were continuously recorded for EEGs (n=16) and LFPs (n=8), starting at ZT0 when the welfare checks were also performed. On SD days with or without monocular FLS stimulation, mice were subjected to 4 hours of SD through the presentation of novel objects from light onset under continuous monitoring (ZT0-ZT4), as previously described (McKillop et al., 2018;Yamagata et al., 2021a). FLS consisted of 8Hz trains of white light emitted from a small LED device, lasting for 2 seconds and repeated every 30s during the entire duration of the 4-h SD. LED intensity was optimised to reliably induce visually detectable cortical responses at a single trial level, and maintained constant during the stimulation. The temporal frequency was chosen based on previous work in rats (Manning et al., 2007;Uhlrich et al., 2005) where it was shown to elicit the strongest evoked EEG response in the visual cortex and potentiation of responses across repeated sessions. Stimulation was presented using custom-made headstages containing one light-emitting diode (Luxeon Star LED, product code: LXML-PWC2 5650K) at a viewing angle of 30 degrees, 6-8 mm from the corneal surface of the eye, positioned over the centre of the pupil. The LED device was attached at the beginning of the 4-h SD period and removed immediately before the animals were left undisturbed. Stimuli were triggered externally by the computer, using the software and hardware from Tucker Davis Technologies (11930 Research Circle Alachua, FL 32615 USA), which allowed precise synchronisation of EEG signals and LED stimulation for subsequent analysis. Electrophysiological recordings were acquired with an RZ2 High-Performance Processor and Synapse software (Tucker-Davis Technologies Inc., Alachua, FL, USA). EEG, EMG, and LFP signals were continuously recorded, concomitantly with extracellular neuronal spike data from the same electrodes used for LFP monitoring (PZ5 NeuroDigitizer preamplifier, TDT, USA). EEG, LFP, and EMG signals were filtered between 0.1 and 100 Hz and stored at a sampling rate of 305 Hz. The signals were resampled offline at a sampling rate of 256 Hz using custom-made Matlab scripts (The MathWorks Inc., Natick, MA, USA). For subsequent analyses, EEG and LFP power spectra were computed by a fast Fourier transform of 4-s epochs (Hanning window), with a 0.25-Hz resolution in Matlab. Signals between 0.5-20 Hz were analysed as changes in this range have been most consistently related to sleep pressure. Extracellular neuronal activity was continuously acquired at a sampling rate of 25 kHz and filtered between 300 Hz and 5 kHz. For spike acquisition, amplitude thresholds were manually set on Synapse on each recording channel. This threshold was set at least 2 standard deviations above noise level using automatic thresholding tool from Synapse that was manually reviewed afterwards. When the voltage crossed this predefined set threshold, 46 samples around the event (0.48 ms before and 1.36 ms after the threshold crossing) were extracted and recorded. Spike waveforms were processed using custom-made Matlab scripts. To screen out putative units of good quality for the 12-h light phase data of each channel, K-means analysis was performed using principal components from PCA analysis based on waveform data recorded via thresholding. Clustered waveforms were then visually inspected and screened. Subsequently, firing rate of each day were plotted and 6 std cutoff (or in two cases, 1 or 3 std) from the mean was applied for noise rejection. OFF periods were detected in each channel (selected best quality 2-3 channels per animal) as neuronal silence lasting at least 50 ms. Sleep scoring was performed offline. Resampled EEG, LFP and EMG signals (256 Hz) were transformed into European Data Format (EDF) using custom made scripts in python (Python 3.10). These signals were visualized in 4-s epochs using the software SleepSign (Kissei Comtec Co., Nagano, Japan) and manually scored for vigilance state. Wake was defined as low-voltage, high-frequency EEG activity accompanied by a high level of EMG activity lasting more than 4 epochs. NREM sleep was defined as EEG signal with high voltage and slow frequency, predominantly characterized by the occurrence of slow waves (0.5 to 4 Hz) and sleep spindles (10-15 Hz), and low EMG activity. REM sleep was defined as low-voltage, high-frequency EEG oscillations, with predominance of theta (6 to 9 Hz) activity in the occipital derivations, which was distinguished from waking by reduced level of EMG activity. Brief awakenings (microarousals) were defined as transient periods of low-voltage, high-frequency oscillations in the EEG accompanied by elevated EMG tone, lasting ≥2 s and ≤16 s. Epochs containing artefacts, resulting from eating, drinking or gross movements were excluded from spectral/MUA analysis. For RNA analyses, undisturbed (BL), sleep-deprived (SD) or sleep-deprived with monocular flickering light stimulation (SD+FLS) mice were sacrificed by cervical dislocation at ZT4 (see MethodsFig 1for summary of experimental groups). Brains were rapidly removed and placed into a brain matrix (Kent Scientific). A skin graft blade (Swann-Morton) was used to dissect 1 mm thick brain slices. Tissue punches were taken from frontal cortex and visual cortex using a sample corer (1 mm internal diameter, Fine Science Tools GmBH), flash frozen on dry ice and stored at -80°C until use. For tissue RNA extraction, the tissue was firstly mechanically disrupted in 100 µl of Trizol. The sample was then made up to 500 µl with Trizol, 100 µl chloroform added and then thoroughly mixed. Following a 5 min incubation at RT, the sample was then centrifuged for 15 min at 15,000 xg, 4°C. The clear top layer was then carefully collected, mixed with an equal volume of 70% ethanol, and RNA extracted using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA concentration and quality was determined using a NanoDrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer and cDNA synthesized using the qScript cDNA synthesis kit (QuantaBio). RT-PCR was then conducted using the Quantifast SYBR Green PCR Kit (Qiagen) and a StepOnePlus thermal cycler (Applied biosystems) with the following thermal profile: 95°C for 5 mins and then 40 cycles of 95°C for 10s, 60°C for 30s and 72°C for 12 s. Quantification of transcript levels was conducted using the relative standard curve method, for comparing within a gene, or the 2-ΔCt method for comparison across genes or samples, using GAPDH and RPL19 as housekeeping genes for the normalisation. GraphPad Prism Version 10.4.1 was used for all statistical analysis. For RT-PCR analysis, Analysis of Variance for comparison of different experimental conditions were performed using two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests corrected for multiple comparisons with Šídák multiple comparison test, alpha 0.05 for SD vs baseline (n=8 mice for baseline and n=11 mice for SD). Similarly, for SD+FLS vs SD comparison, Welch’s t-test was used (n=16 mice for SD and n=16 or 32 mice for SD+FLS). For both absolute and relative power density spectrum analysis of EEG recordings, two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s multiple comparisons test with factors “frequency bins” and “derivations” or Wilcoxon matched-paired signed rank test were used, alpha 0.05. Matlab was used for statistical analysis of MUAs. Statistical comparisons were performed using a two-tailed paired t-test was performed with units from best quality selected channels in the visual cortex, n=14 channels from n=5 mice, each with SD and SD+FLS conditions as well as respective baseline days. To evaluate the relationship between cortical activity, sleep-wake dynamics and gene expression, mice were implanted with frontal and occipital EEG electrodes and recorded during undisturbed 24-h baseline and SD (Fig. 2A). Baseline recordings under 12h-12h light-dark cycle allowed the determination of vigilance states (Fig. 2B) and showed that mice spent a high proportion of time asleep during the light period and awake during the dark phase. As expected, slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.5–4 Hz) during NREM sleep was greater in the frontal than in the occipital derivation, whereas the opposite pattern was observed for theta activity during wakefulness and REM sleep (Fig. 2C). Mice were recorded continuously, with SD performed from ZT0 to ZT4 following 24 h of baseline recording (Fig 2D). Compared to spontaneous wakefulness, SD resulted in increased EEG power in both SWA and theta ranges in both derivations, with the increase at SWA being more pronounced in the frontal cortex. During subsequent NREM sleep, consistent with previous findings (Guillaumin et al., 2018), the increase in SWA was greater in the frontal than in the occipital derivation (Fig. 2E). For molecular assays, a separate cohort of animals were perfused at ZT4, with or without 4h of preceding SD. Unlike its more pronounced effect upon frontal EEG, the effect of SD upon gene expression tended to be comparable across cortical regions, or were more pronounced in occipital cortex (Suppl. Fig. 1). In the frontal derivation, SD resulted in a 2-fold or higher increase in bothFosandArcexpression, although high variability among animals inFosexpression was noted (Arc: p=0.0001;Fos: p=0.006; Holm-Šídák’s multiple testing correction). SD alone also increased by at least 1.5-fold the expression of multiple UPR-related genes in the frontal cortex, includingHspa5/BiP,Xbp1-spliced and unspliced,Gadd34andHyou1(Hspa5/BiP: p<0.0001;Xbp1-spliced: p<0.0001;Xbp1-unspliced: p=0.02;Hyou1: p<0.0001;Gadd34: p<0.0008; Holm-Šídák’s multiple testing correction). In contrast, the expression of genes associated with later-stage UPR signalling and pro-apoptotic pathways, includingAtf4andDdit3/Chop, was not altered by SD alone in the frontal derivation. In the occipital cortex, SD resulted in at least a 2-fold increase in bothFosandArclevels (Arc: p<0.0001 andFos: p=0.015; Holm-Šídák’s multiple testing correction). Likewise, expression ofHspa5/BiP,Xbp1-spliced and unspliced, andHyou1was increased at least 2-fold following SD (Hspa5/BiP: p<0.0001;Xbp1-spliced: p=0.003;Xbp1-unspliced: p=0.0006;Hyou1: p=0.0008; Holm-Šídák’s’s multiple testing correction), while Gadd34 was still increased approximately 1.4-fold (Gadd34: p=0.021; Holm-Šídák’s’s multiple testing correction) (Fig. 2F). Because both forms of the XBP1 transcript are increased during SD, it may reflect increased XBP1 transcript abundance in addition to IRE-1 dependent splicing. To further explore whether expression of ER-stress-related genes was associated with neuronal activity, we performed correlation analyses between activity-dependent genes (i.e.,FosandArc) and UPR-related transcripts. Overall, the analyses revealed positive associations, with correlations betweenArcand UPR-related genes generally stronger than those involvingFos, although rested and sleep-deprived animals formed largely distinct clusters (Supplementary Fig. 2). As SD leads to global changes in electrophysiological and molecular markers of neuronal activity, we hypothesised that the changes in cortical activity during SD are responsible for the molecular signatures associated with ER stress. To address this question, we combined SD with monocular FLS in a separate cohort of mice. The stimulation paradigm consisted of pulses of bright white light delivered to one eye via a skull-mounted LED, which allowed the animal to move freely throughout the stimulation (Figure 3A). Trains of 10-ms light pulses at 8 Hz were delivered for 2 s every 30 s throughout the 4-h SD period, and reliably affected activity in the contralateral primary visual cortex as recorded by intracranial laminar probe (Figure 3B). We chose the 8 Hz frequency to further enhance the spontaneous oscillatory activity typical of active exploratory behaviour and high arousal levels (Yamagata et al., 2021b). In both D) and E) the raster plots below LFP traces represent the occurrence of spikes in individual channels of the laminar probe.F)Comparison of OFF period incidence for 2s before and during the 2s FLS train, mean±SEM (before stimulation: 99.28±0.32; during stimulation: 201.9 ±39.74 (One-tailed t-test, p=0.0147, alpha=0.05)). All values are relative to baseline OFF incidence (n=10 LFP channels with good MUA from n=5 mice).G)Frontal (left) and occipital (right) relative EEG power density spectra for the first hour after SD or SD+FLS (mean ± S.E.M.). Two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s multiple comparisons test with factors “frequency bins” and “experiment”; Frontal: Frequency - F (120, 2142) = 42.78, p<0.0001, experiment - F (1, 2142) = 58.74), p<0.0001, interaction - F (120, 2142) = 2.482, p<0.0001. Occipital: Frequency - F (120, 2142) = 29.11, p<0.0001, experiment - F (1, 2142) = 56.91, p<0.0001, interaction: F (120, 2142) = 1.603, p<0.0001.H)Comparison of the relative OFF period duration in artifact-free NREM epochs during 4 hours after SD or SD+FLS, expressed as percentage of baseline NREM OFF period duration. It was analysed using a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA for each hour interval, with experimental condition (SD and SD+FLS) and time (4 consecutive 15-minute intervals) as within-subject factors. The Geisser– Greenhouse correction was applied, and post hoc comparisons between conditions at individual time points were adjusted for multiple testing, showing significant differences, represented by black lines, only during the first hour after SD or SD+FLS; Time Interval: F (3, 24) = 5.936, p=0.0035; Condition: F (1, 8) = 8.952, p=0.0173; Interaction: F (3, 24) = 0.8221, p=0.4945. Directly observing the animals confirmed that they tolerated the stimulation paradigm well and did not manifest obvious alterations in spontaneous behaviour. Furthermore, the total amount of waking during SD was not significantly affected by the procedure (3.57±0.11 vs 3.64±0.08 hours for SD vs SD+FLS respectively, unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-test, p=0.6). As the animals were handled to disconnect the device at the end of the SD+FLS procedure, they took slightly longer to fall asleep, as compared to the SD alone condition (NREM during the 1st hour after SD and SD+FLS was 0.37±0.04 and 0.22±0.05 hours respectively, unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-test, p<0.05). As expected, FLS elicited a strong theta (8Hz) oscillation in the EEG and LFP in the visual cortex, which was present, although in a somewhat attenuated form, also in the frontal derivation (Figure 3C). Overall average firing rate during wake was lower in the SD+FLS condition as compared to SD alone (SD alone = 138.1 ± 12.1%; SD+FLS = 125±9.9%, as percentage of baseline; p=0.043 two-tailed paired t-test). This change in average firing rate was explained by the markedly altered firing pattern during stimulation. Neuronal activity recorded from the visual cortex was strongly entrained by the FLS, showing brief bursts of activity, that were followed by a prominent suppression in neuronal spiking (Figure 3D). These suppressions in MUA resembled OFF periods typically observed during sleep (Figure 3E) (Harding et al., 2023), and a quantification of OFF periods revealed that their incidence doubled during delivery of the FLS compared with the immediately preceding period (Figure 3F). Despite the increase in the incidence of sleep-like OFF periods induced by stimulation, we did not detect a significant difference in subsequent sleep duration of animals subjected to light stimulation during SD, when compared to those subjected to SD alone (ZT4-ZT24, 10±0.38 hours (n=8) vs 8.78±0.37 hours (n=12) for SD alone or SD+FLS respectively, paired two-tailed Wilcoxon test, p=0.0781). However, the subsequent sleep was characterised by higher EEG SWA in both the occipital and frontal derivations (Figure 3G), as well as longer duration of OFF periods (Figure 3H). This suggests that there was a global increase in sleep pressure in response to physiological stimulation, even if it was associated with the induction of local OFF periods. To investigate whether local stimulation led to changes in neuronal activity-related and ER stress-related genes, we repeated the transcriptomic analysis on cortical tissue punches collected immediately after SD+FLS and compared these results to the SD only condition. Gene expression in the hemisphere contralateral to the eye that received stimulation was compared with the averaged gene expression across both hemispheres in SD only brains. Remarkably, the increases in activity-related genes due to SD were no longer observed in visual cortex. BothFosandArcshowed a marked decrease (1.96-fold forFosand 3.7-fold forArc;p<0.0001 for both genes, Holm-Šídák’s’s multiple testing correction) in the SD+FLS condition when compared to SD alone (Figure 4A). The expression of genes encoding members of ER stress pathways upregulated by SD was also attenuated following FLS. Hspa5/BiP,Xbp1-spliced and unspliced, andHyou1were all reduced in the SD+FLS condition by at least 1.8-fold (p<0.0001 for all four genes; Holm-Šídák’s’s multiple testing correction;Figure 4B). Expression ofHspa5/Bip, which acts as a main sensor of UPR pathways during ER stress, was also attenuated (2.90±0.91 vs 1.45±0.48 for SD alone vs SD+FLS respectively; expression levels: AU, mean±s.d.). SplicedXBP1(XBP1s), which encodes a potent transcriptional activator, and unspliced XBP1 (XBP1u), which encodes an inhibitor of the UPR (Yoshida et al., 2006), were both attenuated (XBP1s0.3±0.06 vs 0.16±0.05, andXBP1u0.93±0.35 vs 0.5±0.14, for SD alone vs SD+FLS, respectively) suggesting that FLS primarily attenuated the SD-associated increase in XBP1 transcription rather than selectively altering the balance between the spliced and unspliced isoforms. Meanwhile, the expression ofHyou1, a chaperone with a similar function toBiP(Kusaczuk & Cechowska-Pasko, 2013) was also attenuated (0.70±0.30 vs 0.33±0.07 for SD alone vs SD+FLS respectively). These population data were pooled from three different experimental batches and consistent effects were observed across each of the three batches. A)Gene expression levels of the immediate early genesFosandArcas measured by qPCR in frontal and occipital cortices of mice that were either sleep-deprived (SD) or sleep-deprived with flickering light stimulation (SD+FLS) for 4hrs. Tissue samples were taken from the hemisphere contralateral to the eye receiving the stimulation in the preceding 4h period. Expression ofArcis significantly reduced by FLS in frontal cortex, while both genes are downregulated in occipital regions (Frontal cortex:Arc: p<0.0001;Fos: p>0.9999; Occipital cortex; p<0.0001 for both genes, Holm-Šídák’s’s multiple testing correction).B)Gene expression levels of members of the ER-stress pathway. Three genes were significantly downregulated following FLS in both frontal and occipital cortices (at least p<0.001 for all four genes; Holm-Šídák’s multiple testing correction). *p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001, **** p<0.0001. SD is n=15 of which 4 are implanted and 11 are unimplanted and SD+FLS is n=32 of which 28 are implanted and 4 are non-implanted. Dashed line represents the expression of the gene presented in undisturbed condition, when animals are allowed to sleep at will. Solid symbols represent mice not implanted with EEG headstages. A similar profile was observed in frontal cortical regions, where the FLS attenuated upregulation of SD-induced genes, with the exception ofFos. Specifically, the activity regulated geneArcwas expressed at 2-fold lower levels when FLS was delivered compared to SD alone (1.60±0.72 vs 0.71±0.41 for SD vs SD+FLS, p=0.0003 Holm-Šídák’s’s multiple testing correction). Similarly,Hspa5/BiP,XBP1u,XBP1s,andHyou1were all approximately 1.6-fold reduced after SD+FLS compared to SD alone (Hspa5: 2.76±0.68 vs 1.71±0.45, p<0.0001;XBP1u: 0.98±0.19 vs 0.58±0.15 p<0.0001;XBP1s: 0.25±0.04 vs 0.16±0.04 p<0.0001;Hyou1: 0.79±0.21 vs 0.47±0.12 p=0.0002; mean±s.d. and Welch’s t-test using Holm-Šídák’s’s multiple testing correction). Previous work has established that prolonged wakefulness is accompanied by increased neuronal activity, elevated expression of immediate early genes, and activation of multiple branches of the UPR (Abdalla et al., 2026c;Basheer et al., 1997;Cirelli et al., 2004;Mackiewicz et al., 2007;Mongrain et al., 2025b;Naidoo et al., 2005,2007;Popescu et al., 2025). These observations have been interpreted as reflecting the increasing biosynthetic demands imposed on cortical neurons during sustained wakefulness (Vanrobaeys et al., 2023;Vyazovskiy & Harris, 2013). We reveal that although electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure (recovery sleep SWA) exhibit substantial heterogeneity across cortical regions, the molecular response to prolonged wakefulness appears to be more uniform across the cortex. This observation suggests that cortical activity underlying transcriptional regulation is not simply reflected by the spatial distribution of SWA. When neuronal activity was manipulated during sleep deprivation by flickering light stimulation, we observed transient suppressions in neuronal firing, while the total duration of wakefulness was unchanged. Critically, however, manipulating neuronal activity in this manner prevented the increase in activity-dependent and UPR-related gene expression induced by sleep deprivation. These results suggest that the UPR is influenced not simply by the duration of prior wakefulness, but by the temporal pattern or type of neuronal activity during waking. Interestingly, reduction of UPR-related gene expression during SD occurred despite a further increase in subsequent SWA. To our knowledge, this is the first experimental demonstration that molecular markers of ER stress and electrophysiological markers of sleep homeostasis can be uncoupled through physiological manipulation of cortical neuronal activity. While SWA remains one of the most robust measures of accumulated sleep pressure, our findings suggest that it does not fully capture the molecular state of cortical neurons. Instead, different components of neuronal activity may regulate distinct aspects of the response to prolonged wakefulness. One possible interpretation of the differential effects of neuronal activity changes in markers of sleep pressure such as SWA and ER-stress related gene expression could be that the UPR is primarily sensitive to action potential firing and the associated metabolic and biosynthetic demands, whereas SWA may be more strongly influenced by synaptic and subthreshold network activity. Repeated firing generates large intracellular calcium transients, increases vesicle recycling, membrane trafficking, and protein synthesis, all processes that place considerable demands on endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis (Brini et al., 2014;Cohen & Greenberg, 2008;Ma et al., 2023;Rangaraju et al., 2017;Walter & Ron, 2011). By repeatedly interrupting neuronal firing through induced sleep-like OFF periods, FLS may reduce these biosynthetic demands sufficiently to attenuate activation of UPR pathways. At the same time, repeated stimulation may favour the recruitment of cortical inhibitory neurons such as somatostatin positive neurons and contribute to the accumulation of sleep pressure (Funk et al., 2017), explaining the enhanced SWA observed during subsequent recovery sleep. Although this model remains speculative, it provides an explanation for the apparent dissociation between transcriptional and electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure observed in the present study. This interpretation is also consistent with recent work showing that experimentally induced OFF periods promote synaptic renormalisation and weaken excitatory cortical synapses (Driessen et al., 2026). Our findings extend these observations by suggesting that OFF periods may not only influence synaptic physiology but also regulate activity-dependent transcriptional programmes associated with ER stress. The broader implication is that distinct features of cortical activity may regulate different biological processes. We speculate that sustained action potential firing may primarily determine activity-dependent transcription and engagement of protein quality-control pathways, whereas other forms of neuronal activity, including synaptic and subthreshold signalling, may contribute more strongly to the accumulation of sleep pressure reflected by SWA. Future experiments combining intracellular recordings, calcium imaging, and direct measurements of protein synthesis and ER function will be required to test this hypothesis. Finally, the findings of the current study may have implications beyond sleep physiology. Dysregulation of ER proteostasis and UPR signalling has been implicated in several neurological disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease and epilepsy. Notably, non-invasive sensory stimulation has emerged as a potential strategy for modifying disease-associated cellular processes. 40-Hz visual stimulation reduces amyloid-β burden and alters microglial responses in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease, while prolonged or multisensory gamma entrainment influences neuronal and synaptic integrity, glial responses, and cognition (Adaikkan et al., 2019;Adaikkan & Tsai, 2020;Iaccarino et al., 2016;Martorell et al., 2019). Although our stimulation paradigm differs in frequency and experimental context, our findings raise the possibility that sensory stimulation can additionally influence cellular stress pathways through activity-dependent mechanisms. Determining whether modulation of ER proteostasis contributes to the beneficial effects reported for sensory stimulation in disease models will be an important direction for future studies.
