title: Toward naturalistic reaching: Intermediate reaches under uncertainty generalize to walking, but are not obligatory
author: Seavey, C. V.; Seegelke, C.; Cooke, D. F.; Marigold, D. S.; Heed, T.
text: Highly-constrained laboratory-based experiments have provided important insights into movement planning. When people reach toward one of several stimuli before knowing which to target, their hand trajectories are situated intermediate to direct reaches to each stimulus. Real-world reaching, however, involves a greater decision landscape than typical laboratory tasks. We extended the go-before-you-know paradigm to a walk-to-reach task resembling unconstrained natural behavior. Participants walked three steps toward a touchscreen before reaching for one of two stimuli, marked as the target either at walk onset or after reach onset. Under uncertainty, intermediate reaches occurred, but only for some stimulus layouts and participants. Individual reaches varied considerably; many directly targeted one stimulus and corrected late. Body position at reach onset was anchored to the screen more than the stimuli and was partly intermediate. Thus, intermediate movements generalize beyond the laboratory, but as one flexible strategy among several, not as obligatory motor plan averaging. Movement-related decisions are a prime example of how cognition and environment interact in complex ways in naturalistic environments: actions shape the environment, and the changing environment shapes actions (Lepora & Pezzulo, 2015;Pezzulo & Cisek, 2016). The information necessary to make movement-based decisions accumulates over time (Gold & Shadlen, 2007), and ongoing movement as well as movement choices influence which subsequent choices become available (Cisek & Kalaska, 2010;Pezzulo & Cisek, 2016). For example, when cleaning up a messy desk, new information becomes available over time as one moves and uncovers items, and this new information shapes subsequent choices of which item(s) to pick up. This continuous movement-and-decision process implies uncertainty about which movement targets may be available in the (near) future, and how to best reach them. This uncertainty, in turn, affects which movements are executed, and how. An influential experimental paradigm for studying human reaching movements under uncertainty is the go-before-you-know task. Participants must initiate a reaching movement before they know where the movement must end. Several stimuli are shown on a monitor as potential reach targets; one of them is marked as the final target only after the participant has begun moving their hand. Reach trajectories in go-before-you-know situations lie intermediate to the trajectories participants produce when each stimulus is presented alone and there is no uncertainty about target location (Chapman et al., 2010;Gallivan & Chapman, 2014;Wispinski et al., 2018). The occurrence of intermediate reaching movements is considered a behavioral reflection of movement uncertainty. However, there are two opposing interpretations of which mechanisms produce them. The first is that the behavior reflects an averaging of several motor plans the brain has planned in parallel (Basso & Wurtz, 1997,1998;Chapman et al., 2010;Cisek & Kalaska, 2005;Enachescu et al., 2021;Gallivan et al., 2016;Gallivan & Chapman, 2014). Several findings support this view. First, even small differences in the stimulus layout evoke a modulation of the intermediate reach trajectory; for example, when one of several stimuli was placed slightly more left than before, the intermediate reach trajectory under target uncertainty, too, was executed slightly more to the left (Chapman et al., 2010). Second, when participants had to swiftly move, by their own choice, to one of two identical visual stimuli, early electromyographic activity reflected an influence of both stimuli (Selen et al., 2023). Third, intermediate trajectories are based on motor, not visual, information when these two aspects are disentangled using motor adaptation (Gallivan et al., 2017). The second interpretation of intermediate trajectories is that they reflect a single motor plan that has been constructed based on the current (uncertain) context (Alhussein & Smith, 2021;Contemori & Carroll, 2025;Dekleva et al., 2018;Haith et al., 2015;Nashed et al., 2017;Wong & Haith, 2017). This notion is supported by the finding that not all uncertain situations evoke intermediate trajectories. For instance, participants used different reach strategies depending on the instructed reach speed in a go-before-you-know task (Wong & Haith, 2017): when reaches were slow, participants produced intermediate reaches; in contrast, when reaches were fast, they were directed to one of the potential targets. Likewise, when obstacles were placed such that a safe, non-collision trajectory deviated from an average trajectory, participants exhibited safe rather than intermediate trajectories (Haith et al., 2015). These strategies ensured the highest possible success rates in the respective contexts. Therefore, intermediate movements may be produced strategically to maximize task success, rather than reflecting mandatory averaging of multiple active plans. Whereas sensorimotor decision making is often framed using natural behaviors – such as the desk cleaning example above – it is not clear whether the types of behavior identified in the lab occur in the same way in natural contexts. Studies that employed the go-before-you-know paradigm have typically implemented various constraints to tease out the described modulation of reaching movements. Some studies have participants respond quickly, with the movement completed in a narrow time interval such that trials are invalid otherwise (Alhussein & Smith, 2021;Chapman et al., 2010;Contemori & Carroll, 2025;Enachescu et al., 2021;Gallivan et al., 2016;Gallivan & Chapman, 2014;Nashed et al., 2017;Wong & Haith, 2017). Other studies have also restricted movement to a single plane of motion (Alhussein & Smith, 2021;Contemori & Carroll, 2025;Nashed et al., 2017). Such constraints thus enforce highly stereotypical movements to help uncover movement strategies. It seems plausible that the production of intermediate reach trajectories can emerge in lab experiments because the experimental context is usually narrow and overlearned, with dozens or hundreds of highly similar trials, all produced in close temporal succession. In everyday life, reaching movements do not usually require stereotypical execution, particularly in uncertain contexts, and they often occur in tandem with full-body movement, including postural changes and walking toward the object to be handled. The decision landscape of a walk-to-reach action is considerably richer than that of typical lab-based experiments. For instance, where the foot is placed during a step affects what targets can be reached thereafter. Therefore, the hand likely starts its reach from a different location in space in each new trial, depending on where walking has positioned the body. Both the expanded decision landscape and the substantial variability of naturalistic contexts may preclude processing strategies that result in intermediate trajectories. One reason is the comparably high complexity of natural contexts. Conversely, however, participants may in fact exploit the expanded decision landscape to modulate not only reaching but also other movements: For instance, they might use walking to place their body strategically before the reach begins, similar to how participants adjust their body posture when they prepare grasping an object (Land et al., 2013;Marteniuk & Bertram, 2001). In this latter case, the laboratory-based findings about reaching movements may be viewed as a blueprint of a general, body-wide movement principle. We addressed these questions in a go-before-you-know experiment that required participants to take several steps toward a screen on which two stimuli were displayed. As in prior, reach-only experiments, one of the stimuli changed color to mark it as the reach target. The onset of this change occurred either at the beginning of walking, so that participants were certain about the target; or it occurred after the participant had walked to the screen and begun to reach toward it, so that the reach had to be initialized under uncertainty. Twenty-two healthy adults participated in this study (4 males and 18 females; mean age = 22.6 ± 3.0 years) based on sample sizes of similar studies (Alhussein & Smith, 2021;Chapman et al., 2010;Contemori & Carroll, 2025). Participants did not have any known history of neurological, musculoskeletal, or visual diseases that could affect their walking or reaching behavior. All participants were right-hand dominant (Edinburg Handedness Inventory: 94.6 ± 9.3) and right leg dominant (based on the leg a participant would use to kick a ball). The ethics committee of the University of Salzburg approved the study protocol, and all participants gave informed written consent prior to the experiment. Participants performed rapid reaches to a visual target. Participants performed the experiment while standing and when required to walk three steps to approach the touchscreen. We counterbalanced the order of the standing and walking blocks of trials. However, we do not include details on the standing trials because of poor data quality. Thus, we only describe the walk-to-reach protocol and report results on these trials. We displayed circular stimuli (white) and targets (green; both with diameter = 27 mm; black background) using the Psychophysics Toolbox, version 3 (Kleiner et al., 2007) on a 23” touchscreen (1920 × 1080 px; refresh rate of 60 Hz). We positioned the top of the touchscreen at 75% of the participant’s body height, measured from the floor. To track finger and walking trajectories, motion capture cameras (Visualeyez VZ4000v, Phoenix Technologies Inc., Vancouver, Canada; sampling rate 100 Hz) recorded active LED position markers placed on the right index finger (three total markers placed on the midline and medial and lateral aspects of the fingertip) and suprasternal notch. We placed additional markers on the radial styloid process, midline of the dorsal aspect of the wrist, suprasternal notch, and right and left midfeet, anterior superior iliac spines, and acromions; however, the motion tracking system did not record all positions with sufficient reliability, and we therefore used only the finger markers for our report. Prior to experimental trials, participants stood in front of the touchscreen and completed ten reaches toward each target without time constraints. We used their average touch location as the target location in motion capture coordinates for our data analysis. During experimental trials, the touchscreen displayed two visual stimuli, 255 mm apart (center-to-center). One of them changed its color during the trial to designate it as the reach target. This color change occurred either at walk onset (‘reach while certain’) or 50 ms after reach onset (‘reach while uncertain’), thus creating two decision contexts. Each stimulus became the final reach target with equal probability. There were two stimulus configurations; they differed only in their left-right placement on the screen, centered 88 mm to the left or right of the monitor’s center. (“stimulus set”,Figure 1B). This manipulation allows testing whether participants make adjustments of their their intermediate trajectories even to small changes of the stimulus display (Chapman et al., 2010). (A) Participants walked toward a touchscreen initially displaying two white stimuli and reached, ultimately touching the target indicated by changing its color to green. Trials began with the participant standing, looking at the screen, and holding 2 buttons for 500 ms: their right index finger on a button on their hip and the heel of their starting foot on another button. At walk onset, the touchscreen presented the potential targets (white circles). The target was revealed (green circle) either at walking onset (“Certain” decision context) or 50 ms after reach onset (“Uncertain”). (B) There were two stimulus configurations that were shifted by 176 mm, with the stimulus midpoints shifted 88 mm to the left or right side of the touchscreen center. (C) For each trial, we calculated the reach angle between a straight line from the reach onset to the center of the target and the reach point 100 ms along the trajectory (top). Reach angle was signed positive for reaches directed medial to a straight line to the target (bottom). (D) Aim analysis (inset) with example reach trajectories and progression of reach aim. Every 5% along each reach trajectory (+, aim analysis points), we projected the aim to the touchscreen. Rasters above indicate left/right position of the aim. Each raster row indicates the progression of the aims across trials in increments of 5% of the reach. Inset shows expanded view of boxed area with one example reach trial trajectory highlighted and annotated to show how aim rasters were determined. Aim lines with arrowheads extend from consecutive aim analysis points from the example trajectory and end at the anterior-posterior position of the targets. This left/right position is projected vertically (dashed lines). Later aim rasters are plotted progressively higher up. A single example aim line and raster are plotted in black. Additional description inFigure 4. Participants began each trial standing at a marked location about three steps away from the touchscreen and were required to depress two buttons for 500 ms: Their right index finger was placed on a hip button, and the heel of their preferred starting foot was placed on a button located on the ground. At walk onset, the touchscreen presented the potential targets. To encourage rapid reaching, we constrained the total walking time to 2300 ms (foot button release to finger-screen contact) and the total reach time (which occurred during walking) to 800 ms (hip button release to finger-screen contact). At the end of each trial, the touchscreen indicated whether the participant had met these timing constraints. Our task consisted of two target decision contexts (‘reach while certain/uncertain’), two stimulus midpoints (stimulus sets shifted left and right), and two endpoints (target endpoint: left and right target of a stimulus set) for a total of eight conditions. Participants completed 25 trials per condition that met timing constraints for a total of 200 trials. To avoid fatigue, we divided the experiment into five blocks. Each block consisted of five repetitions of each condition, randomized within the block for a total of 40 reaches. If the participant did not meet timing constraints for a given trial, that trial was repeated at the end the block. Participants could rest between blocks. Prior to starting the task, participants completed one practice block of trials. We analyzed kinematic data using custom code written in MATLAB. We interpolated missing data for gaps under 16 frames using a cubic spline; we left larger gaps marked as missing data. Then we filtered the data using a zero-lag, fourth-order, low-pass Butterworth filter with a cutoff frequency of 6 Hz. We defined walk onset as the time of release of the foot button, and reach onset as the time of release of the hip button. We defined reach endpoint as the time the touchscreen registered the participant’s touch. We removed five participants from the analysis due to poor data quality (< 5 useable trials for all conditions; these data are, however, included in the available dataset). From remaining participants, we excluded trials if the frame at reach onset and/or the data point at 100 ms after reach onset was missing after interpolation (31% of trials were excluded for this reason), or if the participant touched the wrong side of the screen (< 1%). For one of the four target locations, three participants contained < 5 useable trials for one decision context (reach while certain/uncertain) but not the other. In these cases, we removed the participant’s data of both decision contexts for the respective target from analysis. Subsequent analyses thus included data from 17 participants, three of which had some target locations excluded. For all statistical analyses, we used JMP 18 software (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC). We considered effects significant at an alpha level of 0.05. We used Tukey’s post hoc tests to follow up significant interactions. We asked whether participants’ initial reach strategy depended on the decision context. We expected participants to reach between the two stimuli when initiating their reach before knowing which stimulus was the target (“uncertain”). In contrast, we expected a direct reach to the target when it was already known at the beginning of the trial (“certain”). We used the initial reach angle as a measure of reach direction at the beginning of the reach. Initial reach direction indicates the feedforward motor plan prior to any online corrections, because sensory information is not yet available due to neural transmission times (Scott, 2016). We defined initial reach angle as the angle between a straight line from the fingertip position at reach onset to the target and the location of the fingertip marker 100 ms after reach onset, calculated using the inverse tangent function. We designated angles directed medial of the straight line as positive (i.e., clockwise angles for left targets, counterclockwise angles for right targets; seeFigure 1C). We tested differences in initial reach angle between factors decision context (reach while certain vs. uncertain), target endpoint (left vs. right), and stimulus set (sets shifted left vs. right) with a three-way linear mixed-effects model, and using participant as a random effect. While initial reach angle quantified the deviation of the initial aim from a straight-line trajectory to the target, it was not informative about whether a participant aimed at the same location across trials because the starting position varied between reaches. Thus, we performed an aim analysis. We first time normalized the data and then identified the position of the fingertip along the reach trajectory at every 5 percent of the reach time to determine the location of the aim. We constructed a line between consecutive points along the trajectory and extrapolated the line to the anterior-posterior position of the targets. We indicated the projected aim for each trajectory as vertically dash lines and represented time upward across rows (Figure 1D). This analysis assesses how aim evolved over the duration of the reach and whether participants adopted different reaching strategies in the different decision-context conditions. Subsequently, we averaged trials for each condition within participants and also computed group averages. Participants did not receive specific instructions about how or where they had to walk beyond the general instruction to take three steps and reach for the target. Therefore, participants could theoretically position their body strategically relative to the screen or stimuli prior to reach onset. Participants held their pointing finger on the hip button until they began their reach. We used finger position prior to hip button release as a proxy of body position in space and identified the left/right fingertip position at reach onset relative to the center of the touchscreen. We analyzed the left/right position of the finger at reach onset with a three-way linear mixed-effect model with fixed factors decision context (reach while certain vs. uncertain), target endpoint (left vs. right), and stimulus set (sets shifted left vs. right), and participant as a random effect. We first asked whether reach trajectories are adjusted based on (un)certainty, even when a person walks toward the potential targets. Reach trajectories were mostly straight and directed toward the target when the target had been specified at walk onset (reaching while certain,Figure 2). In contrast, when the target was specified only after the reach had been initiated (reaching while uncertain,Figure 2), reach trajectories often curved toward the target after it was cued. Whereas this finding is, at first glance, compatible with the previous reports of intermediate reach trajectories (Chapman et al., 2010;Gallivan & Chapman, 2014), trajectories were not all intermediate under uncertainty: In some cases, participants produced trajectories akin to those observed in previous go-before-you-know experiments that lie between the direct reaches initiated with certainty about target location (e.g.,Figure 2, Participants 8 and 14, right column). In other cases the trajectory was initially directed toward one of the two stimuli. If the opposite stimulus became the target, the reach turned at the very end toward the correct stimulus (e.g.,Figure 2, Participant 17). Not all cases are easily classifiable. For example, for both Participants 8 and 14, uncertain reaches toward the left stimulus set were strongly biased toward the right target, but the average trajectory nonetheless shows a slight leftward bias visually. The same is true for the average of the full sample (Figure 5, left side). Example reach trajectories from three partic-ipants. Blue and orange traces: reach while certain. pink and green traces: reach while uncertain. Bold lines indicate condition-wise average trajectories, and fine lines indicate individual trajectories. Darker hues indicate the first 100 ms of the trajectory. Initial reach direction differed depending on decision context. When reaching while certain, participants directed their initial reach toward the cued target (Figure 2, blue and orange colors). When reaching while uncertain, some participants directed their initial reach more toward the center of both potential targets (e.g., Participants 8 and 14,Figure 2, pink and green colors) when presented with the right stimulus set. However, when presented with the left stimulus set, participants generally biased the direction of their reach toward the right stimulus. Other participants (e.g., Participant 17,Figure 2) biased the direction of their reach toward the right stimulus irrespective of the stimulus set. To quantify this behavior, we calculated initial reach angle (seeFigure 1C). Initial reach angle differed based on decision context, target endpoint, and stimulus set (three-way interaction: F1,103= 7.43, p = 0.008). To interpret this interaction, we evaluated the decision context × target endpoint interaction for the left and right stimulus sets separately. For the left stimulus set, reaching while uncertain increased the initial reach angle compared to reaching while certain for the left but not for the right target (Figure 3A, left side;Figure 3B, left side; decision context x target endpoint interaction: F1,39= 37.08, p < 0.001). This is also evident in the examples shown inFigure 2. For the right stimulus set, reaching while uncertain increased initial reach angle compared to reaching while certain for both the left and right targets (Figure 3A, right side;Figure 3B, right side; F1,47= 11.31, p = 0.002). This result indicates decision context affected initial reach direction for both targets (see also examples inFigure 2, Participants 8 and 14). (A) Mean ± SE initial reach angle across participants (n=17). *Significantly different based on post hoc tests after significant decision context x target endpoint interaction (P< 0.05). Black * and brackets, significant comparisons of primary interest. (B) Mean ± SE difference in initial reach angle between reaching while certain vs. uncertain. Positive values indicate greater initial reach angle when reaching while uncertain. The means for each participant are superimposed. Previous research used the initial reach angle to characterize initial reach bias (Contemori & Carroll, 2025), just as we did in the present study. Here, with each reach starting at a different location, the direction to the target, too, differs in each trial. Our initial reach angle measure compensates for this potential confound because it is computed relative to a straight line to the target (seeFigure 1C). However, by removing the relevance of the starting location, the measure removes the absolute information about where the reach was directed. In particular, if a participant started their reach more toward the left versus right on a trial, analyzing (non-zero) initial angles alone would not tell us whether the participant was aiming at a common location across trials. Moreover, focusing on the initial reach angle disregards whether and how the aim evolves throughout the reach. Therefore, we computed the reach aim at different points along the reach (seeFigure 4) and extended it to the frontal plane on which the potential targets lie. Progression of reach aim over time for four example participants. Fine trajectories are individual, time-normalized trials. Rasters above indicate left/right position of the aim projected to the anterior-posterior position plane of the targets. Each raster row indicates the progression of the aims across trials in increments of 5% of the reach with later aim rasters plotted progres-sively higher up. SeeFigure 1for details of aim analysis shown in in-set. Initial aim strategy was highly variable within and between participants. When reaching with uncertainty, some participants aimed toward the midpoint of the two potential targets (Figure 4, Participant 8, right stimulus set, both targets: pink and green rasters). However, when reaching with uncertainty toward the potential targets with the other stimulus set, the same participant aimed toward one of the potential targets (Figure 4, Participant 8, left stimulus set, both targets: pink and green rasters). These differences between the two stimulus sets thus mirror the results of the initial reach angle analysis. Yet, even within the same condition, participants varied their reach behavior from trial to trial, suggesting individuals did not aim consistently. This is demonstrated by the spread of the aim rasters spanning the width of the potential targets (e.g.,Figure 4; all Participants, right stimulus set, left target: pink rasters). This can also be seen in the wide spread of pink trajectories in allFigure 4participants. Indeed, Participant 1 appears to have a bimodal distribution of trajectories in this condition. Aiming also varied between participants. The spread of rasters for the initial aim in the group figure demonstrates variance in where participants each aimed on average (Figure 5). Each raster row indicates the average progression of the aims in increments of 5% of the reach. Each raster of a given color in a row is the mean aim of one participant at that timepoint. The trace superimposed on the raster plots indicate condition-wise group average aim. Lines and shading below indicate condition-wise group average trajectories and 2D SE error bands, respectively. Error bands can be conceived of as exactly enclosing the series of standard error ellipses (xSE, ySE) centered on each datapoint along the path. Previous lab-based studies enforced a very precise, fixed starting position for the finger. In our experiment, however, walking toward the screen made the finger’s starting position variable. In fact, participants may have positioned their body—and accordingly, the hand’s starting position— strategically to reduce the motor cost of reaching toward the target. For instance, when reaching with uncertainty, they might have positioned their body (and thus, fingertip) between the visual stimuli. Consequently, participants may have reduced the overall minimal cost of reaching to either stimulus. In other words, it would have been possible for participants not only to adjust their reach (as shown above and in previous experiments), but also its starting point (through strategic body placement). The example trajectories illustrated inFigure 2show that, regardless of decision context, the fingertip’s (and hip’s) starting location varied across conditions. Specifically, finger starting position was often between the two visual stimuli when they were presented toward the right side of the touchscreen (right stimulus set; see e.g.,Figure 2, all depicted participants, right column). In contrast, some participants positioned their fingertip more in front of the right visual stimulus when the stimuli were presented toward the left side of the touchscreen (left stimulus set, see e.g.,Figure 2, Participants 8 and 14, left column). Thus, those participants did not position their body based on just the stimuli, but probably used other scene characteristics, such as the position of the touchscreen, to place themselves. At the group level, participants placed their body in front of the visual stimuli prior to reach onset differently depending on the experimental condition. We determined left/right finger starting position relative to the left/right center of the touchscreen. Thus, if participants placed their body only relative to the monitor as a landmark, we would expect no difference in body position for the two stimulus sets, and if participants tried to position themselves in the middle of the monitor, start positions should be near zero. However, finger starting position differed significantly between stimulus sets (Figure 6; main effect: F1,106= 105.22, p < 0.001). Specifically, finger starting position relative to touchscreen center for the left and right stimulus sets was 73.7 ± 48.0 mm and 97.7 ± 40.0 mm, respectively; thus, the finger started in front of the right half of the monitor for both stimulus sets, but 24 mm further to the left for the left stimulus set. Effect of stimulus set, decision context, and target endpoint on left/right finger position at reach onset Left/right finger starting position relative to touchscreen center at reach onset across participants (mean ± SE, n=17). The means of each participant are superimposed. Dotted gray lines indicate stimulus center for each stimulus set, illustrating that participants started their reaches overall biased to the right also for the left stimulus set. The black dashed line indicates the touchscreen center, illustrating that reaches began on the right side of the screen for both stimulus sets. * After separating left and right stimulus sets, post hoc tests for significant decision context x target endpoint interactions revealed differences in finger starting position between several conditions (P< 0.05). Black * and brackets, significant comparisons of primary interest. In addition, finger starting position depended on decision context and target endpoint (interaction of decision context x target endpoint: F1,106= 51.0, p < 0.001). As is evident inFigure 6, the finger’s starting position differed for the left and right target when participants knew they had to reach these locations (orange vs. blue difference of 28.2 mm and 41.9 mm for the left and right stimulus sets, respectively). In contrast, finger starting position was indistinguishable for left and right targets under uncertainty—as would be expected, because the target wasn’t known at reach start (green vs. pink difference of 0.2 mm and 1.9 mm for the left and right stimulus sets, respectively). However, we had additionally expected that participants would place their finger intermediately in the uncertain relative to the certain decision context, in analogy to the modulation of reach trajectories. BothFig. 2andFig. 6suggested that participants indeed showed this behavior, but only for the right stimulus set—just like intermediate trajectories had been evident primarily for the right stimulus set. Therefore, we analyzed the data of the left and right stimulus sets separately, although interactions with stimulus set were not significant (3-way interaction: F1,106= 1.45, p = 0.232; stimulus set x decision context: F1,106= 1.27, p = 0.262; stimulus set x target endpoint: F1,106= 0.51, p = 0.475). This analysis confirmed the visual result pattern. For the left stimulus set, finger starting position differed depending on decision context and target endpoint (F1,44= 25.28, p < 0.001). Post hoc tests revealed that finger starting position for certain left-target reaches (Figure 6, top half; blue bar) differed significantly from all others (p < 0.001), whereas those did not differ significantly from each other (p = 0.826 – 0.988). Thus, participants positioned their finger under uncertainty in the location they also placed it when reaching directly toward the right target. This result pattern resembles that of the reach trajectories (seeFigures 2and5) and does not indicate intermediate finger placement when uncertain. For the right stimulus set, the decision context x target endpoint interaction was again significant (F1,46= 74.95, p < 0.001). Post hoc tests revealed a significant difference in finger starting position between decision contexts for both the left (p < 0.001; blue vs. pink, lower half ofFigure 6) and right (p = 0.001; orange vs. green) targets, whereas the finger starting position did not differ between the uncertain reaches that later had to be directed to the left and right target (p = 0.997; pink vs. green). Thus, the finger starting position was intermediate for uncertain reaches. Taken together, both touchscreen and stimulus-set locations affect finger starting position. Overall, these results suggest that movement adjustment is not confined to hand trajectories but rather extends to other body parts and movement types as well as to the movement that precedes the actual reach. We expanded the well-known go-before-you-know reaching paradigm by requiring participants to approach the stimulus-displaying touchscreen with several walking steps. This manipulation increases the decision landscape of the task and the variability of multiple movement parameters, such as body posture and the hand’s starting position, and frames the experiment in a natural walk-to-reach context. Previous research showed that in an uncertain, go-before-you-know decision context, people initiate reaches intermediate to direct trajectories to potential targets. (Chapman et al., 2010;Gallivan & Chapman, 2014;Wispinski et al., 2018). Our experiment revealed three key findings. First, intermediate reach trajectories occurred when participants walked toward the screen and the target was only revealed after reach onset. Thus, intermediate reaching under uncertainty occurs in a context that is less constrained than typical sensorimotor laboratory experiments. Second, the decision context affected body placement at reach onset, measured as the finger’s starting position on the hip. This effect was small compared to both variability and the size of the stimulus set shift. Third, in contrast to previous work using this paradigm, we observed variable walking/reaching behavior across specific stimulus configurations and across and within participants. Some variability may be related to the increased decision landscape of our experimental design compared to reaching that is isolated and highly stereotypical, indicating that the expanded task context modulated how trajectories are planned. Variability may have also been present in prior work but hidden by averaging. Inter-and intra-participant variability may imply that participants chose among several strategies. Below, we further discuss and integrate these three findings. Laboratory experiments in sensorimotor neuroscience often place strong constraints on how participants may execute their movements. This approach allows for teasing out small and difficult-to-observe systematic movement modulations. Yet, laboratory designs may not generalize to real-world contexts: they may fail to elicit cognitive processes and decision-making strategies that are relevant in real-world settings, or, conversely, induce processing strategies that are rarely employed outside the laboratory (Cisek & Green, 2024;Gordon et al., 2021;Ingram & Wolpert, 2011;Krakauer et al., 2017;Maselli et al., 2023;Nastase et al., 2020). Our experiment demonstrates that the go-before-you-know intermediate trajectory strategies identified in isolated reaching experiments do generalize to far less constrained, natural walk-to-reach behavior. Our experiment, therefore, principally validates the strict methodology applied in previous work for more complex and closer-to-real-life contexts. At the same time, the modulation of movement with action (un)certainty was not restricted to arm reaches. Because participants rested the reach hand’s finger on a button attached to the hip before each reach, we could use finger position during the walking phase as a proxy for hip or body position. The finger’s (and with it, the body’s) placement differed for the left and right stimulus sets as well as for the decision context. However, these adjustments were small. Body placement remained closely aligned to the monitor (or the room overall): participants only compensated for roughly 14% of the spatial displacement between the two stimulus sets (24 mm of the 176-mm shift). Distributed movement modulation across the entire body would be in line with theoretical proposals of continuous sensorimotor decision-making (Gordon et al., 2021;Lepora & Pezzulo, 2015;Pezzulo & Cisek, 2016) as well as balance recovery responses involving coordinated muscle activity across body parts following perturbations (Lowrey et al., 2017;Marigold et al., 2003;Pijnappels et al., 2010). Moreover, previous walk-to-grasp experiments suggest that participants trade off between walking and reaching depending on their relative cost or effort (Potts et al., 2018;Rosenbaum, 2008). Therefore, body placement might exhibit clearer preparatory effects if some aspects of our walk-to-reach task were adjusted—for instance, if no screen edge were visible that could serve as reference frame for the walking approach. Our findings are in conflict with the idea that reach trajectories reflect average movements derived from direct reaches to the various target options (cf.Chapman et al., 2010). Such averaging cannot explain why intermediate trajectories in our study were pronounced for only one stimulus set. Moreover, if intermediate reach trajectories reflected obligatory averages of individual reach plans, then all trajectories of a given condition should be comparatively similar. However, within a given participant and condition, single trajectories were highly variable and not aimed consistently at a hypothetical target between the two stimuli of a stimulus set. Rather, the present results may fit two alternative interpretations. The first interpretation is that uncertain trajectories are all produced under one common reach strategy that involves no early averaging of movements. This strategy entails coarsely propelling the hand forward in the general direction of the stimuli, and then performing a late, visually-guided correction toward the instructed target. In this propel-and-correct view, the largely stereotypical placement of the body and hand at reach start and the high variability of individual reaches suggest that participants do not even try to prepare, because the reach target is revealed so late. Our experiment implemented a time constraint to avoid participants simply stopping their movement to wait for the target to be revealed. Although the time constraint was twice as long as the original reach-only study (Chapman et al., 2010), participants may still have judged it too short in our more complex task context to use detailed planning. As a consequence, biomechanical constraints— which differed for the left-and right-shifted stimulus sets because participants always began their reaches on the right side of the screen—and the variability of the hand’s start point may have largely determined the trajectory before the final corrective movement. Moreover, the average-like trajectories observed for the right stimulus set may have occurred because participants could simply propel the hand forward from their preferred, right-side starting point, to guide the hand in the general direction of the stimuli. Given that the hand began the reach from the right side of the body, we would expect propelled reaches to be biased toward right side of the left stimulus set. This interpretation may also explain why participants did not exploit the possibility of positioning their body strategically: the uncertainty inherent in the task may have induced late-correction strategies, which in turn may have led to discounting fine-grained preparatory positioning. In the second interpretation, people make average movements to potential targets but do so only sometimes, and/or other factors obscure or cancel out the intermediate strategy. People may choose different reaching strategies based on individual preferences and contextual factors. Various findings point toward the availability of multiple strategies rather than an obligatory integration of all potential targets into an intermediate trajectory. For instance, one study reported that participants sometimes appeared to initiate reaches directed to one stimulus, though they more often produced intermediate trajectories (Contemori & Carroll, 2025). Others have observed more switching than intermediate reaching when the motor cost for switching was low (Burk et al., 2014), again suggesting weighing of multiple decision aspects. Finally, participants produced stimulus-directed rather than intermediate movements when stimuli were so far apart that they could not be reached by late correction in the given time constraint (Wong & Haith, 2017), and when a non-intermediate trajectory avoided collision with an obstacle (Alhussein & Smith, 2021). Thus, in our task, uncertain reaches directed toward one stimulus may have reflected, after choosing for that trial, a late-correction strategy; intermediate reaches may, in contrast, have reflected integration of all target locations for that trial (Chapman et al., 2010;Gallivan et al., 2017;Selen et al., 2023). Alternatively, movement averaging may always take place, but other factors like biomechanical constraints (e.g., contralateral—or cross-body—reaches, more on this below) may erase behavioral evidence of this computation. Overall, we lean more strongly toward the second interpretation, which allows for strategic use of averaging depending on preference and context. Participants only propelling their hand (our suggested first interpretation) cannot explain the intermediate positioning of the hand’s starting position. Moreover, many individual trajectories of the uncertain conditions project clearly between those of the direct reaches to the left and right targets. These factors make it unlikely that participants exclusively used a propel-and-correct strategy. Our experiment did not disentangle which concrete aspects participants might integrate into their decisions. However, it seems likely that at least the precise position of the last step before the reach and biomechanical constraints that emerge between body position and target locations play a role. For instance, ipsilateral reaching requires an elbow extension, whereas cross-body reaches typically require elbow flexion, trunk rotation, and shoulder movement (cf.Gallivan & Chapman, 2014). Thus, participants may have prioritized the ipsilateral reach to the right target in the uncertain decision context because of the resulting lower motor cost. Moreover, participants may have perceived contralateral reaches as more effortful: longer movement duration is associated with higher perceived effort (Morel et al., 2017), and contralateral reaches typically have a longer duration (Carey et al., 1996). Others have argued that it is the transformation from visual to proprioceptive space that induces reach biases (Wang et al., 2026). Finally, the task context, such as pacing and time constraints, likely affects strategic choices. Thus, multiple factors probably shape each single reach in concert. In conclusion, people make intermediate reaches when faced with multiple potential target locations even when the decision landscape is expanded. This extends findings from highly constrained laboratory settings that isolate and standardize reaches to more naturalistic behaviors. However, our naturalistic extension of the paradigm revealed higher variability between participants and stimulus sets than implied by previous, highly constrained reaching-only tasks. This finding suggests that the higher complexity of the walk-to-reach task’s decision landscape prompted participants to use various decision strategies. Moreover, reaching was shaped by additional aspects such as scene characteristics and the spatial characteristics of the stimulus set. Intermediate reaching, therefore, appears to be strategically chosen rather than obligatory. Another strategy may have been to rely on late, visually guided correction of generic reach movements. However, intermediate pre-reach positioning of the body and hand argues against the propel-and-correct interpretation as a dominant or exclusive strategy participants applied throughout. In sum, these findings lead us to favor a nuanced interpretation: that intermediate reaches are sometimes deployed strategically among several possible approaches, explaining their absence in some contexts and trials. From a methodological viewpoint, the rich behavioral variability makes the walk-to-reach approach an excellent candidate paradigm for further exploration of movement decisions in dynamic, real-world environments. title: Sex-Dependent Effects of Creatine Hydrochloride on Neuroinflammation, Neuronal Survival, and Inhibitory Synaptic Remodeling Following Traumatic Brain Injury in Mice.
author: Zigmond, J. W.; Lamberty, B. G.; Simon, G. J.; Wood, J. M.; Elliott, N. M.; Miller, D. W.; Stauch, K. L.
text: Despite traumatic brain injury (TBI) being a leading cause of death and disability in the United States, there is currently no FDA-approved medication that can prevent, heal, or reverse brain damage caused by TBI. TBI is caused by primary and secondary brain damage resulting in loss of neurons, astrocytic gliosis, and microglial activation which culminate in complex neurological disorders. The goal of the current study was to investigate the neuroprotective potential for Creatine Hydrochloride (C-HCl) supplementation following TBI in wild-type mice. Four C-HCl supplementation paradigms were examined including both 7 day pre-injury and 14-day post-injury treatments consisting of the following: 1) water/water, 2) water/C-HCl (100 mg/kg), 3) C-HCl (100 mg/kg)/C-HCl (100 mg/kg), 4) C-HCl (100 mg/kg)/C-HCl (450 mg/kg). Following controlled cortical impact (CCI) injury at a parietal location, measures of tissue and cellular (neuronal and glial) damage were assessed at 14 days post-injury (dpi). At 14 dpi, there were no significant effects on gross anatomical cavitation, tissue loss, third ventricle expansion, or systemic fluid biomarkers with any treatment group, though female mice exhibited larger baseline lesion boundaries overall compared to male mice. However, microstructural evaluation revealed a profound and sex-dependent effect of C-HCl supplementation in the hippocampus with female mice showing reduced neuroinflammation and male mice displaying reduced neurodegeneration (Fluoro-Jade C staining of neurons) across the CA1 and dentate gyrus (DG) compared to placebo control. Furthermore, mice receiving C-HCl pre-injury followed by high-dose C-HCl post-injury demonstrated distinct remodeling of inhibitory circuits to restore network balance with males significantly modifying presynaptic machinery via vesicular GABA transport (VGAT puncta) in the DG, whereas females reinforced postsynaptic architectural framing through scaffolding elements (gephyrin puncta) in both the CA1 and DG. These results suggest C-HCl supplementation holds promise as a neuroprotective therapeutic strategy for TBI. Crucially, the molecular mechanisms utilized to achieve this brain cell homeostasis are radically distinct between the sexes, females benefit primarily via upstream glial stabilization, while males derive protection via direct downstream neuronal survival. These outcomes highlight a critical requirement for sex-stratified profiling in translational pipelines for neurometabolic interventions for TBI. Ultimately, these data indicate that C-HCl successfully counteracts chronic secondary injury cascades, mitigating neurodegeneration, dampening neuroinflammation, and remodeling inhibitory circuitry to prevent post-traumatic network hyperexcitability. Creatine (N-[aminoiminomethyl]-N-methyl glycine) is an amino acid-like compound that plays a central role in cellular energy metabolism1. Creatine and the creatine kinase/phosphocreatine system play an important role as reserved sources of energy in tissues with high and fluctuating energy requirements. The role of creatine in energy metabolism involves the transfer of N-phosphoryl groups from phosphorylcreatine to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) to regenerate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) through a reversible reaction catalyzed by phosphorylcreatine kinase. Creatine from either dietary or endogenous sources are distributed via peripheral circulation to tissues with approximately 95% of the total creatine pool stored in skeletal muscle, while the remaining 5% is distributed amongst other metabolically demanding organs, such as the brain, heart, and kidney. Historically, research on creatine has focused primarily on skeletal muscle; however, over the past decade there has been an increased appreciation for the potential value of creatine supplementation for supporting brain health and cognitive function1,2. There is growing evidence that creatine may be of value in the treatment of a number of neurological and psychiatric disorders. Traumatic brain injury (TBI), a leading cause of disability and death in the United States, induces both focal damage as well as more diffuse disruption in neural function3. The primary injury occurs due to the direct mechanical forces acting upon the brain tissue, while secondary injury evolved over time and results from the cellular and molecular processes initiated by the initial trauma, including cerebral edema, glial and neuronal dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, and metabolic alterations. Based on results of both animal and human studies2, creatine represents a promising nutritional supplement for increasing resilience to and treating TBI. Controlled cortical impact (CCI) is a commonly used and highly regarded model of brain trauma that uses a pneumatically or electromagnetically controlled piston to induce a reproducible and well-controlled injury4. Animal models of TBI are of immeasurable value to better understand outcomes of brain trauma and in testing potential therapeutic agents. While creatine treatment holds promising translational value for improving brain health, studies on creatine supplementation in the context of TBI remain limited. This study aims to fill this gap by evaluating the neuroprotective effects of Creatine Hydrochloride (C-HCl) supplementation when administered after or prior to and after TBI. Mice were divided into four treatment groups: 1) water for 7 days prior to and 14 days after CCI, 2) water for 7 days prior to then 100 mg/kg C-HCl for 14 days after CCI, 3) 100 mg/kg C-HCl for 7 days prior to then 100 mg/kg C-HCl for 14 days after CCI, 4) 100 mg/kg C-HCl for 7 days prior to then 450 mg/kg C-HCl for 14 days after CCI; with post-injury treatments starting 30 min after surgery completion. The impacts of C-HCl treatment on tissue damage, blood biomarkers, glial activation, neuron degeneration, and synapse loss were investigated. While neither male nor female mice showed changes in TBI-induced tissue damage when supplemented with C-HCl/ C-HCl (450), the number of degenerating neurons found in the hippocampus were significantly lower in C-HCl/C-HCl (450) treated male mice. Further, the numbers of synaptic puncta were significantly higher in the C-HCl/C-HCl (450) treated male and female mouse hippocampus. Reduced astrocytic gliosis and microglial activation were observed in the hippocampus of female mice treated with C-HCl/C-HCl (450) and while not significant in male mice similar trends were observed. These findings indicate that while C-HCl therapy fails to alter macroscopic tissue pathology, it drives targeted, sub-cellular neuroprotection and restores inhibitory networks within the injured hippocampus in a sex-dependent manner with females demonstrating reduced glial activation and males exhibiting neuronal survival. Male and female C57BL/6NCrl (from Charles River Laboratories) wild-type (WT) mice were randomly assigned to the four treatment groups. TBI surgeries were performed when the mice were 2 months of age. Mice were sacrificed at 14 days post-injury (dpi). Following surgery, mice were single-housed in a temperature-controlled environment with 12-hour light/dark cycle with free access to food and water at the Department of Comparative Medicine at the University of Nebraska Medical Center (UNMC). Experiments were approved and conducted according to the UNMC Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). C-HCl was obtained from Vireo Systems. The C-HCl was prepared fresh daily in sterile water and administered to the mice daily via oral gavage. The four treatment groups included: 1) water for 7 days prior to TBI and 14 days after TBI starting 30 min after surgery completion (water/water), 2) water for 7 days prior to TBI then 100 mg/kg C-HCl for 14 days after TBI starting 30 min after surgery completion (water/C-HCl), 3) 100 mg/kg C-HCl for 7 days prior to TBI then 100 mg/kg C-HCl for 14 days after TBI starting 30 min after surgery completion (C-HCl/C-HCl), 4) 100 mg/kg C-HCl for 7 days prior to TBI then 450 mg/kg C-HCl for 14 days after TBI starting 30 min after surgery completion (C-HCl/C-HCl (450)). Using the human equivalent dose calculations based on body surface area5, the mouse doses of 100 and 450 mg/kg would be equal to 8.13 and 36.59 mg/kg (animal dose in mg/kg divided by 12.3 equals human equivalent dose), which when using the reference body weight for a human (60 kg) equals 487.8 and 2,195.4 mg (or 0.487 and 2.1954 g). Two-month-old mice were anesthetized using 2.5% isoflurane through inhalation in an anesthesia induction box. Their heads were shaved and they were placed in a stereotaxic frame (RMD) where they were maintained on isoflurane delivered by a nose cone. A midline incision was made to expose the skull, and a 3.5 mm craniotomy was made using a trephine and Dremel centered at -2.5 mm bregma and 2.75 mm lateral to the midline over the left parietal cortex. Mice were subjected to CCI injury at a 0.5 mm depth, 3.5 m/s speed, and 200 ms dwell time. The 68099 II Precision Impactor Device (RWD) uses a computer controlled pneumatically driven piston to rapidly impact the brain. After injury, the incision was closed using wound clips and the mice were administered 1 mg/kg of buprenorphine ER (Epicur Pharma) by subcutaneous injection for pain and allowed to recover on a heating pad. Mice were then given appropriate C-HCl treatment or vehicle control (water) by oral gavage 30 min post-surgery and every subsequent 24 h for 14 days. Once the brains were gently dissected, prior to histology tissue processing, photographs of the whole dorsal brain were taken to analyze the injury area fraction. For analysis, ImageJ was used to outline an ROI around the injury, and its area was measured and normalized to the area of the contralateral hemisphere to obtain an injury area fraction. Brains were gently removed and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in 1x PBS for 24 h at 4°C. After fixation, brains were rinsed with 1x PBS three times for 10 min prior to cryoprotection using 30% sucrose in 1x PBS for 48 h at 4°C. After cryoprotection, the brains were rinsed with 1x PBS three times for 10 min prior to embedding in 3% agar in 1x PBS for tissue sectioning using a vibrating microtome (Leica). Coronal sections were placed on Super Frost Plus microscope slides and stored at -20°C until staining. 50 μm thick coronal sections were sent to the UNMC Tissue Core Facility for processing and staining with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) followed by imaging under a slide scanner (Leica Aperio CS2 brightfield) at 40x magnification power and analyzed using QuPath software. For analysis, an ROI annotation was drawn around the contralateral hemisphere, ipsilateral hemisphere, ipsilateral hippocampus, and third ventricle. The are for each structure was measured and normalized to the area of the contralateral hemisphere to obtain an area fraction. Coronal sections were stained as previously described by our group6. In brief, 50 μm thick coronal sections were stained with the following primary antibodies: GFAP (1:1000, Cat ab68428, Abcam), Iba1 (1:1000, Cat #234009, Synaptic Systems), PSD95 (1:500, Cat #124008, Synaptic Systems), VGLUT1 (1:500, Cat #135316, Synaptic Systems), Gephyrin (1:500, Cat #147318, Synaptic Systems), and VGAT (1:500, Cat #131008, Synaptic Systems). For secondary antibody conjugation, the following antibodies were used: Alexa Goat anti-Rabbit 568 (1:1000, Cat #A11011, Invitrogen), Alexa Goat anti-Chicken 647 (1:1000, Cat #A21449, Invitrogen), Alexa Goat anti-Guinea Pig 647 (1:1000, Cat #A21450, Invitrogen), and DAPI for nuclear counterstain. Coronal sections were stained with Fluoro-Jade C (Cat #NC0859611, Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, slides were prepared with sodium hydroxide, 70% ethanol, and potassium permanganate solutions. Fluoro Jade C stain was coupled with DAPI Nissl counterstain and incubated in a dark environment at room temperature for 10 minutes. After drying on a slide warmer (50-60℃) for 5 minutes, slides were submerged in xylenes, and DPX mounting media was used to place the coverslip. Stained slides were imaged at 40x-oil immersion using a Nikon A1R upright confocal microscope. Images were obtained at 1024 x 1024-pixel size with 561 and 640 nm lasers. Stained slides were imaged at 0.5 μm steps with 21-29 steps per z-stack. Data represented as a volcano plot ofn= 4-6 per treatment group. At 14 dpi, exogenous C-HCl treatment did not yield a macro-structural repair, showing no significant impact on gross lesion size, hemispheric tissue loss, or third ventricle expansion in either male or female mice. Concurrently, systemic fluid biomarkers of acute neuroaxonal degradation (NfL, t-Tau) and astrocytic damage (GFAP) remained statistically unaffected by the treatment. However, baseline TBI-induced lesion areas were significantly larger in female mice compared to male mice across all groups. This prominent sex-based divergence in baseline damage reflects established literature characterizing differential vulnerabilities to biomechanical forces and early pathophysiological cascades between male and female rodents7,8. The absence of treatment-induced gross anatomical shifts or changes in late-stage peripheral protein shedding suggests that the neuroprotective action of C-HCl operates downstream of macroscopic cavitation. This aligns with historical models demonstrating that neurometabolic interventions frequently rescue local cellular architecture and bioenergetic viability without fundamentally altering the primary, macro-scale mechanical lesion boundary9. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed a distinct, sex-specific anti-inflammatory effect localized predominantly within the hippocampal CA1 region of female mice. The higher dose C/C-HCl regimen significantly blunted microglial activation (Iba1 MFI) relative to water controls and reduced both astrocyte density and activation (GFAP % area and MFI) in female mice. Conversely, reactive gliosis in male mice remained unaltered by treatment at 14 dpi. These findings directly complement the growing understanding of creatine as a metabolic buffer capable of modulating energy-demanding inflammatory cascades. In the context of TBI, reactive astrocytes and microglia experience severe bioenergetic strain to maintain ion homeostasis and drive cytokine production. By stabilizing intracellular ATP pools, creatine appears to dampen this hyper-reactive state9. Crucially, the restriction of this anti-inflammatory effect to female CA1 regions highlights a metabolic or hormonal gatekeeping mechanism. This suggests that the capacity of C-HCl to suppress chronic gliosis is highly dependent on sex-stratified cellular environments or baseline neurochemical profiles10. In direct contrast to the glial results, microstructural neuroprotective effects of C-HCl were heavily skewed toward male mice. C/C-HCl (450) and W/C-HCl regimens significantly reduced the number of degenerating Fluoro-Jade C+ neurons within the male hippocampal CA1 and DG regions. Female mice showed no significant treatment shifts in neurodegeneration. This localized reduction in Fluoro-Jade C staining supports wide-ranging literature characterizing creatine as a classic neuroprotective agent capable of mitigating secondary cell death. The preservation of hippocampal neurons in males, but not females, underscores a complex inversion of target mechanisms between sexes. While females benefited via upstream glial stabilization, males derived downstream advantages through direct neuronal survival pathways, reinforcing the need for sex-stratified analysis in neurometabolic therapies. The localized preservation of hippocampal neurons in males validates long-standing preclinical literature identifying creatine as a classic neuroprotective countermeasure against secondary metabolic failure9. TBI routinely triggers an excitotoxic energy crisis characterized by mitochondrial depolarization and intracellular calcium overloads. Creatine supplementation mitigates this decay by maintaining mitochondrial membrane integrity and optimizing bioenergetics9. The paradoxical inversion of targets between the sexes, where females demonstrated upstream glial stabilization but males exhibited direct downstream neuronal survival underscores a complex, sex-dependent therapeutic mechanism that requires explicit stratification in translational TBI models. While sweeping changes in excitatory synaptic markers (VGLUT1 and PSD95 puncta) were largely absent, C-HCl treatment drove profound, targeted alterations in inhibitory synaptic machinery (VGAT and gephyrin). However, the molecular strategies deployed were distinct. Males demonstrated presynaptic modulation, marked by a localized increase in presynaptic GABAergic transport (VGAT+ puncta) within the hippocampal DG, alongside a simultaneous decrease in the parietal cortex under the high-dose C-HCl (450) regimen. Conversely, females exhibited structural postsynaptic modulation, driving significant increases in scaffolding elements (gephyrin+ puncta) in both the CA1 and DG regions. Post-traumatic circuitry is heavily defined by a breakdown of recurrent network inhibition, a pathological hallmark that directly precipitates post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) and cognitive deterioration11. These findings indicate that creatine aids in restoring network balance by selectively fortifying the GABAergic framework. Preclinical literature confirms that delayed or chronic creatine administration counteracts TBI-induced losses of GABAergic functional components12. The novelty of our current data lies in its mechanistic divergence: males primarily adjust the presynaptic vesicular supply lines (VGAT), whereas females reinforce the postsynaptic receptor-anchoring architecture (gephyrin)13. This implies that while the ultimate therapeutic goal (enhanced circuit inhibition) is uniform, the underlying molecular pathways affected by C-HCl treatment in the context of TBI are dictated by biological sex. The effects of creatine on cellular energy reserve, mitochondrial function and inflammation1,14,15supports its potential use in TBI. Indeed, studies examining creatine supplementation on TBI in pre-clinical animal models have reported improvements ranging from significant reductions in cortical damage to reductions in brain lactate levels following creatine administered in food or given as ip injection prior to injury9,16. In these studies, creatine monohydrate, was used prophylactically at relatively high doses (1% of the daily diet16or 3000 mg/kg ip injection9). An open label trial by Sakellaris and colleagues17administered a daily dose of creatine monohydrate (400 mg/kg or approximately 20 g per day) to adolescents with TBI and reported improvement in cognitive and behavioral measures. Such findings are in line with the 20-30 g daily doses of creatine monohydrate being used for neurodegenerative diseases15,18. While these studies suggest high dose creatine supplementation may provide prophylactic and treatment advantages for recovery from TBI, the high-volume loading phase and large doses required limit extended use and effectiveness. Creatine HCl, is a newer form of creatine with increased aqueous solubility and bioavailability compared to creatine monohydrate19. Both clinical case reports and clinical trials suggest creatine HCl dosing, especially for applications involving brain related outcomes, is significantly reduced compared to standard creatine monohydrate20. Given the effectiveness of creatine HCl, the present study examined creatine HCl supplementation in various pretreatment and post-treatment regimens at doses that are more clinically realistic. To put the current dosage regiments in context, using the FDA-based guidelines for determining human equivalent dose, the doses used in the present study ranging from 100 mg/kg to 450 mg/kg would represent approximately 0.5 g and 2 g daily human equivalent doses. The FDA guidelines are intentionally conservative estimates, thus using allometric dosing calculations accounting for both surface area and metabolic differences puts the estimated human dose equivalents at 1.5 g and 6 g21. While confirmational studies are required, the doses of creatine hydrochloride supplementation used in the current study represent a substantial reduction from previous studies using creatine monohydrate. The findings of the present study suggest C-HCl supplementation holds promise as a neuroprotective therapeutic strategy for TBI. In summary, this study demonstrates that while a 14-dpi regimen of exogenous C-HCl does not alter macro-structural lesion boundaries or systemic fluid biomarker profiles (NfL, t-Tau, GFAP), it exerts a potent, highly localized neuroprotective influence within the hippocampus. Crucially, this therapeutic window is governed by a profound biologically sex-dependent split in target pathways. Rather than operating uniformly across both sexes, the mechanism of action of C-HCl diverges into distinct cellular domains. Females derive primary benefit via an upstream glial stabilization cascade, marked by a robust reduction in reactive astrogliosis and microglial activation within the hippocampal CA1 region, accompanied by the structural reinforcement of postsynaptic inhibitory elements (gephyrin). Males bypass glial modification entirely, instead showing a direct downstream preservation of cellular survival pathways (reduced Fluoro-Jade C+ neuronal degeneration in the CA1/DG) alongside an optimization of presynaptic inhibitory machinery (VGAT). Ultimately, these data indicate that C-HCl successfully counteracts chronic secondary injury cascades, mitigating neurodegeneration, dampening neuroinflammation, and remodeling inhibitory circuitry to prevent post-traumatic network hyperexcitability. However, the molecular strategies deployed to achieve this functional homeostasis are entirely distinct between male and female mice. These findings underscore a critical translational insight: neurometabolic interventions for TBI are not one-size-fits-all, and preclinical therapeutic pipelines must explicitly stratify mechanistic targets by biological sex to maximize efficacy. Future studies aimed at determining the optimal dose of C-HCl for neuroprotection following TBI in male and female mice will be essential. To put the current dosage regiments in context, there are two different human equivalent approaches; (i) one uses the FDA-based guidelines for determining human equivalent dosing, and the doses used in the present study ranging from 100 mg/kg to 450 mg/kg would represent approximately 0.5 g and 2 g daily human equivalent doses. However, FDA guidelines are intentionally conservative estimates, thus (ii) using allometric dosing calculations accounting for both surface area and metabolic differences puts the second estimated human dose equivalents at 1.5 g and 6 g21. While confirmational studies are required, the doses of creatine hydrochloride supplementation used in the current study represent a substantial reduction from previous studies using creatine monohydrate. The findings of the present study suggest C-HCl supplementation holds promise as a neuroprotective therapeutic strategy for TBI. And while behavioral outcomes were not formally assessed in the present study, mice receiving creatine supplementation in general were more active post injury suggesting a more quantitative assessment of behaviors is also warranted. title: Neuro-Metabolic and Vascular Dysregulation are Functional Biomarkers of Acquired Brain Injury
author: Chong Chie, J. A. K. H.; Persohn, S. A.; Jullienne, A.; Yan, J.; Bright, M.; Obenaus, A.; Territo, P. R.
text: Emerging clinical and neuropathological evidence suggests a direct link between traumatic brain injury (TBI) and neurodegenerative diseases (ND), but the mechanisms by which TBI contributes to ND onset and progression remain unclear. To bridge this gap, the NINDS TBI-ADRD consortium developed a diagnostic framework to guide the design and evaluation of TBI-ADRD experiments using translational neuroimaging (DCE-MRI,18F-FDG-PET) and advanced image-processing pipelines. Neuro-metabolic and vascular dysregulation (MVD) and metabolic functional connectomics (MFC) were evaluated in 8-month C57BL/6J mice at 30- and 60-days post-injury (DPI). Both MVD and MFC revealed significant changes at 30- and 60-DPI that were sex- and injury side-dependent. Female mice showed greater regional MVD alterations, while MFC identified sex-dependent changes at 30-DPI that diminished by 60-DPI. These findings suggest that a single mid-life closed-head injury induces sexually dimorphic MVD and brain network remodeling, supporting the potential of MVD as a sensitive biomarker for improved clinical monitoring post-TBI. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a global health concern, affecting an estimated 50 to 60 million individuals annually. TBI results in long-term disabilities, including cognitive, emotional, and physical impairments, which impact both affected individuals and their caregivers.1,2The associated worldwide economic burden approaches hundreds of billions of US dollars each year.1–3Beyond its acute effects, this substantial burden raises important questions about whether TBI may accelerate or amplify downstream neurodegenerative processes.4–8One such process is Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and related dementias (RD) which affect over 55 million people worldwide and are characterized by progressive cognitive and memory decline, typically emerging later in life, and are a leading cause of disability and dependency among the older population.9 Dependent upon injury severity, TBI initiates a cascade of immediate changes in the brain, beginning within minutes to days after injury.10,11These changes include neuroinflammation,12,13which results in a cascade of cyto- and chemokine14release that reduces cerebral blood flow,15resulting in continued hypometabolism,16edema,17and blood-brain barrier leakage.13These effects may persist or worsen due to chronic neuroinflammation12and increased oxidative stress,18driving amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau tangles accumulation,19resulting in incomplete cerebrovascular recovery20and ongoing degeneration of both white and gray matter.21These pathological conditions alter the brain’s immune response,22exacerbate tissue damage,18and induce vascular dysfunction,23,24collectively impairing cognitive and neurological function,12,20,25as well as hindering proper cellular post-injury recovery.12Importantly, emerging studies reveal that TBI-induced outcomes are sexually-dimorphic and are influenced by endogenous brain recovery mechanisms.26–28For example, females may experience more pronounced cerebral blood flow deficits and delayed repair of vascular integrity compared to males.29 Emerging clinical and neuropathological evidence suggests an overlap between TBI and ADRD, proposing that TBI may accelerate AD-like pathological processes in certain individuals.4–7TBI disrupts neuro-metabolic and vascular homeostasis,16,30resulting in impaired cerebral perfusion,15,20,23blood-brain barrier dysfunction,13altered neurovascular coupling,31and persistent abnormalities in glucose and mitochondrial energy metabolism.16,23,32These abnormalities persist beyond the acute injury phase.16Such changes may facilitate chronic tissue injury,33promote Aβ and tau accumulation,34impair protein clearance,34and drive progressive neurodegeneration.4,33Similar neurometabolic and vascular dysregulation (MVD) is observed in ADRD,35–38supporting the idea that TBI may initiate or amplify pathophysiological pathways that lead to later-life neurodegeneration.4 Beyond MVD alterations, evidence suggests that TBI also disrupts brain neural connectivity and the organization of brain networks,39–42affecting both their structure and functions.41,43Disruptions in network organization,39hub integrity,44and inter-regional communication represent both adaptive and maladaptive response,41,42altering the efficiency of information processing and coordination across brain regions.39,40,42These network-level changes often accompany shifts in metabolic complexity and regional coupling,16,45suggesting that TBI affects distributed brain systems rather than isolated regions.16Similar network and metabolic alterations in ADRD further support the idea of shared pathophysiological mechanisms between TBI and neurodegeneration.6,34,46Despite these advances, a substantial gap remains in understanding how TBI contributes to the onset and progression of neurodegenerative diseases (ND), especially regarding the temporal evolution of MVD, disturbances in brain connectivity, and their roles as drivers of neurodegeneration. Through the NINDS PAR-23-218(“Development and Characterization of Experimental Models of post-TBI ADRD”), our labs sought to develop, validate, and standardize a preclinical closed-head injury (CHI) model, and establish the construct and face validity of this model by exploring the utility of longitudinal clinically relevant translatable imaging biomarkers to characterize post-TBI pathology for alignment to clinical ADRD endophenotypes. As a first step towards this goal, we characterized CHI-driven MVD, metabolic functional connectomics (MFC) changes, and alterations in region-set enrichment analysis (RSEA)47in middle-aged C57BL6/J mice using our novel imaging biomarker framework. Wehypothesizedthat TBI would induce sex-specific changes in MVD and MFC, resulting in evolving regional and temporal changes in MVD phenotypes, metabolic brain networks, and RSEA outcomes. Accordingly, we aim to provide a diagnostic framework to guide the design and evaluation of TBI-ADRD, thereby advancing insight into the shared and distinct mechanisms underlying TBI and neurodegeneration prior to conducting these experiments in models of ADRD. The brain regional MVD phenotypes were determined by projecting the z-scored mean values (relative to a reference) for cerebral perfusion (x-axis) and cerebral metabolism (y-axis) readouts in a 2D Cartesian coordinate system, per our published methods.36,48This approach yields four possible MVD phenotypes (Figure 1A): Type 1 Uncoupling (↑perfusion, ↓metabolism; T1U), Type 2 Uncoupling (↓perfusion, ↑metabolism; T2U), Prodromal Coupled (↑perfusion, ↑metabolism; PC), and Neuro-Metabolic-Vascular Failure (↓perfusion, ↓metabolism; NMVF). Then, using our MVD analysis framework (Figure S1),36,48we assessed regional metabolism and perfusion changes in the closed-head injury (CHI) model in midlife (8-months) C57BL/6J mice relative to Sham at 30-DPI and 60-DPI in each hemisphere (ipsilateral/contralateral; injured/uninjured) according to the study design (Figure 1B). (A)Conceptual 2D diagram in which the x-axis and y-axis represent the cerebral perfusion and cerebral metabolism, respectively. Each quadrant depicts one of four neuro-metabolic and vascular phenotypes, with conceptual illustrations of the corresponding metabolic and vascular/perfusion alterations.(B)Study workflow diagram, which describes the experimental timeline, procedures, sexes, and readouts used in this proof-of-principle study. Briefly, 8-month-old male and female mice (n=4-5/sex/treatment) received a single closed-head injury (CHI) or Sham (anesthesia only) over the left Primary (M1) and Secondary (M2) Motor cortexes, and behavior, perfusion-weighted MRI (PWI), and18F-FDG PET imaging were conducted at 30 and 60 days post-injury (DPI). MVD and metabolic connectomics analyses were conducted on the 30-DPI and 60-DPI datasets. At 30-DPI, the ipsilateral hemisphere (ILH) exhibited MVD in numerous key brain regions (e.g., Primary Motor Cortex (M1), Secondary Motor Cortex (M2), Retrosplenial Dysgranular Cortex (RSC)), which were directly impacted in CHI. For a complete list of brain regions, seeTable S1. In male ILH of CHI relative to Sham, most regions (10 of 20;Figure 2A) were in the PC phenotype, whereas in females, they were predominantly in T2U (12 of 20;Figure 2A). A similar pattern was observed in the contralateral hemispheres (CLH): most regions in males (13 of 19;Figure 2B) were PC, and most regions in females (15 of 19;Figure 2B) were T2U. The spatial locations of regional p-values that significantly changed were projected onto the Allen MRI Template for males (Figure 2C) and females (Figure 2D), showing that altered MVD occurs not only at the impact site and neighboring regions but also on the opposite hemisphere.
