Regional MFC analysis was performed using metabolic covariance matrices (Figures S3/S4) to evaluate network-level changes across the sixteen possible groups, defined by all combinations of sex (females/males), CHI/Sham status, hemisphere (ILH/CLH), and time points (30-/60-DPI). These matrices quantify the extent to which metabolic activity covaries across brain regions, reflecting coordinated inter-regional metabolic organization at the network level; higher covariance values indicate stronger metabolic coupling between regions, while lower values suggest reduced coordination.47,49 The analysis was performed by constructing regional MFC modules (module) using the metabolic covariance matrices and multi-resolution consensus clustering (MRCC),50a method for identifying communities across spatial scales and quantitatively determining a consensus partition.50In addition, matrix similarity was calculated using the Frobenius norm (FRO),51,52a matrix norm that can be used to measure the distance between two matrices by applying it to their difference, with smaller values indicating greater similarity and no upper-level bound.51,52 Metabolic covariance matrices (Figures S3/S4) are symmetric matrices in which each element reflects the pairwise correlation between brain regions, with diagonal elements corresponding to self-correlations. Black squares denote module identified using MRCC. Clinical and preclinical males start with more integrated networks (fewer modules) that degrade under ADRD pathophysiological conditions (more modules), whereas females follow the opposite trend (from fractured to integrated networks).38,47Analyzing these matrices reveals that, regardless of sex, the number of module varies across hemispheres and time points in CHI mice. In Sham mice, females exhibit consistent module counts across hemispheres at matched time points (e.g., ILH and CLH at 30-DPI), while males show hemispheric differences, although the relative pattern is preserved (e.g., CLH has more modules than ILH). Notably, module composition is not stable across conditions, and regions dynamically reassign between module. For instance, in male CHI mice at 30-DPI, M1 clusters with 12 regions (e.g., S1, S2, TeA) in ILH, but clusters with 14 regions (e.g., Entorhinal Cortex (ECT), Perirhinal Cortex (PRH), Caudate Putamen (CPu)) in CLH. Surprisingly, female CHI CLH at 30-DPI showed a single MFC module, suggesting a relatively homogeneous network organization with weak modular segregation. These findings suggest metabolic network reorganization driven by both injury and aging. The complexity of the results makes simultaneous comparison using the module across hemispheres, time points, and experimental conditions challenging. However, because these matrices are symmetric, they can be reordered to facilitate comparisons by defining one group as the reference and the other as the comparison group, per our previous work.47,49In this study, we combined two matrices such that the upper triangular matrix represents the metabolic covariance matrix of the comparison group, while the lower triangular matrix represents that of the reference group. Subsequently, the module of the reference group is applied. Then, three different comparisons are made: CHI relative to Sham (Figure 6), Sham relative to CHI (Figure S5), and ILH relative to CLH (Figure S6). This provides insight into changes in the interregional relationships associated with injury and aging. At the regional level, these findings indicate that the metabolic brain networks are reorganizing to compensate for, and recover connectivity towards, their pre-injury state, with females exhibiting earlier stabilization or partial recovery than males. However, these differences begin to diminish at 60-DPI. Collectively, whole-brain and regional analyses demonstrate a temporal, sex- and injury-location-dependent evolution in metabolic complexity. Notably, module #1 in females showed a marked increase in the learning category, accompanied by concurrent changes in motor, perception, and integration, suggesting a learning-related network reorganization alongside suppression of sensorimotor networks at 30-DPI. Male mice exhibit a pronounced early reduction in learning, perception, and sensory categories in the ILH at 30-DPI, which largely normalizes by 60-DPI relative to Sham. In contrast, females showed early hemisphere-specific increases in learning, perception, and integration categories, superimposed on reductions in sensorimotor categories, which also return toward Sham-like patterns by 60-DPI. Overall, CHI induces lateralized network restructuring, with more pronounced widespread downregulation in males, while females exhibit both metabolic upregulation and downregulation. This study evaluates the construct and face validity of our CHI model in middle-aged C57BL6/J mice and leverages our novel MVD and MFC analysis methods to assess regional phenotypes (Figure 2) in key brain regions on the ILH (i.e. S2, RSC, DLIVEnt, M1, M2, Cg, TeA). These regions showed accelerated MVD trajectories, as indicated by the size and location of the circles along the x-axis in the MMC (Figure 3). As expected, the ILH exhibits greater MVD compared to the CLH. Analysis of the MMC reveals sex-specific differences at 30-DPI, where males (Figure 3A-D) showed a greater number of regions in the PC phenotype, indicating severe dysfunction, while females (Figure 3E-H) had greater number regions in the T2U phenotype, and differences are present across both brain hemispheres. By 60-DPI, most regions in both sexes and brain hemispheres transition to the T1U phenotype, suggesting a capacity for MVD recovery toward a pre-injury state. The normal MVD sequence is T1U◊T2U◊PC◊NMVF, and has been shown to be initiated by acute neuroinflammation, that progresses to a chronic state, yielding the PC phenotype.36,48Overall, while sex influences the rate and pattern of recovery following TBI, these findings indicate that, regardless of sex and at the time of assessment, the brain demonstrates a substantial ability to partially recover MVD function over time. These findings are consistent with current research, which shows that TBI induces pronounced, region-specific MVD dysfunction in the hemisphere closest to the injury site, with a characteristic pattern of initial dysregulation followed by recovery.31,53,54From the sex-specific response perspective, recent studies report that males experience more severe early dysfunction55,56, while females exhibited a distinct recovery profile, potentially linked to hormone-mediated neuroprotection and differential inflammatory responses.55–58Given this, MVD may serve as both biomarker of TBI pathology and recovery, thus supporting its relevance for outcome assessments and individualized therapeutic strategies in both animal models and human patients.31,53 From the MFC perspective, our analysis revealed both sex- and hemisphere-dependent changes in network connectivity at whole-brain (Figures 4/5) and regional (Figures S3/S4/6) levels. Whole-brain analysis (Figures 4/5) supports these findings by revealing CHI changes, relative to sham, align with the network alterations observed in migration uncoupling charts (Figure 3) and in metabolic covariance matrices (Figure S3/S4). At a regional-level (Figures 6/S5/S6), male CHI animals generally exhibited more fractured networks at 30-DPI, as indicated by changes in the number of MRCC modules. By 60-DPI, these alterations begin to diminish as measured by FRO (Table S2), indicating a network recovery between time points. In contrast, females showed more integrated networks at 30-DPI, which became more fractured by 60-DPI. These results suggest that, following TBI, brain regions reorganize their network structures adaptively to mitigate injury effects and are consistent with patterns observed in mice and humans.40–42,44,45 Taken together, MVD and MFC observations support the hypothesis that the brain dynamically reorganizes its metabolic network architecture to compensate for cerebral perfusion and metabolic disruption caused by TBI, with patterns that differ by sex and injury location. Current TBI studies consistently demonstrate disruptions in brain network structure and function, particularly in the ILH regions,39,59–61as showed by alterations in clustering coefficients after injury, with recovery manifesting as normalization of these network metrics over time.61Importantly, these network alterations exhibit both sex- and hemisphere-dependence, supporting the growing consensus that post-TBI recovery mechanisms are influenced by biological sex and intervention strategies.59–61 Comparison of RSEA results indicates that our framework detected changes across multiple functional categories following TBI, when compared with Sham mice (Figure 7). Males exhibit widespread metabolic downregulation across functional categories on the injury side. By contrast, females show a mixture of both up- and down-regulated metabolic demands across categories. In this context, negative changes reflect a reduction in function, while positive changes indicate an increased metabolic energy demand to sustain functions. Temporal analysis shows that alterations observed at 30-DPI shift towards the Sham counterparts by 60-DPI, suggesting progressive brain recovery. These metabolic changes are likely associated with neuroinflammatory processes following TBI, which have been previously reported.12,13,16,27Our study supports these findings whereby TBI produces both sex- and region-specific changes in brain metabolism, with males exhibiting greater metabolic downregulation and heightened vulnerability to TBI-induced dysfunction compared to females.27,29,62–64Furthermore, the more pronounced early-stage energy dysfunction and downregulation in males is attributed to the more aggressive neuroinflammatory responses and increased neuronal death.27In contrast, in some experimental TBI models, females exhibit differential cerebrovascular responses26and reduced neuroinflammation65compared with males, an effect often attributed to hormonally mediated neuroprotection and differences in inflammatory signaling.26,65These findings, combined with current research,27,66suggest that males may be more susceptible to TBI-induced vascular and metabolic dysfunction than females at early time points, implying that females could possess a greater adaptive response to neuroinflammation. Analyses using different reference groups show similar patterns; Sham relative to CHI (Figure S7) shows that CHI-induced changes reduce overall network-level metabolic demand at early stages with partial recovery over time, while ILH relative to CLH (Figure S8) reveals a persistent reduction in the metabolic demand over the injury location. These data suggest that age, sex, genetics, and time of injury may be important factors in recovery and residual disease post-TBI and may impact future ND progression. There is emerging clinical and neuropathological overlap between TBI and ADRD, suggesting that TBI may accelerate individuals into AD-like pathology.4–7In ADRD, our understanding of disease mechanisms has advanced through the use of transgenic37,67–69and knock-in70mouse models that can reflect human phenotypes, including Aβ and tau deposition (key pathological hallmarks of AD),71chronic neuroinflammation,67increased oxidative stress,68and immune,72metabolic,73,74and vascular dysfunctions.37,69However, the 2025 ADRD Summit8highlighted a substantial gap in our understanding of the mechanisms by which TBI may act as a potential driver in the onset and progression of ADRD through gene-by-environment interactions. The MVD alterations observed in our study parallel those reported in AD mouse models bearingApolipoprotein E4 risk alleles, although these effects are predominantly observed in females.36Moreover, the MFC patterns identified in CHI mice are consistent with prior clinical and preclinical findings in ADRD reported by our lab and others,38,47,49in which male controls exhibit more integrated networks that fracture with disease onset and progression, while females begin with more fractured networks that become more integrated under pathological conditions.38,47,49Collectively, these converging findings highlight the need for strong collaboration between TBI and ADRD researchers to bridge the gap in understanding post-TBI pathology and its influence on onset and progression of ND. As with any research, it is important to acknowledge the limitations of this study. First, the study focused on the impact of a CHI delivered to a single hemisphere (left) and did not test whether injuries to the opposite hemisphere, different cortical locations, or repeated injuries would produce distinguishable effects. Second, behavioral testing was not performed, and all imaging data were acquired under resting conditions; consequently, there is limited insight into how these neuroimaging findings relate to behavioral outcomes or how the brain responds under conditions that require increased metabolic activity or vascular flow. Finally, because perfusion and metabolic images were acquired on different days, simultaneous assessment of both readouts was not possible, precluding a fully integrated evaluation of the temporal relationship between blood flow and metabolism. In summary, this study demonstrates that the data processing pipeline is a reproducible framework that produces a reliable and quantifiable CHI phenotype, establishing a foundation for diagnostic and monitoring in TBI research. The findings further suggest sex-dependent alterations in neurometabolic and vascular regulation, as well as in brain metabolic connectivity networks, following CHI, resulting in temporal changes in brain networks and functional alterations. Consequently, this framework provides a basis for evaluating the impact and interaction of TBI on other pathological conditions (e.g., ADRD, Parkinson’s disease) in both temporal and long-term perspectives. Obenaus moved to University of California Riverside after these data were collected).75Male and female C57BL/6J (B6) mice at 8-months-old were randomized by sex on each injury day. Mice were administered a single TBI over the left mid-brain using the closed-head injury (CHI) protocol.76,77Sham mice underwent the same procedure without the impact (N=4 CHI males, N=5 CHI females, N=4 sham males, N=5 sham females). Mice were then followed for 30- and 60-days post-injury (DPI) for metabolism and perfusion. Brain perfusion and cerebral blood flow (CBF) were captured using dynamic contrast enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) images were acquired as a temporal series of a T1-weighted gradient echo flow compensated (GEFC) images at 3.97 sec/image with the following image parameters: FA (15); TE (3.5ms); TR (61.7ms); 100 repetitions; 4 slices at the level of the dorsal hippocampus, 1mm slice thickness. A pre-contrast baseline of 1.5min was acquired and then mice were intravenously injected with Gadolinium (Dotarem, 0.1mmol/kg) and images were acquired for an additional 3.5min. CBF maps were computed using Jim software (XINAPSE, 9.0) where arterial input voxels automatically derived. All arterial input curves were assessed manually and then CBF maps were computed using a two-compartment model. Brain metabolism was evaluated using18F-FDG PET. All PET/CT imaging was performed on an Inveon PET/CT scanner (Siemens Medical Systems, Knoxville, TN). Awake, overnight-fasted (18 hours) mice (maintained in an enclosure at 25-27°C) were administered 3.9-4.6 MBq of18F-FDG intraperitoneally. Following injection, mice were returned to their cages at 25-27 °C with free access to water. Forty minutes post-injection, mice were anesthetized with 3% isoflurane, placed in the supine position in a mouse holder, and maintained with 3% isoflurane in the PET/CT scanner. Sequential CT and PET imaging of the mice were carried out in the same bed position. A 7.5-minute-long CT scan for attenuation correction and anatomical delineation of PET images was followed by a 30 min-long static PET scan. Upon completion of imaging, mice were returned to their home cages for recovery. PET data were reconstructed as 128×128×159 matrices with a trans-axial pixel of 0.776 mm and a slice thickness of 0.796 mm using the OSEM3D algorithm (two OSEM iterations, 18 MAP iterations). PET images were corrected for random coincidences, attenuation, and scatter according to the manufacturer’s instructions. All images were calibrated in units of Bq/cm3 by scanning a Ge-68 cylinder (6 cm diameter) with known activity. CT images were spatially transformed to align with the reconstructed PET images. CT projections were acquired with the detector-source assembly rotating over 360°, collecting 180 projections at 80 kV, 500 mA, and 23.46 μm pixel resolution. CT images were reconstructed using a Feldkamp reconstruction protocol and a Shepp-Logan filter with a cutoff at the Nyquist frequency and a binning factor of 2, resulting in an image matrix of 512×512×1008 and a voxel size of 0.052 mm3. The study workflow diagram (Figure 1B) outlines the experimental timelines, procedures, sexes, and readouts used. Briefly, 8-month-old male and female mice (n=4-5/sex/treatment) received a single CHI TBI (sTBI) over the left M1 and M2 cortex, MRI and PET imaging were conducted at 30- and 60-DPI. MVD, metabolic connectomics, and RSEA analyses methods were conducted on datasets from both time points. As described in our previous work,36imaging data (DCE-MRI,18F-FDG PET) were co-registered to the Paxinos-Franklin atlas,78which contains 40 bilateral regions over the region covered by the DCE-MRI images. MVD analyses were performed by extracting mean cerebral blood flow for each bilateral brain region from the registered DCE-MRI as a measure of regional perfusion and the registered18F-FDG PET as a surrogate of cerebral metabolism.79To minimize the dose effect, scanner variability, and brain uptake normalization, regional intensities values were ratioed to the corpus callosum.80Similarly, perfusion regional values were also ratioed to the corpus callosum to maintain the same reference region across both modalities. Subsequently, 30- and 60-DPI CHI values were converted to z-scores relative to Sham 30- and 60-DPI, respectively. Regional z-scored data were projected onto a 2D Cartesian plane, where the x-axis represents the z-scored perfusion and the y-axis representing the z-scored metabolism, as measured by their respective surrogate readouts. This mapping yielded four possible MVD phenotypes: Type 1 Uncoupling (↑ perfusion, ↓ metabolism; T1U), Type 2 Uncoupling (↓ perfusion, ↑ metabolism; T2U), Prodromal Coupled (↑ perfusion, ↑ metabolism; PC), and Neuro-Metabolic-Vascular Failure (↓ perfusion, ↓ metabolism; NMVF). Lastly, for improved MVD monitoring the Cartesian space regional data were transformed into MMC as described in our previous clinical work.48Graphical depiction of this process is shown inFigure S1. Metabolic functional connectomics (MFC) analysis was performed using the SUVR18F-FDG data, in which bilateral brain regions (56 total, 28 for each side) were ratioed relative to the whole brain, following established procedures.81SUVR values were analyzed using open-source packages including Brain Connectivity Toolbox (BCT), generalized Louvain modularity, hierarchical consensus clustering, and CovNet.49As previously described,47,49each of the eight possible groups (all possible combinations between CHI/Sham, ILH/CLH, and 30-/60-DPI) produced a covariance matrix of size 28-by-28 representing the similarity between regions in the18F-FDG readouts across all region pairs. In addition, the following network measures were computed for each covariance matrix: (1) network density, indicating the number of connections; (2) nodes degree, representing the number of connections per region; (3) positive and negative nodal strengths, defined as the sum of positive or negative covariance values for each region; and (4) clustering coefficient, quantifying the number of fully connected triangles around a node based on connection weight and sign. Modularity maximization was performed using multi-resolution consensus clustering (MRCC) to identify groups of nodes in a network from an intra-group connectivity perspective, as described in our previous work.47,49These modules were subsequently used to assess alterations in module connectivity within each group. Graphical depiction of this process is shown inFigures S2A/S2B. Region-set enrichment analysis (RSEA) is a technique developed in our lab to quantitatively detect brain functional changes by analyzing regional metabolic readout variations between experimental and reference groups.47This method works by weighting changes in each region (experimental group minus the reference group) and then associating these changes to functional-set enrichment categories (FSEC), which include: auditory, learning, motor, perception, sensory, integration, and visual domains. Using the modules identified by MRCC in the metabolic connectomics analysis, modular FSEC scores were generated for each experimental group relative to the reference group by summing the columns corresponding to the regions within each module. Graphical depiction of this process is shown inFigure S2C. Statistical analysis of at-risk regions was evaluated using Student’s t-test (p<0.05), without Bonferroni correction since regional independence was maintained (i.e. region “x” vs. region “x” between experimental stage and the reference stage),82,83where MVD phenotype was determined by the Cartesian location of glycolytic metabolism and perfusion z-scores per our previous works.36,48Significant regions were then projected onto Allen MRI Temple object maps to provide spatial localization, where the sign of the z-score was applied to the p-value to indicate directionality of change (i.e. 0<z increasing, z<0 decreasing). Whole-brain connectomics metrics significance testing between time points was determined via Student’s t-test with a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.05. Analysis was performed in MATLAB R2024a. JAKCC performed MVD, metabolic functional connectomics, and region-set enrichment analyses, and wrote the paper. SAP performed image processing, registration, and analysis on the images. AJ performed image processing of the MRI images and wrote sections of the paper. JY and MB performed the live phase for the TBI and imaging studies. AO and PRT designed the experiments, performed MVD and connectomics analysis, and wrote sections of the manuscript. All authors reviewed and approved the manuscript prior to publication. title: The Intermediate CA1 and CA3 Subfields of the Hippocampus Differentially Encode Social Recognition
author: Dykstra, B.; Lin, A.; Kim, P.; Sevinc, C.; Berman, G. J.; Murugan, M.
text: Social recognition requires linking information about others to the spatial contexts in which they are encountered, a computation thought to engage the hippocampus. Although this process depends on coordinated activity across the hippocampal network, it remains unclear how specific subfields differentially contribute to social recognition. Of particular interest are the intermediate CA1 (iCA1) and CA3 (iCA3) subfields, which have both been shown to be causally involved in social recognition. Historically, the dense feed-forward projections from CA3 to CA1 led to the view that these subfields form a hierarchical circuit, with CA1 primarily integrating and refining computations from CA3. However, recent causal manipulations of the iCA1 and iCA3 have revealed distinct and separable contributions to approach and avoidance behavior, suggesting functional specialization across the subfields. This functional divergence suggests that iCA1 and iCA3 may differentially encode social recognition information. To test this possibility, we performed one-photon calcium imaging in freely behaving mice to record endogenous activity from the iCA1 and iCA3 during a novel behavioral paradigm that disentangles social identity from spatial position. Notably, we found that iCA3 neurons more robustly discriminated between novel and familiar conspecifics, while iCA1 neurons more strongly encoded spatial position. These results identify the iCA3 as a key locus for social novelty encoding and suggest distinct contributions of the iCA1 and iCA3 to social recognition. Almost every social encounter an animal engages in begins with an assessment: am I interacting with someone I know or someone new? Recognizing familiar individuals allows animals to make informed behavioral decisions based on prior interactions with that individual. Equally important is the ability to detect novel conspecifics who may pose potential threats or present opportunities. In mice, the ability to discriminate between novel and familiar conspecifics is well established1, and depends on hippocampal circuitry2,3. The rodent hippocampus is composed of several subfields that are thought to differentially contribute to social recognition. Among these subfields, the CA2 has been the most intensively studied4–8. Lesioning or inactivating the CA2 disrupts rodents’ natural preference for investigating novel conspecifics over familiar conspecifics9,10. Furthermore, electrophysiological recordings in the CA2 have identified neurons that encode the identity of novel and familiar conspecifics11. However, recent evidence suggests that social recognition relies on a broader hippocampal network. In particular, the intermediate CA1 (iCA1) and CA3 (iCA3) have emerged as important contributors. Inhibiting the intermediate and ventral CA1 and CA3 regions disrupt social novelty preference, whereas inhibition of the dorsal CA1 and CA3 does not12,13. Additionally, Okuyama et al., 2016 and Tao et al, 2022 found that ventral CA1 neurons encode social recognition information, with a larger proportion of neurons responding to familiar conspecifics over novel conspecifics12,14. Yet no studies have directly recorded neuronal activity in the iCA3 during social behavior, leaving its contribution largely unknown. Given the strong monosynaptic projections from the iCA3 to the iCA115,16, understanding how these two subfields interact is critical for revealing how social recognition signals emerge and are transformed within hippocampal circuits. Furthermore, the iCA1 and iCA3 may implement distinct but complementary computations relevant to social recognition processing. Historically, the strong feed-forward projections from CA3 to CA1 led to the view that these subfields operate within a hierarchical circuit, encoding shared information at distinct representational levels17. While this hierarchical organization suggests complementary processing of related inputs, emerging evidence indicates that the subfields also make distinct behavioral contributions. Both regions send direct projections outside the hippocampus18–20, and recent causal manipulations of iCA1 and iCA3 projections to the lateral septum have been shown to differentially bias approach and avoidance behaviors21. Together, these findings suggest that, in addition to processing information at different levels of abstraction, iCA1 and iCA3 may also exhibit functional specialization. Whether this divergence extends to encoding social recognition information remains unknown. A major obstacle in addressing these questions is the strong spatial encoding observed in both the iCA1 and iCA322, potentially masking or modulating more subtle social signals. In the most widely used behavioral assay to study social recognition and memory, the social discrimination test (SDT), different conspecifics are presented at distinct spatial locations.12,23While the SDT has provided valuable insight into social recognition, the spatial constraints of the assay make it difficult to disentangle social from spatial encoding. This challenge is amplified when studying the hippocampus, which is thought to contextualize diverse forms of information, including social representations, into a spatial framework22,24. Thus, location of the conspecific can often serve as a proxy for social identity. These limitations highlight the need for new behavioral paradigms that preserve naturalistic social interactions while minimizing social–spatial confounds. Here, we used one-photon cellular-resolution calcium imaging to record the endogenous activity of iCA1 and iCA3 neurons in two separate cohorts of mice. Mice participated in both a standard SDT and a novel paradigm, the Linear Presentation Assay (LPA), which aims to disassociate social from spatial encoding. In the SDT, we found that social recognition representations in both the iCA1 and iCA3 subfields were conjunctively encoded with spatial information. In the LPA, an automated assay where multiple conspecifics are randomly presented at the same spatial location, we found that both iCA1 and iCA3 neurons carry purely social information, but that iCA3 neurons more distinctly discriminate between novel and familiar conspecifics relative to the iCA1. Longitudinal tracking further revealed that, unlike spatial representations, social novelty representations did not persist across days, suggesting that the iCA3 novel/familiar signals may support real-time social discrimination rather than a general signal of social novelty. These results identify the iCA3 as a key site for social novelty encoding and reveal a functional dissociation of roles between the iCA1 and iCA3. Together, they support a broader view of the hippocampus as a multiplexed system that segregates social information into distinct representations across subfields. To determine whether the iCA3 encodes social recognition information and how these representations compare to those in the iCA1, we performed one-photon cellular resolution calcium imaging in two separate cohorts of mice. We expressed the calcium indicator GCaMP6f in the intermediate hippocampus and implanted a gradient-index (GRIN) lens targeting either the iCA1 (n =15 male mice) or the iCA3 (n = 12 male mice;Fig. 1A). For each subfield, we used two different lens targeting strategies, straight lenses (iCA1 n = 5; iCA3 n = 1) and prism lenses (iCA1 n = 10; iCA3 n = 11;Suppl. Fig. 1D, E). Prism lenses were implanted posterior to the target region, enabling imaging from coronal planes (Fig. 1B;Suppl. Fig. 1B, C), and straight lenses were implanted dorsally to capture horizontal planes (Suppl. Fig. 1A). Because this approach produced distinct lens trajectories, it mitigates the likelihood of consistent off-target damage across animals. GRIN lens placement and viral expression were verified post hoc by histological analysis. In total, we recorded 1506 neurons from 15 mice in the iCA1 and 1017 neurons from 12 mice in the iCA3 (Fig. 1D). A)Schematic of viral injection of GCaMP (left) and GRIN lens implantation (right) targeting iCA1 (top panels) and iCA3 (bottom panels).B)Representative coronal sections showing imaging planes (left) and the corresponding fields of view (FOVs) from two example mice: iCA1 (top) and iCA3 (bottom). Anatomical sections were adapted from the Allen Brain Atlas.C)Reconstruction of imaging planes across all iCA1 and iCA3 mice.D)Average number of neurons collected per mouse in iCA1 (left) and iCA3 (right) across imaging sessions. Example calcium traces of individual neurons from representative animals are shown to the right of each pie chart.E)Schematic of the social discrimination test (SDT) behavioral assay used to assess novelty preference.F)(left) Mice preferentially investigated novel conspecifics over familiar conspecifics during the SDT in lens implanted mice and a no lens control cohort (lens implanted mice: paired-test (t(24) = 3.173, p = 0.004, n = 25; no lens: paired t-test t(25) = 5.674, p < 0.001, n = 26). (right) Lens implanted mice and no lens control mice did not differ in their discrimination score (t-test, t(49) = 0.398, p = 0.692). Throughout this manuscript, we refer to our recording site as the intermediate hippocampus to be consistent with anatomical and molecular boundaries that divide the rodent hippocampus along the dorsoventral axis25. However, the terms “intermediate”26–28and “ventral”12,29–31hippocampus are applied inconsistently across the literature, and studies using these terms often show substantial coordinate overlap. Given known functional gradients along the dorsoventral axis12,13, we have provided our stereotaxic coordinates (Methods), histological verification (Suppl. Fig. 1), and reconstructions of lens placement (Fig. 1C) to encourage comparisons with other studies that may use different naming conventions or anatomical boundaries. We confirmed that the lens-implanted imaging mice retained the ability to discriminate between novel and familiar conspecifics. Imaging mice were run on the Social Discrimination Test (SDT) in which mice freely investigated a novel and a familiar conspecific confined at opposite ends of a behavioral arena (Fig. 1E). Imaging cohorts spent significantly more time investigating a novel conspecific than a familiar conspecific, similar to a control cohort without implants (Fig. 1F; statistics reported in figure legend). We also conducted a free interaction test in which imaging mice were placed into a cylindrical arena with either a novel or a familiar conspecific (Suppl. Fig. 2A). This assay captures naturalistic social interactions beyond the structured choices measured during more constrained tests. Behavioral recordings were annotated using a supervised SimBA network32trained to detect social investigation (Suppl. Fig. 2B, C). In this assay, imaging mice showed a significant preference for investigating the novel mouse over the familiar mouse (Suppl. Fig. 2D; statistics reported in figure legend), matching the behavior of a control cohort lacking implants. Together, these findings demonstrate that imaging mice retained the ability to discriminate between novel and familiar individuals, indicating that the surgical procedures and implants did not compromise their ability to preferentially investigate novel over familiar conspecifics. Next, we recorded neural activity from the iCA1 and iCA3 while imaging mice investigated two conspecifics confined to cages placed in opposite corners of a large SDT behavioral arena (70 × 70 cm). The large SDT arena was chosen to account for the larger place fields sizes in more ventral portions of the hippocampus33,34, reducing potential overlap in place fields centered on either corner. Additionally, in this arena, it took several seconds for the imaging mouse to run from one conspecific to the other, thereby reducing the chance that neural activity from one interaction would carry over into the next (see Movie 1). The imaging mice were allowed to explore the SDT arena in two different behavioral conditions to probe different aspects of social encoding (Fig. 2A). In the first condition, we recorded activity while mice investigated two novel conspecifics to determine whether iCA1 and iCA3 neurons encode the identity of individual mice. In the second condition, we recorded activity while the imaging mice investigated one novel and one familiar conspecific (a same-sex cagemate of the imaging mouse) to determine if neurons encode social novelty. Because the CA1 and CA3 regions of the hippocampus encode spatial information22, we swapped the positions of the conspecifics midway through a 40-minute behavioral recording to dissociate social and spatial information (Fig. 2B). A)Timeline of behavioral experiments in the SDT assay.B)Schematic of the SDT showing the placement of conspecifics before and after the swap.C)Trial-by-trial responses of an example neuron during investigation of novel and familiar conspecifics in two distinct spatial locations. Trials organized in ascending order of time spent in the social zone in each condition. Boxes are color coded by the average response across trials with dark red representing high activity and white representing low activity. Below, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and corresponding area under the curve (AUC) for spatial (left) and social (right) discriminability of the example neuron shown above, computed by comparing the cumulative distribution of neural activity across conditions (see Methods). This example neuron is spatially modulated but not socially modulated.D)Example neuron that is socially modulated and not spatially modulated.E)An example social–spatial neuron. This neuron preferentially fires in the bottom left but only in the presence of the familiar conspecific.F)Proportion of iCA1 neurons that display significant social– spatial preferences, neurons that only display a significant social preference and neurons that only display a significant spatial preference. Neural preferences for the 2-novel session are shown on the left and neural preferences in the novel-familiar conspecific session are shown on the right. In both conditions, there is a significantly larger proportion of spatial than social neurons (2-novel: z = 12.857, p < 0.001; novel–familiar: z = 13.876, p < 0.001) and a significantly larger proportion of social–spatial neurons than social neurons (2-novel: z = 16.523, p < 0.001; novel– familiar: z = 16.770, p < 0.001).G), Same as (F), but for the iCA3. In both conditions there is a significant difference in the proportion of social and spatial neurons (2-novel: z = 4.499, p < 0.001; novel–familiar: z = 4.128, p < 0.001) and there is a significantly larger proportion of social–spatial neurons than social neurons (2-novel: z = 9.318, p < 0.001; novel–familiar: z = 9.178, p < 0.001).H)SVM decoding accuracy in the iCA1 (blue), iCA3 (pink) and shuffled traces (gray) when decoding conspecific identity from population neural data. Each point represents the average decoding accuracy of one mouse. Decoding accuracy was significantly above chance in both the two-novel condition (iCA1: Δ = 5.87%, p < 0.001, d = 4.07; iCA3: Δ = 7.69%, p < 0.001, d = 4.68) and the novel/familiar condition (iCA1: Δ = 3.67%, p < 0.001, d = 3.45; iCA3: Δ = 10.44%, p < 0.001, d = 7.22), with iCA3 decoding accuracy significantly higher than iCA1 in the novel/familiar condition, but not the two-novel condition (2-novel: Δ = 1.40%, p = 0.67, d = 0.65; novel/familiar: Δ = 6.72%, p = 0.009, d = 3.85).(I)Same as (H), but decoding whether the imaging mouse was in the bottom-left vs. top-right corner of the arena. Decoding accuracy was significantly above chance in both the two-novel condition (iCA1: Δ = 26.93%, p < 0.001, d = 15.56; iCA3: Δ = 15.79%, p < 0.001, d = 11.28) and the novel/familiar condition (iCA1: Δ = 28.82%, p < 0.001, d = 22.64; iCA3: Δ = 19.57%, p < 0.001, d = 9.93), with decoding accuracy significantly higher in the iCA1 than the iCA3 in both conditions (2-novel: Δ = 11.37%, p < 0.001, d = 5.13; novel/familiar: Δ = 10.03%, p = 0.002, d = 4.35).(J)Same as (H,I), using a multi-class SVM decoder to decode all four social-spatial conditions. Decoding accuracy was significantly above chance in both the two-novel condition (iCA1: Δ = 56.8%, p < 0.001, d = 28.09; iCA3: Δ = 55.5%, p < 0.001, d = 33.2) and the novel/familiar condition (iCA1: Δ = 56.03%, p < 0.001, d = 26.18; iCA3: Δ = 56.83%, p < 0.001, d = 29.23), with no significant difference in decoding accuracy between subfields (2-novel: Δ = 0.63%, p = 0.90, d = 0.23; novel/familiar: Δ = 0.63%, p = 0.91, d = 0.22). Next, we classified neurons as spatially selective, socially selective, or selective for a specific social–spatial combination using a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis (Fig. 2C-E). In both the iCA1 and iCA3, the proportion of spatially selective neurons was significantly greater than the proportion of socially selective neurons in both the two-novel conspecific condition and the novel/familiar condition (Fig. 2F,G; statistics reported in figure legend). Similarly, the proportion of conjunctive social–spatial neurons was significantly greater than the proportion of socially selective neurons in both conditions (Fig. 2F,G). Together, these findings indicate that iCA1 and iCA3 neurons were more likely to represent purely spatial information or a conjunction of social–spatial information, rather than purely social responses in the SDT. In addition to the pooled analysis across mice (Fig. 2F,G), these trends held true when examining the proportions of social, spatial, and social–spatial neurons across individual mice (Suppl. Fig. 3A). Furthermore, distributions of AUC values revealed a range of stimulus response strengths within each category (Suppl. Fig. 3B, C). In both the iCA1 and iCA3, neurons with purely social preferences were evenly distributed between those preferring each conspecific (Suppl. Fig. 3D). We found iCA1 and iCA3 neurons with social–spatial selectivity for all four social–spatial combinations, with a larger fraction preferring conditions before the conspecific swap (Suppl. Fig. 3E). Next, we used support vector machines (SVMs) to decode conspecific identity from population activity in the iCA1 and iCA3 (Suppl. Fig. 4). In both the two novel conspecific and novel/familiar conspecific conditions, both the iCA1 and iCA3 could decode conspecifics above chance levels (Fig. 2H). In the two novel conspecific condition, there was no significant difference between iCA1 and iCA3 decoding. However, in the novel/familiar condition, the iCA3 was able to decode conspecifics with significantly higher decoding accuracy compared to the iCA1 (Fig. 2H). We next tested whether spatial location could be accurately decoded from the same neural populations. SVMs significantly decoded whether the imaging mouse was located in the top right or bottom left corner in both conditions in both the iCA1 and iCA3, with the iCA1 having significantly higher decoding accuracy than the iCA3 in both conditions (Fig. 2I). Finally, we used multi-class SVMs to decode all four social–spatial combinations simultaneously. In both the two-novel and novel-familiar conditions, decoding was significantly above chance in both the iCA1 and the iCA3 (Fig. 2J). We next compared decoding accuracy across social, spatial, and social–spatial decoders by normalizing the accuracy relative to chance levels to allow for direct comparisons (Suppl. Fig. 5A). Across both iCA1 and iCA3 cohorts, spatial decoding was significantly higher than social decoding and social–spatial decoding was significantly higher than social decoding and spatial decoding (Suppl. Fig. 5A). To assess how decoding performance scaled with population size, we repeated each decoding analysis using increasing subsets of randomly sampled neurons within each mouse. For social, spatial, and social–spatial decoding, accuracy increased with neuron count and approached saturation (Suppl. Fig. 5B, C), implying that the sampled populations were large enough to capture most of the decodable information in both subfields. Given that many neurons preferentially fired for specific social–spatial combinations, we next asked whether social and spatial representations at the population level remained stable across the entire session or whether they were similarly influenced by the conspecific swap. By comparing classifier confidence (distance to the decision boundary) and accuracy across time bins (Suppl. Fig. 5D, F), we found no consistent differences between pre-swap and post-swap decoding for either social or spatial classifiers (Suppl. Fig. 5E, G), suggesting that decoding performance was stable across an imaging session. Together, these results demonstrate that in the SDT, in both the iCA1 and iCA3, social recognition representations are heavily influenced by spatial information. To better dissociate social and spatial representations, we next developed a novel behavioral assay designed to more directly test encoding of social identity independent of spatial location. To investigate social recognition while rigorously controlling for spatial coding, we developed a novel behavioral assay: the Linear Presentation Assay (LPA). In this paradigm, an imaging mouse interacts with two conspecifics that are presented at the same spatial location. The assay consists of a long, narrow behavioral arena that the imaging mouse can freely explore. At one end of the arena is a barred interaction window. The stimulus cage, positioned behind the interaction window, sits on a programmable and automated conveyor belt that allows for multiple stimulus cages to be sequentially presented at the same spatial location (see Movie 2 andFig. 3A). A)Schematic of the linear presentation assay (LPA). The imaging mouse (gray) can freely explore the linear arena. On the right end of the linear arena there is a barred window through which the imaging mouse can interact with a stimulus cage presented. An automated conveyor belt allows us to present multiple stimulus cages at the same spatial location.B)Schematic depicting the imaging mouse entering the trigger zone to initiate a new trial and trigger presentation of a new stimulus cage.C)Example time series of the imaging mouse’s position in the arena during a 30-min session on the LPA. Below, the corresponding time series of stimulus cage presented at the window is shown. The dashed line indicates instances when the imaging mouse triggers a new trial to begin.D)Timeline of behavioral recordings on the LPA. The colored boxes indicate the identity of the stimuli being presented for a given behavioral session. A horizontal black line connecting two colored boxes indicates that the same individual was reused as a social target across subsequent sessions.E)The total number of trials completed on the LPA in both iCA1 and iCA3 across behavioral conditions.F)Total time spent by the imaging mice in the interaction zone oriented toward the conspecific during 30-min sessions.G)The length of time that the imaging mouse investigates each stimulus cage on the first presentation of each cage (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: 2 empty cages: W = 176, n = 29, p = 0.370, effect size r = 0.191; 2 novel mice: W = 343, n = 38, p = 0.898, effect size r = 0.024; novel/familiar conspecifics: W = 235, n = 40, p = 0.0187, effect size r = 0.427; 2 familiar mice: W = 137, n = 25, p = 0.508, effect size r = 0.157; Novel/familiar food: W = 168, n = 30, p = 0.185, effect size r = 0.277) We track the imaging mouse’s position in real time, and the belt automatically advances to the next cage when the mouse crosses to the side of the arena opposite of the window (Fig. 3B,C). Although the same stimulus cage can be presented multiple times in a row, an anti-biasing algorithm discourages long repeats of the same cage. This design enforces a pseudo-trial structure in which distinct social stimuli are presented repeatedly and unpredictably at a fixed location. By dissociating social identity from space, the LPA offers a powerful framework for probing hippocampal representations of social recognition independent of spatial confounds. We ran several experimental conditions using the LPA (Fig. 3D). After habituating the imaging mice to the assay for two days, we first recorded neural activity while the mice investigated two empty stimulus cages. This condition served as a control to test whether mice could discriminate subtle manufacturing differences between the stimulus cages. Mice were then run through the assay in a series of different configurations, including presentations of: (i) two novel conspecifics, (ii) one novel and one familiar conspecific, (iii) two familiar conspecifics, and (iv) novel (Froot Loops cereal) and familiar food (rodent chow). In the food condition, mice could not access the food directly but could smell it through the interaction window. Each LPA session lasted for 30 minutes, and the total number of trials per session varied (Fig. 3E). We excluded any session with fewer than four trials with each stimulus to ensure reliable statistical comparisons. On average, the imaging mice spent the majority of each session in the interaction zone, oriented towards the stimulus (Fig. 3F). Each session began with a fixed presentation of one stimulus cage followed by the other, after which stimulus cages were presented in a randomized order. Periods when the imaging mouse investigated each cage were hand-scored for bouts of active investigation, defined as periods of visible sniffing and/or whisking. In the novel/familiar conspecific condition, during the first two trials, the imaging mice preferentially investigated the novel conspecific longer than the familiar conspecific (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: W = 235, n = 40, p = 0.0187, effect size r = 0.427). The imaging mice did not display a significant behavioral preference in any other conditions (Fig. 3G; full statistics reported in figure legend). We next determined that both the iCA1 and iCA3 neurons exhibit strong spatial encoding in the LPA (Suppl. Fig. 6A-D). Across all experimental conditions, the iCA1 consistently contained a higher proportion of place cells than the iCA3 (Suppl. Fig. 6E). At the population level, we assessed whether neural activity could decode the mouse’s spatial location. SVM classifiers decoded the mouse’s location from both iCA1 and iCA3 activity at well above chance levels in every condition. Notably, spatial decoding accuracy was significantly higher in the iCA1 than in the iCA3 across most conditions (Suppl. Fig. 6F, G). Next, we used an ROC analysis to identify neurons that preferentially fired during investigation of one conspecific over another (Fig. 4A,B). In the two empty cages condition, 5.2% of iCA1 neurons and 6.3% of iCA3 neurons displayed a significant preference, consistent with the expected false-positive rate given our statistical threshold (Fig. 4C). Similarly low proportions of neurons (7-9%;Fig. 4C) displayed a preference in the two-novel and two-familiar conspecific conditions in both regions. In contrast, in the novel-familiar conspecific condition (Day 5 inFig. 3D), a significantly greater proportion of iCA3 neurons (16.4%;Fig. 4C) displayed a preference compared to iCA1 neurons (8.6%, proportion z-test; z = 5.70, p < 0.001). Lastly, in the novel-familiar food condition, a larger subset of neurons showed preferences in both regions (14.9% in iCA1 and 12.4% in iCA3;Fig. 4C). Together, these findings suggest that while spatial coding in the iCA1 and iCA3 is stable both at the individual-neuron and population level, social novelty coding is comparatively more labile. Social interactions require integrating information about who an animal encounters with where the encounter occurs, a computation thought to engage the intermediate hippocampus. Here, we provide the first recordings of endogenous activity in the iCA3 during social behavior and directly compare its function to the iCA1. Both iCA1 and iCA3 activity could discriminate between two novel conspecifics, but only modestly above chance, suggesting that both subfields carried some information about conspecific identity. However, iCA3 activity discriminated between novel and familiar conspecifics more clearly than the iCA1 and more clearly than it discriminated two novel conspecifics revealing a specific role in encoding social novelty. Decoders trained on one session did not generalize to a second session in which the novel conspecific was replaced, suggesting that the iCA3 supports real-time discrimination of a novel from familiar conspecifics rather than a general signal of social novelty. Together, these findings identify the iCA3 as a key site of social novelty encoding and establish a functional dissociation between the iCA1 and iCA3 in processing social recognition. These findings were made possible by a novel behavioral assay, the LPA, which controls for spatial position to isolate social representations. The CA2 has been the hippocampal subfield most strongly implicated in social recognition, with lesion, inactivation, and recording experiments establishing the subfield as a critical hub for social computations9–11. The CA2 receives input from the CA3 and strongly projects to the CA19,32. This connectivity positions CA2 as a potential conduit for transmitting social information through the hippocampal circuit. Our results reveal that social encoding extends beyond the CA2, engaging a broader network within the intermediate hippocampus. To test how social recognition signals are embedded within broader hippocampal networks, we examined coding in the iCA1 and iCA3. In the SDT, we could decode spatial position more accurately than social recognition information in both the iCA1 and iCA3 (Suppl. Fig. 5A). Similar experiments recording from the CA2 have reliably decoded social recognition information, with spatial decoding accuracy varying across studies8,11. Furthermore, in our LPA paradigm, both iCA1 and iCA3 place cells mapped onto stable spatial locations across days (Fig. 5F,I), while CA2 place cells have been reported to rapidly remap across days36. These findings suggest a functional division of labor within the hippocampus. In the intermediate hippocampus, sparse social recognition signals are embedded within stable spatial frameworks, while in the CA2, stronger social representations are maintained in the context of more flexible spatial coding. One potential mechanistic basis for this divergence lies in differences in synaptic plasticity across these regions. Both the CA1 and CA3 exhibit robust long-term potentiation37–39whereas CA2 neurons are relatively resistant to conventional LTP induction40,41. Nonetheless, neuromodulatory inputs, such as oxytocin or vasopressin, can transiently enable plasticity in CA2 under certain conditions42. Reduced plasticity in the CA2 may favor the stability of abstract, identity-based social representations43,44, while greater plasticity in the CA1 and CA3 may support the integration of dynamic social information and spatially anchored representations. In the SDT, a larger fraction of iCA1 and iCA3 neurons encoded conjunctive social–spatial information than social information alone (Fig. 2F,G). These findings underscore the intermediate hippocampus’s inherent bias towards contextual representations, where diverse forms of information are bound into relational codes22. In addition, population-level decoding revealed that joint social–spatial representations in the iCA1 and iCA3 were better represented than either component alone (Suppl. Fig. 5A), suggesting that the integration of these factors might be an active computational process rather than a random overlap between responses of individual neurons. This type of conjunctive coding might enable the hippocampus to link individuals to where they were encountered, facilitating the flexible retrieval of context-appropriate information. Both the iCA1 and iCA3 project outside of the hippocampus18,19,45, raising the possibility that social–spatial codes are read and interpreted by downstream regions. Both subfields send strong projections to the lateral septum20, and we previously demonstrated that inhibiting ventral hippocampus–lateral septum neurons disrupts social novelty preference46. The iCA1 also projects to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)19, and CA1–mPFC projections are likewise necessary for social novelty preference47. Notably, the mPFC itself contains neurons with conjunctive social–spatial selectivity48, similar to those observed in the iCA1 and iCA3, suggesting that the mPFC may inherit contextualized representations from the hippocampus. To disentangle how the hippocampus represents social versus spatial information, we developed the LPA in which conspecifics are presented unpredictably and repeatedly at a fixed location. We show that mice are consistently motivated to investigate both social and non-social stimuli in this assay. Notably, we also found that both the iCA1 and iCA3 failed to robustly discriminate between two empty cages (Fig. 4D,E), suggesting that the presence of a meaningful stimulus is necessary to drive hippocampal representations. While the LPA provides a controlled environment for probing hippocampal encoding, it also has several limitations. Because the presentation of targets is externally controlled, experimental mice do not have the opportunity to choose what conspecific to approach and investigate. This limits the ability to assess whether a brain region encodes motivated social approach towards a specific individual. Nonetheless, the LPA’s ability to isolate social identity encoding independent of spatial encoding makes it a powerful complement to previous paradigms for disentangling social and spatial information. This study contributes to a growing body of literature that social recognition representations in the CA1 are topographically organized along the dorsal-ventral (DV) axis25,49,50. In rodents, inhibiting the dorsal CA1 (dCA1) does not disrupt social novelty preference in mice12, and endogenous recordings of the dCA1 have revealed less social modulation and social recognition encoding relative to more ventral CA1 neurons12,51. In contrast, recordings from the dCA1 in bats have revealed socially modulated place cells and neurons that encode both sex and identity52–54, suggesting that social representations may be more prominent in the dorsal hippocampus of some species. In this study, when controlling for spatial confounds, we find that few neurons in the intermediate CA1 display a social preference (Fig. 4C), and population-level decoders can decode conspecifics just above chance levels. This finding largely mirrors those of Okuyuma et al, 2016, who recorded from a similar location in the CA1 and also found that a small number of neurons display a social preference12. However, recordings from more ventral portions of the CA1 have revealed strong social modulation and strong sex, strain and identity encoding51,55. Together, these results suggest that there exists a functional gradient along the DV axis of the CA1, with the intermediate portion encoding sparse social recognition representations. Interestingly, we found that the iCA1 discriminated more robustly between novel and familiar food than between novel and familiar conspecifics. This result aligns with the well-established role of the CA1 in foraging and food-related memory56–58and suggests that iCA1 may engage distinct coding strategies for social versus non-social forms of novelty. Future work directly comparing how hippocampal subfields represent novelty across social and non-social stimuli, including food, would help clarify whether these differences reflect stimulus-specific coding strategies. Far less is known about how the CA3 contributes to social recognition. In the dorsal CA3 (dCA3), there are conflicting reports regarding its necessity for social novelty preference. Chiang et al., 2018 reported that inhibiting the dCA3 does not disrupt social novelty preference13whereas Liu et al., 2022 found that optogenetic inhibition of dCA3-lateral septum neurons reduced social novelty preference59. In the intermediate/ventral CA3, Chiang et al., 2018 demonstrated that this region is necessary for social encoding but not for social recall. More recently, Li et al., 2025 expanded on this finding by showing that chemogenetic silencing basolateral amygdala inputs to intermediate/ventral CA3 also disrupts social novelty preference60. Building on these results, our study fills an important gap by providing the first recordings of endogenous iCA3 activity during social interactions. We provide evidence that the iCA3 contains robust and separable representations of novel and familiar conspecifics (Fig. 4D,E). In this study, we found that both iCA1 and iCA3 share several functional properties. Each region contained conjunctive social–spatial representations (Fig. 2J), abundant place cells in both the SDT and LPA behavioral assays (Fig. 2F,G;Suppl. Fig. 6E), and spatial codes that were stable across sessions (Fig. 5F,G, I,J). Despite these similarities, the two regions diverged in how they represented social novelty. In the iCA1, social signals were sparse, and decoding performance was similar for discriminating between two novel conspecifics and between novel-familiar pairs. In contrast, the iCA3 showed significantly stronger separation for novel-familiar pairs than for two novel conspecifics (Suppl. Fig. 7E). One possible explanation for this difference relates to the underlying circuit architecture. The CA3 is often described as an autoassociative network, which is classically associated with pattern completion, the retrieval of a stored representation from partial or degraded input61. Such a mechanism could produce more categorical, attractor-like representations of familiarity than the more distributed coding observed in the iCA1. Consistent with this, we found that the iCA3 discriminated between two familiar cagemates with significantly higher decoding accuracy than the iCA1 (Fig. 4D). However, the interpretation of this finding is complicated by the fact that the two social targets were co-housed with the imaging mouse for an uneven length of time, raising the possibility that this result partly reflects residual novel/familiar discrimination. An interesting future direction would be to systematically explore how co-housing duration or behavioral dynamics between the imaging mouse and each conspecific affect the strength of identity-specific recognition representations. In both the iCA1 and iCA3, we found that a subset of neurons displayed significant place fields across two behavioral sessions (Fig. 5E,H), and those neurons exhibited highly stable spatial representations (Fig. 5F,I), consistent with longitudinal imaging recordings from the dCA162. Such stability is expected from classical place cell studies63and further indicates that our cross-session approach reliably captured meaningful neural dynamics. In contrast, social representations remapped across sessions (Fig. 5K,M). We suggest hippocampal social representations may support real-time social discrimination during the social encounter, rather than serving as a long-term storage site of social memory. This interpretation echoes the long-standing view that non-spatial hippocampal codes are more labile than spatial ones22. One prominent counterexample to this interpretation is Okuyama et al. (2016), who reported that familiar-preferring neurons in the CA1 maintained a small but significant preference for familiar conspecifics over 24 hours. We find that after 48 hours, social representations remap almost completely, which may reflect a continuation of Okuyama’s findings with social novel/familiar representations continuing to drift over a longer timescale. Another notable exception to this pattern comes from recent work showing that ventral CA1 neurons can maintain highly stable representations of female odorants in male mice64. This discrepancy may reflect differences in social motivation, as our experiments used only same-sex conspecifics, which may be less behaviorally salient than opposite-sex conspecifics.
