title: Task-evoked flexibility of intrinsic neural timescales is hierarchically organized, behaviorally relevant, and refined across two developmental stages
author: Parkes, L.; Sydnor, V. J.; Howell, A.; France, J. M.; Westbrook, A.; Larsen, B.
text: Cortical regions integrate temporal information over different timescales at rest, ranging from fast in sensorimotor regions to slow in the association cortex. Here, we study how far regions adapt these timescales to meet task demands, as well as how thistimescale flexibilityis organized across the cortical hierarchy, and how it develops in humans. We quantified rest-to-task changes in intrinsic neural timescales, referred to astimescale deflections, using fMRI data from four independent datasets totaling 1,712 participants aged 8–64 years. We found that timescales reduced under cognitive load in all four datasets, most strongly in association cortex, which partially flattened the resting-state timescale hierarchy. Individual differences in timescale deflections were organized along the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis and tracked cognitive performance, both in adults and in youth. Next, in youth, deflections followed a two-stage developmental course: a generalized reduction throughout childhood, followed by a selective expansion in association cortex from mid-adolescence. Furthermore, the timing of these stages aligned with cortical gradients of inhibitory gene expression and intracortical myelin content, both features implicated in the opening and closing of critical periods of neural plasticity. Overall, our results demonstrate that task-evoked timescale flexibility is hierarchically organized, behaviorally and neurobiologically relevant, and refined across adolescence. The brain’s ability to support complex behavior depends upon integrating information across multiple timescales [1]. Reacting to a sudden change in the environment requires rapid sensorimotor processing on the order of milliseconds, whereas following a conversation or reasoning toward a goal requires integrating information over seconds, minutes, or longer. To meet this range of processing demands, cortical regions vary in terms of their temporal receptive windows (TRWs), the length of time over which a region can integrate information [1–3]. Each region’s baseline TRW is calibrated to the temporal structure of the information it preferentially processes. This produces a hierarchy of resting-state TRWs across the cortex. Primary sensory and motor regions exhibit short baseline TRWs suited to high-frequency stimulus processing, while higher-order association regions exhibit longer baseline TRWs suited to integrating information across extended time frames [4,5]. This hierarchical organization is a fundamental feature of cortical function, observed consistently across species and measurement modalities, and its patterning is refined systematically throughout development [6–8]. However, this resting-state hierarchy reflects a single state and primarily indexes regions’ baseline capacity for temporal integration. It remains an open question how far a region’s TRW departs from this baseline with behavioral demands, how any such flexibility is organized across the cortical hierarchy, and how it emerges throughout development in humans. Empirically, regions’ TRWs are most commonly inferred from their intrinsic neural timescales (hereafter, timescales), which quantify the rate at which a region’s local activity decorrelates from itself over time. Across species—including mice [9], macaques [10–12], and humans [13–15]—and across imaging modalities spanning electrophysiology, MEG, EEG, and fMRI, timescales reliably exhibit a hierarchical organization consistent with the cortical hierarchy of TRWs: fast timescales in primary sensorimotor cortices, progressively slower timescales in higher-order association regions. This organization is evident in the infra-slow fluctuations of the BOLD signal, where timescale gradients span the entire cerebral cortex [16,17]. It also aligns closely with the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis, a canonical gradient of cortical variation that captures the continuous transition from unimodal sensorimotor cortex to transmodal association cortex [18]. This hierarchical patterning of timescales is thought to arise from systematic regional differences in cortical microstructure, such as dendritic spine density, receptor and interneuron composition, and intracortical myelination [14,15,19,20], which shape local circuit properties including the balance of excitation and inhibition and the strength of recurrent connectivity [19,21]. Yet timescales are not static properties of a region. Rather, evidence suggests that regions can shift their baseline timescales as task contexts change. Evidence for thistimescale flexibilityspans diverse modalities, species, and behavioral contexts [22,23]. In humans, MEG [24], EEG [25], ECoG [14], and fMRI [26,27] studies report flexible speeding or slowing of timescales in different task contexts, e.g., during working memory tasks. In calcium imaging performed in rodents, timescales show relative slowing during continuous behaviors such as locomotion [25]. Thus, the task-dependent modulation of timescales may be an important feature of brain function that allows brain regions to tune their computational window within and between task contexts [12,28,29]. Timescales are also sensitive to changes in arousal. In human intracranial recordings, timescales slow progressively with the depth of non-rapid eye movement sleep, and the hierarchical gradient present during wakefulness is attenuated [30,31]. Finally, recent work showed anesthesia consistently alters timescales across a diverse range of species [32]. Taken together, these cross-species and cross-modality data suggest that brain regions can be characterized by both their baseline timescale, measured at rest, and their ability to adapt their timescales in response to context and task demands, with both features being critical to understanding healthy brain function. In humans, three dimensions of this timescale flexibility remain unresolved. The first is cognitive. If timescale flexibility represents an important computational resource in the brain, then the extent to which a region’s timescale shifts during cognitive tasks should covary with how well people perform those tasks. Direct evidence comes from human intracranial recordings, where task-evoked change in neuronal timescales tracks working memory performance [14]. However, this evidence comes from a small set of regions in a single task context, and the relationship has not been tested across the whole cortex or in relation to the hierarchy that organizes baseline timescales. Establishing this relationship would identify timescale flexibility as a source of individual variability in cognitive ability. The second is developmental. Resting-state timescales undergo pronounced maturational change that follows the S-A axis [8,33,34], as do other features of cortical function, including local activity [35], as well as long-range functional and structural connectivity [36,37]. This work establishes how baseline timescales develop, but whether the capacity to depart from that baseline in a task-dependent manner also changes with age, and whether any such change is organized along the S-A axis, remains unknown. Additionally, cognitive ability improves markedly across childhood and adolescence, with refinements to higher-order executive function occurring relatively late in adolescence [38]. This pattern suggests that context-dependent modulation of brain function may itself be maturing during mid-to-late adolescence. In turn, timescale flexibility may be one overlooked component of this developmental change, and it may mature in step with the cortical hierarchy. The third is neurobiological. The hierarchical organization of baseline timescales along the S-A axis is thought to be underpinned by regional variation in cortical microstructure and excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) balance. E/I balance determines how long activity persists after input [19,20], and timescales measuredin vivotrack regional variation in microstructure [15] and in the transcriptomic programs that underpin excitatory and inhibitory synaptic signaling [39–41]. Critically,in vivoproxies for these same properties mature along the S-A axis in humans: association cortex undergoes a selective, S-A-axis-organized shift in E/I balance across adolescence [42,43], and intracortical myelin growth peaks late and in a graded fashion along the same axis [44]. Because these properties set the circuit dynamics that determine baseline timescales, they may also constrain how far a region’s timescale can move from that baseline, and their protracted maturation in association cortex would predict that timescale flexibility matures later in association cortex than in sensorimotor cortex. However, whether the developmental course of timescale flexibility aligns with the cortical distribution of these properties is untested. Such alignment would be consistent with the S-A critical period framework, in which the maturation of inhibitory circuitry and the accumulation of intracortical myelin open and close windows of heightened plasticity in a cascading manner along the cortical hierarchy [45–47]. In turn, these processes may facilitate the refinement of cortical microstructure that subserves timescale flexibility. Here, we leverage four independent fMRI datasets totaling 1,712 participants [48–51] to address the following questions about the capacity of timescales to change in response to task demands: (i) how are rest-to-task timescale changes organized across the cortex, (ii) how do they vary between individuals to explain cognition, (iii) how do they emerge across development, and (iv) how does their developmental emergence align with the cortical distribution of gene expression and intracortical myelin features linked to inhibitory circuit maturation. The gaps outlined above motivate three predictions. First, if timescale flexibility is a computational resource organized by the cortical hierarchy, then its magnitude, its inter-individual variability, and its relationship to cognitive performance should each be patterned along the S-A axis. Second, if timescale flexibility matures along the cortical hierarchy, its developmental course should be heterochronous along the S-A axis rather than uniform. Third, the timing of these developmental effects should track the cortical distribution of features linked to E/I balance and intracortical myelination. We find that timescales shorten under cognitive load in all four datasets, most strongly in association cortex, and that individual differences in this rest-to-task timescale flexibility are organized along the S-A axis and track cognitive performance. In youth, this flexibility matures in two stages, a generalized reduction through childhood followed by a selective expansion in association cortex from mid-adolescence, with a timing profile that aligns with cortical gradients of inhibitory-interneuron-related gene expression and intracortical myelin. We studied regions’ intrinsic neural timescales using fMRI data from four independent datasets, totaling 1,712 individuals aged 8–64 years (seeSection 4.1). These datasets comprised two healthy adult cohorts (HCP-YA and WAND) and two developmental cohorts (HCP-D and Penn LEAD). Following our previous work [8,52], timescales were quantified by calculating the decay lag of the autocorrelation coefficient computed separately for resting-state, movie-watching, and task-based regional fMRI time series (seeSection 4.4). Here, lower values indicate faster decay of the ACF tor= 0, and thus faster timescales, which we interpret as shorter TRWs. For movie-watching and task-based data, we regressed out the block-design or event-related task structure from each subject’s scan before computing the ACFs (seeSection 5.1for discussion of this choice and for results without this regression applied). This choice meant that our movie-watching and task-based timescales captured fluctuations in intrinsic neural rhythms that are elicited by attentional or cognitive engagement, but that do not simply reflect the statistical structure of the scan design (e.g., the timing of the stimulus blocks). That is, the regression removed the response time-locked to the task design, not the task-related change in ongoing dynamics that we sought to measure. Across both adults and developing youths, we found that timescales systematically reduced during tasks relative to rest (pairedt-tests, all FDR-correctedp <0.001;Fig. 1B–C), indicative of faster timescales when engaging cognitive processes. Additionally, in the HCP-YA dataset, timescales for movies also decreased relative to rest (pairedt-test,p <0.001), but not to the same extent as tasks, suggesting that timescale deflections scaled with cognitive load. (A) Simulated time series (top) and autocorrelation functions (ACFs; bottom) from three cortical regions spanning the sensorimotor-to-association (S-A) axis: sensorimotor (orange), transitional (light purple), and association (dark purple) cortex. The shaded area represents the timescale, computed as the area under the ACF up to the lag at which the ACF first crosses zero (dashed vertical line), multiplied by the scan repetition time. Timescales increase across the S-A axis (1.9 s→4.1 s→9.5 s), reflecting progressively slower autocorrelation decay in higher-order cortical regions. (B) Timescales reduced under cognitive load. Distributions of regional timescales, averaged over subjects, across conditions for each of the four datasets. Each point is the timescale for a single brain region averaged over subjects and colored by the S-A axis (orange = sensorimotor pole; purple = association pole). Lines connect the same region across scans, and annotatedρvalues indicate the Spearman correlation between timescales and the S-A axis. Brackets denote pairedt-tests across the 400 parcels, comparing each task or movie condition to rest (FDR-corrected within dataset;***p <0.001). (C) Subject-level timescale distributions grouped by S-A axis decile. Each point represents a timescale from a single subject, averaged across regions within a single decile, and the black curve traces the group-mean trend across deciles. (D) Timescales decouple from the S-A axis under cognitive load, assessed at the subject level. For each dataset, distributions of per-subject S-A coupling (Spearmanρbetween a subject’s regional timescales and the S-A axis) at rest and during each condition are shown. Asterisks denote one-sided pairedt-tests comparing each condition’s coupling to rest (Fisher-ztransformed, FDR-corrected across all dataset×condition comparisons;***p <0.001,*p <0.05). (E) Timescales decouple differently for movies than for tasks. For HCP-YA, each subject’s S-A coupling during movies (left) and tasks (right) is plotted against their resting-state coupling; the annotatedrvalues indicate the cross-subject Pearson correlation. A Steiger’s test confirmed that the rest–movie correspondence was significantly stronger than the rest–task correspondence (z= 3.97,p= 7.16×10−5;n= 163). Note, for brevity, only theN-back working memory task is shown here for HCP-YA, alongside movie-watching and resting-state data averaged over the respective multiple runs (seeFig. S1for all scans and runs). Importantly, these task-induced changes in local activity timescales, ortimescale deflections, were not uniform across the cortex. Instead, timescale deflections were larger in association cortex, which resulted in a relative decoupling of regional timescale variation from the cortical hierarchy. Specifically, across all datasets, resting-state timescales correlated positively with the S-A axis (Fig. 1B;ρ= 0.34, 0.31, 0.57, 0.41 for HCP-YA, WAND, HCP-D, and Penn LEAD, respectively), consistent with previous literature. This hierarchical coupling diminished when participants transitioned from rest to watching movies (ρ= 0.09, HCP-YA) and performing tasks (ρ= 0.19, 0.26, 0.36, 0.26, where the HCP-D value is averaged over its three tasks; averagedρ= 0.27 across datasets). Thus, while timescales were consistently slower in association cortex than in sensorimotor cortex at rest, this gradient partially flattened under cognitive load, driven by greater timescale flexibility in association regions relative to sensorimotor. We assessed hierarchical decoupling at the participant level by correlating the S-A axis with participant-level timescale maps. Compared to rest, we found that S-A coupling was significantly reduced during every task and movie condition across all four datasets (one-sided pairedt-tests, all FDR-correctedp <0.05;Fig. 1D). Furthermore, in HCP-YA, we found that this participant-specific decoupling was topographically different for movies compared to the working memory task (Fig. 1E). That is, while participants’ S-A coupling was reduced under both conditions relative to rest, coupling during movies remained correlated, across subjects, with resting-state coupling (r= 0.46,p= 5.88×10−10), whereas coupling during working memory showed no reliable correspondence with rest (r= 0.13,p= 0.11). A Steiger’s test confirmed that this difference between movies and tasks was significant (z= 3.97,p= 7.16×10−5). This result suggests that movies and tasks may decouple timescales from the cortical hierarchy through distinct routes: movie-watching attenuates hierarchical coupling while preserving its between-subject variability, whereas task engagement substantially reconfigures that variability, leaving no reliable correspondence with participants’ resting baseline. Thus, individuals whose timescales are more stratified along the S-A axis at rest show stronger stratification during movies, but this resting-state hierarchical organization does not predict individuals’ task patterning. Collectively, these results demonstrate a consistent modulatory effect of cognition on brain dynamics, in which timescales deflect from rest when the brain is driven exogenously by a diverse range of movies and cognitive tasks—with the largest deflections consistently concentrating in the association regions, indicating greater timescale flexibility relative to the rest of the cortex. The analyses in the previous section characterized timescales within each condition, and showed that they sped up and decoupled from the cortical hierarchy, when participants engaged in cognitive tasks. Hereafter, we change our measure of interest from timescales to the timescale deflections themselves, computed for each participant and region as the absolute difference between task and resting-state timescales (Section 4.4), and treat these deflections as an index of timescale flexibility. Thus, here, larger timescale deflections reflect greater reductions in timescales going from rest to task. This participant-level measure allowed us to ask how deflections varied between individuals across the cortical hierarchy, and whether this variation explained participants’ behavior. All analyses in this section used the working memory task from HCP-YA (n= 966), which yielded the largest timescale deflections relative to rest across all tasks examined (Fig. S1). UnlikeFig. 1, where resting-state timescales were averaged over all available scans, here each participant’s resting-state timescale was estimated from their 3T resting-state runs truncated to the length of the working memory run, so that rest and task estimates were matched on scan duration (seeSection 4.4for more details andSection 5for sensitivity and robustness analyses). We first characterized how inter-individual differences in timescale deflections were distributed across the cortical hierarchy (Fig. 2A). Both the between-subject mean and standard deviation of absolute timescale deflections increased along the S-A axis (r= 0.33,psmash= 0.010;r= 0.34,psmash= 0.007, respectively), indicating that association cortex not only exhibited larger deflections on average, but also showed greater inter-individual variability in the magnitude of those deflections. This result demonstrates that individual differences in timescale flexibility are disproportionately concentrated in higher-order cortex. Furthermore, this between-subject variability was highly reproducible: the spatial pattern of deflection variability estimated from the left–right (LR) acquisition was almost perfectly correlated with that estimated from the independent right–left (RL) run (r= 0.97;Fig. 2B). Together, these findings indicate that timescale deflections capture a stable, hierarchically organized axis of inter-individual variability in brain dynamics. All panels show HCP-YA working memory data (n= 966) with resting-state timescales estimated from 3T rest runs length-matched to the task run. (A) Between-subject mean (left) and standard deviation (right) of absolute timescale deflections plotted as a function of the S-A axis. Each point represents one brain region, colored by the canonical Yeo-7 functional systems [53]. Here, positive relationships indicate that regions higher on the S-A axis exhibit both larger and more variable timescale deflections across individuals (r= 0.33,psmash = 0.010;r= 0.34,psmash = 0.007, respectively), indicating greater flexibility. (B) Between-subject variability (standard deviation) of absolute timescale deflections estimated from the L–R scan acquisition plotted against the same quantity estimated from the independent R–L run. The near-perfect correlation (r= 0.97) indicates that the spatial pattern of timescale deflection variability was highly reproducible across independent acquisitions. Note that this panel indexes measurement reliability rather than spatial correspondence, so no spatial null was applied. (C) Region-wise partial correlations between absolute timescale deflections and working memory accuracy (left), working memory reaction time (middle), and an out-of-scanner measure of cognition (right), each plotted as a function of the S-A axis. Behavioral correlations were systematically organized along the S-A axis (r= 0.58,psmash<1×10−4;r=−0.40,psmash<1×10−4;r= 0.52,psmash<1×10−4, respectively). These results indicate that larger timescale deflections in association cortex corresponded to better performance across all three measures, while larger deflections in sensorimotor cortex showed the opposite relationship. Next, we examined whether the magnitude of timescale deflections correlated with cognitive performance, controlling for participants’ resting-state timescales, age, sex, and in-scanner motion (Fig. 2C). Region-wise correlations between timescale deflections and working memory accuracy significantly varied along the S-A axis (r= 0.58,psmash<1×10−4). In association cortex, larger deflections corresponded to greater accuracy. This relationship was reversed in sensorimotor cortex, where larger deflections corresponded to lower accuracy. This same pattern emerged for reaction time (r=−0.40,psmash<1×10−4): larger deflections in association cortex corresponded to faster responses, while larger deflections in sensorimotor cortex corresponded to slower responses. Thus, individuals whose fMRI-based timescales reduced more markedly (larger deflections) in higher-order association cortex—but less so in sensorimotor cortex—were both more accurate and faster on the working memory task. This result suggests that optimal cognitive performance is associated with a spatially differentiated pattern of timescale modulation, in which timescales are selectively reduced in the association cortex while sensorimotor timescales are relatively preserved. A parallel result was observed for an out-of-scanner measure of cognition (r= 0.52,psmash<1×10−4), where the same hierarchically organized pattern of behavioral correlations was present, indicating that the behavioral relevance of timescale deflections generalizes beyond in-scanner performance. Together, these results demonstrate that individual variability in the task-evoked modulation of infra-slow neural timescales is hierarchically organized and behaviorally meaningful. Note, this hierarchical organization depended on regression of the task design. Without it, neither the mean nor the variability of deflections was significantly organized along the S-A axis, and neither were the brain–behavior correlations, even though the magnitudes of those correlations were unchanged (Figs. S9andS10; seeSection 5.1). In our previous work, we found that both the amplitude of regions’ low-frequency fluctuations [35] and their timescales [8] change systematically throughout development while participants are at rest. These developmental patterns were organized along the S-A axis: primary sensory and motor cortices tended to exhibit linear developmental decreases that onset relatively early (8-12 years), while higher-order association cortices showed non-linear trajectories that onset relatively late (18–22 years) [35]. Extending on our previous work, we next characterized the developmental course of task-based timescale modulations, including quantifying age-resolved effects to study distinct developmental phases. Using the CARIT task in HCP-D (n= 552; ages 8–22 years) [50], we characterized the developmental trajectories of timescale deflections by fitting generalized additive models (GAMs; seeSection 4.6)—either to regional data or to data averaged over S-A axis deciles—and examined the resulting annualized rates of change (Fig. 3). The regional heatmap of annualized change provides an overview of these trajectories across the full cortical hierarchy and age range (Fig. 3A). Qualitative assessment of this heatmap suggested that developmental refinements in timescale deflections were not uniformly expressed across age (e.g., blue and pink inFig. 3A). Rather, reductions in timescale deflections dominated early, while deflection increases could be observed in late adolescence. To quantitatively delineate different phases of development in neural dynamics, we used change-point detection analysis, which is capable of uncovering inflection points in multivariate data. We identified that the spatial developmental pattern of regional developmental trajectories was organized into two phases: an early childhood phase that spanned from 8 to 15 years of age, and an adolescent phase that started at 15 years and continued through to 22 years. (A) Heatmap of the annualized rate of change (1st derivative of GAM fits) in timescale deflections across development (x-axis) for each cortical region ordered by the S-A axis (y-axis; association pole at the top, sensorimotor pole at the bottom). Cool colors indicate reducing deflections, and warm colors indicate expanding deflections. The dashed vertical line marks the stage boundary at age 15. (B) GAM-fitted developmental trajectories of timescale deflections for each S-A axis decile (orange = sensorimotor; purple = association). Fits are mean-centered. Association deciles reduced steeply before reversing course and expanding, whereas sensorimotor deciles reduced gradually throughout development. (C) First temporal derivatives of the trajectories inB, which provide the annualized rate of change per decile. Early in development, all deciles showed negative rates, with the association cortex reducing fastest. At older ages, association deciles crossed into positive rates while sensorimotor deciles remained negative. (D) Second derivatives of the trajectories inB, which provide acceleration per decile. The developmental reduction decelerated through adolescence, most steeply in association deciles. (E) Pearson correlation between regional rates of change in timescale deflections and S-A axis rank, computed at monthly intervals across development. The shaded band shows the subject-level bootstrap 95% confidence interval (CI); vertical labels mark 14.8 and 21.6 years, the window over which the lower CI bound exceeded zero. Across this window, the correlation peaked atr ≈0.36. In the early phase (8–15 years), timescale deflections became smaller across the cortex. In other words, with increasing age, timescales sped up less when participants changed from being at rest to engaging in a task. In the adolescent phase, timescale deflections began to increase in association cortex while they continued to decrease in sensorimotor cortex. To confirm this pattern, we fit GAMs to data averaged within each S-A axis decile (Fig. 3B–C; seeFig. S2for fits without mean-centering). Sensorimotor deciles showed protracted declines in timescale deflections across the full age range, whereas association deciles showed large initial declines followed by smaller increases from late adolescence. The second derivatives (Fig. 3D) showed the change in acceleration of this developmental reduction, and the peak of this change was aligned to 15 years of age. Together, these analyses describe a two-stage developmental course of timescale deflections: (i) a childhood-into-early-adolescence stage of generalized reductions across the cortex, followed by (ii) a late-adolescence stage of selective expansion in association cortex. For an extended summary of these two developmental phases seeFig. S3. Hierarchical organization of this developmental course emerged only in mid-adolescence. To determine when, we correlated regional rates of change in timescale deflections (first derivatives fromFig. 3A) with S-A axis rank at monthly intervals, with subject-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals around each estimate (Fig. 3E). Throughout childhood, this coupling was weak, crossing zero only at approximately 12 years. It then became reliably positive from 14.8 to 21.6 years, peaking atr ≈0.36. Notably, the age at which this coupling first reached significance (14.8 years) aligned closely with the stage boundary estimated from our change-point analysis (15 years), which was estimated independently of the S-A axis. Additionally, while we focused here on timescale deflections computed for the CARIT task, the same two-stage course was evident for both the Emotion (Fig. S4) and Guessing (Fig. S5) tasks, indicating that these effects were task-general. See alsoFig. S6for an analysis of task-based timescales in the CARIT task, instead of deflections. Together, these results indicate that the cortical hierarchy governs the maturation of timescale deflections predominantly during mid-to-late adolescence, when a generalized childhood reduction gives way to selective, hierarchically organized expansion in association cortex. Finally, as in the HCP-YA dataset, we examined whether individual differences in timescale deflections were related to task performance in HCP-D. Unlike in HCP-YA, here, regional correlations between timescale deflection magnitude and CARIT no-go accuracy were negatively organized along the S-A axis (r=−0.34,psmash<1×10−4;Fig. 4A). That is, larger deflections in association cortex were associated with lower accuracy, not better accuracy as in HCP-YA. Furthermore, this S-A patterning was more pronounced in the second developmental stage compared to the first (Fig. 4B). These results suggest that the behavioral relevance of timescale flexibility changes with maturation and is context specific. In youth, better inhibitory control is accompanied by smaller timescale deflections in association cortex, whereas in young adults, larger deflections are accompanied by better working memory performance. Each point is a cortical region, colored by the Yeo-7 systems and ordered by the S-A axis (x-axis). The y-axis shows the partial correlation between regional timescale deflection magnitude and CARIT no-go accuracy, controlling for age, sex, head motion, and mean resting-state timescale. (A) Region-wise partial correlations for no-go accuracy computed across the whole sample (n= 536, 8–22 years). (B) Region-wise partial correlations for no-go accuracy computed separately across participants younger than 15 years (left) and participants aged 15 years and older (right). InB, age was still included as a covariate within each group; the 15-year split corresponds to the stage boundary inFig. 3. *p <0.05; ***p <0.001. The two-stage developmental trajectory outlined above raised the question of what distinguishes the childhood reduction of timescale deflections from their adolescent expansion. Because E/I balance and microstructure shape baseline timescales [15,19] and mature along the S-A axis [42,44], we asked whether the two stages track the cortical distribution of these properties. To address this question, we examined three cortical maps: two gene-expression components and intracortical myelin (Fig. 5A). The two gene maps were derived from principal components analysis (PCA; seeSection 4.10) applied to a curated set of∼2,000 brain-related genes from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), previously used to study timescales [14]. The third map was intracortical myelin measuredin vivoin HCP-D (seeSection 4.11). The first gene component (Gene-PC1; 18.9% of variance) separated regions expressing fast-spiking interneuron machinery (e.g., parvalbumin, the Kv3 potassium channelsKCNC1/KCNC3, and the Nav1.1 sodium channelSCN1A/SCN1B) from those expressing slow, tonic-modulatory signaling genes (e.g., the extrasynaptic GABAAsubunitsGABRA5/GABRB1and the somatostatin receptorSSTR1). Thus, the fast-spiking pole of Gene-PC1 indexes the inhibitory machinery thought to open critical periods [54,55]. By contrast, intracortical myelin is one of the structural brakes thought to close them [56,57]. The third gene component (Gene-PC3; 9.0% of variance), separated regions expressing oligodendrocyte genes (e.g., the transcription factorSOX10and the newly-formed oligodendrocyte markerENPP6) from those expressing synaptic-signaling genes (e.g.,STX1B,SYT7/SYT11,DLGAP1, and the metabotropic glutamate receptorGRM7). Unlike Gene-PC1, which was strongly aligned with both intracortical myelin (r=−0.72,psmash<1×10−4) and the S-A axis (r= 0.68,psmash<1×10−4), Gene-PC3 was aligned with neither (r= 0.05,psmash= 0.55;r=−0.11,psmash= 0.21). This suggests that Gene-PC3 indexes a glial-versus-neuronal axis of cortical composition that is spatially distinct from the hierarchy, rather than a specific opener or closer of critical periods. Note, the second gene component was not associated with developmental change and is not reported further. (A) Top-loading genes at each pole of Gene-PC1 (left) and Gene-PC3 (right), with variance explained. Gene-PC1 contrasts fast-spiking interneuron machinery with slow, tonic-modulatory signaling; Gene-PC3 contrasts oligodendrocyte genes with genes related to synaptic signaling. (B) Pearson correlation between each of the three reference maps—Gene-PC1, Gene-PC3, and intracortical myelin measured in HCP-D—and the regional rate of developmental change in timescale deflections, as a function of age. Bold segments mark pointwise BrainSMASH nulls wherep <0.05, filled markers indicate the age of peak|r|among significant ages, and the dashed vertical line shows the stage boundary at age 15. (C) The regional scatter at each age peak (Gene-PC1:r= 0.22,psmash = 0.01, age 16.1; Gene-PC3:r=−0.21,psmash = 0.005, age 13.7; myelin:r=−0.29,psmash<1×10−4, age 18.5). Each point is a cortical parcel. We found that these maps aligned with the development of timescale deflections in sequence (Fig. 5B). Specifically, we correlated each of the above brain maps with the regional developmental rate of timescale deflections (cf.Fig. 3A) at each age. The oligodendrocyte-versus-synaptic axis (Gene-PC3) showed significant alignment with development first. In late childhood, regions rich in oligodendrocyte genes reduced their deflections fastest, and regions rich in synaptic-signaling genes reduced them least (Gene-PC3; significant across 10.9–15.9 years, peaking at 13.7 years,r=−0.21,psmash= 0.005;Fig. 5C, middle). The fast-spiking inhibitory axis (Gene-PC1) correlated significantly with development next, starting around the transition between stages. This result suggests that regions rich in fast-spiking machinery were still reducing their deflections, whereas regions rich in tonic-modulatory signaling were changing least (Gene-PC1; 14.9–21.2 years, peaking at 16.1 years,r= 0.22,psmash= 0.01;Fig. 5C, left). Finally, intracortical myelin aligned with development last and most strongly, in late adolescence. Here, heavily myelinated regions continued to reduce their deflections, whereas lightly myelinated regions expanded them (myelin; 15.0–21.9 years, peaking at 18.5 years,r=−0.29,psmash<1×10−4;Fig. 5C, right). These results demonstrate that each brain map marked a distinct moment in development: Gene-PC3 correlated with the childhood reduction, Gene-PC1 correlated with the transition between stages, and intracortical myelin correlated with the hierarchical divergence that followed later in adolescence. Here, we characterized the task-evoked modulation of infra-slow intrinsic neural timescales across four independent datasets totaling 1,712 participants. We found that timescales reduced under cognitive load across all datasets and that the magnitude of these deflections was organized along the sensorimotor-to-association (S-A) axis. Additionally, in young adults, we found that individual variability in this magnitude predicted in-scanner working memory performance and reaction time, as well as out-of-scanner cognitive ability, and in developing youths, that the same hierarchical pattern explained individual variability in response inhibition. Furthermore, in the developing brain, we found that timescale deflections followed a two-stage course, with a childhood phase of generalized reduction across the cortex followed by a late-adolescent phase of selective expansion in association cortex, and that these stages aligned in sequence with cortical patterns of gene expression and intracortical myelin. Together, these findings characterize timescale flexibility as a hierarchically organized, biologically grounded, and developmentally acquired property of the cortical hierarchy. A hierarchical organization of resting-state timescales along the S-A axis has been documented across species, modalities, and across development [8–10,13,14]. This hierarchy is thought to reflect systematic differences in cortical microcircuits—including regional variation in recurrent excitatory connectivity, inhibitory interneuron composition, and long-range white matter pathways—that calibrate regions’ local temporal dynamics to the demands of their specialized computational role [15,19]. Our finding that this hierarchy is partially flattened during cognitive task engagement adds to a growing body of evidence that timescales are not static temporal-processing features but a dynamic resource [7,24,25,58,59]. By averaging over sustained task epochs across four independent datasets, we consistently observed timescale reductions under cognitive load [26,27,29]. This finding was robust across tasks spanning working memory, response inhibition, reinforcement learning, and naturalistic movie watching, as well as across samples ranging from childhood to adulthood. Critically, this reduction was not uniform across the cortex but caused a systematic reduction in the spatial coupling between timescales and the S-A axis, suggesting that the timescale hierarchy is selectively reorganized rather than globally compressed under cognitive demand [17]. In the HCP-YA dataset, where both movie-watching and task data were available, timescale deflections scaled with cognitive load, providing further evidence that infra-slow timescale modulation is graded by the degree of cognitive engagement rather than reflecting a binary switch between rest and task. More broadly, this selective, state-dependent reorganization fits an emerging principle whereby dynamic properties of cortical activity—beyond baseline timescales—are organized along the S-A axis and reconfigure with cognitive state. Thus, the cortical hierarchy may be a common scaffold along which the brain reallocates distinct dynamic resources as processing demands change. Our findings of task-evoked changes in timescales builds upon an emerging body of work demonstrating that timescales flexibly adjust according to context and state. Using intracranial recordings in humans, Krauseet al.estimated timescales from local field potential data and tracked them across sleep stages [31]. Timescales slowed progressively with the depth of non-rapid eye movement sleep, and the hierarchical organization present during wakefulness diminished. Thus, cognitive load and sleep appear to move timescales in opposite directions—faster under task, slower under sleep—yet both attenuate the cortical hierarchy. Furthermore, cognition and sleep also appear to attenuate the hierarchy from opposite ends. During sleep, hierarchical flattening was driven by a selective slowing of sensorimotor timescales toward association values [31]. By contrast, in our data, it was driven by a speeding up of association timescales toward sensorimotor values (Fig. 2A). Anesthesia, however, shows a different set of results. Deep anesthesia speeds up infra-slow fMRI timescales, most strongly where baseline timescales are slowest [32], resembling the effect of task engagement in our data. This effect may also depend on dose: propofol sedation slows fMRI timescales, whereas surgical-level anesthesia speeds them up [60]. Because propofol acts largely by potentiating GABAA-mediated inhibition [32], this dose dependence suggests that inhibition can either slow or speed infra-slow timescales. This interpretation is consistent with evidence that focal inhibition can strengthen slow cortical rhythms [61,62]. Taken together, these comparisons indicate that different brain states depart from the resting-state hierarchy in distinct, spatially patterned ways. Whether these different states lie along a common axis, or share underlying mechanisms, warrants further investigation. We found that the S-A axis not only organizes the magnitude of timescale deflections, it organizes between-subject variability in timescale deflections and explained cognitive performance. Association cortex exhibited not only larger mean deflections but also greater inter-individual spread in deflection magnitude. Behaviorally, in young adults, individuals whose timescale deflections were largest in association cortex and relatively preserved in sensorimotor cortex were both more accurate and faster on the working memory task, and showed higher out-of-scanner cognition. To our knowledge, the most direct prior evidence for the behavioral relevance of task-evoked timescale change comes from intracranial recordings, in which prefrontal deflections during working memory maintenance predicted individuals’ task accuracy [14]. Our findings extend this result from a small subset of regions to the whole cortex, where the behavioral relevance of timescale deflections followed the S-A axis, and from electrophysiological to infra-slow fMRI dynamics in large samples. Thus, in adulthood, individuals who most effectively shift their infra-slow dynamics in higher-order association cortex are better positioned to respond when cognitive demand is highest, yielding advantages in both response accuracy and speed. In youth, however, we found that the direction of this hierarchical relationship was reversed. Specifically, in HCP-D, larger timescale deflections in association cortex were accompanied by poorer inhibitory control on the CARIT task (Fig. 4). Furthermore, this negative hierarchical patterning was more pronounced after mid-adolescence (Fig. 4B), when timescale deflections began to expand selectively in association cortex. These results demonstrate that the behavioral relevance of timescale flexibility may be context specific, with both larger and smaller deflections in association cortex linking to improved task performance depending on the needs of the behavioral domain. Thus, our findings suggest that it may be the capacity for larger deflections in association cortex that supports behavior, not the direction itself. In turn, this implies that greater timescale flexibility in association cortex confers a functional advantage not necessarily through greater deflections, but through greater precision of timescale tuning to a specific task context. Confirming our prediction that timescale flexibility develops heterochronously along the cortical hierarchy, we observed a two-stage developmental pattern: a childhood phase of broad reductions in timescale deflections that was followed by a mid-to-late adolescent phase of selective expansion in higher-order association cortex. Notably, these stages map onto well-established models of neurodevelopment. The first stage coincides with several key global developmental processes that are prevalent throughout childhood and early adolescence. For example, synaptic pruning proceeds throughout this window, beginning earlier in primary sensory cortex than in prefrontal cortex [63], where spine density continues to decline into the third decade [64]. Inhibitory interneuron circuitry matures in parallel. In the human prefrontal cortex, markers of fast-spiking interneurons rise across childhood and peak in the teenage years [65]. Theoretical work suggests that the maturation of inhibition suppresses spontaneous activity to a greater extent than it suppresses stimulus-driven activity [66]. In turn, this is thought to shift the cortex toward an externally driven operating mode and enhances the signal-to-noise ratio of cortical processing [18]. Consistent with this account, the genetic axis separating oligodendrocyte genes from synaptic-signaling genes (Gene-PC3) coupled to developmental change predominantly during this first stage, peaking at 13.7 years, with regions rich in oligodendrocyte machinery reducing their timescale deflections fastest. Because Gene-PC3 was aligned with neither the S-A axis nor intracortical myelin, this early coupling is not attributable to the hierarchy. Instead, it may reflect regional differences in the balance of oligodendrocyte-lineage and neuronal synaptic components during the period when broad synaptic refinement is underway. By contrast, the second stage—the selective expansion of timescale deflections in association cortex—emerged in mid-to-late adolescence, becoming robustly organized along the S-A axis between approximately 14.8 and 21.6 years. This timing aligns with the protracted, late maturation of transmodal association cortex that distinguishes human neurodevelopment [18].In vivo, association cortex undergoes a selective, S-A-axis-organized shift in its E/I balance across adolescence [42], accompanied by graded, late-arriving intracortical myelination [44]. Consistent with these mechanisms, recent cross-species work has shown that resting-state timescales in frontal and parietal association cortex are refined throughout adolescence in concert with E/I and deep-layer myelination changes [67]. Our results extend this account from resting-state dynamics to their task-evoked flexibility, suggesting that the same protracted maturation that refines association-cortex timescales at rest may also elaborate the capacity of these systems for context-dependent modulation. These effects complement those we previously reported for the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations [35]. In that work, the alignment between age-resolved developmental change and the S-A axis was strongest in childhood and early adolescence, peaking near age 15 and then weakening through late adolescence. The hierarchical organization of timescale-deflection development followed the opposite trajectory over the same period: it was absent in childhood and emerged only in mid-adolescence, becoming reliable after age 14.8. The two, therefore, overlap in time but move in opposite directions. As the cortical hierarchy’s relationship with resting-state development diminishes from its early-adolescent peak, its connection to the task-evoked flexibility of timescales rises and plateaus. Thus, rather than maturing in separate windows, the two succeed one another within a shared mid-adolescent window, as hierarchical organization shifts from resting-state activity to its task-evoked modulation. Consequently, the cortical hierarchy appears to shift from organizing regions’ intrinsic activity at rest to organizing how flexibly that activity can be reconfigured under cognitive demand. This crossover coincides with the canonical stabilization of executive function in mid-to-late adolescence [38], raising the possibility that the hierarchical elaboration of task-evoked timescale flexibility helps consolidate higher-order cognition as the earlier, resting-state mode of hierarchical development resolves. Prior work suggests that critical periods of heightened neural plasticity open as parvalbumin-expressing interneurons mature and shift E/I balance [54,55,68], and that these critical-period windows close as perineuronal nets, oligodendrocytes, and intracortical myelin accumulate across development [57,69–71]. Importantly, these windows close earlier in sensory cortex than in association cortex [45,72–75], and we have previously proposed that this cascade partly drives the S-A axis of human cortical development, with adolescence forming a late critical period in association cortex that coincides with the refinement of executive function [46,47,76]. The order of the couplings we observed is consistent with this account. The fast-spiking pole of Gene-PC1, which contains inhibitory machinery thought to open critical periods, coupled to development from around the stage transition. Regions at the fast-spiking pole, predominantly in sensorimotor cortex, continued to reduce their deflections, while association regions changed least and then expanded. The adolescent expansion was therefore concentrated in association regions that are relatively sparse in this machinery in adulthood, which fits with evidence that inhibitory circuitry in association cortex matures late [65]. Intracortical myelin, a principal brake on plasticity [56,57], coupled later and for longer, peaking at 18.5 years, when heavily myelinated sensorimotor regions continued to reduce their deflections while lightly myelinated association regions expanded. Thus, the order of developmental couplings in our results is consistent with the order in which critical-period windows are thought to open and then close. Several limitations of the present study warrant acknowledgment. First, all findings are derived from fMRI, which is constrained by its temporal resolution and the indirect hemodynamic coupling between neural activity and the BOLD signal. As such, the infra-slow timescales we measured here represent macroscale aggregates of many underlying neural processes, and findings based on BOLD fluctuations do not always align with those from methods that capture faster neural dynamics [22,23,32,77]. For example, timescales measured with intracranial electrophysiology lengthened in prefrontal cortex during working memory maintenance [14], whereas we observed infra-slow timescales shortening under working memory load. Whether such differences reflect distinct processes operating at different frequencies, or differences in what different modalities measure, remains an open question that will require multi-modal validation, including against the spiking-level timescales documented in non-human primates [10–12]. Second, the task regression approach we applied—removing block-design or event-related task structure from the BOLD time series before computing ACFs—is a necessary step for estimating intrinsic dynamics during task engagement, but it cannot fully disentangle intrinsic neural fluctuations from residual stimulus-evoked variance, particularly in densely-sampled event-related designs [78]. Third, our developmental analyses were cross-sectional; the two-stage trajectory we describe is inferred from age-related differences across participants rather than tracked within individuals, and longitudinal studies are needed to confirm the timing, shape, and inter-individual variability of this trajectory. Fourth, our molecular analyses relate static, group-level maps of gene expression and intracortical myelin to the rate of change of a functional phenotype. The correspondence we report is therefore between spatial patterns and developmental timing, and does not establish that these molecules cause the flexibility of intrinsic timescales. Gene-PC1 and the myelin map are both strongly aligned with the cortical hierarchy, and with each other, so their ordering rests on the temporal separation of their couplings rather than on their spatial independence. Gene-PC3, by contrast, was correlated with neither, so its earlier coupling is not attributable to the hierarchy. Fifth, regional fMRI timescales cannot distinguish a fixed circuit whose dynamics are modulated between rest and task from the differential engagement of local subpopulations with distinct intrinsic timescales. Either would shift the regional timescale, and we leave disentangling these underlying mechanisms to future work. In this work, we characterized how intrinsic neural timescales reconfigure from rest to task, and showed that the flexibility of infra-slow cortical dynamics was hierarchically organized. The magnitude of this flexibility was graded along the sensorimotor–association axis and tracked how well individuals performed during cognitive tasks. We also found that this flexibility may be acquired in two developmental phases: a broad childhood reduction, followed by a mid-adolescent reorganization tightly aligned to the cortical hierarchy, with each phase tracking distinct molecular features of the cortex. In this later phase, hierarchical organization shifted from the resting-state dynamics that dominate earlier development to task-evoked modulation, coinciding with the consolidation of higher-order cognition. Together, these findings establish task-evoked timescale flexibility as a distinct, developmentally acquired axis of cortical function and position its mid-adolescent, hierarchically organized emergence as a candidate substrate for the maturation of complex behavior. We analyzed neuroimaging data from four independent datasets, totaling 1,712 participants spanning ages 8.1 to 63.7 years. These included 966 adults from the Human Connectome Project Young Adult dataset (HCP-YA; ages 22.0–37.0,M= 28.7,SD= 3.7) [48], 95 participants from the Welsh Advanced Neuroimaging Database (WAND; ages 18.7–63.7,M= 28.7,SD= 9.0) [49], 552 youth from the Human Connectome Project Development dataset (HCP-D; ages 8.1–21.9,M= 14.9,SD= 3.9) [50], and 99 youth from the Penn LEAD study (ages 8.6–16.5,M= 12.6,SD= 2.0; first session only) [51]. Across the combined sample, 916 participants (53.5%) were female. All datasets received ethical approval from their respective institutional review boards, and all participants—or their legal guardians for minors—provided written informed consent prior to participation. Analyses involving HCP-YA movie-watching data were restricted to the 163 HCP-YA participants with 7T sessions (ages 22.0–36.0,M= 29.5,SD= 3.3; 98 female, 60.1%), as movies were acquired only at 7T. Owing to known confounds between head motion and development neuroimaging [79–81], subjects were excluded from analysis if they exceeded a mean framewise displacement (FD) threshold of 0.2 mm in any included functional scan. This criterion was applied to HCP-D, yielding the 552 subjects noted above (mean FD = 0.128±0.033 mm; range 0.033–0.200 mm), and to WAND, which reduced from 160 to the 95 subjects noted above (mean FD = 0.131±0.030 mm; range 0.062–0.183 mm). For HCP-YA, no subjects were excluded based on motion. Instead, relative RMS displacement was extracted for use as a nuisance covariate (mean relative RMS = 0.088±0.031 mm;n= 966). Similarly, we retained the full sample for Penn LEAD to preserve sample size (mean FD = 0.352±0.354 mm; range 0.075–2.497 mm). For all datasets, motion was included as a nuisance covariate where between-subjects analyses were performed. Full MRI acquisition parameters for each dataset—including scanner hardware, sequence design, and acquisition structure—are detailed in the original protocol and data-descriptor publications, to which we refer the reader: HCP-YA [48,82,83], HCP-D [50,84], WAND [49], and Penn LEAD [51]. All datasets were processed to produce a common set of regional BOLD time series parcellated according to the Schaefer-400 atlas [85]. Pre-processing proceeded along one of two paths: (i) minimally pre-processed data was sourced from the HCP-YA and HCP-D consortiums and additional steps outlined below were applied, and (ii) fMRIPrep and XCP-D were used in conjunction to process WAND and Penn LEAD. We describe these processing streams in more detail below. The HCP datasets [48,48,50,82–84] consist of multi-modal neuroimaging data from young adult (HCP-YA) and developing youths (HCP-D). For both HCP-YA and HCP-D, minimally preprocessed fMRI data were parcellated using the 400-region variant of the Schaefer parcellation [85]. Concretely, this involved using, for example, rfMRI_REST1_LR_Atlas_MSMAll_hp2000_clean.dtseries.nii for resting-state data and tfMRI_WM_LR_Atlas_MSMAll.dtseries.nii for task data from the S1200 release for HCP-YA. Thus, these data differed in terms of their minimal preprocessing, with the former including ICA-FIX denoising and high-pass filtering not applied to the latter [86]. For HCP-D, minimal processing was consistent across rest and task, and we used files labeled [scan]_Atlas_MSMAll_hp0_clean.dtseries.nii. For both datasets, additional nuisance regression was performed that comprised the global signal (GS). For HCP-YA, we extracted in-scanner accuracy and reaction time from theN-back working memory as well as a composite measure of cognition measured outside the scanner (CogTotalComp_Unadj). We correlated these variables against timescale deflections, controlling for age, sex, in-scanner motion, and resting-state timescales. For HCP-D, we extracted in-scanner performance on the CARIT go/no-go task. Specifically, CARIT no-go accuracy was computed as the proportion of no-go trials on which participants correctly withheld a response (i.e., one minus the no-go false-alarm rate), pooled across previously rewarded and previously punished no-go stimuli. Raw, bids-compliant fMRI data from the WAND [49] and Penn LEAD [51] datasets were both processed usingfMRIprep[87,88] andXCP-D[89]. Full details of these processing steps can be found in theboilerplatecontent included below inSection 5.1.3. As above, regional fMRI time series were extracted using the 400-region variant of the Schaefer parcellation [85]. We quantified each region’s intrinsic neural timescale (timescale) by calculating the integral to zero-crossing of the autocorrelation function (ACF) [8,52,90,91]. For each subject, scan, and Schaefer-400 parcel, we computed the ACF of the regional BOLD time series and defined the timescale as the area under the ACF from lag 0 to the lag at which the ACF first crossed zero, multiplied by the scan’s repetition time to express the timescale in seconds. Lower values indicate faster decay of the autocorrelation, and thus faster timescales or shorter temporal receptive windows. For task-based and movie-watching data, we first regressed the task structure—the block or event-related design for task runs, and the alternation between movie clips and interleaved rest periods for movie runs—from each subject’s regional time series [78,92] and computed the ACF from the residuals. Note that this step was not possible for WAND, for which the task design was not available; WAND task timescales were therefore estimated from unregressed time series. Regressing out task structure meant that timescale estimates reflected intrinsic neural dynamics during cognitive engagement rather than stimulus-locked responses. SeeSection 5.1for a close examination of this choice, and its impact on our key results. To capture task-evoked modulation of intrinsic dynamics, we defined a timescale deflection per region per subject as the difference between that subject’s resting-state and task-based or movie-watching timescales (task/movies minus rest). With the exception ofFig. 1, all analyses used the absolute value of this deflection quantity,|Δtimescale|, for which larger values index greater task- or movie-evoked speeding up of timescales. For the HCP-YA working memory analyses inFig. 2 and theHCP-D CARIT analyses inFigs. 3and5, each subject’s resting-state timescale was estimated from their resting-state runs truncated from scan onset to the duration of the corresponding task run, so that rest and task timescales were matched on scan length [93]. For HCP-YA this differs fromFig. 1, in which resting-state timescales were averaged across all available 3T and 7T resting-state scans at full length. Throughout, we organized cortical regions along the sensorimotor–association (S-A) axis, a dominant axis of cortical organization running from primary sensory and motor cortex to transmodal association cortex [18,35]. We used the S-A axis map projected to the Schaefer-400 (7-network) parcellation, and rank-transformed its values to yield an integer S-A rank from 1 at the sensorimotor pole to 400 at the association pole. We used this rank primarily in two ways. For region-level analyses, we correlated cortical maps directly against the S-A rank. For decile-level analyses, we sorted regions by ascending S-A rank and averaged them into ten equally sized bins of 40 regions, from the sensorimotor pole (decile 1) to the association pole (decile 10). To characterize developmental trajectories of timescale deflections, we fit generalized additive models (GAMs) using the pygam library. GAMs capture non-linear predictor–outcome relationships through penalized smooth basis functions, making them well-suited to modeling development. Here, our outcome variables were the absolute timescale deflections,|Δtimescale|. We fit a separate GAM for each Schaefer-400 parcel, and, in a parallel analysis, for deflections averaged within S-A axis deciles. Each model took the form. Because each deflection is defined relative to rest, its magnitude depends partly on a participant’s resting-state baseline; participants with longer resting-state timescales have more room for their timescales to reduce during a task. Resting-state timescales also change across development [8,33,35]. As such, we included each participant’s whole-brain mean resting-state timescale as a covariate, so that age effects on deflections reflect changes in timescale flexibility beyond those attributable to developmental shifts in the global resting baseline. The age terms(age) was a penalized cubic B-spline with five basis functions, with the smoothing penaltyλselected separately for each region by generalized cross-validation (GCV). Sex, mean framewise displacement, and each subject’s whole-brain mean resting-state timescale were entered as linear terms, and each series was mean-centered before fitting. To recover the age trajectory, we evaluated each fitted model at 200 equally spaced ages spanning the observed range, holding the covariates at their sample means. The rate of developmental change was estimated using the first derivative of this curve, approximated by finite differences between adjacent ages. For the age-resolved hierarchical analysis (Fig. 3E), we computed the Pearson correlation between regional rates of change and S-A axis rank at each age. We estimated 95% confidence intervals by resampling participants with replacement over 5000 iterations, refitting all GAMs and recomputing the correlation within each iteration. To assess the statistical significance of spatial correlations between cortical maps we used BrainSMASH (Brain Surrogate Maps with Autocorrelated Spatial Heterogeneity) [94]. BrainSMASH generates surrogate maps that preserve the empirical spatial autocorrelation of an input map by fitting the relationship between map values and pairwise inter-region distances (the empirical variogram), then reproducing this variogram through randomization and smoothing. Distances were surface geodesic distances between parcel centroid vertices, defined within each hemisphere; surrogates were generated per hemisphere and concatenated. For any given comparison between two brain maps, we generated surrogates for one of the two maps 10,000 times and computed its correlation with the other, unpermuted map. Then, we compared the observed correlation to the surrogate correlation-null to obtain a non-parametric p-value, denotedpsmash, as the proportion of surrogates whose correlation was at least as extreme as the observed value. This test was two-tailed—comparing surrogate and observed|r|—for all analyses. To relate timescale deflections to behavior, we computed, separately for each Schaefer-400 parcel, the Pearson partial correlation across subjects between the absolute timescale deflection (|Δtimescale|) and each behavioral measure (seeSection 4.3.1). In HCP-YA, covariates were age, sex, in-scanner motion (relative RMS displacement) during both the resting-state and working memory runs, and each subject’s mean resting-state timescale across parcels (n= 966). In HCP-D, covariates were age, sex, mean framewise displacement, and each subject’s mean resting-state timescale across parcels; these analyses included the 536 of 552 participants with CARIT performance data. This procedure yielded, for each behavioral measure, a cortical map of regional brain–behavior correlations. We quantified the hierarchical organization of each map as its correlation with S-A axis rank, and assessed significance against 10,000 BrainSMASH surrogates of the S-A axis (Section 4.7). For the age-split analysis in HCP-D (Fig. 4B), we repeated this procedure separately in participants younger than 15 years (n= 288) and in those aged 15 years and older (n= 248), retaining age as a covariate within each group. As discussed in the main text, the regional rates of change in timescale deflections (|Δtimescale|) transitioned from a broad reduction to a hierarchically patterned mixture during adolescence (Fig. 3), which we modeled as a two-stage developmental process. To locate the boundary between stages, we applied change-point detection to the age-resolved first derivative of the regional deflection fits using the ruptures library [95], configured to return a single change point, which it placed at 15 years (subject bootstrap 95% CI 14.8–15.1 years). We then defined an earlier window (stage 1; ages 8–15) and a later window (stage 2; ages 15–22). For each Schaefer-400 parcel, we integrated the fitted GAM first derivative across each window to obtain the net change in|Δtimescale|over that stage. This integral equals the difference in fitted values at the window endpoints. Dividing each net change by its window duration yielded an annualized rate of change, giving a stage-1 map and a stage-2 map across the cortex (Fig. S3). The 15-year boundary was corroborated by an independent criterion: the age at which the correlation between regional rates of change and the S-A axis first became reliably positive (14.8 years;Fig. 3E), which fell within 0.3 years of it. To characterize the molecular organization of the two developmental stages, we related cortical gene expression to the regional rate of developmental change in timescale deflections. We analyzed microarray data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), the full details of which can be found elsewhere [96]. Briefly, the AHBA includes normalized genome-wide microarray data (58,692 probes) for 3702 tissue samples taken from the cortex and subcortex of six post-mortem adult brains. We have used these data previously in combination within vivoneuroimaging to bridge across multiple scales of neuroscience [52,97]. Using the abagen toolbox (v0.1.3) with default parameters [98], we extracted parcellated whole-brain maps of gene expression following an established processing pipeline [99]. Microarray probes were reannotated [99], and probes not matched to a valid Entrez ID were discarded. Probes with expression intensity below background in at least 50% of samples across donors were removed [100], and, where multiple probes indexed the same gene, we retained the probe with the most consistent pattern of regional variation across donors (i.e., differential stability) [101]. Tissue samples were assigned to parcels using MNI coordinates derived from non-linear registration if they fell within 2 mm of a parcel; unassigned samples were discarded, and samples were not mirrored across hemispheres. Expression values were normalized across genes within each tissue sample, and then across tissue samples within each gene, using a scaled robust sigmoid function [102]. Samples assigned to the same parcel were averaged within each donor and then across donors, yielding a matrixXgeneofNgenes (rows) byPbrain regions (columns). FromXgenewe retained a curated panel of 2,031 brain-expressed genes previously used to study timescales [14], restricted to 347 of 400 Schaefer parcels that had AHBA coverage. We decomposedXgeneusing principal components analysis (PCA). We retained the first three components (PC1–PC3; 18.9%, 11.6%, 9.0% of variance) and report the two that were associated with developmental change (PC1 and PC3) in the main text. To relate each component to development, we correlated its regional score map (Pearson) with the regional rate of change in|Δtimescale|—the first derivative of the deflection GAM (Fig. 3A)—at each of the 200 evaluated ages. This process gave an age-resolved coupling curve per component (Fig. 5B). Significance was assessed against a spatial null. For each component we generated 10,000 BrainSMASH surrogates of its score map and recomputed the correlations at each age. This process created age-specific empirical null distributions that corresponding age-specificp-values were derived from. To characterize each component, we identified the genes with the strongest positive and negative loadings at each pole, retaining only those that were reproducible under resampling. Specifically, we refit the PCA on 500 bootstrap resamples of parcels. Within each resample, every component of the full-sample (reference) solution was matched to the bootstrap component with which its loading vector shared the highest absolute correlation, and that bootstrap component was sign-flipped to align with the reference. For each reference component, we then counted how often each gene re-entered the top 40 loadings of its pole across resamples. A gene was deemed stable, and thus eligible for retention, if it did so in at least 50% of resamples; the 20 most strongly loading eligible genes were shown at each pole. Under this criterion, PC1 loadings were near-perfectly reproducible (median gene stability 100%), whereas PC2 and PC3 were progressively less so (medians of 84% and 76%). We note that loadings formed a long, shallow tail—by participation ratio, roughly 1,400 of the 2,031 genes contributed substantially—so the displayed genes represent a stable but arbitrary cut, and their rank order within a pole should not be interpreted. As anin vivoproxy for intracortical myelin, we used the ratio of T1-weighted to T2-weighted image intensity (T1w/T2w), which is sensitive to cortical myelin content [103]. For each HCP-D participant, we took the MyelinMap_BC_MSMAll T1w/T2w surface map generated by the HCP minimal preprocessing pipelines [86], and averaged vertex values within each Schaefer-400 parcel. We then averaged these parcellated maps across all participants in our HCP-D sample for whom a T1w/T2w map was available, yielding a single group-level map of intracortical myelin. We related this map to the regional rate of developmental change in timescale deflections using the same age-resolved procedure as for the gene-expression components (Section 4.10), with significance assessed against 10,000 BrainSMASH surrogates of the myelin map. As discussed in the main text, a key methodological decision in our analyses was to regress out the influence of scan structure from the fMRI time series prior to estimating timescales from the autocorrelation function (ACF). For task-based data, this involved removing the influence of the block or event-related structure of the task design. For movie-watching data, this involved removing the movie-clip structure, which resembled a block design. Here, we document the rationale for this decision, as well as its impact. Given the temporally slow nature of fMRI BOLD data, the presence of a block-design or a movie-clip structure necessarily increases the ACF of the underlying time series data, which in turn increases the timescale. This is because the temporal structure of the task is itself autocorrelated. For example, block designs alternate between task conditions that can span tens of seconds, with interleaved periods where no task is presented that may also last several seconds. As such, the corresponding regressors carry most of their power at low frequencies. Additionally, the convolution with the hemodynamic response function extends that dependence further in time. The consequence is that any brain region whose activity tracks this design inherits this dependence. Critically, because we estimate timescales from the decay of the ACF, this inherited structure affects the timescale estimate directly because the ACF is driven by both an intrinsic component and a task-evoked component, and the task-evoked component decays on the timescale of the design rather than that of the region.Fig. S7shows this effect in a single subject from the HCP-YA. As noted above and in the main text, timescales for task scans were estimated from the residuals of a GLM designed to remove scan structure, while timescales for rest were estimated without that GLM. Importantly, projecting a task design out of our fMRI timeseries removes low-frequency variance, and because the timescale is a product of the decay of the ACF, that projection shortens the estimate (as we demonstrate above). As such, part of the task–rest difference that we calltimescale deflections(Figs. 1–5) may be a property of the processing rather than of the various task conditions, and our inferences rely on assuming an effect of those conditions. Here, we conduct a sensitivity analysis designed to address this issue by regressing scan structure out of the resting-state data in the HCP-YA and HCP-D datasets. Specifically, for each task run we constructed a matched control GLM by fitting that task run’s design matrix to a resting-state run from the same participant, matched on acquisition, phase-encoding direction and scan length. Scan length was matched by truncating resting-state runs to the length of the task run, as in the main analyses ofFigs. 2–5(seeSection 4.4), so this control differs from those analyses only in that the task design was additionally projected out of the resting-state data. Critically, this control contains no task-related variance in the underlying data, so any reduction in resting-state timescales following regression is solely a product of processing, and any difference in timescales between a task residual and its own resting-state control is what survives this processing. Applying this control, we found that timescale deflections remained negative in every condition across both datasets (Fig. S11), though their magnitude did diminish. [115]). FD and DVARS are calculated for each functional run, both using their implementations inNipype[following the definitions by 117]. The implementation differs from that of Behzadi et al. in that instead of eroding the masks by 2 pixels on BOLD space, a mask of pixels that likely contain a volume fraction of GM is subtracted from the aCompCor masks.
