title: Task-specific topographic organization of neural activity in the primate lateral prefrontal cortex
author: Xiang, J. D.; Roussy, M.; Corrigan, B.; Gulli, R. A.; Luna, R.; Mofrad, M. H.; Muller, L.; Diedrichsen, J.; Schmitz, T. W.; Martinez-Trujillo, J.; Mur, M.
text: Neurons in the primate lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) flexibly adapt their activity to support diverse cognitive demands. Whether this flexibility is accompanied by changes in the spatial organization of neural population activity remains unclear. Here, we characterized the functional topography of LPFC neural activity in awake, behaving macaques performing three distinct cognitive tasks. Using chronically implanted multi-electrode arrays and topographic similarity analysis (TSA), we found that LPFC topographies were reproducible within tasks but less consistent across tasks. We then separated neural activity into task-tuned and trial-to-trial residual components to determine the basis of these effects. Task-tuned topographies mirrored the overall pattern: they were less consistent across than within tasks, whereas residual topographies remained comparatively stable across tasks. Moreover, task-tuned and residual topographies showed opposing patterns of consistencies. Within tasks, task-tuned topographies were more consistent than residual topographies; across tasks, the pattern re-versed. This dissociation suggests a reproducible spatial organization of task-related activity that reconfigures across tasks. Nevertheless, task-tuned topographies remained significantly correlated across tasks, revealing a shared component of spatial organization. Across all three tasks, topographies exhibited a common spatial scale comparable to that of patterned afferent inputs to LPFC reported in previous anatomical tracing studies. Together, these findings suggest that LPFC functional organization combines a shared spatial scaffold with selective, task-dependent reconfiguration of task-tuned population activity. Flexibility is a defining property of the higher-order cognitive functions supported by the primate lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC). Unlike neural populations in primary sensory areas, where activity is strongly shaped by stimulus features such as frequency and orientation (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968,Merzenich and Brugge, 1973), LPFC neurons adapt their activity according to rules, behavioral context, and feedback, even when sensory inputs are held constant (Duncan, 2001,Freedman et al., 2001,Miller and Cohen, 2001,Lennert et al., 2011,Lennert and Martinez-Trujillo, 2013). This flexibility is shaped in part by the diverse inputs received by LPFC neurons, which are more heterogeneous than those of sensory neurons (Goldman-Rakic, 1988,Fuster, 2015). Consistent with this connectivity, LPFC neurons often exhibit selectivity for combinations of task features, such as firing maximally for a specific conjunction of rule, context, and feedback (Rigotti et al., 2013,Fusi et al., 2016). The heterogeneous and context-dependent selectivity of individual LPFC neurons creates challenges for understanding their functional organization. In visual cortex, neurons with similar stimulus preferences are often spatially clustered, giving rise to functional organizations that can be delineated using stimulus mapping techniques (Wandell et al., 2007). Mapping visual field location (Brewer et al., 2002), stimulus orientation (Fang et al., 2022), or object category (Bell et al., 2009,Bao et al., 2020) reveals spatially organized populations with distinct feature preferences in striate and extrastriate cortex. These stimulus-tuned populations can remain spatially organized over days, weeks, and months (Margolis et al., 2012,McMahon et al., 2014,Cossell et al., 2015), forming stable topographic maps. Such maps are organized at a columnar spatial scale (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968,Tanaka, 1996) that can be detected using multi-electrode arrays and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) (Brewer et al., 2002,Yacoub et al., 2008,Sato et al., 2013). Whether analogous topographies exist for task-related activity in the LPFC remains unclear (Constantinidis et al., 2001,Markowitz et al., 2015,Masse et al., 2017,Bullock et al., 2017,Leavitt et al., 2018). In particular, it is unknown whether LPFC topographies are stable over time (Driscoll et al., 2017,Muysers et al., 2024), reorganize according to task demands, and operate at a spatial scale comparable to topographic organization in other cortical areas. Testing these possibilities has been challenging because the task space sampled in individual experiments is typically limited in both complexity and diversity (Yang et al., 2019a). Primate electrophysiology studies often examine a single task or task features that are insufficiently distinct, and few have examined changes in the spatial organization of population activity across recording sessions or tasks. If task-dependent functional topographies exist in LPFC, two properties are particularly important for understanding their contribution to flexible cognition. First, a functional topography should be sufficiently stable within a task to provide a reproducible spatial organization of task-related activity. Second, it should be sufficiently adaptable across tasks to allow a common LPFC network to support different cognitive demands. Thus, a central question is whether LPFC topography primarily reflects a stable spatial architecture or is reorganized according to task demands. These possibilities are not mutually exclusive. A stable spatial architecture could provide a scaffold for reliable task-specific population codes while allowing their spatial organization to be selectively reconfigured across tasks. Here, we tested these possibilities using a unique dataset of multi-electrode array recordings from the LPFC of two macaques trained to perform three distinct cognitive tasks (Luna et al., 2019,Roussy et al., 2021,Corrigan et al., 2022). The tasks sampled a diverse task space by differentially engaging cognitive demands, embedding stimuli within rich behavioral contexts, and using virtual-reality environments to promote engagement of the LPFC (Doucet et al., 2016). The same tasks were performed across recording sessions spanning multiple days, allowing us to assess the stability of population topography over time and its reorganization across tasks. To identify task-specific functional topographies, we adapted representational similarity analysis (RSA) (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a) to develop topographic similarity analysis (TSA). RSA is widely used in fMRI (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008b,Mur et al., 2013) and electrophysiology studies (Kiani et al., 2007,Freiwald and Tsao, 2010) to characterize the distributed response patterns across measurement channels, such as voxels or electrodes, evoked by individual stimuli. Comparing these response patterns across stimuli yields an estimate of representational geometry that is independent of the specific measurement channels used to obtain the responses (Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013) (Fig. 1). TSA reverses this perspective by focusing on the transpose of the response matrix: the response profile of each measurement channel across multiple task features (Kiani et al., 2015). Comparing these profiles across channels yields an estimate of their functional topography while abstracting from the specific task features used to characterize the response profiles (Fig. 1). Topographic similarity analysis. To test for task-specific functional topographies in the LPFC, we adapt representational similarity analysis (RSA) to topographic similarity analysis (TSA). a) Simulated neural data across experimental conditions (rows) and measurement channels (columns). Higher spike rates in a given channel are denoted by lighter shades. b) RSA abstracts from measurement channels to infer representational geometry. c) TSA abstracts from experimental conditions to infer functional topography. TSA allows for quantitative comparison of functional topographies across time and tasks. TSA offers two advantages for characterizing functional organization in the LPFC. First, it incorporates the full response profile of each channel across multiple task features, allowing spatial organization to reflect context-dependent combinations of neural selectivity rather than tuning to a single predefined feature. Second, by comparing channel-level response profiles through their pairwise similarities, TSA provides a framework for characterizing functional topography across tasks, even when the tasks involve different features (Xiang et al., 2025). We found that LPFC topographies of task-tuned activity were stable within tasks but selectively reorganized across tasks. Task-tuned topographies were more stable across recording sessions than topographies of trial-to-trial residual activity, but showed greater task-dependent change. Despite this reorganization, task-tuned topographies retained a significant shared component across tasks. Finally, the task-specific topographies exhibited a common spatial scale that was consistent with the scale of patterned afferent projections to LPFC described in previous anatomical tracing studies (Goldman-Rakic, 1984,Goldman-Rakic and Schwartz, 1982,Leichnetz et al., 1981). These findings suggest that LPFC functional organization comprises a spatial scaffold that is sufficiently stable to support reproducible task-related activity while remaining adaptable to changing cognitive demands (Xiang et al., 2026,Nettekoven et al., 2026). We recorded the responses of neurons in layers II/III of LPFC areas 8A and 9/46, dorsal and ventral to the principal sulcus, using 96-channel multi-electrode Utah arrays (seeSupplementary Fig. 1for array placement). Each array covered a 4 mm×4 mm cortical area with 10×10 electrodes (∼0.4 mm spacing). Both monkeys performed multiple measurement sessions for each task on separate days (Supplementary Fig. 2). In each session, we simultaneously recorded neural activity from multiple channels on each array (seeSupplementary Table 1for details on active channels). Action potential times were extracted and synchronized to task events. To enable spatial mapping of response preferences across the array, we pooled spiking activity from putative units identified on the same recording channel, summing their activities to create multi-unit activity. Units measured by the same channel exhibited similar response preferences (Supplementary Fig. 3). The pooled activity reflects the activity of subpopulations of neurons within the area covered by each array channel. To characterize the spatial organization of population codes in the LPFC, we first computed task tuning profiles, one for each channel in each session in each task (Fig. 2d-f). Task tuning profiles are vectors that store the firing rates of a channel to the experimental conditions. The time windows for estimating spike rates vary from a few hundred milliseconds up to a few seconds (see Methods for details). These time windows were determined based on task structure, monkey behavior and population decoding results. Next, we computed a channel-by-channel tuning similarity matrix for each array in each session in each task (Fig. 2g). Each element of the matrix represents the Pearson correlation of tuning profiles between a channel pair. The matrix as a whole reflects the similarity of task tuning for all channel pairs, thus capturing the functional topography of task-tuned LPFC activity. This characterization enables quantitative comparison of functional topographies across time and tasks (Figs. 1,2g). For comparative purposes, we also analyzed trial-to-trial fluctuations around the trial averages that define the tuning profiles (see Methods). Topographies based on these spontaneous fluctuations, or residuals, are expected to be consistent across tasks (Cole et al., 2014,Kiani et al., 2015). We first asked whether the functional topography of LPFC neural activity is stable over time and consistent across tasks (ODR, VWM, and CDM). We used TSA to quantify topographic consistency as the correlation between channel-by-channel similarity matrices across sessions (Fig. 2g). Correlations between sessions within the same task quantify the stability of topography over time, whereas correlations between sessions from different tasks quantify its consistency across tasks. For each array in each monkey, topographies were estimated from the overall time series of each channel, independent of task condition. This definition allowed us to assess topographic organization without introducing differences arising from the specific task conditions sampled across sessions. To minimize the effects of changes in array position across recording sessions, we restricted both within-and between-task comparisons to session pairs separated by no more than 20 days. Because some tasks were recorded more than 20 days apart (Supplementary Fig. 2), each monkey contributed between-task comparisons for two of the three tasks. We focus below on the ventral array in both monkeys because recordings from the dorsal array in mT had a lower signal-to-noise ratio (see Methods). For within-task comparisons, topographic consistency was significantly greater than zero for all task pairs examined (one-sided permutation tests,p <0.05;Fig. 3a,b). Thus, despite changes in recording session, neural populations with similar response structure tended to retain similar relative organization within a given task. This pattern indicates that task-dependent changes in LPFC topography occur on top of a partially shared spatial organization, rather than through complete reorganization of the neural landscape. Notably, this combination of task-dependent flexibility and shared organization is also consistent with our companion human fMRI studies, which identified reproducible, taskinvariant organization of the human prefrontal cortex (Xiang et al., 2026,Nettekoven et al., 2026). Together, these findings suggest that prefrontal functional organization can provide a stable spatial scaffold while allowing neural population activity to be flexibly configured according to task demands. We next asked whether the stability and adaptability of LPFC topography differed between task-tuned responses and residual activity. Specifically, we compared topographies derived from task-tuned responses with those derived from trial-to-trial residual fluctuations in neural activity. This comparison allowed us to determine whether the temporal stability and task dependence observed above were characteristic of task-tuned neural activity or instead reflected more general properties of population activity. Within each task, the consistency of task-tuned topographies across sessions was significantly greater than zero (one-sided permutation tests,p <0.05;Fig. 4a,b). Thus, task-tuned topographies exhibited greater task-dependent change than the topographies of concurrent trial-to-trial fluctuations. Together, these results reveal a selective organization of task-tuned LPFC activity: tasktuned topographies were more stable across sessions within a task, yet more adaptive across tasks, than residual topographies. This suggests that the spatial organization of task-tuned neural activity is not only reproducible over time but also selectively reconfigured according to task demands. The analyses above quantified topographic consistency by averaging correlations across session pairs. To complement these comparisons and quantify the relative contributions of temporal separation and task context to topographic variation, we fitted a linear regression model predicting session-pair consistency from time and task (Supplementary Results 1;Supplementary Fig. 6a). Across sessions and arrays, models including both predictors explained, on average, 87% of the variance in session-pair consistency (Supplementary Fig. 6b). Time uniquely accounted for 15% of the explainable variance, whereas task accounted for 40% (Supplementary Fig. 6c). Although the relative contributions varied across arrays, task context accounted for substantially more topographic variation than elapsed time. These results complement the session-pair analyses and further support a greater contribution of task context than temporal separation to changes in LPFC topographic organization. Finally, we tested whether our estimates of topographic consistency were robust to the specific conditions used to derive the low-dimensional projections. Using a split-half analysis with non-overlapping conditions, we asked whether tuning similarity matrices derived from disjoint subsets of conditions yielded consistent topographies. Within-task consistency remained significantly greater than zero for both same-session (Supplementary Fig. 7a) and cross-session comparisons (Supplementary Fig. 7b; one-sidedt-tests,p <0.05), demonstrating that the observed topographies were not driven by a particular subset of task conditions. Importantly, the between-task results also reproduced the main findings. Between-task consistency remained significantly below the corresponding noise ceiling estimated from withintask consistency (Supplementary Fig. 7b; one-sidedt-tests; mB ventral: VWM-CDM,t(36) =−15.04,p <0.001; mB dorsal: VWM-CDM,t(36) =−43.68,p <0.001; mT ventral: VWM-ODR,t(3) =−5.08,p= 0.007). These results demonstrate that the task-dependent component of LPFC topographic organization is robust to variation in condition sampling. Together, these analyses reveal that LPFC functional topography is both stable over time and adaptive across tasks, with these properties particularly pronounced for task-tuned neural activity. Task-tuned topographies were more stable across sessions within a task than residual topographies, yet showed greater task-dependent variation across tasks. At the same time, task-tuned topographies remained significantly correlated across tasks, indicating that task-dependent reorganization occurs on top of a partially shared spatial organization. Thus, task-tuned neural activity exhibits a distinctive combination of temporal stability and taskdependent flexibility, suggesting that LPFC maintains a structured spatial organization that can be selectively reconfigured according to task demands. Given that feature-tuned neurons are known to cluster in populations at the spatial scale of cortical columns (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968,Merzenich and Brugge, 1973,Tanaka, 1996,Masse et al., 2017), the observed task-specific functional topographies in the LPFC (Fig. 4;Supplementary Fig. 5) may be expressed spatially by clusters of similarly tuned neurons with an adaptive task-dependent ‘fingerprint’. These observations suggest that the task-specific functional topographies in the LPFC converge on a common spatial scale. To quantify this spatial scale, we fit Laplacian functions to the observed ACFs. Modeling the ACFs with Laplacians provides a concise description of the observed spatial decay using a limited set of parameters, allowing us to derive a scalar estimate of spatial scale. This estimate, represented by the full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) of the fitted Laplacians, captures the spatial extent of similarity in tuning. The FWHM is interpreted as the width of the 2-dimensional kernel needed to smooth spatially independent tuning profiles to yield the same degree of clustering we observe in the data (Diedrichsen et al., 2011). The median of the FWHMs across sessions and tasks is 369 +/-107µm (SD), suggesting the existence of fine-grained, or mesoscale, clusters of similarly tuned neural populations on the arrays. To visualize the spatial structure of tuning similarity across the arrays, we applied two-dimensional (2D) multidimensional scaling (MDS) to the correlation distances between channel tuning profiles. Channels were color-coded according to their positions in the 2D MDS space, and these colors were projected back onto the corresponding arrays (Kiani et al., 2015) (Fig. 5b). Within each session, channels with similar tuning profiles across all conditions of a given task were assigned similar colors, allowing the spatial clustering of functionally similar channels to be visualized. Importantly, the color mapping was defined independently for each session; therefore, similar colors indicate similar response profiles only within a session and do not imply similarity across sessions or tasks. Despite this session-specific color coding, the spatial distribution of similarly tuned channels revealed clear clustering, with highly similar organization across sessions within tasks and moderate-to-weak similarity across tasks. Across all maps, these clusters exhibited a consistent spatial scale (Fig. 5c;Supplementary Fig. 8c,d). To further emphasize the spatial scale of these clusters, we smoothed the 2D MDS array maps using 2D Gaussian kernels with full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) values matching the empirically derived cluster sizes from the fitted Laplacian functions. Across all three tasks, this visualization highlighted the mesoscale organization of task-tuned population activity, with clusters spanning a spatial scale similar to that observed in sensory cortical areas such as V1, where mesoscale functional organization reflects tuning to stimulus features (Fang et al., 2022,Yacoub et al., 2008) (Fig. 5d). Our findings suggest that task-tuned LPFC responses are spatially clustered at the mesoscale, similar to sensory cortical areas (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968,Merzenich and Brugge, 1973,Tanaka, 1996,Fang et al., 2022,Yacoub et al., 2008). We next asked what properties of cortical organization might shape this spatial scale. One possibility is that the afferent input projections from different regions of the brain may exhibit a spatial scale of clustering in the LPFC similar to that of the functional topographies observed in the present work. This would suggest that the structural organization of long-range inputs into the LPFC shapes the functional topographies of its task-tuned responses. We used TSA to characterize the functional topography and temporal stability of task-tuned LPFC neural activity in awake, behaving macaques performing three distinct cognitive tasks (Luna et al., 2019,Roussy et al., 2021,Corrigan et al., 2022). We found that task-tuned LPFC topographies were stable across recording sessions within a task but selectively reorganized across tasks. This within-task stability was greater for task-tuned activity than for concurrent trial-to-trial residual activity, whereas task-tuned topographies showed greater task-dependent reorganization. Thus, the spatial organization of task-tuned LPFC activity was both more reproducible within a task and more sensitive to task context than that of residual activity. Despite this reorganization, task-tuned topographies retained a significant shared component across tasks. Finally, all three task-specific topographies exhibited a common spatial scale consistent with the scale of patterned afferent inputs to LPFC reported in previous anatomical tracing studies. Together, these findings suggest that LPFC functional organization comprises a partially stable spatial scaffold on which task-dependent population activity is selectively configured. Similar principles of shared and task-dependent organization were observed in our companion human fMRI studies (Xiang et al., 2026,Nettekoven et al., 2026). TSA provides a flexible approach for characterizing the spatial organization of high-dimensional LPFC response profiles. Unlike traditional stimulus-mapping approaches (Wandell et al., 2007), TSA does not require topographic organization to be defined along a single, explicitly parameterized feature dimension. Instead, it identifies spatial patterns of similarity among channels based on their complete response profiles across task conditions (Kiani et al., 2015) (Fig. 1). This distinction is particularly relevant for LPFC, where neuronal responses can reflect mixtures of task features and their interactions (Duncan, 2001,Miller and Cohen, 2001,Rigotti et al., 2013). TSA therefore provides a means of characterizing spatial organization without prespecifying which task features should define a map, while allowing topographies derived from different tasks to be compared within a common framework. The use of a noise ceiling further provides a useful reference for interpreting the magnitude of topographic consistency (Nili et al., 2014). Nevertheless, TSA does not by itself distinguish whether spatial similarity arises from shared task tuning, intrinsic connectivity, common afferent inputs, or other sources of correlated activity. Interpreting LPFC topography therefore requires consideration of both task structure and underlying connectivity (Xiang et al., 2025). Task mapping in LPFC presents challenges that differ fundamentally from stimulus mapping in sensory cortex. Visual stimulus dimensions such as location, orientation, and object category can be precisely parameterized, whereas task features often involve abstract relationships among rules, contexts, goals, and temporal contingencies (Duncan, 2001,Miller and Cohen, 2001,Rigotti et al., 2013,Kiani et al., 2015,Bullock et al., 2017,Leavitt et al., 2018). This distinction may help explain why the task-specific topographies observed here were not completely independent. All three tasks contained visual stimuli and shared aspects of their temporal structure, including successive cue and target phases. Some of the shared topographic organization may therefore reflect tuning to task features common across tasks, including shared temporal abstractions or task structures (Bein and Niv, 2025). Future studies could more systematically sample a high-dimensional task space in which task, stimulus, context, and behavioral demands are independently manipulated (Yang et al., 2019a,Xiang et al., 2025). Such designs would make it possible to determine whether LPFC topographies vary continuously with task similarity and to test computational accounts of prefrontal function, including biased competition (Desimone and Duncan, 1995,Schmitz and Duncan, 2018) and compositional coding (Duncan et al., 2017,Yang et al., 2019b). The comparison between task-tuned and residual activity provides an additional constraint on the interpretation of LPFC topography. The greater within-task stability of task-tuned topographies suggests that task-related activity is embedded within a reproducible spatial organization rather than being a transient property of individual recording sessions. In contrast, the greater cross-task consistency of residual topographies indicates that some aspects of population organization are comparatively insensitive to task context. Together, these findings indicate that task context selectively reorganizes the spatial organization of task-tuned activity while leaving other aspects of population organization more conserved. Importantly, this distinction argues against a simple model in which the entire LPFC population is globally reorganized whenever task demands change (Cole et al., 2013). Instead, task context appears to modulate a pre-existing spatial organization, producing task-specific configurations of population activity. The spatial organization observed here may reflect, in part, the heterogeneous connectivity of LPFC. Unlike sensory cortices, in which relatively local and homogeneous connectivity contributes to the formation of fine-scale stimulus maps (Yacoub et al., 2008), LPFC receives a diverse set of long-range projections as well as local intrinsic connections (Goldman-Rakic, 1988,Xu et al., 2022,Levitt et al., 1993, González-Burgos et al., 2000,Constantinidis et al., 2001,Arnsten, 2013). Anatomical tracing studies have demonstrated patterned long-range projections to LPFC from multiple cortical areas, including posterior parietal cortex and contralateral LPFC, with some projections forming elongated stripes of connectivity (Goldman-Rakic, 1988,Levitt et al., 1993). We estimated the spatial scale of these afferent patterns from a structural connectivity map reported by Goldman-Rakic and colleagues (Goldman-Rakic, 1984). The resulting scale was similar to the∼300–400µm spatial scale of the functional topographies observed here, despite the substantial methodological differences between the structural and functional measurements. Patterned long-range inputs, together with local horizontal connections that form patchy networks (González-Burgos et al., 2000), could therefore contribute to the spatial clustering of task-related responses. Recent multimodal studies of macaque LPFC have begun to bridge this structure-function gap using microstimulation (Xu et al., 2022) and diffusion MRI (Griffa et al., 2023). Consistent with the present findings, these studies suggest that heterogeneous long-range structural projections may provide a scaffold for functional organization on which task-dependent activity patterns are expressed (Cole et al., 2016,Xu et al., 2022). The correspondence between the spatial scale of macaque LPFC topographies and that of patterned afferent inputs also raises the possibility that analogous functional organization could eventually be investigated in humans. The∼300–400µm scale observed here is challenging for conventional task-based fMRI, but submillimeter functional organization can be resolved in other cortical systems using ultra-high-field imaging (Yacoub et al., 2008). If comparable LPFC organization can be detected with high-resolution fMRI, TSA could provide a common analytical framework for linking human and macaque functional organization. Human fMRI would permit exploration of a substantially broader task space, including abstract cognitive operations that are difficult to manipulate systematically in macaques, whereas macaque electrophysiology provides the temporal and spatial resolution needed to characterize the underlying neural dynamics (Sejnowski et al., 2014). Such cross-species approaches could help establish whether the spatial scaffold identified here represents a conserved organizational principle of primate LPFC. Several limitations should be considered. First, our ability to compare tasks was constrained by the recording schedule and by potential changes in electrode-array position across sessions. We therefore restricted comparisons to sessions separated by no more than 20 days, limiting the number of task pairs that could be examined in each animal. Second, the three tasks necessarily shared some sensory and temporal features, making it difficult to attribute cross-task similarity to a particular computational or cognitive factor. Third, the correspondence between functional topographic scale and anatomical input patterns is suggestive rather than causal. The observed spatial scale could reflect a combination of long-range afferent inputs, local connectivity, anatomical geometry, and properties of the recording array. Future experiments combining electrophysiology with direct measures of structural connectivity and systematically varied task spaces will be important for determining the mechanisms that generate and reconfigure LPFC topography (Xiang et al., 2025). In summary, TSA revealed that task-tuned LPFC activity has a reproducible spatial organization that is stable within tasks but selectively reorganized across tasks. The greater within-task stability and greater cross-task reorganization of task-tuned activity relative to residual activity indicate that task context selectively configures, rather than globally reorganizes, LPFC population organization. At the same time, the persistence of shared topographic structure across tasks suggests that this flexibility operates within a partially conserved spatial scaffold. The common spatial scale observed across tasks, together with its correspondence to previously described patterns of long-range cortical connectivity, further suggests that anatomical organization may constrain the spatial structure within which task-dependent activity is configured. These findings provide evidence for a mode of prefrontal organization in which stable spatial structure and flexible task-dependent population coding coexist. We recorded LPFC neural activity in two male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta, monkey B and monkey T, 10 and 9 years old) while they were performing three different cognitive tasks across multiple measurement sessions. Then a target was presented for 1000 ms before it disappeared. The monkeys were asked to maintain fixation for a variable length delay period (1400 ms −2500 ms, median = 1800 ms) and upon extinction of the fixation point, make a saccade towards the remembered target location to get a reward. More information on the ODR task can be found in (Luna et al., 2019). During the cue period, a visual cue (red rectangle) was presented in one of the nine target locations for 3 seconds, then disappeared. After a 2-second delay, the monkeys navigated towards the remembered target location at a constant speed using a joystick. Upon reaching the correct target, the monkeys received a reward. More information on the VWM task can be found in (Roussy et al., 2021). In other words, the decision context was specified by the texture of the walls. We will refer to the coloured disks as goals in subsequent text. More information on the CDM task can be found in (Corrigan et al., 2022). Two 96-channel Utah arrays (4 mm×4 mm coverage, 10×10 electrodes, spaced at 0.4 mm, 1.5 mm in length) (Blackrock Microsystems) were chronically implanted in the left LPFC in each animal. They were located anterior to the arcuate sulcus and on the ventral and dorsal side of the posterior end of the principal sulcus, targeting layers II/III of cortical areas 8A and 9/46 (seeSupplementary Fig. 1for array placement). Neural data were recorded using a Cerebus Neural Signal Processor (Blackrock Microsystems). The neural signal was digitized (16 bit) at a sampling rate of 30 kHz. Data were online sorted to identify putative units on each recording channel in real-time. Action potential times were extracted and synchronized to task events. For all tasks, eye positions were monitored using SR Research EyeLink 1000, at a sampling rate of 500 Hz. Both monkeys performed multiple measurement sessions for each task. Sessions were acquired on separate days. Monkey B performed 4 sessions for the ODR task, 11 sessions for the VWM task, and 6 sessions for the CDM task. Monkey T performed 4 sessions for the ODR task, 8 sessions for the VWM task, and 9 sessions for the CDM task. Three sessions were excluded from analysis in the VWM task for monkey T due to low trial numbers across experimental conditions. See Supplementary Figure 2 for further details on the included sessions. The dorsal array in monkey T was excluded from analysis due to low signal-to-noise ratio of recordings at the time of the experimental sessions, which makes it difficult to map the topography of the array. Quality assurance data generated by the Blackrock software before each recording session indicated potential crosstalk in 4 out of the 60 sessions analyzed across monkeys and arrays. This affected only one monkey, array, and task (monkey B, dorsal, CDM) in 4 of the 6 measurement sessions for that task. To assess the robustness of the spatial scale results (Fig. 5) to potential crosstalk, we performed a conservative control analysis. For the affected sessions, we removed any shared spikes for channel pairs with more than 10% shared spikes, which impacted approximately 50 channel pairs on average per session. Results from this analysis confirmed that spike removal had minimal effects on the estimated spatial scale (Supplementary Fig. 8) and did not affect the pattern of results for the consistency analyses reported in Supplementary Figure 5. To enable spatial mapping of response preferences across the array, we pooled units recorded from the same channel by summing up their spiking activities. Units recorded from the same channel exhibited similar response preferences (Supplementary Fig. 3). We refer to the pooled activity as multi-unit activity. The pooled activity reflects the activity of subpopulations of neurons within the area covered by an array channel. This area has an estimated diameter of 300 microns based on the impedance of the electrodes. For each channel in each session in each task, we first computed trial-specific spike rates for each experimental condition and applied a square root transformation to the spike rates to account for the Poisson-like increase of variability with increasing mean firing rates (Yu et al., 2009,Arbuckle et al., 2020). We next computed trial-averaged spike rates by averaging across trials of the same experimental condition, which yielded a task tuning profile for each channel. More specifically, in the ODR task, the tuning profile for a channel was defined as the trial-averaged spike rates for the 4 quadrants (16 targets were grouped into 4 quadrants based on their location in the retinotopic reference frame, labelled 1-4 starting from bottom left, clockwise) during cue (1000 ms), delay (1400 ms −2500 ms, median = 1800 ms), and response (first 500 ms) epochs. In the VWM task, the tuning profile for a channel was defined as the trial-averaged spike rates for the 9 target locations during cue (3000 ms), delay (2000 ms), and response (first 500 ms) epochs. In the CDM task, the tuning profile for a channel was defined as the trial-averaged spike rates for the combinations of decision contexts and goal configurations in time windows before and after context onset (50 ms before, 600 ms after), goals onset (500 ms before, 300 ms after), and decision onset (500 ms before, 500 ms after). Goal configuration refers to the location of the disk colour that is associated with wood. If the colour associated with wood is on the left-hand side at the bifurcation, the trial is in configuration 1, otherwise configuration 2. We then subtracted out the mean firing rate across all experimental conditions. The meancentered tuning profile reflects the modulation in firing rate by the experimental conditions, providing a rich characterization of channel tuning in each task. The time windows used for computing tuning profiles were based on trial structure, monkey behavior, and neural population decoding results. Results of subsequent analyses do not critically depend on the exact time windows used. For each array in each session in each task, we computed a channel-by-channel tuning similarity matrix. Elements in this matrix reflect the Pearson correlation of tuning profiles between channel pairs. The matrix reflects the similarity of task tuning for all channel pairs, thus capturing the similarity structure of tuning across the array. As such, it provides the basis for mapping of tuning similarity across the cortical sheet. This approach can be used to study functional topography (Kiani et al., 2015,Ito and Murray, 2023). Importantly, the tuning similarity matrices abstract from the specific experimental conditions used in a single task, which enables comparison of functional topographies between tasks. For comparative purposes, we also analyzed trial-to-trial fluctuations about the trial averages that define the tuning profiles. Topographies based on these spontaneous fluctuations are expected to be consistent across tasks (Kiani et al., 2015,Cole et al., 2014). We partitioned the measured spiking activity in two components: task-tuned activity and spontaneous activity or residuals. For each channel in each session in each task, we computed task-tuned activity by replacing the firing rate of each trial with the mean firing rate across trials of the same experimental condition. This corresponds to a tuning profile where the trial-averaged spike rate for each condition is repeated as many times as the number of trials for that condition. We computed residuals by subtracting out the task-tuned activity from the measured spiking activity. We then computed topographies for task-tuned activity and residuals as described in the previous section, but replaced tuning profiles by task-tuned or residual activity vectors. Results reported inFig. 4are based on the task-tuned and residual topographies, allowing for a direct comparison between the two. To assess whether the functional topographies are consistent across time and across tasks, we computed the Pearson correlation of tuning similarity matrices across session pairs within and between tasks (seeFig. 2g). Because the matrices are symmetric, we computed correlation coefficients using the upper triangular vector of the matrix. The consistency of functional topographies within and between tasks was estimated as the mean across session pairs. To control for array shifting across time, we only included sessions spaced apart no more than 20 days for within-as well as between-task comparisons. Given that data for some tasks were acquired more than 20 days apart (seeSupplementary Fig. 2), between-task comparisons are based on two out of three tasks for each monkey. To determine whether the estimated consistencies are significantly higher than chance, we permuted channel locations on the array to simulate the null hypothesis of no consistent spatial organization. We performed 1,000 permutations, each yielding an estimate of our test statistic under the null hypothesis. If the actual consistency fell within the top 5 percent of the simulated null distribution, we rejected the null hypothesis of no consistent spatial organization. This corresponds to a one-sided test usingp <0.05 for significance thresholding. For between-task consistencies, we did not only test if they were higher than expected for no consistent spatial organization, we also tested if they were lower than expected for a fully consistent spatial organization. We did so by estimating a noise ceiling for between-task consistencies. For each task pair, the noise ceiling is defined as the geometric mean of the within-task consistencies, which reflects the expected maximum between-task consistency given the noise in the data (Vul et al., 2009). We compared the observed between-task consistencies against the noise ceiling using a one-sided one-sample t-test across session pairs. We compared consistencies of task-tuned and residual topographies using a two-sided paired-samples t-test across session pairs. To assess the spatial scale of the functional topographies, we computed spatial autocorrelation functions (ACFs) of channel tuning profiles on the array. The spatial ACFs were computed in a cross-validated fashion to reduce the impact of spatially autocorrelated noise. Trials in a measurement session were split into two halves. Tuning profiles were estimated for each half. We used global Moran’s I as a measure of spatial autocorrelation (Moran, 1950), which is defined as:whereNis the total number of channels on the array;XAiis the mean-centered tuning profile for theithchannel in the first half;XBjis the mean-centered tuning profile for thejthchannel in the second half;X-is the mean-centered tuning profile averaged across all channels, estimated for each half separately; andwijis either 1 or 0 (if channeliand channeljare spaced within a specified spatial range,wijequals 1; otherwise 0). The numerator estimates the cross-validated covariances of tuning profiles between channel pairs spaced at a certain distance. The denominator estimates the cross-validated variances of tuning profiles across all the channels on the array. To account for the fact that some channels appear more frequently than others in the covariance estimates, the variance can be estimated using the following formula as in (King et al., 2019): Using this formula for estimating the variance ensures thatIis bounded between −1 and 1. A positiveIindicates that channels spaced at the given distance have similar tuning profiles; a negativeIindicates that channels spaced at the given distance have dissimilar tuning profiles. To compute spatial ACFs, we systematically varied the spatial distance between channels, from including only immediately neighbouring channels (0<distance≤0.4 mm) to channels that are spaced apart more than one channel width but no more than two (0.4 mm<distance≤0.8 mm), continuing these steps up and till nine channel widths (3.2 mm<distance≤3.6 mm), and computed the spatial autocorrelation for each distance. At distance 0, the cross-validated covariances are the same as cross-validated variances, leading to a spatial autocorrelation of 1. We computed an ACF for each array in each session in each task. To quantify the spatial scale of the functional topographies, we fit a Laplacian function to the spatial ACFs. The Laplacian function captures the exponential decay of channel tuning similarity as the distance between channels increases. The Laplacian function used is defined as follows:whered ≥0 reflects the distances; andsis a fitted value, reflecting the smoothness of the curve. The full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) of the Laplacian curve can be computed usingsvia the following formula:The FWHM of a fitted Laplacian function is equivalent to the FWHM of the 2-dimensional kernel required to smooth an array whose channel tuning profiles are spatially independent, to yield the degree of spatial autocorrelation we observe in the data (Diedrichsen et al., 2011). We therefore use the FWHM as an estimator of spatial scale. To visualize the spatial structure of tuning similarity on the arrays, we converted the correlations in the tuning similarity matrix to correlation distances, and applied 2D multidimensional scaling (MDS) to the distances. Channels were colour-coded based on their location in the 2D MDS space and projected back to the arrays. In the colour space, hue reflects polar angle, and saturation reflects eccentricity. Similar colours indicate similar tuning profiles. As a check, we computed the variance explained in the high-dimensional distances by the low-dimensional distances for a range of MDS dimensions (1-10). We computed the variance explained by first correlating the correlation distances between points (channels) in the original high-dimensional space with the Euclidean distances between points in the low-dimensional MDS space, and then squaring the correlation coefficients (Kiani et al., 2015). The 2D MDS space explains around 80% of the variance in the original high-dimensional space across monkeys, arrays, and tasks. To relate the spatial scale of the observed functional topographies to prior anatomical tracing work, we repeated the spatial autocorrelation analysis on a reconstructed structural map of afferent input to macaque LPFC (Goldman-Rakic, 1984). This structural map shows the terminal field distributions of callosal fibers projecting from the principal sulcus in one hemisphere to the principal sulcus in the other hemisphere (Goldman and Nauta, 1977). The fibers terminate in a stripe-like pattern, reflecting interdigitation of the contralateral callosal fibers with associational fibers from the ipsilateral parietal cortex (Goldman-Rakic and Schwartz, 1982). The structural map suggests the existence of cortical columns in LPFC, which have been reported to have a width of 300 to 700 microns (Goldman-Rakic, 1984,Goldman and Nauta, 1977,Leichnetz et al., 1981,Goldman-Rakic and Schwartz, 1982,Bugbee and Goldman-Rakic, 1983). To assess the spatial scale of the structural map, we randomly sampled 210 cortical patches with 4×4 mm2coverage from the map, simulating array placements. Sampled cortical patches were downsampled to 10×10 to match the measurement resolution of the Utah arrays used in our study. We assessed the spatial ACF for each sampled patch and plotted the distribution of ACFs across samples. We then examined whether the ACFs observed for the task-tuned topographies fall within the distribution derived from the anatomical tracing map (seeFig. 6). Source Data are provided with this paper. Raw data supporting the findings of this paper are available from MR, BC, RL, JMT upon reasonable requests. MATLAB code used for analyzing the data is available from github (https://github.com/jkderrick028/topoPFC) or from JDX. JDX, TWS, JMT, MM conceptualized the work. MR designed the VWM task, collected and preprocessed the data. BC, RAG designed the CDM task, collected and preprocessed the data. RL designed the ODR task, collected and preprocessed the data. RAG performed surgical implantations. JMT contributed to experimental design. JDX analyzed the data and wrote the manuscript. MHM, LM, JD, MM provided analysis advice. JDX, TWS, JMT, MM edited the manuscript. Similarity of tuning profiles of units measured by the same channel. Functional topographies in the LPFC are stable across time but adaptive across tasks. Comparing functional topographies for task-tuned responses and residuals. To assess the relative contributions of task and time to topographic change, we quantified the unique variance explained in the consistency of tuning similarity matrices by task and by time. This was achieved using linear regression, with the full model defined as follows:whereyis the consistency of tuning similarity matrices between session pairs (seeSupplementary Fig. 6a),X1andX2are indicator predictors for task (task A:X1= 1,X2= 0; task B:X1= 0,X2= 1; between task A and B:X1= 0,X2= 0), andX3is a continuous predictor for time (days between sessions in a pair). We first computed the variance explained by the full model. We next built a reduced model by removing the task predictors (X1andX2), and computed the variance explained by the reduced model. The difference in variance explained by the full model and the reduced model is the unique variance explained by task. We used the same strategy to compute the unique variance explained by time (X3). Results for each monkey and array are shown inSupplementary Fig. 6b,c. The full model provides a strong fit to the variance in the consistency of topography across session pairs, explaining 93% of the variance in the mB dorsal array, 78% in the mB ventral array, and 90% in the mT ventral array (Supplementary Fig. 6b). In two out of three arrays, the unique variance explained by task is substantial (Supplementary Fig. 6c): 32% of explainable variance in the mB dorsal array, 5% in the mB ventral array, and 82% in the mT ventral array. For comparison, the unique variance explained by time in these same arrays is 4%, 36%, and 5% of explainable variance, respectively. Explainable variance here refers to the variance explained by the full model. In summary, across monkeys and arrays, task uniquely accounts for 40% of the explainable variance, while time explains 15%. These results underscore the adaptability of the LPFC topography across tasks relative to its stability over time. Unique contributions of task and time to topographic change in the LPFC. Robustness of functional topography to different low-dimensional projections of the data. Robustness of observed spatial scale to removal of shared spikes in sessions with potential crosstalk. Linking task-specific functional topographies to structural maps for varying stripe sizes. This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), Neuronex (ref. FL6GV84CKN57) grants, Ontario Graduate Scholarship, Jonathan & Joshua Memorial Graduate Scholarship in Mental Health Research, Mitacs Globalink Graduate Fellowship and McGill David G. Guthrie Fellowship. This work was further supported by BrainsCAN at the University of Western Ontario through the Canada First Research Excellence Fund (CFREF). This version of the manuscript has been revised to clarify the analytical framework and interpretation of task-specific topographic organization in the macaque lateral prefrontal cortex. We have refined the description of the topographic similarity analysis and clarified the distinction between task-related activity and residual trial-to-trial fluctuations. We have also strengthened the presentation of within-task stability and across-task reorganization, highlighting how task-related neural activity retains a shared spatial component while reorganizing across cognitive tasks. Finally, we have refined the discussion of the spatial scale of functional topography and its relationship to previously described anatomical input patterns, while avoiding causal interpretations not directly supported by the data. title: A note on the responsiveness of neurons
author: Wernecke, H. O.; Kumar, A.
text: The time constant of biological neurons is typically around 5-20ms. This raises the question of how a system made of slow devices can generate and respond to faster signals. A potential solution is a population of uncorrelated neurons that, as a whole, can respond arbitrarily fast despite individual slow neurons. The response speed of a neuron or a population of neurons is often defined as how quickly neurons increase or decrease their firing rate given a change in the input, similar to a reaction time. Less emphasis is placed on the recovery time - the duration to transition and settle in a stationary state again in response to the change in the input. Here, we investigate the reaction time and the recovery time of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons given a change in, either the mean input drive, or input fluctuation level. In general, neurons react faster and fire quicker the larger the change in the input. Moreover, the closer the membrane potential is to the threshold, the faster the reaction. We observe that neurons react faster to increased input fluctuations than to stronger mean drive. Complementary, the recovery time is systematically longer the larger the input change. Also, the closer the neurons’ potentials are to the threshold, the longer it takes the neuron to recover. Most interestingly, the baseline firing of the neuron strongly determines whether recovery is faster when the change happens in the mean drive or the fluctuation level. This observation suggests that communication via the mean drive and the fluctuation level could target different aspects of the overall response - quick reaction time and the recovery speed - based on the initial baseline activity. The membrane time constant of biological neurons is considerably slow (5-20ms) (Destexhe, Rudolph, and Paré 2003). This raises the question of how a system made of slow devices can generate and respond to faster signals. A potential solution to this is that when neurons in a population are uncorrelated, the population as a whole can respond arbitrarily fast despite slow neurons (Ekeberg 1993;Tchumatchenko et al. 2011). In anin vivosetting, the balance of excitation and inhibition can render the population uncorrelated and thereby increase the response speed (Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky 1996). When considering the response time of a neuron or population of neurons, the emphasis is often placed on how quickly neurons react to the change in the input, measured by the instantaneous increase (or decrease) in the output firing rate (Silberberg et al. 2004;Tchumatchenko et al. 2011). Given a stimulus to a system or a neuron, the concept of the time scale can be interpreted as the time the system, or the neuron, takes until it reaches a steady state again. A neural population may exhibit a fast initial response, but the time to reach steady state may be slower – dominated by an ‘effective’ refractory period or even entail oscillatory activity (Knight, Omurtag, and Sirovich 2000;Ekeberg 1993;Tchumatchenko et al. 2011). Consequently, the population may display various activity responses to different perturbations or stimuli. Response transients pose a serious challenge for information representation in the neurons and can even cause large decoding errors (Lenninger et al. 2023). Earlier investigation of reaction time assumed that the network was operating in a linear regime and neurons and synapses had a single time constant. This is far from reality. Even the simplest neuron models (e.g. leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron) display non-linearities, and hence can express various time scales depending on the operating point and the stimulus. On the far side of this scale, the dynamics of a biological neuron are shaped by a multitude of ion channels, and hence invariably display a temporal manifold (Marom 2010). Non-linearities may shape the temporal manifold and consequently affect the reaction time, as well as the recovery speed. In this work, we focus on the recovery time, i.e., the time the population requires to settle in a steady state after a stimulus is presented. To this end, we injected Gaussian white noise (GWN) into neural populations and varied the noise parameters to mimic a stimulus. We found that recovery time was much longer than the reaction time. Interestingly, the non-linear reset mechanism is sufficient to introduce various time scales. The reaction time as well as the recovery time depended strongly on the baseline set point and the stimulus modality (whether the stimulus was a change in the input mean Δµ, the variance Δσor both Δµ &Δσ). When the stimulus pushed the neural population from baseline to the steady state, and then being relaxed again, the comparison of recovery times revealed that neurons exhibit a hysteresis in their activity. Furthermore, the presentation of transient stimuli exposed a non-monotonic relationship of the recovery time to both, the number of stimuli as well as the stimulus duration. These insights indicate the trade-off between fast, memoryless communication and history-dependent processing. Consequently, these findings suggest that the communication among neural networks may be finely tuned to typical activity (persistent or pulse-like stimuli) and connectivity characteristics (which affect the activity set point and the stimulus modality) of the transmitting population. Furthermore, the activity and connectivity can be adapted by neuromodulation in a context-dependent manner. We simulated a population of 100 000 LIF neurons whose sub-threshold membrane potentialU(t) dynamics were governed bywhereτ= 15ms was the membrane time constant andI(t) was the external input current. The input resistance wasR= 60MΩ. A neuron elicited a spike when the membrane potential crossed a thresholdθ= 20mV, and then its membrane potential was reset toVr= 0mV. After which, the neuron was refractory for tref= 2ms. The external currentI(t) is the total input received by the neurons. All parameters of the network are given inTable 1. The external inputI(t) consisted of a mean driveµand the fluctuation levelσ: Here,η(t) was the Gaussian white noise with ⟨η(t)⟩ = 0 and ⟨η(t)η(t′)⟩ =δ(t−t′). Each neuron received an independent noise term. The input pushed the neural activity to the baseline firing rate (FRpre). At tΔ= 500ms, mimicking the presence of a stimulus, the input was modified to reach the target activity FRpost. The simulation continued for tstim= 1000ms, which sufficed to reach a stable FRpost. A neuron can be driven to a firing rate by a pair ofµandσ, we refer to such a pair as set point. For the baseline activity FRpre, we set the mean driveµpreand derive the correspondingσpreutilizing the Siegert formula (Siegert 1951). Similarly, the fluctuation level can be set to obtain the required mean drive. The stimulus altering theI(t) was either a change in the mean current Δµthe fluctuation level Δσor both parameters Δµ &Δσ In case both parameters were changed, the magnitude of the change is half compared to individual parameter changes. We term these the three stimulus modalities. The reaction time was quantified by the change in FR in response to a stimulus (Tchumatchenko et al. 2011). Specifically, the time to the first spike of each neuron was measured for t>tΔ. The recovery time was determined as the time until the neural population reached steady state after presentation of the stimulus. Steady state was considered to be reached once transients were no longer detectable. In stochastic systems, such transient is called the initialization bias. A common approach to estimate the duration of the transient is the Mean-Squared-Error-Reduction (MSER) and its variations (White 1997;Franklin and White 2008). The idea of MSER is to discard initialdsamples that are unrepresentative, as they are far from the sample mean. For a sequence of lengthn, the optimal truncation pointd*is found by minimizing the confidence interval (CI) around the sample mean: Here,s(d) is the large-sample standard deviation of the remaining sequence, andzα/2is the value to calculate the 100(1 −α) CI. More explicitly, for a constantzα/2, the expression becomeswithbeing the sample mean of the remaining sequence starting with sampled+ 1. Note that the length of the whole sequence is largen≫ 30, and the number of discarded samples is low, typicallyd≈ 5% ·n. Moreover, the estimate of the confidence interval is biased for sequentially correlated observations which can be corrected. The application of the Philips-Perron correction, however, does not yield an improvement (Franklin and White 2008). In stochastic systems, bootstrapping is a technique to resample the observations to attain a distribution of estimates. However, the estimates are no longer uncorrelated since the same observation may be observed multiple times. Here, we split the neural population into subgroups of 500 neurons. Next, we pooled the spike times of neurons inb= 50 subgroups corresponding to a total of 25 000 neurons. Then, the peristimulus time histogram (PSTH; binwidth of 2ms) was derived, and the duration of the transient was estimated using MSER. We repeated this processB= 100 times to obtain individual trials. Importantly, the binwidth parameter had only a minor quantitative effect (Suppl. Fig. 1). When analyzing the recurrent neural networks, the excitatory populations were considered the subgroups. Here, the neural spike times ofbRNN= 10 subgroups were pooled, this is equivalent to a total of 50 000 neurons (BRNN=B). The neural activity was characterized as overshooting when the FR was higher than 1.1 FRpost. Given the noise in the activity, many trials fulfilled this criterion. However, the distinction from an undershoot arises from the constraint that an overshooting kernel is required to be larger than the margin for an extended period, that is, for a minimum of 8 consecutive time points. Furthermore, the oscillatory kernel was based on at least one period that the activity is above the margin, as well as a following period of the activity being below 0.9 FRpost. The recurrent neural network (RNN) consisted ofNE= 5 000 excitatory andNI= 1 250 inhibitory neurons, resembling a ratio of 4:1 (Braitenberg and Schüz 1998). The connection probability among the populations wasp= 10% (Braitenberg and Schüz 1998).
