The time of thekth pre-synaptic spike is denoted by. A pre-synaptic excitatory spike evokes a jump in membrane potential ofJE= 0.025mV. The inhibitory synapses wereJI= − 8JEstronger. Thus, the network operated in an inhibition-dominated regime. Moreover, the network exhibited asynchronous-irregular (AI) activity (Brunel 2000; Kumar et al. 2008). The FR of the inhibitory population was set to FRI= 5Hz, driven by the external input with meanµI= 260pA (and corresponding fluctuation levelσI). The stimulus was only presented to the excitatory population to reach FRpost. However, the change in the excitatory population changed the recurrent excitation. Therefore, the external input to the inhibitory population was tuned to maintain its FR, as well as its AI state. All parameters of the network are given inTable 2. Statistical comparisons were performed by applying the one-sided Mann-Whitney U rank test (non-parametric) to evaluate whether the network activity recovered more slowly for the stimulus duration of tstim= 15ms than the other stimulus durations. The significance threshold ofp <0.05 was adjusted using the Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons (3 modalities, 3 numbers of stimulus pulses, 6 set points, 3 stimulus durations). The corrected significance thresholds were:, and. The recovery times for the stimulus duration tstim= 15ms were compared to the other stimulus durations. The recovery was considered to be slower if the significance threshold was crossed in all three comparisons. Only the least significantpvalues are reported in the figure captions. No statistical method was used to predetermine the sample size. All simulations were performed in NEST (Terhorst et al. 2025). The simulations and analyses were performed using custom python scripts. Here, we are interested in characterizing how neurons as a population or as a part of a recurrent network respond to persistent or transient changes in the input. In particular, we want to quantify how much time neurons take to reach a steady state given a perturbation in their inputs. Starting from time tΔ, we injected an external input into neurons already operating at a baseline firing rate FRpreand measured when the neurons’ firing rates reached a stationary target activity FRpost(see Methods). We modeled the input to the neuron as GWN (Brunel 2000), and we considered three different types of input modalities: First, we considered a scenario in which a single LIF neuron fired at baseline and received a persistent step-like stimulus (Fig. 1a). Irrespective of the stimulus modality (Δµ, Δσ, or Δµ &Δσ), we observed three different types of responses (Fig. 1b, c): (1) Undershoot: the neuron firing rate (FR) approaches FRpostasymptotically (Fig. 1c, left and middle column: red and yellow traces). (2) Overshoot: the activity briefly surges before decaying towards the steady state (Fig. 1c, left and middle column: turquoise traces). (3) Oscillatory Response: neural activity displays damped oscillations before reaching FRpost(Fig. 1c, right column: all traces). In our model, the shape of the response kernel depended on both the set point (the pair ofµpreandσpre) as well as the stimulus modality (Δµ, Δσ, or Δµ &Δσ). The response kernel shape varied smoothly as we changed inputs or the operating point. Based on these observations, we can argue that the neurons behave approximately like a second-order filter. Previously, all these response kernels have been observed in both experimental data and numerical simulations (Silberberg et al. 2004; Tchumatchenko et al. 2011;Khorsand and Chance 2008;Knight, Omurtag, and Sirovich 2000;Gerstner 2000). Network architecture, response kernels and reaction time(a)Network architecture: Unconnected neurons receive external GWN input. At timetΔ, the input is changed and the neurons are driven towards a target firing rate FRpost.(b)Response kernels: three response kernels are observed across different setpoints (µpre,σpre) and the stimulus modality (Δµ, Δσor Δµ &Δσ).(c)FR traces for three setpoints, increasing mean driveµprefrom left to right.(d)Individual traces neuronal subgroups (N= 500 neurons) displaying large variability.(e)Reaction time: (left) distribution of the first spike per neuron after the stimulus was presented. (right) Mean and median of the distributions, respectively. One part of the responsiveness of neurons is the time required until a neuron spikes after a stimulus is presented - we call this the reaction time. Here, we observed faster reaction times whenever the fluctuation level was increased as compared to the change in the mean drive of the stimulus (Fig. 1e). Not only was the average reaction time lower, but the distributions were more skewed towards faster reaction times when the fluctuation level was changed. The baseline set point (the pair ofµpreandσpre) to the neurons also affected the reaction time. Increasing the mean input (while reducing the fluctuations to maintain the baseline firing rate) resulted in faster reaction time (Fig. 1e). These observations are consistent with previous results that suggest fast signal transmission when the information is encoded in the input variance (Silberberg et al. 2004). The second part of the responsiveness of neurons is the time to reach a steady state again - we call this the recovery time. Assuming that information is encoded in the FR of neurons, the responses must reach a steady state quickly for fast and accurate encoding of information otherwise transient fluctuations can impair fast inference of inputs (Lenninger et al. 2023). In our model, the recovery time depended on the input modality (Δµ, Δσ, or Δµ &Δσ) as well as the difference between baseline and target FR (Fig. 2a, c). Interestingly, the variance of recovery times was larger when the fluctuation level was increased (Δσ; see turquoise distributions inFig. 2b). This phenomenon may arise from the generally stronger initial response (i.e., overshooting response kernel) for Δσ(seeFig. 2a, c). Note that the variance of both base-line and target firing rates was similar across the input modalities during steady state (Suppl. Fig. 1a-c). Recovery time across various set points.(a)Effect of the target FRpost: Larger differences between the baseline and the target FR exhibit longer recovery times. Moreover, the response kernels changed qualitatively. From left to right: Increase in the target FRpost.(b)Recovery time estimates: (top) Distribution of recovery times across various set points (µpre∈ (220pA, 320pA)). (bottom) Mean (solid) and median (dashed) recovery times.(c)Mean recovery times across target FRpost(low alpha is FRpost= 3Hz, and high alpha is FRpost= 8Hz). Markers indicate the predominant response kernel(▼: undershoot/overdamped; ▲: overshoot/underdamped; : ∼ oscillatory response), and the stronger the alpha, the more prevalent the kernel. Red arrows indicate the mean driveµprethat results in the fastest recovery. When the neurons were in a high-mean set point (i.e., highµprepaired with lowσpre), the recovery times were usually longer (Fig. 2b, c). This happened when the response kernel was of overshooting or oscillatory type - or transitioning towards it (Fig. 2c: response kernels indicated as markers, and their prevalence by the respective alpha value). However, when the responses were undershooting (being overdamped), the minimum recovery time was observed for intermediate values of the mean drive (Fig. 2c: red arrows). While very weakµpredelayed the recovery, strongµpreshifted towards the overshooting (underdamped) re- sponse. Hence, a sweet spot was comparable to a critically damped second-order low-pass filter. In general, large differences in the estimate of recovery time were seen when the response kernel changed qualitatively, e.g., from the asymptotic undershoot to a quick overshoot, or from the overshoot to an oscillatory pattern. Lastly, towards high-mean (and low fluctuation) set points, the response kernels were pre-dominantly of an oscillatory nature. Therefore, the recovery time distributions tended to become bimodal (Fig. 2b) as the steady state is identified either before or after the last low-amplitude cycle (Franklin and White 2008). Naturally, step-like inputs are rare. Continuously varying stimuli or a set of brief discrete events are biologically more plausible. Here, we investigated how pulse trains consisting of one, two, or five discrete stimuli affected the recovery time of neurons. While a single stimulus may provide a metric for a neuron’s bandwidth, multiple stimuli would also emphasize history-dependent activity. Again, neurons were driven towards a target FRpost. However, after a stimulation period Tstim, the input was reset to baseline. The edge case is a long stimulation period Tstim, which is similar to the standard onset (5 →10Hz) and offset (10 →5Hz) dynamics, respectively (Fig. 3a). Input modality affected the onset and offset recovery times. For Δµ, the offset recovery was faster (Fig. 3a: red ✦). For Δσ, in contrast, the onset recovered more quickly (turquoise •). Recovery time for transient stimuli.(a)Onset (left) and offset (middle) of a persistent stimulus, and their respective recovery times (right) across all modalities; •: Onset, ✦: Offset.(b)One stimulus pulse: neural activity over time in response to a single stimulus pulse(left). Recovery times for a stimulus of varying duration (Δµ: red; Δσ: turquoise; Δµ &Δσ: yellow).(c)Same as (b) for two consecutive stimuli separated by Tpause= 5ms.(d)Same as in (b) for five consecutive stimuli. Building on these observations, we reduced the stimulation period to shorter periods than the recovery time of the persistent onset stimulation (except Tstim= 30ms) and estimated the recovery time from the last offset of the pulse train. A pulse-like stimulus revealed how stimulus duration also affected the recovery time had a non-linear relationship with the stimulus duration (Fig 3b). Next, we presented stimuli with two or five pulses (Fig 3 c, d). These experiments revealed that the recovery time also depended on the number of pulses, especially when the neurons were operating in a high-mean set point (highµpreand lowσpre). Although the underlying mechanism is unclear up to now, it was apparent that in several cases the recovery time varied non-monotonically with the number of pulses (Suppl. Fig. 2). Furthermore, in a few cases, the recovery was the slowest for an intermediate pulse duration. This phenomenon was more noticeable when input was modeled as Δσor Δµ &Δσ, e.g., compare the recovery time forTstim= 15ms (dotted; ■) andTstim= 30ms (dash-dotted; +). Finally, the difference in the onset and offset dynamics and dependence of recovery time on pulse duration and count suggest that even unconnected neurons can and do exhibit hysteresis (Fig. 3;Deger et al. (2010)). Thus far, we focused on unconnected neurons. Next, we estimated the recovery time when neurons were part of a recurrent network of excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Fig. 4a; see Methods). We tuned the network (balance of excitation and inhibition) to operate in an asynchronous-irregular state (Brunel 2000; Kumar et al. 2008). Here, the stimulus was only presented to the excitatory population to drive the activity to FRpost. Even the stimulated network’s activity remained asynchronous-irregular with a small increase in the Fano factor (weak correlations) for stronger external mean driveµpre(FF;Fig. 4e). At high mean set points (µpre≥ 300pA), the network dynamics crossed a bifurcation point and displayed synchronous-irregular activity. Recovery time in a recurrent neural network(a)Network architecture: The excitatory and inhibitory populations receive external input. Only the input to the excitatory population was stimulated (see Methods).(b) (c)(left) Activity of the excitatory (solid lines) and the inhibitory (dashed lines) populations (µpre= 260pA). (right) Distributions of recovery times across set points and stimulus modalities.(d)Same as in (c) for the unconnected population receiving feedforward external input.(e)(top) The network exhibited asynchronous-irregular activity in steady state. (bottom) The Fano factor was very low, and displayed a slight increase for higherµpre. Qualitatively, the same three response kernels were observed in the network responses (Fig. 4cleft). Similar to the unconnected population, the recovery time strongly depended on the set point and the stimulus modality (Fig. 4cright). While the response kernels were similar, there were two crucial differences in the network and unconnected neuron population. First, the recurrent network dynamics reduced the total mean drive (Sadeh, Cardanobile, and Rotter 2014). Consequently, the fluctuation level to attain the same FR was higher in the network than in the unconnected population. Hence, a recurrent network with the same external input operated at a set point with higher fluctuations than a comparable population of unconnected neurons (Fig. 4b). Second, in the network setting, the neurons received two different inputs: (1) the external feedforward drive (µpre/postandσpre/post), and (2) the time-varying recurrent synaptic input. To better understand the contribution of the time-varying input, we performed a control experiment: we calculated the total input currentISS(into the exc. population) at steady state (FRpreand FRpost) and then injectedISSinto an unconnected population. Through this approach, we removed the time dependency (and the weak correlations). We found that for matched response kernels, the recovery times were longer for the network than for the unconnected population. This is because of the time-varying component of the input received by the neurons in the network. When the response undershot, the currentI(t) during the transient phase was lower thanISS. Therefore, the unconnected population reacted and recovered faster. On the other hand, an overshooting kernel caused temporarily stronger recurrent excitation (I(t)> ISS). This in turn led to a stronger overshoot and consequently, longer recovery times of the network activity compared to those of the unconnected population. In rare cases, the temporarily weaker recurrent excitation evoked an undershooting kernel compared to a (slightly) overshooting kernel in the control experiment. Then, the RNN exhibited faster recoveries. These observations warrant cautious interpretation as weak correlation in the RNN may partly account for differences in recovery times. Moreover, the pooling of neurons differs for the RNNs and the unconnected populations. The resampling of larger subgroups (RNNs) causes the samples to be less independent than with small subgroups (control; see Methods). The response properties of a neural population are commonly analyzed in terms of how fast neurons react, how strong, or even how accurate the response is. However, the time the neural population requires to reach a stationary state is rarely investigated. Here, we characterized the recovery time of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons to persistent and transient stimuli. First, we found consistently shorter reaction times when the stimulus was a change in the variance of the input current (Δσcompared to Δµ; cf. Silberberg et al. (2004) Next, we confirmed the presence of response kernels to persistent stimuli: being undershooting, overshooting, and oscillatory responses (Fig. 1; Silberberg et al. 2004; Tchumatchenko et al. 2011;Khorsand and Chance 2008;Knight, Omurtag, and Sirovich 2000). For a given stimulus modality, oscillatory responses were slowest to recover, while undershooting responses were the fastest. Quantitatively, the recovery time strongly depended on the set point (the pair ofµpreandσpre) and the stimulus modality (Δµ, Δσ, or Δµ &Δσ). In general terms, the higher theµpre, the more likely an overshooting or even an oscillatory response was. Interestingly, when the predominant kernel transitioned from an undershooting to an overshooting response (for increasingµpre), we observed the minimum recovery times (Fig. 2c). As neural populations are usually embedded into neural networks, we also studied recurrently connected networks. In our networks, the inhibition dominated the excitation, and thus displayed larger fluctuations with lower mean drive (Fig. 4;Sadeh, Cardanobile, and Rotter 2014). As for an unconnected population, we found that the recovery time of the network depended again on the set point and stimulus modality. A crucial difference was that the total current input (feedforward and recurrent) in the network was activity- and thus time-dependent compared to the external input received by an unconnected population. For matched conditions (set point and modality), the network recovered more slowly than an equivalent unconnected population. This is due to the recurrent excitation in the network: the total input was lower than in steady state, resulting in a slower rise. When the activity is above the target FRpost, it led to temporary over-excitation that supported a stronger overshoot. Regardless of the nature of the stimulus,Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky (1996)proposed linear network responses based on large networks and cancellations of excitation by quick inhibition. Their results indicate low-pass filtered responses with a single time constant, and that implies a quick recovery. This neglects the second-order dynamics that LIF neurons display (Hahn et al. 2014). Moreover, their network operated in a (biologically plausible) fluctuation-driven regime. While we observed similar dynamics (especially for Δµand lowµpre), this might not be the optimal set point. The optimal set point resembles a critically damped second-order filter that balances quick reaction time and fast recovery (Fig. 2c). As we observed that RNNs often tend to recover more slowly than an unconnected population, it is of interest whether such an optimal set point has advantages in the network setting. Moreover, it remains an open question which brain regions ought to have such filter properties. Many factors influence the optimal set point: among others, the balance of excitation and inhibition, but also the recurrent connectivity, which is likely to be non-random (Fig. 5b, c). More generally, heterogeneity in the neural and synaptic properties can shape the reaction and the recovery speed individually, and consequently, likely also on a population level. Furthermore, neuromodulation can alter several properties of a network temporarily, or even permanently through synaptic plasticity (Fig. 5c). How heterogeneity and modulation affect the response properties of neural networks remains an important topic for future research. The communication between neural populations is influenced by network characteristics, inter-areal connectivity profiles, and can be modified across timescales.(a)The change in excitation and inhibition determines the communication modality. If either or both change, the default modality is Δµ &Δσ. Only if excitation and inhibition increase proportionally (inversely proportional), the communication is through the modality Δσ(Δµ).(b)Neuromodulation, synaptic plasticity or other means effect the set point of the network.(c)Inter-areal connectivity profiles support different modalities (e.g. Δµ: disinhibition and feed-forward (FF) excitation; Δσ: FF inhibition and FF excitation; Δµ &Δσ: FF excitation). The network characteristics of the receiving network are shaped by its internal connectivity (e.g. convergence or divergence, or the balance of excitation and inhibition), its heterogeneity in neural types. Additionally, these features can be dynamically altered by neuromodulation or synaptic plasticity across various timescales. While the optimal set point is a property of the receiving network, the communication between networks incorporates more: namely, the modality of communication (Δµ, Δσ, or Δµ &Δσ), features of the activity (persistent or stimulus pulses of varying duration), and the connectivity profile. The characteristics of the response dynamics depend on the features of the communication and can be altered or tuned. One major point is that the response properties were contingent on the modality of the communication. Only changing the mean drive or the fluctuation level is a special case, while most often, both parameters are intertwined (Fig. 5b;Brunel 2000). Here, the projection pattern of the sending population becomes crucial. If projections are only excitatory, both output parameters are affected. On the other hand, the addition of feedforward inhibition of equal strength effectively alters only the fluctuation level. In contrast to feedforward disinhibition, in which solely the mean drive is changed. For the latter two cases, this only holds under the condition of equal strength in the projection strength (Fig. 5a, c). Thus, neural activity could transmit different information based on the projection pattern between networks. Moreover, the communication among networks may have different features, be it persistent or transient stimuli. With the assumption that a single stimulation pulse encodes one bit of information, the recovery time indicates the information bandwidth of the neural population. When more than one pulse was presented to the neural population, the recovery sped up in some cases, while in others it slowed down (Suppl. Fig. 2). Those experiments also revealed that neurons exhibit hysteresis (Fig. 3a) that depended on the properties of the pulse trains (number of pulses and pulse duration). We observed that the longest recovery time for transient stimuli depended non-monotonically on the number of pulses as well as their stimulus duration (for a given set point and modality). Therefore, the network’s set point and the communication modality ought to be fine-tuned to the typical stimulus properties of the sending network. Heterogeneity could also play a crucial role in decoding a wider range of stimuli. In contrast to typical stimuli, a surprising event may be encoded predominantly in a fast reaction time, while the recovery speed only plays a subordinate role. These insights dismiss a simplified view of information encoding and make information bandwidth history- and stimulus-dependent (Fig. 3b-d). Long recovery times impose strong limits on how fast neural networks can respond to time-varying signals. The importance of fast reaction time may not be underestimated, as stimuli are constantly reaching the brain. However, this becomes meaningless if the neurons recover sluggishly. This entails the question of which neural mechanisms can calibrate the response properties along both axes - fast recovery while keeping quick reaction properties. One way out of this problem would be to have a tight balance of excitation and inhibition (Hennequin, Vogels, and Gerstner 2014), but such a balance is untenable inin vivosettings. Alternatively, neural networks could rely on compressed sensing to recover the full input despite low sampling frequency (Ganguli and Sompolinsky 2012) using internal models of the input. In the absence of proper internal models, neural networks would have to use the notion of temporal interleaving or spatial interleaving to process fast stimuli. In temporal interleaving, the slow neurons would sample the same signal at different phases, and in spatial interleaving, different phases of the signal are measured in different parts of the brain. The solutions from electronic communication theory are tempting, but it would be necessary to test their biological plausibility. With the technology currently available to stimulate and record hundreds of neurons simultaneously, it is in principle possible to replicate the simulation experimentsin vivo. However, heterogeneities in the neural properties or even the connectivity profiles are likely to affect the response dynamics. Moreover, we assumed no short-term synaptic dynamics by using static synaptic properties. The same holds for the neural properties that did not allow for adaptation features. A major challenge is also the comparison of biological neurons and LIF neurons. However, the crucial common ground is the non-linearity due to the reset mechanism. We believe that more complex neuron models or even biological neurons share fundamental properties in the response dynamics, namely that the recovery speed is finite and depends on neuron, network, and even stimulus properties. Lastly, It should be pointed out that in our simulations, all neurons in a population had the same membrane properties, including the membrane time constant. And yet the neuron populations displayed a large range of reaction and recovery times depending on the experimental setup. The reset mechanism after a spike introduces non-linear effects (Deger et al. 2010), and thus fitting a single or a double exponential function to the response was not applicable (see autocorrelation functions in Suppl. Fig. 3). Although matching the dynamics to a linear second-order filter seemed more promising, certain responses could not be fitted, as the initial response jump exceeded the step input by more than twice. Consequently, we advocate focusing on analyses that are agnostic to a single time scale. Ultimately, the dynamics of neurons, neural populations, and the whole brain evolve on temporal manifolds (Marom 2010). Hence, an interesting line of research would involve temporally more complex stimuli, from coloured noise to experimentally obtained inputs. title: iFLiP: accessible and low-cost lifetime fiber photometry for robust longitudinal and quantitative measurements of neural dynamics
author: Yahiro, T.; Chen, Y.; Bayless-Edwards, L.; An, S.; Mao, T.; Zhong, H.
text: Fluorescence lifetime measurements overcome the limitation of widely used intensity-based measurements in quantifying tonic activities and longitudinal changes in neural dynamics. However, while lifetime sensors are rapidly emerging, their applications have been limited by the complexity and expense of required hardware and software. Here, we report a simple, low-cost lifetime fiber photometry system, named iFLiP, that uses entirely off-the-shelf products and can be assembled without specialized expertise. We also develop software that enables turn-key operation. The integrated system can accurately monitor lifetime changes at up to 5000 Hz for days. We demonstrate the utility of iFLiP in monitoring the activity of protein kinase A (PKA) in vitro and in vivo, and uncover striatal subregion– and cell-type-specific PKA dynamics elicited by locomotion in mice. Additionally, multi-day continuous measurements in the basal forebrain reveal previously unappreciated PKA activity associated with sleep/wakefulness. Overall, iFLiP may make lifetime measurements broadly accessible in neuroscience research. Brain function relies on its underlying neural activity. Genetically encoded sensors, such as those for calcium, voltage, neurotransmitters, and intracellular signaling events, have begun to enable measurements of diverse neural activities in living animals.1–3To date, most studies have relied on intensity-based sensors, which excel in monitoring short-term, relative changes. However, long-term changes and tonic analyte levels are also critical determinants of cellular, circuit, and behavioral function. Yet, quantifying these dynamics remains challenging because the intensity measurements are confounded by common variables, such as light scattering, signal or sample drifting, photobleaching, and sensor expression levels. There is growing recognition that these limitations may be overcome by measuring fluorescence lifetime changes of appropriate sensors. The fluorescence lifetime of a fluorophore is independent of the fluorescence intensity and therefore insensitive to the aforementioned confounding factors.4–6Lifetime measurements have been used to monitor longitudinal analyte changes, compare absolute signaling activities across samples or recording sessions, and improve the signal-to-noise ratio in vitro and in vivo (e.g., ref7–14). At present, lifetime sensors are becoming increasingly available.9,12,13,15–18However, despite previous efforts, fluorescence lifetime measurements remain inaccessible to most laboratories due to the high cost, complicated software and hardware, and specialized expertise required. Towards making the technology more accessible, lifetime measurement has been integrated with fiber photometry.15,19The first fluorescence lifetime photometry (FLiP) system used the time-domain measurement principle, which is advantageous under low photon flux conditions.19Mechanistic insights―different lifetimes of two sensor states (sensor properties) and their relative fractions (biologically-relevant readout)―can be obtained from a single measurement. However, this system required both optical engineering expertise and expensive components. Additionally, this system had a limited sampling rate of ∼1 Hz and was prone to errors even at moderate signal intensities (>1×106photons/s). Another FLiP system, FLIPR, utilized the frequency-domain measurement principle.15While it improved upon many issues of the first system, it also required advanced expertise in both optics and electronics, making it challenging to adopt in typical biological laboratories. The system also remained relatively expensive (∼$38k). Importantly, with a single stimulation frequency using the frequency-domain measurement, the system may encounter difficulties in dissecting the contributions of different lifetimes versus the relative abundance of multiple lifetime populations.20–22As a result, while intensity-based fiber photometry has proven to be accessible to many laboratories, the current FLiP systems remain challenging to adopt and apply. Here, we develop iFLiP, a simple, low-cost, yet flexible and robust system for lifetime fiber photometry. This system uses entirely off-the-shelf components and can be assembled using standard connectors and cables. It is alignment-free, requiring no specialized expertise in optics or electronics. Once assembled, our custom-developed software enables turn-key data acquisition and streamlined analysis. By employing strategies to eliminate the “pile-up” effect, which causes systematic errors at high intensities, and by optimizing single-photon data processing, iFLiP can monitor lifetime at sampling rates up to 5000 Hz and intensities of up to 2×107photons/s. We demonstrated the utility of iFLiP across multiple preparations, including organic dyes, cultured cells, acute brain slices, and in vivo recordings in behaving animals. Using a well-characterized lifetime sensor for protein kinase A (PKA), which plays a central role in mediating neuromodulatory regulation, we found that animal locomotion elicited PKA dynamics with subregion– and cell-type-specific characteristics in the striatum. Additionally, continuous recording over days in the basal forebrain revealed novel dynamics of PKA activity that were associated with locomotion and circadian rhythms. Taken together, these results establish iFLiP as an accessible platform for quantitative and longitudinal fluorescence lifetime measurements of brain activity. To develop iFLiP, we chose to use the time-domain measurement for two reasons: i) its sensitivity under low-light conditions, which are common in biological samples, and ii) its ability to quantify, from a single measurement, the relative populations of different lifetime components for mechanistic dissection. To eliminate the need for specialized expertise and minimize complexity, we optimized each key component (Figure 1A). First, we chose gain-switched, picosecond-pulsed diode lasers, which are inexpensive and available in fiber-coupled formats.23Second, we used modern fiber optics that enable the use of filter cubes without mirror-based optical alignment. Third, we designed a simplified light path so that the emission light returning from the sample is routed through the same filter cube into a fiber that is fed directly to a detector without collection lenses. Effective light collection can be achieved by positioning the fiber close to a detector with a relatively large active area (ϕ > 1 mm). Fourth, we selected a low-cost, sensitive (quantum yield ∼40%), temperature-compensated silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) detector, which features fast response kinetics for single-photon measurements, high resistance to strong light exposure, and a sufficiently large active area. (A) Schematic illustrating the key components of the iFLiP hardware. (B) Conceptual flowchart of data acquisition and processing. (C) Schematic illustrating the data iFLiP records and displays live: the intensity, MPET, and lifetime curve. Em.: emission, sync.: synchronization, phtn: photon, disp.: display, calc.: calculation. See also Figures S1 – S3. The timing signal from the laser (i.e., the sync signal) and the photon signal from the detector are fed into a computer board for time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC),4,5,22from which the lifetime is determined (Figure 1A). Single-photon signals are identified using a constant fraction discriminator (CFD), which detects the timing of pulses with different amplitudes (due to noise in amplification gains) with high precision.24The CFD triggers a time-to-digital converter (TDC) to digitize photon timing with a shorter deadtime (25 ns) and reduced cost compared to previous systems. The previous time-domain FLiP system was limited to detecting low signal intensities due to an effect called “pile-up”.25,26This is caused by the deadtime in the TCSPC process: when a photon is detected, a second photon arriving within the deadtime cannot be measured, thereby distorting the probability of photon detection over time at high photon fluxes (Figure S1A and S1B). However, when the inter-pulse interval is an integer fraction of the dead time (i.e., the multiplication of laser frequency and dead time being an integer), the photon detection probability is uniformly affected throughout the inter-pulse interval, thereby eliminating distortion of lifetime measurements (Figure S1A and S1B). Thus, we set the laser frequency at 80 MHz, which corresponds to an inter-pulse interval of 12.5 ns, half of the deadtime of the TCSPC board we used (25 ns). This allows for a greatly increased intensity limit, which is imposed by the loss of photons due to deadtime (Figure S1C). In parallel, we developed software with a graphical user interface (GUI, in MATLAB) for flexible and intuitive hardware control (Figure 1Band S2). To achieve reliable sampling at high frequencies with live display and without signal losses, we streamed the information of each photon, encoded in different bits of a 32-bit binary number, from the TCSPC boards to the computer. Individual photons were then assigned to individual lifetime bins (25–100 ps/bin) within a macroscopic sampling duration (0.1–5000 Hz sampling frequency). The total intensity, the mean photon emission time (MPET), and the lifetime decay curve (Figure 1C) can be displayed in real-time during recording. This integrated hardware and software system offers the following features: i) measurement at an intensity up to 2×107photons/s and a sampling rate up to 5000 Hz, ii) acquisition triggering by an external Transistor-Transistor Logic (TTL) pulse to enable synchronization with other experimental setups, iii) continuous acquisition durations up to 100 hours, iv) automatic recording loops at programmable time intervals, and v) integrated data visualization and data analyses. We first characterized the basic properties of the iFLiP system, including the instrument response function (IRF) and detector afterpulses, by measuring attenuated laser light fed directly into the detector (Figure S3). The IRF represents the combined timing spread from the laser pulse, detector, and electronics, and defines the temporal resolution of the system. Across intensities in multiple hardware systems, the IRF exhibited a full-width half-maximum (FWHM) of ∼0.21 ns (Figure S3A and S3B), corresponding to a sigma of 0.1 ns when approximated using a Gaussian distribution. This is an order of magnitude lower than the lifetime of most fluorescence sensors (∼1–3 ns), confirming the sufficient temporal precision of the system. Afterpulses, which are artifactual counts occurring at microsecond to millisecond timescales after a true photon arrival event in many types of detectors, contribute to an intensity-dependent uniform background in the laser repetition window (12.5 ns at 80 MHz). They were estimated to be 3–6% of the total intensity, specific to each hardware setup (Figure S3C). This afterpulse probability was largely consistent across the typical intensity range of iFLiP (Figure S3D), allowing it to be subtracted in analyses. In addition, other system background signals, which include a combination of light-independent dark counts of the detector, system autofluorescence, and Raman scattering from the fibers, could also be measured and subtracted from experimental data (Figure 2A). (B and C) MPET (B) and lifetime decay curve and the fit of the 10 Hz curve (dashed line) on the semi-log scale (C) of 5 µM fluorescein across sampling frequencies. (D) Fitted lifetime of fluorescein at various intensities resulting from different fluorescein concentrations (from left to right, n = 4, 4, 5, 8, 5, 5, respectively). (E) Normalized mean photon counts of fluorescein (0.5 µM, n = 5), GFP (0.5 µM, n = 3), and a mixture (n = 6) of fluorescein (0.125 µM) and GFP (0.375 µM). Dotted line: linear fit, lifetime0/lifetime = 8.278×[KI]+1. SD: standard deviation; KI: potassium iodide. Throughout, error bars: standard error. See also Figure S4. To verify that iFLiP can reliably measure fluorescence lifetimes, we imaged well-characterized fluorophores in vitro (Figure 2). iFLiP was used to measure fluorescein across a broad range of sampling frequencies (10 to 5000 Hz). MPETs were consistent across these frequencies, although, as expected, fewer photons per time bin at higher frequencies resulted in increased standard deviations that matched theoretical predictions based on the photon counts (Figure 2B; STAR Methods). When integrated over the same duration, all sampling frequencies produced nearly identical lifetime decay curves. As expected from a single species of fluorophore, these curves were well fitted by a single exponential with a time constant (i.e., lifetime) of 4.04 ns (Figure 2C), consistent with previously reported fluorescein lifetimes in aqueous solutions.27–29Furthermore, under the same excitation condition, the measured lifetime of fluorescein was consistent across four independent rigs (s.d. 0.038 ns, <1% of lifetime; Figure S4A) over a 15-fold change in the concentration and, therefore, in intensity (Figures 2DandS4B). We then tested the analytical capability of iFLiP. First, we examined a mixture of two fluorophores: fluorescein and purified recombinant mEGFP. iFLiP measurements showed that the mixture exhibited a lifetime clearly distinct from that of each ingredient alone (fitted lifetime [ns; mean±sem]: fluorescein, 4.016±0.002; mEGFP, 2.699±0.005; mixture, 3.061±0.020) (Figures 2EandS4C). When fitting the mixture lifetime decay curve with two exponentials, the mEGFP-to-fluorescein fluorescence ratio was estimated to be 0.724:0.276. Based on the known extinction coefficient and quantum yield of these fluorophores (FPBase.org), a molar ratio of 3.05:1 was derived (STAR Methods), closely matching the mixture composition (0.375:0.125 μM). Additionally, in a separate experiment, iFLiP reliably detected a decrease in fluorescein lifetime upon potassium iodide (KI) quenching, which scaled linearly with KI concentrations to yield a Stern-Volmer constant of 8.3 (Figure 2FandS4D), in agreement with prior reports.30,31Overall, these results indicate that the iFLiP system can reliably measure and analytically quantify the fluorescence lifetimes of multiple fluorophores. We next examined iFLiP’s ability to report fluorescence lifetime in biological samples using two widely employed preparations: cultured cells and acute brain slices. First, we expressed mEGFP or the cytosolic PKA lifetime sensor, tAKARβ9, in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells (Figure 3AandS5A). As expected, mEGFP expression resulted in a single exponential lifetime decay (Figure S5B) after subtracting background, which was measured when the fiber was pointed towards an area without expression. In contrast, the tAKARβ sensor exhibited multi-exponential lifetime decays (Figure 3B), as expected from its two activity states. Consistent with literature,9,32iFLiP detected a decrease in the sensor lifetime (measured as MPET), indicating an increase in PKA activity, following the administration of the β-adrenergic agonist norepinephrine (1 µM), a physiological neuromodulator that activates the PKA pathway. The PKA response was further enhanced by strong activation of adenylate cyclases with forskolin (25 µM) and inhibition of phosphodiesterases with IBMX (50 µM) (Figures 3Cand3D). (B) Example normalized lifetime decay curve of tAKARβ in HEK cells under the indicated conditions, displayed on a semi-log scale. Here, we present a simple, low-cost, yet flexible, robust, and turn-key system for lifetime fiber photometry. Although the advantages of fluorescence lifetime measurements have long been recognized, and lifetime measurements have been implemented with microscopy and fiber photometry in certain laboratories,10,15,19this technology remains inaccessible for most laboratories because it requires complex, expensive custom setups and specialized expertise in optics and electronics. iFLiP addresses this critical need by providing a simple hardware design and user-friendly software for turn-key operation. The total cost (∼$22k, Supplemental Table 1) is over 40% lower than that of any previously published systems.46At the same time, this system achieves robust performance, including a sampling rate of up to 5000 Hz and a maximum photon count of 2×107/s. At 20 Hz, this corresponds to up to 1×106photons per sample point and 0.1% precision in lifetime quantification (δτ/τ= 1/√N; STAR Methods). Given that many modern sensors exhibit lifetime dynamics of 25% or more,9,12,13,17,47the sensitivity of the current system enables reliable lifetime detection across a broad range of applications. In addition, the system has an IRF with a FWHM well below the lifetime of most sensors and fluorescent proteins. This is essential as the IRF defines the lower limit of detectable lifetime, analogous to how the point spread function defines the resolution of microscopes. The system presented here is designed for single-channel detection of green fluorescence (e.g., EGFP). The laser and filters can be adjusted to detect sensors of other colors. Multiplexed imaging of multiple sensors or simultaneous data collection at multiple brain regions using a multi-channel TCSPC board is, in principle, possible. However, this is often associated with greatly increased cost and light path complexity. Future efforts to simplify the design for robust multiplexed imaging will be needed. Compared to lifetime measurements based on two-photon microscopy, fiber photometry exhibits significantly higher background signals. As the excitation light is required to pass through meter-long optical fibers, fiber autofluorescence and Raman scattering become substantial. Careful selection of the emission filter is therefore critical. The dark count of the detector is also non-negligible. Another source of background is the detector afterpulses, which scale with the detected intensity. Other detectors, such as photomultipliers (PMTs) or single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD), have lower afterpulse probabilities. However, these alternatives add significant cost and have their own limitations: PMTs may become saturated or damaged at high intensities, whereas SPAD detectors often have a very small active area, making light collection challenging. In iFLiP, hardware optimization combined with background and afterpulse subtraction still enables accurate lifetime measurements (e.g.,Figure 2). When compared to systems based on two-photon microscopy, the iFLiP approach is simpler, more broadly accessible, more readily compatible with freely moving paradigms, and less invasive for imaging deep brain regions (ϕ = 200 μm for optical fibers, c.f. 1400 μm for gradient-index [GRIN] lenses with a cannula), although the gains come at the expense of single-cell resolution. By using iFLiP to measure PKA activity in the striatum, we obtained several observations that extended the current understanding of striatal neuromodulation. First, in acute brain slices, PKA activity in the DMS and DLS exhibited similar sensitivity to dopamine and cocaine manipulations ex vivo. Thus, the recently reported spatial heterogeneity in dopamine release across striatal regions likely propagates to intracellular signaling activity.48,49Second, our result that an nAChR antagonist attenuated PKA activation induced by electrically elicited dopamine release corroborates recent observations that nAChRs expressed on dopaminergic axons mediate local dopamine release driven by cortical inputs.38–40Additionally, in vivo iFLiP measurements in the striatum largely verified our previous observations using in vivo two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging that animal locomotion drives cell type specific PKA signaling.11Furthermore, this approach allowed us to readily compare responses across multiple striatal subregions. We found that PKA activity of dSPNs in the DLS, but not the DMS, exhibited a clear peak at the offset of enforced animal locomotion, which may be related to recently described dopamine release that occurs upon stress relief.50Finally, we found that PKA activity on-kinetics in iSPNs were much faster than those in dSPNs. Such differential kinetics may provide a dynamic temporal window critical for striatal function, such as movement control, warranting future studies. The iFLiP system measures fluorescence lifetime by counting individual photons with high sensitivity (quantum efficiency ∼40%). Because of this sensitivity, in vivo iFLiP experiments often require excitation powers an order of magnitude lower than those of typical intensity-based fiber photometry experiments (e.g., less than 1 μW was used for all experiments inFigure 6). This, together with the aforementioned advantage of lifetime measurements, allows for long-term continuous recordings in freely moving mice. Such recordings in the basal forebrain revealed PKA activity dynamics correlated with the animal’s circadian rhythm: tonic PKA activity increases in the dark phase but decreases in the light phase. The potential role of this PKA activity in driving sleep-wake state transitions is supported by its sensitivity to manipulations of arousal-related neuromodulatory pathways, including the adenosinergic, cholinergic, and orexinergic systems. Future experiments combining iFLiP with EEG/EMG, cell-type-specific recordings, and receptor-specific manipulations will be necessary to define the receptor, cellular and circuit mechanisms by which PKA bridges neuromodulatory activation and animal behavior. Nevertheless, our results demonstrate that iFLiP can reveal previously unresolved intracellular signaling states in freely moving animals that are important for brain function. Multiple factors collectively impose a practical limit on the maximal intensity measurable with iFLiP. First, although the system minimizes the distortion by TCSPC deadtime in lifetime determination by implementing a compatible laser frequency, photon losses caused by the deadtime still limit the collectible light flux. Second, the detector has a finite speed, such that each photon generates a pulse with a FWHM of ∼4 ns (Thorlabs.com). Individual photons arriving within this time duration cannot be resolved from each other, thereby effectively imposing another deadtime that may distort lifetime at high signal intensities. Third, the need to process every photon also imposes challenges for data transfer and CPU computation at high count rates. Achieving a higher intensity limit using the TCSPC mechanism will require improvements on all of these fronts. Nevertheless, as demonstrated, the current intensity limit is sufficient for most in vivo lifetime measurements. Similar to other single-photon excitation methods, the autofluorescence from brain tissue can be substantial. Although the background from the hardware system is typically stable and can be measured and subtracted, background from the sample, particularly in vivo, is usually variable across experiments and can be challenging to remove reliably. Additionally, although lifetime measurements are more resistant to factors affecting fluorescence intensity, they might still be perturbed by certain biological factors. For example, it is known that temperature may affect the lifetime of many fluorophores44,45. Therefore, iFLiP results should be compared with those obtained from a corresponding functionally deficient mutant sensor and interpreted with care. Care was taken to ensure a relatively smooth cut surface, minimizing light scattering. Before recordings, the iFLiP hardware was allowed to warm up for 1–3 hours or longer, and the fiber was bleached until the autofluorescence reached a plateau. Depending on the setup and laser power, this took between 15 minutes (3 mW) and 90 minutes (40 µW). To measure background, the laser power was kept consistent while fluorescence was measured with the sample absent—either in solvent alone or in a bath without the cell coverslip present. To record the lifetime of fluorescein and mEGFP, the exposed fiber end was submerged into fluorescent solutions (0.6–1.6 ml) of fluorescein, GFP, or a mixture of the two made in ddH2O (Figure 2Band2C) or 25 mM HEPES-buffered HBSS solution (pH = 8,Figure 2A, 2D–2F) in a 4-chamber glass-bottom Petri dish (Cellvis). The laser power (typically 0.3 – 10 μW) was adjusted such that the measured photon counts were ∼0.1×107to 1×107. To record from fluorophores expressed in HEK cells, the coverslip was placed on the bottom of the chamber perfused with carbogen (95% O2/5% CO2) gassed artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) containing (in mM) 127 NaCl, 25 NaHCO3, 25 D-glucose, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH2PO4, 2 CaCl2, and 1 MgCl2. The chamber was covered in black electrical tape to reduce ambient light. The fiber was placed in an area with medium expression and over cells with healthy morphology. Specifically, the fiber tip was lowered until it touched the coverslip and was then retracted slightly. The measured photon counts read ∼3×106to 10×106. Drugs were bath-applied. The fiber and chamber were washed between experiments with 70% ethanol and ddH2O. All animal experiments were conducted according to the US National Institutes of Health guidelines for animal research and were approved by the Oregon Health & Science University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC protocols IP00000955 and IP00002274). The following mice were used in this study: wildtype C57BL/6 mice (Charles River Laboratories, Wilmington, MA, USA);Drd1a-Cre(Mutant Mouse Resource and Research Centers, 036916) andAdora2a-Cre(Mutant Mouse Resource Research Centers, 036158). All transgenic mice were backcrossed at least five generations to a C57BL/6 background. Mice of 1.5-8 months old with approximately equal proportions of both sexes were used. All mice were housed in groups when possible and maintained in a standard 12-hour light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water. All in vivo experiments were performed in the light cycle, except for freely moving experiments, which were performed in both light and dark cycles. Mice were randomized to treatment groups, and sexes were approximately equal between groups. The following viruses were used: AAV9-CAG-FLEX-cd-tAKARα (custom production; 1.16×1012GC/mL), AAV9-hSyn-cd-tAKARα (custom production; 1.98×1012GC/mL). The flexed virus was diluted 1:5 in PBS prior to injection. 150-200 nL of the diluted viral vector was injected into one of the following locations using a glass pipette, as previously described51. The coordinates are (in mm relative to bregma): for the DMS, 0.4–0.7 anterior, 1.1–1.15 lateral, 2.8 ventral; for the DLS, 0.2–0.5 anterior, 2.4 lateral, 2.8 ventral; for the basal forebrain 0.5 anterior, 1.2 lateral, 5.0 ventral. Stereotaxic injection was performed under isoflurane anesthesia (5% induction, 2% maintenance). Mice were administered 5mg/kg carprofen for 3 days following surgery and were allowed to recover for 1-3 weeks prior to fiber implantation. Wildtype animals injected with codon-diversified (cd)-tAKARα in the DMS and DLS were sacrificed at P40-60 and decapitated for brain extraction. Brains were sliced coronally on a vibratome (VT1200S, Leica Biosystems, Nussloch, Germany) at 300 µm thickness in fresh ice-cold cutting solution (in mM: 25 NaHCO3, 1.25 NaH2PO4·H2O, 25 glucose, 2.5 KCl, 7 MgCl2·6H2O, 0.5 CaCl2, 110 choline chloride, 11.5 sodium ascorbate, and 3 sodium pyruvate). Slices were incubated at 37 °C for 30 minutes and then at room temperature for 0.5–10 hours in carbogenated aCSF before use. Brain slices were separated along the midline to isolate two half slices each containing one hemisphere. A half slice was then stabilized to the perfusion chamber with a custom-made U-shaped harp. The recording fiber (at a 30-degree angle to the slice) was lowered into the bath toward the expression center, or an area without expression as a control, in the DMS or DLS, until positioned right above the slice. For the intensity drift experiments, the fiber was moved upward for 10 µm to induce intensity change and then moved back to baseline position (Figures S6B and S6C). Alternatively, with the fiber position unchanged, the baseline laser intensity (∼0.8–2µW) was decreased by 5–10% using an inline optical attenuator (V450A, Thorlabs; controlled by a voltage signal generator, TKXEC, QH-VISG2-ED) and then restored to baseline (Figures S4D and S4E). All drugs were bath-applied at the following concentrations (in µM): dopamine 20 or 1, forskolin 25, IBMX 50, cocaine 3. Dopamine and cocaine stocks were prepared in ddH2O, and forskolin and IBMX were dissolved in DMSO. The chamber and fiber were cleaned with at least 6 rounds of wash with ddH2O and 70% ethanol between experiments. The pharmacology experiments (Figures 3F–3J) were performed at room temperature. For electrical stimulation experiments (Figures 3J–3O), a theta-tube was pulled from capillary glass tubing (TG150-4, Warner Instruments), connected to a stimulation box, and positioned below the slice surface 150–200 µm away from the fiber tip at 32–34 ℃. A train of 3 electrical stimulations (25–75 µA) was delivered at 25 Hz with a dwell time of 0.1–0.5 ms to induce an MPET change typically between 0.03 ns and 0.12 ns. A cocktail of glutamatergic and GABAergic blockers (in μM: 10 NBQX, 10 CPP, 20 SR95531, and 1 CGP55845) was added to the bath to isolate putative dopamine-induced responses. CGP55845 stock was prepared in DMSO; NBQX, SR95531, and CPP stocks were prepared in ddH2O. Parameters were kept consistent across stimulations within each experiment. For the mutant control, parameters matched the strongest stimulation applied to the experimental group on the same day. Drugs were applied at least 5 minutes after a stable baseline was reached and incubated for at least 15–20 minutes before the next stimulation. For in vivo photometry experiments, optical fiber cannulas were implanted under isoflurane anesthesia (5% induction, 2% maintenance). 1–2 weeks after stereotaxic viral injections, fiber cannulas (200 μm diameter, 3.5mm long, 0.39 NA; RWD) were implanted at the same coordinates as the injection site by inserting them while recording signals with a custom-built spectrally resolved photometry system52. Using a 488 mm LED to excite green fluorophores, the spectrum was observed during fiber implantation, and the fiber was implanted to the depth of the greatest signal and secured with dental cement mixed with cyanoacrylate. Mice were administered 5 mg/kg carprofen for three days following surgery and were allowed to recover for at least two weeks prior to recording. Before each recording session, the background signal was measured by connecting the patch cable from the iFLiP setup to an unimplanted fiber cannula. The cannula tip was directed toward a black surface in a dark room to minimize reflected excitation light. Because the background signal depends on excitation intensity, a separate background recording was obtained for each laser power used in the experiment. Laser power was approximately 3–10 µW for head-fixed recordings and less than 1 µW for freely moving recordings. For the head-fixed photometry experiments shown inFigure 5, mice were placed on a custom-built one-dimensional rotary treadmill with a 20-cm diameter wheel. The iFLiP recordings were performed with a sampling rate of 10 Hz. For enforced locomotion experiments, a motorized treadmill was driven at approximately 5 cm/s. Each session consisted of at least 10 min of baseline recording, 5 min of enforced running, and 15–20 min of post-running rest. Locomotor activity was measured using a rotary encoder (US Digital, MA3-A10-250-N) coupled to the treadmill axle. The encoder generated an analog voltage signal of approximately 0–5 V, which was digitized at 1 kHz using a National Instruments DAQ board (PCIe-6259), the MATLAB DAQ Toolbox, and custom MATLAB code. For the in vivo pharmacology experiments shown inFigures 4and5, mice first underwent one enforced running session. Drugs were then administered, followed by a 20– 30 min observation period and a second enforced running session after drug treatment. SKF83566 hydrobromide (Tocris) and eticlopride hydrochloride (Tocris) were dissolved in saline at a final concentration of 100 and 50 μg/mL, respectively. For the freely moving open-field experiments shown inFigure 6, a two-channel iFLiP system, in which signals from two independent channels were detected simultaneously using a two-channel TCSPC board (TH260P-DUAL), was used to simultaneously record from two mice. For each recording, a mouse was connected to the optical patch cable through a pigtailed fiber-optic rotary joint (Doric) and placed in an open-top arena measuring 38.5 × 38.5 × 38.5 cm. The iFLiP recordings were performed with a sampling rate of 1 Hz. Mice were maintained on a standard 12-h light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to food and water. An overhead-mounted night-vision camera (ELP, ELP-USBFHD05MT-KL156IR) was used to record mouse position, and mouse motion was analyzed using ezTrack (Pennington et al., 2019). For freely moving pharmacology experiments, drugs were administered intraperitoneally 3 h after the light-to-dark or dark-to-light transition. Istradefylline (Tocris) and ACT-462206 (MedChemExpress) were dissolved in DMSO and then diluted in saline to a final concentration of 2.5 and 50 mg/mL, respectively. Scopolamine (Tocris) was dissolved in saline at a final concentration of 250 μg/mL. All iFLiP data quantification was performed using custom MATLAB software. Because a reduction in MPET indicates an increase in PKA activities, the y-axes of MPET plots were flipped. Statistical tests were performed with MATLAB 2013b–2022a or GraphPad Prism 11. Data distribution was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, and equality of variance was assessed using the F test or Brown–Forsythe test, as appropriate. Data that were normally and equally distributed were compared using a two-tailed paired or unpaired Student’s t-test or a one-way or two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni’s or Dunnett’s post hoc test. Data that were not normally or equally distributed were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Welch’s test, the Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s post hoc test, the Friedman test with Dunn’s post hoc test, or Welch’s ANOVA test with Dunnett’s post hoc test. For the kinetics analysis of striatal tAKARα, the outliers were removed based on the ROUT method. All statistical results are in Table S2. title: A new neural code for position: generalizable spatial maps in mouse medial frontal cortex
author: Sen, R.; Posani, L.; Medoff, A.; Zhang, B.; Abbott, L.; Axel, R.; Fusi, S.
text: Navigation requires the brain to encode spatial relationships that support extrapolation from explored to unexplored regions of space. We identified a novel neural code for space in the mouse medial frontal cortex (mFC) that is well suited for this form of spatial generalization. Using calcium imaging of excitatory neurons in mFC, hippocampus (dorsal CA1), and lateroventral orbitofrontal cortex (lvOFC) as mice explored a square arena with landmarks, we found that mFC activity supports extrapolation. Linear regression of the animal’sxorycoordinates trained in one region of the arena generalized to a completely different region. This property was observed in mFC but not in dCA1 or lvOFC. A model in which neurons encode the squared distance from the animal to multiple landmarks explains several properties of the geometry of the mFC representation, including extrapolation. The neural map that we observed in the frontal cortex may provide a basis for vector computation in navigation and complex route planning. Animals navigate by building internal models that allow them to infer relationships between locations, estimate distances, and plan routes through regions they have never explored. Neural representations of spatial location have been studied intensively in two populations, place cells in the hippocampus (1,2) and grid cells in the entorhinal cortex (3), but have now been described in many other brain areas (4–7). In its simplest form, an internal model of space that provides a basis for navigation and complex planning resembles a map in an atlas, and preserves the geometry of physical space. Such a map is compositional: spatial displacements can be combined as building blocks to construct routes through space. This is possible because, in a map, a given displacement represents the same change in position, regardless of where the movement begins. Consider the street grid of Manhattan in New York City (Fig. 1a). Moving 8 blocks uptown along 8th Avenue takes us from 51st Street to Central Park at 59th Street. This movement defines a displacement of 8 blocks northward, represented by a vector on the map. The same displacement can be applied along a different avenue: moving 8 blocks uptown along 5th Avenue would also take us from 51st Street to 59th Street, even if we had never explored that avenue. This ability to apply a displacement independently of its starting location arises because a map captures the underlying geometry of space rather than representing a collection of individual locations or routes. a, Schematic illustrating spatial generalization using the Manhattan street grid. A displacement learned along one avenue, such as moving eight blocks uptown from 51st Street to 59th Street, can be applied at a new location along another avenue. Likewise, an east-west displacement learned between 8th and 5th Avenues at 51st Street can be generalized to the same displacement at 59th Street.b, Top, mice were injected with an AAV expressing GCaMP6f under the CaMKIIαpromoter and implanted with a GRIN lens over one of three brain regions - the medial frontal cortex (mFC), dorsal CA1 of the hippocampus (dCA1), or lateroventral orbitofrontal cortex (lvOFC) - for one-photon calcium imaging of excitatory neurons. Bottom, mice explored an arena containing four salient corner landmarks: either four identical cups positioned in the corners (cups assay) or four individually housed stimulus mice (social assay). In both assays, the spatial configuration was systematically varied every 3 min by shuffling the positions of the four corner stimuli across 24 configurations.c, Photograph of the 45 × 45 cm arena containing four salient corner landmarks, along with additional environment-specific landmarks, including a door and a holder.d-e, Example linear decoding of position along thex-axis(d)and y-axis(e)from population activity in mFC, dCA1, and lvOFC from the cups assay. Predicted position is shown in color and actual position in black. Scale bars, 30 cm (vertical), 1 minute (horizontal).f-g, Linear decoding error for position along thex-(left) andy-axes (right) in the cups assay(f)and social assay(g)across mFC, dCA1, and lvOFC. Each colored circle represents data from one mouse; horizontal lines and error bars indicate the mean ± SEM. Here and in subsequent figures, unless otherwise indicated, comparisons across three brain regions were assessed using a one-way ANOVA followed by pairwise Welch’st-tests with Holm correction for multiple comparisons. For shuffle analyses, 100 shuffled controls were generated for each animal by circularly time-shifting calcium activity relative to position and evaluating each shifted recording across all cross-validation folds. Gray dots show the pooled shuffle-derived decoding errors, and gray horizontal lines indicate their means. For each brain region, the observed decoding error for each mouse was compared with the mean of that mouse’s shuffle distribution using a two-sided pairedt-test across mice. (*p <0.05, **p <0.01, ***p <0.001, ****p <0.0001; n.s., not significant). We have discovered a spatial code in the mouse medial frontal cortex (mFC) that exhibits this fundamental property of geometric maps. Linear regression of the animal’sxandycoordinates trained in one region of an arena can predict position in regions not used for training, a property we did not observe in hippocampal dorsal CA1 (dCA1) or lateroventral orbitofrontal cortex (lvOFC). This ability to extrapolate across physical space suggests that the mFC representation preserves spatial relationships in a form that may support abstract route planning and navigation. We used GCaMP6f and head-mounted miniscopes to record excitatory neurons in medial frontal cortex (mFC), hippocampal dorsal CA1 (dCA1), and lateroventral orbitofrontal cortex (lvOFC) as mice explored a square arena containing four salient corner landmarks, either four empty cages (cups assay) or four individually caged conspecifics (social assay) (Fig. 1b-c,Extended Data Fig. 1a-f). Activity was recorded across 24 sessions (3 min each), with the corner locations of conspecifics swapped between sessions (Figure 1b). This protocol supported sustained exploration (Extended Data Fig. 1g) and, while it was originally designed to study representations of social identity, it revealed a striking generalizable representation of space in mFC that was independent of social identity and became the focus of this study. We explored neural representations of position along two orthogonal spatial axes. We performed linear regression independently for thexandypositions by reading out the activity recorded as animals explored the full arena. We tested the linear regression performance on held-out temporal blocks. Bothxandypositions could be read out independently from mFC and dCA1 population activity, with markedly lower performance in lvOFC. In mFC and dCA1, the decoded position closely tracked the mouse’s actual position as it navigated the arena. This correspondence was weaker in lvOFC (Fig. 1d-e). To quantify decoding accuracy, we calculated the median absolute difference between the decoded and actual mouse positions along each axis (in cm) and compared it with a null distribution generated by circularly shifting neural activity relative to position. Decoding errors were significantly lower than those obtained from shuffled controls in mFC and dCA1, whereas the effect was weaker in lvOFC (Fig. 1f-g). Consistent with this, two-dimensional position could also be decoded using a nonlinear Bayesian decoder from both mFC and dCA1 populations, with greater decoding accuracy in dCA1. Decoding from lvOFC was substantially poorer (Extended Data Fig. 2). Linear regression forxandypositions from the full arena does not establish that the underlying representation supports extrapolation across space. To test for extrapolation, we trained linear regression to predict eitherxoryposition using activity from only one half of the arena. We then tested de-coding accuracy on the other half, calculating the median absolute difference between the predicted and actual positions, which we refer to as generalization error. (Fig. 2b-d,Extended Data Fig. 3). Importantly, the linear regression model was constructed using only neural activity recorded when the animal was in the training half of the arena, without any information from the opposite half. Forxposition, linear regression was trained on the top half of the arena and tested on the bottom half, and vice versa; foryposition, linear regression was trained on the left half and tested on the right half, and vice versa. Generalization error was averaged across the two train-test directions. As a control, we also trained and tested linear regression within the same half (Fig. 2a,c-d), which we refer to as decoding error. a-b, Linear regression was trained to predict nose position along one spatial axis using population activity sampled from only one half of the arena along the orthogonal axis. Forx-position, the arena was divided into top and bottom halves; fory-position, it was divided into left and right halves. Linear regression was tested(a)within the same arena half (decoding) or(b)on the other half (generalization), thereby testing prediction at positions along the orthogonal axis that were not represented in the training data. Examples showx-position in the social assay; both axes and both assays are quantified in(c–d). Black traces show actual position; colored traces show predictions for each brain area.c, Decoding vs. generalization error across brain regions in the cups assay. For each mouse, generalization error was averaged across the two directions of cross-half testing, and decoding error was averaged across the two arena halves. Each circle represents data from one animal; filled points and error bars indicate the mean ± SEMd, Same as(c), but for the social assay.e,. Schematic of the cross-half weight-correlation analysis. Forx-position, independent linear regression models were trained on the top and bottom halves of the arena; fory-position, independent linear regression models were trained on the left and right halves. For each axis, the correlation between the weights assigned to individual neurons by the two half-specific linear regression models was calculated and compared between mFC and dCA1.f-g, Weights assigned to individual neurons by linear regression models trained on opposite halves are compared forx-(left) andy-(right) position for mFC(f)and dCA1(g)populations in the social assay. Neurons were pooled across animals. For each animal and spatial axis, the two linear regression model weights for each neuron were divided by the Euclidean norm of all weights from both models. Each point represents one neuron. Pearson’s correlation coefficients (r) and numbers of neurons (n) are shown. We restricted the comparison of decoder weights across halves to spatially selective neurons, identified using a mutual-information test for position (see Methods).h-i, Correlation of cross-half decoding weights across animals in the cups assay (h) and social assay (i). Left, Pearson correlation coefficients between weights from the twox-position linear regression models. Right, Pearson correlation coefficients between weights from the twoy-position linear regression models. Each circle represents one animal; horizontal lines and error bars indicate the mean ± SEM. We observed that mFC representations extrapolate across space. The position predicted by linear regression trained on one half of the arena closely tracked the animal’s actual position in the opposite half, for bothx(Fig. 2b) andycoordinates. In contrast, predictions from dCA1 populations deviated substantially from the animal’s actual position when tested on the opposite half (Fig. 2b). To quantify this difference, we compared generalization error with decoding error. In mFC, generalization errors remained low and were comparable to decoding errors. In contrast, dCA1 exhibited substantially higher generalization errors despite accurate within-half decoding, resulting in a much larger ratio of generalization to decoding error (Fig. 2c-d,Extended Data Fig. 3). Generalization remained robust when neuron numbers were matched across animals and brain regions (Extended Data Fig. 4) and across days in a subset of mFC recordings repeated on multiple days (Extended Data Fig. 5). In contrast, lvOFC performed poorly in both decoding and generalization (Fig. 2a-d,Extended Data Fig. 3). Generalization performance in mFC was typically higher forxposition than foryposition, potentially reflecting asymmetries in environmental cues (Fig. 2c-d,Extended Data Fig. 3-4). Removing corner landmarks reduced generalization in mFC, whereas replacing conspecifics with empty cups had little effect (Extended Data Fig. 6), indicating that environmental landmarks are needed to shape and anchor the mFC spatial map. The ability to extrapolate both thexandycoordinates that we observed in mFC implies that the neural displacement vectors across the two coordinate axes are approximately parallel in different parts of the arena. Any arbitrary movement in the 2D physical environment explored by the animal can be decomposed into displacements along these axes. As a consequence, arbitrary movements would be approximately represented by displacement vectors in neural activity space that do not depend on the animal’s initial position, a property that is important for planning and navigation, as discussed in the Introduction. We next asked whether individual neurons contribute similarly to decoding a given spatial coordinate (i.e., have similar decoding weights) across opposite halves of the arena, and whether this consistency supports generalization in mFC. We trained linear regression models independently on different halves of the arena and compared the weights assigned to individual neurons in predictingxandypositions (Fig. 2e). We restricted the comparison of linear regression weights across halves to spatially selective neurons identified using a mutual-information criterion for position (8). Pooling neurons across all animals within each brain region, we found that linear regression weights were strongly correlated across opposite halves of the arena in mFC, whereas correlations were substantially weaker in dCA1 (Fig. 2f-g,Extended Data Fig. 7). In dCA1, we can clearly see that the distribution has the shape of a cross, indicating that the neurons important in the two halves belong to two non-overlapping populations. This difference was also evident when correlations were calculated separately for each animal, with significantly higher weight correlations in mFC than in dCA1 across the cups and social assays (Fig. 2h,i). These findings suggest that the contributions of individual mFC neurons to position decoding remain consistent across space, providing a basis for the generalization of the population code. What properties of mFC neuronal responses allow the population to extrapolate from explored to unexplored regions of space? The simplest way to construct a neural representation that generalizes across an environment is to have neuronal firing rates (fkfor neuronk) depend linearly on thexandycoordinates of the animal (fk=akx+bky), whereakandbkare constants (Fig. 3a). The model’s ability to support extrapolation can be understood by examining the geometry of its neural encoding manifold. The neural activity space forNneurons is anN-dimensional space describing all possible population activity patterns. The encoding manifold is the subspace within this full activity space that describes how population activity varies as the animal occupies different locations in the environment. Ignoring noise, this manifold is a two-dimensional surface parameterized by thexandycoordinates of the animal’s position. Equation 1describing individual neural responses in the squared distance model is clearly an idealization. Neural responses are typically very diverse and often seemingly disorganized (10,11). Neurons respond nonlinearly to multiple task-relevant variables (mixed selectivity), especially in cognitive brain areas such as the prefrontal cortex (12). The hippocampus and entorhinal cortex are no exception: the representations in both CA1 and dentate gyrus are highly distributed, and the individual responses are very diverse (8). Analogously, even selected grid cells exhibit mixed selectivity and are highly heterogeneous (13). Because of this diversity of responses, it is difficult to draw conclusions from analyzing firing patterns of individual neurons, and this is also the case in our recordings of mFC. The key results from our idealized model are thatx2+y2,x, andyshould be strongly represented across the neural population, which will happen if the firing rates of a sufficient number of cells are at least partially described byequation 1. In other words, there can be additional terms in the expressions for the firing patterns of individual neurons, but the squared distance model should account for a large fraction of the total responses across the population.
