The spatial fields of neurons well described by the squared distance model were nevertheless diverse, with a broad distribution of parametersak,bk,xk, andyk(Fig. 6d). There are cells withak<0 that look somewhat like large place cells. Some cells withak>0 exhibit strong activation near the edges of the arena, similar to border cells (14). Other cells could also be interpreted as boundary vector cells (15), as seen in the subiculum and entorhinal cortex, or object vector cells (16), as seen in MEC, which fire when an animal is at a specific distance and allocentric direction relative to a boundary or object. Nevertheless, this diverse population of neurons, each at least partially encoding squared distance from different landmarks, can collectively form a low-dimensional spatial manifold capable of extrapolation. We identified a new spatial code in mFC that possesses a property critical for planning and navigation. This representation encodes physical displacement in a manner invariant to the starting point, enabling predictions of future locations along arbitrary routes in unexplored environments. An arbitrary route can be decomposed into a sequence of displacements, each represented by a vector connecting two successive positions. When using a map in an atlas, we can predict our final location after a series of movements (e.g., move East, North, East, South) by simply adding these displacement vectors to our initial position vector. This additivity property also holds for thex,ysubspace of mFC neural maps—a coordinate system that can be inferred by exploring a restricted portion of the environment. This principle does not apply to idealized place cells with localized fields. For place cells, the neural representation of a displacement depends on its location within the environment. Two identical physical movements (such as equal eastward displacements from different starting locations) evoke distinct changes in population activity, each silencing the cell active at the starting location and activating a different cell encoding the final location. In mFC, we showed that parallel physical movements along one of the two coordinate axes are represented by parallel vectors in neural activity space. This property manifests itself in the ability to cross-generalize (17): a decoder trained to extract the animal’sxandycoordinates in one region of the arena successfully generalizes to other regions. This is possible only because thexandyencoding directions in neural activity space are independent and remain approximately constant throughout the environment. While thexandyaxes represent just two orthogonal directions in physical space, any arbitrary displacement vector can be formed by a linear combination of vectors aligned to the axes. Consequently, the highly desirable property of starting-point invariance extends to any arbitrary displacement in the environment. Ultimately, this reveals that the mFC spatial code is fundamentally compositional: every route can be decomposed into a series of displacements, and the location reached after each displacement can be predicted by simply adding the corresponding vectors in neural activity space. Compositionality is fundamentally important for achieving difficult forms of generalization—a computational principle essential not only for flexible navigation but also for abstract reasoning and cognition more broadly. The neural maps in the hippocampus, MEC and mFC, are markedly different, with distinct computational properties, which may result in different functions in spatial navigation. In all three cases, the coding manifold is curvilinear, but it is high-dimensional in dCA1 and relatively low-dimensional in both mFC (paraboloid) and EC (torus, at least when the analysis is restricted to grid cells (18)). What are the computational implications of these different geometries? It is possible to extract the animals’xandycoordinates by reading out place cells. To see why, consider a population of neurons with highly localized place fields. By computing the weighted sum of the neurons, we can readily obtain the animal’sxcoordinate, provided each cell’s weight scales with the coordinate of its peak firing rate. In dCA1, in contrast to mFC, linear regression must be trained over the entire arena. Because the neural code varies across the arena, with different place cells activated in different regions, linear regression does not generalize, as shown by our analysis of dCA1 activity. This high-dimensional neural code of space, however, has an advantage, not necessarily for navigation, but for memory. In artificial neural networks, the memory capacity scales with the dimensionality of the neural representations (19). Grid cells share some properties with the mFC representation we have identified. Because the grid cell pattern repeats, activity in an unexplored region can be predicted from observed grid cell activity once the phase, orientation, and periodicity of a grid cell have been determined. Furthermore, if, as is widely believed, MEC integrates velocity signals that shift the grid pattern (20), a displacement in an unknown area will produce the same phase change as in a known area. However, translating a representation by integration is not ideal for planning long trips, because it requires simulating them mentally. Grid cells provide a highly efficient, combinatorial spatial code. By leveraging multiple modules with distinct spatial periods, the grid system can represent very large environments without sacrificing spatial resolution (21). However, extracting spatial coordinatesxandyfrom the grid code is challenging using simple linear regression. Position information can be accurately recovered only if the multi-scale grid modules are processed through a non-linear decoder. For instance, the grid code can be non-linearly transformed into localized place cell responses (22), from which position can subsequently be read out linearly. In mFC, due to quadratic distance scaling, firing rates can easily saturate, limiting the coding range in large environments. One possible solution is the existence of multiple mFC maps operating at different inherent spatial scales. Alternatively, the spatial scales may be dynamically adjusted to fit the environment. A direct analog of this dynamic rescaling is found in experiments on time encoding, where the time elapsed since a relevant event is encoded by ramping neural activity. This activity peaks at the next relevant event. Interestingly, when the time interval between two events increases, the slope of the ramp is dynamically adjusted so that it always reaches the same peak at the next relevant event (23–25). Similar mechanisms could stretch or compress the mFC spatial map depending on the current environment’s physical boundaries. The hippocampus plays an important role in learning and memory, whereas it is less clear whether it is important for navigation in familiar environments. Rodent experiments using the Morris water maze established that while hippocampal lesions severely impair the learning of new hidden platform locations, animals trained extensively prior to surgery retain intact spatial navigation capabilities, relying on consolidated remote spatial representations (26,27). Likewise, studies of amnesic patients demonstrate that remote spatial representations acquired decades before hippocampal damage remain intact, enabling accurate mental navigation and vector planning through childhood neighborhoods (28). MEC lesions severely impaired the acquisition of new spatial platform locations in the Morris water maze (29). Animals with MEC lesions exhibited learning deficits comparable to those with complete hippocampal damage, but could achieve good spatial performance in highly familiar environments. However, sometimes their underlying behavioral flexibility is impaired. When tested on novel starting configurations or flexible memory demands, animals without MEC input show persistent navigation deficits (29). In familiar openfield navigation, MEC-lesioned animals show impairments in updating their trajectories when distal landmarks are altered, indicating an inability to flexibly adapt path integration to visual landmarks (30). Causal manipulation studies demonstrate that while mFC inactivation leaves simple locomotion and familiar spatial memory intact, it severely impairs goal-directed planning, flexible route switching, and prospective trajectory generation in complex or dynamically changing environments (31–35). We showed that linear regression on the animal’s coordinates successfully generalizes to an area of the arena excluded from the decoder’s training set. This is a difficult form of out-of-distribution generalization that necessitates highly structured neural representations. For linear generalization to succeed, the coding directions forxmust remain parallel across all values ofy. In a high-dimensional state space, such parallelism is exceptionally rare, as random vectors are nearly orthogonal. When representations encodexandyalong independent, parallel axes, they are referred to as “disentangled” in the machine learning literature and are important for robust generalization. In neuroscience, we have previously termed these representations “abstract,” because they contain low-dimensional subspaces dedicated exclusively to single variables (e.g., an axis that encodesxwhile remaining invariant toy). Such abstract representations have been observed across diverse species and brain regions, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and hippocampus in macaques (17), the hippocampus in humans (36), inferotemporal cortex (37), sensory cortices (38), area CA2 (39) and mFC in navigation tasks(40) in rodents. Crucially, the presence of these geometric structures is correlated with the capacity for cognitive inference (36). How these disentangled representations naturally form remains a significant, unresolved challenge in machine learning (41). In our study, the latent variables are the relatively simple spatial coordinates,xandy. If our quadratic distance model holds, these disentangled subspaces do not require complex learning rules; they emerge naturally simply by encoding the squared Euclidean distances to multiple environmental landmarks (Methods). The neural maps that we observed in the frontal cortex may provide a basis for vector computation in navigation and complex route planning. In addition, given the simplicity of the quadratic distance model, the same principles might apply more broadly to any cognitive map in which “navigation” in a non-spatial latent space describes a general form of abstract reasoning. All procedures were performed in accordance with the U.S. NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Columbia University. Adult male C57BL/6J mice (Jackson Laboratory) were used as subject mice, beginning at 12-25 weeks of age. Animals were housed either individually or, whenever possible, in groups with littermates (2-5 per cage). Stimulus mice were age- and sex-matched and were primarily of the C57BL/6J strain. In a subset of experiments imaging medial frontal cortex (mFC) (2 of 10 subject mice), two stimulus mice were C57BL/6J and two were CD1; as no differences were observed, data were pooled for analysis. Mice had ad libitum access to food and water and were maintained on a 12-hour light/dark cycle. To enable calcium imaging, stereotactic viral injections were performed in each target region in separate cohorts of mice followed by implantation of a gradient refractive index (GRIN) lens above the injection site. Injection coordinates (relative to bregma) were: mFC (ML: ±0.3 mm, AP: +2.0 mm, DV: −1.8 mm), dCA1 (ML: +1.4 mm, AP: −1.9 mm, DV: −1.35 mm), and lvOFC (ML: −1.0 mm, AP: +2.4 mm, DV: −2.45 mm). Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and administered analgesia (buprenorphine XR, 3.25 mg/kg, subcutaneous) for all surgical procedures. The scalp was shaved and mice were positioned in a stereotactic frame. Eyes were protected with ophthalmic ointment (Patterson Veterinary) to prevent corneal drying. Body temperature was maintained using a heating pad with a feedback controller. Lidocaine was applied topically to the scalp to locally anesthetize the incision site. The skull was exposed and cleaned using sterile cotton swabs. A machine screw was secured to the skull to serve as an anchor for the dental cement. Prior to injection, a circular craniotomy (ĩ.2 mm diameter) was made over mFC and lvOFC. For these regions, overlying tissue was gently aspirated to minimize tissue pressure prior to viral injection. For dCA1, a burr hole was made at the target site prior to injection. Injections were performed using a Nanoject III (Drummond Scientific) with a pulled glass micropipette. A total volume of 500 nL of AAV1.CaMKIIa.GCaMP6f.WPRE.bGHpA (Inscopix) was delivered in 10 nL pulses (10 or 23 nL/s) with a 10 s inter-pulse interval for 50 cycles into mFC or lvOFC (3.35 × 1012vg/mL) or dCA1 (1.34 × 1012vg/mL). Injections into mFC were performed in either hemisphere, given its proximity to the midline, whereas dCA1 and lvOFC injections were performed in the right and left hemispheres, respectively. The pipette was left in place for 8-10 min following injection for mFC and lvOFC, and for 25 min for dCA1, before slow retraction. For dCA1, the craniotomy and aspiration were performed after viral delivery. A GRIN lens (1.0 mm diameter, 4.0 mm length; Inscopix) with an integrated baseplate was implanted above the craniotomy and centered over the injection site. The lens was secured using Metabond (Parkell), and the baseplate assembly was further stabilized and covered with black dental cement (Ortho-Jet). After 6-8 weeks, the level of GCaMP6f expression was evaluated using the miniscope. Imaging experiments began once viral expression was deemed sufficient based on visual inspection. Mice were deeply anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine and transcardially perfused with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Heads with implants were collected and post-fixed in PFA for 24-48 h, after which brains were extracted and further post-fixed for 24 h. Coronal sections (100 µm) were prepared using a vibratome (Leica). Sections were stained with far-red NeuroTrace (640/660; Thermo Fisher Scientific) to label neuronal cell bodies. Images were acquired using a fluorescence microscope (Nikon AZ100 Multizoom) equipped with a motorized stage and automated acquisition software for high-throughput imaging. Histological analyses were performed to verify GRIN lens placement and to assess GCaMP expression based on native fluorescence. Male subject mice explored a 45 × 45 cm square arena with an open top (Noldus). The arena was positioned on a table within a three-walled enclosure, also open at the top. A commutator and overhead camera were mounted above the arena, with cables routed from the ceiling into the enclosure. One wall of the arena contained a door through which the experimenter introduced the subject mouse and repositioned stimuli (empty cages or caged conspecifics, see below) at 3-min intervals during the experiment. For consistency, spatial references (left/right, upper/lower) were defined relative to this door: the wall containing the door was designated as the “left” side of the arena. The wall perpendicular to the door wall (to the left when facing the door) was defined as the “upper” wall and contained an empty holder as a landmark (seeFig. 1c). The arena walls were transparent, allowing animals visual access to distal cues in the surrounding room. We performed three behavioral assays during the light phase of the 12 h light-dark cycle. In the first (empty arena), animals freely explored the arena for 30 min. Exploration was not sustained beyond this duration, with animals exhibiting limited movement. The remaining assays used a four-chamber paradigm. In the cups assay, four empty carousel cages (10 cm diameter, 20 cm height; acrylic with gray top; Noldus) were placed at the four corners of the arena. The positions of the cages were shuffled every 3 min such that all 24 possible permutations were presented to the animal in a pseudo-random sequence. In the social assay, four novel male mice were placed within the corner cages, and the same shuffling protocol was applied. For mFC recordings, animals experienced these assays in varying orders across days, and some experienced subsets of assays across multiple days. In addition, a subset of animals was tested in related assays (e.g., with one or two conspecifics in the same chamber), as the experiments were originally designed to probe social-spatial behavior. Decoding and generalization results were consistent across assay orders, both when pooling across all animals and experimental days and when analyzing cohorts with matched assay sequences separately. For analyses presented inFig. 2, we used the first experimental day on which each mFC-implanted animal experienced the given assay (cups or social) in cases where animals were tested on multiple days. For recordings in lvOFC and dCA1, most animals followed a fixed sequence: empty arena (day 1), cups assay (day 2), and social assay (day 3). Two lvOFC- and three mFC-implanted animals experienced only the social assay, and two dCA1 animals were tested in a variable assay order similar to that used for mFC mice. Overall results were comparable across conditions. Entire recording sessions (i.e., full assay) with fewer than 50 identifiable neurons or insufficient exploration (defined as having fewer than 7,000 frames available for linear regression analysis after downsampling in the cups and social assays; see below) were excluded; when necessary, assays were repeated on subsequent days. Recordings of GCaMP6f activity were obtained at 20 Hz using Inscopix miniaturized microscopes and acquisition system (predominantly nVoke 2.0; 5 mFC-implanted mice were recorded using nVue 1.0. We switched to the nVoke 2.0 system for the majority of experiments due to improved signal quality and a higher yield of identifiable cells). Awake mice were connected to the recording system via commutators in passive mode, and the miniature microscope (Inscopix) was attached to the implanted baseplate prior to each experiment. For assays conducted in the empty arena (30 min), recording was continuous throughout the session. For the cups and social assay, neural activity was recorded during each 3-min session, paused during animal or cups repositioning between sessions, and then restarted, resulting in a total recording duration of 72 min for assays with cup or social landmarks. LED illumination was set to the lowest level that reliably captured calcium transients (typically 0.4-0.7, with most recordings<0.7). The focal plane (Z-focus) was adjusted across sessions to maintain a consistent field of view, using anatomical landmarks such as blood vessels. Following each 72-min or 30-min experiment, the microscope was removed and replaced with a baseplate cover or dummy microscope before returning the mice to their home cages. Overhead video was acquired using a Blackfly S USB3 camera (1.6 MP, monochrome; Teledyne) and synchronized with calcium imaging via a hardware trigger from the Inscopix data acquisition (DAQ) system, which generated a pulse after capturing each imaging frame. Hardware-triggered acquisition and synchronization were implemented using custom Python code adapted fromhttps://github.com/nicthib/FLIR-Multicam. Video was thus aligned frame-by-frame with the imaging data, and both were acquired at 20 Hz. Sessions in which synchronization failed were excluded from analysis. The mouse’s nose and tail-base were tracked using DeepLabCut, a pose-estimation software (42). Motion correction and cell extraction were performed using a custom pipeline based on previously described methods (43), with minor modifications. Briefly, raw calcium imaging videos were spatially downsampled (4×) and processed to enhance stable anatomical features (e.g., blood vessels) using spatial band-pass filtering. This was followed by a difference-of-Gaussians filter to further emphasize high-contrast, stationary landmarks, as described previously (43). In brief, images were smoothed using a Gaussian filter (imgaussfilt, MATLAB) with a small kernel (radius 2 pixels for our downsampled 200×320 pixel images), and the result was subtracted from images smoothed with a broader kernel (radius 6 pixels) to emphasize high-frequency, stationary features. Pixel intensities were then thresholded (values<4 set to 4). This yielded videos with a largely suppressed background and high-contrast landmarks, which were used for motion correction; the resulting shifts were then applied to the corresponding unfiltered videos. For each recording day, an anchor 3-min session was motion-corrected to generate a reference template using the NoRMCorre algorithm (44); this corresponded to a middle 3-min session for the cups and social assays and the full session for the 30-min empty arena assay. Motion correction was then performed on the filtered (difference-of-Gaussians) videos from all other sessions relative to this template, using NoRMCorre with the following parameters: bin_width = 500, init_batch = 1000, max_shift = 10, and iter = 2. The shifts were subsequently applied to the corresponding unfiltered (raw) videos. For both the social and cups assays, individual 3-min motion-corrected session videos were concatenated prior to further processing. Motion-corrected videos were then processed using the MATLAB implementation of CNMF-E to extract spatial footprints and temporal activity of individual neurons (45). CNMF-E default parameters were used, except for min_corr = 0.8, min_pnr = 9, gSig = 3, and gSiz = 11. For initialization, min_pixel was set to 25. For identification of cells in the residual after background subtraction, min_corr_res and min_pnr_res were set to 0.8 and 9, respectively. Following two iterations of CNMF-E, additional filtering steps were applied to remove false positives as in (43), based on criteria implemented in the CaImAn Python package (46). Briefly, cells were filtered based on temporal sparsity (>0.003), peak-to-noise ratio (>8.5), and stability of baseline fluorescence across the session. Baseline stability was assessed by computing the difference in mean activity between the first and last 10% of session frames; cells with absolute differences greater than 3 were excluded. Putative neurons were further curated by visual inspection using the CNMF-EviewNeuronsinterface to confirm appropriate spatial footprints and calcium dynamics, and remaining false positives were removed. CNMF-E performs frame-by-frame background subtraction and deconvolution, producing a denoised calcium trace (C) and an inferred spiking trace (S). For all analyses except spatial information content (Skaggs information) and determining the native decay constants of neurons, we used CNMF-E-extracted event amplitudes from S convolved with a fixed exponential kernel (2s decay constant), rather than raw fluorescence traces, and z-scored across the entire experimental session. This procedure standardizes decay kinetics across neurons and animals and enhances signals from temporally sparse activity. Hereafter, “z-scored calcium activity” refers to this 2-s kernel-convolved CNMF-E event trace after z-scoring across the full experimental session. Spatial information content was computed using inferred spike events as a mutual information measure between activity for each cell and the animal’s position (8,47), because this measure assumes discrete, sparse activity and can be biased when applied to continuous fluorescence traces. To estimate decay time constant (τ), we divided each neuron’s calcium activity (z-scored denoised calcium trace, C obtained from CNMF-E) into temporal segments bounded by consecutive inferred spike events (non-zero entries in S). Segments shorter than 2 s or lacking a clear decay (i.e., the z-scored signal remaining entirely above zero) were excluded. For each remaining segment, the signal was normalized to the range [0, 1] and fit with a single-exponential decay to estimateτ. This yielded a distribution ofτvalues per neuron, and the medianτwas taken as the neuron’s characteristicτ. We used principal component analysis (PCA) to examine the organization of spatial population activity. For each neuron, we computed an 8 × 8 spatial rate map by averaging z-scored calcium activity within each spatial bin. PCA was performed separately for individual animals and on neurons pooled across animals within each brain region and assay. Individual-animal PCA results were used for the decoder-PC alignment analysis (see below), whereas pooled-neuron PCA was used to characterize population-level spatial structure. Spatial maps were vectorized across bins and concatenated across neurons, such that spatial bins were observations and neurons were features. PCA was then performed by eigendecomposition of the neuron-by-neuron covariance matrix. To quantify the dimensionality of population variance, we calculated the participation ratio of the full PCA variance spectrum for each animal:whereλiis the fraction of total population variance explained by principal componenti. Larger participation ratios indicate that population variance is distributed across a greater number of principal components, whereas smaller values indicate that variance is concentrated in fewer components. Participation ratios were compared across brain regions using a pairwise two-sided Welch’st-test. To determine how the spatial information used by linear position decoders was distributed across principal components, we measured the alignment between each decoder’s weight vector and the principal component loading vectors obtained from whole-arena PCA performed separately for each animal. For each animal, we used the linear decoders trained to predictxfrom the upper and lower halves of the arena, andyfrom the left and right halves. Decoder weight vectors were matched to the neurons included in PCA, preserving their original ordering. For each decoder and principal component, alignment was quantified as the absolute cosine similarity between their weight vectors,wherewis the decoder weight vector andvkis the loading vector of principal componentk. Absolute cosine similarity was used because the sign of each principal component is arbitrary. We calculated alignment across principal components in order of decreasing explained variance. To quantify how broadly decoder alignment was distributed across principal components, we calculated the participation ratio of the absolute cosine similarity values across the first 20 PCs:Lower values indicate that decoder alignment is concentrated in fewer principal components, whereas higher values indicate a broader distribution. Participation ratios were calculated separately for decoders trained in each half of the arena and then averaged within each animal for thexandydecoders. To assess the consistency of decoder alignment across spatial regions, we calculated the Pearson correlation between the absolute cosine similarity profiles of decoders trained in opposite halves of the arena, using the first 60 PCs. Higher correlations indicate that decoders trained in different spatial regions rely on similar distributions of principal components. Each animal contributed one participation ratio and one alignment-profile correlation for each spatial axis. Differences between brain regions were assessed using pairwise two-sided Welch’st-tests. To characterize the dominant spatial patterns of neuronal activity, we pooled the spatial activity maps of all neurons across animals within each brain in mFC and dCA1, separately for the cups and social conditions. Each neuron’s activity map was represented on an 8 × 8 spatial grid. The four corner bins were excluded, leaving 60 spatial bins per neuron. The matrix was mean-centered by subtracting the mean activity across neurons at each spatial bin. We then performed singular value decomposition (SVD) on the centered matrix. The first three spatial modes were obtained by multiplying the corresponding left singular vectors by their singular values. For visualization, we plotted the reconstructed spatial maps without the fitted intercept. Spatial information content was computed from inferred spike events using the Skaggs information measure. For each cell, the arena was divided into an 8 × 8 spatial grid, and a spatial rate map was constructed by dividing the number of inferred events in each spatial bin by the total number of frames spent in that bin. Here, inferred events were defined by thresholding the CNMF-E-derived deconvolved spike trace (S) to obtain a binary event vector. To assess significance, inferred event trains were circularly shifted relative to the animal’s trajectory 1000 times for each cell, and spatial information was recomputed for each shuffle. Cells were classified as spatially selective if the observed spatial information exceeded the shuffle distribution by a z-score greater than 3. All decoding and generalization analyses were performed separately for each animal. For each animal, z-scored calcium activity was represented as an N x T matrix, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time points. We then trained linear regression models to predict the animal’s frame-by-frame nose position along either thex- ory-axis from population activity vectors. X and Y axes were defined relative to a fixed arena reference frame, with the door located on the left side of the arena, such thatx-values increase from left to right andyvalues increased from top to bottom. For full-arena decoding (Fig. 1d-g), models were trained and evaluated using frames spanning the entire arena. Decoding was performed independently forx- andy-position. To control for non-uniform spatial sampling, frames were balanced with respect to the decoded coordinate: forx-decoding, the arena was divided into four vertical strips spanning thex-axis, and an equal number of frames was randomly sampled from each strip; fory-decoding, the arena was divided into four horizontal strips spanning they-axis and sampled analogously. Decoding performance was then evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation with contiguous folds (KFold, shuffle=False). The data were divided into 10 consecutive temporal blocks; on each fold, the model was trained on nine blocks and tested on the remaining block, with each block serving once as the test set. Predictions from held-out folds were concatenated to obtain predicted positions across the session. Analyses were restricted to moving frames, defined using centroid speed>2 cm/s, with centroid position taken as the midpoint between nose and tail-base coordinates. Decoding performance was quantified as the median absolute error between true and predicted position and converted from pixels to centimeters using a calibration factor of 14.49 pixels/cm (constant across all videos due to the fixed camera position relative to the arena). As a null model, neural activity for each neuron was independently circularly time-shifted, preserving its temporal autocorrelation and activity distribution while disrupting its alignment to behavior. 100 shuffled datasets were generated for each animal and analyzed using the same procedure. For all decoding and generalization analyses, observed performance was compared across animals with each animal’s mean shuffle performance using two-sided pairedt-tests. For generalization decoding ofx-position, we trained on frames when the nose was on the top/bottom of the arena and tested on frames when the nose was on the other half, ensuring thatxposition could be predicted independently ofy. Conversely, for generalization decoding ofy-position, we trained on frames when the nose was on the left or right half and tested on frames when the nose was on the other half, ensuring thatycould be predicted independently ofx. This partitioning was critical for evaluating generalization, as it ensured that the coordinate to be decoded spanned its full range within each half, while the orthogonal coordinate was restricted, enabling assessment of generalization to spatial regions that were out of distribution with respect to the orthogonal coordinate. Spatial partitions were further defined with a 5 percent gap between adjacent halves to exclude frames near the dividing boundary. In addition, brief crossings between adjacent halves were removed: if the animal traversed the gap in less than 2 s (40 frames at 20 Hz), frames surrounding the transition were symmetrically excluded to yield a total exclusion window of 2 s. To control for non-uniform sampling of the decoded coordinate, frames were spatially balanced prior to decoding, similar to full-arena decoding. Forx-position, frames from the top and bottom halves were separately subdivided into four vertical strips spanning thex-axis, and equal numbers of frames were randomly sampled from each strip. Fory-position, frames from the left and right halves were analogously subdivided into four horizontal strips spanning they-axis and equally sampled acrossy-ranges. Following downsampling, experiments with fewer than 7,000 frames available for either coordinate were excluded. Generalization was evaluated in both directions: forx-position, models were trained on the top half and tested on the bottom half, and vice versa; fory-position, models were trained on the left half and tested on the right half, and vice versa. Generalization performance was quantified on the test set as the median absolute error between true and predicted position. Median generalization errors were computed for each train/test configuration, and their mean is reported as generalization errors in the figures. Decoding within individual spatial partitions was evaluated using the same 10-fold contiguous cross-validation procedure described above, separately for each half and each coordinate. The median error was calculated within each half, and the mean across the two halves was reported. The same movement restriction, spatial downsampling procedure used to balance sampling along the decoded coordinate, exclusion criteria, and circular time-shift shuffle procedure described above for full-arena decoding were applied to both within-partition decoding and cross-partition generalization. For comparisons across experimental conditions (empty, cups, and social), analyses were restricted to the first 30 min of each session. For each recording session, separate linear models were trained on the two halves of the arena for decodingx- andy-position. For each spatial axis, decoder weights from the two arena halves were normalized jointly by the Euclidean norm of the concatenated weight vectors. Neurons were then pooled across animals within each brain region. Decoder-weight consistency across halves was quantified as the Pearson correlation (r) between the corresponding population weight vectors, separately for each spatial axis. To assess whether neurons well described by the squared distance model contributed more consistently to position decoding, we divided neurons into two groups based on the model’s RMSE threshold. For this analysis, each decoder’s weight vector was normalized independently by its Euclidean norm. Within each group, we computed the Pearson correlation between decoder weights obtained from opposite halves of the arena, separately forx- andy-position. To examine whether differences in calcium dynamics could account for decoder-weight consistency across arena halves, we tested the relationship between each neuron’s native calcium decay constant and the consistency of its decoder weights across halves. We found no strong correlation between these measures (Extended Data Fig. 13). A Bayesian decoder was used to decode the animal’s two-dimensional position from z-scored calcium activity, as described above. Neural activity and position were averaged in non-overlapping 250-ms bins, and bins were included when at least 80% of frames were classified as movement. The arena was divided into 8 × 8 spatial bins. For each neuron, mean activity was estimated separately for each spatial bin, whereas a single activity variance was estimated across all training samples. Spatial rate maps were smoothed with a 2D Gaussian kernel (σ= 1; kernel truncated at 3σ), and spatial bins containing fewer than five training samples were excluded from decoding. The decoder assumed Gaussian activity distributions and conditional independence between neurons. A uniform prior was used across valid spatial bins. The center of the bin with the maximum posterior probability was selected as the decoded position. Decoder performance was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation, with the recording divided into five contiguous temporal blocks. Four blocks were used for training and the remaining block for testing, with each block serving once as the test set. Decoding error was calculated as the Euclidean distance between the true and decoded positions. For each cross-validation fold, the mean decoding error was calculated across all held-out samples. For each animal, decoding performance was summarized as the mean of the five fold-wise mean decoding errors. To generate a null distribution, neural activity was circularly shifted relative to behavior 100 times, with shifts of at least 30 s. For each brain region and assay, observed decoding errors were compared with the corresponding mean shuffled decoding errors across animals using a two-sided pairedt-test, with each animal contributing one observed value and the mean of its 100 shuffled values. Neural spatial representations were analyzed by modeling the firing rate of individual neurons as a function of the animal’s spatial coordinates (x, y). Raw empirical spatial firing rate maps,Z(x, y), and their associated standard deviation maps,S(x, y), were extracted for each neuron. The four unexplored extremities (corners) of the square arena were excluded from the fitting procedure. Spatial coordinates were normalized to the range [−1, 1] across both axes. We fitted a pure distance model to the measured fields:Model parameters were estimated using a weighted non-linear least squares optimization (trust-region-reflective algorithm). The residual objective function was weighted by the inverse of the empirical standard deviation at each spatial bin:W(x, y) = 1/max(S(x, y),ϵ). Initial parameter guesses were derived from a closed-form weighted linear least squares fit on the expanded polynomial forms to prevent convergence on local minima. title: A multiverse analysis of stomach-brain coupling in humans
author: Ngo, T. T. T.; Hsu, T.-Y.; Duncan, N. W.
text: The gastric-brain axis is a burgeoning field of neuroscience; however, inferences from neuroimaging research are often constrained by the high dimensionality of methodological choices potentially leading to disparate outcomes. This study addresses such concerns by performing a multiverse analysis of gastric-brain coupling in humans. We systematically evaluated 5,184 unique analytic pipelines using electroencephalography (EEG) and electrogastrography (EGG) data to survey the methodological sensitivity of gastric-brain coupling. Our results reveal that whilst analytic decisions influence the magnitude of observed coupling, at the group level the phenomenon remains relatively consistent across the parameter space. High inter-individual variance can, however, be observed. Coupling was observed in the alpha, theta, and beta bands, with the latter two bands showing coupling at the largest number of electrodes. Coupling across frequency bands was primarily seen in medial electrodes, with some left lateral coupling also observed. Overall, these findings suggest that EEG-EGG based measurement of gastric-brain coupling is likely to be consistent across a significant range of plausible analytic pipelines at the group-level in healthy participants, providing useful context for future studies. The connection between the digestive system and the brain is a topic of increasing interest. A burgeoning literature is elucidating how these organ systems interact and how these interactions can influence our experience and behaviour [1,2]. Levels of investigation range from circulating factors arising from gut biota to the effects of bidirectional direct innervation between the systems. Importantly, evidence indicates that interactions between the systems may play a role in pathological conditions [3,4]. There are thus both scientific and clinical motivations for developing our understanding of this axis as part of a wider research programme probing the relationship between the brain and the body [1,5,6]. In this context, neuroimaging studies in humans have begun to map patterns of dynamic influences of stomach contractile activity on the brain [7]. This gastric-brain coupling was first shown with the amplitude of brain alpha oscillations being linked to the slow rhythm of the stomach [8]. Subsequently, the spatial extent of gastric-brain coupling was mapped with functional MRI (fMRI), showing a network of brain regions that are coupled to the contractile rhythm of the stomach [9,10]. A similar spatial pattern of gastric-brain coupling has also been seen with MEG measures of brain activity [11]. These studies together introduce a complex interaction between the stomach and brain and open up important avenues of future research. Although such neuroimaging studies of the gut-brain axis are likely to play an important role in our understanding of how the brain and body interact, there are known issues within the imaging field related to analytic flexibility. Across different modalities, it has been highlighted that the high dimensionality of possible methodological choices available when analysing neuroimaging data may lead to variable analytic outcomes [12,13]. Empirical work has shown that such variability can result in false negatives, false positives, or outcomes in the opposite direction from the true effect [14–20]. This can lead to a lack of robustness in a research domain and, particularly if connected to publication bias, may lead to invalid inferences being made by the research community. With gastric-brain coupling research at a relatively early stage, we therefore sought to quantify the ‘multiverse’ of analytic outcomes [21,22]. By systematically varying preprocessing and estimation parameters, we aimed to identify which nodes of the analysis pipeline are most influential in determining the presence or strength of observed coupling. It is hoped that surveying the influence of analytic choices on outcomes in this way can contribute to a strong methodological foundation that future research can build upon for robust and replicable results. This may be of particular importance for the gastric-brain field as the need to combine multiple complex measures from two separate organ systems presents a large set of possible decisions to researchers. For this work we chose to focus on EEG-based measures of brain activity for estimating the gastric-brain coupling. This was for three reasons. Firstly, EEG appears to be a fast growing modality for gastric-brain coupling, with a number of studies using that modality being published around the time of writing [23–27]. Secondly, EEG is a convenient approach for studies of pathological states. Thirdly, EEG is also more accessible to those living in lower-resourced areas, which may help reduce potential bias in our understanding of the gastric-brain system from selective sampling [28,29]. It should be noted, however, that the use of EEG has downsides in the context of measuring potential gastric-brain coupling. In particular, the low spatial resolution limits separation between different brain networks, which may show coupling within specific frequency bands [11]. This could limit the effects that can be detected. Simultaneous EEG and electrogastrography (EGG) data were therefore acquired from a group of healthy young adults. These data were then entered into a multiverse analysis and the resulting set of outcomes further analysed to establish the methodological sensitivity of any group-level evidence for coupling between the EEG and EGG data. Forty-six adults were recruited for the study. Participants were required to have: no history of eating disorders; no acute or chronic gastrointestinal disorders; no current or past diagnosis of psychiatric or neurological disorders; normal or corrected-to-normal vision; and a body mass index (BMI) of 18-25. Of the 46 recruited, six were excluded due to a lack of a reliable EGG signal. This left a sample of 40 participants (20 female; mean age = 27.7 ± 3.2 years; mean BMI = 21.0 ± 1.8). The study was approved by the Taipei Medical University Institutional Review Board (N202408044). Participants provided written informed consent and were financially compensated for their participation. Participants were asked to refrain from eating in the four hours prior to their session, and to limit fluid intake in the two hours prior. They were also asked to not consume nicotine on the day of the study or alcohol from the day before. Upon arriving, participants were informed about the study and consent was obtained. After this, EEG and EGG electrodes were placed on the head and abdomen. Participants were seated in a semi-recumbent position that allowed them to fully relax their abdominal muscles to facilitate the measurement of the gastric slow-wave signal. Data acquisition was conducted in a lit room. All sessions began at 16:00 to minimise variation due to circadian or metabolic factors. During the study, each participant completed two resting state sessions lasting ten minutes each. During these periods, they were instructed to keep their eyes open, relax, and minimize movement. A fixation cross was located in their eyeline, upon which they were asked to maintain their gaze. A short break was provided between the sessions. The experimental procedures, including preparation, questionnaires, EEG, and EGG acquisition, required approximately 1.5–2 hours. Gastric myoelectrical signals were recorded using a nine-channel OpenBCI Cyton biosensing board (OpenBCI, New York City, USA). Adhesive Ag/AgCl electrodes were positioned following a standardised abdominal montage for capturing gastric slow-wave potentials [30]. In more detail, the first electrode (E1) was placed approximately 2 cm above the umbilicus on the midline, with two additional electrodes (E2 and E3) positioned superiorly along the same axis at intervals corresponding to one-third and two-thirds of the distance to the xiphoid process. Another vertical column of electrodes was placed beneath the midpoint of the left clavicle. These electrodes (E6 and E7) were aligned horizontally with the E1 and E2. When necessary, the upper left electrode (E7) was shifted medially to avoid interference from the costal margin. Two intermediate electrodes (E4 and E5) were placed midway between these vertical columns, positioned at the midpoints between E1-E2 and E2-E3, respectively. A reference electrode was located contralateral to the midline at a site symmetric to E5, and a ground electrode was placed on the lower left abdomen above the iliac crest. Details of abdominal electrode placement are given inFigure 1A. Data were sampled at 250 Hz. (A) Illustration of the location of the seven abdominal electrodes (E1–E7) used for electrogastrography (EGG) recordings. Marker colour shade reflects the proportion of participants for whom that electrode is identified exhibiting the highest peak power within the gastric slow wave range (0.033–0.067 Hz). (B) Participant power spectra for included EEG data. (C) Participant power spectra for included EGG data. As raw signal amplitude naturally varies across individuals [30], spectra were calculated from standardised time EGG time series to allow comparison of peaks across participants. Prior to analysis, EGG recordings were cropped to the trigger indicating the start of the recording session. Slow drifts were removed from each channel using a polynomial regression (Legendre basis functions, orders 1–3). After removing faulty cycles, participants had a median of 29 (range = 24 - 32) valid gastric cycles included in the analysis (seeTable S1andFigure S2for details). Brain electrophysiological signals were acquired using a 32-channel Brain Products system configured according to the international 10–20 electrode placement scheme. Four electrooculography (EOG) electrodes were positioned around the eyes to facilitate removal of ocular artifacts. Two electrodes were placed on the mastoid processes as reference channels. Data were sampled at 1000 Hz and electrode impedances were kept below 10 kΩ for all participants. Continuous data were recorded using Brain Vision Recorder software (Brain Products, Munich, Germany). Prior to data analysis, EEG signals were downsampled to 250 Hz to match the EGG. BrainVision files were imported into MNE-Python (v1.7) [31] and cropped to the trigger indicating the start of the recording session (see Supplementary Methods for details). A 1-30 Hz FIR band-pass filter was applied using MNE’s zero-phase forward–backward filtering, selecting a linear-phase design to avoid phase distortion in subsequent phase–amplitude coupling (PAC) analyses. Bad channels were detected via visual inspection and replaced using spherical spline interpolation. Analysis of the data was split into three stages: EGG preprocessing, EEG preprocessing, and coupling quantification. Each of these stages then has multiple decision points. For the multiverse analysis, sets of plausible decisions for each decision point were determined based upon approaches previously reported in relevant literature. Note that limited sets of plausible decisions were used rather than aiming for an exhaustive potential set as the limited set will allow a demonstration of whether outcomes are sensitive to methodological decisions or not while remaining computationally viable. An overview of decision sets is given inTable 1. These pipelines were run for a set of four EEG frequency bands: delta (1-4 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), and beta (13-30 Hz). In total, 5,184 different analysis pipelines were calculated. Pipelines were implemented in Python (v3.11) through a combination of MNE-Python (v1.7), SciPy (v1.15.3), NumPy (v2.3.5), and NiTime (v0.9). ICA = independent component analysis; FIR = finite impulse response; STD = standard deviation; IIR = infinite impulse response; IQR = interquartile range; MAD = median absolute deviation; MI = Modulation Index; CLC = circular-linear correlation. One run out of the two acquired was selected for the multiverse analysis based upon which had the better data quality. This was established based upon the following criteria: the presence of a clear alpha peak in the EEG data following basic preprocessing; a clear peak within the gastric slow wave range (i.e., 0.033–0.067 Hz) in the EGG; and more than 70% of EGG cycles falling within the normative human normo-gastric range (15–30 s) [30]. Two further quality assurance steps were applied to the EGG data of the selected runs. The first of these involved quantifying the proportion of time within the run where the normogastric rhythm was dominant (compared to bradygastric and tachygastric rhythms). A threshold of 70% of the run was applied, based upon prior literature [32]. Following this, the standard deviation of participant’s gastric cycle durations was calculated. Any participant with a cycle duration standard deviation of greater than six was excluded. One subject was found to have a dominant normogastric rhythm in below 70% of the run and was excluded (Figure S3). All 39 of the remaining participants had a cycle duration SD below six (Figure S4). Group EEG and EGG power spectra for the selected runs are shown inFigure 1B&C. For the processing of the EGG data, the EGG power spectrum was calculated within the gastric rhythm range of 0.033–0.067 Hz [30] using either (i) Welch’s method (window length = 200 s, 75% overlap) or (ii) a multi-taper estimator implemented in the NiTime python package. Selection of the dominant channel(s) was then done by either (i) selecting the channel with the maximal spectral power, or (ii) according to an averaged-channel approach that took the mean signal across channels whose peak power exceeded 90% of the maximum. The selected channel(s) were then filtered using either (i) a finite impulse response (FIR) filter with a passband of ± 0.015 Hz centered on the individual normo-gastric peak frequency or (ii) a fourth-order Butterworth band-pass filter centered on the individual normo-gastric peak. Instantaneous phase and amplitudes were then obtained using the analytic signal of the Hilbert transform. Gastric cycles were identified at negative phase-wrap transitions (π → −π), and their durations were computed. Artifact detection was implemented as a multiverse of nine cycle-based rejection configurations (3 statistical criteria x 3 thresholds). Central tendency and dispersion were estimated using one of three methods: standard deviation (SD), median absolute deviation (MAD), or interquartile range (IQR). For each method, admissible durations were defined as lying within k ∈ {2.5, 3.0, 3.5} units of the center. Cycles were rejected if their durations exceeded method-specific bounds or if their phase progression was non-monotonic (e.g., noise-induced phase reversals). Only cycles satisfying both criteria were retained. A binary valid mask was generated for each pipeline, marking timepoints belonging to accepted cycles. This mask was later applied to the EEG, such that EEG signal amplitude was extracted only during intervals in which gastric activity was deemed physiologically plausible. Following the basic EEG data preparation steps outlined above, the first decision steps for the EEG pipelines was a combination of which reference to use (mastoid or the common average) and the method for ICA artifact removal. For data using the common average reference, both (i) a manual identification of artifact components based on visual inspection of topographies and component time courses, or (ii) automatic classification using ICLabel, implemented viaMNE-ICALabel[33,34]. Components classified aseye, muscle, line noise, heart,orchannel noisewere removed, while those labeled asbrainorotherwere retained. Only manual identification was used for data using the mastoid reference as ICLabel requires an average reference. Band-limited EEG signals were then obtained for the relevant canonical frequency bands [11,35] via finite impulse response (FIR) filtering. The amplitude envelope was extracted using the Hilbert transform. The coupling between the phase of the EGG and the amplitude of the EEG was calculated through two different approaches: (i) the modulation index (MI) [8,36], and (ii) circular-linear correlation (CLC) [11]. MI quantifies coupling by assessing how far the empirical distribution of amplitudes across phase bins deviates from uniformity. The gastric phase time series was divided into 18 equidistant bins spanning the interval [-π,π], following previous relevant literature [8,25]. For each bin, the mean EEG amplitude was computed, yielding a phase–amplitude distribution. The MI is then defined as the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the observed distribution and a uniform distribution, normalised by the maximum possible divergence [36]. The CLC coefficient was calculated based on correlations between EEG amplitude and the sine and cosine components of EGG phase across the same 18 bins [37]. Three surrogate methods were used to generate null distributions of PAC values: one-block swapping, circular time shifting, and five-block shuffling. For the one-block method, the EEG amplitude time series was cut at a random time point and the two resulting segments were concatenated in reverse order. For circular time shifting, the amplitude time series was shifted by a random temporal offset and wrapped around at the recording boundaries. For five-block shuffling, the amplitude time series was divided into five contiguous segments that were randomly reordered. These manipulations preserve the amplitude distribution and spectral properties of the EEG signal while disrupting its temporal alignment with the gastric phase. One-thousand surrogate coupling values were calculated for each pipeline. Empirical PAC values were then standardized relative to its corresponding surrogate distribution aswhereμsurrogateandσsurrogatedenote the mean and standard deviation of the surrogate PAC distribution, respectively. Positive ΔPAC values indicate stronger empirical coupling than expected by chance. To evaluate whether gut–brain PAC was present across the set of preprocessing pipelines, we conducted a specification curve analysis (SCA) following the general framework proposed by Simonsohn et al. [21]. The input to the SCA consisted of subject-level channel-wise ΔPAC values obtained for every preprocessing pipeline. Group-level coupling across participants was then tested through a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of ΔPAC being greater than zero. Three inferential summary statistics were computed from the set of Wilcoxon outcomes across all pipelines [21]. Firstly, we calculated the median Wilcoxon effect sizeracross all specifications for a given channel, indexing the typical magnitude of coupling across the multiverse. Secondly, we calculated the proportion of specifications yielding statistically significant positive coupling, indexing the consistency with which that channel exceeded chance-level PAC across pipelines. Thirdly, we computed a Stouffer-type summary statistic by converting specification-levelp-values to Z scores and averaging them across pipelines, thereby capturing the aggregate strength of evidence for that channel across the full specification space. Statistical significance of these channel-level SCA summary statistics was evaluated using permutation-based null distributions. Under the null hypothesis of no systematic coupling, subject-level ΔPAC values were sign-flipped within the channel, while the same subject-specific sign was preserved across all pipelines for that channel within a permutation iteration. For each permutation, the full set of channel × pipeline Wilcoxon tests was recomputed, followed by recalculation of the three SCA summary statistics. Empiricalp-values were then obtained by comparing the observed statistics against their corresponding permutation-derived null distributions. A linear mixed-effects model (LMM) was used to investigate which preprocessing decisions systematically influenced gut–brain coupling strength. Taking ΔPAC values across all pipelines as the dependent variable, the different decision steps and frequency bands were modeled as fixed effects. Participant ID and EEG channel were included in the model as random effects. The model was specified as:The analysis was conducted in R (v4.5.1) with thelme4package. Follow-up comparisons were performed using estimated marginal means implemented in theemmeanspackage. Pairwise contrasts were corrected using the Holm method to control the family-wise error rate. Owing to the large sample size, post-hoc contrasts were evaluated using asymptotic z-tests. Whereas the SCA assessed the robustness of gut–brain coupling across the full multiverse of preprocessing pipelines, the LMM provided a complementary analysis aimed at identifying which analytic choices were systematically associated with stronger or weaker PAC estimates. Evidence for consistent EEG-EGG coupling was found when considering all channels and frequency bands (Figure 2). CP1 showed the most consistent evidence, showing an elevated proportion of significant pipelines (19.6%, p = 0.009) and mean Stouffer’s Z (0.55, p = .039), although its median correlation was not significant (r = .087, p = 0.055). Two additional channels survived one test each: F4 for mean Stouffer’s Z (0.56, p = 0.038) and FC5 for the proportion of significant pipelines (14.7%, p = 0.023). Overall, significant findings were sparse and were distributed across frontal and centroparietal/parietal electrodes, with the strongest evidence observed at CP1. Outcome from multiverse analysis across all frequency bands. A) Specification curve illustrating the top 20% of pipelines averaged across channels with robust coupling. B) Scalp topography of the number of significant inferential tests passed by each EEG channel C) Topography of average coupling strength across pipelines and frequency bands. The LMM analysis of influences on overall ΔPAC identified a number of factors that were significantly related to outcomes (seeTable 2for model coefficients). For EGG processing, PSD method, channel-selection method, and cycle-rejection criterion all showed differential ΔPAC across analytic choices. Post-hoc tests showed that ΔPAC was higher when the selected EGG channel was estimated by averaging EGG channels exceeding 90% of peak power compared to selecting a single dominant channel, while the multi-taper method resulted in a higher ΔPAC than Welch’s approach. For cycle handling, the standard deviation criterion resulted in higher ΔPAC than alternative methods. Reference levels were common average reference with automated ICA classification, Multi-taper PSD estimation method, IIR filtering, max-power channel selection, IQR cycle-rejection criterion, threshold value of 3.5, theta band, one-block swapping surrogate method, and MI coupling method. Coefficients represent differences relative to these reference levels. Positive coefficients indicate higher ΔPAC than the reference category. ICA = independent component analysis; FIR = finite impulse response; IIR = infinite impulse response; IQR = interquartile range; MAD = median absolute deviation; MI = Modulation Index; CLC = circular-linear correlation. SD = standard deviation; SE = standard error. CIs are 95% Wald confidence intervals. For EEG processing, the reference and denoising approach was found to have an influence on ΔPAC, with a common average reference with automated ICA being associated with highest values. For surrogate generation, the one-block swapping and circular time-shift methods did not differ (p = 0.724), whereas both produced higher ΔPAC than the five-block shuffle method (both Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). All post hoc comparisons are reported inTable 3 We note, though, that fixed analytic factors accounted for only 0.2% of the variance in ΔPAC (marginalR² = 0.002), whereas the full mixed model explained 5.9% (conditionalR² = 0.059). It may also be noted that the analysis outcome is strongly influenced by data quality, as shown by a supplementary comparison between the selected and rejected runs. An LMM analysis showed strongly reduced ΔPAC values in the rejected run (β= −0.117,t= −167.43,p< 0.001), meaning that no significant coupling is found in those runs assessed to have less prominent alpha peaks and EGG activity within the normogastric range (seeFigure S5). The LMM analysis also identified a difference in ΔPAC values across frequency bands. Post hoc analyses revealed that ΔPAC differed across all EEG frequency bands (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), with theta producing the highest values, followed by beta, alpha, and delta. This pattern is also seen when running SCA on the bands separately, where we see no channels with significant coupling across pipelines in the delta and alpha range (Figure 3& seeFigures S6-S9for band-specific SCA). Theta-band coupling exhibited a predominantly left frontocentral–centroparietal region, with consistent evidence at FC5, C3, and CP1 (all surviving the three inferential tests). Beta-band coupling was observed at right frontoparietal electrodes, with CP2, Fz, and P4 surviving all three inferential tests, F4 surviving two inferential tests, and additional evidence at FC2 and P3 from one inferential test. Band-specific multiverse outcomes for delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Upper panels show scalp topography of the number of significant inferential tests passed by each EEG channel. Lower panels show topography of average coupling strength across pipelines. The present study employed a multiverse analysis to systematically evaluate the methodological sensitivity of gastric-brain coupling in humans, as measured through EEG and EGG. By traversing 5,184 unique analytic pipelines, we aimed to determine the extent to which reported coupling is a product of specific methodological choices or represents an analytically stable phenomenon. Our results demonstrate that while analytic decisions do influence the magnitude of observed coupling, evidence for EEG-EGG coupling can be observed across a significant subset of the multiverse of analytical choices studied. This coupling is, however, relatively sparse and weak in this dataset, with large inter-individual variation. Our identification of coupling in all frequency bands other than delta fits with other work showing coupling across a wide frequency range [11]. We do see some differences from prior results, however, where delta coupling has been reported [11] and where alpha coupling has been more centred [8]. These prior results were obtained with MEG and so the contrast may reflect differences in the capabilities of that methodology compared to EEG. In particular, the lack of spatial specificity inherent to EEG means that anatomically localised frequency-specific coupling may be obscured. Alternatively, our work used canonical frequency bands for the analysis, meaning that more frequency specific coupling may have been missed. A more extensive multiverse analysis varying this factor may therefore be justified. Topographically, the channels showing the strongest evidence for coupling were distributed across frontal and centroparietal/parietal electrodes, with CP1 emerging as the most consistent measurement location across frequency bands. Although scalp electrodes cannot be interpreted as direct indicators of underlying cortical sources, this distribution would appear to be broadly compatible with previous MEG and fMRI studies describing a distributed “gastric network” involving sensorimotor and higher-order cortical regions [9,11,38]. This potential consistency with prior work may be further supported by the frequency specific topographies of significant coupling, where coupling in the beta and theta bands follow a general frontal and central distribution. Beyond investigating how sensitive coupling outcomes are to analytical choices, our results may provide some guidance for optimising future EEG-EGG research pipelines. The LMM analysis indicated that certain choices systematically yielded higher coupling estimates. For EGG processing, we found that estimating power spectra using the multi-taper method and utilising an averaged-channel approach (taking the mean of channels exceeding 90% of peak power) were superior to Welch’s estimation or selecting a single dominant channel. This average-channel approach differs from that suggested in prior work [30]. Regarding EEG, the combination of a common average reference and automated ICA denoising was associated with the highest coupling values. It can be noted that the second best approach was an average reference with manual rejection, pointing to the average reference being generally preferable. The method for generating null distributions for measuring coupling was also found to be relevant, with one-block swapping and circular time-shift surrogates generating similar outcomes and both exceeding the five-block shuffle approach. This fits well with recommendations that surrogates for continuous recordings should minimize distortion of phase and amplitude dynamics, with single-point block swapping preferred over resampling at multiple cut points [39]. Importantly, it must be noted that although differences between approaches were found, the ultimate magnitude of these differences was generally not high. Large inter-individual variation in gastric-brain coupling was seen in this dataset. Notably, the regression model suggests that this variation had a considerably larger influence on ΔPAC values than did methodological choices. Prior work with MEG has estimated that only around 8% of the variance in alpha amplitude was accounted for by the gastric oscillation [8]. This relatively small effect may be diluted further when using EEG and so apparent individual variation may arise from a lack of measurement precision [40]. Alternatively, the individual variability may reflect true differences in communication between the stomach and brain between participants. Although efforts were made to ensure consistency in the data recording context for all participants, there are still factors which could influence the level of input to the brain and how that affects ongoing brain activity. Importantly, gastric signals do not reach the cortex directly. Instead, gastric information is conveyed to the central nervous system through vagal and spinal afferent pathways [7]. Vagal afferents terminate primarily in the nucleus tractus solitarius, from which visceral information can influence hypothalamic and distributed brain networks [41]. Thus, variability in autonomic state or in the sensitivity and efficacy of these afferent pathways could influence how strongly gastric rhythms modulate cortical activity. One potential source of such variability is differences in circadian time between participants. Circadian rhythms are endogenously generated but are entrained by multiple environmental and behavioral cues, including light exposure, habitual sleep timing, feeding schedules, and physical activity [42–44]. The central circadian system coordinates peripheral physiology through sympathetic and parasympathetic autonomic pathways [45–47], together with hormonal, thermal, and behavioral signals [48]. Consequently, participants recorded at the same clock time, as was done here, may nevertheless have differed in internal circadian phase and autonomic state. Overall, we can note that the presence of identifiable gastric slow waves and cortical oscillations should be regarded as a prerequisite for assessing coupling but are in themselves not evidence that strong coupling must occur. The use of EEG in this study was motivated by its increasing prevalence in the field and its availability in clinical contexts. Our demonstration that gastric-brain coupling could be observed within this dataset across a meaningful subset of analytic choices points towards the potential of EEG as a tool for probing brain-body interactions in diverse settings. Importantly, as EEG is more accessible than fMRI or MEG, it allows for the inclusion of participants from lower-resourced areas, thereby reducing potential selective sampling bias in our understanding of the gastric-brain system [28]. The relative consistency across analytic pipelines that we observed suggests that EEG-based gastric-brain coupling may have the potential to serve as a useful tool for investigating gastrointestinal or neurological disorders characterised by dysregulated brain-body communication. However, as noted above, use of EEG limits the spatial specificity of the measurement of brain activity. Some evidence suggests that different brain networks may be associated with gastric activity in frequency-specific ways [11]. The mixing of signals between networks that could occur due to low spatial resolution would therefore potentially obfuscate such specificity. This means that the results obtained may only reflect a subset of gastric-brain associations and may omit others that exist. Any results should therefore be interpreted with this context in mind and method choice should follow the specific aims of a given investigation. Several limitations of the current study should be acknowledged. Firstly, our participant sample was restricted to individuals with a BMI between 18 and 25 and no history of gastrointestinal or psychiatric disorders. While this was necessary for establishing a baseline in a healthy population, it is unclear if the same level of analytic robustness would be found in clinical populations where signals might be more attenuated or noisy. Secondly, a proportion of our initial sample (approximately 13%) was excluded due to poor EGG signal quality. This exclusion may bias results towards particular subsets of the population from whom clear signals can be obtained. Thirdly, our work presents outcomes from multiple SCA analysis across the 26 EEG channels. This raises questions about the appropriate approach to potential corrections for multiple comparisons for this analysis type. It must be noted that the results given here have not had such a correction applied. Fourthly, 1000 surrogates were used in the analyses. It is possible that the choice of surrogate number could influence outcomes. However, it was not computationally plausible for us to extend our multiverse to include this factor. This leaves the effect of this decision point open. Finally, this work focused on resting-state data; future multiverse analyses could investigate if analytic flexibility has a greater influence during active tasks or following metabolic challenges (e.g., meal ingestion). In conclusion, this multiverse analysis helps add to the methodological foundation for the study of the gastric-brain axis. Gastric-brain coupling could be observed at the group-level in this dataset across a meaningful set of analytic decisions. This coupling was, however, relatively weak, with large inter-individual variability. The epistemological issue motivating multiverse analyses also remains. We as investigators do not know whether a reported outcome from any particular analysis pipeline is a chance product of the specific decisions made or not [22,49]. As such, a more general adoption of this form of analysis may be justified within the brain-body research field to support more robust inferences. A multiverse analysis of stomach-brain coupling in humans To achieve temporal correspondence between the cortical and gastric recordings, a hardware-based synchronisation system was implemented (Figure S2). The synchronisation mechanism is centered on an isolated trigger interface designed for use with the OpenBCI Cyton biosensing board (Electools, China). This trigger board incorporates optical isolation circuitry and digital input–output channels, enabling safe bidirectional communication with external acquisition systems while electrically isolating participant-connected hardware. The trigger board was directly mounted onto the OpenBCI 9-channel biosensing unit and linked to the EEG amplifier through a DB25-to-terminal block connected to the EEG amplifier USB 2 port (BUA). This configuration provided a stable TTL-level pathway between the two independent acquisition systems. Optical isolation components (rated to approximately 4000 V) ensured full galvanic separation, eliminating the risk of current transfer between devices. A dedicated digital channel (D17) on the trigger board was used as the synchronization marker. This line is hardwired to a physical push-button. Activating the button generated a TTL pulse that was dispatched simultaneously along two routes: To the OpenBCI system, where it was recorded as a digital event embedded directly in the EGG data stream; and To the BrainAmp amplifier, where it was received by the trigger input of the BrainVision system and registered at the corresponding sampling time in the EEG recording. During preprocessing, EEG and EGG signals were cropped at the first detected D17 pulse, yielding precisely matched temporal windows for subsequent phase–amplitude coupling analysis.
