title: Identification of QTL for yield potential under heat stress conditions through a tomato MAGIC population
author: Lin, Y.-P.; Hussain, E.; Hsu, Y.-C.; Lin, C.-Y.; Chen, Y.-S.; Hsu, L.-H.; Hung, C.-Y.; Huang, S.-m.; Yen, J.-Y.; Eybishitz, A.; Hanson, P.; Kang, S. W.; Hoshikawa, K.
text: BackgroundHigh temperature severely limits tomato reproductive development and yield, particularly in tropical production systems. Pollen viability and fruit set are commonly used as indicators of reproductive heat tolerance, but much of the supporting evidence has been obtained under controlled conditions. Their relevance to breeding under variable open-field environments remains less clear. This study investigated reproductive performance and its genetic basis under open-field heat stress using a multi-parent advanced generation inter-cross (MAGIC) population. ResultsWe developed a MAGIC population from eightSolanum lycopersicumparents combining heat tolerance and multiple disease resistances and evaluated 262 F5:6lines under natural open-field heat stress. Flower number showed the highest heritability (0.64), followed by pollen viability (0.56), fruit number (0.48), and days to flowering (0.25), whereas fruit set showed negligible heritability (<0.01). Despite its moderate heritability, pollen viability was only weakly correlated with fruit set (r= 0.22). In contrast, fruit number was strongly correlated with fruit set (r= 0.86), supporting fruit number as a practical selection criterion for reproductive performance under open-field heat stress. Restriction enzyme-associated DNA sequencing generated 16,350 high-quality SNPs for genome-wide association analysis, which identified multiple QTLs for reproductive traits, several overlapping previously reported loci. A region on chromosome 6 at approximately 31–33 Mb was particularly notable because it was associated with multiple reproductive traits and coincided with a previously reported heat-responsive QTL region. Candidate-gene analysis highlighted floral developmental regulation, represented by positional candidatesSlAGO7,ENO, andSlWUS, and cellular and protein homeostasis, supported by direct candidates including MON1, ECM29, and ubiquitin-related genes. ConclusionsSelection criteria established under controlled environments may not fully predict reproductive performance under open-field heat stress. Fruit number provides an integrative and moderately heritable indicator of realized reproductive success under field conditions. The identified QTLs and candidate genes provide targets for validation and development of heat-tolerant tomatoes adapted to tropical open-field production. Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is a globally important crop for both fresh consumption and processing. Its production is increasingly threatened by heat stress, which is intensifying due to climate change [1]. Optimal growth occurs at 26–28°C (day) and 22°C (night), while temperatures above 32°C (day) or 26°C (night) disrupt plant development [2]. Heat stress impairs photosynthesis by reducing the maximum quantum yield (Fv/Fm) of photosystem II, damaging chlorophyll function and overall capacity [3,4]. It destabilizes membranes, proteins, and enzymes, and induces oxidative stress through reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation [5]. The reproductive phase is especially sensitive, with high temperatures affecting microsporogenesis, pollen viability, and fruit set [6–11]. Prolonged exposure to mild heat (32°C, 70% RH, 14-h light) can reduce pollen viability by 86%, pollen number by 56%, and female fertility by 39% [12]. The rising frequency of heatwaves in major production regions exacerbates these impacts, highlighting the urgency of identifying the genetic basis of heat tolerance for breeding resilient cultivars [13]. Domestication has narrowed genetic diversity in cultivated tomatoes, limiting stress tolerance [14–17]. Breeding programs have historically focused on yield and fruit quality under optimal conditions, often at the expense of resilience [18]. Wild relatives such asSolanum pimpinellifoliumretain key adaptive traits, including high pollen viability, sustained chlorophyll content, and stable photochemistry under heat stress [4,19,20], making them valuable for breeding. However, introgression is hindered by linkage drag and the need to restore desirable fruit traits. The polygenic nature of heat tolerance, involving flowering time, pollen viability, and fruit set, further complicates breeding, necessitating quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping and targeted trait selection. In the past decade, QTL mapping has identified genomic regions underlying heat tolerance. Previously research reportedqPN7andqPV11on chromosomes 7 and 11 [8], explaining 18.6% and 36.3% of variation in pollen number and viability. QTLAB7.1_T2on chromosome 7 for pollen viability and several loci on chromosome 2 for flower number, fruit number, and fruit set were identified [20]. In addition, a QTL hub on chromosome 3 (53–65 Mb) controlling multiple reproductive traits was also found [21]. Meanwhile, a locus on chromosome 1 (82–86 Mb) linked to relative electrical conductivity and chlorophyll content was detected [4]. These studies highlight chromosomes 1, 2, and 3 as key regions for heat tolerance. However, most mapping has relied on bi-parental populations, limiting allelic diversity and resolution. Multi-parent advanced generation intercross (MAGIC) populations overcome these constraints by incorporating multiple founders, increasing recombination, and balancing allele frequencies. The first tomato MAGIC population, developed by Pascual et al. (2015) from eightS. lycopersicumaccessions, increased recombination frequency by 87% compared to bi-parental designs, enabling fine mapping of fruit weight QTLs [22]. This resource has also been used to study genotype × environment (G × E) interactions, aiding climate-resilient breeding [23]. The ToMAGIC population, developed fromS. lycopersicumvar.cerasiformeandS. pimpinellifolium, captured broader genetic diversity for discovering loci associated with fruit size, pigmentation, and leaf morphology [24]. By integrating diverse founder genomes, MAGIC populations reduce candidate polymorphisms and improve mapping precision, making them powerful tools for dissecting complex traits like heat tolerance. In this study, aligned with the World Vegetable Center’s breeding objectives, heat tolerance is defined as the ability to maintain high reproductive performance, i.e. yield potential, under heat stress. A MAGIC population derived from heat-tolerant crossing disease-resistantS. lycopersicumlines was evaluated and subjected to genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to identify loci linked to reproductive traits. These results identify key QTLs associated with maintaining yield potential under heat stress, providing valuable targets for breeding heat-resilient cultivars adapted to climate change. The MAGIC population was designed with two primary objectives: (1) to identify genes underlying heat tolerance in tomato, and (2) to develop elite heat-tolerant lines for breeding new varieties suited to tropical and subtropical regions. Parent selection also considered traits beyond heat tolerance. In tropical production systems, begomoviruses causing tomato yellow leaf curl disease (TYLCD) are a major constraint, and high temperatures often coincide with high TYLCD pressure, complicating field evaluation of heat-related traits. Therefore, candidate founder parents were screened with molecular markers for theTy-1/3gene, which confers tolerance to a broad spectrum of begomoviruses. Parents were genotyped for other disease resistance genes includingBwr-12 (tolerance to bacterial wilt disease caused byRalstonia solanacearum,a common soilborne pathogen in the tropics) andPh-3 (a gene conferring resistance to some strains ofPhytophthora infestanscausing late blight). The marker information is listed in Table S1. Candidate parents were also evaluated for horticultural (vigor, plant habit, maturity) and fruit (weight, color, cracking) traits. Ten breeding materials (eightS. lycopersicumand twoS. pimpinellifolium) were evaluated for pollen viability and high temperature fruit set in a greenhouse from August to October 2017 at the World Vegetable Center, Shanhua, Tainan. Mean day and night temperatures during this period were 35.4℃, and 28.1℃, respectively; the highest temperature was 43.4℃ and the lowest was 24.4℃. The candidate heat-tolerant parents were selected from literature review and breeders’ experience (Table 1). We used a randomized complete block design with three blocks and four plants per plot. Pollen was collected from the most recently opened flowers on the second to sixth inflorescences of the main stem for each plant. The pollen viability was assessed using a protocol adapted from Abdul-Baki [25]. Briefly, anther cones were removed from the flowers, opened, and squashed using tweezers. The released pollen was then stained by vortexing in 150 µL of 0.5% acetocarmine solution. A 10 µL aliquot of the stained pollen was placed on a glass slide, covered with coverslip, and observed under 40x magnification. Viable pollen grains (stained red) and non-viable pollen grains (transparent) were counted. Fruit set was determined as the ratio of the total number of fruits to the total number of flowers on the second to sixth inflorescences of the main stem. A detailed workflow of the crossing process is presented inFig. 1A. Eight cultivated tomato lines were selected as the foundation parents of the MAGIC population based on the greenhouse trial. To develop F1hybrids, we initially crossed heat-tolerant lines with disease-resistant lines. To enhance recombinant events, crossing the double crosses was performed by growing 120 plants each of CLN4430 and CLN4433. Each plant in both populations was used once as a male and once as a female in crosses. This process resulted in a total of 240 intercrosses between the double hybrids, allowing for the mixing of all eight genomes. The progeny derived from these crosses was advanced through successive generations using the single-seed descent method. To mitigate the risk of losing progeny under open-field conditions, four plants per progeny were initially planted. To preserve genetic integrity and avoid the effects of artificial selection on gene flow and pool structure, the first plant from each progeny was retained and harvested for the next generation. Additionally, superior plants were identified, selected, and harvested. As a result, 262 progenies were ultimately maintained and advanced to the F5:6generation. AEight parental lines used to develop the MAGIC population and the crossing scheme.BPrincipal component analysis (PCA) of five reproductive traits.CPrincipal coordinate analysis (PCoA) showing genetic relationships among the parental lines and population structure within the MAGIC population. InBandC, red, blue, and grey points represent disease-resistant parents, heat-tolerant parents, and MAGIC progeny, respectively. For phenotypic evaluation, a total of 262 F5:6lines were planted in two replications. Four plants per progeny per replication were evaluated in the field under natural heat stress conditions during the summer season in 2021 at the World Vegetable Center, Headquarters, Shanhua, Tainan. The seeds were sowed on the 15thof July; the seedlings were transplanted on the 12thof August; fruit was harvested on the 18thof October. The daily mean, maximum, and minimum temperatures were recorded at 27.9℃, 37.2℃, and 19.7℃, respectively. We evaluated lines for multiple traits, including days to flowering (DF), pollen viability (PV), flower number (FLN), fruit number (FRN), and fruit set (FS). Days to flowering were recorded as the days until 50% of the plants had flowered. Flower number, fruit number, and fruit set were counted and estimated on the second to sixth inflorescences of the main stem. Pollen viability was measured using Ampha Z32 Impedance Flow Cytometer (Amphasys AG, Switzerland) to determine the number of viable pollen grains and total pollen count. Pollen viability tests were conducted on the second and fourth inflorescences, with two open flowers randomly collected from two plants within each plot. The anther cones were removed from the flowers, placed in a 2.0 mL Eppendorf tube containing 750 µL of AmphaFluid 6 (AF6) buffer (Amphasys AG, Switzerland), and vigorously scraped along the tube bottom to release pollen until the solution became turbid. The turbid solution was filtered, and an additional 750 µL of AF6 buffer was used to wash any remaining pollen on the filter membrane. After the measurement, pollen viability was quantified using AmphaSoft 2.1.6 software (Amphasys AG, Switzerland). The correlation and principal component analysis (PCA) among traits were conducted with the R cor() and prcomp() functions, respectively, and visualized by corrplot and ggplot2 packages, respectively [26–28]. For the eight parents, young leaves of individual seedlings were collected for 10x coverage of the whole genome resequencing. The sequencing was outsourced using Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform of paired-end reads. After data was retrieved, we processed the raw reads following the GATK Best Practice to perform the reference genome-based single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) calling [29]. In brief, we used SolexaQA++ “dynamictrim” to clean the reads [30]. The cleaned reads were mapped to SL4.0 using BWA [31,32]. The individual SNPs were called by gatk functions “HaplotypeCaller” and “GenotypeGVCFs” and then merged by Picard MergeVcfs [33]. The SNP variants were filtered with the threshold of sequencing quality > 20 and mapping quality > 40. Then, we removed all the missing and heterozygous SNPs. Meanwhile, young leaves of the F5:6progenies were collected, and we divided the samples evenly into three groups to prepare theApeKI-digested DNA libraries. The sequencing was outsourced using Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform of paired-end reads. After data retrieval, we processed the raw reads following the similar procedure with what we did for the whole genome sequencing. In brief, we used Stacks function “process_radtags” to demultiplex the data and to check quality scores of the reads [34]. The SNPs were developed following the GATK Best Practice and filtered with the threshold of sequencing quality > 20 and mapping quality > 40 [29]. Samples with more than 50% missing sites and SNPs with more than 25% missing sites were removed from the dataset. We aligned the progeny SNP matrix with the parents SNP matrix, and the missing sites were imputed using Beagle 5.5 [35]. Phenotypic distributions were examined for the five reproductive traits using histograms and kernel density estimates. The normal distribution expected from the observed mean and standard deviation was overlaid for visual comparison, and skewness was calculated to assess departures from symmetry using skewness_fun() function in R. To reduce skewness and the influence of extreme observations, phenotypic values were log10-transformed prior to GWAS analysis. For traits containing zero values, log10(x + 1) transformation was applied to retain zero-valued observations. The genetic distance of the parental lines and the progeny was first estimated in TASSEL v5.2.89 [36]. Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was performed using the prcomp() function in R, with the genetic distance matrix obtained from TASSEL as input. The result was visualized using R ggplot2 package [27]. Since this population was generated from multiple parents, we considered it germplasm and conducted association mapping using the Genome-wide Efficient Mixed Model Association (GEMMA) software [37]. GEMMA utilizes a linear mixed model framework that effectively controls for confounding due to both population stratification and sample relatedness. In this study, we used a linear mixed model treating SNPs as fixed and the kinship matrix estimated by GEMMA as a random effect. The heritability was estimated using the Bayesian Sparse Linear Mixed Model implemented in GEMMA software [38]. The candidate SNPs were defined asP score< 0.001 due to the limitation of the replication in the field evaluation. FDR-adjustedPvalues were calculated using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure in R and reported as complementary measures of statistical evidence rather than as the primary threshold for declaring significant marker–trait associations. To define QTLs and facilitate the development of practical markers, significant SNPs located within 5 Mb of each other were grouped into single QTL regions. This 5 Mb window was determined based on the uneven and often extensive linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay observed in tomato populations [39]. From each QTL group, the SNP with the most significant association was chosen first as the representative marker for downstream analyses. A direct candidate gene was defined when a significantly associated SNP was located directly within the gene. The QTLs of reproductive traits in the four previous studies [8,11,20,21] were browsed on the SL4.0 genome using Genome Browser hosted on the Sol Genomics Network (https://solgenomics.sgn.cornell.edu/) to confirm the consistency with the QTL identified in this study. To assess heat tolerance, ten tomato materials were evaluated for pollen viability and fruit set, revealing significant genotypic effects for both traits (P value< 0.01). Among theS. lycopersicumaccessions, the highest to lowest pollen viability was observed in the following order: CLN1621L, Tomato 337, Nagcarlang, Siberia, Divisoria-2, Saladette, NCHS-1, and TstarD (Table 1). However, the rankings for fruit set differed, with Saladette, Siberia, CLN1621L, and Nagcarlang showing superior performance. As expected, the two small-fruitedS. pimpinellifoliumaccessions exhibited higher pollen viability and fruit set than the cultivatedS. lycopersicum. Given the goal of developing high-yielding tomato varieties without the linkage drag associated with wild tomatoes, fruit set amongS. lycopersicumwas prioritized as the key selection criterion for identifying heat-tolerant parental lines. Based on this criterion, Saladette, Siberia, CLN1621L, and Nagcarlang emerged as the most promising heat tolerant candidate although each is begomovirus and bacterial wilt susceptible. Consequently, four additional multiple disease resistant lines with superior fruit and horticultural traits were also included as parents. Field trials further elucidated the heat tolerance of the parental lines under open-field conditions that reflected realistic agricultural practices. CLN1621L and Nagcarlang exhibited superior pollen viability in open-field environments (Table 2). Additionally, Nagcarlang and Saladette demonstrated the highest fruit set and fruit number among the materials tested (Table 2), underscoring Nagcarlang’s robustness across multiple experiments essential for reproductive success under heat stress. Interestingly, TstarD exhibited high fruit set and fruit number in field conditions despite its low pollen viability. This contrasted with its greenhouse performance, where it ranked among the lowest for both fruit set and pollen viability, indicating that TstarD is highly sensitive to environmental conditions. These findings highlight the importance of considering environmental adaptability when selecting heat-tolerant parental lines for breeding programs. Days to flowering ranged from 10.5 to 44.0 days, pollen viability from 1.35 to 69.40%, flower number from 1.5 to 12.1, fruit number from 0 to 45.75, and fruit set from 0 to 56.95% (Fig. 2). Analysis of the relationships among reproductive traits under heat stress revealed that days to flowering was negatively correlated with all other reproductive traits, with Pearson’s correlation coefficients (r) ranging from −0.14 to −0.38 (Fig. S1), indicating that earlier flowering was generally associated with better reproductive performance under high-temperature conditions. Among the reproductive traits, fruit set was most strongly correlated with fruit number (r= 0.86,P< 0.001), followed by a moderate negative correlation with days to flowering (r= −0.36,P< 0.001). In contrast, pollen viability showed only a weak positive correlation with fruit set (r= 0.22,P< 0.001). Histograms represent the original phenotypic values for five reproductive traits. Skewness before and after log10 transformation is shown for each trait to assess changes in distributional symmetry. Consistent with these pairwise relationships, PCA revealed similar loading directions for fruit number and fruit set, whereas pollen viability and flower number were oriented in a different direction, indicating partially distinct patterns of variation among these reproductive traits. Days to flowering showed an opposing loading direction to fruit number and fruit set. The first two principal components explained 67.7% of the total phenotypic variation, with PC1 and PC2 accounting for 47.0% and 20.7%, respectively (Fig. 1B). Together, the correlation and multivariate analyses indicate that fruit number was more closely associated with realized fruit set than pollen viability under open-field heat stress, supporting its potential as a practical selection index for reproductive heat tolerance. Whole-genome resequencing of the eight parental lines identified 4,075,083 SNPs, providing a high-density genomic reference for the MAGIC population. Following SNP filtering and genotype imputation, 16,350 high-quality SNPs were retained for subsequent GWAS (Fig. 3). The average marker interval across the genome was approximately 48 kb, ranging from 17 kb on chromosome 6 to 195 kb on chromosome 1 (Table 3). Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) revealed relatively close genetic relationships among most heat-tolerant parents, with CLN1621L showing greater differentiation, whereas the disease-resistant parents exhibited broader genetic diversity (Fig. 1C). Within the MAGIC population, PCoA revealed two partially differentiated groups with substantial admixture, indicating residual population structure following intercrossing and recombination during population development (Fig. 1C). This structure was accounted for in the subsequent GWAS using a kinship matrix. SNP density across the 12 tomato chromosomes was calculated in 1-Mb windows. Colors indicate the number of SNPs per window, ranging from low (green) to high (yellow–red) density; grey regions indicate windows without SNP markers. Chromosome positions are shown in megabases (Mb). Given the genetic diversity among the parental lines, the MAGIC population was treated as a diverse association panel for GWAS. In total, 62 significant trait–SNP associations, representing 54 unique SNPs, were detected for five reproductive traits under heat stress conditions (Fig. 4; Fig. S2; Table S3). Of these associations, 20 were detected for days to flowering, 8 for pollen viability, 18 for flower number, 12 for fruit number, and 4 for fruit set. Three SNPs were associated with multiple reproductive traits: SL4.0CH01_7511997 with days to flowering, pollen viability, and flower number; SL4.0CH01_24105448 with pollen viability, flower number, and fruit number; and SL4.0CH01_62158112 with days to flowering, flower number, and fruit number. In addition, SL4.0CH01_63692426 was shared between days to flowering and fruit number, whereas SL4.0CH04_61821975 was associated with both fruit number and fruit set. Manhattan plots show marker–trait associations for days to flowering, pollen viability, flower number, fruit number, and fruit set across the 12 tomato chromosomes. The horizontal dashed line indicates the significance threshold used to identify significant SNPs. To account for the extensive heterochromatic regions and large linkage intervals in tomato, significant SNPs for each trait located within 5 Mb of one another were grouped into QTL regions. This resulted in 29 trait-specific QTLs, including 7 for days to flowering, 5 for pollen viability, 9 for flower number, 5 for fruit number, and 3 for fruit set (Table 4). Several genomic regions showed associations with multiple reproductive traits. Notably, regions on chromosome 1 contained overlapping QTLs for days to flowering, pollen viability, flower number, and fruit number. A region on chromosome 6 at approximately 31.6–32.5 Mb was also associated with days to flowering, flower number, and fruit number, suggesting that these genomic regions may contribute to the coordinated genetic regulation of reproductive responses under heat stress. The heritability of the five reproductive traits varied considerably, ranging from < 0.01 to 0.64, indicating substantial differences in the relative contributions of genetic and environmental effects. Flower number showed the highest heritability (0.64), followed by pollen viability (0.56) and fruit number (0.48), suggesting moderate to strong genetic control of these traits under heat stress. Days to flowering showed relatively low heritability (0.25), whereas fruit set had negligible heritability (< 0.01), indicating that variation in fruit set was predominantly influenced by environmental effects. Although pollen viability was moderately heritable, its relatively weak correlation with fruit set suggests that it may not adequately predict reproductive success under field heat stress. In contrast, the combination of moderate heritability and a strong association with fruit set supports fruit number as a useful selection criterion for improving reproductive performance under heat stress. Flower number, with the highest heritability, may provide an additional genetically stable trait for selection, although its relationship with final reproductive success should also be considered. Because the present experiment was conducted only under heat-stress conditions, the identified QTLs were compared with previously reported loci to assess their consistency across populations and experimental conditions. Several genomic regions overlapped or were located near previously reported QTLs for reproductive traits, providing independent support for the loci identified here. The strongest consistency was observed for flower number. On chromosome 1, previously reportedqFPI1andqIN1near 68 Mb [8] overlapped our flower-number QTL at 62.16–68.77 Mb. On chromosome 2, our QTL at 45.23–45.49 Mb co-localized withnflw2.3[21] and was also close to the heat-responsivefln2.1_T3_2Eidentified in an interspecificS. lycopersicum×S. pimpinellifoliumpopulation [20]. The repeated detection of this region across different genetic backgrounds provides strong support for its role in controlling flower number. Another notable region occurred on chromosome 6, where a QTL hub for fruit set and yield under heat stress was previously reported near 32.95 Mb [11]. In our study, QTLs for days to flowering, flower number, and fruit number were detected between 31.61 and 32.53 Mb. The convergence of multiple reproductive traits with a previously reported heat-responsive locus suggests that this region may contribute to reproductive performance under high temperature. In addition, for pollen viability,qPV11, previously mapped near solcap_snp_sl_36066 at approximately 2.5 Mb on chromosome 11 under heat stress [8], was located near our QTL at 5.09 Mb. Notably, Nagcarlang was used as a heat-tolerant parent in both studies, suggesting that these loci may represent the same or closely linked genomic region. For days to flowering, the previously reportedflw3.3[21] was located near our QTL at 58.37–59.83 Mb on chromosome 3, supporting the involvement of this region in flowering-time variation. Overall, the alignment with previous studies provides independent support for several QTLs detected under heat stress, particularly the chromosome 2 region at approximately 44–45.5 Mb for flower number and the chromosome 6 region at approximately 31–33 Mb for multiple reproductive traits. These regions represent strong candidates for further validation and candidate-gene analysis. The World Vegetable Center has conducted long-term breeding for heat-tolerant tomatoes adapted to tropical production systems, where open-field cultivation exposes plants to considerably greater environmental variation than controlled greenhouse conditions. Reproductive traits, particularly pollen viability and fruit set, have traditionally been used as indicators of heat tolerance in tomato because male reproductive development is highly sensitive to elevated temperature. Much of the experimental evidence supporting pollen viability as a selection criterion, however, has been generated under greenhouse, growth-chamber, or other controlled-temperature conditions. For example, heat stress under controlled conditions substantially reduces pollen viability and fruit set in heat-sensitive genotypes, whereas tolerant genotypes maintain higher pollen viability [8,20]. A major QTL for pollen viability was also identified and validated under continuous mild heat, explaining approximately 36% of the phenotypic variation [8]. Our results suggest that the relative importance of these reproductive traits changes under open-field conditions. Among parental lines previously selected for heat tolerance under greenhouse conditions, only two maintained high fruit set in the field, indicating that reproductive performance identified under controlled conditions does not necessarily translate directly to the target production environment. Under field conditions, plants experience fluctuations in temperature together with other environmental factors that can affect successive stages of reproduction, including flowering, pollination, fertilization, and flower and fruit retention. Indeed, previous comparisons between controlled screening and field performance have highlighted the importance of validating physiological heat-tolerance indicators under field conditions. This distinction was evident in the relationships among reproductive traits. Pollen viability showed moderate heritability (0.56) but was only weakly correlated with fruit set (r= 0.22), suggesting that pollen thermotolerance alone did not adequately predict realized reproductive success under open-field heat stress. In contrast, fruit number showed moderate heritability (0.48) and was strongly correlated with fruit set (r= 0.86), whereas fruit set itself exhibited negligible heritability (<0.01). These contrasting patterns suggest that fruit set is highly sensitive to environmental variation, while fruit number integrates the successful progression through several reproductive stages, from flowering and fertilization to early fruit retention. Our results therefore do not diminish the importance of pollen viability as an indicator of reproductive thermotolerance; rather, they suggest that the most informative selection criterion may depend on the target production environment. Pollen viability provides a relatively heritable and physiologically informative trait for controlled screening, whereas fruit number may better represent realized reproductive performance under variable open-field conditions. Flower number could provide an additional complementary criterion because it showed the highest heritability among the reproductive traits (0.64). Thus, combining controlled-environment screening for specific physiological components such as pollen thermotolerance with field-based selection for fruit number and other reproductive outcomes may provide a more effective strategy for breeding heat-tolerant tomatoes adapted to tropical open-field production. Because linkage disequilibrium in tomato can extend over relatively long and heterogeneous genomic regions, causal genes cannot be confidently assigned from GWAS signals alone. We therefore distinguished direct candidates, in which significant SNPs intersected annotated genes, from positional candidates located within 5 Mb of the corresponding QTL. Among these genes, two biological processes were particularly prominent: regulation of reproductive development and maintenance of cellular and protein homeostasis under stress. Several positional candidates have established functions in tomato reproductive development.ARGONAUTE7(SlAGO7;Solyc01g010970) is located approximately 0.85 Mb from the chromosome 1 SNP associated with days to flowering.SlAGO7regulates the trans-acting siRNA pathway, and its overexpression alters tomato inflorescence architecture and increases fruit yield [40]. Similarly,EXCESSIVE NUMBER OF FLORAL ORGANS(ENO;Solyc03g117230) lies within the chromosome 3 QTL region and regulates floral meristem size and floral organ number through the CLAVATA–WUSCHEL regulatory network [41]. On chromosome 2,SlWUSCHEL(SlWUS;Solyc02g083950) is located close to the flower-number QTL at approximately 45 Mb. Regulatory polymorphisms nearSlWUSunderlie the classicallocule number(lc) locus and affect floral meristem activity and locule number [42]. Together, these positional candidates suggest that variation in floral meristem and inflorescence development may contribute to reproductive performance under heat stress. This hypothesis is particularly relevant because high temperature can disrupt floral meristem termination in tomato through regulation ofSlWUS, resulting in abnormal flower and fruit development [43]. Several direct candidates point toward a complementary role for cellular homeostasis. A significant SNP within the chromosome 3 days-to-flowering QTL intersectedSolyc03g115810, encoding the vacuolar trafficking protein MON1. MON1 forms a complex with CCZ1 that activates Rab7-family GTPases and regulates prevacuolar compartment-to-vacuole trafficking and vacuole biogenesis [44]. MON1/CCZ1 from the wild tomatoSolanum chilensehas also been shown to enhance salt-stress tolerance when expressed inArabidopsis, supporting a broader role for this trafficking pathway in abiotic-stress responses [45]. Although its role in heat-stressed reproductive tissues remains unknown, the direct association ofSolyc03g115810makes MON1 a strong candidate for further investigation. Protein turnover was also implicated by direct candidates on chromosomes 11 and 6. Significant SNPs within the chromosome 11 days-to-flowering QTL intersectedSolyc11g062310, encoding an ECM29-like proteasome-associated protein. ECM29 regulates the 26S proteasome and promotes its disassembly in response to oxidative stress [46], suggesting a potential role in maintaining protein homeostasis during stress. More notably, the chromosome 6 region at approximately 31.6–32.5 Mb was associated with days to flowering, flower number, and fruit number and contained significant SNPs within ubiquitin-related genes, includingSolyc06g051090andSolyc06g051230. The latter encodes an RMA1H1-like E3 ubiquitin ligase. RMA1H1 regulates aquaporin abundance and trafficking through ubiquitination, and its overexpression enhances drought tolerance [47]. Although these functions have not been directly demonstrated under reproductive heat stress, the convergence of multiple reproductive traits and several protein-regulatory genes within the chromosome 6 QTL suggests that protein homeostasis may contribute to reproductive stability under high temperature. Overall, the candidate genes point to two complementary mechanisms: regulation of floral development, represented by positional candidatesSlAGO7,ENO, andSlWUS, and maintenance of cellular and protein homeostasis, supported by direct candidates including MON1, ECM29, and the chromosome 6 ubiquitin-related genes. Among these, the chromosome 6 QTL is particularly noteworthy because it was associated with multiple reproductive traits, overlapped a previously reported heat-responsive QTL region, and contained several direct candidate genes. Nevertheless, these genes remain candidates for functional validation rather than confirmed causal determinants of heat tolerance. The MAGIC population used in this study combines allelic diversity from multiple parental lines with increased historical recombination, providing advantages over conventional biparental populations for dissecting complex reproductive traits. The reduced confounding between population structure and relatedness in MAGIC populations can also facilitate the detection of marker–trait associations [22]. Importantly, several QTLs identified in the present study co-localized with loci previously detected in independent tomato populations, including the chromosome 2 region at approximately 44–45 Mb associated with flower number and the chromosome 6 region at approximately 31–33 Mb associated with multiple reproductive traits. The recurrence of these regions across different genetic backgrounds provides additional support for their potential relevance to tomato breeding. Nevertheless, the transferability of individual markers should be validated in independent breeding populations before their routine application in marker-assisted selection. Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. First, the population was evaluated under open-field heat-stress conditions without a corresponding non-stress control environment. Consequently, the detected associations represent genetic variation in reproductive performance under high-temperature field conditions but cannot unequivocally be attributed to heat-specific responses. The overlap of several QTLs with previously reported heat-responsive loci provides independent support for their relevance, but multi-environment experiments including both optimal- and high-temperature conditions will be necessary to quantify QTL × environment interactions and distinguish constitutive effects from heat-specific responses. Second, despite the increased recombination provided by the MAGIC design, several QTL intervals remain relatively broad because of the extended and heterogeneous linkage disequilibrium in tomato. The candidate genes identified here should therefore be regarded as hypotheses rather than causal genes. Fine mapping, haplotype analysis, and functional validation will be required to resolve these regions and establish causal relationships. Integration with transcriptomic analyses of contrasting genotypes under control and heat-stress conditions could further prioritize candidate genes and clarify the molecular mechanisms underlying reproductive thermotolerance. This study provides new insights into the genetic and phenotypic basis of reproductive performance in tomato under open-field heat stress. Evaluation of a genetically diverse MAGIC population revealed substantial differences among reproductive traits in their heritability and relationships with reproductive success. Although pollen viability has been widely used as an indicator of heat tolerance under controlled conditions, its relatively weak association with fruit set suggests that it may not fully predict reproductive performance under variable field environments. In contrast, fruit number showed moderate heritability and a strong association with fruit set, supporting its use as a practical selection criterion for open-field heat tolerance. GWAS identified multiple QTLs for reproductive traits, several of which overlapped previously reported loci. Particularly notable were regions on chromosomes 2 and 6, with the chromosome 6 QTL associated with multiple reproductive traits. Candidate-gene analysis further implicated floral developmental regulation, intracellular trafficking, and protein homeostasis as potential mechanisms underlying reproductive responses to high temperature. Collectively, these findings emphasize the importance of evaluating heat tolerance in target production environments and provide genomic regions and candidate genes for further validation. Multi-environment evaluation, fine mapping, and functional studies will be essential to translate these findings into robust molecular tools for breeding heat-tolerant tomatoes. title: Cell type-specific epigenomic variation and its association with genotype in the human breast
author: Hauduc, A.; Steif, J.; Bilenky, M.; Moksa, M. M.; Cao, Q.; Ding, S.; Eaves, C. J.; Hirst, M.
text: BackgroundUnderstanding the interplay between genomic variation and the epigenome is fundamental to the study of development and mechanisms of disease. Previous studies have leveraged population-scale genotype surveys to associate alleles with epigenomic states in heterogenous tissue types. However, epigenomes are inherently cell type-specific, giving rise to unique genome–epigenome interactions that can influence distinct functional states and susceptibility to disease. Moreover, the extent of individual variation in cell type-specific epigenotypes remains poorly understood, posing additional challenges to accurately link genotypes with epigenomic features. ResultsWe generated comprehensive genomic and epigenomic profiles of four functionally defined human breast epithelial cell types from eight healthy individuals. To quantify inter-individual epigenomic variation, we developed a statistical framework that measures variability in histone modification landscapes across individuals. This analysis revealed substantially greater variation in repressive chromatin marked by H3K27me3 than in active chromatin marked by H3K27ac and H3K4me3. Integrative chromatin state analysis further identified enhancer elements as the principal source of epigenomic divergence between individuals. Stable enhancer states corresponded to high-confidencecis-regulatory elements that underpin cell type-specific transcriptional programs, whereas variable enhancer states were enriched for environmentally responsive regulatory circuits. Mapping genetic variants associated with chromatin state variation uncovered extensive cell type-specificity, with nearly 90% of regulatory variants detected in only a single cell type. These associations were strongly enriched within active regulatory chromatin and, when integrated with gene expression, enabled the prioritization of functional regulatory variants. We experimentally validated one such variant, rs75071948, demonstrating allele-specific regulation ofANXA1expression using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing. ConclusionsOur study defines the landscape of normal epigenomic variation across the major human breast epithelial cell types and demonstrates that genome–epigenome interactions are highly cell type-specific. These findings establish cell type as a critical determinant of the functional interpretation of regulatory genetic variation and provide a framework for understanding how inherited genetic variation shapes normal breast biology and disease susceptibility. Following the widespread availability of reference human genomes, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have become an invaluable tool for studying the impact of genetic variation by associating specific alleles with traits and diseases [1–3]. A key finding of GWAS is the significant enrichment of variant–trait associations in non-coding regions of the genome, where more than 90% of these loci were found [4,5]. These variants are enriched within regulatory elements and are thought to act by modulating the affinity of DNA-binding proteins such as transcription factors (TFs). TFs play a critical role in various regulatory processes, including directing the addition of covalent post-translational modifications to DNA-associated histone proteins (histone marks) and, ultimately, gene transcription [6–8]. Thus, through the action of TFs, genetic variants influence transcriptional and functional states. However, the functional consequences of genetic variants emerge from their interactions with the surrounding epigenomic landscape, which varies systematically across both cell types and individuals. Defining how genetic variation is translated into regulatory function therefore requires parallel characterization of this epigenomic variability. Epigenomic states are highly cell type-specific, and comprehensive profiling of purified cell populations has established consensus reference maps across diverse tissues and individuals [9–11]. More recently, single-cell epigenomic approaches have refined this view, revealing that functionally defined cell types occupy continuous distributions of epigenomic states within a set of bounds rather than discrete regulatory entities. [12–15]. These reference maps have provided the foundation for large-scale studies linking genetic variation to molecular phenotypes through molecular quantitative trait loci (molQTLs) [16–19]. Integrating histone modifications and chromatin accessibility with genetic variation substantially improves the functional interpretation of non-coding variants compared with transcriptome-based analyses alone. Whereas only approximately 43% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci colocalize with expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), the incorporation of chromatin accessibility and histone acetylation QTLs explains a much larger fraction of disease-associated regulatory variation [20]. A defining feature of molQTLs is their context specificity. Both GWAS loci and molQTLs are strongly enriched within tissue-specific regulatory landscapes [21], while an increasing number of studies demonstrate that many regulatory associations are further restricted to individual cell types [22,23]. In blood, approximately 30% ofcis-eQTLs are cell type-specific [21,24–30], whereas in the brain this proportion reaches nearly 46% [31,32]. Population-scale single-cell QTL mapping has reinforced this principle: the OneK1K study, profiling 1.27 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 982 individuals, found that mostcis-eQTLs exhibit cell type-specific allelic effects, including dynamic regulatory effects that emerge along differentiation trajectories [33]. Similarly, approximately 40% of histone quantitative trait loci (hQTLs) identified in immune cells are restricted to individual cell types [26]. Despite these advances, nearly all high-resolution molQTL studies have been performed in blood-derived cell types or immortalized cell lines. Consequently, the extent to which genetic variation shapes epigenomic regulation across purified cell types within solid human tissues remains largely unknown, representing a major gap in our understanding of genome–epigenome interactions in normal tissue biology and disease. Furthermore, beyond variant–epigenome interactions themselves, the landscape of epigenomic variation within which these associations arise remains poorly understood. Histone marks are among the most dynamic epigenomic modifications and are organized into cell type-specific patterns that define cell type function and identity [9,34,35], yet our understanding of histone mark heterogeneity within functionally defined cell types remains limited [36]. The foundational characterization of inter-individual variability in chromatin states was performed in lymphoblastoid cell lines, where enhancer activity was identified as particularly diverse across individuals while gene expression remained comparatively stable, establishing the regulatory enhancer layer as the principal substrate of inter-individual epigenomic variation [37–39]. This pattern was extended to primary immune cell populations through the BLUEPRINT consortium, which profiled approximately 200 donors across three immune cell types and demonstrated that hQTLs are more cell type-specific than eQTLs or methylation QTLs measured at matched loci in the same dataset [40]. Among primary solid tissues, only brain has been characterized at comparable population scale through bulk H3K27ac profiling of several hundred postmortem samples [41] and a recent multi-tissue extension that included heart, lung, and skeletal muscle [42]. Cell type-resolved population epigenomes within solid tissues remain rarer still, restricted to a small number of brain-specific efforts including FANS-sorted neuronal and neuron-depleted H3K4me3 and H3K27ac profiling in 157 prefrontal cortex samples [43] and a microglia-specific chromatin accessibility study in 150 donors [44]. No equivalent cell type-resolved characterization of histone modification stability and variability has been reported in other primary solid tissues. The human breast provides an ideal system for investigating cell type-resolved epigenomic variation and genome–epigenome interactions, as its major cell populations can be isolated from normal tissue by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). Here, we generated International Human Epigenome Consortium (IHEC)-compliant reference epigenomes for four purified breast cell types from eight healthy individuals and paired these with matched whole-genome sequences. We quantified inter-individual variation in histone modifications and chromatin states, defined stable and variable regulatory compartments using ChromHMM concordance analysis, and integrated these with transcription factor motif enrichment to identify the regulatory programs underlying epigenomic variation. We further mapped genetic variants associated with chromatin-state variation, which we termcishistone binary trait loci (cis-hBTLs), which we prioritized through orthogonal evidence and validated in vitro. Our analyses reveal a two-compartment organization of the breast enhancer epigenome. Stable enhancer states define the core regulatory architecture of each epithelial cell type and are enriched for lineage-specifying transcription factor networks, whereas variable enhancer states are associated with environmentally responsive regulatory programs shared across cell types. Genome–epigenome associations are highly cell type-specific, with the vast majority ofcis-hBTLs restricted to a single cell type and preferentially occurring within active regulatory chromatin. Finally, integration with gene expression enabled the prioritization of functional regulatory variants, including experimental validation of an allele-specific regulatory variant at theANXA1locus. Together, these findings define the stable and variable components of the normal human breast epigenome and demonstrate that both cell identity and inter-individual epigenomic variation are fundamental determinants of the functional interpretation of regulatory genetic variation. We performed whole-genome sequencing (WGS), chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) targeting histone modifications, and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on four functionally characterized breast cell types from eight individuals (Fig. 1a). Fresh breast tissue was collected from reduction mammoplasties and, following single cell dissociation, subjected to FACS sorting using EpCAM and CD49f surface markers to define four constituent cell types [45]: luminal cells (LCs), luminal progenitors (LPs), basal cells (BCs), and stromal cells (SCs), with the latter primarily being composed of fibroblasts, as well as adipocytes and tissue-resident immune cells [46] (Fig. 1a). Across all individuals, WGS was performed from genomic DNA extracted from one of four cell types per individual, and following sequence alignment [47], single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) were called [48]. On average, 3.8 million SNVs were identified per individual, of which 99.5% were previously annotated in dbSNP [49], and 88% were shared between two or more individuals (Additional file 1:Fig. S1). ChIP-seq for six histone modifications (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K36me3, H3K27me3, and H3K9me3) marking active promoters/enhancers, poised enhancers, active promoters, active gene bodies, facultative heterochromatin, and constitutive heterochromatin, respectively, was performed on each of the 32 unique samples as previously described, following IHEC standards [11,50]. ChIP-seq alignments were adjusted [51,52] to remove reference-bias-sensitive reads identified from variants called in each individual, and peaks were called [53]. We found that reference bias-robust alignment of ChIP-seq reads shifted a small proportion of overall peak coverage across histone marks, with median Jaccard correlation of variant-aware and hg38-aligned peaks within samples being 0.92 (Additional file 1:Fig. S2), corresponding to approximately 8% of peak territory being reassigned. Per-mark Jaccard medians ranged from 0.88 for the broader H3K9me3 mark to 0.95 for the sharper H3K27ac and H3K4me3 marks, indicating that broad chromatin domains are more susceptible to alignment-bias artifacts than narrow peaks. RNA-seq reads were processed through JAGuaR [54], and gene transcription across protein-coding genes was quantified [55]. a, Data collection overview. Left, cross-sectional diagram of ductal structure of the breast illustrating the four cell types included in the study; middle, representation of histone modification peaks across cell types; right, representation of genotype and variation in histone modification peaks across different individuals. Dendrograms representing unsupervised clustering of Spearman distances using complete linkage agglomerative clustering on;b, protein-coding gene expression;c, H3K27ac coverage of the top 1000 variable enhancers [50];d, H3K27me3 coverage of the top 1000 variable promoters. Branches are shaded by cell type (luminal cell (LC), orange; luminal progenitor (LP), red; basal cell (BC), blue; stromal cell (SC), gray; mammary cell lines, green). Bootstrap Probability (BP, green) and Approximately Unbiased (AU, red) values are provided for all major branches. To define cell type-specific epigenomic states, we performed unsupervised hierarchical clustering on histone mark occupancy in genomic regions relevant to each mark profiled (promoters, enhancers, or gene bodies), and independently on protein-coding gene transcription (Fig. 1b–1d, Additional file 1:Fig. S3). Cell type clustering based on histone peak landscapes recapitulated known relationships established from cellular characterizations of breast cell types, with LPs and LCs being the most closely related cell types [45,50]. As a comparator, we included matched ChIP-seq datasets of three previously published breast epithelial cell lines that consistently clustered together, away from the primary cell types, reinforcing the importance of studying epigenomic states in primary cell types. Depending on histone mark, the cell lines clustered either closest to basal or luminal cells or formed a distinct branch, potentially reflecting their previously reported mixed basal and luminal characteristics [56], which are distinct from those of primary cells. Active histone marks associated with promoters or enhancers (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3) proved to be the most effective in distinguishing between cell types, followed by the repressive and transcription-associated marks H3K27me3, H3K9me3, and H3K36me3. As predicted from their functional relationships, and as previously reported [50], LPs and LCs are more similar to each other than BCs as viewed through their epigenomes and transcriptomes, and this relationship is observed consistently across the eight individuals in this study (Fig. 1b–1d). We next assessed cell type epigenomic variation across the cohort, focusing on H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3, and H3K27me3, which are associated with promoter and enhancer regions linked to gene regulation and best classified samples into their respective cell types. In order to do this, we developed an approach to adjust for the contribution of measurement variability within total observed variability. For this, genomes were tiled into 50 base pair (bp) bins and variation in bin occupancy across individuals was calculated for each cell type. Bin values were computed using a Bayesian hierarchical model that accounted for sample-specific effects when estimating the group epigenomic state within each bin (see Methods). The resulting estimates represent likelihoods of histone mark peak presence from zero to one across individuals for each cell type, with zero indicating the absence of an observation in any individual, one indicating stable presence across all individuals, and fractional values indicating different levels of variability (Additional file 1:Fig. S4). The degree of variation observed by this measure differed by histone mark, with active marks displaying lower variability compared to H3K27me3, a feature that also varied by genomic context (Fig. 2a, Additional file 1:Fig. S5). Cell type did not significantly impact mean histone estimates within histone mark and feature categories. We found the most stable histone marks were H3K27ac and H3K4me3 in the context of promoter regions, where median histone estimates were 0.94 and 0.97 across cell types, respectively. H3K27ac and H3K4me3 were also distinct from other histone marks in that their variability significantly differed between promoters and enhancers (t-test,p< 2.2 × 10-16, mean Δ = 0.087, 95% CI = 0.085–0.088)), with their enhancer regions having median histone estimates of 0.49 and 0.37, respectively. Interestingly, H3K27me3 was significantly more variable than other marks across both promoter and enhancer regions (t-test,p< 2.2 × 10-16, mean Δ = 0.132, 95% CI = 0.131– 0.133), with the exception of H3K4me3 at enhancers. Previous work has noted that H3K27me3 is highly variable across different cell types and linked with both cell type-specific gene transcription and methylation [57], and we find that in breast cell types, this variability extends to inter-individual variation within a cell type. To better understand the structure of this variability across genomic features, we classified histone bin values into quartiles with variability described in increasing order as stable, low, moderate, and high (Fig. 2b). This revealed generally bimodal variability signatures across histone modification and cell type contexts, where most bins were either stable or highly variable, and fewer bins captured intermediate levels of variability across individuals. Although this bimodal structure was common within modifications, the proportions of stable versus variable bins differed significantly between them. For example, H3K27ac and H3K4me3 at promoters were the most stable overall, with an average of 59% and 69% of promoter regions classified as stable, and only 19% and 13% classified as highly variable, respectively. In contrast, H3K27me3 was predominantly classified as variable, with average of 47% promoter and 51% enhancer regions classified as highly variable. a, Box and whisker plot of Bayesian theta values (histone modification variability estimates) in promoters and enhancers across breast cell types (* forp< 0.05, ** forp< 0.01, and *** forp< 0.001).b, Bayesian theta values reported as quartiles excluding unobserved (0) bins in promoters and enhancers across breast cell types as stable (0.75 – 1), low (0.50 – 0.75), moderate (0.25 – 0.50) and high (≤ 0.25).c, Heatmap showing the association of mean promoter Bayesian theta with gene expression and variability quartiles.d, Correlation of H3K27ac promoter ChIP-seq read depth and gene expression ofCXCL10(left) in luminal progenitors (LP) andEPSTI1in luminal cells (LC) (right). We next sought to characterize the functional implications of histone mark variability by focusing on active, promoter associated marks H3K27ac and H3K4me3. Mean histone at gene promoters was computed, gene expression was quantified across individuals, and genes were subsequently grouped into expression quartiles to calculate mean expression and expression relative standard deviation (RSD) within each quartile (Fig. 2c). Promoter histone was only weakly associated with gene expression (Spearman’s = 0.25 for H3K27ac and = 0.12 for H3K4me3) and showed little relationship with inter-individual transcriptional variability (Spearman’s = −0.08 for H3K27ac and = −0.09 for H3K4me3). We next asked whether loci exhibiting variable promoter also displayed variable transcription. Restricting our analysis to genes with a transcriptional relative standard deviation (RSD) ≥100 and a mean RPKM ≥1 across individuals identified 468 associations, of which 431 involved promoter- and enhancer-associated active histone marks (Additional file 1:Fig. S6). Several had known relations to mammary gland function and disease (e.g.,ADORA1[58],ANKRD12[59],ANXA1[60–64],AZGP1[65],CXCL10[66–69],CYP24A1[70,71],EPSTI1[72–75],IGFBP5[76,77],MMP7[50,78–80],MUCL1[81,82],PDGFRA[83–87],PI3[88,89], SAA2[90],SERPINE1[91],SFRP1[92], andTPM2[93]). For example,CXCL10exhibited high inter-individual variation in both promoter H3K27ac and gene expression in LPs, with promoter H3K27ac levels strongly correlated with transcript abundance (Pearson’s = 0.70;Fig. 2d, left), a relationship that was not observed in LCs or BCs. AsCXCL10has been implicated in cell proliferation, invasion, and immune cell infiltration in breast cancer, these findings suggest that its regulatory activity may be modulated in a cell type-specific manner [66]. Likewise,EPSTI1displayed substantial variation in promoter H3K27ac and gene expression in LCs (Fig. 2d, right). Given its reported role in degradation of the mammary duct basal membrane during breast cancer progression, the concordance between promoter H3K27ac and gene expression suggests cell type-specific regulatory control in luminal cells. Whereas variable histone marking identifies regulatory elements that differ between individuals, stable histone marking is expected to define the core regulatory architecture of each breast cell type. We therefore asked whether promoters exhibiting stable histone marking were enriched for genes and transcriptional programs underlying shared and cell type-specific functions. To test this, we examined genes associated with stable promoter histone marking, focusing on H3K27ac. Comparison of stable and variable H3K27ac regions using monaLisa [94] showed that variable regions were broadly depleted for TF binding motifs across all cell types relative to stable regions (Additional file 1:Fig. S7), consistent with stable regulatory elements harboring the principal transcriptional programs, whereas variable regions may represent more environmentally responsive regulatory activity. Consistent with this model, stably H3K4me3-marked promoters in LPs were enriched for lactation-associated genes, potentially reflecting lineage priming related to parity [95] (Additional file 1:Fig. S8). H3K4me3-marked promoters in LCs were enriched forSERPINA1-associated functions, whereas stably H3K27ac-marked promoters in LPs were enriched for RAGE receptor binding, both linked to breast cancer biology [96–100]. Stable promoter marking also coincided with cell type-specific expression of numerous genes implicated in mammary development and breast cancer, includingAFF3,PTHLH,LTF,RASAL1,PAK5,MAMDC2, andCOL17A1(Additional file 1:Fig. S9a–e) [101–115]. Because stable chromatin states are expected to reflect lineage-defining regulatory programs [116], we next examined TF motif enrichment within stable and highly variable H3K27ac regions using HOMER. Stable regions were enriched for established lineage TFs, including EHF in LPs and TP63 in BCs, consistent with previous studies [50,117], whereas SCs were enriched for PITX1:EBOX motifs previously associated with vertebrate stromal cells [118] (Additional file 1:Fig. S10). LCs showed enrichment for AP-1 family motifs, including FRA1, FRA2, FOS, and JUNB. By contrast, highly variable H3K27ac regions exhibited substantially less cell type specificity, with AP-1 family motifs predominating across all cell types (Additional file 1:Fig. S11). To determine how inter-individual histone mark variability is organized within higher-order regulatory elements, we characterized chromatin states across all breast cell types using a unified ChromHMM segmentation framework (see Methods). We then quantified chromatin state concordance between individuals using pairwise Jaccard similarity, comparing both matched cell types across individuals and each cell type against the remaining three (Fig. 3a). To assess whether these patterns extended beyond the breast epithelium, we performed the same analysis in naïve CD4+and CD8+T cells from the IHEC EpiATLAS (Additional file 1:Fig. S12). a, Boxplots of base-pair-weighted Jaccard index for each of 18 EpiAtlas chromatin states, comparing within-cell type and cell type-versus-other-three pairwise individual comparisons across breast cell types.b, Fraction of ChromHMM enhancer segment genomic territory (merged across all enhancer states: EnhA1, EnhA2, EnhG1, EnhG2, EnhWk, EnhBiv) overlapping ENCODE Registry v4 enhancer-class cCREs, stratified by inter-individual variability category (not present: no individuals call an enhancer state; high: ≤25%; moderate: 25–50%; low: 50–75%; stable: >75%).c, Percentage of significant GREAT Reactome terms matching a curated mammary relevance keyword set is shown across variability bins, with points representing individual cell types and crossbars indicate the cross-cell type mean. JT tests were applied across the four variability bins with BH correction (* forp< 0.05, ** forp< 0.01, and *** forp< 0.001).d, TF motifs enriched in stable versus variable enhancer chromatin across breast cell types. Motifs reaching adjustedp< 0.05 and log2enrichment > 0.4 in at least one cell type are shown (55 stable, 21 variable). Motifs are grouped by the set of cell types in which they reach significance and sorted within blocks by mean log2enrichment. Chromatin state concordance varied markedly across functional chromatin compartments (Fig. 3b). Quiescent chromatin and active promoters were the most conserved chromatin states between individuals within each cell type, whereas enhancer states showed substantially lower concordance. Across all enhancer states combined, the median within-cell type Jaccard index was only 0.13, indicating that most enhancer-associated genomic intervals differ between any two individuals despite sharing the same cell identity. Bivalent chromatin exhibited the lowest concordance of all chromatin states, consistent with its dynamic regulatory nature [119]. Despite these differences, chromatin state concordance was significantly higher within matched cell types than between different cell types for all 18 chromatin states (BH-adjustedp< 0.001; Additional file 1:Fig. S13), demonstrating that cell type remains the dominant determinant of chromatin state organization. Together, these analyses identify enhancer and bivalent chromatin states as the principal source of inter-individual epigenomic variation, whereas promoter and quiescent states constitute a stable regulatory framework that is largely conserved across individuals. To further characterize the level of chromatin variation at enhancers, we annotated enhancer segments with the proportion of individuals calling any enhancer state and assigned it to one of four variability categories (high variability, >0 to ≤25% of individuals; moderate variability, >25 to ≤50%; low variability, >50 to ≤75%; stable, >75%), then assessed how each category distributed across cell types. Strikingly, we found that stable enhancers were the most widely shared, with 36.1% of stable enhancer regions shared with enhancers of any stability in all three other cell types, while 14.7% were specific to a single cell type. By contrast, only 17.0% of highly variable enhancer regions were also present across all cell types, and 33.6% present in only one cell type (Additional file 1:Fig. S14a). Enhancers that were consistently stable across individuals in one breast cell type were therefore more likely to be shared across other cell types, albeit at lower levels of stability consistency, and, on average, 53.9% of any cell type’s stable enhancer territory was uniquely stable in that cell type. Enhancer state composition further tracked this partition, with the share of enhancer state calls assigned to the active EnhA1 state rising from 7.6% in the most variable category, to 23.7% in the stable category. By contrast, weak (EnhWk) and bivalent (EnhBiv) calls declined (76.6% to 70.8% and 1.6% to 0.2%, respectively; Additional file 1:Fig. S14b). Having established that enhancer states account for most inter-individual epigenomic variation, we next asked whether enhancer stability reflects regulatory function. Stable enhancer positions were more likely to overlap independently annotated enhancer-class candidatecis-regulatory elements (cCREs) from the ENCODE Registry [120] than variable enhancers, although fewer than half of stable enhancer intervals overlapped an annotated cCRE (40–44% across breast cell types;Fig. 3b, Additional file 1:Fig. S15). Variable enhancer positions showed progressively lower cCRE overlap and encompassed substantially more genomic territory (Additional file 1:Fig. S16), indicating that much of the variable enhancer compartment remains uncatalogued. Among overlapping cCREs, enhancer stability was positively associated with regulatory strength, measured by H3K27ac maximum Z-score (Jonckheere–Terpstra trend test,p< 0.0001 in all cell types; Additional file 1:Fig. S17a), with the strongest relationship observed for active enhancers (Additional file 1:Fig. S17b). Enhancer state calls depend on histone mark signal crossing a detection threshold in each individual, so a weakly marked region is called inconsistently between individuals and is also more likely to go undetected in another cell type. Because enhancer stability and regulatory strength covary, the enhancer sharing described above could be generated by detection sensitivity alone rather than by any difference in how broadly enhancers are used. To disambiguate this, we matched enhancers of different variabilities by H3K27ac maximum Z-score, and this showed that within every Z-score decile, stable enhancers remained more widely shared between cell types compared to highly variable enhancers (25.3% versus 11.2% in the lowest decile, 52.6% versus 26.3% in the highest; Additional file 1:Fig. S18). Functional enrichment analysis showed that stable active and weak enhancers were progressively enriched for mammary-specific biological pathways, whereas bivalent chromatin became depleted for mammary-relevant functions with increasing stability (Fig. 3c, Additional file 1:Fig. S19). Together, these findings support a two-compartment model of the enhancer epigenome. Stable enhancer states define the core regulatory architecture of each breast cell type: they preferentially overlap independently annotated regulatory elements, exhibit stronger regulatory signatures, and are enriched for mammary-specific biological functions. By contrast, variable enhancer states comprise a larger, weaker, and functionally less resolved regulatory compartment that likely captures context-dependent regulatory activity, including environmental responses and epigenomic drift. To define the regulatory logic underlying the two enhancer compartments, we compared transcription factor motif enrichment and associated gene programs between stable and variable enhancer states (see Methods). Stable enhancers were consistently enriched for lineage-defining transcription factors characteristic of each breast cell type (Fig. 3d). Luminal cells were enriched for forkhead, ETS, AP-2, and nuclear receptor families, basal cells for TP63/TP53, and stromal cells for TCF21, RFX, and CEBP family motifs, recapitulating established mammary lineage regulators [50]. Across all four cell types, stable enhancers were additionally enriched for NFI family motifs, extending their established role in differentiated mammary epithelium to the stromal compartment [121]. In contrast, variable enhancers displayed remarkably little cell type specificity. The only transcription factor family consistently enriched across all four breast cell types was the interferon regulatory factor (IRF) family, while AP-1 motifs were shared between both compartments, consistent with their established roles in both lineage maintenance and inducible stress responses [122,123]. These findings indicate that stable enhancers encode cell identity programs, whereas variable enhancers preferentially capture environmentally responsive regulatory activity. Pathway enrichment analysis mirrored this partitioning (Additional file 1:Fig. S20; Additional file 1:Table S5). Stable enhancers were associated with canonical lineage-specific biological processes, including estrogen signaling in mature luminal cells, Notch signaling in luminal progenitors, TGF-β signaling in basal cells, and extracellular matrix organization in stromal cells. In contrast, variable enhancers were enriched for broadly shared, inducible pathways, including interferon, TP53, nuclear receptor, and immune-response signaling, with relatively little cell type specificity. Together, these findings provide a regulatory framework for the two-compartment model of the breast enhancer epigenome. The stable enhancer compartment concentrates lineage-defining transcription factors and their associated biological pathways, thereby encoding the core regulatory architecture of each breast cell type. Conversely, the variable enhancer compartment is dominated by broadly shared, environmentally responsive regulatory programs that likely underlie inter-individual epigenomic diversity.
