Our study identifies a previously unrecognized two-compartment organization of the human breast enhancer epigenome. Stable enhancer states define the core regulatory architecture that underpins mammary cell identity, whereas a complementary variable enhancer compartment captures inter-individual epigenomic diversity arising from genetic, environmental, and stochastic influences. By integrating histone modification landscapes, chromatin state segmentation, transcription factor binding logic, and genotype, our findings provide a unified framework for understanding how epigenomic variation is organized within normal human tissues. Although the overall epigenomic landscapes of the four breast cell types closely recapitulated their established developmental relationships [45,50,127,128], substantial inter-individual variation was evident within each cell type. Active promoter states were generally highly conserved, whereas active distal regulatory states and H3K27me3 states displayed considerably greater variability, suggesting that enhancers and repressive chromatin are more permissive to inter-individual divergence. Extending these observations to chromatin states demonstrated that enhancer chromatin constitutes the principal locus of inter-individual epigenomic variation. Promoter and quiescent chromatin showed the highest concordance between individuals, while enhancer and bivalent states exhibited markedly lower concordance. Together, these findings indicate that cell identity is maintained through a remarkably stable promoter architecture, whereas enhancer landscapes provide the principal substrate for individual variation. Multiple independent analyses converged on the same biological model. Stable enhancers preferentially overlapped independently annotated ENCODE candidatecis-regulatory elements, exhibited stronger regulatory signatures, and were enriched for mammary-specific biological pathways and lineage-defining transcription factor motifs. Conversely, variable enhancers showed reduced overlap with annotated regulatory elements, were enriched for interferon regulatory factor and AP-1 family motifs, and were associated with broadly shared inflammatory and environmentally responsive pathways. Rather than representing poorly defined regulatory elements, these regions appear to constitute a dynamic regulatory compartment through which developmental identity is integrated with lifetime environmental exposures. Somewhat counterintuitively, stable enhancer positions were the most widely shared between the four breast cell types, and high variability positions the most cell type-specific. This points to cell type-specificity of enhancers being a measure of the consistency with which a given cell type engages a specific enhancer region from a broader set of candidates, together with the TF grammar and biological programs encoded within it. The fact that this relationship survived matching on regulatory strength indicates genuine differences in how broadly enhancer regions are engaged, rather than the greater detectability of strongly marked regions in any one cell type. I observed that while 85.3% of a cell type’s stable enhancer space was also called as an enhancer in at least one other cell type, only 46.1% was stable in any other cell type, leaving 53.9% uniquely stable in that cell type. Cell type-specific motif enrichments observed in stable enhancers therefore derive from the majority of stable enhancer positions unique to each cell type. Consistent with this partition, the one family enriched in the stable compartment of all four cell types was NFI, whereas the lineage-defining families were each confined to the cell type whose identity they specify. This relationship is consistent with observations in other systems. In brain, heart, muscle and lung, regulatory elements shared by all four tissues were enriched for promoter annotations, while tissue-restricted elements were enriched for enhancers [42], matching my observations in different chromatin classes, where promoter and quiescent states were both the most concordant between individuals and the most shared between cell types. Within the enhancer-called chromatin, equivalent ordering by inter-individual variability has been described in lymphoblastoid lines, where bivalent enhancers were the most individual-specific, followed by weak enhancers, and finally strongly active enhancers [37], concurring precisely with the ranking I recovered in purified primary breast cell types. Consistency of deployment across individuals and breadth of use across cell types therefore appear to be linked attributes of a shared landscape of regulatory potential, observable both between chromatin classes and within the enhancer compartment itself. The distinction between stable and variable enhancers may also reflect two complementary biological timescales encoded within the enhancer landscape. Stable enhancers likely represent regulatory programs established during development and maintained by evolutionary constraint to preserve cell identity. In contrast, the variable enhancer compartment appears to capture regulatory programs that remain responsive throughout life to hormonal exposure, immune activation, ageing, and other environmental influences. Such a model provides an explanation for how genetically identical cell types maintain stable lineage identity while remaining capable of adapting to changing physiological conditions. The genetic analyses further refine this framework. We identified more than 245,000cis-hBTLs, nearly 90% of which were unique to a single breast cell type, demonstrating that genetic effects on chromatin state are highly cell type-specific. However, these variants did not preferentially regulate lineage-defining biological pathways. Instead,cis-hBTLs localized within the enhancer landscape of the cell type in which they were identified, at every level of within-cohort concordance, while influencing biological processes broadly shared across breast cell types. This apparent paradox suggests that inherited genetic variation rarely rewires the regulatory circuitry responsible for establishing cell identity. Rather, genetic variants fine-tune regulatory activity within an existing lineage-specific enhancer architecture, modulating the magnitude or responsiveness of conserved biological programs without fundamentally altering cell fate. This interpretation is further supported by the distinct behavior of active and repressive histone modifications. Active marks exhibited greater densities ofcis-hBTLs, significant allelic imbalance, and preferential disruption of lineage-relevant transcription factor binding motifs, whereas repressive chromatin showed comparatively weak genetic associations. Previous histone QTL studies have largely focused on active chromatin, and our findings suggest that the mechanisms linking genotype to chromatin state differ fundamentally between active regulatory elements and repressive chromatin domains. Moreover, the enrichment of environmentally responsive transcription factor motifs within the variable enhancer compartment suggests that many genotype-dependent chromatin effects may only become phenotypically manifest under particular environmental or inflammatory contexts. The functional validation of rs75071948 at theANXA1locus provides direct experimental support for this model. Introduction of the alternate allele was sufficient to establish de novo H3K4me3 deposition and increaseANXA1transcription, confirming that naturally occurring genetic variation can directly modify both chromatin state and gene expression. The observation that, in primary tissue, this effect was detected in LCs, while the edited allele was also sufficient to have an impact in MCF10A cells, further emphasizes that the functional consequence of a regulatory variant depends on the regulatory architecture of the cell in which it is assessed. Given the diverse and sometimes contradictory associations betweenANXA1expression and breast cancer subtypes, these findings further illustrate how the same regulatory variant may have distinct biological consequences depending on cellular context. More broadly, our findings carry important implications for interpreting non-coding genetic variation. Increasing evidence demonstrates that disease-associated variants frequently reside within regulatory DNA, yet predicting their functional consequences remains challenging. Our results suggest that regulatory variants should not be considered independently of the epigenomic landscape in which they occur. Instead, cell type-specific enhancer landscapes provide the regulatory scaffold upon which both inherited genetic variation and environmentally responsive regulatory programs act. Integrating genotype with cell type-resolved epigenomic maps therefore offers a powerful framework for interpreting non-coding variation in normal biology, disease susceptibility, and cancer initiation. We define a two-compartment organization of the human breast enhancer epigenome in which stable enhancers encode the lineage-defining regulatory architecture of each cell type, whereas a variable enhancer compartment captures environmentally responsive and genetically influenced regulatory activity. Genetic variation acts predominantly within this regulatory framework to modulate chromatin state and gene expression in a highly cell type-specific manner, as demonstrated by functional validation of rs75071948 at theANXA1locus. Together, these findings provide a conceptual framework for understanding how cell identity, genotype, and environmental exposure interact to shape the human epigenome and influence disease susceptibility. The registry was filtered to distal enhancer and proximal enhancer cCRE classes. For each cell type, genome-wide segments produced and annotated with the proportion of individuals in which any enhancer ChromHMM state (EnhA1, EnhA2, EnhG1, EnhG2, EnhWk, or EnhBiv) was called and classified into variability categories: stable (>75% of individuals), low (50–75%), moderate (25– 50%), high (≤25%), and not present (0%). Enhancer cCRE coverage was computed per segment as the union base pair overlap with enhancer cCREs divided by segment width, using join_overlap_intersect() followed by GenomicRanges::reduce() to avoid double-counting overlapping cCREs. Among segments overlapping at least one enhancer cCRE, the weighted mean H3K27ac max Z score of the intersecting cCREs was computed, weighting by intersection width. JT trend tests (DescTools::JonckheereTerpstraTest, alternative = “increasing”) were used to assess monotonic trends in cCRE strength across variability categories. This analysis was also extended to CD4+and CD8+naive T cells from the IHEC EpiAtlas to assess generalizability. Eight samples of each T cell subtype were selected from the IHEC metadata, and their pretrained 18-state ChromHMM segmentation BED files were downloaded from the IHEC post-processed data repository (Additional file 11:Table S10). To test for sharing of enhancer regions across cell types, the full enhancer territory of each cell type was first defined as all segments assigned to any variability category and merged into a set of non-overlapping ranges with GenomicRanges::reduce(). For each focal cell type and category in turn, that cell type’s category territory was pooled with the full enhancer territory of the other three, then partitioned using GenomicRanges::disjoin(), cutting pooled ranges at every breakpoint contributed by any of the four sets, and resulting atomic intervals were restricted to those falling inside the focal territory with IRanges::subsetByOverlaps(). Enhancer interval widths were obtained with width() and summed within each combination of focal cell type, variability category and sharing count, then expressed in megabases. Pooling across focal cell types was performed on these base-pair totals, and proportions were then computed within each variability category, giving the fraction of that category’s coverage shared with zero, one, two or three other cell types. Sharing was further computed on a category-matched basis, in which the four cell types’ regions in a given variability category were pooled, disjoined, and each interval labelled with the number of cell types assigning it to that same category. Because intervals shared by any number of cell types contribute to that grouping’s territory, proportions were reweighted by the number of cell types in that grouping to place them on the same per-cell type denominator as the presence measure. Specific enhancer state compositions were also computed per cell type and variability category as the share of enhancer state calls assigned to each of the six enhancer states, weighting each segment by its width and by the number of individuals making each call, so that the result reports the composition of state calls rather than of segments. To test whether the sharing gradient reflected differences in marking strength rather than breadth of use, segments overlapping an enhancer cCRE were assigned to deciles of ENCODE Registry H3K27ac maximum Z-scores computed across all cell types and categories jointly, and the proportion of territory shared with all three other cell types was recomputed within each decile. Sharing was computed on the disjoined partition as above, with each atomic interval inheriting the Z-score of the segment containing it. Pathway enrichment was performed using two complementary approaches. GREAT [140] was used for region-based enrichment, associating genomic intervals with nearby genes using the basal-plus-extension gene regulatory domain model with hg38 TSS annotations and testing for enrichment in Reactome pathways (MSigDB C2:CP:REACTOME). Enrichments were computed separately for each combination of cell type (LC, LP, BC, SC, CD4+T cell, CD8+T cell), enhancer state (merged enhancer and each individual enhancer state), and variability category (high, moderate, low, stable). To quantify the degree to which enriched terms reflected expected cell type- and tissue-specific biology, a relevance scoring framework was developed. A curated pattern legend of 10 categories was defined, spanning mammary-specific terms (mammary/breast/ductal, lactation/milk, ductal branching morphogenesis), cell type-lineage terms (luminal, basal/myoepithelial, stromal/fibroblast), and broader developmental signaling terms (estrogen/progesterone, WNT/Notch/TGFβ/EGFR, epithelial development, ECM/basement membrane) (Additional file 2:Table S1). Each significant enrichment term (p< 0.05) was matched against the pattern legend using case-insensitive regular expressions. Hits were tallied as a percentage of all significant terms, and this percentage of significant terms matching the relevance pattern was computed per variability category and used to compare the functional specificity across enhancer stability (Fig. 3c, Additional file 1:Fig. S19). To test for directional changes in mammary relevance across the variability gradient, JT tests for ordered alternatives were computed for each merged enhancer category, with observations pooled across all four breast cell types (n = 16 per enhancer type: 4 cell types × 4 variability bins ordered from high variability through moderate, low, and stable). The JT test evaluates whether the distributions of mammary relevance fractions across the four ordered variability groups are stochastically ordered, with the test statistic counting concordant pairs between groups of increasing stability rank.P-values were computed using the normal approximation with tie correction (DescTools::JonckheereTerpstraTest), which is appropriate for grouped data with n = 4 per group and accounts for tied fraction values across cell types within the same bin.p-values were corrected for multiple testing across the five enhancer categories using the BH method. Spearman’s between the ordered bin rank and the mammary relevance fraction is reported alongside JT statistics as an interpretable effect-size measure of the monotonic trend. To identify sequence-level features distinguishing stable from variable enhancer chromatin compartments, binned transcription factor binding site motif enrichment was performed using monaLisa [94]. For each cell type, ChromHMM enhancer segments (merged across EnhA1, EnhA2, EnhG1, EnhG2, EnhWk, and EnhBiv) were annotated with the enhancer_prop score, defined as the proportion of individuals in which any enhancer state was called at that locus. We tested the stable bin (enhancer_prop > 0.75) and the high-variability bin (enhancer_prop < 0.25) independently against a GC-matched random genomic background. Segments were resized to a fixed 500 bp width centered on the segment midpoint using GenomicRanges::resize() with fix = “center”, filtered to the canonical autosomes and X chromosome, deduplicated, and sorted. Sequences were extracted from hg38 using BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38 via Biostrings::getSeq() and filtered for greater than 30% ambiguous base content. Motif enrichment was computed using calcBinnedMotifEnrR() against the full JASPAR2024 CORE vertebrate position weight matrix collection (879 motifs) [141] with GC content correction enabled. Motifs were classified as significantly enriched if they reached BH-adjustedp< 0.05 and log2enrichment > 0.4 in at least one cell type and compartment. To reduce redundancy from highly similar PWMs, the full motif set was clustered using universalmotif::compare_motifs() with Pearson correlation coefficient ≥ 0.7 and average linkage, yielding 113 archetype clusters across 828 clustered motifs. The clustering approach is inspired by Vierstraet al.2020 [142] but uses our own per-set clustering rather than published archetype assignments. Pathway-level enrichment of compartment-specific genomic regions was performed using rGREAT [143] against MSigDB C2:CP:REACTOME gene sets retrieved via msigdbr [144], using the default basal-plus-extensioncis-regulatory association rules and hg38 RefSeq TSS annotations. Enrichments were computed independently for each cell type (LC, LP, BC, SC) and compartment (stable, variable), yielding 8 panel-level enrichment tables. Binomialp-values were Benjamini–Hochberg-corrected within each panel and the full enrichment table (one row per cell type × compartment × Reactome term, with BH-adjustedp, log2enrichment, and observed region hit count) is provided as Additional file 6:Table S5. We built an in-house R pipeline using bedr [145], GenomicRanges [146], and plyranges [147] to define and annotate loci where alleles overlapped consistently with peak presence/absence across the cohort of eight individuals for each cell type and histone mark combination. Genomic loci where, across all eight individuals, individuals that carried a particular variant allele, whether reference or alternate, also had an overlapping histone mark peak, and, at the same locus, individuals that did not have that variant allele also had no overlapping histone mark peak, were counted ascis-hBTLs.Cis-hBTLs were linked to their nearest gene and corresponding RPKM value from each individual/cell type combination. At eachcis-hBTL, genotype was used as the independent variable and RPKM as the dependent variable, and a Welch’st-test was performed, withp-values adjusted for false discovery rate using the BH method [148]. Positions with the largest shift in transcription between genotypes were prioritized by computing RPKM variance at eachcis-hBTL, and ChIP-seq peaks and treatment pileups surroundingcis-hBTL variants were manually verified on IGV to prioritize positions where individuals with peak absence had no nearby peaks. To assess enrichment with sequence features, UCSC knownGene [149] sequence features (transcripts, promoters, introns, exons, coding sequences, five prime UTRs, three prime UTRs, and intergenic regions) were intersected withcis-hBTLs and corresponding histone modification peak sets (H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K9me3, H3K27me3, H3K36me3), and the fraction of eachcis-hBTL set covered by a sequence feature was divided by the fraction of each corresponding peak set covered by a sequence feature, then log2transformed. To assess the enrichment ofcis-hBTLs with known eQTL, GTEx v8 eQTL variant sets were downloaded fromhttps://www.gtexportal.org. Variant calls from the breast cohort were annotated withcis-hBTL status, either present or not present, as well as eQTL status for all GTEx tissues. For each GTEx tissue, a Fisher’s exact test forcis-hBTL and eQTL status was performed, and the odds ratio for representation of eQTL within thecis-hBTL set was calculated. To compute the relative enrichment of histone modification peak sets for a given histone mark across the eight individuals withcis-hBTLs, peak sets were tiled into unique sections of the genome with the potential to form acis-hBTL, i.e. having any permutation of 1 to 7 individuals carrying a peak at a given locus. The fraction of the genome covered by tiles intersecting correspondingcis-hBTLs carried by the same permutation of individuals was computed for all histone mark and cell type combinations and normalized to the total genomic coverage for the corresponding mark. To quantify allelic imbalance in ChIP-seq read counts at heterozygouscis-hBTL positions, paired reference- and alternate-allele depths were extracted from the variant-aware (WASP-derived) ChIP-seq alignments using the VariantAnnotation Bioconductor package (readVcfAsVRanges). For each of the 192 unique (individual × cell type × histone mark) combinations available in the cohort, the corresponding sample’s WGS-derived high-confidence SNV call set was filtered to heterozygous positions, defined as positions with a phased allele frequency of exactly 0.5 in the GATK joint-called VCF. The intersection of this heterozygous SNV set with the cell type- and mark-matchedcis-hBTL set defined the position pool eligible for allelic imbalance testing for that sample. Positions were further restricted to those at which the ChIP-seq treatment alignments produced at least one read carrying each allele (refDepth > 0 and altDepth > 0), excluding monoallelic pileups where allelic ratio is undefined. For each retained position, reference and alternate read depths were tallied. Two complementary statistical tests were performed. First, per-position raw paired depths were tested across all positions within each histone mark using a one-sided pairedt-test with the directional alternative testing whether the reference-allele depth was lower than the alternate-allele depth atcis-hBTL-driving positions, consistent with the prior expectation that thecis-hBTL-driving allele recruits the histone mark. Second, to control for the within-individual correlation among positions and to weight individuals equally regardless of how many heterozygouscis-hBTL positions each contributed, per-(individual, cell type) mean depths were computed for the reference and alternate alleles, and a one-sided paired Student’st-test was performed on these aggregated means across the 32 (individual × cell type) combinations contributing to each histone mark. The aggregated form is the test reported in the Results text and used to annotateFig. 4d, while the figure itself displays the per-position log2depth distributions overlaid with significance brackets derived from the aggregated test. To assess whethercis-hBTLs preferentially overlapped enhancer regions of their own cell type, and whether this depended on the consistency of enhancer calls across individuals, the variability category assignments described above were used directly. The four categories partition each cell type’s entire enhancer territory. Because this enhancer stability value is computed on the merged enhancer class, a segment in the stable category is one at which > 75% of individuals received some enhancer state, not one at which every individual received the same enhancer state.Cis-hBTLs were then filtered to those uncovered in active, enhancer-associated histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3) and tested for overlap with each cell type’s enhancer sets. For eachcis-hBTL source cell type by enhancer cell type combination, log2enrichment over genome-wide expectation was computed as observed overlap count divided by expected count under a uniform null. Becausecis-hBTLs are ascertained within histone mark peaks rather than distributed uniformly, this null inflates fold enrichment for all peak-like territory equally, so values are comparable between enhancer variabilities and cell types, but not calibrated in absolute terms. To assess whethercis-hBTLs unique to each cell type preferentially enriched for that cell type’s biology at the functional pathway level, we applied GREAT [140] via the local rGREAT implementation [143] tocis-hBTL sets stratified by cell type and active histone mark (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, H3K4me3). Variants were reduced to non-overlapping intervals using GenomicRanges::reduce() to avoid double-counting in the GREAT binomial test. Enrichment was computed against two gene set collections: the MSigDB Hallmark (H) and Curated (C2) gene sets retrieved via msigdbr. TSS annotations from the TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.knownGene package were used to define GREAT regulatory domains under the default basal-plus-extension model (5 kb upstream, 1 kb downstream, extended up to 1 Mb). Enrichment tables were extracted with getEnrichmentTable() using min_region_hits = 2. To classify enriched terms by their biological relevance to each breast cell type, a curated keyword reference table was constructed with regex patterns drawn from canonical marker studies of breast cell type identity [45,46,50,90,128] (Additional file 3:Table S2). The keyword set comprised 25 functional categories distributed across the four cell types, covering BC-associated terms (myoepithelial identity, contractile/smooth muscle, ECM/adhesion, basement membrane, polarity, epithelial barrier), LP-associated terms (progenitor/stemness markers, proliferation, ELF5/SOX9, hormone response sensitization, alveolar markers, lineage plasticity), LC-associated terms (luminal identity, hormone response, FOXA1/GATA3 transcription factors, secretory function, tight junction biology, milk protein production), and SC-associated terms (fibroblast identity, adipogenesis, angiogenesis, immune signaling, growth factor secretion, ion transport). A parallel cancer/pathology keyword set covered breast cancer specifically, general cancer hallmarks, cancer signaling pathways, EMT, and breast-specific pathology terms (Additional file 4:Table S3). Regex matching was performed case-insensitively against term descriptions with GO accession prefixes stripped. For eachcis-hBTL cell type by mark combination, the proportion of significant terms (FDR < 0.05) matching each of the four cell types’ keyword sets and the cancer/pathology keyword set was computed. A self-versus-other specificity metric was defined as log2((proportion matching own keyword set) / (mean proportion matching other cell types’ keyword sets)), where positive values would indicate preferential enrichment for own-cell type biology. To query for instances of TF binding site disruption mediating breast cell typecis-hBTLs, SNV-level motif disruption scoring was performed using motifbreakR [150] with JASPAR2024 [141] CORE vertebrate position weight matrices. The cell type-specific TF reference set was constructed from the leading cell type-discriminating TFs identified in Pellacaniet al.2016 [50] Fig. 7B, manually resolved to single HGNC gene symbols with matching JASPAR2024 PWMs. The reference set comprised LC-specific TFs (FOXA1, JUN, FOSL2, FOSL1, FOXP1), LP-specific TFs (EHF, ELF5, NFIB, ETS1), and BC-specific TFs (TP63, TP53, NFIB, TEAD4). For allcis-hBTL positions across all six histone marks, reference and alternate allele information was retrieved from dbSNP build 155 via SNPlocs.Hsapiens.dbSNP155.GRCh38, filtering to single-nucleotide variants with unambiguous REF and ALT alleles. Motif disruption was computed with motifbreakR using the information-content (IC) scoring method, which quantifies the change in motif match score caused by the alternate allele relative to the reference allele, weighted by position-specific information content of the PWM. Ap-value threshold of 1 × 10-4was applied to identify motif matches, and variants producing “strong” or “weak” effect classifications (as defined by motifbreakR’s internal IC-based thresholds) were counted as disrupting the motif. IC scoring was chosen over the default log-odds scoring because it is more sensitive to subtle but biologically meaningful disruptions at high-information positions within the motif. To test whethercis-hBTLs from a given cell type preferentially disrupted TF motifs of their own cell type, the motif disruption results were pivoted to a long-form design in which eachcis-hBTL variant contributed one observation per focal TF epithelial cell type (LC, LP, or BC), yielding three rows per variant. For each row, a binary disruption outcome was defined as whether the variant disrupted at least one PWM belonging to the focal TF cell type’s reference set, and a binary predictor (is_match) was defined as whether thecis-hBTL’s source cell type matched the focal TF cell type. Per-mark inference was performed by fitting a logistic generalized linear model (GLM) of the binary disruption outcome onis_matchseparately for each histone mark, using all three breast cell types with defined TF reference sets (BC, LP, LC). Because each variant contributes three rows to the long-form dataset, observations from the same variant are not independent. To account for this within-variant correlation, cluster-robust standard errors were computed using the sandwich HC0 estimator (sandwich::vcovCL, clustered by variant coordinate identifier), and coefficient inference was performed via the Waldz-test (lmtest::coeftest). The exponentiated GLM coefficient foris_matchis reported as the odds ratio (OR), with 95% confidence intervals derived from the cluster-robust standard error. Two-sided Waldp-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the BH method across all six histone marks, and one-sidedp-values (testing OR > 1) were derived from the Waldzstatistic. MCF10A cells were a gift from the Connie Eaves Lab (Terry Fox Laboratories, BC Cancer Research Centre, Vancouver, BC, Canada). Cells were cultured in DMEM/F-12 (STEMCELL Technologies, cat. no. 36254), insulin (10 ug/ml) (Sigma-Aldrich, cat. no. I6634), hydrocortisone (0.5 ug/ml) (Sigma-Aldrich, cat. no. H4881), cholera toxin (100 ng/ml) (Sigma-Aldrich, cat. no. C8052), EGF (20 ng/ml) (Sigma-Aldrich, cat. no. E9644), and horse serum (5%). When cells were 80% confluent, they were trypsinized for 15 minutes, and cells were pelleted by spinning down at 150G for 10 minutes at 20°C. Pelleting in preparation for RT-qPCR or sequencing was done at 300G for 5 minutes at 4°C. Pellets were then flash frozen in an ethanol + dry ice mixture and stores at -80°C. Alt-R S.p. Cas9 Nuclease V3 (Integrated DNA Technologies, cat. no. 1081058) and Alt-R CRISPR-Cas9 sgRNA (Integrated DNA Technologies, custom design specified in Additional file 9) ribonucleoprotein along with Alt-R HDR Donor Oligo (Integrated DNA Technologies, custom design specified in Additional file 9) and Alt-R HDR Enhancer V2 (Integrated DNA Technologies, cat. no. 10007910) were electroporated into MCF10A using the Neon electroporation system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to manufacturer protocols. The region of interest surrounding the edit site was lifted out through PCR (primer design specified in Additional file 9). To test the efficiency of electroporation, libraries were indexed, pooled, and sequenced with Illumina P3 reagents for 200 cycles (Illumina, cat. no. 20040560) using 100 bp paired-end sequencing chemistry on the Illumina NextSeq 2000 platform, following manufacturer protocols (Illumina). Reads were aligned to hg38 using BWA MEM [47] and the haplotypes of reads around rs75071948 were tallied using a custom R script. In the electroporated MCF10A population, around 1% of reads contained the rs75071948-G genotype with no off-target edits within the amplicon window, with another 13% of reads carrying the alternate genotype as well as at least one off-target edit within the amplicon window. To acquire clones containing only the desired variant allele, a series of sorting steps were undertaken. Single-cell sorting did not yield any clones with the desired genotype in the 51 lines that were grown and sequenced. However, sorts of 100 cells per well yielded one line containing the desired genotype at a high frequency of 31%, so additional single-cell sorts were clones out of this line, yielding 10 clones with a biallelic knock-in of rs75071948-G and no off-target edits which were pelleted for downstream validation steps. RNA was extracted from parental and rs75071948-G MCF10A frozen cell pellets using an AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (QIAGEN, cat. no. 80204) and quantified on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer System using an RNA 6000 Nano Kit (Agilent, cat. no. 5067-1511). RT-qPCR was performed with TaqPath 1-Step RT-qPCR MM, CG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat. no. A15300), and TaqMan probes targetingANXA1(Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat. no. 4453320, assay ID Hs00167549_m1), andANXA12-ΔCtin parental and rs75071948-G MCF10A lines was calculated against the parental mean. H3K4me3 ChIP-seq libraries for parental and rs75071948-G MCF10A lines were constructed according to standard operating procedures available athttps://thisisepigenetics.ca/for-scientists/protocols-and-standards. Cells were lysed in mild non-ionic detergents (0.1% Triton X-100 and Deoxycholate) and protease inhibitor cocktail (EMD Millipore, cat. no. 539134-1ML) in order to preserve the integrity of histones harboring epitope of interest during cell lysis. In brief, 100,000 cells were digested by micrococcal nuclease at room temperature for 6 minutes and 0.25mM EDTA was used to stop the reaction. Antibody H3K4me3 (Cell Signaling Technology, cat. no. 9751S) was incubated with anti-IgA magnetic Dynabeads (Invitrogen, cat. no. 10002D) for 2 hours. Digested chromatin was incubated with magnetic beads alone for 1.5 hours. Digested chromatin was separated from the beads and incubated with antibody-bead complex overnight in IP buffer (20mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 2mM EDTA, 150mM NaCl, 0.1% Triton X-100, 0.1% Deoxycholate). The resulting IPs were washed 2 times by low salt (20mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 2 mM EDTA, 150mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS) and then high salt (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 2 mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS) wash buffers. IPs were eluted in elution buffer (1% SDS, 100mM Sodium Bicarbonate) for 1.5 hours at 65°C. Remaining histones were digested by QIAGEN Protease (QIAGEN, cat. no. 19155) for 30 minutes at 50°C and DNA fragments were purified using SeraMag magnetic beads in 30% PEG. Illumina sequencing libraries were generated by end repair, 3’ A-addition, and Illumina sequencing adaptor ligation (New England BioLabs, cat. no. E6000B-10). Libraries were then indexed, PCR amplified (8 cycles) and 150 bp paired-end reads were sequenced on 4 lanes of the Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform (Illumina) following manufacturer protocols. Adaptor sequencing trimming was performed with skewer-0.2.2 [151], and sequence reads were split by index and aligned to human reference genome GRCh38 with BWA (v0.7.6a) MEM [47]. Prior to testing for coverage at rs75071948, BAMs were normalized using DeepTools [152] bamCoverage --minMappingQuality 10 --samFlagExclude 3332 --normalizeUsing RPKM --exactScaling --extendReads --binSize 1 --effectiveGenomeSize 2634848028. All scripts used in this thesis can be found in the following repository:https://github.com/hauduc/cis-hbtl. Additional file 2: Table S1. Mammary cell type GREAT term pattern legend. GREAT curated breast terms (Fig. S20) Additional file 9: Table S8. Top manually verifiedcis-hBTLs and literature annotations. title: Genetic and environmental factors associated with DNA methylation across childhood and adolescence in individuals with and without attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
author: Wrigglesworth, J.; Chirokoff, V.; Fransquet, P. D.; Anderson, V.; Bellgrove, M. A.; Silk, T. J.
text: BackgroundGenetic and environmental factors both contribute risk to the development of childhood Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet the molecular mechanisms conferring this risk remain unclear. We investigated the genetic and environmental factors influencing DNA methylation (DNAm) at sites linked to ADHD symptom trajectories. MethodsWe used two overlapping subsamples from a longitudinal paediatric cohort: (1) children with genetic and epigenetic data at first wave saliva sampling (Wave 3, n=113, 9.47-11.86 years) underwent methylation quantitative trait loci (meQTL) analysis; (2) children with environmental (Waves 1-3) and one or more waves of epigenetic data (n=126, 9.5-11.9 years) were analysed using LASSO regression to identify predictors of ADHD (Remitted ADHD/Persistent ADHD/Controls) and Wave 3 DNAm. In a subset with multiple DNAm timepoints (n=75), linear mixed models tested whether environmental predictors associated with longitudinal DNAm change, and whether ADHD moderated these associations. Analyses were conducted on 12 CpGs in which we previously identified change in DNAm according to the ADHD clinical outcome. ResultsNineteen meQTLs for 5 CpGs explained up to 40% of DNAm variance. We identified 17 environmental predictors of ADHD and wave 3 DNAm. Higher household income and school quality of life (QoL) were associated with reduced DNAm at cg02208776 (household) and cg11124426 (QoL) over time. Critically, higher income in Remitted ADHD showed greater DNAm declines than Controls, with opposite patterns in Persistent ADHD. ConclusionDNAm patterns linked to ADHD outcomes were associated with genetic and environmental factors. Notably, household income and school functioning were associated with epigenetic change, with income effects varying by ADHD trajectories - characterising higher income as protective in remittent individuals. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition, impacting approximately 5% of children and adolescents worldwide (Cortese et al., 2023). There is considerable heterogeneity in symptom profiles between individuals, which can also fluctuate within an individual throughout the course of development (Franke et al., 2018;Sibley et al., 2022). For some children with ADHD, their symptoms remit (reduced to subthreshold levels) by the time they reach young adulthood, while for others the symptoms remain chronic (Sibley et al., 2022;Van Meter et al., 2024). Recent evidence-based consensus suggests that both genetic and environmental factors influence the emergence and course of ADHD (Faraone et al., 2021). It is evident that there is a significant genetic component to ADHD, with heritability estimates as high as 74% in twins (Faraone & Larsson, 2019). However, genome-wide studies revealed how only a small proportion of genetic risk for ADHD (22%,Demontis et al., 2019) can be attributed to common genetic variants (variation found in more than 1% of the population,Faraone & Larsson, 2019). At the same time, ADHD has been linked to several environmental factors (Faraone et al., 2021). More recently, there has been growing interest in epigenetics, which might provide a mechanistic account of how environmental factors may play a role in regulating gene expression to influence health outcomes. The most widely studied epigenetic mechanism in ADHD is DNAm. DNAm can regulate gene expression in response to genetic and environmental stimuli through the addition of a methyl molecule to a cytosine of a cytosine-phosphate-guanine ‘CpG’ dinucleotide (Jaenisch & Bird, 2003). Interest stems from evidence of DNAm playing a regulatory role in brain development (Gapp et al., 2014) and the association with other neurodevelopmental disorders (Dall’Aglio et al., 2018). Moreover, the ease of collecting and evaluating DNAm from peripheral tissue is especially useful when studying paediatric populations (Cecil & Nigg, 2022). Several cross-sectional epigenome-wide studies (EWAS) have identified CpGs where DNAm differed between children and adolescents with and without ADHD (e.g.,Mooney et al., 2020;Walton et al., 2017;Wilmot et al., 2016). Longitudinally, our own work has identified 12 CpGs where change in DNAm varied according to the clinical outcome of ADHD remittance versus persistence (Wrigglesworth et al., 2026). DNAm trajectories are shaped by genetic and environmental influences. Genetic influences on DNAm variation appear to remain relatively stable from childhood onwards, whereas the influence of environmental exposures on DNAm variation increases across the lifespan (Gaunt et al., 2016). Among individuals with ADHD, epigenetic studies have identified methylation quantitative trait loci (meQTL, single nucleotide polymorphisms ‘SNPs’ associated with DNAm at nearby or far away sites) which suggest a genetic contribution on differences in DNAm (Barker et al., 2018;Goodman et al., 2020;Mooney et al., 2020). Studies have also highlighted several early life and childhood risk factors for ADHD that are associated with DNAm, particularly those during the prenatal period (e.g.,Breton et al., 2016;Sharp et al., 2017). The most robust finding relates to maternal smoking, where long-term perturbations in DNAm have been linked to prenatal exposures (Joubert et al., 2016;Kupers et al., 2015;Lee et al., 2015;Richmond et al., 2015;Rzehak et al., 2016;Toledo-Rodriguez et al., 2010). The biological embedding of adverse childhood experiences is also widely studied through epigenetics, with findings linking ACE-related DNAm patterns with mental health outcomes (Nothling et al., 2020;Parade et al., 2021). While prenatal environments have been examined by ADHD-related DNAm studies (Chaumette et al., 2023;Choi et al., 2023;Frey et al., 2018;Gervin et al., 2017; Olstad, Nordeng, Lyle, et al., 2023; Olstad, Nordeng, Sandve, et al., 2023), investigations of childhood risk factors are lacking. A comprehensive epigenetic analysis incorporating both periods, and examining variation across clinical trajectories is needed. Extending our prior work (Wrigglesworth et al., 2026), this study aimed to determine whether 1) genetic variants (i.e., meQTLs) are cross-sectionally associated with late childhood DNAm; 2) early life and childhood predictors of ADHD status (Remitted ADHD/Persistent ADHD/Controls) are cross-sectionally associated with DNAm in late childhood, and 3) clinically relevant early life and childhood environmental predictors of late childhood DNAm are also associated with intra-individual (within-person) change in DNAm across adolescence, and whether this varies according to ADHD status. Data were derived from the larger longitudinal Children’s Attention Project (CAP,Sciberras et al., 2013) and its ancillary neuroimaging study, the Neuroimaging of the Children’s Attention Project (NICAP,Silk et al., 2016). Briefly, a community sample of children (aged 6–8 years) were initially recruited from 43 socioeconomically diverse primary schools in Melbourne, Australia, with follow-up for up to five timepoints with 18-month intervals. Participants were screened for ADHD using independent parent and teacher reports on the Conners 3 ADHD index (Conners, 2008), before receiving a confirmed ADHD diagnoses using the NIMH Diagnostic Interview Schedule for Children-IV (DISC-IV,Shaffer et al., 2000). Diagnosis was reassessed at the third and fifth wave follow-up. For this study, participants were classified as meeting criteria for including in the ADHD group if they met diagnostic criteria at the initial recruitment or wave 3 follow-up. The ADHD group was then further parsed into those who continued to meet diagnostic criteria at their last assessment (Persistent ADHD), and those who no longer met criteria by their last assessment (Remitted ADHD). Control participants did not meet criteria for ADHD at any wave. At each wave, multiple direct assessments were performed, and parent- and teacher-reported questionnaires were collected, providing measures pertaining to several potential protective and risk factors including individual, health, and retrospective prenatal, school, home and life stress factors (SeeSupplementary Table 1for details). Across waves 3-5, a subset of participants also contributed saliva samples for epigenetic and genetic analysis. The current study included participants who met at least one of the following criteria (Figure 1): 1) complete genotypic and epigenetic data at the first wave of biological sampling (Wave 3=113); 1) available historical environmental data (Waves 1-3) plus epigenetic data collected at one or more waves (n=126). The study protocol, including all assessment procedures, was approved by the ethical committees of The Royal Children’s Hospital and Deakin University (Melbourne, Australia), and written informed consent was obtained from the parents or guardians of all participating children. DNA extracted from saliva was genotyped using the Illumina Global Screening Array (GSA-MD-24v1- 0; Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) and initially pre-processed at the Stanley Center for Psychiatric Disease, Broad Institute (Cambridge, MA, USA). A series of quality control (QC) steps were performed, and are detailed in theSupplementary Methods. Briefly, initial QC procedures were executed using the Ricopili pipeline (Lam et al., 2020), which removed low-quality samples and variants after three consecutive runs. Genetic ancestries were inferred using the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel (1000 Genomes Project Consortium et al., 2015), and samples clustering within the European ancestry were retained for downstream analyses. Missing genetic data were imputed using the TOPMed Imputation Server (https://imputation.biodatacatalyst.nhlbi.nih.gov) with the NHLBI TOPMed Reference Panel (Version r3, GRCh38). Low-quality variants were removed during post-imputation QC either if the imputation quality score R² ≤ 0.3 or the minor allele frequency (MAF) ≤ 0.05. A total of 8,231,947 variants were retained for downstream analyses, with 96.02% of the input variants overlapping the reference panel. The World Federation of ADHD summarised evidence on the environmental correlates of ADHD risk in an international consensus statement in 2021 (Faraone et al., 2021). We used this knowledge to focus our epigenetic analyses on environmental factors related to ADHD. For interpretation purposes, we grouped exposures according to the ‘Child’s health’, ‘Home environment’, ‘Perinatal’, ‘School environment’ and ‘Stressful life events’, and provide a list of the analysed variables inSupplementary Table 1. Environmental data on the child’s overall health, sleep habits, medication use, perinatal factors, bullying exposure, parental mental health, and socio-economic characteristics were collected using a combination of standardised scales and study-designed questionnaires. Assessments include the Conners’ 3 ADHD index (Conners, 2008), the Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale (Spence et al., 2014), the Social Experience Questionnaires (SEQ,Crick & Grotpeter, 1996), the Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL,Varni et al., 2003), the Conners’ Adult ADHD Rating Scale (CAARS,Conners et al., 1999), the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K6,Furukawa et al., 2003), the five positive affect items on alertness, inspiration, determination, attentiveness and activeness from the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule Short Form (PANAS-SF,Watson et al., 1988), the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC) Parenting Scale (Wake et al., 2014), and the Stressful Life Events Questionnaire (SLEQ,Brugha & Cragg, 1990). Ground-level ambient air pollution exposure was quantified for fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) by sourcing openly shared datasets, made available by NASA’s Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS) Project. This includes the Global Annual PM2.5 average (Battelle Memorial Institute; Center For International Earth Science Information Network-CIESIN-Columbia University, 2013) and the three-year average NO2 grids (Geddes et al., 2017). Using QGIS software (version 3.40.11,https://github.com/qgis/QGIS), the median exposure levels from PM2.5 and NO2 grids, at a time that aligns with the preceding year of epigenetic assessment, were extracted for the postcode associated with the participant’s home residence in the Melbourne region. The current study derived ‘Absolute’ (coded ‘1’ to perinatal factors, parental mental health history, child medication history, and all stressful life event exposures if ‘Yes’ at any timepoint) and ‘Overall’ (applied to continuous exposures, representing median across Waves 1-3) measures of environmental exposure using data collected across Waves 1-3. Measures are the final output after coding and QC procedures were performed, which we describe in theSupplementary Methods. DNA from saliva was bisulphite treated and hybridised to the Infinium Human Methylation 850 (EPIC) BeadChip arrays, version 1.0 (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) at NTX-Dx (Diagenode, Ghent, Belgium). DNAm data underwent QC procedures which follow theMaksimovic and colleagues (2016)Bioconductor workflow (Maksimovic et al., 2016), using the Rminfipackage (Aryee et al., 2014). Details regarding QC are described elsewhere (Wrigglesworth et al., 2026). Briefly, data across all visits were normalised collectively using subset quantile normalisation (Touleimat & Tost, 2012;Wu & Aryee, 2010). Probes were removed if they had a poor-quality signal (113,011 with detection p>0.01), were located on a sex chromosome (n=16,376), overlapped a SNP at the CpG or extension site (n=26,455), or were cross-hybridising (n=34,471 mapped to multiple locations) (Pidsley et al., 2016). Probes were originally mapped to genomic features of the human genome assembly GRCh37 (hg19) usingIlluminaHumanMethylationEPICanno.ilm10b4.hg19.For the current study, after preprocessing was complete, probes were lift-over to the GRCh38 (hg38) genome assembly. M-values, representing the ratio of methylated/unmethylated intensity, were extracted from the entire epigenome (n=675,546) and used in downstream analyses (Du et al., 2010). Extending on our previous study findings (Wrigglesworth et al., 2026), we analysed 12 CpGs where longitudinal patterns of DNAm differed between ADHD groups. Cell-type heterogeneity on DNAm was controlled using the EpiDISH ‘centEpiFibIC.m’ reference panel (Zheng et al., 2020). This panel has been shown to be appropriate when estimating epithelial and immune cells from paediatric saliva samples (Chan et al., 2026). Given that these cell types are inversely proportional, we only included epithelial proportion as a covariate in downstream analyses, which is mathematically equivalent to adjusting for leukocyte proportion. The aims of determining whether genetic and environmental factors are associated with DNAm were addressed using two independent approaches: 1) focuses on the role of genetic variation through meQTL analyses; 2) examines whether early life and childhood environmental predictors of ADHD status were cross-sectionally associated with wave 3 DNAm, and whether those significant predictors were associated with longitudinal intra-individual change in DNAm. We summarise these two approaches in the subsections below. This study used theMatrix eQTLR package (v2.3,Shabalin, 2012) to test both local ‘cis’ (SNPs within ±1Mb of a CpG site) and distant ‘trans’ (SNPs beyond 1Mb, including inter-chromosomal) genetic effects on wave 3 DNAm, adjusting for age, sex, ADHD status, batch (processing plate), epithelial cell-proportion and population stratification (first 10 PCs of the genetic data). Multiple correction was applied separately to each analysis using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR,Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). A custom greedy LD-clumping algorithm was then used to reduce FDR-significant associations at each CpG to independent lead SNPs. This custom algorithm follows a similar logic to PLINK, which we described in detail in theSupplementary Methods. Each lead SNP’s effect was characterised by its regression beta coefficient (estimated change in DNAm M-value per additional copy of the effect allele under the additive model) and partial R2(unique variance in DNAm explained beyond the covariates). To investigate early life and childhood environmental predictors of ADHD-related DNAm, we conducted a series of cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses. Cross-sectionally, we identified clinically relevant early life and childhood environmental predictors of DNAm using a two-step approach. This approach sequentially applied Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression models: the first step identified nominally significant environmental predictors of ADHD status, and the second step determined whether these environments are also associated with wave 3 DNAm. This two-step approach is detailed inSupplementary Methods. Longitudinally, we incorporated our cross-sectional findings to determine whether clinically relevant environmental predictors of wave 3 DNAm were also associated with intra-individual change in DNAm. We further examined whether associations were moderated by ADHD status. The identified environmental factors were used as predictors in linear mixed models (LMM), first testing longitudinal associations with intra-individual change (within-person) in DNAm across the whole cohort, using thelmerTestpackage (Kuznetsova et al., 2017). LMMs were run separately for each environmental predictor and its associated CpG, along with the interaction between environment and time. Time represents a person-mean centred change, calculated as the difference between each participant’s chronological age at each wave and their age at the first assessment (age at any wave – age at first wave). All models were adjusted for ADHD (Remitted ADHD/Persistent ADHD vs. Controls), sex, epithelial cell-proportion, batch (i.e., plate), and medication use (unless main predictor was medication use); each participant was included as a random intercept. The moderating effect of ADHD status on the relationship between environment and intra-individual change in DNAm was examined using the same adjusted LMM, but included ADHD status as a three-way interaction (ADHD status * environment * time) rather than as a covariate. We performed two sets of group comparisons: 1) ADHD groups (Remitted or Persistent ADHD) vs. Controls, and 2) Remitted ADHD vs. Persistent ADHD. FDR-significant associations were further interpreted within each diagnostic group (Remitted ADHD, Persistent ADHD and Controls) using adjusted LMM, stratified by follow-up diagnosis. Across all analyses, we removed models which were non-converging due to insufficient random-effects variance across participants. For each remaining CpG model, p-values for environmental predictors were corrected for multiple testing using the BH-FDR (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), with a significance set at FDR < 5%. Continuous predictors were standardised, and binary categorical variables were centred (using -0.5, and 0.5 values). Diagnostic plots visually confirmed that each model fitted data from our smaller subsample of participants with repeated biological samples. We examined local (cis) and distant (trans) genetic effects on Wave 3 DNAm using data from 113 children (mean age of 10.37 years, ranging 9.47 to 11.86 years, 63% were male). Among these participants, 55 had a diagnosis of ADHD at recruitment. Across all analyses, we identified 19 independent meQTL signals (2 cis and 17 trans), which involved 5 of the 12 CpG sites (cg02208776, cg12881363, cg17601216, cg17657037, cg21443143). We determined whether clinically relevant early life and childhood environments are cross-sectionally associated with DNAm (‘Cross-sectional DNA methylation in late childhood’), and longitudinally associated with intra-individual change in DNAm across the whole cohort (‘Longitudinal change in DNA methylation’). Longitudinal investigations include additional analyses to test for moderation by ADHD status. We cross-sectionally examined clinically relevant early life and childhood environmental predictors of wave 3 DNAm. Analyses involved 126 children (ages ranging between 9.5 to 11.9 years, 64% were male) with available environmental data and Wave 3 epigenetic data (63% were also eligible for meQTL analyses). We characterise this sample using all the surviving QC environmental factors inSupplementary Table 2. Of these participants, 64 had a history of ADHD, of which 59% continued to meet criteria for ADHD at their last wave (Persistent ADHD); the remaining 41% no longer met criteria (Remitted ADHD). Across two steps of analysis, we applied LASSO models to identify environmental predictors associated with ADHD status (Step 1), and that are also associated with Wave 3 DNAm (Step 2). We describe the findings in theSupplementary Results. Briefly, 23 environmental factors were selected as predictors of ADHD status: 14 predicted Remitted ADHD vs. Controls; 10 predicted Persistent ADHD vs. Controls, and 6 predicted Remitted ADHD to Persistent ADHD (Figure 3). These predictors covered a range of environmental categories, including Air pollution, Home environment, School environment, Perinatal, and Stressful life events, with most relating to the Child’s health (n=12). Among the environmental predictors of ADHD status, 17 were associated with DNAm at 6 CpG sites (Figure 3) - cg02208776 (HSPE1;HSPD1), cg02968116, cg11124426, cg12577151 (ACAD9), cg1281363 (MOV10L1)and cg17657037 (ITGB1BP3). This study extends previous findings (Wrigglesworth et al., 2026) which identified 12 CpGs with varying longitudinal DNAm across ADHD groups, by examining genetic and environmental influences. Our cross-sectional work found 19 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that explained a large proportion of variation in DNAm at five CpGs (cg02208776, cg12881363, cg17601216, cg17657037, cg21443143), which were located near (cis-meQTL), or further away (trans-meQTL). We also identified 17 early life and childhood environmental factors associated with ADHD status and DNAm. We used longitudinal analyses to test whether these environmental factors were also associated with intra- individual change in DNAm, and if these effects varied by ADHD status. Across the whole cohort, a higher school quality of life was associated with an intra-individual decrease in cg11124426 DNAm over time. We also highlight in the whole cohort an association between higher amounts of household income and decreases in intra-individual change in DNAm at cg02208776 (HSPE1;HSPD1). This relationship was moderated by ADHD status, extending our previous finding of elevated DNAm in Remitted ADHD relative to Controls (Wrigglesworth et al., 2026). Notably, higher-income individuals with Remitted ADHD showed greater decreases in DNAm over time than Controls, which contrasted patterns observed in Persistent ADHD, thus emphasising income as a protective influence on epigenetic change in Remitted ADHD. Genetic and environmental variation are well established contributors to ADHD risk, though the underlying biological mechanisms have remained poorly understood. When looking at ADHD diagnostic outcome, this study demonstrated that DNAm at 5 of the 12 CpGs were influenced by genetic variation. This is consistent with previous epigenetic studies in ADHD, which also demonstrate genetic control of differentially DNAm sites, though at CpG’s not investigated here (Goodman et al., 2020;Mooney et al., 2020). We identified 19 independent meQTLs, most of which were trans-chromosomal. Many of these trans associations were polygenic, with groups of variants converging on one of two CpG sites (cg02208776 and cg17657037). By contrast, all cis-meQTLs had a one-to-one relationship with CpG DNAm. This pattern corroborates previous findings (Gaunt et al., 2016), which showed variants closer to a DNAm site tend to have a stronger effect on DNAm than more distal variants; therefore, suggesting trans-meQTLs must act collectively to influence DNAm. However, it should be noted that while we accounted for clumping linkage disequilibrium (LD, i.e., a non-random association between alleles at different loci) on the same chromosome, we did not correct for LD between SNPs found on non-homologous chromosomes (Huang et al., 2023;Lv et al., 2026). The genetic variants discovered here were mostly linked to protein-coding genes, among which four are important for glycosylation (ST3GAL1,B3GLCT) or lipid metabolism (ELOVL6,NUDT12)– two biological processes found to be altered in ADHD (Kianickova et al., 2023;Pivac et al., 2011;Predescu et al., 2024). Genome-wide association studies also link these and other discovered protein- coding genes to brain structures (Alliey-Rodriguez et al., 2019;Fan et al., 2022; N.Liu et al., 2023;van der Meer et al., 2021), and ADHD (Mick et al., 2010). Notably, previous work in this cohort (Dipnall et al., 2024) reported nominal ADHD-DNAm associations at aST3GAL1-annotated CpG, which the current study linked to a cis-meQTL . Lastly, one trans-genetic variant was identified (rs897378832), annotated to a long-non-coding RNA (LINC01440), which defines a group of molecules known for their crosstalk with DNAm to regulate gene expression (Yang et al., 2022). Whether these findings represent a genetic modulation of downstream DNAm patterns, or the influence of DNAm on variant transcription would require further investigation. Whilst the genetic influence on DNAm can be relatively stable across development, the contribution of environment is expected to fluctuate over the life span (Gaunt et al., 2016). We first identified 17 clinically relevant environmental predictors of DNAm, characterising the individual (e.g., child’s health including quality of life, physical health, BMI, psychiatric history and sleep quality) and their surrounding environment (air pollution, perinatal environments, parental mental health history, parenting, stressful life events, income, teacher relationship), which replicate consensus ADHD risk (Faraone et al., 2021). Apart from childhood psychiatric history, all these factors were cross-sectionally associated with DNAm at target sites, emphasising an environmental influence on ADHD that might operate through DNAm. From this selection of environmental predictors, we also identified two FDR- significant longitudinal associations across the whole cohort. First, better school functioning was associated with intra-individual reductions in cg11124426 DNAm, a site where a lower average DNAm level was associated with Remitted ADHD, when compared to Controls in our previous study (Wrigglesworth et al., 2026). Secondly, higher household income was also associated with reductions in cg02208776 DNAm over time, for which a higher average DNAm level at this site was also associated with Remitted ADHD, when compared to Controls in our previous study (Wrigglesworth et al., 2026). School functioning, representing indices of quality of school engagement (e.g., parent reports of how much a child pays attention in class or keeps up with schoolwork), has been associated with mental health problems, including ADHD (Lee et al., 2016;Wen et al., 2026). Interestingly we identified no significant moderating effect of ADHD status on this relationship, but rather represented a link across all groups. While there are currently no studies to our knowledge that have investigated a relationship between school functioning and DNAm, there are a few candidate and epigenome wide studies (EWAS) on related areas that tend to overlap with school functioning, including attention and academic performance (Burenkova et al., 2024;Camerota et al., 2024;Ehlinger et al., 2023). Evidence from these studies corroborate our negative association through links between early life DNAm (infant) and early childhood attentional problems (at 2 years of age) (Camerota et al., 2024), and a cross- sectional relationship between DNAm and measures of academic performance in middle-childhood (writing composite scores, picture vocabulary) (Burenkova et al., 2024). However, positive relationships with attention and academic performance have also been reported (Ehlinger et al., 2023), even within these aforementioned studies. Given the scarcity of epigenetic research on school functioning, there remains a need for longitudinal investigations to validate our finding. A higher household income was linked to an intra-individual decrease in cg02208776 DNAm (HSPE1;HSPD1) over time, and these associations varied between Remitted ADHD and Controls, and by clinical outcome (Remitted ADHD vs. Persistent ADHD). While there have been several studies which associate composite measures of socioeconomic (SES) status with DNAm (Beach et al., 2014;Beach et al., 2016;Laubach et al., 2019;Swartz et al., 2017), few have investigated individual household income. Among three known studies on household income, only one prospective EWAS identified CpGs where early childhood income-per-dependent was associated with later childhood DNAm, representing CpGs with either a negative or positive association with income (Bush et al., 2018). The two other studies, one candidate and one EWAS, reported null findings (Coker et al., 2018; J.Liu et al., 2023). We also identified significant ADHD group differences in the relationship with household income, highlighting a greater reduction in intra-individual change in cg02208776 DNAm in Remitted ADHD at higher levels of income, compared to Persistent ADHD and Controls. To our knowledge this is the first study to test these comparisons, though there is evidence associating higher incomes with a reduced risk of ADHD, and a better clinical outcome, which support our study finding (Kim et al., 2019;Law et al., 2014). Moreover, neuroimaging studies demonstrate how income can influence brain structures (Machlin et al., 2020;Pan et al., 2026;Xie et al., 2026), with links between income and ADHD related to the prefrontal working memory system (Carlsson et al., 2021;Hackman et al., 2010). What cannot be inferred from the current study findings is whether household income is directly associated with intra-individual change in DNAm, or if there is a third mediating factor through which income can influence epigenetic change. One potential explanation may be that individuals with higher incomes are more financially capable to invest in ADHD medication, better nutrition, housing, schools and recreation (Adler & Newman, 2002). Moreover, our finding also shows that genetics explains variance at this CpG site. Thus, we cannot rule out the possibility of familial confounding, whereby associations are driven by genetic differences across the population. Statistical adjustment for genetic variation would have addressed this potential confounding, though this may not have been feasible given our small sample size. From a recent registered systematic review, findings highlight evidence showing a link between income and ADHD, even after adjusting for genetic differences (Carlsson et al., 2021). This study has several strengths. First and foremost, the current study is one of the first to investigate environmental associations with longitudinal DNAm, and whether these vary by clinical outcomes of remittance and persistence in ADHD. We used prior knowledge from an international consensus statement (Faraone et al., 2021) to select environmental correlates of ADHD risk. In addition to investigating known environmental predictors of ADHD, we addressed its genetic contribution (Demontis et al., 2019) by testing whether genetic variants were associated with ADHD-related DNAm – which we assessed through our meQTL analysis. Notwithstanding these strengths are several limitations that warrant consideration. While this cohort had epigenetic data across three waves, most individuals attended two assessments, and across a limited age range. This is also applicable to historical exposures of early life and childhood environment which were collected from questionnaires conducted at two waves prior and at the same time of biological sampling, though not all participants had attended all three visits. Moreover, 40% of the whole environmental cohort did not contribute longitudinal epigenetic data. Although these individuals were comparable to the remaining cohort in baseline characteristics, they reported significantly lower QoL scores, including school functioning; more peer relational victimisation, and were more likely to have a history of internalising disorder. Diagnostic status was assessed at recruitment, and wave 3 and 5, but was not reassessed at the intervening waves. Consequently, while participants with persistent ADHD or without ADHD continued to meet their respective diagnostic criteria at the final wave, it was not possible to determine a more precise timing of remission within a 36month window. Another limitation is that we did not adjust environmental analyses for potential genetic confounding. This is particularly relevant for home environment variables like household income. However, given our relatively small sample size, this additional adjustment may not have been feasible. Lastly, these findings are limited to epigenetic markers measured from saliva, and therefore cannot inform directly on DNAm in brain tissue. Thus, while some studies report relative stability of DNAm across tissue types (Nishitani et al., 2023), patterns are highly tissue- and cell-specific, and these findings should be interpreted with caution. In conclusion, in children and adolescents with and without ADHD we extend the current literature with novel findings that highlight genetic control over some, though not all epigenetic markers of ADHD. Moreover, we provide evidence which suggests better school functioning and higher levels of household income are associated with decreases in DNA methylation over time, with this negative association most relevant to individuals with remitted ADHD symptoms. Given the novelty of these findings, which were conducted on a relatively small cohort of individuals assessed over a short duration, it is necessary to validate these findings using longitudinal studies with larger cohorts investigated over longer periods of time. In addition, future studies would benefit in considering the interplay of genes on physical and social environments.
