title: Improved 1H NMR and ATR-FTIR approaches for structural characterization of high-G-block and high-M-block alginic acids isolated from sugar kelp by a two-step gelation method
author: Xing, X.; Bajwa, B.; Low, K. E.; Tingley, J. P.; Weiler, V.; Montina, T.; Serin, S. C.; Abbott, W.
text: Two low-molecular-weight alginic acid fractions, G-block-rich SKP-G1 and M-block-rich SKP-G2, were sequentially isolated from a hot-water extract of sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) alcohol-insoluble residue by acetic acid-induced and subsequent freeze–thaw-induced gelation. High-field (700 MHz) 2D1H–1H COSY and TOCSY spectroscopy enabled comprehensive cross-peak assignments for selected alginate diad and triad sequences, supporting interpretation of 1D1H NMR spectra. Sequence frequencies were combined with previously established inequalities [1] to calculate constrained frequency ranges for homoblocks beyond the triad level. For selected homoblock lengths up to a degree of polymerization of 18, comparison of the experimentally derived frequency ranges with frequencies predicted by chain-growth statistical models ruled out the Bernoulli model for both fractions and the first-order Markov model for SKP-G1. Applying the recently developed logarithmic cosine transformation (LCT) algorithm [2] to first- and second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra enhanced the visualization of subtle spectral features and produced distinct fingerprints for the two fractions. As a proof of concept, LCT-transformed derivative ATR-FTIR spectra yielded distinct score distributions for the fractions in principal component analysis, suggesting their potential for chemometric differentiation of alginates with different block structures. In conclusion, extending1H NMR-based sequence analysis to calculate constrained frequency ranges for homoblock polyads beyond the triad level, together with LCT-transformed derivative ATR-FTIR fingerprinting, expands the analytical toolkit for alginate block structure characterization. -Low-molecular-weight high-G and high-M alginic acids were isolated from sugar kelp by two-step gelation. -Logarithmic cosine transformation enabled extraction of key features from derivative ATR-FTIR spectra. -High-field (700 MHz) 2D1H–1H NMR facilitated complete assignment of alginate homoblock triad signals. -Alginate homoblock frequency ranges were calculated from 1D1H NMR data using an improved approach. -Alginate homoblock frequency ranges were used to evaluate Bernoulli and Markov chain-growth models. Saccharina latissima, commonly known as sugar kelp, is a perennial macroscopic brown alga widely distributed across the Northern Hemisphere, from the high Arctic to cold-temperate regions along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, with its southernmost range extending to the Iberian Peninsula in Europe, New Jersey on the Atlantic coast of North America, central California on the Pacific coast, and the Korean Peninsula in the Far East [3–5]. As a key primary producer, sugar kelp supports marine ecosystems by providing both food and habitat for diverse organisms [6]. Rich in carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, polyphenols, and other bioactive compounds, it exhibits antioxidant, antitumor, immunomodulatory, antiviral, and anti-inflammatory properties, contributing to its nutritional and functional value [7]. Its major carbohydrate-related constituents include mannitol, alginic acids, fucoidans, laminarins, and cellulose, which can be extracted as value-added products for diverse applications [7–9]. Its ecological and economic significance has led to the expansion of sugar kelp farming in Western countries such as Canada [10], the USA [11], Norway [8], and the UK [12]. Alginic acids are anionic polysaccharides consisting of linear chains of 1,4-linked β-D-mannuronic acid (M) and α-L-guluronic acid (G) residues, arranged in homopolymeric (MM- or GG-rich) or heteropolymeric (MG- or GM-rich) blocks [13]. Both alginic acid and its salt form, alginate, are widely utilized in the food, pharmaceutical, and other industries as bioactive carbohydrates, dietary fibers, functional additives, and biomaterials [13,14]. First extracted from brown seaweed by E.C.C. Stanford in 1881, alginate has since been conventionally produced via alkaline extraction, with insoluble alginic acid or calcium alginate precipitated to facilitate collection [15]. Calcium alginate is typically converted to alginic acid by treatment with a mineral acid and then transformed into water-soluble sodium alginate via reaction with sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate [16]. Conventional alkaline extraction is often preceded by pretreatment with solutions of formaldehyde, hydrochloric acid, or alcohol [17]. Microwave-, ultrasound-, and enzyme-assisted extraction techniques have attracted interest for reducing processing time and enhancing yield [17]. Attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) is a useful tool for the compositional and structural characterization of alginate and alginic acid, enabling rapid, non-destructive identification of functional groups and molecular interactions associated with processes such as gelation, hydration, and crosslinking [18–20]. First- and second-derivative spectra enhance spectral resolution and reduce baseline shifts, facilitating accurate peak assignment and the detection of subtle structural variations [20–23]. Recognized as a powerful fingerprinting technique, ATR-FTIR provides spectral features for chemometric analysis, including principal component analysis (PCA) [24,25]. These features facilitate precise classification, authentication, and quality control, making ATR-FTIR a valuable tool for both research and industrial applications [24,25]. Solution-state1H NMR is the gold standard for characterizing purified alginate, enabling determination of the monosaccharide composition (M/G ratio) and the full set of diad and G-centered triad frequencies via integration of specific peaks in the anomeric region of the1H NMR spectrum [24,26]. Although13C NMR can provide complete diad and triad frequencies, including M-centered triads [27,28], it is less commonly used because of longer acquisition times and higher spectral noise. NMR-derived diad and triad frequencies also enable analysis of homoblock polyad frequency ranges using recently derived inequality relations [1], facilitating evaluation of chain-growth statistical models, such as Bernoulli processes and Markov chains, for homoblock elongation [1,28]. Advances in high-field1H NMR have improved spectral resolution, and 2D techniques such as1H–1H correlation spectroscopy (COSY) and total correlation spectroscopy (TOCSY) facilitate the assignment of alginate signals [29–32]. Prior to1H NMR analysis, the purity and molecular weight distribution of alginate samples are usually assessed using chromatographic methods. High-performance size-exclusion chromatography (HPSEC), combined with refractive index (RI) and multi-angle light scattering (MALS) detectors, enables direct measurement of molecular weights based on the physical principle of static light scattering, obviating the need for conventional column calibration [33,34]. Monosaccharide composition is typically determined by depolymerizing alginic acid under acidic conditions (e.g., acid methanolysis [34], aqueous acid hydrolysis [35,36], or a combination thereof [37]), followed by chromatographic analysis using techniques such as high-performance anion-exchange chromatography with pulsed amperometric detection (HPAEC-PAD) [34] or gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry and/or flame ionization detection (GC-MS/FID) [38,39]. Although quantitative depolymerization of alginate remains challenging due to the resistance of its block structures to acid hydrolysis and the partial degradation of liberated uronic acids, these methods are sufficient for assessing purity and estimating M/G ratios [34–36]. This study introduces a two-step gelation method for sequentially isolating two structurally distinct low-molecular-weight alginic acid fractions from a hot-water extract of alcohol-insoluble residue (AIR) prepared from sugar kelp. Purity and molecular weight distribution were assessed using GC- and HPLC-based chromatographic techniques, followed by structural characterization using improved1H NMR and ATR-FTIR approaches. Saccharina latissimawas harvested from the Pacific Northwest of Canada on May 1, 2022, by Cascadia Seaweed Corporation (Sidney, British Columbia, Canada). Following harvest, the seaweed was rinsed to remove debris and air-dried at temperatures not exceeding 30 °C for 96 h [10]. The dry samples were then shipped in sealed bags at ambient temperature to the Lethbridge Research and Development Centre for analysis. The dry seaweed sample was ball-milled into a fine powder using a Mixer Mill MM 400 system (Retsch, Germany). The powder was transferred into nineteen 50 mL tubes and weighed, with each tube containing 3.1–3.5 g of powder (Table S1). Subsequently, 40 mL of 95% (v/v) ethanol was added to each tube. The tubes were capped, vortexed, and incubated at 60 °C for 2 h; this treatment was performed twice. After each incubation, the samples were centrifuged (3000 ×g, 30 min) at room temperature, and the pellets were collected for the subsequent incubation. A similar procedure was performed using 80% (v/v) ethanol at 40 °C for three cycles (8 h, 16 h, and 8 h), followed by two 30-min incubations with absolute ethanol at 60 °C. The final residues were vacuum-dried directly in the tubes without heating using a SpeedVac vacuum concentrator (Thermo Fisher, USA). The AIR preparation yields for each tube are shown in Table S1. Sugar kelp AIR (32.287 g) was divided among sixteen 50 mL tubes, each containing approximately 2 g of sample. To each tube, 40 mL of deionized water was added, followed by vortexing and incubation at 70 °C for 24 h. This extraction was performed for three cycles. After each incubation, the mixture was centrifuged at 3000 ×gfor 30 min at room temperature to separate the residues for subsequent extraction cycles. The supernatants from all extractions were pooled, filtered through six layers of clean cheesecloth, and allowed to stand at 4 °C for 24 h. The pooled extract was then centrifuged at 3000 ×gfor 30 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatant was extensively dialyzed against deionized water with a molecular-weight cutoff (MWCO) of 14 kDa to facilitate the removal of low-molecular-weight components, including residual laminarin. The dialyzed solution was adjusted to a final volume of 2 L with deionized water, followed by the slow addition of 222 mL of acetic acid. The mixture was gently shaken at 30 °C for 24 h in an incubator. After centrifugation (3000 ×g, 30 min, room temperature), the pellet was washed with a water–acetic acid mixture (9:1, v/v) and collected by centrifugation. The pellet was resuspended in deionized water, extensively dialyzed (MWCO 14 kDa) against deionized water, and freeze-dried to yield 1.990 g of material, designated SKP-G1. The supernatant was transferred to 50 mL tubes, frozen at −20 °C for 24 h, and then thawed at 4 °C for 24 h. This freeze–thaw cycle was repeated once, followed by centrifugation (3000 ×g, 30 min). The resulting pellet was resuspended in deionized water, extensively dialyzed (MWCO 14 kDa) against deionized water, and freeze-dried to yield 0.315 g of material, designated SKP-G2. A flow diagram of the isolation process is shown in Scheme S1. Approximately 2 mg of each fraction was stirred in 1 mL of 2 M trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) at 120 °C for 2 h [40]. After evaporation to dryness, the hydrolysates were co-evaporated to dryness twice with 1 mL of anhydrous methanol and subsequently redissolved in 25 mL of deionized water. An aliquot (1.5 mL) of each resulting solution was filtered through a 0.2 μm nylon syringe filter, and 10 μL was injected via an autosampler into a Dionex ICS-3000 HPAEC-PAD system (Thermo Scientific, USA) equipped with a CarboPac PA20 guard column (3 × 30 mm) and a CarboPac PA20 analytical column (3 × 150 mm). The column compartment was maintained at 15 °C, and the mobile phase, delivered at 0.3 mL/min, was composed of three aqueous solvents: 100 mM NaOH (Solvent A), 1 M sodium acetate in 100 mM NaOH (Solvent B), and water (Solvent C), using the following gradient: 20% A/0% B at 0 min; 19% A/1% B at 20 min; 15% A/5% B at 20.1 min; 80% A/20% B at 60 min; 100% A at 60.1 min (held until 70 min); and 20% A/0% B at 70.1 min (held until 80 min). PAD detection was performed using a gold-on-polytetrafluoroethylene disposable working electrode with the standard quadruple-potential waveform for carbohydrate analysis. Peak assignments were made by comparing retention times with those of monosaccharide standards. Data acquisition and analysis were performed using Chromeleon CDS software version 6.80 SR10 (Thermo Fisher, USA). Two separate experiments were conducted for each sample. The analysis was performed following previous reports [41,42], with modifications. Approximately 5 mg of each fraction was heated in 1 mL of 1.25 M methanolic HCl at 80 °C for 16 h under gentle magnetic stirring [37]. The reaction mixture was evaporated to dryness under N2, followed by two rounds of co-evaporation to dryness with 1 mL of anhydrous methanol. The resulting methyl esters of uronic acid methyl glycosides were then stirred in 1 mL of deionized water containing 10 mg/mL sodium borodeuteride (NaBD4) at 4 °C for 24 h to achieve carboxyl reduction and 6,6′-dideuteration [10,43]. Excess reductant was quenched with glacial acetic acid, and the mixture was evaporated to dryness under N2. The residue was acetylated by heating in 0.5 mL of TFA and 2.5 mL of acetic anhydride (Ac2O) at 60 °C for 1 h [10]. Alginate has been detected in hot-water extracts of various brown seaweeds [54–56]. Hot-water extraction is a green alternative to conventional alkaline extraction. A previous analysis of 16 brown seaweeds revealed that, although hot-water extraction produced a lower overall yield, it generated extracts with higher M levels than alkaline extraction [54]. Hot-water extraction has been employed to isolate alginates and fucoidans from the AIR of sugar kelp, with alginate subsequently precipitated by the addition of CaCl2[16]. In this study, AIR samples were prepared from ball-milled sugar kelp powders with good yields (Table S1). The AIR was extensively extracted with hot water, followed by a two-step gelation process to sequentially isolate two alginic acid fractions from the water extract acidified with acetic acid: first, gelation was induced by mixing the extract with acetic acid (9:1, v/v) to yield SKP-G1; subsequently, two cycles of freezing at −20 °C and thawing at 4 °C produced SKP-G2, as detailed inSection 2.3and Scheme S1. It was apparent that acidification alone triggered gelation in some alginates, whereas others required additional freeze–thaw cycles to form a gel. This phenomenon could be explained as follows: during freezing, ice formation concentrates both alginate and acetic acid in the remaining solution [57]. The increased alginate concentration promotes closer packing of alginate chains, while the elevated acetic acid concentration lowers the pH, protonating carboxylate groups (−COO-) to form carboxylic acids (−COOH) [57]. This conversion reduces electrostatic repulsion and enhances hydrogen bonding between closely packed chains, thereby favoring gel formation [57]. It is well established that acid-induced formation of stable gels is favored in alginates rich in homo-G-blocks compared with those rich in homo-M-blocks [58,59]. Differences in monosaccharide composition and homoblock types between SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 were examined using solution-state 700 MHz1H NMR experiments (Section 3.2). As part of the sample quality assessment prior to NMR analysis, the chromatographic studies described below were conducted to confirm that the purity and molecular weights of SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 met the requirements for high-resolution1H NMR analysis. Acid-catalyzed depolymerization, via acid methanolysis or aqueous acid hydrolysis, is widely employed to release uronic acids from alginate for monosaccharide composition analysis [34–36]. However, the strong glycosidic bonds in alginate necessitate harsh conditions that, while promoting depolymerization, also degrade the liberated uronic acids [13,34–36]. Hydrolysis efficiency depends on both monosaccharide composition and glycosidic linkage; for example, G residues are more readily released than M residues [13,34–36], and G–M linkages cleave more easily than M–G and M–M linkages [60], leading to uneven release of G and M residues during hydrolysis. Moreover, once liberated, G and M degrade at different rates, further complicating quantitation of the constituent monosaccharides [13,61]. Despite extensive optimization, both acid methanolysis and aqueous acid hydrolysis remain unreliable for absolute quantitation due to non-synchronous release, degradation, and low and uneven recovery, although they are acceptable for estimating M/G ratios in similarly treated samples for comparative purposes [13,34–36]. In this study, HPAEC-PAD analysis of SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 following 2 M TFA hydrolysis showed major peaks corresponding to the alginate-derived uronic acids, together with a minor fucose peak (Fig. S1). Although hydrolysis with 2 M TFA (120 °C, 2 h) enabled quantitative fucose release for evaluating minor fucoidan contamination [40,62], it may result in low recovery of M and G residues from alginate [63]. A previous report showed that, even under optimized conditions, 2 M TFA hydrolysis achieved only ~29% total recovery of uronic acids, with recoveries of 24% for G and 5% for M residues [36], suggesting that the relative fucose peak areas (2.7% for SKP-G1 and 14.3% for SKP-G2) were substantially overestimated (Table S2), with the larger relative fucose peak area in SKP-G2 likely due in part to the lower recovery of M residues during hydrolysis. Consequently, further quantitation based on these HPAEC-PAD data was not pursued. Carboxyl reduction has been employed to convert the acid-resistant polyuronate chains of alginate into the corresponding neutral sugar chains, thereby facilitating subsequent acid hydrolysis [38,64]. The resulting gulomannan or mannogulocan depolymerizes more readily during acid hydrolysis, with liberated mannose remaining relatively stable under the hydrolysis conditions, while some of the liberated gulose is converted to 1,6-anhydro-β-L-gulopyranose (hereafter referred to as 1,6-anhydrogulose), yielding a mixture of these three products [38,65–67]. This conversion is accounted for in the quantitative analysis: the constituent M and G residues in the original alginate are determined from the amount of mannose and the combined amounts of gulose and 1,6-anhydrogulose, respectively, as measured by GC or HPLC, allowing calculation of the M/G ratio [38,65,66]. Alternatively, carboxyl-reduced alginic acid can be subjected to methylation-GC-MS to determine glycosidic linkages [64]. In this approach, 1,6-anhydrogulose is not generated during hydrolysis of the permethylated gulomannan or mannogulocan because methylation atO-6 prevents formation of the 1,6-anhydro bridge required for its production. In the present study, the uronic acid residues in SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 were depolymerized using 1.25 M methanolic HCl at 80 °C for 16 h, followed by carboxyl reduction of the resulting uronic acid methyl esters with NaBD4to yield the corresponding 6,6′-dideuterated neutral sugars. These products were subsequently converted through a multistep derivatization procedure into mixtures of alditol acetates and 1,6-anhydrogulose acetates, as detailed inSection 2.4.2.Peaks in the GC-MS chromatograms (Fig. S2) were identified based on retention times and EI-MS spectra (Figs. S3–S6), and the corresponding compounds were quantified using GC-FID responses (Fig. S7; Table S3). The results showed that SKP-G1 contained 94.2% combined M and G residues and 1.24% fucose, whereas SKP-G2 contained 83.3% combined M and G residues and 7.48% fucose, with only minor amounts of other monosaccharides detected in both samples (Table S3). Bojorges et al. (2023) reported that the use of strong acid methanolysis for depolymerization in monosaccharide analysis of high-M-block, low-molecular-weight alginates could lead to substantial underestimation of M residues compared with values obtained by1H NMR [34]. This underestimation of M in SKP-G2 was further supported by linkage analysis (Figs. S8–S10), which revealed a higher proportion of 4-linked mannopyranuronic acid residues (4-ManpA) than of 4-linked gulopyranuronic acid residues (4-GulpA) in SKP-G2 (Table S4). Although the relative proportion of M residues determined by linkage analysis remained lower than that determined by1H NMR (Section 3.2.1), it was closer to the value obtained by1H NMR than to that obtained from the GC-FID-based monosaccharide analysis described above. It is worth noting that the linkage analysis in this study focused on the predominant alginate components rather than the minor fucoidan contaminants in the fractions. Accordingly, the aqueous phase obtained by DCM–water partitioning of the methylation reaction mixture, which contained the methylated fucoidan components, was not collected for linkage analysis, and fucoidan-derived backbone fucose linkages were therefore not detected (Table S4). Nevertheless, minor amounts of terminal fucopyranose (t-Fucp) were detected in both fractions, possibly arising from fucose that was released from minor fucoidans and desulfated during the mild methanolysis step used to esterify the uronic acid residues of alginate prior to NaBD4treatment for carboxyl reduction. These results supported previous reports that both methanolysis- and TFA hydrolysis-based monosaccharide analyses could lead to an underestimation of uronic acid residues, especially M residues in high-M alginate samples, although these methods remain valuable as rapid approaches for comparative analysis of similarly treated samples and for purity estimation prior to1H NMR analysis [34,35]. It was apparent that these depolymerization-based monosaccharide analyses overestimated the relative proportion of fucose in the fractions, particularly in the M-rich SKP-G2. However, no characteristic fucose signals were observed in the 1D and 2D1H NMR spectra (Sections 3.2.1and3.2.2), suggesting that residual fucoidan did not substantially interfere with the NMR analysis. Both SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 readily dissolved in 0.1 M sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), allowing for HPSEC analysis (Figs. S11–S13, Table S5). Each alginate fraction exhibited a single, broad peak in the RI chromatogram, and the DAD chromatogram at 280 nm showed a broad, low-intensity UV signal synchronous with the corresponding RI peak (Figs. S11 and S12), suggesting that the UV absorbance was associated with the polydisperse alginate fractions rather than a separately eluting protein component. The absence of prominent amide bands in the ATR-FTIR spectra (Section 3.3.1) further suggested a lack of substantial protein contamination. The molecular weight distributions were determined by HPSEC using a MALS detector to measure static light scattering and an RI detector to measure concentration. The resulting weight-average (Mw) and number-average (Mn) molecular weights were 40.8 and 22.3 kDa, respectively, for SKP-G1, and 38.5 and 23.8 kDa, respectively, for SKP-G2 (Table S5). Based on these molecular weight values, both fractions were classified as low-molecular-weight alginates. According to the literature [68], alginates produced by fractionation or selective processing typically exhibit a polydispersity index (Mw/Mn) below 2. The resulting polydispersity indices were 1.8 for SKP-G1 and 1.6 for SKP-G2 (Table S5). Using a differential viscometer, the number-average, weight-average, and z-average intrinsic viscosities were determined to be 101.2, 179.9, and 368.2 mL/g, respectively, for SKP-G1, and 68.8, 106.8, and 211.2 mL/g, respectively, for SKP-G2 (Table S5). These relatively low intrinsic viscosities indicated that the alginate chains occupied relatively small hydrodynamic volumes in solution, consistent with their low molecular weights. The power-law exponent α of the Mark-Houwink-Sakurada (MHS) equation was 0.975 for SKP-G1 and 0.937 for SKP-G2 (Table S5), within the typical range of 0.91–1.13 for alginates in a solution with an ionic strength of 0.1 M [68]. In general, α values in the ranges of 0–0.5, 0.5–0.8, and 0.8–1.8 correspond to spherical, random-coil, and rod-like conformations in solution, respectively [68]. Thus, the α values of both fractions were consistent with relatively extended, rod-like chain conformations in solution. Alginate chain stiffness increases in the order of MG alternating blocks < homo-M-blocks < homo-G-blocks [69]. The higher α value for SKP-G1 was consistent with the1H NMR data, which indicated that this fraction was G-block-rich, whereas SKP-G2 contained more M blocks, as detailed inSection 3.2.1. Small hydrodynamic radius (Rh) values of 16.4 nm for SKP-G1 and 12.9 nm for SKP-G2 were determined by differential viscometry (Table S5). In addition, using a right-angle DLS detector, Rhwas independently measured (Table S5), complementing the Rhvalues obtained from differential viscometry. The radius of gyration (Rg), or root-mean-square radius, was determined from the angular dependence of scattered light by MALS. As expected for low-molecular-weight alginates such as SKP-G1 and SKP-G2, the Rgand Rhvalues measured by light scattering exhibited low precision (Table S5) because of the weak scattering intensity associated with their low molecular weights [70]. Although the accuracy of these size measurements could be improved by increasing the sample concentration to enhance light scattering intensity, such experiments were not pursued because molecular size determination was not a primary objective of the present study. In SKP-G2,FMMMranged from 0.52 to 0.62, whereasFGMMranged from 0.00 to 0.10 (Table 1). Notably, the minimumFMMMwas more than five times the maximumFGMM, indicating that 1MMM contributed at least five-sixths of the peak area of 1MM, with 1GMM accounting for at most one-sixth. Based on this substantial difference, it was reasonable to assign the sharp, dominant 1MM peak predominantly to 1MMM in SKP-G2. The combination of high magnetic field strength, elevated sample concentrations enabled by the low molecular weights of the fractions, and optimized NMR acquisition parameters resulted in high-quality 2D1H–1H COSY and TOCSY spectra acquired at 80 °C (Figs. 2–5) and 65 °C (Figs. S14–S17). In SKP-G1, the underlined G residue in the GGG triad exhibited the strongest signals, and cross-peaks from the underlined residues in theGM andMM diads were also detected and assigned (Figs. 2,3, S14, and S15). In SKP-G2, the underlined M residue in the MMM triad exhibited the strongest signals; notably, no GGM triad signals were detected by 1D1H NMR (Fig. 1B,Table 1), indicating that allGM diad signals arose from MGM rather than GGM and thereby supporting the assignment of allGM cross-peaks to MGM (Figs. 4,5, S16, and S17). In addition, weak signals corresponding to reducing-end G and M residues were detected, and partial chemical shift data extracted from these signals are listed in Table S7. These chemical shifts obtained from 2D1H–1H NMR enabled peak assignments in the 1D1H NMR spectra beyond the 4.4–5.2 ppm region (Figs. S18 and S19). Chain-growth statistical models, including the Bernoulli, first-order Markov, and second-order Markov chain models, provide a robust framework for predicting the sequence distribution and block architecture of linear polysaccharides such as alginate [1,27,28]. In these models, the probability of monomer addition is conditioned on preceding units: the first-order Markov model depends on the immediately preceding monomer; the second-order Markov model depends on the preceding diad; and the Bernoulli model assumes independence from prior units [1,27,28]. Traditionally, evaluation of these models has relied on NMR-derived diad and triad frequency data [27,28]. However, a recent study introduced rigorous inequality relations that enable direct calculation of frequency ranges for homoblock polyads, extending model evaluation beyond triads [1] For the G-block-rich SKP-G1, the frequency ranges of homo-G-blocks (G)nwere calculated from the triad frequenciesFGGGandFGGMusing inequality relation (12), whereas for the M-block-rich SKP-G2, the frequency ranges of homo-M-blocks (M)nwere calculated from the diad frequenciesFMMandFMGusing inequality relation (13), as detailed inSection 2.5.These homoblock frequency ranges, derived directly from experimental NMR data rather than from statistical approximations, provide a robust basis for evaluating chain-growth statistical models. As shown inFig. 6, individual frequency values, such asFG,FGG, andFGGGfor SKP-G1 andFMandFMMfor SKP-G2, are presented as discrete points, whereas homoblock frequency ranges are depicted as bars up to a DP of 18. Across all DPs, the upper limits of these bars remain constant, whereas the lower limits decrease progressively with increasing DP until they reach zero and remain constant thereafter. This trend reflects the mathematical properties of inequality relations (12) and (13), in which the maximum value is independent of DP, whereas the minimum decreases with increasing DP until it reaches zero. The C2 curve in (A) represents the predicted values of, whereas the C2m curve in (B) represents the predicted minimum possible values of, both based on the second-order Markov chain model, as detailed inSection 2.5.5. The frequencies of (G)nfor SKP-G1 and (M)nfor SKP-G2 were predicted using the corresponding monad frequencies for the Bernoulli model according toequations (14)and(17), respectively, and the corresponding monad and diad frequencies for the first-order Markov model according toequations (15)and(18), respectively. For the second-order Markov model, the frequencies of (G)nfor SKP-G1 were predicted based onFGGandFGGGusingequation (16), whereas for SKP-G2, whereFMMMis provided as a range rather than a single value, the minimum of that range was used to calculate the minimum possibleat each DP according toequation (20). The predicted values, shown as discrete points along the model-predicted curves, were then compared with the experimental frequency ranges of homoblocks presented as bars inFig. 6. For SKP-G1, the Bernoulli model curve (C0 inFig. 6A) fell below the experimental points or bars for homoblock (G)nat DPs 2–13, and the first-order Markov model curve (C1 inFig. 6A) fell below the experimental bars for (G)nat DPs 3–12, indicating that both models are invalid for homo-G-block growth in this G-rich fraction. In contrast, the second-order Markov model curve (C2 inFig. 6A) remained within the experimental bars, suggesting that its validity cannot be conclusively refuted based on the available data. Similarly, for SKP-G2, the Bernoulli model curve (C0 inFig. 6B) fell below the experimental points or bars for homoblock (M)nacross DPs 2–13, confirming its invalidity. However, both the first-order Markov model curve (C1 inFig. 6B) and the curve representing the minimum predicted homo-M-block frequency calculated using the second-order Markov model (C2m inFig. 6B) remained within all experimental bars shown for (M)nin SKP-G2, indicating that the validity of these models cannot be ruled out based on the current dataset. The1H NMR results presented inSection 3.2established the contrasting G- and M-rich block structures of SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 and provided homoblock polyad frequency ranges for evaluating chain-growth statistical models. We next investigated whether these structural differences were reflected in distinct features in the ATR-FTIR spectra and their first- and second-derivative spectra, and whether LCT-transformed derivative spectra could make these features more visually discernible and provide distinct spectral fingerprints for potential chemometric differentiation of the two fractions. Derivative treatment improves spectral resolution, enabling precise identification of closely spaced bands and subtle spectral features in ATR-FTIR spectra [20–23,31]. In the first-derivative spectrum, zero-crossing points correspond to local extrema in the original spectrum; with increasing wavenumber, a zero crossing from positive to negative indicates a local maximum (peak apex), whereas a transition from negative to positive indicates a local minimum (valley) [22,23]. In the second-derivative spectrum, a local maximum in the original spectrum corresponds to the lowest point of a negative peak, whereas a local minimum corresponds to the highest point of a positive peak [20,21,31]. In the ATR-FTIR spectra (Fig. 7), SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 exhibited major broad bands at approximately 3355 and 3302 cm−1, respectively, corresponding to O–H stretching vibrations [72–74], along with minor bands near 2926 and 2921 cm−1, respectively, corresponding to C–H stretching [21,75]. The bands at 1731 cm−1(SKP-G1) and 1730 cm−1(SKP-G2) were assigned to C=O stretching in carboxyl groups (–COOH) [72,76,77]. Signals at 1633 and 1614 cm−1corresponded to O–C–O asymmetric stretching in carboxylate groups (–COO-) [31,78], while those at 1403 cm−1(SKP-G1) and 1410 cm−1(SKP-G2) were attributed to C–OH deformation, with contributions from O–C–O symmetric stretching in carboxylate groups [78]. These findings indicated the coexistence of protonated and deprotonated carboxyl groups in both samples, consistent with previous studies [79,80]. Slight shifts in O–C–O asymmetric and symmetric stretching between the two samples likely resulted from differences in metal ion coordination and block structures. Relevant bands were also observed in the corresponding regions of the first- and second-derivative spectra (Figs. S20–S23). ATR-FTIR spectra of (A) SKP-G1 and (B) SKP-G2. The blue vertical lines indicate the wavenumbers of selected bands. The bands at 1326 cm−1(SKP-G1) and 1319 cm−1(SKP-G2) were attributed to C–C–H and O–C–H deformation in pyranose rings [73,81], with the latter band associated with M residues [13,14,25]. The band at 1223 cm−1in the SKP-G1 spectrum (Fig. 7A) corresponded to C–O stretching in carboxylic acids [82]. A small band at 1232 cm−1in SKP-G2 (Fig. 7B) likely originated from sulfated esters (S=O) of fucoidan, a common minor contaminant in extracted alginate [76]. Notably, although this band could also arise from amide III vibrations in proteins, the absence of amide I (C=O at 1670 cm−1) and amide II (N–H bending at 1540 cm−1) suggested that substantial protein contamination was unlikely [83]. The band at 1121 cm−1in SKP-G1 (Fig. 7A) was assigned to C–OH stretching vibrations [20,77]. Weak bands at 1174 cm−1(SKP-G1) and 1168 cm−1(SKP-G2) were attributed to C–O stretching, C–C stretching, and C–C–C bending in the pyranose rings of uronic acids [72,84], as well as to C–O symmetric stretching of glycosidic linkages [31]. The strong band centered around 1030 cm−1in alginate and alginic acid was primarily attributed to C–O stretching in the pyranose ring [21,31,72,78,85], although some studies associated it with pyranose-ring C–C stretching [31,73,85,86] or O–H bending [20], assigned it to asymmetric C–O–C stretching in glycosidic linkages [74,87], or left it unclassified because of its complex bonding environment [84,88]. The major shoulder near 1080 cm−1was typically linked to C–O and C–C stretching vibrations of pyranuronate rings [21,31,81,82,84,85], although other reports attributed it to carboxylic C–O stretching [89,90], C–O stretching in glycosidic C–O–C bonds [86], or C–O stretching in weakly hydrogen-bonded C–OH structures [91]. SKP-G1 exhibited a sharp, intense band at 1029 cm−1and a major shoulder at 1082 cm−1, while SKP-G2 displayed a sharp band at 1032 cm−1with a strong shoulder at 1074 cm−1(Fig. 7); these features closely aligned with zero-crossing points in the corresponding first-derivative spectra (Fig. 8). In the second-derivative spectra (Fig. 9), the 1029 and 1082 cm−1bands in SKP-G1 resolved into pairs at 1032/1025 and 1084/1070 cm−1, respectively, while the 1032 and 1074 cm−1bands in SKP-G2 resolved into pairs at 1028/1036 and 1079/1066 cm−1, respectively, reflecting the underlying bonding complexity. Slight shifts between fractions (e.g., 1032 cm−1vs. 1029 cm−1) may reflect differences in metal ion binding, monomer composition, and block structures [21,74,88,92]. Some studies linked the 1030 cm−1band to G residues and its shoulder at 1080 cm−1to M residues [72,86], while others assigned the bands in the opposite manner [25,85]. However, spectral analyses using fractions with varying M/G ratios or block structures did not support direct residue assignment [75,92], and monomer ratio estimation based on these bands was deemed unreliable [93]. For instance, absorbance near 1080 cm−1exhibited minimal variation with changes in the M/G ratio because it reflected pyranose-ring stretching in both M and G residues [88], a conclusion further supported by the present study. The small bands at 947 and 927 cm−1in SKP-G1 and at 929 cm−1in SKP-G2 (Fig. 7), along with their corresponding first- and second-derivative signals (Figs. 8and9), were attributed to C–O stretching vibrations of uronic acids [21,78,93]. The LCT algorithm was previously developed in our study of per-O-ethylated carrageenans as part of a novel workflow for post-processing 2D1H–13C HSQC NMR spectra [2]. In that study, first-derivative processing followed by LCT was applied to individual 1D1H spectral slices at each13C spectral position, producing a 2D spectral representation with enhanced local resolution that facilitated the subsequent extraction of1H and13C chemical shifts. In the present study, the LCT transformation was extended to ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and applied separately to the first- and second-derivative spectra of SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 to investigate its utility for spectral feature extraction and visualization. The mathematical form ofequations (21)–(25)inSection 2.6.2ensures that as a derivative value approaches zero, its corresponding LCT-converted value increases, enabling the LCT algorithm to extract major features from derivative spectra by assigning greater weight to points closer to zero. Zero-crossing points in the derivative spectrum correspond to sharp spikes in the LCT-transformed spectrum, while peaks near but not crossing the zero line generate weaker, broader peaks in the LCT-processed signals. In both cases, peak intensity and sharpness depend on the proximity of the derivative value to zero and the rate at which neighboring derivative values deviate from zero. Additionally, the appearance of LCT-processed derivative spectra depends on the size of the selected Savitzky-Golay smoothing window applied to the raw spectrum prior to differentiation, as it governs the extent of noise reduction and suppression of minor signals. LCT-transformed spectra for SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 were presented separately for the ranges 750–1250 cm−1(Figs. 10and11), 1250–1750 cm−1(Figs. S24 and S25), and 2800–3200 cm−1(Figs. S26 and S27). The effect of increasing the smoothing window was more pronounced in the latter two regions, which exhibited higher noise levels than the 750–1250 cm−1region. LCT-transformed first-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra of SKP-G1 in the 750–1250 cm−1region, with the lowercase letter n denoting increasing Savitzky-Golay smoothing points from 5 to 19. LCT-transformed first-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra of SKP-G2 in the 750–1250 cm−1region, with the lowercase letter n denoting increasing Savitzky-Golay smoothing points from 5 to 19. The LCT-transformed first-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra of SKP-G1 (Figs. 10, S24, and S26) and SKP-G2 (Figs. 11, S25, and S27) exhibited sharp spikes at zero-crossing points in their first-derivative spectra, corresponding to alternating local maxima and minima in the Savitzky-Golay-smoothed original spectra. This spiking effect made spectral features more visually discernible and facilitated identification of peaks in the original spectra and their corresponding zero-crossing wavenumbers in the first-derivative spectra. In contrast, broader, weaker peaks arose from local extrema of derivative features that approached but did not cross the zero line, reflecting unresolved shoulders and troughs in the smoothed original spectra. These features were particularly useful for identifying unresolved shoulder signals in the original spectra. Distinct spectral features also emerged in the LCT-transformed second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra of SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 (Figs. 12and13). Sharp spikes appeared at zero-crossing points in the second-derivative spectra, corresponding to alternating local maxima and minima in the first-derivative spectra. In addition, these zero-crossing points coincided with inflection points in the smoothed original spectra, marking transitions in concavity between concave-up and concave-down regions. Broader, weaker peaks resulted from local extrema of derivative features that approached but did not cross the zero line in the second-derivative spectra, indicating unresolved shoulders and troughs in the first-derivative spectra. LCT-transformed second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra of SKP-G1 in the 750–1250 cm−1region, with the lowercase letter n denoting increasing Savitzky-Golay smoothing points from 5 to 19. LCT-transformed second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra of SKP-G2 in the 750–1250 cm−1region, with the lowercase letter n denoting increasing Savitzky-Golay smoothing points from 5 to 19. Both LCT-transformed first- and second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra preserved key features of the original spectra while enhancing the visibility of previously indistinct details, with the latter highlighting additional spectral features owing to the additional differentiation step. LCT-processed derivative spectra emphasized features often overlooked in conventional analysis, including valleys and shoulder troughs, thereby enabling effective spectral feature extraction and visualization. The distinct spectral patterns of SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 suggest that LCT could provide a fingerprinting approach for characterizing alginic acid or alginate samples with varying M/G ratios and block structures. It is important to note that, in the fundamentalequation (21), the LCT-converted valueZis a monotonically increasing function of cosθ, where cosθranges from 0 to 1. As the absolute value of the derivative, |D|, approaches 0, cosθapproaches 1, andZtends toward +∞, becoming undefined. To ensure practical applicability, a thresholdTwas introduced to cap the value ofZ, as detailed inSection 2.6.2. Conversely, as |D| increases toward +∞, cosθapproaches 0, andZtends toward −∞. A zero crossing ofZoccurs when cosθ= e−1, corresponding to(approximately 2.53). This indicates thatZis positive when |D| is smaller thanand negative when |D| is greater than. In this study, the maximum observed |D| for the first-derivative analysis was on the order of 10−2, whereas those for the second-derivative analysis were even smaller. Thus, all LCT-converted values obtained in the current study remained strictly positive. For broader applications beyond ATR-FTIR-based fingerprinting, particularly when processing derivative values exceeding, an additional constraint may be applied to ensureif maintaining positiveZvalues is required. PCA was applied to assess the variation introduced by different Savitzky-Golay smoothing window sizes in the first- and second-derivative spectra of each fraction, with and without LCT conversion (Fig. S28), and to explore its utility for differentiating SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 based on these spectra as a proof of concept. PCA was performed over the 750–1250 cm−1wavenumber range because of its higher peak density, greater spectral information content, and superior signal-to-noise ratio compared with other regions of the spectra. For overall smoothing-induced variability, PCA of the first-derivative data (Fig. S28A) revealed broad dispersion of SKP-G1 along the dominant PC1 axis, whereas SKP-G2 exhibited a narrower distribution along PC1. Following LCT conversion (Fig. S28B), SKP-G1 showed substantially tighter clustering along PC1, accompanied by a slight expansion along PC2, whereas SKP-G2 remained narrowly distributed along PC1 with little change along PC2. Compared with the first-derivative data (Fig. S28A), the second-derivative data (Fig. S28C) exhibited a different dispersion pattern, with SKP-G1 showing reduced dispersion along PC2, whereas SKP-G2 showed increased dispersion along PC2 while remaining narrowly distributed along PC1. Following LCT conversion of the second-derivative data (Fig. S28D), SKP-G1 exhibited tighter clustering along PC1 with little change along PC2, whereas SKP-G2 showed a slight expansion along both axes. Overall, these visual patterns suggest that LCT may reduce sensitivity to changes in smoothing window size, particularly for SKP-G1 along PC1, which accounted for the largest proportion of variance in each PCA analysis. However, the effects on SKP-G2 and along PC2 were less consistent, and the two fractions remained visually distinct in all four PCA score plots. For within-fraction variation under individual smoothing settings, the PCA score plots revealed differences in the dispersion of replicate measurements across smoothing window sizes (Fig. S28). However, a consistent reduction in replicate dispersion with increasing window size from 5 to 19 points was not evident for both fractions or derivative orders. Following LCT conversion, tighter clustering along PC1 was apparent under some smoothing conditions, particularly for SKP-G1, although this pattern was not consistent across all conditions (Figs. S28B and S28D). To facilitate visualization of the individual smoothing conditions with reduced overlap, a simplified plot showing three selected smoothing windows (5, 11, and 19 points) is provided inFig. 14. The two fractions remained visually distinct along PC1 in all four PCA score plots, while their within-fraction dispersion varied among the different spectral treatments. PCA score plots for SKP-G1 (blue) and SKP-G2 (red) based on (A) first-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra, (B) LCT-transformed first-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra, (C) second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra, and (D) LCT-transformed second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra. Symbols in the shapes of a circle, triangle, and diamond represent Savitzky-Golay smoothing windows of 5, 11, and 19 points, respectively. The 95% data ellipses are calculated from the pooled PCA scores across all three selected smoothing windows for each fraction. Despite the limited dataset of three independent measurements per fraction, SKP-G1 and SKP-G2 remained visually distinct, primarily along PC1, in the PCA score plots generated using 5-point and 19-point smoothing windows (Figs. S29 and S30, respectively). For SKP-G1, LCT conversion resulted in visibly tighter clustering along PC1 in both first- and second-derivative analyses, although this pattern was less consistent for SKP-G2. Given the limited number of independent measurements, these findings should be considered exploratory and require further validation using larger datasets. Nevertheless, this proof-of-concept study illustrates the potential of the approach for distinguishing alginate fractions with different structural characteristics. In conclusion, two-step gelation of a hot-water extract of sugar kelp AIR, involving acetic acid-induced gelation followed by freeze–thaw-induced gelation, yielded G-block-rich and M-block-rich alginic acid fractions, providing contrasting materials for the characterization of distinct alginate block structures. High-field (700 MHz) 2D1H–1H COSY and TOCSY NMR facilitated comprehensive assignment of homoblock triad signals. Previously established inequality relations [1] were applied to diad and triad frequencies derived from 1D1H NMR spectra to calculate constrained frequency ranges for homoblock polyads beyond the triad level. These experimentally derived frequency ranges provided a basis for evaluating predictions from Bernoulli and Markov chain-growth statistical models for homo-G and homo-M-block elongation over a selected range of lengths up to DP 18. Applying the recently developed LCT algorithm [2] to first- and second-derivative ATR-FTIR spectra made subtle spectral features more visually discernible and generated distinct fingerprints for the two fractions. A proof-of-concept application of LCT-transformed derivative ATR-FTIR spectra to chemometric differentiation yielded distinct PCA score distributions for the two fractions. Together, these improved1H NMR and ATR-FTIR approaches broaden the analytical toolkit for alginate block structure characterization. From an industrial perspective, these approaches could support improved structural characterization and quality assessment of seaweed-derived alginates, facilitating their selection for applications where alginate block composition and sequence influence gelation behavior and material properties. title: Chromatin states coordinate diurnal gene expression in the Drosophila retina
author: Meng, G.; McGovern, S. E.; Kramer, L. D.; Martinez Zamudio, R. I.; Weake, V. M.
text: Daily biological rhythms enable organisms to anticipate and respond to predictable diurnal environmental changes. While the circadian clock maintains rhythms under constant conditions, it remains unclear what gates the time-of-day expression of genes that are rhythmic under light:dark cycles. In the retina, restricting biological processes to specific times of the day is crucial for homeostasis because disrupting these rhythms causes retinal degeneration. We show that in light-sensitive photoreceptor neurons ofDrosophila, the circadian transcription factors only account for the timing of a minority of rhythmic genes. Instead, integrative analysis of the daily chromatin landscape and transcription factor footprints reveals that promoter, enhancer, or repressive signatures strongly correspond with phase. Further, genetic modulation of the repressive and promoter chromatin states altered gene expression in a phase-specific manner. Together, our data support a model where the genome is organized into discrete chromatin signatures that collaborate with transcription factors to restrict diurnal transcription to distinct phases of the day. Daily biological rhythms are maintained by a molecular circadian clock that is largely conserved fromDrosophilato humans1. Environmental cues orzeitgeberssuch as light entrain this molecular clock by resetting the transcription-translation feedback loop1,2. At the heart of the molecular clock are two basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors, Clock (Clk) and Cycle (Cyc), which heterodimerize and bind to E-box motifs upstream of clock output genes1. Clk:Cyc-activated genes include those encoding their own repressors,period(per) andtimeless(tim), generating a negative feedback loop with a period of ∼24 h1. In flies, clock neurons in the brain act as the central pacemaker, analogous to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in mammals1. This central clock provides synchronizing cues to peripheral clock cells, including the photoreceptor neurons in the retina, which in turn contribute to light entrainment of the central clock3. Although the molecular clock is required to maintain rhythms in the absence of zeitgebers, environmental cues also strongly contribute to daily rhythms1. In the retina, light is a major zeitgeber; 10-fold more genes in the mouse retina exhibit rhythmic expression under light:dark versus constant darkness4. Dietary intake plays a similarly important role: dietary restriction doubles the amount of circadian transcripts in whole flies and delays visual senescence in a Clk-dependent manner5. Thus, environmental cues interact with the molecular clock to dictate daily biological rhythms; here, we define those rhythms that occur under standard light:dark cycles as “diurnal rhythms”, in contrast to “circadian rhythms” that persist under constant darkness. The retina is an integrated circadian system that receives multiple environmental inputs to coordinate robust oscillations in its morphology, physiology, and function6. Many retinal biological processes show diurnal rhythms, occurring at specific times of the day with respect to the light cycle, including the retinal light response and sensitivity, synaptic structure, and susceptibility to light damage6. Diurnal rhythms are critical for retinal homeostasis because genetically disrupting the molecular clock affects retinal development and accelerates retinal degeneration. In mice retinal progenitor cells, knockout ofBmal1(ortholog ofcyc) impairs retinal neurogenesis7and vascular development8. InDrosophila, photoreceptor-specific expression of dominant negative Clk results in light-dependent retinal degeneration5,9with similar degeneration observed inper01flies10. In mice, retina-specific knockout ofBmal1accelerates the age-dependent loss of cone viability and function11. Even mild defects in Per2 (ortholog ofper) in homozygousPer2lucmice lead to premature aging of photoreceptor cells and retinal pigment epithelium12. Clock disruption also exacerbates inherited retinal dystrophies because the rod-specificBmal1knockout increases degeneration in mouse models of retinitis pigmentosa13. Notably, diurnal rhythms can also be extensively rewired without loss of the core clock itself. During aging14–17, neurodegenerative disease18, and altered nutritional states19,20, many genes lose, gain, or shift rhythmic expression, while core clock genes remain largely intact and oscillate normally, a phenomenon termedcircadian reprogramming19,20. Such reprogramming is widely present in the retina of aged flies and diabetic mice10,21–23. Therefore, maintaining healthy diurnal rhythms in the retina is critical, and requires additional mechanisms to the molecular clock. Although the molecular clock components have been extensively characterized over the past few decades1, an outstanding question remains: how is diurnal gene expression organized into different time windows across the 24-hour day? The circadian transcription factors cannot account for the varied phases (timing of peak gene expression) of the diurnal transcriptome. This is evident because BMAL1 in mice and Clk:Cyc in flies, show synchronized DNA binding at specific times of the day (ZT4 in mice, ZT12 in flies) across all of their binding sites, but the timing of this transcription factor binding is largely uncoupled from the phase of most target gene expression24–27. Although cooperation between BMAL1 or Clk:Cyc and tissue-specific transcription factors contributes to determining which genes are rhythmic in a given tissue26,28, the impact of this collaboration on the phase of expression is limited. Even the phase of cyclic enhancer RNA, regulated by circadian transcription factors, correlates with only a portion of pre-mRNA phases29,30, suggesting additional mechanisms regulate the timing of expression. Here, we explored the mechanisms that regulate the phase of rhythmic gene expression across the genome in a single, light-responsive cell type – photoreceptors inDrosophila. We show that while Clk and Cyc contribute to rhythmicity of about half of diurnal genes in photoreceptors, their occupancy is uncoupled from the phase of transcription for most of their bound genes – the molecular clock genes are a notable exception. Instead, we find that most diurnally rhythmic genes exhibit distinct repressed, promoter, and enhancer chromatin signatures that correspond and contribute to their expression phase. Using ATAC-seq footprinting, we identified transcription factors that are preferentially enriched at promoters or enhancers of genes expressed at specific phases. In contrast, the repressive state lacked these phase-enriched transcription factors, and may be less dependent on transcription factors for transiently low-level expression. Together, our data support a model in which the genome is organized into discrete chromatin signatures that collaborate with transcription factors to restrict diurnal transcription to distinct phases of the day. This model provides a framework to understand and predict how disruptions to the epigenome would result in circadian reprogramming during aging and pathological conditions. To explore the mechanisms underlying the timing of transcription inDrosophilaphotoreceptors, we enriched GFP-tagged photoreceptor nuclei and profiled the diurnal transcriptome and epigenome of young (10 days post-eclosion) flies. We generated H3K27ac, H4K16ac, and H3K27me3 CUT&RUN profiles at six time points across a 12-h light:12-h dark cycle, and integrated them with our published nuclear RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and H3K4me1/2/3 data from the same time points10(Figure 1A-B). Time points are indicated in zeitgeber time (ZT) with ZT0 marking lights on. Because our photoreceptor transcriptome data derive from nuclear RNA-seq, rhythmicity parameters from intronic reads and exonic reads were highly correlated (r2= 0.9)10, indicating these data reflect pre-mRNA rather than steady-state mRNA levels. In young photoreceptors, about half of all expressed genes exhibited rhythmic transcription by dryR analysis (Figure 1C, Table S2). These rhythmic genes fell into three broad phase waves in the morning (ZT0-8, n=2558), afternoon (ZT8-16, n=1471), and late night (ZT16-24, n=1588,Figure 1D). This triphasic pattern persisted under more stringent expression and rhythmicity cutoffs, indicating that these transcription waves do not arise from lowly expressed genes or rhythm-detection noise (Figure S1). A similar triphasic pattern was observed in the baboon retina, although many other tissues exhibited predominantly unimodal or bimodal phase distributions31. Intriguingly, genes in these three phase groups show different average expression levels: the morning phase group showed significantly lower average expression than the afternoon or late-night groups (Figure 1E). Correspondingly, the most highly expressed genes most often peak in the afternoon or late-night (Figure 1F). As observed by other studies, highly expressed genes were also more likely to be rhythmic16,17. Diurnal gene expression rhythms are thought to be important for both temporally separating incompatible biological processes and optimizing energy expenditure34,35. Our data align with both theories: genes involved in cytoplasmic translation, one of the most energy-consuming processes in the cell36, including ribosomal proteins and translation initiation factors, were enriched in the highly expressed afternoon group (Figure 1G, Table S3). In contrast, autophagy genes, whose activity is antagonistic to translation, were temporally separated showing peaks late at night, consistent with nighttime autophagy rhythms reported inDrosophila37. Similarly, while genes involved in sensory perception and G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling pathway peak in the morning, genes involved in negative regulation of response to stimulus peak towards the end of the light phase. ATP levels in the avian retina oscillate across light:dark cycle6,38, suggesting that production and consumption of energy may be tightly regulated across the diurnal cycle. Indeed, ATP levels in fly heads were significantly higher at the end of light phase (ZT12) than at its beginning (ZT0;Figure 1H). InDrosophilaphotoreceptors, because phototransduction is an energy-demanding process39and illumination substantially increases ATP cost40, the timing of energetically costly gene expression programs, such as translation, may be constrained to times with higher ATP availability to balance biosynthetic and visual signaling demand. Together, these results suggest that daily transcription is temporally partitioned across the 24-h day according to both the relative expression level and biological function of each gene. The molecular clock is regarded as the major regulator of circadian gene expression1. However, inDrosophilaphotoreceptors, Clk and Cyc binding sites10only mapped to 232 unique genes (Figure 2A, Table S4), suggesting that Clk:Cyc do not directly regulate most of the 5617 rhythmic genes. When we clustered Clk:Cyc-bound genes into three groups (strong, moderate, weak) based on average Clk and Cyc CUT&RUN signals, only 68% of the Clk:Cyc-bound genes were classified as rhythmically expressed, regardless of the signal group (Figure 2B). Moreover, although Clk:Cyc occupancy is highly rhythmic, peaking at ZT12 and almost absent at ZT4, the phase distribution of Clk:Cyc-bound genes resembled all other genes, broadly peaking in the morning, afternoon, and late-night (Figure 2A-B). The discrepancy between the timing of circadian transcription factor binding and the phase of target gene expression has also been reported in mouse liver24,25. We also noted that rhythmic Clk:Cyc-bound genes displayed a similar range of amplitudes and gene expression levels, except for the core clock genes that showed both the strongest Clk:Cyc signal and the highest expression amplitudes (Figure 2C, Table S4). Thus, while Clk and Cyc contribute to the likelihood of a gene being rhythmically expressed (Figure S2D), their binding alone is not sufficient to restrict the phase of their target expression to a specific time of day (i.e., ZT12.) Next, we asked if circadian transcription factors were necessary for all diurnal transcription in photoreceptors. When we profiled the diurnal photoreceptor transcriptome ofClkjrkmutant flies41that are behaviorally arhythmic (Figure S2A-B), we found that only half of the genes that were rhythmic in control flies lost rhythmicity in theClkjrkmutant (Clk-dependent genes, n = 975,Figure 2D, Table S5). These Clk-dependent genes include core clock genes, such asClock interacting protein circadian (Cipc),period (per), andtimeless(tim)(Figure 2E). However, other Clk:Cyc-bound genes, such asfruitless(fru), stripe(sr)andAcyl-CoA synthetase long-chain(Acsl), either remained rhythmic in theClkjrkmutant (Clk-independent, n = 890), or showed altered rhythmicity parameters such as phase or amplitude (Clk-modulated, n = 252,Ald1,CG46385,Pak). While Clk-dependent genes were involved in circadian rhythm and metabolism, the genes that remained rhythmic in theClkjrkmutant were associated with sensory neuron function processes, such as signal transduction, axon guidance, and synapse organization (Figure 2F, Table S6). Intriguingly, we observed a compression in the overall phase of rhythmic transcription in theClkjrkmutant, where the phases of rhythmically expressed genes were concentrated into two dominant time windows at ZT8 and ZT20 (Figure 2G). The same compression of phase windows occurs in mouse liver upon genetic disruption of the circadian clock, and has been termedsystem-driven rhythms42,43. Overall, these results suggested, apart from the core clock genes, Clk and Cyc alone are insufficient to determine the phase of most of their direct target genes under light:dark conditions. Moreover, Clk appears to be dispensable for roughly half of rhythmically transcribed genes in photoreceptors, suggesting that light itself, or its absence, may contribute to transcription at the middle of the day and night. Clk:Cyc are proposed to act combinatorially with other transcription factors – both by binding on shared targets, and by regulating the expression of downstream transcription factors9,44,45. We therefore extended our analysis to other transcription factors by performing footprint analysis on our diurnal ATAC-seq data10. Using TOBIAS46, we characterized the temporal footprints of 220 expressed transcription factors based on their experimentally determined binding motifs from the CIS-BP database47,48(Figure 3A). Across accessible regions, the vast majority of transcription factors showed the highest activity at ZT12, the same time when chromatin shows highest accessibility at promoters10. However, their putative rhythmic target genes were not expressed in a concerted manner at ZT12, but were broadly distributed into the same three phase groups observed previously (Figure S3A-B). Moreover, only 43.7% of rhythmically expressed genes had transcription factor binding events (Figure 3B). Thus, like Clk:Cyc, the inferred temporal binding of most transcription factors does not match the phase of their target gene expression, and many rhythmic genes do not in fact have transcription factor footprints. We then wondered if, rather than dictating the phase for all their target genes, certain transcription factors may promote phase-specific transcription for a subset of their targets. Using a Chi-square enrichment test, we found that 163 transcription factors showed significantly different phase distributions for their target genes relative to all rhythmic genes (Figure 3C, Table S7). For example, Mef2 (Myocyte enhancer factor 2) targets were enriched at ZT4-8, cyc targets at ZT8-12, and Pdp1 (PAR-domain protein 1) targets at ZT20-24, while targets of other transcription factors, such as Adf1 (Adh transcription factor 1) showed no such enrichment (Figure 3D). Nevertheless, even phase-enriched transcription factors such as Pdp1 still bind many targets with broadly distributed expression phases, reminiscent of Clk:Cyc. In total, 75 transcription factors had targets enriched in the afternoon (phase bin ZT8-12,Figure 3C), including the clock transcription factors, Clk, cyc and cwo (clockwork orange); the architectural factors, BEAF-32 (Boundary element-associated factor of 32kD), Dref (DNA replication-related element factor), M1BP (Motif 1 Binding Protein) and CTCF; and Myc transcription factors, Mitf, Mondo, bigmax and Max (Figure 3E). 71 additional transcription factors had enriched targets in the late-night (ZT16-20 and ZT20-24), including the circadian transcription factors acting downstream of Clk:Cyc, vri (vrille) and Pdp1; and stress-responsive transcription factors, sima (similar), Irbp18 (Inverted repeat binding protein 18 kDa), crc (cryptocephal) (Figure 3E). In striking contrast, only a single neuron activity-dependent transcription factor, Mef2, had targets enriched among the morning genes (ZT4-8) and none was enriched between ZT0-4. These results suggest that transcription factors may favor the timing of a subset of their targets towards the afternoon or late-night, whereas morning genes may be governed by a distinct process. Transcription factors often act cooperatively or antagonistically, and co-binding of Clk:Cyc with other transcription factors contributes to the transcriptional heterogeneity of Clk targets26,28,49. We therefore asked whether co-binding by transcription factor pairs further restricts the expression phase of their shared targets beyond what either transcription factor achieves alone. We defined co-binding as inferred binding of two transcription factors at the same gene at the same ZT. Among the 163 transcription factors, shared targets of 2809 transcription factor pairs were phase-enriched relative to all rhythmic genes (Table S8). However, no pair showed stronger phase enrichment than the targets of either constituent transcription factor alone (Table S9). Although co-bound targets appeared to be more phase-enriched than individual target sets, such as genes co-bound by her (hermaphrodite) and M1BP tend to peak between ZT8-12 (Figure 3F,Figure S3D), this gain of phase enrichment may be largely due to the smaller size of co-bound targets. Instead, clustering of these co-binding transcription factors indicated that certain transcription factors constrained the phase of their target genes towards the same time window, regardless of their co-binding partner (Figure 3G,Figure S3C). These “phase-locking” transcription factors included Dref, M1BP, BEAF-32, Clk, cyc and cwo for the afternoon genes, and Pdp1, vri, Hnf4 (Hepatocyte nuclear factor 4), and Irbp18 for late-night genes. We next asked whether transcription factor binding predicts a gene’s phase group. Using multinomial logistic regression based on individual binding events of the 35 most robustly enriched transcription factors (p.adj ≤ 0.05, fold of enrichment > 1.5, with 5-fold cross validation), we observed poor predictive performance for all three phase groups (AUC ≈ 0.55) (Figure 3H). Thus, like Clk:Cyc, although some transcription factors favor afternoon or late-night transcription, the binding of these transcription factors is not sufficient to predict the phase of gene expression. Because the average expression levels differed significantly between the morning, afternoon, and late-night genes (Figure 1E), we considered if other genomic or epigenomic features might contribute to their phase of expression. HOMER motif analysis of promoters revealed that the morning-peaking genes were enriched for the Initiator (Inr) motif (Figure 4A), a simple core promoter element that is recognized by transcription factor IID (TFIID) and is sufficient for low level basal transcription50. In contrast, afternoon-peaking genes were enriched for Dref and M1BP motifs that are associated with strong promoter activity and high expression levels51,52, as well as E-box motifs bound by bHLH factors such as Clk, Cyc, and Myc53. Importantly, the target genes of these architectural and E-box-binding transcription factors also preferentially peak in expression at ZT8-12, identified by phase enrichment analysis (Figure 3E). The late-night genes instead showed enrichment of the GAGA factor (Trl) motif, which is associated with RNA polymerase II (Pol II) pausing and chromatin accessibility54. Thus, these phase groups differ in promoter architecture, suggesting that morning peaking genes rely more on Inr-associated basal transcription, while the afternoon and late-night genes are activated by sequence-specific transcription factors on more permissive chromatin. We previously found that genes with high levels of H3K4me2/3 tend to peak between ZT8-16, whereas genes with low levels peak between ZT0-410. To extend this, we profiled H3K27ac and H4K16ac, as well as a repressive mark, H3K27me3, using CUT&RUN across the diurnal cycle in young photoreceptors. Building on the pattern suggested by H3K4me2/3, genes expressed at different phases displayed distinct epigenetic features: morning-peaking genes showed the highest overall levels of H3K27me3 and the lowest levels of all four active histone marks and RNA Pol II (Figure 4B). Conversely, both the afternoon and late-night genes carried relatively high levels of enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1), with the afternoon genes showing substantially higher levels of the promoter marks H3K4me3 and H4K16ac (Figure 4B). We noted that while individual histone marks oscillated across the day, their oscillatory patterns were the same in all phase groups (Figure S4A-B), consistent with what we and other have previously observed10,27,57. Thus, baseline chromatin environments, including both the type and levels of histone marks, rather than their oscillations, best distinguish rhythmic gene expression phases. To further interrogate the association between chromatin features and transcription timing, we binned the genome into 200-bp segments and assigned each segment to one of 32 (25=32) chromatin states defined by the presence of five histone marks58–60, including H3K4me1, H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H4K16ac and H3K27me3 (Table S10). Most genomic segments stayed in the same chromatin state throughout the day or switched only between a given state and unmarked chromatin. The largest changes occurred in H3K27me3-marked repressive regions, many of which became unmarked from ZT0 to ZT4 (Figure 4D,Figure S4C). Using correspondence analysis, we compared the phase of expression and chromatin states for each rhythmic gene and identified a significant correlation (Figure 4E). H3K27me3 and bivalent states were associated with morning peaking genes (ZT0-8), with ∼ 70% of genes in H3K27me3-marked state peaking at ZT0-4. In comparison, regions marked by H4K16ac and H3K4me3 correlated with peak expression in the afternoon (ZT8-16), while those marked by H3K27ac and H3K4me1 modestly correlated with late-night genes (ZT16-24) (Figure 4E-F). We compared the enrichment of the phase-enriched transcription factors in each of these chromatin states and found that many of the afternoon and late-night transcription factors were preferentially enriched for specific chromatin states (Figure S4D). Matching HOMER analysis, M1BP and Dref from the afternoon transcription factor group were associated with promoter regions marked by H3K4me3 but were largely depleted at H3K27ac-marked regions, where instead the night transcription factor GAGA factor (Trl) was enriched (Figure S4D). Finally, we asked if these chromatin signatures could predict the phase of gene expression. For each gene, we stratified the levels of each histone mark into 4 groups (high, medium, low, and none) and used these as predictors in a multinomial logistic regression model of phase group. This chromatin-based model outperformed the transcription factor-based model (overall AUC = 0.68 vs. 0.55) and performed the best for the morning genes, suggesting this group may be more responsive to chromatin-based regulation (AUC = 0.71,Figure 4G). Together, these results show that chromatin signatures corresponding to modes of transcription regulation are associated with the phase of gene expression, suggesting that different chromatin environments promote specific diurnal timing of transcription. If chromatin signatures contribute to expression phase, then manipulating specific histone marks should alter gene expression in a phase-specific manner. To test this hypothesis, we focused on the H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 marks that showed strongest distinction across phase groups. Morning genes showed high levels of H3K27me3, low average expression levels, and enrichment of the Inr motif, suggesting they are basally transcribed in the morning and repressed at other time points. Since these genes are enriched for processes associated with sensory neuron function, we speculate that their expression might be rapidly induced in response to light onset. In developing neurons, activity-regulated genes often show a bipartite chromatin signature with H3K27ac-marked promoters and H3K27me3-marked gene body61. While transcription is overall less productive on these bipartite genes, this chromatin signature enables rapid removal of H3K27me3 and stimulus-dependent gene induction61. Notably, ∼ 3% of the genome was co-marked by H3K27me3 and either H3K27ac or H3K4me3 (Figure S4C), including the loci of activity-dependent transcription factorsHr38 (Hormone receptor-like in 38,ortholog of humanNR4A2)andsr (stripe,ortholog of humanEGR1)(Figure S5)62,63. Therefore, we hypothesized that H3K27me3 sets the threshold for morning gene induction, and that reducing H3K27me3 would further enhance transcriptional induction. To test this, we overexpressed the H3K27me3 demethylase Utx or its catalytic inactive control UtxJmjCin photoreceptors and performed nuclear RNA-seq at ZT4 and ZT12, corresponding to the peak and trough of morning gene expression. The main effect of ZT and genotype identified 247 and 133 differentially expressed genes, respectively. Only 11 genes showed a significant genotype and ZT interaction effect (Figure 4H, Table S11). These genes included activity-dependent genesHr38,sr;CG14186, involved in Wnt signaling pathway and implicated in neuron activity64,65; and the nutrient- and light-responsive genes,FASN2 (Fatty acid synthase 2), andDgk (Diacyl glycerol kinase). These five genes showed higher expression only at ZT4, but not at ZT12 and carried a similar bipartite or repressive chromatin signature (Figure S5). Although the effect is modest, these results suggested that a subset of morning genes shares a similar regulatory mechanism with activity-dependent genes that enable their rapid transcriptional induction in response to stimulus.
