Next, we examined the afternoon-peaking genes that are marked by high levels of H3K4me3 and enriched with promoter-associated transcription factors. To test whether H3K4 methylation is required for their afternoon expression, we turned to our previously published diurnal nuclear transcriptomes with individual Set1, Trx, or Trr knockdown across the 24-h light:dark cycle in young photoreceptors10. Set1 is the major H3K4 tri-methyltransferase in larvae, and knockdown of either Trr or Trx also reduces H3K4me1/2/3 levels in adult photoreceptors10. If H3K4me3 is necessary for rhythmic expression in the afternoon, then afternoon-peaking genes should be overrepresented among the genes that lose rhythmicity upon methyltransferase knockdown. Indeed, genes that peaked in the afternoon (ZT8-16) dominated the genes that lost rhythmicity (312 out of 576) in all three Set1/Trx/Trr knockdowns (Figure 4I,Figure S4E). Moreover, 58% of these 576 genes that lost rhythmicity were marked by H3K4me3 in the control knockdown. Notably, the H3K4 methyltransferase knockdowns did not affect all rhythmic genes equally: many genes with decreased amplitude – rather than completely lost rhythm – instead peaked preferentially in the late-night in these knockdowns (Figure 4I). These results suggested that afternoon genes are the most sensitive to the decrease of H3K4me3 and require all three methyltransferases for their rhythmic expression at around ZT12, whereas late-night peaking genes are affected but less sensitive to the knockdown of methyltransferases. Overall, our data show that the phase of expression corresponds to chromatin states that are differentially bound by transcription factors. Afternoon genes were enriched with architectural, E-box transcription factors, and exhibited signatures of strong promoters, including high levels of H3K4me3, H4K16ac, and overall expression. Knockdown of H3K4 methyltransferases preferentially abolished rhythmicity of these afternoon genes. In contrast, genes peaking in the late-night had enhancer signatures, such as H3K27ac and H3K4me1, and were enriched for transcription factors that are either antagonistic or act downstream of the afternoon transcription factors. The morning genes differed from the other two groups and lacked phase-enriched transcription factors. Overexpression of Utx enhanced the morning expression of a subset of genes, including activity-dependentHr38andsr, suggesting that relief of H3K27me3-mediated repression contributes to their morning induction. Together, we propose that these chromatin signatures restrict transcription to specific times of the day, at least in this light-responsive neuronal cell type. Overall, our analysis suggests that the phase of diurnal transcription is shaped by a combination of chromatin signature and phase-enriched transcription factors, particularly the afternoon and late-night peaking genes. The insulator/architectural transcription factors enriched in the afternoon group, including M1BP, Dref, and BEAF-32, bind promoters and mediate long-range interactions that partition the genome into topologically associating domains (TADs)66–68. Together with H3K4me3, they define TAD boundaries associated with high gene expression66–68. We propose that these architectural transcription factors establish and/or maintain the TADs that segregate afternoon genes into a chromatin environment favoring high levels of transcription. E-box transcription factors69, including Clk and Cyc, function within this environment, to promote phase-specific transcription of their targets towards the end of the light cycle. One way this compartmentalization could work is through biomolecular condensates, which concentrate the transcription machinery at target genes or sequester it away from non-targets70. In mice liver, both BMAL1 and REV-ERBα form dynamic circadian condensates that are important for rhythmic gene expression71,72, and in fly clock neurons, Period forms discrete puncta whose subnuclear localization, size and number oscillate over 24 h73. The different levels of histone marks associated with the phase groups in our analysis may be important because histone marks can nucleate transcriptional condensates through multivalent interactions with the transcription machinery70. For example, the local density of H3K4me3 and H3K27ac marks, measured by super-resolution microscopy, correlates with Pol II cluster sizes and transcriptional burst size74. Thus, the chromatin states identified here may influence the spatial organization of the transcription machinery within the nucleus, thereby contributing to the temporal partitioning of gene expression across the day. Late-night-peaking genes are distinguished from the afternoon group by both their enhancer-like chromatin signatures and transcription factor networks. Many late-night transcription factors are themselves transcriptionally controlled by afternoon-enriched transcription factors. For example, Pdp1 and vri, enriched in late-night genes, are direct targets of Clk:Cyc that require Clk activity for rhythmicity75, and their mammalian counterparts REV-ERBα and NFIL3 have been implicated as master regulators of late-night genes in mouse liver30. Other late-night transcription factors are known to antagonize or be suppressed by the function of afternoon-enriched transcription factors, suggesting that their opposing roles could lead to a switch between transcription of the afternoon and late-night genes. For example, BEAF-32 binding has been postulated to weaken pausing induced by the late-night transcription factor Trl76,77, and M1BP not only promotes ribosomal gene transcription78, but also suppresses expression of autophagy and apoptosis genes79, which typically peak at late-night. Because late-night genes showed enhancer-like chromatin signatures, we propose that they depend more on transcription factor activity at enhancers. Consistent with this, enhancer RNA analysis in mouse liver indicates that enhancers were most active at late-night, while transcriptional regulation in the afternoon seems to occur primarily at promoters29,30. It is unclear whether the chromatin signatures we observe in fly photoreceptors are also found at rhythmic genes in mouse liver, but the parallel association of enhancer- and promoter-based regulatory mechanisms with distinct phase groups suggests that a combinatorial model of chromatin signatures and transcription factor binding may be a conserved mechanism to temporally regulate gene expression in peripheral clock tissues. The morning genes differed from the other two groups and seem to be regulated predominantly via chromatin state rather than transcription factors. In neurons, activity evoked by external stimulation or spontaneous firing induces the expression of activity-dependent genes, many of which encode transcription factors that activate downstream gene expression important for synapse formation and function80. InDrosophilaphotoreceptors, light activates a G-protein coupled receptor phosphoinositide signaling cascade that leads to influx of cations such as calcium, and depolarization of the neuron81. Thus, light onset at ZT0 would be expected to induce the expression of activity-dependent genes, and indeed, the immediate early transcription factorsHr38andsrare present in the morning group. Notably,Hr38orsroverexpression expands the projection of small ventrolateral neuron (s-LNv), which is circadian regulated occurring in the early morning63. Our data indicated that H3K27me3 normally keeps morning gene expression at low levels and restricts their induction to a specific time window, a mode of regulation similar to the induction of activity-dependent genes in developing neurons that carry bipartite chromatin signature61. Reduction of H3K27me3, whether via its transient dip at ZT4 or by Utx overexpression, may lower the threshold for inducing this morning wave of transcription. Indeed, in cultured cells, degron-induced depletion of the PRC1/2 complexes leads to rapid induction of H3K27me3-marked genes, with lowly expressed ones showing the earliest transcriptional response within 2h of depletion82. Thus, unlike afternoon and late-night genes, morning genes may be gated mainly by chromatin state and induced by environmental stimulus. The transcription factor networks associated with specific phases in photoreceptors include both core clock regulators and many other transcription factors. While critical for maintaining rhythmic behavior and gene expression in the absence of zeitgebers83, the circadian clock may have a more nuanced role in diurnal rhythmic gene expression, particularly in the retina. We found that the transcriptional waves at ZT8 and ZT20 are largely maintained in theClkjrkmutant. In the mouse liver, similarsystem-driven genesremained rhythmic at comparable times in bothBmal1andCry1/2knockouts, which has been postulated to be regulated via signals from the SCN42. However, because rhythms in the pacemaker neurons are also disrupted in theClkjrkmutant84, system-driven rhythms are unlikely to depend on the central clock and may be driven by external stimulus. In mouse liver, mTOR signaling is both necessary and sufficient to mediate hepatic system-driven rhythmic gene expression in the absence of a functional clock43, suggesting that phosphorylation may represent a critical signaling mechanism through which zeitgebers exert their temporal control on transcription. While nutrient levels are a crucial zeitgeber in the liver, light has a more critical role in the retina4,6. Indeed, light exposure increase phosphorylation of more than 1000 proteins inDrosophilaheads85and many phosphorylation sites show circadian rhythms86. In the mouse forebrain, around half of phosphoproteins exhibit rhythmic phosphorylation, nearly all of which is abolished by sleep deprivation87. These diurnal phosphorylation events may provide clues to the transcriptional mechanisms that drive light-dependent expression rhythms, independent of the molecular clock. We propose that regulating diurnal gene expression rhythms through a combination of chromatin signature and transcription factors enables both the temporal segregation of biological processes and optimization of transcriptional timing based on energy availability. Photoreceptors are among the most energetically demanding cells: visual responses including active ion transport, maintenance of ionic gradients, and synaptic transmission consume vast amount of ATP88,89. Therefore, timing high levels of transcription, and the translation that follows, to time windows of lower phototransduction demands40could reduce the competition for metabolic resources such as ATP and GTP90, especially for highly expressed genes which impose greater energy demand. Consistent with this possibility, afternoon and late-night genes were expressed at higher levels than morning genes, and ATP is more abundant at the end of the light phase at ZT12 compared with early morning at ZT0 (Figure 1H). In addition, translation inDrosophilaclock cells peaks at CT9 and CT2091, which overlaps with the latter two transcriptional waves observed in this study, suggesting global transcription and translation are temporally synchronized. As in the mammalian retina,Drosophilaphotoreceptors are long-lived neurons that maintain their function over the lifespan of the organism, up to 80 days in flies92. The chromatin signatures associated with the afternoon and late-night genes may both promote their diurnal expression and help maintain these rhythms over time. Supporting this idea, H3K4me3 has been proposed to promote transcription consistency by retaining memory about prior transcriptional status93. We propose that these chromatin signatures provide long-term and efficient regulatory mechanisms that collaborate with transcription factors to maintain diurnal rhythms and optimize photoreceptor function across the light cycle. title: Common and Sex-Biased Muscle Transcriptomic Aging Signatures Across Diverse Species
author: Randolph, E. C.; Fang, Y.; Meisel, R.; Walters, J.; Gamble, T.; Wilkinson, G.; Larschan, E.; Webb, A.; IISAGE Consortium,  ; Biga, P.; Riddle, N.; Duan, J. E.
text: Sex differences in lifespan are widespread yet inconsistent across the animal kingdom. In mammals, XX females outlive XY males in over 60% of species, while this pattern reverses in birds, where ZZ males have a higher life expectancy. These sex differences raise the question of whether sex-biased aging biomarkers (age-associated molecular signatures that reflect biological aging processes) can be identified based on transcriptomic data and whether such markers are shared across taxa. To identify sex-biased aging biomarkers, we analyzed sex-specific skeletal muscle transcriptomes (RNA-seq) from young and old individuals of six species spanning major evolutionary lineages. Four female-biased and 18 male-biased aging biomarkers were identified across all species. Three shared aging biomarkers were also identified in both sexes of all species: Na Channel, Heat Shock Protein 70 (HSP70), and Secreted Protein Acidic and Rich in Cysteine (SPARC). Particularly, age-associated changes in the HSP70 family are suggestive of a shared decline in proteostasis, a hallmark of aging observed across both model and non-model organisms. Furthermore, using an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model applied to orthogroup phylogenies, we identified lineage- and sex-dependent expression shifts in shared aging biomarkers. In addition, sex-biased orthogroups revealed age-associated alterations in muscle structure and function in females, whereas mitochondrial and metabolic pathways were predominantly changed in males, indicating divergent mechanisms in muscle aging between sexes. Together, these findings identified a set of transcriptional aging signatures, both shared and sex-biased, that are detectable across diverse evolutionary lineages, providing insight into shared and divergent molecular mechanisms underlying aging. Significance statementAcross the animal kingdom, there are many instances of sex differences in longevity, suggesting the presence of sex differences in the underlying biological processes that drive longevity. This study investigated gene expression differences occurring in age among six species spanning large evolutionary time scales to investigate whether sex differences in biological processes are shared across evolution and whether they can serve as identifiers of aging biomarkers. This investigation yielded three ubiquitously shared transcriptional aging biomarkers along with four female-biased and 18 male-biased transcriptional aging biomarkers. These findings reveal a semi-concerted evolutionary aging pattern that aligns well with preestablished aging biomarkers. In addition, these findings reveal a sex-biased evolutionary aging pattern. Across the animal kingdom, males and females frequently differ in lifespan (Bronikowski et al 2022), and these patterns vary systematically across major clades. In mammals, females outlive males in roughly 60% of surveyed species (Lemaître et al 2020), whereas in birds the opposite pattern is common, with males typically living longer (Marais et al 2018). These differences between birds and mammals often are interpreted in light of the heterogametic sex hypothesis, which posits that the sex possessing two different sex chromosomes (ZW females in birds, XY males in mammals) experiences greater deleterious effects associated with hemizygosity (Marais et al 2018, Staerk et at 2025). Fish also exhibit sex-biased longevity, although the direction of this bias varies by species. For example, male yellow tang (Zebrasoma flavescens) outlive females (Claisse et al 2009), while the opposite pattern is observed in the Maori snapper (Lutjanus rivulatus) (Wakefield et al 2020) and African annual turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri) (Reichard et al 2021). Many invertebrates experience sex-biased longevity as well, includingDrosophila melanogaster(Iliadi et al 2009, Millington and Rideout 2018) andCaenorhabditis elegans(McCulloch and Gems 2003,Barr et al 2018). These widespread yet inconsistent patterns strongly suggest that intrinsic, sex-specific mechanisms are influencing aging; however, the underlying molecular basis of these differences remains poorly understood. While substantial progress has been made in defining common biological processes underlying aging, further work is needed to determine the extent to which these mechanisms are shared across species and between sexes. The updatedHallmarks of Agingframework (López-Otín et al 2023) outlines key processes, such as loss of proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and genomic instability, that are thought to contribute broadly to organismal aging. However, these hallmarks were largely derived from studies in a limited set of classical model organisms, includingD. melanogaster,C. elegans, andMus musculus(Biga et al 2025). Importantly, many of the studies informing this framework either excluded one sex or were conducted predominantly in males, introducing a bias that may obscure sex-specific aging mechanisms (Biga et al 2025). This limitation reflects a broader and well-documented trend in biomedical research, where sex bias historically has been prevalent (Beery and Zucker 2011,Holdcroft 2007,Ballantyne and Rogers 2011) and continues to persist despite increased awareness (Carmody et al 2022). Consequently, it remains uncertain whether the established hallmarks of aging adequately reflect the full molecular diversity of aging across sexes and species, as current knowledge is disproportionately derived from model organisms and male-biased studies. Comparative transcriptomics provides a powerful framework for determining whether the molecular processes underlying aging, and particularly sex-specific aging, are shared evolutionarily. By incorporating species that span deep phylogenetic divergence, this approach enables the identification of transcriptional signatures that are either ubiquitous across taxa or restricted to specific lineages or sexes. Analyzing these data with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) modeling framework further enables the detection of adaptive expression shifts and evolutionary divergence along a phylogeny (Bedford and Hartl 2009). Despite these advantages, most prior transcriptomic studies of aging have focused on within-species analyses. Such studies, including large-scale fly aging atlases (Lu et al 2023), have been highly effective at identifying age-and sex-associated transcriptional changes within individual organisms. However, they provide limited insight into whether these patterns are shared across species or represent lineage-specific changes. As a result, there remains a critical gap in aging biology: the lack of rigorous, cross-species comparative analyses that systematically evaluate shared versus divergent transcriptomic hallmarks of aging across both model and non-model organisms. Muscle (skeletal muscle in vertebrates and striated muscle in invertebrates) represents a particularly informative tissue for interspecific comparisons of aging. It is highly conserved in both structure and function across metazoans (Augustin and Partridge 2009,Mukund and Subramaniam 2019,Mendoza et al 2023), undergoes well characterized age-related decline (Tieland et al 2018), and is sensitive to systemic and sex hormone–mediated aging processes (Sipilȁ et al 2013,Velders and Diel 2013,Critchlow et al 2025). Importantly, muscle can be sampled in a minimally invasive manner and allows broad inclusion of both model and non-model species, including taxa for which other tissues cannot be ethically or feasibly obtained. Here, we perform a comparative, cross-species transcriptomic analysis that integrates both model and non-model organisms while explicitly incorporating both sexes to assess whether aging signatures exhibit sex bias and whether they are species-specific or shared across evolutionary lineages. Using muscle RNA-seq datasets from six species, we first characterize sex-associated transcriptional changes within species during aging. We then evaluate the extent to which molecular pathways show shared age-related regulation across taxa and applied an OU modeling framework to identify lineage- and sex-biased expression shifts in key aging-associated gene families. Our analyses reveal a combination of shared, lineage-specific, and sex-biased transcriptional signatures of aging, identifying a set of aging biomarkers that are detectable across diverse evolutionary lineages. These findings provide insight into both shared and divergent molecular mechanisms underlying sex-specific aging. To determine whether sex-biased aging biomarkers can be identified across a broad phylogenetic spectrum, and whether such markers are shared across major animal clades, we integrated previously published RNA-seq datasets with newly collected datasets. These datasets included young (sexually mature) and old (post-median lifespan) individuals from six species spanning deep evolutionary divergence (Fig. 1A-B): two insects (D. melanogasterandPlodia interpunctella), one fish (N. furzeri), and three mammals, including two rodents (M. musculusandRattus norvegicus) and humans (Homo sapiens). Overall, these species span hundreds of millions of years of evolution while also including closely related pairs, enabling comparisons of aging signatures across both short and long evolutionary time. Following a standardized bioinformatics analysis pipeline (Fig. 1C), we performed principal component analysis (PCA) on normalized transcript counts within each species to assess whether transcriptional profiles could distinguish samples by age and sex. Distinct clustering by age and/or sex was observed in all species (Fig. 2A), indicating robust biological signals. Specifically,P. interpunctella,R. norvegicus, andN. furzerishowed a strong separation by age, whereasD. melanogaster,R. norvegicus, M. musculus, andH. sapiensexhibited a strong separation by sex. To examine how aging alters sex-specific transcription within each species, we identified age-associated differentially expressed genes (agDEGs) using three contrasts: female old vs. young, male old vs. young, and the age-by-sex interaction. Across species, females exhibited anywhere from 1,249-4,984 agDEGs, while males exhibited anywhere from 2,149-6,073 agDEGs (Table 1; Supplemental File 1), indicating substantial species variation, including sample size, power, and variance that affect the magnitude of age-associated transcriptional changes (Supplemental Fig. 1). Additionally, the direction of transcriptional change varied between sexes, within species (Fig. 2B,Table 1). In females,D. melanogaster, N. furzeri,andM. musculusshowed a significant bias (Chi-square test,p <0.05) toward upregulated agDEGs, whereasR. norvegicusandH. sapiensexhibited a predominance of downregulated agDEGs (Chi-square test,p <0.05), andP. interpunctellashowed no significant directional bias. In males,D. melanogasterwas the only species with a significant (Chi-square test,p <0.05) enrichment of upregulated agDEGs, whileP. interpunctella, N. furzeri, R. norvegicus, andH. sapiensshowed a higher proportion of downregulated agDEGs (Chi-square test,p <0.05), andM. musculusshowed no significant bias. These patterns highlight substantial diversity in both the magnitude and direction of transcriptional aging responses across evolutionary lineages. To assess sex differences in aging, we quantified the proportion of agDEGs that were female-specific, male-specific, or shared between sexes within each species (Fig. 2C;Supplemental File 2). Interestingly, across species, 12-44% of agDEGs were female-specific, while 19-54% were male-specific across species. The proportion of common agDEGs ranged from 25-48%, withP. interpunctellaexhibited the greatest overlap whileR. norvegicusshowed the least overlap (Fig. 2C;Supplemental File 2). Together, these results demonstrate that muscle aging processes are associated with widespread transcriptional changes that are highly variable across species and sex, in both magnitude and regulatory direction. To further investigate sex differences in aging, it is important to identify the genes that show age-associated transcriptional trajectories that differ between the sexes. Thus, we evaluated DEGs identified from age-by-sex interaction effects (absDEGs) and compared them with agDEGs identified within each sex (Fig. 2C, Supplemental File 3). Interestingly, absDEGs that overlapped with shared agDEGs often exhibited differences in the magnitude of expression change between sexes within a given species. In some cases, these genes showed opposing regulatory trajectories, with age-associated upregulation in one sex and downregulation in the other (Fig. 2D). For example, inH. sapiens,TPRG1, with its antisense transcriptTPRG1-AS1are implicated in cardiovascular aging (Ren et al 2022), exhibited age-related upregulation in males but downregulation in females (Fig. 2D), suggesting a potential link to the higher incidence of cardiovascular disease observed in males (Freedman et al 2026). These patterns indicate that sex differences in aging are not necessarily driven by entirely distinct gene sets, but rather by quantitative and directional differences in specific gene regulation. Together, these findings demonstrate that aging induces widespread yet highly variable transcriptional changes across species and sexes. While some species exhibit strong concordance between males and females, others display pronounced sex-biased aging signatures, reinforcing the importance of incorporating both sexes in comparative analyses of aging. To gain functional insight into agDEGs and absDEGs, we classified all genes into orthogroups, which are sets of genes descended from a single ancestral gene that may include both orthologs and paralogs across species (Emms and Kelly 2019). Among six species, 95.2% of all annotated genes were assigned successfully to 23,024 orthogroups containing one or more species using OrthoFinder2 (Supplemental File 4), with only 8% of these orthogroups being classified as species-specific, and the remaining 4.8% of annotated genes being unassigned. This result indicates that the vast majority of genes belong to conserved gene families shared across at least two species. Overall, 5,343 orthogroups contained representatives from all six species, reflecting substantial evolutionary conservation. However, only 449 orthogroups were strict single-copy (1:1) orthologs (Supplemental File 5), highlighting the limited prevalence of highly conserved, non-duplicated gene families across these phylogenetically distant taxa. Together, these orthogroup assignments provided the comparative framework for downstream functional and comparative analyses of aging-associated genes. To assess whether well-characterized human aging genes exhibit shared transcriptional responses across species, we compared 307 aging-associated genes from the GenAge database (de Magalhães et al 2024) with the set of 1:1 orthologs identified in our dataset. Only eight genes overlapped across all six species:CDK7, CISD2, ERCC2, GCLM, MLH1, PARP1, STUB1,andXPA(Supplemental Fig. 2). Among these,CISD2exhibited one of the most consistent signatures.CISD2localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial membranes and plays a role in cytosolic Ca²⁺ homeostasis (Shen et al 2021). We observed significant age-related downregulation ofCISD2inM. musculus, H. sapiens,andP. interpunctella, suggesting a shared decline inCISD2expression during aging across both vertebrates and insects. This finding is consistent with prior studies linking reducedCISD2expression to mitochondrial dysfunction and accelerated tissue aging (Chen et al 2009). The remaining species exhibited a mixture of expression patterns among these eight shared human aging genes, reflecting lineage-specific divergence in canonical aging regulators. Although these genes are well-established in human aging biology, their transcriptional trajectories vary substantially across species and between sexes, highlighting both shared elements and species-specific adaptations. Moreover, only four of the eight genes were identified as downregulated agDEGs in human skeletal muscle, which may be due to tissue specific expression patterns as many genes cataloged in the human aging database were derived from brain or other non-muscle tissues. This highlights the importance of tissue context when interpreting shared aging signatures. Furthermore, the relatively small number of shared 1:1 orthologs limited the number of previously defined aging genes that could be compared directly across all species. This limitation highlights the need for more inclusive comparative frameworks, such as incorporating paralogs within broader orthogroups, to better capture the full spectrum of shared and divergent aging mechanisms across species. Together, these findings emphasize the importance of comparative analyses for interpreting the evolutionarily shared aging pathways and caution against assuming that transcriptional aging signatures identified in a single species, a single sex, or a single tissue type readily generalize across taxa and biological contexts. This definition captures gene families exhibiting shared sex-biased transcriptional responses to aging across taxa. Using these criteria, we identified four female-biased and 18 male-biased age-associated orthogroups (Fig. 5A-B; Supplemental Fig. 3-4; Supplemental File 8). Similar to the globally shared aging signatures, the degree of orthogroup conservation decreased with increasing evolutionary distance, indicating that sex-biased aging programs become progressively more lineage-specific across phylogeny. To identify the biological processes most affected by aging across species and sexes, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses were carried out for each species and sex. Despite the substantial phylogenetic diversity of the dataset, several core aging-associated pathways emerged consistently as the most significantly enriched across taxa (Fig. 6A). For example, pathways involved in proteostasis, including proteasome, protein digestion and absorption, and autophagy, all were enriched significantly in multiple species. These pathways mediate cellular responses to age-associated stress, such as the accumulation of misfolded proteins, oxidative damage, and impaired protein turnover (Kourtis and Tavernarakis 2011). As central components of protein quality control, these systems typically are challenged during aging, reflecting an increased cellular stress burden (Higuchi-Sanabria et al 2018). Additionally, when KEGG pathways were cross-referenced to known aging pathways from the Aging Atlas online database (Aging Atlas Consortium 2020), additional pathways relating to proteostasis were identified such as protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum (Fig. 6B), further reflecting the increase of cellular damage in age within the majority of the species studied. A full list of all enriched KEGG pathways for both sexes in each species can be found inSupplemental File 10. Interestingly, the direction of age-associated expression changes differed across species. InH. sapiens, proteostasis-related pathways, including autophagy, proteasome, and protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum were expressed lower in muscles with age (Fig. 6A-B), suggesting a reduced capacity for cellular proteostasis proteasome activities (Saez and Vilchez 2014,Njomen and Tepe 2019) and consistent with increased proteolysis in human muscle aging (Ubaida-Mohien et al 2019). In contrast, many non-human species, such asN. furzeri, M. musculus,andR. norvegicus,exhibited increased expression in some of these pathways, consistent with a compensatory mechanism to to increased proteotoxic stress (Morimoto and Cuervo 2014,Hamazaki and Murata 2024). These contrasting patterns highlight both shared involvement and divergent regulation of cellular stress response mechanisms during aging. In addition to proteostasis pathways, several metabolic and structural processes were enriched broadly with age across species (Fig. 6). These included thermogenesis and pathways associated with muscle fiber organization and cytoskeletal integrity. The decreased expression in pathways of oxidative phosphorylation, PI3K-Akt signaling, calcium signaling, and muscle contraction pathways is consistent with well-established declines in skeletal muscle function, metabolic flexibility, and mitochondrial efficiency during aging (Chen et al 2021). This pattern was not witnessed in all species, or in both sexes within species, demonstrating sex-specific and evolutionary divergent patterns of enrichment. Comparative analysis across taxa revealed that the most consistently enriched pathways involve proteostasis, reinforcing its central role as a core feature in aging biology. At the same time, the presence of sex-biased and lineage-specific enrichment patterns highlights evolutionary divergence in how organisms respond to cellular stress and allocate resources during aging. Together, these findings indicate that aging is characterized by a shared increase in cellular stress, while the transcriptional strategies used to manage this process diverges across species and between sexes. This study provides a cross-species analysis of sex-biased transcriptional aging across diverse animal lineages. We identified three aging markers shared by all species and both sexes, including proteostasis-related genes such asHSP70, highlighting the evolutionary importance of this core aging process. Aging signatures were predominantly sex-biased, defined as genes or pathways that were significantly altered with age in the same sex of all species but not consistently represented in the other sex across all species This is in contrast to sex-specific signatures, which would entail being represented in only one sex across all species and never in the other sex. These signatures relayed involvement of structural and functional properties in female-biased agDEGs and mitochondrial and metabolic properties in male-biased agDEGs. In parallel, we observed substantial lineage-specific divergence, with decreasing overlap of aging-associated orthogroups across evolutionary distances and lineage-dependent expression shifts in key gene families. Functionally, we identified shared proteostasis disruption and male-biased regulation in mitochondrial functions, demonstrating that aging reflects both shared molecular mechanisms and divergent regulatory strategies across species and sexes. Our study advances the field of aging biology by moving beyond single-species analyses to a comparative, cross-species framework that explicitly incorporates sex as a central biological variable. While previous transcriptomic studies have largely focused on a limited set of model organisms in mice (Jin et al 2025,Bilgic et al 2025), flies (Lu et al 2023,Sang et al 2025), and worms (Wang et al 2022,Ham et al 2022), our approach integrates both model and non-model species and includes both sexes, enabling a systematic evaluation of shared and evolutionary divergent sex-biased aging-associated transcriptional programs. Importantly, this study demonstrates that the biology of aging cannot be described fully from single-species or sex-biased perspectives. Instead, it emerges as a comprehensive process shaped by shared cellular stress responses and modulated by lineage specification and sex-specific physiology. By integrating comparative transcriptomics within an evolutionary framework, our work provides a scalable approach for identifying robust, cross-species aging biomarkers, and offers new insights into how fundamental aging processes are both shared and diversified across the animal kingdom. We were able to identify three shared orthogroups (Na⁺ channel proteins, HSP70, and SPARC) demonstrating that similar core transcriptional features of aging are present across deeply divergent species and both sexes. Importantly, these orthogroups map to fundamental muscle biological function, including cellular structural integrity (SPARC), muscle membrane excitability (Na⁺ channels), and proteostasis (HSP70), suggesting that aging consistently impacts these core cellular functions in muscle. While the manner in which these orthogroups are altered with age differs between species, and sometimes between the sexes, their identification provides an exciting opportunity to explore these nuances in future aging studies. One can begin to parse out some of these nuances in orthogroup regulation between species by investigating the fold change of agDEGs within these shared orthogroups. For example,SPARCexhibited consistent age-associated downregulation across species, with the exception ofD. melanogaster. SPARC is a matricellular glycoprotein strongly associated with muscle fibrosis, degeneration, and sarcopenia (Ghanemi et al 2022a), and its decline during aging is consistent with previous observations in mammalian muscle aging (Gruber et al 2005,Ghanemi et al 2022b). In contrast,D. melanogastershowed increasedSPARCexpression, potentially associated with the tissue-specific extracellular matrix remodeling and fibrosis-like accumulation during aging (Vaughan et al 2018). Similarly, Na⁺ channel genes (SCN) were predominantly upregulated across species, again with the exception ofD. melanogaster. This pattern may represent a compensatory response to maintain cellular excitability in the context of declining Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (NKA) activity during aging (Wyckelsma and McKenna 2016). The HSP70 orthogroup is a particularly strong candidate for a shared aging mechanism because HSP70 proteins are central to maintaining proteostasis. The change in HSP70 expression with age across all species supports the idea that proteostasis efficiency is declining, or at the very least being altered with age, consistent with previous findings (López-Otín et al 2023). The observation of both upregulation and downregulation of agDEGs within the HSP70 orthogroup within a given species likely reflects distinct strategies of proteostatic responses. Increased expression of HSP70 genes may represent a compensatory response to accumulating cellular stress, as HSP70 proteins function as molecular chaperones that protect against elevated oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, as observed in agedD. melanogaster(Tower 2010) and duringH. sapiensmuscle aging (Cumming et al 2021). On the other hand, decreasedHSP70expression may indicate a progressive decline in proteostasis capacity, resulting in reduced ability to manage misfolded proteins and increased susceptibility to cellular damage, including muscle atrophy and impaired regeneration, as reported in skeletal muscle of agedR. norvegicus(Vasilaki et al 2002) and elderlyH. sapiens(Senf 2013). These variations suggest that different species may employ distinct transcriptional mechanisms to fine-tune proteostasis during aging. Together, these findings highlight that aging involves shared disruption of core biological systems, while the regulatory responses to these disruptions diverge across species and sexes, reflecting evolutionary differences in how organisms cope with cellular stress and functional decline. The identification of sex-biased orthogroups across species establishes that aging is not a uniform process, but is driven instead by sex-dependent regulatory programs. These molecular signatures arise from coordinated, pathway-level changes, revealing fundamentally distinct strategies by which females and males undergo aging. Our comparative framework further demonstrates that these sex-biased patterns are shared across evolutionary lineages, rather than being species-specific phenomena. For instance, the distinct separation of transcriptomic profiles by sex in five of the six species highlights that sex can be a dominant driver of aging-associated transcriptional variation. While some aging-related pathways, such as those involved in proteostasis (HSP70), are shared across sexes, others exhibit clear sex-bias, for example, the consistent involvement of muscle degeneration pathways in females and mitochondrial and metabolic pathways in males. Consistent with this divergence, aging in females was characterized by enrichment of orthogroups associated with sarcopenia and structural components such as collagens, suggesting the degeneration of normal muscle functioning in age. The downregulation of agDEGs ofDYRKin females of all species, exceptP. interpunctella, could be an indicator of muscle degeneration as some paralogs ofDYRKhave been linked to sarcopenia (Jiao et al 2025). Interestingly enough, the consistent downregulation of the agDEGs phosphodiesterase (PDE4specifically) in females of all species, exceptN. furzeri, is suggestive of a compensatory mechanism to combat muscle degeneration, as inhibition ofPDE4has been identified as a therapeutic target in sarcopenia drug treatments (Balasubramaniam et al 2018,Angelino et al 2025). Finally, the variable expression patterns between species of agDEGs of kinase heavy chain and collagen in all females relays species specific alterations in muscle function and tissue stability with age respectively (Holwerda et al 2025). Together, these findings support a model in which aging in females involves a multi-level perturbation of muscle homeostasis, ultimately impacting muscle function. In contrast, male-biased agDEG orthogroups were enriched for genes involved in mitochondrial function and cellular metabolism, including voltage-dependent anion channels (VDAC) and enzymes involved in acetyl-CoA metabolism and redox regulation, indicating age-associated mitochondrial functional decline in aged males (Viña et al 2003,Camus et al 2012,Demarest and McCarthy 2014). Additional male agDEGs associated with ATP production and ion homeostasis, such as creatine kinases, V-type proton ATPase components, and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase subunits, further indicate alterations in energy production and cellular energetics during aging (Wyckelsma and McKenna 2016). These changes directly correlate with diminished ATP replenishment, reduced metabolic rate, and impaired ion homeostasis (Alves et al 2023). These patterns suggest that aging in males is characterized by a more pronounced disruption of mitochondrial function and metabolic homeostasis, which are essential for sustaining muscle performance. Despite these distinct molecular trajectories, both sexes converge on a similar physiological outcome, age-associated decline in muscle function (Trombetti et al 2015). However, the underlying mechanisms differ: females exhibit more alterations in muscle structure, whereas males show greater alterations in mitochondrial and metabolic pathways. This divergence highlights that similar aging phenotypes can arise from different molecular regulatory mechanisms, shaped by sex-specific physiology. Together, this work extends our current understanding of aging by the systematic analysis of transcriptomes from both young and old individuals of both sexes from six very diverse species. Until recently, aging studies have been male-biased, which reflected a long-standing bias in biomedical research (Beery and Zucker 2011). The presence of distinct, shared molecular pathways underlying aging in each sex suggests that interventions targeting age-related decline may need to be sex-specific, as the efficacy of lifespan extending interventions often differs between males and females (Hajdarovic et al 2026). More broadly, this work highlights the importance of incorporating both sexes in comparative and translational studies to more accurately capture the complexity of aging biology. A key methodological strength of this study is the use of orthogroup-based analysis, rather than relying solely on 1:1 ortholog matching across taxa. Although 1:1 orthologs are used commonly to infer direct evolutionary relationships and functional equivalence (Altenhoff et al 2012), this approach excludes duplicated or lineage-expanded genes, which often play critical roles in adaptation and species-specific biology (Koonin 2005). Moreover, the assumption of strict functional equivalence among 1:1 orthologs increasingly has been questioned (Studer and Robinson-Rechavi 2009,Stamboulian et al 2020). Furthermore, while the number of 1:1 orthologs is relatively high in closely related species, the number decreases substantially with greater evolutionary divergence, limiting their application in broad comparative analyses such as ours. By contrast, orthogroups, including gene families descended from a common ancestral gene, enable a more comprehensive representation of evolutionary relationships. Using this framework, we analyzed 23,024 orthogroups across six species, compared to only 449 1:1 orthologs, substantially expanding the scope of cross-species comparison. This approach allowed us to identify shared functional modules while accommodating lineage-specific gene expansions and losses (Gabaldón and Koonin 2018), which are particularly relevant in the context of aging. Although orthogroup-based analyses may introduce some ambiguity in precise functional equivalence, they provide a more integrative and evolutionarily informative view of transcriptomic divergence (Sheng et al 2022). Future studies combining this approach with functional validation, such as protein modeling or experimental validation, will be important to resolve gene-specific roles within complex orthogroups. This study reveals that muscle aging is governed by a combination of shared and sex-biased molecular programs that operate across vast evolutionary distances. The consistent age-associated expression change of proteostasis-associated HSP70 orthogroups across taxa provides compelling evidence that cellular stress response and proteostasis remodeling represent universal features of aging (Haigis and Yankner 2010). At the same time, our analyses highlight sex divergence in aging, with the consistent involvement of mitochondrial and metabolic pathways in males, demonstrating that aging trajectories can diverge systematically between sexes even within shared biological systems. Our integrative framework, combining comparative transcriptomics, orthogroup-based evolutionary mapping, and OU modeling, establishes a scalable and evolutionarily informed strategy for dissecting the molecular architecture of aging beyond traditional model organisms. By moving beyond single-gene comparisons to pathway- and orthogroup-level analyses, this approach captures both shared functional modules and lineage-specific regulatory divergence, providing a more comprehensive view of aging biology. As transcriptomic resources expand, non-model species will enable increasingly powerful comparative analyses, allowing researchers to disentangle how sex, ecology, and life history strategies shape the evolution of aging. Ultimately, these insights will be critical for advancing a more generalizable and mechanistically grounded understanding of aging, with direct implications for the development of sex-informed and evolutionarily robust therapeutic anti-aging strategies. D. melanogaster(DGRP 304 strain, Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center, RRID: BDSC_25177) were reared at the University of Alabama at Birmingham in incubators with 12 hours light/12 hours dark conditions at 25 °C in 65% humidity and fed Jazz-Mix Drosophila Food (Fisher), supplemented with active dry yeast. Virgin flies from both sexes were collected over the course of 48 hours and housed in single sex groups of 20 in separate vials, totaling about 15 vials per sex, used for aging. For the young group, at 8 days post eclosion, flies were flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and thoraxes were dissected on a dry ice-cooled surface. Five to ten thoraxes were pooled for each sample (n = 4) for both sexes to be used in RNA extraction. The same procedure was repeated at the old time point (54 days post eclosion). Total RNA was extracted using the Monarch Total RNA miniprep kit (New England Biolabs) following the manufacturer’s protocol. P. interpunctellawere raised from pools of larvae housed in 32 oz. plastic cups, held at 25 °C in 14 hours light/10 hours dark conditions, and fed a custom mix of cracked wheat, wheat bran, wheat germ, yeast, honey, glycerin, and water (Silhacek and Murphy 2008). When larvae reached the fifth larval instar, they were transferred to individual 1 oz. deli cups for the remainder of their lifespan. Young samples were collected on the day they eclosed, while old samples were collected at 13 days post eclosion. The cup housing the animal to be collected was placed on ice for 5-15 minutes until the animal stopped moving. The body was then segmented into head, thorax, and abdomen. Individual thoraxes were placed into 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes containing 300 μL TRIzol (Invitrogen, ThermoFisher, US) and stored at -80 °C. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol following the manufacturer’s protocol. For both insect samples described above, 400ng of total RNA was submitted to Novogene (Sacramento, CA, USA) for library preparation and sequencing. Briefly, RNA concentration and integrity were assessed using Qbit and Bioanalyzer. High-quality RNA was poly-A selected and reverse transcribed using random hexamer primers. cDNA libraries were prepared by Novogene and were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq platform, generating on average 40 million paired-end 150 base-pair reads per sample. RNA-seq datasets of four species were obtained from NCBI public datasets (Table 2). Raw reads were retrieved from the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database. Details of each dataset, including replicate numbers (Fig. 1B), accession numbers, and experimental metadata, are provided inTable 2. All samples were from bulk RNA-seq studies that included both sexes and at least two age groups representing young and old timepoints. For species with multiple timepoints, such asM. musculus(Shavlakaez et al 2023) andR. norvegicus(Yu et al 2014), only the youngest sexually mature and the oldest available age group were included to represent young and old. In theR. norvegicusdataset containing technical duplicates (Yu et al 2014), no significant differences were observed between these duplicates. Therefore, the corresponding raw reads were concatenated before processing. We note that sequencing strategies varied across studies. For example,R. norvegicus(Yu at al 2014) andH. sapiens(DeJong et al 2023) studies used single-read sequencing, while all the other studies used paired-end sequencing. Library preparation methods also differed: ribo-depleted libraries were used forR. norvegicus(Yu et al 2014),M. musculus(Shavlakadze et al 2023), andN. furzeri(Xu et al 2023), while poly-A selected libraries were used for the remaining species. All studies included had RNA-seq data derived from skeletal muscle tissue, with sampling sites as follows: vastus lateralis (H. sapiens), gastrocnemius (R. norvegicusandM. musculus), and steak (N. furzeri). Raw reads were processed using kallisto (Bary et al 2016) for species-specific pseudoalignment and transcript quantification. Reference genomes obtained from NCBI (Table 2) includedD. melanogaster(Release 6 plus ISO1 MT, dm6),P interpunctella(ilPlolnte3.1 alternate haplotype),N. furzeri(UI_Nfuz_MZM_1.0),R. norvegicus(GRCr8),M. musculus(CRCm39, mm39), andH. sapiens(GRCh38.p14, hg38). Transcript quantifications for all species were imported into the statistical environment R (R Core Team 2023) using the tximport package (Soneson et al 2015). Transcript abundances were summarized to the gene level and converted to counts using the tximport option “tx2gene” and a generated TxDB transcript to gene object generated from the reference Gene Transfer Format files (gtf) from each species using the R package GenomicFeatures (Lawrence et al 2013). Differentially expressed genes in age (agDEGs) were identified for each species using DESeq2 (Love et al 2014). These agDEGs were identified within each sex, and additional contrasts were performed to detect age-by-sex interaction effects. Genes were considered differentially expressed based on an adjusted p-value (p.adjust) < 0.05. Differences in the proportion of up-versus downregulated agDEGs for both sexes of each species were then investigated using a Chi-Squared Goodness of Fit Test. Orthogroups were identified using the online tool OrthoFinder2 (Emms and Kelly 2019), with the complete proteome of each species obtained from Ensembl (release version 110;Dyer et al 2025) as input. To account for isoforms, or multiple transcripts from the same gene, only the longest (primary) transcript variant from each gene was used for this analysis. OrthoFinder2 was run with its default settings, which performed all-verse-all BLAST searches and used sequence similarity scores to construct gene trees and identify orthogroups. OrthoFinder2 outputs a tab-separated values file (Supplemental File 10) and arbitrarily names each orthogroup. Then, the names of the orthogroups were changed to reflect the proteins that make up the orthogroup. The protein identifier names for each species within an orthogroup were searched in NCBI, and the consensus protein name was used to name the orthogroup. Next, species-specific agDEGs were mapped to their encoded proteins and assigned to corresponding orthogroups. Orthogroups containing agDEGs from two or more species were classified as common aging markers. Species-specific agDEG contributions to shared orthogroups were visualized using the UpSet R package (Gehlenborg 2019). For universal and sex-biased common orthogroups, the median log2 fold-change (old:young) across species and sexes was plotted using ggplot2 (Wickham 2016). An illustration of the complete bioinformatic workflow used in this manuscript can be found inFig. 1C. Species-specific gene functional annotation databases were constructed forN. furzeriandP. interpunctellausing AnnotationForge (Carlson and Pagès 2023). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was performed using clusterProfiler (Wu et al 2021,Yu et al 2012) on the full set of results from each contrast for each species/sex combination to identify enriched KEGG pathways. AsP. interpunctellawas not listed in the KEGG database, their KEGG pathways were obtained using GhostKOALA (Kanehisa et al 2016) and incorporated into the GSEA analysis in clusterProfiler. Enriched KEGG pathways were then compared across all species and sexes to identify shared and sex-biased functional patterns of aging. To detect evolutionary shifts in agDEG expression, OU models were applied to orthogroup gene trees generated by OrthoFinder. For each orthogroup, mean log-TPM values were calculated for each age-sex group combination (young-female; young-male; old-female; old-male), which were treated as multivariate traits. Expression evolution was modeled as a multivariate model using the R package l1ou (v1.43), which identifies branch-specific shifts in expression optima (θ) along a phylogeny. Conceptually, this approach compares evolutionary models with and without allowing changes in optimal expression levels on specific branches and determines whether introducing such shifts provides a better explanation of the observed expression patterns across species. Model comparison was performed using the Akaike Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc), a widely used metric that balances model fit and model complexity. A branch was inferred to have an expression shift when allowing a change in expression optimum on that branch resulted in a better-supported evolutionary model than one assuming a single expression optimum across the tree. We applied the l1ou framework following its standard assumptions (Khabbazian et al 2016), which uses the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process along a phylogenetic tree to provide functions to study trait evolution from comparative transcriptomics and detect past changes in the expected mean gene expression values. The strength of stabilizing selection (α) and the variance of the stochastic component (σ²) were assumed to be constant across branches, yielding a single global stationary variance (γ). Expression levels across four sex-age groups were modeled as correlated multivariate traits, with α and σ² estimated jointly. Shifts in expression optima were assumed to occur along the same branches across traits. All scripts for this project can be found at this link: https://github.com/ecr77/Defining_Ubiquitous_and_Sex- Biased_Aging_Biomarkers_Using_Transcriptional_Data_across_Evolutionar… E.C.R. curated publicly available RNA-seq datasets for four of the species, and performed the cross-species transcriptomic analyses to identify agDEGs. Y.F. contributed to RNA-seq dataset collection, data analysis discussions, bioinformatics pipeline construction and conducted the OU model analyses and result interpretation. C.K. collectedP. interpunctellasamples for RNA sequencing. R.P.M., J.W., T.G., G.W., E.L., A.W., P.R.B., N.C.R., and J.E.D. contributed to result interpretation and discussion. E.C.R. and Y.F. drafted the original manuscript and designed the figures under the supervision of J.E.D., P.R.B., and N.C.R. All authors involved reviewed, revised, and approved the final manuscript.
