title: Acute scalp EEG signatures of anterior thalamic DBS in epilepsy:reproducible gamma power enhancement within an aperiodic spectral-state shift
author: Sabbaghi, E.; Mattila, H.; Siitama, E.; Hyttinen, J.; Peltola, J.; Puthanmadam Subramaniyam, N.
text: BackgroundDeep brain stimulation (DBS) of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) is an established treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy, but acute scalp-EEG signatures of stimulation remain incompletely characterized. ObjectiveTo identify acute scalp-EEG signatures of ANT-DBS and assess their cross-year reproducibility in a proof-of-concept repeated-session cohort. MethodsScalp EEG from five patients recorded one year apart (10 sessions) was analyzed during nominal cyclic DBS (1 s ON, ~5 s OFF). DBS ON was compared with the within-cycle OFF mean and consecutive post-offset OFF windows using power spectral density (PSD), spatiotemporal–frequency (STF) analysis, and spectral parameterization. ResultsDBS ON showed higher 30–70 Hz gamma power than OFFmeanin all sessions (median +0.94 dB), with significant PSD clusters overlapping gamma in 10/10 sessions. STF identified gamma increases as the most reproducible spatiotemporal effect. Exploratory frontal 34–44 Hz and central 56–70 Hz components showed cross-year support, and the broader pattern persisted when 48–52 or 45–55 Hz were excluded before clustering. Lower-frequency effects were more heterogeneous and weakened from early to late OFF windows. Aperiodic parameterization showed lower ON exponent and offset in all sessions (ΔX= −0.20; Δb= −0.25). After correction, theta suppression was not preserved, whereas a smaller low-gamma residual remained. ConclusionsANT-DBS was associated with consistent acute scalp-EEG state signatures comprising raw gamma enhancement, lower aperiodic exponent and offset, and a modest residual low-gamma effect. These hypothesis-generating findings show that scalp EEG can capture acute ANT-DBS state changes, while larger prospective studies are needed to establish clinical relevance. Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) remains a major clinical challenge and is defined as failure of two tolerated and appropriately chosen antiseizure medication regimens to achieve sustained seizure freedom [1]. For patients who are not candidates for resection, or who continue to have disabling seizures after surgery, neuromodulation provides an evidence-based non-resective treatment option [2,3]. Among neuromodulation approaches, deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT-DBS) is particularly relevant for focal epilepsy because the ANT is a key node in limbic and thalamocortical circuits involved in seizure propagation and network regulation [4,5]. The SANTE trial, long-term follow-up studies, and subsequent registry data have shown sustained clinical benefit with an acceptable safety profile [6–10]. However, although ANT-DBS is clinically established, the acute neurophysiological effects detectable noninvasively at the scalp remain incompletely defined. Existing electrophysiological studies show that ANT-DBS modulates epileptic networks, but they leave important questions about acute scalp-EEG stimulation-state effects unresolved. Invasive recordings have linked high-frequency ANT stimulation to hippocampal desynchronization and decoupling of large-scale epileptic networks [11]. More recently, longitudinal intracranial ANT recordings over four years showed that responders developed a progressive shift toward higher-frequency activity, with increasing β1and gamma and decreasing delta and theta power relative to non-responders [12]. Other studies have focused on seizure monitoring and risk tracking [13], while recent reviews have considered biomarkers of longer-term DBS response [14]. Preclinical work has similarly reported reduced theta and increased gamma power [15]. Together, these studies support the view that ANT-DBS acts through distributed epileptic and thalamocortical networks, but they do not directly define reproducible acute scalp-level spectral signatures of the DBS ON state. Scalp EEG studies of ANT-DBS are fewer and have addressed related but distinct questions. Concurrent scalp EEG has linked effective cyclic ANT-DBS to temporal-lobe theta-band desynchronization and broader theta/alpha reductions in responders [16]. Retrospective EEG analyses have reported responder-associated decreases in beta- and gamma-band power together with reduced gamma-band phase synchronization [17]. More recently, time-locked scalp EEG analysis identified an offset-related event-related potential and corresponding limbic source activity during clinically delivered high-frequency ANT-DBS [18]. These studies indicate that scalp EEG can capture ANT-DBS-related effects. However, the immediate within-cycle spectral pattern during repeated cyclic stimulation remains insufficiently characterized. In particular, it is unclear which spectral changes are most reproducibly associated with DBS ON, which depend on the timing of the OFF reference window, and which remain stable across repeated recordings. A further methodological issue is that raw band-power changes may not reflect isolated oscillatory modulation. Shifts in aperiodic exponent or offset can reshape apparent theta, alpha, beta, or gamma power even when narrowband activity is not selectively changed [19,20]. This distinction is especially important in DBS–EEG because within-cycle ON–OFF contrasts occur close to stimulation transitions and may reflect both stimulation-linked changes during ON and rapid recovery after offset. Evidence that aperiodic activity is sensitive to stimulation state comes from subthalamic DBS, where the aperiodic exponent distinguished stimulation states, and from intracranial epilepsy recordings, where the exponent decreased after responsive stimulation [21,22]. Together with the longitudinal ANT-LFP findings, these studies suggest that stimulation-related spectral states may be expressed through both higher-frequency and aperiodic changes. To our knowledge, a noninvasive scalp-EEG counterpart that captures acute ANT-DBS effects while explicitly separating periodic and aperiodic contributions has not been reported. Concurrent DBS–EEG/MEG is also vulnerable to stimulation-related artifacts, making careful interpretation essential [23,24]. Therefore, acute ANT-DBS scalp EEG should be examined not only through raw band-power summaries, but also through analyses of post-offset timing, spatiotemporal reproducibility, and aperiodic spectral structure. To address this gap, we conducted a proof-of-concept study of scalp EEG from five ANT-DBS patients recorded twice, one year apart, allowing us to examine within-patient cross-year consistency. We asked which scalp-EEG changes were reproducibly associated with DBS ON, how these changes evolved across the first five seconds after stimulation offset, and how their interpretation changed after separating fitted aperiodic and residual band-limited spectral components. We combined frequency-resolved PSD analysis, sensor-level spatiotemporal–frequency analysis, and spectral parameterization to characterize acute stimulation-related spectral dynamics. Our aim was to identify and characterize acute scalp-EEG signatures of ANT-DBS, assess their cross-year reproducibility, and provide a framework for future source-level, connectivity-based, and prospective validation studies. We analyzed scalp EEG from five adults with drugresistant focal epilepsy treated with deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT-DBS) at Tampere University Hospital. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Pirkanmaa Hospital District (decision R17132; approved 19 September 2017). All participants provided written informed consent, identifiers were removed before analysis, and the study followed the Declaration of Helsinki [25]. Each patient was recorded in 2018 and 2019, yielding 10 patient-year sessions for within-patient cross-year assessment. The cohort was heterogeneous in age, epilepsy duration, etiology, and epileptogenic-zone distribution. The study characterized acute stimulation-state EEG effects rather than therapeutic efficacy. There was no randomization, blinding, or separate sham condition; within-cycle DBS OFF periods served as the physiological comparator. Clinical characteristics are summarized inTable 1, with stimulation-programming details in the Supplementary Material. Age and epilepsy duration are reported at each patient’s 2018 DBS–EEG recording. Epilepsy duration was calculated from age at the 2018 recording and age at epilepsy onset. The predominant seizure type was FIAS in all patients. M, male; F, female; CD, cortical dysplasia; FIAS, focal impaired awareness seizure. Recordings comprised repeated nominal 1 s ON / ~5 s OFF cycles. Each ON window was compared with five consecutive 1 s OFF windows (OFF1–OFF5) to characterize the DBS ON state and early post-offset dynamics (Fig. 1). The schematic shows the analyzed windows relative to stimulation offset (t0= 0). The ON window spanned −0.98 to 0.02 s. After a 120 ms guard interval, OFF1–OFF5covered 0.12–5.12 s. The next stimulation burst began after OFF5had ended. OFFmeandenotes the mean of OFF1–OFF5when at least 3 windows were valid. EEG acquisition followed Mattila et al. [18] using a 64-channel 10–10 cap. All patients had Medtronic Activa PC pulse generators and received voltage-controlled bilateral monopolar ANT stimulation at 5.0 V per side, 140 Hz, and 90 µs during nominal 1 s ON / 5 s OFF cycles for approximately 10 min. Settings were unchanged across years. This acute time-locked paradigm preserved the 1:5 duty ratio of conventional 1-min ON / 5-min OFF cycling while providing repeated transitions during a short recording; it was not intended to reproduce chronic therapeutic cycling. Leads and contacts were reconstructed in MNI space and visualized relative to the bilateral ANT labels from the DISTAL atlas using Lead-DBS v3 (Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Methods). This visualization was descriptive, and no quantitative spatial analysis was performed. Continuous EEG was visually screened, and bad channels were marked before 64-component InfoMax ICA was estimated in Brainstorm after resampling to 2 kHz [18,26]. Components reflecting ocular, small-amplitude muscle, or stimulation-related activity were removed by visual inspection of their time courses, scalp topographies, and the EEG distortion produced by their removal. The cleaned continuous data were retained at 2 kHz for cycle extraction. The source recordings had different prior filtering histories: the 2018 data had been filtered over 0.5–100 Hz, whereas the 2019 data had been filtered over 0.5–80 Hz with an additional 50-Hz notch. We therefore applied the same MNEspectrum_fit50-Hz notch to all sessions, rereferenced each 1-s window to the common average of channels valid for that cycle, restricted analyses to 4–70 Hz, and compared ON and OFF windows from the same cleaned recording. Each 7 s epoch was time-locked to stimulation offset (t0= 0). The ON window spanned −0.98 to 0.02 s, followed after a 120 ms guard by five consecutive 1 s OFF windows from 0.12 to 5.12 s. The next burst began at approximately 5.13 s. OFFmeanrequired at least three valid windows; further details are provided in the Supplementary Methods. Power spectral density (PSD) was estimated for each channel and window using multitaper DPSS methods over 4–70 Hz and expressed in dB [27]. Delta activity (< 4 Hz) was excluded because 1 s windows provide limited reliability at very low frequencies. Band summaries comprised theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), beta (12–30 Hz), and gamma (30–70 Hz) and were interpreted as broad spectral ranges because of the short windows and multitaper smoothing. Spatiotemporal–frequency (STF) representations were computed with complex Morlet wavelets from 4 to 70 Hz in 1 Hz steps [28]. The primary STF analysis retained the complete notch-cleaned frequency range. To assess dependence on the line-frequency neighborhood, cluster inference was repeated after excluding 48–52 Hz and, more conservatively, 45–55 Hz before cluster formation. Line-noise-robust gamma summaries used 30–44 and 56–70 Hz. Sensors were grouped into five macro-regions for visualization and descriptive ROI summaries, but these regions did not define the cluster-permutation tests. Spectra were parameterized withspecparamusing a fixed aperiodic model, log10P(f) =b−Xlog10(f), fit over 4– 70 Hz after interpolation across 49–51 Hz in log10-power space [19]. Models allowed up to six peaks (width 2–12 Hz; minimum height 0.05; threshold 2.0), and channel–cycle estimates required an aperiodic-lineR2≥ 0.20. Residual spectra were obtained after removing the fitted aperiodic component; further quality-control details are provided in the Supplementary Methods. Stimulation effects were estimated within each session using cycles as paired observations. PSD and aperiodic analyses used ON–OFFmeanas the primary contrast, whereas STF tested ON–OFF1through ON–OFF5separately. Two-sided sign-flip cluster tests used 5000 permutations [29–31]. Cluster-forming nodes required an uncorrectedp< 0.05 and at least 10 valid paired cycles for PSD and aperiodic-derived metrics or 8 for STF; sensor adjacency was defined by a 5-cm Euclidean distance. A shared maximum-cluster null controlled family-wise error across the five OFF references. Across sessions, sign replication, prevalence, and cross-year consistency were summarized descriptively; the 10 patient-year sessions were not treated as independent population-level observations. Full procedures are provided in the Supplementary Methods. Analyses were performed in Python 3.13.9 using MNE-Python 1.11.0 [32] andspecparam2.0.0rc7 [19]. We analyzed five ANT-DBS patients in two yearly sessions (2018/2019), yielding 10 patient-year sessions and 973 retained cycles (467 in 2018; 506 in 2019; 90–106 per session). Each cycle provided one ON and five OFF windows. PSD and aperiodic analyses used Δ = ON − OFFmean, whereas STF used separate ON–OFFkcontrasts. Session-wise QC yield is provided in the Supplementary Material. We first present raw spectral changes, then their spatiotemporal and cross-year reproducibility, and finally the fitted aperiodic and residual components. We first tested whether DBS ON was associated with consistent raw spectral-power changes relative to the withincycle OFF state. PSD analysis showed reduced low-frequency power and increased gamma-range power during DBS ON (Fig. 2). Across 4–70 Hz, the median ON–OFFmeancontrast crossed from negative to positive at approximately 24 Hz (Fig. 2A). The strongest median decrease occurred near 6 Hz (median Δ = −0.90 dB; negative in 8/10 sessions), whereas the strongest median increase occurred near 58 Hz (median Δ = +1.33 dB; positive in 10/10 sessions). Within-session channel-by-frequency cluster-permutation tests identified significant clusters overlapping gamma and beta frequencies in 10/10 sessions and theta and alpha frequencies in 8/10 sessions (Table 2). (A) PSD overlays for each annual session: DBS ON versus OFFmean. Curves show the median channel-mean PSD across retained cycles within each annual session; shaded bands indicate the interquartile range across cycles. (B) Band-limited changes Δ (ON−OFFmean) in 2018 and 2019. Points are patient-year/session mean Δ values; bars show the descriptive mean ± SEM across patients within each year. (C) OFF-window trend across OFF1–OFF5. Lines show the median Δk(ON−OFFk),k= 1, …, 5, across the 10 patient-year sessions; shaded bands show the interquartile range. (D) Patient-wise cross-year comparisons. For each band, dumbbells show each patient’s mean Δ in 2018 and 2019. OFFmeandenotes the within-cycle mean of OFF1–OFF5. In panels B and D, colors identify patients consistently across figures, while marker shape identifies recording year. At the band level, gamma was the most reproducible raw PSD effect (Table 2;Fig. 2B). It increased in all sessions (median Δ = +0.94 dB [IQR 0.73, 1.34]; year-replicated sign in 5/5 patients), with a median within-session paired effect size ofdz= 1.50, and remained positive after 5-cycle block averaging (median +0.96 dB [IQR 0.73, 1.33]). Theta, alpha, and beta generally showed negative raw ON–OFF differences, but their reproducibility was weaker. Beta had within-session cluster support in 10/10 sessions, whereas theta and alpha were more heterogeneous across patients and recording years. However, beta effects were smaller in magnitude and showed weaker cross-year sign replication than gamma; therefore, gamma was emphasized as the more reproducible raw spectral feature. We then examined whether ON–OFF effects depended on the timing of the OFF reference window. Low-frequency ON–OFFkdifferences were largest for early OFF windows and weakened toward OFF5(Fig. 2C), suggesting short-timescale post-offset dynamics rather than a fixed ON– OFF difference. This trend was clearest in alpha, followed by beta and theta, whereas gamma showed minimal OFF-window progression. Cross-year comparisons showed preserved gamma enhancement in every patient, while lower-frequency decreases were less consistent (Fig. 2D). Having established the raw PSD pattern, we next examined how the ON–OFF differences unfolded across time, frequency, and scalp location, and whether they were reproduced one year later. The patient-year STF maps showed a broadly similar organization across sessions: lower-frequency activity tended to decrease during DBS ON, whereas gammarange activity increased (Fig. 3A). This pattern became clearer at the cohort level, where the median and signconsistency maps identified gamma enhancement as the most consistent STF feature (Fig. 3B). Cross-year scalp maps showed positive support both below and above the line-noise neighborhood, at 30–44 and 56–70 Hz, while negative support was concentrated mainly at lower frequencies (Fig. 3C). When these two line-noise-safe gamma ranges were combined, the mean effect was positive in all 10 sessions and retained the same direction across years in all five patients. Theta effects were less consistent: they were negative in 9/10 sessions and reproduced across years in 4/5 patients (Fig. 3D). (A) Patient-year mean within-session STFt-statistic maps, averaged across sensors and ON–OFF1through ON–OFF5. Warm colors indicate ON>OFF and cool colors ON<OFF. (B) Cohort median effect and sign consistency across the 10 patient-year sessions. Sign consistency is the number of positive minus negative sessions at each frequency–time bin. (C) Scalp distribution of cross-year replicated signed support. Values are the fraction of patients with replicated ON>OFF support minus the fraction with replicated ON<OFF support; open circles mark sensors with |support|≥ 3/5. (D) Descriptive within-session summaries for gamma outside the conservative guard (30–44 and 56–70 Hz) and theta (4–8 Hz). Lines connect recording years within patients. All panels use the primary notch-only analysis; the lightly shaded 48–52 Hz interval marks the conventional line-noise neighborhood for display only. Atlas and cohort maps were smoothed for display only. OFF-reference analysis showed distinct temporal profiles (Fig. 4A,B). Gamma ON>OFF support outside 45– 55 Hz remained high across OFF1–OFF5(95.0–97.8%), whereas 4–15 Hz ON<OFF support fell from 67.3% to 27.5%. Thus, lower-frequency effects depended more on the post-offset reference, while gamma remained comparatively stable. (A) Region-level cross-year replicated signed support from the primary notch-only analysis. Warm colors indicate ON>OFF and cool colors ON<OFF. (B) OFF-reference sensitivity for gamma ON>OFF outside 45–55 Hz and low-frequency ON<OFF over 4–15 Hz. (C) Selected line-noise-safe gamma ROIs. Scalp maps show support collapsed across each fixed ROI, and rectangles show its frequency–time boundaries. ICC(3,1) values are descriptive cross-year consistency estimates calculated over the same fixed ROI in all five patients. (D) Temporal evolution of the selected ROIs. Open circles mark sensors meeting |support| ≥ 3/5. The lightly shaded 48–52 Hz interval is a display marker only. Guarded analyses were used as sensitivity tests and are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2. We next summarized the most reproducible gamma patterns as exploratory ROIs. These were derived from the primary notch-only analysis but constrained to frequencies outside the conservative line-noise neighborhood. The selected components were a frontal 34–44 Hz pattern extending from 0.05 to 0.95 s and a central 56–70 Hz pattern extending across the full 0.00–0.95 s window. Sign-level cross-year support reached 5/5 patients for both ROIs, whereas descriptive ICC(3,1) values were moderate (0.56 and 0.52, respectively;Table 3;Fig. 4C,D). Because these ROIs were selected from the same data used to assess their consistency, they should be interpreted as descriptive summaries rather than independent validation results. Candidates were constrained to 30–44 or 56–70 Hz. The frontal low-gamma and central high-gamma components were selected forFig. 4as the highest-ranked positive candidate in each interval. Finally, the line-noise sensitivity analyses closely reproduced the primary pattern. Excluding 48–52 or 45–55 Hz retained 99.5% and 98.8% of positive nodes in the common line-noise-safe gamma domain. Gamma support remained in 50/50 and 49/50 patient-year/OFF comparisons, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S2). Together, these findings support a broad gamma-range enhancement that extends below and above the 50-Hz neighborhood, rather than a narrow effect confined to frequencies immediately adjacent to line noise. Because raw PSD changes can reflect both band-limited and aperiodic components, we next separated fitted aperiodic changes from residual spectral effects. Both aperiodic parameters decreased in all 10 sessions (Fig. 5B,C;Table 4). The exponent decreased (median ΔX= −0.200 [IQR −0.272, −0.131]), indicating a flatter fitted spectrum, and the offset decreased (median Δb= −0.254 [IQR −0.301, −0.131] log10-power), indicating a lower fitted spectral intercept. Patient-year/session summaries (Npy= 10) describe DBS ON relative to OFFmean, reported as Δ = ON − OFFmean. (A) Observed ON–OFFmeanspectral change expressed in decibels as 10 ×Δ log10PSD(f), the change predicted from the fitted aperiodic exponent and offset, and the residual after subtraction of the aperiodic prediction. Observed and predicted contrasts used the same fit-qualified channel–cycle observations. Curves show the patient-year median and interquartile range on a common 1-Hz frequency grid. The 49–51 Hz region was excluded when calculating predictionR2. The dashed vertical line marks the median aperiodic pivot frequency, at which the predicted change crosses zero. PredictionR2is distinct from the fit-qualityR2used during spectral parameterization. (B,C) Paired OFFmeanand ON values for aperiodic exponent (B) and offset (C), with lines connecting conditions within each session. Offset is shown in log10-power units. (D) Raw and aperiodic-adjusted theta, low-gamma, and high-gamma changes. Bars show the median, error bars show the interquartile range, and markers show individual patient-year/session values. (E,F) Median sensor-level ON–OFFmeanchanges in exponent (E) and offset (F) across patient-year sessions. Separate color scales are shown because exponent and offset represent different quantities. In panels B–D, colors identify patients and marker shape identifies recording year. Paired exponent and offset changes were then used to predict the frequency-resolved ON–OFFmeancontrast. The predicted contrast captured a substantial but variable fraction of the observed spectral change (median predictionR2= 0.64 [IQR 0.50, 0.71];Fig. 5A) and crossed zero at a median pivot frequency of 14.1 Hz [IQR 10.8–18.3 Hz]. Aperiodic correction changed the band-level interpretation (Fig. 5D). Raw theta decreased (median −0.83 dB), but adjusted theta was modestly positive (+0.17 dB), arguing against selective suppression. Raw low- and high-gamma increased in all sessions (medians +0.91 and +1.07 dB), yet residuals were much smaller: low gamma remained modestly positive (+0.12 dB; 7/10 sessions), whereas high gamma was inconsistent (−0.05 dB; 4/10 sessions). Exponent and offset changes were spatially widespread (Fig. 5E,F). Thus, the raw low-frequency decrease and much of the gamma increase reflected a broader aperiodic spectral-state shift, with a smaller residual most evident in low gamma. In this repeated-session proof-of-concept study, DBS ON produced a reproducible acute scalp-EEG state shift: raw gamma power increased in every session, lower-frequency differences depended on post-offset timing, and aperiodic exponent and offset decreased consistently. After aperiodic correction, theta suppression was not preserved, whereas a smaller low-gamma residual remained. The central result is therefore gamma enhancement embedded within a broader change in spectral shape, rather than an isolated band-limited effect. These findings build on three lines of ANT-DBS literature: clinical studies establish therapeutic benefit but not acute scalp-EEG stimulation-state signatures [6–10]; invasive and network-level studies show modulation of hippocampal, thalamocortical, and broader epileptic networks, but rarely with repeated scalp EEG across yearly sessions [11,34–37]; and prior scalp EEG studies report theta desynchronization, altered synchronization, and offset-locked responses, but not clearly the roles of OFF-window timing and aperiodic spectral structure [16–18]. We address the remaining gap by combining repeated within-patient recordings, time-resolved ON–OFF comparisons, STF mapping, and separation of aperiodic from residual spectral components. The shortened stimulation paradigm was central to this design. The 1 s ON / 5 s OFF protocol was not intended to reproduce conventional 1 min ON / 5 min OFF therapeutic cycling [6–10]. Instead, it provided many repeated transitions within a short EEG session, enabling within-session ON–OFF comparisons and analysis of the first seconds after offset. The OFF-window analysis showed that this timing matters: low-frequency ON–OFF differences were strongest immediately after stimulation offset and weakened toward later OFF windows. The finding extends the offset-locked analysis of Mattila et al. [18] by showing that spectral effects evolve across the early post-offset interval. The low-frequency findings are consistent with previous evidence that theta and other low-frequency dynamics are relevant to ANT-DBS network physiology. Scherer et al. [16] reported temporal theta-band desynchronization during effective ANT-DBS, and Aiello et al. [35] showed that theta-band anterior thalamus–cortex interactions contribute to stimulation-related network dynamics. Invasive studies have also linked ANT stimulation to hippocampal and seizure-network modulation [11,34,36]. The present results support the relevance of low-frequency dynamics, but refine their scalp-EEG interpretation: raw theta/alpha/beta decreases were not stable isolated band-limited effects, because they depended on post-offset timing and were strongly reduced after aperiodic correction. Thus, these low-frequency changes are better understood as part of a broader stimulation-state transition with early post-offset recovery, rather than as stable selective theta or alpha suppression. The gamma-range finding fits the view of ANT-DBS as a network intervention and suggests that acute stimulation influences high-frequency activity detectable at the scalp. Gamma power increased during DBS ON in every session, with exploratory cross-year support for frontal low-gamma and central high-gamma patterns. A smaller low-gamma residual remained after aperiodic correction, indicating that the raw increase reflected both the broader spectral shift and a remaining band-limited component. This is biologically plausible because gamma activity has been linked to local circuit coordination and communication between neuronal populations [38,39]. However, gamma rhythms, broadband gamma, and high-gamma activity can have different physiological origins [40], so the residual effect should be viewed as a candidate scalp-level feature rather than evidence for a single neural generator. At first sight, our increase may seem different from reports of reduced beta/gamma power after chronic ANT-DBS and reduced 20–70 Hz activity during intraoperative stimulation [17,35]. However, those studies examined different timescales, recording settings, and comparators, whereas we captured repeated acute ON–OFF transitions within the same recordings. Longitudinal intracranial ANT recordings provide a complementary timescale: responders developed progressive increases in β1/gamma and decreases in delta/theta activity over several years [12]. Such context-dependent effects are consistent with reports of hippocampal and temporal-lobe desynchronization and reduced large-scale epileptic-network coupling during stimulation [11,16]. Further support comes from Liu et al. [41], who showed that ANT stimulation increased hippocampal gamma power and improved working-memory precision. Together, these observations support context-dependent ANT-DBS network effects rather than a direct contradiction between studies. Because our analysis was sensor-level, however, we cannot determine whether the residual low-gamma effect reflects cortical generators, thalamocortical interactions, hippocampal– anterior thalamic circuits, or mixed neural and non-neural sources. The aperiodic results changed how the raw band-power effects were interpreted. Spectral parameterization showed that much of the apparent low-frequency decrease and gamma increase reflected a broader change in spectral shape: DBS ON consistently lowered the fitted aperiodic exponent and offset, and the aperiodic-predicted contrast reproduced a substantial portion of the frequency-dependent shape of the raw ON–OFF spectrum. Apparent low-frequency suppression may therefore partly reflect a flatter spectral background rather than selective theta or alpha suppression, illustrating the value of separating aperiodic background activity from periodic peaks [19]. A lower exponent may be consistent with a relative shift toward excitation [20,42,43], while recent neuromodulation studies show that aperiodic activity varies with DBS state and relates to seizure state or treatment response [21,22,44]. However, the slope– E/I relationship is context-dependent and not universally supported [45,46]; sensor-level changes may also reflect firing dynamics, synaptic or membrane time constants, and spatial mixing. We therefore interpret the lower exponent conservatively as an acute spectral-state feature rather than a direct measure of cortical E/I balance. Artifact-related explanations require explicit consideration because active DBS–EEG is susceptible to stimulation artifacts, line noise, and cranial muscle activity [23,24,47]. We therefore evaluated the gamma finding using three convergent robustness checks. First, continuous EEG was cleaned before cycle extraction, and ON and OFF windows were drawn from the same cleaned recording within each patient-year, ensuring matched recording and preprocessing histories. Second, the 140-Hz carrier and its integer harmonics were outside the analyzed 4–70 Hz range, while excluding 48–52 or 45–55 Hz retained 99.5% and 98.8% of significant positive STF nodes, respectively. Third, gamma support extended across a broad frequency range, showed spatial, temporal, and cross-year consistency, and a smaller low-gamma residual remained after aperiodic correction. This residual does not, by itself, establish a neural origin. Together, these checks argue against the stimulation carrier or narrowband 50-Hz contamination as sufficient explanations for the effect. They cannot exclude aliasing, spectral broadening, broadband muscle activity, or other stimulation-related contamination; source-level and dedicated artifact-focused validation therefore remain necessary. The clinical relevance of this study is methodological and hypothesis-generating. Reproducible gamma enhancement may provide a noninvasive readout of acute stimulation-state engagement, while OFF-window dependence shows that reference timing can change ON–OFF interpretation. Aperiodic correction further shows that raw band power may overstate selective oscillatory effects. These points are relevant for future EEG-DBS studies comparing stimulation parameters, evaluating target-network engagement, and relating acute EEG responses to longer-term clinical outcomes. The present data do not establish clinical-response, cognitive, or outcome biomarkers, but define measurable acute EEG features that can be tested in those future contexts. Several limitations define the next validation steps. The cohort was small (n= 5; four male and one female), limiting population-level inference and precluding sex-stratified analyses. No sham condition was included, and the within-cycle OFF windows were post-offset physiological comparators rather than an independent stimulation-free base-line. These constraints should be considered alongside the depth of this longitudinal clinical DBS–EEG dataset: 10 sessions recorded one year apart under unchanged stimulation programming, yielding 973 retained stimulation cycles. The repeated within-patient design supports cross-year consistency but does not replace independent validation. Repeated cycles may also have been temporally dependent, although the main PSD direction was preserved after cycle-block averaging. The analyses were sensor-level, so effects cannot be localized directly to ANT, hippocampal, cortical, or thalamocortical sources. The short 1 s windows limit low-frequency spectral resolution, and band-power and aperiodic estimates should be interpreted as short-window spectral-shape descriptions. Although stimulation contacts were anatomically localized relative to ANT, the small sample did not allow separation of the contributions of contact location, patient-specific anatomy, and seizure-network organization. Because all recordings used the same nominal bilateral voltage amplitude, amplitude-dependent effects could not be evaluated. Future studies should include head-model-based source localization, connectivity analysis, larger prospective cohorts, and clinical or cognitive follow-up to test behavioral or outcome relevance. Across five ANT-DBS patients recorded at two time points, PSD, STF, and spectral-parameterization analyses identified reproducible acute scalp-EEG stimulation-state signatures. DBS ON was associated with increased raw gamma-range power and lower fitted aperiodic exponent and offset. STF showed cross-year frontal 34–44 Hz and central 56–70 Hz support. After aperiodic correction, a modest low-gamma residual remained, whereas low-frequency suppression was not preserved and depended on OFF-window timing. Overall, these findings suggest that gammarange enhancement occurred within a broader stimulation-related spectral-state shift and define candidate acute EEG signatures for future source-level, connectivity-based, and prospective validation studies. title: Semaglutide Increases Striatal Leptin Sensitivity, Impacting Dopaminergic Response to Cocaine
author: Muldowney, J. J.; Umlauf, M. C.; Bocarsly, M. E.
text: There is accumulating evidence that the GLP-1 analog, semaglutide, might effectively curb intake of cocaine via brain dopaminergic functioning, despite limited brain penetrance. However, there is currently no established mechanism elucidating how chronic semaglutide treatment regulates the dopaminergic response to cocaine. Cocaine is a highly addictive substance that produces rewarding effects primarily through antagonism of the dopamine transporter (DAT). Therapeutics for cocaine use disorder (CUD) have long targeted DAT in the hope of reducing cocaine intake. Metabolic hormones such as leptin and insulin have been shown to influence DAT, and for that reason have been explored for the regulation of cocaine reward and behavior. Interestingly, while semaglutide does not penetrate the brain, it does peripherally modulate metabolic hormones that enter the brain. Through fast-scan cyclic voltammetry and behavioral experimentation, we examined the effects of chronic semaglutide treatment on dopamine signaling, cocaine-induced dopamine release, and locomotor sensitivity. We determined that chronic semaglutide inhibits dopaminergic reward induced by cocaine. Surprisingly, semaglutide’s effects on cocaine reward were blunted in mice fasted overnight, suggesting a mechanistic dependence on metabolic hormones. Semaglutide administration generated significant reductions in fasting blood leptin, as well as enhanced striatal leptin sensitivity compared to vehicle controls. Preceding cocaine exposure, application of leptin to fasted mice restored semaglutide’s regulation of cocaine. Our results exhibit a potential mechanism for semaglutide-induced cocaine reward inhibition, emphasizing the potential of central leptin signaling as a therapeutic target for CUD. Nearly 50 million Americans suffer from a substance use disorder, with 5 million reported users of cocaine and 1.3 million patients of cocaine use disorder [1]. Interestingly, there is accumulating evidence that GLP-1 analogs, initially marketed for diabetes and weight loss, might also work to curb intake of substances, including cocaine [23]. However, the mechanism of action is unknown. Research on the blood-brain penetrant glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist exendin-4 and exenatide exhibits their ability to alter the reward system [24-26]. Studies have shown these analogs effectively reduce self-administration of cocaine, cocaine-induced locomotion, cocaine conditioned place preference, and cocaine-induced evoked dopamine in rodents [26-28]. Despite these findings, exenatide did not significantly decrease cocaine self-administration in CUD patients [29]. The development of a more potent GLP-1RA, semaglutide, has reinitiated the examination of GLP-1 analogs for CUD treatment. Chronic semaglutide treatment causes significant metabolic changes, such as a reduction in fasting blood leptin concentration in obese and lean models [30]. Though semaglutide demonstrates very limited CNS access compared to previous analogs [31-34], with no evidence of reaching deeper midbrain regions such as the striatum, new findings reveal modified dopamine dynamics and reward behavior. Despite its inability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier, acute semaglutide treatment increases dopamine release in the striatum during food reward while reducing eating behavior [35]. Further, chronic and acute semaglutide administration reduces alcohol intake and relapse behavior in male and female rats through regulating alcohol-induced dopamine release [36]. A case study on an obese patient receiving semaglutide treatment for weight loss detailed a substantial decline in cocaine craving [37]. Recently, acute semaglutide administration was shown to decrease cocaine self-administration and cocaine-induced dopamine signaling through microdialysis and fiber photometry [38]. Currently, there is no established mechanism elucidating how chronic semaglutide treatment regulates the dopaminergic response to cocaine, especially with limited brain penetrance. Cocaine’s addictive properties can be attributed to its affinity for the dopamine transporter (DAT), blocking synaptic reuptake of dopamine [2-4]. Modulators of DAT functionality and models of altered striatal DAT expression emphasize the potential of DAT as a therapeutic target for CUD [5-10]. With the discovery of metabolic hormones’ influence on dopamine release and reuptake [11-13], the signaling pathways of insulin, leptin, and GLP-1 have been explored for the regulation of cocaine reward and behavior [13-19]. Further, semaglutide is known to affect peripheral hormone levels of insulin and leptin, which do effectively cross the blood-brain barrier. This led us to hypothesize that semaglutide could exert its overall effects on striatal dopamine function through its modulation of peripheral hormones such as insulin and leptin. In this study, we examined the effects of chronic semaglutide treatment on dopamine signaling, as well as semaglutide’s control over cocaine-induced dopamine release and locomotive behavior. We further investigated the mechanism of cocaine response regulation through evaluating the necessity of leptin signaling, emphasizing the potential of central leptin signaling as a therapeutic target for CUD. Adult C57BL/6J male mice (JAX, 12-20 weeks) were group housed in ventilated cages (Nexgen System, Allentown Inc., PA, USA) with controlled temperature, humidity, and light (21 ± 2 °C, humidity 60 ± 10 %, 12:12 h light/dark cycle) with free access to food and water, unless specified. Mice were randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups: semaglutide (Novo Nordisk; 40 μg/kg s.c.) or vehicle (0.4% DMSO in saline (0.9% NaCl), 10 mL/kg, s.c.). Injections were given every three days for five weeks. Mice were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane, decapitated, and brains were rapidly harvested and placed in warm cutting solution (in mM): 225 sucrose, 13.9 NaCl, 26.2 NaHCO3, 1 NaH2PO4, 1.25 glucose, 2.5 KCl, 0.1 CaCl2, 4.9 MgCl2, and 3 kynurenic acid. Coronal brain slices were made using a vibratome (230 μm) in warm cutting solution. Brain sections containing dorsomedial striatum or the nucleus accumbens were allowed to recover in oxygenated ACSF containing (in mM): 124 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 2.5 CaCl2,1.3MgCl2, 26.2 NaHCO3, 1 NaH2PO4, and 20 glucose (∼310-315 mOsm) at 33°C for 30-60 min and maintained at room temperature until recording. Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry was performed in the dorsomedial striatum of semaglutide and vehicle-treated mice to determine levels of evoked dopamine. Carbon fibers (7μm diameter) were inserted into glass pipettes to create carbon fiber electrodes (CFEs), which were hand-cut to expose ∼150μm of the fiber past the pipette tip. Before use, CFEs were backfilled with 3M KCl internal solution. CFEs were conditioned before recordings with a triangular voltage ramp (−0.4 to 1.2 and back to -0.4V versus Ag/AgCl reference at 400V/s) delivered every 15ms. During recordings, CFEs were held at -0.4V versus Ag/AgCl while the same triangular voltage ramp was delivered every 100ms. Dopamine transients were evoked by a single pulse (0.2ms) of electrical stimulation administered every 2 minutes by a glass micropipette filled with ACSF that was placed near the CFE tip. To generate input-output curves, the intensity of electrical stimulations was varied (10, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 150, 200, or 300µA) with each episode. Experiments were conducted in ACSF and maintained at 31-33ºC. In a subset of experiments, slices were treated with semaglutide (Medex, GLP-1 receptor agonist, 100 nM), GBR12909 (Cell Signaling, DAT inhibitor, 5µM), ML375 (Millipore Sigma, muscarinic receptor 5 antagonist, 10µM), Dihydro-β-erythroidine hydrobromide (DhβE) (Tocris, nAchR inhibitor, 1µM), cocaine hydrochloride (Cayman Chemical, 1 µM and 10 µM), porcine insulin (Medex Biochemica, 100nm), or recombinant mouse leptin (R&D Systems, 100nM), all in aCSF. Data were acquired and analyzed using a Chem-Clamp amplifier (Dagan) and I/O board (National Instruments) with custom-written software VIGOR using Igor Pro (Wavemetrics) running mafPC (courtesy of M.A. Xu-Friedman). All data were analyzed with VIGOR and peak current amplitude of dopamine was converted to concentrations according to the post-experimental calibration. Locomotion testing was conducted in the light cycle either in a fasted (16 hours) or fed state, as indicated in the data. Mice were transferred to the experimental room and allowed to habituate for 30 minutes, then transferred into polycarbonate chambers (20 cm H x 17 cm W x 28 cm D) equipped with infrared photobeam detectors (Columbus Instruments). Baseline locomotion was recorded for 1 hour, and 1.5 hours for leptin. On days 1-3, fed mice were then treated with saline (10 mL/kg, i.p.), and locomotor activity was collected for an additional hour. On days 4 and 5, instead of saline, mice received either the DAT inhibitor GBR12909 (i.p., 1, 10 mg/kg, each day respectively), cocaine (i.p. 10 mg/kg), or the D1-like agonist SKF-81297 (i.p., 5, 7.5 mg/kg). Mice used for fasted locomotion experiments received saline in a fed state (for habituation to injections and handling) on days 1 and 2, then saline in a fasted state on days 3 and 5. Drugs were administered to fasted mice on days 7 and 9. Data was extracted and analyzed using IGOR Pro (64-bit). Mice were euthanized using isoflurane and dorsal striatum samples were taken. Samples were flash frozen and stored at −80°C. Each tissue sample was lysed in 150 μL of RIPA buffer with protease inhibitor (Thermoscientific 89901), homogenized by a hand homogenizer, and then sonicated for 15 minutes. Protein was estimated using a Pierce BCA protein assay (Thermofisher 23225) at a 1:5 dilution. 20 µg of protein from each sample was boiled for 7 minutes at 95 degrees Celsius in loading buffer. Samples were loaded onto TGX stain-free mini gels (Bio-Rad) and run at 100 V for ∼2 h. Gels were transferred to a 0.2 µm nitrocellulose membrane using the Bio-Rad Trans-Blot Turbo at 2.5 amps, 25 V for 6 min. Ponceau staining was utilized to determine equal protein loading across wells. Membranes were blocked in 1% BSA in tris-buffered saline solution with tween (TBST) for one hour at room temperature with rapid shaking. Primary antibodies (listed inTable 1) were diluted in TBST and incubated at 4°C with gentle shaking. Following primary incubation, membranes were rinsed with TBST 3×for 10 min with shaking and then incubated with secondary HRP (Gt, Thermo Fisher, 18-4818-82, 1:5000 or Rb, Thermo Fisher, NA9340V, 1:5000) in 1% BSA in TBST for 2 hours at room temperature with gentle shaking, followed by 3×rinses with TBST for 10 min each. To develop, membranes were covered in ECL (GE Healthcare, 17030484) for 2 min and imaged using chemiluminescence on the Chemi-doc imaging system. In addition to using the stain-free feature to ensure equal loading, actin was used as a loading control. For blots in which multiple proteins were detected from a single membrane, membranes were stripped between hybridizations with a stripping buffer consisting of 20 mL 10% SDS and 12.5 mL of Tris HCl, pH 6.5, with 0.8% beta-mercaptoethanol added immediately prior to stripping. Membranes were placed in stripping buffer for 15 min shaking at room temperature. Membranes were moved to TBST and rinsed 3×for 10 min each. Membranes were re-imaged to ensure adequate stripping before re-blocking. Primary and secondary incubations were repeated as described. Band intensity was quantified using the Image Lab software (Bio-Rad). Mice were fasted (16 hours), and tissue was collected. Blood glucose was determined via tail blood using a handheld glucometer (Contour Next One). Trunk blood was collected in non-heparinized capillary tubes, centrifuged at room temperature and serum was collected. Serum concentrations of leptin (EZML-82K, Millipore), insulin (#90080, Crystal Chem), and adiponectin (#80569, Crystal Chem) were determined via commercially available ELISAs. Fat pads were dissected bilaterally and weighed; eWAT was slightly cranial to the epididymis. Analyses were performed in Prism 10 (GraphPad). Data making three or more comparisons were analyzed using two-way ANOVA, with the addition of repeated-measures (RM) or a mixed-effects model, as appropriate (ex. voltammetry input/output curves and time courses, locomotor behavior, etc.). For RM-ANOVA, sphericity was assessed with Mauchly’s test. Significant main effects or interactions were followed up with pairwise tests corrected for multiple comparisons (Sidak or Tukey). Linear mixed effects models were utilized when multiple tissue slices from a single animal were examined. Data comparing two groups (ex. blood analysis, protein levels, etc. between treatment groups) were analyzed with an unpaired Student’s t-test. Mann-Whitney tests were run when comparing groups that failed the Shapiro-Wilk test for normality. One-sample t-test was used to determine deviations from the mean or baseline. Results were considered significant at an alpha ≤ 0.05. All data are presented as mean ± SEM, and individual animal data are shown whenever possible. Full statistics are presented in the figure legends. Sample sizes were chosen based on previous research employing similar approaches and are sufficient for detecting effects while using the minimal number of animals. FSCV experiments with drug applications were normalized to steady-state baseline values preceding drug introduction to the well. Locomotor experiments were normalized to the group average locomotion during saline control trials preceding drug injection days. To model clinical, chronic use of semaglutide, mice were injected with semaglutide (40 µg/kg, s.c.) every 3 days for five weeks [30,45,46]. The control group received vehicle injections on the same schedule. Following treatment, sensitivity to an acute dose of cocaine (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was tested using locomotor response (Figure 1A). While no differences were seen in locomotion in response to a novel environment (Supplementary Figure 1A) or following a saline injection (Supplementary Figure 1B), mice previously treated with semaglutide showed a blunted locomotor response to cocaine compared to vehicle-treated controls (Figure 1B). Because diminished locomotor responses to cocaine suggest alterations in striatal dopamine transmission [47], we assessed striatal dopamine release capacity. Following semaglutide or vehicle treatment,we used ex vivo fast-scan cyclic voltammetry to measure dopamine signals evoked by electrical stimulation in striatal tissue. We focused our recordings on the DMS given its distinct dopamine dynamics and established roles in cocaine seeking, value-guided action selection, and behavioral flexibility [39-44, 48-50]. We found that mice previously treated with semaglutide had a blunted dopaminergic response to cocaine (1 µM) compared to controls (Figure 1D,E). Interestingly, the decay of the dopamine signals, as determined by the decay time constant tau, was significantly faster in mice treated with semaglutide compared to controls (Figure 1F). Across all mice, we observed a correlation in evoked dopamine release and cocaine-induced inhibition of dopamine (Figure 1G), emphasizing the role of dopamine reuptake for regulating the dopaminergic response to cocaine. (A)Schematic demonstrating injection protocol and experimental design.(B)Average locomotor counts in cocaine-injected (10 mg/kg) mice over 60-minute trial, normalized to group-average saline control trial (t(15)=2.22, p=0.04, n = 8-9 mice/group, unpaired t-test).(C)Schematic of recording site: coronal mouse brain slice, with dorsomedial striatum highlighted in red.(D)Time course of evoked dopamine in response to cocaine (1 µM) application, normalized to steady-state baseline values (interaction effect: F(24,552) = 9.92, p < 0.0001; main effect of semaglutide treatment: F(1,23) = 10.61, p = 0.004; main effect of drug application: F(1.39, 31.95) = 115.4, p < 0.0001, n = 12-13 slices/3 mice/group, RM two-way ANOVA).(E) Left:Representative 3D voltammograms showing background-subtracted current (false color scale) as a function of time (x axis) and voltage applied (y axis).Right:(top) representative CV plots of the electrochemical current (background-subtracted) evoked by electrical stimulation in the DMS showing the characteristic current peaks at 0.6 V and –0.2 V that match the oxidation and reduction potentials for dopamine. (bottom) Representative traces of dopamine signals from the DMS of mice previously treated with vehicle (black) or semaglutide (red).(F)Time course of tau values with cocaine application (1 µM), normalized to steady-state baseline values (Interaction effect: F(24,474) = 2.56, p < 0.0001; main effect of semaglutide treatment: F(1,20) = 7.05, p = 0.02; main effect of drug application: F(24,474) = 44.62, p < 0.0001, n = 10-12 slices/3 mice/group, mixed-effects analysis).(G)Positive correlation between normalized dopamine and normalized tau following cocaine (1 µM) application (R2= 0.47, p = 0.0005, n = 22 slices/6 mice, simple linear regression). Data is presented as mean ± SEM; symbols are individual sample data. For all panels, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01. As cocaine predominantly has its actions on dopamine via blocking the dopamine transporter (DAT), preventing dopamine from being cleared [51], we evaluated the effects of the DAT inhibitor, GBR-12909 (1 mg/kg, i.p.), on locomotor output following chronic semaglutide or vehicle treatment. The semaglutide-treated mice demonstrated a diminished response to DAT inhibition compared to vehicle controls (Supplementary Figure 1D,E), mimicking the response to cocaine. Expression and phosphorylation of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting step in dopamine production, were quantified through Western blotting and showed no changes following semaglutide treatment compared to vehicle controls (Supplementary Figure 2A). Given no changes in this dopamine synthesis parameter, to better understand how semaglutide alters cocaine-mediated dopamine release, we looked into modulators of dopamine reuptake and locomotor behavior. Previous research has shown that the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 5 (M5) present on dopamine neuronal synapses regulates dopamine release and reuptake [52,53], possibly contributing to the dopaminergic response to cocaine [54,55]. Semaglutide caused no significant alteration in M5 expression (Supplementary Figure 2B) nor evoked dopamine and reuptake in response to inhibition (Supplementary Figure 2C,D). Additionally, prior studies have shown how the D1 receptor can regulate the behavioral response to cocaine [56]. We used multiple doses of SKF-12987, a D1-like receptor agonist, to assess locomotive responses and determined no differences between groups (Supplementary Figure 2E). These experiments suggest that M5 and D1 signaling are not significant for semaglutide’s control of the cocaine response. Evaluation of baseline evoked dopamine in the absence of cocaine could grant insight into how semaglutide alters cocaine-mediated dopamine release. Interestingly, we found that evoked dopamine was elevated in mice chronically treated with semaglutide compared to vehicle (Figure 2A,B). This was accompanied by a decreased decay time constant tau (Figure 2C), indicating faster clearance of the dopamine from the synapse. In a complementary study, we determined the mean amplitude of dopamine signals evoked by electrical stimulation of increasing intensities in the dorsomedial striatum of mice chronically treated with semaglutide or vehicle (Figure 2D). This experiment replicated our previous finding, with semaglutide-treated mice showing elevated levels of evoked dopamine compared to controls. (A)Schematic demonstrating injection protocol and experimental design.(B)Average nanomolar concentration of evoked dopamine signals at 200uA stimulation in the DMS following chronic semaglutide or chronic vehicle treatment per mouse (t(15)=4.53, p = 0.0004, n = slices X/8-10 mice/group, unpaired t-test).(C)Corresponding values of the decay constant tau compared between semaglutide and vehicle treatment (t(15)=2.26, p = 0.04, n = 8-9 mice/group, unpaired t-test).(D)Evoked dopamine concentrations at varying stimulation currents in the DMS of mice chronically treated with either vehicle or semaglutide (Interaction effect: F(7,175) = 2.57, p = 0.02; main effect of semaglutide treatment: F(1,25) = 4.63, p = 0.04; main effect of current: F(1.54,38.44) = 72.65, p < 0.0001, n = 12-15 slices/3 mice/group, RM two-way ANOVA).(E)Evoked dopamine concentration following incubation in 100 nM semaglutide, normalized to a steady-state baseline concentration (t(7)=1.67, p = 0.14, n = 8 slices/3 mice, one sample t-test). Data is presented as mean ± SEM; symbols are individual sample data. For all panels, *p < 0.05, ***p < 0.001. Again, using ex vivo FSCV, when a 100 nM concentration of semaglutide was applied directly onto brain slices containing the dorsal striatum, no changes in dopamine were detected (Figure 2E). In correspondence with previous research displaying semaglutide’s limited penetration across the blood-brain barrier, this shows that semaglutide is not working locally in the dorsal striatum to affect dopamine levels [31-34]. Because the brain pharmacokinetics do not align well with their behavioral effects, it remains unclear how this drug is influencing central reward processing in deeply buried brain structures like the striatum. Further experimentation revealed that the effect of semaglutide on cocaine-evoked dopamine release depended on metabolic state. As described above, mice received semaglutide or vehicle for five weeks. Prior to ex vivo FSCV, mice were fasted for 16 hours (Figure 3A). Following a 16-hour fast, cocaine-evoked dopamine release and decay time constant tau were comparable between semaglutide- and vehicle-treated mice (Figure 3B,C). Moreover, there was no significant correlation of cocaine-induced inhibition of dopamine reuptake with evoked dopamine released in each slice (Supplementary Figure 3A). Consistent with these findings, when injected with cocaine (10 mg/kg), semaglutide- and vehicle-treated mice showed similar locomotor phenotypes (Figure 3D). trend toward increased cocaine-evoked dopamine release in the fasted state (Figure 3E). However, the difference in the cocaine-induced dopamine response was much more pronounced in animals in the fasted and fed states following chronic semaglutide (Figure 3F). Consistent with these findings, cocaine administration produced a trend toward increased locomotor activity in fasted compared with fed control mice. This effect was more pronounced in semaglutide-treated mice, with fasted animals exhibiting greater cocaine-induced locomotor activity than their fed counterparts (Figure 3G). Data is presented as mean ± SEM; symbols are individual sample data. For all panels, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001. When we replicated this study, replacing cocaine with the DAT inhibitor, GBR-12909 (1 mg/kg, i.p.), locomotor and evoked dopamine were likewise normalized across semaglutide and vehicle-treated groups following an overnight fast (Figure 3H,I). It is important to note that while fasting abolished the dopaminergic and locomotor effects of chronic semaglutide, baseline evoked dopamine was still elevated in semaglutide-treated mice compared to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 3J-L). Together, these findings suggest that fasting may attenuate the effects of chronic semaglutide treatment on cocaine-evoked dopamine signaling and prompted us to investigate the metabolic factors that differ between fed and fasted states. Although the metabolic effects of semaglutide treatment are well characterized in obese mice, its effects in lean mice remain less well understood. One study reported that chronic semaglutide administration alters circulating leptin levels and fat accumulation in lean mice [30]. Here, we found that chronic semaglutide treatment had no effect on body weight in lean mice (Figure 4A). Likewise, fasting blood glucose and insulin levels were not statistically different between treatment groups (Figure 4B,C). However, we did find semaglutide-induced reductions in fasting leptin concentrations (Figure 3D), similar to the previous study. As leptin is proportionally secreted to the mass of adipose tissue and predominantly regulated by visceral fat in male mice [57], epididymal white adipose tissue (eWAT) was extracted from semaglutide and vehicle-injected mice and subsequently measured to determine the ratio of fat weight to total body weight. This resulted in a decrease in the ratio in semaglutide-treated mice compared to vehicle controls (Figure 3E). We also looked at fasting blood adiponectin levels. Like leptin, adiponectin is an adipokine secreted by adipose tissue; however, circulating adiponectin levels generally vary inversely with leptin levels [58]. In the current study, while adiponectin was trending upwards following semaglutide treatment, it was not statistically significant (Figure 4F). While the reduction in peripheral leptin is not surprising because it is consistent with previous findings following semaglutide treatment [30], it identified a potential mechanistic link between peripheral metabolic changes and striatal dopamine signaling, as leptin crosses the blood–brain barrier and modulates dopamine function in the striatum [12,53]. This led to investigating leptin’s potential significance in cocaine regulation following semaglutide treatment. Again, mice were chronically treated with semaglutide or vehicle, fasted overnight to normalize and minimize leptin levels across mice, and locomotor activity was recorded following an acute injection of leptin (Figure 5A). The literature suggests that central leptin activation following an i.p. injection occurs approximately 30 minutes after peripheral injection [59] and lasts for as long as 3 hours [12], leading us to use the last 60 minutes of the 90-minute trials for analysis. Leptin injections resulted in a significantly increased locomotor response from semaglutide-treated mice compared to vehicle controls (Figure 5B). Further investigation of the underlying dopaminergic state was conducted using FSCV. Following the application of a 100 nM leptin solution, the evoked dopamine response was greater in semaglutide-treated mice compared to vehicle controls (Figure 5C). Data is presented as mean ± SEM; symbols are individual sample data. For all panels, *p < 0.05, ****p < 0.0001. Importantly, the current findings are specific to leptin and not all peripheral hormones in general. Previous research has shown that insulin regulates dopamine release in the striatum in the same fashion as leptin [60], and it has also been investigated for regulating addiction [14]. However, when insulin was applied to brain slices from mice chronically treated with semaglutide or vehicle, no changes in the dopaminergic response were observed (Supplementary Figure 4A). Leptin influences striatal dopamine release through two distinct mechanisms: activation of cholinergic interneurons (CIN) to increase local dopaminergic release (as depicted inFigure 5D) and actions directly on the dopaminergic neurons (not shown). CIN depolarization from leptin generates acetylcholine release, subsequently binding to nicotinic receptors on dopamine neurons to increase dopaminergic firing [59]. In parallel, leptin directly influences dopaminergic neurons by elevating DAT activity [12]. With leptin application in our FSCV experiments, along with elevations in evoked dopamine concentration, the semaglutide-treated mice exhibited a significant increase in the decay constant tau (Figure 5E). This can be attributed to the expected rise in acetylcholine from leptin application, which increases dopamine release, particularly in semaglutide-treated mice. To assess leptin-induced dopamine reuptake alterations, we sought to uncouple the local CIN-regulated dopamine release and the effects of leptin on DAT functionality. To do this, we applied the nicotinic receptor antagonist, DhβE, to block the CIN contributions before the addition of leptin during FSCV. Tau values were assessed as a readout of dopamine clearance, showing that in the presence of DhβE and leptin, semaglutide-treated mice showed a significant reduction in tau, whereas vehicle-treated controls did not (Figure 5F). This demonstrates that when CIN-mediated release of dopamine is taken offline, we can clearly see semaglutide’s effects on leptin’s regulation of dopamine reuptake, which we hypothesize reflects a semaglutide-induced increase in DAT activity. We next aimed to determine the relationship between leptin and cocaine in semaglutide-treated mice. Mice that had been chronically administered either semaglutide or vehicle were fasted overnight, then given a peripheral injection of leptin, followed by cocaine, in order to assess leptin’s inhibition of cocaine-induced locomotion (Figure 6A). Locomotor activity following cocaine was normalized to locomotor response following leptin. Semaglutide-treated mice demonstrated a stark reduction in locomotion compared to controls (Figure 6B), which resembled the locomotor response to cocaine observed in a fed-state (Figure 1C). Again, we looked at evoked dopamine in the dorsal striatum of fasted mice chronically treated with either semaglutide or vehicle, this time applying leptin to the bath preceding cocaine. We found that mice previously treated with semaglutide show less evoked dopamine and increased dopamine reuptake compared to vehicle-treated mice (Figure 6C,D). Data is presented as mean ± SEM; symbols are individual sample data. For all panels, *p < 0.05, ****p < 0.0001. When we plotted the evoked dopamine following leptin vs. leptin and cocaine, the mice chronically treated with vehicle and fasted overnight showed a robust increase in cocaine-induced striatal dopamine compared to leptin-induced striatal dopamine alone (Figure 6E). However, mice chronically treated with semaglutide and fasted overnight showed no difference in evoked dopamine with leptin vs. leptin and cocaine bath applications (Figure 6F). This data demonstrates leptin’s restoration of semaglutide-induced regulation of cocaine in fasted mice, indicating the significance of leptin’s role in the mechanism. In control mice, there was no difference in dopamine reuptake following leptin or leptin and cocaine, while semaglutide-treated mice showed slower dopamine reuptake kinetics following leptin and cocaine vs. leptin alone (Figure 6G,H). Together, these data suggest that leptin’s contribution to diminishing the cocaine response in semaglutide treatment is DAT-mediated. Expanding on prior research demonstrating GLP-1 receptor agonists are effective in reducing cocaine use, our work provides novel insight into how chronic semaglutide reduces the rewarding effects of cocaine. Similar to recent findings on acute semaglutide administration [38], following chronic semaglutide, we demonstrate a reduction in the dopaminergic response to cocaine without inducing sedation effects. This study offers the first mechanistic insight into semaglutide’s inhibition of the dopaminergic and behavioral response to cocaine. DAT has been a proposed therapeutic target for CUD due to cocaine’s strong binding affinity, inducing reward signaling through dopamine reuptake antagonism [5-8]. Here, we show that chronic semaglutide caused a significant reduction in the dopamine released from cocaine through decreased inhibition of dopamine reuptake, aligned with previous research [61,62]. Additional work has utilized DAT overexpression models to show that increased basal reuptake generated a decreased dopaminergic response to cocaine [63]. Some studies have suggested that increased striatal dopamine reuptake velocity may produce conditions more susceptible to cocaine inhibition, generating an elevated reward response and motivational state for cocaine [64,65]. Despite heightened dopamine reuptake capability in baseline conditions, our semaglutide-treated mice displayed resistance to cocaine in FSCV and behavioral experiments. We propose that this phenomenon may be attributed to dependence on the contributions of striatal leptin’s regulation of DAT, as seen through the loss of semaglutide efficacy for cocaine regulation in a fasted state. Our findings reiterate the significance of DAT as a therapeutic target, propose a potential mechanism for GLP-1 receptor agonists’ regulation of addiction in leptin, and strengthen semaglutide’s case as a potential treatment option for chronic cocaine use. In this study, we found that overnight fasting nullified the beneficial effects of semaglutide on cocaine despite long-term administration. By evaluating alterations in satiety hormones known to modulate the cocaine response, we determined leptin as a candidate for mediating semaglutide-induced inhibition of cocaine. We were able to replicate the finding of reduced fasting leptin concentrations in the periphery and decreased visceral fat in lean mice chronically treated with semaglutide [30]. In our FSCV and behavioral experiments, we also observed semaglutide-induced striatal leptin sensitivity for the regulation of dopamine release, reuptake, and locomotion. Leptin is known to generate a significant increase in dopamine release in the striatum through CIN activation, as well as an increase in dopamine reuptake by binding to its receptor present on dopaminergic neurons in the DMS [59]. Through application of DhβE, we isolated leptin signaling in dopaminergic neurons to observe the expected increase in dopamine reuptake upon leptin receptor activation. The reduction of tau in response to activation supports our hypothesis that leptin boosts reuptake of dopamine in semaglutide-treated mice. This effect may be driving semaglutide’s control over cocaine, as demonstrated by leptin rescuing the restriction in the cocaine response of fasted animals. In our locomotion and FSCV experiments, mice given chronic semaglutide show particularly diminished responses to cocaine when pretreated with leptin after fasting overnight. As semaglutide has been shown to decrease visceral fat and fasting blood leptin concentrations in addition to increasing leptin sensitivity in the hypothalamus of obese models [46], we suspect that repeating these experiments in mice maintained on a high-fat diet would produce similar results. In some models, obesity causes increased sensitization to cocaine [21]. It is likely that semaglutide’s effects on dopamine and leptin during cocaine use would translate to a patient population with a range of body weights. Previous research has demonstrated the significance of leptin for both DAT and cocaine regulation, as well as other markers downstream of leptin receptor activation. Specifically, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation produces DAT phosphorylation at Thr53, causing translocation to the synaptic cleft in which dopamine reuptake increases [66]. Importantly, ERK signaling facilitates leptin signal propagation within the striatum [67]. Investigating ERK as a target for increased DAT translocation to reduce the dopamine response to cocaine may lead to insight into how to directly influence striatal reward signaling in CUD patients. Additionally, the leptin signaling pathway leads to the inhibition of GSK3β, known to manipulate DAT trafficking [68]and cocaine sensitivity and behaviors [22,69,70]. Further exploration into the distinct molecular mechanisms generating leptin-induced cocaine insensitivity through semaglutide treatment could reveal the significant mediators of GLP-1’s reward regulation. A common concern of the use of an anorexigenic drug for cocaine use disorder is the often observed reduction in fat mass and leptin in models and patients [71-74]. A study tracking the eating habits, weight, and leptin concentration of cocaine use disorder patients determined an increase in food intake with cocaine dependency despite weight loss and a trend in decreased leptin levels [75]. This confounding finding may be caused by elevated sympathetic nervous system activation from cocaine [76] that can reduce leptin secretion [77]. Self-administration of cocaine reduced glp-1 levels in rodents [78], and infusion of cocaine reduced GLP-1 levels in chronic users [79]. Peripheral GLP-1R activation was shown to reduce sympathetic nerve activity [80], adding to its potential for cocaine regulation and leptin signaling restoration in chronic users. It is also possible that GLP-1 treatment in cocaine use disorder may restore leptin production and signaling through its action on adipocytes [81]. Additionally, semaglutide may regulate substantial weight gain often seen in cessation of chronic cocaine use [82]. It would be of high importance to carefully monitor eating behaviors and leptin levels of CUD patients administered semaglutide. Importantly, semaglutide may also act on hindbrain GLP-1Rs to indirectly modulate striatal function [83]. In support of this, previous research has demonstrated that GLP-1R expressing neurons in the nucleus tractus solitarius regulate cocaine seeking [78]. Our findings do not exclude contributions from hindbrain circuits, which may also be shaped by leptin-dependent or -independent mechanisms [84], a topic which requires future study. Our findings are limited to male mice, but evidence supports testing this mechanism in females: female heterozygous DAT-knockout rats show increased locomotor sensitivity to cocaine [62], exogenous leptin reduces cocaine intake and accelerates extinction in female rats [20], and semaglutide lowers circulating leptin in female mice [85], consistent with our findings in males. We focused FSCV experiments on the dorsal striatum, where dopamine reuptake [39,50] and its enhancement by leptin [59] are greater. Although this region contributes to cocaine-motivated behaviors and is altered in cocaine use disorder, future studies will examine semaglutide’s effects on cocaine and leptin sensitivity in the ventral striatum. Cocaine self-administration studies will assess relevance to chronic use, while striatal leptin receptor antagonism or knockdown will test whether leptin signaling is necessary for semaglutide’s effects.
