All data utilised in this study were obtained from the Harvard Electroencephalography Database version 4.1 (HEEDB) [35], which aggregates clinical recordings from four medical centres: Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH), Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH), Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Centre (BIDMC), and Boston Children’s Hospital (BCH). While MGH and BWH provide more raw EEG files, many are short outpatient recordings with higher noise levels and sparse labels. These are less suitable for training deep learning models. In contrast, the BIDMC cohort predominantly features 24-hour continuous EEG (cEEG) recordings, providing prolonged observation windows and a higher density of localised spike and seizure labels that are essential for model training. This study focuses on the BIDMC cohort. This single-site selection, while ensuring annotation density and recording standardisation, may introduce site-specific biases in patient demographics and referral patterns; the external validation on the BCH cohort is designed to provide preliminary evidence of cross-institutional generalisability. To select the target clinical cohorts, we implemented a two-stage screening process consisting of automated lexical scoring followed by manual expert-report verification. A customised natural language processing (NLP) script was used to parse the official clinical reports authored by epileptologists. Patient sessions were quantitatively evaluated using a weighted rule-based grading matrix: High-Relevance Indicators (+2 points): Explicit positive descriptors signalling localised or active ictal events, such as “focal”, “electrographic seizure”, and “clinical seizure”, were assigned a weight of +2 per occurrence. Moderate-Relevance Indicators (+1 point): General epileptiform findings, including “discharge”, were assigned +1 point. Exclusionary Modifiers (-1 or -2 points): Negative qualifiers demonstrating the absence of relevant activity (e.g., “no electrographic seizure”) resulted in a deduction of 1 or 2 points to mitigate false positives from keyword matching. Sessions achieving scores above a predefined threshold (2) were selected for the next stage, 3874 reports passed the lexical selection. Following lexical scoring, a manual audit of the candidate clinical reports was conducted by reviewing the expert clinical summary for each session. For each report, we extracted: Seizure onset side: documented as left, right, or bilateral (bilateral excluded) Seizure onset lobe: documented as frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital, or combinations (e.g., temporo-parietal) Semiology concordance: whether clinical seizure semiology matched the electrographic onset. Based on these clinical descriptions, each session was assigned a six-region multi-label ground-truth vector according to the anatomical mapping defined inSection 1.1. For example, a report stating “seizure onset in the left temporal lobe with propagation to the left parietal region” was labelled as [0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0] - where the ‘1’ indicates the left temporo-parietal region (R3). Sessions with documented bilateral onset, ambiguous localisation, or lacking a clear SOZ in the final report were excluded for this proof-of-principle study. All data utilised in this study were obtained from the Harvard Electroencephalography Database version 4.1 (HEEDB), a publicly accessible repository that aggregates de-identified clinical EEG recordings from four partner institutions: Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH), Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH), Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Centre (BIDMC), and Boston Children’s Hospital (BCH). EEG recordings vary in channel layout. We standardised all recordings by: (1) removing non-EEG channels (e.g., oxygen saturation, pulse rate); and (2) applying a consistent spatial referencing scheme. We applied band-pass filtering (0.3–70 Hz) to remove slow drifts and high-frequency noise, plus a notch filter at 60 Hz to remove electrical interference from power lines [36]. Automated epileptiform labels (spikes and seizures) were parsed from CSV files generated by the Persyst software. There was a small time offset between the EEG signal and the Persyst annotation file. We corrected this by aligning both to the “start recording” marker. To remove non-epileptiform behavioural or environmental markers logged during the session, a vocabulary exclusion filter was applied. Irrelevant textual descriptions, such as ocular movements (“eyes open/closed”), physiological artefacts (“chewing”, “movement”), and operational event logs (“montage review”, “video fault”), were removed to isolate objective spike and seizure annotations. Using these spike and seizure markers as temporal anchors (t=0), the continuous streams were segmented into 16-second windows (from −8.0 seconds to +8.0 seconds). We did not perform manual verification of individual windows, as this was infeasible at the scale of our dataset; instead, use an NLP filter to exclude artefact-contaminated segments, reducing false positives. Moreover, our spatial ground-truth labels derive solely from the final expert clinical reports, not from Persyst confidence scores. Recordings had different sampling rates (256 Hz, 512 Hz, or 1024 Hz). We resampled all windows to 256 Hz, giving each window 4,096 time steps (16 seconds × 256 Hz). Spatial or temporal boundary variations were resolved via centralised trimming or symmetrical zero-padding, ensuring a uniform tensor shape of 18 × 4096 across all windows. The standardised segments were serialised into binary PyTorch tensors. Implementation details of the parallel processing pipeline are provided in Appendix B. To ensure signal integrity and avoid mathematical instabilities during training, an automated data-cleaning and quality-control protocol was applied to all extracted EEG segments (standardised shape 1 × 18 × 4096). Infinite values were converted to NaN. A two-tiered quality control protocol was applied: segments exceeding either a maximum consecutive NaN threshold or a global missing ratio threshold were discarded. For remaining segments, missing values were imputed per channel using 1D linear interpolation, with nearest-neighbour extrapolation at sequence boundaries. The full set of rejection thresholds and interpolation parameters is provided in Appendix B. Following serialisation and quality control, the verified .pt segments underwent a digital signal processing (DSP) pipeline to remove transient high-frequency noise and normalise amplitude scales before model training. Temporal Baseline Correction: We applied temporal baseline correction to mitigate low-frequency drift and baseline wander caused by slow movement or electrode-tissue polarisation. The initial 100-time steps of each segment were designated as the reference window, and its localised channel-wise mean was subtracted from the entire sequence to realign the signal’s electrical baseline to zero [37]. To suppress high-frequency muscle artefacts and line noise without attenuating neural spikes, a discrete wavelet transform denoiser was applied. Each channel was decomposed into four levels using the Daubechies 4 (db4) mother wavelet, with adaptive universal thresholding (VisuShrink) [38]. Soft-thresholding was applied to detail coefficients across all scales, and the signal was reconstructed via inverse DWT. Detailed parameter settings are provided in Appendix C. Spatial Re-referencing (Common Average Reference): To eliminate residual environmental common-mode noise remaining after the initial bipolar montage, a Common Average Reference (CAR) filter was applied spatially. The instantaneous mean voltage across all 18 channels was calculated and subtracted from each channel.[38] Z-Score Standardisation and Incremental Logging: Finally, to optimise numerical stability and ensure stable gradient flow during training, channel-wise Z-score standardisation was executed, scaling each channel sequence to possess zero mean and unit variance. Interictal events occur at very different time scales: brief spikes (20–70 ms), longer sharp waves (70–200 ms), and slow-wave rhythms (4–12 Hz, lasting hundreds of milliseconds). A single fixed-size detector cannot capture all of these. Our MultiScaleConvBlock uses four parallel convolutions with different kernel sizes to detect events at all these scales simultaneously. We introduce a parallelised multi-receptive-field front-end, the MultiScale Temporal Scanning Block (MultiScaleConvBlock). This module processes the input through four independent 1D-convolutional pathways with distinct kernel sizes:At 256 Hz sampling rate, kernel sizes of 16 and 32 correspond to corresponding to receptive fields of 62.5 ms and 125 ms, which cover the 20–70 ms duration of brief spikes. The larger kernels (64 and 128) extend to 250 ms and 500 ms, encompassing the longer sharp-wave and slow-wave complexes (70–200 ms) that frequently follow interictal spikes. The micro-scale branches (ks=16,32) are designed for sharp spike contours, while the macro-scale branches (ks=64,128) target sustained slow-wave rhythms. These branches jointly capture multi-scale temporal features for downstream modules. Let the input segment be denoted as X ∈ RB×1×C×T, where B signifies the batch size, C = 18 represents the number of bipolar channels (num_electrodes), and T indicates the discrete temporal sequence length (chunk_size). Within the MultiScaleConvBlock, the input tensor passes through a bank of parallel 2D convolutions (nn.ModuleList)with kernels constrained to (1, ks) for k ∈ {16, 32, 64, 128}. This restricts early feature extraction to channel-isolated temporal filtering, preserving the spatial dimension for later fusion. Symmetric padding of k//2 is applied to maintain temporal length across branches. Each branch produces an intermediate feature map of depth F1=8. These are concatenated along the channel dimension:followed by Group Batch Normalisation and ELU activation. To fuse cross-channel spatial information without the quadratic parameter growth of standard 2D convolutions, we apply a depthwise spatial convolution (self.depthwise). This operator uses a kernel of size (C,1) with groups equal to the input feature depth F1×∣K∣=32, thus pooling across all 18 spatial channels independently per feature layer. An output multiplier D=2 yields an amplified depth:A second Batch Normalisation and ELU activation follow. Subsequently, the tensor is passed through four sequential 2D average-pooling layers with kernel (1,2) and stride (1,2), compressing the temporal dimension by a factor of 24: T to T’ = T // 16 (T’_prime = 128). Finally, x.squeeze(2) removes the singleton spatial dimension, producing the regularised spatiotemporal token tensor: Unlike invasive sEEG with high SNR, scalp EEG suffers from severe volume conduction and spatial smearing, where a single cortical source projects diffusely across multiple channels. In standard Transformers, flattening time (T) and space (H) into a single sequence forces the attention matrix to model cross-products between temporally distant samples and spatially distant channels simultaneously. This is computationally prohibitive, O((H × T)2), and conflates temporal phase shifts with spatial topography. That is, the model cannot distinguish whether a signal arrived 20 ms later or originated from a different electrode, yet these scenarios have entirely different clinical implications. Our factorisation explicitly disentangles these two physical entities, allowing temporal attention to model waveform evolution and spatial attention to model inter-channel propagation independently To enforce strict geometric factorisation, the proposed network splits the tensor Xout into two parallel, decoupled embedding paths using distinct linear projection layers (self.time_proj and self.chan_proj). Spatial Channel Path Projection(self.chan_proj): Concurrently, the tensor is processed along its spatial coordinate, treating the H channels as the sequence length. A linear layer projects the downsampled temporal steps T’ into the same latent dimension:This dual-path projective embedding maps the raw data into two symmetrical matrices, allowing the downstream encoders to process pure, unmixed temporal dynamics and pure spatial topology independently. This projection maps the raw EEG into two separate representations: one encoding temporal waveform evolution, the other encoding spatial electrode topography. We inject asynchronous positional encodings tailored to each branch. Because time and space have fundamentally different physical meanings in EEG, time is sequential and causal, while space is discrete and topological, we introduce an Asynchronous Positional Encoding mechanism customised for each branch: Sinusoidal Temporal Encoding (self.temporal_pos): The temporal path contains strict sequential constraints (i.e., the chronosynchronous flow of the spike waveform). Thus, a deterministic, non-trainable sinusoidal positional matrix Psin ∈ R1×max_len×128is added to Xtime: Learnable Spatial Channel Encoding(self.channel_pos): Conversely, the spatial pathway maps discrete channels across the 10–20 grid. Since these channels lack a natural linear order, we use a fully trainable parameter tensor Pchan ∈ R1×1×128is initialised and added via broadcast mechanisms to Xchan:Following coordinate alignment, the matrices are routed into their respective isolated Transformer Encoders (self.temporal_encoder and self.channel_encoder). Each encoder block is configured with a depth of num_layers=2 and utilises num_heads=4 parallel attention heads. The feedforward network multiplier is set to dim_feedforward = hidden_dim × 4 = 512, employing Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) activations and a regularisation dropout of 0.3 (EEGNetEnhanced) to prevent over-parametrisation. The final critical operation of the FactorizedTransformer block is the reconciliation of these decoupled time and space embeddings into a singular, unified diagnostic representation. Because the pathways possess different sequence lengths (T’=128 vs. H=64), they cannot be directly fused via element-wise addition or matrix multiplication. To address this dimensional mismatch, we fuse the two pathways via low-rank consensus. The temporal feature matrix emerging from the encoder, Ztime ∈ RB×T’×128, undergoes a global temporal reduction pooling along its sequence axis (dim=1):This global average pooling compresses the temporal sequence into a fixed-length summary vector that preserves waveform morphology while discarding phase shifts. Finally, this global temporal token is broadcast across the spatial sequence axis and added directly to the spatial output matrix Zchan ∈ RB×H×128coming out of the channel encoder:This broadcast fusion scheme establishes a powerful, low-rank additive synthesis. The unified output tensor Xfused overlays the global temporal morphology of the spike onto the localised cross-channel spatial connectivity weights. To ablate the factorised design, we implemented two single-axis Transformer variants that share the identical front-end (MultiScaleConvBlock) but differ in the back-end aggregation. Variant A replaces the factorised dual encoders with a single Transformer that processes time only (no separate spatial pathway). Variant B makes the same single-axis design deeper (6 layers, 12 heads) to test whether increased model capacity alone can match the factorised design. Given that the downstream task is formulated as a six-class multi-label classification problem (where each anatomical region is independently predicted as either involved or not involved in the seizure onset network), the choice of the loss function and the incorporation of domain-specific anatomical priors are critical for stable convergence and clinical reliability. As shown inFigure 5, the label distribution is imbalanced, with common temporo-parietal regions and rare occipital regions (∼10%). This poses a training challenge because pure occipital labels are scarce and mostly appear in complex, noisy multifocal epilepsy cases, hindering model adaptation. Furthermore, signals from the deeper parts of the occipital lobe do not always project clearly to standard surface electrodes [40], which exacerbates classification difficulty. Consequently, during early training, the model tends to exploit easier, more frequent regions as a shortcut to achieve a high score. To mitigate this class imbalance without resorting to computationally expensive resampling, we adopt the Multilabel Focal Loss mechanism [41]. Unlike BCE, Focal Loss introduces a dynamic scaling factor (1−pt)γto its standard cross-entropy formulation:Where N is the batch size, c ∈ {1…,6} indexes the six anatomical regions, p i,c is the model’s predicted probability for sample i and region c, γ=2.0 is the focusing parameter, and αc is the class-specific positive weight (α=3.0 for occipital regions, 1.0 otherwise). In our implementation, the focusing parameter is set to γ=2.0. Additionally, to counteract the extreme scarcity of occipital lobe samples, we apply a positive weight factor of α=3.0 to the occipital regions during loss computation, while keeping α=1.0 for all other anatomical regions Where pi,cdenotes the model’s predicted probability for the i-th sample and the c-th region, and γ(set to 2.0 in our implementation) serves as a focusing parameter. For well-classified, high-confidence samples, (1−pt)γ→ 0, effectively down-weighting their contribution to the loss. Conversely, for hard-to-classify or rare samples where pt is small, the scaling factor approaches 1, preserving the full gradient magnitude. These mathematical priors force the network to allocate more representational capacity to the challenging occipital and frontal polar regions, drastically improving the recall rate for low-prevalence focal epilepsies. While we apply a hard hemispheric constraint at inference time (seeSection 2.10.4), we additionally introduce a soft hemispheric penalty during training. This dual approach ensures that (i) the model learns to suppress cross-hemispheric false positives during gradient updates (L_hemi), and (ii) the final output strictly respects unilateral anatomy via post-processing thresholding. The soft penalty during training is critical because it guides the network’s internal representations toward physiologically plausible solutions before the hard constraint is applied at test time. Although the model processes each window independently as a multi-label task, allowing multiple regions within the same hemisphere to be simultaneously active, consistent with the spatial propagation of interictal discharges, the hemisphere-level penalty enforces unilateral focus at the loss level, aligning with the clinical definition of focal epilepsy. This hybrid formulation preserves within-hemisphere multi-regional discriminability while penalising cross-hemisphere confusion. To forcibly align the network’s spatial attention with this clinical ground truth, we introduce a novel Hemispheric Mutual Exclusivity Penalty (L_hemi) that is directly injected into the optimisation objective. Let the sigmoid-activated probability vector be denoted as p ∈ R6. We define the maximum activated probability for the left and right hemispheres as:The penalty term is then formulated as the product of these two maxima:This penalty is minimised (to zero) only when one hemisphere’s maximum probability is zero, aligning with the clinical axiom of unilateral focal epilepsy; it peaks when the model confidently predicts bilateral activity, which is anatomically impossible. Minimising this product during training repulses the probability landscapes of the two hemispheres, guiding the network toward physiologically plausible solutions. The penalty is weighted by λ = 0.1, determined via grid search over {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5} on the validation set. During inference, after the hemispheric penalty term has guided the network toward unilateral spatial focus during training, we apply a hard anatomical decision rule at the session level. For each continuous recording session, the per-window probability vectors are first averaged to obtain a session-level probabilityp∈ R6. The hemisphere with the higher maximum probability is selected as the putative seizure onset side, and the probabilities of all three regions in the opposite hemisphere are forced to zero:Finally, A fixed binarisation threshold τ = 0.5 (the natural decision boundary of the sigmoid output) is applied to the retained probabilities to produce the final multi-label prediction:This two-stage decision pipeline, side selection followed by region-level thresholding, ensures that the final output strictly respects the clinical axiom of unilateral focal epilepsy while maintaining fine-grained regional discriminability. The final combined loss function for end-to-end training integrates the discriminative power of the Focal Loss with the anatomical prior of the Hemispheric Penalty, weighted by a scalar hyperparameter λ:The implementation details of this loss function (including the grid search for λ) are described in Appendix A. To reduce variance from stochastic training dynamics without incurring the inference-time cost of conventional ensembles, we adopt uniform weight averaging (model soup) following Wortsman et al. [42]. For each architecture, we train three independent variants differing only in random seed and mini-batch order. Because these variants converge to proximate regions of the loss landscape, their parameter vectors can be averaged element-wise without performance degradation. Let {θ1,θ2,θ3} denote the checkpoints of the three runs; the fused model is obtained as:This yields one fused model per seed family. Specifically, we fuse three M1 variants (seeds 100, 101, 102), one M2 variant (seed 42), and one M3 variant (seed 43), totalling five models for the final heterogeneous ensemble. This hierarchical approach eliminates the need to run multiple M1 variants separately at test time while preserving the benefits of multi-run consolidation. Specifically, after the initial training converges, we apply a light fine-tuning stage with three distinct Gaussian noise injection levels (as detailed in the supplementary figure) to the gradients, generating three perturbed checkpoints per converged model. These perturbed weights are then averaged to form the final fused model, further smoothing the loss landscape and improving out-of-distribution robustness. While weight averaging consolidates models sharing the same backbone, ensembling structurally distinct models offers complementary inductive biases. Our empirical analysis (Section 3.1) reveals a dissociation: while SOZNet achieves higher global Exact Match, model 1showssuperior recall on the rare occipital class at the single-model level. Occipital spikes are characterised by brief, low-amplitude transients that may be better captured by content-based retrieval, whereas temporo-parietal propagation benefits from explicit spatiotemporal factorisation. Aggregating these structurally distinct models therefore reduces both bias and variance by covering neurophysiological regimes that no single architecture captures equally well. The ensemble thus reduces both bias (via architectural diversity) and variance (via soft voting), yielding a more stable and generalisable decision boundary. We trained five independent copies of each architecture variant (M1, M2, M3) with different random seeds to select the final ensemble members from the candidate pool. In total, we obtained 15 candidate models. Then we performed an exhaustive search over all non-empty subsets of these 15 candidates on the validation set, with a cardinality cap of five, to maximise exact match rate and recall. Our final ensemble comprises five constituent models: Three M1 variants (seeds 100, 101, 102), each obtained via the model soup procedure described previously. These share the same architecture but diverge due to different random initialisations and fine-tuning trajectories. One M2 model (seed 42), fused from its three fine-tuned variants. One M3 model (seed 43), fused from its three fine-tuned variants. This composition balances intra-architecture consolidation (three M1 models capture training stochasticity) with inter-architecture diversity (M2 and M3 introduce distinct structural priors). At inference time, each constituent model independently processes the same input EEG window X ∈ R18×2048and produces a six-dimensional probability vector p(m) = σ(z(m)) ∈ R6, where σ(⋅) denotes the sigmoid function applied elementwise to the raw logits z(m). The ensemble prediction is obtained via soft voting, i.e., arithmetic averaging of the probability vectors:We used soft voting to preserve confidence information. This is particularly critical for scalp EEG, where low-SNR windows produce low-confidence probabilities; soft voting naturally attenuates overconfident but potentially spurious predictions from individual models. All experiments were implemented in PyTorch and executed on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPU. Models were trained for 30 epochs using the AdamW optimiser (initial learning rate 1 × 10−4, weight decay 1 × 10−4) with a warmup-cosine annealing learning rate schedule. Early stopping with a patience of 20 epochs was applied based on validation exact-match accuracy; the checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy was retained for final evaluation. Full hyperparameter details are provided in Appendix A. A two-stage learning rate schedule was applied to stabilise early training and facilitate fine convergence: Warmup phase (5 epochs): A linear warmup scheduler (LinearLR) increased the learning rate from 1 × 10−6(1% of the initial LR) to 1 × 10−4over the first 5 epochs. Cosine annealing phase (remaining epochs): Following warmup, a CosineAnnealingLR scheduler decayed the learning rate from 1 × 10−4to a minimum of 5 × 10−5over the remaining E − 5 epochs, where the total number of epochs E = 30 (config.EPOCHS). Early stopping with a patience of 20 epochs (config.PATIENCE) was applied based on validation exact-match accuracy; the checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy was retained for final evaluation. The total training time for the largest variant (M3) was approximately 18 hours on the 80-patient training set. Notably, SOZNet achieves this performance with only 0.8M trainable parameters, which is substantially smaller than the 11M-parameter M3, confirming that the factorised design, rather than raw parameter count, drives the performance gain. Baseline models (EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet, TSCeption) were re-implemented from their original public codebases [18,19,43] and trained under the identical data split and hyperparameter tuning protocol as SOZNet (Appendix A). No task-specific modifications were made to these architectures to preserve a fair comparison. Window-level: Each 8-second EEG chunk (18×2048-time steps) was fed independently into the model. The six sigmoid outputs were thresholded at 0.3 (as used in the training code’s preds = (torch.sigmoid(logits) > 0.3).float()) to produce a multi-label prediction for that window. This threshold was chosen empirically to balance precision and recall during early validation. The lower window-level threshold (0.3) compensates for single-window noise. At the session level, averaging across hundreds of windows attenuates transient artefacts, allowing a more conservative threshold of 0.5 without sacrificing sensitivity. Session-level: For each continuous recording session, the per-window probability vectors were averaged over all windows belonging to that session. The hemisphere with the higher maximum average probability was selected as the putative seizure onset side; probabilities in the opposite hemisphere were set to zero, and a threshold of 0.5 (config.SESSION_PROB_THRESHOLD) was applied to the remaining three regions to produce the final multi-label prediction. This post-processing step mimics clinical decision-making, where a full session’s worth of data is aggregated. We reported the following metrics for both window- and session-level predictions: Precision, Recall, and F1-Score: Computed per region (macro-averaged across the six labels) using precision_recall_fscore_support (sklearn) with average=’binary’ per region and zero_division=0. Exact Match Ratio (EM Rate): The proportion of samples (windows or sessions) for which all six predicted labels exactly matched the ground-truth labels, calculated via accuracy_score(sklearn). Hamming Loss: The fraction of incorrect label predictions, reported for completeness at the session level. For each architecture variant, three independent runs were conducted with different random seeds (42, 43, 100, 101, 102). All random seeds were fixed using set_seed() in the training script, covering Python’s random, NumPy, and PyTorch’s CUDA random generators. The best-performing checkpoint (by validation EM rate) was saved for each seed; these checkpoints were subsequently fused via weight averaging (model soup) and then used in the heterogeneous ensemble. Five key findings emerge from our experiments. First, the ensemble achieved 88.46% session-level Exact Match on the internal test set, outperforming all generic EEG baselines (≤50%) and the best single model (80.77%). Second, systematic ablations confirmed that the factorised spatiotemporal design, rather than model capacity, drove performance, with the full augmentation pipeline contributing a +2.66 p.p. macro-F1 gain and model soup recovering the best single-model performance without inference-time cost. Third, performance generalised robustly across three clinically realistic scenarios: annotation-sparse holdout (82.76% EM), cross-institutional paediatric data (84.62% EM), and mixed with unlabelled random windows (66.67% EM on single model M1). Fourth, mechanistic interpretability was supported by case-level trajectory analysis tracking expert summaries, and by zero false positives on 108 healthy controls. Finally, the entire 24-hour recording pipeline completed in 4.26 minutes, with inference under 8 seconds. Each finding is expanded in the subsections that follow. Finally, we benchmarked the end-to-end processing pipeline on a full 24-hour continuous unlabelled EDF recording across three sampling rates. The total execution time was 4.26 minutes at 256 Hz, 7.26 minutes at 512 Hz, and 10.76 minutes at 1024 Hz (Figure 16). Execution profiling revealed that data ingestion and signal harmonisation (including EDF parsing, filtering, and resampling) consumed over 82% of the total runtime. In contrast, deep learning model inference required less than 8 seconds under all tested configurations, indicating that neural network computation is not the primary performance bottleneck of the pipeline. For context, a 24-hour EEG recording typically requires 60–120 minutes of expert visual review to identify and annotate epileptiform events [18]. The current pipeline’s 4.26-minute processing time represents a 14-to 28-fold acceleration over manual review, even in the unlabelled scenario where no spike timestamps are available. This comparison is not intended to suggest replacement of clinical expertise but to quantify the potential for workflow triage in high-volume epilepsy centres: a tool that can process an overnight recording before the morning ward round could flag high-probability cases for early expert review. Our results suggest a broader point: the spatial information needed for SOZ localisation survives the spatial blurring of volume conduction, provided the model respects EEG’s physical structure. That is, temporal dynamics and spatial propagation should be processed through separate pathways, with anatomical priors explicitly encoded in the loss function. Three observations support this interpretation. First, the factorised architecture (M1, 0.8M parameters) matched the performance of a much deeper single-axis variant (M3, 11M), indicating that architectural inductive bias matters more than raw capacity. Second, the hemispheric penalty reduced anatomically implausible bilateral predictions without harming within-hemisphere discriminability. Third, the model’s zero false-positive rate on healthy controls suggests it learned propagation dynamics rather than simple waveform templates -a point we return to below. With this framing, we turn to the detailed findings. The ensemble model achieved 88.46% session-level exact match (EM) on the internal test set, much higher than all baseline models (≤50%). Single lightweight Model 1 maintained 66.67% EM on random windows with a non-spike labelling setting. The ensemble model also produced zero false positives on 108 healthy controls, and processed a full 24-hour recording in 4.26 minutes. These results indicate that routine scalp EEG can provide lobar SOZ localisation, extending prior evidence from invasive [46] and high-density [47] recordings to the low-density, low-SNR clinical setting. Standard baseline architectures rely primarily on localised convolutional layers with fixed receptive fields. Deep variants such as DeepConvNet stack layers to capture abstract representations, but successive downsampling sacrifices fine temporal resolution and fails to preserve transient paroxysmal features such as brief spikes (20–70 ms). EEGNet is shallow but lacks the capacity to bridge long-range temporal dependencies. Our architecture combines parallel multi-scale convolutions with subsequent Transformer layers. The multi-scale convolutions preserve both frequency components and sharp transients, while the self-attention mechanism enables non-local temporal modelling without loss of structural resolution. Within this framework, the smaller Model 1 (0.7M) performed similar with the deeper Models 2 (3M) and Model 3 (11M), providing insights into spatiotemporal regularisation. Models 2 and 3 use standard Transformer encoders on an unflattened spatiotemporal grid, incurring quadratic complexity (O(N²)) and potential overfitting on sample-constrained clinical data. Model 1 instead uses a factorised architecture that separates attention into distinct spatial and temporal dimensions. Physically, this factorisation reflects the orthogonal properties of scalp EEG: temporal dynamics reflect neural synchrony, while spatial dynamics reflect volume conduction and topographic distribution. By encoding this inductive bias, the factorised transformer reduces parameter redundancy and improves generalisation. Our results indicate that these architectures have complementary feature extraction abilities. The factorised transformer (Model 1) is tailored for canonical spatiotemporal landmarks, while the deeper standard transformers (Models 2 and 3) better capture unconstrained global network dynamics. Their prediction errors are largely uncorrelated. Soft voting averages their continuous probability distributions, reducing idiosyncratic false positives or false negatives. This aggregation yielded a 7.69 percentage-point gain in EM (from 80.77% to 88.46%) over the best single variant. Comparing the ensemble against individual sub-models using McNemar’s exact test on paired session-level predictions (Section 3.1) yielded two-sided p-values of 0.25 and 0.50, both above the 0.05 threshold. This reflects the limited sample size (n = 26 sessions). McNemar’s test depends on the frequency of discordant pairs; with few discordant sessions, statistical power is low regardless of the percentage improvement. The ensemble consistently matched or outperformed all individual models, with zero negative discordant pairs (n₁₀ = 0). It corrected single-model errors in 2–3 sessions, raising EM by 7.69 percentage points. Random variance would produce a symmetric distribution (n₁₀ ≈ n₀₁), so this asymmetry supports systematic error correction. This pattern is consistent with the generalisation metrics on the larger holdout and multi-centre cohorts. The performance contributions of different augmentations (Section 3.2) provide insights into model regularisation. Gaussian noise injection yielded the largest individual improvement (Macro F1 +1.42%). This complements the preprocessing denoising procedures. Preprocessing filters (e.g., bandpass and notch filtering) remove macro-level, high-amplitude artefacts; training-time stochastic noise injection simulates micro-level residual variations, such as subtle fluctuations in electrode-skin impedance and hardware thermal drift that standard filters cannot fully eliminate. Random Gaussian perturbation encourages the model to learn signal rather than noise, improving robustness in unlabelled test settings. The optimisation objective incorporated two domain-specific priors. Focal Loss (γ = 2.0) with class-specific positive weighting (α = 3.0 for occipital regions) was introduced to counteract the epidemiological under-representation of occipital lobe epilepsy (8.2–8.7% of positive instances). This weighting directs the gradient toward rare classes and helps the ensemble achieve recall of 1.000 for the right occipital region. The hemispheric mutual exclusivity penalty (λ = 0.1), by contrast, enforced a different prior: unilateral focal epilepsy. Its primary effect was not to improve overall accuracy but to suppress anatomically implausible bilateral predictions. Together, these two components operated at different levels: focal loss addressed inter-regional class imbalance, while the hemispheric penalty enforced inter-hemispheric anatomical plausibility. In the expanded holdout dataset, the global EM rate remained stable (82.76%), but right frontal (RF) recall decreased to 0.714. This drop likely reflects a shift in data distribution: the internal test set (26 sessions) primarily captured dense ictal periods, whereas the holdout cohort (87 sessions) introduced longer continuous recordings with lower discharge density. The inclusion of annotation-sparse windows may increase variance and reduce per-session discharge density, leading to localised sensitivity loss. Nevertheless, RF precision remained 1.000, indicating that positive predictive boundaries stayed reliable. Performance heterogeneity was more evident in the unlabelled test on randomly extracted windows (Figure 14). Macro-averaged F1 decreased from 0.870 to 0.831, with varied regional effects. Marginal improvements occurred in bilateral frontal regions (LF, RF), while the largest drops were observed in bilateral occipital regions (LO, RO). These differences likely reflect cortical physiology. Frontal lobe discharges propagate broadly and appear frequently in random windows, allowing the multi-scale convolutions to learn regional features. In contrast, occipital paroxysms are typically transient, focal, and state-dependent (e.g., eye-closure or visual suppression) [48]. These brief events are easily masked by background alpha rhythms and physiological noise and thus depend more on structured temporal anchors. The model achieved 84.62% EM on the external dataset, suggesting cross-institutional generalisability. This validation cohort had a specific demographic profile: all subjects were under 25 years, including five infants aged ≤1 year. Regional accuracies remained high, particularly in temporal and frontal regions, indicating that the learned representations are robust to age-dependent morphological differences in infant cranial structure and developing EEG backgrounds. However, left occipital (LO) recall was lower at 0.667. Although this suggests regional susceptibility, the small BCH sample size (n = 13 sessions from 9 patients) is a clear statistical limitation. The localised LO sensitivity drop may also reflect physical differences in infant EEG recording: open fontanelles and higher CSF-to-brain volume ratios alter volume conduction properties [49], potentially attenuating occipital signals more than frontal or temporal sources. Larger multi-centre trials are needed to validate these regional variations. The longitudinal case studies (Figure 15) provide a framework for evaluating temporal interpretability. For Patient 150003760, the model produced a continuously elevated probability trajectory (>0.80) for the right temporal and right frontal regions, which corresponded to the clinical report documenting four electrographic seizures originating from the right temporal structures. At the 22nd smoothed epoch index, the right-hemisphere probability curve transiently decreased while the left frontal trajectory showed a reciprocal increase. This crossover coincided with a sharp reduction in prediction confidence (Figure 15, upper right panel). When the discharge remained localised to the primary right temporal focus, the model output a highly certain regional classification. However, during propagation across the corpus callosum to the contralateral hemisphere, the multi-scale convolutions registered conflicting epileptiform features from both sides. The resulting spatial ambiguity flattened the softmax distribution, causing the confidence metric to dip. This alignment between reduced confidence and documented cross-hemispheric propagation supports the model’s ability to produce time-indexed network transitions without relying on post-hoc saliency maps. The zero false-positive rate on 108 healthy control recordings is noteworthy. Generic transient detectors, whether rule-based or learned, often flag high-amplitude artefacts such as eye blinks, muscle activity, and electrode pops. Our model did not, despite lacking explicit artefact rejection modules. This suggests that the factorised spatiotemporal attention mechanism distinguishes true epileptiform spikes from benign events, likely by learning propagation dynamics. The distinction makes clinical sense: benign artefacts, however large in amplitude, lack the organised spatial propagation patterns that characterise true cortical discharges. Eye blinks project diffusely but without the evolving field topography of an epileptic spike; muscle activity is spatially circumscribed and transient. By learning this topological signature rather than a waveform template, the model approximates a clinical rule of thumb that spikes are defined by field distribution and propagation trajectory [50].] That a purely data-driven model captures this contextual distinction without explicit feature engineering suggests that the ensemble learns network-level dynamics rather than isolated waveform templates, extending the intracranial evidence of Jiang et al. [11] to the noisier regime of routine scalp EEG. Clinical deployment also requires computational efficiency. Evaluation on a 24-hour EDF recording (Figure 16) showed that end-to-end execution scales linearly with data volume and sampling rate. Runtime profiling shows that data ingestion, signal harmonisation, and hardware operations (EDF parsing, filtering, downsampling) consume over 82% of execution time. In contrast, the 5-model ensemble inference phase requires under 8 seconds for the full 24-hour sequence. Thus, neural network computation is not the primary bottleneck; throughput is limited by CPU-bound data I/O and signal processing. Total processing time remains under 11 minutes at the highest density (1024 Hz), indicating that the framework operates faster than real-time and could serve as an automated screening tool for long-term video-EEG data. Label granularity and causal limitations. A key limitation is the spatial resolution of the ground-truth labels. Our six-region mapping, which combines temporal and parietal lobes, was a pragmatic alignment with the 18-channel bipolar montage. This coarse labelling presents a ceiling for supervised learning: the model may learn electrophysiological features that contain sublobar information, but it is never incentivised to express them during training. Similarly, the model learns statistical associations between EEG patterns and lobar labels derived from clinical reports, not direct measurements of the epileptogenic zone. It may pick up on correlated features that are not themselves causative, such as secondary propagation patterns or co-occurring structural abnormalities visible on MRI. Prospective comparison with surgical outcomes, the definitive gold standard, would be required to establish causal validity. Data-related limitations. Occipital lobe epilepsy is an inherent minority in our cohort, reflecting its epidemiological rarity rather than a sampling bias. While Focal Loss and ensemble aggregation improved sensitivity for this rare class, this optimisation reflects a small absolute number of test-set samples. Consequently, these findings should be treated as hypothesis-generating regarding rare-event learning rather than definitive proof. Dedicated occipital-specific cohorts would be required for prospective validation. Clinical translation limitations. The framework is positioned as a decision-support tool for use after routine scalp EEG acquisition, prior to sEEG implantation planning. Its output is a six-region probability vector that requires interpretation by an experienced epileptologist; it is not a standalone diagnostic. The current implementation is retrospective; prospective validation in real-time clinical settings is essential. The inference-time hemispheric hard constraint assumes confirmed focal epilepsy and is not designed to differentiate focal from generalised cases. However, we tested the model on a small subset of sessions with documented bilateral or multifocal onsets—cases explicitly excluded from training. In these instances, the ensemble rarely produced a false-positive unilateral localisation. Instead, probabilities across all six regions remained below the 0.5 threshold, yielding a “no prediction” output. When inspecting the longitudinal probability trajectories, regions consistent with the bilateral SOZ showed elevated probabilities (typically 0.3–0.45) relative to other regions, while completely healthy controls (PhysioNet) produced uniformly low probabilities across all regions (typically <0.15). This suggests that the model’s probability magnitude encodes graded information about the presence of epileptiform activity, even when the unilateral assumption is violated. Clinicians could therefore interpret uniformly low probabilities across all regions as a flag for inconclusive or non-focal cases, rather than accepting a forced lateralisation as valid. We excluded ambiguous cases, bilateral onsets, and genetic epilepsies from this proof-of-principle study; generalising to these more complex presentations will require further work. First, the label granularity limitation identified above could be addressed through teacher-student distillation. A teacher model trained on high-density EEG (128 channels) or ESI source imaging could generate soft spatial probability maps over individual anatomical parcels. These maps could then serve as supervisory signals for distilling sublobar discriminative features into our low-density 18-channel architecture, potentially recovering finer-grained information that our current six-region labels cannot express. Second, the dissociation between M1 and M2 performance on occipital versus temporal classes suggests that no single architectural prior is optimal for all epilepsy subtypes. A subtype-adaptive ensemble could address this: rather than a fixed heterogeneous ensemble, one could train specialised models for different electroclinical syndromes (e.g., temporal lobe epilepsy vs. occipital lobe epilepsy) and route inputs to the most appropriate model based on preliminary spectral features. This builds directly on our observation that M1 captures sustained spatiotemporal propagation patterns while M2 better detects sparse, transient discharges. Such an approach would require larger, subtype-stratified cohorts but could improve performance across the full spectrum of focal epilepsies. Third, the factorised attention mechanism provides a basis for interpretable source localisation. Unlike standard transformers where attention weights are difficult to interpret due to flattened time-space sequences, our architecture produces separate temporal and spatial attention maps. Projecting spatial attention weights onto the 10–20 electrode topology could generate a dynamic topographical heatmap showing, in real time, which electrode clusters the model is attending to, providing clinicians with visualisation directly mappable to the EEG montage. Fourth, the computational profile-less than 8 seconds of inference versus over 4 minutes of data I/O for a 24-hour recording-suggests that model compression is not the primary engineering priority. Instead, developing streaming EDF parsers and edge-AI deployment could enable continuous, window-wise inference directly on ICU or EMU bedside devices. Coupled with an automated summariser, this could transform the pipeline from a batch screening tool into a live decision-support system that flags high-confidence localisations without waiting for full-recording download. Finally, integrating multimodal imaging could generate more precise spatial ground truths. ESI has demonstrated the ability to localise averaged interictal discharges to within 10 mm of the surgical resection margin in up to 67% of patients with favourable outcomes [51]. Instead of training on coarse lobar labels, one could project EEG source localisation results onto individual structural MRI scans and use the resulting 3D coordinates as continuous or fine-grained anatomical targets, leveraging EEG’s temporal precision and MRI’s spatial resolution. In conclusion, this work demonstrates proof-of-principle that a deep learning framework can reliably localise the seizure onset zone at the lobar level from routine 18-channel scalp EEG. We curated and annotated a large, clinically heterogeneous cohort of 100 patients (262 sessions, >6,000 hours), and introduced a targeted online augmentation pipeline—Gaussian noise, amplitude scaling, temporal cropping, and hemispheric channel swap—that mitigated overfitting with systematic ablations confirming each component’s contribution. The factorised spatiotemporal Transformer, combined with a hemispheric mutual exclusivity penalty and a heterogeneous five-model ensemble, achieved 88.46% session-level exact match on the internal test set, outperforming generic EEG baselines by over 38 percentage points. Performance generalised to annotation-sparse holdout data (82.76%), a cross-institutional paediatric cohort (84.62%), and wholly unlabelled random segments (66.67% with single M1), with case-level trajectory analysis confirming that predictions track expert clinical summaries across continuous recordings. Critically, by offering a non-invasive, computationally efficient (4.26 minutes for a 24-hour recording), and interpretable pathway to expedite presurgical evaluation, this approach has the potential to reduce reliance on prolonged inpatient monitoring and invasive implantation, thereby lowering patient risk and accelerating surgical decision-making for those with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. DeepSeek-R1 was used as a functional tool during the preparation of this thesis. It was utilised solely to assist with preliminary structural planning and the grammatical refinement and polishing of my original text. The AI did not generate any academic content, arguments, or data analyses, and the final work remains entirely my own. Focal Loss Positive Weighting. The α values were selected based on the inverse class frequency in the training set. Labels 5 (Left Occipital) and 6 (Right Occipital) represented 8.2% and 8.7% of positive instances, respectively; an α of 3.0 was applied to these rare classes to amplify their gradient contribution. All other regions (Labels 1-4) used α=1.0. Hemispheric Penalty Coefficient Search. The coefficient λ was tuned on the validation set over {0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5}. λ=0.1 yielded the highest validation EM (78.85%), compared with76.92% (λ=0.05), 76.92% (λ=0.2), and 73.08% (λ=0.5). All subsequent experiments use λ=0.1. To manage the computational overhead of processing long-term continuous recordings, a multiprocessing pipeline was implemented using Python’s multiprocessing module with a dedicated CPU worker pool. Epochs were batched into chunks of 100 segments and distributed across worker processes. Each worker independently performed resampling, trimming, and serialisation. Memory management was enforced via explicit del statements and gc.collect() at the end of each session loop to prevent memory leaks. -Maximum consecutive NaN: 512 time steps (2 seconds at 256 Hz) -Global NaN ratio: 30% of the total 18×4096 matrix (>22,118 NaN values) -Interpolation method: 1D linear interpolation per channel -Boundary handling: Nearest-neighbour extrapolation for NaN values at sequence start/end The original EEG recordings varied in sampling rate (256 Hz, 512 Hz, and 1024 Hz in the BIDMC cohort). title: Frequency-Resolved Connectivity Graphs for EEG-Based Classification of Alzheimer and Frontotemporal Dementia
author: Radwan, M.; yazidi, A.; lind, P. G.
text: In this study, we build EEG based graph model that uses frequency-resolved connectivity features, with Coherence, phase locking value (PLV) and phase lag index (PLI) in five frequency bands as multi-dimensional edge features. The model is used to classify Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) against healthy controls (CN). This paper extends our earlier work on FTD [1] with AD vs CN as the main new task, a feature ablation for it, and a joint analysis of both tasks. With leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation, the model reaches an accuracy of 81.13% for AD vs CN and 76.06% for FTD vs CN, which is competitive with the baselines reported with the dataset with far fewer parameters (159 and 282 thousand versus 170.5 million). Under the random cross-validation setting used for the DICE-net model, our model has a comparable accuracy for FTD and a lower accuracy for AD. Node and edge saliency maps highlight occipital and temporal electrodes, the Alpha band for node features and the Theta band for edge features, which is consistent with earlier EEG studies. In an ablation on the AD task, using all 15 edge features performed better than using a single connectivity measure or edge features averaged over the bands. Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder that causes cognitive decline, memory loss and changes in behavior, and its pathogenic mechanism is still poorly understood [2]. Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is another neurodegenerative disorder, which mainly affects the frontal and temporal lobes. One route to understanding these diseases and diagnosing them is to find reliable biomarkers. Studying functional connectivity between brain regions can be helpful in the biomarker discovery. Changes in connectivity patterns can appear before clinical symptoms emerge and before structural changes are visible [3], and they may be detectable before the accumulation of beta-amyloid plaques and tau proteins [4]. Studying connectivity separately in different frequency bands can give more detail about the pathology. Electroencephalography (EEG) is a useful tool for studying brain connectivity because it is non-invasive and has a high temporal resolution. Conventional statistical methods have been used to extract EEG features that separate patients from healthy individuals, and deep learning methods are increasingly used for the same purpose. Deep learning models are often seen as black boxes, which makes it hard to understand why a model makes a prediction. This is a concern in clinical settings, so there is a growing interest in interpreting what these models learn, in the hope of identifying robust biomarkers. Graph neural networks (GNNs) represent EEG electrodes as nodes and the relations between electrodes as edges. In many GNN studies the adjacency matrix is built from the spatial distance between electrodes, with the assumption that close electrodes are more strongly connected. However, spatial closeness does not guarantee functional connectivity, and binary adjacency matrices discard the strength of the connection. Using functional connectivity to build a weighted adjacency matrix avoids these problems. Several studies have used graph-based models for EEG. The authors of [5] used graph attention networks for general EEG classification without an interpretation. The authors of [6] introduced a dynamic graph CNN (DGCNN) that learns the adjacency matrix during training and applied it to emotion recognition. The authors of [7] developed a graph input layer attention convolutional network that uses Pearson correlation as the adjacency matrix, with activity, mobility, complexity and power spectral density as node features, on a depression dataset of 60 subjects. They used the weight matrix of the input layer to find important edges and nodes, but did not study frequency bands. A Chebyshev-polynomial GNN with explanations was developed in [8] to detect Parkinson’s disease from EEG. It quantifies the importance of nodes and edges to identify abnormal connectivity, and it uses microstates to study brain dynamics, but it does not use different frequency bands. Interpretation has also been studied for CNN-based EEG models. The authors of [9] classified mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in two EEG datasets using four frequency bands separately, and found that the Beta band (15–30 Hz) gave the best performance. The authors of [10] classified abnormal EEG in the TUH dataset [11] using five frequency bands, and found the Delta band (0.5–4 Hz) to be the most important. That study uses a large dataset but a general normal and abnormal labels with limited conclusions about specific diseases. Frequency content can also be related to higher brain functions such as memory and learning, which can help both explainability and performance [12]. The work most related to ours is [13], which used GNNs for Alzheimer’s disease and epilepsy and studied feature importance for Alzheimer’s disease on the dataset of [14]. The authors report the importance of the Alpha band and of occipital (O1) and prefrontal (Fp1) regions, using PLV, Pearson correlation and cross spectral density to build the adjacency matrices. Their work focuses more on model development, while our focus is on the interpretation of the model, the ablation of the input features, and the salient features that the model uses. This paper extends our earlier work on FTD vs CN [1]. The main task here is AD vs CN, which is new, and we add a feature ablation and node and edge saliency maps for it. The FTD vs CN task from the earlier paper is included to compare the two diseases with the same model, and its results are the same as in the earlier paper. A frequency-resolved multi-edge GNN that uses Coherence, PLV and PLI in five frequency bands as edge features, evaluated for AD vs CN and, from our earlier work, for FTD vs CN, with leave-one-subject-out validation. An ablation of the edge features on the AD vs CN task, comparing each connectivity measure alone and edge features averaged over the frequency bands with the full set of 15 edge features. An interpretation of the model with saliency maps for nodes, edges and frequency bands in both tasks, compared with findings from earlier EEG studies. The rest of the paper is organized as follows.Section 2describes the data, the model, the features and the experiments.Section 3presents the classification results, the saliency maps and the ablation.Section 4discusses the results, andSection 5concludes and lists the limitations. We use the EEG dataset of [15], which contains resting-state, eyes-closed recordings from 88 subjects (36 with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), 23 with frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and 29 healthy controls (CN)) collected at the AHEPA University Hospital in Thessaloniki, Greece. The AD vs CN task therefore uses 65 subjects and the FTD vs CN task uses 52. The recordings have 19 scalp electrodes (plus 2 reference electrodes) and a sampling rate of 500 Hz. We use the preprocessed version provided by the dataset authors, in which the signals were band-pass filtered between 0.5 and 45 Hz, re-referenced to A1–A2 and cleaned of artifacts with Artifact Subspace Reconstruction (ASR) and Independent Component Analysis (ICA) following the preprocessed dataset from [15]. As said, we are proposing a graph model in this study. For each time window, a graph is built with the 19 electrodes as nodes, the node features ofSection 2.3, and 15 edge features for each pair of electrodes which are three connectivity measures in five frequency bands (Section 2.4). The graph is passed to Transformer Convolution layers [16], which use attention message propagation and also use the edge features in the attention. Here, we use five attention heads. The outputs of the attention heads are concatenated and followed by a ReLU activation and batch normalization (Fig. 1). After the last layer, global mean pooling over the nodes gives a graph embedding, which is passed to a fully connected layer. The model has two layers for AD vs CN and three layers for FTD vs CN, so the numbers of trainable parameters are 159,234 and 281,954. Model architecture. ReLU is the rectified linear unit, BN is batch normalization and FC is a fully connected layer. Edge and node features are calculated from the EEG data, which gives a graph for each sample. The Transformer Convolution layer followed by ReLU and BN is repeated twice for AD vs CN and three times for FTD vs CN, and the node embeddings are pooled by global average pooling and passed to an FC layer. The number of attention heads is five. The signals are decomposed with Morlet wavelets into five frequency bands, Delta (1–4 Hz), Theta (4–8 Hz), Alpha (8–13 Hz), Beta (13–30 Hz) and Gamma (30–45 Hz), and the node and edge features are calculated separately for each band. The recordings are divided into windows of 30 seconds with an overlap of 15 seconds, which is the window size used in [17] on this dataset. Each window is one sample, so the classification is window-based. The node features are hand-crafted: differential entropy, spectral entropy, permutation entropy, entropy power, approximate entropy, Hjorth mobility and complexity, fractal density and power spectral density, together with the mean, standard deviation and kurtosis of the signal. Spectral coherence, the phase locking value (PLV) and the phase lag index (PLI) quantify the relation between pairs of electrodes in each of the five bands. All three are symmetric, so the graphs are undirected, and the 15 edge features form a tensorA ∈ℝ19×19×15. The magnitude-squared coherence is estimated with Welch’s method,wherePxandPyare the power spectral density estimates of the signalsxandy, andPxyis their cross spectral density. The PLV [18] measures how consistent the phase difference between two signals is over time, ignoring the amplitudes,where Δφnis the phase difference at time pointn, the instantaneous phases are obtained from the Hilbert transform, andNis the number of time points. The PLV takes values between 0 (no phase synchrony) and 1 (constant phase difference). The PLI [19] is less affected by a common source or volume conduction, which can inflate the PLV, because it ignores phase differences centered around 0 orπ. It measures the asymmetry of the distribution of phase differences,and takes values between 0 (symmetric distribution around 0 orπ) and 1. We use saliency maps, the gradient of the model output with respect to the input, to find which nodes and edges the model relies on. The absolute value of the gradient is taken as the feature importance [20], and the values are averaged over the data to obtain a global importance. The data are split with leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation, as in the baselines of [15]. In each fold, one subject is held out and the model is trained on the remaining subjects. Because the classification is window-based, the predictions for the windows of the held-out subject are combined by majority voting. We report accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and F1 score, averaged over the folds. With 65 subjects for AD vs CN and 52 for FTD vs CN, one subject corresponds to about 1.5 and 1.9 percentage points of accuracy, respectively. The two binary tasks are AD vs CN, which is the main task of this paper, and FTD vs CN, which comes from our earlier work. The model is trained with the Adam optimizer, a learning rate of 0.00001, a batch size of 100, a dropout of 0.5, mean pooling and 35 epochs (Table 1). The small learning rate was used to avoid instability, and beyond 35 epochs the training showed signs of overfitting. The source code is available athttps://github.com/mhmdrdwn/ftd_graph. Two comparisons are made, and they use different evaluation settings.Tables 2and3compare our model with the classical baselines reported with the dataset [15] using LOSO validation.Tables 4and5compare it with the deep learning models of [17], whose results come from random cross-validation (ten runs, with six subjects in the validation sets), so our model was also evaluated in that setting for these two tables. The numbers of the two groups of tables are therefore not directly comparable. Using LOSO validation, the model reaches an accuracy of 81.13% for AD vs CN and 76.06% for FTD vs CN. These are 4.1 points above the best baseline for AD (Random Forest, 77.01%) and 2.9 points above the best baseline for FTD (MLP, 73.12%). The sensitivity is also higher than for the best baseline, by 4.7 points for AD and 6.6 points for FTD. This comes with a lower specificity than the best baseline, by 2.1 points for AD and 5.9 points for FTD. The F1 score is the highest for AD vs CN but not for FTD vs CN, where our model has 65.44% and the MLP baseline has 72.82%. Against the deep learning models in the random cross-validation setting, DICE-net has the highest accuracy for AD vs CN (83.28% versus 77.11% for our model), and the two models are close for FTD vs CN (74.96% versus 74.16%). Our model has the highest sensitivity for both tasks. DeepConvNet, EEGNet [21] and EEGNetSSVEP [22] have a considerably lower performance than our model on both tasks. Fig. 2shows the importance of the nodes for AD vs CN, andFig. 3shows it for FTD vs CN. The maps show the importance of each node relative to the minimum and maximum importance in the map. For AD vs CN, the Alpha (8–13 Hz), Theta (4–8 Hz) and Gamma (30–45 Hz) bands are the most important, and the electrodesO2 andP4 are the most important nodes in these bands. The electrodeT4 is also important in the Alpha, Theta and Gamma bands. For FTD vs CN, the Alpha band is clearly the most important, with the highest values atO2 andP4, andT6,T4 andT3 are also highlighted, while the other bands have a much lower importance. Compared with AD vs CN, the frontal electrodesFp1 andFp2 have a higher importance for FTD vs CN. Importance of the nodes in the AD vs CN classification, using all node features and averaged over the LOSO subjects. Importance of the nodes in the FTD vs CN classification, using all node features and averaged over the LOSO subjects. Fig. 4shows the importance of the edges for AD vs CN. Like the node maps, the edge maps show the importance relative to the minimum and maximum values over all the edges. The Theta band is the most important band, followed by the Alpha and Delta bands, and the PLV edges have the highest importance, followed by Coherence. For FTD vs CN (Fig. 5), the Theta band is also the most important, followed by the Gamma and Alpha bands, and the PLV edges again have the highest importance, followed by Coherence. The edge maps of the two tasks are therefore similar. Relative importance of the edges for AD vs CN, for the different connectivity measures and frequency bands. Relative importance of the edges for FTD vs CN, for the different connectivity measures and frequency bands. We look more closely at the networks that the edge maps highlight. For AD vs CN these are PLV in the Theta band and Coherence in the Theta, Alpha and Delta bands (Fig. 6). All three measures are symmetric, so the connections in these maps are symmetric by construction. In the Theta PLV network (Fig. 6a), the connections to and fromO2,O1,C4,P4 andT4 are highlighted. This is in line with the node maps, whereO2 andP4 are the most important nodes. In the Alpha and Delta Coherence networks (Fig. 6cand6d), the highlighted connections involveO2,P4,T4 andT6 together withFz, Pz, Fp1,F3,O1 andFp2, which belong to different brain regions. The connections betweenCzand the other electrodes are also highlighted. Relative importance of the edges for AD vs CN for the most important networks. Each plot is normalized to its own minimum and maximum to highlight the most important edges. For FTD vs CN, the same networks are highlighted, and in addition the Gamma band networks of PLI and Coherence (Fig. 7). The Theta PLV network (Fig. 7a) is similar to the one for AD vs CN. The connections to and fromO2,C4 andP4 are highlighted, which is consistent with the node maps, whereO2,T6 andP4 are the most important nodes. In the Coherence networks of the Alpha, Delta and Gamma bands (Fig. 7c, 7dand7f), the highlighted connections involveO2,P4,T4 andT6 together withFz, Pz, Fp1,F3,O1 andFp2. The connections betweenCzand the other electrodes are highlighted inFig. 7a, 7b, 7c, 7dand7f, and the connection betweenPzandCzis important inFig. 7eand7f. Relative importance of the edges for FTD vs CN for the most important networks. Each plot is normalized to its own minimum and maximum to highlight the most important edges. To complement the saliency maps, we ran an ablation of the edge features on the AD vs CN task. In one set of variants, only one connectivity measure is used with its five frequency bands, so there are 5 edge features instead of 15. In another variant, the three measures are each averaged over the frequency bands, so there are 3 edge features, one per measure. The ablation was run for AD vs CN, which is the task that is new in this paper and has more subjects than FTD vs CN (65 versus 52). Table 6shows that Coherence is the best single measure in terms of accuracy (76.61%), while PLV and PLI are almost equal (73.72% and 73.59%). Using Coherence alone gives an accuracy 4.5 points below the full model, and averaging the edge features over the bands lowers the accuracy by 9.7 points. All of the ablated variants have an accuracy below the best classical baseline ofTable 2(77.01%). One subject corresponds to about 1.5 points of accuracy in this task, and the ablation was run once for each variant, so the smaller differences, such as the one between PLV and PLI, should not be interpreted. Under LOSO validation the model has a higher accuracy and sensitivity than the baselines reported with the dataset, on both tasks (Tables 2and3). The higher accuracy is accompanied by a higher sensitivity and a lower specificity than the best baseline. A high sensitivity is useful when the cost of missing a patient is high, but a lower specificity means more false alarms among the controls. The gain over the best baseline is 4.1 points for AD and 2.9 points for FTD, which corresponds to about three subjects for AD and one to two for FTD, and we have not tested whether the differences are larger than the variation between runs. Against the deep learning models evaluated with random cross-validation (Tables 4and5), the accuracy of our model is close to DICE-net for FTD but about 6 points lower for AD, and it has a higher sensitivity on both tasks. The settings of the two groups of tables differ, so these comparisons are indicative only. The size of the models is very different. Our models have about 159 and 282 thousand parameters, while DICE-net has 170.5 million parameters according to [17]. This means that a competitive performance for FTD is reached with a model that is much smaller. EEGNet and DeepConvNet, which use the raw EEG amplitudes, have a much lower performance than the models that use extracted features, which are ours and DICE-net, whose inputs are built from spectral coherence and relative band power. A possible explanation is that raw amplitudes are noisy and not comparable across recordings, because of differences in electrode placement and recording conditions. This is a hypothesis that we did not test, and the small size of the dataset may also play a role. In our own experiments, models trained on raw time series did not converge. For the node features, the Alpha band is the most important in both tasks, followed by the Gamma, Theta or Beta bands. For the edge features, the Theta band is the most important, followed by the Alpha, Gamma or Delta bands, depending on the task. The importance of the Alpha band for node features is in line with the findings of [13] for Alzheimer’s disease. In the ablation, edge features averaged over the bands gave a lower accuracy than the band-resolved edge features, so keeping the bands separate helped in this experiment, although the number of edge features also differs. The ablation does not test the bands one by one. The literature reports consistent abnormalities in the Delta, Theta and Alpha rhythms in Alzheimer’s disease [23,24,25,26,27,28]. Relative Theta power is increased in patients with dementia due to AD [24], and global Theta power is increased in AD patients [23]. Other studies report an increase in Delta and Theta and a decrease in Alpha and Beta in AD patients [25,26,27,28]. In patients with cognitive impairment, higher Theta and lower Beta relative power are reported in a longitudinal study [29]. For FTD, Alpha power is generally decreased, particularly in frontal and temporal regions [30], and lower Alpha activity was found in patients compared with controls in orbital frontal and temporal lobes [31]. FTD patients also show increased Theta power compared with controls [30,32,33]. Our saliency maps show a similar pattern, as Alpha and Theta are the most important bands, but saliency shows what the model uses and not the direction of the change in power, so we only claim that the bands match the literature. The occipital electrodeO2 and temporal electrodes are the most important in the decisions of both classifiers. The occipital importance is strongest in the Alpha band, but it is present in nearly all bands. In addition, the frontal electrodesFp1 andFp2 have a higher importance in the FTD vs CN classifier. These results agree with those of [17], who analyzed the same data. The connectivity maps show the same regions as the node maps, with important connections to and fromO2 and the temporal electrodes. A reduced occipital and frontal activity peak has been reported in mild Alzheimer’s disease compared with healthy individuals [34], and atrophy of the anterior temporal lobes is associated with semantic dementia [35,36,37,38,39]. Functional connectivity between the medial temporal lobe and the anterior-temporal system is reduced in the earliest stages of Alzheimer’s disease [40], and medial temporal lobe networks change with age and in MCI and are related to cognition and to later cognitive decline [41,42]. These studies support the relevance of the regions that the model highlights, but scalp electrodes cannot be mapped directly to these deep or anterior structures, so the match is approximate. In the ablation, the full model with 15 edge features performs better than any model with a single connectivity measure or with band-averaged edge features. This is consistent with the idea that the different measures and bands carry information that the model can use. However, the variants also differ in the number of edge features (15, 5 and 3), so the ablation cannot separate the value of the information from the effect of the model input size. It was also run on the AD task only, so we do not know whether the same pattern holds for FTD, and once for each variant. We therefore treat it as a first indication and not as proof of complementary information. The saliency maps and the ablation do not rank the measures in the same way. The saliency maps give the highest importance to PLV edges, followed by Coherence, while Coherence is the best single measure in the ablation. This is not a contradiction, because the two analyses ask different questions: saliency measures how sensitive the full model is to each input, and the ablation measures how informative one measure is on its own. It does mean that the saliency ranking should not be read as a ranking of how useful the measures are. We studied a GNN with frequency-resolved Coherence, PLV and PLI edge features for AD vs CN and FTD vs CN. Under LOSO validation it has a higher accuracy and sensitivity than the classical baselines reported with the dataset, and it is much smaller than DICE-net. Compared with DICE-net it has a comparable accuracy for FTD and a lower accuracy for AD, although the two were evaluated in a different setting. The saliency maps point to occipital and temporal regions, to the Alpha band for node features and to the Theta band for edge features, which agrees with earlier EEG studies. In the AD ablation, the full set of edge features performed better than a single measure or band-averaged edges, but the design does not separate information from model size. The study has several limitations. The dataset is small (36 AD, 23 FTD and 29 control subjects), comes from one hospital, and has no external validation, and one subject changes the accuracy by about 1.5 to 1.9 points. The results are from single runs without confidence intervals or significance tests. The ablation was run on the AD task only, so we do not know whether the same pattern holds for FTD, and it does not control for the number of edge features. The saliency maps are compared with the literature, but we did not test their faithfulness, for example by removing the highlighted features. The input features are hand-crafted, and models on raw time series did not converge in our experiments, which we attribute to noise and the small dataset without testing it. The deep learning comparisons use results from another setting and not our own runs of those models. All windows are treated as independent samples, which ignores how the windows of one subject are related over time. Future work could address these points by validating on an external dataset, running the ablation on both tasks with repeated runs and a control for the number of edge features, and testing the faithfulness of the attribution maps. Since Coherence, PLV and PLI are symmetric, directional measures such as Granger causality could be used to capture the direction of the coupling. Dynamic graphs could model how the windows of one subject are related, and cross-frequency features could be added as candidate biomarkers.
