title: Learning to Pursue Goals that Conflict with Prior Experience Relies on Fast Revaluation and Slow Value Updating
author: Pan, T.-F.; Molinaro, G.; Collins, A. G. E.
text: Humans can flexibly pursue novel goals, learning to reach them from goal-dependent teaching signals. However, the breadth of this flexibility and its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. For example, can humans flexibly learn to reach a typically avoided outcome (e.g., +0) while avoiding a typically sought one (+1)? We hypothesized that humans are sufficiently flexible to learn from counterintuitive goals, but at a cost, and this ability is supported by complementary temporal dynamics of rapid cognitive control and slower, iterative outcome value updating. In two experiments, we confirmed that participants learned when pursuing counterintuitive goals, but less effectively than standard goals. Furthermore, extended practice reduced performance gaps. To characterize the underlying mechanisms, we developed a novel computational model incorporating fast goal switching and slow outcome value updating. This model best captured group-level behavior; individuals differed in the efficiency of these processes, capturing differences in the cost initially incurred by counterintuitive goals. Crucially, a stronger initial cost did not permanently limit performance: slower value updating compensated for early inefficiencies in rapid adaptation. Furthermore, comparing early and late goal-switch learning revealed that greater goal alignment was associated with faster outcome processing, suggesting a transition from effortful control to efficient outcome evaluation. Thus, despite individual differences in initial flexibility, repeated attempts to reach counterintuitive goals decreased initial biases. More broadly, our findings show that goal-dependent outcome valuation leverages complementary fast and slow processes to enable flexible and efficient goal pursuit over time. Humans exhibit an immense capacity to pursue novel and sometimes counterintuitive goals, such as rock climbing without ropes (free solo) or restricting calorie intake against ingrained survival instincts. Prior work has shown that humans are flexible in learning from abstract and novel goal outcomes (McDougle et al., 2022;Molinaro & Collins, 2023,2026), with neuroimaging evidence highlighting how the prefrontal cortex (PFC) dynamically updates neural representations of outcome values given current goals (Frömer et al., 2019;Castegnetti et al., 2021). Beyond abstract and novel goals, converging evidence indicates that humans can flexibly remap outcome values under counterintuitive goal conditions (e.g., minimizing gains;Shi et al., 2026) and learn from goal outcomes that run counter to prior experience (e.g., pursuing +0 over +1;Pan et al., 2025). Brain imaging studies have attributed this flexibility to support from multiple regions, including PFC, the reward network (McDougle et al., 2022;Hjort et al., 2026;Koszeghy & Passecker, 2026), and the hippocampus (Edelson & Hare, 2023;Chericoni et al., 2026). Despite this flexibility, pursuing counterintuitive goals often reduces performance, reflecting persistent influence from prior experience (Pan et al., 2025;Shi et al., 2026). Yet, the cause of this impairment remains unclear. In particular, we do not know whether this impairment reflects a fixed cost of processing counterintuitive goals by recruiting executive function, or whether this cost is temporary and one that practice can mitigate. This gap more generally reflects our poor understanding of what computational mechanisms underlie humans’ goal-dependent learning flexibility (Molinaro & Collins, 2023). To address this gap, we used goal-dependent learning tasks to test whether practice can overcome learning inefficiency imposed by prior experience, and how distinct computational processes dynamically support goal-congruent value update. Drawing on hierarchical frameworks of goal-directed behavior (O’Reilly, 2020;Koszeghy & Passecker, 2026;Xu et al., 2026), we hypothesized that goal-dependent valuation and learning recruits two complementary mechanisms: a fast and effortful process that governs rapid goal-dependent outcome evaluation, and a slow process that trains a goal-congruent outcome-reward association (i.e., an association between the current goal outcomes and the positive reward associated with them;Molinaro and Collins, 2026). Specifically, in this framework, the fast process depends on the active goal representation maintained in executive control, which modulates the slow, gradual updating of goal-congruent mappings while remaining constrained by prior experience. To test the dynamics of the goal-dependent valuation framework, we first designed a self-determined goal task in which participants determined their own goals in a stimulus-action learning task, establishing baseline behavioral flexibility and prior bias across standard versus counterintuitive goal outcomes (e.g., pursuing +1 vs. +0; green vs. red outcomes). To dissect the dynamics of goal-dependent learning, we then implemented an extended stimulus-action learning task involving explicit, instructed goal switches between opposing goal outcomes. Our behavioral results showed that participants initially pursued standard outcomes (+1 over +0), but extended practice enabled flexible adaptation to counterintuitive goals (pursuing +0) and eliminated the performance gap between goals. Computational modeling through a goal-dependent reinforcement learning (RL) framework revealed different degrees of efficiency in fast and slow valuation mechanisms, leading to individual variation in susceptibility to prior experience. Over the time course of learning, practice attenuated these prior constraints through complementary fast and slow valuations, driving a transition from effortful, controlled processing to flexible, automated goal execution. We first designed a goal-dependent stimulus-action learning task to investigate whether humans select different goals during learning based on prior experience, and how these prior preferences impact learning when explicit goals align with or contradict them. Participants completed two sequential blocks: an initial self-determined block followed by an instructed block. Each block consisted of 26 trials comprising 13 iterations of two distinct visual stimuli, with an entirely novel stimulus set introduced in each block. Across both blocks, the core task followed a deterministic stimulus–action learning paradigm (Fig. 1A). On each trial, participants observed a stimulus, selected one of three key presses, and received deterministic outcome feedback (Fig. 1A). In the instructed block (the second block), the goal was instructed and remained fixed throughout the block. On each trial, participants were first informed of which outcome (+1 or +0) was their goal, and were instructed to select actions leading to the goal outcome. By contrast, in the self-determined block (the first block), participants were not told which goal outcome to pursue, only what the possible outcome values were (+1 or +0); the stimulus-action outcome remained deterministic based on the experimenter-defined goal (unknown to the participants). For example, in a Goal 0 self-determined goal, one correct action (e.g., J for the mushroom in Supplementary Fig 6) systematically led to the goal outcome (e.g., +0), while the other two actions led to the non-goal outcome (e.g., +1). Participants were told that instructions were lost and to try to play the game (see Methods for more details). Administering the self-determined block first allowed us to capture participants’ initial biases toward desirable goal outcomes while precluding carryover effects from explicit instruction. After completing the self-determined block, participants rated their preference for each outcome from 0 to 100 and indicated the strategy they used during the task (e.g., collecting as many +1 as possible). They then proceeded to the second block, the instructed block, with the same goal but a new set of stimuli. Experiment 1 paradigm and behavior results:A)The goal-dependent learning experiment comprised two short blocks: a self-determined and an instructed block. Top: Goal 0 group (Goal:+0, Non-Goal:+1). Bottom: Goal Red group (Goal: Red, Non-Goal: Green).B)Goal and non-goal outcomes of six different groups.C)Average choice accuracy across goal groups in the self-determined block (top) and instructed block (bottom). Each dot is a single participant’s data. Error bars indicate 95% CI. Sample sizes for each group: Goal 1 (n = 46), Goal 0 (n= 49), Goal Red (n= 48), Goal Green (n= 46), and Goal Blue (n= 46).∗p <0.05;∗∗∗∗p <0.0001; Unpaired two-sided t-test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. To investigate different outcomes’ impact, we designed six different goal/non-goal pairs: +1/+0 (Goal 1), +0/+1 (Goal 0), green/red (Goal Green), red/green (Goal Red), blue/yellow (Goal Blue), yellow/blue (Goal Yellow). Each participant was randomly assigned to one of the groups. We expected that the Goal Blue and Goal Yellow groups would show no strong preference for outcomes and thus serve as control groups (Fig. 1B); by contrast, given the majority Western cultural associations of our participant cohort, we anticipated that outcomes +1 and green would be strongly preferred in the absence of instructions. In the self-determined block, participants in the Goal 0 and Goal Red groups exhibited lower accuracy compared to the Goal 1 and Goal Green groups, respectively (Fig. 1C; Goal 0 vs Goal 1:t(67.88) = −16.46,p< .001, Bayes factor (BF10)>100; Goal Red vs Goal Green:t(70.42) = −10.90,p< .001, BF10>100). Specifically, Goal 0 and Goal Red groups systematically selected actions leading to non-goal outcomes, driving performance well below chance (one-samplet-tests against 0.33; Goal 0:M= 0.14,t(48) = −11.22,p< .001, BF10= 1.33 × 1012, 95% CI [0.10, 0.17]; Goal Red:M= 0.18,t(47) = −6.78,p< .001, BF10= 7.27 × 105, 95% CI [0.14, 0.23]). This systematic bias suggests that participants viewed 1 and Green as the “correct” outcome to pursue based on prior experience. Self-reported strategies corroborated this finding: participants in Goal 0 and Goal Red groups frequently reported collecting non-goal outcomes (+1 and Green; Supplementary Fig. 7 A). Furthermore, these self-determined rules strongly correlated with participants’ subjective preferences for different outcomes, as indicated by their post-block ratings (Supplementary Fig. 7 B-D). As expected, participants in the Goal Blue and Goal Yellow groups, lacking strong preferences given past experience, exhibited more dispersed behavior, achieving around chance-level accuracy (33%) in the self-determined block. Moreover, we found no difference in accuracy between these goals (Goal Yellow vs Goal Blue:t(81.91) = −1.42,p= .159, BF10= 0.53, with median posteriorδ= 0.26, 95% CI [−0.12, 0.65]). Notably, few participants reported collecting rare outcomes, which corresponded to the correct rule in our task (Supplementary Fig. 7 A). Discovering this strategy requires extensive trial-and-error learning and is considerably more cognitively demanding than relying on standard rewarding outcomes guided by intuitive bias. Having confirmed that participants came into the experiment with strong priors for +1/Green as desirable goals and +0/Red as outcomes to avoid, we next examined how flexibly participants could override those priors. In the full instruction block, participants achieved high average accuracies ranging from 71.2% to 85.1% across all goal types (Fig. 1C). Crucially, performance in every condition was significantly above the 33% chance level (one-samplet-tests: allts ≥ 9.88, all degrees of freedom between 45 and 48, allpadj< .001,], all BF10≥ 1.70 × 1010, 95% CIs within [0.63, 0.89]). These results showed that humans can flexibly learn to pursue arbitrary and even counterintuitive goal outcomes when given clear instructions. Despite the behavioral flexibility observed in the instructed block, participants exhibited attenuated learning performance in Goal 0 compared to Goal 1 (t(84.31) = −2.47,p= .016, BF10= 2.879, with median posteriorδ= 0.451, 95% CI [0.06, 0.854]). By contrast, no significant performance differences emerged between color-pair goals (Goal Red vs. Goal Green, or Goal Yellow vs. Goal Blue). This is particularly notable in the case of the Red group, which exhibited a pronounced prior against Red outcomes observed in the self-determined block. This asymmetry between Goal 0 and Goal Red suggests that intuitive priors for numerical magnitude are stronger and more uniform across individuals than those for color outcomes. While nearly everyone prefers a +1 outcome to a +0, color preference is more subjective and culturally dependent, leading to more individual differences (e.g., some individuals may prefer red over green; Supplementary Fig. 7 B). This pattern was further supported by a linear mixed-effects model (LMM) predicting accuracy from block (self-determined vs. instructed), pair type (color vs. numerical), goal counterintuitiveness (Goal 0 and Goal Red coded as counterintuitive), and their interactions. While the three-way interaction was not significant, the model revealed a significant interaction between goal counterintuitiveness and pair type (β= 0.094,SE= 0.044,t(373.81) = 2.158,p= .032; Supplementary Table 2) alongside an interaction between counterintuitiveness and block (β= 0.493,SE= 0.03,t(373.81) = 16.446,p< .001). Accuracy was higher for numerical than color pairs under standard goals (Goal 1 vs. Goal Green), whereas the pattern was reversed under counterintuitive goals (Goal 0 vs. Goal Red), indicating a stronger prior bias for numerical over color outcomes across blocks. In addition, we conducted a control experiment to assess potential practice effects between blocks, particularly for conventional goals such as Goal +1 and Goal Green. We found that practice effect alone cannot account for the performance differences across blocks, suggesting that our instructional manipulation drove the observed learning differences. For further details, see Supplementary Fig. 8. Together, Experiment 1 showed that without explicit rules, prior experience steered most participants to pursue conventional rewarding outcomes (e.g., +1, green). However, under explicit instructions, they were able to flexibly learn from counterintuitive goals (e.g., +0, red). Nonetheless, this flexibility could be costly, as participants learned less effectively from Goal 0 relative to Goal 1. This performance deficit likely reflects the heightened demand placed on limited executive control resources to dynamically update outcome values (Molinaro & Collins, 2026;Shi et al., 2026). While these results confirmed a fast dynamic for goal value setting, a key question remains: is there also a slower dynamic for outcome-value update, and can extended practice overwrite the influence of prior experiences? Experiment 1 showed that humans have strong pre-existing outcome-reward associations and can override them in a goal-dependent way at a cost, showing evidence for a rapid outcome valuation process. In Experiment 2, we examined whether a slower outcome evaluation process also exists, such that practice decreases the learning inefficiency that the rapid process cannot overcome. To do so, we designed a goal-dependent learning task with both slow and fast dynamics of changes in goals. As in Experiment 1, participants learned deterministic stimulus-action mappings. Unlike Experiment 1, participants were always explicitly instructed which outcome to pursue. Additionally, to assess outcome processing efficiency, we introduced a Go/No-go “collect” mechanism: participants were instructed to use a separate key press tocollecttarget outcomes and to ignore non-goal outcomes (Fig. 2A). For counter-intuitive goals, we used Goal 0, informed by the results of Experiment 1, where the Goal 1 and Goal 0 conditions exhibited the largest performance contrast. Experiment 2 paradigm and predicted dynamics.A)Goal-dependent learning task with explicitly instructed goals.B)Task structure for the two goal sequence groups: Group E1 (goal sequence: 111, 000, 0, 000, 111, 0) and Group E0 (goal sequence: 000, 111, 0, 111, 000, 0).C)Predicted behavioral dynamics for sequence group E1. Hypothesis 0: fast only, a fast goal switch across block sets (e.g., Set 1 - Block 3 to Set 2 - Block 4). Hypothesis 1: fast+slow, fast alongside slow reward adaptation within a block set across mini-blocks (e.g., Blocks 4 to 6). The experiment comprised 14 blocks across three distinct conditions: Goal 1, Goal 0, and one-shot Goal 0. In Goal 1 and Goal 0 blocks, the designated target outcome was displayed at the onset of each trial and remained constant throughout the block. By contrast, during one-shot Goal 0 blocks, the goal (+0) and non-goal (+1) reminders were presented only on the initial trial, requiring participants to maintain the active goal representation across the entire block. Within each block, participants learned new mappings between 6 novel stimuli and 3 actions, with 5 iterations per stimulus (30 trials per block). This brief block structure kept participants in an active learning regime where outcomes remained informative, enabling us to isolate how shifting goals affect new learning. To dissociate fast and slow dynamics of goal-dependent valuation, we structured the block order using alternating runs of repeated and switched goals across two between-subject groups (Fig. 2B). A “set” was defined as three consecutive blocks sharing the same goal, with individual constituent blocks serving as mini-blocks. Participants were randomly assigned to one of two sequence structures consisting of these block types. The E1 group (Early 1 Late 0) began with three consecutive Goal 1 blocks (Set 1; Blocks 1–3) before switching to three consecutive Goal 0 blocks (Set 2; Blocks 4–6). Following a one-shot Goal 0 block (Block 7), the E1 group completed another three Goal 0 blocks (Set 3; Blocks 8–10), three Goal 1 blocks (Set 4; Blocks 11–13), and a final one-shot Goal 0 block (Block 14). Following a parallel structure, the E0 group experienced an inverted set sequence (Goal 0, Goal 1, Goal 1, and Goal 0), with one-shot Goal 0 blocks likewise at Blocks 7 and 14. These sequence manipulations were designed to isolate fast (at goal-switch blocks) from slow dynamics (across repeated goal blocks, and the entire task;Fig. 2C). Based on the rapid adaptation observed in Experiment 1, we predicted that participants would quickly update their goal representations across sets to learn from feedback (fast dynamics), with a cost to counterintuitive goals. Concurrently, if present, slow dynamics would manifest as a gradual updating of the outcomes’ intrinsic reward properties within sets (across mini-blocks), thereby improving overall learning efficiency (Fig. 2C, H0 vs. H1). Furthermore, we expected one-shot blocks to provide more sensitivity to slow dynamics, with only one opportunity to apply task instructions rapidly. Consequently, performance in the late one-shot Goal 0 block would surpass that of the early one-shot block, driven by progressively stabilized goal-congruent outcome–reward associations. To test these hypotheses, we analyzed stimulus–action learning at both the trial and block levels. We focused specifically on goal-switch sets (Sets 2 and 4) to evaluate the learning costs of goal-switching and the influence of prior experience. Additionally, we measured reward collection (RC) precision (d’) and response times (RT) to determine how practice and prior experience affect the accuracy and speed of goal-dependent outcome processing. We first analyzed learning in the initial block (Block 1) to replicate Experiment 1’s results, showing successful but impaired Goal 0 learning. As expected, both groups performed significantly above chance (33%): participants in the E1 group achieved a mean accuracy of 60.2% (95% CI [56.0%, 64.0%],t(35) = 12.97,p< .001, BF10= 1.07 × 1012; two-sided one-samplet-test), and participants in the E0 group achieved 54.6% (95% CI [50.0%, 59.0%],t(39) = 9.16,p< .001, BF10= 3.31 × 108). A generalized linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) predicting trial-level accuracy from sequence group and stimulus iteration revealed a positive learning slope across iterations (b= 1.06,SE= 0.06,z= 17.39,p< .001, OR = 2.88, 95% CI [2.56, 3.25]; Supplementary Table 3). Critically, the group under Goal 0 exhibited significantly lower overall accuracy than those in the Goal 1 condition (b= −1.20,SE= 0.10,z= −11.51,p< .001, OR = 0.30, 95% CI [0.25, 0.37]). Block 1 results thus replicate Experiment 1 findings: learning efficiency was lower for Goal 0 than for Goal 1 in the initial learning block. To further validate the flexibility of goal-dependent learning, we examined the first goal-switch block (Block 4). We predicted that both groups would adapt to the new goal, but that switching to Goal 0 would incur a higher cognitive cost. Analysis of Block 4 confirmed that participants demonstrated fast and flexible goal-switching, achieving above-chance accuracy whether transitioning to Goal 0 or Goal 1. Both sequence groups performed significantly above chance (33.3%) in Block 4, confirming rapid goal switching: the E0 group (switching to Goal 1) achieved a mean accuracy of 53.1% (95% CI [46%, 60%],t(39) = 5.52,p< .001, BF10= 7440.63; two-sided one-samplet-test), and the E1 group (switching to Goal 0) achieved 51.1% (95% CI [44%, 58%],t(35) = 5.10,p< .001, BF10= 1765.20). Next, to confirm that switch cost exists in both groups, we compared accuracy between the pre-switch block (Block 3) and the post-switch block (Block 4) within each group. We found significant drops in accuracy for both the E1 group (switching to Goal 0:t(35) = 4.41,p< .001, 95% CI [0.08, 0.21], BF10= 263.73; two-sided pairedt-test) and the E0 group (switching to Goal 1:t(39) = 3.38,p= .005, 95% CI [0.05, 0.21], BF10= 19.50). Contrary to our prediction, a two-sided unpairedt-test showed no significant difference in accuracy drops between the groups. Thus, reconfiguring outcome valuation imposed a substantial cost, regardless of whether participants switched to Goal 0 or 1. Lastly, to further examine the difference in switch costs between groups, we fitted an analogous GLMM to Block 4 trial-level accuracy. Consistent with the lack of switch cost difference, there was no effect of group, but only a main effect of stimulus iterations (b= 0.92,SE= 0.09,z= 10.72,p< .001, OR = 2.50, 95% CI [2.12, 2.96]; Supplementary Table 4). However, a significant two-way interaction suggests that participants switching to Goal 1 (E0) exhibited a steeper learning slope than those switching to Goal 0 (E1) (b= 0.37,SE= 0.17,z= 2.14,p= .032, OR = 1.44, 95% CI [1.03, 2.01]). This indicates that learning under Goal 0 in Block 4 did exhibit a learning deficit, although its effect was too weak to significantly decrease overall accuracy. Together, the above-chance performance points to a fast valuation mechanism capable of rapidly adapting to changing goals. However, the substantial switch costs observed across both goals led us to ask whether a complementary, slower valuation mechanism also exists—one that makes the typically rewarding pursuit of Goal 1 less efficient after sustained exposure to Goal 0. In our sequence manipulation, participants learned the same goals across consecutive blocks, which we refer to as “mini-blocks”. We hypothesized that learning efficiency would incrementally improve across these mini-blocks. To test whether a slow process contributes to goal outcome valuation, we fitted an LMM model predicting accuracy from sequence group and mini-block in Set 1 and Set 2. There was no main effect of the sequence group nor a two-way interaction, however, the main effects of mini-blocks in both sets indicated a slow improvement across mini-blocks (Set 1:b= 0.042,SE= 0.010,t= 4.31,p< .001; Set 2:b= 0.070,SE= 0.012,t= 6.04,p< .001; Supplementary Table 5& 6). Specifically, in the goal-switch set (Set 2), this improvement across mini-blocks suggests the presence of a slower valuation mechanism that complements the fast valuation, regardless of whether participants switched to Goal 0 or Goal 1. Although accuracy was higher under Goal 1 (61.5%) than under Goal 0 (58.2%) in Set 2, the lack of a significant difference indicates that the initial learning impairment associated with Goal 0 decreases as slow valuation unfolds over consecutive blocks. Note that this cannot be interpreted as an effect of time on task, as performance drops in Block 4 from Block 3 when goals switch. Our early-learning findings suggest that goal-dependent learning reflects complementary fast and slow valuation mechanisms: participants rapidly adapted to changing goals, while learning efficiency improved across consecutive mini-blocks. However, the high switch cost observed in early learning prompted us to test whether in later goal-switch blocks (Blocks 8 and 11), continued practice enhances learning efficiency when facing changing goals. In Block 8, following a one-shot Goal 0 block (Block 7), the E0 group switched goals (learning under Goal 1), whereas the E1 group continued learning under Goal 0. Indeed, a trial-level GLMM predicting accuracy from sequence group, stimulus iteration, and their interaction revealed main effects of iteration (b= 1.70,SE= 0.09,z= 17.99,p< .001, OR = 5.47, 95% CI [4.55, 6.58]; Supplementary Table 7), sequence group (b= −0.64,SE= 0.18,z= −3.52,p< .001, OR = 0.53, 95% CI [0.37, 0.75]), and two-way interactions (b= −0.58,SE= 0.19,z= −3.15,p= .002, OR = 0.56, 95% CI [0.39, 0.80]), indicating the consequences of a goal switch on learning performance. By Block 11, however, we found no evidence of a switch cost in either group. Within-group comparison of accuracy between the pre-switch block (Block 10) and the post-switch block (Block 11) showed no significant decrease. Furthermore, we observed a significantly greater drop in accuracy during the early switch (Blocks 3 to 4) compared to the late switch (Blocks 10 to 11) in both the E1 group (t(35) = −3.07,p= .008, 95% CI [−0.20, −0.04], BF10= 9.11) and the E0 group (t(39) = −2.98,p= .008, 95% CI [−0.23, −0.04], BF10= 7.51; two-sided pairedt-tests). These results suggest that a stable goal-congruent outcome-reward association was trained to complement the fast goal switch. Despite the reduced switch cost, we found a performance difference between sequence groups at Block 11 (main effect of sequence group in GLMM:b= 0.46,SE= 0.18,z= 2.54,p= .011, OR = 1.58, 95% CI [1.11, 2.25]; Supplementary Table 8). We therefore examined the final block set (Set 4; Blocks 11–13) to determine whether slow valuation persists in reducing this between-group difference. An LMM predicting accuracy from sequence group, mini-block, and their interaction revealed a significant effect of mini-block (b= 0.018,SE= 0.008,t= 2.12,p= .034, 95% CI [0.001, 0.035]; Supplementary Table 9), indicating that accuracy improved across mini-blocks in the late learning stage. Importantly, the main effect of sequence group was not significant, suggesting no overall difference in accuracy between groups. The significant two-way interaction indicated that the E1 group, learning under Goal 1, had a steeper increase in accuracy across mini-blocks than the E0 group, learning under Goal 0 (b= −0.051,SE= 0.017,t= −3.03,p= .002, 95% CI [0.018, 0.084]). This finding confirmed that slow valuation persists in the late learning stage, reducing the initial learning difference across groups. Finally, in addition to evaluating adaptation across learning blocks, we assessed whether practice mitigated switch costs during one-shot Goal 0 blocks (Blocks 7 and 14), in which the goal reminder appeared only once at the beginning of a block and thus placed higher demands on internal goal maintenance. Within each sequence group, we tested the interaction between trial-level learning slopes and goal switch. For the E0 group, which experienced an early goal switch from Goal 1 to Goal 0, the interaction was significant (β= 0.38,SE= 0.16,z= 2.31,p= .021; Supplementary Table 10). This reflects a marked goal-switch cost during early learning that was absent at the late stage (Fig. 3A). By contrast, the E1 group, which underwent a late goal-switch, exhibited no such interaction (β= 0.02,SE= 0.18,z= 0.11,p= .911; Supplementary Table 11), showing stable learning slopes across stages. This confirms that practice accrued by the E1 group effectively counteracted the goal-switch cost at the later stage. Experiment 2 behavioral performance.A)Stimulus-action learning performance. Left: Block-level mean choice accuracy across groups. Right: Mean accuracy across stimulus iterations. Error bars: 95% CI. Red dashed line: chance level (33.3%); Grey dashed line: 80% accuracy.B)Reward collection (RC) performance. Left: Block-level RC accuracy (d′) across groups. Right: Median RC reaction time across stimulus iterations. Error bars: 95% CI. Red dashed line: 250 ms; Grey dashed line: 800 ms. Together, these findings indicate that slow valuation continues to enhance performance in the later stages of learning. By establishing stable, goal-congruent outcome–reward associations, extended practice complements fast goal switching, ultimately mitigating goal-switch costs across both learning and one-shot blocks. Having shown that practice mitigates initial learning inefficiencies under Goal 0 and goal-switch cost in stimulus–action mappings, we next asked whether this pattern reflects a systematic change in outcome processing efficiency, measured by reward collection (RC). We first examined the goal-switch sets (Set 2 and 4) to determine whether switching to Goal 0 incurs a higher cost (Fig. 3Bleft). An LMM predicting each block’s RCd′showed significant main effects of block set (b= 0.57,SE= 0.10,t= 5.52,p< .001, 95% CI [0.37, 0.78]; Supplementary Table 12), mini-block (b= 0.42,SE= 0.06,t= 6.54,p< .001, 95% CI [0.29, 0.54]), and two-way interaction between block set and mini-blocks (b= −0.48,SE= 0.13,t= −3.74,p< .001, 95% CI [−0.72, −0.23]), revealing practice improved outcome processing in both sequence groups. Furthermore, a significant two-way interaction between block set and sequence group emerged (b= −0.50,SE= 0.21,t= −2.41,p= .016, 95% CI [−0.91, −0.09]). Follow-up simple-effects analyses showed that average RC accuracy across mini-blocks differed only in the early stage between groups, with significantly higher performance in the E0 group learning under Goal 1 over the E1 group learning under Goal 0 in Set 2 (Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means: Δ = 0.389,SE= 0.178,t(162) = 2.19,p= .030), but not in Set 4. Consistent with stimulus-action learning, the results showed that outcome processing accuracy under Goal 0 also improved with practice. Next, we tested within-group switch costs in outcome processing accuracy (d′). Indeed, early in learning (Set 1 to Set 2), switching goals led to significantly lowerd′in both the E1 group (Goal 1 to Goal 0:M= 3.54 vs. 2.65; two-sided pairedt-test:t(35) = 2.96,p= .006, 95% CI [0.28, 1.50],d= 0.66, BF10= 7.06) and the E0 group (Goal 0 to Goal 1:M= 3.49 vs. 3.15;t(39) = 2.07,p= .045, 95% CI [0.01, 0.68],d= 0.37, BF10= 1.17). However, unlike stimulus-action learning, where late-stage switch costs were absent, switching from Set 3 to Set 4 still loweredd′for the E1 group (Goal 0 to Goal 1:M= 4.01 vs. 3.77;t(35) = 2.51,p= .017, 95% CI [0.05, 0.43],d= 0.56, BF10= 2.71), but not for the E0 group (Goal 1 to Goal 0:M= 3.77 vs. 3.59;t(39) = 1.78,p= .083, 95% CI [−0.03, 0.39],d= 0.32, BF10= 0.71), with no significant difference in the switch cost between the groups. This residual cost in the E1 group may reflect the preceding one-shot Goal 0 block (Block 7), which reinforced the Goal 0 representation and increased the cost of switching back to Goal 1. Conversely, an LMM predicting outcome processing speed (RC RT) from block set, mini-block, and sequence group revealed significant main effects only for block set (b= −0.32,SE= 0.04,t= −8.92,p< .001, 95% CI [−0.39, −0.25]) and mini-block (b= −0.16,SE= 0.02,t= −7.11,p< .001, 95% CI [−0.20, −0.11]; Supplementary Table 13), with no significant main effect of sequence group or interactions (ps ≥ .074), reflecting a general practice-induced acceleration in response execution across both groups. Finally, we evaluated within-group changes in the RC RT difference across goal switches. Across both early (Set 1 to Set 2) and late (Set 3 to Set 4) goal switches, we found no significant change (ps ≥ .586, BF10≤ 0.20) across switches, except that the E0 group exhibited a significant acceleration when switching from Goal 0 to Goal 1 in the early stage (M= 0.01 vs. −0.13;t(39) = 2.26,p= .030, 95% CI [0.01, 0.26],d= 0.45, BF10= 1.64, two-sided pairedt-test). Together, these findings demonstrate that extended practice improves both the accuracy and speed of goal-congruent outcome evaluation, especially in overcoming the initial cost of processing Goal 0 outcomes; this improvement raises the critical question of whether outcome processing directly drives the efficiency of stimulus–action learning. To test whether accurate outcome valuation supports stimulus–action learning, we next examined how participants’ trial-by-trial outcome processing related to their choice performance. We hypothesized that an individual’s outcome collection behavior reflects their internal goals (e.g., either collecting outcome +1 or withholding collection for outcome +0 was classified as having Goal 1 as the internal goal). To formalize this, we quantified goal alignment as “instructed goal occupancy” — defined as the proportion of trials on which a participant’s inferred internal goal matched the instructed goal of the block. A three-way GLMM predicting choice accuracy revealed no significant interaction among instructed goal occupancy, goal-switch block (Block 4 vs. 11), and stimulus iteration. However, instructed goal occupancy interacted significantly with stimulus iteration (β= 3.888,SE= 0.0.541,z= 7.183,p< .001; Supplementary Table 14), indicating that higher goal occupancy was associated with steeper learning curves. This aligns with the expectation that synchronizing internal representations with instructed goals facilitates learning valid stimulus–action–outcome associations. We next asked whether this goal alignment also predicts the speed of outcome processing. An LMM predicting block-level RC RT from instructed goal occupancy (inferred from outcome key presses), goal switch sets (Set 2 vs. 4), and stimulus-action learning accuracy, showed that RC RT was significantly faster with higher instructed/correct goal proportion (β= −1.036,SE= 0.265,t= −3.911,p< .001), higher accuracy (β= −1.397,SE= 0.161,t= −8.658,p< .001) and in later block sets (β= −0.186,SE= 0.041,t= −4.528,p< .001; Supplementary Table 15). Although there was no three-way interaction, instructed goal occupancy interacted reliably with block set (β= −1.493,SE= 0.527,t= −2.833,p= .005). Interestingly, follow-up estimated marginal means showed that RC RT decreased more strongly across block sets only among participants with high instructed-goal occupancy (b= −0.467,SE= 0.087,t(442.35) = −5.360,p< .001), whereas no reliable change was observed among those with low instructed-goal occupancy. Taken together, these results show that with practice, greater goal alignment was associated with increasingly faster outcome processing, marking a transition from effortful goal reconfiguration early in learning toward more efficient goal-switching after extended practice. The behavioral results in Experiment 2 suggest that goal-dependent learning involves both rapid alignment with instructed goals and slower adjustment of outcome-reward properties. We next used a reinforcement learning (RL) framework to determine whether these dynamics could be dissociated computationally and to characterize their contribution to individual differences in learning (Fig. 4A). Specifically, we aimed to examine whether the subjective outcome valuation is governed by two components: (1) afast componentreflecting executive control that switches goal representations across block sets, and (2) aslow componentcapturing the gradual updating of associations between outcomes and their reward properties (positive vs. negative, with initial association set by prior experience; operating within a block set). In summary, rapid alignment with the instructed goal supported flexible adaptation following goal switches, but initially incurred a switch cost that diminished with practice. In parallel, the rate of outcome-reward updating (γ) modulated learning across both early and late stages and was positively associated with accelerated outcome processing. Together, these results suggest that a fast component governs the flexible updating of goal representations, whereas a slow component stabilizes value representations to support automated execution. Human goal-dependent learning exhibits great flexibility. Beyond adapting to abstract and novel goals (McDougle et al., 2022;Molinaro & Collins, 2023), our results showed that this flexibility extends to counterintuitive goals (pursuing +0 over +1), consistent with prior work (Pan et al., 2025;Shi et al., 2026). However, this flexibility in fast goal-dependent valuation is not perfect, and increases with more exposure to the same goal. Indeed, we found that initial learning was less efficient under Goal 0 than under Goal 1, suggesting that overriding the default tendency to pursue standard rewarding outcomes (+1) imposes additional cognitive demands. In addition to this fast flexible process allowing us to rapidly learn from changing goals, we additionally observed slower dynamics. Specifically, repeatedly pursuing the same goal improved performance; in particular, it attenuated the initial learning inefficiency under the counterintuitive Goal 0. Consistent with the existence of a slow process that strengthens our valuation of a repeatedly pursued goal, we found that goal switching incurred a substantial cost on learning, regardless of switching to Goal 0 or Goal 1. The cost of switching to Goal 1 was particularly striking given participants’ strong default tendency to pursue Goal 1 in Experiment 1: three consecutive blocks of pursuing Goal 0 led to a strong impairment in subsequently learning from Goal 1. While switching costs are well documented in the task-switching literature, where changing tasks or response rules typically impairs performance (Monsell, 2003;Robbins, 2007), our findings differ from typical rule switching. Specifically, in our case, the goal switch doesn’t impact the rules the participant follows to make stimulus-action choices (as those are learned); instead, it impacts how outcomes are interpreted. We showed that switching the goal that guides outcome evaluation impairs goal-directed learning. In addition to a fast goal valuation process, enabling rapid new goal pursuit, and a slower one, enabling adjustment across repetitions of the same block, we additionally found evidence for slower dynamics across the whole task, whereby effects in the first half of the experiment decreased or disappeared in the second part. In particular, the effect of Goal 0 vs. Goal 1 largely (though not completely) disappeared. Similarly, the learning cost incurred after a goal switch was markedly reduced and absent at later stages of learning. Goal 0 evaluation and Goal switching therefore became more efficient with experience, even when the newly instructed goal conflicted with the previously established one. This practice-driven improvement reflects a slow establishment of stable, goal-congruent outcome–reward associations that complement the rapid goal-switch process; crucially, in a form of meta-learning, participants became more effective at retrieving previously learned outcome-reward associations from Goal cues. This practice-dependent stabilization of goal representations was also corroborated by outcome processing speed (measured via RC RT). Participants with high goal alignment (a strong match between their internal and instructed goals)) exhibited a pronounced acceleration in RC RT over time, whereas those with low goal alignment showed no reliable change. In line with prior work in goal-dependent automaticity (Verplanken & Aarts, 1999;Aarts & Dijksterhuis, 2000), this suggests that practice strengthens efficient binding between current goals and their corresponding outcome-reward mappings, enabling even initially slow-updating individuals to flexibly adapt. To dissect the cognitive mechanisms underlying this phenomenon, we developed a computational framework that incorporates complementary fast and slow valuation processes to account for goal-dependent learning under changing and opposing goals. Although a model integrating both processes best captured group-level behavior, our model comparison revealed substantial heterogeneity in individual goal-dependent valuation. This heterogeneity reflects varying efficiencies in the fast and slow processes, leading to differences in individuals’ susceptibility to prior experience. For instance, some learners exhibited rapid goal-switching that quickly aligned with instructed goals (best captured by the RL-based and RL-S models), while some were effective at forming goal-congruent outcome-reward associations (best captured by the RL-based and Goal RL models). Crucially, an initial susceptibility to prior experience did not impose a permanent limit on performance, as early inefficiencies can be compensated for by the slower learning mechanism. Consequently, two individuals may ultimately achieve equally successful goal-dependent learning, even if they differ substantially in how much prior experience influenced their behavior during early practice. Furthermore, our finding of stabilization in goal-dependent learning aligns closely with prefrontal-striatal modulation frameworks from neuroscience studies (Terra et al., 2020;Gore et al., 2023).Koszeghy and Passecker (2026)posited a dual mechanism underlying goal-directed behavior: fast switching via direct matrix projections and slower, learning-based adaptation via a striosome-dopamine pathway. In early learning, goal switching necessitates slower adaptation via prefrontal cortex (PFC)-modulated striosomal compartments to establish new goal-dependent outcome-reward associations. Following extended practice, the PFC can exploit direct matrix projections to execute rapid switching over these stabilized mappings. This physiological distinction accounts for late-stage learning dynamics, where most participants switch effectively between opposing goals regardless of initial learning discrepancies. Future neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies could leverage this experimental paradigm and computational modeling framework to delineate the precise mechanisms by which the PFC coordinates both striosome-mediated learning and direct matrix projections. Our computational framework also provides a principled approach to disambiguate whether initial goal adaptation failures stem from poor goal-switch control (Goal RL), outcome sensitivity (RL-S), or a combination of both (Goal RL-S). The behavioral heterogeneity captured by our model converges with evidence that working memory constraints (limiting goal-switch control) (Molinaro & Collins, 2023) or outcome sensitivity (intrinsic outcome preference) can affect outcome valuation (Zhu et al., 2025;Shi et al., 2026). Future work combining this paradigm with secondary measures (e.g., working memory batteries or outcome-preference questionnaires) and clinical populations could test whether these computational phenotypes characterize meaningful individual differences in goal-dependent learning. Finally, our observed practice-dependent attenuation of experience-driven biases parallels research on overcoming Pavlovian biases, which are traditionally viewed as automatic and hardwired. Although evidence for overwriting Pavlovian biases through cognitive training is mixed (Ereira et al., 2021;Schurr et al., 2024),Fleming et al. (2025)showed that practice reduces Pavlovian bias only when paired with high-conflict training. Our task design incorporated alternating, opposing goals, mirroring key elements of high-conflict regimes (albeit without a separate control condition). Crucially, our claim is limited to an attenuation of prior influences rather than the lasting bias reduction achieved through multi-day training. Because our experiment was restricted to a single one-hour session, it remains unclear whether these improvements would persist on subsequent days. Future research should systematically vary learning curricula and utilize multi-day practices to assess the durability of this effect. In conclusion, our findings showed how complementary fast and slow goal-dependent valuation processes enable extended practice to overcome constraints imposed by prior experience or limited cognitive control, ultimately establishing flexible goal pursuit. Furthermore, the proposed novel computational framework allows future research to pinpoint distinct computational phenotypes across individuals by examining the dynamic interplay among multiple valuation mechanisms. A total of 300 participants completed Experiment 1 online through Prolific (151 female; age:M= 27.8,SD= 6.11). We recruited 50 participants for each goal pair. Seventeen participants were excluded based on predefined criteria: excessive missing trials (more than 5 consecutive missing trials or 10 missing trials in a block), more than 15 repeated responses, and fast average response times (mean lower than 300ms), yielding a final sample of 283 participants. In both experiments, we applied the elbow method to identify the exclusion threshold. In Experiment 2, a total of 126 participants participated online (73 female; age:M= 26.7,SD= 7.0): 54 were recruited from the undergraduate participant pool at the University of California, Berkeley, and 72 were recruited via Prolific. We excluded 47 participants who did not reach 50% accuracy across the practice and learning phases, and an additional three participants who failed to recognize the goal outcome on the questionnaire following one-shot blocks. The final sample consisted of 76 participants (n= 40 in sequence group E0;n= 36 in sequence group E1). In both experiments, all participants provided informed consent online. Undergraduates received partial course credit as compensation, while Prolific participants were compensated at a rate of $12 per hour (10 min in Experiment 1; 1 h in Experiment 2). All experiments started with an informed consent form and ended with a demographic survey. The study procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Berkeley. In Experiment 1, participants went through a brief introduction to the task, explaining that they needed to learn the associations between 2 stimuli and 3 actions by trial and error. Participants were then told that“The game’s rules have been lost. Please try to figure out how to play on your own by pressing keys after each image and observing the outcomes.”(Supplementary Fig. 6), followed by a self-determined block. Afterwards, they rated in a brief survey their preference for each outcome and the strategy that best describes the rule they used to match the images with keys in the game. Participants were then told that “The rules of the game have been found. Your job is to try to obtain a specific goal.” and then finished with an instructed block with an explicit instructed goal and non-goal. Experiment 1 comprised two blocks of 26 trials each (13 iterations × 2 stimuli). Each trial began with the possible outcome (1,800 ms), followed by stimulus presentation (1,500 ms), feedback (1,500 ms), and an inter-trial fixation cross (500 ms). On average, participants completed the task in approximately 10 minutes. Experiment 2 began with a brief instruction of the task, explaining that they needed to learn the associations between 6 stimuli and 3 actions by trial and error and collect the goal outcome with a separate key press. Participants then went through a brief practice round, where they learned the associations between 2 stimuli and 3 actions with 13 iterations per stimulus. Both the instruction and practice round used a yellow and a blue solid circle as goal and non-goal outcomes, respectively, to avoid any prior practice on specific goal outcomes from influencing the main learning blocks. After the practice round, participants started the learning phase, where they experienced one of two goal sequences (Fig. 2B). Participants were assigned to one of two sequence structures consisting of four 3-block sets interspersed with one-shot Goal 0 blocks at Blocks 7 and 14. The E1 (Early 1 Late 0) group completed sets in a Goal 1, 0, 0, and 1 order (Blocks 1–3, 4–6, 8–10, and 11–13, respectively). Conversely, the E0 group followed an inverted set sequence (Goals 0, 1, 1, and 0), with the one-shot Goal 0 blocks at Blocks 7 and 14. Crucially, in each block, participants needed to re-learn different pairs of stimulus-action mappings, ensuring that outcome processing can be dissociated from stimulus-action learning throughout the whole experiment. After each one-shot block, participants reported the correct goal outcome in the previous one-shot block in a short questionnaire. We excluded participants who answered incorrectly from further analysis (3 out of 126). Overall, Experiment 2 consisted of 14 learning blocks (5 iterations * 6 stimuli = 30 trials per block). Each trial began with the possible goal outcome (1,800 ms), followed by stimulus presentation (1,500 ms), feedback (1,500 ms), and an inter-trial fixation cross (500 ms). Importantly, 88.7% of participants in the G ≫ Non-G group were from Goal +1 and Goal Green types, suggesting that +1 and green carry strong positive associations from prior experience. However, individual preferences alone cannot fully explain the observed learning differences. We found no evidence of performance differences between the G ≳ Non-G group and groups that favored non-goal outcomes (slightly favor non-goal:t(279) = 1.293,p= .568, BF10= 0.332; strongly favor non-goal:t(279) = 0.378,p= .982, BF10= 0.119). Notably, the G ≳ Non-G group consisted primarily of participants in Goal Yellow and Goal Blue types—outcomes that typically lack strong positive or negative associations. This pattern may reflect the influence of our task instructions, where participants were told to “figure out the lost rule.” This framing may have led participants to infer underlying design principles, making their learning dependent on objective prior associations rather than purely subjective preferences. Specifically, +1 and green are objectively associated with positivity in real-world contexts, while yellow and blue lack such clear associations. To isolate the effects of practice between blocks, we conducted a control experiment using a Goal 1 task with two instructed blocks, where participants received complete instructions throughout the entire task. We compared this fully instructed (I-I) design with the Goal 1 group in the original self-determined + instructed (SD-I) design. An LMM showed a three-way interaction effect among block (Block 1 vs. Block 2), task type (I-I vs. SD-I), and iteration (log-transformed) (β= 0.79 ± 0.29,z= 2.8,p< .01;Table 1). This suggests that the rate of learning varied depending on both task type and block. Specifically, block/practice effect alone cannot account for the behavioral patterns observed in our main SD-I task (Fig. 8B). Even when pursuing the same outcome across blocks, participants still required cognitive effort to re-engage controlled processing when transitioning from self-determined to explicit instructions in the second block, which is also suggested by the strong evidence of the differences in response time between blocks in SD-I (BF10= 56.6, with median posteriorδ= −0.525, 95% CI [−0.835, −0.221]) but not in fully instructed (BF10= 0.265, with median posteriorδ= 0.143, 95% CI [−0.146, 0.434]). This implies that the instructional manipulation influences the observed learning differences, even in Goal 1. title: Mapping the Fragment-Binding Landscape of SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 for Antiviral Drug Discovery
author: Shi, X.; Wang, Q.; Dong, D.; Xu, M.; Al Busaidi, F.; Bowler, M. W.; Haider, S.; Kozielski, F.
text: Non-structural protein 14 (nsp14) is a bifunctional coronavirus drug target, combining a 3’-to-5’ exoribonuclease domain with an N7-methyltransferase domain. Proof-of-concept data have demonstrated beneficial effects in animal models upon inhibition. Using microscale thermophoresis and X-ray crystallography, we screened full-length nsp14 for fragment hits and developed SAR-by-catalogue analogues with five-to eight-fold improved affinity. Several scaffolds showed pronounced overlap between distinct pockets, complicating structure-based optimisation. Analysis of mutational frequencies across over 14 million SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences identified nsp14 residues with markedly high and very low mutation rates, highlighting sites best suited to pan-coronavirus inhibitor design. Combining these data with all 19 publicly known fragment- and ligand-binding regions on nsp14, most of which have never been directly compared, we introduce a systematic site-naming system and rank every site by its potential for future structure-based development. Weighing criteria include proof-of-principle inhibitor data, cross-coronavirus conservation, mutation frequency, the number of fragments bound per site, and susceptibility to crystallographic artefacts from symmetry mates. This ranked, unified binding-site atlas resolves which of the many previously reported nsp14 sites merit prioritisation, providing a practical resource for future coronavirus antiviral drug development. More than 779 million confirmed Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) cases have been recorded worldwide by the World Health Organization (WHO) since the start of the pandemic (World Health Organization, 2026). COVID-19 is caused by a positive-sense single-stranded RNA (+ssRNA) virus named Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). SARS-CoV-2 consists of four structural proteins, sixteen non-structural proteins and six accessory proteins (Marianoet al., 2020;Briggset al., 2023). Non-structural proteins are important in the synthesis of negative-sense single-stranded RNA (-ssRNA), the replication of +ssRNA and the transcription of -ssRNA to subgenomic messenger RNA. One of the key proteins in the Replication Transcription Complex (RTC) is nsp14, a bifunctional protein, which contains both 3’-5’ exoribonuclease (ExoN) and N7-methyltransferase (N7-MTase) activities (Minskaiaet al., 2006;Chenet al., 2009). The ExoN domain can remove mismatched nucleotides from the 3’-end of RNA following viral RNA replication (Minskaiaet al., 2006;Bouvetet al., 2012). The activity of the nsp14 ExoN domain has been shown to be enhanced by the binding of nsp10 (Hsuet al., 2021). The N7-MTase domain transfers the methyl group from its substrate S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) to the 7thposition of guanine of viral mRNA (Chenet al., 2009;Ghosh and Lima, 2010), generating the by-product S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) during the reaction. The viral methylated RNA cap can increase the stability of the mRNA as well as the chances of the virus of escaping from the host immune system (Kakavandiet al., 2023). Nsp14 is considered a potential drug target, as its inhibition disrupts virus replication (Subissiet al., 2014) and ExoN active site mutants result in non-viable virus (Ogandoet al., 2020). N7-MTase mutants have also been shown to affect nsp14 translational inhibition activity (Hsuet al., 2021). The understanding of nsp14 function was further advanced by the determination of its structure. Various SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 crystal structures and cryo-electron microscopy reconstructions are available including unbound nsp14 (Czarnaet al., 2022;Imprachimet al., 2023), the nsp14 ExoN domain in complex with nsp10 (Linet al., 2021;Moelleret al., 2022), the nsp14 N7-MTase domain (Kotturet al., 2023), a nsp10-nsp14-RNA ternary complex (Liuet al., 2021) and nsp14 as part of the RTC (Yanet al., 2021). To develop nsp14 inhibitors one of the strategies is to disrupt the binding between nsp14 and nsp10 by targeting the binding interface (Arabi-Jeshvaghaniet al., 2023). As SARS and SARS-CoV-2 N7-MTase domains do not contain the canonical Rossman fold, the N7-MTase was selectively targeted with inhibitors (Ferronet al., 2017;Czarnaet al., 2022). Several bisubstrate inhibitors, targeting both SAM and RNA binding sites, were designed and developed (Ahmed-Belkacemet al., 2022;Junget al., 2022;Georgiouet al., 2026). A total of 72 fragment hits has been identified using fragment-based screening by X-ray crystallography (Imprachimet al., 2023). Fluorescence-based assays (Basuet al., 2021;Bobiļevaet al., 2021;Kasprzyket al., 2021;Ronaet al., 2022;Cokeret al., 2026) and mass spectrometry (Pearsonet al., 2021) have also been employed to identify inhibitors. In this project, nsp14, and its individual ExoN and N7-MTase domains, were screened for fragment hits using microscale thermophoresis (MST). Subsequently, the initial hits were subjected to X-ray crystallography and further investigated with orthogonal biophysical techniques to obtain estimates of their Kdvalues. An initial Structure-Activity Relationship (SAR)-by-catalogue study was conducted by testing commercially available fragment hit analogues for binding. Here we report the identification and characterisation of novel fragment hits targeting nsp14. An initial SAR-by-catalogue study using X-ray crystallography allowed us to conduct a detailed analysis of binding modes. Through a combination of various criteria, all currently known binding sites on both functional domains of nsp14 were ranked for their potential as real binding sites. Various nsp14 constructs were expressed and purified for thermal shift assays (TSA), MST and structural studies followed by fragment soaking. For fragment screening using MST binding assays as well as the estimation of Kdvalues, three nsp14 constructs containing histags were purified. SUMO was also purified and served as a control. Full-length nsp14 (nsp141-527) cDNA was subcloned into ppSUMO-2 resulting in an expression vector coding for an N-terminal histag and a SUMO fusion protein, an Ulp1 cleavage site and, forE. coliexpression, codon-optimised cDNA coding for nsp14. The resulting plasmid was transformed into Tuner (DE3)E. colicells and incubated on an agar plate supplemented with 50 μg/ml kanamycin at 37°C overnight. A single colony was picked from the plate and added into 30 ml TB medium supplemented with 50 μg/ml kanamycin. The small culture was then placed in a shaker-incubator at 37°C overnight. Then, the small culture was separately added into six 2 L Erlenmeyer flasks each containing 1 L TB medium supplemented with 50 μg/ml kanamycin. The cultures were placed in a shaker-incubator at 37°C until their OD600reached 0.8. The cultures were then induced with 0.1 mM IPTG and incubated at 20°C for 24 h. The culture was harvested by centrifugation at 4000 rpm (Avanti® J-E centrifuge from Beckman Coulter, rotor: JLA 16.250) for 20 min at 4°C. The cell pellet was resuspended with 200 ml 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.4, 300 mM NaCl and 10 mM imidazole, frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C. For purification, the cell pellet was thawed and sonicated for ten rounds on ice. The lysate was centrifuged for 90 min at 20000 rpm, 4°C (Avanti® J-E centrifuge from Beckman Coulter, rotor: JLA 25.50). The supernatant was collected and loaded into a 5 mL HisTrap FF crude column (Cytiva) pre-equilibrated with buffer A (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.8, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM Imidazole and 1 mM PMSF). The column was then washed with 50 column volumes (CVs) of buffer B (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.8, 300 mM NaCl and 30 mM Imidazole). Protein bound to Ni-NTA was eluted with buffer C (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.8, 500 mM NaCl and 500 mM Imidazole), collected in 2 ml fractions and the fractions were analysed by SDS-PAGE. The fractions containing nsp14 were combined and quantified using the Bradford reagent. The nsp14 ExoN domain (ExoN1-289) and the N7-MTase domain (nsp14283-527) were expressed and purified following methods described previously (Kozielskiet al., 2022). SUMO was a purification by-product when cleaved off by Ulp1 protease before the second Ni-NTA column as it retains its histag and binds to Ni-NTA. It was subsequently eluted with imidazole to yield pure SUMO for subsequent control measurements. Nsp14 was expressed, purified and crystallised as previously described (Imprachimet al., 2023), with minor modifications. The nsp147-527cDNA was subcloned into expression vector ppSUMO-2. BL21-Gold(DE3) cells (Agilent Technologies) and TB modified medium (Melford) with 50 µg/ml Kanamycin were used for expressing nsp147-527at 37°C. When the OD600reached 0.6-1.0, IPTG was added to the culture to a final concentration of 1 mM. After incubating at 220 rpm at 18°C for 20 to 24 h, the culture was centrifuged at 4°C at 8000 g for 20 min. Cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 10 mM Imidazole, 5% Glycerol, 1 mM TCEP and 1 mM PMSF) and flash frozen in liquid nitrogen. The cell suspension was thawed and sonicated on ice 14 times for 30 sec to break the cells. Between each sonication cycle, the cell suspension was placed for 1 min on ice. The sample was then centrifuged at 4°C at 20000 rpm for 1 h. The supernatant was loaded into a 5 ml HisTrap FF column (Cytiva) previously equilibrated with lysis buffer. The column was connected to a Biorad FPLC and washed with 50 CVs of wash buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Imidazole, 5% Glycerol and 1 mM TCEP), followed by 15 CVs of 1stcolumn elution buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 300 mM Imidazole, 5% Glycerol and 1 mM TCEP). Samples showing an elution peak were tested using SDS-PAGE. The samples containing nsp14 were added into a 10K MWCO SnakeSkinTMdialysis tubing with 1 mg Ulp1 for every 30 mg nsp14 and placed in 2 L dialysis buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT and 5% Glycerol) for 18 h. The sample was then loaded into a fresh HisTrap FF column. Cleaved nsp14 was eluted with six CVs of 2ndcolumn elution buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 30 mM Imidazole, 5% Glycerol and 1 mM TCEP). Gel filtration was then performed with the eluted sample as described (Imprachimet al., 2023). Fractions containing nsp14 were concentrated to 10 mg/ml for subsequent crystallisation and TSA experiments. For TSA experiments, nsp14 constructs were purified by two affinity purification steps to remove the SUMO and histidine tags. The nsp14 ExoN domain was expressed and purified as previously described (Kozielskiet al., 2022). ExoN was then pooled and cleaved overnight with Ulp1 protease supplemented with 3 mM DTT. Simultaneously, the protein was also dialysed against buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 300 mM NaCl. Thereafter, the protein was passed through the Ni-NTA column for a second time and was eluted with 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl and 20 mM imidazole. The cleaved protein, without the His-SUMO fusion tag, was captured in the flow-through, which was then pooled and dialysed for 18 h in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 300 mM NaCl. The protein was then concentrated to 2 mg/mL using an Amicon ultraconcentration device (Millipore). The N7-MTase domain (nsp14289-525) was expressed and purified as described above for nsp147-527using BL21-Rosetta2 (DE3) cells. The following buffers were used during purification. Lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.8, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole and 1 mM PMSF), 1stcolumn wash buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.8, 300 mM NaCl and 20 mM imidazole), 1stcolumn elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.8, 300 mM NaCl and 200 mM imidazole), Dialysis buffer (60 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl and 3 mM DTT), 2ndcolumn elution buffer (60 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl and 35 mM imidazole) and final buffer (60 mM HEPES pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl). To label nsp14 constructs for MST measurements, SUMO-nsp141-527, SUMO-nsp141-289and SUMO-nsp14283-527were diluted in MST assay buffer to 800 nM. The MST assay buffer for nsp141-527and nsp141-289was 50 mM NaPO4pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl and 0.05% Tween-20, and for nsp14283-527was 60 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 0.1 % PEG-8000. The Red-Tris-NTA 2ndgeneration dye was diluted to 100 nM. 50 μl nsp14 constructs were incubated with 50 μl dye on ice for 1 h and centrifuged at 4°C at 13000 rpm for 5 min. One hundred fragments were tested for binding to nsp14 constructs using the “binding check” procedure. Labelled nsp14 constructs were further diluted to 20 nM in MST assay buffer. Fragment stocks (200 mM) were diluted with MST assay buffer to either 20 mM or 10 mM. DMSO was diluted with MST assay buffer with the same 10-fold or 20-fold ratio as the fragment stock. For the target-only sample, diluted nsp14 constructs were mixed with the same volume of diluted DMSO. For the complex sample, diluted nsp14 constructs were mixed with the same volume of 20 mM or 10 mM fragments. After 30 min incubation at room temperature, the samples were then loaded into Monolith standard capillaries and measured by the Monolith NT.115 instrument. The measurements were performed under 5 - 15 sec MST on time, 100% excitation power and 40% MST power. The data was analysed using MO.Control and MO.Affinity Analysis software. Nsp147-527labelled with RED-NHS 2ndgeneration dye was used to measure the binding affinity between nsp14 constructs and fragments. Protein labelling followed the instructions in the NanoTemper Protein Labelling Kit RED-NHS 2nd Generation manual. Specifically, 100 µL 10 µM nsp147-527was buffer exchanged with the A-column in the kit to labelling buffer NHS (130 mM NaHCO3pH 8.2-8.3 and 50 mM NaCl). 90 µL 10 µM nsp147-527was then mixed with 10 µL 300 µM RED-NHS dye. After incubating for 30 min at RT in the dark, the mixture was loaded onto the B-column provided in the kit. 550 µL PBS-T (Phosphate-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20) buffer was added to the column to remove the free dye. The labelled nsp147-527was then eluted by adding 450 µL PBS-T buffer. For cysteine-directed labelling of nsp147-527, the NanoTemper Protein Labelling Kit RED-MALEIMIDE 2nd Generation was used according to the manufacturer’s protocol. 20 nM labelled nsp14 constructs were mixed with each fragment in 16 wells in 384-well microplates. Each ligand was diluted to final concentrations of 10 mM to 305 nM by a two-fold dilution series. The final concentration of nsp14 constructs in each well was 10 nM. The mixed samples were incubated at room temperature for 1 h and loaded into 16 Monolith NT.115 Premium capillaries and measured by the Monolith NT.115 instrument. The measurements were performed under 5 - 15 sec MST on time, 40% MST power, 100% excitation power for nsp14283-527and 30% excitation power for nsp147-527. As a DMSO control, 3.5µL of 14 mg/mL nsp14 and 1µL of DMSO were mixed with 95.5µL buffer A (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol and 1 mM TCEP). 10µL of 0.5 mg/mL nsp14 with 1% DMSO were loaded into Tycho capillaries and measured in triplicate. For subsequent measurements in the presence of fragments, 3.5µL of 14 mg/mL nsp14, 1µL of 200 mM fragment, and 95.5µL buffer A were mixed and loaded into Tycho capillaries and measured in triplicate. As a control, 10µL of 5 mg/mL nsp141-289, 1µL of DMSO and 89µL buffer B (50 mM HEPES pH 7.0 and 300 mM NaCl) were mixed. 10µL of 0.5 mg/mL nsp141-289with 1% DMSO were loaded into Tycho capillaries and measured in triplicate. For measurements of fragments, 10µL of 5 mg/mL nsp141-289and 1µL of 200 mM fragment were mixed with 89µL buffer B and loaded into Tycho capillaries and measured in triplicate. 5µL of 10 mg/mL nsp14289-525, 1µL of DMSO and 94µL buffer C (60 mM HEPES pH 8.0 and 500 mM NaCl) were mixed as control. 10µL of 0.5 mg/mL nsp14289-525with 1% DMSO were loaded into Tycho capillaries and measured in triplicate. 5µL of 10 mg/mL nsp14289-525, 1µL of 200 mM fragment, and 94µL buffer C were mixed and loaded into Tycho capillaries and measured in triplicate. The heating temperature increased from 35°C to 95°C in 3 min. The inflection temperature (Ti) of the proteins was automatically calculated by the Tycho NT.6 instrument following the heating process. Crystallisation drops were set up using the reported condition of 1.26 M sodium phosphate monobasic (NaH2PO4) and 0.14 M potassium phosphate dibasic (K2HPO4) using the hanging drop vapour diffusion method. Crystals appeared after 30 days at 4°C. To reduce crystal growth time and increase the crystal size, seed stock 1 was prepared with crystals from the initial drops. Seed beads (Hampton Research) were used following the reported protocol (Hampton Research, 2024), 1 µl of 5 mg/ml nsp14 was mixed with 1 µl seed stock 1. Rod clusters appeared five days after setting up drops at 18°C. These new crystals were used to prepare seed stock 2 and diluted to a 1:10 ratio resulting in seed stock 3 to reduce the number of seeds. New drops were set up by mixing 2 µl of 5 mg/ml nsp14 with 2 µl seed stock 3 and incubated at 18°C. Large single crystals were observed seven days after setting up drops. The reservoir in all wells contains 500 µl 1.26 M NaH2PO4and 0.14 M K2HPO4. Crystals were soaked with solutions containing 1.5 M NaH2PO4, 0.17 M K2HPO4and 50 mM fragments dissolved in DMSO for 1 h, then harvested with cryo-loops and flash frozen in liquid nitrogen. Fragment data were collected at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF), beamlines ID23-1 and ID23-2. Analogue data were collected at ESRF beamline ID30A-1 MASSIF-1 (Bowleret al., 2015) and Diamond Light Source (DLS) beamline I03 using unattended data collection. X-ray centring was used to locate the optimal crystal region for data collection (Svenssonet al., 2015). Images (980 to 2300) were collected with either 0.1° or 0.05° oscillation and 0.01 or 0.02 sec exposure time. Diffraction data were automatically integrated and scaled by autoPROC (Vonrheinet al., 2011), EDNA Autoprocessing, GrenADES parallelproc (Monacoet al., 2013) and XIA2_DIALS (Winter, 2010;Winnet al., 2011;Winteret al., 2018). Molecular replacement was performed using Phaser-MR (McCoyet al., 2007) from the PHENIX suite (version:1.19.2-4158-000) (Liebschneret al., 2019) and SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 (PDB entry 7QGI) was used as the search model. The models were manually refined in Coot (0.9.8.6) (Emsleyet al., 2010) while inspecting electron density and difference density maps. The structures were then refined using phenix.refine (Afonineet al., 2012). MW, ClogP and tPSA were obtained from Chemdraw, version 20.0.038 whereas the number of hydrogen bond acceptors and donors as well as the calculated solubility was obtained using the Molsoft server (https://molsoft.com/mprop/mprop.cgi). Nsp14-ligand interactions were analysed using PLIP (Protein Ligand Interaction Profiler) using the default thresholds (Schakeet al., 2025). Figures showing protein structures were generated using Open-Source PyMOL (version 2.5.0). The chemical structures of small molecules were generated in Chemical Sketch Tool (https://www.rcsb.org/chemical-sketch). Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID) is a global online database that provides genomic data for influenza viruses and coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 (https://www.gisaid.org) (Khareet al., 2021). In this study, the whole genome sequence of all uploaded SARS-CoV-2 strains was downloaded in FASTA format. The nsp14 sequences were then extracted from the dataset, and any sequences containing unknown residues (represented as ‘X’) were removed. After this filtering process, 14,246,785 NSP14 sequences remained for further analysis. To improve computational efficiency, we did not conduct a global multiple sequence alignment across all 14 million sequences. Instead, each sequence was individually aligned to the reference Wuhan/WIV04/2019 genome using Parasail (Daily, 2016), allowing for a more effective identification and quantification of mutations. In-house Python scripts were used to process the large dataset, and the mutation rate of each mutation was calculated as the total occurrence of the mutation divided by the total number of sequences. The compiled mutation data were then stored in an Excel sheet. The main criterion for ranking all described binding sites was the existence of proof-of-concept data for nsp14-targeting compounds developed by structure-based design. The second criterion was the potential impact a fragment binding to a particular site, evaluated by combining available structural information about nsp14 and its binding partners. These include the nsp14-SAH complex (PDB entry 7R2V), the nsp14-TDI-015051 complex (PDB entry 8R7B), the RTC (7EGQ), nsp14 bound with 7MeGpppG (PDB entry 7QIF) and a ternary nsp14-nsp10-RNA complex (PDB entry 7N0B). A third criterion was to assess if fragment binding sites in the nsp14 crystal are formed by nsp14 and one of its symmetry mates. We individually and visually inspected all binding sites by generating nsp14 and its symmetry mates in Coot. The availability of binding data was also evaluated. Estimates of Kdvalues from orthogonal biophysical assays for sites formed by nsp14 and a symmetry mate would indicate that these are still valid binding sites. A further criterion was the number of fragments bound per site, as many fragments binding to the same site would allow for future fragment merging and linking. In contrast, a single fragment bound to a particular site would only allow fragment growing, reducing its potential for future development. We also ranked which of the 19 binding sites on nsp14 are the most conserved between SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 coronaviruses with potential to develop pan-nsp14 inhibitors. Therefore, we carried out protein sequence alignments for these three medically relevant CoVs and calculated the conservation of the 19 binding sites. Finally, to assess which of the published nsp14-targeting fragment hits are potential Pan-Assay Interference Compounds (PAINS), the chemical structures of the fragments were extracted from the PDB entries and submitted to the following two PAINS servers:http://www.cbligand.org/PAINS/(Baell and Holloway, 2010);https://mobyle2.rpbs.univ-paris-diderot.fr/cgi-bin/portal.py#forms::FAF-Drugs4(Lagorce et al., 2015). SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 consists of two major domains connected via a central hinge region (Fig 1A). The ExoN domain is located at the N-terminus whereas the N7-MTase domain is positioned at its C-terminus. Its binding partner, the scaffolding protein nsp10, attaches to nsp14 through the ExoN domain (Fig 1B). To carry out biophysical and structural assays and experiments, a variety of nsp14 constructs covering nsp14 and its individual functional domains, ExoN and N7-MTase, were expressed and purified (Fig 1A). For fragment-based screening via MST, nsp14 constructs containing an N-terminal histidine and SUMO tags were purified. SUMO was subsequently used as a control to exclude false positives that were identified in the assay by binding to SUMO rather than nsp14. TSA and crystallisation experiments were conducted using the cleaved nsp14 construct, lacking the histag and SUMO fusion. A) Bar diagram of nsp14 showing the two major ExoN (blue) and N7-MTase (magenta) domains connected via the central hinge region (purple). B) Overlay of the crystal structure of unbound nsp14 (PDB entry 7QGI) and the ExoN-nsp10 complex (PDB entry 7MC5). The three zinc finger domains are shown in light yellow, nsp10 is coloured in orange. C) Summary of MST screening results using full-length nsp14, N7-MTase and ExoN domains. The fragments listed on the chart were those identified in the binding check mode with three distinct nsp14 constructs. The fragments that were also found to bind to SUMO are shown in black and excluded from the list of positive hits. Fragment hits binding to nsp14 constructs but not to SUMO are highlighted in red. One hundred fragments from the Maybridge Ro3 fragment library were investigated by MST for binding to nsp14. Thirty-eight initial hits were identified for nsp14, 65 hits for the ExoN domain and 46 hits for the N7-MTase (Fig 1C). Considering that these constructs were expressed with a SUMO fusion, which may also bind fragments, we conducted a second round of MST experiments using purified SUMO. Subsequently, the hits binding to SUMO were excluded from the first-round screening results. Eight fragments were identified to bind to nsp14, 15 hits to bind to ExoN and 15 hits for N7-MTase. Some of the fragments showed binding activity for more than one nsp14 construct. For example,12H9bound to all three nsp14 constructs and12A9and12D8were found to bind to nsp14 and the ExoN domain, indicating that their shared binding site is localised in the ExoN domain. In total, 27 potential unique hits were identified with a success rate of 27%. All remaining fragment hits from MST were subsequently subjected to nsp14 crystal soaking and data collection at ESRF beamlines ID23-1 and ID23-2. We also recollected data for nsp14 in the absence of any fragment, which served for comparison between unbound and fragment bound electron density. This was necessary as we did not use PanDDA for automated fragment identification and did not collect diffraction data for the ground state. Out of 27 initial MST fragment hits, six resulted in nsp14-fragment complexes, a drop in the success rate to 6% (Table S1). The chemical structures of the six fragment hits are shown inFig 2A. Data collection and refinement statistics for the nsp14-fragment complexes are summarized in Table S2. A) Chemical structures of the six fragment hits targeting SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 identified by MST and x-ray crystallography. B) Fragment binding sites on nsp14 and residues involved in the formation of these sites. Residues coloured in orange are from symmetry mates that are implicated in forming the pocket and residues shaded in green establish hydrogen bond interactions. The six chemically divergent fragment hits bind to five distinct binding sites on nsp14, with three of those being located in the ExoN domain and two being in the MTase domain (Fig 2B). We named these sites according to the location within the two domains, ExoN and MTase. Fragments12A2and12F3bind to the ExoN 1 site, whereas12D8,12H4, 13C4 and 12F3are located in the ExoN 2 site. The only fragment hit binding to the ExoN 3 site was13A3whereas12F3exclusively binds in the MTase 2 and MTase 10 site of the MTase domain. Binding of12A2to nsp14 induces a space group shift fromP212121toP21and is in the same location and conformation in both nsp14 molecules of the asymmetric unit (AU).
