Orthogonal assays such as TSA and MST were employed to detect possible stabilisation of nsp14 or its domains and to estimate the strength of binding between nsp14 and fragment hits. We first measured TSA data for nsp14, ExoN and MTase domains in the absence and presence of DMSO. Whereas DMSO has no influence on the stability of nsp14, we observed an increase of ExoN stability in the presence of DMSO (47.4 ± 0.1°C versus 48.0 ± 0.1°C) and a slight decrease of MTase stability. However, there is no systematic trend of protein stabilisation in the presence of fragment hits for any of the nsp14 constructs tested, similar to our previous TSA experiments for other SARS-CoV-2 proteins (Table S4). To initiate an initial SAR-by-catalogue study, we ordered commercially available fragment analogues for five of the six fragment hits. In total, we purchased 80 analogues and five additional analogues that were selected based on merging of fragments binding to the same site (Table S5). The majority of commercial analogues, 42 in total, belonged to the13A3scaffold. For the other hits, four to eleven analogues could be obtained, and no analogues were available for12D8. All analogues were subjected to crystal soaking, data collection and structure determination (summarized in Table S2). Many13A3analogues had a clear impact on crystal quality. After soaking, crystals with 21 distinct analogues did not diffract anymore or showed weak diffraction, even after varying analogue concentration and soaking times. For the remaining 21 analogues, only two,3A23and1G7,could be identified as analogue hits (Figure S1A). Analogues for hits12A2,12H4and those representing merged analogues of two distinct fragment hits did not bind to nsp14. For13C4, one out of 11 analogues did bind to nsp14 with a Kdof 1.07 + 0.57 mM, an approximately five-fold improvement over the original hit (Figure S1B). For fragment hit12F3, six out of 11 analogues did bind to nsp14, with the best analogue showing an estimated Kdvalue of 0.44 ± 0.37 mM, an almost eight-fold improvement compared to12F3. Rationally explaining their binding activity, even in the presence of structural data, was impossible as analogues did bind to varying pockets on nsp14 with a preference for the ExoN 2 and MTase 1 sites although other sites were also frequented such as ExoN 1, ExoN 7, MTase 2, MTase 8 and MTase 10 (Figure 7,Figure 8). In conclusion, although five-to eight-fold improvements in affinity of analogues from mM to uM could fairly easily be achieved by SAR-by-catalogue, challenges were crystal stability in the presence of certain analogue classes and “binding site hopping”, significantly complicating our SAR interpretation. Estimates of Kdvalues were reported because some data points could be missing at high ligand concentrations in the Kdfit curves (Figure S4). Certain data points at high ligand concentrations (5-10 mM) had to be removed as aggregation was observed in the measurements. For binding affinity measurements with fragments that typically exhibit mM range Kdvalues, a ligand concentration greater than 10 mM would be needed to complete the Kdcurve. However, this was challenging due to the limited solubility of compounds in the MST assay buffer. Furthermore, the DMSO concentration in measurements had to be kept at a maximum of 5% (v/v) due to its effect on protein stability. As most compound stock solutions were prepared at 200 mM in 100% DMSO, 10 mM was the highest feasible final ligand concentration in most cases. In order to identify important residues in nsp14 a total of 14,246,785 sequences were extracted from the GISAID database and used in this study. Using the Wuhan/WIV04/2019 sequence as reference, the nsp14 sequences were pairwise aligned to the reference, and 3435 unique types of mutations could be identified. Mutations were observed at every residue position, ranging from rare variants detected only once to highly prevalent mutations found in over eight million sequences (Fig. 6Aand6B, Fig. S2). Among the 537 residues in nsp14, 107 residues showed a very low mutation rate that exhibited a mutation count lower than 100 from more than 14 million sequences. These residues remain highly conserved, suggesting that substitutions at these positions are rarely tolerated. For example, Phe73, Arg84, Trp86, Arg310, Asp331, Gly333, Pro335, and Tyr368, which are essential for the MTase activity in SARS-CoV (Jinet al., 2013), also remain unchanged and highly conserved in SARS-CoV-2 (Fig. 6C). A total of 25 mutations were classified as highly common, each occurring at a frequency exceeding 0.1% (Fig. 6). Among these, the three most frequent mutations were Ile42Val, Ala394Val, and Asp222Tyr. The mutant Ile42Val was detected in nearly 60% of all SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 sequences, making it the most prevalent mutation in the dataset. Ala394Val appeared in more than 20% of sequences. In this study, we used a combination of techniques to identify novel nsp14-targeting fragment hits, characterised the hits and conducted an initial SAR-by-catalogue study. At the start of this fragment screening project, structural information for SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 was not available and we turned to MST for screening. Later, X-ray and cryo-EM structures appeared in the literature for full-length nsp14, its individual domains, the nsp10-nsp14-RNA complex and several forms of the RTC (Linet al., 2021;Liuet al., 2021;Yanet al., 2021;Czarnaet al., 2022;Kotturet al., 2022;Moelleret al., 2022;Imprachimet al., 2023). In one study, conducting fragment-based screening via X-ray crystallography, more than 72 distinct fragment hits targeting unbound nsp14 have been described (Imprachimet al., 2023). In our approach, we employed a two-step cascade by first employing MST followed by X-ray crystallography. Our approach has a lower hit rate as we did not use PanDDA for fragment identification. Therefore, we could only identify fragment hits with clear positive electron density in the single crystal system, but miss low occupancy fragment hits, which are more difficult to spot in the single crystal system due to their incomplete electron density. A comparison of our fragment hits with those previously described (Imprachimet al., 2023) shows that these are novel hits and that there is no overlap between these two sets. Another important question was whether we were able to identify new binding sites. By overlaying all available fragment hits, we identified a new binding site, which we named the ExoN 7 site. Due to the large number of fragment hits and associated binding sites for nsp14, we suggest introducing a naming convention for the sites, based on the location of the hits on SARS-CoV-2 nsp14, either in the ExoN domain, the central hinge region or the N7-MTase domain (Figure 5and Table S6). Next, we explored whether, by comparing our fragments with those previously published (Imprachimet al., 2023), we could increase the potential for linking and merging of our new fragment hits. To investigate potential linking options, we overlaid our fragment hits binding to the ExoN domain with one representative member of previously published fragments binding in the established sites on the ExoN domain. However, the ExoN sites are located too far away from each other to be used for fragment linking. A total of 19 binding sites has been identified on nsp14. To assess their potential for further development into potent inhibitors, we established a range of criteria for evaluation (Table S7). One criterion was the identification of nsp14 inhibitors with proof-of-principle data, demonstrating inhibition in animal models. TDI-015051 is the only inhibitor to date that has shown such characteristics. It is a picomolarin vitroinhibitor against nsp14 and demonstrates antiviral efficacy in a transgenic mouse model of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Meyeret al., 2025). TDI-015051 binds near the SAH binding site in MTase 1, which also accommodates the cap analogue7MeGpppG. Interestingly, 20 distinct fragment hits bind to this site, leading us to rank this binding site first in our evaluation. An additional criterion was to relate the binding sites to the function of nsp14. For example, fragments binding at the nsp10-nsp14 interface may disrupt protein-protein interactions (ExoN 1, ExoN 2, ExoN 4 and ExoN 5), while those binding at the interface between nsp14 and RNA may interfere with protein-RNA interactions. Furthermore, fragment hits binding near the hinge region could potentially affect the conformational flexibility between the ExoN and MTase domains, such as at Hinge 1 and Hinge 2. Another criterion considered the mutation frequency of residues in SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 (Figure 6). We hypothesize that residues in binding sites with high mutation frequencies will mutate under selective pressure. For example, the ExoN 6 site, which is near the ExoN active site and contains four residues with very low mutation frequencies, was ranked higher than the ExoN 2 site, which has three residues with one of the highest mutation frequencies in nsp14. A further criterion involved a protein sequence alignment between the three medically relevant CoVs SARS, SARS-CoV-2, and MERS (Fig. S3 and Table S8). Binding sites with high sequence conservation were ranked higher than those with low sequence identity. Interestingly, the three highest-ranked binding sites also showed high sequence conservation, while the lowest-ranked sites consistently exhibited low sequence identity. Additional criteria, though considered less stringent, were also evaluated. Specifically, we assessed whether the sites represent true binding sites or if they are likely to be artifacts due to the involvement of symmetry-related molecules. Out of 19 sites, only six were formed by a combination of nsp14 and one of its symmetry mates in the crystal structure. The remaining 13 sites were determined to be “real” binding sites. We combined this criterion with the existence of orthogonal biophysical evaluations, such as MST, to support binding to a site. Estimates of Kdvalues from solution-based experiments provide further evidence of binding. Biophysical assays have been conducted for a reduced number of sites, such as ExoN 1 to ExoN 3, ExoN 7, Hinge 1, MTase 1, and MTase 2. The remaining sites require further evaluation through orthogonal assays. Another important criterion was the number of bound fragment hits per site and the formation of subpockets. Sites that accommodate a higher number of fragments are more likely to benefit from fragment merging, and the existence of subpockets offers the potential for fragment linking. The binding sites with the highest number of fragment hits are ExoN 1, ExoN 2, Hinge 1, MTase 1, and MTase 2. Binding sites that accommodate only a limited number of fragments have reduced potential for subsequent development, as they only allow for fragment growth. Notably, the MTase 1 site, despite having 24 distinct fragments bound, was ranked low due to unfavourable factors such as high mutation frequency and low sequence conservation. The final criterion involved the frequency of Pan Assay Interference Compounds (PAINS) per binding site. Although not directly related to the ranking of the sites, a high number of PAINS would lower the ranking of binding sites with fewer hits. However, we identified only three PAINS among all nsp14 fragments, and these occurred in sites with a high number of fragments bound. Therefore, these PAINS are not problematic when excluded from further development. In summary, we have presented a naming and ranking system for all currently known nsp14 binding sites, which should aid in the prioritization of future development efforts for nsp14-targeting inhibitors. During our project, we identified novel fragment hits, structurally characterised their binding sites, estimated binding affinities, and contextualised our new results with existing data. By combining data from all known binding sites on nsp14, we propose a systematic naming system and ranked these binding sites based on their potential for subsequent structure-based design. Particular attention was given to mutational frequency in nsp14 and amino acid identity across the three medically relevant coronaviruses SARS, MERS, and SARS-CoV-2. It is widely accepted that viral pandemics are likely to occur again in the future, potentially originating from coronaviruses. Therefore, our work contributes to pandemic preparedness. Large conformational changes between nsp10-bound and unbound nsp14 have recently been described (Kozielskiet al., 2025). We hypothesise that by using different approaches one may identify additional previously unidentified binding sites on nsp14.
